Its substance is entirely Jambūnada gold, five yojanas in width, illuminating the world like a second sun;
such are the primary qualities of this wheel-treasure.
Furthermore, the second merit of the wheel-treasure is that it moves without obstruction, traveling through the air; in a single day, it can travel a hundred thousand *yojanas*.

Furthermore, the third merit of the wheel-treasure is that according to the king’s intention, wherever he may think of going—whether to Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, or the abode of the Four Great Kings—the thousand-spoked wheel flies through the air to those respective places.
By the power of the wheel-treasure, it enables the fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—to all follow along, flying through the air.

Furthermore, this is the fourth merit of the wheel-treasure: if there are those who do not submit to the Wheel-turning King, the golden wheel-treasure follows him and is able to bring them into subjection.

Furthermore, this is the fifth merit of the wheel-treasure: that golden wheel-treasure has no rival; whether it be kings or those like them, upon seeing it they immediately submit. This is all due to the power of the Dharma, for as the Wheel-Turning King follows after it, he is thus able to bring this about.
Thus, the wheel-treasure is endowed with and corresponds to these five kinds of meritorious qualities.
Thus has the third great treasure been explained.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—observing the course of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does one practice wholesome karma free from hatred so as to obtain the fourth elephant-treasure of a Wheel-turning King appearing in the world?"
He sees, hears, knows, or perceives with his divine eye:

this Dharma-practicing Wheel-Turning King follows the course of the Dharma and has attained the foremost state of tamed obedience in his elephant, which is capable of conquering other cities. Its seven parts support the ground—namely, its four feet, tail, penis, and tusks—and thus these seven limbs all rest firmly upon the earth.

If an elephant possesses these seven characteristics, its great strength exceeds that of other weak elephants by a thousandfold; its trunk is supple when severed, and its color is white as snow, like that of King Śakra’s Airāvaṇa.
All other elephants submit upon merely smelling its scent and do not dare look directly at it;
it is capable of fighting in three places—namely, in water, on land, and in the air.
It can travel with great speed, circling Jambudvīpa three times in a single day.

That elephant is so well-tamed that it may be led by a single thread tied around its throat. When the Wheel-Turning King mounts it for a journey, the elephant’s discipline is in perfect accord with the king’s mind.

Wherever the Wheel-Turning King wishes to go, he need not give any instruction; the elephant arrives there swiftly, walking with level and even gait—without trembling or swaying, with measured steps, the body remaining motionless. It lifts its feet one after another, neither skipping nor galloping, nor exerting excessive force, performing all manner of excellent movements.
When children see it, they feel no fear;
whether on four-way roads, in alleys, or atop multi-storied houses, it can go wherever one leads it, and women are able to seize it, grasping it by the hand and stroking it.
When engaged in battle, it is exceedingly fierce and valiant, yet when walking, it is docile and compliant, remaining within the tether without straying.

Such a great dragon-elephant treasure of a wheel-turning king is obtained from the seed of practicing even a single path of action among the ten paths of wholesome conduct; how much more so for one who fully and harmoniously practices all ten paths of wholesome action.
Thus, one who practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma perceives with the divine eye that fourth elephant-treasure of the wheel-turning king.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—observing the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does the wheel-turning king obtain that horse-treasure?"
As for that Horse-Jewel, with what qualities is it endowed and how does it correspond?
He perceives this through hearing, knowledge, or vision with the divine eye:

the Horse-Jewel has a pure color like that of a swan or a *kumuda* flower; its entire body is adorned with celestial markings such as the *āvarta*, which constitute its primary characteristics of measure, color, and shape. Endowed with all these marks, it is preeminently well-trained.
In a single day, he can circumambulate Jambudvīpa three times without his body becoming fatigued.
Thus does the wheel-turning monarch obtain this fifth precious possession, the horse-treasure.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does a Wheel-Turning King come to possess the treasure of the military commander?"
He knows this through seeing, hearing, or inference, or he sees it with his divine eye:
what are the merits of that Jewel of the Military Commander?
It is this: whenever the Wheel-Turning King reflects or contemplates, the Jewel understands the King’s intention without waiting for a command, and is able to accomplish whatever the King requires.
He stays far removed from what is contrary to the Dharma and acts in accordance with the True Dharma;
whatever is required at the proper time and place, he provides to the king's satisfaction, doing so without causing suffering or distress, and acquiring things in accordance with the True Dharma.

Just as the king intends and according to his heart’s desire, all that he does accords with the principles of the Dharma, and whatever is required within the king’s domain, he is able to accomplish it all.

Thus, through the wholesome karma of being free from anger, the Wheel-Turning King obtains the treasure of the military commander; he constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action and benefits all sentient beings in the world, just like a father and mother.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—observing the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does the Wheel-Turning King obtain that seventh treasure, the minister-treasurer who is a wealthy householder?"
What are the qualities of that Householder-Treasure?
He is seen, heard, known, or perceived by divine eye:
as for the Householder-Treasure belonging to the Wheel-turning King, what are his qualities?

He is able to fill all pits, ravines, deep mountains, secluded valleys, perilous cliffs, treacherous places, and uneven terrain with various exquisite jewels such as diamond, the blue Indra-gem, mākara-pearls, and musāragalva; these jewels are inexhaustible even without the King’s command, let alone gold and silver.
This householder-treasure, Bṛhaspati, is foremost; he does not deceive, he is not sycophantic, and he does not cause distress to others. All who see him find him refreshing and hold him dear.
Such is the wheel-turning monarch’s householder-treasure.
"Such a wheel-turning monarch, endowed with the seven treasures and ruling over the four continents, is able to sit together with the hosts of nāgas and the hosts of devas.
There are two celestial abodes:
the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Śakra, King of Devas, shared his seat with him.
Thus, being endowed with these seven kinds of wondrous jewels, he became a Wheel-Turning King.

Furthermore, there are another set of similar seven jewels, which are inferior to the former seven: namely, the sword jewel, the skin jewel, the bed jewel, the grove jewel, the palace jewel, the robe jewel, and the footwear jewel.
What are the meritorious qualities of that sword-like treasure of the wheel-turning king?

If there is a kingdom that gives rise to a rebellious or resistant mind, this sword-treasure will swiftly travel there; all kingdoms, upon seeing the sword, will immediately submit without a single person being killed.
Such are the merits of this sword-treasure:
without punishment or killing, all kingdoms naturally submit.
Such are the merits of this foremost sword-treasure.
"How does the Wheel-Turning King obtain that second treasure, which resembles skin?
What are the virtues of that second treasure?
That skin-treasure is produced within the great ocean."
Once it had been born, the merchant obtained it and brought it before the king.
As for the virtues of that jewel:

it was five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long; it was the skin of a sea dragon, which neither rain nor water could rot, wind could not move, and fire could not burn; it could ward off cold and heat, providing warmth in cold times and coolness in hot times.

Wherever the Wheel-Turning King travels—following the king’s host and wherever that Jewel of the Military Commander leads—it can serve as a dwelling, fully accommodating the king and his army. Each unit is partitioned separately so that wives and consorts are not intermingled and do not see one another;
its color is brilliant white, like the radiance of the sun.
Such are the merits of the second treasure, the hide.
How does the wheel-turning king obtain that third treasure, which resembles a couch?
What are the merits of that third treasure?
As for that precious couch, it is soft, supple, and smooth; when one sits upon it, it sinks down, and when one rises, it returns to its original level.
If one sits upon it to practice dhyāna, mindfulness, and reflection, one attains a mind of tranquility within liberation.
If one sits upon that couch while the mind dwells on sensual desires, one immediately becomes free from desire.
In this same sequence, it is likewise for anger and delusion.
From that very couch, small meditation chambers emerge; even those women who harbor extreme passion for the king, upon seeing this precious couch, find their minds free from defilement.
Such are the merits of the third jewel, the throne.
How does the wheel-turning monarch obtain that fourth jewel, which resembles a grove?
What are the merits of that fourth jewel?
If the king remembers his past sporting in the groves, he goes to those groves.

By the power of the virtues of that forest and the king’s own wholesome karma, it becomes like the Nandana Grove in the celestial realm: flowers and fruits grow there, *śārikā* birds abound, and lotus ponds flow at its fords. Celestial songs, court ladies, laughter, dancing, and singing fill the air; all the goddesses gather there together.
Like a god, the king is endowed with all the qualities of the five sensory pleasures.
In that grove, women follow him as he wanders about in pleasure and amusement due to the power of his wholesome karma.
The practitioner observes all of this.
Such is the fourth forest jewel’s merit.
"How does the Wheel-Turning King obtain that fifth jewel which resembles a palace?
What are the qualities of that fifth jewel?

It is said that when the Wheel-Turning King lies down at night within that palace and wishes to see the moon, a star and moon appear within the palace; having seen them, his eyes rejoice, and he calls them 'jewels.'"

When celestial maidens sing and chant, hearing them brings freedom from sorrow; one sleeps joyfully and peacefully, and upon waking, experiences auspicious dreams, beholding wondrous and delightful things.
In the cold season, one is fanned by warm breezes; in the heat, one experiences the pleasant touch of coolness.
Dividing the night into three parts, one sleeps for two parts and rises from sleep during the third part to experience the joy of practicing the Dharma.
Such is the fifth precious jewel, the Hall of Merit, which the wheel-turning king enjoys as a karmic reward.
What is the jewel of clothing?
What are its qualities?

Woven with fine threads, it is dense and exquisite, supremely soft, and cannot be defiled by impurities. Once the King has put it on, he experiences no extremes of cold or heat, hunger or thirst, emaciation or exhaustion; fire cannot burn it, nor can a sword cut it.
Such are the merits of the sixth jewel, the garment.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the practice of dharmas in accordance with the true Dharma—as to how the Wheel-Turning Sage King obtains that seventh merit, the jewel resembling a foot-ornament.
What are the virtues of that seventh treasure?
It is seen, heard, known, or perceived by the divine eye:
it is the *pādukā* (shoes) treasure; if the king wears them, he travels upon water as if upon dry land.
When traveling, he proceeds with deliberate slowness; even if it be a hundred *yojanas*, he can travel there without impairing his dignified demeanor and without physical exhaustion.

Thus, the Wheel-Turning King is endowed with the seven treasures, as well as seven secondary treasures similar to them, which he may enjoy at will. The four continents and the two celestial realms are the domains over which this king rules.
He possesses a full thousand sons, all of whom are brave and strong, capable of defeating the armies of others.
That wheel-turning king is worthy of respect by all people;
having abandoned anger through wholesome karma, he attains such happiness as this, which is the residual power of the ten paths of wholesome action.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma: "How is it that this entire world, from time immemorial, has taken the darkness of ignorance and false views as its seed, such that all fetters are likewise so?"
Furthermore, how does one abandon wrong views, practice right view, and thereby attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death in the world?
Through what is seen, heard, known, or perceived by the divine eye, one understands:

that practitioner who accords with the true Dharma and contemplates the course of dharmas—if they abandon wrong views and cultivate right view—all fetters and unbeneficial factors will be completely severed and extinguished; thus, they will attain nirvana and remain far removed from birth and death.
For those who have abandoned wrong views, the five faculties are unobstructed.
Such virtuous persons take delight in the True Dharma.
Thus, they first hear of the Buddha’s merits and contemplate the various sufferings within the five realms of birth and death; they contemplate the extreme terror of those five abodes:
In the heavens, there is the suffering of heedlessness and the suffering of subsequent decline;
among humans, there is the suffering of agriculture and other such labors;
and within the hells, there is the suffering of being tormented and harmed by others.
Among the hungry ghosts, there is the suffering of affliction by hunger and thirst;
among the animals, there is the suffering of devouring one another.
Thus, if these five realms were explained individually and in detail, they would be of immeasurable kinds.

Having contemplated in this way, one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment toward birth and death, like the radiance of light; through the thorough penetration of the True Dharma, the aspiration for renunciation arises;
and because this mind has arisen, wholesome dharmas flow forth.
If people are in harmony and have given rise to this mind, the yakṣas of that realm will rejoice and praise them, their body hairs standing on end, and they will give rise to this thought:

"This son of good family, with such a name and such a lineage, has resolved his mind to sever greed, hatred, and delusion from beginningless time; he desires to destroy the realm of Māra and takes no pleasure in the realms of afflictions and defiled desire; his mind finds no joy in the love of a mind stained by desire."

"Furthermore, being free from wrong views, that son of good family possesses the aspiration for renunciation; he constantly delights in practicing and performing much, stays close to spiritual friends, delights in hearing the true Dharma, maintains a perpetually pure mind, pays homage to the Buddha and the Dharma, and keeps his physical, verbal, and mental actions well-purified and tranquil."
When that person has thus stilled their speech and mind, they become a practitioner of wholesome conduct. The yakṣas of that realm, having perceived this, rejoice and give rise to this thought:

"This son of good family possesses a virtuous mind and a pure mind; he does not delight in the household life, for all homes and dwellings are like traps or cages. His heart finds no joy in the beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion; he takes no pleasure in the realm of Māra; he does not delight in sensual craving, but desires to battle with Māra and to sever the afflictions."

"Furthermore, in this way, once that son of good family has thus contemplated the suffering of birth and death, his resolve for renunciation increases ever further; he distances himself from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, drinking alcohol, and false speech, fully undertaking and maintaining the precepts of an upāsaka."
When the yakṣas of that realm see this, they become even more joyful and, in turn, inform the yakṣas of the air in succession, saying:

"In such-and-such a kingdom, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a settlement, there is a certain son of good family, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name. Possessing such right faith, he is capable of going forth; he desires to shave his hair and beard, to don the dharma robes, and to go forth with right faith. He will diminish the faction of Māra, increase the assembly of the True Dharma, sever the bonds of Māra, and cut off greed, hatred, and delusion."
"All fetters and bonds have wrong view as their root;
transcendental nirvana has right view as its root.

One who practices by contemplating all phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma first praises right view in this way: they do not despise, revile, debase, or loathe it, and they also teach others to abide in right view. They do not praise wrong view, but rather despise, debase, revile, and loathe it. They constantly explain the karmic retribution of the two opposing paths of wrong view and right view, so as not to allow sentient beings to dwell in wrong view."
The fundamental bondage of all ignorant, ordinary people in the world is what is called wrong view;
because of wrong view, all sentient beings fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
That son of good family abandons wrong views and shall fully attain immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, that son of good family contemplates how household life is oppressed and bound by immeasurable suffering and affliction; having made this contemplation, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, desires to leave the home life, and wishes to wage war against Māra.

When the yakṣas of that earth recognize such a noble person, they rejoice and announce it upward to the yakṣas of the air. The yakṣas of the air, with hearts full of joy, speak to the Four Great Kings:

"In such-and-such a kingdom, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a settlement, there is a son of good family of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, who possesses such right faith and is capable of going forth. He desires to shave his hair and beard, to don the dharma robes, and to go forth in right faith; he will diminish the faction of Māra and increase the host of the True Dharma."
When the Four Great Heavenly Kings heard this, joy arose in their hearts:
"When such a true person hears the True Dharma, they become weary of and detached from the defilements of desire."
Having shown reverence to his preceptor and the noble śrāvakas, that son of good family shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and received the prātimokṣa precepts.
The yakṣas of that earth and the yakṣas of the air, having learned this, rejoiced and spoke thus to the Four Great Kings:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a hamlet, a certain son of good family—of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name—has abandoned false views and cultivated the karma of right view; he has practiced correctly according to the Dharma, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the religious robes, and received the prātimokṣa precepts."

Having abandoned all that is disadvantageous in the world, the confinement of the household life, and the poison of attachment to wife and children, he has gone forth with right faith; having relinquished all mental activities associated with the household life, he desires to wage war against Māra and to sever ignorance.
At that time, having heard this, the Four Great Kings were filled with joy.
Being thus delighted, they spoke to the Four Heavenly Kings as follows:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a settlement, a certain son of good family—of such a lineage and such a name—has abandoned wrong views and practiced right view; he has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and with right faith has gone forth from home. Such-and-such a bhikṣu has accepted him as a disciple."
Upon hearing this, those devas said with joyful hearts:
"The faction of Māra is diminished, and the assembly of the True Dharma increases.
When the Four Great Kings had spoken thus, the Four Heavenly Kings heard it and were likewise filled with joy.

"Furthermore, such a son of good family, upon seeing even a speck of unwholesome or evil dharma, feels deep dread; he is able to endure it and refrain from committing it, and his mental conduct is upright.
He does not delight in much talk, does not cultivate intimacy with families, does not socialize with them, and does not associate with evil friends.

He has no desire to see places of great crowds and clamor; he does not go to evil assemblies, nor to places where many people gather for amusement; and he does not crave delicious flavors or eat excessively from large vessels."
One does not frequently visit friends or spiritual mentors;

rather, one always acts with right mindfulness within the sphere of sensory objects, always exerts diligent effort, consumes food according to the Dharma, and conducts oneself according to the Dharma; one diligently severs the bonds of Māra and diligently cultivates right view.
"Such a virtuous person brings benefit to all sentient beings in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one does not kill sentient beings, And always practices patience with a compassionate heart,"
Toward sentient beings as toward a father, he is able to contemplate the world.
Having abandoned theft, the wise one always restrains his senses;
with bodily action always performing what is good, he is able to cross over all evils of existence.
Even regarding painted women, one does not wish to look upon them;
having shattered desire with firm and clear wisdom, one is therefore said to have attained liberation.
Viewing gold and earth as equal, one departs from sorrow and dwells in right practice.
The serpent of afflictions does not bite him; he attains immeasurable bliss.
His mind is equanimous toward gain and loss, and likewise toward success and failure.
His mind does not waver between suffering and joy; therefore, he is called a bhikṣu.
Seeing no difference between enemy and kin, guarding the senses with heedfulness,
and not being wounded by sensory objects— for these reasons one is called a *brāhmaṇa*.
Viewing sensory objects as poison, one courageously abandons them as one would avoid an enemy.
Nirvana is not far for him, as taught by the One of Perfect and Universal Knowledge.
Seeing arising and ceasing as they truly are, his right view leaves no room for craving;
with a mind as immovable as a mountain, he is liberated from birth and death.
Regarding sandalwood and common grass, they are equal in their mind toward fine or coarse food;
regarding the *kāṣāya* and silk cloth, they cannot be bound by attachment to them.
Without craving for gain or offerings, they find contentment in a mat of grass as their bedding.
Seeing gain and offerings as fire— only thus can one be called "seeing.
Not being swept away by the river of craving for external objects,
and knowing with certainty the fruits of one's own karma— the Buddha calls such a person a bhikṣu.
One does not grieve over what has passed, nor does one long for the future;
practicing according to the Dharma in the present, one does not defile the mind.
If one does not corrupt the intention toward the Dharma and always dwells within the Dharma, [one attains peace].
Then one does not undergo birth and death; such a person is fully endowed with the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
If a person uses the fire of wisdom to burn away the afflictions within the mind, then sensory objects become like servants; that person shall have no suffering.
If a person’s faculties are tranquil, and the faculties do not attain mastery, the mind does not cling to forms and the like; such a one is free from afflictions like a Buddha.
If a person can restrain the faculties, the five faculties will no longer be autonomous.
Form and the like cannot plunder it; it is free from afflictions and is tranquil.
If a person’s mind cherishes it, and if there is one who possesses patience, likewise, the seer’s mind is awakened—such a one is a Moon-like Muni.
If one delights in dwelling in seclusion, And does not delight in multi-storied towers,
But finds joy beneath trees or in the open air, One is called a bhikkhu who begs for alms.
Courageous, serene, disciplined, and wise, One knows suffering and pleasure as they truly are.
One will surely reach the unsurpassed state, forever free from all sorrow and grief.
With a heart of pure sincerity and compassion, practicing dhyāna at all times with equanimity toward victory or defeat, one shall thus cultivate and attain the Truth.
“Because they have abandoned wrong views, they attain such a Dharma.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—contemplating the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the True Dharma: ‘How does that person abandon wrong views, cultivate right view, and free himself from doubt, thus practicing the untainted dhyāna in successive stages, so that the yakṣas of that earth and the yakṣas of the air, up to those of the Four Great Kings, see and hear it and rejoice?’”
He knows this through hearing and seeing, or sees it with his divine eye:
those Four Great Kings and those Four Heavenly Kings go to the abode of Śakra and speak thus:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, or such-and-such a settlement, there is a certain son of good family, of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and out of right faith has gone forth from the household life. He is endowed with virtuous precepts and right conduct, possesses unimpeded and joyful eloquence, maintains constant and correct mindfulness, and even regarding minor offenses feels deep dread; he diminishes the faction of Māra and increases the host of the True Dharma."

When those Four Great Kings had spoken thus to King Śakra, King Śakra, Lord of Devas, was filled with great joy upon hearing it, and the entire assembly of the Thirty-three Gods under King Śakra rejoiced together.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Two;
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.

Chapter 2: On Birth and Death (3–5) Section 1: On Birth and Death, Chapter Two Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma:

"How does a bhikṣu gradually abandon the outflows (*āsrava*), first abandoning unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) and subsequently practicing wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*), correctly contemplating and reflecting so as to cultivate the mind and abide in right stability?"
He sees, hears, and knows this, or perceives it with the divine eye:

that monk first contemplates in this way how the sense faculties and their objects correspond and serve as mutual causes and conditions, such that all worlds have been revolving in the cycle of birth and death since beginningless time.
He contemplates in this way:

"The causes and conditions of these births, the great ocean of objective realms—all are entirely without self; there is only the internal mind and its objective conditions that circulate through the world."

In this way, one who first practices the conduct of seclusion should leave behind places of clamor and bustle, delighting instead in empty, quiet places—such as aranyas, mountain wilds, forests, thickets of rice straw, beneath trees, in the open air, or among burial mounds—and by dwelling there, one can bind the monkey-like mind.

Through such cultivation, the mind becomes tranquil; one takes no pleasure in villages, nor in places of singing, dancing, jesting, and clamor, nor does one delight in seeing men and women of all ages, nor does one delight in much talk.
There are two types of *kaṇḍu* that destroy the holy life:
first, the harlot; second, excessive speech. One should abandon both entirely.
Having abandoned them, the mind becomes unified and tranquil; in this way, that person’s mind can abide [in concentration].
"What is right contemplation?
What is the first dharma to be contemplated?

With his initial mind, that person thus observes the eighteen mental activities (aṣṭādaśa-manopavicārāḥ), which give rise to roots of goodness, roots of unwholesomeness, and roots of the indeterminate."
What are the eighteen?
They are as follows: A bhikṣu correctly observes the mind;
having seen a form with the eye, if the mind becomes attached with joy, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to a mind of sorrow or a mind detached from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to a mind of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, it is the same when the ear hears a sound: if one’s mind becomes stained with joy, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to a mind of sorrow or a mind detached from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to a mind of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, it is the same when the nose smells an odor: if one’s mind becomes attached with joy, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to a mind of sorrow or a mind detached from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to a mind of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, it is the same when the tongue perceives flavors: if one’s mind becomes attached with joy, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to a mind of sorrow or a mind detached from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to a mind of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, it is likewise: once the body has perceived a touch, if one is stained by a joyful mind, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to a mind of sorrow or a mind detached from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to a mind of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, it is likewise: once the mind has cognized a phenomenon, if the mind becomes stained by joy, one obtains an unwholesome retribution.
If one gives rise to thoughts of sorrow or thoughts free from desire, one obtains a wholesome retribution;
if one gives rise to thoughts of equanimity, one obtains an indeterminate retribution.
Through such eighteen mental activities as causes and conditions for these three types of retribution, beings in the world undergo birth and decline.

"If that bhikṣu thus contemplates the eighteen mental activities and attains the first stage, the yakṣas of that stage, having seen this, become even more joyful and successively pass the news on to the yakṣas of the air."
The terrestrial yakṣas and the celestial yakṣas of the air—those two classes of yakṣas spoke with joyful hearts to the Four Great Kings.
Those Four Great Kings spoke with joy to the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a settlement, a certain son of good family, of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and gone forth from home out of right faith;..."
"Having already gone forth, dwelling in a secluded place away from the clamor of the world, he now further observes the eighteen mental activities and has realized those dharmas.
When the Four Great Kings had spoken thus, the Four Heavenly Kings, hearing them, felt even greater joy and said:
"The faction of Māra is diminished, and the assembly of the True Dharma increases."
Those Four Great Kings, having thus spoken, further addressed Śakra, the King of the Gods of the Thirty-three, with joyful words:

"In Jambudvīpa, there is a certain son of good family, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma-robes, and out of right faith has gone forth from home. Having left behind the clamor and bustle of the world, he dwells even among burial mounds, observing the eighteen mental activities according to the Dharma; he has realized that Dharma and abides therein correctly according to the Dharma."
After those Four Great Kings had spoken thus to King Śakra, Kauśika, the Lord of the Thirty-three, heard them and his heart was filled with great joy.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma: "Once this bhikṣu has thus contemplated the eighteen mental activities in accordance with the Dharma and attained the first stage, what other distinct stage does he subsequently realize?"
He knows through hearing and seeing, or sees with the divine eye:
he further examines the four families in succession; these four are the family of wisdom, the family of truth, the family of equanimity, and the family of renunciation.
How does a bhikṣu abide in the house of wisdom?
It is said:

that bhikṣu thus contemplates his own body as the true dharma; he understands it correctly and in accordance with reality, part by part, knowing: "In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element."
"What is the earth element?
The earth element is of two kinds:
first, internal; [second, external]."
2. External. What is internal?
All the various parts within the body are called internal; that which is internal possesses sensation.
What is that which is perceived?

It is perceived when combined with skin, flesh, and so forth; that is to say, the sense organs such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, which are comprised of solidity and roughness, are termed "perception" when they enter within.

What, then, are those? They are the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, veins, bones, and marrow; the spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, and liver; mucus, saliva, and the like; the raw stomach, the cooked stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine, the abdomen, the stomach, the head, and the brain—all such internal components within the body that are solid, coarse, and possess sensation are called the internal earth element.
What is called the external earth element?
Whatever is external earth that is solid, rough, and insentient is called the external earth element.
Whether it be the internal earth element or the external earth element, when they are unified as one, this element is merely an element.
Contemplate this earth element:
it has no agent and no experiencer; it is not without causes and conditions; it is impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity.
When a bhikṣu observes in this way, he attains liberation through wisdom: "All is not-self, there is nothing belonging to self, and there is no self.
Having thus understood the earth element as it truly is and seen it as it truly is, his mind becomes detached from desire.
In this way, a bhikṣu attains liberation within the house of wisdom.
What is the water element?
The water element is of two kinds:
First, internal;
second, external. What is internal?
All that constitutes the category of water possesses the characteristic of the water element, namely, the characteristic of moisture.

Whatever is within the body—moisture, tears, saliva, spittle, brain matter, blood, lymph, fat, marrow, bile, urine, sweat, and so forth—such internal constituents of the body, which are included within the factors of awakening, are called the internal water element.
What is called the external water element?
It consists of all external things categorized as water that are characterized by moisture; namely, those that are insentient.
Because they are insentient and categorized as such, they are called the external water element.
Whether it be the external water element or the internal water element, they are unified as one; this element is merely an element.
Contemplating this water element, one sees that all of it is not self, nor does it belong to a self, nor is it the self.
Having thus understood the water element as it truly is and having seen it as it truly is, the mind attains detachment from desire.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells in the house of wisdom.
"What is the fire element?"
The fire element is of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
What is internal? It refers to the various constituent parts existing within the body.
If fire is subsumed under fire, that which is internal and possesses sensation is what is called bodily warmth, which does not burn.
This is what is called "being able to digest.
What is it that is able to digest?
It refers to the consumption of food and drink, which, having obtained the correct pleasure of flavor, is transformed and digested.
Within this body, that which is internal or part of the internal, and which is fire or included within fire, and which possesses internal sensation, is called the internal fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is called the external fire element?

Whatever external fire or categories of fire there may be—whether characterized by heat or included within warmth—if it is not apprehended through sensation, it is called the external fire element because of its lack of sensation.
Whether it be the internal fire element or the external fire element, when these are unified as one, this element is merely an element.
Contemplating this fire element, one realizes that it is entirely not-self, nor does it belong to a self, nor is it a self.
Having understood this fire element as it truly is and having seen it as it truly is, the mind attains detachment from desire.
Thus, this fire element has no agent and no experiencer.
What is the wind element?
The wind element is of two kinds:
First, the internal;
second, the external.
What constitutes the internal?

Whatever exists within the body, whether internal or internal parts, which is comprised within the category of wind, which is light and mobile, and which is comprised within the category of the factor of sensation— what, then, is that?
That is to say:

upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, sideways-moving winds, or winds such as those involved in childbirth; winds like the prick of a needle or the stroke of a sword; winds of distorted discrimination, and whirlpooling winds—such winds as these are of eighty kinds, moving like the crawling of insects.
Such winds as these—these eighty types of winds that function in eighty distinct locations;
thus, within the body, in every part and place, those things comprised by the category of wind, which are light, mobile, maturing, and associated with sensation, are called the internal wind element.
What is called the external wind element?
Whatever external winds are categorized as light and moving, being a composite and devoid of sentience, is called the external wind element.
Whether it be the internal wind element or the external wind element, when they are unified as one, this element is merely an element.
Contemplate this element of wind: all of it is not self, nor does it belong to a self, nor is it the self.
Thus, this element of wind has no agent and no experiencer.
In this way, thus, having known it as it truly is and seen it as it truly is, the mind attains detachment from desire.
In this manner, a bhikṣu realizes the abode of wisdom.
"What is called the space element?"
The realm of space is also of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
What is the internal?

It refers to all internal components within this body, the internal voids, that which is comprised by the void, the locations of sensory awareness, that which is neither universal nor pervasive, the locations where matter moves and shifts, the places where food and various flavors move downward for digestion, and the openings;

furthermore, the voids within the throat, the ears, the eyes, and the nose, the void at the location of the tongue, the voids within the mouth and so forth, and the void at the location where the tongue moves and acts within the mouth—these are called the internal space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What is called the external space element (*bāhyākāśadhātu*)?

It refers to all that is space which is not included within the sphere of perception, which does not fill everything, and does not pervade everything—namely, the space between the branches, twigs, and leaves of trees; all the spaces within caves; the valleys, rivers, and mountain torrents; and all such spaces as external apertures. This is called the external space element.
Whether the space-element is included within internal forms or included within external forms, they are unified as one; this element is merely an element.

Contemplating this space-element as entirely non-self, nor belonging to a self, nor being a self—thus contemplating the space-element with suchness and right knowledge, and having seen it as it truly is, the mind attains detachment from desire.
Having observed thus, one is not negligent: this realm of space is entirely non-self, nor does it belong to a self, nor is it the self; there is no agent and no experiencer.
Having known this, the mind attains detachment from desire.
"What is the element of consciousness? It is as follows:"
The twelve bases (āyatana) are a combination of the internal and external. Visual consciousness sees objects, while mental consciousness discerns them;

likewise for the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses. Thus, within these realms of consciousness, the mind (manas) is the root, and all are known by mental consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The practice of the Dharma has the mind as its precursor; the mind possesses power and swiftness.
Once the mind has first moved and turned, one is then able to speak and act."
Shaking off all evil karma, one can understand decline and rebirth;
by clearly knowing the retribution of karma, one attains the deathless state.
Able to restrain all the sense faculties and delighting in benefiting sentient beings—
With all faculties stilled and serene, this is the bhikṣu at peace.
Riding the carriage of the six sense-faculties, he can slay the enemy of desire;
brave and wise, practicing in the araṇya, he is able to reach the place of tranquility.
Content with dwelling in the forest, lying upon the ground with a peaceful mind,
one can shake off unwholesome states as the wind disperses thick clouds.
With wholesome deeds of body and speech, one delights in practicing virtuous conduct.
Seeing clearly and practicing with reverence, one can destroy the armies of Māra.
Desire and the like cannot bind such a one; their mind is virtuous and free from greed.
Possessing great compassion, this bhikṣu has emerged from the world and dwells in the Way.
“Objects of perception are the cause of bondage; if one does not crave forms and the like, one attains supreme tranquility and reaches the state free from suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the practice of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—and thinks as follows:
The bhikṣu observes the eighteen mental activities and accomplishes the first stage; by truly knowing the six elements, he attains the second stage.
He then reflects: "By contemplating what dharma does one attain the third stage?"
Through seeing, hearing, and knowing, or through the divine eye, he knows the five faculties of sensation as they truly are; thus, he attains the third stage.
How does he know with truth that a pleasant sensation is about to arise?

He knows them as they truly are; he knows in this sequence the arising of painful feeling, the arising of joyful feeling, the arising of sorrowful feeling, and the arising of equanimous feeling. He knows all that is pleasant, and he knows that pleasant feeling arises with contact as its causal condition.
Having understood pleasant feeling, he knows it as it truly is: "I know pleasant feeling.
If that bhikṣu knows that pleasant feeling arises with contact as its condition, he does not give rise to craving for the pleasant feeling or the contact associated with it.
Knowing that contact with pleasant feeling arises, once the pleasant feeling has arisen, it then ceases;
when that pleasant feeling ceases, one knows it as it truly is:
"My pleasant feeling has ceased."
He reflects thus: "My painful feeling arises through causes and conditions.

He understands that this painful feeling arises in the same manner as a pleasant feeling; he knows it just as it has been taught regarding how a pleasant feeling arises conditioned by contact, and so forth, within this painful feeling.
Thus it is explained in detail:
How does a bhikṣu know the feeling of joy?
The feeling of joy arises with contact as its causal condition.
How does a bhikṣu know the feeling of sorrow?
The feeling of sorrow arises with contact as its causal condition.
If one contemplates that feeling of joy in accordance with reality, then the feeling of joy ceases; [and when that has ceased, the feeling of sorrow likewise ceases].
Having seen its cessation, he becomes free from desire for the feeling of joy:
"If my feeling of joy, which had first arisen, ceases, then having seen its cessation, I shall know that feeling as it truly is, and my mind will become detached from desire."
"In this way, there is the feeling of sorrow," and so it is explained in detail;
the same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*). "Knowing thus, he attains the third stage.

The yakṣas of that stage, having known this, rejoice and successively report it upward to the yakṣas of the sky. The yakṣas of the sky report it to the Four Great Kings, and those Four Great Kings report it to the Four Heavenly Kings. Those Four Heavenly Kings then speak to Kauśika Śakra, King of the Gods:"

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a settlement, a certain son of good family—of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name—having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, has gone forth with right faith and attained the third stage."
"I wish to wage war against Māra, to diminish the faction of Māra, and to increase the assembly of those who uphold the True Dharma.
Having heard this, he was filled with even greater joy.

Then Śakra, the King of Devas Kauśika, mounted his great elephant named Airāvaṇa, accompanied by the foremost host of devas endowed with great supernormal powers, and arrived at the Suyāma Heaven, where he spoke with joy:
“In Jambudvīpa, following in succession even unto such-and-such a son of good family— expounding at length until he has attained the third bhūmi—
he desires to engage in battle with Māra, to diminish the faction of Māra, and to increase the assembly of the True Dharma.”
Having heard this from King Śakra, those Yāma devas became even more joyful.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—observing the practice of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does a bhikṣu attain the third stage, and how does he successively further cultivate it to attain the fourth stage?"
He sees, hears, and knows this, or perceives it with the divine eye:
A bhikṣu who wishes to attain the fourth stage observes in this way:
"Due to the causal condition of contact, my pleasant feeling arises."
If those causes of pleasure and conditions for pleasure cease, become tranquil, and vanish, then there is no feeling of pleasure.
Through the condition of contact, my painful feeling arises.
"In this way, he abandons the contact of suffering, the sensation of suffering, the accumulation of suffering, and all other causes and conditions of suffering.
He understands the causal relationship between contact and sensation thus:
'My sensations arise moment by moment together with contact; they arise because of contact.'"

Regarding pleasant feeling, his mind does not give rise to joy, nor does it give rise to delight; he does not praise that feeling, nor does he cultivate it excessively, nor does he become attached to its flavor. Thus, painful feeling cannot oppress him; he is neither afflicted nor disturbed. In this way, he practices equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Regarding these three feelings, all other mental states are entirely free from defilement;
he relinquishes them all. Such relinquishment is pure and pristine.
That bhikṣu reflects thus in his mind:
‘This renunciation of mine is thus pure and thus bright; how may I now attain the sphere of infinite space?
That person thus hopes and desires to attain the practice of the sphere of infinite space:
‘How may I obtain that state of mind belonging to that sphere?’
I have realized equanimity, which is ultimate and firm.
This equanimity of mine is ultimately joyful and blissful; it is constantly maintained and never abandoned. By means of this equanimity, I take up the sphere of infinite space.

Furthermore, this equanimity of mine is thus pure, thus bright; it takes up the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness, and it takes up the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. I aspire to those realms and practice correctly in this way.
That person, thus practicing correctly in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, forms this thought:
"I shall now attain this equanimity based on that state, according to the nature of that state, so that I may obtain it."
‘By means of this equanimity, I delight in that state, I take hold of that state, and I practice rightly in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It is just as when a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice places refined gold in the fire, blows upon it with a blowpipe, and using tongs, strikes and blows it repeatedly to make it perfectly malleable.

That produced gold is malleable, genuine, and pure, with a brilliant and beautiful luster; whatever is fashioned from it according to need is worthy of praise, and wherever it reaches in any land, no one speaks ill of it.
When polished, it is free of impurities, neither adulterated nor rough, being supremely soft; everything made from it is exquisite, and its radiant purity surpasses all other jewels.
However, if that master craftsman or his disciple knows how to skillfully refine that genuine gold and recognizes it as a true treasure,
then having known this, he reflects according to his intention:
"What should I fashion so that all who see it will give rise to joy?"
He then fashioned bells: to adorn the body, whether in places not visible or in places visible to the eye;
to serve as ear-rings to adorn the ears;
or to serve as necklaces to adorn the throat.
If used to adorn and make offerings to the sūtras and śāstras;
or if made into a signet ring with an engraved inscription to adorn the finger;
or if made into a golden garland or a topknot crown to adorn the hair-knot.
"In whatever place it is used for adornment, in each such case it is successfully accomplished through corresponding application.
Thus, a wise bhikṣu of good conduct gives rise to this thought:
'This renunciation of mine is now thus pure, thus bright white, and thus right practice; by taking up the sphere of infinite space, I shall be in accord with it.'"
Relying upon this equanimity, I fix my mindfulness on that sphere, delight in that sphere, and take up that sphere.

By means of this equanimity, I practice the sphere of infinite space; likewise the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and likewise the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He reflects thus: "How may this relinquishment of mine become permanent, immovable, indestructible, and not subject to momentary cessation?
Having reflected, he next takes the four formless bases as his object of focus.
He abandons what is not eternal, yet it is not non-eternal; it is neither moving nor unmoving, neither eternal nor non-eternal.

He knows thus: "In that sphere of infinite space, likewise in the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and likewise in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—by taking those spheres as an object, they are neither eternal nor non-eternal."
Thus, his mind finds no delight in that state; he knows it is not tranquil, but is impermanent and fluctuating.
He further contemplates feeling: he knows when a feeling is about to arise;
having known that the feeling has arisen, he knows when the feeling is about to cease.

Having known the cessation of feeling, one knows the arising of eye-contact; in this same sequence, one knows the arising of ear-contact, the arising of nose-contact, and the arising of the feelings associated with tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
Having thus realized and understood feeling, he further examines this feeling more deeply:
"I fully know the feeling born of eye-contact—its arising, its having arisen, and its persistence; I know the cessation of my feeling, its desire for cessation, and its having ceased."

Furthermore, he knows: "The feeling born of ear-contact has arisen for me; the feeling born of eye-contact has already ceased, subsided, been brought to weariness, and been abandoned, so that it will not come again. Once this feeling has ceased, he next contemplates the feeling born of ear-contact:
conditioned by suffering, conditioned by pleasure, or conditioned by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure."

Regarding the feeling born of ear-contact, he observes it accordingly in this way; having understood it thus, he does not give rise to delight or pleasure toward that ear-feeling, and knowing that feeling, he becomes detached and liberated.

“When the feeling born of ear-contact has thus ceased, one contemplates the feeling born of nose-contact and knows the feeling born of nose-contact, [understanding] the causal condition of nose-contact:

‘This feeling of mine arises; because of a pleasant condition it arises as pleasure, because of a painful condition it arises as pain, and because of a neither-painful-nor-pleasant condition it arises as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.’”

"In this way, as he observes accordingly, he understands with reality and correctness that feeling arises from the contact of the nose; when the feeling ceases and vanishes, he knows that the feeling has ceased and vanished."
Once that has ceased, he knows that in dependence upon the nose, there arise painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings:
"If at a later time, feelings arise in dependence upon the nose, they will likewise arise through such observation, and having arisen, they will again cease."
“Once that has ceased, he contemplates the feelings arising in the tongue; these feelings arising at a later time are likewise of three kinds, as previously described.
Proceeding in sequence, he even contemplates the feelings arising in the mind, which are also of three kinds.”
Having thus known feeling as it truly is, he attains the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) and exerts diligent effort, desiring to be liberated from the bonds of Māra.

The *yakṣas* of that stage, knowing this, rejoice; they then likewise proclaim it with joyful hearts to the *yakṣas* of the sky. The *yakṣas* of the sky likewise proclaim it to the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārāja*), and those Four Great Kings likewise proclaim it to the Four Heavenly Kings (*caturmahārājika*). Those Four Heavenly Kings likewise proclaim it to Śakra, King of the Gods.
That King Śakra spoke thus to the Yāma-devas:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a hamlet, a certain son of good family, of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma-robes, and out of right faith has gone forth from the household life. He maintains the precepts with diligence; through this sequential process, he has realized the truth as it is and attained the fourth stage."
"Just as I have now declared to you, O Deva, the faction of Māra shall diminish and the assembly of the True Dharma shall increase.
When those Yāma devas see King Śakra riding upon that white elephant Airāvaṇa, having seen him thus, they give rise to joy in their hearts and speak to King Śakra in this way: "O Śakra, you now—!"
"The people of Jambudvīpa follow the practice of the Dharma and are able to give rise to affectionate thoughts; this is what you ought to do.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—observing the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does that bhikṣu, having cast off the bonds of Māra, observe the feeling of equanimity?"
He knows through seeing, hearing, or inference, or sees with the divine eye:
that monk thus observes feeling with precise attention; conditioned by visual consciousness, an unwholesome feeling arises.
When that feeling seeks to give rise to a second, wholesome condition, the unwholesome feeling ceases and a wholesome feeling is produced.
When those determinate conditions cease, determinate feelings cease, and indeterminate feelings arise;

in this same sequence, ear-contact gives rise to feeling, nose-contact gives rise to feeling, tongue-contact gives rise to feeling, body-contact gives rise to feeling, and mind-contact gives rise to feeling. Thus knowing feeling, one becomes fulfilled in wholesome dharmas and afflictions become thin and sparse.
“Practicing in this manner, he further minutely observes feeling (*vedanā*).
He observes that mental feeling (*dharma-vedanā*) is obstructed by mental feeling, just as the light of a lamp is obstructed by sunlight;
the obstruction between these two types of feeling is likewise so. One should understand that once wholesome feeling has arisen, it obstructs unwholesome feeling.”
For example, just as the light of one lamp cannot obstruct the light of a second lamp,
so too one should reflect upon feeling: "By what kind of feeling might another kind of feeling be ultimately obstructed?"
He sees that wholesome feeling and unwholesome feeling are ultimately mutually obstructive; for example, a lamp’s light and the light of the stars do not obstruct one another.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu reflects and examines:
"Which feeling, which feeling, and what, what, can thus destroy [others]?
He observes in this way that feelings conditioned by the outflows (āsrava) destroy feelings conditioned by the absence of outflows, just as the light of fire can obstruct the light of snow.
Furthermore, what is feeling?
What is superior feeling?
Thus, one again gives rise to such an investigation:
Those unwholesome feelings obstruct wholesome feelings, yet they arise again later on.
It is like the moonlight being covered by the daylight during the day; that moonlight cannot be obstructed or covered within the darkness of night.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu correctly contemplates feeling:
"A multitude of feelings may come together, yet a single feeling can obstruct them; this single feeling is superior to those many feelings.
He observes that those many feelings are worldly feelings.
That single feeling is the supramundane, untainted mental feeling; this feeling is superior and capable of obstructing tainted feelings.
It is like the light of the full moon at night, which can obscure the multitude of stars.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes those subtle feelings in accordance with reality:
"Which are the many feelings?
They are those arising from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; these are outflowing feelings."
What is meant by "skillfully manifesting"?

It refers to observing that the world abounds in tainted sensations (*sāsrava-vedanā*) and lacks untainted ones (*anāsrava*). The world lacks power, like the light of the stars in the darkness of night, which cannot illuminate effectively when the moon is present.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates those sensations:
"For how long do these sensations of mine endure?
He observes that his sensations abide with the characteristic of arising and ceasing, like a flash of lightning.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes in this way:
"What is the meaning of this?
Does nose-consciousness arise with eye-consciousness as its causal condition?"
When he correctly observes that the mental faculty (manas-indriya) takes objects as its support, his feeling then destroys all sensory feelings;
it is like the distinct destruction of the characteristics of oxen, horses, camels, donkeys, and water buffaloes, which do not arise from a single cause or condition.

It is thus, it is thus: arising from the five sense faculties, they have delighted in grasping at objects since beginningless time; not limited to a single object, they are destroyed by the objects of their own perverted perceptions, like oxen, horses, camels, donkeys, pigs, and the like.
As that bhikṣu contemplates feeling in this way, he attains subtle wisdom.
That bhikṣu is able to delight in cultivating and frequently practicing that wisdom; having contemplated pleasant feeling, he contemplates feeling in accordance with it;
contemplating its exhaustion in accordance with it, he reflects thus:
"Regarding this sensation of mine, which arises from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: from where does it come when it arises, and to where does it go when it ceases?
That bhikṣu, observing in accordance with reality, sees the exhaustion and cessation of sensation and contemplates its principle;
having observed thus, he knows that the sensation of the eye comes from nowhere when it arises and goes nowhere when it ceases.
"This visual sensation of mine was originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence.
This eye of mine has no place from which it comes, like water in the ocean;
its cessation reaches nowhere, like a river flowing downstream to the great sea."

"This visual sensation of mine was originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence. It arises through causes and conditions. The sensations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all likewise.
"It is like a potter or his apprentice who, by means of a wheel and a lump of clay, through human effort and power, and conditioned by water and a stick, produces a jar."
Such a jar does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere when it ceases; yet this jar arises through causes and conditions.

In this very way, conditioned by the eye, by visible forms, by light, by space, and by attention, visual sensation arises—namely, suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Just like that jar, if the causes and conditions are excellent, an excellent jar is produced; if the causes and conditions are inferior, an inferior jar is produced.
It is thus, it is thus: if one conditions oneself with wholesome objects, wholesome eye-sensations arise; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
If one unites with wholesome sensations and proceeds accordingly in sequence, one will reach Nirvana.

If, however, there are unwholesome causes and conditions, unwholesome eye-sensations arise, conditioned by desire, hatred, and delusion, whereby one falls within the realms of the evil paths—hell, the animal kingdom, and the realm of hungry ghosts—amidst the cycle of birth and death.

"That bhikṣu, regarding all his virtuous conduct and its fruits, observes those sensations through the binding thoughts of conformity as being without any basis; they have no agent, they do not arise from causes, nor do they arise without cause, nor are they a collection; they are not permanent, not material, not momentary, and not subject to inversion."

When a bhikṣu perceives this aggregate of feeling in this way, he extinguishes craving for existence and the birth associated with delight and pleasure. Seeing that all births and deaths, which are tainted by evil craving, are impermanent, he joyfully cultivates and practices extensively the path leading out [of suffering].
"When that bhikṣu has practiced in this way, all fetters (saṃyojana) are severed and he becomes free from all underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

What are the fetters? They are the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana), the fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana), the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana), the fetter of existence (bhava-saṃyojana), and the fetter of pride (māna-saṃyojana); he severs these fetters."
What are the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)? They are:

the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of obstruction (*pratigha-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), and the fetters of deliberation (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).

By these causes and conditions, one wanders through the three realms of existence, traverses the three stages, revolves within the three evil destinies, and follows along with the three times; within the three grades, one is perfumed by the three types of sensation, and according to the three births, one turns through the causal conditions of birth and death.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—observing the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does that bhikṣu come to perceive such causal conditions for the eye?"
He contemplates in this way:
"By what cause and by what condition does the eye arise?
He sees, hears, knows, or perceives with the divine eye:
Karma is the cause of the eye; the eye arises from the cause of karma. Thus it proceeds in succession.
It is like the world’s nyagrodha tree: from its seed the nyagrodha tree is born, and the tree again produces seeds, bound by causes and conditions.

In this way, in this way, one knows that birth arises from karma, and karma in turn gives rise to further birth; when there is birth, there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, weeping, suffering, and affliction.
Thus, bound by the snare of craving through the cause of karma, all foolish, ordinary worldlings revolve in this manner within the ocean of birth and death.
By this causal condition, all perceptions of craving—if one does not perform karma, then because there is no karma, there is no craving;
because there is no craving, there is no feeling.

As for those causal conditions: it is like a lamp wick and a brazier; through the causal conditions of oil and fire, the flame of the lamp arises moment by moment. In this way, a bhikṣu observes the cause of feeling (*vedanā*).
He carefully contemplates that the cause of karma, the nature of karma, and the power of karma give rise to all feelings.

The brazier is a metaphor for the body; the oil is a metaphor for the sense faculties (*indriya*); the wick is a metaphor for feeling; the flames arising moment by moment from the fire of desire, hatred, and delusion are a metaphor for moment-by-moment wisdom; and the light is a metaphor for insight (*prajñā*).

“That practitioner thus perceives and knows that throughout the entire triple world there exists this sensation; it is like a goldsmith or his apprentice who, having obtained fine, genuine gold, is able to fashion exquisite ornaments.”
In this way and so forth, that skilled artisan represents the practitioner; that pure gold represents wholesome objects of focus (*ālambana*).
If one focuses on what is wholesome, there is wholesome karma, and one attains the path to *nirvāṇa*;
if one focuses on what is unwholesome, one incurs unwholesome karma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Clearly knowing causes and conditions, Resolving upon the subtle meaning,
Delighting in the stream of liberation— Such a one cannot be moved by craving."
Sentient beings follow the flow of karma, being born within all realms of action;
once bound by the fruits of karma, they travel through the narrow passages of existence.
If one abandons unwholesome karma and always delights in wholesome karma, [one will not suffer].
Thus the practitioner is like the stainless moonlight;
he can incinerate evil karma as fire consumes dry grass.
He is the illumination of the three realms, liberated from all unwholesome dharmas.
If a person aspires for liberation and their mind finds no delight in birth-and-death,
then birth-and-death cannot bind them, like a bird soaring through the void.
Knowing truly from whence feeling arises, and skillfully understanding the retribution of feeling—
Thus one attains liberation;
neither suffering nor pleasure can move them, and neither good nor evil passes through their mind,
for they view the world as a mirage.
With a mind ever free from error, always delighting in the practice of the Dharma,
and finding joy in the way of the bhikṣu— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
He does not delight in frequent social visits, but delights in seeing virtuous people.
Having left home and abandoned the defilements of the household, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Tranquil in all the sense-faculties and without craving for sensory objects,
walking while looking only a fathom’s length ahead, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
One who does not frequent the homes of those who revile others, who never engages in trade,
and who takes no pleasure in wandering through the four-way streets— such a person is called a bhikṣu.
One who does not delight in watching singing and dancing, and who does not take pleasure in crowded places.
One who delights in dwelling among burial mounds is called a bhikṣu.
One who takes only food for that very day and does not take food for the next day,
and who ceases after eating two portions, is called a bhikṣu.
Having cast aside fine garments, he delights in clothes of dust;
his eating and conduct are both in accord—such a one is called a bhikṣu.
If he does not perform worldly work, nor hope for the fruits of worldly work, [he is a bhikṣu].
One who does not strive painfully for what is required— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Liberated from desire and hatred, having cast off the mud of the deluded mind,
and whom evil dharmas cannot defile— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Having transcended all fetters, Having abandoned all underlying tendencies,
And being liberated from all bonds— Such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Wandering upon the Noble Eightfold Path, He proceeds toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
Free from malice and afflictions, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
With firm resolve and tranquil faculties, having abandoned the mire of desire,
always dwelling with a single-minded focus on the right— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
If one has attained the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*), perceives with a tranquil mind,
and knows the virtues and faults of all stages— such a person is called a bhikṣu.
Whether phenomena are tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), they all arise from causes and conditions.
One who knows all things in their various forms is thus called a bhikṣu.
Upright in practicing the holy life, tranquil and free from indolence,
rising early with purity and reverence— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Delighting in the cultivation of concentration and wisdom, Further delighting in the four dhyānas,
And also delighting in the araṇya— Such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Just as when a bird flies through the void, Its shadow always follows it.
If the mind accords with the True Dharma, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
One who can slay all afflictions, observes with equanimity and a benevolent mind,
and well understands the inhalation and exhalation of breath— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
If one can know the sequence, clearly seeing the practice of the Dharma, and skillfully discerning the path from what is not the path—one such as this is called a bhikṣu.
Finding joy, the mind does not exult; encountering suffering, one does not grieve.
With a mind equanimous toward sorrow and joy, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
If one truly understands old age and death, gods and asuras pay him homage;
Knowing the good and evil of sentient beings, such a one is called a bhikṣu.
Always content with robes and bowl, not hoarding wealth or treasures,
possessing few desires and practicing the holy life— one such as this is called a bhikṣu.
Eating but one meal and free from defilement, not craving various flavors.
One who can renounce gain and honor— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
One who practices a mind of equanimity and compassion, who has abandoned envy, jealousy, and evil,
and has already incinerated all faults— such a one is called a bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu reflects within his mind—in accordance with the True Dharma—thus contemplating feeling (*vedanā*).

Having contemplated feeling, he attains subtle wisdom and observes even more deeply: "Feeling arises from eye-contact; it proceeds by taking an object as its condition. Thus I observe that the second condition, the eye, perishes together with its characteristic.

'My feeling born of eye-contact has perished along with its condition; sound was the co-condition, yet I produced a feeling of craving. If a feeling of non-craving were to arise, the mind would not perish together with it.'"

That bhikṣu binds his mind with the rope of non-distress to the pillar of the focal object; once that auditory sensation has ceased, the ear-sensation together with the focal object of sound ceases as well.
“Dependent upon the nose and odors, nasal sensation arises. That bhikṣu further contemplates this nasal sensation and reflects thus:
‘My nose, together with odors, gives rise to nasal sensation—whether wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate;
may my mind not cease along with this nasal sensation.’”

If that bhikṣu contemplates the destruction of the mind, thus taking it as an object of focus, practicing this repeatedly, cultivating the taming of the mind, and perfuming the mind with wholesome dharmas, then at that time the untainted wholesome dharmas will remain unshakable.
“The tongue takes flavors as its object; this object may be wholesome, unwholesome, specified, or unspecified.
Once that monk has realized the object, he next examines feeling—whether it be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.”
Having observed thus, he reflects and recollects:
"Is this mind of mine subject to destruction or not?
Furthermore, he examines that feeling produced by the object-condition of taste, which is capable of destroying the mind.

Having observed in this way, one binds that mind with the rope of non-sorrow to the pillar of objective support; practicing and grasping in this manner, if the mind is thus, it cannot be carried away by the craving for flavors experienced by the tongue.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates those bodily contacts; such bodily contacts are bound to and take as their objective support the same contact-feelings—whether wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate.
He contemplates that contact and sensation:
if the mind becomes agitated and disturbed, he again binds it to the pillar of the focal object and subdues it so that it no longer breaks apart.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu next examines the mind:
When the mind is bound by the reception of phenomena—whether they be wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate—the view-reception destroys the mind.
That bhikṣu binds that mind with the rope of non-sorrow, fastens it to the pillar of the focal object, and subdues it; thus, it is not destroyed.
“Having observed the body as it enters into the six sense-spheres and feelings, that bhikṣu thoroughly knows the five types of feeling and attains the state of non-exhaustion;
with the lamp of wisdom, he observes the feeling born of eye-contact: what kind of feeling does he perceive?”
He contemplates the mental consciousness:
conditioned by this, feeling arises; the mind is bound and the heart grasps. All ignorant, ordinary people in the world burn themselves with the fire of conceptual discrimination.
In this, there is no experiencer; it is merely the arising of a collection of formations and merely the ceasing of a collection of formations, bound by causes and conditions.
Having observed the feeling born of eye-contact with conformity, one acts with conformity; one does not grasp at it, the mind does not waver, and one is neither dead nor distracted.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu examines auditory sensation.
What is auditory sensation?
Who perceives this sensation?
He sees that the mental consciousness follows and is bound by [the object]:
in this way, the ear-sensation is bound together with the mind; depending upon that mind, this arises through causes and conditions, without an agent and without an experiencer.
In this way, auditory sensation has no agent and no experiencer; there is only the power of the causal conditions of the aggregate of formations, whether arising or ceasing.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates olfactory sensation: "Who perceives this sensation?"
He observes feeling:

bound together with mental consciousness, it takes that mind as its object, relies upon that mind, and arises in accordance with those causes and conditions; there is only a collection of formations, with no agent and no experiencer, yet it continues to revolve in bondage.
Having observed the sensation of the nose, he becomes detached from the experiencer of that sensation.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu next observes the sensation of the tongue: "Who perceives the sensation of the tongue?
Upon examining this sensation, he sees it is bound by the mental consciousness.

In this way, the experience of the tongue depends upon that mind, is bound by that object of perception, and arises through those causes and conditions; it has no agent and no experiencer, nor is there any other entity, but exists only as a collection of formations produced by the power of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the body’s contact and sensation: “Who perceives this sensation?
What is it that experiences this?
Thus he observes the bondage of the mental consciousness.
