Such bodily sensations have no agent and no experiencer; there is nothing else besides, for they are merely a collection of formations that proceed through the power of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu examines mental sensations: "Who perceives these mental sensations?"
Contemplate mental feeling (*manas-vitti*):
when the mind takes dharmas as its object, mental consciousness arises; the coming together of these three is contact (*sparśa*), and from contact, feeling arises simultaneously.
It is like various and immeasurable fragrant substances: when many are combined, a pleasant fragrance is produced. This production of the pleasant fragrance does not arise from a single cause.
This is also like this: through the harmony of causes and conditions, all sensations arise; there is no agent and no experiencer.
For example, through conditions such as the stalk, leaves, filaments, and fragrance, that which is called a "lotus flower" arises; it does not arise from a single cause.

In this way, depending on the eye, with color as condition, with space as condition, with mindfulness as condition, and with light as condition, there arises the feeling born of eye-contact, which arises in dependence upon the eye.

Such a feeling does not arise from a single cause; it is not produced by a single entity, nor produced by a single combination, nor produced by a single characteristic, nor produced by an accumulation, nor produced through transformation.

As that bhikṣu thus and so forth earnestly seeks this sensation, thus and so forth do pure and white dharmas arise. It is like sugarcane juice being boiled with fire in a vessel: when it first becomes free from impurities, it is called *phāṇita*;
when boiled a second time, it gradually becomes more refined and is called *guḍa*;
when boiled a third time, its color becomes white, and it is called white candied sugar (*śveta-matsyaṇḍikā*).
This sugarcane juice is boiled and boiled again in such a manner that it becomes free from impurities and gradually thickens until its color turns white.
In the same way, a bhikṣu uses the fire of wisdom regarding the vessel to boil the sugarcane juice of the continuous mind;
the initial dhyāna-contemplation is like *phāṇita*, and the second stage is like *guḍa*.
Next, the third stage is like white rock honey.

In this way, when a bhikṣu’s mental continuum is boiled with the fire of wisdom, it becomes the stainless and pure dharma; free from defilement and unmixed, the supramundane dharma arises, transcending birth and death. It is pure, stainless, and bright, just like washed clothing.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu again observes feeling through another method with subtle discernment:

"Feelings born of eye-contact are coarse or subtle, heavy with defilements and not light, accompanying delusion; such-and-such a being experiences them, or so-and-so experiences them. Because they are superior, they are able to destroy [the remainder]; only a small residue remains, and he does not rely upon it."

In this same way, for the ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—once that bhikṣu has cultivated them thus, he achieves the contemplation of feeling, and the host of Māra seeks to destroy him.
The yakṣas of that realm became even more joyful and reported this upward to the yakṣas of the sky;
those yakṣas of the realm and the yakṣas of the sky reported it to the Four Great Kings;
and those yakṣas of the realm, the yakṣas of the sky, and those Four Great Kings reported it to the Four Heavenly Kings.
The yakṣas of that realm, the yakṣas of the sky, and the four great kings, together with the four heavenly kings, reported this to Śakra.
Then, King Śakra mounted his white elephant Airāvaṇa and, with a joyful heart, reported it to the Suyāma devas, in full detail as before.

Upon hearing what Śakra had said, the devas of the Yāma heaven felt great joy in their hearts. Adorning their bodies with various celestial jewels, exquisite garlands, ornaments, and perfumes, they mounted diverse vehicles—possessing desirable sounds, textures, tastes, forms, and fragrances—and experienced an ineffable variety of delightful pleasures, their minds filled with immense rapture.

“The assembly of the Yāma devas proceeds forty thousand yojanas toward Tuṣita Heaven, where there are palaces of the seven treasures with supreme and wondrous radiance, various mansions, and the city of Manovibhakti extending ten thousand yojanas, known as the ‘Pavilion of Untainted Joy’ for bodhisattvas; there the World-Honored One Maitreya resides, together with five hundred bodhisattvas.”

That Yāma-deva approached the Blessed One with a heart full of great joy; he adjusted his celestial robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and having paid homage with palms joined, placed his joined palms to his forehead and spoke these words:
"O Deva, you should now know:

In the land of action within Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a settlement of Jambudvīpa, there is a certain son of good family, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and gone forth out of right faith. He upholds the precepts, practices cultivation, honors his elders and superiors, and has attained the fourth stage of seeking untainted goodness. Having clearly perceived the ground of reception, he destroys the hosts of Māra; he firmly establishes the bridge of the True Dharma, reveals the white dharmas, and causes the faction of Māra to lose its power while increasing the celestial allies, who possess great might.
"Just as I have now spoken to you, O deva.
Having heard this, Maitreya Bhagavān spoke thus to the Yāma devas: "The faction of the devas is powerful, while the division of Māra is weak;
the side of the True Dharma increases, and the bonds of affliction are loosened. The army of Māra trembles in battle; hearing this, I rejoice."
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Birth and Death, Part Two:
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the practice of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma.
That bhikṣu, regarding the stages of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), has briefly attained what is known and seen by the six heavens; furthermore, how does he attain the fifth stage?

Furthermore, that bhikṣu has clearly perceived sensation; having performed his work, those six classes of devas contemplate the characteristics of the aggregate of perception, analyzing and deliberating:
"In which realm shall I practice the white dharmas together with them?"

Having engaged in correct reflection, he practices in one part, observing the characteristics of that perception as a wholesome dharma (*śukla-dharma*). Initially, he thoroughly understands these dharmas part by part: how is it that by taking as an object that which is visible and resistant, there arises a perception that is invisible and non-resistant?

That bhikṣu further expands his contemplative visualization; that visualization takes eleven kinds of forms as its object, namely: long, short, square, round, triangular, circular, and blue, yellow, red, white, and purple.
“Based on that characteristic of length, one gives rise to the perception of length.

Thus, in this world, those who are deluded and possess little wisdom undergo boundless birth and death; they fall from their karmic fruits and are reborn, suffering the afflictions of separation from loved ones, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and being made to serve others like slaves and servants. They prey upon one another; thus they gather together in a manner that is empty, false, and unreal—all things that are of no benefit. Such immeasurable and unbearable things exist;

for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of lifetimes, they have used all the actions of body, speech, and mind to create karma that results in suffering and affliction, adorning themselves with falsehood and deception. Foolish ordinary beings are constantly like this.”

Among human beings, there are the sufferings of agricultural labor and the like; mutual deception; the use of false weights and measures; litigation, quarreling, and fighting; seeking profit through business; serving kings and officials; traveling far across the sea; various forms of contention; farming and herding cattle.

When born among the barbarians, they take pleasure in giving rise to wrong views, their faculties are incomplete, and they are deprived of hearing the True Dharma. Born in places where no Buddha resides, they lack the favorable conditions for goodness. Even if they encounter no hardships, their minds constantly delight in drinking alcohol, sexual misconduct, theft, greed, anger, lying, double-tongued speech, harsh words, and frivolous talk.
Such people prolong the cycle of birth and death; because of those prolonged characteristics, they give rise to the perception of length.

Furthermore, within the heavens, there is the characteristic of long-term birth and death. Conditioned by those signs and perceptions, one fails to attain the true realm within the heavens; instead, one delights in sensory realms—sounds, tastes, forms, and fragrances—as well as greed, hatred, and delusion. One indulges in various forms of negligence, consorts with women, and finds pleasure in sporting amidst gardens adorned with diverse ornaments. There are palaces interspersed with jewels, groves, ponds, and exquisite lotuses where one enjoys play and happiness. Attached to the joy of celestial flower scents, various flavors and foods, dancing, feasting, and wandering, one becomes obsessed with such pleasures. Whether scattering or anointing oneself with celestial sandalwood powder, or taking delight in *mandārava* flowers and celestial songs, one departs from the True Dharma; this is long-term birth and death.
If one is born among the gods, such things occur; by taking those long characteristics as a condition, the perception of length arises.

Furthermore, regarding the long characteristics of birth and death among the hungry ghosts (preta), because they take those characteristics as perceptions and due to their practice of evil karma, they suffer from hunger, thirst, emaciation, and exhaustion; rain falls upon them like fire, and it descends upon their bodies. Their throats are like needles, their ribs are shaped like mountain crags, and they are like broken jars in the void. Because of envy and jealousy, they hack and slash one another with swords, blades, and the like. In places of pitch darkness, they fall down precipitous cliffs and run swiftly toward rivers, canals, and ponds, where the henchmen of Yama, holding swords, staves, sharp mattocks, and other weapons, strike, beat, and hack them, causing them to undergo great suffering.
They eat foul food such as human saliva and vomit; for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, they cannot endure it and undergo various kinds of suffering.

Tears flow from their eyes; their hair is disheveled, covering their bodies and faces. Hundreds of thousands of worms swarm over their entire forms. They carry these wretched bodies, burdened by every kind of disease, wandering long through the cycle of birth and death.
There are always iron crows with flaming claws and beaks that peck and claw at their eyes;
their mouths are like scorched trees, as they devour one another in turn.

They travel through wildernesses spanning thirty-six hundred thousand *koṭis* of *yojanas*, without a master and without a guide, oppressed by hunger and thirst, their bodies aflame as they enter regions of pitch-black darkness.
Such hungry ghosts are deceived by false views and deprived of hearing the True Dharma; this is the prolongation of birth and death.
Due to perceptions of those signs, furthermore, animals prey upon one another, engage in unrighteous sexual desire, and do not know what is appropriate.

If they are born in the water, they move within it with parched minds and constant hunger, always fearing they will be seized by others—such as soft-shelled turtles, tortoises, stingrays, otters, and the like; as for fish, there are the *timi* and *timitimingila*, the one known as the jar-fish (*kumbhīra*), the *nāgara* fish, the one called the large-mouthed fish, the clam, the snail, and other such creatures, who at all times the larger devour the smaller and constantly fear being caught by nets and the like through obstruction.

Furthermore, as for those that travel on land—such as deer, wild boar, water buffalo, pigs, elephants, oxen, horses, donkeys, and yak, as well as elk, bears, rhinoceroses, and so forth—they are bound by various sufferings, slain by blades, afflicted by illness, old age, and death, and mutually harass one another with hundreds of thousands of agonies.

As for those that travel through the air—such as crows, ravens, foxes, geese, peacocks, starlings, chickens, pheasants, doves, pigeons, water cranes, green birds, water-fowl, thrushes, herons, *jīvañjīvaka* birds, and *tāyika* birds—these and countless other such birds, as well as other species, are likewise subject to killing, binding, hunger, and thirst; they are tormented by mutual devouring and the pressing sufferings of cold and heat.
Thus, these animals, whether moving in water, on land, or through the air, are fearful in all three realms; this is the prolongation of birth and death, conditioned by the perception of those signs.

"Just as in the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, the Burning Heat Hell, the Great Burning Heat Hell, and the Avīci Hell, there is the foremost suffering and affliction, inconceivable and immeasurable. One faces hundreds of thousands of fears regarding fire, blades, and the like; one falls into various foul pools where the blood flows from one's limbs, enters the forest of sword-leaves, enters amidst great fires, falls into the River of Ashes, walks upon ground ablaze with fire, and undergoes the agony of being burned by flames. One is oppressed by immeasurable kinds of evil sufferings, such as being bound by rigid shackles, which are unbearable."
Such hells constitute long-term birth and death, conditioned by the perception of those signs.
That bhikṣu, with his accumulation of wisdom, observes:
he perceives the presence of resistance, conditioned by the causal conditions of the karmic fruit of long-lasting form, and thereby contemplates the Four Noble Truths.

He observes the various activities of sentient beings across hundreds of thousands of yojanas; thus, through his practice on the path, he reflects upon them part by part, examines their causes and conditions, and develops weary detachment from birth and death.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does that bhikṣu, through successive analysis, contemplate that mark of shortness?"
He sees, hears, knows, or perceives with the divine eye:
that bhikṣu, wishing to move the army of Māra, how does he analytically contemplate and examine the characteristics of the brevity of birth and death?

They receive the precepts and practice the dhūtas; they are diligent in giving, uphold the precepts, and cultivate wisdom; they show reverence to their elders and superiors with a straightforward mind and joy;

thus possessing right view, they respect and honor their parents; they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, reverently making offerings; they act without flattery or crookedness, without arrogance or deception; they draw near to virtuous friends, maintain faith and upright conduct, initiate actions with a straightforward mind, and discipline their body, speech, and mind.
For such a person, birth and death are brief.
Yet, conditioned by those perceptions and conceptions, if they are born among the gods, they will become heedless:

amidst the Nandana Grove, with its interspersed jeweled palanquins, various groves of trees, ponds of lotuses, fine sandalwood, and exquisite, wonderful necklaces that are beautifully adorned; there are kalpavṛkṣa trees, rivers, springs, and forests, where they enjoy the pleasures of wandering and feasting.

Having renounced such pleasures, they observe the precepts, partake of food, and wander about; they engage in various forms of meditation and recitation, delight in seeing virtuous people, and teach others to recite; they practice generosity and self-restraint, correctly maintain the holy life (*brahmacarya*), keep their sense faculties tranquil, speak little, delight in the Dharma, and consume food in accordance with the Dharma.
"If it were so for the gods, their cycle of birth and death would be short.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Various kinds of suffering and affliction, Hunger and thirst that parch the mouth and dry it out,"
The flames burn his body as if it were a withered tree being consumed;

his suffering is beyond counting. Yet, if for even a single thought-moment he calms his faculties and briefly takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, that person’s cycle of birth and death will be short.
“A bhikṣu thus contemplates the perception of signs:
‘There is constant fear of being beaten, of rain, cold, and heat,
and of devouring one another— such are the manifold sufferings.’”

That suffering is incalculable; yet if one stills the mind for even a single thought-moment and takes temporary refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, the cycle of birth and death as an animal will be short.
Thus does the bhikṣu attend to the perception of signs.
"In the Reviving, Black Rope, Crushing, Screaming,
Great Screaming, and Avīci hells, one is oppressed by various extreme sufferings;
those pains are beyond counting, yet within a single thought-moment,"
With a tranquil mind, one takes up the precepts; thus, the cycle of birth and death in hell is shortened.
"In this way, the bhikṣu conditions his mind upon the perception of signs.
That bhikṣu contemplates in this manner the characteristic of the shortness of birth and death."
What are the four edges?
He observes correctly:
the people of Uttarakuru possess no sense of "mine" regarding any object; this is their definitive practice.
That person thus has four-edged birth-and-death.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates upon the perception of signs: "What is circular?"
In the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, there is a wheeling about through ignorance; this is not the functioning of one's own mind, but is rather circular birth and death.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates upon signs and perceptions.
"What is the 'triangular' [rebirth]?
It refers to when a person performs various mixed karmas—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and is reborn in various places such as the hells, heavens, and the human realm."
Those unwholesome karmas lead to birth in the hells;
wholesome karmas, to the heavens;
and mixed karmas, to the human realm.
If one performs the three types of karma and is reborn in the three realms, this is called the triangular cycle of birth and death.
A bhikṣu thus contemplates the perception of signs: "What is the mass?"

The Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Yāma, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin—beings born according to their similar karma—fall from among the devas and are reborn again among the devas;
they fall from among humans and are reborn again among humans.
This is the cycle of birth and death, a sphere that is not a place of hardship.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the perception of signs: "What is blue?
It is the blue of birth and death for those who, being comprised of unwholesome karma, enter the dark hells."
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the perception of signs:

"What is yellow? Those whose karmic actions of the yellow color lead them to be reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta), where they inflict harm upon one another and mutually destroy each other—such is the yellow cycle of birth and death for hungry ghosts."
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the perception of signs:
"What is red? That which is comprised of red karma leads to birth among animals who devour one another's blood; they conceive a craving for blood—this is the cycle of birth and death that is red."
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the perception of signs:

"What is white? White karma, which is comprised of wholesome deeds, gives rise to birth among the devas; by means of that person's white karma—the precious price for the path of the virtuous—they purchase birth as a deva."
When a deva is about to fall from heaven, other devas say to him:
"Go to the human world; it is a good path for you.
When a person is about to die, their relatives, friends, and acquaintances, as well as their wife and children, weep and cry out, their tears covering their faces as they speak these words:
"How deeply pitiable that you now leave me; you shall be reborn in a good realm, born among human beings.
Such is the white cycle of birth and death for devas and humans.
A bhikṣu thus contemplates the perception of signs. That bhikṣu reflects as follows:

"Having obtained a human body, if one does not practice virtue, cultivate generosity, morality, and wisdom, that person deceives themselves and wanders through the wilderness of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts."
In this way, foolish worldlings fully accumulate such paths of karmic action.

That bhikṣu carefully observes feeling and observes how the aggregate of perception proceeds by taking objects as its support; he sees clearly and seeks with clarity that, conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises, and from the conjunction of these three comes contact, which repeatedly cultivates perceptions.
Observing analytically, one perceives the beauty or ugliness of forms—whether near or far, long or short, square or round, white, or triangular; these are the characteristics of form.

Observing analytically, one contemplates those various perceptions of characteristics, contemplates the causes and conditions of perception, and contemplates the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as the causes and conditions of such perceptions.

Observing analytically, one correctly realizes each aspect of the retribution for evil karma, corresponding to its causes and conditions, awakening to the correspondence of causes and conditions, and subsequently relinquishing them.
Whether they be beneficial or non-beneficial, each having its own distinct characteristic, one knows past perceptions, thinking:
"Regarding this karma, I have already received a favorable retribution, or I have already received an unfavorable retribution," as previously described.
Thus one knows perception: if there is perception, it must still be recollected;

that recollection arises conditioned by that perception, just as light exists because of a lamp—depending on the lamp and conditioned by the lamp, it is due to the lamp as a cause and condition that light exists.
"In this way, indeed, through perception as cause and perception as condition, by the power of perception, there arises recollection; thus that bhikṣu attains the fifth stage.
Having thus understood the contact of perception, the bhikṣu does not give rise to craving for the pleasures of those heavens, nor does he give rise to fear regarding the sufferings of the hells."
He views them with equanimity, perceiving them as being like pure gold.

That monk, having broken through such perceptions, contemplates phenomena differently and is liberated from those perceptions; he then further observes that other people are false and unreal, thinking:
"I now investigate: by what cause, by what condition, and by what causal conditions do these perceptions arise?"
He observes that this perception arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
if those causes and conditions cease, that perception ceases as well, just like the moonstone.
For example, when a moon-crystal (candrakānta) encounters the moon and the crystal, clear water is produced; perception likewise arises through causes and conditions.
Such perception is not without causes and conditions, nor does it have a creator, nor a recipient, nor is it born spontaneously.
In this way, a bhikṣu closely contemplates the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Having thus closely contemplated perception, he understands its arising and ceasing with precision, and further observes it subtly:
"Just as the current of a river flows rapidly, so too is perception; once a wholesome perception has arisen, through the power of other conditions, it is transformed into something unwholesome."
When unwholesome perceptions arise, they are transformed into wholesome perceptions through the power of other conditions;
that monkey-like mind is initially subdued, and the indeterminate is rendered determinate.
He contemplates the perception of pleasure without giving rise to craving for pleasure, and within untainted bliss, he gives rise to the perception of pleasure.
Regarding the perception of suffering within pleasure, one knows pleasure in this way: How does one see it?

When the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—whether arising or ceasing—are neither delighted in nor clung to as pleasant feelings, and when one does not take up the cessation of perception, then formations arise; they neither abide nor cease, and the mind harbors no longing as consciousness arises, abides, and ceases.

When a bhikṣu thus knows these aggregates with clear discernment, he does not dwell within the realm of Māra; he cannot be bound by greed, hatred, or delusion; he is free from the views of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self; and ignorance cannot bind him within saṃsāra with the snare of craving for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. He does not lose his mindfulness, and through the arising of that mindfulness, he is able to exhaust all outflows (āsravas) and reach nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Any bhikṣu who associates with those who are indolent, Who does not constantly exert themselves with diligence— Such a person is no bhikṣu.”
If one does not delight in beds and seats, the Buddha calls such a person a bhikṣu;
yet if the mind delights in indolence, that person is not fit for wholesome dharmas.
The root of affliction is but one, and that is called indolence.
If there is one who is indolent, that person shall not attain the Dharma.
It is not merely by wearing the dharma-robes that one is named a bhikṣu;
if one lacks the intent for recitation, lacks meditative concentration, and lacks the exhaustion of outflows, [one is not a true bhikṣu].
One who possesses only the outward form of a bhikṣu, yet is not such a bhikṣu in reality;
one who merely delights in wandering through the forests, yet finds no joy in the realm of the Path;
one whose greedy mind takes pleasure in wine and sensual beauty—such a person is not a bhikṣu.
If one can sever the bonds of Māra and further cut off evil karma,
the Buddha says that such a bhikṣu does not consume the saṅgha’s food in vain.
It would be better to eat snake venom, datura, or molten copper than [to eat the saṅgha’s food without merit].
One who never breaks the prohibitions and precepts yet eats the food and drink of the Saṃgha acts thus improperly; eating what should not be eaten,
such a person who feeds on afflictions is a denizen of hell.
If a person has abandoned the afflictions like a snake emerging from its hole, that bhikṣu should eat; he does not delight in seeing women.
Taking his own body as collateral, yet his mind delights in evil—
This person defiles the Jewel of the Saṅgha; how can he be called a bhikṣu?
If he craves gain and offerings, delights in sense objects, and feels lustful attachment toward women, he is neither a follower of the Way nor a layman.
If one can burn away afflictions as fire consumes a forest, they are called a true Brahmin; they do not crave food or drink.
They always delight in frequenting villages and take pleasure in bathing repeatedly.
The deluded, who deceive both themselves and others, are all submerged in the ways of the world.
Those who settle their minds in secluded places and constantly practice meditation without abandoning it are called *brāhmaṇas*; they enter the realm of the noble path.
The forest hermitage is excellent; it is not for those who are unworthy to dwell there.
Only those who have abandoned desire can abide therein—those who delight in compassion and joy.
If one delights in much speech and takes pleasure in sense objects, [one cannot dwell there].
He does not head toward the city of Nirvāṇa, nor toward the place where there is neither birth nor death.
He stays close to kings and fine foods, constantly drinking wine and delighting in anger;
he is a bhikṣu in name only, using false speech to deceive his donors.
If one falsely employs expedient means, frequently visiting the gates of kings to afflict and distress laypeople,
and to bring ruin upon those who dwell in seclusion;
if such a person abandons wife and children to rely on a tranquil forest—
If there is still a lingering attachment, it is like having vomited food only to eat it again.

That bhikṣu, transcending this state of agitation, contemplates the aggregates with discernment and perceives them as they truly are; he diligently cultivates liberation and consults his elders, asking:
"What is the path? What is not the path?"

Because of knowing and seeing with clarity, one seeks the city of liberation via the Noble Eightfold Path, constantly and diligently practicing the Way. With right view that is impartial, the mind is free from defilement and its nature is tranquil; thus, one joyfully cultivates and frequently practices the path upon which one travels.
That bhikṣu, thus practicing in conjunction with these wholesome dharmas and the untainted paths of action, diminishes the hosts of Māra and increases the faction of the True Dharma.
When the yakṣas of that earth have thus learned this, they in turn announce it upward to the yakṣas of the atmosphere;
the yakṣas of the atmosphere then successively report it to the Four Great Kings.
From those Four Great Kings up to Yama and Maitreya, the World-Honored One of Tuṣita Heaven, it is as previously described.
In the realm of Tuṣita, there was a bodhisattva who felt extreme joy and spoke thus to the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven:
"In Jambudvīpa, a certain son of good family has shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, as previously described."
That emanated deva became even more joyful, as previously described.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—observing the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does that bhikṣu attain the fifth stage?"
He knows through seeing, hearing, or learning, or sees with the divine eye:
he contemplates the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).

The ten are as follows: the base of the eye, the base of forms; the base of the ear, the base of sounds; the base of the nose, the base of odors; the base of the tongue, the base of tastes; the base of the body, and the base of tangibles.
How does one observe these ten bases of form?
With the eye-base as condition and the form-base as condition, this perception of "self" arises in me.
One observes it in this way:

Due to the condition of the eye and the condition of visible forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is contact, and with contact there arise simultaneously feeling, perception, volition, and so forth.

That bhikṣu, whether experiencing feeling, knows it as feeling; whether experiencing volition, knows it as volition; whether experiencing perception, knows it as perception. Such as: "this form is long," "this form is short"; "this form is attractive," "this is unattractive"; "this form is visible," "this is invisible"; "this form is resistant," "this is non-resistant"—and so on, up to this mental name-and-form, which consists of eleven kinds.

"By such analysis, one knows that from the meeting of the three arises contact; contact arises together with feeling, perception, volition, and so forth. One knows that from eye-contact, feeling, perception, and volition are produced."
What is the meaning of that?

To discern and know is the meaning of *vedanā* (feeling); to know the temporal sequence is the meaning of *saṃjñā* (perception). This is called the turning of the mind (*manas*), and when these dharmas arise, they possess distinct characteristics and distinct entities.
The meaning of "distinct" is like the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); such distinct characteristics are the distinct characteristic of volition (*cetanā*).

Mindfulness, wisdom, and liberation; feeling, perception, volition, contact, desire, diligence, and concentration—these share a single object of focus, yet they possess distinct and differing characteristics.
Thus, feeling and perception, as well as their respective characteristics, are diverse and not one, just as the rays of sunlight, though having a single object, possess different natures.
In this way, there is a distinct entity of feeling, a distinct entity of volition, and one clearly knows that from eye-contact, feeling, perception, and volition arise.
He observes correctly that the eye is thus empty, devoid of substance, and without solidity.
In this way, the bhikṣu truly sees that eye; he understands the path with clarity, abandons wrong views, and right view becomes manifest before him.

He relinquishes such defiled conduct associated with delusion—namely, the impure perception of the eye and the perception of it as unreal—and contemplates this eye with discernment as being merely a lump of flesh, a confluence of fat, pus, blood, tears, and other impure substances. Having understood it thus, he is able to sever desire.
Having understood that this eye is impermanent, he perceives it as impermanent;
having understood that this eye is merely a lump of flesh within a bony socket, his mind becomes detached from desire;

furthermore, understanding that this eye is bound by tendons, he knows that this eye-base, whether belonging to self or others, is mutually unrelated and non-corresponding—this thing is not solid, and all things are without self.
"To state it briefly: such an eye is nothing but a source of suffering.
Having observed and understood this, one becomes detached from desire for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Having thus observed and known the eye-base, one next observes visible forms (*rūpa*):"
Such form is subject to love and non-love; it is an indeterminate phenomenon, a false discrimination. What solidity, what purity, what permanence, what self, or what pleasure can there be in this?
Observing form in this way and having understood it through reflection, one knows that all forms are entirely without solidity and consist of nothing but conceptual construction.

Such is form: there are the pleasant and the unpleasant; yet this pleasantness and unpleasantness cannot be found as an intrinsic essence. These are merely the world’s grasping through the conceptual constructions of love and hatred; thus one reflects upon love and hatred.
Furthermore, once that bhikṣu has thus observed the sense base of the eye and its objects, he observes the sense base of the ear and its sounds. He examines how sound arises:
this sound arises from the mutual encounter of the faculty and the object.

He contemplates in this way: "Due to the condition of the ear and the condition of mindfulness, auditory consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is contact (*sparśa*). Contact arises together with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). He knows that contact arises together with those feelings, perceptions, and volitions. If he knows that contact arises together with volition, he perceives the mental formations (*saṃskāra*), namely the characteristics of length, distance, and so forth, as well as the conditions by which he hears sounds—whether they be heavy or coarse, subtle or gross, and whether they are pleasant or unpleasant."

That bhikṣu knows such sounds; he knows them through reflection, knows them through perception, and investigates them part by part, knowing them with the mental consciousness, knowing them through reflection, and knowing them through feeling, while recollecting and deliberating upon them.

Regarding that ear and the sphere of sound, one reflects and discriminates, and subsequently realizes that such sounds have no intrinsic nature; they are neither desirable nor undesirable, for it is only through discrimination that one perceives these sounds as being thus desirable or undesirable.

Such sounds have no intrinsic nature; they are neither permanent nor substantial. They are fragile and unstable, devoid of pleasure, self, or that which belongs to a self; they are merely sounds of attachment, aversion, ignorance, and the pleasant or unpleasant.

Having thus correctly contemplated the sense-sphere of the ear and sounds, when hearing a sound, one is not deluded; one does not give rise to delight, does not grasp, does not cling, and does not consider it to be substantial.
Having thus observed the sense-spheres of the ear and sounds, one does not delight in ear-consciousness and becomes free from desire for ear-consciousness:
"Ear-consciousness is not self, and I am not ear-consciousness. It is the same for contact, feeling, perception, and volition.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the nose and the sphere of odors:
through the condition of the nose, the condition of odors, and the condition of mindfulness, olfactory consciousness arises.

Whether near or far, whether pleasant or unpleasant, whether fragrant or foul, when wind brings them together and they arrive, one smells them by means of the wind. The nose is the internal sense-sphere (*āyatana*), and odors are the external sense-sphere; from the conjunction of these three comes contact (*sparśa*), and with contact arise simultaneously feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

Having known those characteristics, one thus contemplates the characteristics of the nose and fragrance bases; knowing the characteristic of internal contact, one then knows that the characteristics of contact and volition are equal. Regarding such phenomena, there is a single characteristic as the object of focus, yet they function through diverse causes and conditions.

"Different" means that there are distinct characteristics and distinct entities. As for distinct characteristics, they are like the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), as previously explained.
All these phenomena possess such distinct characteristics; they do not share a single characteristic, nor are they produced by a single cause or condition.
That bhikṣu thus knows the nose and the field of odors with clear discernment, and thus seeks with clear discernment:
"In such things as these, what substance is solid?
What substance is permanent?"
What is indestructible?
This nose-consciousness-element (ghrāṇa-vijñānāyatana) is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
When that person thus knows the nose-consciousness-element—that all things are not self and do not belong to a self—and understands this correctly, there remains only conceptual discrimination.
"This nose and the sphere of odors are thus bound only to the foolish worldling and not to the wise one.
In this manner, the bhikṣu performs such an investigation.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the tongue and the sphere of tastes:

With that mindfulness as a condition, tongue-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is contact (*sparśa*). Contact arises simultaneously with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

That which accords with awakening is called the characteristic of feeling; knowing is the characteristic of perception; resistance is the characteristic of contact; perception is the characteristic of volition; and perception takes the characteristic as its object.
These phenomena each have their own specific characteristics and, moreover, a common characteristic; they arise from distinct causes and conditions.

In this way, all these factors together accomplish a single task—just as, for example, by means of a tube, tongs, husks, water, and a crucible, a goldsmith through these conditions fashions a finger-ring or a bracelet. Thus, these phenomena do not arise from a single characteristic;
the tongue and the taste-base (*rasāyatana*) are likewise so.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu carefully contemplates the sense-base of the tongue and the sense-base of tastes. Having contemplated them in this way, he finds that within these bases of the tongue and tastes there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is permanent, blissful, self, or pure. Through all manner of profound and subtle reflection, he does not find a single dharma [possessing such qualities].
In this way, in this manner, they correspond to a single characteristic.

They experience the tongue as an entrance, an entrance into flavor, and an entrance into defilement; all sentient beings sink into this sea, delighting in the sea of flavors and mutually obstructing one another. Therefore, they are further bound within the great ocean of the five realms—humans, devas, hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—in this very way.
In this way, a bhikṣu, though desiring liberation regarding the tongue and the sphere of tastes, [realizes]:
"The tongue-sphere is not self; I am not the tongue-sphere; it is neither permanent, nor a substantial entity, nor immovable, nor indestructible, nor is it the tongue and the sphere of tastes."
"In this way, the bhikṣu becomes free from defiled desire.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the body-contact base (*kāya-spraṣṭavyāyatana*): conditioned by body and contact, body-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is contact; and with contact, feeling, perception, volition, and so forth arise simultaneously. Just as previously described regarding the eye-base and other bases, this body-contact base should be understood in the same manner."

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does a bhikṣu, having thus contemplated the ten bases of form (rūpāyatana), contemplate the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?"
He knows through seeing, hearing, or cognition, or sees with the divine eye:

within that sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), three kinds of phenomena are subsumed—namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and all non-existent phenomena such as space; all these are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects.
Having observed in this way, that space is also a sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

As for cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), this phenomenon is called "knowledge. Having realized it in its immeasurable varieties, one proceeds in accordance with deliberation; having performed this, one realizes the abandonment of afflictions, causing those afflictions to be exhausted, extinguished, and destroyed, such that all is untainted (*anāsrava*).

As for that which is not conditioned by calculation (*apratisaṃkhyā*), it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it is not feeling (*vedanā*); it is neither cognition (*jñāna*) nor awakening (*bodha*), nor is it doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The consciousnesses of other people, though they have undergone hundreds of thousands of births, are all lost.
The consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already been destroyed and will not arise again; this is called cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This non-deliberative cessation is the third emptiness. Knowing these three dharmas, one understands that what does not arise is permanent, is not subsumed within the three periods of time, and is neither presently arising, nor has it arisen, nor will it ever arise.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu analyzes the two types of the dharma-āyatana individually, namely: the material and the immaterial.
That which is called "material" refers to the ten material āyatanas.
How is it that visual consciousness, which is neither seeing nor an object of sight, sees forms as objects of sight?
Likewise, how is it that auditory consciousness, which is neither seeing nor an object of sight, apprehends sounds?
Likewise, how is it that olfactory consciousness, which is neither seeing nor an object of sight, apprehends fragrances?
In this way, the tongue-consciousness is neither seeing nor encountering; how then does it apprehend flavors?
In this way, the body-consciousness is neither seeing nor encountering; how then does it apprehend tangibles?
How is it that these five external bases and these five internal bases, being neither seeing nor encountering, come into contact with what is seen and encountered?
How do they correspond? That bhikṣu observes in this way:

when visual consciousness arises, there are two kinds of objects; likewise, up to mental consciousness, each has two kinds [of objects]. Thus consciousness arises like a seal impressing an object: if the object does not resemble the seal, or if the seal is soft while the object is hard, then it cannot be impressed.
When a seal is applied to a hard object that is soft, the impression is produced.

In this way, and in this way, consciousness does not directly perceive the object; rather, it takes up the perception of the object, and among all phenomena, the third seal arises: dissimilar things arise from dissimilar things.
That these various phenomena are dissimilar things arising from dissimilar things is the first *koṭi*.
The second *koṭi* (alternative): two phenomena are similar and arise from what is similar; that is to say, white threads produce a white cloth. The third *koṭi*:
two things are non-associated and arise from what is non-associated, such as fire produced by a fire-drill; the wood and the fire are seen to be non-associated.
The fourth position is that one perceives thick substances arising from thin substances, such as curd arising from milk; since milk is thin and curd is thick, such a principle is inconsistent.
"In this way, in this way, these dissimilar phenomena—namely, eye-consciousness and the rest—arise from distinct causes and distinct conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one delights in the knowledge of phenomena, Practicing meditation while dwelling in the forest,"
One who correctly awakens to the characteristics of the truths, Then attains the unsurpassed state.
Always delighting in the practice of a compassionate mind, Diligent within the realm of the Dharma,
And truly knowing the characteristics of the body— Such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
If a person observes correctly, desire and anger cannot destroy them;
such a one may be called a bhikṣu,
but one who differs from this is not a bhikṣu.
Compassionate toward all sentient beings, Having abandoned all craving and attachment,
And liberated from all bonds— Such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
If one disciplines the mind, The sensory realms cannot destroy it.
Stainless like pure gold, he is called a bhikṣu who knows contentment.
If one’s mind is not defiled by what is liked or disliked,
know that such a person practices virtue and has abandoned all faults.
One whose deportment is beyond reproach, who practices the Dharma and disciplines the sense faculties,
and who possesses a courageous and pure mind— such a person is called a bhikṣu.
If a person always delights in [the teachings] and understands the meaning within all treatises, [he is a true practitioner].
Not craving for food or drink, he is called a bhikṣu of tranquil mind.
Practicing in the forest as an araṇyaka, using grass among the graves as his mat—
if one finds joy in this, such a person is called a bhikṣu.
Truly knowing the faults of karmic offenses, Skillfully understanding the fruits of all actions,
Profoundly recognizing causes and conditions— Such a one is a bhikṣu who has left evil behind.
He breaks through the vast wilderness of birth and death, Destroys evil, and disciplines the sense faculties.
Furthermore, he is well able to discern his friends; his name is the bhikṣu Śāntamati.
His mind does not rejoice in praise, nor does it grieve at disparagement;
like the depth of the great ocean, such is the bhikṣu who practices.
One who conceals the faults of others with a firm mind, Who does not relish soft and flattering speech,
But speaks at the proper time with skillful respect— Such a one is called a bhikṣu of tranquility.
He knows the causes of karma in the desire realm, And likewise knows the causes of the form realm.
One who understands the formless realms as well is a bhikṣu who knows the doctrine.
One who does not delight in worldly talk, who always rejoices in severing all faults,
and who regards sense objects as poison— of such a person the Buddha says, "He is a bhikṣu."
If a person desires [purity] as one treats clay, and always acts with such an intention,
opening their mind through wisdom, they will be liberated from the bonds of birth and death.
If a person engages in the practice of meditation and recitation, remaining far removed from indolence, they shall attain liberation.
One who benefits all sentient beings is called an araṇya bhikṣu.
If one can answer difficult questions, possesses eloquence, and has disciplined the sense faculties, know that such a person is a Dharma teacher; otherwise, they are like mere grass.
Whether in physical or mental activities, they never grow weary; whatever tasks the Saṅgha has, they are able to perform them all,
yet they seek no wealth, nor do they act for the sake of riches, pleasure, or fame.
With a mind solely intent on benefiting the Saṅgha, he is liberated from all bonds.
He observes the precepts without desiring rebirth in heaven, nor does he seek fame or profit;
he observes the precepts for the sake of Nirvāṇa—he is a bhikṣu of tranquility.
Always abandoning all evils, Delighting only in practicing wholesome deeds,
And not associating with evil associates— Such a one is a bhikṣu of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Always cultivating the mind with loving-kindness, With a respectful and upright intention,
One whose training is unimpaired is not far from Nirvana.
Constantly fearing old age, illness, and death, and having no desire for worldly pleasures,
one who cultivates dhyāna without negligence is not far from Nirvana.
If a person, through impermanence, And the selflessness and emptiness of self and others, Cultivates dhyāna and supreme wisdom, They are not far from nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—observing the course of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does that bhikṣu, having attained the fifth stage, attain the sixth stage?"
He knows through seeing, hearing, or inference, or sees it with the divine eye:
that bhikṣu understands the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*). What is this teaching?
It is that from a similar cause, a similar fruit is obtained.
There is a dissimilar cause and a dissimilar effect;
there is a dissimilar cause and a dissimilar effect;
and there is that which is half-similar and half-dissimilar.
What is meant by "a similar cause producing a similar result"?
It is like rice seeds producing rice;
in this same way, internal similarity refers to the similarity of wholesome karma, through which one obtains results in the realms of gods and humans.
This is the first stage of attainment.
What is meant by "dissimilar cause and dissimilar effect"?
It is, for example, like sweet milk producing sour curds, which are not pleasant or desirable.

In this way and that way, internal dissimilarity refers to how, through attachment to sounds, tangibles, tastes, forms, and fragrances in this world, one obtains undesirable and unpleasant fruits in hell, just like sour curd;
this is the second *koṭi*.
What is meant by "the cause being dissimilar and the fruit being dissimilar"?
For example, when blue and other colors combine to produce a different color, the resulting color is dissimilar [to its components].

In this same way, internal dissimilarity refers to the fact that karma and its retribution are entirely dissimilar; it is not the case that the fruit corresponds to its specific karma, as in the following wrong view:
Regarding the sacrificial rites of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they slaughter sheep in hopes of reaching heaven, yet fall instead into hell;
this is the third case of *kuśala* (merit). What is meant by "half-similar and half-dissimilar"?
For example, it is like white threads used to make a white garment: the threads are fine while the garment is coarse, and thus they are dissimilar.
In this same way, there is both similarity and dissimilarity within; through subtle unwholesome karma, one obtains the coarse and unwholesome retribution of the great hells.
This is the fourth *kuśala*.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, having reflected and contemplated, does not grasp at the fruits of karma; he further reflects and contemplates the diverse fruits of karma, which proceed through existence like the turning of a wheel, possessing four modes of occurrence.
There are actions that have not yet arrived, yet when performed collectively by many people, they can cause oppression and affliction;
this is the first case of accumulation.
There are actions that must have already arrived before they can cause oppression and affliction.
The second *upādāna* (appropriation) is that by which karma, whether it has already arrived or has not yet arrived, is capable of causing affliction;
this is the third *upādāna*.
There is karma that neither reaches nor does not reach, which constitutes the fourth category (*koṭi*).

There is karma that has not yet reached its object but is capable of afflicting many people collectively; this is like worldly phenomena where a country suffers calamity even though the [ominous] stars have not yet arrived.

In the supramundane sense, although visual consciousness has not yet reached the object, the ocean of karma can still afflict it—namely, by the afflictions of desire, mental distress, sorrow, grief, and so forth.
This is the first stage of proximity (*pratyupasthāna*).
Regarding "only when karma has arrived can it exert its pressure": it is like worldly phenomena, where fire burns only upon arrival and a blade cuts only when it reaches the flesh;
likewise, in the supramundane realm, when unwholesome karma arrives, one is oppressed and afflicted by the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
The second point concerns the nature of karma:

there are actions that can cause affliction whether they have already arrived or have not yet arrived. This is like worldly phenomena, such as the power of spells or poisons, which can cause affliction both when they have reached their target and when they have not;
or as in the supramundane case, when a person is about to die, there are signs of hope that have not yet reached the hells.

The third case concerns karma that is neither "arrived" nor "not arrived. For example, in the world, various medicinal seeds do not produce their power by having already arrived [at the sprout], nor do they produce it by not yet having arrived;

it is the same for supramundane matters. When an Arhat Bhikṣu has determined karma as vast as Mount Sumeru, whether that Arhat enters Nirvāṇa or has not yet entered Nirvāṇa, this karma cannot oppress the Arhat.
The fourth permutation:
"There is karma that is experienced in the present life but not in a future birth;
this is the first permutation."
There is karma that is to be experienced in a future birth but not in the present life;
this is the second category.
There is karma that is to be experienced in a future birth and also experienced in the present life.

The third category consists of those that are neither to be experienced in the present life nor to be experienced upon rebirth; the fourth category consists of those that are to be experienced in future lives.
"What is karma that is experienced in the present life but not in a future birth?
Regarding worldly matters, it is like violating the laws of a king and being punished by the king's law; such karma is experienced in the present life but not in a future birth.
Regarding supramundane matters, it is the practice of generosity praised by virtuous people; such karma is experienced in the present life and not in another world."
This is the first cause.
What kind of karma results in retribution to be experienced in a future life rather than in the present?
It is like a worldly person who enters fire and obtains fire.
Regarding the supramundane: it can be seen in this very life that if one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, one will obtain the fruit in another world;
this is the second acquisition (*adhigama*).
What karma results in both birth-reception (*upapadyavedanīya*) and present-life reception (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?
That which is mundane refers to what is experienced in the present life and what is experienced upon being born into a future life;
that which is supramundane is likewise so;
this is the third *koṭi*.
What karma is neither to be experienced in the present life nor in the next life?
Regarding worldly karma, it is such as the precept of silence or the act of giving;
regarding supramundane karma, it refers to indeterminate (avyākṛta) karma, which is neither to be experienced in the present life nor to be experienced in the next life.
The fourth dwelling place:

"That bhikṣu sits thus in one corner, observing in this way the net of karmic retribution consisting of immeasurable varieties of branches that pervades the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. Having seen this, he practices in accordance with the Dharma."
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does a bhikṣu know the retribution of karma?"

That is to say, he knows this karma and knows the fruit of this karma; he knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. He knows that certain sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, accomplished misconduct of speech, and accomplished misconduct of mind; they revile the noble ones and are possessed by wrong views. Because of these causes and conditions of karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall among hungry ghosts.

If there are sentient beings who have accomplished good conduct of body, accomplished good conduct of speech, and accomplished good conduct of mind; they praise the noble ones and are possessed by right view. Because of these causes and conditions of karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the world of the gods in the happy realms.

“That bhikṣu thus contemplates the dharma of the retribution of his own karma; having contemplated it in this way, he does not associate with the beings of the realm of Māra and will ultimately reach nirvāṇa.
Practicing the Dharma in this manner, cultivating the practice of disenchantment, and diligently following the path of goodness, he brings an end to birth and death.
Having taken others under his care, he causes them to cross over birth and death just as he has crossed over himself, as well as all his donors.”

That bhikṣu, knowing the dharma of karmic retribution, contemplates the sequence of karmic retributions in the various realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas; it is like a pure vaidūrya gem that has been strung with a cord for the sake of adornment.
Just as one sees the colors of that cord— whether blue, yellow, red, white, purple, or otherwise—
so too does one see the beads of karma threaded upon the cord of retribution.
In this regard, that bhikṣu perceives, hears, and knows all within these karmas, or sees them with the divine eye, clearly and purely.
Furthermore, whether seeing or hearing, that bhikṣu knows the law of karmic retribution just as he does that jewel.

It is like a jewel whose color is exceedingly white, universally pure and flawless, clean and ready for threading, well-refined, and preeminent in all its aspects; it is praised by all people of the world and is fit to be possessed and used by kings and those like them.
Such a pure jewel endowed with these qualities—only kings and those like them know the value of this pure jewel—and having taken this jewel, they place it upon their ornaments.

In this way, in this way, that bhikṣu’s jewel of the pure portion of the ten paths of wholesome action is universally white, virtuous, and pure; free from faults and blemishes; clean and ready for boring; a portion of the remedial dharmas; possessed of great power; and a dharma that answers difficult questions. It is bored by the dharma-drill of a Dharma-preacher and skillfully refined. In this way, in this way, he vows to bestow [the fruits of] precepts and wisdom;

and in this way, having refined the jewel of the ten paths of wholesome action, he takes up whatever he desires according to his vow—whether becoming a Wheel-turning Sage King, a Heavenly King, a Māra King, or a Brahmā King—and cultivates untainted dhyāna with mastery over samādhi.
In this way, in this way, when that jewel of the True Dharma has been well-refined, it is called the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*); this Universal Gate refers to the gate of devas and humans.

That jewel of the True Dharma is named "Universal Gateway. Having emerged from within the city of the world, one enters the gate of Nirvana. It is that which is praised by all people of the world—that is, praised by those of right view and those in training—and it is that which is fit for application by kings and their like; it is what should be employed by the Mind-King who has entered the path of the True Dharma.
If a person has faith in that Vaiḍūrya jewel, all its merits will be fully complete; such a precious jewel is similar to and corresponds with the jewel of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the law of karmic retribution as being like that gem.

For example, suppose there is a gem that has flaws; it is not entirely pure, is not bright and white in all its facets, cannot be drilled or pierced, and cannot be polished. When seen by anyone, it is not praised, and it is not fit to be possessed or used by a king or those like a king.
It is just so, it is just so. Those teachings of the non-Buddhists are merely semblances of the Dharma, like a flawed pearl.

As for what is called "flaw," it refers to the flaw of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the flaw of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the flaw of doubt; they do not lead to all gates [of liberation], but are only gates to the three realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. They are not excellent teachings;

furthermore, they are not associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), they cannot be penetrated by investigation, and they are not a method capable of answering difficult challenges. They are not the kind of teaching that can be pierced by the Dharma-pearl drill of a true Dharma-preacher, nor are they fit to be possessed or used by kings or those like them.
The practice of the Eightfold Path of the True Dharma for the eight types of persons (*pudgala*) is the king of the mind; those beads of the non-Buddhists are not suitable for it.

Such dharmas are similar in appearance yet opposed in nature: if a flawed bead that is not the true Dharma were tied around a person's neck, and that person, having tied such a counterfeit bead around their neck, remains in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, they will continue to transmigrate through birth and death from time immemorial.

In this way, that bhikṣu observes the jewel and the counterfeit jewel; for example, there may be a lapis lazuli bead in the world that resembles vaidūrya, and someone seeing it might call it vaidūrya—foolish ordinary people are just like this.
"When that bhikṣu has thus correctly understood what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, he attains the seventh stage."

The yakṣas of that realm, seeing that bhikṣu maintaining pure precepts and having attained the seventh stage, were filled with even greater joy. Thus it was passed on to the yakṣas of the air; the yakṣas of the air heard the Four Great Kings; those Four Great Kings heard the Four Heavenly Kings; those Four Heavenly Kings thus passed the news to the Heaven of the Thirty-three; the Heaven of the Thirty-three likewise spoke to Śakra, King of Devas; Śakra, King of Devas, in turn spoke to the Yāma Heaven; the Yāma Heaven successively heard it from the Tuṣita Heaven; the Tuṣita Heaven then reported this in full to Maitreya, the World-Honored One; Maitreya, the World-Honored One, informed the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven further spoke to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, saying:
"In Jambudvīpa, such-and-such a son of good family [proceeds] in this sequence, as previously described."

"Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma: How does a bhikṣu contemplate the dharma of karmic retribution? The eleventh is called 'non-action' (avijñapti), which is comprised within form (rūpa)."

Among all phenomena, it is associated with form (*rūpa*). If a person receives the precepts, once the precept has been generated, even if they are asleep, fainting, have lost their mind, or are insane, such wholesome dharmas continue in succession and proceed, just like a river that flows constantly without interruption.
For such a person, even when asleep, fainting, unconscious, or insane, this non-action (avijñapti) continues to flow constantly and without interruption.
This non-action, consisting of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), cannot be seen or confronted.
Furthermore, how is that matter subsumed under karma?
This unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is the pillar of all wholesome dharmas.
Such are these eleven kinds of matter.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Volume Four.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Volume Five.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Birth and Death, Part Three:
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes in this way:
"How is it that sentient beings possess various colors, various forms, various paths, and various bases?"

Furthermore, he observes that there are various minds, various bases, various inclinations, and various karmas; these various forms, various shapes, various paths, and various bases are like a skillful and wise painter or his apprentice who, having observed a well-levelled, firm, and smooth piece of ground, and having obtained this ground, uses various pigments and various mixtures—whether beautiful or ugly—to create whatever he desires according to his mind, exactly as those forms appear.

The painter of mental karma, or his disciple, is likewise so: upon the ground of the ripening of karmic fruits—which is even, firm, smooth, and slippery—and within the realm of birth and death, they create various forms, various paths, and various bases according to their understanding;
the painter of mental karma fashions sentient beings through karma.

Furthermore, regarding various pigments: if one takes white, it becomes white; if one takes red, it becomes red; if one takes yellow, it becomes yellow; if one takes the color of a pigeon, it becomes the color of a pigeon; and if one takes black, it becomes black.
The painter of mental karma is likewise: by taking up the white through conditions, it becomes white among devas and humans.
In what sense is it called "white"?
Because it is not defiled by the stains of outflows such as desire, it is therefore called "white."
Furthermore, it is like this:
the artist of mental karma takes the red pigment and produces the color red among gods and humans.
In what sense is it called "red"?
That which is called the attachment to sounds, tastes, touches, fragrances, and forms is like painting and observing a garment.
Furthermore, it is like this:
the painter of mental karma takes yellow pigment and is able to produce the color yellow within the animal realm.
In what sense is it called "yellow"?
Because they drink each other's blood and devour one another's flesh, and because of their greed, hatred, and delusion, they kill and harm one another; therefore, it is called the color yellow.
Furthermore, it is also like this:
The painter of mental karma takes the color of a pigeon and, through the process of objective observation, creates the appearance of a soiled pigeon within the realm of hungry ghosts.
For what reason is it called a "pigeon"?
Their bodies are like trees in a forest scorched by fire, tormented by hunger and thirst, and oppressed by manifold sufferings.
The painter of mental karma is gripped by envy and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance.
Furthermore, it is like this:
the painter of mental karma takes black pigments and paints the color black within the hells.
In what sense is it called "black"?

Because of black karma, one is born within the hells; there are black iron walls where one is burned and bound, resulting in a blackened body. One undergoes various diseases and a body afflicted by the sufferings of hunger and thirst, oppressed by immeasurable pains—all of which are one's own karma and not created by another.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates this robe of the painting of birth and death, with its five colors representing the three realms and five destinies, abiding within the three stages:
namely, the stage of the desire realm, and the stages of the form and formless realms.
The mind, like a painter, habitually frequents sensual desire and grasps at the various forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm as its objects of painting, taking form as its support.

With the twenty types of detachment from desire and the four *dhyānas* as its brushes, and relying upon the sixteen stages as the site of painting, it paints the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Having detached from the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the realm of form as their object, it takes the formless realm as its object, painting it as the four [formless] abodes.
The painter of mental karma extensively paints this great garment of the triple world.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes how this painter of mental karma creates sentient beings through yet another method.
The mind is like a painter; the body is like a painting board; greed, hatred, and delusion serve as its sturdy foundation;
the攀緣 (pān-yuan) mind is like a ladder; the sense faculties are like painting brushes; external objects—sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and various fragrances—are like the various pigments;

birth and death are like the ground; wisdom is like light; the diligent exertion of vigor is similar to the hands; sentient beings are like the painted figures; and the supernatural powers are like their immeasurable forms and garments. Just as a painting is brought to completion, so too do immeasurable kinds of karmic fruits and retributions arise.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, relying on dhyāna, observes that the painter of mental karma possesses various kinds of phenomena.
Just as that painter does not grow weary, skillfully prepares the pigments so that each is bright and pure, and is well-versed in fine brushes to paint beautiful colors; so too is it with this.

The mental karma artist is likewise tireless; when practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he skillfully prepares the colors of dhyāna, and his focal objects are luminous and pure. Like the light of the colors, he is a master of the path of cultivation; like a fine brush, he knows the higher and lower levels of dhyāna.

Like one who possesses excellent discernment, he knows when to grasp and when to relinquish. Thus, without weariness, this mental karma artist paints those stages of dhyāna with the beautiful colors of that concentration.
Furthermore, in this way, if the painter of mental karma becomes weary, he paints what is unwholesome—the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—which share the same karmic causes and conditions.

Using an iron pestle as a brush and being unskilled in colors, he painted figures of those who are unworthy of such treatment—namely, those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Such colors are not beautiful paintings; the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu next observes the monkey-like mind as if he were seeing an actual monkey;

just as that monkey is restless and never still, moving without obstruction through various trees, flowers, branches, fruits, forests, and such, as well as through mountain valleys, rocky caves, and winding places.

The monkey of the mind is likewise: the distinctions of the five realms of existence are like various forests; the paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts are like the trees therein; the immeasurable sentient beings are like the various branches;
craving is like the flowers and leaves;
and the discrimination of sounds, scents, tastes, and textures constitutes the manifold fruits.
When traversing the mountains of the three realms, the body is like a cave; that which moves without obstruction is the monkey of the mind.
This monkey of the mind constantly wanders through the lands of birth and death in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, relying on dhyāna, observes the mind as an actor, seeing it just as one sees an actor.
Just as that actor takes up various musical instruments and performs all manner of plays upon the stage, so too does the mind.
The puppet of the mind is likewise: its various karmic transformations serve as its clothing;
the performance arena refers to the ground of the five destinies;
and its various ornaments, various conditions, and various musical instruments refer to its own objective spheres.
"The performance of an actor is the play of birth and death;
the mind is the actor, and its various performances are the long cycle of birth and death, without beginning or end.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, relying on dhyāna, observes the mind as a *miṇi* fish, seeing it just as he sees a *miṇi*.

It is like the *miṇi* fish dwelling in a river; if the waters are swift, turbulent with waves, deep, and flow rapidly, making it difficult to move about, and they can carry away immeasurable varieties of trees, their force being so violent and rapid that it cannot be obstructed.
In mountain torrents and river currents that are swift, violent, and treacherous, the *miṇi* fish is able to enter and exit, and to move and stay.
The *miṇi* of the mind is likewise: within the turbulent waves of the swift river of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is able to enter and exit, and to move and stay.

In hell there is a river named Vaitaraṇī; that river is extremely deep, its surging waves swift and violent, never pausing for a moment. It is most terrifying, a turbulent current of rapid speed, with wholesome and unwholesome karmas serving as its flowing waters. It is difficult to traverse, and no foolish worldling can cross it.

This river of the five destinies has constantly drifted sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas; its currents of sensory objects flow swiftly and without ceasing, its violent power is impossible to obstruct, it continues incessantly through impermanence, and being dragged by its forceful momentum, it cannot be checked or severed.

The river of craving is swift and treacherous; the fish Mīṇa dwell within its depths. One can traverse this river, either entering it or emerging from it: those who emerge are devas and humans, while those who enter are hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"The *mimira* fish dwells within the river of craving, entering and exiting it in this manner.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—contemplating the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does that bhikṣu cultivate the foundations of mindfulness through meditative concentration and know the law of karmic retribution? He observes how the minds of all sentient beings always act with autonomy, yet are driven by the mind and bound by the mind."
Observing in this way, he sees, hears, knows, or perceives with the divine eye that all sentient beings possess mastery over their mental karma;
they act in accordance with their mental karma and are driven by the mind.
Furthermore, he observes: how is it that sentient beings are bound within birth and death, without beginning or end, wandering through immeasurable cycles?
Through what he sees, hears, and knows, or through his divine eye, he perceives:
because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are fettered.
Because the mind is pure, sentient beings attain liberation.
Such a mind possesses immeasurable and various modes of disintegration: the disintegration of objective conditions, the disintegration of its own essence, and the disintegration through common karma.

The mind is of five kinds; that is to say, within the five destinies, it freely grasps and clings, conjoining with and corresponding to the mind of the fetters (saṃyojana), and thus constantly abides in saṃsāra, separated from the supreme reliance, namely the three unconditioned dharmas such as space.
There are five types of mind regarding the signs of the deterioration of the five faculties; these are based upon immeasurable and boundless signs of attachment to various forms of deterioration.
In brief, this constitutes the defiled portion.
What is the skillful means for becoming free from the three afflictive roots?
There are three remedies; all the Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past and future have taught this right path:
[remedy] desire with the contemplation of impurity, hatred with a mind of loving-kindness, and delusion with dependent origination.

"He contemplates desire within the body in this way; having thus attended to the bodily formations, the bhikṣu contemplates the body part by part, from the fingernails and so forth up to the head, observing part by part:
'Of these gross parts of the body, which one is the self?'"
"What is 'mine'? Within the parts of my own body, I observe such things as my toenails, seeing them apart from the body:
'The nails are not the body; the toes are not the body. What, then, is the body? "
What is "I"? What is "mine"? The sole of the foot is not the body; where, then, does the thought arise that it is "mine"?
This inner ankle is not my body; this heel is also not my body;
the calf is not my body; the knee is not my body; the ball of the foot is not my body; the genitals are not my body; this skull is also not my body; the anus is also not my body;
likewise, the forty-five bones of the back region are all not my body.
"The head is not my body; the bones within the face are also not my body; the bones within the head are also not my body.
As that bhikṣu observes in this way, he does not perceive a body within each constituent part; in every single part, he does not perceive a body, nor does he perceive such parts themselves.
