Furthermore, he contemplates the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, yet in none of these does he perceive a body.

Again, he observes that within the self there is no self; all such things are merely subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). Thus, he analyzes that body part by part, seeing it as being like a mustard seed, and even down to the level of subtle particles.
Furthermore, he analyzes each of the great elements individually:
"Which of these is the self? Which is the earth element?
He proceeds in this manner in successive order:
"What is 'I' and what is the water element?
What is 'I' and what is the fire element?
What is 'I' and what is the wind element?"
He contemplates in this way:
"The elements are not the self, and the self is not the elements;
there is no self separate from the elements, nor are there elements separate from the self."
"The self is not something distinct from the aggregates; there is no other separate entity.

Thus, all this is according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For example, when countless trees are combined, one perceives a "forest"; yet the trees are not the forest, and apart from the trees there is no forest—this is the ultimate truth.
Outside of the trees, there is no separate thing named "forest."
Furthermore, when one examines a tree, apart from its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves, there is no separate tree;
in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), such a tree does not exist, yet in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), there are forests and trees.
The body is also like this: it is a mere designation resulting from the combination of the feet and other parts; it is only by relying on conventional truth that one can say "there is a body.
Once that bhikṣu has understood the nature of the body, he becomes free from desire for the body;
being free from desire for the parts of the body, he attains freedom from all desire for the sense faculties, sensations, and elements.
Once he has become detached from desire, that craving for joy and desire can no longer bind him.
In this way, he diligently contemplates the antidote to the mind of desire.
Furthermore, how does that bhikṣu diligently contemplate the antidote to the mind of hatred?
Abiding in a mind of loving-kindness, he constantly and diligently observes that sentient beings of evil conduct—
those who undergo the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence— are perpetually in a state of terror, no different from being dead.
The bhikṣu contemplates them as a mother pities her child, thinking:
"How can I feel anger toward those sentient beings who are thus afflicted by suffering?
If I were to become angry with them, it would be like inflicting yet another wound upon an existing sore."
"Since sentient beings are by nature afflicted with suffering, one should not feel anger toward them.
Anger is the second greatest affliction; thus, one should diligently observe the antidotes to the angry mind."
Furthermore, how does that bhikṣu successively and diligently observe the third greatest affliction?

Delusion shrouds sentient beings, leading them to unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into evil realms and are born within the hells.

If he is free from delusion and practices right view, he engages in wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind, clearly discerning both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.

Thus, by truly knowing the mind of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, one extinguishes the third and greatest affliction; in this way, one diligently contemplates the antidote to the deluded mind.

Furthermore, as that bhikṣu diligently contemplates these three types of afflictions and their three types of antidotes, once those three are extinguished, all afflictions, fetters, and latent tendencies are extinguished. It is like cutting the root of a tree: the bark, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and surrounding conditions all wither away entirely.
In this way, one is able to sever these three afflictions, whereby all afflictions are completely extinguished.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the practice of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does that bhikṣu, while in the seventh stage, cultivate the eighth stage and attain the eighth stage?"
Through hearing, learning, or by seeing with the divine eye, he perceives:
how is it that when a foolish worldling sees a form with the eye, they become attached, or feel aversion, or give rise to delusion? He thus observes the eye as it truly is for the first time.
When those ordinary worldlings see a friend or a woman, greed arises in their minds;
if they see something else, anger arises.
Seeing others possessed by and shrouded in greed and anger, they do not see forms with their eyes as they truly are, for their minds are obscured by delusion.
Ignorant ordinary beings possess only conceptual construction; when the eye sees forms, they are shrouded by greed, hatred, or delusion.
Deceived by craving, such people conceptually construct "I" and "mine" within their own minds and thus become stained by attachment.
It is like a dog gnawing on a bone from which the meat has been stripped, mixing saliva with it in the hope of finding marrow.
In this way, when that greedy dog has blood flow from between its teeth and experiences its taste, it thinks it is the marrow of the bone, not realizing that its own blood has such a flavor.

Because of its craving for the taste, it does not perceive that it is gradually eating its own tongue; further craving that flavor and being shrouded by greed, it continues to think it is the taste of bone marrow.

Foolish ordinary beings are likewise like this in their false conceptualization: when the eye-consciousness sees forms, they become greedily attached to them with joy and pleasure. They deliberate and discriminate, placing a withered bone of form into the mouth of the eye; the sensory object is like the teeth, and they gnaw upon it thus. Their defiled mind is like saliva, and from the blood of craving, the flavor of greedy attachment flows forth. They deem form to be beautiful and find a taste in form, just like that dog.
Ordinary worldlings, being ignorant and deluded, perceive those forms with their visual consciousness as being like bones; they engage in false conceptualization, just as a dog gnaws at a bone.
Thus one should observe:
when the eye sees forms, it is just like gnawing on dry bones.
Thus all these foolish worldlings are deceived and deluded by false conceptualization.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"How does a bhikṣu give rise to fear toward craving, become weary of and detached from birth-and-death, and renounce all desires?"

It is like a dragon-elephant that has reached sixty years of age; though its strength is at its peak, a skilled elephant trainer captures it by force, binds its five limbs, and places it within a sturdy enclosure. He then provides it with many kinds of delightful foods, such as *modaka* cakes, sugarcane, and sugarcane wine, and entertains it with various musical instruments and songs, hoping thereby to prevent it from feeling sorrowful and to make it forget the pleasures of the forest.
If one forgets the pleasures of the forest, one may dwell together with ordinary elephants, being thoroughly tamed and brought under the control of others.

Although that elephant is thus cared for and provided for, it cannot cause its mind to be free from sorrow and distress; for it does not forget the pleasures of roaming freely in the forest, nor does it forget the flowers and fruits of the mountain groves, the songs of various birds, or the joys found by the riverside.

Having reflected thus, he broke his bonds and departed. Because he remembered that pleasure, he felt no apprehension toward the elephant trainer; he shattered his sturdy enclosure and headed for the forest. His mind paid no heed to the many *kaṇṭaka* fruits, the delicious and delightful morsels, the sugarcane, the sugarcane wine, the lute music, or the songs. His mind could not be subdued nor deceived; not forgetting the joys of the forest, and taking no pleasure in walking or dwelling with ordinary elephants, he returned to the forest.
The bhikṣu who practices the path is likewise: since beginningless time, he has wandered through the world, bound by five fetters.
What are these five?
They are attachment to sound, touch, taste, fragrance, and form.
Who is it that is well-tamed?
It refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six consciousnesses.
What is the cage?

That which is called the joy of wife, children, and kinsmen; one’s dwelling place; servants and wealth; that which is obstructed by the defilements of attachment; and the abundance of joyful morsels, sugarcane wine, and various delicious foods and drinks.

The discriminating mind is the ball of dough for joy; lust is the food and drink; the net of mental attachment serves as the sounds of music, song, and laughter. Ordinary people with false views are like wild elephants;

those who dwell together with them are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the net of doubt. That which is sweet in their mouths is the talk of delighting in false views; being bound to others means being subject to desire, hatred, and delusion.

The well-trained elephant refers to the practitioner; all defilements and delusions serve as his offerings. Mindfulness of renunciation is called the mountain; dhyāna and samādhi are the mountain cave; the arising of the mind of the right path is called the flower; and nirvāṇa is the fruit. The voices of the various birds refer to the Dharma-preacher; wisdom is the river; the crossing point of the river is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā); and the divisions of the ground refer to the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāras): loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
That practitioner is like a mighty elephant; contemplating and following the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he proceeds toward the monastery as if returning to the forest.
A bhikṣu who practices the Path in this manner is like a mighty elephant;
if he does not do so, he is no different from a dog.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—observing the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma: "How does that bhikṣu cultivate the ninth stage upon the basis of the eighth stage, and thereby attain the ninth stage?"

Through seeing, hearing, and knowing, or by means of the divine eye, he perceives that all three realms are vessels of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and so forth; he contemplates all desires in this same way.

For example, in a forest there is an extremely high mountain precipice, a place of steep and rugged terrain, where stands a great, tall tree named *khaśūri*. It has immeasurable thorns, and at its crown there are few fruits which are moreover difficult to obtain. If one were to take those fruits, there would be many dangers; fearing that the tree’s fruit might fall into the abyss, and further fearing for one's life;

there is a hollow in the trunk of the tree, and the cavity is brittle and decayed. Desiring to climb the tree, one fears the hollow may collapse and endanger one’s life. That tree is exceedingly high; falling from it would still result in death, let alone falling from such a high, treacherous precipice.
Foolish ordinary people, blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, crave various flavors; they gaze only at the fruit and fail to see the steep precipice and the rotten hollows in the trunk of the tree.
Those foolish people, greedy for the taste of the fruit, climb that tree; before they have even reached the fruit, they fall down and immediately lose their lives.

Furthermore, there are others who possess some knowledge of skillful means or have karmic merit such that they do not fall; yet they obtain but a small taste of the fruit while undergoing much suffering.

In this way, as the practicing bhikṣu contemplates the forest of the five destinies, he sees therein a hollow and an exceedingly perilous precipice, which represent all diseases; the *khaśūli* tree represents the mind of desire; the immeasurable thorns represent the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of afflictions (*kleśa*); the seeking of those bitter fruits represents suffering itself; and the fruit at the top of the tree represents all intentional desires—the fruit of desire being those things difficult to obtain, such as various sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances.
That which is called "entering the sea," or facing the fear of swords, attending upon kings, or making a living as a thief—such are the sufferings through which one obtains what is desired.

Just as those who undergo such suffering and possess many faults are driven by greed, hatred, and delusion; those who fall from a high precipice refer to falling into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; "the end of life" refers to the exhaustion of the Dharma-life; and "a tree rotting with holes" means it is entirely empty and devoid of substance, being utterly insubstantial.

Those foolish people who go there are those of ignorance and false views. There are immeasurable faults such as these, and even more besides; such are the fruits of desire, where the flavor is meager while the faults are many.
In this way, that bhikṣu contemplates all thoughts of desire and does not give rise to discrimination.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the mind of desire as being like a flame or like the wick of a lamp: its bright color is lovely, yet its touch is extremely hot; because of their delusion, flying insects see that bright flame, become greedily attached to it with longing and joy, and perish as soon as they enter within.

Ignorant worldlings are just like this: covered by desire, hatred, and delusion, they give rise to attachment toward all sensual desires, just as those flying insects see the color of a lamp’s light. If they enter the lamp of desire, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, just as those flying insects enter the lamp and die.
As that bhikṣu observes in this way, his mind attains detachment from desire.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu reflects within his mind—contemplating the practice of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma: "By what bonds are all sentient beings in this world bound, such that they revolve in birth and death?"
He sees, hears, knows, or perceives with the divine eye:
that one is bound by two fetters and remains tethered to the world. What are these two?
First is the bondage of food, and second is the bondage of contact.
There are four kinds of the bondage of food: first, edible morsel food; [the others being contact, volition, and consciousness].
The second is the food of volition;
the third is the food of meditative concentration;
and the fourth is the food of contact.
What is edible food?
It refers to four [realms]:
human beings, the six heavens of the desire realm, eight of the great hells, and one portion of the hungry ghosts.
2. Those who subsist on the food of volition are those among the fish.
3. Those who subsist on the food of meditative absorption are those such as the gods of the form realm who practice dhyāna.
4. Those who subsist on the food of contact are those among the various birds.
What is contact? Contact refers to desire;
there are those who grasp hands, those who laugh, and those who gaze with their eyes—all such as these are deceived by the contact of desire.
Thus, all such ignorant worldlings—namely humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings within the desire realm—practice desire; therefore, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) take meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) as their object of sustenance.
Bound by these two fetters, they constantly remain in the world, unable to transcend desire, and are perpetually bound by all the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the eye as it truly is:
when the eye-consciousness sees forms, if a pleasant contact arises, it clings to pleasure; this is not karma that results in a pleasant retribution.

Again, he contemplates as it truly is: in such and such a way, when the eye-consciousness sees forms, if it is a basis for an evil intention and an eye-contact arises, it clings to suffering; this is karma that results in a pleasant retribution.
He knows it as it truly is:
what is it that is called "eye-consciousness seeing forms" which, while taking pleasure as its object, is not a karmic action resulting in a pleasant retribution?

Within this phenomenon, having observed with the eye after seeing forms, one engages in improper reflection and observation, and by recollecting and becoming attached to the flavor [of the experience], a mind of pleasure arises; though there is pleasure in the present, one later receives a bitter retribution, bringing about rebirth in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
What karma results in an unpleasant retribution in the present but a pleasant retribution later?

When visual consciousness perceives forms and gives rise to eye-contact, if one engages in wholesome mental reflection, observation, and focused attention, the mind does not become attached in the present life. This is a karma that is unpleasant in the present but not a karma of bitter retribution; it leads to rebirth among humans or devas where one experiences superior and wondrous happiness, ultimately reaching nirvana.
In this same way, it is also so for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the practice of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: "How does that bhikṣu, when the eye-consciousness sees forms, maintain equanimity in his mental activity?"

That is to say: when that bhikṣu has seen forms with the eye, his mind is neither delighted nor undelighted; he is neither greedy nor hateful; his mind neither longs for them nor does not long for them; he neither recollects them nor does not recollect them; and he is neither one who fails to observe them well nor one who is obscured by them. Practicing equanimity in this way is called the basis of equanimity, which is neither a state of suffering nor pleasure.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu attains the practice of the six stages of the tenth ground, namely the stages from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna of the anāgāmin; he attains and ascends to those grounds.

He contemplates the emergence and disappearance, the arising and ceasing, of all phenomena, and constantly and diligently practices the Noble Eightfold Path, desiring to awaken to and reach the gateway of liberation.

As that bhikṣu thus exerts himself with diligence, the palace of Māra is shrouded in darkness. The yakṣas of that realm, having seen this, rejoice and immediately report it to the yakṣas of the air; the yakṣas of the air report it to the Four Great Kings; the Four Great Kings report it to the Four Heavenly Kings; the Four Heavenly Kings likewise report it to the Heaven of the Thirty-three; the Heaven of the Thirty-three reports it to the Yāma Heaven; the Yāma Heaven reports it to the Tuṣita Heaven; the Tuṣita Heaven reports it to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven then speaks of it to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven likewise speaks of it to the Brahmā Heaven, saying:
"In Jambudvīpa, a certain son of good family—as explained extensively as before—up to the eighth stage being subsumed within the sixth stage."
Having heard this, they were filled with great joy.
The Brahmakāyika devas, emerging from their practice of dhyāna-bliss, were even more joyful upon hearing it as a reality.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Whether wholesome or unwholesome, the fruits of karma are all determined.
One reaps what one has sown; all are bound by their own karma."
Such is the ground of afflictions: sweet at first, but bitter in the end.
One should abandon sense objects as if they were poison, for they bring no benefit.
Wisdom does not belong to the afflictions; it belongs to the sphere of wisdom.
In this world and in the next, one shall experience happiness at all times.
Wisdom constantly incinerates afflictions, just as fire can burn away grass.
Because afflictions shroud wisdom and purity, the Buddha spoke of the Triple Gem.
If one delights in the realm of wisdom, as tranquil as a Muni;
yet if bitten by the serpent of afflictions, that person loses everything.
If a person knows the two truths and possesses courageous, discerning insight, [they shall not fall].
He practices the foremost path, abandoning the realm of birth and death.
If a person delights in birth and death, rejoicing in the enemies that are the afflictions,
that person is constantly bound, wandering through the narrow passages of existence.
If a person possesses the intent for transcendence and constantly practices the conduct of tranquility,
they will die and be born among the celestial hosts, reaching the abode of the Brahma-world.
If one is free from desire and the like, and makes offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, [one shall likewise attain such a state].
That person abandons birth and death, Like the wind blowing dry grass.
If one is not driven by the mind, But can instead master the mind,
Then one can eliminate afflictions, Just as the rising sun dispels darkness.
The mind is the foremost enemy; there is no enemy like it.
The mind constantly burns sentient beings, just as fire consumes trees when set loose.
If the mind acts according to its own will, the foolish fail to discipline their faculties.
That suffering is not stilled, and one remains far from Nirvana.
By knowing suffering and the retribution of suffering, and further being able to know the cause of suffering,
one is then liberated from all bonds and universally freed from all afflictions.
Wisdom is the foremost light; ignorance is the foremost darkness.
One who takes up such illumination is called a person of wisdom.
Ignorance is the foremost evil; the wise are able to abandon it.
If one allows delusion to be sovereign, tranquility will be difficult to attain.
If one desires personal peace and security, it would be better to enter a great fire or dwell with venomous snakes than to ever draw near to the afflictions.
Wisdom is the foremost nectar, the supreme refuge;
wisdom is the foremost kinsman, wisdom is the foremost treasure.
Such a fire of wisdom constantly burns away the mountain of afflictions.
Those who burn away the mountain of afflictions reach the place of peace and bliss.
If a person lacks wisdom, they are like a blind man entering a dark place;
they do not weary of birth and death, which is a cage of unrighteous strife.
If a person constantly contemplates the Dharma, having well attained this human body and not being deceived by the mind, they should receive the offerings of virtuous people.

When that bhikṣu thus knows the Dharma and the non-Dharma, practicing correctly in accordance with the Dharma and possessing such a purified mind, he is able to destroy the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of high and great mountains of birth; leaving no residual traces, he is never born again, is freed from the sword of afflictions, and draws near to Nirvāṇa.

3. Chapter on the Hells (5–15), Part One: The Sūtra on the Stages of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Chapter Three: The Hells. Furthermore, that bhikṣu, reflecting in accordance with the law of karmic retribution, contemplates what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma: "How is it that immeasurable and manifold evil karmas all arise from the mind and continue to flow and circulate?"

Just as a river flows with a deep current, sweeping away sentient beings and causing them to fall into the realm of the retribution of evil karma, where they undergo extreme suffering and affliction in the hells.
That bhikṣu contemplates the wholesome and the unwholesome, reflecting with focused attention:

"How is it that these sentient beings, thus deceived by their own minds and deceived by craving, are born within the evil places of the hells—namely, Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci?"

Each of those hells has its own distinct locations, all of which have officials who, according to the similarity of their karma, each serve as witnesses and knowers; what are the names of those hellish places?
By what karma do sentient beings reach which hells?
In which places do they fall?
That bhikṣu, through seeing, hearing, knowing, or by means of the divine eye, perceives this:
There is a great hell named Saṃjīva (Reviving Hell), and there are also separate locations within it.
How many are these separate locations,
and what are their names?
There are sixteen locations:
the first is named Excrement Mud;
the second is named Wheel of Blades.
The third is named Vessel-Ripened;
the fourth is named Much-Suffering;
the fifth is named Darkness.
Sixth is named "Displeasure";
seventh is named "Extreme Suffering";
eighth is named "Multitude of Diseases."
The ninth is named Two Irons;
the tenth is named Evil Staff;
the eleventh is named Black Weasel.
The twelfth is named Diverse Revolutions;
the thirteenth is named Oppression by Suffering;
the fourteenth is named Padmāmālā.
The fifteenth is named Pond;
the sixteenth is named Suffering in Mid-Air.
These are called the sixteen locations of the Reviving Hells.
By what karma is one born in that Saṃjīva hell?
That bhikṣu, through seeing, hearing, knowing, or by means of the divine eye, perceives:

if there is one who kills living beings, who delights in and frequently performs this action, making it pervasive, bringing the act of killing to completion, and acting in accordance with its conditions, such a person falls into the fundamental region of the Saṃjīva hell.
The karma of killing is of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and the suffering experienced in hell is likewise of three grades.
Among those karmas of hell, which is the superior?

It is when a killer kills a virtuous person, one who has received the precepts, or one who practices wholesome conduct; where there is another sentient being, the perception of that being as a sentient being, and the intent to kill; where one severs their life-faculty, brings this karma to completion, feels no regret in one's heart, speaks of it with praise to others while committing it again, further instructs others to kill, encourages killing with sympathetic joy, praises the act of killing, or causes another to kill.

Such deluded people, having committed these deeds themselves and incited others to do so, bring their sinful karma to fruition and, at the end of their lives, are reborn in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.

If fifty years among humans constitute one day and night for the Four Great Kings, that calculation is likewise applied there: thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year;
fifty years by that reckoning for the Four Great Kings constitute one day and night in the Saṃjīva Great Hell.

Because there are inferior, middling, and superior grades of evil karma, the lifespan in the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*) is likewise inferior, middling, and superior; there is also death midway. According to the quantity and gravity of the seeds of karma, one may experience [retribution] in one place, two places, three places, four places, five places, or six places within the Reviving Hell, and so on up to sixteen places. This continues until the evil karma is destroyed and decayed, and the potency of the karma is exhausted. The lifespan in that hell is five hundred years, calculated according to celestial years, not human years.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of phenomena in accordance with the True Dharma—as to how that bhikṣu observes the Reviving Hell and understands the karmic distinctions of its various locations.

The mind, like a master painter, uses its own karma as a brush to paint the various regions of karmic fruition; with diverse and distinct states of mind, one suffers in different places, encountering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of terrifying and evil events that have no equal and are beyond all comparison.
He examines each part of the Reviving Hell to see by what karma sentient beings are born in the place of excrement and mud.
Through hearing, learning, or seeing with the divine eye, he perceives:
by what evil karma and unwholesome seeds are they born in the place of excrement and mud?
What is called killing:
if one kills with a desirous mind, such as commanding a bird to kill—
releasing hawks or releasing eagles.

Furthermore, there are other forms of killing: if one surrounds and kills deer, or hunts and kills deer, and does not repent, these acts of karma become pervasive; the karma of killing reaches its ultimate fulfillment through their convergence and correspondence, as previously described.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and their life ends, they are born in that hell, where they undergo various sufferings in a particular region called the Excrement Mire. The burning excrement is extremely hot and its taste is most bitter; it is mixed with molten copper, and within the excrement there are worms with diamond-like beaks that cover the surface of the mire everywhere.

Those sinful beings eat such excrement; worms enter their bodies and first devour their lips, then their tongues, then their gums, then their throats, then their hearts, then their lungs, then their bellies, then their spleens, then their stomachs, then their small intestines, then their large intestines, then their receptacles for digested food, then their sinews, all their vascular channels, and finally their flesh and blood.
In that manner, those people undergo extreme suffering within that hell for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, as calculated by human reckoning.

Those who take life commit evil karma—whether by surrounding and killing deer, hunting and killing deer, or raising birds, sparrows, hawks, eagles, and the like to be killed, and having them slaughtered, seizing the meat for themselves to eat.
Such is the karmic retribution for that act of killing: after he has been killed, those people take his flesh to eat due to the power of that evil karma.
Within that excrement there are many worms with adamantine beaks, which enter his body and devour him in this manner.
The fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma correspond to their respective actions.

If that sinner’s evil karma is exhausted, he may escape from this hellish place of excrement and mud; once the patterns painted by his mental karma have been fully consumed, he escapes from that place in such a manner.
However, if the person’s karma for future retribution has not yet ripened, he will be born among animals, taking the body of a flying bird to be killed by other birds.
If one receives the body of a deer and is killed by a hunter’s snare, it is because in a previous life one killed birds or deer.
That person experiences the retribution for that karma in hell; as for the residual karma, one is born among animals.
If, through subsequent karmic momentum, one is born among the devas or among humans, due to the causal conditions of that karma, one will be short-lived upon birth.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Reviving Hell and its second distinct location, called the Place of the Wheel of Blades.
Regarding the karmic retribution there, by what karma do sentient beings take birth in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:
if one’s mind is greedy for things, through such causes and conditions one kills sentient beings, desiring to obtain the cause of life by killing with a blade.
That person, acting thus through these causes and conditions, does not repent; furthermore, they teach others to kill, so that their karma becomes pervasive, as previously described.
Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into that hell and are born in the Place of the Blade-Wheel (*kṣurapracakra*).
There, fires blaze and iron walls surround it, ten *yojanas* high.
In that hellish realm, great fires burn perpetually.
Compared to the fire there, the fire of the human world is like a mere cloud.

In that hellish realm, fiery iron constantly strikes their bodies; that hot iron fire cuts the bodies of those people, shattering them like mustard seeds, burning, splitting, and cleaving them apart. A rain of all these iron fragments falls just as the summer rains fall upon Jambudvīpa in this world.
In that place, hot iron rains down everywhere throughout the ten directions, inflicting great suffering and affliction.
Although those hell-beings are split and torn asunder, they never die; because of the retribution for such evil karma, their bodies are thus cut, yet as soon as they are cut, they grow back again.

In that place of the Wheel of Blades (Kṣuradhāramaṇḍala) there is a forest of sword-leaves; their edges are extremely sharp and double-edged, with the tips pointing downward. From afar, that forest appears green and moist, resembling water.

Those sinners, tormented by hunger and thirst, cry out and rush toward it, driven by the suffering of their shared karma. Once they have entered that forest, due to the causes of their past actions, swords rain down from all sides, hacking their bodies to pieces.
Furthermore, because that person craves their own life, they consume and nourish living beings, which is to deceive others.

Such is the ripening of that karma; the mental karma-artist paints the garments of hell. Thus painted by the unwholesome karma of hell, one experiences suffering in hell accordingly, being encompassed by that very karma.

In that hell, they are thus constantly split asunder for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years; this continues until their evil karma is destroyed and decayed, and the residual force of the karma is exhausted, for the patterns drawn by the mind-karma artist do not vanish—explained at length as before.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Sañjīva hell, its third distinct location called the Pot-Baking Place (Kumbhapacyana).
Regarding the karmic retribution there, by what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows this:

those people who take life—whether they kill camels, pigs, or sheep; various birds, horses, or rabbits; or hairy animals such as brown bears or black bears—do so for the sake of eating their flesh. Desiring to strip the hair from them, they burn them alive or boil them alive, or place them in boiling water.
Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*), being born in the "Boiling Cauldron" section.
As a result of seeds of evil karma, a corresponding retribution occurs: they are placed within an iron cauldron and boiled over an intense heat, like parched beans.

Thus, for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, they are boiled in the great fires of that hell; only when the garments painted by the artist of mental karma are completely destroyed and rotted away do they finally escape from that place of hell.

Next, they undergo the retribution of residual karma, and next, the retribution of karmic tendencies, as previously described; even if they are born among gods or humans, their lifespan will be short.
That practitioner, within internal phenomena, follows the true Dharma and contemplates the course of phenomena, reflecting thus:
"After that bhikṣu has observed the 'Jar-Ripening' section of the Reviving Great Hell in this manner, what will happen next?"
He sees, hears, and knows this, or perceives it with his divine eye:

that bhikṣu is foremost in valor; he can shatter the armies of Māra, cross the ocean of birth and death, extinguish the fire of the lustful mind with the water of precepts, extinguish the fire of the hateful mind with the water of loving-kindness, and dispel the darkness of the deluded mind with the lamp-light of profound dependent origination.
Such a bhikṣu is able to swiftly cross the great ocean of birth and death.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Reviving Hell and its fourth distinct location, named the Place of Much Suffering (*bahuduḥkha*).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
It is because the seeds of karmic causes produce corresponding fruits of retribution.
If there are people who afflict sentient beings with various kinds of suffering, yet the lives of those beings are not yet exhausted—namely:
by pressing them with wood to cause them to suffer; or by suspending them with ropes; or by burning them with firebrands; or by tying their hair to a pillar and hanging them;
or by fumigating them with smoke to cause them distress; or by making them run swiftly along a road; or by placing them upon the ground amidst thorns to cause them distress.

Whether they throw them to the ground, or push them from high and precipitous places to cause them to fall; whether they pierce them with needles, or bind them with ropes, or have elephants trample them;
whether they hurl them into the air and catch them with a blade before they reach the ground to inflict suffering upon them;

whether they place them on sand, or weigh them down with stones, or strike them with sticks, or clutch their heads, or have small children repeatedly beat and toy with them to torment them with manifold sufferings.

Whether they are placed in a hot location, or cast into ice, or submerged in water, or drowned; or if their faces and mouths are covered with wet clothes; or if they are tied to trees or suspended from tree branches to inflict suffering and distress upon them;
or if they are cast over a precipice onto a steep, terrifying cliff;
or if they are delivered to an enemy to be subjected to various forms of painful treatment by means of diverse expedients.
Whether it be by pulling out their genitals, or pinching their fingers, or plucking out their hair, or by spinning iron wheels to split open their heads, causing them to suffer;

or by pouring molten white tin, lead, pewter, copper, and so forth over their bodies; or by cutting off their noses; or by piercing the anus and private parts with sharp iron or pointed wood, causing them to suffer;

or by dousing them with water, or binding them with ropes to blocks and dragging them along, or roasting them all over with lamp-wicks, or pulling out their hair, or having evil insects bite and devour them, or twisting their skin, or pulling, pushing, or violently shaking their bodies, or placing them in cauldrons to be boiled in fire and water—causing them to suffer.
If one strikes them with bricks; or smears their bodies with salt and the like;
or covers their mouths and faces with dust, soil, or flour;
or inserts a reed pipe into the anus and blows into it with a bellows; [these are all offenses].
Whether one splits their toes with a sharp knife;
or blows upon them so that they cannot make a sound;
or rubs their body vigorously with a pumice stone; or cuts off their hands and feet; or drives them to walk long distances; or obstructs what they require.
If they bind their throats, they drag them back and forth through yellow and blue flowers;
if they pour various kinds of mixed fats and greases into their mouths;

if they use gold, jewels, or various wealth—whether by beating, pressing, making musical instruments, or shooting at them; or if they beat them until they swell, and then beat them again upon the swelling.
If one were to suspend them by a rope and push them so that they reach an extreme height, and then let them fall to the ground,
causing them to experience suffering and affliction— such immeasurable and various kinds of painful matters as these torment sentient beings.
Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall into the Reviving Hell, known as the Place of Much Suffering.
In accordance with their evil karma, they receive a corresponding fruit.
Such hells are of ten thousand billion kinds and cannot be fully described; this extreme suffering has been detailed above.
All those sufferings are experienced by each individual according to their own karma within the locations of the hells.

Drawn by the artist of mental karma with the brush of craving, one lacks skillful discernment; through attachment to various colors—the beloved wife and children—one takes these as the cause and condition for clinging, regarding them as solid and firm. Having performed the actions oneself, one receives the bitter retribution oneself; it was not created by parents. Until that evil karma is destroyed and decayed, and until the potency of the karma is exhausted, one will constantly experience this without cessation at all times.
Having fallen away from that state, if there is no ripening of wholesome karma from the distant past of previous lives, they will not fall among animals or hungry ghosts;

rather, if born among humans in a place of similar karma, they will experience the remnants of their remaining karma by being constantly punished by kings—whether beaten or bound—and by facing strife, fear, and false accusations from all people;
they will always endure heavy suffering and be detested by good friends, spiritual teachers, wives, children, kinsmen, and hosts.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Reviving Hell and its fifth distinct location, named the Place of Utter Darkness (*andhakāra-sthāna*).
Regarding the retribution of karma, by what kind of karma do sentient beings are born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

sentient beings hold wrong views and act with inverted understanding of karma and its results; that is to say, during the sacrificial feasts of heretics regarding directions and times, they slaughter sheep by stuffing their mouths and nostrils;
they place turtles upon bricks and press them down with more bricks on top until they die.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*), born in a place of blinding darkness where they are scorched by dark fires.
Because of their evil karma, powerful winds blow against diamond mountains, grinding them together until they are crushed like scattered sand; there is not even a moment’s respite from suffering.

There, the sinners cannot see one another; driven by hot winds as if being sliced by sharp knives, their bodies are dismembered. Their bodies burn with hunger and thirst, yet though they cry out with all their might, no sound issues forth—like a sheep’s mouth being muffled or a tortoise being crushed under bricks—they are constantly burned by great fires and perpetually oppressed.

Thus, for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, they constantly dwell in blinding darkness, such that there is not even the slightest glimmer of light, no larger than the tip of a needle; yet they burn their own bodies with their own body hair, and at all times, fire breaks out across their entire bodies as they undergo such suffering until their karma is exhausted—all of which is the work of the monkey of the mind.

That mind-monkey ranges over the mountain of the proclivities (*anuśaya*). It dwells upon the high peaks of delusion, stubbornness, and pride; the rocky crags of wrong views are its domain of movement; it roams through the forest of arrogance and resides within the caves of anger on the mountain of hatred. It takes the virtues of envy as its manifold fruits. Drifted by the river of craving and submerged in unwholesome karma, it remains there until its evil karma has rotted away and dispersed, at which point it finally gains release from the dark places of hell.
If, in a past life long ago, there was the ripening of wholesome karma, one will not be born in the realms of hungry ghosts or animals;
yet, if one is born among humans, one will frequently be bound in fetters as the result of residual karma, and one's lifespan will be short.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Bactrian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Hells, Part Two:
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Sañjīva Hell and its sixth distinct location, named the Place of Displeasure (*Aratisthāna*).
Regarding the karmic retribution of that place, by what karma do sentient beings take birth there?
He sees, hears, and knows:

A person who commits evil deeds constantly dwells in his mind on the desire to kill sentient beings. For the sake of hunting and killing, he roams through forests and wilds, employing various means such as blowing conch shells and beating drums to produce all manner of great, evil sounds. These sounds are most terrifying, yet the forest-dwelling beings—beasts such as deer, birds, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, brown bears, and monkeys—roam about without fear. However, those who perform evil karma produce such terrifying sounds because they wish to kill;
for the sake of hunting and killing, they roam through forests and wilds, desiring to present their prey to a king or to those like a king.
Because of these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*), being born in a place of no joy.

In accordance with the causes of their karma, they receive a corresponding fruit: just as when they were committing the deed, they caused other sentient beings’ hearts to feel no joy, so now, having fallen into hell and entered among the flames, birds with burning beaks utter extremely foul cries; jackals, crows, vultures, dogs, and wild jackals devour their ears, causing their hearts no joy.
Those evil sounds are most extreme and wicked, unpleasant and not to be delighted in, and a sound the heart finds unbearable to hear—the most terrifying of all sounds.

The Vajra-beaked insect enters its bones, moves within them, and devours its ears; this continues until its evil karma is exhausted. Its mind is like the *mimani* fish swimming in the river of craving;

it whirls in the turbulent waves of anger and drifts away. It constantly dwells within the mountains of birth and death, divided by desire, anger, and delusion. Greeding for a mere taste of sensual pleasure, it is caught on the hook; it constantly wanders through the deep waters of false views, passing through decline or rebirth within the three realms. Taking these as its own slippery domain, it is ever-thirsty for sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances. Such are its sinful karmas: it laughs with joy when committing them, yet it wails and weeps when receiving their calamitous retribution.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The deluded mind is like a mīna fish, Dwelling within the house of craving;
It laughs with joy when performing karma, But wails and weeps when suffering arises.”
"When their evil karma is exhausted there, they finally emerge, only to be reborn among the hungry ghosts or animals.

If, due to some slight wholesome karma from a long-past previous life, they are born among humans, they will constantly harbor sorrow and suffering; at all times they hear inauspicious sounds and their minds are never joyful. That is to say, they constantly hear of harmful matters:

the death of wives and children, the loss of wealth and goods, calamities befalling their kin, being killed or bound, and they are perpetually filled with grief and distress, their hearts never finding joy."
Those unwholesome karmas have corresponding causes and effects.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the Reviving Hell and its seventh distinct location, named the Place of Extreme Suffering.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows this:
when those who perform evil deeds commit their evil karma, they do so with deep-seated fetters and intense malice, killing many sentient beings while acting with heedlessness.

Because of these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall into the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*), born into a place of extreme suffering. There they undergo the most grievous torments of hot iron fire, falling down precipitous cliffs while being pierced by flaming iron hooks;
thus they suffer without respite, day and night without ceasing.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, clearly understanding the fruits of karma and seeking the city of Nirvāṇa, clearly understands the suffering and affliction of birth and death in the world, and observes the location of the Black Rope Great Hell.
Within this Black Rope Great Hell, what distinct locations are there?
He perceives, hears, and knows that in the Black Rope Hell, there is a place called Equal Shouting Suffering; there they are horribly incinerated, experiencing uninterrupted agony.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:
if there are people who preach the Dharma based on treatises of evil views, using causes and analogies that are entirely unreal;
Disregarding everything, they throw themselves from cliffs to commit suicide;
they possess no correct or virtuous precepts.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the Black Rope Great Hell, born in the Place of Equal Shrieking where they undergo great suffering and affliction. There, they experience extreme agony:

They are hoisted up onto a precipice many *yojanas* in height; once bound and fettered with glowing black ropes, they are then pushed down onto a ground of sharp iron blades. There, they are devoured by dogs with iron-flaming fangs, until every part of their bodies is torn limb from limb.
They cry out and roar, yet there is no one to rescue them, no one to protect them, no one to whom they may appeal, and no one to offer comfort and release them from their suffering.

Deceived by one's own mind, one remains within the wheel of birth and death, which turns constantly and rapidly; blinded by the darkness of ignorance, one’s body is like a scorched black forest, resembling the grounds of that hell.
There, one sees the messengers of Yama, who rebuke and reproach with these piercing verses:
"You are of wrong views and deluded, A person bound by the snare of folly."
Now you have fallen into this hell, dwelling within a great ocean of suffering;
burned by evil views, your merit is exhausted, and you are the most base among men.
You feared the bonds of hell, yet this is now your abode.
Those who belong to wrong views are not wise;
they perform all manner of deeds leading to hell, deceived by the mind of an enemy.
The mind is the foremost enemy, and this enemy is the most evil of all.
This enemy can bind a person and deliver them to the abode of Yama.
With a mind that constantly races toward sensory objects and never practices the True Dharma,
one becomes deluded regarding the path of the True Dharma and is sent to be slain in hell.
The mind is difficult to subdue, more so than a great, raging fire;
moving swiftly and impossible to restrain, it drags people into hell.
The mind is the foremost thing that is hard to tame; this fire is more intense than ordinary fire.
Difficult to tame and swift in its course, it goes from hell to hell.
If the mind is left unrestrained, one wanders through the hells;
if one can master the mind, one will not suffer affliction.
Desire is the foremost fire; delusion is the foremost darkness;
hatred is the foremost enemy—these three govern the world.
When you previously committed evil, you did so through the deliberations of your own mind.
What you did in the past with a deluded mind, you now receive as this evil retribution.
Your heart was fond of stealing the property of others, you secretly committed adultery with the wives of others,
and you constantly harmed sentient beings— all these were the deceptions of your own mind.
Thus, by the sovereignty of karma, you have been brought to this place;
it is your own original evil karma—why do you groan and lament?
If a person has committed an evil deed and later feels remorse, they are merely deluded.
He shall not obtain the fruit of his reward, like sowing seeds in salty soil.
Desire yields little flavor and profit, yet the retribution of suffering is great;
the deluded person who clings to desire goes from darkness into darkness.
Fools commit various evils for the sake of benefiting their wives and children,
yet they alone suffer the torments of hell, deceived by their own karma.
If, for the sake of wife and children, one creates various evil deeds—
Thus one arrives at this hell, now undergoing these torments.
Neither wife nor children, nor wealth, nor friends can provide rescue;
when one is on the verge of death among humans, there is no one able to protect or save them.
If a person’s mind is stained by desire, deceived by craving,
and they follow along with it, they now undergo such suffering.
Originally plundered by sense objects, they have already been deceived by craving.
"Having committed these evil karmas yourself, why do you groan and wail now?

While they suffer such agonies in that place of crying out and distress, the Yama-wardens thus inflict punishment upon them. Those hell-beings suffer in this manner, enduring the foremost suffering for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years. Only when their evil karma has dissipated, been destroyed, and utterly decayed will they finally gain release.

If, due to the ripening of wholesome karma from a long time past in previous lives, one is born among humans, yet because of unwholesome karma, one dwells in a borderland— such as the country of Devīra, the country of Pāpā, the coastal regions, the regions of the Indus River, or the regions of sandbanks— one will have one's wealth plundered by others, becoming a slave in a place of extreme suffering and poverty;
or if one serves as a gate-guard, one’s body will be maimed and crippled, with all one’s limbs being base, deficient, and incomplete.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, and assailed by the extremes of cold and heat as if struck by arrows piercing a mound of earth, they undergo extreme suffering;
they are constantly subjected to false accusations and beaten with sticks, stones, bricks, and the like by small children;
and they are held in contempt and loathed by all people.
Without wife and without children;
among all people, he is the most base and lowly, suffering the foremost misery.
The retribution of residual karma accords with its cause and accords with its conditions: as one acted in the past, so one receives in the future.
If that bhikṣu thus contemplates the dark hells and the karma of extreme suffering and affliction, he attains liberation from the bonds of desire within birth and death.

Furthermore, the practitioner observes that bhikṣu who is constantly diligent and energetic, who clearly perceives the fruits of karma, and who practices wholesome and correct conduct; such a one feels weary of and detached from all birth and death in the world, severs the foremost and most firm fetters of Māra, refuses to dwell within the realm of Māra, takes no pleasure in cohabiting with the ground of afflictions, and his mind finds no delight in defiled attachment or craving.

The yakṣas of that realm, seeing that the bhikṣu was endowed with such corresponding merits, further reported it upward to the yakṣas of the void, as previously described, proceeding in succession up to the Mahābrahmakāyika devas, as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the great hell of Black Rope (Kālasūtra) and sees another distinct location within it, a place named Caṇḍakālasūtra Hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place? He sees:
there are people who consume bedding, mats, and medicines required for illness in great quantities, even though such things are not their due.
Worldly people, obscured by ignorance, conceal their evil karma; whether they kill sheep themselves or incite others to kill them, they are deceived like the Brahmin heretics.
By reason of such evil karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realm of the Black Rope Hell, born in the Candāla section where they undergo great suffering.
This includes being plucked of their eyes by wicked birds—whether crows, vultures, or fierce pigs—and so forth.
The lord of that hell, with mallets and shackles, or with great axes, or with fierce fires, being extremely enraged and full of urgent hatred, torments them with various kinds of suffering.
Having already been born within such hells, they further undergo various kinds of most grievous suffering, namely:
having their eyes gouged out, or having their tongues torn out, and having every part of their bodies torn limb from limb;
and drinking molten copper.
Three red-hot iron spikes pierce their bodies all over;
their feet are hacked off and devoured by crows and birds;
every kind of disease gathers upon them as they wail and lament, without protector or companion.
The Yama-rodha beings strike them with extreme fury.
Thus, in this Black Rope Hell, they remain for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years until their evil karma is exhausted and decayed, at which point they finally obtain release.
If, due to virtuous karma from long ago in past lives not yet having matured, one is born among hungry ghosts or animals;
or if born among humans, one suffers from a hunched back, blindness, and a short lifespan, and after dying among humans, enters the evil realms once again.

Thus, sentient beings are bound by the shackles of karma: those who perform wholesome deeds receive wholesome retributions, while those who commit unwholesome deeds receive unwholesome retributions; bound by the fruits of their actions, they remain perpetually within birth and death.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the region of the Black Rope Great Hell called the Place of Fearful Vultures. By what karma are sentient beings born there? He sees:
there are people who, for the sake of coveting wealth, kill others—whether by binding them, starving them, or depriving them of food and drink.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into the Black Rope Hell within the evil realms, being born in the Place of the Fearful Vultures, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

In that hell, the iron ground is ablaze with fire yet appears entirely the color of water; ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference, it is surrounded by rising flames. There are iron caltrops upon which the hell-beings, struck violently with wrathful staves, run constantly day and night.
Blazing fires, swords, halberds, drawn bows, crossbows, and arrows pursue them from behind as they flee;
iron awls pierce them as they run in perpetual haste.
The Yama-wardens hold iron swords, iron hammers, and iron arrows, all ablaze with fire, with which they hack, strike, and shoot them;

as they wander through that place, driven by hunger and thirst, their lives are constantly on the verge of being severed; without rescue or refuge, their breath nearly exhausted, they exist only by the thread of life, held in the grasp of others, and undergo every manner of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Many people may follow one another In committing unwholesome deeds;
But when those evil deeds ripen in the future, There is birth where one must experience the fruit alone."
Fire, blades, and poisonous malice—though they cause harm, they may still be endured;
yet if one creates evil karma for oneself, the subsequent suffering will exceed even this.
All kinsmen and relatives are separated, but karma alone does not abandon us.
Good and evil follow one throughout all times in future lives;
Just as wherever a flower goes, its fragrance follows it,
So too does one's karma— whether good or evil— follow after.
As various birds rely upon a forest, departing at dawn and gathering again at dusk, so it is with sentient beings: in time, they shall once more be reunited.
By destroying the superior achievements of others and taking them for oneself to overstep them, one brings ruin upon oneself.
Whatever evil karma one commits, that person is deceived by delusion.
If they do not proceed toward Nirvana, nor turn toward the celestial realms, that delusion is the primary cause; from darkness, they enter further into darkness.

"Having thus committed evil karma for themselves, that person undergoes the sufferings of hell, wandering through the hells for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years until their evil karma is destroyed and exhausted, at which point they finally attain liberation."
Thereafter, they are reborn again as animals or hungry ghosts;

if they are born among humans, they become herdsmen—whether tending camels, other livestock, oxen and donkeys, or wild horses—and like elephants or dogs, they are constantly driving donkeys and camels, sustaining themselves by engaging in various trades everywhere;
or they serve as soldiers in an encircling army or as commanders of such troops, remaining impoverished and short-lived.
These are the results resembling the causes of base and evil deeds, as well as the remaining residual karmic causes.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the location of the Black Rope Great Hell, examining its sixteen subsidiary regions in their entirety, just as he did with the Reviving Hell.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the Sañjīva Hell and the Kālasūtra Hell; having observed them, he understands the law of karmic retribution: that the fruits of all evil karma are firm and solid, and that there is karma which is performed and accumulated, karma which is accumulated but not performed, and karma which is performed but not accumulated.
That which is both performed and accumulated will certainly be experienced;
that which is accumulated but not performed will not necessarily be experienced;
and that which is performed but not accumulated will not necessarily be experienced.

Having seen, heard, and known these three kinds of evil karma and their karmic retributions, and having understood them as they truly are, he gives rise once more to a sense of weary detachment. He observes the places where the ropes of karma bind one another;
furthermore, he observes the immeasurable varieties of karma, and further observes the immeasurable varieties of mental movements and objective attachments.
As that bhikṣu observes in this way, having seen that the minds of all sentient beings are subject to their own mastery, he further examines the other hells.
He perceives through seeing and hearing that the third hell is named the Saṃghāta Hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born there?
It is by having performed and accumulated evil and unwholesome karma that burns and cooks sentient beings.
They see, hear, and know this:

Sentient beings accumulate three kinds of evil karma through their actions, which leads them to be born in conjunction with the hells and causes them to undergo evil retributions: namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
These three kinds of evil and unwholesome karma lead to rebirth in the conjoined hells (*saṃghāta-naraka*).

Among them, superior evil karma leads to rebirth in the fundamental hells, while middling and inferior evil karma leads to rebirth in the individual locations (*pratyekanaraka*), where there are three types of painful sensations—superior, middling, and inferior.
Furthermore, at the time of performing an action, because the power of the mind differs, the lifespan experienced therein is categorized as superior, middling, or inferior.

Moreover, at the time of performing an action, because the mental power’s focal object (ālambana) is superior, middling, or inferior, the suffering experienced therein is likewise categorized as superior, middling, or inferior.
There are three determinate types of karma: three types of bodily karma, and three each for vocal and mental karma—namely, superior, middling, and inferior;
furthermore, there are three types, namely:
those born in the desire realm, those born in the form realm, and those born in the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three kinds: namely, the past, the present, and the future; again, there are three kinds:
namely, those to be experienced in the present life, those to be experienced in the next life, and those to be experienced in subsequent lives;
yet again, there are three kinds, namely:
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;
furthermore, there are three kinds:
bondage in the present, bondage in the intermediate state, and bondage in the place of rebirth for ordinary beings.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of bondage: bondage by humans and non-humans, bondage by non-humans and humans, and self-bondage within one’s own state—namely, having abandoned a human existence yet again obtaining a human body.
One performs karma for the hells; through the power of that karma, one acts in accordance with it, and through the similarity of that karma, one is born accordingly.
"Furthermore, there are three types of bhikṣus who have attained liberation and supernormal powers:
first, those who act; second, those who do not act; and third, those who act while bound.
As for 'those who act,' they are those who first become śramaṇas."
To speak of "one who acts" refers to being bound by subsequent continuity;
to speak of "one who does not act" refers to attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, "one who acts" refers to having become a śramaṇa and performing the practices of a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the bound agent: having passed away from this place, one is born in another place.
Moreover, there are three types:
first, the bond of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bandhana*); second, the bond of non-concentration (*a-dhyāna-bandhana*); and third, the bond of no retribution (*avipāka-bandhana*).
Those bound by dhyāna refer to the stages of the first dhyāna and the stages bound by the second dhyāna, but not the third or fourth dhyānas;
those not bound by dhyāna refer to [the practice of] giving, precepts, and so forth;

those without the bondage of retribution refer to Arhats, whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, such that although they possess karma that would certainly lead to fruition, they no longer receive its retribution.

That bhikṣu contemplates the ocean of the world, bound by the net of karma, where the fruits of actions arise from mutual causes; there is no creator, no experiencer, and it is not without causes and conditions—there is only the power of karma.

As that bhikṣu reflects in this way, he destroys the army of Māra, cultivates and accumulates wholesome dharmas, and further contemplates with even greater excellence the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions associated with the hells.
How is it that sentient beings are born into the fundamental Great Earth Hell? They see:
there are those who commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, delighting in such acts and performing them frequently;
When such karma is pervasive and ultimate, and is practiced with pleasure and performed extensively, that karma leads to birth in the root hells as well as the secondary locations.

That person undergoes great suffering and affliction in those root hells; having performed actions as previously described—whether by stealing or by committing sexual misconduct—such a person is called one who practices sexual misconduct.
What is meant by "perverse"?
It refers to acting in one way and conceptualizing in another.
If a person commits an illicit act with the wife of a venerable one, that person will be born in the Saṃjīva Great Hell and undergo great suffering. As for what constitutes such suffering:
Iron-flame-beaked vultures, having extracted their entrails, hang them upon the treetops and devour them;

there is a great river there named Abounding Iron Hooks, where iron hooks are all ablaze with fire, and the Yama-wardens seize the hell-beings and hurl them into that river so that they fall upon the iron hooks.

Furthermore, within that river are flaming knives; there, the sinners undergo great suffering and affliction. That suffering is peerless and beyond comparison, specifically the suffering of being struck by flaming hooks: they strike their bodies with flaming hooks.
The *Yama* wardens seize the hell-beings and cast them into that river, pressing them down to make them submerge;
once submerged, those hell-beings sink one another, and having thus sunk, they cry out and wail.
The river is not water, but molten red copper; it carries those offenders along like drifting logs, flowing without ceasing, so that they are thus swept away, burned, and undergo great suffering.
After having been scorched and swept away by that River of Iron Hooks, some of those hell-beings have bodies like the sun first rising;
some have bodies that sink down like heavy stones;
and some cling to the riverbanks without being submerged.
Some sinners have bodies like aquatic moss;
some are devoured by iron vultures with flaming beaks as if they were eating fish;
and some have bodies that melt away until their forms resemble lumps of fresh butter.
Some are struck with iron bricks;
some have their bodies shattered into hundreds of thousands of fragments like a handful of sand;
and some are in rivers as if in molten copper.
Some have their bodies scorched with hot ashes;
some have their bodies pincered with flaming tongs and placed within hot ashes, while further being repeatedly stabbed and pierced with iron pincers;
some have their bodies torn apart like fine threads and are beaten as they are pulled.
Some have their heads pulled down so that they are below while being beaten from above;
some are placed in cauldrons and boiled in boiling water like hot beans;
and some are tossed up and down repeatedly and rapidly within the cauldrons.

Some are placed in the cauldrons near one side, raising their hands toward heaven and wailing; others are close together, wailing as well, enduring great suffering for a long time without a protector or a savior.

Within that place, there are many fire-tongued vultures, jackals, dogs, and the like; they consume their prey upon the hot ground without killing them, while those suffering in secluded spots cannot see one another.

Through various causes and conditions, they undergo various sufferings; they experience immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of suffering, deceived by their own minds, obtained through the root of the ten unwholesome actions and improper conduct—obtained through the condition of killing and obtained through the condition of stealing.
Furthermore, it is like this:
the Yama-wardens strike those sinners with iron pestles ablaze with flames. Terrified, the sinners flee, looking in all four directions for refuge or rescue, crying out: "Who will save me?"
"Where shall I go for refuge?

Running and looking in the four directions, as he travels thus, he is struck by flaming pestles and cast into places of extreme peril and evil—such as rivers of blazing fire, trees of blazing fire, or among mountain crags, rocks, caves, and pits—where he undergoes various sufferings. That is to say, he is placed upon the tops of trees and then pushed down onto ground covered with iron hooks; his body is torn and split in this manner a thousand times, or even hundreds of thousands of times.
Furthermore, it is like this:

The Yama-wardens seize the hell-beings and place them in the Forest of Sword-Leaves—where the sword-leaves are exceedingly numerous and ablaze with flames. When these sinners see beautiful, upright, and elegantly adorned women at the tops of those trees, upon seeing them, they give rise to extreme passion and attachment.

Thus, these women are adorned with exquisite garlands, their bodies sprinkled with powdered incense and anointed with fragrant unguents; their physical forms are the most superbly decorated, their bodies exceedingly supple, their fingers and nails slender and long, and they wear joyful smiles. Adorned with various jewels and employing every kind of seductive artifice, they captivate the hearts of all foolish, ordinary worldlings upon seeing them.
Once those hell-beings have seen such beautiful women upon the trees, they give rise to this thought:
"These are those whom I saw in my former human existence; these are those who belonged to me in the past."
Those hell-beings, deceived by their own karma, perceive things in this way;
having perceived them thus, they immediately climb that tree, whose leaves are like knives, which cut the flesh of their bodies;
once the flesh has been cut, it next cuts their tendons.
Once the tendons have been cut, he next cuts his bones;
once the bones have been cut, he next splits his marrow.

Having thus split and cut every part of his body, he is finally able to climb the tree. Desiring to approach the women, his mind becomes increasingly focused on them, yet deceived by his own heart, he suffers in this manner while upon that tree.
Having already climbed the tree, he saw that woman still on the ground.
Upon seeing her, the woman looked up at him with seductive eyes and called out to him in a beautiful voice, first speaking these sweet words:
"It was because of you that I came to this place; why do you not now come near me?"
"Why do you not embrace me?

Thus, in this hell, created by the transformations of karma, the sinner sees [the apparition] and his lustful mind becomes intensely inflamed; he then descends one after another to the tops of the trees with sword-leaves.

Once that person has descended, the blade-edges turn upward—blazing with fierce flames and as sharp as razors. These sharp blades first cut through his flesh, then sever his tendons, then cut through his bones, then cut through his veins, and finally cut through his marrow, leaving sores over his entire body.
Those hell-beings are thus cut and thus split; once their veins have been severed, they gaze upon that woman, their hearts consumed by lustful craving.
As they gaze thus, the fire-tipped vultures immediately peck at their eyes, and the flaming sword-leaves first cut their ears. Being thus cut, they cry out and shriek;
the flaming sword-leaves next cut their tongues, then their noses, cutting through every part of their bodies as their hearts are dragged on by lustful craving.
Having thus reached the ground, and once he had reached the ground, that woman was again at the top of the tree; seeing her, the man climbed the tree once more, as previously described.

Due to the power of that karma, for thus immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, and for thus immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years, deceived by their own minds, they wander about in that hell.
Those hell-beings are thus scorched; for what cause are they scorched? Lust is the cause.
Such people do not abandon lust even in this state; with a mind that has operated thus since beginningless time, they wander through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The minds of sentient beings cannot be tamed or brought into harmony; even while in the hells, they remain thus. One should know that this mind is untrustworthy.

Furthermore, within the Saṃjīva Great Hell there is a mountain named Gṛdhra-kūṭa (Vulture Peak). The denizens of that hell, their bodies burning with hunger and thirst, run toward that mountain. Throughout that mountain, there are iron vultures with flaming beaks, possessing massive bodies and great bellies. Within the bodies and bellies of those iron vultures dwell the hell-beings known as "Fire-Men."
Those hell-beings, seeking rescue and seeking refuge, rush toward that mountain;
once they have reached it, those iron vultures first shatter their heads, split open their skulls to extract the brains, and then gouge out their eyes;
the hell-beings wail and cry out, yet there is no one to save them.
Once their heads have been split open and the brains have been completely drunk, they cast the heads aside;
those hell-beings, now headless and eyeless, run again toward the Dark Hell due to the power of their karmic offenses.
Furthermore, there are iron vultures with extremely large bodies; within the bellies of these vultures are fire-people who come toward the offenders and swallow them as soon as they arrive.
When those hell-beings enter the vultures' bellies, they immediately become fire-people;
this is caused by the karmic retribution for their original sin of violating the wives of others.
"Because he delighted in and frequently committed the act of killing, he shall be constantly burned for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, yet still not die."
Due to the cause of sexual misconduct, having delighted in and frequently committed it, one sees women in the Forest of Sword-Leaves (*asipattravana*).

Due to the cause of theft, having delighted in and frequently committed it, one enters another hell in a certain location; that place is a river called *Anantapāra* (Boundless Shore), which is filled with boiling molten copper.

The sinners in hell see on the opposite bank of the river many kinds of foremost pure food, *khādaniya* food, and *bhojaniya* food; there are excellent bedding and seating, beautiful groves with deep shadows, as well as ponds and rivers of clear water.
Having seen this, those hell-beings immediately let out a great cry, calling out to one another in succession, saying:
"Come here! Come here!"
"I have now attained happiness.
Now there are various kinds of khādaniya food and bhojaniya food, as well as excellent bedding and seating," as previously described.
As those hell-beings cry out in this manner, the other hell-beings, having heard the sound, all run together, thinking there is one who can rescue them and one to whom they may return for refuge.
Gathering in one place, they ask one another: "Where shall we now find happiness?"
"Who can save us? To whom can we turn for refuge?
Then another person, who had not been called, approached and pointed out to them, saying:

"Look now at this shoreless further bank, the other side of the great river! Here there are many kinds of *khādaniya* food and *bhojaniya* food, as well as groves of trees providing cool shade and bedding."
As previously described,
all those hell-beings gather together in this manner and run as one toward the shoreless further bank, the other side of the great river.
In this river, molten white tin and molten lead and tin flow with foam covering their surfaces.
As those hell-beings run in such a manner, they fall into that river;

once fallen, some have bodies like lumps of fresh butter, some are melted away, some are devoured by crows with flaming beaks, some are eaten by evil fish with flaming mouths, and some have their limbs scattered and dissolved.
Those hell-beings in that river undergo all such sufferings in this manner; it is brought about by the accumulated power and conditions of their evil karma, and thus they experience such suffering.
