What he previously heard from afar as the calls of birds are actually this wicked dragon seizing and devouring the hell-beings, inflicting upon them all manner of torments.
Thus these sinners undergo great suffering and wail with loud cries.

After the dragon’s flaming mouth has devoured them in this manner, they are restored to life again within that very dragon’s mouth. By the power of their own karma, they die and are reborn within the dragon’s mouth, living and dying again and again. Thus they are constantly devoured for many years beyond counting; having been eaten, they are born once more, and having been born, they are eaten again.

If, through the exhaustion of karma related to the mouth, one obtains release from that state, yet remains in extreme heat and thirst, one sees a pool of water in another location and runs toward it with haste.

However, that pool is entirely covered by dark fires; the blazing fires of hell are one *yojana* deep. When the hell-being arrives and enters it, they sink down and undergo extreme suffering. This corresponds exactly to their own past actions; no other karma can serve as a metaphor for it, and the suffering they experience is identical to its likeness.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they will experience uninterrupted suffering at all times;
only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place in hell.
Even after escaping that place, one will be born among hungry ghosts and animals for seven hundred lifetimes.
Even if one escapes that state, it is as difficult to obtain a human body as it is for a turtle to encounter a hole in a floating yoke.
If one is born among humans in a place of similar karma, one will be impoverished and frequently ill, subject to the commands of others, begging in the alleys, and having a short stature;
these are the residual karmic fruits of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the Great Intense Heat Great Hell and considers what other places exist there.
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another distinct place called the Place of Great Sorrow, which is the fourteenth location within that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

if a person habitually commits and frequently performs acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, drinking intoxicants, lying, and holding wrong views—their karma and its retribution are as previously described.

Furthermore, there are virtuous people who read and recite sūtras and śāstras from others, or hear of them from them; yet these people, driven by excessive desire, commit adultery with their own wives and concubines, or even with the wives of their teachers and others—women who are in fact chaste and virtuous—deceiving and seducing them while constantly saying to others, "She is my mother."
Because the teacher’s wife resembled his mother, his deluded mind violated his faith, and he thus engaged in sexual desire.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perished and his life ended, he fell into an evil destination; born in that hell in the "Great Compassion" section, he undergoes great suffering and affliction.
As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies endured in the Reviving Hell and other such hells are experienced here in their entirety.
Furthermore, there are even more severe sufferings, namely:

there is a bed of hot iron there, upon which are sharp blades shaped like grinding teeth; the sinner is constantly and violently ground upon it, so that all parts of the body—the skin, flesh, sinews, veins, marrow, and blood—all become fused together.
As they are thus ground, they wail and weep with grief; when the other inhabitants of hell hear their cries, they are overcome by great anguish and no longer perceive their own suffering.

Although they are thus ground, they do not die; they remain alive as they are ground for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years. As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they will experience unceasing suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place of hell.
For six thousand lifetimes, they will be born among hungry ghosts and animals.
Even if they escape that state, it will be as difficult for them to obtain a human body as it is for a turtle to encounter a hole in a floating yoke.

If they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they may die in the womb; or die after birth; or die before being able to sit up; or die before being able to walk; or die after being able to walk; or die while walking about.
Wherever they are born, their sense faculties are incomplete;
this is the residual karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the Great Intense Heat Great Hell: what other places are there within it?
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another place called Non-Darkness (Anandhakāra), which is the fifteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

if a person habitually practices and frequently commits killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, drinking intoxicants, lying, and holding wrong views, their karma and its retribution are as previously described.

Furthermore, there are those who commit adultery with their own sons' wives; because of this causal condition of evil karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into an evil destination and undergo great suffering in that hell in the place called Non-Darkness (Anandhakāra).
As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies experienced in the Reviving Hell and the other hells are fully endured here.

Furthermore, there is something even more severe: the iron ground there is ablaze and seething with heat. The *yama-rākṣasas* seize the hell-beings and toss them up and down upon that hot ground, causing those sinners to alternate between being on top and being underneath hundreds and thousands of times. They are gathered together and boiled until they merge into a single mass, not allowing even a hair’s breadth of space between them; thus, they become one solid block with one another.

The Yama-wardens pound them with mallets, reforming them into different masses that are more compact than the previous ones; thus they are pounded finely until they are so subtly blended together that they can no longer be distinguished.

Thus they undergo harsh and rigid suffering for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years; as long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decomposed, and its residual force has not been exhausted, they shall suffer incessantly at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that hellish realm.
Even after escaping that place, one will be born among hungry ghosts and animals for nine hundred lifetimes.
If one escapes from there, it is as difficult to obtain a human body as it is for a turtle to encounter a hole in a floating yoke.

If they are born among humans in places of similar karma, they will be poor and constantly afflicted by disease; they will be perpetually ruined by enemies, born in evil lands or as barbarians of the sea; they will be the most base and inferior among all people, and furthermore, they will not live long.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, examines the Great Intense Heat Great Hell: what other places are there within it?
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another place called Wood-Turning (Kāṣṭhabhramana), which is the sixteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

if a person habitually practices and frequently commits killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, drinking intoxicants, lying, and wrong views, their karma and its retribution are as previously described.

Furthermore, there may be someone who has saved another’s life—such as one whose life was about to end due to illness or the like, or one who was being executed—and yet, instead of recognizing that kindness, he commits adultery with the savior’s wife.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the Wood-Turning section of that hell, where they undergo great suffering and distress.
As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies experienced in the Reviving Hell and the other hells are fully endured here.
Moreover, there is something even more severe:
in that place there is a river named Great Screaming (*Mahāraurava*), wherein molten white tin flows, boiling and scalding countless hundreds of thousands of beings as they drift along.

The sinners in hell are thus tossed and boiled in that river; those hell-beings are likewise swept along by the current within it, and because of the violent current, they enter headfirst and sink as soon as they have entered, overturning and pressing against one another with the other sinners until they can no longer be distinguished.
Thus, in the upper and lower hells, the sinners are pressed down below; they are scorched and boiled in boiling white tin, crying out as they undergo uninterrupted suffering.
As those hell-beings suffer in this manner due to their evil karma, there further appear great makara fish that devour their limbs; once devoured, their bodies grow back again.
As that wood revolves, they undergo great suffering and affliction; they endure such pain for an immensely long duration, suffering in this way due to their own evil karma.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and its residual force has not been exhausted, they will experience uninterrupted suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that hellish realm.
Even after escaping that state, one will be born among hungry ghosts and animals for five hundred lifetimes.

Once liberated from there, if one is born among humans in a place of similar karma, one will be loathed and despised by all women; one’s own parents, brothers, wife, and children will all feel aversion toward them, and for five hundred lifetimes, one will be unable to engage in sexual desire.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of those evil deeds.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, observes that the Great Hell of Intense Heat (Mahāraurava) consists of only these sixteen distinct locations; he sees no seventeenth location. Surveying them all, there are only sixteen places, and this great, most wicked, and extremely intense Great Hell is thus boundless.

This is the fruit of one's own karma, experienced within hell; the sinner undergoes great suffering through being burned and boiled, corresponding exactly to their deeds. It is not that one person acts and another suffers; what one has done oneself is never lost, and what one has not done is never obtained.
Just as one obtains results corresponding to the actions one has performed, and those actions arise from oneself, so it is with sentient beings:
according to what they have done, they obtain the results of their own karma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, receiving fruits in accordance with their deeds.

That bhikṣu thus contemplates the retribution of the hells and the karmic actions that lead to the hells; having contemplated them, he becomes weary of and seeks liberation from birth and death. He perceives no pleasure, perceives no permanence, perceives no self, and perceives no purity; in this way, he sees only that all of birth and death is entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Having seen this, he becomes detached from all desires; he is detached from the fetters of desire, detached from the conduct of desire, detached from the intention of desire, and detached from the causes of desire. Seeing the faults and evils of desire, his fear increases even further.
Thus, by correctly restraining the conduct of body, speech, and mind—these supreme practices of the three karmas—the Māra finds no opportunity and one is no longer bound to Māra.
Cultivating in this way, one becomes lax toward the cycle of birth and death; the fetters of the continuity of evil are destroyed and dispersed.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma—and forms this thought:
"That bhikṣu is truly rare; possessing superior power, he has attained the eleventh stage."

When the terrestrial yakṣas see that bhikṣu’s tireless diligence and his superior power, they give rise to joy in their hearts and pass the news upward to the celestial yakṣas. The celestial yakṣas inform the Four Great Kings as previously described, and so on in succession until it reaches the Great Brahmā Heaven, who speaks thus:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country and such-and-such a village, there is a son of good family named So-and-so of such-and-such a clan. Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he has gone forth with right faith. His mind takes no pleasure in dwelling within the realm of Māra; he does not delight in living together with desire, lust, or attachment. He finds no joy in the snake of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and seeing the suffering and distress of others, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment from all birth and death in the world."
Upon hearing this, those Brahmakāyika devas were filled with joy and spoke these words:
"The faction of Māra is diminished, and the assembly of the True Dharma increases.

With their divine eye, those practitioners beheld that bhikṣu who had thus attained the eleventh stage and perceived the Right Path; they clearly saw and understood the law of karmic retribution, and they clearly saw his bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions.

“Monks! These three kinds of subtle bodily, verbal, and mental actions are known in their various subtle details; neither the world of devas, nor the world of Māras, nor the world of Brahmās, nor the realm of śramaṇas, nor the realm of brāhmaṇas—neither such gods and humans can know them in their various subtle details, much less could the outsiders, the Carakas and Parivrājakas, ever know them?”
Only I can know this, and my disciples who have heard it from me can likewise know it; they know all the subtle divisions of the three types of action, down to their most minute details.
"O bhikṣus, if other persons, such as those heterodox followers, the Carakas and Parivrājakas, should ask you such questions, you should answer them in this way;
if you answer those heterodox followers, the Carakas and Parivrājakas, in this manner, their minds will become bewildered and submerged, and they will be unable to answer you."
Why is this? O bhikṣus!

Because all sentient beings encompassed within birth and death do not practice therein and it is not their sphere; those people possess only a coarse understanding and cannot understand correctly. Their knowledge is fleeting, defiled, and meagerly inferior regarding those three types of karma—karma of body, speech, and mind.

What that person says is refuted by others; they cannot sever birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and all forms of suffering and affliction. They do not realize the noble Dharma, nor do they reach Nirvana. It is not the ultimate path, not the dharma of tranquility, not the dharma of peace and happiness, and not the way to be born in the heavens. That person contemplates the three paths of action—of body, speech, and mind—with nothing but a mind of pride.

"O Bhikṣus! That outsider, the Cārvāka Parivrājaka, rejoices in his own mind and does not contemplate the faults or merits [of his actions]. Thus, this person possesses these three types of karma—karma of body, speech, and mind—which are greatly evil."
That person has not the slightest resemblance to me; they are like nirvana compared to saṃsāra, having not even the slightest similarity.
Their principles and characteristics are profoundly remote: that person’s knowledge of the three karmas and my knowledge of the three karmas have not the slightest resemblance.

"O Bhikṣus! You should know that the questions of those non-Buddhists consist merely of words; whereas the Buddha possesses the right path, the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and [the realization that] all birth-and-death is impermanent, subject to decay, entirely suffering, and devoid of joy."
"O bhikṣus! You should know this:
there is no entity that is eternal, no entity that is immovable, no entity that is unchanging, and no entity that does not undergo transformation."
"O monks! That practitioner sees that monk thus: through his various bodily, verbal, and mental actions, he perceives them clearly as he proceeds toward the city of Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, he observes:
"How does that bhikṣu attain the twelve stages?

That practitioner observes in this way and sees that the bhikṣu practices with tireless diligence. He then further carefully contemplates the seven great hells and their subsidiary locations as the causes and effects of evil karma, according to the laws of karmic retribution. Having observed this thoroughly, he comes to see, hear, and know:
Furthermore, there is yet another greatest hell named Avīci.
Taking the seven great hells along with their subsidiary locations as one part, the Avīci Hell is a thousand times more intense than them.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that hell?
He perceives and knows through hearing and learning:
if a person, with a heavy heart, kills their mother or kills their father; or further, with an evil mind, sheds the blood of a Buddha, causes a schism in the Saṃgha, or kills an Arhat.
Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, that person is born within the Great Avīci Hell and remains there for one kalpa.

If they remain during a *kalpa* of decrease (*apakarṣa-kalpa*), it is because their karma is equal [to that of those remaining during a kalpa of increase], yet they fall into Avīci by having committed evil karma during the intermediate period of the kalpa; thus, during that *kalpa* of decrease, that person is burned and boiled in Avīci.

Why is this? Because the time has already passed and cannot be turned back; therefore, although their afflictions are intense and their suffering is harsh during that aeon of decrease (*apakalpa*), they experience it for only a short duration due to their many evil karmas.
Thus, when one performs an action leading to Avīci hell, if it is done with a mind of compassion, a firm resolve, or a gentle disposition, the suffering experienced will not be severe.
For example, if a person commits a single act that leads to Avīci hell, yet does so with a heavy heart [of malice], they will experience the most intense suffering.

All karmic actions and their retributive fruits are entirely mental states and mental concomitants; all are governed by the mind, all are the conjunction of the mind, and all proceed in accordance with the mind. Furthermore, there are six fetters that bind sentient beings; if the mind is tranquil, sentient beings are liberated.

According to that sequence, within the Avīci Hell, due to the causes and conditions of their suffering, the bodies they experience are either soft or coarse. If one has committed five heinous crimes (ānantarya), their body in hell is five hundred yojanas tall; if four, four hundred yojanas; if three, three hundred yojanas; if two, two hundred yojanas; and if one, one hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the location of the Great Avīci Hell. He wonders: "How many locations are there in this so-called 'Hair-Raising' Great Hell?
Through seeing, hearing, and knowing, he perceives that this entire hell consists of sixteen locations. What are these sixteen?
First is named Crow’s Beak;
second is named Facing All Directions Toward the Earth;
third is named No Shore, Constantly Suffering Affliction.
The fourth is named Howling Jackal;
the fifth is named Iron Jackal-Eater;
the sixth is named Black Belly.
The seventh is named Body-Ocean;
the eighth is named Dream-Vision-of-Fear;
the ninth is named Body-Ocean-Suffering.
The tenth is named Two Mountains Assembly;
the eleventh is named Yamavardha;
the twelfth is named Star Garland.
Thirteenth is named Urgent Suffering;
fourteenth is named Enveloped in Foul Odor;
fifteenth is named Iron Plates.
The sixteenth is named Eleven Flames.
Throughout that greatest of all hells, Avīci, there are these sixteen distinct locations.

Furthermore, as that bhikṣu thus observes those who are about to die, up to their existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he considers how those who have committed deeds leading to the Avīci hell suffer within it and are reborn in such places of misery.
He sees that sentient beings, shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion, commit evil deeds and thereby bring about the unwholesome conduct of the Avīci Hell.
In this way, those who commit the evil karma that leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell include those who, for the sake of being born in heaven,
burn and kill their own mothers with a great fire; or again, those who push their mothers off high mountains and precipitous cliffs, thus killing their mothers.
Furthermore, there are those who place their mother in water; in this way, they kill their mother.
Again, there are those who starve their mother to death.
These foolish people of the evil paths, deceived by what they have heard, therefore kill their mothers.
With a greedy mind longing for heaven, one kills one's mother in this way:

some starve her to death; some push her off a mountain or a precipice; some burn her with fire; or they kill her in the water. For the sake of attaining heaven, that person, out of love for heaven, kills their own mother.

Some kill with a mind of hatred and poison; some kill because of a frivolous mind, because of mental conditions, or because of mental autonomy. Thus one kills one's mother, and likewise kills one's father; such killings occur due to the faults of the three poisons.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, due to a deluded mind, does not recognize that the Tathāgata is a great field of merit; thus, giving rise to a hateful and evil mind, they shed his blood.
It is through such excessive hatred that they commit the schism of the Saṃgha and kill Arhats.
Such a person, having completely abandoned all such causes and conditions and all karmic actions, is born in the Great Avīci Hell.

When that person of evil karma is on the verge of death, the great fires of the Avīci Hell have already arisen within their very body; or again, when another is about to die, they experience the suffering of Avīci while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as they are being reborn there.

Whenever such individuals as these commit evil karma for the Avīci Hell, they immediately incinerate all their wholesome karma—including the karma of those destined for renunciation and the karma conducive to liberation—and are unable to receive the precepts.
Having been thus burned, his unwholesome and evil karma consumes that person's body.
Because he committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) in the distant past, those superior karmas of his will certainly not bear fruit [in this life].
What is meant by "certainty"?

Certainty regarding hell means it can shorten one's lifespan; if a hundred-year lifespan is reduced to twenty years, and all that one seeks through thought cannot be obtained, it is like sowing seeds in salty soil.

For such a person of evil karma, even their personal protective deity (*svadevatā*) will immediately abandon them; all their undertakings will yield no fruit or benefit, their faculties will become dull and rigid, and they will frequently experience bad dreams amidst their sensory objects. They will constantly encounter all manner of disadvantageous circumstances, and their wife, children, and servants will all desert them. They will perpetually suffer from hunger and thirst; even when encountering fine food, they will not perceive its true flavor. Their voices will be impaired, their touch will be entirely unpleasant, and their facial complexion will be extremely wretched. Their minds will be in constant terror, and they will be base and inferior among men. Even toward their kinsmen, brothers, and others, they will feel fear and dread due to no other cause than their own evil karma. Furthermore, they will see smoke everywhere throughout all worlds.

The various elements within this person’s body are out of harmony; they perceive foul colors even from afar; their bathed skin dries quickly; their body constantly suffers from heat and is prone to jaundice; their mouth is always salty and bitter;
though their bedding is soft, they experience harsh and unpleasant sensations;
even the sounds of flutes, drums, and lutes seem offensive to them, let alone other vulgar noises.

Furthermore, that person’s olfactory consciousness is impaired; when they smell fragrant things, they perceive them as foul odors. All parts of their body become putrid and rotten; all their hair and body hairs fall out and lose their firmness; the color of their teeth deteriorates, and their hands and feet crack open. They completely forget all forms of calculation.
Devas constantly terrify them, and they experience heart-throbbing fear in their dreams. Because of this mental agitation, they are perpetually emaciated and never plump.
If one places fine flowers upon their head or body, they quickly wither and dry up.
His clothes wear out easily and he takes pleasure in becoming soiled; though he bathes and washes his garments, they quickly become dirty again.
When walking on the road, he falls down without cause; once he has fallen, his body is wounded and sores break out, which further increase upon his person and are difficult to heal.
When lying down to sleep, his throat becomes dry, and he constantly craves to drink much.
The cities, towns, and settlements were actually teeming with people, yet he saw them all as empty;
he did not perceive the true colors of the sun, moon, or stars;
when a faint breeze blew, he felt a sensation of solidity, as if iron were touching his body.
Just as when one wishes to approach fire, the body is burned and experiences a twofold sensation of heat;
one perceives warmth even in the moon, and feels heat even in extremely cold water;
and what was once a most excellent grove is seen as a place of horror.
The lovely bird songs they previously heard now sound like those of jackals;
they see all people as no different from corpses in a cemetery; at all times they constantly hear sounds that bring them no joy;
and even when drinking wine, their hearts find no pleasure.
Having never committed evil deeds to incur punishment,
such a person nevertheless voids excrement and urine in main streets, crossroads, and triangular alleys.
Such a person is abandoned by the devas and constantly encounters all manner of disadvantageous circumstances.
That person’s physical appearance is like a forest that has been scorched; all people in the world loathe him and do not love him.
That person of evil karma first manifests such signs of Avīci hell in the present life, and subsequently, the signs of death appear:

One sees the moon in broad daylight and the sun in the middle of the night; one does not see one's own reflection. Without any apparent cause or condition, one hears evil sounds; the nose becomes distorted and inverted; the hair and body hairs become matted together; and the body contracts fatal diseases such as fever. The entire body is steaming with heat, afflicted by the four hundred and four diseases. One perceives only these four hundred afflictions pervading the body, as if being scorched and boiled in a pit of fire. Eighty kinds of worms inhabit the body, permeating all the bodily channels, sinews, fat, skin, and flesh. Eighty kinds of winds blow upon and kill those worms; that is to say, the eighty kinds of worms are killed by the eighty winds.
What are these eighty?
First is the hair-worm (*vālaka-jantu*), which is killed by the *roma-atikrānta* wind;
second is the black-mouthed worm (*kṛṣṇamukha-jantu*), which is killed by the *kāla-anuvartana* wind.
The third is the *abalavāta* worm, killed by the wind of chaotic dreams;
the fourth is the *balavakarmaka* worm, killed by the wind of intolerance;
the fifth is the *mohakarman* worm, whose color and form are killed by the wind of fabrication.
Sixth is the fire-colored *kṛmi*, killed by the *rasapīḍana* wind;
seventh is the slippery worm (*snigdha-kṛmi*), killed by the *ayaḥsāra* wind;
eighth is the river-drifting worm (*nadīpluta-kṛmi*), killed by the *viṣṭhāmūtra-ūrdhva* wind.
The ninth is named the leaping insect, killed by the wind that moves through the anus;
the tenth is named the discriminating-view insect, killed by the wind of recollecting the past;
the eleventh is named the foul-smelling insect, killed by the wind of skin-excess.
12. The worm named Asthija is killed by the flavor-excess wind;
13. The worm named Raktamukha is killed by the pulse-excess wind;
14. The worm named Sūcīviddha is killed by the desire-excess wind.
The fifteenth is named *nāḍīcārāhāra* (Vessel-Walking Food-Eater), which is killed by the *asthigata-vāyu* (Bone-Pervading Wind);
the sixteenth is named *bibhala* (Bibhala), which is killed by the *balahara-vāyu* (Strength-Consuming Wind);
the seventeenth is named *kaṭhina-mukha* (Hard-Mouth), which is killed by the *viśeṣa-go-vāyu* (Superior Ox Wind).
Eighteenth is the hairless worm, killed by the wind of excessive impurity;
nineteenth is the needle-mouthed worm, killed by the wind of excessive moisture;
twentieth is the stomach-piercing worm, killed by the wind of excessive feces.
The twenty-first is the Non-Active Worm, killed by the Conjunction Wind;
the twenty-second is the Excrement-Dispersing Worm, killed by the Tooth-Breaking Wind;
the twenty-third is the Three-Jointed Worm, killed by the Throat-Collecting Wind.
Twenty-fourth is the *antra-bheda* worm, killed by the downward-moving wind;
twenty-fifth is the *ādhmāpana* worm, killed by the upward-moving wind;
twenty-sixth is the *suvarṇa* worm, killed by the three-sided wind.
Twenty-seventh is the worm named Excrement-Orifice-Mature, which is killed by the Joint-by-Joint Moving Wind;
twenty-eighth is the worm named Skin-Maker, which is killed by the Heart-Passing Wind;
twenty-ninth is the worm named Fat-Beak, which is killed by the Dispersing Wind.
The thirty-first is the *saṃghāta* worm, killed by the *vivartana* wind;
the thirty-second is the *durgandha* worm, killed by the *saṃvartana* wind;
the thirty-third is the *pañcavātasamudita* worm, killed by the *saṃnicaya* wind.
The thirty-third is named the *Cucu* insect, which is killed by the *Saṃkṣepa-vāyu*;
the thirty-fourth is named the *Puṣpasaṃcaya* insect, which is killed by the *Gati-āgati-sthiti-dhāvana-kriyā-vāyu*.
Next are the worms named Great Deceit, Snake, Black, Great Eater, Warmth-Walker, and those of the eyes, ears, and nose, which are killed by the body-wind;
next are the worms named Bone-Licker, killed by the wind of Overlooking;
next are the worms named Black-Foot, killed by the wind of Cold Foam.
Next is the worm named Guṇa-cchedaka, which is killed by the marrow-pervading wind;
next is the worm named Māṃsa-cara, which is killed by the nail-relying wind;
next is the worm named Kapāla-cārī, which is killed by the wind that courses along one side of the foot.
Next is the worm named Skull-Walker, which kills by producing the unconsciousness-wind;
next is the worm named Affliction-Giver, which kills by the destruction-wind;
next is the worm named Ear-Walker, which kills by the splitting-wind.
Next is the worm named *Gṛhītaśarīra*, which is killed by the *Piṇḍaka* wind;
next is the worm named *Sarvagata-vasā*, which is killed by the *Ūru-bheda* wind;
next is the worm named *Kheṭa-prakiraṇa*, which is killed by the *Sandhi-bheda* wind.
Next is the worm called *Dantāda* (Tooth-Biter), which is killed by the wind *Pārśvabhedaka* (Rib-Splitter);
next is the worm called *Kheṭāhāra* (Spittle-Eater), which is killed by the wind *Balakledana* (Strength-Rotter);
next is the worm called *Lālāśīta-phena* (Cold-Foam-Spittle), which is killed by the wind *Snāyupreraṇa-stambha* (Tendon-Pushing-Pillar).
Next is the worm named Vamana, which is killed by the internal whirlwind Dravaṇa;
next is the worm named Ghanamada, which is killed by the wind Ghanavilola;
next is the worm named Ṣarasa-abhilāṣin, which is killed by the wind Loma-nakha-śakṛt-vināśana.
Next is the worm named *Vāyu-niḥsaraṇa*, which is killed by the wind *Sāraniḥsaraṇa*;
next is the worm named *Rasa-vardhana*, which is killed by the wind *Bhedana-kara*;
next is the worm named *Svapna-āśā*, which is killed by the wind *Viśāla-stambha*.
Next is the worm named Loma-ja (Hair-born), which is killed by the wind called Śuṣka-viṣṭhā-kṛt (Dry-feces-maker);
next is the worm named Sva-rasa (Good-taste), which is killed by the wind called Pakṣa-bandha (Side-binding);
next is the worm named Krimimātṛ (Worm-mother), which is killed by the wind called Ṣaḍ-gṛdhra (Six-vulture).
Next is the hair-light worm (*loma-prabhāsa-kṛmi*), which is killed by the wind that causes all bodily parts to become like hair;
next is the hair-eating worm (*lomāśa-kṛmi*), which is killed by the wind that violently destroys;
next is the *kṣikṣika* worm, which is killed by the wind that moves all bodily parts.
Next is the worm named *Sukṣu*, which is killed by the heat-wind;
next is the worm named *Vraṇaja*, which is killed by the *saṃnipāta*-wind;
next is the worm named *Yavayava*, which is killed by the downward-and-upward wind (*adhaūrdhvavāyu*).
Next is the worm named *snāyu-saṃvṛta*, which is killed by the life-force wind (*jīvita-vāyu*); when a person's life-force wind departs along with the excrement, that person dies immediately.
Next is the worm named *sirā-spandana*, which is killed by the obstructing wind (*saṃvaraṇa-vāyu*).
"When all sentient beings are on the verge of death, these various worms and these various winds—specifically the discordant winds—kill those worms.
Likewise, for those in the Avīci Hell, due to their inverted evil karma, they are blown by such upward and downward inverted winds."
Due to that evil karma, powerful winds arise and blow throughout his body.
These eighty kinds of winds kill eighty kinds of worms, killing them in accordance with their respective conditions or by overturning them.

There is a wind named Viparācinī that causes all parts of the body to become parched, as if being pressed by a mechanical device like sugarcane; all the blood dries up, all the vessels close, all the sinews snap, and all the marrow melts away, causing one to experience great suffering and affliction.

When those who have committed evil deeds—those destined for the Avīci Hell—are on the verge of death, as their worms are about to die, they perceive certain forms; the person bound for Avīci sees the signs of hell like a house covered by a black curtain, where fire breaks out in one corner and gradually spreads until the entire interior of the black-curtained house is ablaze with flames.

Having seen the house burning in this way, that person is struck with alarm and dread; his face contorts and he groans, his two hands flail about, his eyes roll and saliva flows from his mouth, his teeth chatter with sound, and his lips press against one another.

That person further sees a second mass of great black darkness, becoming even more terrified; it abounds with lions, tigers, leopards, bears, brown bears, as well as snakes and pythons, causing him to give rise to extreme fear.

On a high mountain peak, about to fall over a precipice, with excrement soiling his bedding, and fearing he would fall down that mountain, he stretches his hand upward; when his relatives see this, they all say, "This man is stroking the empty sky with his hand."

Thus the sick person sees those mountain forests, cliffs, and caves abounding in willow trees, all ablaze with fierce flames; wishing to fall upon them, his heart is filled with terror and he cries out with a choked voice. He further loses control of his bowels, his eyes roll about, and his face contorts in fear. Tears stream from his eyes, the hair on his entire body stands on end like thorns or needles, his testicles shrink inward, and saliva flows from his mouth.
"Then, this person’s four great elements become intensely agitated; these four are:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
The earth element becomes enraged:"

All parts of the body are rendered unstable and destroyed, like a mass of water-foam squeezed between two stones, or like a clump of sand being pressed; all the bones of the body and the channels of the limbs are severed and scattered, and that person’s entire body undergoes the foremost suffering.
Such is the wrath of the earth element due to [past] anger.
Because of their evil karma, the water element becomes enraged:
their throats become constricted, they gasp for breath as if dying, their muscles all go limp, and they see great floods rushing in and entering their eyes and ears.
The fire element becomes enraged:

one sees oneself within a great house being set ablaze, undergoing immense suffering; every part of the body experiences harsh and rigid pain. Because of this suffering, one groans and tosses about, with hands and feet moving restlessly and the head unable to remain still for even a moment.
The wind element becomes enraged:

there is a sensation of hardness and roughness, along with various forms of lightness and cold. All parts of the body become rigid and constricted; various winds blow through them, and that which is light rises upward as if ascending into space, falling instead into great precipices. The cold causes all the sinews to contract and curl up.

When that person’s four great elements are about to perish at the time of death, the power of those four great elements becomes intense; thus, the four great elements, like venomous snakes, become enraged, and one undergoes various kinds of suffering and affliction such as these—the magnitude of which is beyond all analogy.

That person’s entire body is thus utterly destroyed, like a mass of foam being washed away by water or consumed by fire; experiencing the foremost suffering, they clutch at their bedding and rub their hands against the empty air.

When the present mind ceases, the intermediate mind arises; it is like standing on a mountain peak and letting one’s body fall to the ground: once separated from the peak and having nothing to grasp, one revolves through the air.

When that person is thus born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), appearing as if from a seal impression, they perceive in that state of mind various hideous faces, hands, and feet—those of pigs, elephants, donkeys, horses, bears, *ṛkṣas*, tigers, leopards, lions, snakes, pythons, jackals, dogs, and other such creatures—as well as the henchmen of Yama holding various terrifying weapons in their hands, striking their bodies.
Only the sinful person sees it; others do not see it.
Because they see it in this way, their faces become extremely contorted and their eyes appear like oil that is gradually being exhausted, and thus they also gradually perish.

That person of evil karma dies and perishes in this manner, and a form arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). It is invisible and intangible; its body is like that of an eight-year-old child, and it dies and falls immediately.

At that very moment of falling, they are seized by the Yama-wardens with flaming iron nooses, which bind their throats and tie their two hands behind their backs; as they look toward the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, they see them ablaze with flames.
He sees within that fire various Yama-wardens with hideous faces; amidst the boiling heat of the flames, they hold various terrifying weapons in their hands and strike his body.

Having seen his arms bound behind his back, that person is struck with extreme terror. The *Yama-rodha* (Yama’s henchmen) rebuke the sinner; having rebuked him, they lead him toward the southern wing. In distress and weeping, he speaks these verses:
“Leaving this world and my life behind, I wander like a fool without a companion.
Evil men lead me away, Surrounded on all sides by wicked people.”
All is but a mass of flames, pervading space without interval;
in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate points, there is no empty space within the realm of earth.
Having no mastery over one’s destination, that place cannot be known.
The wilderness has cast me adrift, and I am without any companion.
No one is there to offer me comfort; no one can rescue me from my suffering.
Powerless and lacking autonomy, my body is consumed by fire as I endure extreme agony.
Sent away against my will, I know not where I am going;
every part of my entire body is bound with iron.
It is no object, nor a kinsman; it is neither wife nor son.
No one comes to rescue me, for they loathe my evil deeds.
Having lost the Dharma, I have no refuge or protector; my mind is shattered by suffering and distress.
Bound by the messengers of Yama, I can find no one to turn to for rescue.
"Because you hate me, you inflict such intense suffering upon me;
who are you, and by whom were you sent?
You bind my entire body."
As I now behold it, all moving and non-moving things—
everywhere like this— are entirely filled with great fire.
Throughout every region of the earth, wicked people are everywhere present.
Now I have no refuge; alone and without companion, I am in a wretched place in the darkness, having entered a great mass of blazing flames.
In the midst of the void, I see neither sun, moon, nor stars.
All these are inversions; all are universally shrouded in darkness.
All the five faculties and the like are entirely views of inversion.
They hook my entire body, tearing it apart and causing me to undergo great suffering.
I have no refuge; how can I attain liberation?
The mass of suffering and affliction increases, as do all those people surrounding me;
moment by moment, the accumulation of suffering grows, and both body and mind undergo suffering.
"Suffering torments my body, and I have no other companion.
When the Yama-wardens heard this verse spoken by the person of evil karma, they replied with a mind of fierce anger to that person who had been deceived by their own evil deeds:
"You previously committed evil; what is the use of reflecting on it now?"
Formerly deceived by delusion, what can your present remorse avail?
The evil karma you have committed is the greatest of evils;
it is the most unwholesome among the unwholesome, and the greatest suffering among sufferings.
Whether in a kalpa or a declining kalpa, the great fire shall burn your body;
since you, a deluded person, have already committed evil, what use is there now in giving rise to regret?
It is not the devas, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, or ghosts [who cause this].
Bound by the snare of karma, no one can save you.
If a person is bound by karma, they are fettered in hell;
sent there against their will, they are driven entirely by the workings of causes and conditions.
Among all evils you have committed, this is the foremost evil:
the karmic act of killing your mother; this deed is now irrevocably fixed.
For that which was born from you, which grew from the very body of your father—
His father was not his own master; you, out of malice, killed him with a blade.
He was the most supreme in the three realms, free from all faults, and liberated from all bonds; yet you committed evil against him.
The treasury of all dharmas, which can open the gate of liberation—you, an evil person who has split the Saṃgha, now receive its fruit here.
All latent tendencies have been transcended; all fetters have been abandoned.
The fool who killed an Arhat now receives the fruit of that deed here.
Like fire among all things, you have destroyed the jewel of truthful speech;
because you constantly spoke falsehoods, you now receive the fruit of that deed here.
The meaning of mutual destruction is recollected in every moment:
you have uttered divisive speech, and thus you receive such a fruit.
Like a sword, like fire, like poison—it is the most scorching among evils.
You constantly spoke with harsh words, and now you receive their fruit here.
Your speech was inverted from beginning to end, meaningless and inconsistent;
you uttered much frivolous chatter, and now you receive its fruit here.
Sentient beings have no autonomy; they always cherish their lives and fear death.
You killed many sentient beings, and now you suffer this bitter fruit of retribution.
With a greedy mind, you oppressed others and seized their wealth and property.
Out of a mind of greed, you committed theft; now the fruit of that retribution has ripened.
Because you were shrouded by the darkness of delusion, you further committed a second evil—having already engaged in sexual misconduct, why do you feel regret only now?
Desiring to obtain the property of others, you dwelt extensively on thoughts of greed;
since that object could not be obtained, you have now received such a fruit.
You have already committed many acts of anger, and you continue to dwell extensively on thoughts of anger.
Having thus attained hell, why do you now feel regret?
Your perverted, evil, and false views have already destroyed both types of karma;
with a mind of false views, you caused others to abide in false views as well.
These various unwholesome dharmas arise from body, speech, and mind;
because of your deluded mind, you have committed them yourself and then attributed them to others.
Having committed many evils, you have certainly performed unwholesome deeds.
Now that you have grasped at a self in this place, why do you give rise to regret?
It is like taking but a single handful of water from the great ocean;
this suffering is like that single handful, while future suffering will be like the great ocean.
If a person commits evil deeds, that person does not love themselves;
since they will be boiled in hell due to those evil deeds, one should not dwell upon them.
When an evil person sees evil conduct, a virtuous person acts in the same way.
One who commits evil deeds and hates virtuous people will thus be born in hell.
The deluded person abandons the good and enters into what is unwholesome;
you, O deluded one, abandon the jewel and take up stones and the like.
Abounding in all manner of excellent dharmas, such as the Buddha-jewel and others beyond measure—
since you have already obtained a human body, for what reason do you not delight in the Dharma?
Constantly abandon evil people and always maintain a virtuous mind.
One attains nirvāṇa, which those of external paths cannot attain;
it is good in the beginning, middle, and end, and brings constant joy regarding the Dharma.
That which brings suffering in the beginning, middle, and end is the retribution for evil karma.
Thus, one should constantly abandon evil and cling to virtuous conduct;
those who renounce unwholesome karma will always experience happiness wherever they are born.
Since beginningless saṃsāra, they have been repeatedly scorched by their evil deeds.
Why are you not weary, you fool who belongs to a deluded mind?
You were scorched by evil karma in the past, and later you will be burned by a great fire;
evil karma is the cause for the hells, where evil-doers are boiled and cooked.
Upon hearing the teaching on the fruits of evil karma, one’s mind should be disciplined;
how much more so after having committed evil deeds, when such agonies of burning and boiling ensue?
Thus, there are immeasurable varieties of great suffering and affliction.
"In this brief moment, you shall undergo such suffering and distress.
Thus do the messengers of Yama rebuke those who have practiced evil deeds.
Having thus rebuked him, they lead him toward the most agonizing and evil places of hell, where he remains bound by the snares of karma for immeasurable time.
Due to that person’s evil karma, every part of his body is set ablaze; like the interior of a tree that has dried out, he is scorched for a long duration.
"The distance from here to the gates of hell is not far; that place of hell is beyond all analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Four corners with four gates, Divided into broad and long sections."
"Scorched and boiled, they lack self-mastery; the beings in hell mostly lie prostrate.

Twenty-five thousand yojanas away from here, one hears the immeasurable, harsh, and evil sounds of their wailing; it is a state of intense suffering and flavorlessness, a ruinous and terrifying place beyond compare."

Those beings born in other hells do not even remember any of the sufferings of all the hells when they hear this; they die upon hearing it—how much more so for those who have not yet been born in hell?

Those hell-beings, having committed evil deeds while in the human world, are now covered by various sufferings within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); furthermore, upon hearing that sound, they faint ten times over.
That person experiences such boundless suffering, with both body and mind tormented; their mind becomes further agitated as if in a dream.

That person draws closer still to the Avīci hell; due to their evil karma, they are blown by cold winds beneath the earth and within the waters—places never touched by humans, where there is no sun—and the power of those winds exceeds that of the winds at the end of an eon.
That wind is extremely cold; its form is like the snow here, no different from ice.

Upon the waters there, the cold wind is even colder; due to their evil karma, the wind is like a sharp blade. The power of this wind can blow away great mountains ten *yojana*s high, causing them to shift and disperse.

When such a malignant wind blows upon those within it, those people suffer from the misery of cold; their form and other aggregates (skandhas) undergo extreme suffering and affliction, such that this suffering and affliction is beyond all analogy.

Just as at the end of an eon, the heat produced by seven suns is increased a thousandfold by the heat of craving; with this grasping as its causal condition, there is the constituent of becoming (*bhava-aṅga*). That very craving causes the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to cease and different aggregates to arise; thus, the aggregates of experience (*upādāna-skandha*) are born.

For example, like the second Heaven of the Thirty-three, beings with bodies similar to those born through the sovereign power of karma—measuring five, four, three, two, or one yojana—fall head-first with their feet upward. As they are about to fall, they are shaken and shattered by great flames of fire; for two thousand years they travel downward, yet they have not yet reached the location of the Avīci Hell.
The Avīci Hell extends downward in this manner, situated in the midst such that it cannot be reached from here.

As for "Avīci," the Avīci Hell is the lowest point of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); from this Desire Realm, ascending through the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), one reaches as far as Akaniṣṭha; beyond these two realms, there is no further place.
The Avīci Hell is likewise; there is no place below it.
Having fallen into that place, one undergoes extreme suffering and affliction due to the power of evil karma.
Thus, those in the Avīci Hell see the offenders of the Mahāraurava Hell as if they were seeing those in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the two appear identical and indistinguishable.
"In that Avīci Hell there is an abundance of flaming wreaths; once born therein, they first burn one's head and then burn one's body, so that the person's head and body are thus scorched and heated."

Now I shall provide a brief analogy: such a mass of flames, encircling Sumeru, the king of mountains, for even a short time, would burn away all its sixty thousand attendant peaks, as well as all its rivers, mountains, ponds, pools, forests, and trees; yet the inhabitants of hell alone continue to burn for a long time without dying.
Now I shall provide a brief analogy: it is like a metal vessel heated until it is intensely hot; if a single drop of fat is placed upon it, it is instantly consumed by fire.

In this same way, the karma of a single transgression can burn a person with the fires of Avīci Hell, and can likewise incinerate all sentient beings throughout the four continents, as well as mountains, devas, asuras, nāgas, mountain caves, islands, forests, and the great ocean.
If a person commits two of the heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), they can burn two oceans, as previously described regarding burning.
If a person commits three of the heinous crimes, they can burn three oceans;
likewise, four such acts can burn four oceans.
His body burns with heat like a heated iron vessel; as he enters, the Cakravāḍa Mountains and the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains are likewise completely consumed by fire at that very moment of entry.

All the nāgas, great asuras, and various classes of animals gathered along the shores of every ocean, as well as those in the four continents who possess good karma and the inhabitants of the six heavens of the desire realm, were all completely extinguished upon merely smelling the odor of hell.
Why is this? Because the inhabitants of hell are extremely foul-smelling.
For what reason does the stench of hell not come here?
There are two great mountains, one named Mount Emergence and the other named Mount Submergence, which block that foul odor.
That evil stench is incomparably intense.
"Because of their evil karma, the hells are vast and expansive."

In that hell there are birds with flaming beaks; their beaks are hard and sharp, white in color like ice. Such evil birds, within that hell, devour the skin, fat, flesh, bones, and marrow of all the sinners.
Furthermore, there are other birds born within the fire, who move within the fire and feed within the fire; such evil birds devour all the flesh of the hell-beings' bodies and then break their bones.
Having broken the bones, they tear the flesh and drink the blood;
once they have drunk the blood, they next drink the marrow.
Those hell-beings wail, lament, weep, and faint in distress.

Next, there are birds called Fire-Crested Wanderers (*Jvālāśikhacara*), which cannot be burned by fire; they are filled with extreme joy as they split open the heads of the beings and first drink their blood.
Next, there are birds called Skull-Eaters, which pierce the skulls with their flame-tipped beaks and drink the brains.

Next, there are birds called Tongue-Eaters, which devour the tongues and the flesh at the roots of the teeth; once eaten, they grow back again, as soft as lotus petals when newly born, and thus they are eaten again, and once eaten, they grow back again.
Next, there is another bird named Tooth-Extractor; its beak is like a flaming tongs, and with great strength, it pulls out all the teeth.
Next, there is another bird named Throat-Seizer; its body is extremely minute, and it devours the throat.
Next, there is another bird named "Pain-Eater" that devours their lungs.
Next, there is another bird named "Raw-Viscera-Eater" that, having torn open their hearts, drinks their blood.
Next, there is another bird named *Plīhaka* (Spleen-Cluster) that eats their spleens.
Next, there is another bird named *Antrāśin* (Intestine-Eater) that eats within their intestines.
Next, there is another bird named *Pṛṣṭhāsthipriya* (Back-Bone-Lover) that breaks open their backbones to drink their marrow; having drunk it, they exit.

Next, there is another bird called the Vein-Treasury (*nāḍīkośa*); once the veins have been severed, it enters the openings of the veins to drink their fluid, while [the victim] suffers and cries out.
Next, there is another bird called the Needle-Hole (*sūcivaktra*); its beak is as sharp as a needle, and it drinks their blood.
Next, there is another bird named Bone-Dweller, which breaks through the cheekbones to eat from within.
Next, there is another bird named Flesh-and-Skin-Eater, which eats its outer skin.
Next, there are birds called "Nail-Extractors" that pull out all the nails.
Next, there are birds called "Fat-Eaters" that break open the skin and drink the fat.
Next, there is another bird named Slow-Tendon, which tears their tendons apart and devours them all.
Next, there is another bird named Hair-Puller, which pulls out the roots of their hair.

In this manner, within the Avīci Hell there is a place extending three thousand yojanas called the "Abode of Evil Birds. Therein, other hell-beings are likewise devoured by them together; thus they are eaten for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, and having been eaten, they are born again.
Thus that person fears being devoured by birds.

Having escaped from that place in the Avīci Hell which is shrouded by the net of all sufferings, and seeking refuge and rescue, they next enter again the place named "Falling into Precipitous Cliffs" where one undergoes suffering.

Surrounded on all sides by eleven masses of flames, solitary and without companion, bound by the snares of karma, and with everything both inside and outside completely obstructed, they wander through the wilderness.

Among all the sufferings and afflictions of the various hells, there is one particularly excruciating place that they hasten toward with great speed; it is called the Place of Falling into Precipices where Suffering is Endured.

When they set foot down, the ground melts away; when they lift their feet, it reforms. As it reforms, it becomes even softer, yet its touch is extremely painful—harsh, sharp, and agonizing, inspiring the utmost terror.
Terrified in this way, with wrinkled faces and distorted mouths, their hands, feet, and all their limbs completely melting away, they then proceed in succession toward that perilous precipice.

When those people fall there at the edge of the precipice, because of their evil karma, a wind lifts them up for three thousand yojanas; before they have even reached the ground below, vultures, eagles, crows, dogs, and jackals devour them, and the wind lifts them up once more.
That evil wind touches them like fire or a blade, lifting them up and then devouring them once more; thus they are tossed up and down for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years.

"If they leave that place, they further run toward the location of the Revolving Wheel-Hole Hell; having arrived there, beneath them a thousand-spoked wheel arises, with a vajra axle, blazing fiercely and spinning rapidly."

When that time comes, those hell-beings' wheels spin rapidly; one wheel shatters their body and another wheel shatters their head. From those shattered places, hot flames and fat emerge, and their two eyes melt away.
Furthermore, two wheels revolve upon his two shoulders, shattering the shoulder bones until they are entirely melted away.
On each of his two hands there is a wheel; these wheels spin so rapidly as if by friction, and fire is produced from his hands.
There are two kinds of fire:
one is wheel-fire, and the other is friction-fire.

Fire issues from within the flesh; thus, an iron wheel, blazing with flames, rotates rapidly. All the bones of that person’s body are shattered and crushed by the swift rotation until they are like a handful of sand.
Furthermore, on the back there is a wheel of fire with a thousand spokes that revolves with great speed, starting from the vertebrae down to the hip bones and reaching the private organs.

There are also iron chains with both ends fastened to pillars; the sinner is placed upon them and pushed back and forth, being struck in succession until it enters the *pakvāśaya* (the receptacle for digested food), then the *āmāśaya* (the receptacle for undigested food). Having pierced the *āmāśaya*, it next severs the intestines.
Furthermore, they are forced to sit upon large seats; wheels grow upon their thighs, which spin rapidly and tear the flesh from them.
Wheels grow upon their inner ankles, tearing through the marrow until it issues forth. Iron hooks beneath their feet pierce both their feet, causing them to undergo great suffering and distress.
Those who practice evil deeds suffer the torments of Avīci for such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years; their suffering is harsh and cruel, unbearable, produced by their own karma.
"If they leave that place to escape from their suffering and distress, hoping for refuge and rescue, they run swiftly to another location.
Once they have fled, they see a great mountain and rush toward it; however, there are many strange insects there, their bodies ablaze with flames, filling the entire mountain."

Those hell-beings enter the place of black insects; the bodies of those black insects have a touch like flames. Thus, these black insects devour those sinners, dispersing and shattering them piece by piece until they are like dust, while the beings wail in agony.

Because of that wailing, flaming black insects enter his mouth; having entered through the throat and so forth down to the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), they devour him, and that person undergoes extremely intense and agonizing suffering.

If those offenders have committed evil karma—such as the five heinous crimes leading to Avīci hell, the ten unwholesome actions, or other corresponding karmic accumulations—they will experience results similar to their deeds for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, being devoured by black insects and undergoing great suffering and distress.

"If one leaves that place, one again sees a forest of meat-eating animals, abounding with fierce dogs, jackals, lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, and the like, toward which they rush with great speed."
Once they have arrived there, they are torn apart limb by limb by various predatory beasts to be devoured; their heads are split open and their brains eaten.

Some eat the throat, some eat the head, some eat the shoulders, some eat the chest, some eat the belly, some eat the intestines, some eat the mesentery, some eat the large intestine, some eat the small intestine, some eat the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*), and some eat the receptacle for undigested food (*āmāśaya*). Some eat the thighs, some eat the calves, and some eat the tops of the feet. After the person has been thus devoured, they are born again; at first, they are soft and tender, and because they are so soft and tender, the suffering of being eaten is even more intense; once they have been eaten, their flesh grows back again.
Furthermore, because they have committed and accumulated evil karma through much killing, they undergo its evil fruits.

Those hell-beings remain in that place of hell for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, experiencing the fruits of their evil karma; the evil karma and its evil fruits are so identical that they cannot be compared by any analogy.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Thirteen [and] Scroll Fourteen,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Yuan Wei dynasty.
Chapter on the Hells, Ten:
Furthermore, that bhikṣu examines the karmic results experienced by those who delight in and frequently commit theft.
He sees, hears, and knows:

Thus, those who have committed the evil karma of stealing perceive within the hells a mass of great wealth that resembles a whirling wheel of fire, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage; there they see gold, jewels, garments, and various other riches gathered together in diverse combinations.
Having seen this, that person of evil karma gives rise to a mind of greed; deceived by the karma of greed and delusion, he conceives such a thought: "Those riches are my riches."
Thus, due to their evil karma, these deluded people pass through a mass of burning charcoal embers and run toward those objects.

By the power of their evil karma, the *yama* messengers immediately seize all the limbs and members of those sinners with nets of blades, hacking, slicing, and burning them until nothing remains but bones.
"Since beginningless time, my greedy mind has not been abandoned; thus I have suffered in this way, yet I still remember it and do not forget.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"With a topknot of pride and the smoke of envy, One discriminates and seizes the property of others."
The fire of greed burns people, just as worldly fire burns wood.
When a person is bitten by the venom of greed, they find no peace;
repeatedly delighting in greed, it grows ever greater.
Just as fire finds fuel, so does the greedy mind grow;
when fire burns a person, they may flee, but when burned by greed, there is no escape.
The greedy person revolves like a wheel; the greedy mind deceives and deludes humanity.
In this world without beginning or end, there is no enemy more primordial than greed.
Deceived by a greedy mind, people enter the waters of the ocean and enter places abounding with blades;
it is because of the greedy mind that they undergo these sufferings.
Driven by the causes and conditions of greed, they become kings and slaughter one another;
they separate mother and son from their union and enter the realm of attachment to objects.
If one can escape the poison of craving, that person shall extinguish the fire of greed.
If one regards gold and earth as equal, one draws near to Nirvana.
Morality is the supreme wealth; the sun is the foremost light.
Material riches may be scattered and destroyed, but morality is never lost or diminished.
By upholding the precepts, one is born in the three heavens, and further, in the realms of dhyāna;
the light of the precepts has no equal, both in this life and in future lives.
If one would extinguish the fire of greed, let wisdom serve as the water.
"One who does not extinguish the mind of greed cannot attain liberation.

Having been thus scorched by that fire of greed, those hell-beings further enter the second fire of Avīci to be burned; they then fall onto a precipice where there are sharp blades, suffering threefold, extreme burning.
That place of hell is like a whirling firebrand, resembling a city of Gandharvas or a mirage; such craving for objects is like what is seen in a dream.
The henchmen of Yama seize the denizens of hell and subject them to great torment for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years because of their karma of theft.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the karmic fruits of the unwholesome actions of the Avīci hell;

he sees that once such a person who has committed evil deeds has escaped from that iron place of suffering and passed beyond the mass of fire, because their evil karma continues to evolve, they enter another place called the Place of Wrong Views (Kudṛṣṭi-sthāna).

Due to that evil karma, he sees a woman who is just like one he previously saw and with whom he previously engaged while among humans; having seen her, the fire of desire practiced since beginningless time is ignited, and he immediately runs swiftly toward that woman.

Those women are made of iron through the power of their evil karma; once he has approached them, he is embraced by them, who then kiss his mouth and devour his lips and so forth until not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remains. His body is likewise devoured until it is entirely consumed; once it is gone, it is born again, and once born, it is eaten again; having been eaten, it is born again. In this manner, that person undergoes such harsh and agonizing suffering.
That person, unable to abandon such fires of desire, again sees a woman in another place; consumed by the fire of lust, he runs toward her swiftly, heedless of his suffering.

Those women have bodies ablaze with vajra-iron flames; they embrace those sinners, and as soon as they embrace them, the sinners shatter like a clod of sand being crushed. Their entire bodies disintegrate, and having disintegrated, they are born again;
having been born, they disintegrate again, and having disintegrated, they are born again.
Furthermore, he runs away again; thus he undergoes suffering, his mind unsettled by desire.
Having seen that place and having heard and known it to be likewise, the bhikṣu speaks this verse:
"Women are the root of evil, They can cause one to lose all things."
If a person delights in women, that delight shall not be obtained.
Among all things, women are the most evil; they are full of flattery and jealousy.
Because of women, a man may cause the loss of both worlds.
Women delight in sensual pleasure; women constantly practice deception.
What they think in their hearts is one thing, while the words they speak are another.
At first their speech is soft and smooth, but later their hearts are like adamant.
Neither for kindness nor for offerings, their hearts are light and they do not remember;
though one has shown them a hundred favors, they reckon only a single wrong.
Their minds are like the body of a mirage, the ground for the evil karma of women.
A man’s mind of lustful passion causes him to lose everything;
in this world and in future worlds, women are the foremost cause of loss.
If one desires to experience true happiness, one should abandon women.
If one abandons women, it is the foremost happiness in the world.
If a person wishes to sever craving, hopes for great wealth and joy,
and desires to reach the state of tranquility, they should abandon women.
"Due to their deluded minds, they are thus burned, boiled, and destroyed for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, only to be born again.
Once those people have escaped from that place, they enter a mass of fire; having been burned and boiled, and driven by hunger and thirst, they run hither and thither."
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the person who has fully committed the unwholesome karma of lying, who delighted in practicing it and performed it frequently, and the retribution they receive.
He sees, hears, and knows:
the person who committed the karma of lying is in that hell, tormented by the confusion of hunger and thirst. There, powerful Yama-wardens seize that sinner and question him, saying:
"What is your ailment? He replied,
"Hunger and thirst."
The Yama-wardens seize the person who has accumulated such karma and, by the power of their evil deeds, pry open his mouth and pull out his tongue.
Because it is the fruit of lying, this wicked tongue measures five yojanas in length.

Once that tongue has protruded, the Yama-wardens immediately seize it and spread it upon the blazing iron ground. Due to their evil karma, they fashion a thousand plows; on that ground, the tips of the plows are ablaze, and extremely powerful oxen—hundreds or thousands of times—plow back and forth across it from every direction. Pus and blood form rivers, and within these rivers dwell worms.

Furthermore, many worms arise within the tongue; the tongue is extremely soft, as supple as celestial garments. Once this soft tongue has been plowed across in all directions, it grows back together again; once joined, it is plowed once more.

In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years, that evil tongue undergoes such bitter suffering; the agony is so harsh and intense that it is unbearable. As that person endures the pain, they cry out and wail, solitary and without rescue.

Such evil karma is not created by the mother, nor by the father, nor by the gods, nor yet by another person; it is not uncreated, nor does it come from another place. What one has done oneself is not lost, and what one has not done is not obtained; one experiences the fruit of the karma one has performed.
As that person thus suffers and cries out, the Yama-wardens rebuke them, speaking these verses:
“One should abandon harsh evil and the unpalatable lie;
The person who speaks falsehoods, With a light heart, will soon be lost.”
Those who lack faith in such a place are abandoned by all virtuous people;
they are as disliked as an enemy, yet the steadfast are able to abandon them.
False speech first deceives oneself, and only thereafter deceives others.
If one does not abandon false speech, both oneself and others will be ruined.
The person who utters such falsehoods first destroys their own mouth;
abandoned by gods and humans, they shall ultimately go to an evil destination.
If one delights in false speech, that person has no good fortune;
they abandon both the mundane and supramundane paths because of their lying.
False speech brings firm retribution; therefore, the wise abandon it.
One who relies on lying goes to the place of hell;
speaking the truth is supreme among humans, for all people honor them.
Abandoning all lies, one should speak only the truth.
If one refrains from killing, speaks truthful words, and possesses a gentle heart with compassion for sentient beings—
truthful speech is the stairway to heaven, and truth is the foremost dharma.
Even if a person is headed for the hells before the messengers of Yama, [truth shall protect them].
The wise have declared that such lies are caused by those conditions;
they are like poisonous snares and hooks, and similar to swords and fire.
Those who speak falsehoods will undergo many evil retributions.
‘If you desire the fruits of wholesome karma and wish to perceive the Truths, you should always speak words of truth and abandon evil, false speech.

Thus those hell-beings undergo such harsh and agonizing suffering; for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years their tongues are ploughed, and the tongue of that liar is drawn back into his mouth.

Terrified, that person fled in all directions with mouth agape and face torn, falling into a mass of burning coals; having entered it, he was scorched, and thus he experienced great suffering and distress, without rescue or refuge.
Furthermore, there are other Yama-wardens who, grasping clubs and swords in their hands, cause those hell-beings to be shattered from head to foot; they cry out and wail, never ceasing for a moment.
The fires of Avīci are constantly and intensely ablaze.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the karmic retribution obtained by those who delight in and frequently practice divisive speech.
He sees, hears, and knows the fruit of the karma of divisive speech of these hell-beings:
Due to the cause of divisive speech, they further arrive within the most wretched hells; there, the *yama-rākṣasas* are even more cruel—when the sinners see them, they ask the sinners:
"What is your affliction?"
He replied, "I suffer from hunger.
The Yama-people then split open his mouth, pulled out his tongue, and held it in their hands; such was the size of the tongue, measuring three hundred yojanas, as it was drawn out completely.

Those merciless and wicked people of Yama take up flaming iron swords with sharp, blazing edges and slice off one side of the tongue; as that side of the tongue is devoured by dogs, jackals, hyenas, and other beasts, the victim undergoes such extreme and evil suffering that the sound of their wailing and crying does not cease.
As those hell-beings cry out in this manner, the Yama-wardens, in order to rebuke them, speak these verses:
"Because you spoke many words with a destructive mind, Which is a defilement within all dharmas, Such is the fruit: you are now boiled [in this state]."
The person who utters divisive speech is born into a state of constant solitude;
who would speak with double-tongued words? Such is not praised by the virtuous.
One is born into a state that is always base and vulgar, taking birth in an evil realm.
If a person speaks with double-tongued speech, they are possessed by delusion.
A person who practices such evil karma is constantly scorched by hell;
if a person delights in committing evil, they will always speak with double-tongued speech.
First, one is deceived by evil; one’s secret words are not kept concealed.
A person who engages in double-tongued speech eats the flesh from the backs of others.
If a person abandons double-tongued speech, that person will always be firm and secretive.
One’s brothers in knowledge and the like are never abandoned;
if a person abandons divisive speech, they always protect the king’s secret words.
By abandoning divisive speech, one attains tranquility; if a person is free from envy and malice.
Why did you not practice the Dharma?
Why did you not abandon double-tongued speech?
Now that you receive the fruit of double-tongued speech, why does remorse arise in your heart?

After the Yama-wardens have thus rebuked the hell-beings, those who are undergoing the suffering of their tongues enter a great ocean of misery; they remain there for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years due to that person’s evil karma.
Once they have been freed from that harsh and rigid suffering, their tongues return to their original state, and they no longer see the *Yama-rākṣasas*.

Having escaped the sufferings within that hell, those hell-beings run frantically in every direction; they undergo the foremost suffering, which is unbearable, as the wind of evil karma blows upon the fuel of retribution while great fires blaze forth, and they continue to run frantically in every direction.
There, the Yama-rākṣasas seize him and ask: "What is your affliction?
Due to the causes and conditions of his evil karma, he immediately replies:
"I am now afflicted by hunger.
The Yama-wardens then split open his mouth and pull out his tongue; men of great strength cut it with knives and drive him to devour it himself.
Afflicted by urgent hunger, he immediately ate his own tongue, from which saliva and blood flowed out.

As that man thus devoured his own tongue, it grew back after being cut, and grew back again after being cut; due to the power of the snare of karma, he rolled about on the ground, crying out and wailing.
That person is tormented; their eyes roll and pupils dart as they undergo great suffering, solitary and without companion, experiencing the fruits of their own actions.
The Yama-wardens rebuke them, speaking these verses:
"Released from the bow of the tongue, The flaming arrows of sharp speech—"
If a person speaks with harsh words, the fruit they reap will be similar to that.
Just as those who eat meat are shunned by all people,
so too is the tongue of one who speaks harshly like poison.
Swords, fire, and poisons—such evils are not the greatest evil.
If a person speaks with malicious words, this evil is the greatest evil.
The tongue-drill can produce fire; it grows within the heart.
The fire of harsh speech among humans is like burning dry wood.
If a person delights in sweet words, all people will honor them as they would their own mother, no different; they will rejoice in them as if they were their own father.
Sweet speech is the foremost good; its cause is joy, and its fruit is likewise joy.
Though it cannot exhaustively eliminate evil, it benefits the entire world.
Sweet speech is the stairway to heaven; sweetness is the foremost treasury.
Sweetness is the eye of the world; sweetness is no different from honey.
Harsh speech is the foremost evil; having spoken it, one arrives in hell.
