Your own tongue has brought this retribution upon yourself; why do you now feel regret?
"In this manner, the Yama-wardens rebuke the hell-beings.

Thus, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, those persons of evil karma—who delighted in, frequently practiced, and committed false speech and harsh words, and who incited others to do so and rejoiced in their doing—undergo such suffering."
If they escape from that place, they run hither and thither, whereupon yet other *yama* demons seize them and burn them intensely, inflicting great suffering upon them.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu contemplates the evil karmic retribution for those who delight in and frequently practice frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
He sees, hears, and knows:

these hell-beings, as the karmic fruit of their own actions, undergo extreme suffering and are oppressed by the foremost of pains. Having escaped such Yama-wardens, they run hither and thither, only to be seized again by other Yama-wardens who interrogate them, saying:
"What is your affliction?"
He immediately replied,
"I am suffering from extreme hunger and thirst," and spoke this verse:
"My own merit is exhausted; produced by my own drilling, the iron fire burns with hunger and thirst, and I undergo the suffering of being scorched by evil."
Like ice and snow before fire, like Mount Sumeru compared to a mustard seed,
or like one famished by the fires of hell— their superiority is likewise such.
The power of the fires of hell does not extend to other places.
Such fires of hunger and thirst can reach even the heavens;
likewise, in this hell, one undergoes other heavy afflictions.
Yet though such sufferings are grave, they do not equal the agony of the fire of thirst.

When the messengers of Yama have heard those words, they pry open his mouth with flaming iron tongs and place a flaming iron bowl filled with molten red copper—boiling and ablaze—into his mouth. Because of the fault of his improper and frivolous speech, it burns his tongue, which immediately melts away like snow in a fire.
The two kinds of suffering endured by those hell-beings cannot be fully described; having been thus scorched, they cry out with loud screams.
Because of these loud screams, even more [molten copper] is poured into their mouths; once the blazing red copper has burned their tongues, it next burns their throats;
having burned their throats, it next burns their hearts.
Having burned the heart, it next burns the intestines;
having burned the intestines, it next burns the large intestine;
having burned the large intestine, it exits from below.
As these sinful beings suffer and cry out, the Yama-wardens address them with a verse, rebuking them as follows:
"Your words were neither bound together in sequence nor coherent; they lacked meaning and were inconsistent.
You originally spoke such frivolous speech, and now you must experience its fruit in this way."
If one always speaks what is untrue, And never recites the scriptures,
that is not a tongue, But merely a piece of flesh.
If a person always speaks the truth, And constantly delights in wholesome merit, [that is truly a tongue.]
"That is the stairway to heaven, and thus it is called the tongue.

Having thus rebuked the hell-beings, the Yama-wardens then pour boiling, molten, red-hot copper into the mouths of those hell-beings. This continues for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years as a consequence of their improper and frivolous speech.

If those hell-beings manage to escape from the people of Yama, they run hither and thither only to enter again into masses of fire; their bodies melt away, and their feet, thighs, and waists, remaining within the masses of fire, all completely liquefy like lumps of fresh butter, only to be born anew once they have melted.
Thus seeking rescue and seeking refuge, that person runs hither and thither; yet because of his evil karma, he sees a city filled with treasures guarded by others.
Due to the causes of such evil karma of these deluded persons, their minds give rise to greedy attachment as they rush toward those objects, claiming them as their own.

Because that person with a greedy mind has delighted in and frequently committed evil and unwholesome deeds, the retribution they receive is such that they perceive things with a perverted view within the hell realms. Having perceived them thus, because of their greedy mind, they hope to enjoy them in great abundance.

Due to their greedy minds, knives grow from their hands as they run toward those objects. Upon reaching the place of the objects, they hack at one another with their knives; these hell-beings slice and carve each other until nothing but bone remains. Afterward, they are born again;
once born, they are sliced again, and after being sliced, they are born once more, continuing in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.

Due to their evil karma, the henchmen of Yama hold sharp knives in their hands and flay the hell-beings; they seize the hell-beings and cut and pare them entirely until all the flesh is gone, not even a grain of mustard seed remaining, and only the bones are left.
Those hell-beings shriek and wail, filled with grief and anguish; thus they are cut and carved, and having been carved, they are born again.

Just as when one cuts with a blade, if the *Yama* wardens place them in a river, they immediately return to life; in this way, in this manner, those hell-beings are born yet again and undergo such suffering, shrieking and wailing.
The Yama-wardens further spoke these verses to rebuke him,
saying: “The man ruined by greed, deceived by greed,
Who covets the property of others— For this, he is thus boiled in this world.”
The greedy mind is evil and unwholesome; the deluded person delights in it.
The greedy mind burns itself, like fire produced from within wood.
Greed is exceedingly evil, leading people to hell.
Thus one should abandon greed, that poisonous and evil thing which brings bitter retribution.
Having seen the wealth of others, the greedy mind hopes to obtain it for oneself;
that greed produces poisonous fruit, which is now experienced here in this place.
"Thus do the Yama-wardens rebuke the hell-beings.

Having finished their rebuke, they then inflict upon them manifold sufferings. In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, until their evil karma is exhausted, they endure these long-lasting periods during which the infliction of suffering never ceases."

When those hell-beings leave that place, they run hither and thither in search of rescue and a refuge; yet they enter again into masses of fire and fall upon ground of glowing, burning red-hot iron, where they wallow and rise again, running everywhere, solitary and without companion.
The practitioner of evil deeds, pursued by the enemies of his own evil karma as he is about to enter hell, flees in every direction if he should happen to escape the *Yama-rākṣasas*.

This person, having delighted in and frequently committed acts born of a mind of hatred, now undergoes their karmic retribution; without rescue and without refuge, lions, tigers, snakes, and other such beings of fierce malice stand manifest before him.

Terrified, that person flees in every direction; yet, due to their evil karma, they are unable to run and are seized by him. He becomes extremely enraged and first devours their head. Once their head has been eaten, the victim cries out in bitter anguish and rolls about on the ground. Furthermore, there are evil snakes with venomous fangs that bite them and devour their ribs; tigers devour their backs, fire burns their feet, and the *Yama* hell-wardens shoot at them from afar. In this manner, they undergo such suffering.
The Yama-wardens further spoke these verses in rebuke, saying:
"Scorched by your own anger, you are the most base among men;
now that you have arrived here and are being burned, why do you cry out now?"
Hatred is the primary cause that leads people to the hells;
like a rope binding you, it brings about this present suffering.
Hatred deceives the deluded person, who constantly dwells upon it without letting go.
Their minds have never been at peace, dwelling like those inside a snake's den.
If a person possesses a stubbornly evil nature and constantly acts with much anger,
that person shall find no happiness, like darkness in the midst of the day.
Neither illegal conduct, nor great wealth, nor wise associates,
nor kinsmen can protect one whose mind is agitated by hatred;
in this world and the next, such a person brings about the fruit of darkness.
Furthermore, one can go to evil realms; therefore, this is called "anger.
One who is without anger is supreme; an angry person is not victorious.
If a person abandons anger, that person proceeds toward Nirvāṇa.
"Because of the causes and conditions of your anger, you have reached this evil place, hell;
only when your karma is exhausted shall you be released. What benefit is there in writhing about?
Having thus rebuked the hell-beings, the Yama-wardens, after the rebuke, further strike them with arrows.
Lions, tigers, and other highly wrathful animals kill and eat [their prey] due to the cause of their anger.
Because that karma is similar, they receive a corresponding retribution; for the fruit resembles the seed.

Such sinners, as the karmic retribution for their evil deeds, are boiled and consumed for a long time; if they escape that place, hoping for rescue and seeking a refuge, they run hither and thither, having attained such a path through the cause of wrong views and the retribution of the five heinous crimes, and are born in the Avīci hell.
Thus, those who commit the five heinous crimes will certainly undergo retribution in accordance with their karma.
"In what place do those hell-beings reside?
Māṣaka, Pūraṇa, Devadatta, Kokālika, and others are scorched and boiled in that very place."
Those hell-beings go to the great hells where they are certainly burned and boiled, experiencing the most intense and terrible suffering.
As for the suffering in that place, what is this torment?
No sentient beings are able to provide a metaphor for it;
such is the great suffering endured by those in the Avīci Hell, where the practitioners of evil karma gather together like a mass of darkness, encompassing all sentient beings.
In the Māṃsotpāda Hell above, knives rain down.

Those in the Avīci Hell are burned, boiled, and split asunder; having been born again, they are split once more, being hacked and burned repeatedly. Furthermore, vajra-yokes rain down, vajra-hail falls, and stones rain down to shatter and pulverize them.
After those who have committed the five heinous crimes have been thus scorched, there further arise eleven clusters of flames that inflict unbearable great suffering.
There are ten flames in the ten directions, and the eleventh is a cluster of fire consisting of hunger and thirst; because of this hunger and thirst, flames issue from their mouths.

That person is surrounded on all sides by ten flames encircling their body; thus they are scorched and boiled throughout their entire frame, such that there is not even a space as small as a pore that is not set ablaze.

Those sinners are burned equally, such that there is not even as much pleasure as the root of a single hair; thus it is named Avīci. Because there is not even the slightest bit of pleasure, it is named Avīci.
All faculties and all objects are completely scorched; because of this improper mind, it is called Avīci (the Unrelenting).
When one falls from this world, there is no other place of rebirth, for one is born only there.
"The suffering within the Great Hell is unsurpassed; because its duration is incalculable, it is called Avīci.
Because it encompasses all sentient beings of the desire realm who are at the very lowest level, it is called Avīci."
Thus, because there is nothing that surpasses this Avīci, it is named Avīci;
thus, because there is nothing that excels this Avīci, it is named Avīci.
Just as there is nothing above the head of that great hell, so too is the location of the Avīci hell intensely hot and likewise has nothing above it; therefore, it is named Avīci.

That place of Avīci has the most intense heat of all, with nothing surpassing it; the boiling red copper burns the flesh and bones until they are crimson, with nothing more extreme than this, and for this reason it is named Avīci.
Because that place is densely packed with earth, it is named Avīci.

In that hellish realm, all fat, flesh, marrow, and bones are ablaze with flames; the inhabitants of that hell are entirely engulfed in fire such that one cannot distinguish between this person and that person, nor can any subtle interval between them be found. Therefore, it is named Avīci.

Just as a river in the mountains flows with unceasing force, rushing day and night, so too in that Avīci realm suffering is constantly endured with unceasing force; the person’s torment cannot cease until the end of the kalpa, and because there is no interval between moments, it is named Avīci.

The suffering and affliction of that person cannot be described; there is but a slight analogy for it: just as the drops of seawater cannot be counted, so too the suffering endured by those who commit evil deeds in the Avīci Hell cannot be counted or described. Among all places of suffering, none is like the place of Avīci; because their karma is heavy, the suffering they endure is likewise heavy.

If one commits a single transgression, that person’s suffering is slight; if one commits two transgressions, that person’s body becomes larger and they suffer much more. Following this sequence, all parts of the body become increasingly vast, and the suffering is likewise so.
Because the causes of karma are so heavy, there is no other cause for such suffering that can serve as a comparison;
just as there is nothing comparable to the experience of bliss in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, so too, these two realms of suffering and bliss, whether above or below, are entirely beyond analogy;
thus, whether above or below, their limits cannot be compared.
Why is this? Because they have committed evil karma.
Due to having committed evil karma, although there is a result that corresponds to its cause within the hells, one cannot find anything even remotely analogous to it on the outskirts of the hells.
Such a person remains there being burned and boiled for either a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa; only when their evil karma is exhausted do they finally attain liberation.
Because the cause is exhausted, its fruit is likewise exhausted; just as when fire is extinguished its heat is also extinguished, or when the seed is lost the sprout is also lost.
In this same way, when the evil karma of those in the Avīci Hell is exhausted, they lose their vitality and their bodies rot away, and only then do they escape from that hell.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, due to the remaining residual karmic fruits, they are born among the hungry ghosts in the Needle-Hole Mountain Clefts.
Having been born in that place, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst, their forms resembling forests of trees ablaze with fire.
If they escape that place and are born among animals, they become śuśumāras; furthermore, they are born in excrement as impure worms.

Among the hungry ghosts (preta), they are scorched and boiled by hunger and thirst for two hundred thousand lifetimes; among animals, they pass through two thousand lifetimes, experiencing all manner of sufferings in various birthplaces due to the residual force of their evil and unwholesome karma.

Among the animals, there are various kinds of foul food; their minds constantly dwell upon being born in places where they kill living beings, and furthermore, in those very places, they prey upon one another, undergoing great suffering and distress.
If they escape that place, by the power of past karma they may be born among humans; for five hundred lifetimes they die within the womb;
for another five hundred lifetimes they die after being born, being devoured by crows;
and for another five hundred lifetimes they die before they have even begun to walk.
This is the residual fruit of that evil karma.

Once the retribution for the remaining karma has been exhausted, one continues to experience results corresponding to the patterns of the net of karma from beginningless time, which are categorized as inferior, middling, or superior.
Having observed in this way, that bhikṣu spoke these verses:
“In the beginningless cycle of birth and death, The net of karma covers the world;
Whether being born or passing away, All is due to the causes and conditions of one’s own karma.”
From heaven one is born into hell; from hell one is born into heaven.
Humans are born into the realm of hungry ghosts; from hell one is born as a hungry ghost.
Through various powers one is born; through various powers one finds pleasure.
All are born from the karma of craving; they are not created by a sovereign lord (*īśvara*).
The karmic actions performed throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*) are constant for sentient beings in birth and death;
others cannot understand them, for only the Tathāgata knows them.
"He clearly understands this karma, and he also knows its causes and conditions;
he explains it to ignorant people and transforms all sentient beings. "O Bhikṣus!"

Having thus observed the sufferings of Avīci, that bhikṣu’s mind becomes detached from all saṃsāra; cultivating his mind with great compassion and maintaining right mindfulness, he attains the eleventh stage.

The yakṣas of that earth, having learned this, rejoiced and further transmitted it to the yakṣas of the air. The yakṣas of the air heard the Four Great Kings, and those Four Great Kings heard the Four Heavenly Kings, as previously described, in succession until it reached the Great Brahmā Heaven. Thus they spoke:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country and such-and-such a village, a son of good family of such-and-such a clan has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and with right faith has gone forth from home. He battles with Māra, does not abide within the realm of Māra, and his mind finds no delight in the spheres of defiled desire; he has attained the eleventh stage."
Having heard this, that Great Brahmā rejoiced and spoke these words: "The faction of Māra is diminished;
the allies of the True Dharma have arisen; the side of goodness increases; they act in accordance with the Dharma; and the Dharma of the bhikṣus is firmly established and flourishing."

"Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within the mind—contemplating the course of dharmas in accordance with the True Dharma—asking: 'How does that bhikṣu, having observed the Avīci hell, practice in accordance [with the Dharma]? "
How does that bhikṣu observe the location of the great Avīci hell? How many locations are there in total within the Avīci hell?
He knows through seeing and hearing:
as other hells possess sixteen locations, this Avīci hell is likewise possessed of sixteen locations.
What are these sixteen?
First is named Crow’s Beak;
second is named All-Facing-the-Earth.
The third is named Endlessly Suffering Torment;
the fourth is named Jackal’s Howl;
the fifth is named Iron Jackal’s Food.
Sixth is named Black Belly;
seventh is named Swollen Body;
eighth is named Dreaming of Fear.
Ninth is the Hell of Suffering from Molten Iron;
tenth is the Hell of the Converging Mountains;
eleventh is the Hell of the Unfordable Howling Yama.
The twelfth is named Star-Garland;
the thirteenth is named Urgent Distress;
the fourteenth is named Enveloped in Foul Odor.
The fifteenth is named Iron Plates;
the sixteenth is named Eleven Flames.
These sixteen locations are the subsidiary realms belonging to the fundamental Avīci Hell.
Those who practice the ten unwholesome paths of action, together with the five crimes of immediate retribution, all collectively accumulate the karma for the Great Hell and enter the Avīci Hell.

There are internal five-fold transgressions and external five-fold transgressions; having fully committed them, they are born within the Great Avīci Hell, being reborn in that place in accordance with their specific karma.

In accordance with the karma they have performed and accumulated—karma that is fully consummated and which they delighted in practicing and frequently committing—they are born in a specific location within that hell.
There are five kinds of such *avīci* karma: namely, killing an arhat; harboring evil thoughts;

shedding the blood of a Buddha; rejoicing in such acts with a mind of approval, delighting in practicing them frequently, and doing so extensively; furthermore, teaching others to do so, establishing them in it, or dispatching others to perform it.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the "Crow's Mouth" section of that hell, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra—with the exception of the torments endured in Avīci—all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another [punishment]:

the Yama-wardens pry open the mouths of the offenders as if prying open the beaks of crows; they are then led to a river named Black Ash, where its deep current flows with such violent rapidity that it pours into their mouths.
Thus, the hot ashes first burn their lips;
having burned the lips, they next burn their teeth;
having burned the teeth, they next burn their throats.
Having burned the throat, it next burns the heart;
having burned the heart, it next burns the lungs;
having burned the lungs, it next burns the intestines.
Once the intestines have been burned, next the small intestine (pakvāśaya) is burned;
once the small intestine has been burned, next the large intestine (āmāśaya) is burned;
once the large intestine has been burned, next the stomach (pakvāśaya) is burned.
Having burned the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), [the fire] exits from below.

Those hell-beings undergo the suffering of the River of Ashes; their internal bodies are completely incinerated until nothing remains within them except for external matter. Sustained solely by their evil karma, they do not die and thus undergo intense and rigid suffering.

For a vast duration, they are constantly burned and boiled for countless years; as long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decomposed, and its residual force has not been exhausted, they shall experience unceasing suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place of hell.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, they will be born among hungry ghosts for a thousand lifetimes, known as "cauldron-hungry ghosts" (*kumbhāṇḍa*).

If they escape that place and are born among animals, they will become elephants, yak-cows, *tuṇḍamukha*, rats, mongooses, venomous snakes, lizards, earthworms, mosquitoes, and other such insects; furthermore, they will also become oxen.

Once liberated from that place, if one is born among humans in a realm of similar karma, one will be born into a family of executioners; for two hundred lifetimes, one will die within the womb, or else die before crawling after birth, or else pass away just as one is about to emerge.
Due to the causal conditions of their remaining evil karma, they further commit evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowledge:
there is yet another distinct location, called Sarvābhimukha-bhūmi (The Ground Facing All), which is the second secondary region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

if a person, having contemplated [the teachings], has attained the realization of the exhaustion of outflows as a noble bhikṣuṇī—an arhat—yet forcibly engages in sexual desire, delighting in its practice and committing it repeatedly.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the separate location called Sarvābhimukha within that hell, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the sufferings experienced in the seven hells—Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, and Pratāpana—all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [form of suffering]:

on that iron ground, with their heads and faces downward and their bodies above, they are inverted top-to-bottom and repeatedly turned over. The Yama-wardens inflict extreme torment upon these hell-beings; as they suffer, they are unable to cry out, cannot produce a sound, and cannot even breathe.
If the lower half of their body is positioned above [the upper half], the Yama-keepers gradually chop it with sharp axes until the flesh is entirely gone and only the bones remain.
Furthermore, they wash them with a lye of bone-ash; having been washed, they fall away, and that person remains there merely as a living soul.

They are then placed in a cauldron of boiling, flaming, and surging red copper and molten iron, where they are turned over and under, boiled until completely disintegrated like large or small beans. Once fully cooked, a pervasive vapor covers everything, rendering it invisible.

Thus they are boiled within iron cauldrons for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years; as long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they shall suffer incessantly at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that hellish place.
Whether for the duration of one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa, the suffering endured from further burning the body is still less than the suffering within the Avīci Hell.
For a thousand lifetimes, one receives the body of a hungry ghost (preta), being born among the reproachful hungry ghosts; hunger and thirst burn the body, and the entire body blazes like a lamp.

If they manage to escape from that, they will be born among animals for a thousand lifetimes, constantly suffering from hunger and thirst as wild birds and the like—namely, *cātaka* birds, jackals, cicadas, *gūḍa* insects, wild horses, wild donkeys, deer, and other such animals.
This is the remaining karmic retribution for those evil deeds.
Having escaped that place, if one is born among humans in a realm of similar karma, one will be born in the land of Horse-Face (*Aśvamukha*), dying in the womb for three hundred lifetimes;
or, if through past karma one survives without dying, one will be impoverished, constantly ill, and undergo much suffering and distress, becoming a eunuch for five hundred lifetimes.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, observes the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:

Furthermore, there is another distinct location called "Without the Further Shore" (*Aparapāra*), where beings undergo long-lasting suffering and affliction; this is the third separate sub-region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

if there are certain persons whose senses are distracted by their environment, or who, due to lustful thoughts, proximity to evil friends, or being intoxicated by liquor, engage in sexual intercourse with their own mother; having done so, their minds are filled with dread, and they seek out the counsel of evil associates.
Such deluded people not only repeatedly take pleasure in and frequently commit such acts themselves, but also instruct others to act in this same way.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination, into that hell named Boundless Suffering, where they undergo great anguish and distress.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [torture], namely:

the Yama-wardens there use glowing iron hooks to hook the person's genitals and pull them out from the navel; they take thorny needles and pierce the person's genitals, or drive iron hooks into the navel, or nail them into the nose, or nail them into the ears. Furthermore, they gape open the mouth and place flaming iron hooks inside until the mouth is filled; with flames filling the entire mouth, the person undergoes great suffering.
That person further undergoes great suffering in the lower realms.

Thus, that person suffers in three places, being burned, crushed, split, and beaten until utterly destroyed. All of these together are called the "Boundless Suffering Place," where one undergoes great anguish within Avīci; the suffering experienced there is beyond all analogy.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they will experience uninterrupted suffering at all times.
They shall be constantly burned for an eon, or slightly less than an eon;
only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place in hell.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, for four thousand lifetimes they are born among the *apāyika* hungry ghosts, their bodies consumed by hunger and thirst.
If they escape that place, they are born among the animals in waterless wildernesses, growing up in bamboo groves with mouths perpetually parched.
Born in a cramped place amidst mountains and valleys, they are constantly afraid of shadows and constantly fear being reborn among animals such as pigeons and vultures.
By what causes and conditions are they born within the bamboo groves?

In that bamboo grove there is always a great wind; the wind blows against the bamboos, producing fire. For four thousand lifetimes, they are constantly burned to death there and are reborn in that very place.

Once they have escaped that place, if they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they will be poor and chronically ill, despised and lowly in the world, and their wives will not be chaste.

If they violate another’s wife or commit adultery with another’s daughter, they will be seized by him; having been seized, they are handed over to the king, and the king or his officials will castrate them.
Having no home, they beg for food from others at crossroads or at three-way junctions to sustain their lives, constantly suffering from hunger and thirst;
they further fall ill and die a bitter death at crossroads or in burial grounds.
This is the remaining karmic retribution for those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, observes the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Jackal’s Howl, which is the fourth secondary location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows this through seeing and hearing:

If a person slanders those who possess all-knowledge, slanders pratyekabuddhas, or slanders arhats; or if they slander the Dharma and Vinaya, or preach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, and furthermore teaches others to abide in sympathetic joy [for such acts].

That person, who proclaims what is unrighteous as being righteous and constantly reviles the noble ones, will, by reason of these causes and conditions of evil karma, fall into an evil destination upon the dissolution of the body after death, and undergo great suffering in that hell known as the Place of the Howling Jackals.

Regarding what is called suffering: as previously described, the sufferings experienced in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, which correspond to one's evil karma—all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there are others who are even more wretched:
namely, jackals created by karma in that place, their iron mouths ablaze with flames that fill the entire area.

These jackals have flaming fangs that are exceedingly sharp; they run swiftly toward those who disparage the Dharma of the Noble Ones, each devouring them in different places—some eating their heads, others eating their necks.

Because of their evil speech with the tongue, jackals come to eat their tongues; furthermore, there are jackals that eat their noses, jackals that eat their breastbones, those that eat their lungs, those that eat their small intestines, and those that eat their large intestines. There are those that eat the bladder, those that eat the thighs, those that eat the calves, those that eat the shins, those that eat the arms, and those that eat the hands and feet. Furthermore, there are those that eat the fingers of the hands and feet; every part of the body is dissected and eaten separately, and once eaten, it grows back again.
That person of evil karma, having accumulated the fruits of their actions, undergoes such suffering for a long and distant time.

If they escape from that place of torment, seeking rescue and seeking refuge, they run hither and thither; there, the *yama* demons further force open their mouths and pull out their tongues, slicing and mincing them with extremely sharp knives. Once cut, the tongue grows back again, because they used their tongues to slander the noble ones and praised what is not the Dharma for the sake of others.
In this manner, that person undergoes such suffering for a vast period of time.
If they escape from that place and, seeking rescue and seeking refuge, run hither and thither, the *Yama* messengers—driven by their evil karma—seize them once again and say to one another:

"This liar spoke with crooked words, harsh words, impure and defiled words, words that preach evil dharmas, and words that preach what is not the Dharma, causing all sentient beings to fall away from the Right Path."

Having seized him again, they force open his mouth and pull out his tongue; such an evil tongue is one *krośa* in length. This soft tongue is placed upon a ground of glowing red copper iron, marked out like a grid of fields, and men are sent to plow it. A hot-flaming iron plow with sharp, blazing blades is used, and oxen with extremely sharp knives upon their hooves, amidst fiercely burning flames, plow back and forth over it a hundred or a thousand times.
Having spoken evil words, he utters speech that is inconsistent with the realization of future lives and undergoes such suffering.
For a long time, he is ploughed, boiled, burned, and cut; thus does that wicked tongue experience various kinds of suffering.
As that person thus undergoes suffering, crying out, repenting in their heart, and weeping, the Yama-wardens, in order to rebuke them, speak this verse:
"Sixty thousand Arbudas and five thousand six hundred Arbudas—
Because of the evil of one’s speech and mental intentions, One who reviles the Noble Ones reaches hell."
You practiced unwholesome deeds with virtuous appearance; you preached what is not Dharma as if it were Dharma.
Because of your previous evil speech, you are now being burned here.
Sentient beings hope for the truth—how could you preach evil teachings?
Because you have spoken wickedly, you shall experience suffering corresponding to that wickedness.
One who speaks deliberate falsehoods, proclaiming what is not Dharma to be Dharma, is the foremost thief; all others are not great thieves.
If a person correctly teaches the Dharma, transcending all evil,
they will reach a state of goodness where there is no suffering or affliction.
Their inexhaustible wealth shall not be lost, and no one can steal it away.
Truthful speech is the stairway to heaven and is also the gateway to Nirvana.
One who always speaks the truth and constantly recollects the practice of the Dharma—
free from sorrow, grief, and old age— is the most excellent among men.
"You have abandoned the True Dharma and reviled the virtuous ones;
having accumulated evil in the past, you now experience its consequences here.
Thus do the Yama-wardens rebuke those who disparage the Dharma of the Noble Ones.
Having already been censured and distanced, they are subjected to much suffering—an indescribable and inconceivable suffering.
Why is this? Because they have committed an extremely grave offense against the Noble Ones, they will obtain a corresponding result, as taught by the Tathāgata.
Thus they are burned and boiled until their evil karma is neither destroyed nor decayed, and until the potency of that karma is exhausted; at all times, their suffering does not cease.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted do they finally escape from the place where the jackals howl.

Once they have attained liberation from that state, they are born among the hungry ghosts for two thousand lifetimes; dwelling in the *Piṇḍa* realm, their bodies are mere lumps, resembling masses of flesh, unable to see or hear, unable to smell or taste, and incapable of speech.
If they escape from that place, they will be born among animals for three thousand lifetimes, constantly becoming dung-worms.

Having escaped from there, if they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they will remain perpetually impoverished for five hundred lifetimes; whatever words they speak will not be trusted by others, and they will suffer from leprosy, deafness, and muteness.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Iron Jackal Feeding; this is the fifth distinct location within that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows this:

if a person, with an evil mind and evil thoughts, rejoices in such acts, and with a heavy, malevolent heart, burns a monastery of the Saṃgha, as well as Buddha images, many bedding spreads, garments, wealth, grain, and various utensils;

because of that evil mind, he sets fire to the monastic quarters, and having burned them, rejoices in it without giving rise to remorse, further teaching others to rejoice in and praise such speech—when these actions are pervasive, the karma is completed, and they are joined in harmony.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination, being born in a specific place within that hell known as "Devoured by Iron Jackals," where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra; all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:
because their karma is heavy, the suffering they undergo is also heavy. Why is this?
Cause and effect are similar, for the fruit resembles the seed.

Once born in that place, due to the causal conditions of their evil karma, all parts of their bodies are universally ablaze with flames; the fire burning upon those bodies extends for a measure of ten yojanas.
There are eleven kinds of suffering, of which the suffering of the Summit (*mūrdhan*) is the heaviest; among all the hells, this suffering is the most intense.

In that place there is also a mountain resembling fire, where all-consuming flames blaze everywhere. Tormented by hunger and thirst, they are constantly burned and beaten for a vast duration of time, with their arms outstretched upward.
That person’s outstretched hand reaches five yojanas high, and its flaming mane burns everywhere like the peak of a mountain being consumed by fire.

As that person is scorched all over, he utters cries of wailing and lamentation, weeping and sobbing; his mouth gapes wide as he calls out, and flames fill his mouth, burning both inside and out until they become a single mass of fire with no space between.
The flames gradually grow longer, and for a long time they are scorched and boiled.

If they escape that place, hoping for rescue and seeking a refuge, they run hither and thither with distorted mouths and broken faces, searching for a place of happiness, yet their own evil karma follows them and binds them.

In that hell, they arrive at yet another place where there are mountains and rivers, and their suffering increases. From above, iron bricks the size of a *krośa* fall like summer rain; these bricks strike those people, crushing and piling them from head to foot like dried jerky, so that no part of their bodies can be distinguished.

Thus that person is constantly rained upon with foul iron, undergoing great suffering and distress; yet he is born again, his body being powerless as flaming-toothed jackals devour him like dried meat. As soon as he is reassembled and reborn, they devour him once more.

For a long period of time, that evil jackal is constantly fed in this manner and thus roasted; having been cooked, it is born again, and due to its evil karma, it is eaten in this way, undergoing great suffering and distress.
One creates for oneself and not by another; what one has created is not lost, and what one has not created is not obtained. It is not obtained without cause, nor does it come from elsewhere.
There is no agent in whom it dwells, nor is there a recipient who sustains it; it is obtained through the cause of one's own action.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they will experience unceasing suffering at all times;
only when their evil karma is exhausted can they finally escape from such an extremely terrible place in hell.

Furthermore, for another thousand lifetimes, they will be born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), their entire bodies scorched by flames as they cry out in lamentation, wailing throughout all lands, all cities, and all villages during the night.

At night it is burned by fire, and during the daytime, the sun rains down fire; thus it is burned by a fire-like heat until the evil karma that produced it is exhausted, rotted away, deprived of its vitality, and utterly extinguished.

If they escape from that place, they will be born among animals for a thousand lifetimes, constantly existing as centipedes in the wilderness. They will perpetually suffer from hunger and thirst; they have two heads, two faces, and furthermore two mouths. For a long time they endure suffering without respite, their entire bodies being devoured by many black insects.

Once liberated from that place, due to a small amount of past wholesome karma from long ago, if one is born among humans in a realm of similar karma, for a thousand lifetimes one will be a person of black complexion, with a color like dark clouds; one will be prone to injury, constantly impoverished, and always wandering about in many places. One will be employed as a camel-driver, enslaved by others, perpetually afflicted by hunger and thirst, finding food and drink only with great difficulty, barely maintaining life.

In this manner, they undergo suffering for a thousand lifetimes as hungry ghosts, a thousand lifetimes as animals, and a thousand lifetimes among humans, all due to the causal conditions of their evil karma.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Volume Fourteen [and] Volume Fifteen.
Translated by the Brahamana Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Hells, Number Eleven:
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, further contemplates the location of the Great Hell of Avīci.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Kṛṣṇodara (Black Belly), which is the sixth distinct sub-region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows through seeing and hearing:

If certain individuals take the property of the Buddha for their own consumption, neither returning it nor making restitution, and without believing in the karmic consequences of such acts, they take more again or incite others to take it, acting as its custodians;
or having already offered it to the Buddha, they subsequently reclaim it;
or when others give them objects to be offered to the Buddha, they instead consume them themselves.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the Black Belly section of that hell, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra; all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundredfold more intense.
Furthermore, there is another even more grievous state, namely:
there, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst, and they eat their own flesh; having eaten, it grows back again, and having eaten, it grows back again.
In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years, they are reborn after eating, and having been reborn, they grow.

They undergo double suffering and the affliction of hunger and thirst; the suffering they endure due to their evil karma is a hundred times more severe than before. Having created their own suffering, they are once again crushed by it themselves.

That person, thus eating his own flesh, runs about everywhere; as he runs in this manner, a black-bellied snake, the color of a dark cloud, seizes him and bites him gradually, starting from the nails of his feet, devouring him down to the bone; once eaten, he is born again;
having been born, he is eaten again; and having been eaten, he is born again.
Thus, for a long time, because of their evil karma, they are devoured in this manner;

for those sinners consumed the property of the Buddha, and since among all fields of merit the field of the Buddha is supreme, they undergo such suffering because they damaged the property of the Buddha.

Once they have escaped that, they enter the ground of flaming iron, which resembles the fiery embers of *khadira* wood. Having entered that ground to a depth of one *yojana*, those people are boiled and burned within the fire for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years; it increases further still, and they are thus subjected to extreme boiling.

Once they have escaped, hoping for rescue and seeking a refuge, there are further *yama-rākṣasas* there who, using flaming iron tongs, seize their bodies and place them in iron cauldrons. They boil until thoroughly cooked, like large or small beans; being scorched and boiled, they are turned over and over, floating and sinking, undergoing harsh suffering and the foremost of evil sufferings—such agonies are beyond all analogy.

The causes and effects within all three realms are similar; compared to the suffering that person undergoes in hell, [the former] does not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, or one *kalā* part of it.
Thus, overwhelmed by hundreds of thousands of forces of suffering and adrift upon the great ocean of primary misery, they experience the fruits of their own karma.
As long as the evil and unwholesome karma they have accumulated has not been destroyed or decayed, and its residual power has not been exhausted, they shall suffer incessantly at all times;
only when that evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place in the Black-Bellied Hell.
Once they have attained liberation from that, for twelve hundred lifetimes they will be born among the hungry ghosts who feed on excrement.
Once they have attained liberation from that, for seven hundred lifetimes they will be born among the animals who feed on vomit.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, it is as difficult to obtain a human body as it is for a turtle to encounter a hole in a floating yoke.
If they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they become heterodox practitioners with wrong views, such as those who consume excrement.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another location called the Body-Melting Place (*kāya-vidahana-sthāna*), which is the seventh distinct sub-region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
They see, hear, and know:

There are those who commit evil, seizing the wealth and property of others to consume for themselves; they act repeatedly and accumulate such deeds until their karma becomes pervasive, completing their actions and further inciting others to do the same.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in that hell at the Place of Boiling Bodies, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [torture], namely:

in that place there are two iron trees, both ablaze with flames. Driven by the winds of evil karma, they strike one another together. The beings in that hell are caught between the two trees; they are crushed with extreme force like *tāla* leaves, their bodies being squeezed until they melt away, only to be born again, and once born, to be crushed once more.
Two trees come straight toward him, and as he is squeezed between them on both sides, he undergoes great suffering and torment. Thus, being crushed and ground down, he falls to the ground.

There, iron birds with fierce vajra-beaks perch upon those trees and peck at the heads of the offenders. Having pecked, they fly back up to the trees; this happens repeatedly until the offenders' heads are shattered. They peck out their eyes and eat them; the offenders wail and weep piteously as the birds continue to devour their eyes.
Once the heads have been broken, they drink the brains; having drunk the brains, they next split open the hearts.
Having split open the heart, they drink the flesh and blood;
having drunk them, they next eat the intestines;
having eaten the intestines, they next eat the stomach.
Once the stomach has been eaten, he next eats the intestines;
having eaten the intestines, he next eats the hips;
once the hips have been eaten, he next eats the thighs.
Having eaten the thigh, he next ate the shin;
having eaten the shin, he next ate the top of the foot;
having eaten the top of the foot, he next ate the toes.

That person undergoes such harsh and agonizing suffering for a long duration of countless years, such that even the number of hundreds of years could not exhaust it; there is not even a slight resemblance [to ordinary pain]. What is now described is but a small portion, like taking a single handful of water from the great ocean and placing it elsewhere—what has been said is merely one part.

Those people of evil karma undergo such harsh and rigid suffering for a long time; thus, as long as the accumulated evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and its residual force has not been exhausted, they shall suffer without ceasing at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be released from that place in hell.

Once they have attained liberation from that state, they will be born for a thousand lifetimes among the hungry ghosts who feed on saliva; possessing only life, their bodies will be scorched by the supreme suffering of hunger and thirst.

If one is released from that place, one is born among animals as a great fish in the salt waters of the great ocean, dwelling constantly within the waters of the great sea—either as a *nāgara*, a *makara*, or a great tortoise—suffering perpetually from hunger and thirst for a thousand lifetimes while moving through the salt water.

Once they have escaped that place, if there is karma from past lives that has matured and they are born among humans in a place of common karma, they will be situated in a borderland between two kingdoms where those two kings are constantly at war with one another.
Once that person has accumulated wealth and possessions, they are seized by others or confiscated by the king's punishment;
having been stripped of everything, they are made to guard and maintain a prison, their bodies scorched by hunger and thirst, receiving food from others while undergoing extreme suffering.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Dream-Vision-Terror, which is the eighth distinct sub-region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
They perceive, hear, and know:

If a certain person, when a large assembly of bhikṣus has gathered in harmony and desires food, takes that food for himself and eats it, thereby depriving the Saṃgha of sustenance, causing them to suffer the pain of hunger, unable to contemplate the wholesome, unable to practice dhyāna, and their minds remaining unpacified.

That person of evil karma takes the food currently being consumed by the Saṃgha; having taken it, he does not confess nor does he give rise to remorse. Furthermore, he delights in taking the Saṃgha’s food and incites others to do so, giving rise to sympathetic joy. Thus his actions are pervasive and his commissioning of the deed is brought to completion.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination; in that hell, they experience great suffering and torment in the terrifying place called Dream-Vision.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is something even more extraordinary:

all sentient beings do not know its name. Those great sufferings are entirely solid and rigid, so acute and unbearable that the afflictions they endure arise from their own karma; now I shall describe but a small portion, like a single drop from the ocean, for what is seen in this hell is as unreal as what is seen in a person's dream.

He sees wicked men who are most terrifying; those men hold various weapons in their hands, such as shackles or pestles. They seize beings from hell who have performed evil deeds and place them upon an iron ground, seating them within an iron casket. With a hot iron pestle, they pound and trample their bodies until both flesh and bone are crushed and scattered like blocks of wax or honey. Yet they are born again; once born, they are struck with clubs, broken, and shattered into pieces. This is the power of the accumulation of their evil karma, through which they undergo such retribution.

If they escape from the suffering endured within that chest, they enter again the Iron Forest (*ayaḥ-vana*). Driven by the paths of their own karma, they enter that Iron Forest; every part of their body is split and torn apart, hacked and severed until scattered, and they fall upon iron beds, where all the limbs and members of those evil-doers are utterly destroyed.

If they escape that place, hoping for rescue and seeking refuge, they run hither and thither; yet iron blades rain down, hacking and slicing their bodies until all their sinews and veins are severed and destroyed, leaving only a skeletal lattice. There is not even a small patch of flesh where a fly could alight; skin, bone, and sinew are joined together, consisting of nothing but a web of bones.
Furthermore, iron rain falls, splitting, cleaving, and shattering them; they run about wailing and crying out in bitter suffering, fleeing everywhere yet unable to escape.

Arising from their own evil karma, arising from their unwholesome karma, as long as the accumulated unwholesome and evil karma has not been exhausted or destroyed, they are intensely scorched and boiled until their entire bodies are cooked, shattered, ruined, and putrefied. Due to this unwholesome karma, they endure this for a vast duration of time without attaining liberation;
only when all that evil karma has been fully experienced and exhausted do they finally gain release.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, they will be born among the hungry ghosts who feed on pus for a thousand lifetimes.

If they escape that place, they will be born among animals for five hundred lifetimes, constantly in places where stones fall and crush them; their bodies will be like reeds, and they will undergo great suffering until they die because of it.

Once they have been liberated from that place, if they are born among humans in a realm of similar karma, they will always be poor and constantly ill, subject to the commands of others, and born in desolate wildernesses, on perilous riverbanks, in places abounding in sand, where grass is sparse, where there is no grass, where there is no water, in places devoid of marshes, in places of constant fear, and in evil lands.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Hell of Avīci.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Body-Melting (Kāya-vilayana), a place of suffering and affliction; it is the ninth distinct section of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

there is a donor’s family who always possesses a kind heart and is accomplished in right faith; they constantly provide wealth and goods to the sick and to renunciants for the purpose of curing their illnesses.
Such wealth and property should be used to ensure that any sick person recovers from their illness.

Yet there are wicked people, those who practice deceitful speech, whose inner minds are unwholesome, who distance themselves from virtuous friends and the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), and who, though wearing the *kāṣāya*, are great thieves. They consume the offerings and the property of the sick; having used them, they do not repent, they feel no remorse, and they neither return nor repay it. Furthermore, they instruct others to go along with them in approval, and they continue to greedily seize more.

Because of these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination, being born in that hell in the place called "Molting Body" (Śarīra-vidagdha), where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [torment]:
in that hell region, there is an iron tree one *yojana* in height, heated and boiling, its flames ablaze, produced by the effects of evil karma.
In that hell region, there are stones of hot flame resembling vajra; their touch is extremely hard and rigid, burning with a hundredfold blaze.

Thus, beneath a tree ablaze with fire and towering high, those born in that hell dwell at its roots; their four hundred and four diseases increase their suffering and affliction, and they remain solitary without companions, with their heads and faces downward and their feet upward.
The intense heat and power of those trees are so fierce that, compared to the fires of the hells, they seem as cold as ice.
The sap from the roots of those trees exerts a singular, agonizing pressure upon the bodies of the offenders, leaving not even a space the size of a hair’s breadth untouched.

The suffering of that illness is a hundred times greater than fire, and the agony of being crushed by the tree exceeds even that; for vast periods of time, throughout countless years, they undergo such suffering.
Furthermore, in that place there are Yama-wardens who, holding iron swords in their hands, slice [the beings] everywhere, vein by vein.

In those hell regions, they undergo five kinds of suffering—namely, the suffering of trees, fire, iron, hunger and thirst, and disease—for a vast duration of countless years. Those who hear this will have the hair on their bodies stand on end; this describes but a small portion of the harsh and rigid afflictions and the afflictions of bitter flavors.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they will experience uninterrupted suffering at all times;
only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place in hell.

Once they have attained liberation from that state, for seven hundred lifetimes they are born among the hungry ghosts who feed on fire and smoke; their bodies are consumed by hunger and thirst as if a forest hut were being set ablaze.

Having escaped from there, for five hundred lifetimes they are born among animals as scorched dragons, constantly rained upon with hot sand falling upon their bodies, where they are burned and cooked.

Once they have escaped from among the animals, if they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they will dwell in thickets and forests constantly carrying bricks and the like; throughout their lives they experience extreme suffering, never once being satiated and never obtaining fine food. They hear only the names of excellent foods and delicious flavors, serving as slaves under the command of others, impoverished, sickly, and lowly.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called the "Confluence of Two Mountains," which is the tenth distinct sub-region of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
They learn through seeing and hearing:
There was a person who committed evil; while a pratyekabuddha was hungry and about to eat, he stole [the food] from him.

Because of this causal condition of evil karma, when his body perished and his life ended, he fell into an evil destination and underwent great suffering and affliction in that hell at the place where two mountains meet.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Sañjīva and Kālasūtra—all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there are even more grievous sufferings, namely:
that place abounds with iron clubs, iron spears, iron cauldrons, and iron coffins; it inflicts torment by making one climb two iron mountains, bestowing all manner of suffering.
In that place, there falls a heavy rain of excellent mountain-clumps; from above, these fall with a measure of one yojana, consisting solely of pairs of mountain-clumps.
They strike those sinners, causing their bodies to disintegrate like balls of sand; having scattered, they are born again;
once born, they scatter again; having scattered, they are born again.
Eleven flames surround and burn their bodies; once the fire has burned their bodies, it next destroys their eyes, which grow back again after being destroyed.
The Yama-wardens then cut off their tongues, which grow back again after being cut, and then they cut off their noses, pouring molten white tin onto the severed places.

Furthermore, their ears were sliced open, and molten red copper was poured into them until they were full; hot iron bowls filled with boiling ashes were then sprinkled over the ears, and they were further cut and pared away with sharp knives.
The four hundred and four diseases are always fully present there.
Blazing flames spread everywhere, merging into a single conflagration, whereby they undergo the suffering of extreme heat.

In that hell-dwelling, for a vast duration beyond reckoning of years, as long as the accumulated unwholesome and evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they are subjected to uninterrupted suffering at all times.
When their evil karma is exhausted, they finally escape from that hellish place.

Having escaped, for five hundred lifetimes they are born as flies and insects that completely cover their bodies and constantly devour them; their bodies are riddled with sores, and within these sores dwell evil insects that eat away at their flesh. They live in secluded places among the hungry ghosts who constantly consume excrement and urine.

If they are released from that place, they will be born among animals for seven hundred lifetimes in desolate and evil wildernesses, constantly taking the body of a deer and being tormented by hunger and thirst.

Once they have escaped from there, if they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, their bodies will always carry heavy burdens; they will be beaten until their bodies are broken, remaining restless day and night, with hands and feet all cracked and mouths perpetually parched. Their physical complexion will be foul and their clothing tattered; this is the residual karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Although born among humans, for five hundred lifetimes they are not true human beings; resembling ghosts, their bodies are constantly afflicted by suffering and they find no peace day or night.
This is the residual karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another distinct place called Yamabādhana, which is the eleventh location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He perceives and knows through hearing and learning:

there are people who dwell in the wilderness by rivers and marshes, taking them as their means of livelihood. That river and marsh environment constitutes their primary karma; all fields, grains, and other provisions for sustenance are obtained from them, whereby they preserve their lives.

A person with an evil mind cut off that river; once the river was severed, all the lands in that region were lost, and even the birds and deer died, let alone human beings. All the cities, villages, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas there perished from thirst.
Because that river was cut off, the people of the land all died out.

Due to the causal conditions of such evil karma, when those people’s bodies dissolved at the end of their lives, they fell into an evil destination and were born in a specific section of that hell called Yamavapradur, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is something even more formidable:
that place extends for seven hundred yojanas like a vast wilderness, with precipitous cliffs, high mountains, and great flames blazing forth, where there are many iron trees.

Because those hell-beings possess perverted views, they see ponds, rivers, and groves in their full abundance. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, and having been burned by the most terrible fires, they cry out and wail as they rush toward those ponds with this thought:
"When I reach that place, I shall drink the water from those ponds."
Having reached that pond, it is found to be filled with boiling hot ashes throughout the river and the pool.
At that location, the henchmen of Yama hold iron blades in their hands; they seize those sinners and slice them with the blades, causing them to undergo two kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of being cut by the blades; [the second is...]
2. The suffering of hunger and thirst.
Thus, that person remains in such a wilderness, their body mangled by blades, enduring great agony for a long period of time.
If they escape that place, they run hither and thither due to hunger and thirst; with their bodies scorched by hunger and thirst, they run everywhere until they see a cool river and hasten toward it.

Once that person has fled, there is a bird in the pond as large as an elephant, named Yama, whose beak is sharp and emits flames. It seizes the hell-being and lifts it up into the air; having lifted it, it flies about, and while the hell-being loses consciousness, it then releases him like a stone falling to the ground.
In that place, the ground is ablaze and possesses a harsh, solid touch; when a sinner falls upon it, he is shattered into a hundred pieces, yet he is joined together again;
having been joined, he scatters once more, and having scattered, he is joined together again.
The birds seize them again, as previously described, inflicting upon them such suffering and distress.
Those inhabitants of hell further suffer from malignant diseases, as previously described.
In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years, they undergo such various torments inflicted by the evil birds.
If they escape from that place, they are again seized by the *yama-rākṣasas* and cast into the river of boiling, red-hot copper that swirls in eddies.

Once placed there, their bodies are completely melted away like the vanishing of water-foam; yet they are born anew. Because of their evil karma and the performance of evil deeds, those people of evil karma are thus burned and cooked for a vast and long duration, beyond counting in years.

When those who destroyed the kingdom and its people have finally escaped, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst as they run hither and thither. Due to their own evil karma, wherever they go, the path is filled with iron hooks; their blades are extremely sharp and cut through their feet, tearing everything from the soles of the feet up to the thighs.

Once their feet are torn apart, their bodies burst into flames, and they undergo extreme suffering. They cry out in lamentation, their hearts filled with remorse and distress, groaning and wailing. Every part of their bodies is completely ablaze; having been burned, they rise again, and having risen, they move on once more. Thus, that person’s mind is deranged and lacks stability.

Furthermore, from that place, dogs with flaming teeth come and bite the offenders everywhere, causing all their limbs and members to be shattered; they devour their skin, flesh, fat, and marrow, and then drink their fluids.

Those practitioners of evil karma who have destroyed their own lands undergo such suffering through the power of their own karma for a vast duration of time. As long as the accumulated evil and unwholesome karma has not been destroyed or decomposed, and its residual force has not been exhausted, they will experience uninterrupted suffering at all times.
Only when that evil karma is fully exhausted will they finally be liberated from that place in hell.
Once they have attained liberation from that state, they are born among hungry ghosts for five hundred lifetimes, undergoing extreme suffering and affliction.

If they escape that place, they are born among animals for five hundred lifetimes as śarabhas; in every lifetime, they enter fire and are burned, or are eaten by snakes, or are consumed by fire, or are killed by the wind.

Once liberated from that place, if they are born among humans in a realm of similar karma, they will be born during a time when there is no moral discipline, becoming the most base and lowly among all people.
This is the residual fruit of retribution for those evil karmas.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Hell of Avīci.
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another distinct place called Tārāmāla (Star-Garland), which is the twelfth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place? He sees, hears, and knows: there is a person who commits evil;

toward a bhikṣu who has attained the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—in whom all afflictions are utterly extinguished—and who has just arisen from it and is extremely hungry, he steals his food and feels joy in his heart. Having eaten it, he greedily takes more, speaks words of praise with his mouth, and further instructs others to do the same. These karmas are pervasive; he brings the actions to completion, performs them again and again, and accumulates them, so that his evil karma becomes firm and hardened.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the Star-Garland section of that hell, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, as previously described, all the agonies endured in the seven great hells—such as Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, and the rest—are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [aspect]:
namely, at the two corners of that hell, throughout the entire hellish region, cauldrons of boiling water blaze like stars in the sky.

At one corner, for a duration exceeding twenty billion, nine nayutas, nine thousand padmas, sixty billion abjas, thirty mahāpadmas, one hundred koṭis, ten koṭis, and twenty thousand mālakas, beings are burned and boiled; they are thoroughly cooked and scorched. Like fish tossing about in a cauldron of blazing, crimson, boiling copper, they are burned and boiled with increasing intensity, suffering firm and evil torments at all times.
That person of evil karma cries out in remorse for the evil deeds of his own mind; he is thus scorched and boiled for a long, vast period of time, as previously described.

Once that person has escaped from such a place of suffering, he enters again the wind of "Exceedingly Hot Flavor," whose harsh touch is like a blade that severs all the vessels. Having severed the vessels, it lifts him up and moves him toward the second corner of the hell.

Once that person of evil karma has reached the second corner of the hell, winds blow forth billions of swords that slice the sinner, causing all his limbs and members to be completely shattered and destroyed, leaving only sinews and veins.

When that person’s body has become nothing but a mere web of sinews, the Yama-wardens then seize them and place them within a cauldron blown by the Star-Garland wind; having placed them there, they stand with their feet above and their heads below, entering first with their heads and faces.

Furthermore, at a later time, boiling red-hot copper first burns their eyes, then their skulls, then their faces, then their teeth, and then their throats; the hot molten copper is poured into their throats, burning everything throughout, so that they cannot cry out or produce a sound. In this manner, those people undergo harsh and agonizing suffering.

Having endured that suffering, there is yet more: the henchmen of Yama seize iron pestles and strike their heads. Once their heads are struck, all parts of their bodies leap and quiver; both head and body leap together like writhing fish for a vast duration of time.

Thus, in the Two-Angled Star-Garland Hell, they are boiled and cooked in its midst; as long as the accumulated unwholesome and evil karma has not been destroyed or decomposed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they shall experience uninterrupted suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be liberated from that hellish place.

Once they have attained liberation from that state, for a thousand lifetimes they will be born among the *preta*s known as "those who harbor expectations," constantly experiencing suffering and affliction; food and drink are difficult to obtain, being found perhaps once, or not at all, within a hundred years.

Having been liberated from that place, they are born among animals for five hundred lifetimes, taking the body of a deer in narrow and confined places. Their minds are constantly filled with alarm and fear; they harbor dread toward all people. In desolate, precipitous places far from human habitation, because they are perpetually terrified, they become emaciated, lose their luster, and their bodies wither away. Due to the power of their evil karma, they are killed by hunters.

Once they have attained liberation, if they are born among humans in a place of similar karma, they will constantly engage in worldly livelihoods as leaders and guides; they will be perpetually exhausted by hunger and thirst, always on the move, and eternally dependent on others, being employed by them and sustaining their lives through others. Though appearing similar to other men, they are not true persons and constantly undergo suffering and affliction.
This is the residual karmic retribution of those evil deeds.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called Sarvaduḥkhāvarta; this is the thirteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

there are people with evil minds who give rise to perverted thoughts, and regarding the words spoken, the drawings, and the written characters of the All-Knowing One, they suppress, obscure, and conceal them so as to cause the loss of the Dharma-body, preventing all sentient beings from gaining faith in the Buddha.
If one hears the True Dharma, then faith arises; because [the Dharma] is not present, sentient beings do not believe.

With such a mind and such wrong views, they accumulate evil karma with a defiled and wicked mind. If they teach others to abide in sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), having done so, they do it again and again; because of their wicked mental state, their karmic actions become pervasive, and as they complete these deeds, they perform them repeatedly in that state.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall into an evil destination and are born in a specific place within that hell called Sarvaduḥkhāvarta, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering, it is as previously described: the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra; all those sufferings are experienced here in their entirety, a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there are even more severe sufferings, namely:
