molten, boiling red copper is poured into their eyes until both eyes are completely filled; or their eyes are rubbed and ground with hot sand and the harsh touch of vajras until they are melted away and scattered to pieces, only to be born again, and once born, to be rubbed and ground once more.
Furthermore, their hands are severed with sharp saws; once severed, they grow back again, and as soon as they have grown, they are severed once more.

They are then placed in a cauldron of blazing flames, with their heads submerged inside and their bodies outside the cauldron. Thus they are boiled intensely, while their bodies remain half-outside the cauldron, being sliced and carved by sharp knives.
Because they viewed the Dharma with their eyes and thereby destroyed it, they receive such retribution;
because they rubbed and ground the Dharma with their hands and thereby destroyed it, they receive the retribution of being sawn asunder;
because they concealed and extinguished the Dharma with their original evil minds, they sit within the cauldrons.
The Vajratuṇḍa birds pluck out their hearts and eat them, drinking the essence of their hearts; because of their evil intentions, they undergo such suffering.

Seated within cauldrons with their backs positioned above so that they do not enter the depths of the cauldron, the Yama-wardens seize sharp axes to flay their skin until it peels away, washing them with intensely hot alkaline lye. Blazing, hot needles pierce their bodies all over, and a flaming, hot iron wheel spins rapidly upon their heads; thus they suffer.

If they are released from that place, they fall into the Ground of Melting and Boiling, where suffering is constant and uninterrupted because of the karma they have accumulated and performed; thus they undergo such suffering within the hells.
As long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and the potency of that karma has not been exhausted, they shall experience unceasing suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be able to escape that hellish realm.

Even after escaping that place, for five hundred lifetimes they are born among the hungry ghosts who feed on smoke; their bodies are shrouded by their own evil deeds, and their minds suffer affliction with unceasing mental agitation.
If they escape from that place, they will be born among animals for seven hundred lifetimes as nocturnal insects, or as foxes, hares, owls, and other such birds.

Having escaped from there, if they possess the karmic seeds of humans from the distant past, they may be born among humans in a place of common karma; they will be born in the Snowy Mountains, eating foul food and drink, remaining perpetually impoverished, and will be born among the Mlecchas for three hundred lifetimes.
This is the remaining karmic retribution of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place called "Enveloped in Foul Odor," which is the fourteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
They perceive, hear, and know:

There is a person who, due to wrong views, recollects and contemplates with an evil mind; following a state of hatred, they give rise to a sense of joy and pleasure. They set fire to the fields or sugarcane plantations belonging to the Sangha, or to groves, fruit trees, or other places used for the consumption of the Sangha. By thus burning the property used by the Sangha, they cause the bhikṣus to suffer loss and ruin; their karma is pervasive, their actions are brought to completion, and they act in full accord with the consequences.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination, undergoing great suffering and affliction in that hell known as the Place Enveloped in Foul Odors.

As for what is called suffering: as previously described, all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [suffering], namely:

in that place there is a net of fiery flames called the "Needle-Hole Net," with fiery flames pervading the entire hell. Once the evildoers have been born there, the *Yama* wardens strike them with flaming, sharp-edged swords and hot arrows; they are driven into the flaming Needle-Hole Net and cannot escape. Those evildoers are bound there and cannot be released.
Those nets are extremely sharp; they slice and cut their hands, then their ribs, then their backs, until every part of their bodies has been completely sliced away, leaving only the bones remaining.
Once they have been cut and sliced like a net, the *yama-rākṣasas* beat them with cane staffs, causing them to fall a hundred times, a thousand times, or even a hundred thousand times.

Those people of evil karma, completely enveloped by their own evil deeds, undergo the suffering of those arrows; for a long duration, they experience great torment, characterized by harsh and cruel contact—the suffering they endure is incomparable and beyond parallel.

In that hell, they undergo extreme great suffering; as long as the accumulated evil and unwholesome karma has not been destroyed or decomposed, and its karmic force has not been exhausted, they shall experience uninterrupted suffering at all times.
Only when their evil karma is exhausted will they finally be able to escape from that place in hell.
Even after escaping that place, one will be born among the blood-eating hungry ghosts for seven hundred lifetimes, consuming only the blood of childbirth.
Even after escaping that place, one will be born among animals for five hundred lifetimes, becoming birds such as chickens, peacocks, and starlings.
Having been released from that place, if one is born among humans in a place of similar karma, one will be born into the family of a caṇḍāla or a butcher.
This is the remaining retribution of that evil karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
there is another distinct place called the Iron Plate Place (Ayastambha), which is the fifteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows through seeing and hearing:
there are those who, with a frivolous mind, a deceitful mind, and evil intent, invite a bhikṣu during a time of scarcity and speak to him thus:
"During this year’s summer retreat at my home, I shall provide all that is required for medicine and the sick; you need have no anxiety at all, nor should you harbor any other thoughts.
Those bhikṣus all conceived faith in their hearts; as the times were again in a famine, they relied upon that person and sought nothing else.
Once they had entered the summer retreat, those people of evil intent gave nothing at all to them and drove them away.

Because the world was suffering from famine at that time, some of those bhikṣus died; some bhikṣus failed to complete their summer retreat; some suffered greatly from hunger and thirst; and some bhikṣus departed for other countries.

Such evil persons abandon monks, obstructing, wasting, and harassing them; by reason of this evil karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into an evil destination and are born in that hell, the Place of Iron Sheets, where they undergo great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering: as previously described, all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is another superior [suffering]:

namely, those hell-beings in that place are surrounded on all sides by eleven masses of flames; constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, the Yama-wardens repeatedly and constantly force them to drink and eat molten red copper and balls of heated iron.
The body of that sinner is constantly burned and boiled, dried up and destroyed, yet is born again, for immeasurable *bhadramukha*, *trayastrimśa*, and *niyuta* kalpas.

Furthermore, there is a more excruciating suffering produced by their own karma: the Yama-wardens take a sheet of hot iron five *yojanas* wide, its flames fiercely blazing and forming a single continuous wreath of fire. They wrap this iron sheet around the body, causing it all to seethe and boil; the entire body is ablaze with fire as they wail and cry out in ruinous agony. There is not even a space the size of a needle’s eye where one might find a point of refuge or any slight pleasure. Thus, the fire from the iron sheet is uninterrupted throughout, and such a painful touch makes the suffering unbearable.

Thus, iron sheets cause them hunger and thirst and create great blazing fires; they undergo such suffering as long as their evil karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and its residual force has not been exhausted. At all times, their suffering does not cease;
only when their evil karma is exhausted are they finally able to escape from that hellish place.
Once released from that place, they will be born among the hungry ghosts who eat brains for a hundred thousand lifetimes.
If released from that place, they will be born among the animals who eat fire for seven hundred lifetimes.

Having been liberated from that place, if they are born among humans in a realm of similar karma, for five hundred lifetimes they will be kings who lack faith; they will be constantly imprisoned and die of hunger and thirst.
This is the residual karmic retribution of that evil deed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, again contemplates the location of the Great Avīci Hell.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another place named Eleven Flames, which is the sixteenth location of that hell.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
They see, hear, and know:

There are those of evil conduct who destroy, wipe away, or extinguish [the offerings at] Buddha images, Buddha stupas, or the monasteries of the Sangha; who with malicious intent destroy the dwellings of noble ones and erase painted images of the Buddha.

Or again, there are those who are not disciples of the Buddha and have no faith in the Buddha, yet claim for themselves to be disciples of the Buddha; they listen to the Buddha-dharma seeking out faults and looking for opportunities to find flaws. Having heard it, they do not give rise to faith or enter into the Dharma, and thus they delight in and frequently practice such disparagement.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into an evil destination; they wander within the fires of the eleventh flaming region of that hell, undergoing great suffering and affliction.

As for what is called suffering: as previously described, all the agonies endured in the seven great hells, such as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, are experienced here in their entirety, yet a hundred times more intense.
Furthermore, there is something even more formidable:
namely, in that place there are a thousand times more fierce and venomous snakes; those snakes abound and pervade the hell, and the inhabitants of that hell come and go amidst them.
The Yama-wardens, wielding iron clubs, beat them so that they flee in haste, only to be bitten by snakes; furthermore, some hold fire that burns with extreme heat.
Thus, those people are scorched by two kinds of fires—namely, the fire of poison and the fire of hell—and as they run about crying out, they wail and weep in lamentation.
Because of their wailing, the Yama-wardens further address them with verses, rebuking them as follows:
"Intoxicated by the poison of craving, Through the power of all your delusion, You were stubborn and dull toward the True Dharma; Now you cry out in vain."
They take delight in evil deeds and crave only present pleasure;
though doing evil is sweet at first, it is like fire or poison in the end.
Those who commit evil acts are reviled by all people.
All who perform good deeds are praised; thus one should abandon evil.
Those who see it do not delight in it; the retribution for evil brings suffering and distress.
Since performing evil yields an evil retribution, the wise abandon it accordingly.
Evil deeds do not perish; all evil has its retribution.
Evil is acquired through performance, for performance arises from the mind.
Because of the mind one performs evil, and because of the mind there is retribution.
All things are created by the mind; all things are caused by the mind.
The mind can deceive sentient beings, leading them toward evil realms.
This place of hell is an evil realm, and it is the most painful and wretched of places.
Do not be bound by the mind; one should always act in accordance with the Dharma.
Acting in accordance with the Dharma brings constant joy, whereas evil conduct lacks tranquility.
Unrighteousness yields no good fruit; therefore, receive [the teachings] without error.
All various kinds of fruits are seen to resemble their causes;
as the fruit resembles its cause, that which has a different characteristic is not cause and effect.
Thus, all impermanent phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
One does not see the fruit without a cause; it is most severe within hell.
Just as cause and effect correspond, one is boiled and cooked within hell.
Having accumulated karma that is firm and hard, one will certainly proceed to an evil destination.
Bound by the continuity of the fruits of karma, one is boiled and cooked within hell.
If one employs the means of repentance, evil karma is destroyed;
thus one does not see the undesirable fruit—so it is taught by those who see reality.
The world exists because of light, just as one obtains fruit because of karma;
karma and its fruit are mutual causes for one another—all phenomena are thus.
Seeing these reciprocal conditions, they proceed with mutual independence.
"Similarity, conformity, and bondage—this is what those who see reality have taught.
All worldly phenomena are not without cause and effect, nor are they created by a sovereign god (Īśvara) and so forth; this is what those who see reality have taught."
Since beginningless birth and death, all things arise through causes and conditions;
as one sees them according to their karma, there is no phenomenon that does not correspond [to its cause].
If one knows that the actions performed through craving give rise to the karma of sentient beings, [one understands that] they are born from the causes of karma.
That person who understands the fruit of karma is therefore called a person of tranquility.
One who commits evil with their own body is constantly bound by the snare of delusion;
having already completed the commission of evil deeds, why does the mind give rise to regret?
Evil always relies upon evil, and the Dharma always relies upon the Dharma;
the wise person abandons both—this is what those who see reality have taught.
If one is deluded regarding the path and the non-path, then one is deluded regarding the Buddha-Dharma.
They do not attain tranquility, just as there is no darkness in the midst of the sun.
If a person is deluded regarding causes and conditions, and is confused about what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma,
they will go to an evil hell, a place of extreme suffering and affliction.

After the Yama-wardens have rebuked him with words appropriate to his deeds, they again seize their halberds and spears; with minds full of wrath, they further bind the hell-beings with immeasurable varieties of weapons. For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *padma* aeons, they cut, pierce, strike, and crush them for a vast duration—suffering thus as the result of their own karma.
As long as the accumulated evil and unwholesome karma has not been destroyed or decayed, and its karmic potency has not been exhausted, suffering will continue without ceasing at all times;
only when that evil karma is exhausted will one finally be liberated from that place of hell.

Once they have attained liberation from that state, for seven hundred lifetimes they will be born among the hungry ghosts who feed on excrement and urine; this is the residual power of that evil karma.
If they escape from there, for five hundred lifetimes they will be born among animals as earthworms and the like; this is the remaining fruit of retribution from the power of that karma.

Having been released from that place, if one is born among humans in a realm of similar karma, one will be born in a borderland with a black body, belonging to the class of fishermen in low-lying marshes where there is no food in the paddy fields; food and drink are difficult to obtain, and one eats insects found in the water.
This is the residual karmic retribution of those evil deeds.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, observes the location of the Great Avīci Hell and sees no seventeenth place; neither below, nor to the sides, nor in coarse or subtle forms, nor near or far—there is nothing further to be encompassed, and he sees nothing at all.
That bhikṣu reflects in this way—observing the limit of exhaustion through the contemplation of the path:

the eight great hells, each with sixteen subsidiary locations; such is the limit of exhaustion, the ground for those who have committed evil karma, where all foolish worldlings have accumulated their deeds, and the place where those who have performed evil karma receive retribution.

Among the eight great hells and their subsidiary realms, I have never seen another great hell, nor another place of birth resulting from a different type of karma; there is no place of evil such as this Avīci Great Hell where sentient beings undergo such immense suffering!
Regarding such a place as the Great Avīci Hell, the Hair-Raising Hell cannot even be described as a single part out of a thousand. Why is this?
It cannot be fully told, it cannot be heard, and it is beyond all analogy.

The suffering and affliction in hell is thus extremely evil, thus hard and rigid, thus great suffering, thus unbearable, and thus an affliction such that there is nothing else similar to it; its pain cannot be compared by any analogy.
Why is this? There is no one who can speak it, and there is no one who can hear it.
If there were anyone to speak it or anyone to hear it, such a person would vomit blood and die.
"This great hell is unpleasant and not to be remembered; its sufferings are the most grievous among all sufferings.

When that bhikṣu has thus observed the great hells, his mind gives rise to weary detachment toward all the suffering and affliction of birth and death. Observing impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, he sees that all phenomena are entirely impermanent. Contemplating the Noble Truths, he again gives rise to weary detachment toward birth and death and reviles birth and death.
Such is birth and death, most base and evil.
Having seen this, that bhikṣu gives rise to this thought:

"These sentient beings lack the divine eye and do not know the past; being deprived of hearing the True Dharma, they are reborn once again in the places of extreme suffering in hell—the foremost place of suffering, the foremost place of evil."
"Such foolish worldlings as these are bound by the snare of craving throughout beginningless birth and death.

Furthermore, the practitioner reflects within his mind—contemplating the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the True Dharma—and knows that the bhikṣu has sequentially observed all the evil realms, from the Reviving Hell up to the Avīci Hell, fully understanding all the karmic retributions therein. Having attained the thirteenth stage, he takes no pleasure in the realm of Māra; craving no longer holds him in its power. To be liberated from the bonds of craving, he does not dwell in the realm of Māra, which delights in impermanence.
That bhikṣu, desiring to sever the fetters and latent tendencies and enter the city of Nirvāṇa, was observed by the yakṣas of that region.
Seeing his diligence, they conceived joy in their hearts and, in turn, reported it upward to the yakṣas of the void, who spoke these words:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a village, there is a son of good family of such-and-such a clan and such-and-such a name. Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he has gone forth out of right faith. He practices the right path with right conduct and right view, free from perversity; he walks the supramundane way, understands the law of karmic retribution, attains the thirteenth stage, and fully perceives the depths and boundaries of all hells, knowing the suffering of the Avīci hell."
The terrestrial yakṣas thus fully transmitted the report to the celestial yakṣas, and the celestial yakṣas reported it to the Four Great Kings, just as previously described.

Those Four Great Kings spoke thus to the Four Heavenly Kings; those Four Heavenly Kings spoke thus to the Heaven of the Thirty-three; the Heaven of the Thirty-three spoke thus to the Yāma Heaven; that Yāma Heaven spoke thus to the Tuṣita Heaven; that Tuṣita Heaven spoke thus to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and that Nirmāṇarati Heaven spoke thus to the sixth heaven. In this manner, it proceeded successively until reaching the Parīttābha Heaven, where they spoke these words: "O Devas, listen now!
One should maintain right mindfulness:

"In such-and-such a country and such-and-such a village within Jambudvīpa, a son of good family of such-and-such a lineage has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and with right faith gone forth from the household life. He practices the Dharma correctly without ever ceasing; his mind takes no delight in dwelling within the realm of Māra, nor does it delight in defiled attachment or the taints of desire regarding the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Having attained the thirteenth stage, he fully knows all karmic retributions of the eight great hells."
Having understood this, that bhikṣu becomes weary of and detached from the darkness of ignorance and the cycle of birth and death.
O Deva, you should now know:
the faction of Māra is diminished, and the True Dharma increases.
Having heard this, those gods of Limited Radiance were filled with supreme joy.
They rejoiced because they had heard that the faction of Māra was diminishing and the assembly of the True Dharma was increasing.
The gods in that place hear the true Dharma and are thus filled with joy.

If even those gods who have not previously heard the Buddha’s teachings feel such joy upon hearing it, how much more so would those who follow with faith, those practitioners who accord with the truth, and those noble beings of right view—not rejoice when they hear that monk teaching the law of karmic retribution and increasing the true Dharma?
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Fifteen, the "Hell Chapter," concludes.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Sixteen,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Four: On the Hungry Ghosts (16–17), Part One.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, surveys everywhere the ocean of suffering in the hells, which is submerged by the swirling eddies of the torrential waters of craving.

The inhabitants of the great hells, such as Pūraṇa and Makkhali, Kokālika and Devadatta—these beings are like fish swallowed by the great makara; from the Sañjīva hell down to the Avīci hell, those hells are vast, like the deep waters of the Voca-jvālā.

And in the great ocean of suffering of the other hells, there are the timi fish, the timingila fish, the nakara fish, the kumbhira fish, the śiśumāra fish, as well as turtles, tortoises, soft-shelled turtles, and crocodiles, circling in eddies and whirlpools.

Driven and tossed by the force of the winds of greed, hatred, and delusion, with surging waves and turbulent eddies flowing together, it is at times like water-foam; one undergoes great suffering and affliction, with tears falling like rain, wailing, weeping, lamenting, and moaning, crying out in bitter pain like crashing billows, as the waves of sorrow and anxiety overwhelm them.
By the power of these evil-karma dragons, they rain down great rains of suffering that fill all the hells.

The Avīci Hell is uninterrupted and exceedingly deep; its flames are so fierce that they resemble the fires at the end of an eon when the Great Kalpa is consumed. These fires fill Mount Cakravāḍa (translated in Wei as "Wheel Mountain," which is the Iron Ring Mountain), constituting the great ocean of suffering and affliction within the great hells.
Those who are weak and inferior lack the power of virtue and are unable to cross over.

Having thus contemplated great suffering, the bhikṣu’s mind becomes weary and detached, and he speaks in verse (*gāthā*—the correct pronunciation of which is *gāthā*; the single character *gā* was corrupted into *jiè*, and in the Wei language it is called *sòng*):
"All sentient beings are deceived by delusion, Bound by the fetters of craving and defilement."
When one approaches the perilous path of the world, that place of terror where old age and death provide no refuge;
having passed away from the three [fortunate] realms, one enters hell; having emerged from hell, one is born in the heavens.
When life ends in those three realms, one falls among the animals; again, when life ends there, one falls among the hungry ghosts.
Deluded by their own evil karma, beings are driven by the mastery of various desires;
ensnared by the net of ignorance, they wander in the swirling currents of the ocean of the three realms.
Having long endured great suffering since time without beginning, And the various sufferings of birth and death for all sentient beings,
They lack the mind of weary detachment from saṃsāra, Because of causes and conditions accumulated since time without beginning.
The gods, through negligence, ruin their own minds; Humans pursue desires and undergo various sufferings;
Hungry ghosts are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst; Animals prey upon one another in turn.
Within the hells are great, fierce fires; in the realm of hungry ghosts, beings are tormented by delusion.
Amidst the birth and death of all sentient beings, not even a hair’s breadth of slight happiness can be found.
Conceiving the notion of pleasure amidst all sufferings, sentient beings are deluded by ignorance and deceived by craving;
lacking anyone to instruct them in the right path, they cannot escape from this suffering.
If one distances oneself from wholesome dharmas, constantly practices falsehood without sincerity or faith,
and is unable to cultivate the methods of meditative concentration, one will long remain submerged in birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering.
The Dharma taught by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, whether in the present or in future ages, surpasses that of parents and kinsmen; it constantly follows sentient beings and never departs from them.
Sentient beings of the three categories are always dominated by the three kinds of faults;
they constantly traverse the three realms without ceasing, taking the three kinds of sensation as their companions.
The three karmas delude sentient beings, causing them to travel the perilous paths of the three evil realms;
they constantly delight in the activities of the three realms of existence, revolving within the phenomena of the three realms.
If there are sentient beings who take refuge in the Triple Gem, Who practice freely for the sake of the three types of enlightenment,
And sever and distance themselves from the three kinds of views, Such persons shall be free from all suffering.
Delighting in right practice throughout the three periods of the day, observing the three kinds of aging as they truly are,
and knowing moderation in food and drink— a person such as this is able to leave behind sorrow and affliction.
Transcending the three aggregates of greed, hatred, and delusion, one who reflects well on the three karmas and does not commit evil—
such a practitioner leaves behind the suffering of birth and forever severs all anxieties and fevers.
If a person knows what is the path and what is not the path, and skillfully contemplates existence and non-existence,
being able to properly cultivate and train in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, then they shall attain the foremost and most supreme path.
If there are sentient beings who are not turbid or distracted, whose minds are always pure and unstained,
and who are able to leave behind all unwholesome and evil dharmas— know that such persons have attained liberation.

If there is one who can practice the right path, because their power of right mindfulness is firm and stable, they will always delight in remaining far removed from all states of existence; such a person will undoubtedly attain liberation.
If a person can sever craving for existence and does not give rise to a mind of longing for existence,
that person will not produce even the slightest attachment toward the suffering of birth, old age, and death.
If there are fools who create various karmas, having committed various evils, they only cause them to increase further;
all desires are like poison and cannot be approached—those with wisdom should abandon them.
If a person abandons all desires and their mind constantly delights in seeking the fruit of liberation,
that person’s unwholesome states are extinguished without remainder, just as sunlight dispels the darkness.
One who thus draws near to wholesome dharmas constantly abandons all that is unwholesome;
they are able to skillfully contemplate the pure and the impure—know this to be a brief explanation.
"In this way, a bhikṣu should keep in mind this world and the other world for the benefit of wisdom.

Once his mind has so reflected, he should benefit the entire world with wisdom; observing the suffering of the hells, he should contemplate all sentient beings and give rise to a heart of compassion, practicing loving-kindness and compassion."
Having thoroughly observed all the places in the hells that are oppressed by fear and suffering, he understands the retribution of karma.
Having understood the retribution of karma, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and further reflects:
"How is it that these sentient beings sink into various evil realms of great terror and wander within the wilderness of saṃsāra?"

Thus, the bhikṣu reflects in this way and gives rise to a heart of compassion. He understands that the karmic retribution of the realm of hungry ghosts is a perilous and evil state resulting from mental greed and envy, deceiving others, hoarding wealth out of greedy attachment with a desire for long-term prosperity, and extensively accumulating various evils.

Enshrouded by wicked greed, they do not practice giving; they do not bestow gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the sick and emaciated, the blind, or the impoverished. When there are those who come to beg, they give rise to stinginess and envy, refusing to grant anything. They perform no meritorious deeds and do not uphold the precepts; thus, in both this world and the next, they suffer decline and affliction. Being stingy toward their wives, children, servants, and slaves, they refuse to share with them, deceiving themselves through their own envy and parsimony.
For these reasons, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Women are often reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts. Why is this?

The nature of women is such that their minds are often full of envy and jealousy; even before their husbands have complied with their wishes, they give rise to feelings of resentment. For this reason, women are frequently reborn within the realm of hungry ghosts.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). Where do these hungry ghosts dwell?
Having made this contemplation, he then uses the wisdom derived from hearing to observe that there are, briefly, two kinds of hungry ghosts."
What are these two?
First, dwelling among humans;
second, dwelling in the realm of hungry ghosts.
These are ghosts among humans; if people travel at night, some may see them.

As for the world of hungry ghosts (preta), it lies five hundred yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa and extends thirty-six thousand yojanas in length. Together with their retinues from other evil realms of hungry ghosts, they are immeasurable in number and possess a vast amount of evil karma. Residing in Jambudvīpa, they are situated both near and far.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the various types of hungry ghosts (preta), which are immeasurable in kind.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he briefly contemplates thirty-six types of hungry ghosts.

All hungry ghosts are born in that place due to the causes and conditions of stinginess, greed, and envy; with various minds they create various karmas and perform various deeds, dwelling in various abodes and burning their own bodies with various forms of hunger and thirst—thus, briefly stated, there are thirty-six kinds.
What are the thirty-six kinds?
First is the *kapāli*, the cauldron-bodied hungry ghost;
second is the *sūcimukha*, the needle-mouthed hungry ghost.
Third are the *pāṇḍapāśa*, hungry ghosts who eat vomit;
fourth are the *viṣṭhāda*, hungry ghosts who eat excrement;
fifth are the *apāśa*, hungry ghosts who have no food.
Sixth are the gandharvas, hungry ghosts who feed on odors;
seventh are the dharmapākṣas, hungry ghosts who feed on vomit;
eighth are the pāriplavas, hungry ghosts who feed on water.
Ninth are the āśāka, hungry ghosts who long for [food];
tenth are the kheṭapiṇḍa, hungry ghosts who eat spittle;
eleventh are the mālyabhakṣa, hungry ghosts who eat garlands.
Twelfth are the *rakṣasa*, hungry ghosts who feed on blood;
thirteenth are the *maṃsapākṣa*, hungry ghosts who feed on flesh;
fourteenth are the *sugandha*, hungry ghosts who feed on the smoke of incense.
Fifteenth are the *abhi-cara*, the swiftly moving hungry ghosts;
sixteenth are the *cit-tara*, the hungry ghosts who watch for opportunities;
seventeenth are the *pātāla*, the hungry ghosts of the subterranean realm.
The eighteenth is Ardi, the hungry ghost with supernatural powers;
the nineteenth is Javali, the blazing hungry ghost;
the twentieth is Citra, the hungry ghost who watches for the vulnerability of infants.
Twenty-first are the Kākuloma, the hungry ghosts of desire and form;
twenty-second are the Samudratīpa, the hungry ghosts of the ocean islands;
twenty-third are the messengers of King Yama, the hungry ghosts who wield staves.
Twenty-fourth are the *Bharabhaṭṭa*, hungry ghosts who devour small children;
twenty-fifth are the *Uśubhaṭṭa*, hungry ghosts who consume the vital essence of humans;
twenty-sixth are the *Brāhmaṇa-rākṣasa* hungry ghosts.
Twenty-seventh are the *kuntāpāhuka* hungry ghosts, who consume burnt food;
twenty-eighth are the *aśuparata* hungry ghosts, who dwell in impure streets and alleys;
twenty-ninth are the *vayubhakṣa* hungry ghosts, who subsist on wind.
The thirty-second is the Aṅgārāśana preta, who feeds on glowing embers;
the thirty-first is the Viṣāśana preta, who feeds on poison;
and the thirty-second is the Āṭavika preta, who dwells in the wilderness.
Thirty-third are the Śmaśānikas, hungry ghosts who dwell among burial mounds and eat hot ashes and soil;
thirty-fourth are the Vairūpakas, hungry ghosts who dwell within trees;
thirty-fifth are the Cāṭaputras, hungry ghosts at the crossroads.
The thirty-sixth are the *māra-kāya*, the hungry ghosts who kill their own bodies.

This is a brief explanation of the thirty-six kinds of hungry ghosts; if explained extensively, they are immeasurable. Having committed evil with a heavy heart, their karmic actions differ from one another; due to various types of stinginess and failing to practice giving, they receive these various bodies through the conditions of a greedy mind.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the various hungry ghosts (preta), who suffer from great hunger and thirst that burn their own bodies.

Because in previous lives they frequently gave rise to envy and jealousy, destroyed others with malicious intent, and extensively committed the three types of unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind—the ten non-virtuous actions—they were born among the hungry ghosts."

Because that person has committed the ten unwholesome paths of action as causes and conditions, they experience all manner of suffering; due to their evil karma, they are born among the hungry ghosts.
Drawn by evil karma and with karma as the root, they enter the evil realms and are bound by them.

Because of karma as their cause, they do not escape birth and death; for since time immemorial, the monkey-like mind has been restless, agitated, and fickle, wandering through perilous and obstructed places, grasping at various nets and branches, swiftly coming and going, dwelling upon the mountain of birth and death, and sleeping within its rocky caves, such that the path it travels cannot be perceived.
One should contemplate the mind as a monkey, swift and restless; in this way, one should first subdue the mind.
If the mind is not subdued, it can lead sentient beings to places of great terror and cause them to undergo immense suffering;
such an enemy that is the mind causes sentient beings to wander through the cycle of birth and death.
When the bhikṣu has thus reflected in his mind, he attains detachment from the defilements within saṃsāra and becomes weary of the suffering of saṃsāra, reflecting:
"All of saṃsāra is entirely suffering and affliction."
Thus the bhikṣu reflects and analyzes, seeing that among the hungry ghosts there are immeasurable varieties.

Having reflected thus, he analyzes each one individually, observing that the retributions of karma do not arise without cause; that suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, purity and impurity, good and evil, nobility and meanness, high and low, birth and extinction—all these diverse categories do not arise spontaneously.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the various hungry ghosts, knowing the retribution of karma through the wisdom derived from hearing. How does he contemplate the *kapāla-śarīra* (skull-bodied) hungry ghost?

Their bodies are twice as tall as those of ordinary men; they have no faces or eyes, and their hands and feet are perforated like the legs of a cauldron. Within them, blazing fires burn their bodies as if consuming a forest; tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they are bound by the retribution of their time. No one can save them; they have no refuge and no protector, beset by sorrow, anxiety, and suffering, with no one to offer them rescue or protection.
By what karma was he born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

in a previous life, this sentient being, out of greed for wealth, slaughtered others for hire; he received payment to kill living beings, carving and slicing their fat and flesh with no compassion in his heart.
With a greedy mind, one kills living beings; having killed them, one rejoices in the act, thereby accumulating evil karma without any remorse in the heart.

Such an evil person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls into the evil realms and receives the body of a *kapāli* hungry ghost—*kapālika* meaning "cauldron-bodied" in the Wei language—dwelling five hundred *yojanas* beneath the earth.

When their life here ends, they suddenly pass away and are reborn in a place of great terror and darkness. Once reborn there, two mountains—one above and one below—simultaneously close together, crushing their bodies and causing them intense suffering. Their bodies grow ever larger until they fill an entire yojana, and they are scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst within the realm of hungry ghosts for five hundred years.
One day and night in the realm of hungry ghosts corresponds to ten years by the calculation of days, months, and years in this Jambudvīpa.
A lifespan of five hundred such years constitutes one lifetime; it rarely exceeds this and mostly falls short, so the duration of life is also uncertain.
Furthermore, the second karma leading to rebirth among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) is as follows:
if there are sentient beings who receive deposits from others but refuse to return them, they will be born in that place.

Those who do not give material wealth, do not give the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), and do not give the gift of fearlessness—whether male or female—if they do not practice these three kinds of giving and constantly harbor stinginess and envy, [they will fall into this state].
By these causes and conditions, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the hungry ghosts.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the hungry ghosts with needle-like mouths and considers by what karma they are born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the *suji-muqie* (魏: "needle-mouthed") hungry ghosts and knows:

these sentient beings, in their previous lives, hired others with wealth to carry out killings; they were stingy, greedy, and envious; they did not practice giving, nor did they give food or clothing, nor did they give the gift of fearlessness, nor did they give the gift of the Dharma.

When such an evil person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they receive the body of a needle-mouthed hungry ghost (*preta*). Having received this ghostly body, they are deceived by their own karma; the body they have received has a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a great mountain. They constantly harbor grief and affliction as the fires of hunger and thirst burn their bodies. They undergo various internal sufferings, while externally they are tormented by cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, noxious insects, fevers, and other maladies.
Thus, while their bodies and minds undergo various sufferings, one day and night in the realm of hungry ghosts corresponds to ten years by the reckoning of human days, months, and years.
Receiving such a lifespan, they remain for five hundred years, yet even this life span is not fixed; sons or daughters may be born among them.
Furthermore, by a second karma, one falls into this realm of the hungry ghosts with needle-like mouths:
if there is a man who commands his wife to give food as alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
His wife was stingy and, though things were actually there, she claimed they were not;
she said to her husband, "There is nothing at all in the house—what do we have to give to the śramaṇas and the various practitioners?"

"In this way, such a woman deceives her husband; being stingy with wealth, she does not practice giving. When her body perishes and her life ends, she falls among the hungry ghosts with needle-mouths.
Because she has habitually accumulated many evil karmas, women are frequently reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts."
Why is this? Because women have much greed, desire, envy, and jealousy, they do not equal men;
because women have narrow minds and frivolous minds, they do not equal men.
By these causes and conditions, they are born among the hungry ghosts.
As long as their karma of jealousy has not been exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape from among the hungry ghosts;
only when that karma is exhausted can they escape. Having died there, they are then born among the animals.

Among the animals, they take birth in the body of a *caṭaka* bird; this bird eats only the rain from heaven, catching the rainwater with its upturned beak to drink it, for it cannot eat any other water. It is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, undergoing great suffering and distress.

Dying among the animals and being reborn among humans, due to the remaining effects of their karma, they are constantly distressed by hunger and thirst; their suffering is inexhaustible, and they must constantly beg for food to sustain themselves.
"Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the fruits of karma observes the various hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who feed on vomit, considering by what karma these sentient beings receive the body of a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being was a woman who deceived her husband; she consumed fine food for herself while harboring stinginess and jealousy in her heart, hating her own child and refusing to give anything to him.
Or there was a man whose wife was free of ulterior motives, yet he gave rise to jealousy and ate delicious food alone, not sharing it with his wife or children.

Due to these causes and conditions, they fall among the *panta* hungry ghosts—*panta-bakṣa*, which in the Wei language means "eaters of vomit"—and, having received the body of a hungry ghost, their bodies are constantly scorched by hunger and thirst.
His body was vast, measuring half a yojana in length; in the wilderness, he ran frantically in all four directions seeking water and drink, crying out in a loud voice, "I am hungry! I am thirsty!"

Because these sentient beings, in their previous lives, did not practice the giving of material wealth or the fearlessness-giving, nor did they practice the giving of the Dharma, by reason of these causes and conditions, they are born among the hungry ghosts. Their lifespan is extremely long, as described above; for five hundred years, and until their evil karma is exhausted, unbroken and undestroyed, they shall never attain liberation.
Among the *vāntāśin* spirits (those who eat vomit), they constantly seek to vomit, yet are exhausted and unable to obtain it.
When their lives there end, they are reborn among animals, where they likewise constantly consume vomit and undergo the suffering of hunger and thirst.

Having died among animals and been reborn among humans, due to the remaining causes and conditions of their karma, they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst; in the streets and alleys, they always gather discarded leftovers left by worldly people, or they sustain themselves by begging from śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
"Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the fruit of karma observes the various hungry ghosts (preta).
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:"

In their previous lives, these sentient beings frequently practiced greed and envy; they were constantly harboring stinginess and failed to practice giving. They offered impure food to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, being unaware that it was impure, consumed it.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when this person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms and are born among the hungry ghosts who feed on excrement. Their lifespan, as previously described, is also five hundred years; their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst, yet even as they search for filth and impurities, they cannot find any.

Due to the power of their karma, they are never able to follow their own hearts' desires; in impure places filled with maggots, excrement, and filth, they run about searching for food yet are never satisfied, enduring constant suffering and affliction until the end of their lives.
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape;

only when their evil karma is exhausted do they pass away from there, wandering through saṃsāra according to their karma and undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log, and thus they undergo various evil forms of existence.

If born among humans, they will be poor and frequently ill, constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, perpetually begging for their morning meal to sustain their lives. They will be adorned with immeasurable signs of decay and evil; their bodies will be cracked, impure, and foul-smelling, loathed and despised by others. Their breath will be rank and acrid, and their teeth will be stained black.
Due to the causal conditions of residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the realm of hungry ghosts characterized by stinginess and envy.
All hungry ghosts have stinginess and envy as their root. By what karma are these sentient beings born among the hungry ghosts who receive no food? Through the wisdom gained from hearing, they know:

in their previous lives, these hungry ghosts, because of stinginess and envy, obscured their own minds with falsehoods and deception; relying on their own strength, they falsely accused the virtuous, cast them into prison, and withheld grain and food from others, causing them to die. Having killed them, they felt satisfaction and felt no regret; they took pleasure in the act and further taught others to do the same. Having committed such evil karma, they did not repent at first.

Thus, when such evil persons die and their lives end, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts who have no food. Whether male or female, once born therein, the fires of hunger and thirst increase and blaze fiercely with the force of surging waves from a mountain torrent. Fires arise within their bellies, burning their bodies until nothing remains; once extinguished, they are born again, and once born, they are burned once more.
There are two kinds of suffering that incinerate their bodies:
first, hunger and thirst;
second, being burned by fire.
Oppressed by suffering, that person wails and cries out in grief and distress, running hither and thither in all directions; the inconceivable evil fruits of one’s own karma are thus experienced.

In this way, the person undergoes internal and external suffering; every part of their body is scorched by the fires of karma, and fire issues from within the body to consume its own form, like a great tree that is hollow and dry within.

If a person throws fire upon them so that it blazes fiercely, this hungry ghost is likewise scorched; their entire body is ablaze as they wail and weep piteously, with fire erupting from their mouths. Two flames arise together to incinerate their bodies as they panic and seek a way out. Thorns sprout from the ground, all of them burning with fire, piercing their two feet with unbearable agony. They shriek and lament as the fire burns their tongues until they are completely melted and rotted away, like burnt solid butter, only to be reborn again once extinguished.
Due to their evil karma, they run about seeking water at various ponds, streams, springs, and sources, yet the water is instantly dried up.

Because of the evil karma of those people, when they reach places for recreation in the forest—whether on high plateaus or in marshy wetlands—their perceptions are inverted; they see only great, fierce flames everywhere, and the mountains, earth, trees, and forests all appear ablaze.

As they approach various bodies of water, they see yakṣas guarding the waters at the riverbanks who seize them with weapons in their hands and strike them on the head, causing them to undergo great suffering and distress; all this is due to being deceived and deluded by the resentment of greed and envy in their previous lives.
Their lifespan is long, lasting five hundred years, as described above.

Due to such evil karma, they constantly have nothing to eat; yet because their evil karma is not exhausted, they do not die. As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape. When their karma is exhausted, they may escape;

then, at the end of that life, blown by their evil karma, they transmigrate according to their deeds and undergo the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just as it is for a blind turtle to encounter the hole of a floating wooden plank in the ocean.

If one is born among humans, while dwelling in the mother’s womb, the mother will be unable to eat, causing her physical complexion to become haggard and unsightly; due to the karma of killing, the fetus may suffer injury or miscarry.
Should they not die in the womb, it will cause the mother’s body to become foul-smelling and loathsome, and she will take pleasure in practicing unwholesome deeds;
if they are born, they will be short-lived and encounter many hardships, facing royal punishment and imprisonment, suffering in prison, and dying of hunger and thirst.
"Due to residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who feed on odors, and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being consumed many fine foods for himself alone, without giving any to his wife, children, or other relatives. His wife and children could only smell the fragrance but did not know its flavor, as he ate them all by himself before their eyes.

Out of stinginess and envy, he did not give to his kinsmen who shared the same karma, nor did he encourage others to provide for their wives and children; instead, he rejoiced in such behavior. He repeatedly committed these transgressions without repentance, feeling no shame or remorse.
Thus, when such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts who feed on odors.

Once reborn, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst; they run hither and thither, groaning and wailing, weeping and suffering in bitter grief. They rely solely upon the fragrances from stūpas and shrines, or from offerings provided by those with faith, subsisting on that scent or the residual odors thereof to sustain their lives.

Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts who subsist on odors; because worldly people frequently suffer from illnesses, they set out various sacrificial offerings by the water, in forests, in alleys, and at crossroads, and these ghosts sustain their lives by means of the fragrances thereof.

Thus, these hungry ghosts who subsist on the scent of food endure immeasurable suffering and affliction; because their evil karma is not exhausted, they are prevented from dying. As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot attain liberation. Only when their karma is exhausted do they attain liberation;

then, at the end of this life, they transmigrate according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just like a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating wooden plank.
If born among humans, they will be impoverished, frequently ill, and their bodies foul-smelling and filthy.
Due to the remainder of their karma, they undergo such retribution.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who subsist on the dharma; how do they maintain their bodies and possess power through the causal conditions of the dharma, and by what karma are they born therein?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that when this hungry ghost was among humans, his nature was characterized by much greed and envy; for the sake of sustaining his own life or seeking wealth and profit, he preached the Dharma to others with a lack of reverence in his heart, violating the precepts and lacking faith, not for the purpose of taming sentient beings.
They preach impure doctrines, saying:
"By killing living beings, one obtains the merit of rebirth in heaven";
they forcibly seize wealth, claiming there is no karmic retribution for such acts.
By giving a daughter in marriage, one gains great merit; likewise is it with releasing a bull-king.
Preaching such impure dharmas as these to others, he obtains wealth for his own maintenance, yet he does not practice giving, but instead hoards and accumulates it.
Because this person’s mind was shrouded by such jealousy, at the end of their life they were reborn in the evil realms, receiving the body of a *dharmabhakṣa* hungry ghost.
This person’s lifespan lasts five hundred years, and the length of its days and months is as described above.

In a place of peril and hardship, they run hither and thither seeking food and drink; their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst, and none can save them. They are like dry wood being consumed by fire; their hair is disheveled and their body hair is exceedingly long; their bodies are emaciated with veins like a network; fat and flesh have vanished, leaving skin and bone pressed against one another; their bodies are tall and large, rigid and coarse, with long and sharp claws and nails.

Deceived by their evil karma, with wrinkled faces and deep-set eyes, they shed tears like rain; their complexions are as dark and murky as black clouds, and malevolent insects devour every part of their bodies, while mosquitoes, gadflies, and black worms enter through their pores to eat the flesh of their bodies.

Terrified and fleeing in haste, if they reach a monastery where someone comes to offer two kinds of gifts among the assembly of monks, and because of those offerings the elder preaches the Dharma and others praise the preaching of the Dharma;
by this means, these hungry ghosts obtain life and strength, and their lives are sustained.
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted—neither destroyed nor decayed—they shall never attain liberation.

Only when their karma is exhausted will they be liberated; having passed away from there, because of the various karmas created with various states of mind in previous lives, they will take birth in various places. A human body is difficult to obtain, like a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.

If born among humans, they will constantly serve as Brahmins who guard celestial shrines, performing animal sacrifices by slaughtering sheep to worship the gods; they will act as sorcerers for dragons, lacking self-mastery, and must always depend on others for alms to sustain their lives.
Due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, they fall back into hell because of their residual karma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who subsist on water, considering by what karma they were born therein.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these hungry ghosts, in their previous lives, had their minds shrouded by evil greed; they brewed and sold fermented liquors, deceiving the world by adding water or alkaline ash, or even sinking earthworms and moths into them to delude simpletons. They did not practice giving, nor cultivate merit, nor observe the precepts, nor listen to the True Dharma, nor practice the True Dharma. Furthermore, they taught others to engage in such evil greed, rejoiced in seeing it done, and felt no remorse after having committed it.

Due to such evil karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts who feed on water. Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst that burn their bodies, they run through desolate wildernesses and perilous places, wandering in distress seeking water, yet remain exhausted and unable to find it.

His body’s appearance was hard, coarse, and loathsome like parched salt-encrusted earth; his body was cracked and broken, with flames blazing from every limb. Long hair covered his face so that he could not see, and as his body burned with hunger and thirst, he ran toward the riverbank.
If a person crosses a river, there may be drops of water remaining beneath their feet, with mud and grime dripping from them;

if they quickly catch these to sustain their own lives, and if another person, standing by the riverbank, scoops up water to offer to deceased parents, then that other person obtains only a small portion.
By these causes and conditions, one's life is sustained.

If one takes water for oneself, the various ghosts who guard the water will strike one with clubs; the skin of one's body will be flayed off, and the pain is so unbearable that one cries out in lamentation and runs along the riverbank.

Because they have performed evil deeds and thus deceived their own bodies, the bonds of karma remain inexhaustible, which prevents them from dying; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape. Only when their karma is exhausted do they attain liberation.

Upon passing away from there, driven by the winds of karma, they transmigrate through birth and death; it is difficult to obtain a human body, just as it is for a blind turtle to encounter the hole of a floating wooden plank in the ocean.

If they are born among humans, they will be born in remote borderlands, impoverished and beset by hardship, dwelling in places devoid of forests or water; they will constantly suffer from parching thirst, perpetually afflicted by heat-related illnesses, and remain thirsty day and night.
Due to the remnants of their karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes that there are hungry ghosts named Āśā (translated in Wei as "Hungry Ghosts of Hope"). By what karma are they born therein?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows: These sentient beings are envious and possess evil greed; they conceal their own minds. Seeing other virtuous people obtain even a small amount of goods through trade or barter, they do not act with integrity but instead deceive them to take the goods. Having done so, they rejoice in their actions and feel no remorse. Furthermore, they teach others to commit such evils. They do not practice giving, do not cultivate merit, and do not uphold the precepts. Their minds lack sincerity and faith, and they do not accord with the True Dharma. Their minds are coarse and wild, impossible to subdue; they do not associate with virtuous friends and constantly harbor envy.

Thus, when such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall among the *preta*s of longing. If people of the world perform memorial rites for the spirits of deceased parents, these *preta*s may obtain and eat such offerings, but they cannot eat any other food at all. Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, their bodies are scorched like a forest on fire, yet there is no one to rescue them. Their faces are wrinkled and blackened, tears flow down, their hands and feet are cracked, their hair covers their faces, and the color of their bodies is as loathsome as a dark cloud.
Uttering a bitter and sorrowful cry, he spoke this verse:
“Without giving there is no reward; Without giving, there is no fruit either.
Just as there is no light without a lamp, Without giving, there is no joyful retribution.”
Just as a blind person without eyes cannot see anything, so it is with one who does not practice giving:
there will be no joyful retribution in future lives.
If such a person is born into the realm of hungry ghosts, they will always be impoverished among human beings.
They wander through saṃsāra, suffering affliction, due to the causes and conditions of envy.
Without giving, there is no reward; the karma one creates is never lost.
One receives the fruit of one’s own karma; sentient beings subsist upon their karma as food.
Burned by my own evil karma, I have been born among the hungry ghosts;
suffering from this great hunger and thirst, fierce fires constantly blaze within me.
When shall I be freed from this hunger and thirst?
When shall we attain peace and happiness?
We suffer under the extreme heat of affliction; when shall we attain liberation?
We do not distinguish between the path and what is not the path, nor do we know the fruits of wholesome karma.
Hunger and thirst burn like fire; thus they suffer distress.
Tangled hair covers their faces and eyes, and no one can provide protection.
Veins appear like a binding net; though pressed by suffering, their lives do not end.
“Pacing anxiously through the vast wilderness, they constantly suffer various afflictions;
solitary and without protection, they endure all manner of hardships.
Thus do these hungry ghosts, sighing in longing, run about, fleeing everywhere.
Having observed this, the bhikṣu reflects:
"Birth and death are ablaze, and the realm of desire is predominant.

Such hungry ghosts, if their lineage occasionally performs offerings and sacrifices for the deceased, may obtain and eat them to sustain their lives; they can only eat these, and all other kinds of food they are entirely unable to consume."
Because their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they are made not to die; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape.

When their evil karma is exhausted, they pass away from there and, blown by the winds of karma, transmigrate through the world, undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just like a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating wooden plank.
If they are born among humans, they are born into the households of craftsmen as lowly servants, being driven and commanded by others.
Due to the causes and conditions of their remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts.

With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who consume saliva and spittle, and by what karma they were born therein. With the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows: these beings—whether men or women—had their minds shrouded by stinginess and envy;

they deceived various renunciant śramaṇas and practitioners with impure food, claiming it was pure so that they would trust and eat it. At other times, they gave to those practicing purity food that was unfit for consumption. Having repeatedly committed this deed, they further taught others to practice such deception. They did not practice giving, nor did they uphold the prohibitions and precepts; they did not draw near to virtuous friends and did not accord with the True Dharma, delighting instead in holding impure things to give to others.

Thus, when such evil persons die and their lives end, they are reborn in the miserable realms, receiving the body of a *piśāca* hungry ghost—*piśāca* being the Wei (Northern Wei) term for "one who eats saliva" (*pi-cha*, pronounced with the *qiū-yī* rhyme)—whose bodies are constantly scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst. In impure places, whether on walls or on the ground, they seek out human saliva to eat in order to sustain their lives; they cannot obtain any other food whatsoever. As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape;
only when their karma is exhausted do they attain liberation. Having died from this state, they continue to transmigrate according to their karma, undergoing the sufferings of birth and death.

If born among humans, they will be poor and lowly, frequently ill and emaciated, with a runny and suppurating nose; they will be born into families that serve as latrines, or they will sustain their lives by begging for leftover food from the monastic community.
Due to the causes and conditions of residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).

With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the hungry ghosts known as Māra-āhāra-mālā—Māra being the term for "garland" in the Wei language; this refers to the Nine Sons of Māra worshipped by worldly people—and considers by what karma they are born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being stole flower garlands from the Buddha and from his respected teachers and elders. Because they were pure and clean, he used them to adorn himself; it was not out of malice, but because his mind was driven by greed and envy.

When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn either in a Buddhist stūpa or in a celestial shrine where they possess supernatural powers. If people engage in quarrels or disputes, these beings go to the stūpa and make a solemn vow; thus gaining an opportunity, they are able to manifest evil dreams to terrify the multitude.
If there are others who encounter various misfortunes and seek his grace and power, saying, "This yakṣa is a spirit of great majesty and supernatural powers," they offer him flower garlands.

Because of this act, he obtains food consisting of garlands; thus he is somewhat relieved from hunger and thirst and is not consumed by the fire of hunger. He is praised by the people of the world and is constantly delighted by the ghosts—this is the Garland-Eating Ghost (Mālāda).
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, not destroyed, and not decayed, they cannot escape;
once their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation. Thereafter, at the end of this life, they transmigrate according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death.
If born among humans, he becomes a gardener who sells flowers to support himself.
Due to the remnants of his karma, he receives such a retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who subsist by eating blood; by what karma were they born therein?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that when these hungry ghosts were originally human beings, they delighted in and craved food consisting of flesh and blood. Their minds were stingy and envious; they committed evil in jest, slaughtered living beings for bloody meals, and did not give even to their own wives and children.

When such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall into the evil realms; because of their craving for blood, they are born among the Rakṣasa hungry ghosts—*rakṣasa* meaning "blood-eater" in the Wei language. Having received this ghostly body, people all name them *yakṣas*, making offerings and serving them, and worshiping them by smearing mud with blood as a sacrifice.
Having consumed the blood, they instill terror in people and repeatedly demand offerings; everyone speaks of them and regards them as divine spirits.
In this manner, they successively manage to sustain their own lives.
Their lifespan is as long as described above, lasting five hundred years.

Thus, these hungry ghosts manifest various malevolent apparitions; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape. Once their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation;
having ended their lives from this state, they wander according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death.
If one obtains a human body, one is born into the family of a *caṇḍāla* and eats human flesh;
it is because of the remaining causes and conditions of evil karma that this occurs.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who eat flesh, considering by what karma they were born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these sentient beings were envious and possessed evil greed; they obscured their own minds and fashioned pieces of sentient beings' flesh into meat portions, weighing them out piece by piece. They engaged in buying and selling through deception, claiming much while possessing little, and treating the base as noble.
Thus, when such evil persons die and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born among the flesh-eating *preta*s.

These *yakṣa* spirits are born at crossroads, or in lanes, streets, markets, and shops; or within cities in the dwellings of monks or in shrines to the gods. Their forms are hideous and ugly, causing terror to those who see them, yet they possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
His nature was gentle and mild, and he did not often commit evil; yet, because he practiced impure giving, through these causes and conditions, he attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Because he provided assemblies for sentient beings by offering various kinds of meat—such as that of oxen, sheep, deer, and gazelles—to others, through the karmic conditions of this deed, he possesses divine power (*ṛddhibala*).
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape; only when their karma is exhausted can they escape.

Upon passing away from this life, they will wander according to their karma and undergo the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just like a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating wooden plank.

Possessing a slight amount of wholesome karma, they are born among human beings; yet, due to their remaining karmic conditions, they fall into remote borderlands as outcasts such as Caṇḍālas or barbarians, where they consume human flesh and receive this retribution.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who feed on the smoke of incense, and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

This sentient being, overwhelmed by a mind of envy and evil greed, is a merchant who sells incense. Seeing someone purchase incense for the purpose of making an offering, he does not give the superior incense to that buyer; instead, he gives inferior incense at a price that does not reflect its true value.
Lacking pure faith in his heart, he claims there is no retribution for evil deeds and fails to recognize the Buddhas as the true field of merit.

Thus, when such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they are reborn among the yakṣa spirits who feed on incense smoke; possessing supernatural powers, they wear fragrant garlands and are adorned with scented pastes and powdered incense, delighting themselves with music and song.

Or they may be born in divine shrines, at crossroads, within monasteries, amidst groves, or in places for recreation; they roam everywhere among multi-storied pavilions and watchtowers, where foolish people of the world pay them homage and worship, offering various incenses such as aloeswood.
In a previous life, when he was a merchant, he sold incense and had others make offerings to the most excellent fields of merit, rather than to the field of the mind.

If one practices even a small amount of giving toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one obtains a great reward; it is like the *nyagrodha* tree, whose seed is extremely small, yet when planted in fertile soil, it grows into a vast tree with branches spreading in all four directions.
If one practices giving toward the field of merit consisting of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, the attainment of great rewards is likewise so.
By the power of this field of merit, even a yakṣa who possesses supernatural powers attains the retribution of happiness.

Having been liberated from suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts, they pass away from there and, driven by the flow of karma, undergo birth and death; a human body is difficult to obtain, just as it is for a blind sea turtle to encounter the hole in a floating piece of wood.
If born among humans, one is born into a poor family; yet the fragrance of one’s body resembles that of anointed incense.
Due to residual karma, one undergoes such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the hungry ghosts who move with great speed and considers by what karma they are born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these beings had their minds shrouded by greed and envy; perhaps they were śramaṇas who violated the precepts they had received while wearing the dharma robes, wandering through villages to seek wealth through flattery and deception, claiming to provide for the sick according to their needs, yet ultimately failing to give anything and instead consuming it themselves.
For the sake of begging, they adorned their clothing and traveled through all the cities and towns to seek out whatever they required, yet they did not give anything to the sick.

Because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perished and their lives ended, they fell into the evil realms and were born among the *ābhi-cara* hungry ghosts—*ābhi-cara* being translated in the Wei language as "swift-moving. Having received this ghostly body, they consume impurities in unclean places; constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, they burn their own bodies.

If there are sentient beings who engage in impure conduct, such hungry ghosts will greatly afflict them; they manifest their own forms to instill terror, seeking opportunities to harm them, or show them evil dreams to cause fear;
they roam among burial mounds, delighting in proximity to corpses;
their bodies are ablaze, with smoke and flames rising together.
If they see an epidemic spreading in the world and many people dying, their hearts rejoice.
If there are evil spells, they come as soon as they are summoned, able to bring harm to sentient beings;
their movement is so swift that they can travel a hundred thousand yojanas in a single thought-moment. For this reason, they are called the "Swift-moving Hungry Ghosts."
All the foolish people of the world together make offerings to him, and all call him a yakṣa of great power and supernatural faculties.
In these various ways, he brings calamity and misfortune to people, causing them to be filled with fear.
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, not destroyed, and not decayed, they cannot escape;
once their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation. When their life here ends, they transmigrate according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death.
If born among humans, one will be born into the family of a mantra-practitioner, belong to various spirits and deities, and guard shrines for spirits and deities.
Due to residual karma, one receives such retribution as this.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who wait for an opportunity and constantly seek out the faults of others. By what karma are they born therein?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows: These sentient beings have their minds shrouded by greed and envy; they falsely accuse others to seize their property, or engage in strife and intimidation to coerce people, encroaching upon the wealth of others.
