They plunder the goods of others in villages and cities, constantly seeking opportunities to commit robbery and theft. They do not practice giving, do not cultivate meritorious deeds, and do not associate with virtuous friends. Always harboring jealousy, they covet and snatch the wealth of others; seeing the possessions of others, their hearts harbor malice. Toward their mentors, good friends, brothers, and kinsmen, they always maintain hatred and envy. When people see them, they all point at them together, calling them wicked and evil men.

When this person’s body perishes, they fall into the evil realms and receive the body of a *cetaka* hungry ghost—*cetaka* meaning "orifice" in the Wei language, which in its sense refers to "waiting for an opportunity. Throughout all the pores of their body, flames spontaneously burn their form, like the *cūta* tree (*vijñuṣka*) when its flowers are in full bloom; as these flowers are red like the color of a mass of fire, it is used as a metaphor. Constantly scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, they groan and wail in lamentation, rushing about and fleeing, seeking food and drink to sustain themselves.
In this world, there are foolish people who walk counter-clockwise around a stupa, yet when they see a temple to the gods, they circumambulate it clockwise with reverence;
such persons provide an opportunity for these ghosts, who enter their bodies and consume their vital energy.

If there is another person who approaches a chamber with lustful impurity, this ghost seizes the opportunity to enter their body, consuming the person's vital energy to sustain its own life; it cannot consume anything else at all.
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, not destroyed, and not decayed, they cannot escape;
once their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation. Upon passing away from this life, they wander according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death.

If born among humans, they will encounter many hardships—calamities from kings, calamities from water, calamities from fire, calamities from bandits, and the calamity of famine—and will constantly be born in places of poverty and low station, suffering from many ailments and having bodies that are weak and emaciated.
Due to the remnants of their karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the fruits of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the various hungry ghosts in the dark places beneath the earth and considers by what karma they are born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

These sentient beings, being foolish and committing evil, have their minds shrouded by greed and envy; they pervert the Dharma to seek wealth and bind others, casting them into dark prisons where it is pitch black and their eyes see nothing. They constantly call out to one another with voices of perpetual lamentation, suffering great anguish within their confinement, with no one to rescue or protect them.

Thus, when such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall into a place of black darkness and are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). They dwell in a dark place beneath the earth where great, malevolent serpents fill every corner. Their bodies are immense, twenty *li* in length; they shiver from the cold wind, their bodies consumed by hunger and thirst. Their hair is disheveled and matted, and their emaciated frames are battered and shattered by blows from clubs. They travel through vast, perilous, and dark regions, undergoing intense suffering as they flee in terror, utterly alone without a companion, while fierce winds lash them with a sharpness like the cutting of a blade.

Due to their evil karma, they seek death but cannot find it; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape. Only when their karma is exhausted can they escape;

then, at the end of this life, they wander according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just like a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating wooden plank.

If they are born among humans, they will mostly dwell in deep mountains, remote precipices, or along the seashore where the sun and moon are not seen; born in such lands, their eyes will be blind and dark, seeing nothing at all, and they will be poor and lowly, sustaining themselves by begging.
"Due to residual karma, they receive such retribution as this.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees a class of hungry ghosts named 'Great Power of Supernatural Abilities and Radiance' (Ṛddhibalābhāsvara). By what karma were they born therein?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these sentient beings deceive others with false speech; they are greedy and envious, causing destruction; they steal the wealth of others and take things by deceiving them; or, relying on their power, they forcibly seize the property of others to bestow upon evil friends, rather than giving to fields of merit, practicing impure generosity.

Giving for the sake of seeking favor, for the sake of seeking rescue, for the sake of festivals and gatherings, for the sake of urgent distress, for the sake of gaining intimacy, and for such reasons as these, is called impure giving.

After this person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they will be reborn among the powerful ghosts possessing supernormal powers. Having received a ghostly body, they will be surrounded on all sides by immeasurable numbers of suffering hungry ghosts; dwelling therein, whether in deep mountains or on islands in the sea, they will possess sovereign supernormal power.

Only this one ghost experiences supreme bliss, while his remaining kinsmen have bodies like scorched forests; oppressed by the fires of hunger and thirst, they all gaze upon this ghost who enjoys such pleasure—the retribution for his impure giving.

When their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation; yet, when their life here ends, they flow according to their karma through the cycle of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, just as it is for a blind sea turtle to encounter the hole in a floating log.
If they obtain human birth, they will rule over a kingdom or serve as a high minister during an era of famine.
Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who blaze intensely at night; fire issues forth from their bodies as they groan and wail in lamentation, rushing and fleeing toward cities, towns, villages, and human dwellings in mountains and forests, their bodies like masses of fire burning with the fires of hunger and thirst.
By what karma are they born therein? Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these sentient beings had their minds shrouded by greed and envy; they destroyed others, deceived people with false speech, unjustly seized the wealth of others, demolished the cities and towers of others, and slaughtered the populace. They caused the dispersal and ruin of the kinsmen and relatives of others, plundering them for wealth which they then presented to kings, ministers, and the noble and powerful, thereby gaining the influence of the king.
The king approved of his capability, praising and extolling him, whereby [the man] became increasingly cruel and violent, as described above.

When such an evil person’s body perishes and his life ends, he falls among the *jāvalī* hungry ghosts—*jāvalī* being the Wei-language term for "blazing"—because in a previous life he had robbed at night, bound people, and inflicted upon them bitter torments; by these causes and conditions, fire blazes forth from his entire body throughout the night.
In a previous life, they bound others, causing them to wail and cry out; due to these causes and conditions, their bodies are now consumed by blazing fires as they shriek with grief.
Because their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they do not die; as long as their evil karma remains unexhausted, undestroyed, and unfaded, they cannot escape.
When their lives end here, they wander according to their karma, and a human body is difficult to obtain, like a turtle encountering the hole of a floating log in the ocean.
If one obtains a human body, one will constantly be subjected to destruction by others; even if one possesses wealth and property, it will mostly be plundered and seized by kings and thieves;
and if one climbs to high places or ascends trees, one will fall and injure the body.
Due to the remnants of their karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees hungry ghosts who constantly seek opportunities to harm humans, watching for their shortcomings and killing infants. By what karma are they born therein?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
"In a previous life, this sentient being had his infant killed by another wicked person; filled with great rage, he immediately made a vow, saying:
'In a future life, I shall become a yakṣa to take revenge for the killing of my son.'"

When such an evil person’s body perishes and his life ends, he falls into the evil realms and receives the body of a *cittara* hungry ghost—*cittara* being translated in Wei as "a ghost that watches for an opportunity. Constantly mindful of enemies, harboring hatred and poison, he seeks out the birthplaces of women and watches for an infant's vulnerability to take its life.
This ghost possesses sovereign power and supernatural faculties; upon smelling the scent of blood, it can travel a hundred thousand yojanas in a mere instant.

When a woman gives birth, it seeks an opportunity with its subtle body; with a mind of malice, it constantly seeks an opening, pursuing her everywhere, desiring to kill the infant and seeking every chance to cause harm.
In this way, these hungry ghosts search everywhere for an opportunity regarding infants, seeking the causal conditions for them.
If the mother commits a transgression or fails to follow the proper method in nurturing her child, they seize the opportunity against the infant.

If one is impure and defiled, ghosts will find an opportunity to exploit them; they may peep through windows or lattice screens, or lurk at doors, places where excrement and urine are discarded, or by the side of unclean water, seeking flaws in one's incantations or searching for what one fears.

Whether seeing a reflection, or when clothing is impure, or in the presence of fire, water, earth, or a blade; or when seeking auspicious celebrations, or standing on a high cliff, or ascending a lofty pavilion, or seeking an opportunity by moving up or down—in these various ways they constantly seek an opening, never relinquishing their heart of resentment and anger, as described above.
If it finds an opportunity, it can harm the infant;
if it does not find an opportunity, even when the child reaches ten years of age, it continues to seek various opportunities to kill and will not let go.
Such unwholesome states entangle one's own mind, and though one is burned by hunger and thirst and cannot yet bring about the killing, if it finds its opportunity, it then cuts off one's life.
If this child possesses powerful wholesome karma or is protected by benevolent deities, they cannot be killed; however, that ghost will harbor a heart of malice.

Upon the end of his life there, he will wander through the cycle of birth and death according to his karma, suffering the pains of saṃsāra; it is as difficult for him to obtain a human body again as it is for a blind sea turtle to encounter the hole of a floating log.

If born among humans, due to the habitual tendencies of anger from past karma, they are bound by knots of enmity; even toward those with whom they have no connection, they regard them all as enemies, seeking out the faults and deficiencies of others through various means.
Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 16;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 17.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Pretas, Part Two:
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of pretas."
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the *kāma-ālābuka* hungry ghosts—*kāma-ālābuka* meaning "desire-color" in the Wei language—and considers by what karma they are born therein.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these beings—whether male, female, or eunuch—adorn themselves with various garments and dress in women’s clothes, practicing the ways of courtesans. When desire arises in others, they engage in sexual union with them; for this reason, they obtain wealth and property, which they give to ordinary people.
They give at places that are not fields of merit, with impure minds.
Due to these causes and conditions, after the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts of the desire and form realms.

Having received a ghostly body, they are adorned with various ornaments; whatever they conceive in their minds is obtained according to their will—if they desire it to be good, it becomes beautiful; if they desire it to be evil, it becomes ugly.
If they wish to manifest forms that are either attractive or unattractive, they are able to do so entirely.
They may appear as men with handsome and upright features,
or as women with exquisite beauty and grace.
Or they may be born as animals with extraordinary appearances;
they are able to create various kinds of exquisite adornments and can travel everywhere to all places.
If they obtain food or drink, they can consume it without suffering, because they practiced giving to a small degree.
Being able to enter people's homes in a subtle body to steal food and drink, the people of the world say:
"A piśāca ghost has stolen my food and drink."
Sometimes they take human form and enter others' festive assemblies;
sometimes they take the form of birds and eat the sacrificial offerings of humans.
Their bodies are so subtle and dense that people cannot see them.
This ghost can thus manifest various forms at will; people of the world all call him the "Wish-Fulfilling Yakṣa.
Sometimes he takes the form of a woman and engages in sexual union with men, using such various adornments to deceive people as he wanders among humanity.
Within the realm of hungry ghosts, as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape; only when their karma is exhausted do they attain liberation.

Upon ending their lives there, they wander according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, like a turtle in the ocean encountering the hole of a floating log.

If one is born as a human, one falls among the ranks of performers, wearing various garments and sporting about in unrestrained indulgence to seek a livelihood; using one's own wife, one causes her to serve others in order to seek wealth and goods.
"Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution as this.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes the hungry ghosts on the islands in the ocean and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being saw a traveler who wished to cross a wilderness and was exhausted with the suffering of illness; yet, at that person's place, he took a great deal of payment while giving only a meager amount in return.
Because of their evil greed, they used clever words to deceive travelers who were exhausted and weary in the wilderness.
Due to these causes and conditions, they were born on a desert island in the ocean.

On that island, there are no forests, ponds, or rivers; the place is extremely hot, and even in the winter months the heat and venom are intense, exceeding the heat of summer in the human world by more than tenfold. They sustain their lives solely upon the morning dew.
Although they dwell on an island in the ocean, they are unable to obtain water; because of their evil karma, they see the sea dried up.
Even if they see forests, they all appear ablaze with great flames, causing their hopes to be severed; as all manner of evils converge upon them, there is no peace or security.
Scorched by hunger and thirst, they groan and lament in grief and distress; deceived by their own minds, they run hither and thither, their cries of sorrow reaching a breaking point.

Without rescue or protection, without refuge or reliance, their hair is disheveled and matted, their bodies emaciated and wasted, and all the veins of their bodies are clearly visible like a network. Wherever they go, everything is utterly exhausted; there is no rescue, no home to return to, no refuge, and no one to rely upon.
Because evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, one is thus prevented from dying;
only when karma is exhausted does one attain liberation.

When life ends here, one wanders according to karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death. A human body is difficult to obtain, like a turtle encountering the hole of a floating log in the ocean.
If they are born among humans, they will be born on an island in the ocean, perhaps with only one foot or with short feet, and will suffer from a lack of water and food.
Because of their residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes the *daṇḍadhara* hungry ghosts of Yama; by what karma are they born therein?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

Because these sentient beings are driven by stinginess and envy, they corrupt their own minds; they associate with kings, ministers, and the wealthy and noble, exclusively practicing violence and evil without compassion; they do not act according to the correct principle, and are thus despised and reviled by the virtuous and good.

When such an evil person’s body perishes and their life ends, they receive the body of a staff-bearing yakṣa under King Yama; in the world of ghosts, they serve as a messenger and attendant running errands for King Yama.
If there are sentient beings who have committed various evil karmas, King Yama then commands this ghost to seize their spirit.

This ghost’s body is hideous and terrifying; he holds a blade or staff in his hand, with disheveled hair that hangs down over his body, long lips hanging down, drooping ears, and a large belly. He lets out loud, piercing cries to frighten the other ghosts, and brandishing a sharp blade at the offenders, he seizes them by the hand and binds them with rope. Leading them to the King’s presence, he says to the Great King:
"I have captured this offender from among humans and brought him here, Great King!"
"This person, in his previous lives, performed unwholesome deeds—unwholesome actions of body, unwholesome actions of speech, and unwholesome actions of mind.
We pray that Your Majesty will rebuke him. Then King Yama spoke in verse, rebuking him, saying:
"You were a foolish sort among men, Adorned by all manner of evil karma.
Why did you not cultivate wholesome conduct in the past?
Like one who reaches a treasure island and returns empty-handed.
Through the causal conditions of wholesome karma, one obtains the fruit of happiness; through the causal conditions of the fruit of happiness, a virtuous mind arises.
All phenomena revolve according to the mind, Cycling through birth and death without ever ceasing.
All conditioned formations are entirely impermanent, Like water bubbles, lacking any solidity.
If one can thus cultivate the True Dharma, That person shall obtain a supreme retribution in the future.
If there is one who can constantly cultivate goodness and abandon all evil deeds,
such a person will not come to my realm, but shall ascend by the steps to be reborn in heaven and receive its rewards.
If a person is foolish and lacks awakening, yet comes to me having delighted in evil deeds, they are able to renounce those unwholesome and evil actions; such a person then walks the foremost path.
If one sees the various fruits of karma in the world, and also sees the manifold pleasures in the heavens,
yet still gives rise to a heedless mind— such a person cannot be said to cherish their own self.
For whose sake did you create evil karma, letting yourself run wild with body, speech, and mind?
Such people as these follow various paths; now the retribution for your karma has arrived at my place.
Deceived and deluded by manifold evils, you will certainly travel upon the perilous and wicked path;
for one who delights in committing evil deeds, a human body in the future will be exceedingly difficult to obtain.
If a person stays far removed from all evil deeds, Delighting in practicing wholesome dharmas with a joyful heart,
Such a person will always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life, And will surely attain the fruit of nirvana and liberation.
If there are sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds, they are the most preeminent in the world;
if a person practices and learns unwholesome karma, they are the greatest evil in all the world.
If there are wise people who practice virtue, they are able to leave behind the unwholesome dharmas of the beginning, middle, and end;
if there are those who create and habituate themselves to various evil karmas, they will enter hell to undergo the retribution of suffering.
One who can discipline the faculties with wholesome dharmas will obtain the pure and supreme dharmas of the world;
when such a person’s body perishes at the end of life, they will be reborn in a celestial palace to experience happiness.
Karma binds you with great firmness; held by the messengers of Yama, you are sent to the terrifying evil realms, to the places of great suffering in the world of Yama.
You committed many evils in your previous lives; you shall now receive the retribution for this karma yourself.
What one does oneself, one receives oneself; it is not done by another, nor is what another has done one's own retribution.

"Once King Yama has thus rebuked the sinner, the messengers lead him out; deceived by his own evil karma and the fruits of his own actions, he is led away to undergo various sufferings as retribution."
They are treated with bitter and agonizing punishments; driven by hunger and thirst, they consume only wind and air. Because their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying.
Once they escape from this, they wander according to their karma, undergoing the suffering of birth and death.

If one is born among humans in a remote frontier, in dark mountains, perilous valleys, deep rivers, or on steep and precipitous banks—places of danger and fear—may those who possess mastery travel this path and lead me as their guide.
Due to the remaining karma, one undergoes this retribution for sin.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates phenomena internally: how does a bhikṣu contemplate the five stages?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the ten bases of form with clear vision. What are these ten?
The first is the eye-base.
Second, the sense-base of form;
third, the sense-base of the ear;
fourth, the sense-base of sound.
Fifth, the nose base;
sixth, the odor base;
seventh, the tongue base;
Eighth is the sense-base of taste;
ninth is the sense-base of body;
tenth is the sense-base of tangibles.
How does a bhikṣu regard the eye as conditioned by visible forms?

A bhikṣu contemplates that consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; from the conjunction of these three factors, contact arises; and contact is accompanied by feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness.

Contact has the characteristic of touching; feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of cognizing; volition has the characteristic of intending, such as regarding length and shortness, the pleasant and the unpleasant, or the relative oppositions of what is directly perceived; and consciousness cognizes a single object, yet each of these mental factors possesses its own distinct characteristic and threefold nature—whether material or non-material—and its own individual essence, just like the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
What are the ten? First is sensation;
second is perception.
Third is volition;
fourth is contact;
fifth is attention.
Sixth is desire;
seventh is liberation;
eighth is mindfulness.
Ninth is samādhi; tenth is prajñā.

These ten—beginning with the single object and each being mutually cognizant—are likewise for each single dharma. It is just as when a single ray of sunlight arises, the various rays themselves are each distinct from one another.
Just as the intrinsic nature of consciousness is distinct, so it is for volition as well.
That bhikṣu knows the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) as it truly is; he contemplates the eye as empty, non-existent, without solidity, and without reality.

When a bhikṣu thus knows reality as it is, he is freed from wrong views; with right view his mind is gladdened, and his eye is freed from the defilement of delusion. He sees truly that the eye is merely a lump of flesh, and that what is called "delusion" is nothing but a pore for tears, possessing no knowledge whatsoever.
Having known it as it truly is, one becomes free from desire for the mind and contemplates the eye as impermanent;

having known its impermanence, one knows the eye as it truly is: it is merely a mass of flesh dwelling within a cavity, bound by tendons and sinews, existing through the conjunction of various conditions—thus should one understand the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Such as this eye has no seer; it is without self and without cognition, and even suffering is likewise so.
Having contemplated the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana), one attains the mind of detachment from desire.
“Having thus observed the eye-base as it really is, that bhikṣu analytically contemplates forms:
‘Such forms—whether attractive, unattractive, or entirely neutral—are all produced through conceptual differentiation.’”
What phenomena can be seen? What is pure?
What is permanent?
"What is there to be craved?
A bhikṣu thus reflects and examines, knowing as it truly is that form is neither existent nor pleasant.
He reflects and examines in this way:
The characteristics of form (*rūpa*) are neither solid nor real; it is through discrimination that one gives rise to likes and dislikes, for they are not truly existent!

All sentient beings falsely crave and cling to what is liked and disliked. Such forms have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they are impermanent and non-existent, unreal and unsatisfactory (*duḥkha*), subject to disintegration, neither solid nor self. Because their minds are shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion, they give rise to likes and dislikes; it is not that form itself possesses likes or dislikes!

Because they arise through recollection, a bhikṣu thus contemplates the sense-sphere of form; having seen name-and-form, he is neither greedy nor stained, neither deluded nor grasping, knowing that form lacks solidity.
When that bhikṣu has thus contemplated the eye and contemplated the sense-sphere of forms, he does not cling to eye-consciousness and attains freedom from the defilement of desire.

He contemplates that "eye-consciousness is not self, and self is not eye-consciousness"; it is likewise for contact, feeling, perception, and volition. Thus he contemplates the eye and forms; this is the fifth stage among the thirteen stages of non-attachment.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who devour small children; by what karma are they born therein?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings employ malevolent incantations to command dragons in order to eliminate calamities such as hail, thereby deceiving and deluding the sick;
they employ mantras to command yakṣas to seize people's wealth or even kill sheep.

Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls into the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*) and undergoes immeasurable suffering. Emerging from that hell, they are reborn among the *Pāripatika* hungry ghosts—*pāripatika* being translated in the Wei language as "eaters of small children."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, as a residual retribution for killing, are born among humans as these hungry ghosts (*preta*). They steal and eat [the infants], or go to the places where women giving birth reside to take those infants—whether when they are crawling on their bellies or when they have just begun to walk. In this manner, these hungry ghosts steal various small children and eat them one after another.
"If one finds an opportunity, one can immediately take his life;
if there is no karma of killing, none can cause him harm. A verse says:
“Bound by evil karma, one undergoes bitter fruit; if one performs good karma, one receives pleasant retribution.
The ropes of karma are long and firm, binding people; they bind all sentient beings so that they cannot escape.”
Unable to reach the secure city of nirvāṇa, one undergoes manifold sufferings within the long-flowing stream of the three realms of existence;
yet by using the sword of wisdom to sever these karmic actions, one will surely attain liberation from all burning afflictions.
By severing the ropes of karma, one is free from bondage and reaches the unconditioned state of tranquility;
just as a fish caught in a net is dragged away by humans, so too do sentient beings die, bound by craving.
Just as a wild deer struck by a poisoned arrow runs frantically to the east and west in terror,
yet cannot escape once the venom has spread, so too are sentient beings bound by craving.
Always following sentient beings without abandoning them, one should contemplate craving as poison and distance oneself from it;
foolish worldlings are scorched by craving, just as a great fire consumes dry wood.
This craving, initially stained and difficult to perceive, brings retribution like fire that consumes itself.
If you desire constant joy and peace of mind, you should abandon the fetters of craving and detach from all attachments.
Just as a fish that swallows a hook does not have long to live, so too are people bound by the fetters of craving;
they bind all sentient beings and lead them to evil realms, falling among the hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst.
The various sufferings and afflictions in the realm of hungry ghosts, where beings flee and run in every direction,
and those who undergo torment within the destinies of the hells— all arise from the causal conditions of the fetter of craving.
If there are those who are poor and afflicted by illness, seeking morning meals for their own survival, it is all due to the causal conditions of the fetters of craving;
that they receive such bitter retribution is what the Sage has taught.
"Thus, having fully observed all the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of greed and envy, one becomes weary of and detached from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and abandons all desires.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the fruits of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*)."
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who consume the vital essence of humans, and considers by what karma they were born therein.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
"In a previous life, these beings used clever speech to deceive people, falsely claiming to be their close friends."
"I shall protect you," he said.
Having heard this, the man roused his heart and exerted his courage.

At that time, the man caused another to enter the enemy lines with the intent to take his life; he abandoned him and departed, failing to provide any protection, desiring only to seize the wealth from the king. Consequently, the one who had been deceived perished in the battle.

Due to these unwholesome causes and conditions, when that person’s body breaks up at the end of life, they fall among the hungry ghosts who feed on the vital essence of humans. They suffer from great hunger and thirst, which burns their own bodies; knives hack their limbs until their skin and flesh are torn and destroyed. Knives rain down from the sky as they run in all four directions, finding no place of escape.

If they see someone who commits evil, lacks faith, and does not honor the Triple Gem, they immediately seize the opportunity to enter that person's body and devour their vital essence to sustain their own lives.
It is extremely difficult to seek; one may be exhausted and unable to obtain it, only finding an opportunity once every ten or twenty years, while constantly suffering from hunger and thirst.

Having created evil karma for oneself, one returns to experience its results. Because the evil karma is not yet exhausted, it causes one not to die; as long as the evil karma is not exhausted, lost, or destroyed, one cannot escape.
Only when the karma is exhausted does one attain liberation.

When their life there ends, they are reborn among humans; they constantly guard the altars of the gods, yet remain impoverished and beset by misfortune, lacking self-mastery, subsisting on the remnants of sacrificial offerings.
Due to the residue of their karma, they must depend on others for their livelihood.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees a class of hungry ghosts named Brahma-rākṣasa. By what karma are they born therein?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
in a previous life, this sentient being held great assemblies where he took the lives of living beings, regarding such acts as extraordinary;
he traded food and drink, buying low and selling high, driven by greed, envy, and destruction.

When such beings die and their bodies perish, they fall among the hungry ghosts, known as the *brāhmaṇa-rākṣasa* hungry ghosts. Their bodies are scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst; they run and rush about, appearing in human form to kill and harm sentient beings, or they dwell in empty alleys, thoroughfares, and at the crossroads of four-way junctions, seeking opportunities to prey upon people.
Many of those who kill living beings to host sacrificial assemblies among the Brahmins are reborn therein.
Some conceal their own bodies to kill and harm others, while others enter into the bodies of people to sever their lives.
The practitioners of incantations say:
"A spirit has possessed a person.
Once it has entered the person's body, it causes the mind to become disordered, leading to madness, delusion, and ignorance.

Due to such evil karma, constantly committing various misdeeds, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst as they undergo great suffering and distress while dwelling in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape;
only when their karma is exhausted and their life ends, through the conditions of residual karma, are they born among humans, where they constantly eat human flesh or drink human blood.
"Due to residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who eat [the food] in the fire-pits; by what karma are they born in that place?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings have distanced themselves from virtuous friends; their minds are shrouded by greed and envy, and they delight in consuming the food of the Sangha.
Such persons, when their bodies perish and their lives end, fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Emerging from hell, they are born among the *kūṭa* hungry ghosts—*kūṭa* being translated in Wei as "fire-hearth.
Once born, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst like a forest consumed by fire; they run about in every direction, seeking food and drink.
Deceived by their own karma, they eat the remains of food that has been scorched in the celestial temples, consuming it along with the flames.
Their minds constantly dwell upon the remnants of food from the hearth; as hunger and thirst burn their bodies, two fires arise together, causing them to groan and wail in agony.
Having committed various evil karmas, they will inevitably reach maturation; as long as these evil karmas are not exhausted, one cannot escape them.

Only when the karma is exhausted does one attain liberation; yet due to the remaining causes and conditions of that karma, one is born among humans, impoverished and frequently ill, being constantly burned by fire wherever one goes, consumed by wild fires.
Due to the causal conditions of residual karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes:

Having frequently practiced jealousy and habituated themselves to pervasive karma, they bring that karma to completion and fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), being born amidst the impurities of alleyways.
By what karmic conduct are they born in such a place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings, their minds shrouded by stinginess and envy, give impure food to those of pure conduct and holy life.
By this cause and condition, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are born among the impure *ratha* hungry ghosts—*ratha* being translated in the Wei language as "streets and alleys."
If it is during the day, people cannot see them;
if people travel at night, they see many of them.

Whether in cities, towns, or crowded villages, or if one dwells in the wilderness, in military camps, latrines, or secluded and filthy places filled with maggots and worms—such foul and impure locations;
If anyone sees them, they loathe the sight and vomit in revulsion before departing.

These hungry ghosts are born therein because, in a previous life, they offered impure food to the Sangha; by this cause and condition, they are born in an impure place and undergo great suffering and distress.

Although they dwell therein, they constantly fail to obtain food; various malevolent spirits, holding sharp knives from which flames erupt, stand guard by their side, leaving them perpetually tormented by hunger and thirst.
Only once every month or half-month do they obtain a single meal, yet even then they cannot be satiated;
should they happen to eat their fill, the various *piśāca* ghosts who guard the excrement forcibly strike them until they vomit.
Their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst; they groan and wail in lamentation, running hither and thither in distress, sorrowful and weeping, whereupon they speak these verses in *gāthā*:
"Because the seeds are unwholesome causes and conditions, one obtains the evil retribution of sorrow and suffering;
the nature and characteristics of cause and effect are similar, and through the causes and conditions of evil karma, one receives the retribution of suffering."
Dragged by the hook of evil karma, one enters the miserable realms like a fish swallowing a hook;
while a hooked fish may still escape, no one dragged by evil karma can be exempt.

The great power of various karmas drags sentient beings along; bound by the ropes of unwholesome karma, they are led to the world of hungry ghosts, where they undergo all manner of great sufferings of hunger and thirst.
The suffering of hunger and thirst among the various hungry ghosts exceeds that of fire, knives, and poisons;
such hunger and thirst possess great power, and immeasurable hunger and thirst afflict sentient beings.
Not for a single moment do they find rest; day and night, they are never parted from suffering and affliction.
They do not obtain even the slightest bit of happiness, but constantly endure all manner of hardships and toil.
Because of the causes and conditions of having committed karmic actions that lead to suffering, one is born within the evil realms to undergo the retribution of suffering;
since it is difficult to escape from this retribution of suffering, when shall one ever attain peace and happiness?
All the springs they see are entirely without water; all the ponds and pools have completely dried up.
Running hither and thither in every direction seeking water and drink, they go to the various rivers but find none at all.
I searched for water wherever I traveled, throughout mountains, forests, and vast wildernesses, leaving no place unvisited;
yet wherever I went, though I looked for it to drink, I could find not even a drop.
The fire of hunger and thirst scorched my body, and with no refuge and no savior, I endured great suffering.
"Thus, these hungry ghosts, deceived by their own karma, groan and wail; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, they cannot escape.
When their retribution ends and their lives conclude, due to the remaining karma, they are born among humans, taking the bodies of courtesans or women;
if they obtain a male body, they are born into a family of scavengers, wearing the clothes worn by women and practicing the ways of women."
It is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta): by what karma are they born among the hungry ghosts who feed on wind?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

"These sentient beings, upon seeing śramaṇas, brahmins, or the poor and sick come to beg for alms, promised to give them food; yet when they arrived, they ultimately gave nothing at all, leaving these śramaṇas, brahmins, and the poor and sick hungry, parched, and exhausted, as if struck by a cold wind."
That person who speaks falsely, upon the dissolution of the body after death, falls among the *pāyikṣa*—the hungry ghosts known in the Wei language as "Wind-Eaters.

Having received a ghostly body, they suffer from hunger and thirst just like those in the Reviving Hell (*sañjīva*), without any difference. They run in the four directions, having no hope, no one to rescue or protect them, and being without refuge or reliance.

Deceived by their own minds, they see food and drink in distant places—whether in the forest or at a monastic residence—and rush toward them. Exhausted and weary, with hunger and thirst exceeding the ordinary, they open their mouths to seek food; yet the wind that enters through their mouths serves as their sustenance.
Due to the conditions of their evil karma, they do not die;

their bodies are sustained by that evil karma, and they falsely perceive the thought of food. It is like a thirsty deer who, upon seeing a mirage, calls it water—yet it is empty and non-existent, like a whirling firebrand.
In a previous life, he falsely promised things to others but ultimately did not give them; as a result of this retribution, he can only see food with his eyes but is unable to obtain it.
As the verse says:
"The Sage has taught that cause and effect are similar: A virtuous cause brings about a virtuous fruit."
Virtuous causes do not yield evil fruits; Evil causes never receive virtuous retribution.
Causes and conditions, mutually conforming, bind sentient beings; Birth and death continue in succession like a chain of hooks.
Birth and death fetter all sentient beings, Cycling through the various realms from which none can escape.
If one can sever all fetters— the firm shackles of karma and afflictions—
that person shall reach the state of tranquility, forever cutting off all sorrows and distress.

"When that person thus undergoes the retribution of suffering corresponding to their causes, deceived by their own mind, they run about and flee, constantly subsisting on wind and air to sustain their lives. As long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape."

When their karma was exhausted and their lives ended, they were reborn among human beings; however, they were poor and lowly, despised by others, and though constantly requested by the multitude for the gift of dwellings, food, drink, clothing, or other necessities, there was no one who gave them anything.

When they hear that others have been granted permission, their hearts rejoice in the hope of obtaining it; yet when they do not receive it later, they become filled with anxiety and distress, undergoing two kinds of suffering:
first, hunger and thirst;
second, sorrow and affliction.
They undergo great suffering and affliction as the result of their remaining karma, receiving such retribution. A verse says:
"Thus, beings perfumed by evil karma Fully experience all manner of sufferings and afflictions."
Just as that which is permeated by excrement is utterly loathsome, so too should such evil karma be abandoned.
That which is permeated by wholesome dharmas is most excellent; it enables one to forever leave behind the suffering of the evil realms.
It is like sandalwood oil perfumed by *campaka* flowers: though the flowers perish, the fragrance of the oil remains.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who eat burning coals, and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these beings are jailers in charge of the physical prisons; with their minds shrouded by greed and envy, they beat and bind sentient beings, restricting them from food and drink so that they suffer hunger and thirst, and force them to eat earth and mud to sustain their lives.
Because of these causes and conditions, when this prison warden’s body perishes at the end of his life, he falls among the hungry ghosts who eat fire;
he constantly goes to the charnel grounds to devour the fires of cremated corpses, yet even so, he is never satisfied.

Such evil karma brings joy at the time of its commission, yet the retribution received is extreme distress; the mind finds no pleasure therein. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions—the impurity, the loathesomeness, and the power of the poison of craving—one receives the body of a *preta* who eats fire.
If one obtains food that is like fire, it only slightly relieves the affliction of hunger, just as a person uses water to extinguish a worldly fire.
When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he develops a deep sense of weary detachment toward worldly desires and takes no pleasure in being joined with them; he reflects thus:
"Foolish worldlings are driven by craving and do not attain self-mastery."
"Eating fire to remove hunger is beyond all analogy; having received the body of a hungry ghost, as long as one's evil karma is not exhausted or destroyed, one cannot escape."

When their karma is exhausted and their lives end, they are reborn among humans; however, they are always born in remote borderlands where there is famine and scarcity. Their food is coarse and foul, lacking any delicious flavors, and they do not know the taste of salt.
"Due to the remnants of their karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the fruits of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes those hungry ghosts who consume poison, and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings, their minds shrouded by greed and envy, give poisoned food to others to cause them to lose their lives so that they may seize their wealth.
Such evil persons, when their bodies disintegrate and their lives end, fall into the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva) and undergo all manner of suffering.

Emerging from hell, they are born among the hungry ghosts who consume poison, dwelling within the caves of Mount Minda, or in the remote and perilous mountains of Pāriyātra; or they are born in places of extreme cold upon ice mountains, or on Mount Malaya—a place of extreme danger and difficulty, abounding in venom, lacking water and drink, and filled with poisonous herbs. It is terrifyingly fearsome: a place of dense boulders and steep cliffs where lions and fierce tigers dwell, and therein they are born.
The suffering of cold is a hundred times more agonizing than that of humans; the torment of summer heat is likewise a hundred times greater than that of humans.
For five days during the height of summer, fire rains from the sky and burns their bodies;
when the extreme cold of winter arrives, knives rain from the void for five days.

Due to their evil karma, fire rains down from the sky along with swords and blades; dwelling in perilous places, their bodies are scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, and they cry out in grief and distress as they devour poisonous medicinal pellets.
Having eaten, they die immediately; yet because their evil karma is not exhausted, they are instantly restored to life.
Once they have returned to life, their hunger and thirst are doubled compared to before, and they groan and lament in sorrow.
Sharp-beaked birds come to peck at their eyes, causing them great agony as they cry out loudly;
once the birds have finished pecking and eating, the eyes grow back again.
They suffer in this manner until their evil karma is exhausted, destroyed, and decayed, for only then can they be liberated.

When their karma is exhausted and their lives end, they are reborn among humans, making their living by working at crossroads and thoroughfares; yet, permeated by their evil karma, they still practice sorcery and poisoning, and due to the remnants of their karma, they fall back again into the Great Hell of Reviving and others.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes the various hungry ghosts in the wilderness: by what karma are they born therein?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, when this sentient being was in a wilderness—a perilous place devoid of water—amidst the scorching heat of the sun's rays, he who sought merit planted forest trees and constructed lakes and ponds to provide for travelers.

There were groups of bandits who diverted the water from the pond, causing travelers on the road to become utterly exhausted and parched, their physical strength diminished; they then destroyed, plundered, and stripped them of their wealth, their hearts shrouded by envy such that they were unwilling to practice generosity.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls among the *aṭavī*—meaning "wilderness"—hungry ghosts.

Their bodies are scorched by great fires like lamp-trees ablaze; exposed to the glare of the sun’s flames, they run through the wilderness, wailing as they seek water, food, and drink, crying out for pity to save themselves.

Thus, due to their evil karma, these hungry ghosts see a mirage from afar and mistake it for clear water, tranquil and still. They run toward it with great haste, hoping to find water to drink, disregarding their extreme exhaustion; yet wherever they arrive, they see only empty ground, with not a drop of water to be found.
Why is this? Within a mirage, water does not exist by its very nature; how could it be obtained!

These ghosts, terrified and fleeing through the wilderness, have their two feet pierced by thorns and wicked brambles; utterly exhausted and longing for water, they faint and collapse upon the ground.
Due to the power of their evil karma, after death they are reborn once more, tormented by hunger and thirst to a degree ten times greater than before.

Even before they have fully arisen, crows, ravens, vultures, and eagles compete to peck out their eyes and devour the flesh of their bodies; they tear them apart, rending and scattering their bones. As the three types of suffering arrive all at once, they undergo great agony, having no refuge and no savior, as they lament to one another in mutual grief.
He then spoke in verse, saying:
“Vultures, eagles, crows, and ravens—these various evil birds—with diamond-sharp beaks peck at my body;
they tear and rend it until not a single place remains whole, as I undergo all manner of suffering without any protection.”
All karmas are like shadows, never leaving the body; as in the past we committed evil deeds, so now we receive their retribution.
Because we previously harmed travelers, we now suffer this great affliction.
Encircled by the fence of karma and ensnared by the ropes of karma, one sees no place from which to seek liberation;
only when evil karma is completely exhausted can one finally escape this great suffering and affliction.
Evil karma can lead all sentient beings; dragged by karma, they are brought to places of dread.
Wherever evil karma follows them, there it ripens when the time comes to experience its fruit.
Karma binds sentient beings as they wander through the three realms, Cycling without end and without rest.
If one performs wholesome deeds and abandons all evils, Then one will be free from all suffering and find no further harm.
If a person does not love various evil deeds, but views them as fire and does not cling to them,
that person will not go to the realm of hungry ghosts, nor will they be burned by the fires of hunger and thirst.
In the space of a mere moment, [suffering] constantly increases; the pains of hunger and thirst arise with every thought-moment.
The blazing fire of the body illuminates the mountain valleys, like a great conflagration consuming a forest.
When wild fires burn down great mountain forests, A great dragon’s rain can extinguish them;
When the fire at the end of an eon breaks out and the ocean waters dry up, My fire cannot be extinguished in such a way.
This fire is born from the causal conditions of the fuel of karma;
fanned by the winds of craving and desire, this fire of evil karma burns my body, surrounding it on all sides without any gap.
The waters of ethical discipline, diligence, and wisdom are contained within the vessel of generosity;
when the Great Being who abides in tranquility holds these waters, he is able to extinguish the fires of all karma within the three realms.
If one is driven by the three karmas, and through these three karmas wanders through the various realms of existence,
such a person revolves through the three states, thus deceived by these three factors.
Driven by the thirty-six karmas, they cannot escape the forty modes of conduct;
with the ninety-eight kinds of fetters and afflictions, such dharmas as these circulate within the three realms.
By means of the wisdom of one hundred and eight vidyās, contemplating the profound meaning of the twelve [links of dependent origination],
if a person can discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, that person shall attain immeasurable bliss.
If one can understand these two kinds of characteristics, And contemplate the eightfold and the ninefold special stages of progress,
Having contemplated these sixteen special stages of progress, Such a person will remain far removed from all evil realms.
If a person can perceive these two kinds of paths, they are one who has reached the ultimate consummation of the four dharmas;
having already transcended the ocean of the four currents, such a person is awakened and free from all afflictions.
One who can skillfully practice the Noble Eightfold Path, Who well knows and perceives the meaning of the Ten Powers,
And well understands the causal conditions of the two kinds of suffering— Such a person shall reach the realm of non-arising.
If a person skillfully masters the meaning of the two truths, Is able to skillfully contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness,
And is able to observe the past and future worlds, They will not be obstructed by the net of Māra.
Driven by my own evil karma, I have abandoned all wholesome and pure dharmas;
having reached this world of hungry ghosts, I am deluded by the ignorance of the evil deeds I myself created.

"In this way, there are certain hungry ghosts who possess sharp faculties and wisdom; having performed a small amount of wholesome karma, they remember their past conduct and repeatedly reproach other hungry ghosts."
Although they are rebuked by the various hungry ghosts, they still cannot escape their evil karma; as long as that evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape.
When their karma is exhausted and their lives end, they are born among human beings, yet they constantly travel through mountain crags and follow herds of deer due to the remnants of their karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom born of hearing, he sees the various hungry ghosts dwelling among burial mounds; by what karma are they born therein?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
this sentient being’s mind is shrouded by greed and envy; seeing a person of faith offering flowers to the Buddha, they steal these flowers and sell them for their own sustenance.

Due to these causes and conditions of evil karma, when this person’s body perishes and life ends, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), receiving the body of a cemetery-dwelling hungry ghost. Tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they constantly eat the hot ashes and hot earth from places where the dead are cremated; they may obtain food once a month, or perhaps not at all.
An iron garland of flames blazes upon their heads, and their skulls and faces completely melt and rot; once burned away, they are born again.
Next, an iron garland is placed upon his neck, from which flames burst forth, burning his throat and chest; fire issues from within all his limbs, consuming his entire body.
In a previous life, he stole a flower garland from a Buddha; therefore, he has received this retribution.
His body is hideous and foul, fire erupts from his skin, and various insects devour him.

A strange rākṣasa comes to his side, striking him with a staff and clubbing him, and hacking at his body with a blade. In intense agony, he shrieks and wails, undergoing these three kinds of suffering.
What are the three?
First, hunger and thirst;
second, the iron garland.
Third, they are struck and hacked with swords and staves by rākṣasas;
due to their evil karma, they undergo such retribution, filled with grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress.
Thereupon, he spoke these verses in gāthā:
“I have endured the many hardships of hunger and thirst; my body was pierced by iron garlands burning with fierce flames;
and I suffered the third agony of being struck and hacked by swords and staves—thus I have fully experienced all such sorrows.”
Deceived by my own mind and deluded by various evil karmas and ignorance,
I now undergo this suffering as a hungry ghost, forever separated from my teachers, friends, and kinsmen.
Neither friends nor wife, nor sons, daughters, or any kinsmen, can rescue me from this suffering bound by karma;
for the great power of this karma cannot be taken away.
Suffering and pleasure arise from karma and are not created by another;
I now experience these three kinds of karma because, though I heard the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and the Dharma, I did not practice them after hearing them.
Because I was shrouded by the net of ignorance, I committed various kinds of evil karma;
due to the causal conditions of these foremost evil karmas, I now undergo this great retribution of suffering.
If I may now escape from this world of hungry ghosts, a place of great suffering,
I vow that in future lives, even at the cost of my life, I shall never again commit such evil karma.

"Then, having spoken thus, the hungry ghosts were oppressed by great suffering and repented of the karma they had previously created. Because their evil karma was not yet exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they could not escape;
when their karma was finally exhausted and their lives ended, they were reborn among humans, falling into the families of *caṇḍālas*, serving as butchers, executioners, or corpse-bearers."
"Due to residual karma, they receive such retribution as this.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta).
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the various hungry ghosts dwelling within trees, and considers by what karma they are born therein."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being saw people planting forests of merit trees for the sake of travelers and those suffering from illness, yet out of greed and envy, he cut them down to take the timber and stole the trees from the gardens and groves of the Sangha.

Due to these unwholesome causes and conditions, when this person’s body perishes and their life ends, they fall among the *pīlīccha* hungry ghosts—*pīlīccha* meaning "tree" in the Wei language—and are born within a tree.

Due to their evil karma, when it is cold they experience extreme cold, and when it is hot they experience extreme heat; their bodies are constricted and crushed like wood-boring insects, undergoing great suffering and affliction as their limbs wither and decay, and their bodies are gnawed by various worms and ants.
If there are those who discard food upon trees and obtain it to eat for their own sustenance, they undergo various sufferings among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because their evil karma has not been exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot escape;

only when their karma is exhausted and their lives end will they be born among humans, where they must constantly sell medicinal herbs, timber, flowers, and leaves to survive, being employed by others and lacking autonomy, thus undergoing great distress.
"Due to residual karma, they receive such retribution as this.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of hungry ghosts (preta). He sees a hungry ghost dwelling at a crossroads, from which it derives its name. By what karma was it born there?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

This sentient being, his mind corrupted by greed and envy, stole the provisions for another’s journey; having taken them, he picked them up with a smile and departed, while the owner, deprived of his provisions, wanders through the wilderness suffering great hunger and thirst.
Such a person, by virtue of this evil karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, falls among the *cātapatra*—translated in Wei as "crossroads"—hungry ghosts.
Due to their evil karma, iron saws spontaneously appear to cut their bodies, slicing through them from all four directions; they are then tormented by hunger and thirst that burn their bodies.

If there are many causes and conditions for illness in the world, people cross roads to perform sacrifices. These ordinary, ignorant fools do not understand cause and effect; they practice evil views by performing sacrifices at crossroads, and when their subsequent illnesses are cured, they claim it is due to the grace of spirits.
These are crossroads ghosts who sustain their lives by means of these sacrificial offerings;
they cannot eat any other leftover food.
Because their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they are made not to die; as long as their evil karma is not exhausted, destroyed, or decayed, they cannot attain liberation.
When his karma was exhausted and his life ended, he was reborn among humans, but in a state of poverty and lowliness, born into a family of butchers who slaughter sheep.
It is due to the remainder of his karma that he receives such retribution.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta).

With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees those sentient beings who walk upon deviant paths, acting with deceit and crookedness, committing evil deeds, practicing unwholesome causes, preaching false views as the ultimate truth, and having no faith in the true Dharma."
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls among the hungry ghosts of Māra’s realm and receives the body of an evil spirit.

Whether monks are walking, eating, or practicing seated meditation, this Māra-ghost creates disturbances and obstacles to their minds, or utters evil sounds to terrify them, or causes them to have nightmares.
Thus, these hungry ghosts are possessed by Māra; they harbor malice toward the True Dharma and exclusively practice violence and evil.

Because of the conditions of the evil karma they have created in this present life, large, glowing iron balls enter through their mouths, no different from those of the denizens of hell; they swallow and devour hot iron, enduring great suffering and affliction without respite.
After passing away from among these māra-kāya spirits, they fall into the hells and undergo suffering for many kalpas—whether for ten kalpas or twenty kalpas.
Thus they are certain to remain within the three evil realms, where they may be scorched and roasted, beaten with clubs, or devoured by others;
a human body is difficult to obtain, as rare as a sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.
If born among humans, they will be blind, mute, deaf, and witless; adorned with every form of misfortune and immeasurable suffering from disease, they will be impoverished and lowly.
"Due to the remaining karma, they receive such retribution.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the fruits of karma contemplates the world of hungry ghosts (preta) through the wisdom derived from hearing:

thus, in brief, are the abodes of the hungry ghosts described; if explained in detail, there are immeasurable varieties of kinsmen among the hungry ghosts, some dwelling in the ocean, some dwelling on ocean islands, some dwelling in Jambudvīpa, some dwelling in Godānīya, some dwelling in Pūrvavideha, and some dwelling in the intermediate regions between the great continents such as Uttarakuru."
Although they are designated by a single name, when explained through various gateways, there are rākṣasa demons, kumbhāṇḍa demons, and piśāca demons.
One should understand the subtle karmic activities of those spirits and demons, and by what specific karma each is born in that place.
What food do you eat?
By what practices do you conduct yourself?
What do you desire and delight in?
For what reason are these hungry ghosts born in this place?
It is entirely because they were unable to subdue the monkey of their own minds; their conduct was as unrefined as the flapping ears of an elephant, never remaining still for a moment.
Like a bird in a forest shot by an arrow, it flits from branch to branch; it constantly and unceasingly spies upon all objects of perception, just as a great wind blows and stirs up all the dust.
This mind is to be feared; while beasts such as lions, tigers, leopards, snakes, and poisons may still be tamed, this mind is difficult to tame and exceeds even those in its ferocity.
One obtains results corresponding to the karma one has created; thus, this mind is difficult to perceive.
In this way, the defiled mind binds all sentient beings, whereas if the mind is pure, one attains liberation.

This mind is like a king, with the various sense faculties surrounding it as its retinue. Because the mind creates karma, there is the fruit of karma through its causes and conditions; and because of the causes and conditions of that fruit, there are the five destinies.
The mind is like a mechanical device and the sense faculties are like its threads; if the five faculties and the mind are not skillfully controlled, one wanders through the evil realms.
If they can be skillfully controlled, one performs various wholesome deeds, is born among gods and humans, and even attains the unshakable nirvana.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the subtle movements of the mind, observing them in accordance with reality. Having observed thus, he attains great revulsion toward saṃsāra.

This bhikṣu has previously contemplated the suffering of the hells and developed revulsion for saṃsāra; next, he contemplates the various sufferings of the realm of hungry ghosts and enters the Noble Truth of Suffering. He attains unimpeded practice regarding the Truth of Suffering, though he has not yet realized the Unimpeded Path.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates internal phenomena and practices in accordance with the Dharma.

That bhikṣu contemplates the retribution of karma as it truly is; having previously analyzed and contemplated the various hells, he next contemplates the distinctions among the various realms of hungry ghosts, seeing as it truly is the faults and afflictions of birth and death, which are utterly loathsome and contemptible."

Having observed in this way, they leave the realm of Māra, grow weary of and renounce birth and death, and exert the power of diligence to seek nirvāṇa, thereby achieving and fully attaining the fifteen stages.

Once it was accomplished, at that time the earth spirits, yakṣas, and others were filled with great joy and announced it to the yakṣas of the air; having heard this, the yakṣas of the air rejoiced and announced it to the four great kings (*caturmahārāja*). Having heard this, the four great kings rejoiced and announced it to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*); Śakra and his retinue, having heard this, rejoiced and announced it to the Yāma heaven. The Yāmas and others, having heard this, rejoiced and announced it to the Tuṣita heaven; the gods of Tuṣita, having heard this, rejoiced and announced it to the Nirmāṇarati heaven; and the gods of Nirmāṇarati, having heard this, rejoiced and announced it to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven.
Thus, as they informed one another in succession throughout the desire realm, the sound spread from the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, where all proclaimed these words:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a city, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a town, within such-and-such a clan, a certain son of good family has shaved off his hair and beard and gone forth out of faith. He has left the realm of Māra, seeks to destroy Māra’s army, and causes the messengers of Māra to be struck with great terror. He is able to shake the mountains of all afflictions, has entered the Right Path to radiate light, and now attains such practice of the fifteen stages."
When the Ābhāsvara devas heard these words, they were all greatly rejoiced and addressed the other hosts of devas:

"You devas should give rise to joy! You shall cause the True Dharma to increase, diminish the various Māras and their retinues, ensure that the river of the True Dharma flows without interruption, dry up the pools of false views, subdue greed, hatred, and delusion, destroy the ranks of the heterodox, propagate and honor the True Dharma, and bring about the dispersal of birth and death."

Upon hearing these words, the devas of the desire realm were filled with great joy and uttered sounds of praise; thus, in succession, they informed one another until the message reached all the celestial hosts of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

When a bhikṣu thus practices with diligence, his mind never resting, upright and free from flattery, far removed from crookedness and deviousness, seeking in this way the city of Nirvāṇa, his virtuous voice and fame will pervade all the hosts of devas.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Volume Seventeen, ending with the Chapter on Hungry Ghosts.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Volume Eighteen.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Five: Animals (18–21), Part One. Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the various hells as they truly are.

Having known the karmic retributions within the one hundred and thirty-six hells, and having truly understood the increase and decrease in the lifespans of sentient beings therein, he observes the second realm of immeasurable hungry ghosts; he briefly explains their thirty-six types and likewise truly understands their karmic actions.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes that there are thirty-four billion distinct species of animals, who are born into the five destinies according to the freedom of their own minds.

Among these five destinies, the number of animal species is the greatest; they possess various appearances and diverse physical forms, differing in their behaviors and diets, flying in various groups, and varying in their mutual feelings of hatred or affection, opposition or compliance, whether traveling in pairs or alone, or being born together to roam as companions.
Regarding the so-called birds and various beasts:
crows, magpies, geese, wild geese, and the many species of swans fly and roam in separate flocks and groups, never harboring resentment or harming one another;
whereas foxes, dogs, jackals, and the like harbor mutual hatred and jealousy toward each other.
Crows and horned owls, horses and water buffaloes, vipers and weasels, and so forth, mutually prey upon one another.
Their physical forms differ, and their behaviors and diets vary.
By what karma do they possess such diverse forms, behaviors, and diets?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes:
these sentient beings are driven by various states of mind; they perform various karmas, enter various paths, and consume various foods.
He observes for what reason these beings, being of various different kinds, harbor mutual hatred and jealousy;
through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
"In a previous life, these sentient beings, due to wrong views, practiced and studied false teachings."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who likewise study false teachings and give rise to false pride; they engage in mutual debate using false views and false analogies. Although they converse together, it yields no benefit, brings no peace or happiness, and is not a wholesome path.
When these two individuals die and their bodies perish, they fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.

Upon emerging from hell, because of their original enmity and hatred, they fall among the animals; thus, as enemies, they continue to kill one another—namely, as vipers and snakes, mongooses, horses and water buffaloes, crows and owls, and so forth.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates why certain classes of animals follow one another without harming each other.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
When these beings were among humans, for the sake of birth and death, they practiced giving while simultaneously making a vow together: [text continues]"
"In a future age, we shall always be husband and wife.

After this person's body perishes and their life ends, they will be born among the animals; though they possess some slight pleasure rather than great suffering, they will be such as the *jīvajīvaka* bird, the mandarin duck, or the pigeon.
They take great pleasure in sensual desires due to the causes of their karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the various animals—foxes, dogs, and jackals—and considers by what karma they are by nature prone to mutual hatred and harm.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

when these sentient beings were among humans, they defiled pure food in the presence of virtuous people and renunciants; they constantly engaged in playful quarreling and strife due to the causes and conditions of a greedy mind.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall among the animals, receiving the bodies of jackals, foxes, and dogs, where they harbor mutual hatred and envy.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the various deer and gazelles: by what karma are they born in that place?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

"In a previous life, this sentient being delighted in acting as a violent bandit; beating drums and blowing conch shells, he went to cities, towns, villages, and military camps, destroying people’s fences and raising a great clamor to instill terror."
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls into hell and undergoes all manner of suffering.

Emerging from hell, they are born among deer and wild animals; their minds are constantly filled with fear because in past lives they destroyed people's villages and caused others to be terrified. Therefore, they are born in wildernesses and mountain forests where there is always much terror.
Due to the power of karma, if they are born among humans, their minds are constantly fearful, timid, and weak, and they harbor much dread.
Due to the conditions of residual karma, even in this limited state, they observe animals who are mutually hateful and jealous;
because of their abundant karma, they harm one another, following the dictates of their original karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the animals and considers by what karma they receive a transformation-born body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, these beings, in order to seek silk and gauze, raised silkworms and killed the cocoons—either by steaming or boiling them, or soaking them in water—which produced immeasurable insects called 'Fire-Tuft' insects (*jvālā-śikhā-kīṭa*).
There are certain non-Buddhists who observe false fasting rites; they catch these tiny insects and place them in fire as an offering to the various devas in order to seek merit.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell and undergo all manner of sufferings.
Emerging from hell, they are born among the various diverse classes of spontaneously born beings in the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the animals: by what karma do they fall into the moisture-born state?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings give rise to evil and false views, killing and harming turtles, tortoises, fish, crabs, clams, and oysters;
they kill the many minute insects in small ponds or the minute insects in vinegar; or there are wicked people who, out of greed for wealth, kill various minute insects.
Or, due to wrong views, they worship deities and kill insects for sacrifices.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Emerging from hell, they receive a moisture-born body, becoming either mosquitoes, fleas, or lice.
