"Having observed these two types of birth, he then proceeds in this sequence to observe the karmic retribution with a subtle mind, contemplating those sentient beings born from eggs: by what karma are they born in that place?"

If a person has not yet severed greed, anger, and delusion, yet practices meditative concentration and attains mundane supernormal powers, they may, due to certain causes and conditions, give rise to a mind of malice and destroy a kingdom.
When such a person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Emerging from hell, they take birth from eggs in the form of flying birds, eagles, or vultures.
When their life ends here, if they are reborn among humans, they will frequently be prone to anger due to the remaining karmic residue.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu understands the retribution of karma.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes by what karma various animals receive a womb-born body:
if there are sentient beings who, out of lustful desire, cause oxen or horses to mate for their own pleasure, or cause others to engage in illicit and improper sexual conduct.
After this person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they will fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering.
Emerging from hell, they will receive the bodies of womb-born beings or animals;
or, if born among humans, they will receive the body of a eunuch due to the remaining karma.
"Furthermore, after the bhikṣu has observed the eleven kinds of animals, he next observes four kinds of sentient beings who emerge from hell and receive four kinds of food."
What are the four? First is edible food;
second is the food of mental volition; [the third is the food of consciousness; the fourth is the food of contact].
Third is the nutriment of contact;
fourth is the nutriment of consciousness and craving.
A bhikṣu contemplates and observes the retribution of these four nutriments, perceiving them through the wisdom derived from hearing:

There are sentient beings who give various types of solid food to those of immoral conduct and to thieves; after they have eaten, they command these thieves to kill and eliminate their enemies, and the thieves, having received their instructions, immediately kill those enemies.
Such evil persons, when their bodies perish and their lives end, fall into hell and undergo all manner of sufferings.

Emerging from hell, they fall among the animals that subsist on solid food, taking birth as water buffaloes, cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, elephants, horses, pigs, dogs, jackals, deer, wild oxen, crows, ravens, eagles, vultures, geese, ducks, peacocks, *jīvañjīvaka* birds, swans, and various other species of birds; they are mostly born in vast wildernesses and perilous precipices.
These are called the beings who subsist on a small portion of solid food.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the class of beings who subsist on the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*): those dwelling within an eggshell or those who have just emerged from it, taking contact as their food.

Furthermore, there are various birds that delight in dwelling within the water, building nests upon the banks or boring into the riverbanks to make burrows, where they lay their eggs—such as dragons, snakes, and other similar species. By what karma do they receive the nutriment of contact?
The bhikṣu observes and, through the wisdom derived from hearing, knows:
"In a previous life, this sentient being intended in his mind to practice giving; he contemplated and deliberated upon it, but later his mind regretted it and he did not bestow anything."
Due to unwholesome karma, they fall among the animals; by virtue of their original volitional mind, they receive the retribution of nutriment through mental contact (*āhāra-saṃsparśa*).
"Furthermore, monks, when observing those sentient beings who subsist on nutriment through volition (*saṃcetanika-āhāra*), by what karma do they receive this nutriment of volition?"
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing,

he knows that among the classes of sentient beings— namely, the offspring of red fish, *timi* fish, *cakra* fish, and so forth, as well as the eggs of conchs, clams, and oysters— their food consists of the faculty of volition (*cetanā*).
If the mother remembers [him], she will feel neither hunger nor thirst, and her body and life-force will flourish.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he understands: "By what karma was I born in this place?"
These sentient beings are foolish and lack wisdom; they do not understand the fruits of karma. Having promised to give someone wealth or goods, they say to them:
"In half a month, or perhaps a month from now, I shall give you wealth, food and drink, gold, silver, and precious jewels."
At that time, having heard his promise to give alms, the poor man felt great joy in his heart and offered words of praise; he looked forward to receiving something for a month or even half a month.
When the poor man went to his house, however, the man spoke different words and no longer maintained his original faith.
After such evil persons have passed away, they fall into the Hell of Sorrow and Joy, where they undergo all manner of suffering.
When their lives there end, they fall among the animals, where they take mental volition as food.
Because in a previous life they promised something to another poor person to make them rejoice, yet in the end failed to fulfill it;
due to these causes and conditions, if they are born among humans, they become slaves to others.
This is due to the remnants of their karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the fourth type of consciousness-food among animals.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that there are animals who, afflicted by craving for consciousness, constantly long for food and drink; they are born in the wilderness, taking on the bodies of great pythons, lizards, and the like, subsisting only on the air they inhale.

Furthermore, there are the Radiant Devas (*Ābhāsvara*), also known as those who cherish consciousness and remember food without affliction; upon seeing food, they remember it, and by mere thought, they are satiated.
By what karma do animals experience such a retribution of remembering food?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings, due to excessive hatred or excessive delusion, kill and harm other beings.
When their bodies perish, they are reborn in the evil realms and receive the body of a great python.

In a previous life, they were fond of attachment and enmity, binding their own minds; by these causes and conditions, they were born among the animals and undergo such suffering and affliction, feeding on the wind with craving-consciousness as their food.
If they are born among humans, they will constantly harbor anger and engage in strife in places where there is no cause for it, due to the remaining effects of their karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the immeasurable and boundless world of animals: how do sentient beings receive the body of a water insect?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings are foolish and lack intelligence; they possess no wise mind, and at the time of their death, they suffer intensely from thirst and crave water with longing thoughts.
When their body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms and receive the body of an aquatic insect, becoming various kinds of fish.
When such a person’s life ends, during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), upon seeing water, they give rise to a thought and immediately go toward it, being born within the water.
Taking conditions as cause, there is existence.

Within this intermediate state of existence (*antarābhava*), if one has not previously practiced giving or observed the precepts, that person will be born within warm water; their mouth is constantly parched, as if touching alkaline ash, due to the power of their past karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the various species of flying birds and animals: by what karma do they travel through the unobstructed realm of space?"
Thereupon, with the wisdom derived from hearing, he contemplates the three kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are these three?
The first is the supernormal power of liberation (*vimokṣa-abhijñā*).
Second is the supernormal power of bodily action;
third is the supernormal power of mastery over the mind.

For one who has attained liberation, these powers follow their mental recollection: whether they walk upon the earth like a bird or fly through the air as if walking on the ground, such is not the nature of the dharma of liberation.

The power of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, reaches wherever it is directed by the mind’s intention; it can arrive at will and performs three types of actions. Such are the three kinds of supreme noble supernormal knowledges.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the animal realm.
How does he contemplate the animals of the hells, the gods and humans, those that move in water, on land, or through the air, and the birds and beasts?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he observes that within the various sufferings of hell there are two kinds of animals:
those belonging to the category of sentient beings and those not belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Regarding those categorized as sentient beings: having been born in that place, they are tormented by the suffering of being burned.

Regarding those not categorized as sentient beings: when hell-dwellers, with perverted minds, see various great birds soaring and sporting in the void, a thought arises in their hearts, wishing to be born in this place.
As soon as they give rise to such thoughts, they take birth in the bodies of flying birds and undergo all the aforementioned sufferings of hell.

Due to the retribution of their evil karma, they are born within the hells; there they see various lions, tigers, leopards, great birds, and malevolent insects or pythons of terrifying appearance—some of which do not belong to the category of sentient beings, yet they inflict torment and harm upon the denizens of hell, while others do belong to the category of sentient beings.
What is obtained through karma causes those sinful beings to undergo great suffering and affliction.
Those animal beings who do not experience such suffering [in their own realm] are, within the hells, tormented and harmed by lions, tigers, leopards, and even pythons.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the realm of hungry ghosts whose bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst, as well as those among the animals who undergo the suffering of hunger and thirst.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees various flying birds born within the thirty-six kinds of hungry ghost realms:
having died among humans, they are born among birds, undergoing existence as species that harm living beings, such as crows, ravens, eagles, vultures, hawks, and falcons.

Dying among birds, they are reborn in the world of hungry ghosts (preta) and take the body of a starving bird; their bodies are consumed by hunger and thirst, and they peck at other hungry ghosts, plucking out their eyes or splitting open their heads to eat their brains.
In this way, the eyes and brain-marrow of the hungry ghosts are as hot as molten copper, and these sentient beings all eat them together due to their evil karma.
Having thus observed the hungry ghosts and the birds, the bhikṣu rebuked them with a verse:
"Hot karma yields a hot retribution; One undergoes all manner of great sufferings."
Thus one should abandon and leave behind these evil and unwholesome karmas.
Do not commit such evil deeds; greed and envy bring about one's own ruin.
Those who practice greed and envy will fall among the hungry ghosts and animals.
Mutually harming one another, or being beaten, bound, and imprisoned, they then undergo rebirth as hungry animals; therefore, one should abandon delusion.
Delusion destroys one's own mind and leads one far away from precepts and generosity.
Deceived and deluded by craving, one falls among the animals.
Not discerning what is right or wrong, one eats what ought not to be eaten;
failing to do what should be done, one does not understand what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
"The five faculties are dull and stubborn, performing only the karma of animals.

Thus, the bhikṣu contemplates that these various animals possess but a single type of karma; bound by it for a time, they transmigrate through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births and deaths, receiving existence among animals and being bound by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various nets of suffering.
Due to a single karma of the animal realm, beings are bound by the continuity of immeasurable causes and conditions of successive acts of lustful desire.

They are born in the great ocean at a depth of ten yojanas, where they become makaras, conchs, clams, oysters, timi fish, śiśumāras, nāgas, and crocodiles. There they fear one another and constantly dwell in terror; driven by much lustful desire and the causes and conditions of ignorance, they engage in unlawful and perverse conduct, failing to recognize what is appropriate and what is inappropriate to do.
Born within the great ocean, they are tormented by the water; they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst, harming one another and living in mutual fear and dread.
If they practice anger and delusion excessively, they will be born within the great ocean at a depth of ten thousand yojanas, receiving the body of a venomous dragon.
They alternately provoke one another with anger and vexation; with hearts full of hatred and distraction, they spew poison to harm each other, constantly practicing evil deeds.

The city where the nāgas dwell is named Kṣemavatī (Playful Delight); the city is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is filled with nāga kings. There are two kinds of nāga kings: first, those who act according to the Dharma (dharmacārin);
[the second are those who do not].
The second is unrighteous conduct, which consists of two parts:
first, protecting the world;
second, destroying the world.
Within that city, where the Dharma-practicing Dragon King dwells, hot sand does not fall;
however, where the non-Dharma Dragon Kings dwell, hot sand falls constantly.

If hot sand were to fall upon their heads, as scorching as a blazing fire, it would incinerate the palaces and their retinues, reducing them all to total destruction; yet once destroyed, they would be born again.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the suffering of rain falling as hot sand in the world of the nāgas. By what karmic cause does one receive this retribution?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
when these beings were among humans, being foolish people, they burned monasteries, villages, and cities with hearts of hatred."
Such evil persons, when their bodies perish and their lives end, fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.

Emerging from hell, they are born among the nāgas; because in a previous life they burned villages and monastic dwellings with fire, by this causal condition they receive the body of an animal and are scorched by hot sands.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the world of the nāgas: by what karma are they born in that place?
By what conditions are they not burned or harmed by hot sand?"
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

"In a previous life, this sentient being received the various heterodox and worldly false precepts of non-Buddhists; though he practiced giving, it was not pure—possessing the seven kinds of impurity as previously described—and with a mind of anger, he vowed to be born among the nāgas."
After this person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they will fall into the City of Playful Delight and receive the body of a nāga king.
Having been born in that city, their malice will be thin, they will recollect their merit, and they will act in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the dragon king’s body does not suffer the pain of the hot sands.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the world of dragons: by what karma was the Dharma-practicing Dragon King born in the City of Playful Joy?
What are the characteristics of the City of Playful Delight?

Observing with the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees that the city inhabited by the Dragon King Dharmacara has ramparts and walls made of the seven treasures and radiates the colors of the seven treasures. Its various ponds are filled with *utpala* flowers and all manner of blossoms; its inhabitants enjoy the food of *sudhā* and constantly experience happiness. Adorned with fragrant garlands, necklaces, powdered incense, and ointments, they attain whatever they desire through their supernatural powers and mindfulness.

Yet upon their heads were the heads of dragons and snakes. Within that city dwelt various Dharma-practicing Dragon Kings, namely: the Seven-headed Dragon King, the Elephant-faced Dragon King, Vāsuki Dragon King, Takṣaka Dragon King, Bhadra Dragon King (translated in Wei as "Worthy Dragon"), Lohita Dragon King (translated in Wei as "Red Dragon"), Padma Dragon King, Meghamāla Dragon King, Avarta Dragon King, Sarvamārga Dragon King, and Pāpaha Dragon King (translated in Wei as "Enduring Dragon"). Such meritorious dragons as these followed the practice of the Dharma; because of their virtuous minds, they sent down rain at the proper times, causing the five grains of all worlds to ripen, ensuring abundance, joy, peace, and security, while preventing the falling of calamitous hail.
They have faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; they practice in accordance with the Dharma and protect the relics of the Buddha.
Thus, O Dragon King, being free from the suffering of hot sands, he experiences the foremost bliss.
He pours down sweet rain upon the four continents—namely, Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru.

If people accord with the Dharma, filially support their parents, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and practice the true Dharma, they cause the Dragon King Dharmavṛddhi to increase his great power.

Because the Dharma is supreme, a fine rain falls; the five grains ripen to perfection, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, free from all calamities; fruits are abundant, flowers possess wondrous colors, the sun and moon shine with crystalline brilliance, majestic virtue is pure and clear, and the merit-bestowing Dragon King does not release poisonous winds.
“People of Jambudvīpa lose their lives due to four causes and conditions. What are these four?
First, famine and scarcity;”
Second, weapons;
third, poisonous winds;
fourth, calamitous rains.

If the people of the world follow the practice of the Dharma and cultivate various merits, the Dragon King Dharmapāla will increase his great power; he will not produce evil clouds nor send down calamitous rain, there will be no malevolent winds, and all waters will be harmonious and wholesome. Rice crops will ripen in abundance, and the fruits will be rich in flavor, possessing perfect color, fragrance, and taste. Those who eat them will remain free from illness, be liberated from the afflictions of hunger, be endowed with physical vigor and strength, have their four elements in a state of peace and stability, and thus practice virtuous deeds.
By performing virtuous deeds, they assist in their karmic fruition so that the harvests of the fields ripen in abundance.
In this manner, the Dharma-practicing Dragon King successively protects those sentient beings who accord with the Dharma and cultivate goodness.
“Having observed Jambudvīpa, he observes Aparagoyānī.
How does the Dragon King Anulomika protect Aparagoyānī?
The beings in the realm of Aparagoyānī have gentle minds; they have only one evil:”
Due to the cause and condition of turbid water, those who drink it meet an untimely death.
The Dragon King Anulomadharmika does not rain down turbid water upon that world; because the people of Godānīya drink pure water, they remain free from illness and affliction.
This is due to the power of the nāgas.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates Pūrvavideha: how does the Dharma-practicing Nāga King bestow happiness?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he knows that when the people of Pūrvavideha hear the sound of thunder or see flashes of lightning, they fall ill due to their tender hearts.
The Dragon King Dharmacārin does not produce the sound of thunder nor release flashes of lightning in that world, so that the people of Pūrvavideha do not suffer from the pain of illness;
this is due to the power of the Dragon King.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the people of Uttarakuru: how do they suffer decline and affliction?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
when the people of Uttarakuru encounter black clouds or are struck by cold winds, the fragrant flowers do not bloom."
Having seen the flowers close, his heart was filled with sorrow and distress.

Because black clouds had arisen, the birds on Mount Saṃkhaśaya sang with harsh and evil cries; the sounds of all the musical instruments were devoid of any beautiful tones. Thus he experienced this decline and affliction caused by the wicked dragon.
The Dragon King Dharmacārin does not send forth black clouds or cold, piercing winds.
In this way, within the four continents, the Dragon King Dharmacārin brings peace and happiness through righteousness and benefits all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of the nāgas.
What are the evil nāgas who do not follow the practice of the Dharma?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows: [text continues]"

In the city of Kṛīḍāpura, there dwell several wicked nāga kings who do not act in accordance with the Dharma; their names are Nandana (translated in Wei as "Trouble-Maker"), Vikramin (translated in Wei as "The Impetuous"), Kāla (translated in Wei as "Black One"), and Ghosaghosha (translated in Wei as "Many-Voiced"). They reside within the city of Kṛīḍāpura in the midst of the ocean.
"How do these unrighteous and evil nāgas increase their power?
He knows through the wisdom derived from hearing:

"When sentient beings practice unwholesome dharmas—being unfilial toward their parents, and failing to respect śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—the power of such evil nāgas increases, and they manifest great malevolent bodies within Jambudvīpa."

Due to their evil minds, they raise up clouds and rain of evil; wherever it rains, trees of poisonous venom grow. When evil winds blow upon these trees, the poisonous vapors enter the water, causing the water to become tainted with poison. All five grains become entirely blighted and inferior; those who consume them suffer from illness and pain, and because the potency of the grain is weak, it causes people to have short lifespans.

These corrupt dragon kings, with their evil minds and calamitous poisons, harm one another in turn; because of this wickedness, all people of Jambudvīpa are utterly ruined, for these unrighteous dragons commit all manner of evils.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the powerful and sovereign dragon kings.
How do these dragon kings of unlawful and evil conduct afflict the continent of Aparagoyānī with various calamities and afflictions?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he knows that unrighteous and evil nāgas, in the empty and treacherous mountains of Godānīya, pour down torrential rains, causing all the waters to become turbid and muddy.
If the people of Aparagoyānī should drink [the water], they will suffer great distress because of this cause and condition.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates Aparagoyānī and understands it as it truly is.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates Pūrvavideha.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

when the people of the world do not practice the Dharma, the power and influence of the evil dragon kings increase; they thunder and roar with great peals of lightning like the collapse of a massive mountain, and because the people of Pūrvavideha possess weak minds, they frequently suffer from illness and pain."

In some cases, flashes of lightning illuminate the entire world like a blazing fire; from within the clouds, dragons appear with eyes like chariot wheels, their bodies dark and hideous like black mountains, with three heads upon their necks that burst forth with various flowers, their forms resembling horses or taking the shape of snakes.
Manifesting various such evil bodies, they cause the people of Pūrvavideha to experience great distress upon seeing them.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes Uttarakuru as being like the second heaven; how is it that evil nāgas inflict such distress upon the people of Uttarakuru?

By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows that on Mount Saṃkāśa in Uttarakuru, as previously described, lotuses are perpetually in bloom, their fragrance wafting forth and their colors exquisitely beautiful; the people of that land inhale this scent and rejoice.

If people in the world are unfilial toward their parents and fail to make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, at that time the evil dragon kings, through the increasing power of their sovereign minds, raise great, heavy clouds like black mountains; these clouds hang down in dense masses, obscuring the sunlight, so that the lotus flowers immediately close, lose their fragrance, and forfeit their golden radiance.

When the people of Uttarakuru see that the flowers have closed, they become sorrowful, distressed, timid, and weak; then wind issues from the clouds, blowing the various musical sounds so that they are all disordered and ruined, no longer delightful.
Thus, the power of the evil nāgas throughout the four continents brings about ruin and harm.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes that within the four continents there are both superior and inferior states.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes that the land of Uttarakuru is more joyful, peaceful, and secure than the three other continents.
In Jambudvīpa, people practice both the Dharma and non-Dharma; by these causes and conditions, suffering and happiness increase or decrease.
These three continents are lands where karma increases; there, the ten paths of wholesome action are practiced, and Buddhas appear in the world.
It is because of the causal conditions of Jambudvīpa that there are four continents.

The people of Jambudvīpa contemplate and practice the ten paths of wholesome action and are able to cultivate the holy life; in this world, many are able to contemplate and observe arising and ceasing.
This site of the Vajrāsana in this country is the only one of its kind among all the Jambudvīpa nations in the world.
The Vajrāsana extends for eighty-four thousand yojanas; it was upon this seat that the Buddha sat and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata appears in the land of Jambudvīpa and not in other realms.
Why is this? Because it is here that roots of goodness are perfected, and one attains the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, cannot support it, let alone other lands!
For this reason, the Buddha dwells in Jambudvīpa and not in other countries.
A human body is difficult to obtain; it is through the causal conditions of karma created within Jambudvīpa that one is born among humans.
For this reason, among the four continents, the kingdom of Jambudvīpa is the foremost and most excellent, unlike the other continents.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of the nāgas.
By what karma do the nāga kings who act contrary to the Dharma swallow frogs, devour sand and soil, and subsist by breathing in wind?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

while this sentient being was among humans, he deceived and oppressed his wife and children, eating fine food all alone; when his wife and children saw him, they were filled with longing and attachment, and saliva flowed from their mouths.
This person eats alone until fully satiated, yet gives only coarse and unpalatable food to his wife and children.
Such a person, when the body perishes and life ends, falls among the nāgas, where he swallows frogs, eats sand, and inhales wind, experiencing a karmic fruit corresponding to his actions.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the world of the nāgas.
By what karma do the nāgas cause rain to fall?
And by what karma do they bring down calamitous hail?"
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knew:

these evil dragons harbor poison and malice, do not accord with the practice of the Dharma, and each dragon king, in his anger and contention, raises clouds and rain of ill omen, fierce winds, calamities, and hail, causing all the five grains to be scattered, ruined, and unreaped.
"Because sentient beings practice what is not the Dharma, the evil dragons become enraged, and thus these calamities occur.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the world of the nāgas."
How is it that you cause timely rain to fall upon Jambudvīpa, moistening and benefiting the sugarcane, rice, hemp, groves, wheat, barley, and beans, so that the five grains flourish?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the Dragon King Dharmacārin sends down seasonal rains, bringing peace, happiness, and benefit to sentient beings through the Dharma.
Because all sentient beings follow and accord with the practice of the Dharma, he pours down timely rain, causing the land to be abundant and joyful.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the palaces where all the nāgas dwell: how many hosts of nāgas reside within the great ocean, and how many hosts of nāgas reside within the various streams?"
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
when the people of Jambudvīpa do not practice in accordance with the Dharma, immeasurable nāgas dwell within the various streams;
when the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, five billion seven hundred million nāgas dwell within the various streams.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma, having observed the world of the nāgas, the city of Playful Delight, and the flowing waters of the nāgas, then observes the bottom of the great ocean."
What kind of sentient beings dwell therein?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one knows:
beneath the earth of the great ocean are the enemies of the devas, known as asuras; briefly stated, there are two kinds.
What are the two? First, those comprised within the realm of hungry ghosts;
second, those comprised within the realm of animals.
Regarding those subsumed under the realm of ghosts (*preta*), the māras are hungry ghosts who possess supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
As for the asuras subsumed under the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), they dwell at the base of Mount Sumeru in the great ocean, eighty-four thousand *yojana*s beneath the sea floor.
Briefly stated, there are four levels: the first level is twenty-one thousand *yojana*s deep, which is the dwelling place of Rāhu, the asura king.

"This Rāhu, King of the Asuras, can manifest bodies of various sizes within the desire realm according to his will. Because of the power of the wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed by human beings, the Asura at that time thinks to himself:
'I shall go to observe the pleasure gardens where my enemies sport; there, together with my female attendants, I shall enjoy myself and indulge in pleasures as I please.'"

Having reflected thus, he immediately adorned himself with the Great Blue Jewel King, the Pundarika Jewel King, and the Radiant Majesty Jewel King; or with the Five-Colored Gold-and-Jade Red Jewel King; or with various colored robe-kings—whether blue, red, yellow, or black—in diverse hues he adorned his body as armor, so that its radiance shone brilliantly.

At that time, the body of Rāhu, King of the Asuras, was as vast in size as Sumeru, the king of mountains; from the jewels adorning his entire body issued forth great radiance—great blue jewels emitted blue light, and likewise those of yellow, black, and red hues.

Because of the radiance of the jewel, his heart became greatly puffed with pride, and thinking that there was no one equal to him, he went out from the city desiring to cause the celestial maidens and the asura maidens to love and revere him.

The city where he dwells is named Radiance; it is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is adorned with immeasurable jewel groves, flowing springs, bathing pools, various trees, and lotus flowers. Adorned with flower garlands upon his head and self-anointed with fragrant unguents, he scatters powdered incense as he rises from the city to behold the celestial gardens and places of recreation.

"If the people of Jambudvīpa do not practice the True Dharma, do not filially support their parents, do not respect śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their elders, do not act according to the Dharma, do not honor the Triple Gem, and do not contemplate wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, the power of the devas will all diminish. Then the gods of the Four Great Kings will inform one another and flee in all directions, fearing that Rāhu, the Asura King and son of Siṃhala, will come to slay us."

If the people of Jambudvīpa practice the True Dharma, filially supporting their parents, respectfully serving their teachers and elders, and making offerings to śramaṇas, the aged, and those of long standing, the power and influence of all the devas will increase.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings adorned their bodies with various precious robes, anointed themselves with fragrant ointments and powdered incense, and immediately rained down various swords and blades from the sky above Rāhu, the son of the Asuras and a lion cub. All the celestial hosts felt joy in their hearts and, reaching the side of Mount Sumeru, raised a great shout.

"If the sun does not appear, when the asura kings wish to view the groves and gardens, the hundreds of thousands of solar rays strike their bodies; the brilliance of their ornaments obstructs their vision, such that they are unable to see the places where the devas sport, enjoy themselves, and experience pleasure within the gardens."
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, thought to himself:
"The sun obstructs my eyes, preventing me from seeing the celestial maidens; I shall use my hand to block the solar disk and gaze upon the goddesses."

He immediately raised his right hand to shield himself from the solar disc, desiring to behold the lovely and wondrous form of the celestial maiden. From his hand issued four rays of light as previously described; he stood in the midst of the sea with the water reaching only to his waist, while the radiance of his precious jewel was sometimes blue, sometimes yellow, sometimes red, or sometimes black, as he used his hand to block the sun.
The various heterodox teachers of the world all give rise to divergent views, saying:
"The asura king Rāhu eclipses the sun.
Based on such phenomena as the sun appearing red or black, they prognosticate the lifespans of human beings.

Astrologers and others who do not understand the nature of karmic results speak in this way: some say there will be abundance, while others say there will be scarcity; some say that calamities and misfortunes will befall the king, while others say it will be auspicious and celebratory.
When the asura had blocked the sun with his hands, he gazed intently at the gardens, groves, bathing pools, and pleasure grounds of the devas.

Seeing this, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded the hosts of devas to adorn the palaces and ordered the sons of the gods to embellish their bodies with various jewels; they then proceeded to the abode of Rāhu the asura, desiring to engage him in battle.
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, seeing the hosts of devas, immediately returned to his palace city.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu, how does one contemplate the lunar eclipse?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows this:

when the retinue and ministers of Rāhu, the Asura King, travel upon the ocean, they see that the Moon constantly dwells upon the summit of Mount Udayana; as it traverses Jambudvīpa, it abides within the radiance of lapis lazuli, appearing upright, majestic, and exquisite—a hundred times more excellent than before.
Having seen this, the officials immediately went to the Rāhu Asura and said to him:
"Great King! The full moon is as beautiful and dignified as the face of a celestial maiden."

When King Rāhu heard these words, a heart of affection immediately arose within him; desiring to see the celestial maiden, he rose from the ground with yearning to behold her, and shielding the moon with his hand, he sought to see the celestial maiden.
The body of the Asura King is adorned with immeasurable jewels as described above.
The sorcerers and others within Jambudvīpa recite this incantation:
"May all evils in all lands, villages, and cities be swiftly extinguished; may all evils in the soil of all worlds be swiftly extinguished; may all evils among all Brahmins be swiftly extinguished."

If the moon appears black or yellow, the world’s physiognomists speak thus: some say there will be abundance, others say there will be scarcity; some say the king is in danger, others say there will be auspicious celebration; some say weapons and warfare will arise, while others say they will not.
In the continents of Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru, there is no mention of eclipses occurring in any direction.
For this single reason, the sun and moon are obscured, which is called a lunar eclipse.
"Furthermore, for two reasons, the sun and moon are eclipsed and a great sound descends from heaven.
When the Asura King Rāhu dwells beneath the great ocean, his various ministers and officials address him, saying: 'Great King!'"
The Lord of Devas, Kauśika, dwells within the city of Sudarśana on the summit of Mount Sumeru, residing in the Hall of Good Dharma.
Endowed with the merits of the devas and all five objects of desire, he is surrounded by his retinue, enjoying himself in joy and pleasure.

"Kauśika, Lord of Devas, is the sovereign of all devas; yet now, Great King, you are the one we honor. You possess great power and your supernatural faculties surpass his; you may lead your officials and subordinates to attack the Lord of Devas and destroy the city of Sudarśana."
At that time, the asura accepted these words and, exerting his majesty and venting his wrath, departed from the City of Radiance with a roar like thunder.

Within Jambudvīpa, the various national diviners interpreted this omen: some said it portended the descent of celestial beasts, predicting abundance, joy, peace, and security; some predicted calamity and famine, with the five grains becoming scarce and prices soaring; some spoke of the death of a king; some spoke of auspicious celebrations, spiritual responses, and excellent omens; some spoke of the rise of war and weapons within the borders; some spoke of the people being peaceful and secure without change; and some said that one must observe fasts, maintain purity, and worship the deities to seek blessings.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, thought to himself:
"I shall leave my precious jewels and other treasures within this city to provide great illumination for my sons."

If there were no precious jewel, there would be no radiance; it is the same in the heavens: because there are the sun and moon, there is radiance, and if there were no sun and moon, there would be darkness.
"I would rather now obscure the sun and moon, causing the heavens to become dark.
Having reflected thus, the asura rose from his city and, with one hand, immediately covered and obstructed the luminous wheels of the sun and moon.
The foolish people of the world and various fortune-tellers all predicted signs of calamity and auspiciousness as previously described.
Furthermore, with one hand they stroked the summit of Mount Sumeru, wishing to determine their success or failure against the devas.

These asuras, being animals of little wisdom, seeing the various superior marks, adornments, majestic power, and radiance of the devas, conceived doubt and regret; they returned to their own abodes and dwelt in the City of Radiance.
This is called the second cause and condition by which the sun and moon are obscured, causing solar and lunar eclipses, and the celestial sounds roar and thunder.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the pleasures experienced by the great asura king Rāhu.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes that within the city where the asuras dwell, it is adorned with various kinds of precious jewels. Situated at the side of Mount Sumeru, it is twenty-one thousand yojanas deep and eight thousand yojanas wide. It is fully endowed with lotus bathing pools and lush, flourishing groves of trees. The ground is made of pure gold, its color like a flash of lightning. There are golden palaces and pavilions, and coral jewel-trees from which hang many jeweled bells that emit exquisite sounds; amidst these various musical tones, they enjoy themselves in pleasure and delight.

Each pond is adorned with golden flowers, and the ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks are all of a true golden color, serving as exquisite ornaments; those who see them love and delight in them. Like the birds of the celestial realms, they have beaks made of *maṇi* jewels and sport joyfully; their wings are variegated with the seven treasures and blue *vaiḍūrya*. They frolic and play amidst the railings of the various pavilions, appearing most lovely and delightful; they emit wondrous sounds that bring joy to all who hear them. All the other birds are likewise pure and stainless, upright and magnificently adorned.
The peacocks possess emerald tails with eyes that open and close alternately; they wear magnificent crests upon their heads and travel in pairs.
They feed on the nectar of flowers—such as the *pāṭala* flower—and their voices are elegant and exquisite like the sound of a child.
Their crests are golden or made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and they soar and sport among the balustrades without ever ceasing.
At rest, they indulge themselves in the nectar of flowers; their eyes are deep blue, and the colors of their bodies are variegated like streaks of lightning, with every hue distinct.
Their yellow complexions are fine, soft, and brilliant as lightning as they move through the forest trees and mountain crags, sporting wantonly.
Their flower garlands and necklaces possess the colors of a celestial rainbow, and their radiance encircles them.
Their bodies are adorned like flower garlands; their throats contain a beauty like the color of red pearls;

their two wings are as soft as blooming lotuses, displaying immeasurable varieties of hue; they possess long beaks of mani-jewels; their bodily fragrance is pure and sweet like that of the *pilikā* flower;
they sport within palaces, moving together in pairs with glossy, lustrous plumage.
When they fly, they travel together, bathing in the pure ponds; their soaring over the courtyards and grounds is likewise so.

They call out to one another with mournful cries, producing subtle and wondrous sounds, and uttering notes of desire. Such birds as the kokila, the cakra-vāka, and the parrot fill the city, and their voices are heard throughout the groves and trees.
"It is adorned with many groves of trees and lotus bathing pools; within that city are four parks, all consisting of golden trees, each park being exactly one hundred yojanas in length and breadth:
the first is named Playful Sport (Kīḍā);
the second is named Indulgence in Pleasure (Rati)."
The third is named Haṃsa-vāsinī;
the fourth is named Kokilā. These four groves adorn the city.

Within each grove there are three thousand kinds of wish-fulfilling trees; these trees are golden in color like clouds or shadows, their branches are supple, and birds dwell upon them. Various flowers are always in bloom, their fragrance wafting for a full yojana, and many swarms of bees abound with overflowing honey.
There were trees of golden hue, trees from which flowed springs of wine, and trees of ox-head sandalwood whose fragrance was like the color of clouds.
Seven-leafed incense trees, *citraka* trees, and *pīlu* trees were stirred by a gentle breeze.

There were black aloeswood trees, universal-eye incense trees, bright-lamp incense trees, mani-jewel incense trees, fire-colored incense trees, blue *aśoka* trees, red *aśoka* trees, *bakula* trees, *aciṭa* trees, *aśoka* trees, *nicula* trees, blue *campaka* trees, and *tilaka* trees; such various flowering incense trees as these had their blossoms in full bloom, always appearing as if freshly emerged.

Furthermore, there are various fruit trees: the *mātulunga* tree, the *phoenix-seed* tree, the *panasa* tree whose fruits are like jars, the *unobstructed-fruit* tree, the *hanging-gourd-fruit* tree, the *vīraṇa* tree, the *earth-canopy* tree, the *space-canopy* tree, the *cloud-colored-fruit* tree, the *delightful-to-behold-fruit* tree, the *cloud-obscuring-fruit* tree, the *bird-assembling-fruit* tree, the *bee-mango* tree, the *fragrant-wreath* tree, and the *fragrant-flower* tree; their flowers of various colors always bloom season after season.

When the women see them, they all give rise to delight and attachment for the trees—the *pūga* trees, grapevines, *kapittha* trees, and *pāruṣaka* trees—which possess abundant foliage, are adorned with radiance, cast deep shadows over the channels, and grace the springs and ponds, making them lovely to behold.

Such various kinds of trees as these—some grow within Jambudvīpa, some grow in the land of Uttarakuru, and some grow in the city of Radiance belonging to the Asura kings; among them are flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and even wine-producing trees.

The Asura King wanders everywhere for sightseeing, enjoying himself with pleasure, surrounded by a multitude of court ladies as he amuses himself; yet regarding these defiled afflictions—this impermanent, unstable, and swiftly decaying pleasure—he deems it a realm of ambrosia and immortality.
"The Asura King has four court ladies born from his thoughts:
the first is named Like a Shadow;
the second is named All Fragrances."
The third was named Subhavana;
the fourth was named Jinaśrī.

These four court ladies had twelve nayutas of handmaidens as their retinue, who surrounded the Asura King, providing him with entertainment to his heart's content; they indulged in pleasures of such boundless extravagance that no analogy can describe them.

The Asura King, having accomplished his own karma, was surrounded by immeasurable billions of celestial maidens; they enjoyed themselves in joy and delight within a jeweled palace of a thousand pillars, with rows of precious chambers.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates for what karmic retribution Rāhu, the asura king, attained the path of the asuras,
and by performing what karma did he receive such a retribution?
The verse says:
"Without cause there is no fruit; whatever karma one creates must have its retribution.
Just as a seed yields its fruit, so do wholesome deeds give rise to rebirth among humans and devas."
Through wholesome karma one obtains pleasant fruits, always dwelling among gods and humans;
through unwholesome karma one falls into the three lower realms.
How is it that the asuras receive the path of animals?
"How is it that one receives a pleasant retribution?
Those of little wisdom cannot comprehend this; what are the causes and conditions for it?
Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu then observed with the wisdom derived from hearing:

In the distant past, this asura practiced the dharma of the brahmins; he was preeminent in wisdom and well-versed in the various arts and crafts of the world. He delighted in practicing generosity, providing food, drink, fruits, roots, clear springs, fine water, dwellings, and bedding in the wilderness. Furthermore, at the four crossroads, he gave to the sick, to traveling merchants, and to the blind, the destitute, and the poor, providing them with dwellings, food, drink, and bedding until they were fully satisfied, yet he lacked right view.

“At that time, there was a monastery in the Mithilā forest, twenty yojanas in length and breadth. Within that temple were hundreds of thousands of Buddha-stūpas adorned with jewel-flames, a merit created collectively by King Nimi and five hundred other great kings.”

In the center was a stupa, adorned with necklaces and flaming garlands of pure gold, embellished and decorated with various ornaments of the seven precious gems. According to the names of the Buddhas they had previously heard, images of the Tathāgatas were all depicted there, along with various groves of trees, ponds, streams, and springs, as magnificent and sublime as those described above.

"At that time, within Jambudvīpa, all the groves and trees were present just as they are in the city of the Asura King Rāhu. Just as those trees were seen, artisans depicted and adorned them upon the stūpas; likewise, bathing pools, flowing springs, various wondrous lotuses, and birds sporting about were also as described above."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Bali who recited the Vedas and performed extensive meritorious deeds as previously described.

The brahmin then loaded four thousand chariots with various foods and drinks and traveled along a public road through a vast wilderness, intending to give whatever was needed to those on the way. There he saw a Buddhist stupa two yojanas high and fifty li wide.
At that time, there was an evil man who set fire to the stupa and abandoned it, departing.
When the brahmin saw the stupa burning, he thought to himself:

"I would rather stay here for a while to give merit and rescue the Tathāgata’s stupa—which is wonderfully adorned, exquisitely decorated, vast and rare—by extinguishing this fire so that the stupa shall not be destroyed."
‘If I do not extinguish this fire and the King learns of it, he may impose a severe punishment upon me.
This was neither out of genuine faith nor out of a spirit of reverence;
rather, he simply used four thousand chariots to carry water to put out the blaze.
Having extinguished the fire, he spoke with a smile:
"Did I gain merit or not by saving this stupa? If there is merit, I vow that in my future life I shall obtain a magnificent physical form, peerless throughout the realm of desire."
Although he made this vow, he still did not believe it; his thoughts were not upright, he constantly delighted in combat, and he did not trust in right action.
By the power of the field of merit, however, he was born in the City of Radiance as an Asura king.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 18;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 19.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Animals, Part Two:
"Furthermore, how does a bhikṣu contemplate the second abode of Rāhu, the Asura King?
He observes it with the wisdom of the divine eye: [text continues]"

The dwelling place of the Asura King is thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its gardens, groves, and bathing pools are lush with lotuses, and the sporting grounds are adorned by various species of birds.

The city of the asuras has ground made of gold, adorned everywhere with many mani-jewels and conch shells. It abounds with numerous court ladies who are upright and exceptionally beautiful. It is governed by Rāhu, the king of the asuras, where there is no contention or dispute; one can go wherever one intends by the mere power of thought.
The realms where they dwell consist of thirteen locations.
What are these thirteen?
The first is named Chami;
The second is named Courageous Runner;
the third is named Recollection;
the fourth is named Pearl Necklace.
The fifth is named Bee-Swirl;
the sixth is named Red-Fish-Eye;
the seventh is named Straight-Run.
Eighth, named Water-Walker;
ninth, named Dweller in the Void;
tenth, named Dweller in Mountain Caves.
Eleventh is named Pond of Affection;
twelfth is named Fish Mouth;
thirteenth is named Shared Path.

If in the world people are unfilial toward their parents, do not make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and do not practice the True Dharma, the hosts of devas will diminish and the hosts of asuras will increase;
if in the world people make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and practice the True Dharma, the asuras will diminish and the hosts of devas will increase.
"By means of the two causes and conditions of righteousness and unrighteousness, they cause the gods and asuras to increase or diminish.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the realm inhabited by Rāhu, the asura king, and the karmic fruits of the various asuras' deeds."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
these sentient beings see fishermen and hunters setting enclosures, laying nets, and spreading snares to intercept them;

yet for the sake of benefiting those beings so they may sustain their lives, they break down the fish dams, or by their power compel others to release living creatures. This may be for their own benefit, or to seek fame, or for the sake of kings, or for ministers who prohibit slaughter, or to protect their clans. Thus, through the practices inherited from previous generations, they follow the law of non-killing, though they do not practice other forms of goodness.
When such a person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they fall into the realm of the asuras and receive an asura body, with a lifespan lasting for five thousand years.

One day and night among the asuras is equivalent to five hundred years in the human world; thus their lifespan reaches a full five thousand years, though it may be slightly more or mostly less, and there are also those who die prematurely.
Hereafter, by the power of central causes and conditions, the physical marks and majestic virtue [of beings] receive their retribution according to their karma.
Bhikṣus, you should know this!
Observe the minds of sentient beings and their various inclinations and understandings.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the realm of Rāhu the asura at the bottom of the great ocean.
With the wisdom derived from hearing and with his foremost, pure, and sharp intelligence, he observes:

beneath the earth, in the second stratum, there is a land called Candrāvalī (Moon-Garland). It lies twenty-one thousand yojanas below the realm of Rāhu the asura. There dwells an asura named Dharmāhu (in the Wei language, 'Bone-Throat'), and the king of these asuras is named Puṣpamālī (Flower-Garland)."

There is a great city there named Yuga-līlā, eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its groves and forests are lush and verdant; clear streams and bathing pools are adorned with lotuses; and golden mountain crags and precipices abound. Deep and secluded mountain caves are filled with various birds and beasts, providing a pervasive adornment. The ground is made of blue *vaiḍūrya* gemstone, where soft and lovely green grasses grow, and the songs of diverse birds are harmonious and elegant.

The hosts of asuras all dwell therein; the realm is filled with abundance, joy, and peace, pervaded by wonders that are most delightful. The groves and pavilions adorned with trees of the seven treasures are also as described above.
Furthermore, there were various trees, exceptionally distinguished and twice as magnificent as those before:
the Nāga-dragon tree, the Aśoka-dragon tree, the Tāpa tree, the Khadira tree, and the Aśoka-bala tree.

Furthermore, there are various trees that surpass the previous groves, namely: the night-luminous tree (*rātry-ālokaka*), the night-blooming tree, the *paryuṣita* tree, the *niścanda* tree, the double-flowered tree, the universally beloved tree, the flower-cluster tree, the profusely blossoming tree, the soft-flowered tree, the five-year-flowering tree, the bee-delighting tree, the *gaurī-gaurī* sound-making tree, the tree where birds sport, the white-toothed tree, and the *nārada-leaf* tree.
The city of Yugandhara is situated among four mountains, which are golden in color:
the first is named Mount Nandana;
the second is named Mount Suvarṇajvālāgiri.
The third is named Mount Invisible Summit;
the fourth is named Lovely Light Mountain.

These mountains are five thousand yojanas in height and breadth, adorned with various groves of trees, flowing springs, and bathing pools. The river waters are clear and cool, and herds of diverse animals of many colors roam about according to their hues. There, many celestial maidens enjoy themselves in pleasure, and the gateways are decorated with various kinds of precious jewels.
The fragrant breeze from the *gośīrṣa-candana* trees is cool and refreshing, bringing joy and pleasure when it touches the body.

They constantly roam through fragrant forests, sporting and delighting themselves; various kinds of jewels provide radiance that is unobstructed, and they adorn their bodies with diverse exquisite flowers. There are the sounds of countless hundreds of thousands of peacocks.

Protected by the Great Asura King, the climate is temperate, free from extremes of cold and heat; many people dwell there in constant joy and delight, amusing themselves with music, song, dance, and laughter.

"In the city of Jyotir-mālā there is a great pool of water, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It is supremely pure and possesses the finest flavor; it is free from silt and turbidity, as well as any impurities. It is serene and inexhaustible, beautiful and lovely like the full moon."

In the city of Tārāmālā, there is a lake named Sarvadarśana. By the power of that lake, when the Asura King Dharmarāja wishes to engage in battle, he arrays his weapons and surrounds the lake; he beholds his own body as if looking into a clear mirror, and by observing his own reflection, he discerns whether he will be victorious or defeated in the fight.
In the waters of the pond, as in a clear and bright mirror, they see themselves retreating and fleeing, knowing that the gods will certainly be victorious;
if, within the pond, they see their own bodies lying prostrate, they know it to be a sign of death.
At that time, the asura king Dharmāhu—the asura king Vīryavanta—beheld his own body within the waters of the pond, either running or falling.
At that time, the asuras thought to themselves:
"For what reason do we see such things occurring in this pond?
Having fought with the devas and been defeated and driven back, we have all returned to our respective abodes, where we have remained for ten years, or a hundred years, or even five hundred years."

Then the Asura King Śūra, having arrayed himself with various weapons, diverse spears and armor, and adorned with ointments, powdered incense, and flower garlands, went again to the Sarvadarśana Pond and surrounded it to observe himself: "By what causes and conditions am I seen being destroyed?"

Thereupon, within the pond, he saw the people of Jambudvīpa filially supporting their parents, revering śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, practicing the True Dharma, and delighting in being reborn in the heavens; after their lives ended, they were reborn among the various devas.
Consequently, the hosts of devas increase while the hosts of asuras decline and diminish.
Seeing such signs within the pond, the courageous Asura King Dhamahu then reflects:

"Because humans practice filial piety toward their parents, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and act according to the causes and conditions of the Dharma, it is by the power of human beings that the devas have gained superior strength."
"I shall now perform acts that bring unhappiness and lack of benefit to the people of the world, so that the gods may diminish and we may increase.
Then, the Asura King Dhamahu-yongjian (Dharmāhu-vīryavanta) further reflected:
"It is by reason of human beings that the gods possess superior power."
"How shall I cause these people to lose their sustenance and cause even the gods to be thwarted?
It is because of food that humans obtain life and are able to practice the Dharma; now I must employ skillful means to cut off the food of these people."
Having reflected thus, he went directly to where the evil dragon king of the ocean was.
"This evil dragon king does not follow the practice of the Dharma; harboring poison and full of anger, he constantly causes great ruin and harm to others."
"I shall now go to that dwelling place.
"The Dragon King Nālanda, the Dragon King Vikrama, the Dragon King Kāla, and other such dragons do not accord with the True Dharma."
Then, having arrived at the place where the nāgas were, the asura king Dharmāru said these words:
"You have long enjoyed sovereign power over the people of the world;
yet now, with humans aiding the devas, they cause us to diminish."
"Human beings obtain their life-span by depending on food; you should cut off that food for these people.
If you can do so, there will be no more humans; and if there are no human beings, the gods will diminish."
"Just as the Naga King Vasuki and the Naga King Takshaka are your great enemies, so too am I to the various devas.
You may, for my sake, utterly destroy the human realm, which is my adversary."
At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Asura King Dharmarāja Śūra, the evil dragon replied: "Excellent!
I shall become your companion and assist you with my support."

At that time, the Dragon King entered his own palace and gave rise to great wrath; he caused the great waters to tremble, shaking them for a hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas.
The earth rests upon the water; because the water moves, the great earth also moves.
When unrighteous and evil dragons cause the great earth to move, the various worldly teachers of false views all say:
"Such a sign portends famine and disaster for the land," or they say, "It portends abundance and joy."
Some say that the king has passed away and the high ministers will suffer calamity;
some say it is an auspicious omen of divine blessing for the king;
others say that war will break out.
Some said it would be peaceful and secure;
some said there would be a water disaster;
others said there would be a severe drought.
The worldly prognosticators speak thus regarding the signs of an earthquake, yet they are unable to know the causes and conditions for its shaking.

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions that cause the great earth to shake; it is due to the causes and conditions of the various sentient beings' performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds that the earth shakes violently.
Beneath the earth there is a wind named the Sustaining Wind; because the Sustaining Wind moves, it causes the great waters to move;
because the great waters move, they cause the great earth to quake—fifty yojanas, or a hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas.
As the wind expands or contracts, the water moves accordingly;
as the water expands or contracts, the earth moves likewise.
By what cause and condition does the movement of the wind cause the water to move, and the movement of the water cause the earth to move?
He then observed with the wisdom of hearing and with his divine eye:
the wind sustains the water, and the water sustains the earth; because the wind moves, the great waters move;
and because the waters move, the great earth shakes.
These are the two causes and conditions that cause the earth-element to tremble.
That bhikṣu contemplates these two kinds of movements:
if it moves due to virtuous causes and conditions, sentient beings will enjoy abundance and happiness, free from all decline and affliction;
If sentient beings set in motion unwholesome actions as their causes and conditions, then unwholesome matters arise for those beings.

All karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, arise from causes and conditions; they do not arise without cause, nor is there a creator. The fruit of retribution is obtained in accordance with the similarity between cause and effect.
Astrologers with false views, ignorant of cause and effect, make such claims as:
"The Lord of Devas shakes the earth";

or they say it is moved by the wind; or they predict calamity or prosperity, famine or ruin, the good or ill fortune of kings, wind, rain, drought, or floods, whether wars and military arrays will arise or not, and whether the celestial ox or the Brahmin will be auspicious or malevolent.
The worldly physiognomists who divined good and ill fortune and those who observed the stars did not understand cause and effect;
they merely made such claims, recording a hundred calamities, each of which was verified by a single instance.
Fools all claim that this scripture of mine is supreme and peerless.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the Dāma-hu Aśura, the courageous Aśura King, the unrighteous and harassing evil Dragon Kings, and others.
Having completed his observation, for the sake of benefiting all the worlds, he reflected and examined:
"By what means can the wicked nāgas and base asuras be diminished and rendered powerless, so that they do not cause decay or destruction to the worlds?"
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows this:

when the people of Jambudvīpa practice the True Dharma, filially support their parents, and make offerings to śramaṇas, brahmins, and the elderly; and when kings and great ministers likewise practice the True Dharma—at that time, the earth deities and yakṣas, seeing those evil nāgas and evil asuras intending to act unlawfully and destroy the world, immediately go to the great ocean to the abodes of the dragon kings such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, and report these matters to them. They further inform the yakṣas dwelling in the sky, telling them of the aforementioned events.

At that time, the various yakṣas in the void, having heard these words spoken by the earth deities, immediately manifested great bodies and great supernormal powers, giving rise to intense wrath. Smoke issued from their mouths as they ascended through the air and went to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings, speaking these words: “O Devendra!”
"Those vexing and evil nāgas and wicked asuras now wish to destroy those in Jambudvīpa who practice the Dharma and cultivate filial piety.

When the heretical teachers of Jambudvīpa saw smoke issuing from the mouth of that yakṣa, they took it to be the appearance of a comet and said, "These are the one hundred and one sons of King Yama," not realizing they were actually one hundred and one powerful yakṣas.
At that time, among the people of the world, some saw them while others did not.
The worldly physiognomists said:
"These are the one hundred and one sons of King Yama."
Not knowing things as they truly are, one gives rise to false discrimination, saying that a comet has appeared:

some say there will be abundance and joy, while others say there will be famine; some say it portends good fortune for the king, while others say the king will pass away; some speak of the outbreak of war, while others say there will be no war; some say it is auspicious or inauspicious for oxen and Brahmins; some speak of floods, droughts, or other calamities; and some say a certain country will suffer misfortune and decline, while others say a certain country will have no troubles.
Although he speaks thus, it is false and unreal.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the conduct of evil nāgas and evil asuras.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
that yakṣa of great body and great supernormal power informs the assembly of devas of the aforementioned matter, whereupon the Four Great Kings say to the yakṣa,
"Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!"
The various devas are supreme and honored, while the hosts of asuras are timid, weak, and inferior;
what, then, can they possibly achieve?

Why is this so? It is because the people of Jambudvīpa practice the true Dharma, filially support their parents, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and show reverence to their elders and seniors.
"By this principle, my hosts shall increase, while the asuras shall become weak and powerless.

When the space-dwelling deities, the great yakṣas of vast supernatural powers, and others heard what the devas said, they rejoiced and leaped for joy. They conceived great wrath toward those evil nāgas and asuras, and immediately descended to visit the Dharma-practicing nāga kings Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the other nāga kings, to recount the aforementioned circumstances.
Descending from the sky, all his limbs blazed with surging flames; those who beheld this phenomenon all said, "Ullūka has descended"—in the Wei language, "the heavenly dog has descended."
If it descends at night, all people of the world see it;
if it descends during the day, some may see it while others do not.
It descends into the great ocean and goes to where the Great Nāga King Dharmavṛtti dwells, there to recount the aforementioned causes and conditions.
Having seen these signs, the worldly sorcerers who hold false views all made diverse pronouncements:

regarding the appearance of these signs, some said there would be abundance and joy; some said there would be famine; some spoke of the good or ill fortune of the king; some said war would break out, while others said it would not; some said the people would perish, while others said they would not die; and some said that for the cattle and the brahmins there would be auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
Although they speak thus, they do not understand the fruit of karma; their discourse follows mere appearances and lacks any reality.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates the descent of the fire from the Yauluka heaven, there is another cause and condition for the Yauluka fire to descend.

When the devas wish to travel, their palaces follow them; moving with great speed, two palaces race side by side, grinding against one another until they produce blazing flames. Their brilliant light surges forth and descends from above.
When people see this, various sorcerers and astrologers speak thus: some say there will be famine in the world; others say there will be abundance and joy;

some speak of the auspiciousness or misfortune, and the calamities or blessings, of kings; some speak of the peace and security of the land, while others speak of its ruin; some say that epidemics will spread among livestock and the people will suffer from grave illnesses, while others say that humans and animals will be safe, prosperous, and free from trouble.
Although various worldly heterodox theories make such assertions, they are unable to understand the causes and conditions of marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Why is this? Because they merely speak according to the marks without recognizing the fruits of karma.

Why is this? Because no one in the entire world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, or asuras—is able to know in such a way the subtle causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of action; nor can they contemplate these ten paths of wholesome karma within my Dharma and Vinaya, except for the Tathāgata alone.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the powerful yakṣas who travel through the air: how do they attain such great power that they can roam in the heavens and reach the abode of the Dharmacara Nāga King in the great ocean?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,

he sees that the sky-wandering yakṣas, possessing great supernormal powers, enter the great ocean and go to where the great nāga kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka— who practice in accordance with the Dharma— reside, and speak these words:
"The courageous Asura King Dhama-hu has gone to the Sarvadarśana Lake and is observing his own body (as described above)."
At that time, the great nāga kings, such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, having heard what the yakṣa said, addressed the yakṣa:
"As for those unlawful and evil nāgas, we shall rebuke them and cause them to be subdued."
I shall cause timely rain to fall upon that Jambudvīpa, so that the hundred grains and all crops of the people of Jambudvīpa may fully flourish, and they may enjoy abundance, joy, and peace.
Having heard this, the yakṣa departed with joy.

At that time, the great nāga kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka, along with other nāga kings, having adorned themselves, went to where the unrighteous and evil nāgas—the Nāgarāja who Torments Others and the Nāgarāja Who Is Impetuous—along with various other wicked nāgas, resided, and spoke these words:
"You practice what is contrary to the Dharma and delight in committing manifold evils;..."
I practice the True Dharma and accord with all that is wholesome.
You are no virtuous companion to us.
I now wish to contend with you to determine who shall prevail.

When the Dragon Nāraṇa, the Dragon Vikrānta, and the others heard these words, they immediately arose in full regalia; thunder rolled, lightning flashed, thunderbolts struck with fire, and a great rain poured down.

"If the people of Jambudvīpa are filial toward their parents, and provide offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior dignitaries, then the nāga kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka will attain superior power; they will harass and subdue the wicked nāga kings such as Phena and Veṣṭana, causing them to retreat in defeat, so that Jambudvīpa receives rain in its proper season and the people enjoy abundance and happiness."

At that time, various incantation masters and astrologers falsely propounded heterodox doctrines, claiming that it was due to the meritorious characteristics of the eight celestial bodies (*aṣṭagraha*) and the meritorious characteristics of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*aṣṭāviṃśatinakṣatra*) that great rain falls according to the seasons;
they asserted that it is by the power of the *gopālaka* Brahmins that the heavens send down rain, and not through any other causes or conditions.

If the people of Jambudvīpa are unfilial toward their parents, fail to make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, do not respect their elders, and do not practice the True Dharma, then the *pāśvika* and *takṣaka* nāgas who abide according to the Dharma will decline and lose their strength. At that time, the *kṣobhaṇa* and *vikrānta* nāgas will gain great power, causing the rains in Jambudvīpa to fall out of season, resulting in droughts, floods, and famine among the people.
Those in the world who hold wrong views—such as practitioners of incantations, astrologers, and various physiognomists—make such claims:
"It is due to the transgressions of the eight planets, the transgressions of the seasons, or the transgressions of the signs of divination."

The various non-Buddhists do not recognize the law of karmic cause and effect; they fail to understand that when many people commit evil, it causes calamities and famine in the nation. Instead, they formulate divergent doctrines, which are not based on the vision of reality as it truly is.

Why is this? Whether it be the world of devas, the world of Māras, or the world of Brahmās; whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—none of these constitute its domain. It is only the Tathāgata and my disciples, the various śramaṇas and others, who, having heard my teaching on the retribution of various karmas as well as the definitive characteristics of other karmic retributions, can know these actions; no other person is able to know them.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the abode of the Dharmāraṇya Asuras: if the dragon kings such as Vāsuki and others act in accordance with the Dharma, they attain great power; those who act contrary to the Dharma are destroyed."

The Asura Dāmaho, dwelling in the city of Tārakāmālā or within the forests, felt his heart wither away; his radiance and majestic power were both diminished. Ashamed and filled with sorrowful distress, he entered his own palace and thought to himself:
"When shall I now be able to defeat the devas?"
At that time, having reflected thus, Dharmāhu went to the abode of the Asura Rāhu and spoke these words: "O King of Asuras!"
"You must exert great strength and not be timid; before long, I shall defeat that host of devas.
Having heard these words, Rāhu, the Asura King, addressed the Asura Dharmāṅga-vīrya, saying:
"Do not be sorrowful or afraid; set your mind at ease for a moment. Before long, I shall destroy that host of devas along with their lord, Śakra Devendra."
When the Asura King Dharmāhu-vīrya heard these words, he was filled with joy once more and returned to his dwelling.
Furthermore, having understood the karmic retribution of beings and observed the city of Jyotiṣprabha, the bhikṣu next observes the remaining lands and gardens of the Asura King Dharmāhu.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes that in the realm of Dharmāraṇa there is a distinct grove, measuring thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within this grove are flowing streams and ponds, a place where various species of birds sport; it is adorned everywhere with lotus bathing pools and wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, where beings enjoy themselves and experience pleasure.
In that dwelling place, there are seven groves:
the first is named Cloud-Garland Grove;
the second is named Constant Grove; [and so forth].
The third is named Forest of Musical Performance;
the fourth is named Forest of Constantly Gathering Fruits;
the fifth is named Forest of Wind-Music.
The sixth is named Grove of Music and Dance;
the seventh is named Grove of Miscellaneous Jewels.
These are the seven great groves.
The dwelling place of the Dharmāraṇya Asuras is filled with many companions; through the power of their own karma, they all enjoy wealth and pleasure, which completely fills that realm.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the ripening of the karmic results experienced by the Dharmāraṇya Asuras.
By what karma was he born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In a previous life, this sentient being organized a great assembly of offerings to support non-Buddhists, practicing impure giving that was defiled, unstable, and inconsistent. He gave various kinds of food to those who had broken their precepts and followed mixed practices, his mind lacking right reflection.

Having given such gifts, at the end of his life he was reborn among the animals, receiving the body of a *dharmāhu* asura; according to whether his karma was inferior, middling, or superior, the joyful retribution he obtained was likewise inferior, middling, or superior—the cause and effect being of a corresponding nature.
