"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the karmic retribution of the asura king Vikrānta.
By what karmic retribution does one become an asura king?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

when this sentient being was among humans, he delighted in committing theft and robbery to steal the property of others; with improper reflection, he provided food and drink in abundance to non-Buddhist ascetics who were detached from desire.
By these causes and conditions, they are born among the asuras.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the length of the lifespan of the dharmāruṇa asuras.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing and by observing with the divine eye, he sees:
The lifespan of an asura is six thousand years; six hundred years among the Jambudvīpa people constitute one day and one night for the Dharmāraṇa asuras.
Thus, their lifespan reaches six thousand years, though it rarely exceeds this and mostly falls short; their life span is also uncertain.
Due to the causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, they are encompassed by the karmic fruits of the animal realm, serving as the second stage for the asuras.
Having contemplated the second stage, one accords with the practice of the Dharma and contemplates all sentient beings:

those who follow the Dharma, those protected by the Dharma, and all sentient beings encompassed within birth and death—those who, through wholesome karma, are born among humans and devas, and those who, through evil and unwholesome karma, are born in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, observes what the celestial messenger does after hearing these matters spoken by the yakṣas with supernormal powers in the midst of the sky."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows that the celestial messengers go to the world-protectors, the Mālādhāra gods, and speak thus:

"The hosts of asuras do not follow the practice of the Dharma; they instruct the evil nāgas to bring harm, ruin, and affliction upon those people of merit in Jambudvīpa who practice the Dharma and perform wholesome deeds."
Why is this? It is because he fears that those who practice virtue and accord with the Dharma, upon the end of their lives, will be reborn in the heavens. He thinks to himself:

"The people of Jambudvīpa, by means of food as a causal condition, are able to practice generosity, maintain ethical discipline, and cultivate wisdom; you should go to Jambudvīpa and send down calamitous rain to destroy the people's hundred grains."
"The *kinnaras*, *yakṣas*, and others who follow the Dharma have come to me and related these matters.
I now tell you: you must pass this on in turn to the other hosts of devas—namely, the Kuṇḍinī devas, the Triśaṅku devas, and the Nityotsada devas—and cause them all to hear it."

At that time, having heard what was said, the Four Great Heavenly Kings went to the Hall of Good Dharma within the City of Sudarśana, to the presence of the Heavenly King Kauśika, who was fully endowed with the merits of the five desires and his retinue, and related the aforementioned matter in detail.
The Lord of Devas, Kauśika, then addressed the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, saying: "You should go to Jambudvīpa to observe all sentient beings.

Are there those who have faith in the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Bhikṣu-saṃgha-jewel; who make offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior monks; who recognize kindness and repay it; who are upright and sincere, possessing faith; who filially support their parents; who observe the fasts and precepts; who are neither sycophantic nor devious; and who do not deceive others with false measures or weights, nor treat one another with contempt?"

At that time, having heard these words, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world descended to Jambudvīpa for the benefit of sentient beings. They observed each and every kingdom, each and every village, each and every city, military camp, and hamlet, examining everywhere as they traveled throughout to observe the practice of the Dharma teachings.

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world, seeing that the people of Jambudvīpa were practicing in accordance with the Dharma—filially supporting their parents and reverently believing in the Triple Gem—went upon seeing this to the city of Playful Delight within the palace of the Great Nāga King of the Great Ocean, to where the great Nāga Kings such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka resided, and spoke these words:
"O Dharma-practicing Nāga Kings!..."
Do not fear, do not fear!
Unrighteousness diminishes and the True Dharma increases; darkness is destroyed and light is revealed; the hosts of Māra are shaken, and the celestial hosts increase.

The devas, humans, and dragon kings delight in practicing the True Dharma; they are able to beat the drum of the Dharma and chant the melodies of the Dharma, thereby increasing the assembly of devas and diminishing the various māras, non-Dharmic evil dragons, and asuras.
When the great dragon kings, such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, heard this, they were filled with joy and addressed the four world-protecting heavenly kings, saying:
"We are now joyful, O Heavenly Kings!"
I now have no fear of unrighteous and evil dragons, nor of unrighteous and evil-acting, base asuras; they shall not be able to disturb or trouble the beings who practice the Dharma within Jambudvīpa.
"I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will announce this to the Heavenly King Śakra.
When the dragon kings had finished speaking these words, the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings went to the abode of Śakra and recounted the matter in detail.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard these words, he leaped for joy and spoke this verse in gāthā:
“The Muni truly knows and teaches the path of reality; If a person can practice it, they will be born in the heavens.
Practice giving with sincerity and cultivate a compassionate mind; Protect all sentient beings and speak words of kindness.”
With right view and a pure mind free from defilement, the Buddha taught the path to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
by practicing various virtuous deeds in accordance with purity, one can take right refuge with a wholesome mind.
From a state of bliss to a state of bliss, from radiance back into radiance;
like a *prabhāsa* flower falling at dawn, or as one lamp kindles another lamp—
if a person wishes to be like that lamp, do not act with negligence and destroy your own mind.
If one constantly practices a pure and wholesome mind, stainless and luminously clear like a precious gem,
such a person’s wisdom is free from defilement and can reach the places where the various devas are born.
Maintaining the precepts, practicing dhyāna and samādhi— if there are those capable of cultivating these in their minds,
such people’s wisdom is like pure gold, and they will surely attain rebirth in the palaces of the devas.
If one abandons the taking of life, gives rise to loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings,
and possesses a mind that is merciful, upright, and tranquil— such a person is born in the celestial palaces.
Bestowing gentle words upon all people, they abandon all evil and unwholesome deeds;
since evil karma cannot defile their minds, such persons are born in celestial palaces.
If a person views gold as mere grass and wood, and regards all sensual desires as fire or poison,
such a wise one who has abandoned desire will be born in a celestial palace and experience happiness.

If there are those who are not deluded by the objects of desire, And do not follow the causes and conditions of craving, They shall attain liberation from the terrors of the three evil realms; Such people as these are born in the heavens.
If one sees those engaged in strife and can offer counsel, skillfully reconciling friends, kinsmen,
and brothers so that they are free from contention— such a person is born in the heavens.
If a person leaves behind evil and emerges from the mire of desire, constantly bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings,
and attains liberation through a stainless and tranquil mind, they will be able to destroy the hosts of Māra’s army.
If one can subdue the mind and thought, and is not driven by mind and thought, such a person is pure and destroys their enemies; they shall attain rebirth in the celestial palaces.
If there is one who can purify the actions of the body, Who stays far removed from all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
And who, detached from desire, cultivates the bliss of meditative concentration— Such a person is born in the celestial palaces.
Abandoning negligence and evil associates, severing the poisonous afflictions of craving,
and not being bound by the desires of women— such a person is born in the celestial palaces.
If a person applies diligent effort toward the Dharma— practicing generosity, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating samādhi—
with a courageous will and a firm mind, that person shall be reborn in the heavens.
If a person can, with the sword of wisdom, sever the various fetters without obstruction,
attaining mastery and freedom from bonds without hindrance— such a person is born in the celestial palaces;
free from the defilement of all desires and without craving, they extinguish all faults and evils and eliminate stained attachment.
The valiant and pure one, having severed all longing, Then receives his own karmic retribution;
If there are sentient beings who receive human retribution, They are able to constantly practice all wholesome dharmas.
Such is the karmic fruit of the deeds of virtuous people, which causes the world of devas to flourish;
through human effort, the devas increase in excellence, and through the protection of the devas, humans dwell in peace and security.
Each mutually increasing their power, they abide upon the path that accords with the True Dharma:
the world of humans as the virtuous path for devas, and the realm of devas as the virtuous path for humans.
The grounds of the various evil realms are of three kinds, which those who practice goodness keep far from;
you should be courageous and exert yourself with diligence, and you ought to delight in drawing near to virtuous friends.
In this way, you should constantly increase the Dharma, and strive with all your might to ascend to the celestial palaces.
The Dharma is the root of all happiness; through the causes and conditions of the Dharma, one attains Nirvana.
While sentient beings sleep, the Dharma remains ever awake; the Dharma is the most supreme and foremost path.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having thus instructed the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world, traveled everywhere to observe [the realm], for the sake of protecting the people of Jambudvīpa and causing them to increase in the True Dharma and obtain benefit.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma, having observed the mental conduct of the devas, reflects within himself and practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma, having observed the second realm of the asuras, next observes the third realm of the asuras."
What is the third asura realm? Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that the third realm lies twenty-one thousand yojanas beneath the second realm.

There is an asura realm named Śūṇapa, measuring thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its forests are lush and verdant, its bathing pools and flowing springs are filled with flowers that bloom perpetually, and it is replete with musical instruments and entertainment.
The city is named Kambila, eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within that city dwells an asura king named Mālyāvat, and the asura subjects are known as Līlācarin.

That city of the asuras, Kambila, is adorned with various kinds of precious jewels; it possesses gardens for recreation, clear flowing streams, bathing pools, and lotus flowers, all of which are filled with hosts of asuras sporting therein.
There are four great groves that serve as its adornment, wherein flowers are perpetually fresh and flourishing throughout the six periods of the day.
What are these four? The first is named Ghaṇṭāmāla (Bell-Garland).
Each individual tree in the groves is hung with jeweled bells that emit exquisite sounds.
The second is named Yellow Garlands (*pītamālā*):
its groves consist entirely of trees made of pure gold.
The third is named Jvālāmāla:
the flowers of its trees are like flames.
The fourth is named Miśrakavana (Miscellaneous Forest).
Adorned with various flowers and fruits, these four kinds of groves beautify the asura city of Khambhīra.

The pleasure of the asuras who sport there in their dwelling places is no different from that of the devas; they anoint their bodies with various unguents and powdered incense, constantly delighting in play, song, dance, and laughter, surrounded and protected by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.

The Asura King Puṣpamāla constantly roams through gardens and groves to enjoy himself, his body adorned with various kinds of precious jewels; this is called the place of pleasure enjoyed by the sporting Asuras.
At that time, the second earth-dwelling Asura king, Vīra, dispatched a messenger named Yamapa to the Asura Mālyaputra, who spoke these words:

"Because the people of Jambudvīpa honor their parents, recognize and repay their debts of gratitude, and reverently serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, practicing according to the Dharma, they have empowered the gods. I shall now exert all my strength to destroy the true Dharma practiced by humans and devas."
At that time, having heard these words, the third earth-dwelling Asura King Puṣpamāla, as previously described, harbored a mind of anger and spoke thus:
"How shall I destroy those humans and devas?"
"Because of humans there are devas; thus, both humans and devas are my great enemies.

At that time, the Asura who sports in the third stage immediately arrayed himself in various kinds of armor and took up weapons, intending to go to the palace of the Dragon King in the City of Pleasure.

At that time, the great nāga kings Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others, hearing the sound of the asuras, gave rise to great wrath. From their bodies issued forth lightning and blazing flames of brilliant light, raining down massive, searing bolts of fire. Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas emerged from the ocean and joined the asuras in a great battle.
"If the people of Jambudvīpa practice the True Dharma, the nāgas will prevail and the hosts of asuras will scatter and be defeated;
if the people of the world do not conform to the True Dharma, then the asuras will prevail and the hosts of nāgas will be defeated."
Having been defeated, he went to the White Deity and said, "Great Seer!
I have now been defeated; you should exert all your strength to defeat the asuras."
When the celestial messenger heard these words, anger arose in his heart and smoke issued from his mouth; he went to inform the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O Heavenly Kings!..."
"The Asuras have triumphed; the Nāgas are now defeated.
When the diviners with false views in Jambudvīpa observe these signs of smoke, they all say:
"A comet has appeared; there will be either abundance or famine, or water or drought," as was previously described.
This is the second causal condition for the appearance of a comet:
if the devas and nāgas are victorious, then timely rains fall frequently, pestilence does not circulate, and warfare does not arise.
The diviners with false views further made this claim, elaborating on the aforementioned matters:
"It is the power of the eight planetary deities (*aṣṭagraha*) that acts thus.

If those in the world do not cultivate the True Dharma, do not act in accordance with the Dharma, are unfilial toward their parents, and do not revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, then the asuras shall prevail."
Because the asuras are victorious, rains fall out of season, the people suffer from famine, and weapons are frequently raised.
The various worldy diviners with false views think to themselves:
"This is the work of the eight planets."
He spoke to the people of the world regarding the faults of the stars, explaining them at length as described above.

In this way, all such non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do not understand what is the True Dharma and what is not the Dharma; with minds of ignorance, they engage in conceptualization and discrimination, speaking in a manner that does not accord with reality.
When the asuras were defeated and the dragon kings were overcome, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings addressed the assembly of the four directions with these verses:
“Dharma prevails and non-dharma diminishes; Truth increases and falsehood is abandoned.
The devas defeat the asuras; Light triumphs over darkness.”
Generosity surpasses stinginess; uphold the precepts and do not violate them.
The Buddha is supreme, not the non-Buddhists; immovability surpasses falling back.
Speak the truth and do not be deceitful; compassion surpasses malice.
Loving-kindness conquers hatred; the celestial king conquers the asuras.
The superior overcomes the inferior and shall not yield; abundance overcomes famine and shall not yield.
Wisdom overcomes ignorance and shall extinguish it; the Dharma and the precepts overcome all evils and shall extinguish them.
Diligence overcomes indolence; the man of noble character surpasses the woman;
the elder excels the petty person; patience triumphs over anger.
A human being surpasses an evil dragon; the day is superior to the night.
The moon excels other luminaries; the five grains excel the stalks of reeds.
By extinguishing suffering, happiness increases; free from illness, one is ever at peace.
Gentleness excels coarseness and wickedness; liberation extinguishes all bonds.
“The Dharma-precepts surpass all things; wholesome dharmas constantly increase and flourish, while unwholesome ones are perpetually extinguished.
After the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings had spoken thus, they struck their celestial drums and uttered these words:
"O great assembly of devas!
The Dragon King has been weakened and the asuras have triumphed.
When the host of devas heard these words, they arrayed their weapons and, in a mere instant, arrived at the great ocean.

If people of the world filially support their parents and reverently serve the śramaṇas, when the hosts of asuras see the devas approaching, they immediately retreat and disperse, returning to their own palaces.

If people of the world are unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, even for a brief moment, they will fight with the devas; yet the devas shall prevail, and the asura king Puṣpamāla will be defeated and dispersed, returning to his palace.

In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the battle between the asuras and the devas; having seen it as it truly is, he gives rise to a mind of world-weariness and practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the karmic retribution experienced by Mālyavat, the asura king of the third realm.
By what karma is one born in the third stage?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that these sentient beings, on festival days, engaged in various games of chance and skill such as wrestling, archery, *chuppo* (dice), and *weiqi* (go).
For this reason, one who practices impure giving does so without intention, without thought, and without a field of merit.
When such a person’s body perishes, they fall into the evil realms and are born among the Asuras of the Realm of Playful Activity, where their lifespan is seven thousand years.

Seven hundred years among humans constitute one day and night among the asuras; their lifespan thus reaches a full seven thousand years, yet there are also premature deaths, and their life spans are not fixed.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes and contemplates the asura king Puṣpamāla.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
This asura king gave food to a sick person who had broken the precepts, yet his mind was devoid of pure intention."
By reason of these karmic conditions, he was born among the asuras and became the asura king in the city of Khaṃbirā, named Puṣpamālā.
His food tasted like the *sudarśana* nectar consumed by the devas, and all his articles of pleasure were as previously described.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Nineteen *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
Fascicle Twenty Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Five, Part Three: On Animals.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the fourth realm of the asuras.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There is a realm of animals and asuras located twenty-one thousand yojanas beneath the third earth, named Acala. This land is vast, measuring sixty thousand yojanas in extent; its city is named Khambhīra, spanning thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and is exquisitely adorned.
The Asura King is named Prahāsa, and the host of Asuras is named Sarvakṣānti. This Asura King has attained supreme sovereignty among all Asuras;

he is peaceful, joyful, courageous, and robust, possessing radiant majesty, self-mastery, and fearlessness. He does not even fear Śakra Devendra, let alone the other devas. Possessing great power and influence, yet being heedless, arrogant, and conceited, he dwells beneath the entire earth; below this, there is no further place to dwell.

This is the dwelling place of the asura king, where the ground is composed of mani-jewels; his mind is constantly joyful, like a person delighting in festivities and self-amusement. It abounds in love and pride, and is adorned all around with various lotus flowers, flowing springs, and bathing pools.
The city of Kāmpīla was adorned with palaces made of the seven treasures; free from all enemies, its inhabitants were mutually affectionate, without fear of others, and enjoyed the highest bliss.

In this fourth stage, the city of Khaṃbirā is adorned with groves, gardens, flowing streams, and lotus ponds; its palaces made of the seven precious gems are upright, majestic, and exquisitely wonderful, just as stars situated in the sky are upright, majestic, and exquisitely wonderful.
The verse says: “The mind can create all karma; Because of the mind, there are all fruits.
In this way, through various mental activities, One obtains various kinds of retributions.”
The mind is the masterful painter of all things; it can give rise to manifold activities within the three realms.
Driven by the mind, one wanders through all destinies, taking birth everywhere without end.
The mind is the root of both bondage and liberation; therefore, it is said that the mind is supreme.
By doing good, one attains liberation; by committing evil and unwholesome deeds, one is bound.
Thus, the mental faculty drives sentient beings, causing them to wander and transmigrate through the ocean of the three realms.
Because they are under the sway of the fetters of ignorance and craving, the mental formations cause sentient beings to wander in saṃsāra;
they cannot reach that city of nirvāṇa, like those born blind who have lost the right path.
"Thus, because sentient beings perform various kinds of karma, that city receives various kinds of retribution; this is the fourth stage.

Outside its walls, it is surrounded on all sides by groves, gardens, streams, and ponds, adorned with rivers, springs, lotuses, and various species of birds; such is the dwelling place of the fourth stage of the asuras."

All the Asuras, such as the Sarvāsahas, were valiant and fearless, possessing supreme beauty that adorned their bodies; they took delight together without causing one another any distress, their minds constantly joyful as if at a festival.
Together with his various female attendants, all magnificently adorned, and surrounded by each of his retinues of followers—whether numbering a hundred or a thousand—he sports and delights.
That ground is entirely composed of mani-jewels and pearls serving as female attendants, their radiance shimmering brilliantly.
All the asuras revere and honor the asura king Pāhāsa, gazing upon him without weariness;
yet, though they receive the retribution of pleasure, it is impermanent and destined for decay and dispersal.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the retribution experienced by the asura king Sarva-saha.
By what karma was he born in that place?"

Through the wisdom born of hearing, he sees that when these sentient beings were among humans, their minds were shrouded by wrong views and they did not recognize the fruits of karma; having abandoned the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they encountered a person of supreme diligence and integrity who required something and came to beg from them; though they begged with great hardship, the beings gave but a single meal.
Having already given the food, he spoke these words:
"I have given you this food; what merit is there in it?
It was out of delusion that I gave you this food."
“You base person, you should not have gone forth; to give food to you is like casting seeds into salty, barren soil.
Because of such difficult giving, when his body perishes at the end of life, he falls into the evil realms on account of this difficult gift.

Through impure giving, by virtue of the merit of the field of blessings, one is born in a place of supreme peace and bliss, adorned with various jewels; yet, receiving the retribution of an animal, one is born in the Immovable Realm as an asura named Sarvakṣānti (All-Enduring).
This means that he is equal to the gods and surpasses all other asura kings, being fully endowed with every kind of pleasure and requisite.
Such a retribution is obtained through giving to fields of merit; it does not arise from one's own mind.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the karma and its retribution of the entire host of Asuras of Sarvatovīra.
By what karmic retribution are they born in the realm of the Asuras of Sarvatovīra?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

these sentient beings are attached to delicious flavors; dwelling among the forest trees, they protect these forests not for the sake of other beings, but for the purpose of sustaining their own lives.
Lacking any compassion, they protect all the forests solely for the sake of the causes and conditions that sustain their own physical existence.
By these causes and conditions, when his body perishes and his life ends, he is reborn among the Asuras of Sarvāsaha.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the Asuras as they battle with the devas.
He then observes with the wisdom born of hearing:

The Dragon King Dharmacara dwells in the city of Kridaratna; upon the head of this dragon king are seven heads, which are named the Dragon King Vasuki, the Dragon King Takshaka, the Dragon King Bhadra, the Dragon King Lohita, the Dragon King Meghamala, the Dragon King Padma, the Dragon King Sarvavarta, the Dragon King Pahasa, and the Dragon King Varisa.
These dragon kings possess right view and accord with the Dharma; they delight in renouncing negligence, as previously described.

At that time, the non-Dharmic and unrighteous evil dragon kings—namely, the dragon king Padma, the dragon king Viśāla, the dragon king Kāla, the dragon king Hūhū, and others—having been defeated by the dragon kings who act in accordance with the Dharma, immediately fled to the first dwelling place, where the Asuras of the Twin Games resided, and spoke these words:
"Come quickly! Come quickly!"
"Companions, you should know!
The Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Takṣaka, and the Four Heavenly Kings have destroyed us; you are now our close friends—why do you not assist us?"
When the Asura Viśvāsa heard these words, he immediately went to the city of Prabhā and approached the Asura Rāhu; having arrived, he related the aforementioned matter in full.

If Rāhu, the Asura King, knows that the people of the world are practicing the True Dharma, making offerings to śramaṇas, and recognizing and repaying kindness, he says to the evil dragon kings such as Pāṭhīna:

"Wait for one month and restrain those dragon kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka; I shall inform the Asura King of the second residence so that he will not trouble you," and so on, as explained above in detail.
When the asura Dharmāruṇa heard these words, he entered the city of Tārākāraṇḍaka and went to the place where the asura king was, speaking thus: "Great King!
The Asura King Rāhu sent a messenger to inform me, saying:
"The Naga King Vāsuki, the various Naga Kings such as Takṣaka, and the Four Great Kings are harassing Padma."
At that time, having heard these words, the second earth-dwelling Asura King, Vīrabala, immediately observed himself:
"Do I have the power or not?
If the people of Jambudvīpa were practicing the True Dharma and making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, he would know he lacked the power and would reply to the messenger:
"The devas possess great power.
Why is this? Because the people of Jambudvīpa practice the True Dharma."
"I shall now go to inform the third place and extensively explain these matters above to all the Asuras of Sarvagamin.

Then, the Asura Vikrama immediately went to inform the host of Asuras dwelling in that third abode. When the Asura Sarvagamin heard these words, he entered the city of Khaṃpīra and went to the presence of the Asura King Mālādhāra, where he again related the aforementioned matters.
The Asura King Puṣpamāla then observed the people of Jambudvīpa; seeing those who made offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, he addressed the Asura Sarvacārin, saying:
"I shall inform the Asuras of the fourth abode."
Then the asura of the third stage went to where the asura of the fourth stage was and spoke these words:
"Vāsuki and Takṣaka, together with the Four Heavenly Kings, have defeated my companions, the nāga kings. I shall now bring great distress and ruin upon those hosts of devas."
At that time, having heard these words, the asura hosts of the fourth abode immediately headed toward the city of Kambala and arrived at the place of the asura king Pāhāsa.
Then Bāhuka asked the asuras, "For what reason are you traveling so swiftly?
They answered as above, and then Bāhuka addressed the assembly of asuras:
"Rāhu and the other asuras are powerless; they can only cause the Four Heavenly Kings to destroy the Bhr̥ṅgī and other nāga kings.
As for those in the world who follow the Dharma, making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—what power could they possibly have?"
"I am able to destroy them.
Then, the Asura King Pāhāsa went to where the great assembly of Asuras was and addressed them, saying:
"Quickly prepare yourselves! I now wish to go to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings, such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, to defeat their armies."
Then the various Asura kings, by means of their peerless power, led their armies to battle with the gods.
At that time, the Asura King Pāhāsa addressed the Asuras, saying:
"For what reason do you lack the courage and strength to defeat those Dragon Kings, yet instead bring about your own destruction?"
"I shall now go myself and, by my own physical strength, destroy that dragon-god.
Then the Asura King Pāhāsa commanded his army:
"Quickly prepare yourselves and take up your weapons!"
"In no long time, I shall engage in battle with the gods. You will first witness my enmity with the celestial foes; it shall soon break out.
I have already informed the host of asuras that the gods cannot be tolerated and must be fought."
When the asuras learned of this matter, they immediately equipped themselves with various weapons.

At that time, the powerful Asura King Prahlāda, relying on his own heroic strength and great courage, disregarded the relative superiority or inferiority of his own power versus that of others; he emerged from his city and proceeded to the third earth, arriving at the city of Khaṇḍavīra to reach the presence of the Asura King Mālādhāra.
At that time, the Asura King Pāhāsa, together with immeasurable billions of nayutas of asuras, went to where the asura Mālādhāra was and spoke these words:
"Arise quickly! Arise quickly!"
"For the sake of battle,
we are capable of defeating the various dragon kings such as the Vāsuki and Takṣaka, as well as the celestial kings.
When the Asura King Puṣpamāla heard these words, he addressed his military hosts:
"Now is not the time for battle.

Why is this? Because the people of Jambudvīpa provide filial support to their parents, revere the śramaṇas, and practice the True Dharma; it is because of these matters that the gods possess great power."
"Therefore, this is not the time for battle.
When the asura king Pāhāsa heard these words from the asura king Puṣpamāla, he said:
"Arise quickly! Arise quickly!"
"I am capable of defeating Vāsuki and the rest, as well as the hosts of devas, all by myself;
how much more so with you as my companions!

When the Asura King Puṣpamāla heard these words, his power increased and his heart was filled with joy; together with his immeasurable billions of nayutas of Asura hosts, he proceeded to the second stage.
Then the asura king Pāhāsa, the asura king Vikrānta, and the asura king Mālādhāra followed one another to the abode of the asura Rāhu and said to him:
"Arise quickly! Arise quickly!"
"The Asura King [acts] for the sake of battle and to defeat the devas.
Then Rāhu, the Asura King, addressed the various Asura Kings, saying:
"For us now, this is not the time for battle."

Why is this? Because the people of Jambudvīpa filially support their parents and respectfully honor śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; they are reborn in the heavens, causing the gods to possess great power. For this reason, they cannot engage in battle with the gods.
Because it was not the proper time, the Asura kings said to Rāhu, the Asura:
"Arise quickly! Arise quickly!"
"I have come here for the sake of battle, wishing to fight with the gods.
Then Rāhu, the Asura King, immediately followed his intent and arose, intending to go to the great ocean; he addressed the evil Nāga Kings such as Pāṭhīna and others, speaking these words:
"The various Asura Kings now wish to defeat those Nāga Kings, the Pauṣkas and the Takṣakas."
When Pāṭhī heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy; he immediately went to where Vāsuki and Takṣaka were and said to them:
"Come, my companions! You should come forth now; I shall fight with you. Where shall we stand to do battle?"
Then the dragon kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka emerged from their city and fought against the evil dragon Pāṭala; the unrighteous dragon king was defeated and retreated.
At that time, immeasurable billions of asura hosts rushed swiftly toward the abode of the dragon kings, desiring to engage in battle with them.
Then, Vāsuki and Takṣaka emerged from their city and arrayed themselves against the asuras on the great ocean for a battle so vast it cannot be described.

"In the midst of the void, some rain down great fires while others rain down swords and halberds, attacking one another; scorched by the poison of craving and due to their delusion, they thus engage in such strife."

If the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, filially supporting their parents and revering śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, then a single dragon who practices the Dharma can alone defeat the entire army of the asuras;
if those in the world who practice the Dharma are few, then the asuras prevail and the dragons who practice the Dharma retreat.
"If the nāgas are defeated, they immediately go to the celestial messenger and say:
'Come quickly! Come quickly!
All the hosts of asuras have come to attack me; I have fought them and been defeated, losing out to them.'"
When the celestial messenger heard these words, he armed himself with various weapons and went to where the nāga kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka were, saying to them:
"I have heard that you have been defeated by the asura king; therefore, I have come here to destroy the asura army."
Then the celestial messenger and the Dragon King went together to the abode of the Asuras, desiring to engage them in battle.
Upon hearing of this matter, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, also proceeded toward the gods and drew up his battle lines upon the great ocean to fight.
If people of the world practice in accordance with the Dharma, the celestial messengers will then be able to swiftly defeat the hosts of asuras.
Once the asuras have been defeated, they return to their palaces and cities.
At that time, when the asura hosts of the Second Earth heard these words, they addressed their armies, saying:
"Do not fear! Since my own body still endures, I am capable of subduing those devas; what have you to fear?"
Then the asuras immediately rushed back to the celestial messengers and raised a great battle, engaging in combat and arraying their forces together within the great ocean.
The devas again achieved victory and destroyed the asura army.

Once the asura army had been defeated, the asuras of the third realm, hearing that they had been broken, immediately advanced toward the gods and engaged them in battle, inflicting mutual harm upon one another.
"If the gods are defeated, they shall go to the Four World-Protecting Devas and the Kāla gods and say: 'O Deva Kings!
Haste to our aid; the hosts of asuras are harassing us.'"
At that time, the Kāla devas took up their various weapons and immediately went to where the asuras were.

When the asuras saw the celestial hosts approaching, they gave rise to great wrath and quickly went to where the devas were. They engaged the host of Kāla devas in a great battle in formation, such that those who witnessed it had their hair stand on end.
Among all the battles in the world, none is greater than the war between the devas and the asuras; it is beyond comparison.
If those in the world practice in accordance with the Dharma, the Kālaya devas will achieve great victory and destroy the asuras.
Thus, the battle between the vast multitudes of devas and asuras in the great ocean is beyond all comparison.
By the power of the causes and conditions of Dharma and non-Dharma, there are those who triumph and those who retreat; it is not by their own inherent strength.
"If the Kāla gods are defeated by them, the World-Protecting Gods (Lokapālas) will immediately go and inform the hosts of Mālādhara gods.
Then the Mālādharas, together with the Kālas, the celestial messengers, the Takṣakas, the Vāsukis, and an immeasurable multitude, will assemble in harmony."

At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, resided in the City of Radiance; together with the first-rank Asuras who sport in pairs, the Dharmāhus, and an immeasurable number of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of Asura hosts, he formed a single army to battle the devas in a manner beyond description.

If people of the world practice in accordance with the Dharma, the celestial hosts will prevail, and the armies of the asuras will retreat, disperse, and be destroyed; all this is due to the power and influence of the Dharma, which causes the devas to achieve victory, not through what is contrary to the Dharma.
"If there are no practitioners who follow the Dharma, then the asuras will prevail.
Having witnessed this, the Four World-Protecting Devas went to the realm of the Constantly Indulgent Devas and spoke thus:
"Quickly prepare yourselves; the asura army has gained the upper hand over the celestial hosts."

Having heard these words, the gods of the Constantly Indulgent Heaven, accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, took up various weapons and set out for the great ocean to battle the asuras. Standing within the great ocean, they raised a loud, fierce shout, desiring to swiftly destroy the asura army. They engaged in mutual combat for a long time; it was a great and terrible battle, filled with immeasurable suffering and distress.
"If the asuras are defeated by the devas, they immediately go to where Rāhu, the asura, is and recount all that has occurred.
Then Rāhu, the king of the asuras, consoles the asuras, saying:
'Do not fear now; do not be afraid now.'"
"I possess great power capable of destroying the host of devas; the strength of the devas is weak and inferior, while my power surpasses theirs.
Asuras! You should turn back."
When the various asuras heard these words spoken by Rāhu, the asura king, they immediately turned back again, desiring to fight with the devas.

At that time, the devas and asuras drew up their battle lines for a great conflict; with immeasurable swords and halberds they struck and hacked at one another. During this great battle, the asuras of the first earth, the Yugaṃdharas, and the asuras of the second earth, the Tāmrābhas, joined the hosts of devas in combat against their enemies.
"If the people of the world do not practice in accordance with the Dharma, the asuras will prevail and the hosts of devas will retreat;
if the people of the world practice the True Dharma, the hosts of devas will prevail and will be able to utterly destroy the armies of the asuras."
Such a Dharma is the supreme banner of the devas; the Dharma is foremost, and the Dharma is the true savior.
If one practices what is contrary to the Dharma, then for such a practitioner of unrighteousness, the Dharma shall not save them.
Because all the asuras practice what is contrary to the Dharma, the devas think to themselves:
"The asura kings harass and disturb us; they are neither superior to the devas nor equal to them."

Why is this? Because the people of Jambudvīpa filially support their parents, act in accordance with the Dharma, and show reverence to those of noble lineage, the elderly, and the virtuous; they purely observe the eight precepts of the fast, practice giving and uphold the precepts to cultivate merit, refrain from negligence, and do not associate with evil friends. Such people, when their lives end, are reborn in the heavens.
"The Asuras act contrary to the Dharma and lack the true Dharma;
we must protect all the hosts of devas.

Having reflected thus, the celestial messengers, the Mālava-devas, the Nitya-manorama-devas, and all the other hosts of devas took up the banners of the deva-dharma and rushed swiftly toward the asura army, addressing them with these words:
"Stop, stop! O Asuras! We dwell among the devas; for what reason do you repeatedly harass us?"
Since you are unable to overcome the power of the devas and are not their superior, your weapons cannot defeat them.
I have come here for the purpose of destroying your army; because of your malice toward the devas, you shall not reach the palace city where you dwell.
"Because you all do not practice the True Dharma, you shall obtain neither peace nor tranquility.

Having spoken thus, he went directly to their location; with total resolve and valor, he rained down great swords and halberds, while Vāsuki and others rained down great flaming fires, which fell upon the army of the asuras.
At that time, having witnessed these events, the asuras immediately called out to the various evil nāgas, such as Pāṭhīna:
"You shall be my allies; you must join me in battle against the great nāga kings Takṣaka and Vāsuki by raining down fire."

When Padma had heard these words, he immediately ran toward the abode of Vāsuki; at that time, the two classes of nāgas rained down fire upon one another as the devas and asuras engaged in a great battle.
The gods again achieved victory and shattered the army of the asuras.
At that time, the asuras all joined together and went to the abode of Rāhu the asura, appearing dejected and haggard as they sought protection.
When Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, saw this, he comforted them, saying:
"Do not be afraid, do not be terrified! Because I am here, even if I were alone, I would not fear that Śakra, the Heavenly King; how much less so when you all are my followers and allies."
"The devas are weak and inferior; what can they possibly do?
Of what are you afraid?

I shall now inform the great seer, the valiant Asura King, the Asura King Puṣpamāla, the Asura King Bāhuka, Vemacitra, and the others. Once I have spoken to them, I myself shall go and defeat those hosts of devas."
Then Rāhu, the Asura King, went at once to inform the Asura Kings of the third realm. Having arrived at their abode, he spoke these words:
"All the hosts of devas and the gods of the Four Great Kings have united and come to my place to fight with me. Now we must consider what expedient means to employ to defeat those devas."
When the asuras heard these words, they replied to Rāhu Asura, saying:
"We shall array ourselves and go to battle against Śakra, the King of the Thirty-three Heavens."
"You may go now; the gods shall be defeated and the asuras shall prevail.
Then Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, went at once to the battlefield, desiring to fight with the gods.
Then the hosts of asuras said to Rāhu, the king of the asuras:
"Great King! The devas possess great power! The devas possess great power!"
"They cannot be fought together.
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, immediately advanced toward the celestial hosts and rained down various swords and halberds to battle with the gods.

When the gods saw the Asuras raining down swords and halberds, they caused the nāgas to rain fire; they rushed forward, desiring to break Rāhu’s Asura army. The gods rained down swords and halberds like vajras, and as their ranks interlocked in combat, the battle was beyond description.

"If the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, serve their parents with filial piety, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and show respect to the elders, then the celestial hosts will prevail and the asura armies will retreat in defeat;
if the people of the world do not follow the teachings of the Dharma, then the devas will weaken and the asuras will triumph."
Thus, due to the power of the Dharma and the power of non-Dharma, the gods and asuras engage in unequal combat.
If the asuras prevail and the host of gods is defeated, all the celestial hosts cry out to one another: "O devas! O devas!"
"One should keep the Dharma in mind.

Because of the Dharma, the hosts of devas are victorious; by reason of the Dharma, the devas increase. Therefore, all devas should give rise to faith and reverence, contemplate and keep the Dharma in mind, and proceed once more toward those armies of asuras."
Because all the hosts of devas were mindful of the Dharma, they were protected by the Dharma; their radiance and majestic virtue increased until they surpassed their former state a hundredfold.
When the asuras saw the radiance and majestic virtue of the deva hosts, they became timid and weak, and addressed their armies:
"Why have you now become so timid and weak?"
"The majesty and virtue of Heaven do not equal ours; when it comes to clashing with swords, halberds, and weapons, or wrestling, I have completely defeated them all.
Why, then, do you now give rise to such timidity and weakness?"

At that time, when the various military hosts heard the words of consolation from the Asura King, their strength and vigor increased; thereupon, the army of Rāhu, the Asura, turned back toward the celestial hosts.

At that time, the various devas, having gained power in their bodies, rushed swiftly toward the asuras for a great battle in formation. Then, while the mighty asura king Rāhu stood within his army like a second Mount Sumeru, the devas, by means of their spiritual power, immediately shattered Rāhu’s asura host.
"Among all forms of protection, the Dharma is foremost; among all lights, the light of the Dharma is supreme.
At that time, Rāhu the Asura saw his host shattered, retreating in dispersal, and all were rendered timid and weak.
The Asura King further comforted them, saying: "You Asuras, do not fear! Do not fear!"
"Why is it that you, who are men, are as timid as crows within your own homes?
How can you claim to be brave and heroic, true great men?

You yourselves all understand the principles of debate and possess no fear; you have already witnessed countless armies being shattered and routed. Why, then, do you now give rise to sorrow and terror?"
When the asuras heard these words of consolation, joy arose in their hearts; yet, out of arrogance, they immediately turned back, intending to fight with the devas.
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, with a mind of arrogance, stood at the head of his army; all the asuras relied upon Rāhu, were protected by Rāhu, and regarded King Rāhu as the foremost.
All the asuras went toward the Four Great Kings; relying on the power of the asura Rāhu, they gained renewed vigor and said:
"The asura king Rāhu marches before us; if this king’s power can even defeat that Lord Śakra, how much more so the Four Great Kings!"

He immediately confronted the enemy again, raining down various swords and halberds, and further raining down great stones like massive mountains descending from the sky, intending to destroy the celestial hosts.
At that time, the World-Protecting Devas, seeing the Asura King Rāhu raining down great rocky mountains, addressed the hosts of devas:
"The Asura King Rāhu is raining down great rocky mountains; you all should rain down swords, halberds, spears, and lances, lest the host of devas suffer great decline and distress."

When the World-Protecting Deities (Lokapālas) had spoken these words, they, together with the hosts of devas, went directly toward Rāhu, the King of the Asuras. They engaged Rāhu in a great battle of arrayed forces, raining down swords and stones from the sky that fell into the great ocean, causing the waters to boil and surge. The devas rained down swords and blades, wounding and killing countless hundreds of thousands of species of sentient beings within the sea; some died, while others were struck with terror and fled in all directions throughout the great ocean, where they were covered entirely by foam and bubbles.
When Rāhu the asura fought with the devas, the remaining devas and asuras, having witnessed this event, all thought to themselves:
"This is unprecedented!"
Thus the gods and the asuras engaged in a great battle, fighting without ceasing.

"If the people of the world practice in accordance with the Dharma, then all the asuras—though they possess many arts and skills such as swords, spears, lances, and blades, and though they are of great strength, valor, and courage with hearts free from fear—even with these arts, they are immediately defeated.
However, if the people of the world do not follow the True Dharma, then Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, shall triumph over the host of gods."
Therefore, the Dharma is foremost; the Dharma is supreme. Among all phenomena, none are without causes and conditions.

When Rāhu, the Asura King, was defeated and his power lost, all the Asuras became dejected and weary of their martial intent. At that time, seeing that his entire host was dejected and had conceived a spirit of renunciation, Rāhu, the Asura King, addressed them, saying: "O Asuras!"
Do not distress yourself and cause your mind to become weak.
Do not fear, do not fear!
If I were to go with you to your original palace city, I would not dwell there in peace and happiness.
"Do not harbor such thoughts as to wish to return to the palace city.
Display your martial prowess to increase your physical strength; turn back toward the battlefield and do not return to your original place.

When the asuras heard these words, they again went to where the Four Heavenly Kings were and fought once more. They rained down great stone mountains, with thunder and lightning and pouring rain; black clouds swirled as they drew up their ranks for a great battle, making the hair of those who saw them stand on end.
"The gods again achieved victory and shattered the army of the asuras. All the asuras thought to themselves: 'The gods possess great power;
we should go to the second residence, the city of Tārakāmāla, to seek the protection, benefit, and peace of the asura king there, so that we may defeat the hosts of the gods.'"

Within that city there is an asura king named Vikrānta, who is naturally courageous; he has already fought against the devas hundreds of thousands of times and has even been victorious over Śakra-devendra, the Lord of Devas—thus this asura excels all others.
Having reflected thus, they all went together to where the asura Vīrabala was and spoke these words:
"O Asura King! The celestial hosts possess great power; even when Rāhu, the asura king, fights against them, he cannot subdue them."

You should go quickly now and benefit them with your strength, providing them protection and assistance through your superior power; for if the King were to take up his weapon, even Śakra, the Lord of Devas, could not defeat the army of the asuras, let alone the other hosts of devas.

The King had previously subdued them and attained great renown among the Asuras in all their battles; he swiftly approached them, rushing forward with haste, grasping weapons in his hands and brandishing his armaments to fight the gods and defeat that celestial host.
"You have already shattered those diamond-fists hundreds of thousands of times; in those heavens, you displayed your superior strength, exerting your majesty and shaking with martial prowess.
When the Asura King heard these words, he immediately went to where the Asuras Puṣpamāla and Vemacitrin Bāhuka were and spoke thus:
"The celestial army is superior in strength and has destroyed Rāhu, the Asura King, along with his hosts. Your Majesty, now permit me to fight against the gods so that I may achieve victory."
Then the Asura King Puṣpamāla, the Asura King Vemacitra, and the Asura Bāhuka immediately addressed the Asura Śūra:
"Go quickly! Go quickly!"
"I shall be your companion and am able to destroy the hosts of devas.
If you assist Rāhu, the Asura King, you will be able to shatter all the celestial hosts, let alone the Four Heavenly Kings."
When the Asura King Śūra heard these words, he immediately went to where Rāhu the Asura was, in order to assist in the battle.

When the hosts of Asuras saw Śūra approaching, they were all greatly rejoiced; their courage and strength were fully aroused, and grasping weapons such as swords, spears, arrows, and lances, they advanced directly toward the celestial hosts, deploying various implements of war as arrows fell like rain.
At that time, the gods saw these two asuras leading their great armies and each said:
"These asuras come repeatedly to harass the celestial hosts without any sense of shame; because they are beasts, we have destroyed them many times, yet they still do not cease coming."
Having spoken thus, he firmly armed himself and, exerting his vigorous strength, advanced toward the army of the asuras, desiring to engage them in battle.
At that time, the asura kings Vīrabhadra and Rāhu, seeing the celestial hosts, spoke these words:
"The gods have now descended here; they will surely engage us in combat. We shall set our ranks against the gods and wage a great battle."
At that time, after the two asura kings had deliberated thus, they quickly went to the abode of the Four Great Kings, resolute in their desire to fight, each hoping for victory.

"If the sun is behind the heavenly host and the army of the asuras is in front, because the radiance of the sun shines upon their eyes, they are unable to inflict harm; nor can they rain down swords, spears, halberds, or lances. They cannot gaze directly at the devas with their eyes, and each says to the others:
'The dazzling brilliance of the sun's light strikes our eyes.'"
For this reason, they cannot engage in battle with the gods.
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, immediately obstructs the sun’s rays with one hand; this is the third causal condition.
When people see this, with their deluded minds they all speak thus: "Now there is a solar eclipse;

some say there will be abundance, while others say there will be scarcity; some speak of floods, while others speak of drought; some speak of the auspiciousness or misfortune, the calamities or blessings of the king, while others speak of whether there shall be an epidemic among the people or not."
Thus, though it is without reality, they give rise to false discrimination; not knowing things as they truly are, they speak according to their ignorance.
"In this way, the Asura King Rāhu obstructs the sunlight and says to the Asura Vikrama:
'The heavens are now easy to see! The heavens are now easy to see!'"
"One may destroy those gods with swords, various weapons, and arms such as spears and halberds.
Then the valiant Asura King rushed forward at the head of the host, raining down various swords and halberds upon the abodes of the gods.
When the celestial hosts saw this, they too swiftly advanced, arraying themselves with various weapons of war.
The valiant Asura King rained down a multitude of armaments—swords, blades, spears, and lances—upon the Mālādhāra devas. Upon seeing this, the Mālādhāra devas exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O Asura King! My celestial hosts have defeated you time and again, yet you feel no shame and do not give rise to a sense of weariness.
Because I rely on the Dharma, because I practice the Dharma, because I take refuge in the Dharma, because I cultivate the Dharma, and because I never depart from the Dharma, I am victorious."
Because you are full of greed, you covet the property of others, hoping to use it for your own sake; because you practice much greed, you do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
How can you hope to destroy these gods who follow the Dharma through the ten paths of wholesome action?
"Darkness cannot obscure or obstruct light, for the power of light is superior.
When the Asura King Viryavanta heard these words, he said to the devas:
"What need is there for many words!"

I beheld the supernatural powers and majestic virtue of you all and could not endure it; we relied on our own strength to destroy the celestial hosts because we could not bear seeing the superior majesty and virtue of the gods.
Having spoken these words, he went straight toward the realm of the Mālādharas.

When the Mālādharas saw this, they rained down various arrows, striking the bodies of the asuras so that there was no space left uncovered, raining down a multitude of swords upon the head of the valiant asura.
Then the Mālyadhāra devas said to the asuras:
"Why are you so greedy, O asuras?"
"You have brought about your own destruction through your evil karma; why then do you wage war against the gods?

That which is contrary to the Dharma cannot destroy that which accords with the Dharma. I shall not cause you any further decline or affliction; for what reason do you repeatedly harass the celestial hosts?"
"Although he spoke these words, the asuras nevertheless continued to gallop and rush toward the celestial hosts.
At that time, the Māndhātṛ devas addressed the nāga kings Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the others, saying:
'Now this valiant asura king, out of arrogance, relies on his own strength and remains unsubdued.'"
"You should now rain down great fires upon the asuras, causing them to lose their strength, be destroyed, and retreat.

When Vāsuki heard these words, he immediately rained down fierce, blazing fire from mid-air, burning the evil nāgas such as Padma and others; he then rushed swiftly toward the valiant asuras, discharging great, glowing lightning and the fierce fire of thunderbolts upon the asura army.
When the Asura King had been struck by the dragon-fire, he gave rise to great wrath; seizing a massive boulder eight hundred li in breadth with his hands, he hurled it at the Mālādhāra devas.
When the Kāla devas witnessed this, they immediately rained down great fire, burning that mountain to ashes.
At that time, the Asura King Śūra, seeing the mountain being consumed by fire, immediately lost his power and said to the gods:
"This mountain is already burning; I shall now hurl another great mountain upon your bodies."
"At that time, the Asura King Valavanta held up a great mountain in his hand, intending once more to hurl it at heaven.
Then the hosts of devas said to the Asura:
'Since you possess no Dharma and act contrary to the Dharma, you shall not be able to destroy us.'"
"I abide in the True Dharma, while you abide in what is not the Dharma.
Thus did the devas revile the asura king.
Upon hearing these words, Rāhu, the asura king, led his host and rushed swiftly toward the devas.

Upon seeing this, the hosts of devas also all rushed forward, desiring to engage the asuras in a great battle in formation; they attacked one another with various weapons—swords, halberds, spears, lances, arrows, and javelins.
When the devas had finished preaching the Dharma, they called it to mind with sincere hearts and took refuge in the Triple Gem; they then advanced directly toward the asura army.
Once the celestial hosts arrived, the asura forces were completely routed and dispersed into hundreds of thousands of fragments, seeking to flee down into the ocean.
The unrighteous and evil nāgas, such as Padma-ti and others, said to the asuras:
"Do not fear! Do not fear!
Now that you have abandoned us, where do you intend to go?"
"I can restrain the nāga kings such as Takṣaka and Vāsuki; you alone shall engage in battle with the devas and defeat the celestial hosts."
If you are afraid, why did you originally leave the palace city of your own accord and come here?
Without examining the relative strength or weakness of your own power, why have you made enemies with the devas?
"If you abandon your enmity and return to your original palace city, where shall we, the host of nāgas, go?
Takṣaka and Vāsuki are our enemies; where shall we go?"
When the asuras heard these words, they returned to the realm of the devas and fought with them.

At that time, the wicked nāgas were unable to obstruct those nāgas who acted in accordance with the Dharma; consequently, the asura army soon retreated and dispersed, returning beneath the sea to enter their own palaces.
At that time, seeing his army thus defeated, the asura dispatched another asura to the third earth to the asura Flower-Garland and said to him: "Great King!
"Arise quickly! Arise quickly!
The hosts of devas are victorious; they have shattered the entire army of asuras, scattering them into the four realms of rebirth as they flee in all directions.
Great King, you have long fought with the devas and attained great renown; now, likewise, you must rouse your fierce resolve and destroy these celestial hosts."
"If the King were to go forth, even Śakra, the Lord of Devas, would be unable to stand as his adversary, let alone the other hosts of devas.

At that time, having heard these words, the Asura King Puṣpamāla reflected and deliberated; he was immediately surrounded by immeasurable billions of Asuras, who were themselves firmly arrayed with various weapons—swords, halberds, spears, and lances—and they proceeded to the battlefield, letting out a great roar that filled the ten directions.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, spoke to Śūra, the Asura:
"The Asura King Puṣpamāla is now approaching here; he will augment our power and destroy the hosts of the devas."
"Turn back now! Turn back now! The Flower-Garland Asura has arrived; I am now possessed of great power.
Having heard this, the host returned to the battlefield, desiring to fight with the gods.
Then the Four Great Heavenly Kings said to the asuras:
"You follow the ways of beasts; though the gods have repeatedly defeated you, you turn back once more.
With your foolish minds, you bring ruin upon your own armies."
Having spoken these words, he rushed swiftly toward the host of asuras. Seeing the devas approaching, the Mālyaputra asura addressed his army:
"O asuras, do not be afraid, do not be terrified; go forth to battle with the devas!"
"Why do you gather here?
Break up that host of devas; do not give way to cowardice! Since I exist, what have you to fear?
I alone am capable of destroying all the devas, let alone the valiant Asura King who is my ally and the Asura King Rāhu, son of Siṃhika, who is my companion."
"You all, in this battle, do not give rise to fear; do not give rise to fear!
Increase your power and break through those devas, causing the asuras to increase their victory; exert your great strength and wage war against them."

When the Asura Mālādhāra had thus issued his command, he immediately went together with the other Asuras to the abodes of the Mālādhāra-devas, the Nityotsada-devas, the Kālayaṣṭi-devas, and the Triṃśatkoṭi-devas. There, the ground of lapis lazuli was everywhere magnificently adorned; their hearts filled with joy, they spoke these words:
"We do not require Śakra, the King of Devas of the Thirty-three Heavens, who repeatedly destroys the Asura armies; for by the power of Dharma and having Dharma as our companion, we shall prevail."
At that time, the asuras, dwelling in the great ocean and spread across its surface, gathered at the great ocean, desiring to fight with the devas.
When the devas saw that the great host of asuras had assembled, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"All the third-level flower-garland asuras, those who possessed great power in former times, have now all come together."
After these words were spoken, the hosts of asuras all arrived at that place.
When the gods saw them, they immediately addressed the asuras, saying:
"You have come here in vain, hoping to destroy our celestial host."
I possess great power; why is this?

Because the people of Jambudvīpa follow the practice of the Dharma, provide filial support to their parents, make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, delight in wholesome dharmas, and cultivate wholesome dharmas; thus, at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the heavens.
Therefore, we are now superior to you; we possess great power and are foremost and peerless.
We practice in accordance with the Dharma and in conformity with the Dharma, and we do not afflict you, yet you practice what is contrary to the Dharma and afflict us.
When the asuras heard these words, they did not heed the speech of the devas and immediately engaged them in battle.
Then the various devas, from their respective abodes filling the entirety of space, descended from the sky, desiring to shatter the army of the asuras.

The sound of the two armies clashing shook the great ocean; fish, turtles, crocodiles, sea monsters (*makara*), and *nāga* fish were all seized with great terror, scattering in a hundred or even a thousand fragments.
The gods and others engaged in a great battle, raining down various weapons—spears, lances, swords, and halberds. Thus did the gods and the asuras wage a great war.
At that time, the asura king Puṣpamāla addressed the gods, saying:
"The vanguard is fighting; it is not yet my turn to arrive, so let me shatter them."
"Now that I have arrived here, I shall destroy your host; I alone am able to subdue Śakra, let alone you, the assembly of the Four Great Kings; therefore, I can defeat your celestial hosts."
Having spoken these words, he immediately proceeded toward the Mālidhāra devas.
At that time, the Kāla devas, seeing him approach, immediately went to the place where the Puṣpamāla asuras were.

At that time, wishing to break his army, the asura took up a great boulder from the edge of the great ocean—measuring four hundred li, or three hundred li, or two hundred li, or one hundred li, or one yojana—and, with it ablaze with a great fire, he intended to hurl this mountain at the Kāla gods.
When the devas saw this, they immediately took refuge in the Triple Gem and contemplated the Dharma; they shot arrows at him, shattering him like fine sand that fell into the great ocean.
At that time, seeing his efforts were fruitless, the asura took up a great halberd and engaged in battle against the Kāla devas.
Once the gods had seen this, they rained down vajra-hail from the midst of the sky, shattering their swords and halberds, so that the asura army was utterly dispersed and destroyed.

Then the asura king Vīrabala again rushed toward the Suyāma devas, desiring to engage them in battle; he seized the great mountain named Parikha, five hundred yojanas in breadth, and addressed the gods, saying:
"I shall now defeat all you gods and send your celestial hosts to the abode of King Yama."
Having spoken these words, he went straight toward the Heaven of Constant Indulgence (*Sadāmatta*).

When the World-Protectors (*Lokapāla*) saw this, they seized Mount Vṛtra and struck the chest of the asura with it; the asura was instantly shattered, fled down into the depths of the ocean, and returned to his original dwelling place.
At that time, seeing the Asuras retreat, the entire army of the Dharmāraṇya Asuras also dispersed and fled; exhausted and on the verge of death, they returned to their original abodes.
At that time, Rāhu the asura and his host again rushed swiftly toward the Trāyastriṃśa devas, intending to engage them in battle by relying on his own power.

When the devas saw this, they rained down great, fierce fires upon Rāhu the asura, burning the asura army; the asura king and his host retreated in flight, scattered and destroyed, returning to the depths of the ocean.
At that time, seeing the Asura army completely routed and dispersing, the devas were filled with great joy.
The Asura King was overcome with grief and distress; his manly strength utterly shattered, he fled back toward the waters and entered through the gate, seeking protection and a place of refuge.

At that time, the hosts of devas, knowing that the asuras had all entered beneath the waters, returned to the summit of their own mountain and dwelt upon the Vaiḍūrya mountain, fearing that the asuras might come there once again.
Why is this? "The Asura King Vemacitra Pāhāsa is the most powerful among the asuras, the foremost and most excellent, and capable of rescuing all asuras; yet even he has not yet arrived."
"If they are defeated, all the asuras will be utterly defeated.
Having spoken these words, they were all greatly delighted; their strength increased, and together they gazed afar at the asura army, resolutely determined to do battle.

Then the Dharma-practicing Dragon Kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka, having defeated the remnants of the Pāramati and others who had been wounded, returned to the city of Krīḍāpura. They hoped that Bāhuka, the Asura King, would destroy the gods and protect them; yet if he could not defeat them, the gods would regain the victory and their hosts would increase.
Thus, the Asura allies, such as the evil dragon kings Pāṭhīna and others, dwelt within their own cities, tormented by grief and suffering.
The Asura armies likewise remained in their respective places, filled with sorrow, anxiety, and distress.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty-One.
Translated by the Bactrian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.

Chapter Five: On Animals, Part Four At that time, when the Asura King Vemacitrin heard that the Asura Kings Puṣpamāla, Vikrama, and Rāhu had been defeated and deprived of their power, another Asura said to Bāhuka:
"The army has been shattered and there is no one capable of saving it; only you possess the strength to protect those troops."
Bāhasa said: "Quickly look where those three asura kings are now! The asuras replied:

"Now they have all been defeated by the various devas and have returned to the bottom of the water, staying beneath the gate; having lost all their power, they have sent word from afar to the Great King Sālaghaṣa, seeking his protection and hoping for his assistance. Ashamed and abashed, they remain beneath the gate and are unable to enter the city."
When Vemacitrin Bāhika heard these words, he spoke to the asuras, saying:
"Asuras, when you wage war against the devas, is Śakra, the Lord of Devas, not among them?"
The asura replied, "I have never come before.
Upon hearing these words, Pāhāsa was seized with great rage; his eyes turned red as blood, and exerting his physical strength, he glared at the asura and spoke thus:

"Only the Four Heavenly Kings have destroyed the asuras of the three lower realms and deprived them of their power; the asura army is rendered powerless, having been defeated by a single deity. I shall now go forth to destroy all the devas."
When the Asura King Pāhāsa had spoken these words, all the Asuras were filled with great power.
The Asura King commanded his armies to quickly beat the drums, saying:
"I wish to go forth myself to strike the celestial hosts, so that they shall be shattered, afflicted, and utterly destroyed; even Śakra, the King of Devas, I alone am able to defeat."
"The gods are now destroying the host of asuras, and I cannot endure this.
If it were not for me, one might say that the gods possess great power;
yet since I still exist, how can these gods have such great strength as to desire to seize my asura daughters?"
After Vemacitrī Bāhika had spoken these words, he struck the great war drum and addressed the host of armies:
"Quickly prepare yourselves! I now wish to go and attack that celestial host, so that the asura forces may all increase."

Having issued these commands, he immediately manifested a hundred thousand wheel-palaces (*cakravimāna*). The light of the immeasurable thousands of billions of *asura* armies was like that of the sun; at the very moment they were manifested, the entire earth with its mountains and rivers, Mount Gandhamādana, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all shook violently. Even the city of Sudarśana, the Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), and the place where Śakra, Lord of Devas, sat, trembled and became unstable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"My seat is shaking; the Asura King must be fighting with the gods, which is why my place of sitting is tilting."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the gods, saying:

"If Vemacitrin the Asura rises up, then the groves, forests, mountain valleys, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, will all tremble violently; you, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, must quickly prepare yourselves."
The asuras have arrived; the asura king Vemacitrin Pāhāsa has mobilized his forces, desiring to come and destroy the celestial hosts.
I shall now also mount the elephant Airāvaṇa, and together with the various celestial hosts, proceed to the place of battle.
"Why is this? For I do not see any among the hosts of devas who can engage in battle with this Asura King Vemacitra Pāhāsa.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these words, he commanded all the hosts of devas dwelling in every individual celestial palace within the city of Sudarśana to depart from the city of Sudarśana and proceed to the place of battle against Vemacitra Pāhāsa.
Having heard this, the celestial hosts immediately entered the Caitraratha Grove to take up various weapons.
In this Caitraratha Grove, all manner of martial equipment is fully provided.

At that time, hundreds, thousands, or even trillions of those celestial hosts swiftly entered that forest, all seizing their weapons; their clamor and agitation were like the sound of the ocean tide, as they crowded and rushed together, raising clouds of dust that filled the sky.
In this way, the great assembly had some moving through the void, some along mountain ridges, and some through mountain valleys; the surrounding great array left no empty space.

Furthermore, there were various devas sporting among the groves who, upon hearing the sound of the drums, rushed toward the Caitraratha Grove. Discarding their sensual pleasures, they took up various weapons of war. In groups of hundreds, thousands, ten billions, and millions, all the devas together gazed up at Śakra, King of Devas.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing this host of devas, was filled with great joy and sat upon a palace made of many jewels.

That palace was magnificent and adorned with the seven treasures; it was embellished with some radiant jewels, some with golden ornaments, some with lapis lazuli, some with crystal, some with musaragalva, some with karketana, and various other great gems, or adorned with various mani-jewels. It was draped with jeweled nets and hung with clusters of precious bells, so upright, dignified, and exquisite that it was like the ripening of karmic fruit.
Having obtained these magnificent palaces, their bodies were radiant with a majestic brilliance that blazed forth.

Their ranks were so closely arrayed that there was no space between them for a person to pass; some filled the slopes of Mount Sumeru’s peaks to its utmost extent, while others dwelt in the air by the hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands, all gazing together upon Śakra, the King of Devas. They waited expectantly for the Lord of Devas to engage in battle with the Asura Kings, each devising various expedients and strategies.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to his charioteer: "Worthy sir!
Go and inform that six-headed white elephant Airāvaṇa—who is endowed with all the virtues of a great nāga—that I shall mount this elephant to crush the asuras."
At that time, the minister, having received the command of the Lord of Heaven, immediately proceeded to the place of the Wish-Fulfilling Lotus Pond.
At that moment, Airāvaṇa, the six-headed white elephant, was sporting in the pond with a multitude of other elephants. Then the attendant addressed the elephant’s son, saying:
"The Lord of Heaven, Śakra, wishes to mount this precious elephant to destroy the Asuras."
Upon hearing this, the elephant cub immediately informed the precious elephant.
When Airāvaṇa heard what was said, he went with the keeper to the presence of the royal minister; having arrived at the Sudharmā Hall, the attendant entered and addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"Your Majesty, you should know!"
"The first precious elephant has now arrived.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, by means of his recollection, transformed this precious elephant so that it had a hundred heads. Their faces were pure and free from all dust and defilement; each head possessed ten tusks, all of which were fresh and white. At the tip of each tusk was a pool of flowers; in each pool were a thousand lotuses; on each lotus was a flower pedestal; on each pedestal were a hundred flower petals. Within each petal were a hundred jade maidens who, with the five kinds of music, sang, danced, and played, producing exquisite sounds beyond compare.

Thus, this supreme jewel-elephant Airāvaṇa was manifested by Śakra, the King of Devas; his body was vast, measuring one thousand yojanas, and his color was a pure, bright white beyond compare. Mounted upon him, Śakra set out from the city of Sudarśana, intending to destroy the army of the Asuras. Various musical instruments were played, with some singing and dancing, some laughing and jesting, and others whistling, roaring, or shouting. Radiant, majestic, dignified, and exquisite, he departed from the city.

Having seen this, the various devas each mounted palaces of diverse colors made of various jewels; adorned themselves with various weapons and instruments, and accompanied by various musical performances, songs, dances, and laughter, they uttered cries of joy and delight like the sound of a cackling goose.
