Seeing King Śakra, their joy was doubled compared to before.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sat upright upon a precious elephant, with the King seated within it. It was formed through the accumulation of the power of great merit; surrounded on all sides by immeasurable hosts of devas, its majesty and dignity were beyond compare, as various celestial multitudes gathered around it.

The radiance of the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings surpassed that of a hundred thousand suns, filling the void of space; the sounds of various musical instruments pervaded twenty thousand yojanas as they descended from above to the place where the battle with the asuras was taking place.
"At that time, the four world-protecting Great Kings raised a great cry, ascended into the void, and went to visit Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
While in mid-air, they encountered Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and addressed him, saying:
'O Heavenly King!'"

When Vemacitrin Bāhika desired to wage war against the devas, all the great oceans were agitated and unsettled, and hundreds of thousands of mountain ranges all shook and trembled. The hosts of asuras displayed their martial prowess in sport, emitting sounds of great terror; the fish, turtles, and young nāgas of the great ocean all lost their physical strength, while the minor rākṣasas, piśācas, and immeasurable sentient beings perished, losing their lives.
The unrighteous and evil dragon Brahmadatta rejoiced and leaped about, roaring like a thunderclap;
the righteous dragon kings Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others remained dejected and self-contained.
When the Asura King Vemacitra emerged from beneath the waters, sixty thousand Sumeru mountains of pure gold were all shaken, and the hearts of all sentient beings became timid and weak.

The Māndhātṛ devas, the Nityapramuditā devas, the Kālayaśas devas, and the Trivīṇā devas are all terrified, cowardly, and ill at ease; they have sent me here to the Great Heavenly King’s presence. What skillful means should the Heavenly King employ?

In this way, I have already defeated the asura armies of those three realms; the asura king Rāhu, the asura king Puṣpamāla, and the asura king Vikrānta—these hundreds of thousands who fought together—have all been utterly destroyed.
Having heard this, Śakra addressed the World-Protectors, saying:
"I have already known beforehand that Vemacitrin Bāhika has given rise to the desire to afflict the gods; I now wish to descend and crush the army of the asuras to rescue and protect all the devas."

I take refuge in the Dharma and am rescued by the Dharma; I practice the Dharma, for the Dharma is the supreme banner. I seek the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, taking no pleasure in what is contrary to the Dharma.
"By means of such merit as this, I shall be able to defeat that army; I shall be victorious, and there is none who can defeat me. Do not give way to fear.
I am now leading a great host to the abode of the asuras; do not be timid."

Why is this? Because the people of Jambudvīpa filially support their parents; they revere śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior monks; they recognize kindness and repay it; they practice in accordance with the Dharma, protect the True Dharma, delight in the True Dharma, and faithfully believe in the True Dharma; they make offerings to śramaṇas, understand the retribution of karmic actions, observe the fasts and precepts on the six days of purification, and cultivate merit through giving, uphold the precepts, and practice wisdom.

I constantly recollect and practice in accordance with the Dharma, receiving and observing the precepts of the Dharma; since those asuras possess no such practice of the Dharma, I have not the slightest fear toward them.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these words, he went to the summit of Mount Vaidūrya, the dwelling place of the Four Great Kings.
There, Śakra saw the Four Great Kings and addressed the assembly of devas:
"The four world-protectors have gathered here, desiring to destroy the army of the asuras."
Then the World-Protecting Deities addressed Śakra, saying:
"These hosts of devas are gathered under the protection of the Heavenly King, guarded by the Heavenly King, and rely upon the Heavenly King; they fear neither the asuras nor their armies."
When this had been said, all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with great joy and praised the Heavenly King, saying:
"Victory to the Heavenly King!
Victory to the celestial hosts!"
Having offered these praises, he proceeded to the abode of the Four Great Kings.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial palaces and his divine hosts. He rode upon Airāvaṇa, the great white elephant king, whose body was as exquisite as described above. The blazing radiance of the seven precious jewels was as brilliant as lightning, filling the void of space. The thunderous sound of immeasurable music resounded throughout the ten directions, and hundreds of thousands of devas joyfully surrounded him as he dwelt upon Mount Sumeru.

The hosts of gandharvas adorn the various devas; sages and saints offer incomparable praise through song and hymn. Together they enjoy themselves, experiencing the foremost pleasure as the fruit of their own virtuous karma.
At that time, when the Four Heavenly Kings saw Śakra descend, they were all greatly rejoiced.
Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"I have now come here wishing to defeat the asuras; do not fear, do not fear!"
"The great assembly of devas has all gathered here.
When the four classes of devas heard this, they were filled with joy and said:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"I am already capable of defeating the asuras alone; how much more so now that the Heavenly King has arrived and the great assembly is gathered.
Relying upon the Heavenly King, I have not the slightest fear of the asuras."
Having spoken these words, he immediately circumambulated Śakra and stood to one side, observing the armies of the asura kings Vemacitrin, Rāhu, Vikrānta, and Mālādhāra.

Clad in the adamantine armor of the various devas and grasping diverse weapons and implements in their hands, they desire to crush the army of the asuras; with unceasing resolve, they dwell upon palaces adorned with various jewels. The nāga kings Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Takṣaka, whose minds are intent on battle, stand to one side gazing up at Śakra, ready to carry out his commands as soon as they are given.
They looked together toward the water.

Then the four Asura kings suddenly emerged directly, surrounded by a host of all their troops numbering immeasurable thousands of billions. Holding various weapons of war in their hands, they advanced straight forward, paying no heed to their left or right. Surrounded by a great multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions, all the Mount Sumerus were made to tremble.

Among all the asuras, his strength was supreme; he was well-versed in immeasurable arts of combat. Emerging from beneath the waters like a second Sumeru King of Mountains, surrounded by the unrighteous and evil nāgas such as Pāṭhīna and others, Vemacitrin Bāhusaha arrived at the battlefield.

The great assembly of devas filled the void of space, while the army of asuras covered the great ocean; wishing to engage in a great battle with the host of devas, they each reflected within themselves.
Desiring to observe the battle, he stood to one side.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Takṣaka, Vāsuki, and others said to Śakra:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"The army of the asuras stands before us; O Heavenly King, why do you not command us to engage them in battle?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the hosts of devas and the hosts of nāgas:

"I shall now dispatch the Four World-Protectors to Jambudvīpa among the four continents to observe those sentient beings who provide filial support to their parents, show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and practice in accordance with the Dharma; such people will be able to destroy the army of the asuras."
The devas are protected by the Dharma; relying upon the Dharma and increasing through the Dharma, the devas also increase.
Because the Dharma declines, the hosts of devas also diminish.
"I now send you to Jambudvīpa to reach the world of humans.
Having spoken thus, he immediately commanded the Four Heavenly Kings:

"Go quickly to Jambudvīpa to observe all sentient beings. Are there any who accord with the Dharma—those who filially support their parents, revere their elders, make offerings to śramaṇas, maintain themselves through the observance of fasts and precepts, practice generosity and uphold the precepts, and refrain from negligence while following the True Dharma?"

When the four world-protectors had heard these words, they traveled in the time it takes to shoot an arrow to every single dwelling, every village, every city, every military camp, every crossroads, and every kingdom throughout Jambudvīpa, observing everything: whether people were filially supporting their parents, making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and honoring the elderly and long-established seniors; they observed all of this everywhere.

He saw that the people of Jambudvīpa were practicing in accordance with the Dharma, filially supporting their parents, making offerings to śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, and senior monks, and practicing according to the Dharma.
Having seen this, his heart was filled with joy; in the time it takes to shoot an arrow, he arrived at the abode of Śakra and, overflowing with delight, addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"How truly cause for celebration and joy!"
"Śakra Devānām Indra!

The people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, filially supporting their parents, and showing reverence to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior members of the community. By practicing generosity and cultivating virtue, they increase the hosts of devas and diminish the armies of the asuras."
Upon hearing this, Śakra was filled with great joy and said to the World-Protectors:
"All the hosts of devas should rejoice; I shall now destroy the army of the asuras!"
"I shall now destroy the army of the asuras, for the people of Jambudvīpa have cultivated much merit.
Upon hearing this, the celestial hosts were all greatly delighted; their physical strength increased tenfold beyond what it was before, and they addressed him, saying:
"O Heavenly King!"
For what reason do you remain?
For what reason do you remain?
By means of the majestic power of the Heavenly King, I shall destroy those enemies and cause the devas to achieve victory.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the dragon kings Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the others, saying:
"Go quickly to the place of the unrighteous dragons such as Pāṭhīna; do not go to the army of the Asuras led by Vemacitra."

When Vāsuki and Takṣaka heard these words, they immediately went swiftly to where the non-dharmic nāgas, such as the Asura companion Pārvatī and others, were located, and rained down great, fierce fires upon them.

Then Vemacitrī Bāhika immediately dispatched Padma-ati to discharge great, blazing lightning; all the evil nāgas’ bodies burst into flames as they suffered great agony, and being thus destroyed, they fled toward the army of the asuras, saying these words:
"Each of our separate divisions cannot defeat that great host; we must all unite and fight together, for only then can the gods be broken."
Having spoken these words, he immediately ran back toward the abodes of the nāgas Vāsuki and Takṣaka.
At that time, the nāga Vāsuki, who practices the Dharma, saw that evil nāga and said to Takṣaka:
"He comes with an evil mind and full of anger; I shall cause him distress and affliction so that he will not come again."
"If we do not strike him back, he will continue to harass and disturb us in this manner again and again.

Having spoken these words, the dragon Kālika immediately rushed toward Padma-tīra; from the midst of the sky, he rained down great, fierce fires and released clouds of smoke and flames to burn that evil nāga.
Once they had been burned, they immediately retreated and fled toward the abode of the asuras, hoping to save their lives.
When the asura king Rāhu saw this, he spoke these words:
"These nāgas have been defeated and have retreated here."
"Why do you abandon them and stay here?
Having spoken these words, he rushed forward with all his might.

At that time, the deity Kālayasas, seeing the asura Rāhu approaching, also ran toward him; their armies met in battle, which was most terrifying, like a perilous precipice. All the minor asuras dwelling within the ocean were deafened and overwhelmed, and some, struck with terror, lost their lives.

"Rains of swords fall from the sky, pressing down and descending with great speed, numbering in the hundreds of thousands. When fighting in this manner, if a deva is harmed and his hands or feet are severed, they are immediately restored; he suffers no injury, and all his limbs are likewise free from pain or affliction. His physical appearance remains unchanged, and he is endowed with exquisite beauty, except in the case of decapitation or the severing of half the body."
The devas and asuras are mutual enemies and thus engage in battle.
If an asura is slain by a deva, he does not regenerate once severed; this is according to the law of humans, wherein one undergoes various sufferings, unlike the law of the devas.

At that time, during this great battle between the Kālayaśas devas and the army of the Rāhu asuras, the Kālayaśas devas further seized immeasurable great mountains and rained them down upon the asura army; at that moment, the asura army was scattered and destroyed, divided into hundreds of thousands of fragments.
When Rāhu, the Asura King, saw that his army had been completely shattered, he immediately seized a great mountain three hundred yojanas in breadth and rushed toward the celestial hosts.

At that time, the deity Kālapāda, having seen this, took up his bow and weapons and also ran toward it; he shot an arrow at the mountain, shattering it like fine sand until it fell into the great ocean.
When the sky rains down swords, the asuras, having witnessed this event, because of their animal-like minds, become slightly discouraged and weak, and flee toward the army of the courageous asuras.
Seeing him retreat, the Asura King Vīrabhadra addressed his army, saying:

"This King Rāhu possesses a vast body but lacks even the slightest strength; having been defeated by the gods, he flees toward our ranks seeking protection. He is no different from ordinary asuras, for he is devoid of power."
If one were powerful enough, this body could certainly alone shatter all the hosts of devas; this body is like a second Sumeru King of Mountains.
This Kālayojana Deva is foremost in valor and strength, being able to engage in combat with such a massive body without being destroyed.
Having spoken these words, they immediately set out with the Dharmāraṇa hosts toward the Kālayojana devas, desiring to engage them in battle.
When the [Kālayojana] devas saw this, they said to the Mālādharas:
"Come quickly! Come quickly!"
"Now the Asura King Vīrabhadra is leading a great host toward my abode.
Upon hearing these words, the Māndhātṛ devas immediately rushed again with great speed toward the abodes of the Asuras Vīrabhadra and Rāhu.
Rāhu, again accompanied by the valiant Asuras and having firmly arrayed himself for battle, turned toward the celestial hosts, desiring to wrestle and fight with the Kālayukti devas.

Recalling their ancient enmity, they hurled great mountain rocks; from above, they rained down swords, arrows, various weapons, and large trees, filling the air so that there was no empty space between them and they could no longer see one another. A hundred thousand fought together in an incomparable battle.

When the bodies of the various devas are destroyed, they are reborn again as previously described; however, when the armies of the asuras are decapitated, they do not regenerate, following the same law as humans.
Among the hosts of deva armies, life is not fully restored except in the case of decapitation; likewise, if their waists are severed, they are also unable to survive.
At that time, the host of devas was slightly diminished, while the host of asuras suffered great loss and destruction.
Having been defeated by the devas, the remaining asura forces retreated back beneath the waters, seeking protection.
The celestial hosts raised a great cry; hearing their shouts, the Asura army lost all its power and barely managed to preserve its lives.
Rāhu and Vikrama fled back to their own city and stood at the gate.
At that time, the third earth-dwelling Asura king, Puṣpamāla, seeing that Rāhu and Vikrānta had been defeated by the devas, addressed his army, saying:
"Let all my troops advance; we shall do battle with the devas."
"I possess great power; what can the gods possibly do?

Having spoken these words, he immediately led his army to charge at the celestial hosts. Then Rāhu, along with the remnants of the valiant Asura army, rallied together and returned with Puṣpamāla to join the celestial hosts, saying to one another:
"Why did you falsely claim to be the King of the Asuras and then flee in retreat?"
"Since I am personally powerless and lack swords or halberds with which to skillfully battle the enemy, even if I were to reach the palace, I would only bring disgrace upon my wife and children.

Having said these words, his strength returned; his body became like a great mountain, he grasped weapons in his hands, and his speed was like the wind as he once again turned toward the celestial hosts, desiring to do battle with them.
At that time, the celestial messengers, along with the Māndhātṛ devas, the Nityotsada devas, and the Kālaya devas, all deliberated together:
"All the asuras have gathered together and wish to come to our abode; relying on their own strength, they have become arrogant and do not recognize the power of the devas."

Having spoken these words, he rushed toward the asuras and engaged them in a great battle. From above, they rained down massive mountains or great boulders, and they rained down swords and halberds. They seized and struck one another; there was immeasurable killing, immeasurable oppression, and immeasurable beating, with immeasurable lives lost across the vast ocean. Their various modes of combat were beyond all comparison.
The hosts of nāgas fought with the nāgas in immeasurable varieties of combat.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw this, he addressed the gods of the Thirty-three, saying:
"Quickly prepare yourselves for battle!"
"All the hosts of asuras have now come here, with the exception of Bāhika.
I shall mount the white elephant Airāvata and fight against Bāhika."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having addressed the devas, spoke to Airāvaṇa, the king of white elephants:
"I shall now mount you to defeat Vemacitra, the Asura King, and his host."
Having spoken these words, he grasped the vajra in his hand and surveyed the entire host of asuras to see which side possessed superior power.
He saw that the devas had gained the victory, while the asura army was retreating in defeat.
When the gods saw the asuras being defeated and fleeing, they were all greatly delighted; Śakra, the King of Devas, was filled with joy and gladness.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Pākaśāsana reflected thus:

"The immeasurable billions of asura hosts of the three realms have lost their strength in battle and been utterly defeated as before; what is seen in the Sarvadarśin pool is no different from this—it is exactly so and not false."
"I shall now go forth to defeat Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and destroy those gods.
As soon as these words were spoken, the celestial hosts arrived at the gateway beneath the waters.
At that moment, Vemacitrin Bāhika gave rise to great fury; the mountains shook, the great ocean surged with waves, and the sun’s rays turned the mountain peaks entirely crimson.

When their army came to rest at the bottom of the water, they saw the hosts of devas defeating the asura forces of Rāhu and others; [the asuras] fled toward the depths of the water, powerless and without rescue, all in a state of total turmoil.
The gods raised a great cry, and all the asuras lost their strength, saying to one another:
"We now have no power; there is no protection for us."
An asura said: "Do not fear, do not fear!
Turn back and do not flee!"
When these words were spoken, mountain peaks rained down, striking the Asura army everywhere. The gods rejoiced greatly and cried out:
"Seize the Asuras! Seize the Asuras!"
"Kill this unrighteous beast of evil conduct who constantly torments us!
He is incapable of combat, as cowardly as a crow and devoid of heroic resolve; he is unskilled with sword and spear. Thus, we shall break him so thoroughly that he never turns back again."
"This battle of the asuras knows no bounds of time.

Thus the hosts of devas, each filled with joy, turned toward the asuras, desiring to strike and harm them. Their eyes were red with rage like the color of cinnabar; they rained down swords, spears, and great fires, just as a great rain pours down in the autumn months, thus destroying the asura host.

At that time, the Asura King Bāhika sat upon a mobile palace of a hundred thousand wheels, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of billions of asuras. Raining down various swords and halberds, he seized great mountains with his hands—some one yojana in size, others up to five yojanas—and directed them toward the celestial hosts.
When Rāhu and the other asuras saw this, their strength was restored and they turned back, desiring to fight.
Then Bāhika comforted them, saying:
"Do not fear! Do not fear!"
I have now come here to shatter all the gods, to annihilate and destroy them;
do not be afraid. O Asura King, do not fear, do not fear!
If you return to your own palace, how can you call yourself a man in the presence of your own wives?
"Yet you lack courage and bravery, yet you falsely claim to be men.
When Pāhāsa had spoken these words, he rushed toward the celestial hosts.

Seeing him, the gods also hurried forward. The gods and the asuras engaged in a great battle in formation, their loud roars and shouts filling the mountains, rivers, ravines, and gorges of Mount Sumeru.

At that time, the Asura King Rāhu rushed toward the Karoṭapāṇi devas; the Asura King Śauṇḍa, grasping a great halberd in his hand, rushed toward the Mālādharas; and the Asura King Puṣpamāla, holding a great mountain three yojanas wide in his hands, rushed toward the Trāyastriṃśa devas and their messengers. Such a great battle—merely hearing it described makes the hair of all living beings stand on end, let alone witnessing it.
At that time, the Asura King Pāhāsa again desired to subdue and destroy the devas; like the wind blowing through the clouds, he relied on his own great power and feared not the celestial hosts.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, being thus distressed, went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and addressed Śakra, saying:

"The celestial hosts are fighting alone and are on the verge of being destroyed by the asuras. O Heavenly King, go quickly; do not let the celestial hosts be scattered, extinguished, or ruined, allowing the beasts to achieve victory."
"O Heavenly King, depart quickly! Depart quickly!
With the exception of the Sudharmā Hall, all other devas must depart immediately.

Upon hearing these words, the entire assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas all hurried to where Baka Vemacitra was. They rained down a multitude of swords and arrows; Baka, from above the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, rained down great stone mountains that filled the void of space. All joined together, roaring and engaging in a great battle.
Each side thought to themselves:
"My army has achieved victory.
Thus they fought, and hundreds of thousands of mountains and valleys struck one another until they were shattered into fine dust, filling the void of space for a thousand yojanas.

Within these clouds of dust, they rain arrows and mountains upon one another like the rains of autumn; immeasurable billions of asura hosts perish and do not return, while among the celestial hosts, immeasurable thousands lose their lives and meet their end.
The cowardly asuras, for the sake of protecting their lives, fled back to their own palaces.
Once the remnants of the defeated army had entered the city, the women of the asura host came and asked them: "Where is our husband now?"
The asura replied: "The asura army has been fighting with the devas; having defeated the celestial hosts, they are all greatly rejoicing and will arrive before long."

At that time, the women of the asuras immediately turned toward the Sarvadarśin pool to observe the asura army; they saw that the devas had gained the victory, while the asura army was defeated, scattered, and broken, with corpses strewn about and retreating by the hundreds and thousands.

When the women saw this, they were overwhelmed with grief and distress; they sat down upon the ground, weeping and wailing aloud. With hearts filled with great suffering, they remained by the pond, beating their breasts and crying out loudly, tearing at their hair, striking their bodies with their hands, and shedding tears from their eyes.
At that time, when the women saw their husbands dead in the waters of the pond, they were overcome with grief, sorrow, and great suffering.
Thus do the devas and asuras fight together; such is this great calamity.
"The Asura King Pāhāsa, surrounded by immeasurable billions of asuras, came toward Śakra.
Upon seeing him, Śakra addressed the host of devas:
'This asura now comes to me, desiring to engage in battle; he is difficult to subdue.'"
"Supported by the Dharma as my companion, I shall shatter that army, just as light dispels darkness.

Having spoken these words, he mounted the white elephant king Airāvaṇa, whose speed was as swift as a shot arrow. Surrounded by the hosts of the Heaven of Good Dharma, he descended from above and headed straight for the Asura army. He uprooted great groves of trees and hurled them upon the host, and further cast down massive boulders or rained down great arrows toward Pākaśāsana.
At that time, Pāhāsa mounted the Great Wheel Palace and attacked King Śakra. Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Pāhāsa:
"You are a beast dwelling in the path of unrighteousness; where do you hope to go?"
"I shall destroy you and cause you to retreat, fleeing back into the waters!
Then Vemacitrin Bāhika said to the Lord of Devas:
"I shall now defeat you and the host of all the devas."

At that time, Vemacitrin Bāhika took up a great golden mountain five hundred yojanas wide and hurled it at the celestial hosts. When Airāvaṇa, the white elephant king, saw the golden mountain approaching, he emitted a fierce wind from his mouth that blew the mountain to pieces like fine sand, causing it to fall into the great ocean.
At that time, seeing Mount Suvarṇa shattered, the Asura King took up Mount Vajrasama, which was five hundred yojanas wide, and hurled it at Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Then the white elephant king Airāvaṇa caught it with his trunk and struck the chest of the Asura Pākaśāsana, causing him to stagger and reel.
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven saw this, they raised their voices and cried out, saying:
"O beast! The Heavenly King has defeated you; the white elephant has struck you, causing you to tremble; how much more so when Śakra releases his vajra from his hand!"
Having spoken these words, the entire host of devas rushed toward the army of the asuras;
some took up great rocks, some took up great trees, some took up great mountains, some grasped great halberds, and some grasped great spears;
some caused thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts to erupt into fire, some took up plows, and some engaged in wrestling.
Some wielded wheels of swords, while others wielded single swords; some traveled through the air, while others wielded bows and arrows;
some held encircling mountains, while others engaged in grappling and boxing; some fought according to the Dharma, while others fought by way of logic or gave instructions;
there were many who practiced deceitful arts, and some fought with fire or fought with water.
There are torrential streams, and there are various kinds of combats: some are all-out battles, some are battles in the dark, and some are illusory battles;
some involve saws, some involve talons, some involve palace-wheels, and some involve shrieks so loud that those who hear them cannot endure it;
some involve trampling with feet, and some involve hand-to-hand combat—thus they are fully equipped with all manner of such weapons.
All the hosts of devas stood before Śakra, facing the asuras.
At that time, Bāhāsura, Rāhu-rāja, and the others, seeing the deva hosts grasping various weapons, went together with Bāhāsura toward the place where Śakra was.
At that time, the hosts of devas, seeing the four asura kings heading toward the abode of Śakra, immediately adorned themselves to assist the Heavenly King.
Then, Śakra, Lord of Devas, surveyed his own celestial host and addressed the asuras, saying:
"You beasts! Why are you so deluded and ignorant?"
The combined strength of all the asuras does not equal the power of a single deva; I alone, as one deva, am able to shatter your army.
Why is this? The devas possess the power of the Dharma, whereas you possess no such power.

The Dharma and what is contrary to the Dharma are separated by an abyss; they are like comparing sunlight to darkness, like comparing truthful speech to falsehood, like comparing Mount Sumeru to the various mountains, like comparing liberation to bondage, like comparing benefit to loss, like comparing a virtuous friend to an enemy, like comparing nectar to poison, like comparing the bright day to the gloomy night, like comparing a counterfeit pearl to a genuine gem, like comparing great wealth to poverty, and like comparing a traveler on the road to one who dwells in peace.
It is like comparing a firefly to the light of the sun, or one without feet to the fierce wind; they are worlds apart.
It is like comparing a blind man to one with clear vision, a perilous path to a level road, a non-Buddhist to the Tathāgata, or space to the earth.
Just as one might wish to compare a single thought-moment to an eon, so too is the vast and profound distance between you and me.
You do not accord with the Dharma, whereas I revere it;
you are deluded, whereas I possess wisdom.
"You do not cultivate merit, whereas the devas cultivate meritorious conduct;
you are a beast, while I am a pure deva.
Having recognized this, you ought not to engage in battle with me."
Having spoken these words, he immediately manifested the appearance of departure and directed Airāvaṇa toward the asuras.
A verse was recited:
“The Dharma can destroy what is contrary to the Dharma; Truthful speech destroys falsehood.”
"Wisdom destroys ignorance, as the gods destroy the asuras.

When Śakra had spoken these words, he transformed himself into Airāvaṇa as previously described and advanced toward the asura army with speed surpassing that of a swift wind. Holding a thousand-edged vajra in his hand, he terrified the asuras, yet not with a mind intent on killing.
At that time, seeing Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, also rushing forward, the Four Great Kings and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens likewise ran swiftly.
The devas and asuras drew up their battle lines and fought a great war; all hoped for victory and assailed one another.

Among the devas and asuras, some are wounded and die; some, being timid and weak, retreat and return home; some remain and watch; some think of returning; some are filled with anger; some are deluded and confused; and some are struck with fear.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately manifested a transformation, causing the asuras to see the white elephant king Airāvaṇa, with a thousand Śakras upon each of its heads, all holding thousand-edged vajras and various weapons in their hands, and many lotus ponds as previously described.

Within the lotus pond, he saw immeasurable thousands of Śakra-devānām-indras. Airāvaṇa had manifested as ten heads, upon each of which were a thousand bathing pools; within each pool were a thousand lotuses; each lotus had a hundred pericarps; and each pericarp had a thousand petals. Upon the pericarps of the elephant’s heads were hundreds of billions of Śakra-devānām-indras, with billions of nayutas of various weapons and diamond swords interspersed so that there was no empty space between them.
At that time, having seen this transformation, the asuras were terrified and overwhelmed, thinking to themselves:

"The Heavenly King Śakra pervades the intermediate spaces of the void without any empty place remaining; he holds various swords, halberds, and weapons in his hands, and his physical strength is immeasurable. Various blades and staves fill the intermediate spaces of the void without any empty place remaining, extending throughout the ten directions. We fear that beneath the waters, the celestial armies of the Lord of Devas will likewise fill them."
At that time, the asuras were seized with great terror and spoke to one another;
Pāhāsa said: "Asuras, do not fear! Do not fear!"
"I am able to subdue that Śakra Devānām Indra and Airāvaṇa.

Having spoken these words, he rushed swiftly toward Airāvaṇa, the great nāga-elephant king. At that moment, Airāvaṇa seized the asura with his trunk and whirled him around in the air like a person playing with a bell, releasing him only when he was on the verge of death.
Once the elephant had been released, he regained some composure and said to the asuras,
"How can one man alone defeat Śakra?
We must now all join together to attack him."

Then the four Asura kings again fled toward Airāvaṇa. Seeing this, Śakra released a hail of vajras to strike the Asuras, intending to cause them to retreat and disperse, rather than to take their lives.

At that time, the asuras rained down immeasurable great mountains, swords, knives, spears, and lances upon the Heavenly King; yet, just as summer rain falls in torrents, they descended upon the Heavenly King’s body without causing him any harm, for he was majestic and free from affliction.

Thus, as the celestial king and the asuras engaged in a great battle of immeasurable scale, the other devas, having witnessed it, rushed toward the asura army, while the asura army charged toward the hosts of devas; they fought one another, inflicting immeasurable harm, such that immeasurable sentient beings who saw it were struck with great terror, experiencing incomparable agitation.
In such a great battle, the devas and the asura kings, along with their armies, attacked one another; wielding immeasurable weapons as hard as vajra, they joined together in combat.

At that time, although Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw the immeasurable hosts of asuras standing before him, he did not take their lives; he merely intended to defeat those asura hosts and drive them back until none remained.

Then Bāhuka Vemacitra, the Asura King, together with his host, retreated, scattered, and fled in defeat; seeking protection and a place of refuge, they descended into the great ocean and ran toward the gate, their power utterly lost.
Vemacitrin Bāhika, mounting a celestial chariot of a hundred thousand wheels to repel the enemy, caused the three asura kings to flee before him in terror and distress.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the white elephant king Airāvaṇa, saying:
"Pursue that Vemacitrin with great speed! Out of arrogance, he claims for himself great power; go now quickly and destroy the chariot-palace of a hundred thousand wheels upon which he rides."
"What the Great Sage has taught—that the precept against taking life is the path to Nirvana—is true.
Sentient beings cherish their lives; do not sever their lives.
Go quickly to him and shatter his wheel-palace into hundreds of thousands of pieces."
Having heard this command, Airāvaṇa assumed a transformation body and, swifter than a rushing wind, arrived beneath the great ocean.
When Pāḥasa Vemacitra saw him, he was struck with terror and fled swiftly toward the gate at the bottom of the great ocean, yet he lacked the strength to advance further.

Having arrived at that place with great power, Airāvaṇa seized its wheel with his trunk, causing it to fall from the palace terrace; he caught it before it reached the ground, brought it face-to-face with him, and crushed the great palace as if crushing withered grass.
At that time, the Asura King Puṣpamāla lost all his power and his life was on the verge of ending; remembering his wife and children, he rushed toward the gate.
The Asura King Śūra also fled in haste, running toward the water and heading for the gate to seek his own salvation.
Rāhu, the Asura King, likewise fled and ran toward the depths of the water, hoping to save his own life; though he possessed a massive body, he was entirely devoid of strength.
At that time, the hosts of devas, seeing that the asuras had been utterly defeated, spoke with joy:
"The asuras have received the retribution for their battle; they have been shattered and are fleeing in retreat."
Seeing this, the devas spoke thus:
"We shall go to his gate and witness the defeat of those broken asuras.
Then the devas swiftly rushed toward the waters; the asuras were shattered like thick clouds blown apart by a fierce wind.
Having seen this, the Lord of Devas spoke to the asura, saying:
"For what reason have you committed this evil yourself, causing immeasurable hosts of asuras to lose their lives?"
"You have become an enemy to the devas; there is not the slightest benefit for you.
Now, the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma. Because people cultivate goodness, the devas possess superior power;
if people perform unwholesome deeds, the devas will be destroyed."
"You do not know the time nor the place; you have allied yourself with my enemies to no avail.
In your desire to attack the heavens, you shall only bring ruin upon yourself."
When the asuras heard these words, they again entered beneath the waters in search of their lives.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded the host of devas:
"Turn back! Turn back!"
"The Asura armies have all lost their strength and possess only a flicker of life; release them so they may return to their original abodes.
Then the hosts of devas said to the Heavenly King:

"These Asuras cannot be subdued; they do not know their own power nor discern the power of others. We should now once again destroy the Asura host so that they shall never return, and we may enjoy the fruits of our own karma within the heavens without the Asuras causing us further affliction or harm."
"How can this asura wish to afflict others who practice in accordance with the Dharma?
I shall not retaliate against my enemies; I will never turn back.
Having spoken these words, he took up various weapons such as swords and halberds and rushed swiftly toward the asura army. He struck them with terror to break their ranks, yet did not kill them.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, gave rise to a heart of compassion; fearing that Bāhika might die of terror, he addressed the host of devas:
"You all lack a heart of compassion."
Having spoken these words, he returned with the entire assembly of devas from the Sudharmā Hall toward the celestial palace.
At that time, the Four Great Kings, seeing Śakra returning, addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, saying:
"Since the Heavenly King has returned, you may also turn back."
Having attained this supreme power, they were all filled with joy and returned each to their own palaces.

King Śakra, Lord of Devas, mounted the white elephant king Airāvaṇa while the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens sang praises and hymns; he proceeded to the second heaven, ascended the Sudharmā Hall, and together with the other celestial hosts, they all entered their respective palaces. They all cast off their armor and placed it in the Citraśālā Grove. Airāvaṇa relinquished his transformed body, returned to his original form, and entered the Lotus Pond.
Thus they reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where they enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses; together with the merits of the five desires, they sported and played in the groves and ponds.
Having defeated the asuras, the Naga King Vāsuki, the Naga King Takṣaka, and the others returned to the City of Playful Joy with hearts full of delight.
The remnants of the Asura army, their bodies mangled and shattered, stood with heads bowed in shame; the women, distressed and emaciated by grief, turned toward the Asuras.
Rāhu, the asura, spoke to the defeated asuras, saying:

"I previously told you that this was not the time for you to engage in battle with the devas; rather, humans were following the True Dharma, supporting their parents with filial piety, and showing reverence to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior members of the community, thereby increasing the hosts of devas and diminishing the asuras."
"I spoke these words, yet you did not follow my instructions; for this reason, you have now obtained this evil retribution, causing the gods to slaughter immeasurable sentient beings.
Another asura said to Rāhu, "It is truly as you have said."
"Disregarding the King’s words, you fought at an improper time; for this reason, you have now obtained such an evil fruit.
The Asura Dharmāhu said, "Because my karma was about to ripen, it compelled me not to turn back. Having given rise to such a thought, I have obtained this evil fruit."
Having thus spoken to one another in turn, they returned to their respective realms.

Vemacitrin reached the fourth stage and entered his own city; he was deeply ashamed, dejected, and hung his head down, surrounded by court ladies who were themselves distressed and withered with grief.
The unrighteous and evil nāgas, such as Padma and others, having lost their vital strength, returned to the city of Krīḍāpura.
"In this way, the poison of craving destroys sentient beings; they inflict harm upon one another and transmigrate through the world without the slightest happiness."
Having observed in this way, the noble disciple attains a mind free from desire.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates phenomena internally and practices in accordance with them.
Having contemplated in this way, this bhikṣu attains the seventeenth stage, and his mind constantly delights in contemplating the foremost ultimate truth.

At that time, the earth-dwelling yakṣas, seeing this, rejoice and announce it to the space-dwelling yakṣas; the space-dwelling yakṣas, having heard it, rejoice and announce it to the world-protecting devas (Lokapālas). In this manner, the news is passed on in succession until it reaches the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, where they all say:

"In Jambudvīpa, there is a son of good family residing in a certain village, named so-and-so, who has left the household life out of faith, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the saffron robes. Having departed from the realm of Māra, taking no pleasure in afflictions and wearying of and renouncing birth and death, he has performed such contemplation and now attained this seventeenth stage."
Upon hearing this, all the devas were filled with great joy and spoke thus:
"Such a bhikṣu is a god among gods; he diminishes the hosts of Māra and increases the ranks of the devas."
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty-one, concludes with the "Chapter on Animals.

translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Yuan-Wei dynasty.
6. Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens (22–63), Part One: The Four Heavenly Kings (22–24). Chapter Six, Part One: The Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

"Furthermore, having understood the retribution of karma, and having observed the retribution for unwholesome karma in the hells, among hungry ghosts, and among animals—having examined them thoroughly according to reality—the bhikṣu should next contemplate the retribution of wholesome karma."
Why is this so? Because all sentient beings delight in pleasant fruits and loathe and abandon bitter retributions, and because they gather all manner of pleasures, they are called "devas.

Furthermore, observing their subtle karma, they accumulate various wholesome deeds and receive bodies subject to birth and death, attaining cherished rewards; by means of the sevenfold precepts, they are born among the devas.

What are the seven? There are four types of vocal karma and three types of bodily karma; because they have closely associated with and extensively practiced these, they are born among the gods of the six heavens of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāma-deva*).

Within these six heavens of desire, there are superior, middling, and inferior paths; likewise, their lifespans are of middling and inferior durations; likewise, their food is of middling and inferior qualities; likewise, their physical forms are of middling and inferior qualities; and likewise, their strength is of superior, middling, and inferior degrees.
The retribution of pleasure is likewise twofold: there is that which is middling and that which is inferior.
Among the six heavens of the desire realm, the first two depend upon Mount Sumeru;
the [remaining] four heavens depend upon space, appearing like gathered clouds.
Those first classes of devas belong to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

The first is the Mālidhāra Heaven (Gandharva Heaven), which dwells encircling the four terraces of Mount Sumeru. This Mālidhāra Heaven has ten abodes; on each side, there are different karmas and different names. Thus, through immeasurable karma, beings are born in the Mālidhāra Heaven.
Experiencing pleasure according to one’s karma, one enjoys pleasures of immeasurable forms and colors; yet there is no suffering of old age, for all things are marked by the seal of the net of karma.

Arising from causes and conditions, they do not arise without cause, nor are they subject to annihilation; there is no creator. Therefore, a man who cherishes himself should always exert himself to cultivate all wholesome karmas.

The net of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—has been flowing since beginningless time, binding all sentient beings so that they transmigrate through birth and death like a waterwheel. They wander through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, while regarding the human world as if watching a troupe of performers.

If one performs wholesome deeds and is reborn among the gods, there are sixty thousand mountains surrounding Mount Sumeru. Various kinds of precious gems emit blazing light that illuminates all the mountain peaks, and lotus ponds, bathing pools, and pure flowing springs adorn those mountains.

The mountain is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, composed of the four precious substances, surrounded by devas of virtuous karma, illuminated by immeasurable flames of light, and exceedingly delightful.
"In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the first deva realm, the Mālava-devas. There are ten abodes of the Mālava-devas; what are these ten?
First is named White Maṇi;
second is named Steep Precipice."
The third was named Life of Fruits;
the fourth was named White Meritorious Conduct;
the fifth was named Constant Joy.
Sixth is named "Practicing the Path";

The second is called the Path of Practice.
Toward Uttarakuru, there are four celestial abodes:
the first is named Desire-Love;
The second is named Realm of Desire;
the third is named Movement of the Mind;
the fourth is named Forest of Play.
Each of these celestial abodes is one thousand yojanas in extent and is situated upon the great ocean.
The lifespan of those devas is such that fifty years in Jambudvīpa constitute a single day and night; thus their full lifespan is five hundred years, though there are also those who die prematurely.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates how those gods of the earth-realm play and enjoy pleasures: what kind of karma did they perform to be born in that realm?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the various devas dwelling on the slopes of Mount Sumeru: if a person cultivates goodness and, with a pure mind, takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus for even the duration of ten finger-snap, without giving rise to any other thought.

When that person’s life ends, they will be reborn on the slopes of Mount Sumeru in the White Maṇi Heaven; because they received the three refuges with a pure mind, they shall obtain a body adorned with majestic power and radiance, enjoying sovereign bliss.
Of the sixteen parts of the happiness one experiences [in heaven], the joy of a wheel-turning monarch does not equal even one part.
In that land there is a river named *Kāmanadī* (Flow of Desire), with pearls for its sand spread across its bed.
By what power? By the power of the mental recollection of the two devas on the precipice, various kinds of exquisite drinks emerge from the river.

Furthermore, there is a pearl river called "True Pearl," where coral and jewels flow; from this river flow the celestial hosts and jade maidens, as well as various kinds of treasures, namely: lapis lazuli, fragments of diamond, celestial nila pearls, celestial great-blue pearls, celestial red pearls, celestial conch jewels, and other various kinds of treasures for adornment—all of which are obtained immediately upon thought.

Furthermore, there is a fragrant river named Fragrant Water, adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks; on both its banks are many golden trees that form groves and gardens, filled with various kinds of birds.

When the gods smell the fragrance, their hearts give rise to desire and joy; having experienced sensual pleasure, they are a hundredfold more delighted, and together with the other five objects of desire, they enjoy themselves.

There are many trees with red branches and green leaves, and others with green branches and red leaves; furthermore, there are trees whose leaves are of variegated colors—blue, yellow, and green—and these are adorned by swarms of bees of various hues.
Their minds are constantly joyful, and they produce wondrous sounds as they experience the retribution of their virtuous karma, sporting and enjoying themselves.
Various precious jewels adorn the mountain peaks, or some flat summits are adorned with five peaks.
What are the five? First is named Miscellaneous Species;
second is named Various Flowing Springs.
The third is named Sound of Various Birds;
the fourth is named Fragrant Incense;
the fifth is named Constant Fruit.
Such mountains as these are adorned with the seven treasures.

The devas of these lands sport and rejoice, indulging themselves in pleasure; surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, they sing, dance, play, and laugh, indulging their senses in the five desires with joyful hearts and minds.
The merit of the Three Refuges ensures that until the end of one's life, and in future lives, one shall attain Nirvana.

If born among humans, one will possess abundant wealth and property, always experience joy, and receive the foremost happiness; one will delight in practicing music and arts, and be fully endowed with material riches.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the heavenly world and sees the second abode of the Mālikas, named Steep Precipice (Uccaggha).
By what karma is one born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees:
these sentient beings constructed bridges and boats at river crossings, or, with a virtuous mind, ferried those who observed the precepts across by boat.

Because they are persons who uphold the precepts and further ferry others across, refraining from all manner of evil, such people, at the end of their lives, will be reborn in the happy realms and dwell upon high precipices.

By virtue of their wholesome karma, having been born in that heaven, they experience various pleasures. They are surrounded by and adorned with many flower ponds—pure, cool, and refreshing, with exquisite fragrance and color, free from any mud or turbidity. There is constant laughter, song, dance, and play; they are surrounded by many celestial maidens who adorn their bodies with various jewels. These hosts of celestial maidens respectfully serve and make offerings to them, while the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments provide their music. Together with the celestial maidens, they sport in the groves and gardens, enjoying themselves in pleasure-pools made of various jewels.
There are six bathing pools. What are the six?
The first is named Flowing Bliss;...
The second is named Delightful to Behold;
the third is named All Joy;
the fourth is named Cloud-Garland.
The fifth is named Lake Garland;
the sixth is named Wish-Fulfilling.
Furthermore, there are four groves that are lovely to behold, which produce winds of exquisite fragrance and are adorned with myriad flowers.
What are the four? First is named Gandhavatīvana (Fragrant Wind Forest);
second is named Miśrakāvana (Mixed Forest).
The third is called Playful Bees;
the fourth is called Delightful Pleasure.

There, the devas and their celestial maidens enjoy the pleasures of the five senses within those groves. Following whatever thoughts arise in their minds, they sport in the gardens and groves; their movements are unhindered and unimpeded. Adorning their bodies with various exquisite jewels, their enjoyment increases like deep mountain waters as they amuse themselves with the five desires.

The five faculties surge like waves in the river of craving as they run wild; they sport in various gardens, groves, and bathing pools, and upon golden mountains adorned with all manner of jewels, they frolic with celestial maidens upon mountain peaks.
Surrounded by many celestial maidens adorned with flower garlands, their exquisite beauty beyond compare, they partake of various delicious flavors until fully satiated.
Experiencing such rewards of pleasure, their minds are filled with joy that is beyond description; this continues through the power of their virtuous karma until that karma is exhausted.
When his life there ends, he will be reborn among humans as a virtuous, upright, and immensely wealthy person who serves as the royal treasurer due to the remnants of his karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the Māladhara devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the third abode of the Mālādharas is named Phalajīvī.
By what wholesome karma are beings born in this heaven?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

In an age of famine, this sentient being maintained pure precepts and purified his body, speech, and mind; for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, he planted fruit trees, so that those who ate them were filled with peace and happiness.
By these causes and conditions, they attain peaceful and secure conduct.
At the end of their life, such persons are reborn in the heavens; having been born there, they dwell in the celestial realm as a result of their lives.
Once born in that heaven, they possess immeasurable celestial maidens of incomparable beauty, are fully endowed with a retinue, and experience celestial bliss.

In the gardens and groves, the flowers and fruits grow upon trees of pure gold with branches of coral; various jewels are interlaced as ornaments, and numerous precious bells hang down, emitting exquisite sounds as they play within the woods and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
There are six kinds of groves. What are the six?
First is the Grove of All Meanings;
second is the Grove of the Four Gardens.
The third is named Forest of Softness;
the fourth is named Forest of Universal Joy;
the fifth is named Forest of Bee-Joy.
The sixth is named Golden Reflection Forest (*Suvarṇapratibhāsa-vana*).

Within this grove, celestial maidens constantly sport and enjoy themselves; it is adorned with lotus bathing pools. As they play within the forest, the flowing springs and bathing pools emit wondrous sounds, the trees radiate brilliant light, and various birds warble melodiously. Food and drink are abundant, and amidst various mountain peaks adorned with the seven treasures, they sport and enjoy themselves.
That Mount Sumeru has five mountain peaks; what are these five?
The first is named Radiant Adornment;
the second is named Jambū.
The third is named White Water;
the fourth is named Adorned with Laughter;
the fifth is named Constant Play.

These hosts of devas sport among these various mountain peaks, receiving the rewards of their wholesome karma, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, enjoying themselves together.
The verse says: "By means of a small cause, one is born in heaven and experiences all manner of bliss;
therefore, one should abandon evil and constantly practice virtuous deeds."
With a mindful mind, one practices generosity and upholds the pure precepts;
the precepts can cause rebirth in the heavens and the enjoyment of the merits of the five desires.
This is not due to the benefit of parents, nor of brothers or kinsmen.
By well-guarding the pure precepts, one attains a state of happiness from happiness.
The observance of morality brings benefit in two worlds; indeed, the observance of the Path is most supreme.
One who observes morality is the highest of men, for they attain a state of happiness from happiness.
Maintaining the precepts and practicing right conduct—this is called being a person of pure practice.
Because of these profound karmic deeds, one passes from the human realm to a celestial abode.
The precepts are an inexhaustible treasury; the joy of the precepts is unsurpassed.
The man who maintains the supreme precepts always experiences peace and happiness.
The wise person who upholds the precepts constantly attains three kinds of joy:
praise, material gain, and rebirth in the heavens hereafter.
If a person can uphold the precepts, and thus cultivates ethical discipline,
they will attain happiness in the present life and reach nirvana, forever attaining the state of deathlessness.
From beginningless birth and death, they shall be free from the terrors of desire, ignorance, and the like.
Precepts are a great radiance; therefore, one should always practice them.
One should always praise the precepts; the precepts are like a pure pool.
Neither kings nor thieves, nor water or fire, can plunder the wealth of the precepts.
Therefore, one should constantly cultivate precepts and remain far removed from breaking them;
if a person delights in upholding the precepts, they shall attain nirvana.
One who upholds the precepts is noble; one should draw near to those who uphold the precepts.
Precepts are like the light of the sun and moon; breaking the precepts is base and defiling.
Stainless and free from the wilderness, devoid of sorrow and free from feverish affliction, The precepts are praised by the Buddha; they can lead one to the city of Nirvana.
If a person is fully endowed with it and their pure precepts constantly increase, that person is guarded by the precepts and shall have no fear at the time of death.
The precepts are good in the beginning and the end; they turn all toward the practice of happiness.
Those who uphold the precepts are noble; those who break them are like beasts.
If a person breaks the precepts, they will travel the path of animals;
being ignorant of what should and should not be done, one must therefore constantly cultivate the precepts.
If a person maintains the prohibitive precepts, they are covered by the garment of morality;
if there are those who do not maintain the precepts, they are naked like animals.
For the one who maintains the precepts, heaven is like reaching a place of recreation.
Like a kinsman remembered with longing, one who maintains the precepts comes here.
With pure morality and right conduct, all wholesome deeds are brought together;
this person, having cultivated such wholesome karma, is reborn among the devas.
If a person desires happiness, they should always maintain the pure precepts;
such a person will achieve success and cause their growth in virtue to be complete.
In both the present and the future, the precepts are the foremost companion.
Merit constantly follows one; therefore, one should cultivate ethical discipline (*śīla*).
In the wilderness, amidst the terrors of hunger and thirst, ethical discipline serves as protection.
The practice of upholding the precepts is supreme, following one even into future lives.
If there is one who upholds the precepts and knows that the fruit of the precepts is thus,
they would rather take a sharp blade and sever their own head and body.
All the joys of the assembly gather in harmony, such that they cannot be described by analogy.
The fruit of upholding the precepts is purity; thus has the Sugata taught.
Good in the beginning, good in the middle, and likewise good in the end—this fruit of the precepts is exceedingly vast; from happiness one obtains the retribution of happiness.
Having understood these merits, one should always cultivate pure precepts;
for the precepts are able to provide protection, and there is nothing equal to them.
Thus, when a bhikṣu has contemplated the true merits of upholding the precepts, he should constantly praise the observance of precepts and censure their violation.

Just as they experienced the pleasures of the five desires in that celestial realm, when their karma from observing the precepts was exhausted, they declined and were reborn among humans; there, their spiritual virtues were peerless and their physical form was most exquisite, and the land where they were born abounded in forests due to the remainder of their karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the Māladhara devas.
Through the wisdom born of hearing,
he knows that among the Māladhara devas there is a fourth place where they experience celestial bliss, called White Meritorious Conduct (Śuklakarmācāra).
By what karma is one born in this place?

If a person of little wisdom, upon seeing the Buddha walking, scatters a garland they are wearing over the Buddha, or offers a flower garland to a stupa, and contemplates the merit of the field of blessings with a virtuous mind.
Because they contemplate these merits, at the end of their lives such persons are reborn in the auspicious realm as the White Goddess of Merit (Śuklā Guṇakaraṇī).
Having been born in that heaven, they adorn their bodies with garlands fashioned from merit; its ground is made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, adorned with the seven treasures.
There are many birds with bodies the color of the seven treasures that emit exquisite sounds.
Their radiance shines everywhere, adorned with the wondrous beauty of a hundred merits.
The various trees and groves are infinitely decorated, adorned with *sukha-vasati* trees, trees growing on both cliffs, *gandha-vāsita* trees, and others; these serve as its adornments.
According to their mental inclinations, the fragrance—whether vast or narrow—pervades for many *yojanas*. Flowers and fruits are ever-luxuriant, along with other adornments that grace the ground.

Celestial maidens sing praises, dance, and play; they enjoy themselves in delight and pleasure. In every direction where they sport, they find entertainment and joy, laughing, dancing, and frolicking in merriment. Surrounded by those who revere them, the happiness they experience is beyond description.

The ground is as soft as fresh butter; when devas and humans walk upon it, it rises and falls according to their feet like tūla-cotton. At each place where they step, the ground becomes level again, just as previously described.
From each jewel tree issues forth light of exquisite color; this light is as delightful as the radiance of the sun.
These trees of exquisite golden hue have flowers and leaves that are ever fresh and never wither or fall; born of virtuous karma, they are beyond all comparison.
The sovereign power of the strength of precepts is obtained through wholesome karma, like a seal impressing its mark upon an object.
Thus, these devas sport in groves and lotus ponds; according to their own karma, they receive retributions of superior, middling, or inferior quality, experiencing celestial delights and pleasures.

The physical form produced by their own karma is radiant and lovely; they take pleasure at will in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. Their bodies are free from illness or affliction, and they suffer neither hunger nor thirst; they constantly indulge in the five desires without ever reaching satiety, giving rise to much craving and lust, yet their minds remain never fully satisfied.
If the devas recollect, they obtain everything according to their recollection.

What is obtained through recollection cannot be destroyed by others; it is sovereign and unimpeded, and their minds are constantly joyful. According to their recollection, they can arrive at their destination; their emanated bodies follow their will—large or small as they desire, vast yet light and supple.

In the blink of an eye, they can travel a hundred thousand *yojanas* without the slightest exhaustion, like the wind moving through space without obstruction; the devas are likewise, experiencing no fatigue.

The majestic power of the celestial bodies arises from the mind; they are light, pure, and stainless, with radiant colors that manifest at will wherever they move. There, the gods and goddesses frolic in joy within the groves;

the gods and goddesses delight in the five sensual pleasures, their minds filled with gladness as they experience bliss. Following one another, they enjoy themselves together in their various dwelling places, sporting wantonly amidst the gardens of Mount Gandhamādana. Intoxicated by sensual delights, they do not reflect upon the suffering of decline or impermanence; led astray by heedlessness and the delusions of craving, they continue in their playful indulgence until their passion for them fades.
Having accumulated the causes for birth in the heavens, once their karma is exhausted, they fall back into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there is remaining wholesome karma, they may be born among humans—perhaps as governors of cities or protectors of kingdoms—in places abounding with people where there is constant joy, being free from illness and endowed with physical beauty, all due to the influence of that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the fifth station of the Mālādharas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that among the Mālādharas there is a station named Sarvaprīti."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

those who uphold the precepts possess right faith in their hearts; they offer flowers to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, having acquired the wealth through their own efforts to purchase the flowers for offering.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in a good realm, among the gods of the Heaven of All Joyful Conduct.
Having been born in that heaven, they will experience four kinds of bliss. What are these four?
First, they are without enmity;
second, they are able to act in accordance with mindfulness;
third, no other devas can surpass their majestic virtue.
Fourth, the celestial maidens do not think of other gods.

With five kinds of musical instruments, singing, and dancing, they entertain one another with various diversions: sometimes playing in water, sporting in flower ponds, or playing with flowers, fruits, perfumes, or birds; or they sport in the forests, playing to the sounds of bees. Gazing at one another, surrounded by their companions, they play, laugh, and rejoice together in mutual love, entirely free from the suffering of jealousy.

That land is supremely blissful, surrounded by exquisite fragrant lotus ponds, namely: the pond of excellent fragrance lotuses, the pond of unfading lotuses, the pond of various *utpala* lotuses, and the pond of ever-abundant lotuses; thus, it is adorned with such immeasurable lotus ponds.
They enjoy various pleasures and amuse themselves within the groves.

In those groves, golden trees abound with swarms of bees sporting among them; the various fragrances and the plaintive songs of the birds are so exceedingly delightful that the five musical tones of human beings do not equal even a sixteenth part of their beauty.

Thus, the exquisite forms of these devaputras fill the eyes; the music of the gandharvas delights the ears; and various fragrant winds bring joy to the nose. Such are the realms of the five desires, where immeasurable varieties of forms are exceedingly lovely and delightful.
It is not born of effort, cannot be taken away by others, and is not sought from another; it is the spontaneous accomplishment of one's own joy.
The various supreme flavors of the heavens, with their wondrous colors, tastes, and textures, arise according to one's thoughts, originating from one's own karma.

In this way, each individual grove, each individual lotus pond, and each individual garden is surrounded by retinues of immeasurable celestial maidens; they experience various sensual pleasures, delights, and joys, receiving the fruits of their virtuous karma.
Numerous golden trees radiate light, and flocks of golden birds emit wondrous sounds that bring joy to those who hear them.

Thus, there are immeasurable and incomparable delights; they enjoy such infinite pleasure until their karma of attachment is exhausted, at which point they fall from the celestial realm, perhaps reborn in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.

If there is wholesome karma, one will be born among humans, perhaps ruling over a city or a village, possessing great wealth and sovereignty, with a mind free from stinginess, surrounded by immeasurable attendants, and experiencing the foremost bliss.
"Because they have planted roots of goodness in the field of merit, they proceed even unto nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the Māladhara devas."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the sixth level of the Māndhātṛ devas is named Walking the Path (Caryāpatha).
By what kind of karma are beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:
When a person who upholds the precepts sees a great fire arising that burns living beings, they extinguish the fire with water and save those lives.

At the end of their life, this person ascends to the good realms and is born in the Mālādhara Heaven; by the power of the causes and conditions of giving fearlessness, they receive the retribution of celestial bliss.

Surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens, they enjoy lovely forms, exquisite sounds, various fragrances, flavors, and tactile sensations; amidst manifold musical performances, songs, dances, and laughter, many celestial maidens adorn golden railings with jeweled bells, while windows are covered with nets of pearls and decorated with immeasurable precious gems, wherein countless celestial maidens sport and play.

The host of celestial maidens all conceived feelings of love and joy; they gazed up at the celestial son, never tiring of looking upon him. Adorned with various ornaments and necklaces, their bodies were fragrant and pure, and they were filled with delight and wore smiles; ever harboring joy, they surrounded the celestial son.
Thus, when these celestial maidens behold such exquisite forms, their hearts are filled with supreme love and delight.

Their ears hear all manner of sounds that bring them joy, namely those of flocks of golden birds with coral beaks, sporting and soaring amidst mountain ravines and emitting wondrous, ineffable melodies. Whether in the mountains, in the ravines, or among the flowers; whether in the water, in the air, on level ground, or upon stairways; or whether from within mountain caves, they emit such beautiful sounds. In this way, their celestial ears constantly hear these sublime tones.
They constantly smell wondrous fragrances—namely, the excellent and sublime fragrant winds and immeasurable varieties of flowers—which bring incomparable joy;

from the mouths of the celestial maidens issue wondrous scents and various other lovely, exquisite fragrances, the scent of which delights the mind. Their tongues experience immeasurable *sūdhā* flavors, such that even the superior tastes enjoyed by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) do not equal one hundred-thousandth part of them.

The garments worn upon their bodies lack the patterns of warp and woof or thread and fiber; they are fine, smooth, and soft, giving rise to a heart of love and delight, and providing immeasurable joy in wearing such various kinds of clothing.
If they give rise to a thought, they obtain whatever they desire at will—pure and lovely, which others cannot take away.

Thus, amidst immeasurable objects of the six desires and immeasurable pleasures, they sport within immeasurable lotus groves; in immeasurable forests and groves of golden *maṇi* jewels, where various birds sing with exquisite melodies, they play together in *maṇi* palaces. In this way, they sport by rivers, ponds, lotuses, flowing springs, and bathing pools.
Such are the various fruits of sensual pleasures.
Having observed this with the wisdom born of hearing, that bhikṣu spoke these verses:
"Attached to the six sense faculties, They are consumed by their objects; The fire of craving burns the gods."
Like one who burns down a forest, they obtain pleasure and delight; deceived by that pleasure, they do not consider their own downfall, being utterly deluded by craving.
All pleasures must inevitably end; there is nothing that is permanent. If one wishes to attain eternal bliss, one should renounce craving and desire.
When the gods fall from their realms, they depart from their celestial abodes; the suffering of separation from loved ones exceeds even the torments of hell.

"Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu further observes that all worldly pleasures lack autonomy; they are impermanent and subject to decline, yet people are deceived by craving and do not realize their own downfall."

Having made this contemplation, they grow weary of and renounce celestial desires. Thus, as long as their wholesome karma is not exhausted, they enjoy the pleasures experienced within those heavens; yet when their karma is exhausted, they fall back and take birth according to their remaining karma, perhaps falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, they will experience the foremost happiness, always free from fear, and be beloved by all people; they will be trusted and employed by kings, and until the end of their lives, they will suffer no affliction or disturbance.
Due to the remaining karma, they shall attain nirvana in a future life.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the seventh station of the Māladhara devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings practice wholesome karma; seeing their friends and relatives destroying one another and harboring resentment in their hearts, they are able to bring about benefit by reconciling disputes and restoring harmony.
By virtue of these wholesome karmas, when this person’s life ends, they ascend to the happy realms and are born in the Heaven of Desire-Love (*Kāma-rāga-deva*).

Having been born in that heaven, according to whatever their mind conceives and whatever they think of, they immediately obtain various forms of play and pleasure, various garments, and various celestial ornaments such as crowns and necklaces; they enjoy these celestial articles of luxury.
From each of these, various sounds of song and music emerge, namely the musical sounds of the *candra* lute and the singing voices of the celestial maidens.
Riding upon palaces made of various jewels, they are constantly filled with joy.

There are diverse gardens, groves, mountains, valleys, and ravines, as well as rivers, ponds, and flowing springs where lotuses flourish luxuriantly. Surrounded by celestial maidens, golden lotuses sway in fragrant breezes, emitting wondrous scents.

These are the so-called Vaidūrya groves, Tāla groves, Cūta groves (translated in Wei as "mango" groves), Bird-joy groves, Lotus groves, Various-musical-sounds groves, and Kukkula groves; produced by virtuous karma, they sport therein.

The celestial river is pure and adorned with mani-jewels; lotus ponds and groves of trees reflect its beauty. From the waters of the river, wondrous sounds emerge; such sounds are produced by many birds whose calls are plaintive and elegant. By means of these rivers and ponds, the ground is magnificently adorned.
For example, if a woman possesses all physical beauty but lacks merit or is barren, she is not said to be adorned;
likewise, the abode of the gods is not called pure and wondrous if it lacks the adornment of rivers.
With its various delicious flavors and its perfect color and fragrance, this river constitutes the foremost adornment.

Among all the worldly flavors that provoke attachment, water is supreme; it adorns the gardens and groves, serves as the vehicle for precious ships, and provides constant enjoyment and great benefit for both humans and devas.
Beings enjoy this water endowed with such merits, sporting and finding delight within it.
Having finished their aquatic play, they proceed to the Mirror-Water Forest (*ādarśa-vāri-vana*) to experience celestial bliss.
Entering the Mirror Forest, they look upon their own bodies; the trees are pure and stainless like clear mirrors, through which they observe the signs of their own good and evil karma.
If they have performed virtuous deeds, they see themselves being born in a favorable realm;
if they have committed evil deeds and are about to undergo retribution for suffering, they see themselves first manifesting the signs of those past actions as they fall into the three evil destinies.
He clearly perceives all the suffering and pleasure experienced within the cycle of birth and death across the five realms.

If there is unwholesome karma, he sees [beings] falling into the great hells such as the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Howling Hell, and the Great Howling Hell, where they undergo various sufferings exactly as previously described, seeing them all in their entirety.
Just as the pleasures of the heavens are beyond description, so too are the retributions for sins in hell beyond description.

Having seen their own reflections within the mirror-trees, they completely forget the heavenly joys as if they belonged to another age; beholding immeasurable suffering, they no longer perceive any pleasure.

Just as when a single *liang* of salt is cast into the Ganges River, its taste cannot be discerned, so too the suffering of the mind is like the great Ganges, while its pleasure is but slight, like the taste of that salt.
Although there were sounds of singing, hymns, and music, as well as gardens for strolling and the lamenting cries of various birds, he felt no pleasure at all.

Having seen these things, he departed for another place; yet his mind again became attached to the five desires of the devas.
