Furthermore, beneath another tree, he saw himself falling into various realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*), suffering manifold afflictions with his bodies consumed by hunger and thirst.
Having seen these signs, he was struck with great terror and said to the other devas: "Great Sages!
I have seen a most terrifying sign in the Mirror Tree; do you see it as well?"
Then the deva replied:
"I do not see them. If there were evil karma, I would see the forms of hungry ghosts."
"If one possesses wholesome karma, one does not perceive evil signs.
The Great Seer Devaputra then asked him,
"What signs do you see?"
The deva-son replied, "I see the forms of hungry ghosts, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.

Having seen the hungry ghosts suffering in this way, he completely forgot his celestial pleasures as if they were separated by a thousand lifetimes; he grew weary of and abandoned the grove, and proceeded toward another place.

Furthermore, they crave celestial pleasures and delight themselves in the five desires—forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures—sporting amidst various lotus ponds and the wondrous songs of flocks of birds, enjoying themselves in play with many celestial maidens.

Thus, swept away by the waters of craving, they arrive again at the Forest of Mirrors. Due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, they see the bodies of animals harming one another; seeing themselves receiving the bodies of animals and undergoing various sufferings, their hearts are filled with intense loathing, and they proceed toward the abode of other devas, as previously described in detail.
Having become weary and abandoned [the world], they return to attachment and craving, experiencing the pleasures of the five desires and wandering through birth and death.

Furthermore, when they see human beings in the Mirror Forest, according to the accumulation of their karma, they witness the dissolution and subsequent reunion of their acquaintances, relatives, friends, and brothers; by these causes and conditions, they are born in this celestial realm.

Having seen their own karma, they feel weary and abandon it, yet they return to attachment to sensual pleasures, experiencing the objects of desire—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—and thus, in such negligence, they enjoy the celestial delights.

Furthermore, entering the Mirror Forest, they again see themselves passing away and transmigrating to other realms; or they see themselves falling into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, whereby they give rise to weary detachment, thinking:
"This place is impermanent; I shall certainly pass away from here."
"Separated from the celestial maidens, all conditioned things are impermanent; we shall soon be parted, for all things are subject to movement and decay.
Having thought this, the World-Protector Deity then addressed him, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!..."
It is joyful and delightful.

The people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, filially support their parents, and make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; thus they increase the hosts of devas and diminish the armies of Māra.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has appeared in the world.

He is the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He proclaims the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, stainless and unimpaired, a pure and white teaching, peaceful and tranquil—namely: "This is form; this is the origin of form; this is the cessation of form; this is the practice leading to the cessation of form."
Having seen his own karma within the Mirror Grove and hearing these words, he asked the World-Protectors:

"Where now is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
The World-Protector replied, "In Jambudvīpa,
you shall proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, having heard the World-Protector’s words, the devaputra, fearing the suffering of falling back into lower realms, descended to Jambudvīpa.
Within the human realm, death is a great suffering;
within the animal realm, there is the suffering of mutual predation;
within the realm of hungry ghosts, there is the great suffering of hunger and thirst.
Within the realm of hell, there are various sufferings such as being burned, boiled, and tortured.

Having thus observed these five fears within the five destinies, he approached the place where the Buddha was. From afar, he saw the World-Honored One—dignified and pure, with his faculties stilled, his mind well-extinguished, supremely tamed, and established in *śamatha* concentration; a dragon among men, a charioteer of beings, whose majestic radiance was like a mass of molten gold, surpassing the light of the sun, immovable as Mount Sumeru, profound as the ocean, sitting upright beneath a tree like a mountain of pure gold—he was the God among Gods.
Having seen this, the Devaputra gave rise to a pure mind and approached the World-Honored One; prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"Is there perhaps any place that is permanent, immovable, indestructible, and unchanging?
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately expounded the Four Noble Truths for the devaputra; having heard them, the devaputra returned to his celestial palace.
Having reached the celestial palaces, they experience the pleasures of the five desires until their wholesome karma is exhausted.

Once they have descended from the heavens, they wander according to their karma; if they are born among humans, although they have not yet realized the Truths, they constantly encounter spiritual friends and are endowed with kinsmen, relatives, and brothers, possessing great wealth and abundant riches due to the remainder of their karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the Mālyadhāraṇa devas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the eighth ground of the Mālyadhāraṇa devas is named 'Delightful Realm' (Priyaviṣaya)."
By what karma are these sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
there are sentient beings who organize assemblies for the preaching of the Dharma.

When this person’s life ends, they ascend to a celestial palace and are born in the Heaven of the Realm of Desire (*Kāma-viṣaya-deva*), passing beyond the Heaven of Desire (*Kāma-deva*) to reach the Realm of Desire.

Having been born in that heaven, they experience the retribution of their wholesome karma; all their palaces are of true golden color, adorned with the seven jewels and featuring railings of true gold. There are many kinds of birds—birds of heart-delight, birds of all sounds, birds that play in the rivers, and golden-colored birds—and such birds are there in great numbers.

In the gardens and groves where rivers and ponds flow, one may wander and enjoy the sights; there are a hundred rivers complete with hundreds of thousands of kinds of birds, some of which experience the four desires and others the five desires, delighting themselves therewith.

Beholding exquisite forms with their eyes, they give rise to love and delight; hearing exquisite sounds with their ears, their minds are filled with affectionate joy; smelling exquisite fragrances with their noses, their inner hearts are filled with affectionate joy; tasting exquisite flavors with their tongues, their hearts increase in joy; touching fine and soft textures with their bodies, they are suffused with affectionate joy; and whatever they recollect with their minds, their intellects are filled with joy and rapture.
The qualities of the five desires are deeply cherished by the mind; one experiences the foremost pleasure and receives incomparable bliss within the realms of such objects of attachment.
This continues until the merit of one's beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; when the karma of this world and the next is spent, one falls back again.

If there remains further karma, one will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will be born among humans in a land of great wealth, such as the kingdom of Kāśī or the kingdom of Kośala; or one may be born into a great clan of kṣatriyas or a great clan of brāhmaṇas, due to that remaining karma.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the heavenly realms: by what karma are beings born in the Heaven of the Moving Mind (*Cāritramati*) within the Garland-Bearing (*Mālādharī*) stage?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that these sentient beings, with pure faith, make offerings to the Saṃgha and sweep the stūpas of the Tathāgata; with pure confidence, they recognize [the Saṃgha] as the supreme field of merit.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in the celestial realm of the *Citta-cañcala* (Restless Mind) gods within the happy destinies.

Those born in that heaven have bodies devoid of bone or flesh and free from any impurity; their fragrance can permeate a hundred *yojanas*. Their bodies are as pure as a bright mirror, clearly reflecting the forms and images of all other celestial beings. Thus do they achieve the karmic fruition of such virtuous deeds.
In that celestial abode there are four groves. What are the four?
The first is named the Stainless Grove;
the second is named the Clear Understanding Grove.
The third is named Forest of Exquisite Fragrance;
the fourth is named Forest of Mandārava.

Within those forests are lotus ponds where lotuses grow with coral stems and filaments of pure gold. Geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks emit various wondrous sounds, and there are flowers of diverse colors and fragrances—supremely exquisite, free from dust or impurity, and never withering or falling. The water is not turbid or muddy, but is filled with fragrant milk.

The various birds in the grove constantly sport together; in the lotus ponds, each and every tree is perpetually covered with blossoms as if freshly emerged, never wilting or falling, being exceedingly delightful and remaining unchanged throughout the six periods of the day.
Those who have performed virtuous deeds roam within those groves, accompanied by celestial maidens whose bodies are adorned with various jewels, enjoying themselves in pleasure and delight.

Their minds become stained and attached to the objects of the six desires, lacking even for a moment a heart of weary detachment. Bound by the net of craving like a fish caught in a net, they experience the fruits of their virtuous karma until it is exhausted; once the karma is spent, they fall back into decline.

Due to remaining wholesome karma, he does not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, but attains a human body as a great teacher, possessing great wealth and abundance, and being respected and loved by kings, all because of that residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abode of the Māladhara devas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the tenth station of the Māladhara devas is named Vanakrīḍa (Forest Play).
By what kind of karma is one born in that place?
He perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowing:

if a person maintains the precepts with pure faith, recognizes the Sangha as a field of merit, and for the sake of offering robes, gives even the value of a single fruit as the price for making a robe, their mind constantly delights in it and gives rise to sympathetic joy.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Devakrīḍa Heaven.

Having been born in that heaven, they will sport freely within its celestial gardens and groves, traveling wherever they wish; whether walking upon water as if on dry land or moving through the air, they have no fear.
They wear celestial garments and garlands, experiencing the foremost bliss.
As in the aforementioned stages, they travel without obstruction.
From the ponds, streams, and springs, exquisite fragrances issue forth; there are many celestial maidens whose majestic virtue and radiance are like a second sun, as they enjoy celestial bliss.

Through the causal conditions of karma, one obtains pleasant retributions; it is not the case that what one has done oneself is experienced as retribution by another. Sentient beings experience the fruits of the actions they themselves have committed.
If one performs wholesome karma, one is born among gods or humans;
if one performs unwholesome karma, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Riding upon these merits, they are reborn in higher realms and enjoy pleasures at will; this continues until their wholesome karma is exhausted, at which point they fall back once the karma is spent.

Because there remains residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. If they are born among humans, they are born in lands abounding in forests and trees; their divine virtues are sovereign and indestructible due to that residual karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-Two.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-Three.
Translated by the Bactrian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Observing the Heavens, Part Two; Section Two: The Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma, having observed the ten grounds of the Mālādharas, observes the grounds where the Karoṭapāṇis—here called the 'Elephant-Track' Heaven—dwell. How many kinds of grounds are there where they themselves perform wholesome deeds and experience the retribution of happiness?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the Kāyika devas have ten kinds of grounds. What are these ten?
The first was named Moving Lotus;
the second, Victorious Bee;
and the third, Wondrous Sound.
The fourth is named Fragrant Joy;
the fifth is named Wind-Walk;
the sixth is named Garland-Delight.
The seventh is named Universal Observation;
the eighth is named Constant Joy;
the ninth is named Fond of Fragrance.
The tenth is named Samasira.
These are the ten abodes of the Kāruṣa gods, each born among the devas due to their respective distinct karmas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he perceives them as follows:

These sentient beings, having perfumed their minds with the wholesome karma of observing the precepts, take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and recite "Namo Buddha" while taking the triple refuge three times.

By virtue of this wholesome karma, they will ultimately reach Nirvana; as this merit is not yet exhausted, these persons, at the end of their lives, will be born in the Kāyikas Heaven, where they walk upon lotus grounds and experience the pleasures of the five senses.
Attached to the flavor of desire, his eyes did not blink and his body was like the light of the sun;

he delighted in that land where all the lotuses were the color of white elephants, adorning the ground, their flowers perpetually in bloom, each emitting a fragrance that pervaded a hundred *yojanas*, surpassing the scent of all other flowers.

There were bees of various colors—of the hue of lapis lazuli—emitting all manner of sounds; even the sounds of the various musical instruments of human beings could not equal one hundred-thousandth part of them.
Why is this? Because the celestial sounds of the devas cannot be heard by humans. For what reason?
Because it is not within the realm of non-humans—excluding the Cakravartin kings and those who have abandoned desire.
The Cakravartin kings possess great power in their faculties and are thus able to experience celestial desires;
as for those who have abandoned desire, because their eyes and other faculties are free from both sorrow and joy, they are therefore able to hear it.
If even the humming of bees among the animals is thus, how much more so is the song of the celestial maidens' desire; it is beyond all analogy.

Just as the voices of the celestial maidens are exceedingly lovely and delightful, so too are their forms, fragrances, tastes, and textures; they experience immeasurable varieties of immeasurable love and delight.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall away from the celestial realm; if there remains further karma, they do not fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, but instead obtain a human body, being born into the family of an elder with abundant wealth and possessions.
Due to other virtuous causes and conditions, their merit remains inexhaustible until they reach nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the second dwelling place of the Kalūpāda devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the second stage is named "Joy of the Supreme Bee.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that place?

If a person possesses wisdom, has faith and maintains the precepts, and with a heart of compassion benefits sentient beings, making offerings of flowers, incense, and music to the Buddha’s stūpas—such a person, at the end of life, will be reborn among the superior bees of the Kālaśyapa Heaven. There, amidst various kinds of music, song, dance, and laughter, they sport and enjoy pleasures, experiencing the fruits of their own karma.

They enjoy fragrant flowers at will and listen to the songs of celestial maidens, immediately experiencing bliss. As the wind blows through the wondrous sounds of the immeasurable celestial maidens’ hymns and the extraordinary fragrance of various flowers, they sport with the celestial maidens upon the peaks of the jewel-adorned Mount Sumeru, hearing the music and enjoying celestial happiness.
Having thus observed the retribution of such wholesome karma, the bhikṣu praised wholesome karma and spoke these verses:
“Wholesome precepts are like a flight of stairs; By the power of karma, one is born in the heavens.
If a person mounts this path, They shall reach the realm of celestial bliss.”
The fourfold precepts of verbal action and the three types of pure bodily karma—
by mounting these seven karmic paths, the wise person can reach the heavenly realms.
Observing the precepts is the foremost bliss, which no amount of wealth can equal.
Wealth may be lost, but the observance of precepts is ever firm.
Adorned with the precepts, a person is always upright with the fragrance of virtue.
The Buddha taught that through pure and wholesome karma, one is reborn in the highest celestial realms.
If a person performs wholesome deeds, they can proceed among the devas as if arriving at a place of recreation, experiencing supreme bliss.
Their bodies emit a great radiance, shining brilliantly and illuminating the celestial palaces.
They sport in various gardens and groves, obtained through their own karma;
their minds are always filled with joy, and they experience pleasure and constant serenity as they play within celestial palaces—
all because of the cause and condition of upholding the precepts.

If a person skillfully maintains the precepts, protecting them in their infinite varieties, they will achieve the karmic fruit of rebirth in heaven; therefore, one should cultivate ethical discipline.
Ethical discipline serves as a staircase, providing the causal conditions for attaining manifold joys.
If a person breaks the precepts, there is no place of peace or joy.
The pure water of upholding the precepts is deep and ever-filling;
by bathing oneself therein, one enjoys happiness in the celestial palaces.
Adorned with celestial garlands, enjoying happiness in union,
and sporting within the celestial palaces— all this is obtained through virtuous causes.
Surrounded by celestial maidens, one shines like the radiance of the sun and moon.
The enjoyment of happiness in the heavens arises entirely from virtuous causes.
Whatever one’s mind desires is obtained, and once obtained, it is never lost;
that wholesome dharmas constantly increase is likewise attained through virtuous causes.
One experiences immeasurable happiness, And all things constantly increase;
If a person upholds the precepts, They shall obtain such joy as this.
If a person always practices goodness, They will be held in high esteem by the king.
Virtue is the supreme adornment; therefore, one should practice the precepts.
The virtuous person is always self-restrained, compassionate toward all living beings, and constantly practices loving-kindness and generosity; such a person can reach the heavenly realms.
Not harming living beings, Compassionately pitying all multitudes,
Constantly practicing right action— Such a person is born in the celestial palaces.
Not stealing the wealth of others, With a mind always mindful of giving,
With the faculties stilled and wisdom attained, such a person reaches the heavenly realms.
Not violating the wives of others, always delighting in practicing the right path,
and seeking the stillness of nirvāṇa— that person is born in the heavenly realms.
Do not drink alcohol to the point of intoxication; the intoxicated person is despised by others.
The wise are able to abstain from alcohol, and such people are reborn in the heavens.
Upholding the precepts and practicing well, they abandon all evil karma.
"It can produce immeasurable bliss and bring comfort to all beings.

Having thus contemplated the immeasurable bliss resulting from praising wholesome karma, the bhikṣu rejoiced like a victorious bee; immeasurable swarms of bees emitted exquisite sounds. Until his cherished wholesome karma was exhausted, he fell back from that celestial realm. If he possessed further wholesome karma, he would not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they will be foremost in physical beauty, possessing skillful speech and eloquence; they will constantly experience peace and happiness without any afflictions, and their lifespan will be long due to the remaining power of their past karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the third dwelling place of the Kālapāda devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the third stage is named "Exquisite Sound" (Svaravati).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one knows:
it is those who, while observing the precepts, offer to the Tathāgata with a boundless mind, making offerings of precious canopies.

When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Exquisite Sounds (*Sudrśa*), where they will experience celestial bliss. They will traverse mountains of pure gold and lapis lazuli, adorned with celestial garlands in the company of heavenly maidens. They will roam among mountains of the seven treasures, enter the Gandharva groves, and enjoy various trees, streams, rivers, ponds, and lotuses, as well as ointments and powdered incenses. The radiance of those groves is blue, yellow, and purple.
Upon entering that grove, a fragrant breeze stirs gently, and the leaves produce melodic songs; the songs of all the asuras and gandharvas do not equal even one-sixteenth part of these.
When a gentle breeze blows, they strike against one another, producing wondrous sounds; the music of the five instruments provides entertainment and pleasure.

Having heard these musical sounds, they become ten times more heedless, delighting in the sounds and becoming so stained by attachment that they deceive themselves; it is the same with fragrances, tastes, and tactile sensations.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they descend from the heavens; if there remains further merit, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body. They will have a great fondness for music, possess great wealth and many treasures, live in secure dwellings where the five grains abound, and enjoy long lives with their kin, wives, and children. They will be honored and loved by kings due to the influence of this residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the fourth dwelling place of the Kāla-pāda devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the fourth level of the Kāla devas is named Gandhamada (Fragrant Joy).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings anointed the Buddha-stūpas with incense, maintaining their precepts with faith.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Fragrant Joy (*Gandharvati*), where they will experience celestial bliss beyond all analogy.

They shall take the *sudhā* nectar as their food and drink; their bodies and minds will be free from affliction. Amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, adorned with celestial garlands, they will engage in laughter, song, and dance, constantly enjoying themselves with hosts of celestial maidens like water gushing from a mountain spring, sporting upon the mountain peaks.
There are azure jewels, coral roses, conch shells, and agates; amidst the peaks of golden mountains are various flowing rivers, springs, and flower ponds, as well as groves of *kūṭāgāra* birds.

They see various groves and sport within them; the flowing streams, rivers, and ponds possess a most exquisite flavor, surpassing all the delicious tastes of Jambudvīpa. Born of their own virtuous karma, they partake of these superior flavors and experience such celestial bliss.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall back from the heavens; yet because they possess residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body, being born into a wealthy family with abundant riches and a bountiful supply of the five grains, owing to that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the fifth abode of the Kāyikas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the Kāyika devas have a fifth ground called Vāyu-carin (Wind-Walker).
By what karma are beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one knows:

those beings possessed faith and maintained the precepts; seeing the community of bhikṣus, they offered them fans so that they might obtain coolness—like the medicinal herb named *uśīra*—and enabled the bhikṣus to recite and study the Dharma.
When this person’s life comes to an end, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Wind Movement (*Vāyujavana*), where they shall experience celestial bliss.

Because of their wholesome karma, fragrant winds blow, bringing incomparable joy; the fragrant winds from the four heavens all come to permeate them with a fragrance a hundred-thousandfold more intense than before—cool, refreshing, and lovely, perhaps even one to five times superior.

The fragrance of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is twofold; that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is threefold; that of the Yāma Heaven is fourfold; that of the Tuṣita Heaven is fivefold; and the fragrance of the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens is sixfold.
Because their karma is superior, the celestial hosts are also superior.

Having observed their virtuous karma, the winds blow through the forests where the gods sport; they experience various fragrances and tactile sensations, for the fragrant winds from all six heavens enter this heaven, sharing a single wind-force.
Why is this? The merit of a single wind cannot be fully described; whatever the devas conceive in their minds, they obtain it all from the wind.
If they wish to hear music, the wind blows through the mountain ravines, producing sounds that even the singing voices of the celestial maidens cannot match.

If they wish to contemplate fragrances, even those of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, an unspeakable variety of blended floral scents will come to permeate this heaven.
If they wish for coolness, it shall be according to their heart's desire.
If one travels to other regions desiring to see various jewels, one may go to the peaks of Mount Sumeru, or to the Golden Peaks, or to peaks of Jāmbūnada gold or crystal.
Within these groves and gardens, there are various flowers and fruits, flowing springs, rivers, and ponds, adorned with the fragrances of flowers and the songs of many birds;
it is the dwelling place of various celestial maidens, where immeasurable fragrances and tactile sensations prevail, and exquisite sounds emerge.
The deva-sons ride upon the wind to travel to various gardens, groves, mountains, and valleys for recreation, as previously described.

Thus, this fragrant wind enables these deva-sons to come and go, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses and enjoying themselves together; they play and take delight without giving rise to jealousy, free from any contentious mind, and all love one another.
By means of their own defiled karma—whether superior, middling, or inferior—they receive corresponding retributions, just as a seal impresses its mark upon an object.
They obtain a wind of exquisite fragrance and are free from envy.

When the power of karma is exhausted, one descends from the heavens; since the karma created has superior, middling, or inferior grades, once the retribution for that karma is fully experienced, one descends again when the karma is spent.
Thus, the karmic actions of sentient beings cause them to flow and revolve according to their karma; they do not arise without a cause.
Having observed karma in this way, that bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"Just as one knows the seasons by the sun, and as grasses and trees grow according to the seasons, so too do things arise through the conditions of karma; they do not arise without a cause."
Bound by the fetters of karma throughout immeasurable thousands of births and deaths,
sentient beings are tightly constrained by the three kinds of craving.
Like honey mixed with poison, this is something that should not be consumed.
The celestial music is likewise so; when one falls away, there is great suffering.
When karma is exhausted, one harbors grief and fear;
abandoning all the celestial maidens at the time of decline brings such great anguish that no analogy can suffice.
When wholesome karma is about to be exhausted, like a lamp flame about to go out, one knows not where one will go;
the mind gives rise to great anguish and distress.
Burned by the poison of craving, sorrow and grief shatter one's own heart.
The sounds of speech and the movements of the body cause fear of losing one’s celestial form.
Such flavors of manifold pleasure— the greatest deception of craving—
because they are not abandoned, increase great suffering and affliction.
When one is about to fall from the heavens, the mind gives rise to great anguish;
yet even the manifold poisons of suffering in hell do not equal a sixteenth part of it.
All those wheels of flame are produced by the power of craving.
The fetters of craving bind sentient beings, leading them to all manner of perilous and evil paths.
There is suffering when the gods fall from their celestial realms, and there is suffering when one casts off life among humans;
viewing birth and death as like fire, and having seen this, one leaves all desires behind.
If a person acts with negligence, that person will have no liberation;
deluded by negligence and ignorance, they are very far from Nirvana.
One should abandon negligence, for negligence is a great enemy.
Due to negligence in the heavens, one falls back into the hells.
The three realms revolve like a wheel; the bonds of karma turn without end.
Therefore, abandon craving and desire; by being free from desire, one attains nirvana.

"Thus, having observed the decline of the devas, the bhikṣu develops a mind of weary detachment from desire. He observes that the pleasure of the Vāyu-carā devas is impermanent, born of karmic causes and conditions, and not free from impermanence."

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall back from the heavens; yet, because they possess residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body. Due to that residual karma, they become skilled mariners and great sea captains who are well-acquainted with the winds and routes.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the sixth abode of the Kāla-cara devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the sixth region of the Kāla devas is named 'Joyful Scattering of Flowers' (Puṣpābhikīrṇa-nandana)."
By what karma is one born in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

A person who upholds the precepts possesses pure faith in their mind and maintains rectitude in body, speech, and thought. When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, they give water-pitchers as offerings; or while traveling on a road or in a wilderness, they fill them with pure water and give water-pitchers to others.

When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Joyful Scattered Flowers. Amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and playful melodies, they will sport with many celestial maidens on the side of Mount Sumeru, which is made of various precious *vaiḍūrya* stones. Perfumed by fragrant winds, their bodies adorned with various fragrant garlands and necklaces, and graced by flowing springs and bathing pools, the devas and goddesses enjoy each other’s company, experiencing immeasurable bliss.
For immeasurable periods of time, they enter the groves of flowing springs, where they experience celestial bliss within those forests.
There are trees of *vaiḍūrya* with leaves of pure gold, and trees of pure gold with leaves of *vaiḍūrya*.
Entering this grove, they are constantly filled with joy; their bodies emit radiance as they drink the celestial nectar, all due to the causes and conditions of their virtuous karma.
Compared to what the gods drink, the finest honey-wine of Jambudvīpa is as bitter as mustard seed.
It was replete with exquisite colors and flavors, and its fragrance wafted everywhere, filling an entire yojana.
All the birds were of a true golden hue; drinking from various fragrant waters, they harbored hearts of joy and emitted wondrous songs that filled the entire grove.
Many swarms of bees sport within it.

All manner of fragrances flow forth from the trees—some golden, some the color of lapis lazuli, some the color of musaragalva, some the color of red pearls, and some green—as they stream out to form a river of fragrance named the Flow of Joy (*Nandana-srotas*), two yojanas in width.
The devas and apsaras sported on both banks, enjoying themselves in joy and pleasure.
Having drunk, the devas and apsaras were filled with delight, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing.
There were golden lotuses with stalks of lapis lazuli.

Amusing themselves with songs and hymns, they ride upon palaces made of various jewels and enter a great pond filled with water of eight meritorious qualities. There they sport and enjoy pleasure, splashing one another; this pond is named Aśokā, pure and magnificently adorned, its exquisite beauty being beyond compare.

Thus these hosts of devas enjoy celestial pleasures until their wholesome karma is exhausted; when their life in heaven ends, they do not fall into the three evil realms but instead obtain a human body, being born in a land of abundance and joy where hunger and thirst are unknown. They are born into a great wealthy family and do not encounter an age of famine, being beloved by all people due to the remaining force of their residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the seventh dwelling place of the Kālayaśas gods.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the seventh level of the Kālayaśas gods is named Universal Observation (Samantadarśana).
By what kind of karma is one born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

it is those who maintain the precepts and practice wholesome deeds, who perfume their minds with goodness; who, when encountering a patient who has broken the precepts, do not seek any reward, but instead bestow peace through compassion and serve the sick without weariness of mind.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Universal Observation Heaven (*Samantadarśana*), where they will experience the pleasures of the five senses.

Adorned with celestial garlands, their minds will be filled with joy as they travel about, observing everything at will. Surrounded by celestial maidens, their majestic brilliance will shine like the light of the sun, and all the hosts of devas will revere and honor them.

Wandering amidst the precious Mount Sumeru, clad in various celestial garments and adorned with many jewels, they roam and sport through the forests at will, experiencing the ripening of their own karma in the midst of numerous lotus ponds, mountain ravines, rivers, and springs.

Thus they sport within the celestial gardens, where railings of pure gold and many varieties of birds provide exquisite adornment; when the wind blows through the lattices of bells, it produces a multitude of wondrous sounds. This grove is named Universal Manifestation Adornment, and its majestic radiance surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns.
Mount Sumeru is surrounded by seven mountain peaks that encircle this grove.
What are these seven?
The first is named High Mountain;
The second is named Mount Confluence;
the third is named Rainfall;
the fourth is named Dragon’s Roar.
The fifth is named Light of Love;
the sixth is named Rain of Jewels;
the seventh is named Garland of Stars.

Surrounding that grove, the various trees were adorned with many jeweled bells; celestial maidens, themselves adorned with divine garlands, sported within the forest, their bodies radiating hundreds of thousands of brilliant lights.

Having seen this, the devaputra became indulgent in the five desires; with golden lotuses, they entertained one another with song, dance, and laughter, finding no satiety in exquisite sounds, lovely forms, fragrances, tastes, textures, and mental objects.
Thus surrounded by these thirty-six fires, which burn like a conflagration, they are never satiated.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
“Enveloped by the fire of craving, Pervading the entire world of devas,
Desiring to burn, one lacks self-mastery, being driven by desire and delusion.
Just as adding dry fuel to a fire causes the flames to grow more intense,
so too for one who indulges in pleasure, the fire of craving increases all the more.
Though the fire of fuel blazes fiercely, all people are able to abandon it;
yet the fire of craving burns the world, so entangling that it cannot be cast off.
If a person would cross the river of craving, they must contemplate the fear of its malevolent insects.
One attains the state of ultimate peace by remaining far removed from craving and desire.
If a person is liberated from the net of craving and stays aloof from lust and hatred,
that wise one crosses over the afflictions and is forever freed from all sorrows and calamities.
If one practices giving and observes the precepts while constantly keeping the heavens in mind,
yet this person defiles the pure precepts, it is like water mixed with poison.
Such a person deceives all sentient beings through craving for more than a thousand million kalpas.
The fool cannot relinquish it, being driven by greed.
Deceived by craving, sentient beings still rely upon it,
like a person carrying a heavy burden who drinks hot, salty water.
Having drunk, one immediately thirsts again; for a moment there is no respite.
The fool does not reflect well, laboring in vain and suffering self-inflicted torment.
Therefore, one should abandon craving; the heart of craving is difficult to subdue.
Craving causes all sentient beings to fail to escape birth and death.
The unsurpassed, supreme bliss—the bliss of dhyāna and the realm of contemplation—is the most excellent of joys; it enables one to behold the city of Nirvāṇa.
By accomplishing the causes for supreme bliss, one receives the retribution of celestial joy;
yet, bound by the net of craving, one returns to suffer the pains of hell.
Craving is unwholesome from beginning to end, and one constantly undergoes manifold afflictions.
"Craving is the root of all evils," so the Teacher of the True Dharma has declared.

Thus, the bhikṣu contemplates the world of the devas, seeing how they are swept away and submerged by the eddies of the river of desire, and how they sink back into the suffering of death; having observed this thoroughly, a sense of weary detachment arises in his mind.

Thus, having universally observed the abodes where the devas dwell and the celestial pleasures they enjoy, until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they descend from the heavens; yet they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will be greatly wealthy and possess abundant riches; with wife, children, male and female slaves, servants, and merchants, one’s kin and dependents will live in harmony due to the remaining effects of past karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the eighth dwelling place of the Kāyāvaha devas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the eighth ground of the Kāyāvaha devas is named Constant Joy."
By what karma is one born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one knows:

these sentient beings, with pure faith, saw those who had violated the law and were destined for the suffering of death, bound in prison; they ransomed them with wealth to enable their release—not for the sake of profit, but to benefit sentient beings out of a heart of compassion, seeking no reward in return.

When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the heavens, where they shall always be joyful and experience a hundredfold more delight than other devas, owing to the excellence of their karma.

There, they enjoy themselves with countless celestial maidens who sing, dance, play, and laugh; they sport in mountain valleys and find pleasure in the touch of soft gold and lapis lazuli, as well as in rivers, ponds, and springs, receiving celestial bliss within the groves and gardens.
Of the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of pleasure they experience, the pleasure of a wheel-turning monarch does not equal even one part.
Why is this? Because they are born through shared karma with the hosts of devas; their bodies have neither bone nor flesh, and are free from all impurities.
Beside Mount Sumeru, their bodies are adorned with various precious lotus flowers, celestial garlands, and celestial robes;
if they ascend the golden peaks, their bodies become golden in color;
if they ascend the lapis lazuli peaks, their bodies become the color of lapis lazuli.
Just as when entering pool water, the body becomes the same color as the water;
when ascending the peak of lapis lazuli, the radiance and color of the body are like a second sun due to the power of the lapis lazuli;
and if one ascends the silver peak, the color of the body is like snow or the *kumuda* flower, with every part of the body being upright and magnificently adorned.
Surrounded by celestial maidens, they perform various musical performances and sport in the gardens, enjoying heavenly bliss.

While thus sporting, they see from afar a grove of trees complete in every way, named the Forest of Celestial Play (*devakrīḍāvana*). Mounting a palace made of Jambūnada gold, they enter this Forest of Celestial Play; its woods are soft and supple, and the songs of its many birds are harmonious and exquisite.
Once the Son of Heaven had entered, a bird named Celestial Sound— born through shared karma with the devas and by virtue of their wholesome karma— spoke these verses:
"If there is one who can perform Wholesome deeds that they delight in,
The karmic fruit of those deeds Will result in supreme majesty."
Having already attained celestial pleasures, if one does not act with negligence, one will proceed from joy to a state of further joy, and in the end will surely reach Nirvāṇa.
All pleasures are impermanent; they must inevitably come to an end.
Do not accept these celestial pleasures as your own amusement.
These celestial pleasures are impermanent; when one's lifespan ends, one must inevitably fall away.
Having understood this law, you should seek the path to Nirvāṇa.
All phenomena are subject to exhaustion; that which is high must also fall.
Where there is union, there must be separation; where there is life, all returns to death.
So it is for all sentient beings within the three realms, both present and future.
Those who are born must inevitably die; there is no phenomenon that is eternal.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun are seen by all people, so it is with all living beings:
the law of death is ever-present before them.
Knowing all phenomena in this way— That they are all subject to arising and ceasing— Do not act with a heedless mind; Heedlessness is more harmful than poison.
To be cautious and free from heedlessness— This state is called the Deathless Nectar.
Those who practice heedlessness—this is called the path of death.
Those who are not heedless—these always attain the state of immortality;
those who practice heedlessness—these always proceed upon the road to death.
If a person acts with negligence, it is like poison and like fire;
sentient beings who act with negligence reach a place of suffering at the end of life.
If a person is not negligent, wherever they go, they should be honored.
One who can reach the state of quiescence is forever free from all heedlessness.
All worldly pleasures eventually come to an end, yet the fool does not perceive this;
when the time of death arrives, he forgets everything.
If one loves oneself, one should practice wholesome deeds and cultivate delight in the Dharma as taught by the Buddha.
All things are impermanent; in the end, they lead to great suffering.
"Because of the ultimate truth, the Buddha preaches it for the sake of all sentient beings.

When the deva heard this verse spoken by the bird, his mind was awakened through reflection; he recalled the fruits of his past lives, became slightly free from negligence, and was illumined by the light of contentment. Holding fast his mind, he did not crave the five desires nor engage in negligence.

Before long, their minds will stir again, and they will become attached once more to the five desires, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses. Eventually, when their wholesome karma is exhausted, they will fall back from the heavens.

If they have no evil karma, they will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; instead, they will obtain a human body, avoid royal calamities, constantly experience happiness, and encounter no misfortunes, all due to the remaining traces of their karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the ninth dwelling place of the Kālaya-pāda devas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the ninth station of the Kālaya-pāda devas is named Fragrant Joy (Gandhamada)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows through vision and hearing:

if there are people who maintain the precepts and have faith in the Triple Gem, who offer various powdered incenses and unguents as great fields of merit within the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, making offerings with a pure mind; who acquire wealth in accordance with the Dharma and use it for giving; and who, having performed such acts, reflect upon them with sympathetic joy.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of Fragrant Joy (*Gandharvati*), where they experience celestial bliss.

Their bodies emit radiance, and the five kinds of celestial music play; their minds are constantly joyful, and as they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses for a vast duration, they do not perceive the passage of time as long. Their faculties are immersed in pleasure, restless and greedily attached; thus they have wandered through beginningless transmigration, never knowing contentment.

They sport in the gardens, adorning their bodies with various flower garlands, and are graced by ointments and powdered incenses; the diverse groves are endowed with radiant light, and the ponds, rivers, and flowing springs serve as their adornment.
Their minds are attached to sensual pleasures, unaware of their decline and fall.
Thus deceived by the love for such objects of desire, they experience the delights of the five senses until their karma is exhausted, at which point they fall back from the celestial realm.

If there is wholesome karma, one will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will obtain a human body and be born in a land of cool serenity, where one does not encounter desolation, warfare, or famine, and is honored by all people, due to the remaining traces of that karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the tenth dwelling place of the Kālayojana devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the tenth ground of the Kālayojana devas is named Samtuṣita."
By what karma is one born in that place?
If a person maintains the precepts with pure faith and sees a sentient being who has offended the king, with disheveled hair awaiting execution, and rescues them so they may be set free.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Equal Heads (Suyāma), where they will experience the pleasures of the five senses.
The sensual pleasures enjoyed by the kings of the three directions are fully present and without deficiency for this deity, who possesses the joys of all three heavens.

They delight in desire and seek illumination; they delight in the continuity [of existence]. The pleasures of the three heavens are all obtained according to their thoughts, including the five sensory desires, music, and instruments of enjoyment provided by celestial maidens.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall back from that celestial realm; yet because they possess residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. They obtain a human body, remaining forever free from fear, sorrow, suffering, and agitation. They are healthy and secure, possessing upright and exquisite features, beloved by others, and endowed with great wealth and abundance. Their lifespan is long, varying according to the increase or decrease of the kalpa, due to the power of their residual karma.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma, having observed the ten grounds of the Kālaśodara devas, observes the third dwelling place of the Cāturmahārājika devas, named Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada). How many sub-grounds does it have?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he observes that the Heaven of Following One’s Own Will has ten types of grounds. What are these ten?
First is named Praharṣa-tīra;
second is named Utpala-varṇā;
third is named Puṇḍarīkā.
The fourth is named Various Colors;
the fifth is named Citra;
the sixth is named Mountain Peak.
The seventh is named Mātanga;
the eighth is named Realm of Desire;
the ninth is named Pool of Coolness.
The tenth is named Constantly Sporting.
This is the dwelling place of the gods of Constant Indulgence in the Tenth Stage. By what karma are beings born there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

These sentient beings maintain a pure mind and observe the precepts, remaining free from wrong views; when they see someone cutting down a great tree that is the dwelling place of spirits, yakṣas, or rākṣasas, they protect it and prevent it from being cut down.
These spirits and deities do not harm or afflict people; they find joy by depending on trees and suffer when there are no trees.
Because of this person, the spirits and deities obtain happiness.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Shore of Joy (*Nandana-tīra-deva*) and experience celestial bliss.

The pond is named Cool and Refreshing; its geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks are all golden in body, serving as its adornment, and they produce various wondrous sounds. It is further embellished with lotus flowers made of the seven treasures.

The golden forest trees are called the Golden Grove; they completely surround the lotus ponds, and the reflections of the various immeasurable colors of these precious golden trees appear within the pools. These ponds are exquisitely beautiful, like the ponds of Śakra.

If Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descends from above, wishing to wage war against the asuras, he beholds those lotuses like the sun first rising; such lotuses, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, serve as their adornment.
Having seen this, Śakra addressed the devas, saying:
"This Cool Lake is pure, adorned, and most wonderful.

Regarding such merit-filled lotus ponds, his heart was always filled with love and joy; the Deva Priyāṅga played and enjoyed himself with the celestial maidens in ways beyond analogy, sporting with sovereign ease.
Surrounded by celestial maidens, they experience supreme bliss and exercise mastery over their food.
Whether at the banks of lotus ponds or traveling to other places, their bodies never grow weary and their minds are always joyful and delighted, being perfectly endowed with the highest excellence.

Singing, dancing, and playful laughter resound constantly; surrounded by celestial maidens, they contemplate the bliss of body and mind, which is pure and stainless, ever-increasing and perfected. They enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, their hearts never feeling satiety.
Why is this? Because the heart of craving is like fire; it knows no satisfaction.

Thus, the deva-son sports amidst various mountains, rivers, and palaces, where ponds and lotuses are adorned with the seven treasures. In these places of recreation, he hears various sounds as he sports among the groves with many celestial maidens, enjoying himself in joy and pleasure.
The peaks of Mount Sumeru, with their lapis lazuli jewels, white silver, coral, and golden hues, shine with radiant light as they move about with sovereign ease.

Their radiance is like that of the sun, and their beauty is like that of the moon; some possess a brilliance beyond all analogy. By virtue of their wholesome karma, they have attained these wondrous bodies and experience the fruits of that wholesome karma.

These devas sport and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses until their wholesome karma is exhausted; then, when their life in that heaven ends, if there remains some residual merit, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body—handsome, exquisite, living in abundance, peace, and security, possessing great wealth and many riches, and experiencing the highest pleasure due to the remainder of their karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the second station of the Heaven of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the second station of the Heaven of Constant Indulgence is named Utpala-color."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings practiced in accordance with the Dharma, maintained the precepts with pure faith, and, desiring to make offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, constructed ponds of *utpala* flowers to offer to the Triple Gem.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Utpala-colored Heaven, where they will experience celestial bliss.
They will sport in lotus ponds, rejoicing and finding delight, receiving immeasurable pleasure through singing, dancing, and laughter.
Each of these groves is adorned with lapis lazuli, coral, and pure gold; their ground is soft and supple.
Within them, immeasurable celestial maidens sport and enjoy divine pleasures that are accomplished according to their thoughts, finding joy and delight in countless mountain valleys.

Because of the cause of pleasure, they experience the retribution of pleasure; all that the five sense faculties encounter is entirely blissful, and their bodies are like the color of a lapis lazuli *utpala* flower.
They roam among various lotus ponds amidst *utpala* flowers, the fragrance of which fills a hundred *yojanas* and surpasses all other flowers, like the most excellent of kings.
"Attaining the fruit through its cause is what the Tathāgata has taught.

Having been born in the heavens, they take delight in those lotus ponds, sporting within them and experiencing immeasurable bliss; whatever their six sense faculties encounter, their minds are always filled with joy."

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm. If there remains residual karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body. They are born in a great land abundant with flowers and fruits, endowed with celestial pleasures, and possessed of immense wealth and riches due to the power of that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma perceives, through the wisdom born of hearing,
that the third dwelling place of the Nityotsada devas is named Puṇḍarīka.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings have purified their body, speech, and mind, and for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they constructed lotus ponds to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Puṇḍarīka Heaven; having accomplished virtuous karma, they will experience celestial bliss.
Their bodies will be adorned with various kinds of precious jewels, radiating brilliant light, beloved by all the devas, and graced with flower garlands.
Surrounded by many celestial maidens, he enjoys himself, adorned with various precious jewels such as vajra-blue maṇi gems and mother-of-pearl, experiencing sovereign bliss.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm. If there remains residual karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body. In the land where they are born, there are many marshes and ponds; they are immensely wealthy with abundant riches and experience the highest pleasures. They are cherished and remembered by their parents, siblings, wives, children, and kinsmen, all due to the power of that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the fourth abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the fourth ground of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Varied Ground (Citrapṛthivī)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees:

these sentient beings possessed pure faith in their hearts and dyed robes for the community of bhikṣus—whether they were made of *pi-pa-lo* (bark-cloth), or red, yellow, purple, dark blue, sandalwood-colored, green, light green, black, or azure—using these various colors to dye the Dharma-robes for those who have left the household life.
When this person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of Variegated Grounds (*Citrabhūmi*) and experience celestial bliss.

Adorned with various colored garments and garlands, their bodies constantly emit diverse radiances that illuminate that land; everything is crimson, like the light emitted by red jewel-flowers, and the radiance of that ground is likewise so.
Furthermore, various other kinds of blue and yellow miscellaneous jewels adorned the ground; likewise, all manner of colored garments served as adornments, adorning their bodies in the same way.
Sporting in the groves, they constantly experience incomparable happiness, endowed with immeasurable and supreme merits, enjoying all manner of delights.

Attained through their virtuous karma, they possess various gardens, palaces, and pavilions adorned with many jewels; together with hosts of celestial maidens, they sport within these gardens and pavilions, and wherever they go upon the variegated ground, they become the same color as it.

In each forest tree, each mountain peak, each flower pond, each river, and each flowing spring, they sport and enjoy themselves, engaging in various musical performances, singing, dancing, and laughter.

Together with the many celestial maidens, they indulge in mutual affection and delight themselves in the six desires; they eat the flavor of *sūdā* and drink the celestial nectar, yet remain free from intoxication or confusion.
Surrounded by the hosts of devas, they experience such joyful pleasures.
Having observed this, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
“Wholesome karma is supreme and exalted; More exalted than Mount Sumeru.
Wholesome karma can lead a person To the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.”
Observing various kinds of precepts and protecting them in immeasurable ways,
one experiences happiness among the devas through the retribution of such wholesome karma.
Adorned with the pure radiance of the precepts, the water of upholding the precepts is utterly pure.
Those who bathe and cultivate the path of practice are born in heaven and enjoy happiness.
Through generosity and precepts, they discipline themselves;
benefiting all sentient beings, they advance in wisdom and a compassionate heart—such people are born among the gods.
Practicing correctly and free from all faults, adorned by the jewel of ethical discipline, and possessing compassion for sentient beings—such a person is reborn in the heavens.
One who is upright is like gold; when refined, it is freed from dust and dross.
Those who practice the joy of right action are born among the gods;
those who have compassion for all sentient beings, whose minds are ever mindful of their benefit,
and who are untainted by evil deeds, are born in the celestial palaces.
Maintaining the precepts day and night, and always upholding them with wisdom,
such a person is born among the gods and constantly experiences happiness.
If a person reflects and contemplates, they shall mount the horse of moral discipline.
Reaching the palaces of the various devas, those immeasurable places of play and joy—
if one sports in these celestial palaces and receives the retribution of heavenly bliss,
it is all due to upholding the pure precepts; so has the Tathāgata taught.
If a person is adorned with garlands and celestial flowers of supreme excellence,
sporting within the heavens, it is all due to the power of wholesome karma.
They sport amidst *utpala* lotuses, and their gardens and groves are magnificently adorned.
Sporting amidst the heavens is entirely due to virtuous karma;
dwelling within the realm of space, adorned with celestial jewels,
and possessing the pure light of the devas— all these are attained through the observance of the precepts.
In places adorned with gold and jewels, Where exquisite flowers and fragrances abound, They sport upon mountain peaks; All this is obtained through the observance of precepts.
Like a person entering their own home, Their mind is free from fear.
The observance of precepts is likewise; it can lead one to the heavens.
Neither the scent of jasmine flowers nor that of the māluva or campaka can surpass the fragrance of the heavens;
the fragrance of keeping the precepts is most supreme.
If a person upholds the precepts, that person is truly superior;
if a person abandons the precepts, they are called a dead man.
Having understood this merit, if one loves oneself, [one should protect the precepts].
One who well guards and upholds the precepts, remaining far removed from the mind that violates them;
one who maintains discipline and is ever self-controlled, whose patience makes them a joy for others to behold—
such a person is like one ascending a staircase, reaching the blissful realm of heaven.

"In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the retribution of his own karma as experienced by the devas. Having contemplated the fruits of karma, he develops a mind of weary detachment from desire within the cycle of birth and death.

Those devas of the Painted Ground (Citrapṛthivī) sport and enjoy pleasures until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted. When their life as a deva ends, if they have remaining wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; instead, they obtain a human body, becoming beloved and respected by all people, possessing great wealth and abundance, and being born in the South Heavenly Region (Dakṣiṇāpatha), a place free from affliction and turmoil, due to that residual karma."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the fifth abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the fifth level of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Citrā, which in the Wei language means 'Variegated Ground' (Zadi)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one knows:
these sentient beings, with faith and compassion, gave various kinds of food as alms to those who observe the precepts and those who do not.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, where, through various karmas, they obtain various pleasures.

They enjoy diverse pleasures upon various couches and seats, sporting amidst various groves and gardens, entertaining themselves with celestial maidens and experiencing delight. They frolic within various mountain forests, ravines, and peaks.

In various lotus ponds and springs, amidst *utpala* and *padma* flowers and all manner of fruits and blossoms—places for wandering and viewing—they adorn their bodies with various garments and engage in various forms of speech: skillful words and eloquent rhetoric, playful laughter and endearing talk, and discursive debate; thus creating various causes, they experience manifold pleasures within the various groves.
Having observed this, the bhikṣu was filled with joy and spoke these verses:
“The workings of karma surpass even the skill of a master painter;
The artist of karma, within the heavens, Produces all manner of pleasant retributions.”
Various kinds of pigments can be counted when they appear before one's eyes;
but the colors spread by the karma of the mind, their number cannot be known.
When the wall is destroyed, the painting perishes; both perish at the same time.
When the body perishes and is extinguished, the paintings of karma cannot be lost.
Just as a single painter creates various ornamental designs,
so too does the single mind create all manner of karmic deeds.
The five-colored radiance appears, and upon seeing it, one gives rise to love and delight;
so too are the paintings of the five sense-faculties, which exist according to karma as birth and death.
Just as a skillful painter of this world can be seen before one’s eyes, [so do these faculties appear].
The mind is a subtle painter; no one can see it.
It paints forms, both beautiful and ugly, causing various images to appear upon the wall.
The karma of the mind is likewise: it is able to produce the retributions of good and evil.
This mind, throughout day and night, is constantly restless in its thoughts;
likewise, karma follows the mind, revolving and never departing from it.
Just as wind, dust, smoke, clouds, and heat cause painted colors to fade and perish, so too does karma dissolve the mind.
"When one abandons both the wholesome and the unwholesome, all karmas are thereby lost.
Thus, the bhikṣu contemplates the mind as a painter that freely creates karma; observing karma as it truly is, he becomes weary of and detached from birth and death.

This deva experiences various pleasant karmic results until that karma is exhausted; when his life as a deva comes to an end, if there remains further merit, he will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will obtain a human body, becoming immensely wealthy with abundant riches, constantly practicing the True Dharma, and seeking wealth and treasures by means of great ships, all due to the residue of his remaining karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (*Sadāmada*).
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the sixth stage of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Mountain Peak (*Śikhara*)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings, having cultivated their minds with virtue, constructed shelters for the purpose of warding off cold and heat for others to enjoy.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn on a mountain peak, where they will experience celestial bliss, delighting themselves with the five desires and achieving all manner of excellences.
There are seven groves:
the first is named the Mandārava Play Grove;
The second is named Cloud Forest;
the third is named Forest of Cessation and Joy;
the fourth is named Forest of Play.
The fifth is named Roaring Forest;
the sixth is named Illusion Forest;
the seventh is named Nikāra Forest.

In this grove, accompanied by a multitude of celestial maidens, they frolic and laugh, indulging in song and dance with unrestrained abandon; performing divine music, they wander and gaze as they please, experiencing the foremost of pleasures.

They sport amidst each of the flowering groves, which adorn the mountain with various treasuries of jewels; from every mountain peak issues golden light, and as they sport therein, they are free from all illness and affliction.

Having been born in that place by means of various wholesome karmas, they experience celestial delights, enjoying themselves among flowing rivers, springs, and lotus ponds. This continues until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; when their life as a deva ends, if there remains further merit, they will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will obtain a human body and become a teacher to great kings, beloved by all people, due to the influence of that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the seventh stage of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Māthava, which in the Wei language means 'Beautiful Land' (Meidi)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings practiced wholesome karma and observed the prohibitive precepts; they benefited sentient beings with a gentle and compassionate heart, being upright and free from deceit, never troubling others; they gave food as alms to wandering śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to the poor, the sick, the suffering, and the solitary, doing so for one day, two days, or even many days, constantly providing without ceasing.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn among the beautiful devas and experience celestial bliss.

From the nets of bells in the groves, wondrous sounds issue forth; surrounded on all sides by hosts of celestial maidens, they enjoy immeasurable celestial desires and pleasures, accompanied by many youths.

The heavenly *sūdhā* nectar is sweet and delicious, satisfying all their desires; they wear *mandārava* flowers as celestial garlands and sport amidst flowering groves and mountain peaks of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Many swarms of bees roam the flower ponds, producing exquisite sounds; they sport with hosts of jade maidens in the gardens and groves, where the splendor of the forests surpasses that of hundreds of thousands of suns.
In the Mandāra groves and the Kūṣaja groves, the sounds of flocks of golden birds are lovely; with the sounds of the five kinds of music, they experience celestial bliss.
The ground is composed of gold and lapis lazuli.
There are many ponds, their bottoms strewn with pearls as sand; in each pond is water of eight virtues, produced by the power of one's own karma.
Mount Sumeru has stones of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal; upon this adorned mountain of jewels, he plays and enjoys pleasures with celestial jade maidens, experiencing the fruits of his own karma.

When their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm; if there remains further wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body and constantly enjoy wealth and happiness. By virtue of their residual karma, they receive a fief from a great king near Mount Mīṇḍha.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (*Nityotsada*).
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the eighth station of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Realm of Desire (*Kāmagati*).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings gave to those who maintain the precepts, or to those suffering from wrong views and illness, whatever food, drink, and medicinal decoctions were necessary for their comfort, thereby causing them to be free from the suffering of disease.

When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the heavens of the desire realm, where they will experience celestial bliss, free from all fear, and be venerated by all the devas of that same level.
Because their karma is superior, the retribution of their pleasure is also superior; it is just as when a lamp is large, its radiance is also great.
Thus, they experience supreme celestial pleasures in heaven, having been born in that place through the power of their wholesome karma.
With the golden light of *vaiḍūrya* jewels and *maṇi* gems, they sport and enjoy themselves upon the peaks of Mount Sumeru; with infinite promenades and observations, they adorn that land.
The gardens, bathing pools, rivers, springs, and flowing streams were adorned with the seven treasures and various radiances.
Many celestial maidens respectfully surrounded him as he enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses, sporting at will and experiencing all manner of sensual delights.

They experience pleasure therein until their wholesome karma is exhausted; when their life in that celestial realm comes to an end, if there remains residual karma, they will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will instead obtain a human body—foremost in physical beauty, free from fear, immensely wealthy with abundant riches, respected by kings, honored by the multitude, long-lived, and born in a noble land;
they will be born at a time when the True Dharma exists and will not be born in an evil age.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
In the ninth stage of the Heaven of Constant Indulgence, there is a place called the Pond of Cool Refreshment.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who possess faith and compassion; seeing other sentient beings at the point of death, afflicted by thirst and having encountered the messengers of Yama, they give rise to great fear, and thus bestow honey-melodious syrup or cold water upon these sick persons.
By these causes and conditions, when such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Cool Refreshment (Sīta-vatī), where they shall experience celestial bliss.
That land is fully endowed with flowing waters, rivers, ponds, and places for play and enjoyment.

In those heavens, they experience various pleasures: their sight is satisfied, their sense of fragrance is indulged in at will, their bodies touch what is fine and soft, and the same is true for sounds and tastes.

Their minds are cool and free from the fault of intoxication. That drink is endowed with five kinds of merit; once the devas have drunk it, ten merits increase. When they travel through the air, they do not fall; they ride upon the void without obstruction, as if wandering on level ground, without exerting any effort.
Singing, dancing, playing, and laughing, their minds are constantly joyful as they enjoy the merits of the heavens and the pleasures of a hundred virtues.
Their ears hear sounds without any obstruction.
Thus, within the heavens, they experience the foremost pleasure.
Such are the celestial pleasures enjoyed according to one's will—pleasures of the sensory realm.
There are eight groves of trees formed of the seven precious substances:
the first is named Caturānanda (Four Joys).
The second is named Playful Conduct;
the third is named Cool Intent;
the fourth is named Forest of Wind-Bliss.
The fifth is named Musical Sound;
the sixth is named Leaf Sound;
the seventh is named Flower Forest.
The eighth is named the Forest of Fulfilling Wishes.
In this forest, they sport and enjoy pleasure: their eyes behold exquisite forms, their ears hear delightful sounds, their noses smell wondrous fragrances, and their tongues obtain superior flavors.

Thus free from defilement, their minds are cool and serene; they experience pleasure within the spheres of the five sense-faculties. Yet, being consumed by these six desires, they cause the fires of the six desires to increase day and night; though they burn with unrestrained indulgence, they remain unaware of it.

Born into a state of negligence, their minds were corrupted by heedlessness; eventually, when their wholesome karma was exhausted, they passed away from that celestial realm. Because a residue of wholesome karma remained, they did not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attained a human body. They were constantly free from hunger and thirst and never experienced fatigue; they never encountered the fear of famine and enjoyed the highest pleasure, being beloved and cherished by all people of the world, who provided them with bedding, seating, and medical supplies for their bodies—all due to the power of their residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the abode of the gods of Constant Indulgence (Nityotsada).
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he observes that the tenth stage of the gods of Constant Indulgence is named Constant Play (Nityavihāra).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees:

there are sentient beings who, for the sake of those practicing dhyāna, paint murals on their dwellings to facilitate the contemplation of a corpse (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) so as to engender revulsion and renunciation.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Constant Play (Nityapramada), where they shall constantly experience happiness.
