That land is adorned with gold, lapis lazuli, coral, and indranīla mani-jewels; there they sport and enjoy pleasures, amidst immeasurable sounds that are most lovely and delightful beyond description.
Food, drink, clothing, and articles such as flowers and incense are obtained immediately upon thought.
There are immeasurable modes of play, namely:
play in the groves, play in joyful delight, play with the songs of birds, play with sounds, play at will, play with fine fragrances, and play with tactile garments.
Various incenses are blended together in manifold ways for the sake of playful delight.

Traveling through the void, they behold their kinsmen and friends, and their hearts are filled with joy; as they traverse the mountains of various jewels, they likewise experience delight. Thus they achieve immeasurable pleasures, including the sounds of the five musical instruments, all brought to fruition by their own karma.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm; yet because of residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead attain a human body. Due to this remaining karma, they constantly possess various places for play, wear various silken garments, and delight in various languages and diversions.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 23 [and] Scroll 24,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Contemplation of the Heavens, Part Three; The Third [Section] on the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, having observed the three abodes of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and having examined each of their karmic fruits in detail, now observes the fourth abode."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he observes that the Trayastrimsha Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three) has ten levels. What are these ten?
The first is named Gandhara;
the second is named Yingsheng (Responsive Sound);
the third is named Xile (Joyful Delight).
The fourth is named "Probing the Water";
the fifth is named "White Body";
the sixth is named "Shared Entertainment."
Seventh is named Joyful Conduct;
eighth is named Shared Conduct;
ninth is named Transformation-Birth.
The tenth is named Accumulated Conduct (*saṃcāra*). These are the ten abodes of the *kumbhāṇḍa* gods.
In this way, the bhikṣu analytically contemplates the retribution of those karmas: by what karma is one born in these celestial realms?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that the gods of the *vīṇā* (lute) realm cultivate wholesome karma and are born in that celestial world, obtaining a corresponding fruit.
The first terrestrial region is named Gandhara; by what karma are sentient beings born into this heaven?

If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of faith, cultivate their bodies and offer groves of land, or fields of sugarcane, or groves of mango trees, or groves of fine fruit, to the community of monks, so that the monks may enjoy them.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Gandharva Heaven, where they will experience immeasurable bliss.

Their bodies will be anointed with celestial *candana* and *gośīrṣa-candana*, and they will be surrounded and entertained by countless celestial maidens. These maidens possess various ornaments and diverse appearances, and are skilled in the arts of song, dance, and laughter. They sport in groves and gardens and among various lotus ponds, enjoying themselves in play and delight.

Their bodies are clothed in celestial garments and adorned with flower garlands; their hearts are filled with mutual love and joy. The fragrance of these flowers permeates for a hundred *yojanas*, and when the celestial maidens (*apsaras*) smell this scent, they all rejoice greatly, becoming a hundredfold more unrestrained. They gaze upon the deva-son with insatiable desire, honoring him in a hundred ways through immeasurable modes of conduct.
Thus the minds of these devaputras were unrestrained and indulgent, delighting themselves in sensual pleasures.
There were various rivers:
one was named the Jewel-Flowing River;
The second is named the River of Waves;
the third is named the River of Gold;
the fourth is named the River of Wine.
The fifth is named Beautiful Flowing River;
the sixth is named River of Laughing Bubbles.

In these various rivers, geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks produce manifold exquisite sounds. On both banks of the rivers there are many groves and gardens, their trees lush and interlacing. Various birds of diverse colors, adorned with the seven treasures, emit harmonious and elegant notes that are most delightful.
The hosts of celestial maidens produce exquisite song; upon hearing the voices of the various birds, their desire increases a hundredfold, and they take no pleasure in any other sounds.
Having heard them, they rejoice and experience immeasurable bliss, as the seven musical notes are fully present, harmonious and supple.

In the river, various birds and celestial maidens sing and play; drinking the celestial nectar, they are free from intoxication or confusion. Together with the celestial maidens, they enjoy themselves and experience pleasure upon the many jewel mountains—the peaks of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The gardens, groves, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, and lotuses were adorned by flocks of birds.
Furthermore, together with celestial maidens, they sported upon the blue lapis lazuli ground, which was entirely covered with various kinds of flowers; therein they played and enjoyed themselves.
"By virtue of their wholesome karma, the pleasures of the heavens are accomplished.
Having thus observed the heavenly pleasures through the wisdom of hearing, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"The five faculties constantly experience pleasure, Deceived and deluded by the objects of desire."
The fire of desire has never known satiety; in a mere moment it is quenched.
In every single realm, one sees celestial maidens everywhere;
yet in all these supreme realms, the flames of desire blaze ever fiercer.
Whether joined or separated, whether spoken of or recollected, through the causal conditions of the celestial maidens, fire arises and burns the devas.
The nature of fire exists through conjunction; without conjunction, it does not arise.
Whether in union or not in union, the fire of desire is ever ablaze.
Because of the lack of connection with its causes and conditions, fire does not burn when it is distant;
yet the fire of desire has no distance or proximity—it constantly burns and harms sentient beings.
By the power of the fuel of conceptual thought, driven by wrong mindfulness, the oil of craving is cast into the fire of desire, which burns the foolish person.
If one were to burn the body with fire, once it has burned, it is extinguished in an instant; [but this fire of desire is not so easily quenched].
Even when name-and-form have dissolved, the fire of desire is not yet extinguished.
The fire of desire burns sentient beings more fiercely than an ordinary fire burns a person;
though the harm of the fire of desire is extreme, people do not feel weary of it.
The five faculties arise through causes and conditions, conditioned by the five objects;
blown by the wind of craving, the fire of desire burns sentient beings.
Born from the friction-stick of recollection, it grows by means of the objects.
Though not a visible phenomenon, it burns people more fiercely than a blazing fire.
The fire of desire is likewise; it increases and blazes even more intensely.
Thus blinded by desire, one becomes greedily attached to sensual pleasures.
"Fire possesses radiance, yet the fire of desire is shrouded in darkness;
this desire is like a poisonous enemy—wise people should abandon it.
Thus, as the bhikṣu contemplates how the fire of desire incinerates devas and humans, compassion arises in his heart; seeing their faults, he takes no pleasure in celestial delights.

Thus the Gandharva devas experience various pleasures until their wholesome karma is exhausted. When their life in that heaven comes to an end, if they have residual wholesome karma, they do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but instead obtain a human body. Due to that residual karma, they possess vast landed estates and great wealth.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the realm where the Vīṇā-devas dwell.
With the wisdom born of hearing, he observes:
the second stage of the Vīṇā-devas is named 'Resonance' (Anurava)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

there are sentient beings who correctly practice wholesome deeds and, for the sake of those with wrong views, preach even a single verse of Dharma, causing their minds to become pure and cool, and leading them to have faith in the Buddha.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Responding to Sounds (*Gandharva-saṃcodana*), where they will experience the pleasures of the five senses.
They will sport in the lotus ponds of the celestial river, amidst mountain peaks of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal, to the music of the *gandharvas*.

The hosts of celestial maidens, adorned with various ornaments, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing—peerless in their beauty—surrounded the deva-son, increasing his joy and delight as they sported upon the mountain peaks and experienced manifold pleasures.
Adorned with celestial garlands and powdered incense, they delight themselves within immeasurable realms.
Furthermore, they roam through mountain valleys and golden mountain gardens, sporting and enjoying pleasures therein.

There are various mountains of gold, namely Mount Campaka, the Mountain Without Shadow, the Mountain of All Joys, and the Mountain of Mental Transformations; such mountains as these are adorned with various jewels and graced by golden groves and gardens.
The hosts of devas, filled with joy, sang praises as they roamed among the mountain peaks and even by the various waters.
The many lotus ponds were adorned with water that was pure, cool, delicious, and pristine; there, flocks of birds frolicked at will, emitting exquisite melodies.

The dwelling place on that mountain is exceedingly delightful; there they experience the retribution of their own karma, sporting and enjoying pleasures, surrounded by celestial maidens. Various kinds of birds emit exquisite songs, and swarms of bees produce the sound of desire.
He sports in the forest palaces where the Deva-sons dwell, experiencing the foremost pleasures together with the celestial maidens.

Such is the pleasure experienced by these earth-devas until their wholesome karma is exhausted; then they fall back from heaven and, transmigrating according to their karma, undergo various births and deaths, perhaps being born in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

If there remains further karma, one may receive a human body, being born into a prominent and most wealthy family, respected by all people, with excellence of body, speech, and mind, possessing steadfast kinsmen, and fully endowed with servants, slaves, and attendants—all due to this remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the abodes of the Tūṇava-devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the third level of the Tūṇava-devas is named Nandana (Joy).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings practiced wholesome karma; with pure faith, they gave fine drinks to others, or gave pure, fine water to those on the path, bringing them peace and happiness.

Or one may cover up springs and wells, fearing that venomous snakes, spiders, insects, or ants might fall into them, causing suffering to travelers who drink from them; for this reason, one covers the springs and wells not for the sake of seeking reward, but for the sake of merit.
When that person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Three Lutes within the Land of Joyful Play.
Having been born in that heaven, the radiance of their body is like that of a second sun; by virtue of their wholesome karma, their entire body is adorned with splendor.
They sport in mountain valleys, springs, ponds, and flowing streams, wandering together with the celestial maidens in harmony.
These handsome youths are free from suffering and old age; they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses—immeasurable forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and delightful tactile sensations.
In that land, the mountains and forests abound with trees made of the seven precious gems, free from such things as withered groves.
The various flowers in those forests never wither or change, and their fragrance constantly perfumes the air.
In the forest of Golden Shadow Trees, golden branches spread everywhere, adorned with peaks of lapis lazuli.

Flocks of peacocks and *kūṭāhara* birds, with wings made of the seven precious gems, produce exquisite sounds; beholding their own forms, they feel joy in their hearts, for their plumage is of variegated colors.

According to what the devas thought, exquisite sounds issued forth; having heard these sounds, each of them conceived a sense of wonder, thinking: "This bird is able to know the thoughts within my mind."

They emit sounds at will, their voices exquisite and beautiful; from within the mouths of the birds flows a continuous stream of ambrosial nectar. The birds drink of it and become ten times more unrestrained, their hearts filled with joy. From their mouths they utter sounds of a hundred kinds of merit, the resonance of which is adorned with supreme and wondrous virtues.
Hearing the various songs and manifold wondrous sounds of the birds, his mind of desire and lust becomes a hundredfold more dissolute, and joy arises within him.

Furthermore, there are many birds named *Līlā-vihāra* (Sportive Play) that produce manifold wondrous sounds within the lattice of bells; their voices are so pure and exquisite that they merge with the sound of the bells, becoming indistinguishable from them, and as these sounds blend together, they become twice as wonderful.
Furthermore, there are various birds called "Bank-Walkers" (*tīracārin*) that dwell among the golden lotuses on the riverbanks, from which fragrant drinks flow forth.
There are also various birds called "Shadow-Roamers" (*chāyācārin*); wherever they travel, the ground becomes the same color as themselves.
Furthermore, there are birds called *cakra* (wheel-birds); whenever these wheel-birds fly near, they cause the celestial maidens to become a hundred times more upright and exquisite than before.
They sport and enjoy themselves within the immeasurable groves without interruption, attaining the foremost, supreme bliss at will, which is incomparably pure.
Surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens, they play in the groves or roam upon mountain peaks, traveling through the air to the summits of mountains of gold and lapis lazuli.
In the various lotus ponds, there are geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks; the water is as pure as lapis lazuli, filled to the brim with fragrant waters.
In these places of recreation, streams of various perfumes flow, and the scents of all the groves waft everywhere.
Innumerable golden trees and lapis lazuli trees surround that mountain; its ground is soft and supple, leveling itself as one lifts or sets foot upon it.
Upon this ground, he sports with various celestial maidens, enjoying themselves together.

Beholding lovely forms with their eyes—countless hundreds of thousands of various exquisite colors—and countless hundreds of thousands of lovely, exquisite sounds, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of various exquisite fragrances, these sense faculties experience immeasurable pleasure. This continues until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted. When life ends from this state, if there remains further wholesome karma, they will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will obtain a human body and constantly enjoy peace and happiness. They will be cherished by kings and remembered by the masses, due to the power of that residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the Vīṇā-devas.
With the wisdom born of hearing,
he sees that the fourth abode of the Vīṇā-devas is named Water-Spading (Āloka-vīṇā).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings practiced wholesome deeds with faith, compassion, and a heart intent on benefiting others. Seeing those afflicted by illness whose lives were nearing their end, and who were making gasping sounds from their throats while their remaining life-force was not yet exhausted, they gave them drinks or provided wealth to sustain their lives.

By reason of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, at the end of his life this person is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three), in the region known as "Searching for Water," where he experiences celestial bliss.

His radiance and majestic virtue are like those of Śakra, the King of Devas; surrounded on all sides by hosts of celestial maidens, he constantly enjoys happiness, experiencing the retribution of his own karma for an immeasurable time.

They see immeasurable forests and immeasurable rivers, where hosts of celestial maidens follow one another into the woods; the forest is named Māli, adorned with immeasurable river-lotus bathing pools, while celestial musical instruments emit exquisite sounds.
Many celestial maidens rejoice and enjoy themselves within that grove, which abounds in flowers and fruits and resounds with the music of *gandharvas* and the songs of various birds.

The jewel-trees of that grove include the *mandārava* grove, the *kūṭaśālmali* grove, the indestructible grove, the ever-joyful grove, the perfectly joyful grove, and the grove of wish-fulfilling fragrance.

Thus, the fragrance of these flowers perfumes everything universally. Following the thoughts of the celestial maidens, once they have finished sporting in the Mālatī grove, they proceed toward the Five Flower Groves to enjoy themselves together.
In that grove, there were birds known as "Recallers of Past Lives" (*pūrvajātismara*). Seeing the hosts of devas, they spoke these verses:
"Merit is lovely and delightful; it can bring about superior fruits and rewards.
Therefore, one should cultivate merit; there is no raft or boat equal to merit."
The treasury of merit is inexhaustible; merit is the supreme kinsman.
Merit is like a bright lamp, and it is also like compassionate parents.
Through merit one reaches the heavens; merit can lead one to the good realms.
Because people can cultivate merit, they receive blissful happiness in the heavens.
If a person cultivates supreme merit, they will always be born in pleasant places;
therefore, one should cultivate merit, for there is no happiness that equals the joy of merit.
Benefiting both worlds—through endearment and respect as well as material wealth—one should constantly observe these two causes; this is called the bliss of merit.
Merit always follows the person, never departing like a shadow.
Merit is the foremost happiness; without merit, there is no reward of joy.
When a celestial being’s merit is exhausted, they fall away and are reborn according to their karma.
Since the fruits of the world are both good and evil, one should therefore cultivate merit.
Though I once dwelt in the world of devas, I now receive the body of an animal;
due to the lack of meritorious causes and conditions, I am deceived by my own karma.
If one lacks the discipline of merit, one will constantly wander upon the evil paths.
That person has no peace or happiness, like sand from which no oil can be extracted.
Deceived by their own minds, fools remain far removed from merit;
such people do not attain joy, and their manifold sufferings never cease.
These beings are born again and again, and repeatedly fall back into decline;
because they act with negligence in the heavens, the pleasures of those gods are impermanent.
The net of karma binds sentient beings, who are deceived by ignorance and craving.
Since beginningless birth and death, beings have transmigrated like a waterwheel.
When the gods fall from their celestial realms, they undergo such great suffering and affliction that even the manifold poisons of suffering in the hells cannot be compared to it.
The celestial music must surely end; why do you not awaken?
Because you do not see death and extinction, you are greedily attached to worldly pleasures.
The births and deaths of all worlds cannot be known by mere calculation.
Yet no one can grow weary of it; they are deceived by craving.

At that time, when the assembly of devas heard the bird preaching the Dharma, their minds briefly recollected [the truth], but they returned once more to negligence, driven by the mind, and proceeded toward sensual desire.”
In those groves, they entertain themselves with the sounds of the five kinds of music, singing, dancing, and laughter.
They burn the fuel of sensory objects with the fire of heedlessness.
In each dwelling place, each garden, each mountain peak, each palace, and each lotus pond, they sport among the celestial maidens, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
In this celestial realm, they experience heavenly bliss until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; then, when their life in heaven ends, they transmigrate according to their karma.

If there remains further wholesome merit, they will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will obtain a human body. From birth until death, they will not encounter the suffering of illness, nor will they be troubled by disturbances; they will be loved and respected by others, born in a noble land free from hunger and thirst, and possess a handsome appearance due to the remnants of their past karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the Vīṇā-devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the fifth dwelling place of the Vīṇā-devas is named White Body (Śvetakāya).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?

If there are sentient beings who recognize the field of merit and, with pure faith, see a Buddhist stūpa damaged by wind and rain—or a monastic dwelling—and with a mind of merit, they plaster, decorate, repair, or restore it; and with right faith, knowing the retribution of karmic actions, they rejoice after having performed the deed, and further teach others to repair old stūpas.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn among the Śukra-devas (White-bodied Devas).

Those born in that heaven wear white garments as brilliant as jade, snow, or the kumuda flower; even if one were to divide [the latter] into sixteen parts, their brilliance would not equal even one part. Their palaces are likewise entirely white light, and their bodies are a fresh, radiant white.
They sport among various groves; from the coral tree groves issue manifold exquisite fragrances, and amidst various musical sounds, songs, dances, and laughter, they experience celestial bliss.
Entering the coral grove, it resounds with the cries of many birds; its radiance is majestic and possesses great power, being crimson in color—the most excellent among all colors.
Their own bodies were originally pure white, but due to the red radiance of the trees, their bodies all became red.
Looking at one another, they each said:
"Our original colors have all disappeared, and a different color has arisen."
"This tree is red; we should go to another grove.
He then entered the Vaiḍūrya grove with the celestial maidens. That grove was blue in color, like looking up at the sky from Jambudvīpa, causing the bodies of all the devas to lose their white hue.
The blue light of those trees completely enveloped the bodies of the devas; all the birds and lotuses there were likewise blue in color.

At that time, the sons of the gods, surrounded by their celestial maidens, performed divine music and engaged in play, song, and dance. For a long duration, they enjoyed celestial pleasures, delighting themselves with the five desires for a great length of time.

They then proceeded to the Silver Forest to indulge in unrestrained play; within that Silver Forest, all the adornments were white—white jewel lotuses and white jewel birds—and these were the White-Body Devas.

Entering this grove, it is as if seeing the reflection of the moon's image within milk; dwelling long in this grove, they sport and enjoy pleasures, with the celestial music and performances beyond all comparison.

Having left this grove, they proceed to the Grove of Various Multitudes (Vicitra-vana). That grove is adorned with all kinds of trees—some are golden trees, some are silver trees, and some are beryl trees—adorned with leaves of various colors. The physical forms and complexions of these devas likewise manifest in various colors accordingly.
In this grove, he sports for a long time with the celestial maidens.

Leaving this grove behind, he proceeds to a golden mountain peak named Samantagata. This golden peak is adorned with the seven precious jewels; from its summit, he beholds all sixty thousand golden mountains that are the retinue of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which stands at their center.

They then proceed to Mount Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*). Having ascended that mountain, they sport there for a long time. The surrounding gardens are adorned everywhere with many flowing streams, rivers, and ponds; numerous birds emit exquisite melodies. The White-Body gods (*Śvetakāya*) and others enjoy celestial pleasures on Mount Universal Eye for a long duration, sporting and delighting with various heavenly maidens (*apsaras*).

Having left that mountain, they ascended further to the summit of Mount Mahāmeru. There, other devas also came to this mountain to gather and sport together. At that time, the Śvetakāya devas played and enjoyed themselves with the hosts of devas; the sounds of celestial music were exceedingly delightful.

When the enjoyment of pleasure is exhausted, it is like a lamp whose oil is spent and its light is extinguished; or like the setting sun, whose brightness also vanishes. The devas are likewise: when their karma is exhausted, they fall back and, according to their original karma, are reborn in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

If they are born among humans, their bodies will be as fresh and white as the color of lotus fibers; born in lands such as the northern celestial realm of Han, they will all possess beautiful complexions and be fully endowed with luster, experiencing the foremost pleasures and governing the people due to the remaining force of their past karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the abode of the Vīṇā-devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the sixth station of the Vīṇā-devas is named Saṃkrīḍita (Common Play)."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings possess faith and maintain the precepts; they gather together in harmony for the sake of the Dharma and its meaning, upholding the precepts and practicing generosity.
By these causes and conditions, these people, at the end of their lives here, will be reborn in the Heaven of Shared Play (*Sahamodana*).

Having been born in that heaven, their merit will be perfected; they will all with one mind experience joy in harmony, delighting together in play, movement, and food. Their sensory realms will be delightful, and they will enjoy themselves with the sounds of the five kinds of music, laughing, singing, dancing, and reveling in pleasure.

The hosts of celestial maidens were adorned with various ornaments, and the mountain terrain was embellished with diverse precious jewels; they sported therein, experiencing the fruits of their own karma.

Balustrades made of *vaiḍūrya* gems encircled the area, while rivers were graced by various precious geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, and the riverbanks were adorned with trees of manifold jewels. The hosts of celestial maidens surrounded them as they played.

They went to the Pearl River, where they drank from its immeasurable currents; it was pure, fragrant, and clean, with white pearl sand spread across its bottom and fine gold for its mud. There were many golden fish, their bodies adorned with immeasurable precious jewels.
On both banks of that river, there are trees made of gold with leaves of *vaiḍūrya* gemstone;
there are also *vaiḍūrya* trees with leaves of gold.
All the flowers and fruits are endowed with exquisite colors, always in full bloom, while various birds sport therein, ever filled with joy and delight.
Upon hearing their voices, all give rise to love and joy; if they look upon them with their eyes, their hearts are gladdened by the sight.

Those devaputras, constantly filled with delight, proceed once more to their original dwelling place within the waters of the Pañcaśikha. There, the branches and leaves of the jewel-trees form dwellings and palaces; the ground is soft, rising and falling according to the tread of the feet like celestial blue jewels. They come and go in play amidst a vast, level, and expansive expanse adorned with many lotus groves, where various birds are embellished with exquisite jewels.
There are some lands of golden ground, where beryl tree branches form nets that serve as palaces and dwellings; they are adorned with many fragrant flowers and surrounded by swarms of bees.
Devaputras and devakanyās fill its midst, enjoying the retribution of celestial pleasures.
They further proceed to springs, gardens, groves, and bathing pools; there, flocks of birds with golden bodies sport within the waters, filling the space and emitting exquisite sounds.
The river’s spring-fed waters, pure, fragrant, and clean, flow forth and pour into the Golden Mountain, producing various sounds.

On the banks of that river, celestial maidens hold golden lotuses in their hands and surround the deva-son, providing him with entertainment and pleasure; they take delight in a game of flower-fighting, continuing for a long time.
Furthermore, together with the various devas, they went to the Forest of Desire (*kāmanavana*). In that forest, all such beings had their minds shrouded by negligence.
The flocks of birds in that grove indulged themselves in the flavors of the fruits; the bees, whose appearance was like lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), indulged themselves in the flavors of the flowers;
and the *kapiñjala* birds were constantly intoxicated and dissolute in heart, as if it were the springtime.
Just as the flocks of birds on the riverbank are intoxicated by the fine drink, so too do these devas indulge their will in the five sensual pleasures.
When the hosts of celestial maidens see the devas, their hearts are filled with desire.
For such women, there is no other pleasure superior to the pleasure of desire.

Thus, these women relish the flavor of desire, dwell upon desire, rely upon desire, and by their very nature are mindful of desire; they constantly think of the deva-sons, never letting go of them from their minds. When they see a deva-son sporting and enjoying himself with various celestial maidens, they become a hundred times more intoxicated.

Experiencing such pleasure until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm and, transmigrating according to their karma, fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
If they are born among humans, they will again be born together with their kinsmen in the same country, cultivating merit through shared karma.

Due to the remainder of their karma, they will all be immensely wealthy; they will all practice wholesome deeds, and everyone will collectively experience the results of the same karma, being born in the same place.
That person experiences both good and evil results entirely together without distinction, due to residual karma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the ground where the Vīṇā-devas dwell.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that the seventh stage of the *kōṅhǒu* (vīṇā) devas is named "Delightful Play.

If a person upholds the precepts and transforms sentient beings, causing their minds to have pure faith, encouraging them to rejoice, or teaching them generosity, or teaching them the observance of precepts, and leading them to believe in fields of merit that possess great virtue; [they shall be reborn there].
When this person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of Delightful Play (Nirmāṇarati), their body endowed with radiance.
They then reflect to themselves: "By what karma have I been born here?"
He then reflected and knew:
"In a previous life, when I was among humans, I practiced giving; this person was my kinsman, and we shared in the same merit."
"By these causes and conditions, I have been born in this heavenly realm. He recalled thus:

"It was through the power of the teaching of my spiritual friend, the śramaṇa, that he caused me to practice giving and give rise to a pure mind; for this reason, I am now born in the Heaven of Delightful Play."
Immediately turning his gaze back, he beheld the celestial maidens like a grove of lotuses, fully adorned with all manner of exquisite forms and features.

Upon seeing them, his heart became attached; he no longer recalled even the slightest bit of his former merit, fell into a state of negligence, became enamored with the five desires, and experienced the tactile pleasures of the heavens.

Seeing the celestial maidens with their immeasurable and exquisite forms, his heart gave rise to attachment. Having wandered through beginningless transmigration, he was consumed by the fire of desire, just as a fierce fire burns down a forest of dry trees; so too was he consumed by the fire of desire.

The hosts of celestial maidens directed themselves toward the sons of the gods; from their mouths issued fragrances that pervaded their entire dwelling, and holding lotus flowers adorned with immeasurable ornaments, they approached the place where the sons of the gods were.
The sons of gods and daughters of gods enjoy immeasurable sensual pleasures together, experiencing the delights of the five desires.

Having thus contemplated heedlessness, the bhikṣu becomes weary of and detached from birth and death; feeling timidity toward the great place of terror that is the suffering of saṃsāra, he speaks these verses:
"When the phenomena of pleasure and pain first arise, One then forgets long-standing suffering and joy."
Just as at the break of dawn there is no longer the previous day,
how can those in the heavenly world enjoy celestial pleasures in the present?
Unaware that they must eventually fall away, all things ultimately return to extinction.
Like honey amidst thorny bushes, or like rice mixed with poison, so too are all pleasures;
one does not perceive the suffering of their decline.
Even when experiencing the most exquisite desires within the heavens, one never feels satiated.
The power of all desires within the heavens obscures the mind with great pleasure.
The fire of craving burns sentient beings; though they seek happiness, it cannot be found.
If one can become free from craving and desire, practicing with a single-minded focus, that is true happiness.
The person who is selfless and free from desire can reach the city of Nirvāṇa;
such a person is pure in the beginning and at the end, attaining a state of bliss from bliss.
If a person severs the fetters of craving, leaving nothing remaining in the mind, [they shall transcend all suffering].
Well-restraining the mind and intellect, one does not grasp at any phenomena.
Knowing what should and should not be done, that person always attains happiness;
if one can sever the river of craving, one shall escape the current of birth and death.
The courageous and resolute can cross over and will surely reach the city of Nirvāṇa;
for those possessed by craving there is no joy, because of the conjunction of the three poisons.
If one can be liberated from desire, this is called the bliss of purity.
"In this way, the bhikṣu observes how the fire of craving increases for the devas who engage in heedless conduct, and he gives rise to a heart of compassion.

At that time, those devas, surrounded by celestial maidens, go to the Fragrant Smoke Forest to sport; there they enjoy themselves with various sounds, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing. Some travel through the air like soaring birds, surrounded by celestial maidens; some ride upon swan-palaces, some ride upon swans, and some walk upon the ground. Many celestial maidens offer songs of praise and verses, while their bodies are entirely at ease and free from fatigue."

They went to the Forest of Incense Smoke and saw the various devas who had previously resided in that forest; they were filled with great joy, gathered together in harmony, and their sounds of laughter and play were supremely delightful.

Within the Forest of Incense Smoke, immeasurable sounds fill the air; there are flutes, pipes, lutes, and various kinds of drums and music. Celestial maidens, adorned with garments and necklaces, produce myriad exquisite sounds, songs, and laughter. The flowing waters of the rivers emit various tones, and birds of many precious colors display a diversity of forms and hues.

The various celestial songs, which bring delight to those who hear them, fill the entire grove; this forest abounds with celestial medicinal herbs, phoenixes, springs, ponds, flowers, and fruits, where they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses in these places of play.
Furthermore, surrounded by a retinue of celestial maidens, he proceeded to the Peak of Eloquence on Mount Sumeru, where that mountain was fully endowed with various lotus ponds and groves.

"In the midst of that mountain peak is the dwelling place of the Deva King Virūḍhaka, surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens. He observes the deeds of sentient beings—whether they accord with the Dharma or not—and considers how many sentient beings practice the path of the Dharma."
How many sentient beings practice what is contrary to the Dharma?
By performing what kind of karma do they benefit the world?
By performing what kind of karma do they fail to benefit the world?
By what means can the True Dharma be made to increase and unrighteousness be diminished?
How can the hosts of Māra’s armies be reduced, and how can the valiant asuras, the vexing nāgas, and others all be brought to decline?
Thus, on the path traveled by the sun, not far from the peak of the Mountain of Eloquence, the World-Protecting Heavenly King Virūḍhaka observed its radiance and thought:
"By practicing what dharma does this light exist that illuminates the world?"
He contemplated and observed the radiance of the sun’s course:

"If people in the world practice in accordance with the Dharma, protect the True Dharma, and flourish according to the Dharma, the sunlight will be pure, the seasons will proceed in harmony, the light will shine brightly, the five grains will ripen, and people will be free from disease.
If they practice what is not the Dharma, then the sun will lack radiance, the five grains will not reach maturity, and the people will suffer from illness."
Thus, all these superior fruits are obtained through the power of both the Dharma and non-Dharma; the radiance of the sun does not arise without causes and conditions.
Its brilliance is peerless, and as it moves along the side of Mount Sumeru, it is therefore called the Great Radiance (Mahāprabha).
When King Virūḍhaka had seen the sun, he surveyed the worlds.
Those hosts of devas were joyful and experiencing pleasure; seeing this great radiance moving among the mountain peaks with such majestic splendor, they rejoiced a hundredfold more.
After the Deva King Virūḍhaka had surveyed the world and seen that the celestial radiance and majestic virtue were even more exalted, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these verses:
"Three kinds of wholesome karma are performed, With three types and three causes for each;
In three times and three locations, There are three merits and three fruits."
Not stealing, constantly practicing generosity, and acting in accordance with the True Dharma,
being truly endowed with patience and goodness— one is born among all the devas.
Fully possessed of celestial adornments, one’s body is naturally graced by divine garlands.
Such pleasures in the heavens all arise from the cause of wholesome karma.
If sentient beings are heedless and do not practice wholesome karma,
such foolish people will not be born in the heavens.
Having performed wholesome deeds among humans, and having brought those human deeds to fulfillment,
by the retribution of such karma, one is born in this celestial realm.
If one loves one's own self and desires to experience the fruit of happiness, [one must practice virtue].
By creating the causes for great merit and virtue, one attains birth in the heavenly realms.
If, among the various heavens, one experiences superior, middling, or inferior pleasures—
these three kinds of pleasure arise from the causal conditions of merit and virtue.
"If a person performs various karmas, According to those karmas there is increase or decrease;
Thus, following those various karmas, One receives the retribution of joy among the gods.

At that time, after King Virūḍhaka had observed the assembly of devas and spoken these verses, he sported with the host of devas upon mountain peaks, in groves, by bathing pools, and in places of flowers and fruit, where various birds emitted wondrous sounds.

Many hosts of devas gazed upon the mountain valleys, their hearts filled with love and delight; they experienced the pleasures of the six senses, were greedy for the objects of the six realms, and indulged in heedless play amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.
In the places where they sport in lotus ponds, or by the rivers of the Vaiḍūrya forest where they wander and drink, they enjoy themselves amidst these adorned springs and pools.

This continues until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; then, their life in that heaven comes to an end, and according to their karma, they receive retribution by falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
If they are born among humans, they will possess wisdom and eloquence as teachers of the world, being trusted and accepted by others due to their residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the eighth station of the Vīṇā-devas is named Saṃcāra (Common Roaming).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that these sentient beings practice with faith, uphold the precepts, and practice giving; they attend Dharma assemblies to hear the teachings and assist in their organization, encouraging others with a profound and virtuous mind of sympathetic joy.
With pure faith, one should reflect in this way:
"This person possesses such merit;
I too am like this, and I shall cultivate merit."
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Shared Wanderings (*Sahamāna*). Because they rejoiced in the act of giving, their minds will find delight in immeasurable realms.

Within those groves, they will experience pleasure through various sounds and games; the four banks of the ponds are adorned with railings made of *vaiḍūrya* jewels, covered everywhere with golden flowers, and filled with various birds uttering wondrous songs, where they sport together with celestial maidens.
Within those groves, they sport and enjoy pleasures with various celestial maidens amidst the adornments of *kūṭaśila* birds and peacocks.
Their lotuses have stems of lapis lazuli, leaves of gold, and pericarps of diamond; therein they frolic.
In the beautiful groves where all manner of fruits abound, they drink exquisite flavors with the celestial maidens and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
Or they traverse the peaks of mountains where the ground is made of lapis lazuli and is perfectly level.
Or they roam among the rivers, springs, and flowing streams of Mount King, which are pure, stainless, cool, and refreshing; there they sport with various celestial maidens.
Or they roam by the fords and crossings, where pearls serve as sand spread upon the ground, and they sport within the clear waters.
There were some pavilions adorned with the seven treasures, lofty and vast;
some where musical instruments resounded as they sported and enjoyed pleasures with celestial maidens;
and some where wish-fulfilling trees were adorned with the exquisite sounds of jeweled bells.
In some groves, the six periods of the day are fully present, where they constantly enjoy happiness together with their kinsmen, friends, and hosts of celestial maidens.
In others, the ground is composed of the seven treasures; having ascended these mountains, they observe the other celestial hosts.
In this way, through various and incomparable manifestations produced by their own karma, they experience celestial bliss.

Thus, these devas delight in negligence and know no satiety; their eyes crave immeasurable varieties of exquisite forms without ever knowing satisfaction. It is likewise with their ears, noses, tongues, bodies, and minds as they greedily desire sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

Thus, these six sense faculties become stained with craving for the six objects; they do not know contentment, and as they encounter their respective objects, the heart of craving increases further, like fire fed by fuel. As they encounter more objects, craving grows boundlessly, shrouding the devas so that they do not recognize true happiness.

Experiencing such immeasurable celestial pleasures, they remain until their wholesome karma is exhausted; then, when their life in heaven ends, if they have no further wholesome karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they will gather together in one assembly; whether they enter the great ocean as merchants seeking wealth, or reside in the same city, or dwell in the same village in the mountains, or engage in the same occupation, or are mutual friends, or even become great kings, wealthy, and powerful—all this is due to the influence of their residual karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the ninth abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, called Upapāduka (Spontaneous Birth).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he knows:

this sentient being has given rise to a mind of great compassion; seeing another sentient being oppressed by famine, he plunges into deep water, intending to sacrifice his own life to rescue that drowning person, loving them as if they were his own child, and protecting them with a heart of compassion.

When this person’s life ends, they are reborn in the heavens. Approaching whichever celestial maiden the deva-son frequents, he is born by sudden transformation while sitting in the full-lotus posture within her embrace. At that time, the celestial parents immediately conceive the thought that they have given birth to a son; once the deva-son has been born, he likewise conceives the thought that they are his parents.
The parents' love for their child is just like that of the people of Jambudvīpa.
Likewise, in that celestial realm, they are born through transformation from their seats, and their love for him is even more intense; they say to the devaputra:
"You are the fruit of good karma, born of our transformation; we shall grant you all happiness."

I shall now take you to sport within all the gardens and groves, the various lotus ponds, and upon the mountain peaks; amidst streams and bathing pools covered by golden nets, where the branches of trees completely overspread the lotus ponds filled with golden lotuses adorned by swarms of bees; and there, by the pure flowing waters and the various delicious rivers for drinking, I shall freely sport and enjoy pleasure together with you.
The devaputra said, "I have now been born here and obtained this virtuous fruit; having been born to meet my parents, I shall now make offerings to them.

Then the celestial parents immediately led the devaputra to two Jambūnada forests, and together with various heavenly maidens, they went into that grove. There they saw the Jambūnada trees with their flowers and fruits flourishing luxuriantly, their fragrance wafting everywhere for five yojanas. Flowers of various wonderful colors—blue, red, yellow, and purple—and of various shapes and sizes—long, short, square, and round—were scattered everywhere. With these many flowers, they adorned themselves like the whorls of hair on a celestial being.
Then the celestial father and mother said to their son:
"In these two Jambūnada groves, the *saṃtuṣita* flowers are in full bloom; when the wind stirs the trees, their blossoms scatter everywhere among all the celestial hosts."
"You may now sport in this grove, enjoying yourself with the host of celestial maidens and wandering together.

Having spoken these words, he entered that grove together with the assembly of devas. There they saw a flock of celestial birds called "Life-Callers," who immediately praised the son of heaven with these verses:
"Welcome, O worthy one! Born from the performance of virtuous deeds, ... [you have come here]."
By upholding the sevenfold precepts, one now attains such a fruit as this.
The fruit of maintaining the precepts is peace and happiness; one receives this retribution among the devas.
The precepts are like a boat or raft, capable of crossing over the ford of birth and death.
If a person’s water of precepts is pure, bathing their courageous and steadfast mind,
they will naturally cleanse themselves with the flowers of Jāmbūnada gold among the gods.
Taking the observance of precepts as the seed, one cultivates various forms of ethical conduct.
Sporting within the heavens, you have now achieved your joy.
If a person tames their mind and is always adorned with precepts,
that person will attain a celestial realm and experience immeasurable happiness.
If a person performs wholesome deeds, they will proceed from happiness to a place of happiness,
sporting in celestial palaces because their observance of the precepts has increased.
By ascending the stairway of *śīla* (virtuous conduct), they increase their wisdom.
This person reaches the excellent paths, by virtue of wisdom and wholesome karma.
Therefore, always maintain the precepts, bestow the wealth of generosity and wisdom,
and constantly distance yourself from breaking the precepts, as one would avoid a blade, fire, or poison.
"Thus, well-guarded morality leads a person to the good realms;
if one is devoid of the observance of morality, there will be no place of peace and happiness.
In this way, the Bird of Life praised the deva with verses, causing his heart to rejoice.

Having heard this, the prince felt great joy in his heart; he immediately entered the forest with his father. That forest was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees, whose marvelous splendor was like that of the sun’s radiance. Countless hundreds of thousands of groves were harmoniously joined, and the forest was further adorned by flowing springs and bathing pools. Trees of lapis lazuli were embellished with pure gold, providing immeasurable delight.
When the newly born deva-son beholds these forest trees, he experiences great joy and wanders through that grove. There he sees the celestial maidens, who are not yet attached to anyone.

Seeing this deva-son wandering alone in the forest—his countenance upright and majestic—and finding no other celestial maiden, they all hasten toward him with quick steps, laughing, singing, dancing, and performing divine music.
At that time, having left his parents, that deva-son, overwhelmed by desire, went to the assembly of celestial maidens to enjoy themselves together, their joy being beyond compare.
There, they achieved the enjoyment of celestial music and song.

Amidst mountain peaks of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, and agate, there are gardens, groves, and bathing pools; their floors are strewn with pearls as sand, and they are adorned with celestial lotus ponds and various kinds of birds. There, together with celestial maidens, he wanders and sports in every direction, experiencing pleasure.
In each mountain, in each river, and at every flowing stream, he sports and enjoys pleasures with the celestial maidens.

Having observed such rare wonders, he revels and enjoys himself with the hosts of goddesses until his wholesome karma is exhausted. When his life as a deva ends, he wanders according to his karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
If born among humans, they may become a king or a high minister, beloved by all people and possessing handsome features, due to the remaining force of their past karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the abode of the Tūṇava-devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that among the Tūṇava-devas there is a tenth stage called Samyak-caryā (Right Conduct).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows through vision and hearing:

if there are sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds—such as seeing people who have been ruined or plundered by others and rescuing them so they may escape; or teaching people the right path in desolate wildernesses or perilous places; or ensuring the safety and peace of others in situations of doubt and fear; thus benefiting sentient beings and practicing the three types of wholesome action with purity of body, speech, and mind.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of Right Practice (*Samyak-caryā*).

Having been born in that heaven, their body is as radiant as the full moon; its brilliance shines forth, and their six sense faculties constantly experience the pleasures of the five desires. They always enjoy themselves, with immeasurable celestial maidens providing them with offerings.
Clad in celestial garments and adorned with heavenly garlands, they constantly sport and play in groves and flowery ponds.

They enter the crystal forest, where all the trees are made of crystal; it is universally adorned with radiating light, replete with flowers and fruits. The leaves possess a luster like mica, and the fruits are like bright mirrors, square in shape.

At that time, the deva-son entered the Vaiśravaṇa grove and saw hundreds of thousands of bodies, all of them exquisitely handsome, adorned with scented ointments, powdered incense, and flower garlands; he leaped for joy a hundredfold, thinking that none of the other hosts of devas were his equal.
Then Virūpākṣa entered that forest and surveyed the worlds.
By the power of the forest, within this grove, Virūpākṣa beheld the sky-walking yakṣas, the earth-walking yakṣas, and the phenomena of both dharma and adharma in Jambudvīpa.
He perceives the increase of the fruit;
at the crystal trees, seeing people practicing the Dharma, his mind is filled with joy;
seeing them practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, his mind is displeased.
Vaiśravaṇa, having perceived what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, spoke to Śakra:
"Among the yakṣas, I know whether the people of Jambudvīpa are virtuous or non-virtuous."
At that time, those devaputras enjoy the pleasures of the five senses within this grove; until their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If they are born among humans, by the power of their residual karma, they will be born into the family of a great elder with right view within the city of the Dharma, possessing great wealth and abundant riches.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, having observed the three *kinnara* heavens, observes the Four Great Kings’ Heavens, known as the *Cāra* (Moving) heavens. They dwell in palaces surrounding Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains;
what non-Buddhists call "the luminaries and the constellations."
To speak briefly, by what karma are three billion six hundred million sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
these sentient beings uphold the sevenfold precepts—the precepts of body and the precepts of speech:
The three kinds of bodily precepts and the four kinds of verbal precepts—by being born in those places, one attains these superior fruits.
Because sentient beings create the causes and conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, the signs of good and evil manifest.
The sun, moon, and constellations are called the "Moving Devas," which circumambulate Mount Sumeru;

the wind sustained by space is called the "Wind-wheel," which serves as the dominant condition to turn and sustain the sun, moon, and constellations as they circumambulate the King of Mountains, Sumeru.
In that celestial realm, there are two World-Protectors (Lokapālas):
the first is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
and the second is named Vaiśravaṇa.

These hosts of devas, together with the two Great Heavenly Kings, roam throughout the four continents; their palaces are made of various maṇi jewels in blue, yellow, red, and white, as previously described.

Together with the hosts of devas, they sport in mid-air, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses and delighting as they wish; yet, until their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If they obtain human birth, they will always delight in traveling through all lands; even when there is no specific cause or condition, they will constantly wander among various countries, sometimes experiencing peace and happiness and sometimes undergoing suffering and affliction, due to the force of residual habits and the power of residual precepts.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes that there is no other ground beyond the Four Great Kings, and he reflects thus:
'The heavens of the Four Great Kings are immeasurable and boundless.'"
Thus, they exhaustively observe the enjoyment of pleasures on all four sides of Mount Sumeru, circumambulating it to the right as they travel.
As the sun and moon travel and circumambulate Mount Sumeru, wherever they may be, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, casts a shadow; this is what people call "night."

To the north of Jambudvīpa is that which is called the Wind Circle (vāyu-maṇḍala), which sustains the northern stars so that they revolve without setting; this is because the Wind Circle supports them.

When various non-Buddhists see these morning stars—the seven stars of the Northern Dipper—constantly appearing without setting, they claim that these stars are able to sustain all the lands of the world.
They do not know it as it truly is; they do not understand that which is sustained by the power of the wind. Such is the limited knowledge possessed by these non-Buddhists.

A bhikṣu, however, contemplates the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings as they truly are: he becomes weary of and detached from birth and death; he sees the suffering of the gods' decline. Having contemplated this, he becomes weary of and detached from it, seeing that birth and death are impermanent, subject to total destruction, total fluctuation, and total separation, and that all is a treasury of karma where various karmas flow on.
Thus does a bhikṣu know and see through hearing.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates phenomena internally and practices in accordance with the Dharma.
All foolish worldlings are greedily attached to sensual pleasures; bound by craving, they practice the holy life desiring to be reborn in heaven and seeking to experience celestial bliss.
Thus, the bhikṣu develops a profound sense of weary detachment; he finds no pleasure in it, does not cling to it, does not cultivate it, and does not relish it.
Having contemplated all forms of pleasure, he perceives through the wisdom born of hearing:
that bhikṣu is able to contend with Māra, desires to cross the ocean of birth and death, and attains the seventeenth stage.

Having heard this, the Earth-dwelling yakṣas rejoiced and informed the space-dwelling devas; the space-dwelling yakṣas, having heard it, rejoiced and informed the Four Great Kings. Following the sequence previously described, it continued up to the Heaven of Immeasurable Light:

"In Jambudvīpa, in such-and-such a village, such-and-such a town, such-and-such a city, such-and-such a country, within such-and-such a clan, a certain son of good family named so-and-so has gone forth out of faith, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the dharma-robes; he battles with Māra, desiring to emerge from all states of existence."
Having heard this, the gods of the Immeasurable Light Heaven rejoiced and said to the other gods:
"The people of Jambudvīpa practice the True Dharma; I now rejoice in this."
This person has resolved their mind to transcend birth and death, engaging in battle with Māra by upholding the precepts and practicing correctly.
Desiring to wage war against Māra, they diminish his armies and increase the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Twenty-four and Scroll Twenty-five,
translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
2. The Heaven of the Thirty-three (25–35). Chapter Six, Part Four: Observing the Heavens. Regarding the Heaven of the Thirty-three, first:
Furthermore, a bhikṣu observes the observance of precepts; if one lacks the wisdom of observing the precepts, one cannot be born in heaven.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that those who uphold the precepts are born among the devas and experience celestial bliss.
Because they possess wisdom, when their lives end and they pass away, they do not fall into the evil realms.
By what kind of precepts and how many types of precepts is one born among the devas?
By what characteristics are they produced?
One sees that by means of seven kinds of precepts, one is born among the devas through transformation, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior:
By observing the precept against killing, one is reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings;
by not killing and not stealing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
by not killing, not stealing, and refraining from sexual misconduct, one is reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
By refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech; by refraining from divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, one is reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

By observing the worldly precepts and faithfully upholding the Buddha’s precepts—refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—one is reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; it is the same for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates how sentient beings, bound by the karma of their precepts, are reborn in the heavens.
"How does one uphold the precepts? Where is one born?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that these sentient beings,
having received the precept against killing, are born in the realm of the Four Great Kings, where their physical stature, complexion, strength, wealth, and lifespan are supreme.

If one receives the precepts against killing and stealing, one will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where one’s physical stature, complexion, strength, wealth, and lifespan become increasingly superior.

If one receives the precepts against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and cultivates them through close practice, one will be reborn in the Yāma Heaven, where one’s physical stature, complexion, strength, wealth, and lifespan become even more superior.
Because their faith and wisdom are superior, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where their physical stature, complexion, strength, wealth, and lifespan become increasingly superior.

By refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, they are reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, where their physical stature, complexion, strength, enjoyment of pleasure, wealth, and lifespan become even more superior than before.

By observing the precepts of not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct; and not speaking falsely, divisively, harshly, or frivolously, one is reborn among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), where one’s physical stature, complexion, strength, lifespan, wealth, and happiness surpass those of other heavens.
He is not one who is dispatched by the power of Māra Pāpīyān, nor does he dispatch Māra.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates how subtle causes lead to rebirth in the heavens.

He sees that the volitional mind is the superior cause of precepts; through superior, middling, or inferior precepts, one is born in the six heavens of the desire realm. Because the mind is superior and the karma is superior, one is born in the six heavens; because the mind is superior, the place of birth is also superior.
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates the precepts, how many kinds does he observe?
He sees that there are two kinds of precepts in the world:
first, those that arise spontaneously;"
Second, arising from another.
Regarding "arising from itself," it means the self-nature is able to maintain itself;
regarding "arising from another," it means it arises through combination.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts:
first, those for the laity;
second, those for the ordained.
The precepts for laypeople are the so-called five precepts;
the precepts for those who have left the household life are the observance of the *vimokṣa* (liberation) precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts: namely, the single-practice precepts and the non-single-practice precepts.
"One practice" refers to the single precept;
"non-one practice" refers to either receiving two precepts or observing three precepts.
Furthermore, there are two types:
The first is for a long duration;
the second is not for a long duration.
"For a long duration" means guarding the precepts for as long as one's life lasts.
"Before long" means according to what the mind requires and according to one's capacity to maintain the precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
the first is that which is defiled;
Second is stainlessness.
Those with stained precepts are reborn among the devas;
those with stainless precepts attain nirvana.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts:
first, worldly precepts;
second, world-transcending precepts.
Worldly precepts are subject to fluctuation, whereas supramundane precepts are without fluctuation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts: first, those for self-protection; [second, those for protecting others].
The second is protecting others.
To maintain the precepts oneself is called self-protection;
protecting others means causing others to abide in the worldly, defiled precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, cessation;
second, activity.
The "creator" accomplishes various conditioned formations and revolves within birth and death;
the "stiller" knows causes and conditions but does not advance in study.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is inclusion by wisdom;
the second is inclusion by giving.
Through the inclusion of giving, one observes the precepts and attains great wealth and happiness.
Precepts embraced by wisdom lead to the attainment of nirvana.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, internal practice; [second, external practice].
The second is external practice.
External practice consists of purifying the body;
internal practice consists of purifying the mind, speech, and intention.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, cultivation;
second, non-cultivation.
As for "cultivation," it refers to having practiced over immeasurable lifetimes;
as for "non-cultivation," it refers to observing the precepts for only a single lifetime.
In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates these and other such immeasurable pairs of precepts.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the subtle precepts: how many kinds of precepts are there?
When a bhikṣu contemplates the precepts, there are again three kinds:
first, the limited precepts;"
Second is the precept of many parts;
third is the precept of receiving them in their entirety.
The precept of few parts refers to upholding a single precept.
Those who observe many precepts may maintain two or three;
those who have fully received the precepts maintain all of them.
Furthermore, there are three types:
First is attachment;
second is non-attachment;
third is natural attachment.
One who practices out of attachment does so for the sake of wealth and profit;
one who practices out of aversion does so because of illness;
as for the natural [practice], it is pure conduct by its very nature, and this merit is superior.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of precepts:
first, the precepts of meditative practice;
second, the precepts without meditation.
Third is the avoidance of unwholesome precepts.
Regarding the precepts of meditative practice: one cultivates mundane dhyāna, even entering cities and villages while constantly practicing meditation;
non-meditative precepts refer to being separated from the precepts of meditative practice.

One who abandons immoral conduct does so out of fear of encountering manifold evils; they renounce it and do not engage in it, just as when a person, intoxicated by wine, commits unwholesome deeds, a wise person observes this and cuts off the wine, refusing to drink it.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of precepts:
first, deceitful precepts;
second, non-deceitful precepts.
Third is the precept of natural goodness.
Regarding the precept of crookedness and deceit: it is defiled and impure, yielding only meager rewards;
the precept free from crookedness and deceit yields great rewards.
Regarding the precepts of inherent goodness: if the mind is predominant, one attains a great fruit; if the mind is weak or inferior, the fruit is small.
Furthermore, there are three types:
first, those maintained through causes and conditions.
Second, upholding through non-conditions;
third, that which is not to be done according to the Dharma.
Upholding through conditions means that one guards and maintains the prohibitive precepts because of specific causes and conditions.
Regarding "not through causes and conditions," this refers to observing the precepts without a supporting condition;
regarding "that which should not be done," this refers to performing what is improper for one born into a noble family, because of the need to protect one's lineage.
Furthermore, as for observing the precepts by means of conditions, because it is for the sake of attaining Buddhahood and because the intention is superior, its fruit is great.
If one observes the precepts without a proper basis, the fruit will be small because one does not recognize the fruit;
if one performs what should not be done for the sake of seeking worldly fame, the fruit will likewise be small, resulting only in birth among human beings.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, those who fear their teacher;
second, those who do not fear their teacher.
Third, fearing the evil realms and fearing the preceptor’s observance of the precepts is called inferior observance of the precepts;
not fearing the preceptor’s observance of the precepts is called middling observance of the precepts.
If one observes the precepts out of fear of the evil realms, it is called the superior upholding of the precepts.
Furthermore, there are three types:
first, upholding the precepts oneself without teaching others;
Second, practicing it oneself and teaching others;
third, practicing equanimity toward others.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
First, those with deficient precepts;
second, those with non-deficient precepts;
third, those whose precepts are entirely deficient.
Regarding "deficient precepts": one who initially maintains the precepts well but later breaks them is said to have deficient precepts. Regarding "non-deficient precepts":
one who consistently maintains the precepts well from the beginning through the middle to the end is said to have non-deficient precepts.
Regarding "all-deficient precepts": one who associates with various heterodox teachers to receive their fasting precepts, yet holds wrong views and takes life, is said to have all-deficient precepts.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates four kinds of precepts. What are the four?
They are the abstention from the four faults of speech: [lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter]."
First, false speech;
second, divisive speech; third, harsh speech;
and fourth, frivolous speech.
The fourth is frivolous speech.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of precepts that restrain one from five objects; these are called the five.
Moreover, there are six causes and conditions for maintaining the prohibitive precepts:
First, the fear of others seeking an opportunity to harm;
second, the fear of punishment and execution;
third, the fear of dread.
Fourth is causal conditions;
fifth is non-contemplation;
sixth is intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of precepts: namely, the three precepts of body and the four precepts of speech.
A bhikṣu contemplates these immeasurable observances of the precepts in this way: sentient beings fear the evil realms, yet by observing the precepts they can cross over them.
Thus, the upholding of ethical discipline is briefly explained as being of two kinds:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
“Thus, having observed the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the bhikṣu observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and observes their karmic actions.
By what karma are they born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?”
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees the abodes where the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three dwell. What are these thirty-three?
The first is named the gods who dwell in the Sudharma Hall.
The second is named the Heaven of Dwelling on Peaks;
the third is named the Heaven of Dwelling on Mountain Summits;
and the fourth is named the Heaven of the City of Sudarśana.
Fifth is named the Bhauma-devas;
sixth is named the Cāturmahārājakāyika-devas (the "Cāturmahārāja" being the name of a mountain);
seventh is named the Vaijayanta-devas.
The eighth is named the Heaven of Dwelling in the Nandana Garden;
the ninth is named the Heaven of Radiant Light;
the tenth is named the Heaven of the Pāriyātra Tree Garden.
Eleventh is named the Heaven of the Precipitous Shore;
twelfth is named the Heaven Dwelling on the Mixed Precipitous Shore;
thirteenth is named the Heaven Dwelling in the Maṇi Treasury.
Fourteenth is the deity named Revolving Path;
fifteenth is the deity named Golden Palace;
sixteenth is the deity named Place of Garland Reflections.
Seventeenth is the deity named Dwelling on the Ground of Flexibility;
eighteenth is the deity named Variegated Adornment;
nineteenth is the deity named Ground of Sovereign Will.
The twentieth is named the Heaven of Subtle Conduct;
the twenty-first is named the Heaven of Joyful Delight in Song;
the twenty-second is named the Heaven of Majestic Power and the Wheel.
The twenty-third is named the Candra-gati Heaven;
the twenty-fourth is named the Yama-sāla Heaven;
the twenty-fifth is named the Śīghra-gati Heaven.
The twenty-sixth is named Chāyāprabhāsa Heaven;
the twenty-seventh is named Prajñācaryā Heaven;
the twenty-eighth is named Bahudhātuka Heaven.
The twenty-ninth is named Cakravāḍa Heaven;
the thirtieth is named Ūrdhvasrotas Heaven;
the thirty-first is named Tejorāśimukha Heaven.
The thirty-second is named the Heaven of the Wheel of Majestic Radiance;
the thirty-third is named the Pure Heaven.

"In this way, monks, one contemplates the subtle karmic retributions of the Thirty-three Heavens: by what kind of accumulated karma of virtuous conduct and precept-keeping is one born into these auspicious realms?"
Through the causal conditions of wholesome karma, one obtains the retribution of wholesome fruits and is born in a place of pleasant retribution.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, they hear the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, which is not the dharma of non-Buddhists.

He saw that the places where those devas are born are beyond description in their playful enjoyment of bliss; they are protected by Śakra, King of Devas, and dwell in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
The non-Buddhists claim that it is eternal and indestructible.
First, one contemplates wholesome dharmas; next, one analytically contemplates which precepts should be well-cultivated to give rise to the Hall of Wholesome Dharmas.
He sees, hears, and knows this:

If a person upholds the sevenfold precepts—precepts that are unbroken, unperforated, and without fissures; precepts held with firmness beyond reproach—and cultivates the mind through generosity, giving at the proper time to the field of merit;

whether to an Arhat, a caregiver for the sick, one's parents, an Anāgāmin, a Sakṛdāgāmin, a Srotāpanna, one who has emerged from the meditative attainment of cessation, or a practitioner on the path; bestowing gifts with a heart of compassion and joy; and granting life to those who are terrified.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) as Śakradevendra, of the Kauśika clan, named Lord of the Gods (Devendra).
He will have ninety-nine nayutas of celestial maidens as his retinue, who will reverently surround and make offerings to Śakra, just as a single woman serves her husband.
The various celestial maidens were free from jealousy; they made offerings to the Queen of Heaven and served Śakra together, likewise without any envious hearts.

That Hall of Good Dharma was five hundred yojanas wide, with railings made of *vaiḍūrya* beads, pillars of coral, and adorned with crystal, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha*. Its walls were made of Jambūnada gold, appearing like the color of molten gold.
Their seats were all adorned with vajra-maṇis, red lotus gems, blue pearls, and jade jewels.
The various lotuses had filaments of vajra and stalks of pure gold, and they were further adorned by clear, pure flower ponds.
Furthermore, there were various birds with wings of vaidūrya, beaks made of red lotus gems, and bodies of blue indranīla jewels, filling the entire pond.
The four banks of that pond are adorned with blue maṇi flowers, and maṇi jewels are spread upon the ground.
Furthermore, there are various birds filling the pond, having feet made of blue indranīla gems, beaks of musāragalva, and eyes of coral.
Furthermore, there were many birds in that pond, their bodies complete and entirely like Jāmbūnada gold, with wings made of coral and eyes made of Indra-ratna gems.
There are further bathing pools adorned with swarms of bees; these bees, in color and form like lapis lazuli, adorn the bathing pools.
Within that Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), there are ten great flower ponds.
What are the ten? First is the Lotus Pond named Nanda;
