second is the Lotus Pond named Mahānanda.
The third is named Lotus Pond of Joy;
the fourth is named Lotus Pond of Great Joy;
the fifth is named Lotus Pond of Playful Sport.
The sixth is named the Lotus Pond of Right Mindfulness;
the seventh is named the Lotus Pond of All Meanings;
the eighth is named the Lotus Pond of Right Discernment.
The ninth is named the Lotus Pond of the Wish-Fulfilling Tree;
the tenth is named the Lotus Pond of Great Radiance, Sovereign in the Indra-Avabhāsa Abode.
These are the ten great lotus ponds that adorn the Sudharmā Hall of the gods.
Furthermore, there are other lotus groves and ponds where the flowers are pure, with stems of white silver, filaments of genuine gold, leaves of lapis lazuli, and calyxes of diamond.

Furthermore, there are lotuses with stems of diamond and leaves of variegated colors; each individual leaf is like a flower of red jewel, like *vaiḍūrya*, like *musāragalva*, or like gold. There are such multicolored lotus petals, some with a hundred petals, some with two hundred, and even up to a thousand; these various colored flowers, each distinct from the others, serve as adornments.
In the Sudharmā Hall of Śakra, the King of Devas, there are many birds within the lotuses—namely, the *nityakāma* birds, the *sarvacaryā* birds, and the *nityasvara* birds.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, enters the lotus pond with the celestial maidens to enjoy themselves and play, the birds likewise frolic;
when the devas perform music, the birds likewise utter their songs.

Furthermore, there are various birds named *Kāmacchanda* (Desire-Indulgence); when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wanders among the lotus ponds, these birds also sport about, appearing like celestial maidens.

There are also various birds named *Vicāraṇa* (Wandering); on the banks of the lotus ponds, they hold lotus filaments in their beaks and dance and frolic everywhere along the shores, producing exquisite sounds.
The Deva King Śakra possesses such superior lotus ponds as these.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu contemplates what has been manifested by the virtuous karma of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. He sees:

In the lotus ponds, there are fish made of pure gold, or silver fish, or *vaiḍūrya* fish; their wings are made of red lotus jewels, and their eyes are made of *musāragalva*. When they are angry, they resemble red lotuses; their scales are composed of various miscellaneous jewels, or they have wings of the seven treasures, as they sport and enjoy themselves in the lotus ponds.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu again contemplates Śakra’s lotus grove pond.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes what constitutes the ground of that lotus pond.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees it thus:"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, covered that ground with pearls as its sand, or with silver sand, or with golden sand, or with *vaiḍūrya* as its sand.
Thus he sees all these various multicolored adornments distinctly,
all produced by the virtuous karma of Śakra, King of the Devas.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu thus analyzes and observes the regions of the earth.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees that the grove of those *pāṇḍuraka* lotuses is surrounded on all sides by railings made of pure gold, or railings made of *vaiḍūrya*, or railings made of white silver; it is covered above by nets of pure gold, and various kinds of birds emit wondrous sounds as they sport by the edge of the pond.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the lotus ponds within the Hall of Good Dharma (*Saddharmakūṭa*). In those lotus ponds, various bees of diverse colors produce wondrous sounds: upon golden flowers are silver-colored bees with wings of diamond (*vajra*), their bodies supple;
upon silver-colored lotuses are gold-colored bees.
In this way, various kinds of bees sport within it.
Thus, these wholesome karmas bring about various fruits and rewards.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu contemplates the Hall of Wholesome Dharmas (Saddharmakūṭāgāra).
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he observes the Śakrā devendra in the Forest of Good Dharma (Saddharmavana). How many kinds of groves are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees all the groves belonging to the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), examining each one of the various gods of the Heaven of Good Dharma.
Śakra, King of Devas, together with the celestial maidens, plays and enjoys pleasures in which forest, and amuses himself with the five desires?
He sees: there is a forest named "Play of the Celestial Maidens," where the trees of heaven are fully endowed with flowers and fruits, and which is filled with various birds.
The trees are named "Wish-Fulfilling" (*kalpavṛkṣa*); whatever the gods desire, it all arises from the forest.

When the hosts of gods sport within the grove, exquisite flowers bloom; when the celestial maidens enter the forest and draw near to these trees, the flowers immediately droop downward and present themselves to the goddesses.
When the celestial maidens have taken the flowers, the branches and twigs rise back up.
Thus, these various flowers differ in color, fragrance, and appearance; they arise according to their thoughts, and for this reason they are called "Mind-Trees" (Manojña-vṛkṣa).

If one thinks of music, it is likewise so: hearing various sounds according to what the mind contemplates, the wind of wholesome karma blows upon the leaves of the trees, causing them to rub against one another; their sound is exquisite and beautiful like the music of the devas, and for this reason they are called "Mind-Trees" (Manojña-vṛkṣa).

Furthermore, there are immeasurable *manas-kāma* trees; according to whatever the celestial maidens desire in their minds, ornaments, divine garments, and celestial flowers are all obtained upon mere thought. Therefore, they are called "mind-trees" (*manas-vṛkṣa*).
Furthermore, there are wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) the color of lapis lazuli, with stems and leaves of pure gold, branches of white silver and leaves of lapis lazuli;
or branches of coral with leaves of the seven treasures, which distill delicious flavors.

Furthermore, there are wish-fulfilling trees; if the celestial maidens desire to see Śakra, by virtue of their wholesome karma, they immediately behold a manifested Śakra within this grove and enjoy themselves with him.

Such are the merits of this grove that one beholds a manifested Śakra; likewise, within this forest, ninety-nine nayutas of celestial maidens each perceive themselves enjoying pleasure with him alone, without seeing any other maiden meeting with the Lord of Devas.

According to the mental inclinations of the celestial maidens for adornment, they behold the body of Śakra; because it appears exactly as they have thought of it, it is called the "Tree of the Mind" (*manoratha-vṛkṣa*).
Thus, amidst the immeasurable sensual delights within this grove, they sport in succession until they reach Mount Nandana.

That mountain was magnificent, composed of the seven treasures, adorned with rocky crags of vajra-body, and completely covered by branches of pure gold trees like a palace; it was adorned with deer made of gold, silver, and blue pearls, and many birds there emitted wondrous sounds.
On that mountain there is a hall named Victorious Superior (Jinshang); the hall has a thousand pillars, all of which are fashioned from gold, lapis lazuli, and blue maṇi jewels.

The adamantine floor was inlaid with jewels, and hundreds of thousands of celestial palaces appeared as if colored red; they were magnificent and extraordinary, with lion thrones covered in soft furnishings.
Within the halls were a thousand couches, adorned with *vaiḍūrya* gems.

"When King Śakra defeats the army of the asuras and achieves victory, all the celestial hosts are filled with joy and praise Śakra. Together with the celestial maidens, they ascend this palace to play, sing, dance, and enjoy themselves, each experiencing superior, middling, or inferior pleasures according to their own past karma."
Having finished their play, they enter the mountains again to frolic and enjoy themselves, their minds single-mindedly intent on desire. Why is this?
Because women have much desire, and since celestial desires are superior, those celestial desires burn intensely.

They proceeded further to another river; within that river, food and drink of supreme flavor flowed along with the current, and it was filled with various colors, fragrances, and drinks of the finest taste. If anyone drank from it, they were freed from intoxication and confusion.
There is a beverage named "Joy," which when drunk by the celestial maidens, fills their hearts with great delight.

There is another exquisite drink called "Able to Behold"; once they have drunk it, they are able to survey everywhere all the gardens and the immeasurable mountain ranges within the heavens, seeing them all clearly.
There is also a celestial drink called "All Tastes" (Saṃbhāra-rasa), which is exceedingly abundant; by drinking it, their physical color and strength increase a hundredfold.

After the celestial maidens have drunk, they enter the grounds of food, where they receive such retribution according to the superior, middling, or inferior karma they themselves have created, fully endowed with various colors, fragrances, and exquisite flavors.

Having finished eating and drinking, they proceed again to the realm of music to sport among the mountains. There, *vaiḍūrya* jewels serve as musical instruments, with strings of pure gold and the resonance of drums made of various gems. Flutes and pipes are crafted from agate and assorted precious stones, while the hosts of celestial maidens produce immeasurable sounds. Thus, there are infinite and countless musical performances, including the melodies of the *gandharvas*.

The hosts of celestial maidens were adorned all over their bodies; with various instruments of pleasure, they sported and enjoyed themselves, delighting in song and music whose tones were harmonious and elegant, with melodies perfectly balanced and complete in every respect.
To increase their sensual pleasure, having already produced songs, they further proceeded to the land of the tinkling bells.

In that land, the network of bells was stirred by a gentle breeze, producing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite sounds; hearing them, they rejoiced, dancing, singing, and laughing, their bodies adorned with various kinds of wonderful jewels.

They further proceeded to the Lotus Pond Adorned with Various Birds. That pond was adorned with various birds made of gold, silver, and diverse jewels; celestial maidens entered therein to sport and enjoy themselves, each taking golden lotuses to play together and scattering them at one another, their hearts free from jealousy. They engaged in various diversions, the sounds of which were exquisite and beautiful.
There is water of eight virtues within which they sport.
Having sported therein, because their desire increases, and because their own lust is difficult to satisfy, they are consumed by craving for sensual pleasures and know no contentment.

Again, they go to the forest of mirror trees; within this forest, they see their own bodies adorned with various ornaments and endowed with all merits. Seeing various forms within the various mirrors, they become ten times more dissolute.
Why is this? The nature of women involves three kinds of negligence.
What are these three?
First, giving rise to negligence by relying on one's own physical appearance;
second, giving rise to negligence by relying on one's status as a man;
third, giving rise to negligence through arrogance.
Beholding her own physical form, she looked down upon other women.
Leaving that place, she proceeded further to a grove named Sarvakāla (Always Present).
That grove possesses six distinct periods within a single day; these periods flow on without interruption like a revolving wheel, adorning the forest with their sixfold temporal beauty.

The various birds in the forest are of immeasurable and diverse colors; corresponding to the specific seasons within that forest, they roam together in the woods, free from envy and their hearts filled with joy.
Having seen this grove, according to their inclinations, they enter the Grove of Six Seasons (*ṣaḍṛtuvana*) and enjoy delights as they play at will according to the seasons.

Various seasonal birds gather there spontaneously to frolic, and they amuse themselves with celestial maidens; within this grove, they experience the pleasures of the five senses, no longer thinking of other groves.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arrived at this grove, the celestial maidens joyfully danced, sang, and laughed as they made offerings to Śakra.
Thus, within this single grove, Śakra was endowed with every kind of merit.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the second grove of Śakra, Lord of the Devas: how many kinds of forests are there, and what are their names?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
What are the meritorious qualities of the grove of Śakra named Sarvakrīḍā? He perceives,
hears, and knows them as follows:

The very essence of that grove is named "All-Groves. Within this grove, there are many devaputras who sport and enjoy themselves together with celestial maidens; hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens follow their every thought as they play.

In the pleasure grounds there were eighty-four thousand walking palaces, with wheels made of lapis lazuli, networks of bells made of Jambūnada gold, and canopies of silver lattices covering them above, all adorned with the seven precious gems.

Some of the first sons of the gods rode horses, some rode geese, some traveled through the air, and some moved upon the ground; some played musical instruments while others sang songs as they surrounded Śakra and proceeded toward the place of recreation.
There were eighty-four thousand noble elephants, their bodies covered with golden nets and adorned with precious bells; soft silk cushions were spread upon the backs of the elephants.
Whenever an elephant thought of desire, its temples would swell and open, and fragrant ichor would flow forth.
The foremost and most excellent celestial being, riding this dragon-elephant, gazed up at Śakra while surrounded by his attendants as they proceeded to the place of recreation.

Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, adorned in various ways, gazed up at Śakra; some sang, some danced, some played celestial music, and they engaged in various diversions as they proceeded to the place of recreation.
Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens performed various musical performances, playing, dancing, and singing to entertain Śakra; adorned in diverse ornaments, they gazed up at him.

The Lady Śacī, riding in a celestial palace adorned with a thousand-spoked wheel and the seven treasures—namely, genuine gold, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, sapphire, and great blue gem—is magnificently embellished.

It was drawn by hundreds of thousands of geese, whose bodies were made of Jāmbūnada gold, their feet of coral, their eyes of red jewels, and their bodies of red lotus gems; their beaks were of coral and their wings of pearls, as they drew that palace.

Following the thought of Śakra, wherever he intended to go, Śakra would take his seat, his body adorned with various jewels. His majestic radiance surpassed the simultaneous illumination of a hundred suns; together with his consort Śacī, he proceeded to the pleasure groves. His splendor and adornment exceeded that of all other celestial maidens by a full hundredfold, and he sat sharing a seat with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, as they went to the pleasure groves.
Thus these gods experience the pleasures of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, just as the gods of the Thirty-three [Heavens] proceed toward the Forest of All Pleasures (*Sarvārthasiddha*).
Surrounded by the entire host of devas, they attend upon Śakra and Śacī, experiencing hundreds of thousands of kinds of immeasurable pleasure as previously described.

In the Hall of the Dragon-Elephants, the great ministers and attendants provide entertainment for Śakra with the sounds of song and music; he then proceeds to sport and enjoy himself in the Forest of All Pleasures.

As he approaches that forest, the celestial maidens already dwelling there hear the sound of the heavenly music; holding lotus flowers in their hands, they perform various musical performances to go out and welcome Śakra.
Śakra, seeing this, addressed the assembly of devas:
"These celestial maidens are adorned with various kinds of jewels within all these groves, and they possess every variety of musical sound."
"I shall now sport with him in the forest.
When the assembly of devas heard Śakra’s words, they said to him:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"These celestial maidens are the attendants of the king; they always return to the king and take the king as their master.
Śakra replied: "These celestial maidens are not my servants; they do not return to me, nor are they the result of my karmic power."

By the power of their own karma, they receive bodies according to their own karma; as their karma varies as superior, middling, or inferior, so too do these celestial maidens vary as superior, middling, or inferior—it is not by my power.
At that time, Śakra spoke in verse:
"From inferior karma one receives an inferior retribution, fulfilling the path of sentient beings;
from middling karma one receives a middling retribution; and from superior karma, the body of a great man."
Whatever deeds a person performs, they receive the retribution according to those deeds;
that person experiences the results of their actions within this very body, regardless of time or place.
Even if one were a celestial being with a wheel of radiant light, enjoying various delights in play, [the consequences of karma would still follow].
This person attains a wholesome fruit because of their pure and superior karma.
Whatever actions a man performs, whether wholesome or unwholesome,
when he experiences their retribution, he will either suffer or enjoy happiness.
"These various rewards of pleasure, these manifold celestial diversions—these are not caused by me;
they are obtained through the power of their former karma.

When the host of devas heard this verse spoken by Śakra, Lord of Devas, they all felt sympathetic joy, joined their palms and received it upon their heads, and headed toward the Forest of All Pleasures, desiring to sport together.
There were hundreds or thousands of celestial maidens, each holding lotus flowers and adorned with various ornaments.

The physical forms and features of every single maiden were indistinguishable from one another, and their songs were likewise identical—all brought forth by the transformation of their virtuous karma.
Beholding Śakra’s dance, they proceeded toward the Forest of Play (*Kūṭāgāra-vana*).
In that forest, the jewel-trees had leaves of white silver and the ground was of white silver; it was filled with flocks of silver-colored birds that emitted various sounds.

With Śakra at their head, the hosts of devas entered in succession; various jewel-lights, whether from their bodies or the ground, spiraled through the entirety of space. Having seen this, Śakra was filled with great joy.
The voices of the celestial maidens sang with the notes of *gong* and *shang* perfectly harmonized, like the sounds of divine music.
Eighty-four thousand processional palaces were drawn by dragons and elephants; adorned with nets of bells, they emitted a multitude of wondrous sounds.
Immeasurable sons of gods and ninety-nine billion goddesses praised Śakra and enjoyed the pleasures of the six desire realms.

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with those goddesses, proceeded once more to the Forest of All Pleasures (*Sarvaratavāna*), riding upon the Great Dragon Palace (*mahānāgaprāsāda*), as previously described.

The Lord Śakra and the other hosts of devas then entered a grove of golden trees; its golden leaves and golden fruits were five *puruṣa* in height, their flavor was sweet and delicious, and they were endowed with every fragrance; eating them increased their desire.
When the nāga-elephants eat this, they become intoxicated with desire and move about; hearing the sounds of various musical instruments, they dance and play for their own amusement.
When the devas see them, they give rise to a sense of wonder, for their dancing and play are so lovely.
Having finished eating, they dance and play; amidst the various bird calls in this forest, silver-colored birds dwell within the golden groves, appearing most exquisite and majestic.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with his consort Śacī, the hosts of devas, and the devaputras and apsaras, sport and enjoy themselves. The other devaputras likewise entertain one another with song, dance, and laughter alongside their own apsaras; because of their virtuous karma, they harbor no jealousy.

He went again to the Golden Forest (*Suvarṇavana*). In that forest was a pond named Cool and Refreshing (*Sītā*), where golden lotuses and lapis lazuli flowers gathered in various profusions. Surrounding Śakra’s Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), he enjoyed himself with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and for a long time performed various musical performances on the banks of the lotus pond together with the host of celestial maidens (*apsaras*).

Together with the assembly of all devas in the Hall of Good Dharma, they further enter the Forest of All Pleasures. In that forest, every tree is made of lapis lazuli, fully laden with golden fruit; it is filled with exquisite flavors like those of the *panasa* fruit, possessing perfect color, fragrance, and taste.

When the devas take the fruit, they open it and drink from it; its flavor surpasses the supreme flavors among humans, such as madhu liquor. Yet when the devas drink it, they do not become intoxicated or deranged.
Devas experience pleasure through three kinds of negligence:
first, celestial maidens;
second, eating fruits.
Third are the five desires.
These are the three ways of experiencing the pleasure of negligence.
For example, the flavor of the celestial food *sudhā* consumed by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is accomplished through one's own karma.

Surrounded and venerated by all the hosts of devas, they sport and enjoy themselves in every direction within the Vaiḍūrya groves; various birds and swarms of bees abound there, and the area is covered with nets of bells.
Having finished their play, they returned with the celestial hosts to the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā). There was a third grove there called Anupama (Incomparable).

The Heavenly King Śakra had five hundred sons, who were surrounded by celestial maidens as they played within it; that garden was vast and expansive, and the pleasures enjoyed therein were second only to those of Śakra himself.
Always acting in accordance with the Dharma, they possess right view and are free from deviance;
by virtue of this right view, they triumph over the asuras in times of battle.
If a person makes offerings to their parents, respects śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and follows them without contention, [they shall likewise be victorious].
He thought to himself:
"I shall now take these celestial maidens and go to the Incomparable Grove.
Each son of the gods had a *nayuta* of celestial maidens as his retinue; they were endowed with exquisite beauty and, all with one mind, sported and enjoyed themselves.
Then the sons of the gods went to the abode of Śakra and said to him:
"O Heavenly King!
We now wish to go to the Anupama Grove to sport and enjoy ourselves; we pray that you will come with us to that forest."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the devaputra, saying:
"I have already indulged in play; now I wish to follow the Dharma for my own benefit. Pleasure arises from desire, yet it can never be satisfied."
"I now renounce pleasure, fearing the fault of negligence; negligence is a poison, and for this reason I abandon it.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke in verse:
"Negligence is not death; negligence is the place of death.
Heedfulness is immortality; heedlessness is constant birth and death.
Heedfulness is immortality; heedlessness is the path of death.
Through heedfulness, I have now attained supremacy among the gods.
I now place my faith in the Tathāgata; you should practice the Dharma.
Regarding the Buddha’s teachings, I dare not commit any transgression.
If one violates the words of the Tathāgata, such a person is driven by greed and delusion.
"One shall not escape from the multitude of sufferings, but shall constantly experience all manner of decline and affliction.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these words, he entered the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).

At that time, Śakra’s sons and the various devaputras were filled with great joy; together they went to their own palace, which was adorned with gold and jewels, where they sang, praised, and enjoyed themselves.
Returning to their respective dwellings, they beat drums to summon one another, desiring to go to the groves to sport and enjoy pleasures.
At that time, seventy thousand devaputras each mounted precious palaces, some riding celestial birds, traveling through the air surrounded by hosts of goddesses.
Some wandered amidst lotus ponds, playing celestial music, singing, dancing, and laughing as they proceeded toward the Incomparable Grove (*Anupama-vana*).

At that time, the sons of Śakra were adorned with celestial garlands and rained down sandalwood incense; their radiance was brilliant like the light of the sun, while others possessed splendor like the full moon or the stars. According to their respective karmic actions, they headed toward the Incomparable Grove, each filled with longing and attachment, their minds uninterrupted.
Entering that grove, they experience celestial bliss; the majesty of that forest is beyond description.
Upon entering it, the fragrance is peerless: even sixteen parts of the scent of ox-head sandalwood do not equal one part of it. Having smelled this fragrance, they conceive a sense of wonder.
They enter again into the Forest of Drinks, entering the groves in succession for the sake of seeking pleasure.

Due to their virtuous karma, there are hundreds of various trees made of beryl, gold, silver, and crystal; they possess manifold colors like variegated silks. These trees, adorned with such marvelous colors, likewise manifest immeasurable hues and forms.

When the devaputra saw them—as if looking into countless hundreds of thousands of pure, bright mirrors—he gazed about in all directions and gave rise to great joy; surrounded by celestial maidens and hearing the sounds of various music, his heart was filled with profound delight.

Furthermore, they sported and enjoyed themselves in another place. The various birds in that grove had wings of pure gold, chests of lapis lazuli, feet of coral, backs of white silver, and eyes of red precious gems; they emitted a multitude of wondrous sounds.
Furthermore, there were sons of gods who, hearing this wondrous sound, said to one another:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
The voices of these birds, with their immeasurable melodies and tunes, cannot be distinguished from the voices of the goddesses."
Having heard the birds' cries, he again went to another grove to frolic and enjoy himself.
There he saw thousand-petaled lotuses in various ponds, their radiance like that of the sun.

Arriving at those pools, which were adorned with various ornaments as previously described, he was surrounded by celestial maidens; they sang, danced, laughed, and played together, enjoying themselves in delight.

Again, accompanied by celestial maidens, he went to another forest. In this forest were rivers, springs, and flowing streams; within those rivers were various kinds of water, namely flowing milk and flowing drinks—sweet and delicious waters—which the deva-sons drank.
There were many hundreds of swarms of bees and birds, and gold, silver, coral, and various colored precious gems gathered within the river.
There, the devas and devīs sported and delighted themselves in this grove, and for a long time they experienced the pleasures of the five senses.

He then proceeded to the grove of flowering trees; there, the many flowers were entirely free from withering or change, and their fragrance wafted everywhere, filling ten yojanas. These were the Moonlight Flower, the Moon-Colored Flower, the White Flower, and the Star-Colored Flower, which was cool and free from heat.

He proceeded further to a grove of fruit trees; that grove contained fruits such as those from the *madhūka* tree, those with pungent flavors, those that were soft and tender, and those from the *gandhamālya* tree, the mere scent of which brought satiety.

The fruits of the trees possess six flavors, like fruits that accord with one's desires and fruits that bring no satiety; such fruits as these are fully present within this incomparable grove, produced by virtuous karma.
In this grove, they sport and enjoy themselves, partaking of food and drink.
They then proceed to the Grove of Bird-Dancing, where the various birds frolic, sing, and dance, emitting exquisite sounds; hearing these, the devaputras immediately experience great bliss.

He then proceeded to the Grove of Multicolored Trees (Miśrakāvana). The colors of that grove were extraordinary; all its flowers and fruits were as previously described, and its rivers, ponds, and various birds were likewise so. For this reason, it is called the Grove of Multicolored Trees.
In this grove, they delight themselves with the five desires and enjoy long-lasting happiness through the music of the gandharvas.
King Śakra, the Lord of Devas, reflects thus:
"Where are my sons enjoying the pleasures of negligence, unaware that their merit is waning?"

At that time, the sons of the gods, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, went to where Śakra was; the celestial maidens, for their part, each returned to their own palaces to sport and enjoy themselves.
At that time, Śakra, seeing the sons of the gods, spoke these verses:
“Desiring all sensory objects, the heart of craving is difficult to satisfy;
One who is free from craving knows contentment—such a person has no grief or affliction.”
If a person craves the objects of desire, they shall find no peace;
for such objects are like poison, leading to suffering in future lives.
Whether in the beginning, middle, or end, whether in the present or the future, [they remain thus].
Seeking happiness, it cannot be found; later, one suffers affliction.
Throughout all the worlds, birth and death increase;
one wanders in transmigration without a moment’s pause. Where there is union, there must be separation.
There has never been anyone who escaped;
by immeasurable deceptions and delusions, sentient beings are deceived by ignorance and sport within craving and desire.
There is never satiety; the objects of the senses are difficult to satisfy, like adding dry fuel to a fire.
Difficult to fill is likewise the human condition, even as one draws near the ground of death.
Yet they still do not feel weary or detached,
nor do they seek the provisions for virtue; when they fall from the heavens, lacking self-mastery,
they are deceived and deluded by craving.
I now instruct and rebuke you:
you are deluded by desire; you should act for your own benefit.
The Dharma is the supreme path; if there are those who practice the Dharma, [they shall attain liberation].
From happiness one obtains a happy retribution; one who can practice in this way attains the quiescence of nirvana.
Seeking the bliss of nirvana, if there are those who constantly cultivate merit,
They shall attain the state of inexhaustibility.
Having heard Śakra’s discourse, the devas became tranquil and their minds grew supple.
At that time, the sons of Śakra were subdued and complied with their father’s instruction.
"Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, instructed and admonished his sons to follow the right path and cultivate wholesome deeds, thereby closing the gates to the evil realms.
They then proceeded to the Grove of Mixed Delights (*Miśrakāvana*) to sport and enjoy pleasures born of all manner of virtues."

The Heavenly King Śakra possesses five hundred palaces, adorned with various kinds of jewels: crystal, coral, gold, silver, the celestial sapphire king, the celestial great sapphire, and many other such precious gems.
Śakra, King of the Gods, beheld various groves where the petals of the lotuses were like the newly risen sun, serving as a magnificent adornment.
Having seen this, Śakra spoke in verse:
"The meritorious deeds performed among humans, In infinite varieties among humans..."
By performing various meritorious deeds, all things are accomplished.
By failing to perform manifold wholesome karmas, one is deceived by the enemy that is the mind;
at the time of decline, lacking self-mastery, one falls into the most wretched states.
"All these palaces are adorned by various karmas;
through the increase of wholesome karma, the retribution of devas and humans is accomplished.

When the Heavenly King Śakra had spoken this verse, he proceeded to another palace. That palace was adorned with immeasurable, soft, jewel-ornamented seats arranged within, all manifested by the power of wholesome karma.
At that time, Kauśika beheld this palace and took his pleasure within it.

He then proceeded to a silver palace, which was adorned with immeasurable radiance, immeasurable varieties of jewels, and immeasurable varieties of flowers; there, immeasurable celestial maidens sported and enjoyed themselves.

They further arrived at the gardens where various celestial maidens dwelt; the ground was soft and adorned with many flowers, the groves were vast and expansive, various golden birds emitted wondrous sounds, and swarms of bees surrounded the wish-fulfilling trees.
The Universal Eye of Śakra, King of the Gods, surveys the celestial hosts who surround him as he sports and enjoys pleasures; his physical majesty surpasses that of the sun and moon.
Within a grove of golden trees stands a Vaiḍūrya palace, adorned with pillars of various jewels, while the lotus ponds are embellished with blue gems.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"I shall enter the jeweled palace to sport and enjoy pleasures.
The other devas also thought the same.
"The Heavenly King wishes to enter, surrounded by his retinue and celestial maidens to enjoy himself in pleasure.
At that time, Śakra, knowing the thoughts of the devas, addressed the sons of the gods:
"Each of you should go and sport in the groves."
At that time, having heard the instruction of the Heavenly King, the sons of the gods each entered the flower ponds to sport and enjoy themselves with their celestial maidens.
The Heavenly King entered the hall and sat upon a pure beryl throne.

Due to his virtuous karma, the palace was as pure as a clear mirror. Upon these pure walls, he saw entirely the signs of decline and the names of the various celestial kings of antiquity who had passed away. Their names were:

King Pūṣya, King Īśvara, King Aśoka, King Samyagjñāna, King Sarvasukha, King Susthita, King Samantaprabha, King Sarvapriya, King Sahasradarśana, King Tejasvin, King Guṇadhara, King Nīla, King Anivartin, King Māyāvin, King Upavāsika, King Puṇyavanta, King Vikrīḍita, King Tila, and King Kauśika.
Due to their wholesome karma, they see such kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When the wholesome karma of these heavenly kings is exhausted, they fall back into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, undergoing great suffering and affliction wherever they are reborn.
If one enters hell, one sees on the wall that person undergoing great suffering and affliction;

if one falls among the hungry ghosts, one sees on the wall that person undergoing great suffering and affliction, their bodies scorched by hunger and thirst, emaciated and tormented, with only sinews and bones remaining;
if one falls among the animals, one sees on the wall that person mutually harming one another and undergoing great suffering and affliction.
If one is born among humans, one pursues activities and undergoes various sufferings.

Thus, one perceives that within all births and deaths there is nothing to be delighted in; that within the cycle of birth and death there are many faults and afflictions, and that it is without solidity, impermanent, subject to change, and prone to destruction.
Thus, these celestial kings all decline and perish; by the fruit of their own karma, they are reborn in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
Why do you abandon such great bliss to undergo this suffering and affliction?
How can this be endured?
How marvelous!
Birth and death are truly a great suffering, capable of leading gods and humans to places of extreme terror.
The next day, the Heavenly King suffered this great suffering.

Having witnessed this event, Śakra, the Heavenly King and foremost among superior beings, conceived a profound sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*). He observed his own body as it closed off the three evil realms; dying from the heavenly realm, he was reborn among humans, and at the end of his life among humans, he was reborn once again in the heavens.

If they are born among humans, they will be born in peaceful and blissful kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages; they will be born into families of great lineage in places where the True Dharma is practiced, remaining free from wrong views, arrogance, and deceit.
Furthermore, there are those who see themselves born among humans as the sons of national princes or ministers, born into families of right view, possessing great wealth and sovereignty.
Having ended their lives among humans, where will they be reborn?

He immediately saw himself reborn among the gods, endowed with great supernormal powers and supreme radiance. While partaking of various foods together with the other hosts of devas, he felt shame in his heart; because his karma was meager, he received food according to the deeds he had performed.
Later, in his place of birth, he did not see superior food and thought with a sense of shame:
"For how many lifetimes shall I continue to receive such retribution?

Due to his wholesome karma, he saw his own body within the walls of the palace: seven births among the devas and seven births among humans, coming and going seven times, with no eighth birth—neither among the devas, nor among humans, nor in the hells, nor among the hungry ghosts, nor among animals.
Śakra thought to himself:
"Why is it that my body has no further place of rebirth? Where have I been born such that I cannot be seen?
A sense of wonder and alarm arose in his mind: "For what reason is there no eighth place of rebirth?"
Having reflected for a long time,
he then thought to himself:
"I have previously heard the World-Honored One speak these words:"
“A *srotāpanna* enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* after seven births;
I shall certainly be so.
With a pure mind, he paid homage to the World-Honored One and, with a heart of joy, sat upon his golden throne, a seat adorned with various jewels and made of Jambūnada gold.

Furthermore, within the walls he saw various celestial kings who had passed away in previous lives; he then recalled entering the Hall of Good Dharma, where he beheld the hosts of devas and brought benefit to them.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, rose from his seat and went to the Caitraratha Grove, where he sported and enjoyed himself with his retinue of devaputras and devakanyās, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
Various kinds of birds adorned the forest trees, and lotus flowers served as further embellishments.
Upon seeing this, the devas performed various musical performances with the voices of gandharvas; they went to the abode of Śakra, prostrated before him, and surrounded him.
The devas and devīs sang, danced, and sported, filled with manifold joy.

The Sudharmā Hall was adorned in various ways; surrounded by the devīs, Śakra performed many musical performances and proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall, where everyone rejoiced in song, dance, and laughter.

At that time, the devas dwelling in the Sudharmā Hall followed Śakra’s movements and made offerings to him; they produced various sounds, playing celestial music, and performed diverse songs and dances that emitted exquisite tones, pervading the entire assembly of devas.

When the devas dwelling in other abodes heard this sound of music, they all came to the Sudharmā Hall, where they prostrated themselves before the Heavenly King, circumambulated him to the right, and stood there.
Countless hundreds of thousands [of beings] go to the Hall of the True Dharma (*Saddharmasabhā*), well-versed in song and dance and adorned in various ways.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they are born therein; protected by the goodness of their precepts, they receive this great fruit, with all the celestial hosts achieving the rewards of bliss.

That Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) was five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its color was fresh and wondrous like a mass of molten gold, adorned with trees of lapis lazuli and embellished on all sides by various kinds of precious flowers.
The fragrance of its flowers filled five *yojanas* and was always as if freshly emerged, causing the heart to feel love and delight without ever becoming satiated.

Thus, the celestial hosts attended upon Śakra; ninety-nine *nayutas* of goddesses followed the Lord of Devas into the Hall of Joy (*Nandana-vimāna*), which was adorned with pillars of gold, *vaiḍūrya*, and *musāragalva*. Its couches were soft, spread with celestial garments, and the Heavenly King Śakra commanded them all to take their seats.
The devas, having received the instruction, all took their seats.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-five;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-six.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Observing the Heavens, Part Five; Section Two: The Thirty-three Heavens.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the devas, saying:

"Because of my wholesome karma, I have been born in this heaven; yet when that karma is exhausted, I shall fall away. It is through the causal conditions of karmic fruit that I was born in this heaven.
I will certainly pass away from this heaven; therefore, I must exert myself to seek peace and security."
When the assembly of devas had heard these words spoken by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, they addressed Śakra, saying: "So it is,
O Heavenly King!"
"In this place of joy resulting from our wholesome karma, we dare not again engage in heedless conduct.
They addressed him, saying:
"O Heavenly King!
"By what causes and conditions may I be made not to fall back?
At that time, Śakra addressed the devas, saying:

"In all places where one is born—above, below, or in the eight directions—there is nothing that is not conditioned, impermanent, and subject to destruction; do not give rise to greedy attachment, thinking it can be maintained forever."
Impure afflictions lead later to great suffering; they do not give rise to the dharma of happiness, they are not the causal conditions for wisdom, and they do not constitute right practice.
Recalling this, one will later experience great suffering.
"O sons of the gods!
You have already been born in this heavenly realm for immeasurable lifetimes; yet, when your lives ended, you fell back down into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."
Furthermore, having been born in this celestial realm by means of wholesome karma, they experience the fruits of their own actions and enjoy celestial pleasures.
Deceived by the illusions of karma, they fall once again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
You should not be negligent.
What I have spoken are the dharmas of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; those who hear these dharmas shall attain liberation from within birth and death.

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. In this way, there is only this great mass of suffering that accumulates.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Thus, this entire mass of suffering ceases.
Having thus observed the revolving cycle of birth and death within the heavens, one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Because afflictions are exhausted, one is forever indestructible; without birth or aging, without death or end—this is called Nirvana.
"O sons of the gods!
If you can act in this way, you will be liberated from birth and death.
Within this realm of birth and death, there exists no such dharma as that which is unborn and eternally abiding, indestructible, inexhaustible, and non-extinguishable."
"In the midst of birth and death, there is no such dharma; within birth and death, there exists only the dharma of decline, disappearance, arising, and ceasing.

When the sons of the gods heard Śakra, Lord of Devas, speak this dharma, those who had practiced during the True Dharma of past Buddhas became even more heedful; they placed their faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and with single-minded purity, they planted the seeds for nirvāṇa.

If there are devas or humans who, during the past Buddhas' True Dharma, did not cultivate their minds, becoming negligent and distracted, they were deceived by craving and indulged in the pleasures of the five senses.
"Because they are deceived by craving, they undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction within birth and death.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken this Dharma, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings thought to themselves:
"Where does the Heavenly King Śakra dwell together with the assembly of devas?"
While he was reflecting thus, he immediately saw the Heavenly King seated in his celestial palace, surrounded by a host of devas, possessing majestic virtue and radiance, and enjoying heavenly bliss.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings went to the Hall of Good Dharma and approached Śakra; they prostrated with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
After sitting for a short while, they rose from their seats and addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King!"

The people of Jambudvīpa practice the ten paths of wholesome action, act in accordance with the Dharma, provide filial support to their parents, and show reverence to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior members of the community.
"O Heavenly King!
May you grant us your favor.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the World-Protectors, saying:
"I also rejoice in the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings benefiting the world and causing them to practice the wholesome Dharma; hearing this, I am filled with joy.
You have acquired wholesome karma, and thus the people of Jambudvīpa will follow and accord with the practice of the Dharma."
The World-Protecting Heavenly King said to Śakra:

"If the people of Jambudvīpa do not act in accordance with the Dharma, are unfilial toward their parents, and show no respect for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, or senior monastics, they will increase the hosts of Māra and cause the True Dharma to diminish."
Upon hearing this, Śakra informed the gods of the Thirty-three and the Four Great Kings to quickly prepare for battle.
The Asura kings Tila, Vikrānta, and Bāhuka, as well as the unrighteous and malevolent Dragon King who causes turmoil, dwell beneath the sea and may come to engage in combat.

At that time, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings and their retinues, having heard the instruction of Śakra, returned to the abodes of the four heavens and went to Mount Sudarśana, where they arrayed their weapons as previously described.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of thousands of world-protecting devas, adorned himself with celestial garments and celestial garlands, and accompanied by various celestial maidens, proceeded to Mount Sarvārthasiddha. He was like the full moon surrounded by the myriad stars as they encircle Mount Sumeru, or like the radiance of the sun dwelling amidst the host of stars.

Just as hundreds of thousands of golden mountains surround Mount Sumeru, so too are these adorned with jewel-trees made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, sapphire-blue indranīla gems, and red lotus jewels.
In the places where the Lord of Devas sports, there are many birds that emit wondrous sounds.

There is a celestial lotus pond—the sporting ground of Airāvaṇa, the white elephant king of the nāgas—where golden lotuses with stalks of lapis lazuli grow; he sports therein together with various milk-white elephants, as previously described.
"Though he is an animal, he also enjoys celestial pleasures.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, went to where the elephant was, stroked him with his hand, and toyed with him, saying:
"This white elephant king of mine is skilled at fighting the asuras and enables me to achieve victory."

Having spoken these words, he proceeded again to Mount Sarvādhipati; arriving at the Palace of No-Grief, he sported together with nine *nayuta* of celestial maidens and enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses.
Together with the hosts of devas, they sport amidst the sounds of music and song in places of infinite adornment.

The celestial hosts experience their karmic rewards until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted and the accumulation of joyful retribution is spent; then, at the Hall of Good Dharma, their lives end and they fall back, perhaps falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If one possesses wholesome karma, one will be born among human beings and constantly experience happiness; being intelligent and wise, one will be born in the same city or the same village as others, becoming the foremost in the world, or serving as a relative, friend, brother, or acquaintance, always enjoying peace and bliss.
This is due to residual karma.
Śakra, King of the Devas, closed off the three evil realms and, observing the devas falling from their celestial abodes, spoke this verse:
"These various groves and gardens here, And these various lotus ponds,"
The mountain peaks are most sublime, vast and abounding in rare treasures.
Lotus ponds and rivers are adorned with precious gems;
various flowering trees and groves are where flocks of birds gather in harmony.
Golden trees and wish-fulfilling trees are as pure as lapis lazuli;
with silver jewels or coral, they are adorned in various ways.
Bees emit wondrous sounds as they dwell within the lotus ponds.
The jeweled towers are exceedingly vast, Stately, pure, and most exquisite.
Their adornments are most extraordinary, Worthy of offerings from all the devas;
With such various embellishments, Heavenly beings revolve in saṃsāra.
Like an illusion and like a bubble, like a city of the gandharvas—
deceived by craving for the five desires, the pleasures of heaven are likewise.
Craving harms all the world, causing it to wander through the ocean of birth and death.
The poison of craving is like a fierce fire that destroys all worlds.
There is no satiety in the pleasures of desire; one seeks them without ceasing.
Once scorched by the fires of impermanence, one knows not where one will go.
All sentient beings are thus deceived by the poison of craving;
Obscured by the stains of passion, the gods do not perceive the passage of time.
Devas, asuras, hell-beings, nāgas, and yakṣas—
All things lack sovereignty, shifting from moment to moment.
Within the entire triple world, beings are ensnared by the net of time;
unaware of this lack of sovereignty, they are deluded by craving.
"Thus, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the impermanence of the devas— that they are subject to birth and death—
and having seen this impermanence, he recollected the Supreme Dharma and praised the Buddha in verse:
‘Homage to the Bhagavān, Who brings benefit to all sentient beings.’"
I have explained that craving is like a poisonous harm, analyzing it extensively for the sake of the multitude.
Having thoroughly understood all phenomena, one’s wisdom is without obstruction;
when one is free from both wisdom and its objects of knowledge, there is no third dharma.
"Impermanent, suffering, and empty, And likewise devoid of a creator—
The Tathāgata, having seen the true reality, Speaks it for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, Śakra, having praised the Buddha with a pure mind, returned to his own abode as if marked by a seal, there to enjoy celestial bliss.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the second place is named Śikhara (Mountain Peak).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings taught others to uphold the precepts, even for a single day and night refraining from killing living beings, as well as refraining from stealing and violating the laws of the king; they did not commit theft, nor did they intentionally commit even minor offenses.
When this person’s life ends, they will be born on the second mountain peak; that ground is soft and adorned with the various lights of the diverse karmic merits of the Sumeru peaks.

Within this ground, one beholds the foundations of all Mount Sumerus, adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various jewels; the ground is further embellished by immeasurable celestial garlands and garments, its wondrous color like a mass of molten gold, and the mountain terrain is graced by forests of vaidūrya, where one sports together with celestial maidens.
He further proceeded to the rivers of food and drink:
the first is named the River of Celestial Exquisite Flavor;
the second is named the River of Great Rapid Current.
Third is the River of Flowing Currents;
fourth is the River of Great Flow;
fifth is the River of Meandering Currents.

By drinking from this river, one is freed from intoxication and confusion.
All manner of drinks flow forth from the river, possessing various flavors and various colors.

Some are the color of milk; some are the color of red jewels, the color of blue-jewel kings, or the color of *vaiḍūrya*; some are the color of golden hue, or of variegated colors. Exquisite fragrances waft forth, and it remains serene and ever full.

Furthermore, there is celestial food, all of which is endowed with various colors, fragrances, and flavors; its taste is like rock honey, its fragrance is pure and white, and its flavor is as one desires, manifesting in various tastes according to what the devas think of.

Adorned with various groves, fragrant flowers, and diverse colored birds as ornaments, he sports therein with celestial maidens amidst various musical performances, songs, dances, and laughter—truly most delightful.

There are many groves, namely: the Śāla grove, the Mahāśāla grove, the grove of wish-fulfilling trees, the grove of ever-blooming fragrant flowers, and the grove of wish-fulfilling breezes. When these touch the body, they bring joy and pleasure; they are adorned with golden branches and covered by nets of bells. Hundreds of thousands of birds emit exquisite songs as they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses and delight together.

Free from the affliction of illness, liberated from hunger and thirst, their bodies without exhaustion and needing no further labor, they experience whatever the mind desires, sporting in gardens and lotus ponds while beholding various wondrous sights and enjoying the pleasures of the five senses.

The devas dwelling on mountain peaks possess bodies of radiant light; their size is as they wish, and their supernormal powers are sovereign. Whatever they conceive in their minds is immediately attained, and once attained, it is indestructible and cannot be taken away by anyone.

Thus, while dwelling on the peak, all the hosts of devas experience the pleasures resulting from their own karma, as long as they cherish the fundamental precepts maintained through wholesome karma—namely, non-killing and non-stealing. Once that wholesome karma is exhausted, their lives end and they fall back, transmigrating according to their karma and falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, they will dwell in mountain valleys, possessing great wealth and abundant riches; they will be of supreme physical beauty, surrounded by lush gardens and groves, where cold and heat are perfectly temperate.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the third station of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
There is a place called Mountain Peak.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
There are sentient beings who observe two kinds of precepts:
seeing other sentient beings bound and imprisoned, they release them so that they may be set free;
when traveling on desolate roads, though pressed by hunger, they do not steal others' sugarcane, fruits, or vegetables.
Although they possess power and influence, they do not seize from others water, drinks, food, or meals.

Because they refrain from killing and release living beings, at the end of their lives these people will be reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where they will experience immeasurable bliss.
There are immeasurable river waters, namely the swirling eddies of the flow of desire, with longing for sense-pleasures as its banks and the joyful person’s recollections as its surging waves.

Within these rivers, there are many birds of lovely color, fragrance, and flavor; there are countless dragons and nāgas attached to desire, flowing along in crooked and twisted ways. The foam of the water serves as rafts, the groves of envy serve as gardens, and immeasurable realms serve as the mountain valleys.
In this manner, the gods are submerged and drowned in the river of craving;

none are able to cross it. Revolving since beginningless time, they fail to reach the further shore. Its flow pours on without ceasing, its habitual patterns are profoundly deep, and it courses through the three realms. With torrential waves surging forth, it pervades the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction constitute its great power.
Such is the river of craving that even the people of the world cannot cross.
On the mountain peaks, the gods dwell where the river of craving flows eternally; they sport therein with celestial maidens, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
There are six gardens and groves. What are the six?
The first is named Constant Joy.
The second is named Constant Play;
the third is named White Cloud Accumulation;
the fourth is named Universal Joy Forest.
The fifth is named Moon Forest;
the sixth is named Ganges Forest.
Adorned with such forests as these, they sport upon the mountain peaks, experiencing immeasurable bliss therein.
They proceeded further toward the rivers that flow like a drink, namely the Citrā River, the Sparśavatī River, the Atṛptā River, and the Citravāri River.
On both banks of these rivers, there were groves of trees made of gold, silver, and crystal, complete with flowers and fruits, which were exceedingly delightful.

Due to their virtuous karma, the various rivers and groves of the gods on that ground possess food and drink of exquisite fragrance and purity that flow from the rivers, where tens of millions of celestial hosts sport and enjoy themselves.

The celestial garments they wear have no warp or woof; their bodies are endowed with radiance and lack bone or flesh, nor do they have any moisture or impurity. Their speech and thoughts are free from weariness, and they constantly harbor joy as they move with measured grace, singing, dancing, and laughing.

Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted—their bodily, verbal, and mental karma, their karma of coolness, and their karma of certain retribution for the foremost blissful rewards—is spent, they fall back from the heavens and descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If born among humans, they will always experience peace and happiness; they will be immensely wealthy with abundant riches, delight in cultivating wisdom, and enjoy music, song, and dance; the lands where they are born will mostly consist of high plateaus.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The fourth stage is named the City of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he perceives what karma causes sentient beings to be born in that place:

There are sentient beings who practice and uphold the precepts, rescuing those drowning so as to free them from the peril of water; or when someone is about to be executed, they ransom and deliver them; or they cast their own bodies into deep waters to rescue those who are drowning.

If there is an evil person who instructs one to commit theft, one does not follow that instruction nor engage in theft; even when wandering through a wilderness, oppressed by hunger and thirst, one still does not steal another's grain or fruit.
Revering the precepts, they feel fear toward even the most subtle rules and do not dare to violate them.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in the city of Sudarśana.

That city is ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, with ten thousand stairways; its ground is made of Jāmbūnada gold. It contains ten thousand great palaces adorned with alternating patterns of Vaiḍūrya, Jāmbūnada gold, white silver, Indranīla, and the other seven precious gems. Within its streets and alleys, there are many multi-storied pavilions and jeweled halls, resplendent with brilliant light.
If one were to compare that celestial palace to sunlight, it would be like a lamp in broad daylight.
On its four sides, the city has groves made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, adorned all around, with nets of pearls covering them entirely above.
Furthermore, there are golden trees covered with silver nets, and silver trees covered with golden nets.
There are trees made of the seven precious gems serving as places for recreation.
From these wish-fulfilling trees, according to the gods' thoughts, indranīla blue jewels are produced.
In the great forest of blue gems, flocks of golden birds utter exquisite sounds;

within the golden forest, there are silver-colored birds; in the forest of blue gems, there are birds with red-gem-like plumage; and in the forest of red gems, there are flocks of birds of variegated colors.
Such gardens and groves are adorned with the exquisite songs of various birds.
The streets, lanes, and thoroughfares of the great city of Sudarśana are all adorned with palaces of pure gold and pillars of white silver, with trees of lapis lazuli serving as their ornamentation.
Furthermore, there are golden palaces with lapis lazuli pillars, and golden palaces adorned with golden trees.
Stairways and pathways are embellished with palaces made of various jewels; golden birds emit exquisite melodies, adorning the Great City of Sudarśana in a manner beyond description.
There are four great forests that serve as its adornments:
the first is named Cloud-Garland Forest;
the second is named Great Tree Forest.
The third is named Forest of Radiant Sound;
the fourth is named Forest Delightful to Behold.
Each of these groves measures two thousand five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
In each forest there are ten thousand rivers, all of which are completely covered with golden lotuses upon their waters.
Their two banks are magnificently adorned and exceedingly delightful, embellished by trees of gold, silver, crystal, and the king of blue jewels.
In this grove there are many bees with bodies of white silver and wings made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel.
Their sound is exquisite and beautiful, surpassing the sound of flutes, pipes, strings, and bamboo wind instruments by sixteen times.

The vimala trees have fruits of gold; they are fragrant, beautiful, and soft, with a flavor superior to rock honey. The fragrance of these fruits fills an entire yojana, and when birds smell this fragrance, they experience a hundredfold joy.
There are golden trees with silver fruits of exquisite fragrance and superior flavor;
there are *vaiḍūrya* trees with leaves of gold and fruits of various jewel colors.

Such diverse and immeasurable forest trees surround and adorn the Great City of Sudarśana. According to their recollections, all manner of virtuous karmas are fully accomplished, and they obtain various kinds of retributions.
According to their seeds, they receive retribution in accordance with their karma and dwell in the city of Sudarśana, experiencing immeasurable bliss.
Because this city is thus a place that all delight in beholding, it is named Sudarśana.
That grove is adorned with various kinds of red jewels, and networks of bells made of coral and mother-of-pearl cover the gardens and pleasure grounds.
The gods of Sudarśana dwell therein, their city palaces adorned with flower garlands and jeweled banners.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of jeweled banners, flags, and canopies were stirred by a gentle breeze, producing various subtle and exquisite musical sounds.
Surrounded by a vast retinue of devaputras and devakanyās, he dwelt within the city of Sudarśana on the summit of Mount Sumeru.

Thirty-six billion beings, adorned by their virtuous karma and receiving supreme retribution, were known to Śakra, King of the Devas; they possessed great supernatural powers, radiant majesty, and their minds were always filled with joy.

"Countless hundreds of thousands of deva sons and deva daughters emerged from the city of the Heavenly King and went to the grove to sport, riding upon countless hundreds of thousands of billions of palaces, adorned with hundreds of thousands of billions of various kinds of banners and streamers."
That palace was adorned with various colors and forms; its carriage-box was made of indranīla-blue jewels, and its wheels were made of red lotus jewels.
There were precious palaces upon a ground of purple-gold, with paths of vaidūrya, and the sides of the roads were demarcated by cords of musāragalva, all adorned with precious bells.

Furthermore, there were devaputras riding in palaces made of various jewels; some rode in jeweled palatial halls with mother-of-pearl for their floors, covered above by nets of pearls, with coral for their walls and white silver for their pillars.
Furthermore, there were sons of gods riding in golden palaces, with walls of pearls, floors of red jewels, pillars of white silver, and adorned with coral.
From each adornment issued a thousand rays of light; the hundreds of thousands of such palaces were beyond description.
Surrounded by hosts of devas and adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various ornaments, the deva-son mounts it and proceeds toward the groves.

There are banners of *vaiḍūrya*, or banners covered in red, or banners of purple gold, or banners of red-lotus jewels; banners of immeasurable colors and various precious streamers fill the void as he joyfully sports and proceeds to the four groves.
Immeasurable music, with hundreds of thousands of billions of sounds and all manner of exquisite melodies, is fully present; those who hear it find delight in it.
According to what they have obtained through their karma, they experience joy and pleasure as their superior, middling, or inferior retributions.
They proceeded to the Great Forest.
Each deva, accompanied by a host of celestial maidens—whether numbering a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand—sang, danced, and merrily laughed.
With the full accompaniment of gandharva melodies and musical instruments, they proceeded to the Great Forest to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.

Each celestial maiden enjoys herself with her respective deva-son, indulging in pleasures as they desire; they proceed to various places for recreation, sometimes traveling through the air like blue clouds of the color of lapis lazuli.
Thus the host of devas, situated in the void, their bodies adorned with various garments and diverse ornaments, proceeded toward the Great Forest with beautiful voices and endearing speech.

Some hosts of devas travel upon golden paths; the rims of their countless hundreds of thousands of jewel palaces roll over the golden ground, such that golden dust fills the sky, causing it to be shrouded in shadow yet remaining untainted.
"When the life of a certain deva is about to end, dust clings to his body.
Other devas who have previously seen another deva with such signs—that he will soon fall away and undergo great suffering—give rise to a heart of compassion and speak these verses:
'When the devas travel this path, Whether they return a hundred or a thousand times,'
The fire of time burns the fuel of sensory objects;
seeing the signs of others' sickness and death, one fails to realize it for oneself.
Once the signs of decay have arrived, one then knows one's own suffering.
Heedlessness turbidly stains one's own mind; One constantly delights in sensory objects, Unaware that death pursues one, Never departing from living beings.
Those who enjoy pleasures and engage in play, Who delight in practicing heedlessness—
The army of death is about to arrive, destroying all like a poisonous plague.
Neither the power of mantras nor medicines, nor gods or asuras, can save one who is bound by their own karma;
it is beyond the power of the world to rescue them.
Dust and grime cover their bodies and faces, yet they remain unaware;
when the certainty of death arrives, they will surely pass away before long.
Sentient beings are constantly driven by desire, and their thirst for craving knows no satisfaction.
The thief of death has suddenly arrived, yet you, attached to pleasure, do not perceive it.
The signs of death have already appeared for you; dragged away by death, you will surely perish in an instant, and at the time of your passing, you shall suffer affliction.
The beings on this mountain peak, in places adorned with groves and gardens,
are bound by their karma and lack autonomy, experiencing the retribution of their own deeds.
Engaging in play and heedless conduct, they enjoy pleasures without ever feeling satiety.
The deluded person’s craving increases; they sink and fall, lacking self-mastery.
Where there is smoke, there must be fire; such is the nature of these phenomena.
With such signs of sinking and falling, one will surely return to the suffering of death.
"Thus, having seen these signs, the celestial son’s mind of negligence subsided; he cultivated his original roots of goodness and rebuked his own mind as well as those of the other celestial sons."

When this was being spoken, there were various devaputras riding in diverse palaces, covered with jeweled nets and hung with many precious bells; adorned with immeasurable ornaments that decorated them so that all who saw them were filled with delight.
Adorned with celestial garlands and celestial garments like masses of molten gold, hundreds of thousands of beings filled the summit of Mount Sumeru.

At that time, the devaputra saw the celestial hosts approaching—some riding golden palaces, some walking upon the ground, and some riding swan-palaces—accompanied by celestial maidens singing, dancing, and laughing as they headed toward the Forest of Play.

The celestial lotus trees, rivers, springs, ponds, and streams abound with flourishing flowers and fruits; they are adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels, and all the groves and gardens are exceedingly delightful.
Once the gods of the Sudarśana Heaven had arrived at the grove, they all descended from their palaces and proceeded toward the golden trees.
Those trees were so fresh and radiant that they shone like the light of the sun; the hosts of gods traveling through the air descended from the sky and went to the place of recreation.

All the hosts of devas gathered like clouds, playing drums and stringed instruments, singing songs, sporting and enjoying pleasures without jealousy; they danced, sang, and laughed, delighting themselves with the five desires. Adorned with the sounds of music, they moved together with the celestial maidens through the areas of food, drink, and riverbanks, heading toward the Vaiḍūrya grove.

That beryl forest is adorned with fruits of pure gold; they are perfect in fragrance and color, and their taste is like honeyed wine. Together with many beautiful celestial maidens of exquisite form, they drink the fruit-juice of the *mātuluṅga* and long enjoy celestial delights.
Thus the host of devas enjoyed themselves with song, dance, play, and laughter.
Having heard this, other devas went to the abode of Śakra, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"O Heavenly King!
"O Heavenly King, you should know that all the hosts of devas in the city of Sudarśana have gone to the pleasure groves to sport.
Having heard this, Śakra issued a command:
"The assembly of devas must quickly adorn themselves; I wish to go to the place where the gods of the Sudarśana heaven sport.

When all the devas in the Sudharmā Hall heard the command of the Heavenly King, they mounted various celestial palaces—some mounting golden palaces with lapis lazuli banners, while others mounted lapis lazuli palaces with pure gold banners.
It was adorned with banners made of various seven-jeweled materials;
the golden bird-palaces emitted manifold wondrous sounds;
and there were horse-palaces that moved with great speed.

There were some golden geese with feet of lapis lazuli and wings made of red lotus jewels; the sons of gods mounted them and followed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, toward the place of recreation in the great city of Sudarśana.
Furthermore, there were devaputras riding peacock birds whose bodies were composed of the seven treasures.

Among all the birds in Jambudvīpa, the color of these peacocks surpassed that of every other species; how much more so when they are adorned by the excellent karma of the heavens—their forms, features, and complexions are beyond comparison.
Mounted upon this peacock, he proceeded to the pleasure grounds, where amidst various musical sounds, songs, dances, and laughter, he went to the Sudarśana Heaven to sport and enjoy delights.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, mounted a celestial palace with a thousand spokes and four wheels; that palace was magnificently adorned, being composed of the seven precious gems.
What are the seven?
First, the king of blue jewels;
second, the red lotus jewel.
Third, musaragalva jewels;
fourth, pure vaidūrya jewels; fifth, coral and vajra.
Sixth is crystal; seventh is pure gold.

Thus, adorned with the variegated colors of these seven treasures, it is drawn by a thousand geese whose bodies possess the luster of the seven treasures and various wondrous forms. Their voices are exquisite and surpass the songs of all celestial maidens. Śakra mounts this vehicle.

There were five hundred banners, with gold, silver, and lapis lazuli forming precious standards; blue, yellow, red, white, and purple combined to create a magnificent adornment for the palace, which Śakra mounted.

Innumerable celestial maidens, with voices of exquisite song, preceded him as they danced and sang; whether traversing the void or walking upon the earth, they moved with sovereign ease and without hindrance, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses and delighting in music as they proceeded toward the sporting grounds of the Sudarśana Heaven.
The other devas, seeing this, took up various flowers with stems of lapis lazuli and went to where Śakra was.
When the gods of the Sudarśana Heaven saw Śakra approaching, they all abandoned their play and went out to welcome him.
Śakra declared, "You all should now sport in the waters.

Having heard Śakra’s command, the hosts of the Heaven of Good Dharma received his instruction with reverence; they immediately entered the pool, gathered lotus petals, and ran swiftly toward the Heaven of Good Appearance.
The devas of the Sudarśana heaven also grasped lotuses and rushed toward the devas of the Sudharma heaven, sporting and laughing.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, remained in mid-air, observing the various devas sporting and fighting in the water; they sported for a long time without ever becoming weary or satisfied.

Furthermore, they engage in playful combat with lotuses; using golden flowers, lapis lazuli flowers, and various colored stalks, they strike and toss one another. For a long time in this place, they take delight in fighting with lotuses as a form of play and laughter.
They then proceeded to the Fruit Grove, where they gathered various soft fruits and threw them at one another from a distance.

Having finished their playful combat with the fruits, they went further to the Wine Grove to eat *mātuluṅga* and drink wine; yet, due to the power of their wholesome karma, they did not become intoxicated or disordered.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended from his palace and entered the grove; when the sons of the gods saw Śakra approaching, they were all greatly delighted and made offerings to him.
The sons of the gods joined their palms and said:
"We have obtained a fortunate life and attained a virtuous karmic reward; that we have encountered the Heavenly King who benefits us exceeds even the kindness of our parents."
After the host of devas had thus made their offerings, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the sons of the gods:
"All of you are like my own sons; you are like brothers to me."

Having thus comforted one another, they entered the realm of heedlessness and sported for pleasure within the groves. There, rivers, springs, and lotus ponds were adorned with the various birds emitting wondrous sounds.
The ground is adorned with various golden flowers;
it is exquisite, soft, supple, level, and even.
Those groves of trees are adorned with trees of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Rivers, springs, and flowing streams produce all manner of food and drink, which are fully provided in abundance.
