It is adorned with *mandārava* flowers, *kūṣmāṇḍa* flowers, great lotuses, and other such blossoms.
The devas and apsaras play, sing, and dance amidst the mountain valleys, enjoying themselves in delight.
To the sounds of the five musical instruments and the songs of the apsaras, they experience the pleasures of the five desires.

The sons of the gods within the city of Sudarśana and those within the Sudharmā Hall all sport together in the groves; having spent immeasurable time sporting and enjoying pleasures among human beings, they return toward their own palaces along the various places of recreation on the way, laughing and enjoying themselves.
Adorned with various ornaments, they returned to their original palaces.

The gods dwelling within the city of Sudarśana enjoyed celestial pleasures until their beloved wholesome karma was exhausted; then, at the end of their heavenly life, they fell according to their original karma into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If one possesses virtuous karma, they will be born among humans and constantly experience peace and happiness. They will possess extensive learning and insight, always delighting in music, song, dance, and laughter, and taking pleasure in festivals and gatherings. They will have abundant means of livelihood, avoid epidemics, and remain free from sorrow and affliction.
"Because of residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The fifth stage is named Bṛhatphala.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

When a person who upholds the precepts is poor and begs for wealth, food, or drink, and sees someone in great poverty, they share their own meal and bestow it as a gift, even reducing the portion of their wife and children to give to the destitute.

A person who is blind, solitary, and afflicted by illness, having cultivated and accumulated wholesome faith, sees another who has committed adultery and is seized by the authorities, exiting through the right gate. As the executioners and butchers are about to take his life, he is struck with terror and his vision fails; [the practitioner] then rescues him, causing him to escape.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Pāruṣyaka region of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born in this heaven, by virtue of their wholesome karma, the radiance of their body will shine everywhere, just like the light of the sun.
The appearance of its radiance consists of immeasurable light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and green—which shines everywhere throughout the heavens, ten times more magnificent than before.
Just as among all the stars in Jambudvīpa the moonlight is foremost, so too is the bodily radiance of the sons of gods in this realm.
Possessing a perfection of all colors, when the other gods compare themselves to him, they are like fireflies.
When the goddesses see this deva-son, they all run toward him.
As soon as the deva-son is born, his ornaments also appear simultaneously; upon his head is a crown made of the great king of blue jewels, whose light shines everywhere, filling an entire yojana.
Other great jewels, upon seeing the light of this pearl, were all extinguished and ceased to appear, just as fireflies lose their glow when the sun rises.

Naturally formed from the seven precious gems, it served as a flower crown; its light shone universally for a full hundred yojanas, adorned with every kind of radiance. Blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and green lights appeared spontaneously upon his body.
The jewelry and necklaces of the seven treasures emit radiance that universally illuminates one hundred yojanas.
The necklaces worn upon their bodies, composed of the seven treasures, likewise emit light capable of illuminating one hundred yojanas.

He used a vajra-thread as a waist-cord, hanging down across his chest; the belt he wore was the color of a celestial rainbow, and he wore sandals of various hues upon his feet, their brilliance shining like flashes of lightning, so that he could travel without ever becoming weary.

If one contemplates the practice of emptiness, wherever one directs oneself, by the power of this [practice] as if by the force of a shoe, one can reach whatever destination without ever becoming weary.
The garments worn have no warp or woof; they are composed of various kinds of jewels whose radiance shines brilliantly, being exceptionally sublime and lovely.
Once the son of heaven was born, he immediately reflected to himself:
"By what karma have I come to be born here?
As soon as this thought arose, he saw for himself his past life in Jambudvīpa, in both virtuous and non-virtuous states, and how he passed away from there to be born in this celestial realm.
"If one has cultivated wholesome karma within Jambudvīpa, it ripens here.
'I have come to be born here because I performed wholesome karma.
I am born through causes and conditions; I am not born without cause.'"
In an instant, a multitude of celestial maidens—youthful, of exquisite beauty, and fully endowed with radiant light—all came to approach the newly born deva-son.

The sounds produced by the ornaments adorning these celestial maidens were like the music of the five instruments; their fragrance pervaded two yojanas in every direction, and their flowers surpassed all other flowers.
With a countenance of wondrous color and radiance, adorned with celestial garments, they are born of merit through the power of their heavenly wholesome karma;
like the rising sun, the various flowers bloom in full splendor.

Once the son of heaven was born, celestial maidens of radiant beauty approached the place where the son of heaven was; they entertained and delighted him with various amusements. Taking up the son of heaven, they went to the grove to play, performing various musical instruments, songs, dances, and laughter, gazing up at the son of heaven as they proceeded together into the forest.

That grove is named Lotus-Born; when the devaputras enter the grove to sport, a lotus flower grows beneath each of their feet to support them—having stems of lapis lazuli, filaments of diamond, and petals of pure gold. Their calyxes are soft and are adorned by swarms of bees.
As they lift their feet and are about to set them down, lotus flowers immediately spring up to receive their feet.

From this grove of flowers, they enter the Mātuluṅga forest. In that forest, golden trees exude fragrant drinks superior to grape wine, complete in color, aroma, and flavor; when the gods drink them, they do not become intoxicated or disordered, nor do the celestial maidens.
He then proceeded to the Caitraratha forest; the three qualities of that forest were beyond comparison:
first, the songs of birds;
second, the humming of bees.
Third, there is the sound of the celestial maidens’ songs and hymns.

Within the groves of the three assemblies of those devaputras, in every place of recreation and every lotus pond, they hear the various calls of the birds and find such delight that they never know satiety.
Burned by the fire of craving, until their wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm; bound by their karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will possess exquisite and upright features, be born into a great lineage, and be fully endowed with merit. One will enjoy wealth, happiness, and sovereignty, sporting according to one's heart; free from illness and dwelling in peace, one will have a long life. One will be born in a virtuous age or in a central land, never in a frontier region; one may become a great king or a high minister, possessing abundant treasures as a great merchant leader.
"Due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The sixth place is named Kūṭa.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth there?
He perceives and knows:

If there are sentient beings who have captured a thief, they do not inflict punishment or execution upon them, nor do they cause them suffering; or, if others have seized a thief, they cause that person to escape.
With a heart of moistening benefit, they bring welfare to sentient beings.

He makes offerings to his parents, providing them with medicine when they are ill according to their every need; he does not steal any of his parents' wealth or possessions; he speaks with a pleasing and gentle voice, and uses few words for his own benefit.
He constantly makes offerings of incense and flowers, pays homage, and recollects the Buddha’s merits.
He respects his teachers and elders, prostrating to them and inquiring after their well-being with gentle, kind, and harmonious speech.
Upon seeing those of evil character, he does not associate with them nor take pleasure in their conduct.
Those who are unwholesome and evil, those who practice incorrectly, are despised by the world; one should not associate with them or dwell together with them.
Instead, one should draw near to the elders and revere them with respect.
Having received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, they are fully endowed with wisdom; upholding the precepts with a sincere heart, they do not afflict or harm others.
They are beloved by all people and praised for their virtuous words.
He serves his slaves, servants, and attendants with gentle speech and does not unjustly inflict fear upon them.
He is moderate in food and drink, never consuming leftovers.

He does not afflict living beings, takes no pleasure in anger, and avoids associating with lowly people such as butchers, executioners, or merchants; in all buying and selling, he is upright and honest.

He does not deceive sentient beings; he does not enter wine shops; he is not treated with contempt by women; he does not violate his dignified deportment or fail to maintain orderly composure in his movements.
When he speaks, he acts accordingly.
One does not seek after the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others.
One harbors no resentment in the heart, neither slanders nor speaks of their wisdom.
Seeing others planting in their fields, one does not give rise to envy.
They pay taxes according to the law and do not deceive the king.
They do not steal the water used for irrigating others' fields.
Whether by day or by night, they do not take the fruit belonging to others.
One completely abandons all evil deeds and does not commit them; this may be a single cessation, or it may be a "lower cessation.
What is meant by lower cessation?
To engage in various karmic actions throughout is called lower cessation.
What is intermediate cessation?
Having committed [an offense], one repents and censures it, resolving not to do it again; this is called intermediate cessation.
What is superior cessation?

One does not perform pervasive karma oneself, nor does one instruct others to do so; one exhorts others to abandon it, does not give rise to sympathetic joy for it, and relinquishes the inferior and middling karma of evil persons.
These three types of people obtain three kinds of fruits, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
Thus, those who have practiced virtue and abandoned unwholesome karma, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, are reborn in the Kūṭa Heaven.
Having been born there, their bodies are boneless and skinless, free from all impurities, and they experience an inconceivable perfection of bliss.

For example, the pleasures enjoyed by a wheel-turning sage king—who possesses the seven treasures and a thousand sons and rules over the four continents—when compared to the bliss of this heaven, are like a living hell.

The celestial abode is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is adorned with celestial trees of the seven treasures, rivers, and ponds within that heaven, and is named Gaṇḍavyūha (Forest of Arrays).
In that grove, the golden trees arise from the trees themselves in accordance with the devas' thoughts.
Wherever the devas go, these trees always accompany them, just as the seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) always follow the king according to his mental inclinations.
This celestial grove is likewise: if a deva’s mind remains fixed, the grove immediately stays upon the ground.
Just as a flying bird soars through the air but settles upon the earth when it stops, this celestial grove is exactly like that.
This is the first power of the Kūṭa devas.
Furthermore, by virtue of their wholesome karma, they possess another power:
wherever they go, various birds with exquisite songs always accompany them. This is the second power of the Kūṭa devas.

Furthermore, there are virtuous karmas that follow wherever they go: various lotus ponds adorned with the exquisite sounds of swarms of bees and with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks; these are the three powers of the Kūṭa-devas.

Furthermore, there is another wholesome karma: adorning oneself with celestial flower garlands and traveling through the air, where thousand-petaled lotuses naturally appear with stems of lapis lazuli; celestial maidens sit upon their flower pedestals and sport together—this is the fourth power of the Kūṭa-devas.

Furthermore, there is another wholesome karma: wherever the devas go, they travel through the air; divine jeweled vessels filled with celestial drink naturally appear in their hands, which they drink together with the celestial maidens in succession; they can dance, sing, play, and laugh as they wish and move about at will—this is the fifth power of the Kūṭa-devas.
Furthermore, there is the power of karma by which everything is accomplished according to one's thoughts.

If one has the intention to travel to another region, one can cross mountain peaks where gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits are all fully provided; traveling through the air with celestial maidens, one performs divine music and goes wherever the mind desires.

The gods of the Sudharmā Hall and the gods of the Sudarśana City, seeing this host of deities ascending this lofty palace and looking down upon the mountain valleys, were filled with great joy, like celestial messengers observing Jambudvīpa.
The gods of the Sudharmā Hall and the Sudarśana City, seeing this assembly of gods, said to one another:
"These gods of the Kūṭa realm can act according to their thoughts; they are able to surpass us, moving everywhere without obstruction."
"This is the sixth power of the god Kūṭa.
King Śakra, together with his queen, sits upon a lotus pedestal of a hundred thousand petals and travels through the air, transformed by his virtuous karma."

Upon each petal of every flower sat five celestial maidens, adorned with divine garlands, appearing like masses of molten gold; performing celestial music, they gazed up at Śakra, their forms upright and exquisitely beautiful, as they accompanied the Lord of Devas to the Kūṭa heaven.

At that time, when the host of devas saw Śakra approaching, they all rejoiced greatly and went out to welcome him; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, praised him with eloquent words, and stood surrounding him on all four sides.
Whether on mountain peaks or in pleasure groves, whether on mountain summits, in gardens, or by lotus ponds, they dwell together with Śakra.
After the hosts of the Kūṭa devas have sported for a long time with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, they return to their own palaces, and Śakra, the Heavenly King, returns to the Sudharmā Hall.

The celestial beings here experience the pleasures of the five sensory desires—exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures—and so forth, until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; they then transmigrate according to their karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will experience the foremost peace and happiness, never encountering the suffering of illness; or dwelling on a great continent, one will not fear enemies; or becoming a great king or a high minister, one will constantly enjoy peace and happiness.
Due to the remaining karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 26.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 27.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Observing the Heavens, Part Six; The Thirty-three Heavens, Part Three.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the abodes of the Thirty-three Heavens.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the seventh stage is named Varied Palaces (Citra-maṇḍala).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?

If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing ancient stūpas and monasteries, or when wicked kings and ministers with false views have confiscated the lands and property belonging to the Saṃgha, do not fear royal prohibitions and instead bestow fields and goods upon the Saṃgha; and if they speak to such evil kings of the Buddha’s merits, praising the Buddha with virtuous words.
When such a person’s life ends, they are reborn in the Realm of Variegated Palaces.
Having been born in this heaven, they experience various pleasures through the sounds of the five musical instruments, singing, dancing, and playful laughter.
Furthermore, there are others who, due to different karma, are born in this heaven:
Not killing and not stealing; using wealth to redeem the lives of those at the hands of butchers;
not committing evil oneself and not teaching others to do so;
and if others commit evil, not rejoicing in it with one's heart.
What is non-stealing?
Whether acting as a sovereign of a nation or as a high minister, one does not unjustly levy taxes or seize property, and likewise instructs others to abide by this precept.
By these two types of karma, one is reborn in the Realm of the Variegated Palaces.
That grove is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth; because various palaces serve as the playgrounds for the devaputras, it is named "Miscellaneous Palaces" (Citra-maṇḍala).
Each of the palaces of the devaputras is wondrously adorned; golden lotuses possess the most exquisite fragrance, and beryl bees produce sublime sounds.

In those lotus groves, all things grow together; in each individual lotus pond there are various kinds of lotuses—some ponds have lotuses made of red jewels, while others have lotuses of variegated lapis lazuli.
There are also lotus ponds where various lotuses grow, with golden flowers and beryl flowers growing interspersed.
Each lotus has a hundred petals, some of which are made of gold and others of red jewels.
Furthermore, there were variegated flowers with lapis lazuli leaves, wherein golden bees sported and played.
There were also flower ponds where various lotuses grew, adorned by multitudes of red-jewel bees.
Furthermore, there are flower ponds where various lotuses grow, with stems of lapis lazuli and flowers of pure gold;
or there are flower ponds where various lotuses grow, with stems of pure gold and flowers of white silver.
There are some lotus ponds where various lotuses grow, with stems of musāragalva and flowers of white silver.
There are further lotus ponds where various lotuses grow, with stems of marakata and flowers of Jambūnada gold.
Bees of various colors produced exquisite sounds that filled the spaces between the lotuses;
just as the flowers of the fragrant trees in Jambudvīpa are filled with swarms of bees, so too were the various palatial flower ponds.
Just as a painter or a painter’s disciple might depict various images using a multitude of colors based on things previously heard within Jambudvīpa, so too is the grove of the variegated palace.
Furthermore, there are various birds of diverse colors, their heads and feet being multicolored, and their bodies, chests, and bellies likewise so.
Some birds have golden breasts and silver wings, with backs made of red jewels and eyes like red jewels.

There were also various birds with chests of white silver, wings of pure gold, eyes of blue *vaiḍūrya*, pupils of red jewels, and backs adorned with a variety of miscellaneous gems; they were further embellished by flocks of diverse birds of the colors of the seven precious substances.

Within the Jālinī Grove there are further mountain peaks composed of blue gems, pearls, conch shells, lapis lazuli, red jewels, and pure gold. Their radiance shines everywhere, pervading the entire grove; these elements intermingle and swirl in elegant, circular currents that fill the forest. This adornment is extraordinary and most delightful.

In the Miscellany Hall Grove, there are further various creepers intertwined with one another; they have stems of lapis lazuli with filaments of red jewels forming entangling vines, adorned with fruits;
others have stems of white silver with filaments of blue jewels, surrounded by radiance.
Branches made of musāragalva are entwined with pure gold;
branches made of red jewels are entwined with white silver.
In this manner, these two colors wind around and envelop one another.
In this Mixed Palace Grove, there are further trees adorned with branches of three colors that serve as curtains and canopies: beryl branches entwined with pure gold and red jewels;
likewise, branches of red jewels entwined with gold and silver;
and branches of white silver entwined with musāragalva and red jewels.
Each and every branch is intertwined and entwined within the grove of variegated palaces.
Furthermore, there are various flowers: those with branches of pure gold have blossoms of lapis lazuli;
those with branches of silver have blossoms of indra-color.
If the branches are made of gold, the flowers are of red jewels;
if the branches are of mother-of-pearl, the flowers are of lapis lazuli.
It is likewise for the production of fruits of manifold colors.
Arising from a mixture of mental factors, one performs various mixed karmas; because these mixed causes accumulate, one receives various retributions.

By means of the causal conditions of karma, one experiences mixed fruit-retribution in the Forest of Mixed Palaces (Miśrakavana); cause and effect correspond to one another, just as various seeds yield corresponding fruits.
According to the power of their karma, following what they have done, following the timing, and following the various mental states that arise,
they perform such actions and receive such retributions, just as a seal impresses its mark upon an object.

The fruits of pleasure in the heavens do not arise without a cause; the retribution of suffering in the hells is likewise so. It is not that I create [the karma] while another receives the retribution.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma contemplates the Forest of Variegated Palaces (Citrakūṭa)."
How do sentient beings create karma and are born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three?

If there are sentient beings in the world who practice what is not the Dharma—being unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders, not associating with virtuous friends, lacking faith in the law of karmic fruition, and practicing wrong views.
At such a time, the Māra-king rejoices.
When unrighteousness prevails, there are four assemblies of devas in this world. What are these four?
First is the demon-messenger named Strife;
second is the demon-messenger named Chaos, who creates distraction in the minds of those practicing the Dharma, causing listeners to become dazed and fall into sleep;
third is the demon-messenger named Greed and Delusion, who causes donors to give rise to thoughts of attachment and stinginess, leading them to think thus:

"If I give material goods as offerings to the various fields of merit—the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—what will become of my wife and children? How shall they provide for themselves with food and clothing?"
The fourth is the demonic emissary named "Deviating from Right Mindfulness," who causes those who have left the household life to abandon right mindfulness; this is the first evil.

If a person enters a city or marketplace and sees women in taverns quarreling and beating one another, or dreams of practicing the breaking of precepts—these are called the four kinds of demonic emissaries.
When the people of Jambudvīpa practice what is not the Dharma and commit such evils, the four kinds of Māra’s messengers rejoice in their hearts and say to the King of Māras:
"The True Dharma is being diminished and the armies of Māra are increasing; this is truly a cause for celebration!"
When the Māra King heard this, he asked his messenger:
"In what way does the world cause my dharma to increase and the True Dharma to diminish?
Then the Māra messenger addressed the Māra King, saying:
"The people of Jambudvīpa practice what is not the Dharma; they are unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
I shall cause those who listen to the True Dharma to fall into drowsiness;
I shall cause those who have gone forth to return to the life of ordinary laypeople and cast off their religious robes."
Whether they be renunciants, those who uphold the precepts, or practitioners of the Brahma-faring life, he causes them to manifest in female forms within their dreams, thereby deranging their minds;
he causes donors to become greedy and stingy regarding their wealth, their hearts shrouded by avarice, and to become attached to their wives and children;
and he causes those who have left the household life to practice various forms of trade, commerce, and strife, beating one another.
"I have employed various such skillful means to cause Māra to increase and the True Dharma to diminish.
When Māra heard this, he immediately dispatched messengers to inform Rāhu, Vikrānta, Vemacitrin, and the evil nāgas Pāpīmān and Kṣobhaṇa:
"You all should feel great joy today; the Buddha’s True Dharma has now diminished, and the armies of Māra have increased."

Thus, the Māra messenger went immediately to the bottom of the water to the abode of the Asura Vemacitra; when he had related the aforementioned matters in detail, the Asura heard them and rejoiced, and he immediately informed the malevolent Dragon Kings who cause distress and turmoil.
When the evil dragon in the city of Bhogavatī heard this, he was filled with great joy and began to cause disturbances for the people of the world, as previously described.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard these words spoken by King Virūḍhaka; he entered the Caitraratha Grove and discussed this matter with the gods of the Thirty-three:
"The World-Protecting Heavenly King has come and said to me:..."
"The Māras and Devas possess great power, as do the Asuras and the evil Nāgas who cause affliction, such as Vemacitra.
You should assemble all the hosts of devas and come here; I shall go to that Mountain Arrayed with Jewels to fight the Asuras."
Upon hearing this, the devas replied,
"So be it! and each returned to their own palace to adorn themselves.
The hosts of devas from the Citra Hall also returned to their own palaces; with various sounds of song, dance, and laughter, they entered the Citra Grove.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the hosts of devas, left the Citra Grove and proceeded to another region.

The devaputras dwelling in this Citraśālavana grove experience such pleasures until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; at the end of life, they pass away and decline, wandering according to their karma and falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will achieve happiness, being adorned and upright in appearance; from youth until old age, one will always delight in various colors and diverse ornaments, be fond of various languages, and be beloved by the masses.
If one goes forth into the homeless life, one will ascend the lion throne as a Dharma teacher, understand various languages, and those who hear it will find contentment.
Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The eighth stage of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named the Garden of Joy (*Nandanavana*).
By what karma do sentient beings take birth there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
These sentient beings possess wholesome minds and profound resolve; they refrain from killing and stealing, and they also instruct others to refrain from killing and stealing.
If they see someone killing, they urge them not to kill; they do not teach others to do so, nor do they rejoice when they see it being done.
If one commits an offense, one immediately repents and distances oneself from evil associates.
How does one refrain from killing?
Upon seeing a bird being killed, one rescues it and causes it to be released.
One does not commit evil oneself; should one commit it, one immediately repents and receives the precept against killing.
One ransoms lives with wealth to enable them to escape, and further teaches others to join in sympathetic joy.
What is non-stealing? What is stealing?

When officials commissioned by the king to govern the country and manage the people—whether they be lords of villages or towns, masters of herds, or commanders of frontier garrisons—are ordered to take cattle, sheep, or other property, a person who guards the precepts will refuse to take them.

By these causes and conditions, after the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Joy (Nirmāṇarati), specifically in the Garden of Joy within the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).

Furthermore, they will have the opportunity to hear the Dharma and attend Dharma assemblies; on the six days of the fast, they will listen to and receive the Dharma, listening with single-minded devotion.
After this master of the Dharma assembly passed away, he was reborn among the devas.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of the Dharma is foremost; by virtue of these causes and conditions, upon his death he was reborn in the Joyful Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born in that heaven, they enjoy immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial delights beyond all analogy; I shall now describe a small portion of them.
That grove is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with trees made of the seven precious jewels.
Because the devas of Joy do not go to other gardens, it is therefore called the Garden of Joy;
this is a name derived from its own specific quality.
All the trees in that grove are wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*); whatever the devas think of, all of it emerges from the trees.

If a celestial being conceives the thought that he desires a palace, and having so thought, wishes to ascend, he immediately sees that the grove is a palace made of the seven treasures, possessing one hundred pillars. Each pillar of the palace is made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, ruby, or musaragalva; indeed, all manner of such precious jewels are used to form the pillars of the palace.
Again, he had this thought:
"I wish to obtain a smooth staircase to ascend to this hall.
As soon as he thought it, a staircase appeared, perfectly formed.
Having entered the palace, he further reflected:
"May lotus ponds arise within this palace.
As soon as this thought occurred, various lotus ponds appeared, possessing the colors of the seven precious gems and adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
Again, he thought: "In this hall of mine, there should be celestial maidens singing, dancing, playing, and laughing.
As soon as he thought this, celestial maidens arrived; according to his heart's desire, they provided offerings through their play, laughter, song, and dance.
Again, he thought to himself:
"I should now obtain the musical performances of the celestial hosts.
In accordance with this thought, the wind blew through the leaves of the trees, causing them to strike one another and produce exquisite sounds that surpassed all the music of the devas.
Again, he thought:
"Now, food and drink should arise within this palace.
In accordance with his mental intention, the branches of the trees split open and flowed forth rivers of drink, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.
Again, he thought:
"I should now obtain the flavor of *sudhā*.
As soon as this thought arose, food of the finest *sudhā* appeared, complete in color, fragrance, and taste; the devaputra ate it until he was fully satisfied.

Furthermore, together with celestial maidens, he sports and enjoys himself, entering the Garden of Joy (*Nandana-vana*); within this Garden of Joy, the devas who dwell there achieve such supreme and wondrous bliss.
Descending from the palace, he was born upon this ground in a lotus flower with a stem of lapis lazuli and petals of pure gold;
its stem was soft and supple, bringing joy and delight to all who beheld it.
Perfectly endowed with color and fragrance, they walk by treading upon flowers as they lift and set down their feet.

Thus, with every step they achieve celestial bliss, and in every thought-moment they experience the pleasures of the five desires; all their sense faculties never know satiety within their respective domains.

That which is called the eye is constantly covetous of forms; it gazes in various ways with unceasing attachment and delight, causing the eye to find pleasure, yet even upon seeing such forms, it remains unsatisfied;
the ear hears wondrous sounds and knows no satiety.
Thus, regarding the nose and odors: if one smells various fragrances, great lust arises, and one knows no satiety.
The tongue craves delicious flavors and knows no satiety.
Likewise, it craves tactile sensations and knows no satiety.
All such thoughts are merely attachments; they delight in their own bodies while sporting in the forest of the senses, never satiated in their pursuit of desire.
With sensory objects as the mother, the faculties as the kindling, the wind of recollection blowing upon them, and self-exaltation as the fuel, the fire of lust blazes fiercely.
"Unsatisfied with desire, he indulges in pleasure and sports in the Garden of Joy with a mind of craving.
The Lord of the Śakras defeated the asuras on Mount Citrakūṭa and attained great renown, as described above."
Returning again to the Joyful Grove (*Nandana-vana*), he addressed the hosts of devas, saying:

"You, O assembly of devas, should give rise to joy; enter the Joyful Garden to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, sporting and delighting yourselves. I, too, shall sport and enjoy myself within the Joyful Garden."

Having already defeated the Māra army, Vemacitrin, the evil nāgas, and others, all the hosts of devas and celestial maidens may come to my place of recreation to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; for the four months of the rainy season, let us amuse ourselves with the five desires.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had finished speaking these words to the Trāyastriṃśa gods, his heart was filled with great joy, and he addressed the white elephant king Airāvaṇa, saying:
"You are now adorned; I wish to go with you and the assembly of devas, along with the celestial maidens, to sport and enjoy ourselves in the Nandana Grove."

"You should manifest a transformation body, causing the hosts of devas to mount upon the tip of the tusk on your crown, and lead them toward the pleasure-pool gardens and mountain peaks, just as you previously manifested."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the white elephant Airāvaṇa immediately manifested a vast body with a hundred heads; each head had ten tusks, at the tip of each tusk were a hundred bathing pools, in each bathing pool were a thousand lotus flowers, and each lotus flower had a thousand petals made of the seven precious gems. At the tip of every petal were thousands of bees made of the seven precious gems, and between every two petals were a thousand devaputras.
Upon the head of that elephant, various celestial maidens move about without hindering one another, performing divine music as they travel through the void to the Nandana Grove.
On both flanks of the elephant, two groves are manifested:
the first is named the Grove of Joy; [the second is named the Grove of Delight].
The second is named Forest of Joy (Nandavana).
Within that forest, the rivers, ponds, and lotuses are all complete with trees made of the seven treasures; there, the sons of the gods sport and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
The devas and apsaras filled the grove.
Then the great white elephant king Airāvaṇa, resembling a second Mount Sumeru, proceeded toward the Nandana Grove.

Upon the back of that elephant, there appeared a great city, level and soft; its streets and alleys were adorned with palaces of the seven treasures and groves, resembling the second great city, Sudarśana.
Thus, this transformed palace was composed of the seven treasures and adorned with one hundred pillars.
Within the palace was a flower pond, where Śakra, King of the Devas, sported with various celestial maidens, performing divine music.
The Heavenly King Kauśika sat in the great hall facing the Nandana Grove; his body remained as motionless as the summit of Mount Sumeru.
From within the ears of his elephant, lotus ponds further emerged; the first pond was ten yojanas in length and breadth, and the second pond was eleven yojanas.
The first is named Profound;
the second is named Pure.

It is filled with water possessing the eight virtues. Within the pond grow flowers called *utpala*, with stems of lapis lazuli and blossoms of red jewels, adorned by swarms of bees and endowed with celestial fragrances.
The flowers there bloom as blue lotuses (*utpala*); celestial sons and daughters sit upon the filaments of these blossoms, sporting and enjoying themselves.
Some celestial sons sport in the water, while others sport amidst the lotuses, unaware whether the white elephant is moving or standing still.

The tip of that elephant’s trunk transformed into a palace, five yojanas in width, adorned everywhere with various flowers and māndārava blossoms; it resounded with the exquisite songs of bees, and its roof was covered with leaves of gośīrṣa sandalwood.

Furthermore, there were golden trees with various kinds of flowers covering their tops; celestial maidens sat upon the filaments of these flowers, singing many wondrous melodies in praise of the Heavenly King.
Thus, from within the lotus of the White Elephant King, a long palace manifested by the elephant’s trunk was produced; it was one yojana in width and possessed a hundred thousand petals.
Its leaves are broad and long, and its fragrance is supreme, filling ten *yojanas*.

Within each leaf, devas and devīs sport together, yet they do not see one another; thus they play without mutual interference. As they proceed with Śakra, the King of Devas, toward the Nandana Grove, none perceive the elephant’s walking or standing, as if they were situated upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.

Upon the head of the elephant, he further manifested a great mountain named Realm-Adornment (*dhātu-vyūha*), adorned with various realms. There, amidst places adorned with celestial trees, rivers, ponds, groves, and lotuses, they sported and enjoyed pleasures; this is called the Great Mountain Manifested upon the Head of the Elephant King.
Upon the tusks of that White Elephant King, he manifested groves and gardens resembling one hundred million moons, filled with many varieties of flowers.
The ground was pure white, like the color of *sūta*, and it was filled with many bees whose humming was like the song of the *kucīra* bird.
Countless birds, adorned with various jewels—peacocks, kalaviṅkas, and other such immeasurable varieties of birds—are born from its tusks through transformation.
That white elephant king is vast in body; surrounded by hosts of devas, his great form and great strength move with steady, unwavering steps as he proceeds toward the Nandana Grove.

From the two nostrils of that white elephant king, rivers were manifested; just as the waters of the Ganges and the Yamunā flow down from their pools in Jambudvīpa—waters that are pure, cool, and unclouded—so too did the rivers issued from the trunk of the white elephant descend from above.

Throughout the four continents, in the dwelling places of humans, among the forests, trees, and medicinal herbs, despite the drought and scorching heat, the grains and wheat flourish; on the leaves of the plants and trees, a sign of water appears, which is called dew.
The water from the elephant's trunk descends from the sky; because it falls from a great height, it is buffeted by the wind and becomes dispersed and parched, resulting in little dew.
Within the three continents, this is what is called "dew."

"Furthermore, when the celestial white elephant king emits a misty vapor and travels through the heavens, those in the world perceive its color as white; non-Buddhists call this the path traveled by King Indra, while others call it the path of the white elephant king."
Just as clear white water, sustained by the wind, does not fall but remains in mid-air like a mirage, which is seen indistinctly only because it is so far away;

likewise, upon the head of the elephant is the summit of a great mountain, where jeweled banners and flowered canopies hang suspended with precious streamers, and a wheel of lapis lazuli with a cover of pure gold, its radiance shining like the light of the sun.
Long banners were suspended from the top of the standard, and from within those banners issued forth a great radiance.
When the asuras within the great ocean saw this, they said to one another, "The victory banner of Śakra, King of Devas, has appeared;
he is mounting the white elephant king and proceeding toward the Nandana Grove."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the grove from afar, addressed the gods, saying:
"Do you see this grove? It is exceedingly delightful.
Having defeated the asuras, the Lord of the Śākyas now sports in this grove."
These groves and trees are exceedingly delightful.
During the four months of summer, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven sport and enjoy themselves within these forests.
Then the assembly of devas addressed Śakra, saying:
"We shall carry out whatever Your Majesty commands.
Having spoken these words, they drew near to the Forest of Joy (Nandana-vana).

The devas who previously resided within the Nandana Grove, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, saw the celestial victory banner and the king of white elephants. Their hearts were filled with great joy as they went out to welcome Śakra; they prostrated and made offerings, joining their palms above their heads, and accompanied by celestial music, song, dance, and play, they entered the Nandana Grove.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately descended from the white elephant and entered the Nandana Grove together with the hosts of devas; all the other celestial hosts likewise descended from their elephants.

Thus, from the heads, trunks, and tips of the noses of the elephants, as well as from the flanks of the elephants, all the celestial hosts abandoned the white elephants and entered the Nandana Forest to sport and enjoy themselves.

The various devas who previously resided in the Nandana Grove, along with the Lord of Devas and the hosts of devas who had defeated the asuras, enjoyed celestial pleasures during the four months of summer.
The Śakra-devānām-indra, together with the hosts of devas, enjoys pleasures and amuses himself.

At such a time, if the good karma of any of those sons of gods is about to be exhausted, and eventually their beloved good karma is spent, they pass away and fall back, descending into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will constantly experience peace and happiness; possessing supreme understanding and being foremost in physical beauty, one will be beloved by all people. One will be born in delightful places such as mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds, ruling over a great kingdom with wealth, joy, and sovereignty.
This is due to residual karma.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa: by what karmic conditions did he achieve such a massive body and great supernormal powers, and how did he gain great renown by fighting with the asuras?
By what karma did they receive a birth in the bodies of animals?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these beings had a lifespan of seventy thousand years when they were in the heavens. In a past life, there was a *brahmin* named Unaraṇa who extensively cultivated merit and was fond of practicing charity toward those who were poor, blind, and suffering.
Because of his virtuous mind, he always delighted in giving and benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, there was a king named Sudarśana who, on the day of a festival, left the palace to go out for recreation like the hosts of devas.
Accompanied by eighty-four thousand great white elephant kings, covered with golden nets and adorned with precious bells, appearing just like the Tathāgata;

adorned with all kinds of golden bells and surrounded by eighty-four thousand court ladies, the sounds of eighty-four thousand musical instruments resounded as they proceeded toward the pleasure gardens and palaces.
This was the foremost majesty of King Sudarśana, who experienced the fruit of great bliss.
At that time, a brahmin endowed with full majesty went to the place where King Sudarśana was sporting.

This brahmin, named Samata, saw that this great king was endowed with majestic power. The king possessed a white elephant named Meghasamcaya (Cloud-Cluster), adorned with precious bells and necklaces of pearls and golden nets; it was a magnificent white elephant fashioned by skilled artisans, accompanied by various songs and performances as it proceeded to the pleasure grounds, being foremost in its exquisite beauty.
At that time, the brahmin Samata thought to himself:
"This white elephant king enjoys the foremost happiness; I vow to be reborn as the white elephant king for Śakra, Lord of the Devas."
"By the power of his generosity and the power of his vows, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven as the White Elephant King, the mount of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Having observed this, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
'This artisan of karma, Drawn here and there by his own deeds, ...'"
The power of the mind-king is exceedingly great, producing all manner of retributions.
Driven by superior causes and conditions, it is everywhere impelled by mental factors;
in every single place, it travels along the paths of the three realms.
The karma of all sentient beings causes the mind to act with autonomy;
therefore, by taming the mind, one can reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Lightly shifting and difficult to subdue, it falsely grasps at objects everywhere.
If one well subdues the mind, through such subduing there is peace and happiness.
If one can subdue the mind, then one can sever all faults;
the brave one, having left behind transgressions and evils, shall no longer undergo various sufferings.
Whether it be suffering in this world, or suffering in future lives,
all such lack of self-mastery arises from the cause and condition of a frivolous mind.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, asuras, hell-beings, pretas, or rākṣasas, [they are all subject to this].
The mind is always the guiding master, like a king traveling through the three realms.
The mind leads one to the heavens, and again leads one among human beings;
the mind leads one to the evil paths, as the mind revolves through the world.
The wheel of the mind revolves and destroys people;
deluded by sense objects, sentient beings are swept away by craving and experience boundless suffering in the present.
Constantly hidden and covered, it is a great power difficult to subdue.
Harmful yet invisible, light-moving and swiftly flowing—
if a person possesses wisdom and tames such a mind,
that person will escape the net of Māra and be able to reach the further shore.
Recalling the mind that is crooked, deceitful, and perverse— deep yet extremely fickle and restless—
is a wicked and treacherous precipice that leads people to the evil realms.
Thus, one should abandon all such evils and not be enslaved by the sensory faculties.
Not clinging to any unwholesome dharmas, one attains the state of non-extinction.
The mind arises from causes and conditions; what is required is obtained from the mind.
Conditions turn and flow swiftly; such is the manner of its continuous evolution.
Thus one performs various karmas and obtains diverse retributions;
the subtle mind flows on, never remaining still for even a single thought-moment.
Its sphere of activity cannot be known, and it is forever without form or color.
To what place does he lead people?
By what path does he travel?
Having arrived, in what place does he abide?
The body is produced by karma; one sees the actions performed by the mind, yet the agent cannot be seen.
This mind is difficult to subdue; its form cannot be seen, yet it harms all sentient beings everywhere. Sightless, it swiftly creates karma.
The nature of this mind is like an illusion; from evil, one receives an evil retribution.
The nature of this mind is like an illusion; its sphere of activity is extremely difficult to know, for it can lead all people to immeasurable places of birth and death.
It cannot be cut by a blade, nor can it be burned by fire;
though this mind has no eyes, it consumes and harms all people.
The rope of karma is exceedingly firm and binds those who are afflicted by suffering.
One undergoes hundreds of thousands of births and deaths, yet that which departs cannot be seen.
In an instant one performs wholesome karma; in an instant one gives rise to unwholesome karma.
Since the mind creates both the wholesome and the unwholesome, through its subduing one attains happiness.
"The six sense faculties encounter their objects; With much greed, they know no satisfaction.
Failing to realize that the mind is approaching [its end], One suffers affliction in the evil realms.
Thus, the bhikṣu observed that although the brahmin performed great wholesome deeds, his aspirations were narrow and small. Seeing this, he reflected and admonished his own mind.
Through such wholesome karma, one may either attain a celestial body or transcend birth and death; yet one remains subject to the dictates of the mind.
If one falls among the animals, it is due to the power of the mind's aspirations.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the ninth ground is named Radiance (Prabhāsvara).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place? He sees, hears, and knows:

if there are people who maintain the precepts and teach them to others; who do not commit evil themselves nor incite others to do so; who, seeing others committing evil, urge them to abandon it; who personally guard the prohibitive precepts and teach others to guard them with firmness and without deficiency, causing all to be pure; and who neither kill nor steal.
What is meant by "not killing"?
If one sees a place where there are many sentient beings, for the sake of upholding the precepts, one does not dig it oneself, nor does one instruct others to dig.
Whether it be scorpions, ants, frogs, or various other creatures, knowing the dwelling places of these beings, one does not destroy them oneself, nor does one cause others to do so.
Whether they have received the prohibitive precepts or not, if one sees them committing evil, one instructs them to perform repentance.
How does one refrain from stealing?

If it is another's land, or the site of a potter, or anything belonging to others—even down to a clod of mud—one does not steal it oneself, nor does one instruct others to take it, thereby causing others to abide in the precepts.
When seeing others steal, one does not give rise to approval, but exhorts them not to do so.
This is called non-killing and non-stealing.

After such a person who maintains the precepts passes away, they are reborn in the Heaven of Light (Ābhāsvara), where their minds are constantly joyful; they enjoy themselves with singing, dancing, laughter, and play, and the radiance of their bodies constantly illuminates the celestial hosts.
There are many celestial gardens where devas sport; those who practiced the foremost precepts and performed wholesome deeds are born in this heavenly realm to receive such rewards of bliss.
All the gardens are covered with nets of gold, and the exquisite sounds of precious bells and *vaiḍūrya* chimes are produced by their own wholesome karma.
From afar, they saw the Son of Heaven singing praises within his bells, saying:
"Welcome, O Son of Heaven!
You who have cultivated goodness."
He then composed a verse in a tranquil meter, saying:
"By guarding the precepts with a well-peaceful mind, One who maintains the precepts experiences the coolness of bliss now."
By properly maintaining various practices of the precepts, one later attains nirvana or pleasant rewards;
or, by warding off the evil realms, one reaches a place of excellence. Therefore, the observance of the precepts results in ultimate coolness.
When a person who upholds the precepts faces the end of life, their mind is peaceful and free from fear;
they have no dread of the evil realms, for the pure observance of the precepts can provide protection.
“You have well protected yourself by maintaining the precepts; now that you have reached the heavens, do not be heedless.
Thus, by virtue of his wholesome karma, the sound of the bells in the net recited these verses to awaken the mind of the deva and cause him to abandon heedlessness.

There are certain sons of gods who, having observed the precepts for a long time in previous lives, upon hearing this Dharma, maintain their precepts for a short while and do not fall into negligence.

However, if a god has observed the precepts for only a few lifetimes, he will fall into negligence without realizing it; though he hears the sound of the Dharma, he immediately lapses into negligence, departs from the awakening sounds of the bell-nets, and proceeds to another grove.
The Grove of Radiance is adorned with the seven treasures; it is three thousand yojanas in breadth and length, and except for the four grounds and the city of Sudarśana, nothing else surpasses it.

In the four directions of that grove, there are four wish-fulfilling *vaiḍūrya* trees, pure and stainless; their light shines universally, filling one *yojana*, and with a brilliance like the sun, they are visible for five thousand *yojanas*.
The sons of gods and daughters of gods dwell among the branches of the trees, sporting and enjoying pleasures; whatever they conceive in their minds, they obtain from the trees.

Within these four groves is a forest of radiant light, where lotus ponds are made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. The adornments of the forest trees resemble masses of molten gold. Everywhere there is the flavor of *sudhā*; it is perfectly pure and stainless, clean, fragrant, exquisite, powerful, and spontaneously present as the flavor of *sudhā*.

Furthermore, there were various birds that were lovely to behold; their voices were exquisite and served as an adornment. They had heads of pure gold, wings of white silver, chests of lapis lazuli, beaks of red jewels, and eyes of lotus-colored gems.
Thus these various birds serve as adornments: upon the silver-leafed trees are golden birds;
upon the golden trees are silver birds;
and upon the lapis lazuli trees are red lotus-colored birds.
There are red lotus trees and king-of-blue-jewels birds;
all the various birds drink wine and eat fruit, while seven-jeweled trees and birds of seven-jeweled colors sport upon them.
Furthermore, there are swarms of bees like red jewel-flowers, which have received their bodies as the result of various karmas, sporting and enjoying themselves within the lotuses.
Thus, all the reflections of every merit are fully present within these trees, and the devas and devīs sport and amuse themselves upon them.
That grove is fully endowed with the merits of the devas; when the devas and asuras engage in battle, Śakra, King of Devas, commands the hosts of devas:
"Adorn yourselves with haste!"
"The asura army is harassing the devas dwelling on the summit of Mount Sudarśana.

Having heard these words, the Trāyastriṃśa devas turned toward the Āloka Grove, where all the celestial hosts, together with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, entered the Āloka Grove situated between four trees.
The vaidūrya trees are as pure as clear mirrors; one sees one's own form within them and knows whether one will be victorious or defeated in battle.
If any part of the body is damaged, it is all clearly seen.
Thus, within these trees, one sees one's own body being struck, harmed, or cut; though it is destroyed, it is restored to life.
If one sees [beings] having their heads severed or their waists severed, they immediately vanish;
all of this is clearly seen within these trees.
Just as it was seen, he informed the devaputras: "You should avoid untimely death; this will be of great benefit."
The asuras fought and killed this deva-son.
Having heard this, Śakra said:
"Great Seer!..."
"Do not engage in battle; you will surely suffer ruin and harm, meeting an untimely death.
The bhikṣu, reflecting and observing within the celestial tree, saw the signs of decline and extinction, and through the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), he knew:
"If a person, with a compassionate heart, sees a butcher about to kill a living being and causes that being to escape."
By virtue of this karmic retribution, they perceive their own physical forms within the Forest of Radiance (*Prabhāsvanavana*).

Furthermore, the gods proceed to the Forest of Radiance known as the Mixed Forest (*Miśrakāvana*), where they dwell in the Forest of Radiance, which is adorned with wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
Having entered this grove, they each reflected:
"Between the devas and the asuras, whose power is superior?
By what power do the devas attain superiority?"
"By what power do the asuras prevail?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of devas:
"Those who practice the Dharma are born among the various devas."

At the beginning of the kalpa, the people of Jambudvīpa practiced the ten paths of wholesome action; some instructed others and exhorted themselves to maintain the seven types of precepts, observing them without deficiency or leakage, with firm resolve and without guile.
In this way, these beings, at the end of their lives, are born in the heavens.
It is like a leather bag filled with sand; if its mouth is not tied shut, a person of great strength can empty it quickly when pouring it out.
At the beginning of the kalpa, when beings were born among the gods, it was likewise so.
Therefore, the power of the gods increased while the strength of the asura hosts diminished; the gods dwelling on the summit of Mount Sudarśana were able to repel the asuras.
Furthermore, at a later time, people practice unwholesome deeds; their conduct is flawed and lacking in steadfastness, and they perform only a small amount of wholesome karma.
When those in Jambudvīpa die, they are reborn in the heavens.
It is like when mangoes are about to ripen, and a strong man shakes the tree; only a few fruits fall, and it is the same way for those born in the heavens.

Furthermore, at another time, he performed various defiled actions; he did not maintain the precepts of body, nor did he maintain the precepts of speech; he was neither firm nor pure, and did not practice constantly.
When such persons die, few are reborn among the devas.
It is like the fruit of the great *bīra* tree: while the fruit is unripe, even if a person of little strength shakes it, they cannot make it move;
and even if they manage to move it, very few fruits fall.
If a fruit is ripe, it falls; if it is not yet ripe, it does not fall. It is just so with the beings at the beginning of the eon:
many were born in the heavens, whereas in later ages those born in the heavens become very few. This is likewise because they have been defiled by impurities and have violated the precepts.
"You gods, do not act with negligence; if you act with negligence, you will increase the ranks of the asuras and diminish the assembly of the devas.

Nowadays, sentient beings mostly practice what is contrary to the Dharma and lack the precepts; they do not observe the sevenfold precepts of body and speech, but instead deceive and delude others, causing them to give rise to feverish affliction. They are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, and do not comply with the practice of the Dharma."
When such a person’s life ends, they fall into hell.
It is like a leather bag filled with sand; if its mouth is not tied shut and a strong man pours it out, the sand comes out quickly.
The way sentient beings of the present age fall into the realm of asuras by performing unwholesome deeds is likewise.
If sentient beings observe even half of the precepts, whether through body or speech, such persons, at the end of their lives, will be born among the asuras or perhaps in the heavens.
It is like a mango tree that a person of great strength shakes.
If the fruit is ripe, it falls as soon as the tree is shaken;
if it is not yet ripe, it does not fall even when shaken.
Sentient beings with mixed karma are also like this: some are born among the devas, some fall into hell, and some are born among the asuras.

If all those in the world practice only what is unwholesome—being unfilial toward their parents, not following the path of Dharma, not respecting teachers, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and failing to maintain the precepts of body and speech—[they likewise suffer such consequences].
When such a person’s life ends, they fall into hell or else fall among the asuras; consequently, the forces of the asura armies increase in great power, while the power of the devas diminishes.
"Even so, I am now able to defeat the army of the asuras, and not the other hosts of devas.
You should reflect upon this and practice the way of Dharma, guarding the true Dharma in both this life and future lives."
Among all powers, the power of the Dharma is supreme; none can equal it.
You should contemplate and keep the True Dharma in mind, exerting yourself with diligence to defeat the asuras.
At that time, having heard these instructions spoken by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, the host of devas addressed Śakra, saying:
"We shall carry out what the Heavenly King has taught."
Having spoken these words, he went toward the Forest of Armor (Kavaca-vana), where from the trees emerged indestructible armor with which he adorned himself.
Those who wear this armor can have no enemy; its radiance shines like the sun rising over Mount Udayana, and its brilliant splendor is likewise so.
They headed toward Mount Sudarśana, desiring to array their forces for a great battle with the asuras, as previously described.
Meanwhile, the devas dwelling within the Forest of Radiance amused one another, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses with heedless minds.
In the forests of beryl, golden trees, and red jewel groves, flowers and fruits abound, and various birds emit exquisite songs.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the various birds and beasts within the Heaven of the Thirty-three, which possess diverse colors, diverse adornments, diverse forms, diverse sounds, and diverse jewel-feathers, sporting and enjoying themselves amidst the gardens and groves.
Observing this as it truly is, one understands the subtle causes, conditions, and karmic retributions.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees that sentient beings act as skilled painters; though they receive wages for their labor, they do so without deceitful intent, performing meritorious deeds for others by painting monasteries, lecture halls, and viharas with bright and pure colors, using various hues such as blue, yellow, vermilion, and purple to depict Buddha-stupas, vihara gate-towers, and pavilions.

They fashioned mountains, trees, humans, dragons, birds, and beasts—such as lions, tigers, and deer—as well as gardens, groves, cities, walls, bathing pools, pleasure grounds, lotus forests, ponds, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, military camps, and palaces; they depicted these forms and adorned them for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha and as causes and conditions for his majesty.
Hired for wages, some carve and engrave, while others fashion images from clay, wood, gold, silver, copper, and other materials.

When these various artisans pass away, they are reborn in the heavens; yet because they performed diverse tasks without observing the precepts, they receive the bodies of various birds, or the forms of deer, or the bodies of swarms of bees, where they constantly experience happiness.
According to the nature of the karma one performs, one obtains a corresponding fruit.

Just as the devas experience pleasure, those who perform actions without wisdom—though they possess the faculty of volition—experience pleasure through a body of delusion because of their lack of wisdom; they sport and enjoy themselves within the celestial groves.
The mountain forests and peaks are like paintings carved in relief; ivory, silver, and gold appear as if naturally formed, like objects produced by a seal.
Within the celestial gardens, immeasurable colors arise, just like original pigments.

The devas further sport, sing, and dance within this Forest of Radiance, experiencing various pleasures. When their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from this Heaven of Radiance and, transmigrating according to their karma, fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there is wholesome karma, one will be born among human beings and constantly experience peace and happiness; one may become a king or a high minister, receiving offerings from immeasurable people, delighting in recreation and play, loving festivals and gatherings, with a mind always joyful, a handsome countenance, and food and drink according to one's wish. One will constantly enjoy such peace and happiness that others cannot take it away.
They possess abundant bedding, mattresses, dwellings, gardens for recreation, and male and female servants.
This is due to their residual karma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the tenth stage is named Pāriyātra.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows this:

if a person possesses pure faith and, having long since renounced worldly possessions, gives gifts such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; and furthermore, teaches others not to kill sentient beings, extending even to insects and ants, so that they do not give rise to a murderous intent.
If one sees fruit being eaten by insects, one does not eat that fruit in order to protect their lives; seeing others eating it, one exhorts them not to do so.
Upholding the precepts oneself, one further teaches others to do the same.
What is non-stealing?
Regarding the property of others, one does not take even as much as root-food or fruit-food.
Whether in the forest or in an open space, one neither takes it oneself nor instructs others to do so.
Such a person, benefiting both themselves and others, after the end of their life, will be reborn in the Pāriyātra tree grove.
The Pāriyātra tree is the foremost and most excellent; from this single tree, it is able to manifest the signs of good and evil for the people of Jambudvīpa.
If the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, the flowers and fruits of those trees will become fully abundant.

Because the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, the radiance of the flowers illuminates a hundred yojanas, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwell surrounding them with hearts full of joy.

In this way, when the flowers and fruits of the Pāriyātra tree flourish and thrive, it is known that the people of Jambudvīpa are filial toward their parents and provide offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and senior monks; for this reason, the flowers and fruits of this tree bloom in such abundance.
In the fourth month of summer, the hosts of devas surround this tree to enjoy themselves and experience pleasure.

When the flowers of the Pāriyātra tree have only half emerged, they feel slight joy, knowing that the people of Jambudvīpa maintain the precepts only in small measure, which causes this celestial tree to produce only half its blossoms.

If all people were to practice entirely what is contrary to the Dharma, then the flowers of this celestial tree, the Pāriyātra, would all fall; their color would wither, they would lose their radiance, and they would also lose their fragrance.
For example, it is like the sun in winter when obscured by clouds and mist; its radiance is not clear, and its sight does not dazzle the eyes.
In this same way, the radiance of the Pāriyātra and Kovidāra trees is faint, their fragrance diminished, and their appearance withered.
At that time, when the assembly of devas had witnessed this event, they addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
The radiance of the Pāriyātra tree has diminished, its fragrance has grown weak, and all its majestic virtues are no longer as they were before."
"This must be because the people of Jambudvīpa are unfilial toward their parents and do not respect śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, or senior monks.

Upon hearing this, Śakra took the precious image and, together with the assembly of devas, reverently made offerings to it, honoring and praising the likeness of the Tathāgata and recollecting the Buddha’s merits. He then addressed the assembly of devas:
"The flowers and leaves of this Pāriyātra-kovidāra tree have fallen; I shall now go beneath that tree, and you all should prepare yourselves."

"With a virtuous mind, I shall now take the stūpa of the Tathāgata and the image of the World-Honored One to the foot of that tree, and with celestial ointments and powdered incense, I shall make offerings to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having heard the instruction of Śakra, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of devas went to where Śakra was.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, placed an image of the Tathāgata upon his celestial crown and, wearing it upon his head, proceeded to the Pāriyātra tree grove.
He saw that the hosts of devas there were all devoid of joy; because the leaves of those Pāriyātra trees had fallen and they had lost their original radiance, they were consequently displeased.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, placed an image of the Tathāgata upon a seat of vaidūrya on ground made of the seven treasures beneath a tree. All the hosts of devas gave rise to faith and reverence, conceiving a heart of profound respect; they made offerings with celestial māluṅga flowers, celestial māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, and kauseyaśa flowers—such various blossoms as these—and bathed the image of the Tathāgata with fragrant water.
Having made such offerings, he instructed the assembly of devas: "You should give rise to faith and reverence, abandon stinginess and envy, and leave behind all heedlessness.
This Buddha-Tathāgata is the Great Teacher of the triple world, along with the Holy Sangha of the True Dharma."
Upon hearing the instruction of Śakra, all the sons of the gods conceived respectful faith and prostrated themselves before the image of the Tathāgata, the Honored One among Gods.
At that time, Śakra praised him with these verses:
“The Tathāgata has liberated himself from the poison of affection; He holds all sentient beings as his own kin.”
"Having long since crossed the ocean of birth and death, Homage, homage to the All-Knowing One!

At that time, Śakra joined his palms in reverence toward the image of the Tathāgata; together with the assembly of devas, he knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and further praised the Tathāgata with these verses:
"The Tathāgata has forever severed desire, greed, and hatred; He is eternally free from feverish affliction and is immeasurable."
"Unsurpassed Teacher of all sentient beings, Homage, homage to the All-Knowing One!
Having praised the Buddha with these verses, the entire assembly of devas surrounded the King of Trees, revering the Tathāgata and giving rise to the great faculty of faith.
Thus, all these hosts of devas, with pure and virtuous minds, increased the True Dharma and made offerings to the Buddha image.
At that time, the Pāriyātra tree immediately put forth buds and new leaves were about to emerge; when the devas saw this, they were all filled with great joy.
Before long, that tree will successively sprout flowers and leaves, no different from its original state; its radiance will illuminate one hundred *yojanas*, and its fragrance shall be likewise.
Its leaves will be the color of clouds, surrounded by swarms of bees, and its shadow will be fresh and lustrous, encircled by hosts of devas like a second sun. One shall behold its majestic splendor:
its fragrance will pervade one hundred *yojanas*, its branches will cover one hundred *yojanas*, and its roots shall be the same.
All the hosts of devas were filled with great joy.
The radiance and fragrance of that king of celestial trees were fully restored to their original state.
It was like how, among the sixty thousand mountains, Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is preeminent.
Among all the various trees, the radiance and adornment of the Pāriyātra tree are likewise supreme and foremost.

Beholding its superior light, its magnificent and sublime majesty, which is fully pervasive and complete; its brilliant purity, its manifest appearance, and its perfect blazing flames—the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven see it and rejoice, saying to one another:
"O you sons of the gods!..."
"Do you see how great the power of the Buddha is?
This king of celestial trees, with its flowers, leaves, radiance, and fragrance, is fully endowed and remains no different than it was before.
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three saw the superior power and radiance of the tree, they were all freed from the net of doubt.

“The people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma; as their mindfulness of the Dharma becomes supreme, the armies of Māra shall diminish, and neither unrighteous evil nāgas nor asuras shall be able to destroy them.”
"For those who act in accordance with the Dharma, the True Dharma increases, the hosts of devas do not diminish, and they shall no longer be inferior among the celestial maidens.
The armies of Māra will decrease, while the hosts of devas become mighty."
"By the characteristics of the King of Trees, one should know that the devas possess great majesty and power.
Thus did each of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three speak.
At that time, the World-Protector went from Jambudvīpa to the second heaven, to the grove of the Pārijāta, the King of Trees.
At that time, the World-Protectors saw the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven beneath the Pāriyātra tree making offerings to the Tathāgata with pure minds, their bodies emitting radiance.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of Śakra and addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"The great assembly of devas should now rejoice.
Now, all the people of Jambudvīpa follow the practice of the Dharma; they make offerings to their parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and they show reverence to their elders."
When the assembly of devas heard what he said, they were all greatly delighted; they made offerings to the World-Protector and spoke these words:
"You have brought us joy; may you likewise always experience such auspicious gladness."
Because he had spoken thus regarding how the people of Jambudvīpa practice the Dharma, when the assembly of devas heard these words spoken by the World-Protecting Deva, they again prepared offerings.
Having made these offerings, they took the image of the Tathāgata and proceeded to the Hall of the Good Dharma (Saddharmasabhā).

The devas of the Tree-King [Grove] and Śakra, Lord of Devas, returned to the Pāriyātra tree grove, where for the four months of the summer retreat they enjoyed celestial pleasures, sporting and delighting themselves.
Surrounded by celestial maidens, they sport and enjoy pleasures for four months of summer.
If any son of heaven passes away from this life, he wanders according to his karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there is prior karma such that one is born among humans, one will have a handsome and upright countenance that people delight to behold; the mind will be constantly joyful, peaceful, and free from affliction; one will be loved and respected by all, constantly entertaining oneself with song, dance, and laughter; and whenever any woman sees such a person, she will feel love and respect for them, whether they become a king or a high minister.
Due to the remaining karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 27;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 28.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Observing the Heavens, Part Seven; The Fourth [Section] on the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the ground where the Heaven of the Thirty-three resides."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the eleventh level of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named "Leaving the Precipitous Shore.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He hears and understands:

if a person maintains the precepts to benefit sentient beings, their merit perfumes the mind; or if a person of virtue maintains the precepts with wisdom; or again, if one gives even a single meal to a sick person.
Regarding abstaining from taking life oneself:

if there are insects, ants, or various minute creatures within hollow trees; or if there are people herding oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, camels, or donkeys; or if, during the cold winter months when ice, snow, and frost descend, one sets fire to the wilderness—should there be a virtuous person who extinguishes such a fire with water or earth, seeing the act they urge others to desist from it; one does not intentionally commit such acts oneself, and if one has committed them, one repents, does not give rise to approval, explains the terrors [of such deeds] to others, and causes them to abide in wholesome dharmas.
Causing those sentient beings to abide in wholesome dharmas, one neither steals oneself nor instructs others to do so.
Such a person, at the end of life, will be reborn in the Heaven of the Shore Free from Peril.

The ground was paved with gold, silver, and various kinds of red jewels; it was thus adorned with various combinations of gold, silver, and diverse gems, and filled with various precious stones. It was beautified by various jewel-trees and various birds and beasts that graced the land. Everywhere, including the rugged slopes, there were species of birds and beasts, and all the groves and gardens were adorned with immeasurable seven-jeweled treasures.
