The deva Viṣamapāra resides in this forest; his ornaments are like masses of molten gold, and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, he enjoys the pleasures of the five senses.
Wherever they dwell, their bodies emit radiance, and the light from the trees on the banks is likewise like that of celestial bodies; thus they sport and enjoy themselves within this forest.

Accompanied by various heavenly maidens, they proceed to the river groves; on both banks of the river stand many golden trees with leaves of pure gold, and by the radiance of these trees, the water is turned yellow, entirely devoid of any white color.
The current flows so swiftly that no white color can be seen.
Amidst the groves, the devas and apsaras play and enjoy themselves.
A deva then thinks to himself:
"From within this tree, delicious drinks should now emerge.

Due to their wholesome karma, as soon as they think of them, various kinds of delicious drinks—complete with color, fragrance, and flavor—flow forth immediately, which they drink from vessels made of various jewels.
Drinking the flavors of the heavens, they experience celestial bliss.
Seeing the various goddesses consumed by the fire of passion, they remain unaware because their perception is shrouded by pleasure.
The deva-son then reflects:
"I now wish to hear various sounds.
Due to his wholesome karma, according to his thoughts, the wind moves the trees and produces exquisite sounds that surpass the music of the five instruments.
The Son of Heaven thought again:
"Now, from this tree, the flavor of *srotas* (ambrosia) should emerge.

Due to his virtuous karma, according to his thought, it immediately flowed from the tree like the pouring of contents from a large vessel; descending from above, its flavor could not be compared to that of rock honey.

The deva-son partakes of this food, sings various wondrous melodies, and proceeds to the jeweled ground. There he gazes intently and observes with constant delight and longing, experiencing the pleasures of the five desires within that jeweled ground.

Having left this place, he proceeded further to a grove of plum trees (*pruṇa*). Within that grove there were seven kinds of birds: geese made of the seven precious jewels with pure gold; parrots made of *indranīla* sapphire; mandarin ducks made of vermilion-colored gems; wild ducks made of *vaiḍūrya* beryl; peacocks made of blue gems and musaragalva; *jīvajīvaka* birds made of the great blue seven-jewels; and *kalaviṅka* birds made of coral and silver.

Their voices were as exquisite as the song of the kalaviṅka bird, a sound that all delight in hearing; they soared through the air, sporting and amusing themselves, their voices as beautiful as the songs of celestial maidens.
In the lotus ponds, they sport amidst the adornments of swarms of bees; furthermore, they soar and play upon the land.

There are also golden trees, the shadows of whose various leaves reflect and grace the bodies of the birds. When the devas see these many birds, their hearts give rise to joy; hearing their songs with their ears, their minds are filled with delight.
The deva-sons roam through the sky sporting with the birds, or sport with them in the water, or sport together with them on the land.
Thus the hosts of devas sport with the birds; the deva-sons and deva-maidens entertain one another, and the celestial birds, paired as mates, sport and experience pleasure.
Having observed the birds experiencing celestial pleasures, the bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“Animals engage in desire through the power of delusion; if the devas were likewise so, they would be no different from animals.”
When a person enjoys wealth and pleasure, yet does not become attached to or negligent, they are a wise person; the fool is the opposite.
Negligence leads even a deva to hell; as the wise have said, negligence is like poison.
Foolish and negligent, attached to present pleasures, when the fruits of negligence ripen, one later gives rise to great regret.
Contemplating negligence, one sees it brings not the slightest benefit; if one abandons negligence, one will always be free from sorrow and affliction.
Heedlessness is great suffering; heedfulness is happiness. To state the essential point: one should abandon heedlessness.
If a person loves suffering, they should practice heedlessness; but for one who delights in practicing heedlessness, there will ultimately be no reward of happiness.
Delighting in heedfulness, they reach the state of non-retrogression; by not practicing heedlessness, they are forever free from the retribution of suffering.
These hosts of devas sport with birds; between devas and animals, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The realms, paths, bodies, and minds—all are subject to destruction; so too are gods, humans, non-humans, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts.
The various divisions of karma are likewise the same for the paths; such are the manifold and diverse karmic actions.
Born among the gods, you are attached to pleasure and negligence, unaware of your impending decline.
When the signs of death arrive, you shall know for yourself that you are falling from the celestial realm and will undergo great suffering and distress.
Harmed by delusion and deceived by heedlessness, the gods, driven by craving, fall into hell.
Deceived by their own playful pleasures, they fall into hell; having experienced celestial bliss, they subsequently undergo great suffering.
"Deluded by the mind, they do not weary of birth and death;
deceived by craving, they pass from suffering into suffering.
Thus, with these verses, the bhikṣu rebuked the heedless sons of the gods, who were greedy for the five desires and knew no satiety, like fire finding fuel.
Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall back from the heavens and, driven by the flow of karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they possess remaining wholesome karma, they will be born among humans, constantly experiencing peace and happiness; food and drink will be abundant, the land will be prosperous and joyful, the five grains will ripen in abundance, and they may become kings or high ministers.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The twelfth stage of the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods is named Ravine Precipice.
By what kind of karma are these beings born in that heaven?
They perceive and know thus:
If a person, with a virtuous mind, practices meritorious deeds by giving food to a practitioner of dhyāna who has attained the first dhyāna;
if they give their own food, teach others to give food, rejoice after giving, and teach others to rejoice—this is called generosity (dāna).
Regarding non-killing and non-stealing:

if one practices the Way among people, at places such as wells, springs, ponds, or streams where water is provided for public use, one should offer jars, vessels, and drinking implements to supply those traveling on the road.
Furthermore, suppose there is another person who instructs someone else to steal and carry [goods] across a wilderness, saying:
"If you do not take them, you will surely suffer from thirst and exhaustion.

At that time, although that person knows they would die of thirst, because they fear committing a transgression, they do not accept the instruction; they do not steal the property, nor do they rejoice in the act. They urge others not to take it, leading them to abide in the path of goodness, such that even at the cost of their own life, they do not commit theft.
What is non-killing? It is to personally refrain from killing, to exhort others not to kill, and to disparage the act of killing.

If there are minute insects within the windows or door-panels of a house, or upon the rafters, one does not close the doors or windows when lighting a fire for fear of harming their lives; this is called non-killing.
Furthermore, they teach others to practice non-killing and abide in the path of goodness.
Such persons, at the end of their lives, will be reborn among the gods of the Valley Cliff Bank in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, receiving the retribution of their wholesome karma.

There is a grove of trees named *Anuparivartin* (Ever-Bending); its various trees possess the radiance of many jewels, and it is made of pure, stainless blue *vaiḍūrya*. Various birds emit wondrous sounds, and flowers are always in full bloom. It is adorned with flowing springs, rivers, and ponds, where blue *vaiḍūrya* serves as the lotuses, and golden peaks are adorned like masses of molten gold.
Various colored birds sport therein, whether in the water or on the land, or upon mountain peaks, precipitous cliffs, and mountain caves, emitting manifold wonderful sounds.
Transformed by their virtuous karma, they experience the fruits of that virtuous karma.

Surrounded by various celestial maidens, adorned with divine garlands and celestial garments, their physical forms and majestic virtues are exceptionally beautiful and sublime as they dance, sing, and sport within this forest.
Due to their virtuous karma, the birds and deer in the grove spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds Receive happiness among the devas;
If they perform unwholesome deeds, They suffer painful retribution in hell.”
Having been born among the gods, one is able to attain self-awakening;
from happiness one obtains the fruit of happiness, and is not deluded by craving.
The ropes of karma bind sentient beings, keeping them long within the prison of the three realms of existence.
The power of karma turns with sovereign mastery, like a hub turning the many spokes.
It revolves through the three realms of existence, in the eight directions and above and below.
Blown by the wind of karmic power, it wanders like dust in the void of space.
Born from causes and conditions, like a lotus in full adornment,
such celestial ornaments all arise from virtuous karma.
Like pure, clear water, like the sky free from dust.
With such a purified mind, one can reach the place of peace and happiness.
One who has liberated themselves from the three bonds, who guards the five faculties,
and who stays far removed from the one thing that leads to ruin, shall enjoy peace and happiness among the devas.
One who lacks shame and dread of blame, an undisciplined evil friend, is like poison and like fire; the wise should abandon them.
One who speaks the truth and practices generosity should always be delighted to associate with.
Always maintaining a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings— this path leads to birth among the devas.
With a straightforward mind free from flattery and crookedness, practicing generosity and cultivating right mindfulness,
through these causes and conditions of one's own karma, one is born here in this celestial realm.
All life in the world arises from both the Dharma and the non-Dharma;
there is no protection superior to the Dharma, therefore one should practice the Dharma.
If a person abandons the Dharma and delights in performing unwholesome deeds, [they will suffer].
Burned by the fires of evil, one suffers without end.
Having already attained birth in heaven, if one gives rein to a heedless mind, that person’s wholesome karma will be exhausted;
it is only at the time of falling away that they realize it for themselves.
Ultimate bliss is supreme; there is neither birth nor death.
The net of death binds sentient beings, leaving no place of peace and happiness.
Wherever one follows the pursuit of pleasure, the craving heart only grows stronger.
The fire of craving burns sentient beings, who then suffer the retribution of hell.
Do not practice heedlessness, for it is unbecoming of the gods;
destroyed by the fault of heedlessness, one falls away from the celestial realms.

"When the celestial bird preached this Dharma in this manner, the mind of the deva-son became distracted; he thought of the celestial maidens and neither listened to nor accepted the beneficial Dharma. Thirsting for the five desires, his mind became deeply attached, and he took pleasure and delight in sporting at the lotus ponds."
Again, they went to a mountain peak named Mountain of Joyful Play (*Ratikrīḍā*). There was a bird there called Playful Delight (*Kilakila*), which frolicked in the ponds and entertained one another.
When the gods saw the bird, they thought to themselves:
"How marvelous!"
"This bird, with its various colors and various songs, surpasses all other birds.
At that time, the deva-son further thought:
"I shall now ride this bird to roam and observe the groves and ponds."

Once the deva had thought this, the bird’s body immediately transformed and became massive. Thereupon, the devaputra stroked it with his hand, mounted it, and traveled through the air, soaring about and enjoying bliss.

The Devaputra further thought to transform a seven-jeweled palace upon the back of the bird, complete with gardens, groves, and flower ponds, adorned with various kinds of birds. Ascending into the void, surrounded by celestial maidens in various ornaments, he sported everywhere and experienced manifold pleasures, surveying all the abodes where the devas dwell.
Having observed this, his attachment increased a hundred-thousandfold, beyond all comparison.
Thus the fire of craving blazes within the six sense-desires; it cannot be subdued. To take false craving for pleasure is in truth a great suffering.
Riding upon birds, they travel through the sky; the sounds of the five kinds of music and the voices of their songs are so exquisite and beautiful as to be beyond comparison.

They see everywhere all the devas and devīs upon Mount Sumeru—in the gardens, groves, ponds, streams, mountain valleys, and forests, which are completely covered with lotuses and filled with many birds—and they behold them all.
In each dwelling place, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas reside; though he observes them everywhere, he is never satiated.
His faculties are attached and craving for the five desires; he rejoices without weariness, and his heart of love increases.

Thus, for a long time, they rode upon birds and sported, beholding the sixty thousand mountains surrounding Sumeru, the King of Mountains—the dwelling places of devas of virtuous karma, adorned with the radiant light of immeasurable jewels, and exceedingly delightful.
The four sides of Mount Sumeru possess four kinds of colors, namely: lapis lazuli, white silver, gold, and crystal.

These devas travel everywhere to observe Mount Sumeru, riding upon bird-palaces back to their respective abodes; when they reach their dwellings, the appearance and adornments manifest exactly as those devas had conceived them in their thoughts.
At that time, the devaputra again mounted his bird-palace and arrived at Lake Maśīta; the lake was five yojanas in circumference and adorned with various blue vaidūrya lotuses.

When the birds arrive at this pond, they enjoy the five sensory pleasures together with the celestial maidens, just as swarms of bees greedily savor the nectar of flowers. They drink from the *mautu* and eat the *sudhā* essence, which is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor; clad in celestial jewel-garments, they sport and enjoy themselves with the celestial maidens.
Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that heavenly realm and, driven by the flow of karma, fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they possess remaining wholesome karma, they may be born among humans, constantly enjoying wealth and pleasure; they will have many vehicles and places for recreation, becoming either kings or great ministers, revered and loved by all.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The thirteenth stage is named Maṇiguhya.
What karma do sentient beings perform to be born in this heaven?
He hears and perceives:

If there are virtuous people who benefit sentient beings, they refrain from killing and stealing, and they also teach others to abide in the path of goodness. They themselves abstain from taking life; even when they see moisture-born insects within wine or honey, they will never intentionally drink it unless it has been strained and purified.

Not instructing others to do so, nor rejoicing in such acts; knowing unwholesome karma, one abandons it and does not perform it; seeing others commit evil, one abandons them and does not associate with them; and exhorting others to cultivate goodness—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?

Even when entering a stupa or temple, if there is an offering of light for the Buddha’s stupa, one does not use that light to perform various tasks, nor does one take the smoke to use as ink for writing; fearing every subtle transgression—this is called non-stealing.
Furthermore, there are those who refrain from killing and refrain from stealing.

Regarding non-killing: even if mosquitoes or ants cause annoyance or distress to a person, one does not kill them; one does not even harbor thoughts of killing in the mind. If one sees another killing, one exhorts them to desist, saying to that person:
"If one kills a living being, it is an unwholesome karma, and at the end of life, one shall fall into the Reviving Hell."
"In this way, they instruct others to refrain from evil and to abide securely in wholesome dharmas.
Such virtuous persons themselves uphold the precepts and cause others to abide in them.
Whether traveling through wildernesses or during times of famine, they give gifts of food and drink."
Even when pressed by the distress of hunger, he does not steal the food of others.
In the wilderness, seeing those who are impoverished, starving, and lacking provisions, he is able to diminish his own food and give it to the poor.
Because both the intention of the mind and the field of merit are superior, one obtains a great karmic reward; this is because the gift was given at the proper time.
Why is this so? There is no greater affliction than famine; therefore, giving food yields a great karmic reward.

These two kinds of people who uphold the precepts benefit themselves and others; with upright conduct born of a virtuous mind, they are the foremost of good persons. They always harbor great fear regarding even the smallest transgression, offering various precious jewels to their parents, or perhaps offering jeweled necklaces to images of the Tathāgata.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven on the Maṇigarbha Ground.
Having been born in that heaven, they will experience supreme bliss and delight themselves with the five sensory pleasures.

The majestic power and radiant light of this person of virtuous karma will shine everywhere for five hundred yojanas; just as the rising sun shines universally upon all mountains, so too does the light of this deity illuminate the entire ground.
That ground of various jewels was already endowed with radiance; yet when the light from the bodies of these devaputras shone upon it, it became a hundred times more magnificent.

Their various lights—blue, yellow, vermilion, and purple—were like the colors of a celestial rainbow, and the radiance of their bodies became a hundred times more superior, adorned with exquisite beauty.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, their bodies are like flashes of lightning, surpassing all the hosts of devas.
Just as the moon is foremost among the multitude of stars, so too is the body of this deva.

With flames of light radiating from his entire body, he beheld the precious ground; that ground was adorned with various kinds of maṇi jewels, interspersed in diverse patterns with distinct boundaries, such that all its radiance was like the simultaneous illumination of a hundred suns.
When the Son of Heaven saw this, he was filled with great joy.

Looking further toward another place, he beheld celestial maidens endowed with exquisite beauty, adorned with various kinds of jewels beyond compare, enjoying manifold sensual pleasures. There were drums, lutes, songs, flutes, pipes, and harps, as well as various such melodies of wondrous song.
Some engage in dance and play, adorned with celestial garlands; some sport with birds in flower ponds; others eat celestial fruits.
Furthermore, they take various flowers and fruits from the wish-fulfilling trees, singing songs of sensual delight to bring joy to the multitude.
When the deva-son arrived, he saw that the celestial maidens had been stung by the venomous snakes of the objects of sensual desire; turning from his seat, he looked toward the celestial maidens.
Adorned with celestial garlands, the deva-son beheld them, and the fire of desire scorched his heart as he turned back to gaze at the celestial maidens.

At that time, the celestial maidens saw that their husbands were nearing the end of their lives, with the five signs of death appearing; they were like a swarm of bees abandoning withered flowers to fly toward newly blossomed ones.
The various celestial maidens likewise abandoned their original attendants and approached this deva-son;
adorning themselves with diverse celestial garlands and diverse celestial garments, they entertained the deva-son with hearts of passionate desire, causing his mind to be filled with joy.

This regressing deva, having practiced various sensual desires since beginningless time, feels a burning affliction in his heart upon seeing his celestial nymphs turn their backs on him and pursue other objects.
Just as the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell burn one’s body, so too is the burning affliction of his mind when he sees the celestial nymphs turning away from him to go toward others.

When their allotted lifespan from the mandate of heaven comes to an end, they harm their own bodies out of a mind of jealousy; as their retribution is about to exhaust, they seize upon conditions with a turbid mind and see nothing more, falling back into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
By what causes and conditions does one experience great suffering and affliction upon seeing celestial maidens desert them for others?
It is because, during a previous life among humans, they committed sexual misconduct and acted improperly by violating the wives of others.
Having been born among the gods due to the performance of wholesome karma, one perceives this evil karma because of having violated another's wife.
Thus, within wholesome karma, unwholesome karma reaches maturation; for this reason, even the slightest unwholesome karma should not be committed.
If one can uphold the seven kinds of precepts without deficiency or omission, there will be further fruits.

When the gods of the Yāma Heaven perceive the signs of their impending decline, it is not as [described] here; the retribution for future lives shall be stated briefly and will not be explained in detail.
"The hosts of celestial maidens, adorned with divine garlands, shall quickly go to the newly born deva-son and present him with those divine garlands to adorn him."
The flower garlands were endowed with fragrance and color, never fading or withering; they caused the newly born deva-sons to wear them.
Once the deva-sons had put them on, their hearts were filled with joy, and they immediately drew near one another to roam together through the gardens and groves, enjoying each other’s company.
In this place where the hosts of devas dwell, they see pure water with *vaiḍūrya* flowers, having petals of true gold and filaments of diamond, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of bees.

Some of those bees have wings of pure gold and bodies of *vaiḍūrya*; some have wings of white silver and bodies of pure gold; some have wings of red jewels and bodies of variegated colors; and some have wings of coral and bodies of variegated colors. They constantly sport and enjoy themselves within such lotus ponds that are unfading and unchanging, their voices as pure and exquisite as the voices of celestial maidens.

Thus adorned by swarms of bees, the devas and devīs enter the lotus pond to sport and enjoy themselves, singing, laughing, and playing; they thus find pleasure and delight within the pond for a long time.
He then proceeded to the forest of the *Suvarṇamālā* trees, which were densely covered by two kinds of trees.

Having arrived within the grove, various musical instruments produced exquisite sounds. He beheld Mount Sumeru like a mass of molten gold, and saw the hosts of devas upon its peaks sporting and delighting themselves with music alongside their celestial nymphs. They were adorned with celestial garlands and divine robes, and their bodies were embellished with necklaces made of Jambūnada gold.
In the lotus ponds and blue-lotus ponds, all varieties of fragrances and flavors are fully present; there, the devas and devīs sport and enjoy pleasures.
Geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, and powerful lions form rows, while the various devas sport and enjoy pleasures therein.

Furthermore, he saw hosts of devas moving through the void, accompanied by celestial maidens like bright lamps; they delighted themselves with beautiful songs and melodies, raining down various exquisite flowers, experiencing celestial bliss amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music and their playful entertainments.

Furthermore, he saw the hosts of devas drinking celestial delicacies; they were free from the faults of intoxication and each spoke words of endearment to amuse one another, causing their hearts to rejoice.
He also saw the hosts of devas eating *sudhā*; as the fruit of their own virtuous karma, it was fully endowed with perfect color, fragrance, flavor, and texture.
Furthermore, he saw hosts of devas gathering seven-jeweled flowers from trees made of the seven precious substances to adorn themselves.
He also saw hosts of devas gathering flowers and plucking fruits; some were eating them, while others struck one another with them in playful laughter, enjoying their mutual entertainment.
Furthermore, they see hosts of devas riding celestial birds, adorned with a variety of the seven precious gems; mounting these swans, they roam through the void, sporting together with one another.

Furthermore, he saw celestial hosts and the sounds of musical ensembles; before the sons of the gods, throngs of celestial maidens danced and sported for their amusement, striking one another with celestial lotuses, engaging in flirtatious conversation to arouse desire, and intensifying the realm of passion.
When the newly born deva-son beholds such various celestial hosts and the diverse transformations produced by karma, he reflects to himself:
"Though I behold these things, my eyes are not yet satisfied."
Hearing various sounds, the ear never tires;
encountering various fragrances, the nose is likewise;
tasting various of the six flavors, the tongue knows no satiety.
The body craves subtle touch; likewise, it is adorned with celestial garments and exquisite clothing, and its body is anointed with fragrant ointments, yet it knows no satiety.
Toward all objects of affection, the mind constantly complies, thinking: "I now delight in these things; I shall experience this pleasure."
Having reflected thus, they take mutual delight in one another, experiencing the five sensual pleasures as befits the gods.
In this way, the sixfold mind of attachment in these sons of the gods is completely surrounded and consumed by the fires of craving.

For example, suppose there is a person traveling through a vast wilderness during the extreme heat of midsummer. Suddenly, a great fire breaks out, burning dry grass, tree leaves, and branches; fires erupt from the valleys, forests, and all the trees. In a state of panic and terror, he flees, but there is no place of refuge.

The flames blaze fiercely, surrounding him on all sides until they become a single conflagration that burns the entire forest. Wherever he goes, smoke and flames rise together; scorched by the fire, he cannot escape.
All foolish ordinary beings in the world are likewise thus: they are burned by the fire of craving for dry grass and tree branches.
For those who are about to go to heaven and have performed meritorious deeds, the wind of ignorance and the fetters blow upon the great fire of craving.
Practicing meditation and cultivation, one attains mundane dhyāna; this is likened to a withered tree or the grass and leaves of a mountain valley being consumed by the fire of craving.
The "fierce and blazing fire" is a metaphor for the six types of craving.
Wandering everywhere is a metaphor for the sense faculties being stained by and attached to their objects.
The blazing flames represent the recollection of those objects; fanned by the fierce winds of craving and scorched by the fire of attachment, they destroy the worlds of gods and humans.
"Fire" is a metaphor for the fire of craving.

Because of their wholesome karma, the devas experience immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of pleasure; yet, once their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall back from the heavens and, driven by the flow of karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, they will dwell upon jeweled grounds, being born into a family adorned with all kinds of precious gems; they may become great kings or high ministers, constantly enjoying peace and happiness, beloved by all people, endowed with many descendants, and possessing abundant resources and requisites.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The fourteenth stage is named "Whirling Movement" (Vartanī).
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he perceives what karma causes sentient beings to be born in that stage:
There are sentient beings who neither kill nor steal; when they see others doing so, they urge them not to do it, explaining that unwholesome karma results in evil retribution.
How does one refrain from killing?
Even regarding a leaf of vegetables, if he sees minute insects within the water, he protects them and does not eat it.
If the water has not been strained, he never drinks it intentionally.

He does not discard the insects caught in the strainer onto dry land, but returns them to the water so that the insects may be at ease and do not lose their lives; furthermore, he teaches others to abide in the path of goodness.
What is non-stealing?

Whether it be a field of sugarcane, or fruits, or vegetables, or *āmra* trees—regarding the property belonging to others, one does not give rise to a mind of theft, nor does one instruct others to engage in stealing.
One maintains the precepts oneself and teaches others to maintain the precepts.
What is meant by maintaining the precepts?
It is to refrain from killing and refrain from stealing.
Even at the cost of one's life, one does not drink water containing insects, nor does one consume it; furthermore, one instructs others not to do so—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing? One does not intentionally steal even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf.

One practices generosity; if one sees a sick person, one provides them with medicine to bring them peace and comfort, yet one never gives another medicine containing insects for the purpose of treating their illness.
This is wholesome giving; even unto nirvana, its merit shall never be exhausted.
When this person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the region of Revolving Movement.
Once reborn there, by virtue of their wholesome karma, all the radiance of various jewels will revolve, and exquisite celestial maidens will provide them with offerings.

Having made these offerings, he proceeded to the Forest of Radiant Circles (*Prabhāmaṇḍalavana*). There, amidst various kinds of music, there were birds in the forest called "Adorned Trees" (*Vṛkṣavibhūṣaṇa*), which filled the woods.
By the power of the birds, according to their mental inclinations, wherever they wish to go, they fly through the void and the forest follows them as well.
If the devaputras are beneath the trees, the forest likewise follows them.
Wherever they go, lotus ponds arise, adorned with various kinds of lotuses, having leaves of lapis lazuli, stalks of pure gold, and filaments of white silver.
Upon the lotus pedestals, various celestial maidens sing with manifold exquisite melodies.

Due to their virtuous karma, from within those lotuses flows *madhu-madhu*, a delicious drink commonly known as wine; the celestial maidens drink it. Together with the sons of gods on the lotus pedestals, they dwell upon them, surrounded by the maidens as they drink *madhu* together. Having long enjoyed these pleasures, they descend from the sky, accompanied by birds and the host of celestial maidens, and proceed to the Utpala Palace.
The palace was two yojanas in length and breadth; there were hundreds of thousands of such *utpala* lotuses, and upon each petal sat a celestial maiden, performing songs, dances, and music.

Furthermore, there are blue utpala flowers; by the blue light of these flowers, they cause all the celestial maidens to appear blue. If it is red, they cause all the celestial maidens to appear red; their bodily ornaments are likewise transformed in this same way.

The deva king and his celestial maidens sit upon lotus pedestals; by virtue of their wholesome karma, they are surrounded by various celestial maidens as they sit amidst the filaments of the lotuses. Holding various multicolored jeweled banners in their hands, they sing, dance, and sport, enjoying celestial pleasures for a long time.

Descending from the flower pedestal, he beheld the Kṣaya Palace. There was a river named Priyadarśanā; on both its banks were many trees made of various jewels, complete with branches and leaves and fully formed trunks. Various birds with beautiful beaks and wings, their voices like the *bhṛṅgārava* bird, adorned the riverbanks, emerging from the river according to the thoughts of the devas.
The adornments of that river are such that the singing and dancing of the celestial maidens are exceedingly delightful, as they enjoy themselves in mutual play.
When a deva-son approaches this River of Love, the celestial maidens see him and all rejoice greatly, singing, dancing, laughing, and performing various musical entertainments.

There were other celestial maidens who, performing various musical entertainments, approached the deva-son. At that time, seeing the exquisite and beautiful countenances of these celestial maidens, the deva-son’s attachment increased a hundredfold; he ran toward them and played upon the riverbank with those celestial maidens and others, such as those holding *utpala* flowers.

All the celestial maidens gathered together, performing various musical instruments and producing exquisite sounds; the resonance of their singing filled the midst of the precious peaks of Sumeru, the King of Mountains.

At that time, all the hosts of devas within the mountain peaks, hearing this wondrous sound, gathered together; their minds became attached to the singing voices of the celestial maidens, and the great assembly of devas and devis, in harmonious union, engaged in song, dance, and play without giving rise to jealousy.
They further proceeded to pleasure groves and gardens, where they experienced immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of delights for a long time.
Eventually, when their beloved wholesome karma was exhausted, their lives ended in those heavenly realms; driven by the flow of karma, they fell into the states of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, they will always experience peace and happiness; they will always delight in bathing, and in applying scented ointments and powdered incense. They will love various lotuses—the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *kubjaka* flowers—and will be upright, intelligent, and fond of the True Dharma.
They may become kings or ministers, elders or city governors, or serve as guides; they will manage their livelihoods with success and harmony.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The fifteenth stage is named Golden Palace.
What karma causes sentient beings to be born in that place?
He observes and sees with the wisdom of his divine eye:
A person who upholds the precepts does not kill and does not steal.
How is it that they do not kill?

If they see an enemy coming to harm them, or another person violating their spouse, even if they capture and seize them, they do not beat or injure them; instead, they release them to escape and comfort them with gentle words.
Or one may see someone wishing to harm an enemy, but instead ransoming their life with wealth so that they may be released.
Furthermore, when a wicked person has been captured and seized, one releases them to go their way rather than inflicting harm upon them.

When such evil persons come again to his house, desiring to invade and harm him, he captures them and immediately releases them without inflicting injury, because he guards and upholds the precepts and stands in awe of the fruits of karma.
If an enemy comes with a sword intending to kill one, one protects that enemy so that they may escape and not be slaughtered;
out of fear of breaking the precepts, one sacrifices one's own life rather than harming another—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing? How many kinds of non-stealing are there?
This person who upholds the precepts gives rise to great dread even toward minor offenses; fearing the retribution of karma, they do not commit evil deeds and cultivate wholesome deeds.
Furthermore, there is non-stealing: seeing even a minor offense, down to the size of a mote of dust, one feels fear in one's heart.

Whether visiting a stupa or monastery, or going to a grove—a place of quiet seclusion for recitation and walking meditation—or arriving at the water’s edge, one does not take the property of others; one never intentionally takes various kinds of shoes or sandals.
One does not listen to what others do not permit, nor does one enjoy such things.
Because of guarding the precepts, whether by day or by night, one does not give rise to a mind of theft; this is called non-stealing.
This is called non-killing and non-stealing.
How does one abide in the precepts?
One abandons impurity and does not cherish or delight in unwholesome dharmas; maintaining pure precepts, one is beloved by virtuous people, being true and not false.
Maintaining the precepts in this way, one is reborn among the devas and will certainly reach Nirvana; according to one's heart's aspiration, one shall attain *sambodhi*.

If such a person who maintains the precepts travels through a wilderness—whether alone or with companions, whether on a path or off the path—and sees a malevolent beast that has conceived and is giving birth, being driven by hunger and wishing to devour its own offspring.
When this person saw this, he voluntarily surrendered his own body to these evil beasts, wishing for them to kill him rather than devouring his child.
This practitioner of the precepts, in order to preserve their life and out of compassion for sentient beings, sacrificed his own body and life.
Filially supporting one's parents.
What is giving? It is when a person who upholds the precepts, though poor and destitute, obtains goods through diligent toil while remaining compliant with the Dharma and maintaining their precepts.
Perhaps a śramaṇa might arise from the meditative attainment of cessation and come to his house to beg for alms.
Thus, this poor man would diminish the portion of food intended for his wife and children to give a small amount of rice and food to this bhikṣu, thereby depriving himself of one day’s meal.
Having seen them eat, his heart was filled with joy; he further instructed others not to kill or steal, established them in the path of goodness, and rejoiced in their virtuous deeds.

This person who upholds the precepts benefits both himself and others; after his life ends, he will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, just as a fragrant scent arises within a golden palace.
When these beings of virtuous karma are born in that heaven, they dwell upon a ground of sensual delights, with palaces made of gold and adorned with every kind of precious jewel.
Upon seeing this, Śakra conceives a sense of wonder and experiences a hundredfold joy, praising it with these verses:
"Supreme among pleasures, The virtuous fruit of wholesome karma, That which is experienced by the gods."
Due to the karma of previous lives, the palace of the four wheels is drawn by elephants and horses; with wisdom as its hook, the radiance of the palace is like the sun.

The goodness of upholding the precepts leads one to roam among the heavens; with compassion for sentient beings, as a mother loves her child, the person of loving-kindness and compassion can reach the celestial realms. Those who practice loving-kindness and compassion benefit all beings;
they should always be venerated, for after death they will be reborn in the heavens.
Taming others through compassion, they benefit all sentient beings.
Such people are like celestial beings, revered by all the gods.
Those who possess loving-kindness and compassion are as majestic and serene as the moon; they protect and shelter sentient beings, freeing them from sorrow and affliction.
"Therefore, apply yourself with diligence and practice to seek happiness.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken this verse, he entered his golden palace and sat upon a soft seat, adorned with various forms and features, together with the assembly of devas who were seated there.
Surrounded by celestial maidens, he enjoyed pleasures for a long time;
with their various physical forms and diverse ornaments, they entertained one another.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, emerged from the golden palace and proceeded to the Forest of Universal Delight (*Sarvārthasiddha*), surrounded by hundreds of thousands of various celestial hosts, while manifold musical instruments produced a multitude of exquisite sounds.
The hosts of devas, emitting great radiance, followed Śakra, Lord of Devas.

Not far from the grove, they beheld a place of recreation adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lights; its trees were made of gold and lapis lazuli, brilliantly blazing and universally adorned. The various adornments of that grove of recreation are beyond all analogy; now, I shall describe but a small portion of them.
For example, it was as if seven suns had risen simultaneously; the radiance of that forest was likewise.
Those various radiances possessed manifold colors: blue, yellow, crimson, purple, and white lights.
The splendor of that grove, a place for play and sport, was brilliantly radiant; having seen it, Śakra addressed the host of devas:
"Do you all see this park, adorned as a place for every kind of pleasure and amusement?"
"Yes, indeed, we have seen it.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the assembly of devas:
"In a past age, the Great King Mūrdhaja sat here in this grove sharing a seat with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sporting and enjoying pleasures."
Surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens and ruling over the four continents,

the two heavenly kings experienced the pleasures of the five desires for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, yet they remained insatiable and eventually fell from their celestial realm.
At that time, by virtue of his wholesome karma, King Mūrdhaja possessed radiance, majesty, physical beauty, and power within this forest.
I shall now describe it; you should listen well.
In a past life, there was King Mūrdhaja, who ruled over the four continents; he did not employ the sword or staff, nor were there any punishments, yet his desires remained insatiable.
By virtue of the wholesome karma from previous lives, he has now come to this heaven.
The radiance of his body surpassed that of Mount Sumeru by more than ten times; all the lights of the devas were extinguished and ceased to appear within his light.
When the Four Heavenly Kings saw King Mūrdhaja, they immediately came forth to welcome him and addressed him, saying: "Welcome, Great King!"
"I shall now go forth to welcome the Great King and provide him with all necessary offerings.
Then, having accepted those offerings, King Mūrdhaja ascended once more to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, the radiance and majestic power of Mūrdhagata were like the light of the sun; he was the most supreme among men, and so too was he within this heaven.
Then the four World-Protecting Devas (Lokapālas), seeing that their own radiance no longer appeared, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and said to the other gods:

"This King Mūrdhagata has arrived here in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. This is either due to the power of his own majesty or the power of the wheel-treasure; it is not the power of other gods, nor is it the power of humans. Do not give rise to fear."
"This person follows the Dharma and shall become a Wheel-Turning King.
After the World-Protector had spoken thus, King Mūrdhaja arrived at the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, Śakra was sporting and enjoying himself in the Forest of All Delights; seeing Mūrdhaja from afar, he immediately offered him half of his seat and bade him sit.
At that time, Mūrdhaja sat upon the same couch as Śakra.
For a long period, the two kings enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses; when their karma was exhausted, they fell back from their state.
At that time, among the pleasure grounds of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, none could equal this Forest of All Pleasures (Sarvaratavāna).
"That forest is exquisite, adorned with immeasurable varieties of jewels, its radiance like that of the sun.
Having spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, entered the Forest of All Pleasures.
Having entered the grove, the devas and apsaras enjoy themselves in pleasure, partaking of various kinds of *sūdā* flavors.

Once they have finished eating, they ascend the palace of the seven treasures; its radiance, majesty, and solemnity are like those of the sun, and amidst the sounds of various musical instruments, they return to the Sudharmā Hall.

After Śakra had departed, the resident devas enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses until their wholesome karma was exhausted, whereupon they fell into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If born among humans, they will always encounter a virtuous age and not meet with the calamities of war; they will be born in a noble land fully provided with gardens and groves, abundant in rice, wheat, sugarcane, flowers, and fruits, and in a place of great wealth. They will always encounter the True Dharma, becoming either a great king or a high minister, beloved and respected by all people. They will possess supreme physical beauty, have perfected faculties, and be blessed with many descendants.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the ground where the Trāyastriṃśa devas dwell.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The sixteenth stage is named Mālā-pratibimba.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
These sentient beings possess wholesome karma and wholesome minds; they neither kill nor steal.
How do they refrain from killing?
How do they refrain from stealing?
How many kinds of non-killing?
How many kinds of non-stealing?
As for non-killing, one does not kill living beings oneself.
Whether it be various kinds of fish or turtles, or *śukti* (mother-of-pearl) or *śaṅkha* (conch), one does not take them nor sell them.

Upon seeing one who kills living beings, one instructs them to abide in the precepts; upon seeing another who commits such acts, one does not rejoice in the heart, but exhorts them to dwell securely within the path of goodness—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?
If this virtuous person maintains the precepts with a pure mind and a straightforward mind, and not out of a greedy mind;
if, at a Buddha’s stupa or temple, or in a place where incense is burned among the Sangha, they do not smell the fragrance, nor do they employ any means to let it perfume their clothes.
If fragrances reach the nose and the mind does not become attached to them, this is called the subtle precept against stealing.
Seeing others do so, one encourages them not to do it and leads them to abide in the path of goodness.
Thus, these sentient beings benefit themselves and others.
With what kind of mind do they benefit sentient beings?

When they see one who is killing, it is as if they were seeing their own child being killed; they regard all insects and ants in the same way, and they also instruct others to abide in the path of goodness.
What is giving? If a poor person, through diligent toil, acquires wealth and uses it to give to those who practice the precepts or have attained the first dhyāna;
if they share half of the food in their vessel as an offering, and also teaches others to practice giving.
Such a person, having benefited both themselves and others, will, after the end of their life, be reborn in the Heaven of Garland Shadows (*Mālādharāḥ*).
Once reborn there, there is a tree named Garland Shadow, whose circle of radiance pervades the entire grove.
The fragrance of its flowers fills one *yojana*, surpassing that of all other flowers.
The flowers are long and slender; a single flower can form a head-garland. They are of various colors, adorned in manifold ways—blue, yellow, red, and white—luxuriant and brilliantly radiant.

Furthermore, within the gardens and groves, they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; with the sounds of music and song, their sensual delights are fully provided, and whatever the mind conceives is entirely accomplished.
Through various and extraordinary infinite accomplishments, everything is achieved by virtue of their wholesome karma.

Furthermore, within the grove there is a lotus pond named Variegated Flowers (*Vicitrapuṣpa*), where lotuses of great power grow; these flowers are perpetually in bloom and are adorned with bees of the colors of the seven precious gems.
Within the lotus ponds, various bees produced wondrous singing sounds; hearing these bee songs, the devas and devīs were all filled with great joy and said to one another:
"How marvelous!"
"The bees here produce wondrous songs that delight my heart.
Thus the swarms of bees sang with various exquisite melodies.

Furthermore, there were geese that fanned the lotus pond with their wings, causing the flowers to rise up like golden filaments that completely covered the water. Seeing this, the ducks and wildfowl ran toward them in joy, uttering beautiful cries.
In these lotus ponds there are many birds; with hearts full of joy, the devas and devīs set aside their various musical sounds and go to join the birds in play and enjoyment.

He further proceeded to the pleasure gardens where the palatial halls were arranged in rows; those palaces had pillars made of the seven precious gems and were adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, and crystal.

In that land, there are many various celestial maidens who sport and enjoy themselves, adorned with divine jewels. They anoint their bodies with celestial sandalwood powder and take pleasure together, free from jealousy; they delight one another, devoid of envy, experiencing the fruits of their own karma.
Within various realms, they are born therein by means of various karmas, experiencing the fruits of their own actions and sporting in pleasure.
They further proceed to the wish-fulfilling trees; by the power of those trees, whatever the devas think of is entirely obtained.

In this grove, there are rivers of food and drink, endowed with the foremost colors, fragrances, and flavors; with hearts full of joy, they sport within these rivers and partake of the *sūdāma* essence.
Having finished eating and drinking, they experience a hundredfold joy and proceed once more to the Blue Lotus Grove (*utpala-vana*).
Those flowers possess the foremost color, fragrance, and flavor; from within their petals flows the delicious drink called *ma-thou*, just as wine flows out from fermented dregs.

Their colors are as follows: those that are blue-green like the *puṇḍarīka* produce yellow *puṇḍarīka* drink; flowers of beryl color produce beryl-colored drink; flowers of crystal color produce crystal-colored drink; flowers of musāragalva color produce musāragalva-colored drink; and flowers of variegated colors produce variegated-colored drink.
The leaves and flowers are variegated in color, with stems of lapis lazuli and filaments of diamond.
From these various flowers flow diverse drinks, possessing the most excellent fragrance and flavor.
Having drunk [the nectar], the gods proceeded to the Sarvadarśana forest to sport and enjoy themselves; upon arriving in this grove, they beheld all the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

The entire Grove of Contemplation is exceedingly delightful; within this grove is a lotus pond named Universal Flow, thirty *li* in width, filled with pure, limpid water as clear as the color of lapis lazuli, and surrounded on all sides by geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
All the birds were golden in color, with backs made of the seven treasures, feet of coral, and eyes of red jewels, adorned with various precious gems.
Their voices were exquisite and beautiful as they frolicked and danced.

At that time, the sons of the gods went to their place of recreation. Golden birds emitted exquisite sounds, and the sons of the gods ascended upon golden palaces; the radiance of those palaces was like masses of molten gold.

They said to one another, "Do you see how this place of recreation for the gods causes the bodies of the celestial hosts to emit such brilliance, their yellow hue becoming so wondrous as to surpass [their former state] by more than double?"
Within this palace, they sport and amuse themselves, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses.

Greedily craving sensory objects without satiety, they blaze ever more intensely like a fire fed with fuel; the gods' attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures is likewise such that they know no satisfaction.

In this celestial realm, they experience the pleasures of the five senses until their wholesome karma is exhausted; at the end of their lives, they fall back and, transmigrating according to their karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there remains further karma, they will be born among human beings and constantly experience happiness. Adorned with flower garlands and fragrant ointments, and sprinkled with powdered incense, their minds are always joyful. They may become kings or great ministers, possessing vast wealth and riches, beloved and respected by all people, free from enemies and without the affliction of illness.
Due to the remaining karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 28;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 29.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Observing the Heavens, Part Eight; The Fifth [Section] on the Thirty-three Heavens.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the ground where the Thirty-three Gods dwell."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
the seventeenth stage is named "Gentle and Soft" (Mṛdu).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that celestial realm?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that those who uphold the precepts— refraining from killing and refraining from stealing— are born in this celestial realm.
How do they refrain from killing?

There are sentient beings who, for the sake of greed for wealth and profit, indulge unrestrainedly in the five desires; they take the lives of venomous snakes to obtain their precious jewels to provide for their own livelihood.

A person who upholds the precepts does not do such a thing; this is called non-killing. Furthermore, they teach others to practice non-killing, not intentionally killing even minute sentient beings such as mosquitoes and ants.
What is non-stealing?

It is not taking another's grass or soil with a mind of theft, nor intentionally taking even the most minute thing; furthermore, regarding all writings and records belonging to others, one does not copy them for one's own use with a mind of theft—this is called non-stealing.

What is giving? It is when a person who upholds the precepts, being poor and lacking wealth, with a mind free from greed, diminishes their own resources to give clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities of life to those in the first dhyāna; or they give a single meal, or they level and clear the grounds of a monastery so that the Saṃgha may come and go in peace and without difficulty.
Thus, while practicing giving themselves, they also cause others to abide in the wholesome path and exhort others to abandon unwholesome karma.

These practitioners of ethical discipline refrain from killing and stealing, benefiting both themselves and others; by these causes and conditions, at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Having been born in this heaven, they experience celestial bliss.
The ground is entirely covered with soft celestial silks used as bedding, spread over the whole earth, supple and smooth.
If celestial beings walk upon it, the ground rises and falls according to their feet; when the foot treads down, it sinks, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to levelness.
Just as when a great wind blows over water, waves rise up and down in an unstable manner, yet the water becomes level again when the wind ceases, so too is the softness of that earth.

That ground is pure like a clear mirror; if there were a master artisan or an apprentice capable of polishing a mirror until it was brilliantly clean and clearly reflected all images, such that even a single hair split into a hundred parts could be seen entirely within that mirror.

In this world-system, the sight of all the limbs and members of the various devaputras is likewise so; just as that bright mirror is pure and free from defilement, the purity of this ground is also like that.
Furthermore, a rare phenomenon occurs on that ground:

if a celestial maiden has a thought in her mind, desiring to sport with a celestial son, the celestial son will immediately see written characters appear within the ground where he dwells, and he then sports with and enjoys pleasure together with that celestial maiden.
That land further possesses a rare wonder:
if the gods think of anything they require, it all springs forth from the ground.
Thus, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enjoy celestial bliss upon this soft ground and then proceed to their places of recreation.
In their place of recreation, there is a great grove named Mātanga, completely covered by networks of bells and adorned with immeasurable jewel trees.

Within that forest, various birds abound and flowers and fruits are fully provided; they sport and enjoy pleasure through the sounds of the five musical instruments, experiencing the bliss of karmic retribution within the spheres of the five sense faculties.

Within that land there is also a grove of trees called *bala*; when the hosts of devas enter this forest to sport, the trees shrink in size so that it is not difficult for the celestial maidens to gather fruit.

That forest was composed entirely of the seven treasures; its radiance was as brilliant as the rising sun, serving as its adornment, and it was further embellished by flowers and fruits of immeasurable varieties of color.
Various birds of diverse colors emit exquisite sounds as adornments; such birds dwell within the forest, producing a multitude of wondrous voices.
Within this grove, they enjoy the pleasures of the six senses, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing.

Having left this grove, he proceeded once more to the mountain peak named Uccaya, where he went with various celestial maidens, adorned in diverse ornaments, to engage in song, dance, and playful laughter.

Ascending to the High Peak, its summit is ten yojanas in circumference; upon this mountain peak is a great lotus pond named Radiance, filled with flowers of the seven jewels, kumuda lilies, kuganada lilies, and blue utpala lotuses.

The water is pure and clear; geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks emit various wondrous sounds that are most delightful. Surrounded by celestial sons and daughters at the flower pond, they sing, dance, play, and laugh, drinking the essence of the heavens without becoming intoxicated or disordered.
The fruits of the six flavors may be eaten at will; their juice is fragrant and delicious, and drinking it brings no harm, as both the devas and devīs drink from it together.

Furthermore, in another place, there are various devīs who sing, dance, play, and laugh, accompanied by drums, lutes, flutes, pipes, harps, and all manner of musical instruments. They enjoy themselves and experience pleasure with the devaputras, surrounding the flower pond and long partaking in celestial delights.

Furthermore, there is a flower pond named *Sarvamanoratha-vihāra* (The Place of Play for All Desires), adorned with celestial garlands, their bodies anointed with sandalwood and sprinkled with powdered incense, from which light radiates.

"By the power of the causal conditions of the superior, middling, and inferior karma created by oneself, one obtains three kinds of retribution according to what the mind desires, giving rise to a consciousness that corresponds to the karma.
If a person performs such karma, they obtain such a fruit—the visual consciousness conditions forms and gives rise to a joyful mind."
Why is this? If one performs an inferior action, within a neutral form one perceives it as an inferior form; thus, such a person perceives an inferior form within a single object-condition.
If one performs middling karma, one sees middling forms and gives rise to a mind of middling joy.
If one performs superior karma, one sees immeasurable varieties of exquisite forms with dignified and majestic features.
In this same way, all sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles are likewise.
All the various realms within the heavens of the desire realm that are objects of the eye are also like this; were it not so, the threefold retribution would not be accomplished.
One should know that through these three kinds of karma, they obtain such exquisite physical beauty, dignity, and majesty, as well as the excellence of celestial maidens.
These hosts of devas sport and enjoy themselves within all the pleasure gardens of their minds, becoming greedily attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, never knowing satiety.
Having observed this, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
“The flames at the end of the kalpa dry up the great ocean, yet craving does not perish even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.”
The oceans may yet be filled by all the waters and rains;
but the ocean of craving for sensual forms is never satiated.
Recalling various pleasures, desire can never be fulfilled; only when one is free from sorrow and attachment does desire come to rest and contentment.
Pleasure arises from desire; the wise do not delight in it. The pleasure of being free from desire is the most supreme among all pleasures.
Pleasure mixed with craving is like water mixed with poison.
If one is free from craving and desire, it is like water and milk blending together.
Desire burns the deluded person, who is blind, obscured, and without awakening—like the insects on Mount Malaya devouring the wood.
Craving and recollection—these thoughts are beyond counting; one never finds satiety in such recollection and is thus bound by the King of Death.
One who is not driven by desire and does not dwell within the realm of attachment is a vessel for happiness, as taught by the Tathāgata.
Like what is seen in a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas—false and unsubstantial;
all desires are deceptive, like an illusion or water bubbles, or like the *jambuka* fruit that grows on an island in the sea, which causes one to become intoxicated for seven days when eaten.
Sensual desire causes decay and affliction, like fire that harms people;
if one knows the faults of desire and does not crave its intoxicating fruits, one can perceive the true reality and forever leave behind the afflictions of craving.
All desires are like poison; before they are attained, one longs for them, and once attained, they bring self-affliction.
All evils blaze forth, yet desire knows no satisfaction; one loses celestial bliss and falls into hell, deceived by desire.
Sensual desire is like ripples on water, like lightning, and like a lamp; the lust for women is like poison, like a fish circling in a whirlpool.
When it is contemplated, it increases like fire fed with fuel; unstable from beginning to end, it is abandoned by the wise.
If one associates with them, they increase through mutual reinforcement; their touch is like a flame, and one will suffer the retribution of desire.
Knowing these faults of desire, the wise person abandons them with revulsion; the one who is free from desire attains the bliss of Nirvana.
Countless tens of millions, nayutas of devas, having indulged in desire, fell and underwent the sufferings of hell.
The fire of desire, the sword, and the poison—seeking pleasure, one should abandon them; one should always renounce desire, for it is the cause of hell.
I have never seen anyone who, without being driven by desire and without indulging in the habit of desire, does not undergo suffering and affliction.
Therefore, abandon desire; do not give rise to thoughts of it, for all desires burn like a blazing fire.
"Thus the bhikṣu, observing that the sons of the gods are driven by desire, spoke these verses in rebuke.

The negligent gods then proceeded to the Sarvārthasiddha pleasure grove, where they performed various musical entertainments; adorned in all manner of finery with their celestial maidens, they entered that forest, enjoying themselves amidst the sounds of song and music."
Immeasurable rivers and ponds adorn the gardens and groves, and everywhere one beholds various wondrous forms; thus the faculty of the eye experiences the desire for form.

Furthermore, according to one's recollections, one hears manifold exquisite sounds and various lovely voices; the nose smells various supreme and delightful fragrances; the tongue obtains various extraordinary flavors—all these are obtained exactly as the mind conceives them.

In accordance with whatever they think of in their minds, they obtain various tactile sensations; body and mind are filled with joy and pleasure, and the dharmas of pleasure they conceive in their minds are accomplished.
Thus, these celestial hosts, shrouded by craving, sport in negligence, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses according to what they desire in their hearts.
Until their wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away and fall back into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they constantly experience peace and happiness; they always delight in flower garlands, ointments, and powdered incense; they are immensely wealthy with abundant riches; they possess a straightforward and virtuous mind; they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold; their words are trusted and accepted; they are beloved by the masses; they are provided with a wife and children; they excel in ritual propriety and never fail in ceremonial decorum; their wealth cannot be seized by kings, thieves, water, or fire; they are honored by rulers and are born into a great lineage.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The eighteenth stage is named "Various Adornments.
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing, he perceives: by what karma do sentient beings are born in that place?
One who upholds the precepts does not kill and does not steal, and also teaches others to abide in the path of goodness.
How does one refrain from killing and not harm sentient beings?
One does not kill oneself, does not instruct others to kill, and does not rejoice in such acts.
Furthermore, one should not associate with those who take life, nor even engage them in conversation;
one should not listen to the impure speech of others, nor walk along the same path as them.
Furthermore, there is non-killing:
there are sentient beings who, using the sounds of singing or the music of lutes, harps, flutes, and pipes, deceive various birds and beasts, causing them to fall into nets and traps.

This person who upholds the precepts does not employ such means to kill, nor does he instruct others to practice killing; seeing others do so, he ransoms them to secure their release, and his mind harbors no thought of killing—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?
There are some sentient beings who, through falsehood and deception, engage in unlawful acts in their pursuit of wealth as merchants, committing various forms of theft.
What constitutes such deception?
Or they may weigh and sell sand mixed with other valuables.
Seeing this as wrong, one should advise them not to do it, teaching them through skillful means:
"Do not commit theft for the sake of your wife and children, for your own person, or due to the influence of evil friends."
"If one commits theft, at the end of life they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
As the karmic retribution for theft, one undergoes great suffering.
Thus, one does not commit evil oneself, nor does one encourage others to abandon unwholesome dharmas.
When the conditions have converged, one who is able to relinquish rather than grasp—such a person benefits both themselves and others.
How does such a person practice giving?

Whether they enter the great ocean or traverse vast wildernesses to seek wealth, or earn wealth through labor for others, they bestow it upon those who are poor and afflicted. With a heart of reverence and with their faculties filled with joy, they grant it to them.
To give these things as a gift to those in the second dhyāna, or to give them to the poor—this is called generosity.
What is non-killing?
If there are hunters catching birds with nets, or people catching fish, and someone sees them, ransoms their lives with goods so that they may be released and set free.
Reflecting with joy, their faculties were filled with delight; they also taught others to redeem living beings from death, giving rise to sympathetic joy, thinking:
"I have performed a wholesome deed; I vow to cultivate this constantly."
They also cause others to practice wholesome deeds.
Such wholesome deeds—namely, refraining from killing and refraining from stealing—benefit both oneself and others.

Through these two kinds of benefits of upholding the precepts, which benefit both self and others, at the end of life they are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they dwell within palaces adorned with various inlaid decorations.
“Once those born of virtuous karma have been reborn in this heaven, it is adorned and filled with the shimmering radiance of various mani-jewels.
Their bodies emit light, and they are adorned with garments of various colors, various celestial maidens, and various types of clothing.”
Dwelling there, the newly born deva-son thinks to himself:
"By what karma have I been born in this place?
Reflecting that he has come to be born in this heaven because he cultivated wholesome deeds in his previous life, he exclaims to himself:
"How marvelous! Because I have cultivated wholesome karma, I have been reborn in this place.

Having reflected thus, by virtue of his wholesome karma, the celestial son first hears the sound of music; the songs of the heavenly maidens pervade all places—the mountain peaks and palaces—filled with beautiful sounds, while birds and beasts dance in harmony.
Upon hearing this song, they experience a hundredfold joy.
At first, hearing this sound, their minds give rise to attachment; this is called the first causal condition for the arising of desire.

Once attached to the sound, their minds further give rise to thoughts of desiring these various forms. Immediately looking back, they see the celestial maidens with immeasurable physical features beyond comparison, fully adorned.
"Who is this celestial maiden?
To whom does she belong?
As soon as he thought this, a lustful mind arose within him.
At that time, the goddess spoke in verse:
"Among all causes and conditions for desire, I am the foremost.
I now offer myself to the Son of Heaven, so that we may enjoy various delights in play."

"At that time, having heard the sound of the song and beheld the beautiful form, the deva-son immediately turned his body toward the celestial maidens, desiring to experience the pleasure of touch; this is called the second causal condition for the arising of desire."
Furthermore, there is a third cause and condition for the arising of desire: the mind drives the sense faculties to crave sensory objects, and the mind acts with sovereign freedom.

When the sons of gods, with minds of desire, touch the celestial maidens, and the celestial maidens likewise touch the sons of gods with their bodies—this is called the third cause and condition for the arising of desire.
Furthermore, there is a fourth cause and condition for the arising of desire:
an immeasurable and incomparable fragrance, beyond all analogy. When the devaputra observes it, he wonders from where it comes.
He immediately realizes that this fragrance originates from the heavenly maiden;
he then embraces the maiden with a mind of desire and smells her peerless scent. This is called the fourth cause and condition for the arising of desire.
Regarding the four sensory objects, the mind is stained with craving and delight.
Then, the celestial maidens offer various foods and drinks of *sudarśana* flavor to the deva-son; this is called the fifth causal condition for the arising of desire.
Thus, due to the causes and conditions for the arising of desire—namely, the objects of the five desires which are beyond analogy—one first becomes attached to celestial pleasures.

In this way, when a deva-son receives the retribution of celestial pleasure, at the moment of his birth he remembers his past lives; yet, because of his attachment to sensual delights, he completely forgets them all.

Furthermore, with a mind of desire, he went to where the celestial maidens were; the celestial maidens also came toward the place where the deva-son was. Singing, dancing, playing, and laughing, they entertained one another as they approached the deva-son, engaging in playful dalliance, affectionate speech, and the enjoyment of pleasure.

They then proceeded toward the groves and lotus ponds; the celestial maidens were adorned with various ornaments, and together with the celestial sons, they went to the Grove of All-Wonderful Intent, the Forest of Universal Vision, and the places where the gods of all realms sport.
The trees in that grove are endowed with the power of thought and possess immeasurable adornments.
There are golden trees with silver leaves, branches of red jewels, and fruits of crystal, perfect in color, fragrance, and flavor; such are the countless trees that adorn the gardens and groves.

Furthermore, there is another forest that serves as an adornment, with trees of vaidūrya, their branches of pure gold, their leaves of red jewels, and their fruits of white silver, all embellished with musāragalva.
Furthermore, there are other trees, each one cubit in height, adorned with a single precious substance—namely, gold, silver, red jewels, lapis lazuli, and musaragalva.
Furthermore, there are tree branches measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in length, each composed of a single jewel, fully endowed with flowers and fruits, and adorned with celestial blossoms.
These flowers possess every variety of color and fragrance; their scent pervades an area of sixty *yojanas*, and bees of various colors drink the nectar of the flowers.

This is the grove of the mental dispositions (*āśaya*) of all those who hold such views, adorned by these various trees as its ornaments; they receive this fruit of retribution for their diverse white karmas.

Furthermore, it is adorned with lotuses having stems of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), leaves of pure gold, and filaments of red jewels, adorned by blue *indragopa* bees; their sounds are exquisite and beautiful, and when the celestial hosts hear them, they give rise to great joy.
Furthermore, those groves are adorned with rows of variously colored forests—blue, yellow, crimson, and purple—which appear like flashes of lightning observed in Jambudvīpa.
The groves were thus arrayed in rows as adornments, and the river fords, lotus ponds, and garden parks likewise served as ornaments.
Seeing such a grove endowed with these merits, the deva-son’s heart was filled with great joy, and he went into that forest together with the celestial maidens.

When the other devas see him, they know that the newly born deva-son wishes to come to their abode; they all rise to welcome him, exchange greetings with one another, and praise him with pleasant words. They enjoy themselves amidst the sounds of music and dance, sporting within various lotus groves, and for a long time they experience the pleasures of the five senses in the Forest of Universal Vision.

Leaving this grove once more, they proceeded to a place for joyful play and recreation. That place of recreation was surrounded by various railings; there were flowing streams of exquisite drinks and rows of palaces made of the seven treasures standing like a forest. The ground was of pure gold, and various birds emitted wondrous sounds as they danced and sported for their own amusement.

The sounds of the rivers and ponds flowing there are exquisite and beautiful; the rivers of food and drink possess perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. Amidst these, the deva-sons roam, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses and sporting for their own delight.
Adorned with various ornaments together with the celestial maidens, he enjoyed the fruits of his heavenly virtuous karma for a long time; yet, due to negligence, he remained unaware of it.

Thus, while the devaputra experienced the pleasures of the five senses, his karma was exhausted and he was destined to fall back. Negligence shrouded his mind so that he did not perceive his impending downfall; deluded by craving and scorched by the fire of desire, his heart was attached to sensual delights, and he remained unaware.
When the signs of decline appear and fear is realized, and one perceives impermanence and change, it is certain that one will inevitably fall; only then does the mind awaken.

Thus, these sons of heaven, attached to and indulging in negligence, until their wholesome karma is exhausted, at the end of life they fall back and, transmigrating according to their karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
