If there is remaining karma that causes rebirth among humans, one will experience supreme happiness, be endowed with abundant wealth and treasures, be upright and free from flattery, and be born in a central land. One will discern between wrong and right conduct, know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and be born in a place where all virtuous people follow the Dharma and where the ways of gratitude are known. Such a person will be pleasing to behold for all, inspiring love and respect in both the elderly and the young; they will always be free from illness and affliction, possess the highest degree of physical beauty, have great strength and fearlessness, and bring comfort to all. They will be fully provided with a wife and children, and their possessions—whether wealth or goods—cannot be seized by kings, thieves, water, or fire.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The nineteenth stage of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named "As One Wishes.
By what karma are sentient beings born in this place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who, with a mind of right view, believe in the retribution of karmic actions; they abide firmly in right view, their minds are upright and honest, and they do not harm sentient beings. They filially support their parents, practice in accordance with the Dharma without indolence, and show reverence to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. They refrain from killing and stealing, neither commanding others to do so nor rejoicing in such acts; seeing others commit them, they exhort them to desist.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he explains the retribution of karma, causing them to abide in the wholesome paths by refraining from killing and stealing.

If there are sentient beings who do not maintain the precepts, he teaches them to abide in the precepts; if there are people who already maintain the precepts, he teaches them to remain steadfastly established in them.
Such a person benefits both themselves and others, and after the end of their life, they will be reborn in the good realms among the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
What is meant by not killing?
If one recognizes another sentient being—even down to the likes of lice, mosquitoes, and ants—and does not intentionally take their life, this is called non-killing.
There are sentient beings who kill *gōda* (musk shrews), rats, hares, and other such creatures by setting snares, nets, traps, and pitfalls; [the practitioner] exhorts them not to do so.

Furthermore, there are others who employ evil means, using various nooses and pitfalls, spreading nets to hunt birds and beasts, and employing all kinds of lethal instruments to filter out sentient beings and deprive them of life;
this person who upholds the precepts exhorts them to relinquish these acts—this is called non-killing.
They cause other sentient beings to abide securely on the path of goodness.
How do they refrain from stealing?
They do not give rise to the thought of theft even regarding a blade of grass or a leaf.
Seeing others committing theft, he exhorts them not to do so.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who engage in unrighteous conduct:

at a Buddha-stūpa or within a vihāra, while others are making offerings to the stūpa with various musical instruments, yet another person is there dancing and singing for his own amusement, or joining women in song, dance, and laughter, finding joy therein.

Or if one works as a hired musician in a monastery, or supports oneself by performing various musical offerings at Buddhist stupas, one should not allow such a person to perform music for others; this is called non-stealing.
Furthermore, there is theft:
for instance, when one initially agrees to pay a high price for a prostitute but later pays a smaller amount; this is called theft.
Furthermore, there is theft:
If there are those who sell wine, butcher animals, or engage in trade by fixing prices without compensating the original value, this is called stealing.
One who upholds the precepts completely abandons such acts of killing and stealing; they do not rejoice when seeing them committed, nor do they even entertain such thoughts in their mind.

What is giving? One who is poor and possesses little wealth yet is able to relinquish material goods to give to those practicing the third dhyāna; one who endures the suffering of hunger oneself to bestow gifts upon others, giving with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion as if toward one's own child.
What is meant by upholding the precept of not killing sentient beings?

If one encounters sentient beings being killed while cleaning a latrine, one instructs them not to do so; one provides them with water and drink, and restores them to their place of filth, thereby ensuring their lives are not harmed—this is called non-killing.
A person who performs such wholesome karma, at the end of life, is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Having been born in that celestial realm, this person of wholesome karma experiences the pleasures of the five senses, surrounded by the sounds of divine music and various celestial maidens, enjoying incomparable bliss.

Now, for the sake of this deva, I shall provide a brief illustration: the pleasure experienced by a golden-wheel-turning monarch, when compared to celestial bliss, does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.

The celestial body they receive has neither bone nor flesh, nor is it subject to defilement; they do not give rise to envy, their eyes do not blink, their garments are free from dust and grime, unaffected by smoke or mist, and they are without the affliction of excrement or urine.
The radiance of his body is something that a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) does not possess at all.

He does not show partiality toward his own wife and children, is free from jealousy, has mastery over food and drink, and knows neither sleep nor exhaustion—things that a Wheel-Turning Sage King does not possess at all.

For this reason, the pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch do not equal even one-sixteenth part of it; therefore, using a minor analogy from among humans, he experiences the pleasures of the five desires in such a sequence.
“There is a grove named Kapila, ten yojanas long and five yojanas wide, entirely adorned with golden birds.”

Countless birds, their bodies adorned all over with various jewels, serve as ornaments; the groves are beautified by the radiance of exquisite flowers, and the trees are made of the seven precious gems.

Within these forests, the birds possess a most sublime brilliance, just as a person wearing various ornaments becomes increasingly magnificent; likewise, the birds of manifold colors adorn the celestial trees in this same way.
Furthermore, there are sons of gods within this grove who sport and enjoy themselves with various flowers.

These flowers all have stems, leaves, and filaments made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, while their pericarps are made of red lotus jewels. The fragrance of these flowers fills ten *yojanas* and surpasses all other flowers; when the gods smell this scent, their joy increases tenfold.
Furthermore, together with the celestial maidens, he went toward the Food River in Kapilavastu; it arrived as soon as he thought of it.

There were lofty palaces with various railings, multi-storied pavilions and gateways adorned with various jeweled bells and various jeweled garlands, covered above by nets of pearls. Various jeweled banners were suspended, with many precious streamers hanging down, all magnificently decorated with gold, silver, crystal, and red jewels.
The various pillars were adorned with figures of geese, doves, pigeons, *jīvajīvaka* birds, or wild geese; such diverse flocks of birds as these served to ornament the palace.

The celestial hosts ascended the hall; by virtue of their wholesome karma, they went with various goddesses toward the Great Forest of Kapilavastu to the place of food and drink. Having arrived, they immediately descended and partook of the sweet celestial delicacies.

Having finished eating, they sported; amidst the various musical sounds in the groves, they enjoyed themselves in play for a long time, and because their minds were attached to pleasure, they did not perceive the passage of such a vast duration.

They then proceeded to the Forest of All Views (*Sarvadṛṣṭi-vana*), where they ascended a high peak desiring to behold the various groves; subsequently, together with the other hosts of devas, they returned to the Palace of Transformation (*nirmāṇa-prāsāda*).
There, they delighted one another with various songs and dances, various jests and laughter, enjoying pleasure with a single mind.

Having arrived at the Forest of All-Vision, he stayed upon its peak and beheld one side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which was adorned with many groves and gardens; the flowers there possessed the luster and color of molten gold, their radiance surging like flames.

There are various rivers, springs, streams, ponds, and watering places, with rivers of delicious drink and rivers of various foods, surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens adorned in diverse ornaments.

That Mount Sumeru sustains all the worlds; it stands amidst sixty thousand mountains and is surrounded by those sixty thousand mountains. It is lofty, steep, vast, and expansive—the dwelling place of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and kiṃnaras, and the refuge for devas of virtuous karma, obtained as the fruit of various wholesome deeds.

In each dwelling place where the four jewels are perfected, they see all the various colors used as adornments; they take delight in one another, their minds becoming dissolute with desire, exchanging various pleasant words and engaging in playful banter, while moving about, playing, and eating in their superior, middling, and inferior bodies.
Having seen this, he thought:
"It is not only I who enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; there are many other devas as well, sporting with their celestial nymphs and experiencing such delights."
Thus he beheld various gardens adorned with wish-fulfilling trees of diverse colors and fragrances.
At that time, the gods further beheld another region,
the first of which was named High Mound (Uccaya).
The second is named Mahā-uccaya (Great High Mound).

It is adorned with various rivers; when the sun and moon travel over the summit of this mountain and behold those two mountains, they see hundreds of thousands of bodies within that light, just as was previously described regarding Rāhu the Asura obstructing the sunlight with his hand.

At that time, the devaputra again hovered and circled in mid-air, gazing upon the King of Mountains; he enjoyed himself and took pleasure with the celestial maidens, and while dwelling in his palace, the sounds of his songs and praises were heard throughout the gardens of the King of Mountains, all of which he beheld.

Returning to their own realm and having reached their original palace, they enjoy various pleasures within the gardens, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing; indulging themselves in the five desires, their minds are shrouded by sensual pleasure, and they do not perceive the passage of long time.

He then proceeded to Mount Sālamā, which was five yojanas in length and breadth and ten yojanas in height; he ascended this mountain either by means of a celestial palace or by riding upon a flying bird.

They are adorned with various jeweled pillars and various rivers and ponds embellished with the seven treasures; wish-fulfilling jewel trees radiate blazing light, and amidst various musical performances, they joyfully entertain one another, experiencing the fruits of their own karma.
Due to their negligence, they pass a long time without realizing it; deluded by pleasure, they know no satiety.

They then proceed to an *utpala* grove, where they are surrounded by hundreds of thousands of bees. Entering the grove, they partake together of fine food and drink, enjoying themselves with song and dance, never reaching a point of satisfaction.

They further proceeded to a place of recreation called Vimala (Stainless), where hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of musical sounds provided entertainment together, such that they were never satiated.

The devas, being heedless and indulging in the pleasures of the five desires, eventually exhaust their wholesome karma; at the end of their lives, they fall back and descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
If there is remaining karma, one will be born among humans with a radiant complexion, esteemed by sovereigns, possessing the foremost wealth and happiness,
and being wise and discerning— due to that remaining karma.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who knows the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the twentieth stage is named Subtle Conduct (Sūkṣmacāra).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that heaven? Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

these sentient beings practiced wholesome dharmas for their own benefit and the benefit of others; they did not deceive sentient beings nor cause them distress. Practicing with integrity and performing wholesome deeds, they obtained the retribution of happiness; performing cooling deeds, they obtained a cooling retribution. Possessing the joyful retribution of wholesome karma, they were honored by all sentient beings and beloved by all people, attaining peace, happiness, and benefit in both the present and the future.
If one casts off this body and reaches future lives, the wholesome karma one has performed will be like parents; because it is in accordance with reality, one will experience immeasurable bliss.
One refrains from killing and stealing, and likewise teaches others to practice non-killing and to refrain from theft.

Furthermore, if there are those who kill living beings or steal, one should not dwell together with them, nor associate with them, nor play with them, nor engage in work together; in this way, one does not cohabit with such persons who break the precepts and practice evil.

One draws near to those who uphold the precepts and practice goodness, sharing in their activities and enjoying themselves together, while mutually contemplating what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.

Such a person of wholesome karma neither commits evil themselves nor instructs others to commit evil; such a person universally cultivates wholesome deeds, causing those who have broken the precepts to abide in the path of goodness, showing people the true Dharma so they may enter the right path, and planting seeds of wholesome karma.
The mind of such a person is pure like refined gold; practicing wholesome deeds, they will enjoy peace and happiness in both the present and the future.
This is called non-killing.
Furthermore, there is another form of non-killing:

There are sentient beings who, due to wrong views, kill various snakes, scorpions, centipedes, mosquitoes, gadflies, lizards, and the like; by killing such creatures, they fumigate fruit trees, desiring to make the flowers and fruits in their groves flourish.
Those who uphold the precepts are not like this; in order to protect life, they will never intentionally eat various fruits or foods suspected of containing insects.
As for water, curd-milk, fermented grain drinks, and various other beverages, they will never drink them unless they have carefully inspected them.
Regarding water that has been kept overnight, if one does not examine it closely, there may be fears of tiny insects being present; if it is not filtered and purified, it must not be drunk nor used.
This is called the subtle observance of the precept against killing.
What is meant by not stealing and not being self-indulgent?
Furthermore, how many kinds are there?
If a person reflects, desiring that various kinds of rice, grains, hemp, wheat, millet, and beans be accomplished for them alone;
He causes the five grains to fail to ripen for the people of the world, while he alone achieves a bountiful harvest.

Constantly engaging in such unwholesome thoughts, at another time when sentient beings have little merit and the crops in the fields are not harvested, this evil person sees the world’s famine and feels joy in his heart, thinking:
"It is just as I had intended."
Selling goods in the marketplace with a crooked mind and crafty deceit, he cheats people by mis-measuring grains and wheat; thus, he ultimately completes the karma.
When the mind reflects upon it, it is called the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*);
when the act of deception is performed, it is called the karma of deception (*vañcana-karma*).
Once the act of deception has been committed, it is termed a "completed action.
One should abandon such manifold faults and refrain from committing them.
Although a person who upholds the precepts may be poor, they do not employ unlawful means to deceive others; nor do they feel joy in their hearts when seeing others commit such acts.
If, in a time of famine, one seeks profit through livelihood by engaging in trade according to the Dharma and without deceiving sentient beings, this is called non-stealing.
How does such a virtuous person practice giving?

With a virtuous mind and virtuous conduct, one benefits both oneself and others; though one may have acquired wealth through personal poverty and diligent toil, or obtained it by constantly begging for goods from others, once acquired, one gives it to those who are poor, sick, or destitute.
If one who has studied the third dhyāna and attained the third dhyāna seeks [wealth] from others and, having obtained it through diligent effort, practices giving,
this person’s threefold karma of giving is perfected:
when the mind contemplates and desires to practice giving, this is called determination;
When one gives a gift, it is called "karma";
once the gift has been given and the mind reflects upon it again, this is called "consummation.
Such a person performs one thousand two hundred wholesome karmas; after the end of their life, they will be reborn in a subtle region within the happy realms.

When those who have practiced wholesome deeds are born in that heaven, because of the causal conditions of their subtle karmic actions, the celestial body they obtain conforms to their thoughts; its magnitude, whether vast or minute, follows their will.
The grounds and groves have trees made of the seven treasures; they are supremely pure, perfected by the karma of those who dwell there.

These forests of the seven treasures are twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, fully endowed with rivers, springs, and flowing streams. Those who behold them find joy and delight; they are pure and stainless, like a clear mirror.
The branches and leaves of those trees are pure and stainless, like the color of molten gold; the groves are composed of trees of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various other diverse colors.
When the sons of heaven enter the grove, within the branches and leaves of all the jewel trees, they each see their own physical forms.
Just as they see their own bodies within a single tree, so it is likewise within hundreds of thousands of trees; the physical characteristics of each son of heaven appear clearly in all the trees.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they obtain corresponding fruits.

This tree possesses further extraordinary qualities: according to the superior, middling, or inferior karma they have created, as they are born into this heaven, all the superior, middling, and inferior karma originally performed by them is manifested within the tree; from the roots, trunk, branches, and leaves, everything is clearly visible.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was adorned with celestial maidens and flower garlands; the radiance of his palace shone with such brilliant clarity that it surpassed the combined light of a hundred suns shining together.

When the gods of the Subtle Conduct Heaven saw Śakra from afar, they all went out to meet him; having arrived, they paid homage by prostrating themselves before Śakra and followed the Lord of Devas back into the grove to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
The Deva King Śakra also comforted the various devas with pleasant words, saying:
"You have performed great wholesome deeds!
The birds of that grove emitted exquisite sounds, and the park was adorned with trees made of pure gold.
At that time, the Heavenly King, having observed the retribution of karma, spoke in verse:
“Through virtuous karma one obtains this fruit; The various forests of karma provide witness.
Though there is no speech, One knows it is by way of the retribution of virtuous karma.”
Through various kinds of karmic retributions, one undergoes birth and death in every place;
whether virtuous or unvirtuous, such is the retribution one receives.
If a person cultivates wholesome karma, they shall be reborn among the devas.
If one performs unwholesome deeds, one falls into the three evil realms.
Delighting in both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and deluded by attachment to desire and ignorance,
one does not realize that one shall decline and perish, destined to undergo the suffering of death.
Now, by the signs of this tree, one may know the retribution of these wholesome karmas;
yet they do not grow weary of or renounce desire, for their minds are deluded by pleasure.
Those people who indulge in the flavors of desire and negligence constantly seek after sensory objects with their minds.
Constantly tormented by craving, one is likewise bound by craving.
One desires to dwell together with women; yet women are exceedingly evil, capable of producing feverish affliction, like fire that harms sentient beings.
Such torment of desire exceeds even a great and fierce fire;
the great heat of female form incinerates the minds of sentient beings.
Women destroy the world, causing all that is wholesome to be utterly extinguished.
This is the cause and condition for hell; thus has the Great Sage spoken.
Though her mouth speaks pleasant words, her heart is like a poisonous harm;
she deceives and cheats without a moment's pause—the woman’s mind has no reality.
In an instant they give rise to affection, in an instant their hearts are without love;
their minds do not pause for a moment, like lightning that does not endure long.
Those of clever wit who deceive others draw near when the mind is greedy.
Constantly thinking only of delighting others, harboring arrogance and licentiousness;
gods, humans, piśācas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and yakṣas—all are bound by female form; women are like virulent poison.
She is unmindful of kindness received; she possesses neither noble lineage nor skillful arts.
The nature of women is like the wind: their minds do not rest.
When they see great wealth, their hearts give rise to attachment and delight.
Furthermore, when one sees misfortune arrive, one grows weary of it and abandons it;
yet if someone approaches, one gives rise to a heart of affection and delight,
only to cast them aside in an instant upon seeing their distress arrive.
Just as a bee delights in flowers but quickly abandons them when they wither, so too is it with women: when she is no longer pleased, she departs.
With an evil mind devoid of compassion and kindness, her heart is restless and unstable.
To destroy the ignorant, women have appeared in the world.
Among the fetters of the heavens, none surpasses the color of women;
women bind the devas and lead them to the three evil realms.
If the mind covets the beauty of women, this desire is most extreme;
the lust for female beauty burns the heart, leading later to great suffering.
Regarding the actions performed in the present, one’s own mind is deluded by greed and desire.
The deluded mind cannot awaken, for it is bewildered by the desires of women.
Once a man has placed his trust [in them], he is bound by immeasurable love;
yet he suddenly casts them off, just as a snake sheds its skin.
Such is the nature of women: though served with every skillful means and protected in various ways, they still cannot be won over by the heart.
The nature of women is thus; their minds lack sincerity.
"Deceitful and full of guile and hypocrisy, it is not trusted by the wise.
When the sons of the gods heard Śakra, Lord of Devas, speak these teachings, they felt weary of and detached from worldly existence, and spoke in verse:
"Just so, just so, O King of Devas! What you have spoken is according to reality, true and not false."
“I lacked wisdom and failed to perceive this; I have bound my own mind with the net of celestial maidens.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had heard this verse, he immediately went to the Forest of Bird-Sounds (*Śakunaghoṣa*). It was adorned with immeasurable palaces, and its trees were graced by lotus bathing pools. Its golden mountain peaks resembled masses of molten gold, and it resounded with the exquisite melodies of various musical instruments and songs, where many hosts of celestial maidens gathered.
Śakra, King of the Devas, entered this grove desiring to enjoy celestial pleasures, experiencing the delights of the five senses within the realms of his faculties.
He then proceeded to Mount Gandhamādana, to the peak of Sumeru, which was adorned with the seven treasures; its flowing rivers were magnificent and extraordinary.

The mountain peaks are adorned with pearl necklaces, and the riverbed is strewn with sand made of pearls; on both banks of the river, many birds emit exquisite melodies, and all who behold this river conceive a sense of love and joy.
Śakra, King of Devas, together with various celestial maidens and the hosts of devas, adorned in manifold ornaments, sported and enjoyed pleasures upon this mountain peak.

Having finished his enjoyment, he again went with the sons of devas and celestial maidens to the place of sporting in the Cūḍāmaṇi Palace. Upon arriving there, the devas from other regions, hearing that the Lord of Devas had arrived, also all gathered there.

The palaces upon that peak reside at the summit of Mount Sumeru; they are lofty, vast, magnificent, and pure. Just as the light of the Yāma Heaven illuminates the summit of Mount Sumeru, causing its color to reflect throughout the four continents, so too does the light of the Yāma Heaven illuminate this mountain peak.
Because it is illuminated by the radiance of the Yāma Heaven, this palace is a thousand times more magnificent than all other palaces.
At that time, having finished sporting in this palace, Śakra-devendra, the Lord of Devas, returned with the sons of gods and daughters of gods to the Sudharmā Hall.

These gods of Subtle Conduct experience the pleasures of the five desires until their wholesome karma is exhausted; at the end of their lives, they fall back and descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there remains further karma leading to birth among humans, one will constantly experience peace and happiness, becoming either a king or a high minister. Possessing the foremost conch-like hair, their mind is discerning and profound; they are consulted and honored by others, and do not delight in excessive speech. Their clothing is fresh, clean, and free from stain or defilement; their wives and concubines are chaste, and their hearts are upright and not crooked. They take pleasure in practicing generosity, being straightforward and without flattery; they are loved and respected by their brothers and kinsmen, and they revere teachers and elders. They cherish guests, delight in practicing generosity, maintain the precepts to guard themselves, and by nature love fragrant garlands. They distance themselves from evil associates, are born into a great clan, and are handsome, exquisite, and adorned with various ornaments.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, monks, knowing the retribution of karma, one contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one sees:"
The twenty-first stage is named Joyful Song-Sound.
By what karma are sentient beings born in this stage?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who possess a virtuous mind and virtuous karma, whose body, speech, and mind are wholesome; they practice virtuous deeds for their own benefit and the benefit of others, bringing great advantage to all beings. Their hearts are imbued with compassion, and they have faith in the law of karmic cause and effect. Possessing right view and right action, they uphold two kinds of precepts: their minds are undistracted, they do not lose their dignified deportment, and they do not associate with evil friends. They are filial and supportive toward their parents and make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. They fully practice and perfect the three kinds of wholesome karma and maintain the two types of precepts—namely, refraining from killing and refraining from stealing.
What is meant by "not killing"?

If there are minute insects within rice, millet, or wheat, one does not pound or grind them; knowing that they contain living beings, one protects the lives of these insects and does not pass them on to others.
Furthermore, there is non-killing:

if oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys are carrying loads until their backs are ruined and worms breed in the sores, when one washes these sores with a decoction of grain-water, one does not use medicinal herbs to sever the lives of these worms; instead, using bird feathers to scrub and wipe them clean, one places the worms into other stinking, rotting, or spoiled meat, thereby preserving their lives.
He protects these donkeys and oxen, fearing that their lives might be harmed, and he further protects the lives of insects; even ants he does not kill intentionally.

Whether by day or by night, he does not engage in negligence; his mind does not harbor thoughts of killing, and if there is the perception of a living being—whether it be a louse or an ant—he does not kill it intentionally.
This is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing? How many kinds of non-stealing are there?

If there are sentient beings who see a snake eating insects, a frog eating insects, or a yellow weasel eating insects; or if they see a dog or a jackal seizing various sentient beings, intending to eat them.
If that person sees [the other] and trades what he himself eats for [the other's] life, causing him to escape, such a person protects the lives of both self and other; this is called non-stealing.

Not stealing oneself nor teaching others to do so, one exhorts all sentient beings to abide in the path of goodness; those who have not yet established themselves in the precepts, one teaches to abide in them; those who already uphold the precepts, one causes them to increase [in virtue]; and by explaining the retribution of karmic actions, one brings about their awakening.
This is what is called not killing and not stealing.

Furthermore, there are practitioners who follow the Dharma and benefit sentient beings; seeing honeybees and knowing that others wish to kill them, they ransom them with objects so that they may be set free, bestowing life upon them—this is called the gift of life.
Furthermore, there is giving:

if a practitioner of the Dharma is poor and destitute, one might give them even a single meal; or, seeing an evil person who intends to take another's life, one might ransom that person with goods to ensure their release.

The gift of life and the gift of the Dharma are the foremost among all gifts; such a person practices these two kinds of giving, teaches others to practice them as well, and rejoices in seeing them being performed.
Maintaining the precepts in this manner, after the end of life, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the realm of Song-Sound Delight;
through the transformation of wholesome karma, one receives superior offerings.
Because of their virtuous karma, the groves and gardens of that land are adorned in various ways.

"In the abode of the devas, there is not a single spot that is not a transformation of virtuous karma; there is not a single deva who does not sport, there is not a single deva who does not experience pleasure, and there is not a single deva who does not eventually pass away."
"When their wholesome karma is exhausted, they know it at the time of their decline; yet they remain unsatisfied, bound by the ropes of craving and deceived by craving.
After Śakra, King of the Gods, had spoken these words, he sported and enjoyed himself with the hosts of devas in the groves, where the trees were fully endowed with various flowers and fruits.
The River of Food and Drink is replete with every flavor; together with the hosts of devas, they arrive at the banks of this river to enjoy themselves and experience pleasure.
Then, accompanied by celestial maidens, they proceed to the place of play known as Mātaliṃnana. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beholding the trees of that grove, said to the devas:
"Do you all see this place of play?"
The sons of the gods replied,
"Indeed, we have seen it. Then Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, explained for the sons of the gods the Dharma of past events:

"As I heard from the elder devas in the past, there was once a Buddha named Kakudaṃdavyūha Tathāgata who taught the Dharma to the devas in this grove; it was good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing—a pure and complete teaching of the white dharma."
It is said: "Because this exists, that exists; because this ceases, that ceases.
What is meant by "existence"?
Because desire exists, there are faults.
If one is without desire, then there are no faults.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
This is what is meant by: "Because this thing exists, that thing exists. What is meant by:
"Because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist"?
If there is no desire, then there is no fault of desire; this is what is meant by: "Because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist."
What is meant by "because this thing ceases, that thing ceases"?
Because craving ceases, desire ceases; because desire ceases, the transgression of desire ceases. This is called "because this thing ceases, that thing ceases."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
Because this exists, that exists; because this does not exist, that does not exist.
If one contemplates in reverse the causal conditions of craving and the root from which desire arises, one sees that the causal conditions of desire are able to produce desire."
What is desire? When the mind seeks and recollects, desiring to perform some action, this is called desire (*chanda*).
Because delusion involves seeking something, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of ignorance, one feels no weariness toward sense objects; this is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
O sons of the gods!
Because one does not seek contentment, it is called desire (*kāma*).
O sons of the gods!
This is called: because this thing exists, that thing exists.
What is meant by: because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist?
What is called craving for existence is greed that knows no satisfaction;
if craving is extinguished, then lack of satiety is extinguished as well—this is what is meant by "because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist."
This is called: "Because this thing ceases, that thing ceases.
Furthermore, O Devaputra, because this thing exists, that thing exists; namely, the collective formation of karma.
Because karma exists, there is the retribution of karma;
if there were no accumulation of karma, there would be no retribution of karma.
O sons of the gods!
This is called: "Because this thing exists, that thing exists; because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist.
Furthermore, O Devaputra, how is it that "because this thing exists, that thing exists"?
That is to say: first there is mindfulness; when the eye conditions a form, consciousness arises.
With mindfulness as the precursor, this is called "because this thing exists, that thing exists."
How is it that because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist?
If there is no form, then there is no eye; if there is no eye, then there is no recollection. Because there is no form, no eye, and no recollection, visual consciousness also does not exist.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
This is called: because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!"
What is meant by "because this exists, that exists"?
It is like a potter: through the combination of various factors—the wheel, the string, the clay, and water—a jar is produced.
O sons of the gods!
"It is also thus that because this thing exists, that thing exists. Furthermore, O Devaputra,
how is it that because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist?"
For example, if a potter’s wheel, cord, clay, and water do not come together, then there is no jar.
In this same way, it is also like this: because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
How is it that 'because this exists, that exists'? It is said:
where there is union, there must be separation; this is what is meant by 'because this exists, that exists. "
"How is it that because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist?
If there is no coming together, then there is no parting.
It is thus, O Devaputra!"
This means that because this thing does not exist,
that thing does not exist. "Furthermore, O Devaputra,
how is it that because this thing exists, that thing exists?"
Because there is birth, there is death.
If there were no birth, there would be no death.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

This is called: "Because this exists, that exists; because this does not exist, that does not exist. Since devas do not age, when preaching the Dharma to devas, one does not speak of the factor of aging, but speaks only of death.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
How is it that because this exists, that exists? It is said:
because desire exists, one is inevitably burned; just as where there is fire, there must necessarily be burning."
Thus it is, O Devaputra! This is called:
because this thing exists, that thing exists. What is meant by:
because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist?
It is because of revulsion toward desire that desire cannot burn one, just as without fire there can be no burning.
Thus, O Devaputra, it is said that "because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
How is it that because this exists, that exists? It is said:

because there are the semen and blood of the parents, and because there is karma, the *ālaya*, and the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), just as a fragrance [produces its effect], the body is born."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
This is what is meant by "because this exists, that exists.
What is meant by "because this does not exist, that does not exist"?
If there were no father and mother, there would be no semen and blood; if there were no determinate karma, no womb, and no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there would be no arising of a body.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Because this thing does not exist, that thing does not exist.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 29.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 30.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Contemplating the Heavens, Part Nine; Thirty-three Heavens, Part Six.
"Furthermore, because this exists, that exists; that is to say, because there is the 'other shore,' there is the 'this shore.'"
If there is no "other shore," then there is no "this shore. Thus, O Devaputra, it is because this exists that that exists;
because this does not exist, that does not exist. They arise together through mutual dependence on their respective causes and conditions.
All conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions. As for these causes and conditions:
namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; and so on, up to and including death, which is likewise.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

Regarding these twelve links of dependent origination, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, within this palace, for five thousand years by human reckoning, expounded this Dharma within this very palace."

I shall now proclaim for you a small portion of it; Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time have all spoken this same Dharma as the True Dharmakāya.
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached this Dharma, seven hundred million devas exhausted all outflows and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
"At that time, the World-Honored One returned to Jambudvīpa and preached the Dharma for the sake of human beings with a heart of great compassion."
That is to say: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," and so on, up to "conditioned by birth are old age and death.
At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, having distanced themselves from dust and defilement, attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows regarding all phenomena.
"In this way, the World-Honored One, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, has expounded this Dharma for the sake of all gods and humans.

Having thus extensively preached the Dharma for the assembly of gods, Śakra proceeded to the celestial palace of the Mātaliṃnaha gods. Upon arriving at that palace, he saw various birds, their wings and feathers adorned with the seven treasures.

There were many lotus ponds, and within those ponds were lotuses made of the seven treasures. The colors of these lotuses were the colors of various jewels, and they were adorned by swarms of bees of every kind; like the rising sun, the radiance of these flowers adorned the jeweled palaces.
Beside that palace stands a tree of lapis lazuli; as the light of the tree reflects off one another, it causes this celestial palace to emit a blue radiance.
The leaves of that lapis lazuli tree are made of pure gold; because these leaves reflect one another, they emit yellow and red light.
Furthermore, there was great radiance as an adornment; the palaces and gardens were adorned with various kinds of jewels.
These various jeweled palaces and gardens of the seven precious substances were further adorned with flowering trees, making them exceedingly delightful.
When Śakra saw this, he conceived a sense of rare wonder.
Within his palace was a great flower pond, fashioned from the seven precious gems; its water was yellow like a mass of molten gold, exquisitely adorned and magnificent.
It was inlaid and adorned with various kinds of precious jewels and embellished with birds of diverse colors.
All the hosts of devas, accompanied by various musical instruments, singing, dancing, and laughing together in mutual enjoyment, proceeded toward a great pond named Sarvābhibhū (All-Surpassing).
Seeing that the minds of the devaputras were agitated and dissolute, the birds in the pond spoke these verses for the sake of the devaputras:
"Just as the *śarabha* bird does not dwell among lotuses,
so too should wicked people not reside in such a place of tranquility."
In such a tranquil forest, how can one practice heedlessness?
To act with inverted views and disregard for the Dharma is like the sun emitting cold light.
If one attains freedom from craving and delight, one will be liberated and freed from all suffering.
If one is separated from these two dharmas, celestial bliss is not true bliss.
By practicing dhyāna and abandoning negligence, one is liberated from the snare of desire;
such liberation alone is called bliss, for it is not deceived by your worldly attachments.
"The World-Honored One formerly dwelt here, as did various practitioners;
you, however, are led by desire and should not remain in this grove.
This palace, where celestial pleasures are enjoyed, is impermanent and will not endure for long."
If one is free from craving and desire, this is the supreme bliss.
Those who previously dwelt in this grove have all entered the foremost state;
having attained that foremost state, they are able to sever all suffering.
One whose greedy mind craves fine food, deceived by that very greed,
should not dwell in this forest of tranquility.
Those who cultivate a tranquil mind and delight in purity should dwell here.
If the mind wanders among sensual objects, it does not dwell in the forest of tranquility.
If the mind is tranquil, one should dwell in the forest;
if the mind is disturbed by desire, one should not dwell in this forest.
Fearing the five causes and conditions, one cannot be burned by craving;
the pure person who has abandoned craving will never fall into the evil realms.
Where there is birth, there must be death; the strong are invaded by illness.
Wealth and pleasure end in decline and distress; youth is destroyed by old age.
There must be separation from those one loves; unions do not endure for long.
All phenomena are thus—this is what the Perfectly Awakened One has taught.
If a person within the three realms has a mind that is not deluded,
that person attains tranquility and should dwell in the forest of stillness.
Constantly enslaved by desire and crookedness, they harbor fear in their recollections.
Such a person shall not obtain the joy of tranquility within the forest.
If one’s mind is pure and one relies upon the forest to cultivate tranquility, that person finds joy in the forest;
such is not the case for one who pursues sensual desires.
Cultivating a pure mind in the forest, one enters the village with an unshakable heart;
therefore, one should dwell in the forest and not reside in towns or cities.
If a person enters a town or city, they will be disturbed by the mind of desire.
Devoid of flattery and crookedness, unsullied and pure, one reaches the forest and returns to stillness.
Therefore, within the groves of trees, there is the foremost and supreme tranquility;
this is where the practitioner should dwell, able to leave behind the mind of desire.
With all faculties and mind stilled, the practitioner’s heart is at peace and bliss;
the joy of a thousand Śakras does not equal the heart of such a person.
If one attains the bliss of meditative concentration, all pure and white dharmas [will follow].
Among the gods of the Yāma heaven, none can equal even a fraction of this bliss.
Pleasure born of desire is ever conjoined with manifold suffering;
but the bliss that comes from severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) is forever indestructible.
Within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, the afflictions form a knot of enmity within the mind;
if one severs this knot of enmity, no sensual pleasure can equal it.
That which arises from desire as pleasure is, in truth, the impure and bitter fruit of retribution.
If one attains the bliss of liberation, that bliss is beyond compare.
Relying on the practice of detachment is the foremost path for the practitioner;
the sensual pleasure born of craving cannot lead to the True Path.
When initial craving produces a sweet taste, one receives retribution like fire or poison;
the pleasure born of desire leads eternally to hell.
When initial craving produces a wholesome taste, so too does intermediate craving.
Later, through tranquility and purity, one can reach the state of peace and bliss.
If one acts with goodness in the beginning and the middle, adorning oneself like a compassionate mother,
why would one abandon right mindfulness to dally in the realm of sensual pleasures?
Driven by the swirling eddies of desire, one suffers constant distress from the middle of the day until its end;
how can a foolish person find delight in desire?
It is like a flower of exquisite color that is poisonous, or like touching a fierce flame.
Sensual pleasures are likewise; in the end, they bring great suffering and distress.
Just as adding more fuel to a fire makes its flames impossible to extinguish, and it burns both oneself and others, so too are sensual pleasures.
Just as a moth throws itself into a flame, unaware of the suffering of being burned, so it is with sensual pleasures; the deluded person does not perceive this.
If a person is attached to sensual pleasures, they are constantly burned by those very desires.
Like a moth casting itself into a lamp’s flame, the fire of desire exceeds this even more.
Therefore, abandon the harm of desire and always delight in cultivating wisdom;
do not practice heedlessness, for through heedlessness one falls into the evil realms.
Deceived by heedlessness regarding all sensual pleasures,
once the retribution for experiencing those joys is exhausted, one later falls into the suffering of hell.
When that person’s wholesome karma is spent, they are deceived by desire.
From the heavens down to the hells, one is deceived by desire and delusion;
from birth until the end, if one constantly practices right reflection and keeps the Dharma of the precepts in mind, that person attains quiescence.
Deceit, crookedness, and perverse recollection, The three poisons give rise to attachment;
The waters of negligence are profoundly deep, And the desire for women serves as the aquatic weeds.
Song and music stir the mind, As the waters of craving surge against the boulders.
Enveloped by the snakes of sensory objects, the waves of the mind flow in rapid currents.
The great, violent cataracts of the river of craving flow into the realm of the nāgas;
when foolish people enter this river, they are submerged by celestial desires.
Terrifying like a rushing torrent, the foolish do not realize they are being submerged;
they are like foolish bees drinking from the flowers of a poisonous tree.
Thus, though the poison of desire is harmful, the foolish take pleasure in their greedy attachment.
As bees drink poison and perish, there is no one who does not sink under the power of craving and desire.
Born from the waters of the three poisons and blown by the winds of negligence,
the fires of craving burn the celestial hosts, yet they remain unaware.
Poison is born within the heavens; heedlessness is its dense forest, where the deluded play, deceiving their own minds with craving.
Heedlessness gives rise to all desires, which cling to objects without a moment’s rest.
These desires are like dreams and illusions, which the wise do not believe in.
Although all desires are like dreams, a dream is not the cause of hell;
therefore, abandon all desires and constantly cultivate pure deeds.
Virtuous conduct is supreme; unwholesome karma is not.
Bound by such wholesome karma, one attains a superior realm.
The devas, being attached to sensual pleasures, do not attain the state of tranquility.
"The wise person attains supreme tranquility through heedfulness.
When the celestial bird had spoken this verse for the sake of the heedless sons of the gods, Śakra, King of the Devas, proceeded to another location within that grove.

Having reached that forest, it was entirely adorned with the various merits of virtuous karma; it was the dwelling place of those in training and those beyond training, and the abode of the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kakutsunda.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, together with immeasurable hosts of devas, performed celestial music and entered the grove, where they beheld these forest trees.

Having entered the grove, the majesty and virtue of all the devas were preeminently superior; just as Mount Sumeru stands amidst sixty thousand golden mountains, so too did Śakra, the Lord of Devas, appear among the devas.
Among all the groves of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the radiance of this grove is the most excellent and extraordinary.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the hosts of devas, respectfully surrounded him as they proceeded to the Jambū Grove.
In that Jambūvana grove, all the trees were made of gold as an adornment. When Śakra, King of the Gods, arrived in this grove, he addressed the host of devas, saying:
"Do you, members of the celestial assembly, see this entire, most excellent grove?"
"It is fully endowed with immeasurable flower ponds and groves.
The celestial hosts replied,
"Indeed, we have seen it."
Śakra replied: "This grove is thus fully endowed with all such merits.
Beholding it now, I have conceived a sense of wonder."
Beholding this forest now, it is as if one were seeing the peerless physical body of the Tathāgata Kakutsunda, the dwelling place of the Tathāgata who possesses all wisdom and great compassion.
In this dwelling place, immeasurable hosts of devas, by virtue of hearing the Dharma, have attained happiness from happiness.
Although this Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Great Man, has already entered parinirvāṇa, his residual fruits still remain.
At that time, Śakra again went to the grove of the Kūṭāgāra palace.
It was here that the Tathāgata Kakudha had also entered in the past.

When Śakra, King of Devas, entered this grove, he saw hundreds of thousands of palaces surrounding this central palace, adorned with the seven treasures—namely, the king of blue gems, diamond, musāragalva, and vaidūrya—with various precious jewels interspersed in their ornamentation and decorated with diverse banners and streamers.
Among all the palaces, the supreme palace where the Tathāgata sat shone with brilliant radiance.

Just as in the early summer or autumn when there are no clouds or mists, and the sun and moon are most preeminent among the multitude of stars, so too was the palace where the Tathāgata sat supremely distinguished.
Its brilliance was so radiant that, with the sole exception of Śakra, none among the hosts of devas could gaze upon the majesty and virtue of this palace for long.
It was like the midsummer sun in Jambudvīpa, which no person in the world can behold for long; the palace of the Tathāgata was likewise.
Śakra, King of Devas, addressed the devas, saying:
"Do you all see the majestic power and virtue of this palace? The devas replied:
"Yes, O Heavenly King! I have indeed seen it. Śakra replied:

"In the past, this hall was ascended by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śāstṛ of Gods and Men, Unsurpassed Great Teacher Kāśyapa, together with hundreds of thousands of śramaṇas who had all cast off the net of doubt, perceived the Four Noble Truths, attained the two kinds of liberation, and were endowed with the six supernormal powers and the four bases of psychic power, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all devas and humans."
During the four months of summer, he observed the rains retreat at this place and expounded the True Dharma for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He said: "This is form;

this is the arising of form; this is the cessation of form; this is the realization of the path leading to the cessation of form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this aggregation and accumulation is likewise to be viewed with the perception of its faults, and one should relinquish it and emerge from it."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

That Buddha-Tathāgata, in this sequence, for the sake of the various hosts of devas—who are negligent and arrogant, who do not perceive the suffering of decline and impermanence but cling only to sensual pleasures, and who do not understand the mark of the equality of self-nature—preaches such a Dharma to benefit sentient beings."
"At that time, the Tathāgata again preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the heedless sons of the gods, rebuking them with these verses:
"Heedlessness is the root of birth and death, The dwelling place of all the gods.
Intoxicated by the poison of heedlessness, They sink into the various realms of existence."
If one is free from heedlessness, one will forever escape the ocean of the three realms;
for heedlessness has delusion as its root, leaving one blind, dark, and without awakening.
The arising of light has its source: it is born from fire and the sun.
"From delusion arises heedlessness," so has the Great Sage said.
The fire of heedlessness blazes forth, arising from the mind;
it deceives and deludes the ignorant and foolish, leading them to the paths of the various hells.
Devas and humans indulge in heedlessness, driven by the power of female beauty;
they delight in their union with one another, unaware of the suffering of parting from what is loved.
When the end of life approaches, they experience great suffering right before them.
The court ladies also fade away, and all pleasures are utterly extinguished.
Where there is union, there must be separation; all joys come to an end.
Youthfulness shall inevitably decay and change; all karmic activities come to an end.
All sentient beings, bound by their good and evil karma,
are like performers at play, coming and going with various distinctions.
Bound by the artifice of karma, they wander through birth and death.
Impermanent karma flows and shifts; the wise should not place their trust in it.
Heedlessness is like a poisonous harm; one should skillfully abandon it.
If one is free from heedlessness, one will forever cross the ocean of the three realms.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Kakutsunda subdued nine nayutas of heedless devas, causing them to abandon their heedlessness; having analyzed and explained the Dharma for the benefit of those devas, he went to Jambudvīpa together with the bhikṣus and the great assembly."
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had finished speaking these words to the assembly of devas, he proceeded to the palace and ascended the jeweled hall.

The Kuṭāgaśa Palace was adorned with immeasurable varieties of precious jewels; such rare treasures as these had never been seen before by any of the devas. Upon seeing them, all the devas were filled with joy and gave rise to a sense of wonder.
Having seen this, Śakra addressed the assembly of devas:
"Do you see this preeminent palace? Such a magnificent and exquisite adornment as this has never existed before."
Then the assembly of devas said to the Heavenly King,
“Indeed, we have seen it. Śakra replied:
"This precious palace was offered by the King of the Yāma Heaven as a gift of pure faith to the World-Honored One Kāśyapa.
The radiance of this palace cannot be seen [by others], for such is the supreme excellence of that deity's light."
"Why is this? Because in previous lives, the devas did not practice heedlessness as you do.
At that time, the assembly of devas, realizing their own inferiority and weakness, abandoned their prideful minds.
All the hosts of devas bowed their heads in homage at the feet of the Tathāgata’s palace; they were all filled with joy, their countenances radiant and their hearts feeling a sense of renunciation.

They realized that their own karma was diminished, inferior, and meager. Some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, some gave rise to the mind of pratyekabuddha-bodhi, and some gave rise to the mind of śrāvaka-bodhi. Others attained indestructible faith in the Buddha. All the hosts of devas conceived pure faith, joined their palms in reverence, and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, entered the Kūṭāgāra Hall and proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata’s lion throne stood for preaching the Dharma.
There lay the bedding used by the Tathāgata Kakudha; its frame was made of diamond and was fully equipped with every kind of excellence.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with a pure mind, prostrated his entire body upon the ground before the lion throne, thinking to himself:
"This is the place where the Tathāgata sits."
Because he called the Tathāgata to mind with a heart of reverence, he rose from the ground and saw verses inscribed on the wall of the book-palace.
The text of those verses read:
"If a person throws himself from a precipice, There may be some who do not lose their life."
Those who fall into the state of negligence will never fail to experience suffering.
If a person acts with negligence, then whatever they do—
day and night alike— will ultimately yield no fruit of happiness.
All worldly and world-transcending dharmas of happiness can be destroyed by heedlessness; therefore, one should abandon it.
Heedfulness is immortality; heedlessness is the path of death.
Heedfulness is supreme; one shall become a lord of the devas.
Heedlessness is the root of birth and death; vigilance is the excellent path.
Therefore, abandon heedlessness, and you shall always enjoy celestial bliss.
If one desires happiness, and if one fears all forms of suffering, one should abandon heedless conduct; heedlessness is like fire and poison.
Heedlessness covers a person with sleep; heedlessness is the harm of the poison of delusion.
Committing various unwholesome deeds, one falls into pits and ravines through heedlessness.
Heedfulness is supreme; heedlessness is unwholesome.
Through heedfulness one attains happiness; through heedlessness one constantly suffers.
"In summary, these verse lines are the root of suffering and happiness;
having understood this merit, one should skillfully cultivate what is beneficial for oneself.

At that time, Śakra read and recited these verses, his reverence increasing. With a pure mind, he again prostrated with his head at the lion throne. Having long praised non-heedlessness and censured heedlessness in this place, he departed from the hall toward the assembly of devas.
At that time, the assembly of devas, seeing King Śakra, the Lord of Devas, all conceived feelings of reverence and approached him.
Then, Śakra, Lord of Devas, using the aforementioned verses, expounded them in full for the assembly of devas, addressing them thus:
"These verse lines were inscribed upon the palace walls for the sake of benefiting, bringing peace, and providing happiness to all the sons of the gods."
Upon hearing these words, all the hosts of devas prostrated before the World-Honored One and spoke thus:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Eye of the World, has spoken such verses for our sake."
At that time, the host of devas, having long been free from negligence, again went with various musical sounds to the devas of Subhakṛtsna (the Heaven of Refulgent Purity).

When the gods of the Subtle Conduct Heaven heard of this matter, they accompanied various celestial maidens with diverse musical instruments that produced exquisite sounds and came to this grove, desiring to enjoy themselves together with the sons of gods dwelling in this forest.

When the gods of the Subhakṛtsna Heaven arrive at this grove, the gods of this grove lose their right mindfulness and fall into negligence; they engage in various musical performances, singing, dancing, and laughter, directed toward the great assembly of the gods of the Subhakṛtsna Heaven.
Having seen one another, they all gave rise to joy; within the groves, jewel trees and jewel branches completely covered the gardens as they entertained one another.
This continued until their beloved wholesome karma was exhausted; their lives ended in the heavens, and driven by the flow of karma, they fell into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If there are those who close the gates of the three evil realms and are reborn among humans in a land of peace and happiness, where gardens, groves, streams, and ponds are all fully provided; who constantly perform wholesome deeds, possess great wealth and abundant riches, and may become either kings or ministers, being loved and respected by all people; and who always delight in practicing generosity, uphold the prohibitive precepts, and take pleasure in performing virtuous actions.
This is due to residual karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
There is a second location, named Wheel of Majestic Power (*Vīryacakravartin*).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

All sentient beings practice wholesome dharmas with constant heedfulness; with a mind intent on benefiting others, they benefit sentient beings; they have faith in the retribution of karma; they draw near to virtuous friends; and they refrain from killing and stealing.
Whether it be *śiṃśapā* trees, mango trees, jujubes, or hazel trees—among these various forest trees, there are bird nests upon them, and within the nests are fledglings.

If a bird or a snake were to seize the young of other birds, and that person, seeing this, would with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion benefit sentient beings by rescuing them and causing them to escape—
how is this not stealing?
In the groves and trees of others, one does not take even a single branch or leaf, nor does one incite others to do so.
If, while traveling on a road, one sees fruit left on the ground, one does not take it nor steal it; seeing someone else taking it, one exhorts them to desist and abandon it.
How does one practice virtue by cultivating generosity?
One gives food to the Sangha during times of rain; likewise, one gives food to those suffering from famine or to those afflicted by illness.

One maintains the precepts oneself and causes others to abide in the precepts; seeing those who abide in the precepts, one teaches them to rejoice in it; and for the sake of other sentient beings, one explains the retribution of karmic actions.

One practices giving while recollecting the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—whether giving to parents, to lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), or to those who lack the precepts or are afflicted by illness—one gives to these people whatever they require, such as food, drink, and medicinal supplies; furthermore, one teaches others to do the same and explains the retribution of karmic actions.
They do not associate with evil friends, nor dwell with them, nor converse with them.
They are always able to skillfully restrain the actions of body, speech, and mind, benefiting both themselves and others.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, on the Ground of Majestic Virtue and Wheels.
Having been born in this heaven, by virtue of their wholesome karma, the radiance of their bodies is like that of the full moon.
The ground is magnificently adorned and exceedingly delightful, filled with groves and gardens made of the seven precious gems.
There are various flowing springs and lotus ponds filled with diverse lotuses, their stalks made of lapis lazuli and their leaves of gold, completely covering the waters of the pools.
The banks are formed of various precious stones and metals.
The waters swirl and eddy as if in a dance, while various birds emit wondrous sounds that gladden the heart.
Peaks of true gold and peaks of lapis lazuli adorn the ground.
Geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks emit various wondrous sounds as the sons and daughters of gods joyfully sport around the lotus ponds.
Those rivers flow forth with exquisite melodies, and there are further groves of lotuses made of various jewels, adorned with diverse radiances and many kinds of bees.
The devas and devīs gaze upon the lotus ponds, their bodies adorned with various jewels.
In the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they enjoy pleasure for a long time.
They then proceed to the Miśrakāvana grove to sport and enjoy themselves, delighting one another with various musical sounds.

Upon reaching that forest, there was a lotus grove named *Vīṇā-vihāra* (Lute-like Play). This lotus grove was five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides; it was filled with drinks of supreme flavor, color, fragrance, and taste. Therein, the devas drank, singing, dancing, playing, laughing, and enjoying themselves together.
At that time, there was a celestial bird named Samyag-cārin (Right Conduct) who, seeing the sons of the gods indulging in negligence,
spoke these verses: “Lacking shame and lacking remorse, Lazy and having evil friends—
These are the seeds of hell, Which the wise abandon.”
Shameless and devoid of moral dread, constantly performing unwholesome deeds,
like a person falling from a high cliff who only realizes it later;
greedy, deluded, and lacking sincerity or faith, their minds feel no fear.
Deluded by envy, one cannot be born in the heavens.
Drinking alcohol, speaking falsehoods, the mind being firmly attached to greed and desire,
and not believing in the retribution of karmic results— these are the causes and conditions for hell.
Guard against the faults and evils of the mind; through the evil karma of anger and the evil karma of sentient beings, one falls into the three miserable realms.
With a bold heart one creates evil karma, constantly driven by desire.
Those who constantly practice lying receive no joyful retribution.
If a person violates the precepts, they are like the counterfeit gem musāragalva;
because of their evil karma, such a person falls into the three miserable realms.
If a person dwells in an evil mind, their darkness is boundless;
if a person takes refuge in the Triple Gem, it is like a great light in the night.
When a fool acts with negligence, he is like one intoxicated and deluded, deceiving himself.
Deluded by the two forms of negligence, they revolve within the hells.
All worlds that come into being must inevitably return to extinction;
as there is birth, so there is death—they are ultimately inseparable.
Surrounded by their own negligence, they increase the ocean of sensory realms;
bound by the fetters of craving, they sport within the heavens.
When the gods are first born, their arising pleasure perishes moment by moment.
Heedlessness shrouds one's own mind, so that one does not perceive the turning of impermanence.
Heedlessness causes self-delusion; constantly delighting in sensory objects, one never finds satiation through desire and thus perpetually undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction.
There is no moment or instant when one is not subject to it;
this craving causes sentient beings to experience heavenly pleasures.
The ground of craving is exceedingly violent and evil, filled with immeasurable discursive thoughts and reflections.
Sporting upon the ground of craving, they are driven by desire.
Just as the fires of hell incinerate all sinners,
so too does the fire of craving incinerate all devas.
The fires of hunger and thirst blaze fiercely, Scorching all the hungry ghosts;
Animals harm one another, And humans suffer the pain of seeking.
The fire of craving arises everywhere, Encompassing them all on every side.
"The fire burns with constant intensity, yet none in the world can perceive it.

When the celestial bird had thus spoken this verse for the sake of the heedless sons of the gods, those sons of the gods who had performed virtuous deeds in previous lives, upon hearing this sound of the Dharma, slightly abandoned their heedlessness; they did not drink the celestial wine and distanced themselves from the heedless pleasures of the five supreme sensual desires—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
They further enter the groves and gardens, delighting themselves with music and entertainment, experiencing various pleasures according to their own inclinations.
Within these gardens, peaks of blue *vaiḍūrya* and *musāragalva* gems are adorned with flowing springs, rivers, and many lotus ponds, where bees of various colors gather and roam.

In that lotus grove, the leaves are of vaidūrya and the stalks are of crystal; there are many bees beyond description, and hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens sport and enjoy themselves with the devaputras.
Due to their wholesome karma, they are swept away by the river of desire for various celestial maidens within those manifold realms, never awakening to their condition.

Thus they sport and enjoy themselves together until their wholesome karma is exhausted; then, when their life in heaven ends, they wander according to their karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will be born in a place of peace and happiness, possessing great wealth and abundant resources; his mind will be vast, he will delight in practicing the True Dharma and constantly cherish wisdom, love and revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and his lifespan will be extended.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The twenty-third place is named Moon-Walk (Candracāra).
What karma do sentient beings perform to be born in that place?
He hears and perceives:

If there are sentient beings who, with a pure mind, practice wholesome deeds and cultivate their minds well, they may fashion images of the Buddha or provide offerings for them, washing the images to remove dust and grime, and polishing them by rubbing and scrubbing.

Or they may see images of the Tathāgata made of gold or silver; seeing them, they rejoice, contemplate and revere the merit of the field of blessings, and reflecting upon the merit of their own thoughts, they perfume their own minds and practice wholesome deeds, giving rise to joy in their hearts, refraining from killing and stealing.
What is meant by "not killing"?

Such a person does not even entertain the thought of ending the life of a living being, nor do they instruct others to do so; seeing others do it, they do not rejoice in it, but instead urge them to refrain from doing so, establishing them in the path of goodness, thereby benefiting both themselves and others.
Furthermore, there is non-killing:

not giving rise to the thought of killing, even when there are moisture-born insects upon one's bedding or furniture, one does not conceive the intention to take their lives; nor does one give rise to the intent to kill even the most minute of lives, down to an ant—this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?

Such virtuous persons cultivate wholesome karma without ever knowing satiety; they do not commit theft in any circumstance, even regarding grass, wood, mud, or soil—neither taking them themselves nor instructing others to do so.
Even when suffering from great heat, one does not seize the shade of others, nor does one force another to stand in the sun while one occupies the shaded spot for oneself.

Possessing personal power, one does not seize it from others, nor does one incite others to do so; seeing others doing such things, one exhorts them to desist. This extends even to shade and coolness, which one does not steal; regarding even the most minute matters, one commits no theft.
This is called non-stealing.
Such a person, after the end of life, will be reborn in the celestial realm in the region of the Moon’s Path.
Having been born in that heaven, by virtue of their wholesome karma, they will obtain the retribution of happiness.
The radiance shines universally, just as ten moons joined together would shine; likewise, the bodily radiance of these celestial hosts is pure and stainless in the same way.

Once the Son of Heaven was born, all the celestial hosts became a hundredfold more excellent; the radiance of his body was perfectly balanced in warmth and coolness, and all the other devas beheld him with love and joy.
That light surpasses the light of all other devas; it shines universally for a full ten yojanas, excelling the light of all other precious jewels, due to his wholesome karma.

Thus, surrounded by an immeasurable retinue of celestial sons, performing various musical performances, he proceeded to the pleasure groves for recreation; the grove was named Pañca-rati, which was supremely excellent and most distinguished among all those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

The majesty and virtue of those trees are such that they bear excellent fruits; the birds possess superior wisdom; there are *padma* and *kumuda* flowers, as well as lotus ponds with flowing streams. From the air, fragrant breezes blow upon jeweled bells, producing immeasurable and subtle, wondrous sounds.

At that time, the devaputra, together with the host of devas, performed various musical performances; adorned in diverse ways along with the celestial maidens, he went to the Pañcakaṇḍaka Forest to enjoy himself through various musical entertainments and play.
The celestial maidens sang praises and played the sounds of the five musical instruments, experiencing supreme bliss.
Because they had performed virtuous deeds toward a field of merit, they obtained this superior fragrance; its scent wafted everywhere, filling an area of five yojanas.
Its fruits rest in emptiness like a multitude of stars.
The trees are magnificently adorned, the most excellent among those in the heavens; they are as bright as the light of the sun, yet their radiance is neither hot nor cold.
Its fruits are endowed with color, fragrance, and all manner of flavors; their scent surpasses all other fragrances, pervading five yojanas.

Like stars set in the sky, various fragrant drinks constantly flow from within the fruits; when the devas drink them, they are free from intoxication and confusion, and they obtain every variety of flavor and scent according to whatever they desire in their minds.
They receive such seeds of merit as these.
At that time, there was a celestial bird named "Teaching Heedlessness," who spoke these verses for the sake of the heedless sons of the gods:
"Virtuous karma is about to be exhausted, And one's lifespan passes in vain; One should swiftly practice the Dharma."
Do not practice heedlessness;
youth passes easily, and life is likewise; all possessions will soon be lost—do not practice heedlessness.
The heavens are not eternal, nor are their perfections everlasting; while the time has not yet come for their destruction, one should cultivate merit.
Through the convergence of wholesome karma, guard your mind with mindfulness; for there is no place to be found that is free from suffering and affliction.
If one’s mind is constantly distracted and one acts contrary to the Dharma, such pleasure is false; having departed, one does not return.
Trading one's precepts for worldly pleasure leads to birth among the gods, yet if one fails to guard the precepts, one will feel regret at the time of death.
Therefore, one should uphold the precepts, guarding them so as not to transgress; for fools who depart from the precepts cannot ascend to heaven.
If one experiences the pleasures of the five desires within the heavens, it is because they upheld the precepts with purity, and thus obtained this great fruit.
The various devas are attached to desire; through the poisons of negligence and ignorance, they fail to perceive impermanence, and thus their bodies and lives are destroyed.
Countless hundreds of thousands, nayutas of devas, are all consumed by the fire of desire due to their negligence.
All sentient beings are blinded by heedlessness; only after suffering decline and affliction do they realize their transgression.
Their minds constantly cling to objects of perception without a moment’s rest; the deluded do not perceive this, and later it results in great evil.
The mind delights in sensual objects and does not perceive its own distress; only when misfortune and calamity arrive does regret arise.
The fetters and afflictions are born from recollection; the sovereign of the mind and these fetters constantly follow and pursue one another.
Racing along with the mind wherever it dwells, one is constantly mired in delusion and flows through the ocean of the three realms.
