If one knows the True Dharma and perceives that worldly phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty,
one will forever be free from grief and affliction.
Driven by form, they constantly seek after desires; such people, in their future births, will forever lack celestial bliss.
This coral grove is adorned with myriad jewels, its various branches and twigs embellished with lotus flowers.
Various flowing waters, adorned by many rivers, obtained through the causes of karma, pervade the entirety of space.
How much more so this celestial body, which is like a bubble on the water; having arisen, it perishes once again.
"Through negligence, you deceive yourselves.

At that time, those sons of the gods who had accumulated various wholesome karmas in previous lives were able to understand and awaken upon hearing the sound of this celestial bird preaching the Dharma.
"According to what the bird said, it must indeed be impermanent.

For a short while he reflected and remained free from negligence; yet, he was again deceived and deluded by the objects of the senses—form, sound, smell, and touch—and completely forgot the sound of the Dharma as if it belonged to another age, losing all memory of both what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
They experience sensual pleasures in the present without regarding the future, and do not recall the sounds of the celestial birds preaching the Dharma.

They observe the play and enjoyment of the five desires in the present, without thinking of the great suffering endured in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; they do not think that a celestial body is extremely difficult to obtain, nor do they reflect upon the beginningless cycle of suffering through wandering in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
All sufferings are stubborn and difficult to subdue, except for the foremost superior mind of a deva-son who has long cultivated roots of goodness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu observes by what karma these celestial birds speak the pure, stainless, and true Dharma to instruct the negligent deva-sons.
He hears and understands:

if there are those among human beings who, while in their human state, engage in heedless conduct—whether as performers, strongmen, or actors—who wear the saṃghāṭī robe while playing, singing, and dancing, and who obtain wealth by chanting the virtues of the Buddha.
Having acquired wealth, whether in the form of clothing or food, they give it as alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas or consume it themselves.

By the power of the causal condition of wearing the saffron robe, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens with the body of a flying bird, experiencing supreme bliss due to that karma.
Furthermore, the various devas enjoy themselves with singing, dancing, laughter, and play; beryl trees with golden leaves and crystal branches spread all around them.

Furthermore, there were jewel trees, adorned with various kinds of coral jewel trees; they were embellished by hundreds of thousands of swarms of bees, and their branches were made of gold and pearls.
Furthermore, there are mountain peaks adorned with wheels of flames made of the seven treasures.
There are also lotuses—golden lotuses, crystal lotuses, and lapis lazuli lotuses—in which they sport and enjoy themselves.

Furthermore, there are other celestial palaces and towers made of precious jewels, where the devas sport and enjoy pleasures together with their celestial maidens. Free from jealousy and all fears, their hearts are filled with mutual affection and longing as they experience the highest bliss.

Furthermore, together with the hosts of devas, they enter the Forest of Sovereign Power (*cintāmaṇi-vana*) to sport, sing, and dance. Once they have entered this forest, everything they conceive in their minds is obtained.
For this reason, it is called the Tree of Sovereign Power (*cintāmaṇi-vṛkṣa*).

Having long enjoyed celestial pleasures within this grove, they proceed once more to the Golden Peak of Mount Sumeru. That mountain peak is adorned with rivers, ponds, and flowing springs; there, together with various celestial maidens, they sing, dance, play, and laugh, performing divine music that produces exquisite sounds. Hearing them, they are filled with joy, and beholding various kinds of sublime and wondrous forms with their eyes, they experience great happiness.
Through the transformation of their own karma, they are surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens; on Mount Sumeru, they see all the various and immeasurable lotus ponds.
Furthermore, there are various groves and lotus ponds, their fragrance exquisite and wondrous, bringing joy and delight to those who smell it.

There is also a supreme and most excellent touch; if the body touches it, it is as if touching a kāñcanaprabhāsa (golden-light) bird—a sea-bird that brings great bliss when touched—and which appears whenever a Wheel-Turning King arises. It possesses immeasurable, stainless, pure radiance and a sublime, fragrant scent.
Should anyone behold it, they would find it exceedingly delightful.

While sporting amidst such mountain peaks, whatever thoughts arise in their minds, they shall all obtain immeasurable merit in its entirety; they enjoy these with sovereign ease that cannot be taken away by others, pure and stainless, experiencing celestial bliss within this realm, sporting and entertaining themselves while enjoying manifold pleasures.
His body is radiant, surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens as he enjoys the five desires of the heavens.
Eventually, when his wholesome karma is exhausted, his life ends and he falls back, wandering according to his karma to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, from birth until the end of life they will constantly experience happiness; their physical appearance will be foremost, and they will become either kings or great ministers. They will be born in a land where virtuous dharmas always prevail, a place inhabited by sentient beings of right view, and they will remain free from evil associates.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
There is a twenty-fourth stage of existence called Yama-sāla.
What karma do sentient beings perform to be born in that heaven?
He perceives and knows this:
If there are sentient beings who uphold the prohibitive precepts, who benefit sentient beings with a mind of right view, and who rectify their body, speech, and mind;
whether in remote and dangerous places or in the midst of wildernesses, or if people are drowning and falling into great rivers, they rescue them and cause them to escape.
If one is oppressed by thirst and exhaustion in a wilderness, they provide them with water and drink;
if one is lost on a perilous path and cannot find the way, they show them the correct road—without seeking any recompense for their kindness.
To benefit sentient beings, to rescue and protect sentient beings, and to bestow upon them their life-span.
How does one refrain from killing and refrain from stealing?
It is when one performs wholesome deeds toward this person or toward others.
Not killing sentient beings:

if various living beings—whether born from a womb or born from moisture, whether coarse or subtle—should arise within one's dwelling and damage one's necessities, or frequently fall from the rafters onto people, causing them distress, one shall not kill them out of a heart of compassion.
Regarding frogs, venomous insects, and various stinging creatures: even if one is harmed by them, one does not take their life.
This is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?
What are the various forms of non-stealing?

When such virtuous persons travel through the wilderness, they possess the strength and autonomy to take the water and black salt belonging to merchants; yet, though they have the power to do so, they do not steal, but instead restrain themselves from succumbing to thirst.
If those merchants offer water to them, they drink only after doing so;

if they do not offer it, they trade for it before drinking. Thus, they carefully observe the subtle karmic retribution of actions, practice the Buddha-dharma, and cultivate their minds by recollecting the merits of the Buddha.
In a mere moment, one should not associate with evil friends, nor converse with them, nor travel along the same path.
For what reason should one not travel with them?
Because all wholesome karma is obstructed by associating with evil associates; therefore, one must not speak with them, nor dwell together with them in coming or going.
Why is this? Because evil associates are the dwelling place of greed, hatred, and delusion; a person of wisdom should abandon them just as one would a poisonous tree.
That person is as pure as refined gold; when the body perishes and life ends, they are reborn in the realm of Yama-sāla.
Once born in that heaven, that person of virtuous karma is revered and honored by all good people, experiencing the fruits of happiness as a result of their certain karmic actions.
The radiance of their bodies increases day by day, as does the number of people.
Why is this? Because among the devas there is no distinction between day and night; thus, the bodily light of these devas increases in this manner.
When the other devas saw this, they all felt shame before the celestial maidens.
Surpassing all the devas of other realms, the devas, having witnessed this, all went to Śakra, the King of Devas, to inquire about the cause and conditions, saying:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"In the Yama-sāla grove, there was a deva-son who, upon his initial birth, possessed a radiance surpassing all other celestial hosts.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard these words, he spoke this verse:
"The radiance of the deva-son Is born from the observance of the precepts."
The golden light-wheel of Mount Sumeru does not equal even a sixteenth part [of this].
His body constantly emits radiance, like a mass of molten gold;
this light is perfectly harmonized because the wise have fashioned their karma.

According to these three grades of karma—superior, middling, and inferior—and the three ways of upholding the precepts, the fruits obtained are likewise: there are superior, middling, and inferior retributions.
By upholding the precepts, one leaves behind negligence and increases non-negligence.
One always attains peace and happiness; such is the nature of all phenomena.
If one maintains pure precepts, one now attains a body of radiant light that unites with the brilliance of a thousand suns, such that nothing can surpass its illumination.
If there is a superior person who upholds the seven precepts,
that individual will obtain a virtuous fruit, as taught by the Buddhas of the past.
If one performs wholesome deeds, one shall not lose the retribution of happiness.
If one does not act, there will be no fruit; yet the karma one has created is never lost.
The deluded person takes no pleasure in the cause, but delights only in the retribution of the fruit.
Since there is no fruit without a cause, it is as difficult to obtain as oil from sand.
"If a person practices what is wholesome, they remain far removed from envy;
the unwholesome and foolish person constantly engages in malice.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having thus explained the karmic fruits of wholesome deeds, instructed the heedless sons of the gods.
When the sons of the gods had heard these words, they received them upon their heads in reverence and set out to return to the realm of Yama-sāla.
Upon reaching their abode, the sons and daughters of the gods engaged in play and enjoyment amidst the sounds of music, experiencing celestial delights.
In this place on earth, among all the groves of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, these two śāla trees are the most excellent.

Their dimensions, color, appearance, radiance, flowers, and fruits are preeminent; a network of bells covers them, and the sound of their leaves is like that of the five musical instruments. When the devas hear this sound, they all come toward the trees to play and enjoy themselves.
Once the devas had arrived, they ascended the śāla trees. Above those trees was a lotus pond named *Nandana*.

Within this lotus pond were many geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, which produced various wondrous sounds as an adornment. It was adorned with immeasurable lotuses and water possessing the eight meritorious qualities. Seeing this, the devas marveled at such an unprecedented sight, exclaiming:
"Apart from these two trees, there has never been a lotus bathing pool such as this."
"Among these *śāla* trees, none can equal the *pāriyātra-kovidāra* tree. Having said this, the devas and apsarasas engaged in play, song, and dance,
enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, and for a long time they experienced celestial delights in that place.

He then proceeded to the Forest of Constant Play, wearing a crown of flower garlands and robes of various colors; from his body issued forth various radiances, for which I shall provide a brief illustration.
For example, the color of a lightning flash in summer possesses three qualities:
first, blue light; second, yellow light; [and third, white light].
Third is the Red Light.
In their place of play, the various devaputras experience the pleasures of the five desires; with the force of waves surging from a mountain torrent, they enjoy manifold delights.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was sporting with the entire host of devas in the Sudharmā Hall; he emerged from the Sudharmā Palace and, accompanied by various celestial maidens, performed manifold musical performances and produced exquisite sounds as they proceeded toward the place where the Yama-sāla trees dwell.
At that time, when the entire host of devas in the Yama-sāla grove saw Śakra approaching, they all came forth to welcome him, joining their palms and prostrating at his feet.

The Heavenly King Śakra, the devas of the Sudharmā Hall, and the devas of the Yama-sāla grove all gathered together; they enjoyed themselves with song, dance, and laughter as they proceeded toward the twin trees.
Having arrived beneath this tree, the entire host of devas gathered around it and drank the supreme flavor of the *madya* of the heavens.
Then, Śakra, King of the Devas, addressed the devas, saying:
"Do you see this Yama-sāla tree? Among all the trees of the heavens, with the exception of the Pāriyātra-koṭaraka tree, there is no other tree equal to it."
The devas replied, "Indeed, we have seen it. Śakra said to them:
"O you devas, you do not yet know the merits of such a Yama-sāla tree; you see only its outward form. You should contemplate the power of these two trees."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended from his palace and struck this great tree with a vajra held in his hand; the gate immediately opened.

Within that tree were immeasurable groves, flower ponds, flowing streams, and lotus pools as adornments, along with mountain peaks of *maṇi*, white silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli, all adorned with various flowing waters, rivers, and ponds.
Furthermore, he saw celestial flowers and lotus ponds made of the seven treasures, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of bees.
He also saw groves and gardens with trees of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and the king of blue jewels.

Furthermore, there were various birds with wings made of the seven treasures, which produced immeasurable kinds of exquisite and beautiful sounds; when the devas heard them, they experienced what they had never known before, rejoicing and enjoying themselves.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by the hosts of devas before and behind him, entered the palace of the *yamasaḷa* tree rows. There he beheld the various jeweled pillars of the palace of the rows, adorned with the seven treasures—namely, pillars embellished with the king of blue jewels (*nīlaratnarāja*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), white silver, and various precious gems such as crystal (*sphaṭika*) and musaragalva.

Furthermore, there were various kinds of couches adorned with mattresses, silken spreads, and fine coverlets; these couches had four legs, which were embellished with many jewels, namely vajra-gems, blue gems, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, within the trees and amidst the mountain peaks, he saw the immeasurable voices of various kinds of birds.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of devas:
"Do you all see these extraordinary wonders within the pair of trees?"
The devas replied, "Indeed, we have seen it.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observing that the celestial hosts were negligent and attached to pleasure, led them into the Hall for Manifesting the Retribution of Karma. That hall was pure like a clear mirror, its brilliance shining everywhere.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, instructed the gods:
"You should observe the retribution of karma upon the walls of this jeweled palace, according to the deeds performed through their respective causes and conditions."

If one bestows wealth and treasures upon a field of merit, offering them with faith, giving according to one’s inclination, and giving at the proper time, one will obtain rewards that accord with one’s wishes.
Wherever one is born, one will receive the corresponding retribution; one shall see all the various kinds of retributions one receives.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again showed the celestial host:

"You, members of the celestial host, should observe such observance of the precepts and spiritual practice, which protects sentient beings among all paths like parents; it is real and not false, like pure ground, like excellent jewels, and like the seeds of the devas."
"If a person guards these seven kinds of precepts, wherever they are born—whether among devas or humans—they will experience the fruits of upholding those precepts.
Then, Śakra, Lord of Devas, again showed the reflections in the karma-mirrors to the various devas and addressed them, saying:
"You all observe all karmic retributions."

If there is a man who performs various wholesome deeds and gathers the lamp of wisdom and right view, he will be able to know such superior, middling, and inferior wisdom, as well as the outflowing and non-outflowing fruits.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further revealed to the celestial assembly the ninefold wisdom of giving and maintaining the precepts:
"Within giving there are superior, middling, and inferior levels; through these, the fruits and rewards of the auspicious paths are all fully accomplished."
One who contemplates and cultivates the field of merit is fully endowed with nine kinds of endowments.
O Devaputra!
If one gives without determination, it lacks the corresponding characteristics and is called "meager fruit."
Furthermore, there is a minor fruit, namely the supernatural power of hungry ghosts, or the experience of pleasant fruits by certain animals; this is called "inferior giving.
O Son of Heaven!
You should observe these reflections in the mirror of karma—these various fruits of karma, among which is the fruit of giving.
If one does not cultivate the mind of reflection, the mind will not be perfected, nor will the wealth of merit and material goods be perfected.
By giving to those who are excellent fields of merit and possess great virtue, one obtains a middling karmic fruit, being reborn among humans in the continent of Pūrvavideha or Aparagodānīya.
"If one is born among animals—whether as an asura or a yakṣa—this is called the middling fruit.
Such signs he saw upon the walls of the Mirror Palace.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again revealed the karmic retribution of the celestial hosts, declaring:
"O sons of gods!
You should observe the superior, middling, and inferior karmas; do not fail to cultivate a mind of reflection, for the field of merit is complete."
What is meant by "not cultivating a mind of reflection yet obtaining the karmic fruit"?
It refers to a donor who gives at the proper time, yet causes others to give while his own mind lacks deep faith;
he does not give with his own hand, does not rise when seeing [the recipient], and does not pay respectful homage.
Though endowed with a field of merit and possessed of wealth, because his intention was not perfected, he gave as a matter of necessity.
He was born in a remote region where there is no true Dharma or Vinaya and no codes of propriety; whether serving as a ruler or as a minister, he received no homage from others.
"O sons of the gods!
You should observe this wall of the karma-mirror, and you shall see everything therein.
Thus did Śakra, Lord of the Devas, instruct them.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 30 [and] Scroll 31,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen of the *Devatā-darśana-parivarta*, Section Seven on the Thirteenth Heaven:

"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again showed the fruits of giving to the various heavens. He demonstrated how one performs offerings with the perfection of intention, the perfection of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and the perfection of material goods. The merit of the intention is fully perfected; the field of merit that is superior refers to the Tathāgatas and others; the perfection of goods refers to food, drink, and material wealth; and the perfection of intention refers to deep-seated faith and so forth. Thus, one cultivates the practice of making offerings."
Giving in this manner yields great rewards among gods and humans:

one may be born in the heavens with great majesty and power, or be born among humans as a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), fully endowed with the seven treasures and ruling over the four continents, including the seven types of secondary treasures.
This wheel-turning king practices the True Dharma and possesses all perfections.
By upholding the precepts and cultivating wisdom, he enters nirvana; this is called the supreme gift.
Such gifts as these are seen within the mirror-wall as their karmic retribution.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further manifested the three fruits of giving within the pure vaidūrya wall, appearing in the mirror-like surface.
These were as follows:
through the gift of material requisites, one attains great wealth; its retribution is as previously described.

The gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*): One is born into a great kingdom as a king or sovereign; there is no threat of weapons, nor calamities, famine, pestilence, or untimely death. One does not fear enemies, remaining free from illness and secure. One is exempt from the fear of fire and the fear of water, and free from the fear of epidemics. Whether acting as a king or a high minister, one dwells long in this world—this is the karmic fruit of the gift of fearlessness.
Within the mirror wall, he saw such karma.
Furthermore, within the mirror wall, he saw superior forms of giving, namely:
that the gift of Dharma is supreme and unsurpassed, for it can bring forth the seeds for escaping all conditioned existence and birth-and-death.
This unsurpassed giving attains the unsurpassed fruit, achieving whatever one desires within the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).
Furthermore, within the mirror-wall, he again beholds the fruits of karma:

if one preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of material wealth, and takes that wealth without benefiting sentient beings with a heart of compassion, this is called the inferior grade of the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).

This is the inferior gift of Dharma: preaching the Dharma to others not with a virtuous mind, but solely for the sake of wealth and profit; being unable to practice oneself according to what one has preached—this is called the inferior gift.

If one acquires wealth through the preaching of the Dharma, and uses it to drink alcohol, or to eat and drink together with women in the manner of performers, selling oneself to seek profit—such a gift of Dharma yields very little fruit.
Within the mirror-wall, one sees such people who have given the gift of Dharma being born in the heavens as wisdom-birds, capable of reciting verses;
this is called the lower gift of Dharma.
"What is called the middling gift of Dharma?

It is preaching the Dharma to others for the sake of fame, for the sake of surpassing others, for the desire to excel other great Dharma masters, or preaching the Dharma to others with a mind of envy."
Such a gift of Dharma yields little reward; one is reborn among the devas to receive middling karmic fruits, or is born among human beings.
Thus Śakra, King of the Devas, displays all of this within the mirror-wall; this is what is called the middling gift of Dharma.
"What is called the supreme gift of Dharma?

It is to preach the Dharma with a pure mind for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of sentient beings, not for the sake of wealth or profit, but to cause those sentient beings who hold wrong views to abide in the True Dharma."
Such a gift of Dharma benefits oneself and others; it is unsurpassed and most excellent, and its merit remains inexhaustible even unto Nirvana. This is what is called the supreme gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the gift of Dharma. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further demonstrated to the various devas the remaining fruits of the gift of Dharma.
He explained that the inferior gift of Dharma consists of teaching the dharma of giving without teaching wisdom;
the middling gift of Dharma consists of teaching the observance of precepts.
The superior gift of Dharma consists in teaching wisdom and liberation.
As for those of inferior wisdom, when they preach the Dharma for others, few understand or realize it;
when they teach the Dharma of giving, they speak only of giving.

He does not speak of other dharmas, but speaks of the causes and conditions of the Dharma to cause them to know how to uphold the precepts; subsequently, they attain wisdom, and those people, through faith and compliance, become arhats, exhausting all fetters and outflows to attain the two kinds of liberation.
This is called the inferior gift of Dharma. Why is this?
Because it teaches the Dharma associated with giving.
"What is called the middling gift of Dharma?
It is the teaching of dharmas associated with the observance of precepts in order to cultivate the mind; this is the wisdom therein.
Within a mirror or a wall, one perceives such karmic retributions as these:"
Following wisdom, one attains arhatship and swiftly exhausts all outflows, or else attains the state of a pratyekabuddha; this is the gift of the Dharma at the intermediate level.
To see such signs within a mirror or a wall is what is called the gift of the Dharma at the intermediate level.
What is called the supreme gift of Dharma?
It is to expound the merits of wisdom, cultivating the mind through reflection, seeking no personal reward, and preaching the Dharma solely for the benefit of others.

He spoke of the faults and evils of desire, the fetters of the flavor of desire, and liberation as bliss; he caused those with wrong views to abide in the True Dharma and taught the pure, stainless Dharma.

This is the supreme gift of Dharma, which attains the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; it is the state of one perfected in knowledge and conduct, the unsurpassed charioteer, the teacher of gods and humans, the unsurpassed True Dharma, and the Dharma of discipline. It is good in the beginning, middle, and end, the unsurpassed accomplishment, and all-knowing vision; for the sake of all sentient beings, it extensively expounds the essential points of the Dharma.
This is what is called the supreme gift of Dharma.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again observed the retribution of karma within the mirror.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, showed this to the assembly of devas; upon seeing it, all the devas felt shame. Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of devas:
“O sons of the gods, do not be negligent. Why is this?
Because by creating such causes, one obtains corresponding fruits in every place where one is born.”
"You, sons of gods, should come to my presence to behold the retribution of your karma.
Observe these results of karma—superior, middling, and inferior—and you must now cultivate the practice of heedfulness."
At that time, the assembly of devas, witnessing this rare occurrence of karmic retribution, all conceived a sense of revulsion toward saṃsāra and spoke these verses:
“Sensual pleasures are false and illusory; their inherent nature is weak and inferior. Deluded by sensual pleasures, one fails to see the terrors [they entail].”
If one indulges in the passions of desire, there is no benefit; when wholesome karma is exhausted, one only realizes it at the point of death.
Supreme bliss is inevitably subject to decay and change; thus, by being attached to pleasure, one loses it and increases only suffering.
If one falls from the world of the gods into hell, the body and mind undergo great suffering, with every kind of torment.
This suffering is immeasurable and most acrid; yet the suffering of separation from what is loved exceeds even this.
The manifestation of separation from what is loved is ever-present among the gods; the foolish do not see it, being deceived by their own craving.
Initially beautiful yet empty and deceptive, they are cheated by desire for hundreds of thousands of millions, billions, trillions, and quadrillions [of eons].
What is gained through desire is lost again; it cannot be maintained forever. With wholesome karma as the cause, one obtains the retribution of happiness.
Without cause there is no fruit, just as without a tree there is no fruit; as poison harms life, so too does heedlessness.
Like a fire that consumes, like a sword or a halberd; at first like a kinsman, later it becomes an enemy.
Like a fish swallowing a hook, so too is heedlessness.
Devas, nāgas, humans, ghosts, and asuras alike— due to their heedlessness,
they all suffer great decline and affliction.
O Heavenly King, you should know this!
"By our merit and blessings, we cause the King to see here the prison of birth and death.
When the sons of the gods had spoken this verse, they further said:
"O Heavenly King!
"How can this be known?
Who has shown the Heavenly King such a Dharma?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the sons of the gods:
"Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
When I was first born in this heaven, there was an elder deva named Sumāra, who was my foremost friend."
From him, he heard in succession this account:

"Just as Kāśyapa Buddha came here to discipline the various devas, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, seeing that the hearts of the sons of gods were greatly given to negligence, for the sake of benefiting those sons of gods, employed his supernatural power of recollection to manifest such a wall of karmic reflections, which he left within this tree."
At that time, my mind was negligent, and the deity Sumāra showed me this teaching: "Do not be negligent now.
For what reason?
"All conditioned things are impermanent and subject to destruction.

If you, O sons of heaven, allow your minds to become negligent, you should enter this tree and observe for yourselves the superior, intermediate, and inferior aspects of your own bodies; then you will feel shame."
If there are sons of gods who believe in heedfulness, you should show them this Dharma.

Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata, for the benefit of sentient beings, has manifested such matters to discipline the various devas; at the ground of the karma-mirror, he causes them to abide in the good paths and return to Jambudvīpa.
"I have heard this rare and difficult-to-behold matter from such a venerable deva.
Having heard it, in order to abandon negligence, I have come here with the hosts of devas so that all the devas may attain a sense of shame."
"Therefore, I now show you all the superior, middling, and inferior karmas upon the wall of the karma-mirror; you, sons of gods, must be careful not to be negligent!
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the host of devas:
"We shall go together with you to the second tree to observe the various karma-mirrors."
In the past, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa manifested transformations within this tree to benefit all the heedless devas, causing them to contemplate the net of karmic actions within birth and death.
"I shall now show it to you!

After the Deva King Śakra had spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, immediately departed from the gate, and having exited, closed it behind him.

There were other hosts of devas who sang, danced, laughed, and performed various musical arts, enjoying themselves in delight; upon seeing Śakra, the Lord of Devas, they immediately approached him, prostrating their heads in respectful salutation, and engaged in singing and dancing to amuse one another, throwing various lotuses such as the *padma* at each other.
At that time, the hosts of devas who had emerged from the trees recounted to the Deva of Heedlessness the rare and marvelous things they had witnessed.
However, because the sons of the gods who were heedless were themselves distracted by their own negligence, they neither listened to nor believed these marvelous teachings.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in order to restrain the heedless sons of the gods, also sported together with them in the lotus pond; with various sounds and the celestial music of the devas, they entertained one another.
Adorned with celestial garlands and celestial garments, they enter various groves and gardens to sport and enjoy themselves by virtue of their wholesome karma.
At that time, the assembly of devas and Śakra, Lord of Devas, enter the Mirror of Karma; seeing those who experience the retribution of their karma, they no longer engage in play.

Just as an adept (*aśaikṣa*) who has completed what was to be done, having abandoned heedless conduct, dwells established in stability, sees that the hosts of devas are addicted to heedlessness and gives rise to a heart of compassion, speaking thus:

"These sons of gods are attached in mind to heedlessness; they do not know that they shall fall away, and will wander according to their karma, falling into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals."

Following the karma of afflictions, one does not depart from all karmic activities of birth and death; according to what is performed through karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one receives such a retribution as that karma.
Thus, the devaputra contemplated the heedless devas and gave rise to a heart of compassion.
At that time, the various devaputras in the Sudharmā Hall addressed Śakra, saying:
"By the grace of the Heavenly King, we members of the celestial host enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; we sport among the heavens, enjoying ourselves in various gardens and groves."
"Why does the Heavenly King not take us under his protection?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of devas:
"O Son of Heaven, you are attached to pleasure, And you practice much heedlessness."
Due to negligence and attachment, one does not perceive the true reality.
If the mind is constantly negligent, there will be no virtuous retribution;
being separated from wholesome deeds, one falls into hell.
All forms of attachment and craving must inevitably end in separation;
you do not realize this, yet in an instant you shall surely pass away.
When life is about to reach its end, all the sense faculties will utterly perish.
Only then does one realize that suffering and affliction arrive suddenly and cannot be avoided.
Like a whirling firebrand, like a city of the Gandharvas,
the three realms are all impermanent, just like bubbles on the water or foam.
Just as with a mass of foam upon the water, the fool relies on it for protection;
amidst phenomena that are impermanent, he gives rise to joy and pleasure.
Neither devas nor humans, neither yakṣas, nāgas, nor spirits can [protect him].
Bound by the karma of one's final moment, no one can provide rescue or protection.
While death has not yet arrived, you should cultivate wholesome deeds;
for the King of Death is exceedingly fierce and cruel—do not harbor regrets when it is too late.
I now instruct you: be careful not to act with negligence.
You are shrouded by craving and race through various sensory realms.
These realms bind you; they are the cause of all hells.
"Therefore, you should abandon [these things] to seek the place of peace and security.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, preached this Dharma for the assembly of devas, the devas were negligent and did not keep it in mind; except for those who had already seen the ground of the karma-mirror, they all gave rise to a sense of revulsion and said to Śakra:

"We wish to enter the second śāla tree. This tree is a karmic net manifested by Kāśyapa Tathāgata for the sake of benefiting the negligent devas, displaying the wall of the karma-mirror that reveals the retribution of birth and death to the assembly of devas."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the heedless devas delighted in play, led them to another place and, together with the non-heedless sons of the gods, arrived at the second tree.

Having reached the tree, he took a vajra in his hand and struck the great tree; the gate immediately opened, and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the assembly of devas, felt joy in their hearts and entered the tree together.

Once the celestial hosts had entered, they beheld various groves never seen before, which were exceedingly delightful; everything necessary was fully provided, and there were many kinds of immeasurable birds, lotus ponds, and various flowers as adornments, along with immeasurable golden trees—all of which were objects of great joy.

When a gentle breeze blows, all rejoice greatly; the various birds on the peaks of the mountain of seven treasures utter wondrous songs, and the wish-fulfilling trees are like the light of the sun, their radiance shining everywhere like the light of the sun.
Furthermore, within these śāla trees, the rivers are filled with food and drink, overflowing with fragrances and tastes; there are various exquisite and supreme perfumes.
The pleasures corresponding to the five kinds of sensory objects perceived by the five faculties are exceedingly delightful.
The great virtuous devas, upon hearing this, were filled with joy and attachment; how much more so the other devas.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, showed the assembly of devas that all the gardens were lovely and exquisite, yet even the lotus groves, forested parks, and flowing ponds outside those trees did not equal one-sixteenth part of their splendor.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with all the devas, went once more to Mount Vaidūrya; that mountain was supremely pure and peerless.
Upon its summit stood a hall of a thousand pillars, fashioned from vaidūrya jewels, with railings made of red lotus gems and a floor of gold.
That lapis lazuli palace was five yojanas long and three yojanas wide, accomplished through the transformative power of Kāśyapa Tathāgata.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with the hosts of devas, ascended the lapis lazuli palace by means of stairways made of the seven treasures; there they beheld the image of Kāśyapa Tathāgata, appearing as if Kāśyapa Buddha were actually preaching the Dharma within the hall.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the assembly of devas joined their palms in reverent salutation to the shadow of the Tathāgata, giving rise to profound faith and respect.
Having completed their prostrations, they praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The Tathāgata is the unsurpassed Honored One in the world; He has attained true liberation and the reality of the Truth.”
His shadow is serene and wondrous beyond compare, Able to open the unsurpassed path of liberation.
If a person constantly pays homage to the Tathāgata, Their pure faith is stainless and their mind is tranquil.
Such a person will forever be freed from the fear of existence, And shall always attain a state of peace and supreme bliss.
Such is this tranquil and wondrous Dharma; he expounds these words on the state of cessation.
This is the teaching spoken by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, which reveals to all sentient beings the path to Nirvāṇa.
If there are sentient beings who contemplate this Dharma, they are called brave and fearless persons;
they shall attain the unsurpassed state, always delighting in peace and tranquility of mind, free from affliction.
If there are sentient beings who contemplate the True Truth, they are like those crossing over who board a boat or raft;
through the treacherous whirlpools of the ocean of the three realms, such persons are able to transcend and cross over.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Eye of the World, Universally contemplates all phenomena without exception;
This Buddha’s radiance is peerless, And among all lights, none can equal it.
Sentient beings recall their own turbid minds— The stains of ignorance, anger, and desire;
The great waters of wisdom are profoundly pure, Washing away all the defilements of sentient beings.
All sentient beings are unable to see it; The arrogant followers of external paths cannot comprehend it.
That Dharma is pure and free from defilement; The World-Honored One reveals it universally to all sentient beings.
Those who delight in heedlessness and have no savior—such beings the Teacher of Men saves;
he ferries them across birth and death to the further shore, able to deliver all sentient beings who have no protector.
To benefit all the worlds, there is none but the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Honored One;
because he is able to benefit sentient beings, the Tathāgata is therefore most preeminent.

Thus, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, praised the image of the Buddha with pure faith; bowing his head and joining his palms, he, together with the host of devas, prostrated himself before the image of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, together with the host of devas, he bowed his head and joined his palms to pay homage to the celestial robes emanated by the Tathāgata.
Such garments are sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
When the assembly of devas beheld these reflections, they all became free from arrogance and free from negligence.
The color of the image manifested by the Tathāgata was so upright, dignified, and exquisite that even a thousand Śakras could not compare to it, let alone other devas.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, beheld this miraculous manifestation of the Tathāgata’s image and showed this reflection to those devas who were arrogant and heedless, in order to cause them to abandon their arrogance and heedlessness.
At that time, the sons of the gods said to the Heavenly King:
"Kauśika! For what cause and condition did the Tathāgata Kāśyapa manifest within this Jambū-sāla tree the transformation of the net of karma and the cycle of birth and death?"
"Why did he not manifest his transformation outside the tree?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the sons of the gods:
"I too previously harbored such doubts regarding this matter; that deity showed it to me in order to cause me to abandon my arrogance."
In the past, I also asked about this matter, and at that time the devaputra replied to me:
"This is a rare dharma, not to be seen constantly.
Because it is not seen constantly, one develops deep faith upon seeing it."
For this reason, the Tathāgata leaves behind a transformation-body that does not exist externally; it is not something that all people are able to see.
If the transformation-body were external, the various devas would see it and would not experience a sense of wonder, or might even give rise to faults and evils.
For this reason, within these Yama-sāla trees, he manifests and leaves behind transformational images.
Among these two trees, such divine transformations are rare; the transformations within the trees are the most extraordinary, being invisible to all the devas.
"For this reason, Kāśyapa Tathāgata, within this tree, has manifested a preserved image and a mirror-wall to demonstrate the karma of birth and death.
When the assembly of devas heard Śakra, Lord of Devas, speak these words, they were freed from doubt and regret.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further showed the walls of the various celestial palaces, which were five yojanas wide.
Upon these mirror-like walls, he first beheld the sixteen compartments of the Saṃjīva Hell.
Those who have committed the act of killing fall into this hell, where they undergo immeasurable varieties of agonizing suffering as previously described.
Upon emerging from the hell, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta), where they frequently give rise to anger, their envy increases, and they harm one another with knives.
Bound by the net of karma, they are born among the animals, where they harm one another and are eaten by humans; for the sake of their flesh, their lives are taken.
Or they take the form of fierce beasts such as tigers and leopards, with increased malice and anger, and are killed by humans.
Dying among animals, one is reborn among humans; such a person constantly delights in strife and contention, their mind is base and evil, they die by the blade, and do not attain long life.
Having residual wholesome karma, they are born among the devas, yet their majesty, physical appearance, and characteristics are diminished and inferior, and their lifespan is short.
When the hosts of devas engage in battle with the asuras, they may be wounded and die.
All of these were clearly visible upon the walls of the hall.
"In this same manner, the sixteen compartments of the Black Rope Hell (Kālasūtra) are also as previously described.
Due to the causal power of killing and stealing, beings fall into this hell and undergo immeasurable varieties of agonizing torment."
Once their suffering is exhausted, they emerge from hell and are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). There, they kill one another with various swords and staves as previously described.
Alternatively, they consume impure things such as excrement and urine, which are difficult for them to find even when they seek them.
There are other hungry ghosts who tear one another apart, their bodies destroyed or their lives lost.
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are reborn among the animals; in the wilderness, they take the form of *caṭaka* birds—famished scavengers—their bodies scorched by thirst and hunger.
Dying among the animals, if one is reborn among humans, it will be in a land of weapons and war or a corrupt and evil country; there, one may die by the blade of a soldier's sword or from starvation.
Having obtained food through great toil and hardship, it is snatched away by others; even if they do obtain food, they are unable to digest it.

Dying from among humans, if there remains residual karma, they are born among the devas, yet their physical appearance and facial features are diminished, inferior, and coarse, and the flavor of the food they consume is not like that of other devas.
When they see other gods, they feel great shame; their musical performances are entirely inferior, and their lifespans are short.
All such karmic results are seen here upon this wall.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again beheld within the walls of his palace the sixteen compartments of the Saṃghāta Hell.
As previously described, those who have committed killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct fall into this hell, where they undergo immeasurable varieties of agonizing torment.
Having finished suffering there, they emerge from hell and are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), receiving the body of a *vāntāśin* (one who eats vomit) hungry ghost with a long lifespan.
If they obtain food or drink, it is plundered by other hungry ghosts; even if they have kinsmen, those too are deceived and robbed by hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, there are other ghosts who are hacked and severed with knives, undergoing great suffering and agony until they die.

When their lives end here, they are reborn among the animals, taking the forms of water buffaloes, oxen, horses, or donkeys; their lifespans are exceedingly long, and even when they obtain food and drink, it is snatched away from them by others.
Having died among the animals, if one is born among humans, one's lifespan will be short, one will be poor and low-born, and one's wife will not be chaste.
All such karmic results were clearly visible upon the walls of the palace.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again contemplated the fruits of karma and beheld within the walls of his palace sixteen distinct sections of the Great Hell of Screaming (Raurava).

As previously described, those who have committed killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying fall into this hell, where they undergo all manner of suffering, various agonies, and immeasurable bitterness.
Emerging from hell, they are born among the hungry ghosts (preta), where their lifespan is exceedingly long.

Some take on the form of the "awl-bodied" hungry ghosts, while others take on the form of the "needle-necked" hungry ghosts; according to what they receive through their karma, they are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, and if they have kinsmen, these are seized by others.
Or they are born among the hungry ghosts who consume poison, being burned by poisonous fires.
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are born among the animals, where in vast wildernesses they harm one another and devour each other in turn.
If one dies among the animals and is born among humans, their physical appearance will be haggard and they will lack majesty.

If there remains residual karma such that they are born in the heavens, their stature and physical form will all be diminished and inferior; the radiance of all their various jeweled ornaments will be faint, and they will not be loved or respected by the celestial maidens.
The celestial maidens have betrayed him, abandoning him to go to other heavens.
His *srotāpanna* [attainment] has little flavor, his wisdom is meager, and his mind is not upright; thus he is held in contempt and mocked by the other sons of gods.
When the hosts of devas were fighting with the asuras and were slain by them, it was due to the remaining force of their karma.

At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, again, together with the hosts of devas, beheld upon the walls of the jewel palace the sixteen sections of the Great Howling Hell (*Mahāraurava*), wherein sentient beings undergo various sufferings as previously described.

If there are sentient beings who kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, or drink intoxicants to the point of confusion, they will fall into this hell and undergo immeasurable varieties of agonizing suffering.

Having finished suffering there, they emerge from hell and are born among the hungry ghosts; fleeing everywhere, great malevolent spirits pull out their tongues, which grow back again once they have been removed.

Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are reborn among animals, receiving the body of a *kapinjala* partridge; they lose their lives by their own cries due to the residual karmic conditions of their past false speech.
If one dies among the animals and is reborn among humans, they will receive the retribution of their karma as previously described; whatever they say, people will not believe or accept.

If they have virtuous karma and are reborn among the gods, their voices will be hoarse, broken, coarse, harsh, and turbid; they will be unskilled in singing or chanting, and all the hosts of gods will not trust their words. They cannot proclaim beautiful, lovely, and correct speech like the other gods, due to the residual karmic conditions of their former false speech.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again beheld upon the palace wall the sixteen compartments of the Reviving (Tapana) Hell.
Therein, sentient beings undergo various immeasurable sufferings, agonies, and bitter torments as the karmic retribution for their deeds, just as previously described.

Having completed their punishment, they emerge from hell and are born among the hungry ghosts, receiving the bodies of those hungry ghosts who consume impure food, and undergo great suffering five times greater than before.
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are reborn among animals, taking on the body of a makara fish in the great ocean.
Dying among animals, if they are reborn among humans, their appearance is hideous; their lips and mouths are coarse and large, and they are loathsome for others to behold.

When their life in the human realm comes to an end, if they have residual karma remaining, they may be reborn among the devas; however, the radiance of their bodies will be diminished and inferior as previously described, and they will be held in contempt by all the hosts of devas.
“The Great Intense Heat Hell and the Avīci Hell—these two hells do not manifest as transformations of karmic retribution.
Why is this? Fearing that the minds of the devas are delicate and they might lose their lives upon seeing them.”
If one sees these two hells, one will feel great terror; therefore, this retribution of birth and death is not manifested [to others].
Then Śakra, King of Devas, having observed this, spoke in verse:
"Just as fine dust particles Dwell within the empty sky,"
As the wind blows and causes things to revolve, so too are all karmas.
Union is followed by separation; suffering and joy are likewise so.
They are turned by the power of karma; they do not arise without causes and conditions.
Now, this sphere of karmic transformation, the Muni knows as it truly is;
he transforms immeasurable nets of karma, the seeds of all minds.
The accumulation of karma by the mind is difficult to know, except for the Tathāgatas.
Bound by various kinds of karma, one revolves within the world.
The net of karma possesses great power, enabling one to undergo hundreds of thousands,
even millions of nayutas of kalpas of diverse births and deaths.
"Just as a bird tied by a rope, though it flies far away, is drawn back when the line is pulled;
so too is the matter for sentient beings bound by the ropes of karma.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having shown this rare occurrence to the sons of the gods:

Sentient beings have immeasurable determinate karma and indeterminate karma, which are experienced as retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, or retribution in subsequent lives.
Furthermore, there are three types:
wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and neutral (avyākṛta) karma.

Having displayed such an immeasurable net of karma—the manifested images transformed by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa—and having finished prostrating together with the host of devas, he emerged from this Yama-sāla tree.
Once the host of devas had departed, Śakra closed the doors of the śāla trees.
After Śakra had come out, he saw the remaining devas indulging in negligence and play, amusing themselves and enjoying the pleasures of the five senses.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Heavenly King felt compassion in his heart and spoke these verses:
“Beings of various animal forms, deceived by heedlessness,
Whether eating or indulging in desire, their greedy minds are ever fond of it.”
Having practiced wholesome deeds, one enjoys their karmic retribution among the devas;
yet when such a heedless person’s life ends, where will they go?
Destroyed by the enemy of heedlessness and blown away by the winds of karma—
Just as a tree that has fallen over, they fall into the various realms of existence.
For hundreds of thousands of nayutas of times, they undergo birth and death among the devas,
yet they feel no weariness or detachment, nor do they give rise to a mind of sorrow or fear.
At that time, after Śakra had spoken these verses, he went among the assembly of the negligent devaputras; the devaputras, conceiving hearts of reverence, made offerings and paid him homage.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in order to restrain his mind, played with this son of heaven amidst various groves and gardens, not entering among the Yama-sāla trees, as they enjoyed themselves and took pleasure in those parks.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue and the great assembly of devas, proceeded to the Hall of Good Dharma.

As for the devas dwelling in the Yama-sāla grove who enjoy celestial pleasures, once their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, their lives end and they fall back; driven by the flow of karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
If born among humans, they will experience the foremost pleasures, presiding over great gardens and groves, constantly enjoying peace and happiness.
Due to the remaining karma, they will be born in the country of Malaya, presiding over sandalwood forests, possessing great wealth and abundant joy.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the twenty-fifth ground of the Trāyastriṃśa devas is named the Ground of Swift Movement (Javanā).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that heaven? One sees:

there are sentient beings who practice wholesome karma; their minds are upright and honest, free from flattery and crookedness; they do not afflict other beings; they believe in the retribution of actions; they practice the karma of right view and extensively cultivate generosity, becoming immensely wealthy and possessing abundant riches.
Seeing sentient beings entering the great ocean in search of wealth and treasures, he provides large ships for these merchants.
Having obtained these vessels, the merchants acquire vast amounts of wealth and treasure, which they then use for acts of giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds.
In this way, the boat owner gives the boat as a gift, seeking no favor and receiving no recompense.
What is non-stealing?

If one travels on a road where there are bandit armies destroying village enclosures, or where people, fearing government troops, flee to these villages for refuge—even so much as not taking a single grain of chaff, stalk, or blade of grass—one does so out of fear born from faith in the retribution of karmic results, rather than out of fear of royal law; this is called non-stealing.
What is non-killing? From the smallest moisture-born creatures such as centipedes, one never intentionally kills them, nor does one even entertain thoughts of killing.

If there are sentient beings who set snares, nets, traps, or pits to kill tigers, wolves, birds, beasts, and other such creatures, one immediately ransoms them with wealth and goods to ensure their release.
Their minds feel no regret, and they also teach others to abide in the wholesome path, performing various such virtuous deeds.
These persons who uphold the precepts refrain from killing and stealing; by recollecting their virtuous karma, they achieve success in all things.

If there is anything performed, all the hosts of devas collectively praise it as excellent; their countenances are pure and they receive offerings from the devas—this is called the retribution of manifest karma.
"When this person of virtuous karma passes away from here, they are reborn above the Heaven of the Thirty-three in a place called the Ground of Swift Movement (*Javanā*).

Having been born in that celestial realm, by virtue of their wholesome karma, they possess the foremost adornments such that no sentient beings can fully discern them; such a celestial abode is exceedingly delightful."

Once the son of heaven is born, his body is radiant and he experiences supreme bliss; his body is without bone or flesh, nor is it subject to impurities or sweat. He has no enemies and no fear, nothing to pursue, and is free from envy. There is nothing he does not love and delight in; he is free from the fear of illness, except at the time of his decline, and he knows no fear of kings, though his mind is largely given to heedlessness.
He beholds all the grounds as delightful, sporting and enjoying himself with the five desires, and experiencing pleasure in playing within immeasurable realms.

There are towers of lapis lazuli with railings of gold, and various groves of trees and lotus ponds composed of the seven treasures; these are adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, which emit various subtle and wondrous sounds.

Within the mountain valleys there abound many birds; the peaks of Mount Sumeru are adorned with the seven treasures; the lotus ponds have gold, silver, and pearls for their sandy bottoms; various jewel-trees possess the radiance of the sun, with branches of gold and lapis lazuli, adorned with manifold flowers and embellished by immeasurable swarms of bees.
The cave of Mount Sumeru is adorned with the foremost of all jewels.
Its ground is soft and supple.
Amidst its high peaks made of the seven treasures, various flowers and exquisite fragrances surround and embellish them, appearing spontaneously according to one's thoughts.

Furthermore, there were other places adorned with lamp-trees; these wish-fulfilling trees, adorned with hundreds of thousands of radiances, were most extraordinary, and they were surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who entertained one another with the singing of various wondrous melodies.
Thus, as these celestial hosts touch and behold various things, they all experience happiness; when their ears hear various sounds, their minds find delight in them all.
If they smell various fragrances, they become fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
If he touches with his body, there is nothing he does not find delightful.
Whatever his mind desires, he obtains it all; no cause or condition can ever deprive him of that joy.
Thus, the deva-son, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, proceeds together with the other hosts of devas toward the mountain peak.

That peak is named All-Powerful; its entire summit is adorned with wish-fulfilling trees, and it is further embellished by flowing springs, rivers, and ponds where various lotuses bloom. It is surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, with branches of *vaiḍūrya* gemstone covering it entirely. Adorned with hundreds of thousands of multi-storied pavilions, immeasurable flocks of birds emit exquisite melodies.

Due to the power of virtuous karma, such various pleasures are accomplished within these mountain peaks; virtuous karma is their root, for they do not arise without cause, nor are they created by another.
"This person receives this retribution not because the Lord Īśvara joyfully bestows it upon them.
At that time, the devaputra ascended this mountain peak and saw that the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of radiances of all the other devaputras were entirely equal, no different from his own.
Upon this peak, they perform various musical performances together with the devas and apsaras, producing exquisite sounds as they enjoy their pleasures.

These hosts of devas are fully endowed with bodily radiance, physical form, stature, and the experience of bliss; they gaze upon one another with reverence, adorned with garlands of many lotuses. Hearing the various songs, their hearts give rise to love and delight; all are clothed in celestial garments that are devoid of any distinction between warp and woof.
In this way, the bodies of all these devas were entirely endowed with radiance.
At that time, having ascended the mountain peak, the devaputra saw the various realms of the earth, each distinct from the others, and beheld the luminous wheels of the rivers.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they dwell in two locations within this heaven.
These various pure and adorned lands are perfected with manifold delights, as previously described.
Why is it called the "Swift-Traveling Ground"?

Because these celestial hosts possess such great power that when they engage in battle with the asuras, they can strike the asuras and return to their own abode, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, within the blink of an eye among human beings; therefore, it is named "Swift-Traveling."
Due to past karma, one obtains a corresponding fruit.

Because he formerly gave people swift ships so that they might cross the great ocean and obtain many precious treasures, through this practice of giving and cultivating merit, he has now obtained this swift karmic retribution.
Thus, these devaputras wield weapons with great swiftness.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they enjoy celestial pleasures for a long time.

Once that wholesome karma is exhausted, the five signs of decay appear: sweat flows from their bodies, their physical radiance suddenly vanishes like a lamp when its oil is spent, and all their sensory faculties undergo the same.
Finding no flavor of pleasure whatsoever within the five desires, he feels shame upon seeing other hosts of devas, and all his celestial maidens have deserted him.
At that time, when the deva-son sees his celestial maidens turning their backs on him to pursue others, two kinds of suffering arise: first, the suffering of jealousy;
[the second being the suffering of separation].
The second is the suffering of separation from the beloved.
These two kinds of suffering scorch one's own heart more fiercely than a raging fire.
If, in a previous life, one committed the karma of theft, at that time one will see celestial maidens and others seize the ornaments one was wearing and present them to other devas.
If, in previous lives, one has committed the karma of false speech, when the celestial maidens hear what is said, they will develop a perverted understanding and take it to be abusive language.

If, in previous lives, one gave alcohol to those who observe the precepts, or broke the prohibitions by drinking alcohol oneself, or produced yeast and fermented liquors, at the time of death, one's mind will become confused and lose right mindfulness.
Afflicted and distracted by such twofold remorse and fever, they fall into hell.
If, in a previous life, they committed the karma of killing, their lifespan will be short and they will meet an early death.
If, due to the karma of sexual misconduct committed in previous lives, they see that all the celestial maidens have abandoned them to enjoy themselves with other deva sons,
this is called the fifth sign of decline.
Because their observance of the precepts is deficient in five ways, they are bound by the net of karma and undergo retribution according to their deeds.
If they act with negligence, they will be dragged away by the King of Death.

All such flawed and leaky observances of the precepts—maintaining the prohibitions for the sake of rebirth in heaven—are swiftly destroyed by impermanence; at that time, they will be bound by the ropes of karma and fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

"Thus observing the impermanence of celestial bliss as if with one's own eyes—one sees that although there is attachment at first, it ultimately returns to destruction; it is unstable and impermanent, like lightning that does not abide. Observing the faults and evils of all desires, he spoke in verse:
'Drinking the wine of heedlessness, The gods relish this foolish drink;
They fall away into hell, Enveloped by great, fierce fires.'
Initially stained by craving and desire, with a mind tormented by the heat of anger and deluded by ignorance, it is merely empty and devoid of reality.
Deceived by the sounds of music and performance, one is led astray by what is false and illusory.
They do not perceive the suffering of decline and fall, which is ultimately impossible to avoid.
When they behold the celestial maidens, their minds undergo a transformation;
eventually, they must be parted from them and fall away into other realms of existence.
Observe the nature of women: they do not remain constant as women;
when there is wealth and pleasure, they draw near, but when things decline and change, they abandon them.
Like a wild deer that roams in trust, so too is the trust placed in desire.
Later, when one encounters decline and change, the mind becomes light and abandons them.
One does not remember their kindness or the care they provided, nor does one think of them as kin or friends;
when faced with such decline, one immediately casts them aside and no longer remembers them.
Just as a swarm of bees abandons a flower that has withered and decayed, so too it is with women: when decline arrives, they cast one aside.
They do not regard his virtuous and loving heart; fickle and restless, their thoughts dwell only on sensual desire.
The nature of women is thus: like honey mixed with poisonous medicine.
Deluded by desire, they lead to folly; their clever speech increases delusion.
Women are difficult to trust and are to be shunned by the wise.
The color of women deceives gods and humans, causing their minds to be utterly deluded;
even into future lives, they cannot provide even the slightest benefit.
Gods, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, asuras, and the like—
Rākṣasas and piśācas are all deceived by the illusions of women;
likewise, these various sensual pleasures arise from sensory objects,
yet at the moment of death, all such pleasures vanish.
All the hosts of devas, though adorned with gardens and groves,
are bound by the noose of death and led away by the fetters of desire.
Since sensual pleasures cannot save them, what use are the various court ladies?
"Throughout all the worlds under heaven, the King of Death carries everyone away.
Having thus observed the signs of the devas' decline and passing away, the bhikṣu gave rise to a mind of compassion and developed weary detachment from the realm of desire.
Thus, sustained by their own karma, wherever these devas go, they are led by the ropes of their karma and remain ever heedful.

Yet there are other devas who, out of heedlessness, delight in play and enjoyment; like men riding horses, they rush toward all sensory objects and experience heedless pleasure within every grove and garden. This continues until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; at the end of life, they fall back and transmigrate according to their karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they will always be born in pleasant places, possessing the foremost wealth and happiness, with abundant riches and treasures; they may become kings or high ministers, possessing many elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys for riding, so that they never have to travel on foot and never experience fatigue.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The twenty-sixth stage of the path is named Shadow-Reflection (*Chāyā-pratibimba*).
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that heaven?

If there are sentient beings who can fully uphold the seven types of precepts and thereby attain a corresponding fruit; who, through a mind cultivated by reflection, are endowed with right view; and who refrain from killing and stealing while skillfully maintaining the prohibitive precepts.

Because this person who upholds the precepts acts as a cause for happiness, they observe the mundane precepts, even to the point of not stealing the most minute of objects and remaining free from theft.

Even if they dwell near the seashore in a territory controlled by others, regarding all various things such as conch shells, fish, and oysters brought forth by the tide, they do not take these items with a thieving mind.
This person of virtuous karma has faith in the future and fears the retribution of karmic results; it is not out of fear of royal law that they do so—this is called non-stealing. What is non-killing?

This person of wholesome karma has faith in the future and fears the retribution of karmic results; with a well-considered and upright mind, they do not afflict sentient beings, distance themselves from evil associates, and refrain from killing living beings for the sake of seeking happiness.

Whether wandering in rivers or traveling through mountain valleys, if such a person is seized by a shadow-demon (chāyā-piśāca), they would rather sacrifice their own body than harm the shadow-demon; they would not place poison within the shadow, fearing it might take the demon's life. Although they know the means to do so, they refrain from inflicting injury.

If a *śūdra* ghost knows the means of killing but observes the precepts and does not act upon them—whether by using water to reflect, a mirror to reflect, or the light of the sun—the person, knowing of the intent to kill, will not inflict harm, nor will they seek revenge; instead, they sacrifice their own life rather than kill any living being.
When this person of virtuous karma dies and their life ends, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the region known as Shadow-Reflection.

Having been born in that heaven, by virtue of their good karma, their bodies emit radiance; amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, they experience supreme bliss, fully endowed with all manner of delights.
He sports and enjoys himself upon the ground of Mount Sumeru, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand celestial maidens; the ground consists of Jāmbūnada gold, interspersed with various ornaments.

Furthermore, they sport and enjoy themselves among the peaks of the Jambūnada gold mountains; from wish-fulfilling trees, whatever the mind desires arises entirely from those trees. For a long time, they thus experience celestial pleasures together with their retinues.
He further proceeded to the Forest of External Reflections, where groves of Jāmbūnada gold adorned the park.
The golden trees had silver leaves and fruits of blue lapis lazuli;
the silver trees had golden leaves and fruits of lapis lazuli, thus forming a magnificent array.

Having already played in the Forest of External Reflections, they proceed again to another place, wandering and observing in succession; there are flocks of peacocks and various birds, their bodies adorned and interspersed with the diverse colors of the seven treasures.
Having seen this, the deva-son entered that grove and sported together with the peacocks and various other birds.
When the peacocks saw the deva-son approaching, they emitted all manner of exquisite and beautiful sounds; the singing voices of the celestial maidens did not equal even one-sixteenth part of these.
At that time, the devaputra thought to himself:
"I shall now mount this peacock bird and sport with the celestial maidens upon the mountain peaks, wandering and gazing about in every direction."

Due to his wholesome karma, as soon as he thinks of it, the peacock celestial bird approaches the deva-son, transforms itself into a massive body, and possesses great beauty and power; it is upright, majestic, and exceptionally sublime.

At that time, the devaputra, together with the celestial maidens, mounted this peacock and traveled to every mountain peak throughout Mount Sumeru; according to whatever came to mind, they went to observe them all. They gazed upon every flower pond and every mountain peak, surveying all such peaks and ponds everywhere.
"At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings—the guardians of the world—wished to go to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to proclaim the Dharma and the non-Dharma of Jambudvīpa."
At that time, while traveling through the air, the devaputra encountered the Four Great Heavenly Kings who Guard the World and asked them:
"Where have you all come from, following one another?"
At that time, the World-Protector replied to the devaputra, saying:

"I have come from the delightful realm of the foremost wholesome karma. That place abounds with lotus gardens, groves, rivers, and ponds, fully adorned with every kind of splendor; I have come from there, desiring to go to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to report to King Śakra the presence of both Dharma and non-Dharma in Jambudvīpa."

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world, the deva son gave rise to a sense of wonder. Mounting a great-power peacock adorned with various jewels, he traveled according to his thought without any obstruction, descending from heaven toward Jambudvīpa as if it were the second day.

With a rare and precious mind, he surveyed everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa—the gardens, groves, flower ponds, rivers, springs, villages, camps, cities, and towns—observing them all in their entirety.
When the various Brahmins, heterodox practitioners with false views, and physiognomists within Jambudvīpa saw this omen, they spoke thus:
"The eight-armed deity, riding upon the Garuḍa, the king of golden-winged birds, has descended from heaven toward Jambudvīpa to observe the world."
They merely speak thus with such false conceptualizations.
Furthermore, there are those with wrong views from heterodox paths and various brahmins who say:
"This is Maheśvara, the Sovereign Deva, named Kumāra, the Youthful Deva; he has descended from heaven riding upon a peacock toward Jambudvīpa to protect the world."
Furthermore, there are those with wrong views from heterodox paths, such as certain Brahmins, who speak thus:
"Maheśvara rides upon a white bull; he creates the world and can destroy the world. He is called the 'Maker' and is the one who fashions the world."

"In this way, those heterodox practitioners with such false views, the various Brahmins, engage in manifold conceptualizations and manifold praises, composing various treatises that do not perceive reality as it truly is."
"In this way, all these brahmins destroy the True Dharma; they are supremely ignorant and also teach others to hold false views.
At that time, the devaputra, having completed his observation, returned to his celestial palace.
Thus, these non-Buddhists, with minds clouded by ignorance, speak of the unreal as real and do not see things as they truly are.
At the beginning of the kalpa, when this deity descended from above, the non-Buddhists saw him but did not know him as he truly was.
Thus do these non-Buddhist Brahmins of wrong views give rise to their own conceptual constructions and proclaim them to others; in this way, these non-Buddhists do not see according to reality.
At that time, the deva-son, having arrived at his celestial palace, spoke thus to the other hosts of devas:
"I went to Jambudvīpa and beheld its lands; the ground was level and even, and its gardens, groves, flowers, and ponds were soft and lovely."

At that time, having heard what was said, the devaputras—some riding white elephants, some riding peacocks, and others on various mounts, or traveling through the air—surveyed Mount Sumeru in its entirety and then descended in succession to Jambudvīpa.

Or, when one temporarily descends to dwell in a river, pond, mountain, or forest retreat, all non-Buddhists and brahmins alike designate that place as a "ground of merit"; within such a place, they practice asceticism and observe the precepts, claiming it to be a site of merit.
Thus, through such false traditions passed down in succession, those who hear them become attached to their hearts, claiming they possess reality.
At that time, when the devaputra first descended, a brahmin saw him and gave rise to conceptual discrimination, saying:
