"This is either the Great Brahmā Deva King;..."
Some said, "This is Maheśvara";
some said, "This is the eight-armed Heavenly King";
others said, "This is the Son of Heaven Īśvara, or the youth Kumāra."
Each gave rise to a conceptual discrimination, thinking: "This is the ground where Brahmā resides;
this is the ground governed by Maheśvara, the King of the Īśvaradevas."
"This is the realm presided over by the Eight-Armed Heavenly King;
this is the realm presided over by the Youthful Deva Kumāra.
Having made such distinctions, they may formulate heterodox doctrines or offer praises, establish their own tenets, or state their own reasons and analogies—engaging in all manner of false views.
Having already held wrong views oneself, one further teaches others with those same wrong views; others, having heard this, in turn teach one another.
In this successive manner, it is not seeing according to reality.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-One;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Two.
Translated by the Bactrian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: Contemplation of the Heavens, Part Eight: The Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, the devaputra, longing for his celestial palace, returned to the heavens.
Then, the heterodox Brahmins with wrong views said:
"These various stages are presided over by such-and-such a deity or such-and-such a deity.

Whether they compose treatises or offer hymns of praise, the heterodox Brahmins dwelling in these groves see them and pay them respect, prostrating themselves with their heads at their feet; yet they merely observe their outward appearance and develop faith and reverence, failing to know according to reality that these are the deities of the second heaven.
Furthermore, they give rise to discriminatory views, thinking:

"This deva-son wanders everywhere, his body like a mass of fire; whereas the people of Jambudvīpa enter into fire—by this cause and condition, he has been born in a good realm and received a celestial body."

The non-Buddhist heretics and various Brahmins immediately composed heterodox treatises; some established their own tenets, some stated their own reasons and provided their own analogies, and some offered praises.
Having themselves held such wrong views, they further explain them to others and cause others to accept and practice them, such as burning their own bodies in the hope of being reborn in the heavens.

Being thus unable to see and know things as they truly are, they preach false causes and effects that do not result in true karmic retribution; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.
"Furthermore, those Brahmins of wrong views who dwell in the forest give rise to false views.
Seeing this son of heaven descending from the celestial realm toward Jambudvīpa, because they see him from afar, their vision is not clear."
From afar they saw the deva-son descend from the peak of Mount Alaṃkāra, go to Jambudvīpa, and later return to the heavens.

Having witnessed this event, the brahmins dwelling in the forest conceived a conceptual distinction, saying: "The people of Jambudvīpa throw themselves off high cliffs; by this cause and condition, they are born in the good realms and receive the bodies of devas."

Therefore, those brahmins with wrong views throw themselves from high cliffs, desiring to be reborn in heaven; they further preach this method to others, compose heterodox treatises or offer praises, and proclaim these false doctrines as the results of karma.
Because of their wrong views, they falsely proclaim cause and effect; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms within the hells. This is called wrong view.

At that time, the brahmins among the non-Buddhist followers of wrong views dwelling in the forest saw this deva descending from heaven toward Jambudvīpa. Being at a great distance, they could not see his true form, but only a great radiance like the color of fire. They gave rise to false discriminations and claimed that because the people of Jambudvīpa make offerings to fire, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the good realms and receive the bodies of devas.
Why is this? Fire is the mouth of all the devas; therefore, those who make offerings to fire attain rebirth in the heavens.

Engaging in such false conceptualizations and failing to see things as they truly are, they compose heterodox treatises, establish their own tenets, state their own reasons, and offer their own analogies. They create wrong views for themselves and further teach others to enter into those same wrong views.

Thus, these brahmins with such wrong views bring no benefit to themselves and cause others to suffer; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are reborn in hell.
Furthermore, there were certain heterodox Brahmins with wrong views who lived in the forest; seeing this deva-son, they gave rise to false discriminations.
Seeing from afar that the deva-son neither drank nor ate, the Brahmins then thought:

"The people of Jambudvīpa do not drink and do not eat; by reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the happy realms and receive the bodies of devas."
"I, too, shall now neither drink nor eat.
Furthermore, he teaches others to study his method, composes heterodox treatises or offers praise for them, and proclaims these false teachings as the results of karma.
Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born in the hells.
Thus, these non-Buddhists do not know things as they truly are, and they open the gates to the evil realms.
"If this deva-son remains for even a short time, or for but a moment, it would appear as more than a hundred years in Jambudvīpa.
The heterodox Brahmins with false views then say:
'This deva-son is eternally abiding and immovable; he is neither broken nor destroyed; he creates the world and is able to destroy the world.'"
When non-Buddhists see this, they compose heterodox treatises or offer praise, propounding false causes.
Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into evil realms and are born within the hells.
Thus, through such immeasurable lack of seeing things as they truly are, he composes false doctrines; through such lack of seeing things as they truly are, he deceives his own mind.
Through this lack of seeing things as they truly are, the bhikṣu observes how all sentient beings are deluded by their minds, and speaks in verse:
"The mind is a malignant serpent, The poison of craving pervades it entirely; It stings the five limbs of man."
One will experience great regret for having lived in vain.
The river of craving is vast; the five sense faculties serve as its ferry-crossing. This shore is terrifying, while the other shore is peaceful and secure.
Seeing this, they give rise to false interpretations and do not know it as it truly is; such people of wrong views fall into hell.
These people of wrong views perceive what is not a cause to be a cause; because of their inverted views, they fall into hell.
Foolish people, deluded regarding cause and effect, are bound by the prison of existence and undergo all manner of suffering.
From the retribution of karma, there arise birth and death; yet if one sees according to reality, one reaches the further shore.
The fool seeks sensual desires and is deluded by them, falling into hell like a moth into a flame.
Among humans, it is by maintaining the precepts and practicing right view that one attains rebirth in heaven, not through asceticism.
Practicing the ways of false views, relying on their own wisdom with perverse pride, they deceive and delude others,
entering into the great ocean of darkness and ignorance.
The world suffers because of wrong views;
liberation is not attained by tormenting the body.
As the wise have said: one must subdue the mind to burn away the mountain of afflictions.
Then one attains liberation.
By practicing right view and extinguishing all afflictions, and by seeing the true reality, one then attains liberation.
All non-Buddhists delude the world; there is no place among them where quiescence and freedom from falsehood exist.
The non-Buddhists of the world are full of deception and falsehood; even if one sought for them for a hundred eons, not the slightest bit of reality would be found.
The Dharma that transcends the world is entirely true; worldly discourse is a bondage like poison.
Performing merit with a heart of attachment yields impermanent happiness, whereas the Dharma that transcends the world yields eternal happiness.
Impure and full of evils, these things arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are empty of substance and exist only as verbal designations, lacking any reality.
Those who speak such falsehoods and deceive others will fall into the pitch-black darkness, a place of great terror.
"Thus the bhikṣu, seeing it as it truly is, spoke these verses.
How does a sentient being attain true knowledge and attain true vision, so that wrong views do not arise?"
The discourse of wrong views lacks any genuine insight within itself and induces wrong views in others.
Whether one practices such a discourse oneself or explains it to others, one falls into hell and causes others to fall into hell as well.

Then the assembly of devas, having surveyed all of Jambudvīpa, mounted their celestial birds and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Upon arriving at the heavenly palace, they spoke to the other devas as previously described.
Furthermore, they sport and enjoy pleasures within the groves, delighting themselves with music and song, fully endowed with all manner of meritorious qualities.

They sport and enjoy pleasures in places adorned with every kind of jewel, until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; then, passing away from that heavenly realm, they wander according to their karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, they will always experience peace and happiness without the affliction of illness, remaining free from all decline and disorder; they will be born in a land of abundance and joy, possessing a male body with all faculties complete, and will become either a king or a great minister.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the dwelling places of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The twenty-seventh stage of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named "Practice of Wisdom.
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who maintain the precepts with a great resolve and cultivate wholesome deeds; they perceive the retribution of karma as it truly is, possess faith and delight in their hearts, constantly practice wholesome deeds, and abandon what is unwholesome. Their minds are upright and honest, and they distance themselves from evil friends—to the extent that they do not even travel the same road with them, do not converse with them, and do not dwell together with them.
Having thus fully cultivated such wholesome karma, like refining pure gold,
one becomes beloved and respected by all people in the present life because of having practiced virtue.

If there is a bhikṣu who constantly practices the recitation and study of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, such a bhikṣu diligently cultivates these with a mind that never slackens, whether by day or by night.

If, during the darkness of night, one’s recitation and study are interrupted, there may be sentient beings who revere the Buddha-dharma and this bhikṣu, offering lamps to the Saṅgha. Out of reverence for the Dharma and with faith in the Triple Gem, they further practice such giving so that the merit of their recitation and study may increase.

If, during times of intense heat, one gives a fan as a gift, causing there to be neither darkness nor the distress of heat, and hears the bhikṣus discuss the noble Dharma, the mind becomes exceedingly joyful.

By the power of these two kinds of meritorious causes and conditions, this person of wholesome karma benefits both themselves and others; at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the good destination of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the realm of wise conduct.

Having been born in that heaven, by virtue of his wholesome karma, the radiance of his body surpasses the light of the sun tenfold; he is honored by all the hosts of devas, surrounded and venerated by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who were formerly his close friends—women who are joyful, smiling, and adorned in every way.

Their bodies were sublime and excellent, adorned with all the marks of physical beauty, majesty, and virtue; free from envy and jealousy, they loved and respected one another, never parting for even a moment, and all gave rise to joy as they drew near to the celestial king.
They hold lotuses in their hands, or golden flowers, or silver flowers, beryl flowers, crystal flowers, or flowers made of various jewels.
If they are golden lotuses, they have stems of white silver and filaments of red gems;
if they are beryl flowers, they have stems of pure gold.
The blue jewel lotuses have stems of white silver;
the mother-of-pearl lotuses have stems made of blue jewels and gems;
the red lotus jewels have filaments of diamond.
Thus the celestial maidens approached the place where the deva-son was, scattering the flowers they held over the deva-son like a torrential downpour falling in the height of summer;
the other celestial maidens likewise scattered various precious flowers over the newly born deva-son in the same manner.

At that time, the deva-son, seeing the celestial maidens, felt joy arise in his heart; his desire was immediately stirred and an evil longing took birth. He rose from his seat, experiencing something he had never known before.

They approached the celestial maidens, leaping for joy and filled with delight; together they harmonized in merriment and enjoyment, singing, dancing, laughing, and sporting, thereby causing the desire of this deva-son to increase.
Thus, surrounded on all sides by these celestial maidens, they roam through the gardens.
The various celestial groves are radiant with the light of many jewels, and every desire is there in full abundance.

Under these trees they sport and enjoy themselves; various birds sing with exquisite melodies that are indistinguishable from the voices of the celestial maidens. Adorned with all the requisites of desire, the grove is filled with flowers and fruits and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of varieties of flowing springs, lotus ponds, and rivers.
Thus the deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, sports and enjoys himself, experiencing immeasurable pleasure by virtue of his wholesome karma.

At that time, the deva-son again goes with the celestial maidens to another grove, where they amuse themselves with music; everything is provided according to their thoughts as they enjoy the pleasures of the devas.
This is the fruit of the precepts cherished by the sages; it is the accomplishment of karmic fruition.
Thus, surrounded by celestial maidens, the deva proceeds further to the Maṇicīra forest for recreation.

When the long-established devas see this deva-son, they all come forth to welcome him, their hearts filled with joy as if seeing a kinsman or a brother. They offer words of comfort and inquiry, then enter the grove together to enjoy celestial pleasures amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments.
Thus the deva-son experiences various pleasures; furthermore, within the Maṇicūḍaka grove, he rejoices immeasurably, his eyes beholding manifold colors and his mind giving rise to joy and delight.
The grounds and groves were all adorned with the seven treasures; the trees of the forests were embellished with golden jeweled robes, and thus they were adorned by various kinds of precious trees.
The ground is soft and supple, and immeasurable food and drink flow forth from the rivers; when one looks upon all these various colors, the eyes are filled with great delight.
Thus, the newly born deva-son enjoys himself and experiences pleasure together with the hosts of devas.

The celestial son further proceeded to the Vaiḍūrya ground, where, together with the host of goddesses, he successively beheld mani-jewel robes produced from trees; their color was bright and pure, exceedingly delightful, and as a gentle breeze stirred them, they rose and fell with the wind, adorned by immeasurable colored bees, their radiant luster like that of lamps.

When the devas saw this, they conceived a sense of rare wonder and gave rise to great joy; together with the hosts of celestial maidens, they went to this tree and performed divine music, sporting and enjoying themselves.
At that time, the devas felt a sense of wonder within this grove; immediately from the flowers emerged celestial *māndārava* blossoms, endowed with every supreme and exquisite flavor.

All the hosts of devas, seeing colors, fragrances, tastes, and textures never before seen, experience a hundredfold increase in joy and delight; they drink the celestial *madhu*, the wine of supreme flavor.
The deva-son drinks it and, together with the various celestial maidens, sports and enjoys pleasures, singing many wondrous melodies in praise of Śakra, the Heavenly King:
"By the power of the causal conditions of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, I am able to experience the pleasures of the five desires here within this Maṇicūḍaka grove."
"The flavor is like *madhu*; its color, fragrance, and exquisite taste emerge from the flowers of the tree, being most rare.
Now that I drink it, I experience a hundredfold pleasure.

At that time, the deva, together with the celestial maidens, filled a beryl vessel to the brim with the supreme flavor of the *madhu* of the heavens, and they exhorted one another in turn to drink this celestial nectar.

"When these hosts of devas were among humans, they practiced generosity and observed the precepts; now they have obtained such superior and wondrous rewards as exquisite form, fragrance, and sublime flavors.
According to their original karma—whether of superior, middling, or inferior retribution—they feel shame and remorse in their hearts."
"On the tree there is a bird named Yamastu; seeing the sons of the gods, it feels shame in its heart and speaks this verse for them:
'Beings are driven by delusion, Drinking the wine of *yamastu*;
Manifestly observing how they are bound by delusion, They remain greedily attached to delicious flavors.'"
The snare of the *māda* and *mūrchā* poisons is drunk until the end of life, causing one to fall back into hell; it is the same for all nāgas.
If they see, touch, smell, or taste it, it causes the human mind to become deluded and intoxicated.
Therefore, the wise abandon all nets of entanglement.
Seeing them gives rise to craving; touching them leads to smelling and tasting.
Smelling them, the mind craves their flavor; attachment to flavor becomes a source of decline and affliction.
Among all forms of bondage, none surpasses the craving for flavors;
it destroys one’s reputation, complexion, and strength, because of this attachment to taste.
Bewildered by attachment to flavor, the eyes grow dim and one remains perpetually intoxicated.
The mind is deluded and leads to the wasteland of ignorance, such that one does not know the dharmas of good and evil.
One is treated with contempt and laughter by women,
sleeping amidst filth and excrement without any awareness, unable to move or exert oneself.
Alcohol can destroy one's reputation, surpassing even the fear of death;
it is like drinking poisonous medicine, and like being caught in the snare of death.
The affliction of drinking alcohol brings thirty-six faults.
Having recognized these faults and evils, one should swiftly distance oneself from them.
Even those of noble lineage and great wisdom, when defiled by alcohol,
are held in contempt by all people, like grass tossed about by the wind.
"Thus, although these celestial birds are animals, they revile the gods; how much more so would other gods?

These sons of the gods drink celestial nectars—possessing superior, middling, and inferior flavors, as well as perfect colors and fragrances—according to the seeds of their own virtuous karma, vows, and practices."

Having drunk, he again went to the Tāla-palace grove; desiring to sport within this grove, he heard various sounds and his heart was filled with joy. Taking blue *utpala* lotuses as his primary garland, surrounded by celestial sons and daughters, he sported in delight, his mind constantly dwelling on the golden-light Tāla palace grove.
Having experienced that pleasure, he proceeded again to the Mṛgāra Forest; once he had arrived within the Mṛgāra Forest, he beheld hundreds of thousands of palaces adorned with celestial garlands.

"At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Lord of Devas, mounted upon the great white elephant king Airāvaṇa, surrounded by his retinue of sons and daughters of the gods; with a heart full of joy, he acted for the sake of benefiting those gods who were heedless."

At that time, when the hosts of devas saw Śakra approaching, they all came forth to welcome him; they all prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Lord of Devas, and before him they produced various wondrous sounds, singing, dancing, playing, laughing, and shouting with joy.
Then Śakra, King of the Devas, with gentle words, comforted the various devas; seated upon the white elephant Airāvaṇa, he addressed the devas, saying:
"By your own karma you enjoy celestial pleasures. I now wish to return to the Garden of Joy to eliminate the anger of the asuras and their pride in relying on their great strength."
Then the assembly of devas addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King!
We too shall now follow the Heavenly King to eliminate the anger and arrogance of the asuras."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the gods:
"Do not be in such haste; I myself am now able to defeat the asuras.
Having spoken thus to the gods, Śakra entered the Nandana Grove.
Seeing the asuras in the Nandana Grove like gathering clouds, gradually increasing in size,
the hosts of devas reviled and censured them, whereupon the asuras grew even taller and more massive.
At that time, when the hosts of devas saw him grow, they cursed him incessantly; he grew even larger, his appearance becoming increasingly hideous.
When Śakra saw this, he addressed the hosts of devas:
"Because of your anger, this asura’s body has grown ever greater. I shall employ skillful means to cause him to abandon his anger and arrogance."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke in verse:
"Non-anger can subdue anger; Patience subdues the coarse and evil mind;
The Dharma can subdue what is contrary to the Dharma; And light destroys the darkness."
Truthfulness surpasses false speech; right speech subdues frivolous talk;
gentle words overcome harsh speech, and one is able to restrain the fault of divisive talk;
with a compassionate heart, one cuts off killing and harming; through giving, one eliminates stinginess and greed.
Right mindfulness overcomes wrong mindfulness; wholesome thoughts destroy evil thoughts.
Wisdom can dispel ignorance, just as the bright day removes the darkness, and the waxing moon surpasses the waning moon; in this way, one always attains victory.
Wisdom knows the true reality, surpassing the desires of false views;
The Noble Eightfold Path can destroy all evil realms;
The Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses can destroy all terrors.
Mindfulness overcomes forgetfulness, and wisdom overcomes delusion;
if one dwells in an araṇya, one can overcome all desires—
just as Mount Sumeru surpasses all other mountains and all groves and forests.
The great ocean surpasses all streams, And likewise all rivers and ponds;
The sun’s radiance surpasses all the stars, And also excels the other lunar mansions.
The Dharma excels the absence of Dharma, While generosity destroys poverty.
Sincerity and straightforwardness surpass flattery and crookedness; truth can destroy false speech.
Good fortune can overcome misfortune, just as fire can burn all kinds of fuel;
water can quench thirst, and food can eliminate hunger.
The lion’s heart is brave and strong, surpassing all other beasts;
contentment surpasses longing—thus the wise have said.
The compassionate one always triumphs; the lack of compassion is inferiority.
"Wisdom can subdue them; thus the wise have said.
Amidst those who commit many evil deeds of wrong views and utter much falsehood—among such heterodox practitioners—the Tathāgata is most preeminent."
The gods have triumphed over the asuras because their Dharma is superior;
I shall destroy them all, how much more so you alone?
You, messenger of the asuras, do not harbor such expectations.
"This lion throne is where the wise should dwell.

When the asuras heard these words spoken by Śakra-devānām-indra, they ceased to grow; because they had heard this binding truth, they diminished and did not increase, their physical strength, vigor, and prowess all failing to develop.
Seeing him weak and frail, a certain devaputra grasped his feet with his hands and dragged him down from his seat, immediately driving him out of the Heaven of Joyful Delight (Tuṣita).

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, felt great joy in his heart; he then proceeded to the dwelling place of Maṇicīra, mounting the great white elephant king Airāvaṇa to travel through the air toward the grove of Maṇicīra.
Having completed what was to be done, he went with all the devaputras and devakanyās to the Maṇi ground.

When the devas of the Maṇi ground saw Śakra, the King of Devas, they all came forth to welcome him; bowing their heads to his feet in prostration, and having finished their respectful salutations, they all proceeded together to the Megha Grove Forest.

That land is fully endowed with all manner of desires; it is soft, vast, and wide, covered everywhere with various flowers, and its palaces and all delightful places are fashioned from lotus branches.
Śakra, Lord of the Gods, together with various celestial maidens, enjoys himself through music, song, dance, and play.
The Gandharva kings surround Śakra, singing with exquisite melodies to praise the Heavenly King, while the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments provide entertainment.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was atop the white elephant Airāvaṇa; the elephant was so majestic and sublime that it surpassed a mountain of jewels, and its gait and forward movement were like the shifting of a mountain of jade. The elephant was as pure white as the Snowy Mountains, like the peaks of the Himalayas illuminated by the sun’s rays at the end of spring.
Thus, surrounded by hosts of devas, sons of gods, and daughters of gods, Śakra wanders through the groves.
Those groves are adorned with *vaiḍūrya* jewels, white silver, crystal, *indranīla* sapphires, great *indrāyudha* gems, red lotus gems, and pure gold and *śaṅkha* shells.
The Deva King Śakra, together with the hosts of devas, sons of gods, and daughters of gods, sports within the gardens; he closes the gates to the evil destinies and gives rise to joy in his heart.
Although he has attained the vision of the Truths, he still experiences sensual pleasures, yet he constantly contemplates the birth and death of sentient beings.
Having reflected thus, he was neither angry nor pleased; he observed that all pleasant sensations are impermanent, subject to destruction and dissolution.
Knowing this, he thought within himself:
"When the gods fall and perish, it is due to their own karma; where will they go to experience the fruits of their own karma?"
Blown by the winds of karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, wandering through suffering without a companion.
All the devas and all the celestial maidens are likewise thus; they must inevitably part from one another.
"Such karma creates great instruments of pleasure that mock all foolish, ordinary worldlings.
Having reflected thus, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke these verses:
"Just as clouds in the sky, Driven by the wind,"
What is joined together disperses in an instant; birth and death are likewise so.
From time to time, like a multitude of flowers, one sees people undergo birth and death;
all things are subject to total extinction, just as their coming and going are also thus.
When such wholesome karma ripens, one then experiences celestial bliss;
yet once the favorable time has ended, that experience of pleasure is likewise lost.
The seasons are like a forest: when they first arise, they flourish most luxuriantly.
When the proper time has passed, all things fall away.
The gods are like the leaves of a tree, and the tree is like a place of enjoyment;
as one enjoys pleasure, there is a falling away, for there is no such thing as permanent bliss.
Just as summer rain does not remain suspended in the sky,
so too all pleasures do not pause for even a single moment.
Like a peacock bird, it utters its cry when the winds and clouds arise.
When the wind ceases, the sound is extinguished; the celestial music is likewise.
Just as dry wood placed within a fire is consumed, so too is the celestial music burned by the fire of time.
Having been born, one returns to extinction; this has already happened hundreds of thousands of times.
Deceived by craving, one remains without a sense of weariness.
Enshrouded by the net of delusion and craving, there is no one who escapes.
“They toy with the various devas, receiving the fruits of their unwholesome karma.

Having spoken this verse out of compassion for the devas, Śakra, Lord of Devas, mounted the great white elephant king Airāvaṇa; surrounded by the hosts of devas who played various musical instruments and produced exquisite sounds, he returned to the Sudharmā Hall.
Because they have achieved victory over the asuras, their hearts are filled with joy; thus, revered by the various devas, they proceed to the Sudharmā Hall.

The devas dwelling in Maṇicūḍa’s abode indulge in sensual desires without satiety, enjoying forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures while sporting in the groves and gardens. This continues until their beloved wholesome karma is completely exhausted; they then fall back from the heavens and, driven by the flow of their karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will be born into a great lineage and experience the foremost pleasures; being handsome and exquisite, one will be born in a central land where the True Dharma is practiced. Possessing great wealth and abundant resources, with a full complement of descendants, one will enjoy a long life and harmonious kinship. All worldly requisites will be fully provided, and one will be loved and respected by all people, becoming either a great king or a high minister.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The twenty-eight grounds of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are called the Realm of Multitudes (*Saṃbhūta*).
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that heaven?
He knows and sees this through hearing:

There are sentient beings who practice wholesome karma, rectifying their body, speech, and mind; they are upright and honest, without guile, and do not afflict other beings. They constantly act with benevolent intent, and their minds are straightforward. They distance themselves from evil associates, draw near to virtuous friends, and do not associate with evil companions. They do not converse with them, nor dwell with them, nor travel with them; they always avoid wicked people and do not even draw near to those who are friends of the wicked.

One associates with the virtuous and good, hears the true Dharma, and having heard it, reflects upon it so that the mind enters into the Dharma—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. If there is a wholesome dharma, one then adopts it; knowing an unwholesome dharma, one then abandons it.

Observing with right mindfulness, he subdues his mind; free from greed and desire, he maintains the seven types of precepts, not transgressing even in the slightest detail, and always harboring great fear regarding even minor offenses.
All their wholesome deeds are like refined pure gold, stainless and immaculate.
Such persons neither kill nor steal; they practice giving and cultivate merit, and upon seeing those being harmed, they rescue them and cause them to escape.
How does one rescue those beings who are being executed?

Suppose there is a man who has violated another’s wife and has been seized by the authorities; with the drum of execution beaten, he is led out through the southern gate, about to have his life cut short. Having no savior, no protector, and nothing to hope for, he is emaciated by grief and affliction as he approaches the cemetery.
As they were about to reach the place of execution, such a virtuous person ransomed them, enabling their release.
Furthermore, he practiced giving and cultivated various meritorious deeds.
How does such a virtuous person cultivate meritorious karma?
If a monastic dwelling is in a wilderness without water, causing suffering through thirst and exhaustion, such virtuous persons may construct wells or create ponds for them.
If there is already a pond or well that has collapsed, or if it contains many minute insects, they shall repair it for the sake of the Saṃgha, transferring those minute insects to other water.
In this way, one does not kill even the most minute beings.
If there are water insects caught in a water-strainer, one returns them to the water.
This is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing? It is not taking another’s grass or leaves with a thieving mind;

nor, in the midst of wildernesses, intentionally taking various fruits or vegetables from deserted villages or settlements, even if one suspects they are guarded by others—this is called non-stealing.
This person, having practiced all wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, is reborn in the realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, among the assembly of the Right Gate.
There they are born with a seat made of pure gold; alternatively, their seat may be made of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musāragalva, or ruby.
Upon a seat adorned with such precious jewels—blue indranīla gems, great blue king-gems, and pearls—they are born.
Having been born as devas, they reflect to themselves:
"By what karma have I come to be born here?"
He then reflected and knew for himself:
"In a previous life, I performed this wholesome deed by making offerings to the Sangha.
Such wholesome karma is like parents; it is a cooling treasure that brings birth in the heavens, where one will certainly experience bliss."
Having formed this thought, the deva-son immediately perceived for himself the retribution of karma.
Having seen that retribution, he praised wholesome karma and censured unwholesome karma.
Having recollected his former births, he then recollected the ground of human karma—the ground of immeasurable wholesome karma, which is like a father and like a mother.
At that time, the devaputra, having recollected his former births, spoke these verses:
"By means of merit one obtains a human body; Having obtained it, one must not be negligent."
By performing various wholesome deeds, one attains birth in the heavens because of this.
Human existence is extremely difficult to obtain; having obtained it, if one acts with heedlessness and is deluded by such negligence, at the end of life one falls into hell.
By performing three kinds of wholesome deeds, practicing the sevenfold precepts,
and slaying the three enemies, one receives the body of a deva.
If a person subdues the afflictions but has not yet severed the heart of craving, [they will likewise attain such a state].
Through the causal conditions of loving-kindness, such a person is born among the devas.
Having destroyed the den of great suffering— namely, envy—
and having practiced various kinds of giving, this person is born among the devas.
Regarding others as one’s own self, Compassionately protecting all sentient beings,
With a mind of loving-kindness always subdued— Such a person is born among the gods.
Viewing theft as fire, One practices giving to all.
By cultivating one's own mind, one is born among the gods.
Regarding the wives of others as one’s mother and constantly contemplating the True Reality, one cannot be defiled by the mire of desire; such a person is born among the gods.
Fire arises from one's own mind, produced by the friction-stick of the tongue;
if one abandons this false speech, one will be born in a happy realm.
Harsh words shatter the heart of loving-kindness; the wise are able to relinquish them.
One who always delights in speaking gentle words will be reborn in the heavens.
Viewing frivolous speech as a sword and always remaining far removed from it,
one who constantly practices right speech will be born in the good realms.
If there is a person who practices virtue, who does not engage in double-tongued speech,
who speaks truthfully and knows the proper time, such a person will be born among the devas.
If a person guards these seven kinds of precepts of body and speech, [they shall attain this state].
"One who truly understands the precepts will be reborn among the gods.
Having finished this reflection, the newly born deva spoke this verse and then surveyed his place of birth.
Having recollected his place of birth and become attached to the realm of desire due to his former habits, he spoke these verses.

At that time, the majesty and splendor of the newly born deva-puṃsaka were all gathered together; when the celestial maidens saw him, they rushed swiftly toward the deva, just as a swarm of bees rushes toward a lotus flower, and so it was with the host of celestial maidens rushing toward the deva.
In their hands they held various musical instruments—lutes, harps, and *konghou*—and produced a multitude of wondrous sounds.
These goddesses were adorned with flower garlands; they scattered powdered incense and held bouquets of flowers in their hands.
Furthermore, there were celestial maidens who scattered flowers as an offering to the newly born deva-son.
In this manner, these celestial maidens made various offerings to the deva-son.

Hundreds or thousands of superior celestial maidens, beyond all comparison, seeing this deva-son newly born in heaven, felt love and delight in their hearts; moreover, seeing that the signs of death had already appeared in the deva-son they had previously served, they abandoned their former lord and rushed toward the newly born deva-son of merit.
Just as a thirsty cow abandons a dried-up pond and runs toward clear water, so too do these celestial maidens abandon their original duties and hasten to approach the newly born deva-son.

"At that time, when the newly born deva-son hears the exquisite sounds produced by the ornaments of the goddesses, desire immediately arises; how much more so when he beholds their forms and hears their voices."

At that time, the devaputra beheld the celestial maidens and heard the sounds of music; as he paid them respectful homage and offerings, a heart of attachment and delight arose within him, such that he completely forgot his former birth, as if separated from it by hundreds of thousands of births and deaths.
Why is this? Because they have been born into a realm of negligence within the heavens, and their nature is such.
At that time, because the newly born deva-son does not skillfully contemplate the various emotional displays of the desire-dharmas employed by the celestial maidens, his lustful mind increases.
At that time, the celestial maidens spoke various impure words associated with lustful thoughts; thus they experienced the pleasures of negligence, with the devas and goddesses pursuing one another.

Surrounded by celestial maidens and possessing every kind of sensual desire, he experienced such bliss as he had never attained before. Having now obtained it, his heart was filled with joy; led by his desires, he followed the celestial maidens and could not remain self-possessed.

At that time, the celestial maidens attended upon the deva-son, singing, dancing, laughing, and chanting various melodies, engaging in vulgar and flirtatious conversation to bewilder his mind; wherever those celestial maidens went, he constantly followed behind them.
Bound by the net of desire like a bird caught in a snare, so too is this deva bound by sensual craving; wherever he goes, the [craving] follows him.
Such a place was adorned with the seven treasures, never seen before, and upon seeing it, they felt great love and joy.
Having seen this ground, they experienced immeasurable pleasure, adorned within that place by countless celestial garments and celestial garlands.
He then proceeded to the Forest of Crossing the Wilderness (*Āṭavī*), where celestial music was performed; together with this deva-son, he went to that forest of the wilderness.

There he saw all the various birds within the grove, adorned with diverse appearances, their voices exquisite as they uttered a variety of sounds, as they frolicked and enjoyed themselves among the flocks of birds.
The various birds likewise follow one another, male and female; if they go into the flowers to drink *madhu* wine, the male bird follows them, and it is the same with all the flowers.
If a bird soars through the sky, the male and female follow one another in the same manner.
Wherever it goes, if it eats delicious fruit, the other bird follows it; if it sports again within a lotus pond, it is likewise.
Upon the mountain peaks, two birds roam as a pair; likewise, these celestial birds are also bound by the net of craving and led to another place, and the same is true for the various kinds of bees.

Herds of deer, both bucks and does, roam and play together, yet they too are bound by the snares of desire for the does, just as the celestial son is infatuated with the beauty of the heavenly maidens.
It is like the summer rains that fill a pond until it overflows; likewise, these sons of gods are filled with the love and desire for the heavenly maidens, and are thus bound by craving and lust.
Although it is explained at length, it is extremely difficult to understand.
"Having thus observed this matter, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
'Such a web of female desire binds one with very firm fetters.'"
They cause all sentient beings to revolve within the prison of existence.
While physical bonds may still be untied, mental bonds cannot be released;
since the mind is bound by desire, one constantly undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction.
A net may still be cut, but the net of desire cannot be burned;
wherever one wanders, one will not escape the three evil realms.
A net merely binds the body, but the net of craving is vast and wide.
Though it is not a material phenomenon, it can bind all people.
A snare or net that binds sentient beings can still be seen with the naked eye;
yet such a mind bound by craving, though sought, cannot be seen.
Initial passion gives rise to attachment; when the mind is attached, it is extremely difficult to untie.
Bound by craving, human beings cannot escape birth and death.
The great snare of feminine beauty binds the six sense faculties of sentient beings.
A snare binds only a single body, and it may bind or it may not;
yet the shackles, fetters, and manacles described by the Sage are not considered firm.
It is the mind of the deluded person, stained by craving, that is bound with the most secure of bonds.
"Thus did the bhikṣu disparage sensual desire.
At that time, the devaputra was bound by all the nets of craving for the sake of the celestial maiden."
Upon arriving at the grove, he beheld various kinds of forests, so exceedingly delightful that they were beyond comparison.
At that time, the deva-son wandered among the flower ponds; the pond was named the White Goose Pond, and together with the celestial maidens, he came to its edge.
The devas and devīs sport and enjoy themselves, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses, as various musical instruments produce manifold exquisite sounds.
Furthermore, the Saṃbhavāgra devas go into the midst of the Golden Mountain to amuse one another, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
Having experienced such pleasure, he thinks to himself:
"I shall now go with the entire host of devas to the Sudharmā Hall to sport and enjoy themselves.

Having formed this thought, he goes with the host of devas to the Sudharmā Hall—some traveling through the air, some riding on swans, some on peacocks, and some on palaces—in these various ways they proceed to the Sudharmā Hall and behold Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

With various kinds of musical instruments and the singing of many wondrous sounds, they proceeded to the Hall of the Excellent Dharma. At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra, hearing the sounds of the music, addressed the sons of the gods:
"O Great Sages!..."
"From where do such musical sounds come? Whose music is this?
Which assembly of devas from which realm has arrived here?
When the sons of the gods heard these words, they all went out to observe.
Having seen the celestial hosts, he returned to the Sudharmā Hall and addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King, you should know!
The gods of the Saṃtuṣita realm have now arrived here to inquire after the Heavenly King."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the sons of the gods:

"You should now give rise to supreme joy; play upon all your musical instruments and perform various melodies to go out and welcome the sons of the gods who have come from the realm of the Many Divisions, so that you may engage in various sports and enjoy yourselves together."

At that time, having heard the command of Śakra, the sons of the gods immediately obeyed his instruction; they held various musical instruments such as lutes, harps, and *konghou* in their hands, adorned their bodies with various celestial garlands, and emitted various kinds of radiance from their bodies. Their bodily light was pure white and dazzlingly brilliant, illuminating everything as they went out to welcome the sons of the gods who had come from the assembly hall.

The two assemblies, seeing one another, harmonized and sported together, performing various supernatural feats and playing all kinds of musical instruments while singing many wondrous melodies as they proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall.
At that time, Śakra-devendra, the Lord of Devas, was seated upon a precious hall supported by hundreds of thousands of pillars.

That lion throne is named Victorious Attainment; when the Heavenly King sits upon it, he experiences peace, security, and joy, his majestic virtue blazing with radiant flames. Surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, he enjoys the fruits of his virtuous karma; his majesty and excellence surpass the combined radiance of a hundred suns shining together.
Though dwelling in the celestial palace, he remains free from negligence.

When the assembly of devas beheld the Heavenly King in this manner, they all rejoiced with a joy ten times greater than before. They immediately prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Heavenly King Śakra Devānām Indra, engaging in song, dance, and play, and praising the Heavenly King with these verses:
"Lord of Devas, Kauśika, You constantly protect the world."
The practice of Dharma is ever tranquil; its sphere cannot be destroyed.
One should discipline the world through the Dharma, not by means of what is contrary to the Dharma.
Those who follow the Dharma enjoy constant peace and happiness; those who violate the Dharma suffer affliction.
Practicing the Dharma brings peace and happiness; cultivating wisdom is likewise so.
By not encroaching on others and by refraining from false speech, one constantly experiences peace and happiness.
Whether it be worldly merit or supramundane merit, [it all arises from this].
All these merits are fully possessed by the Heavenly King.
He provides refuge for those who are afraid and shows the good path to those who suffer.
The Heavenly King sustains the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
The Heavenly King is most preeminent; Free from all unwholesome dharmas, he has washed away the stains of the three evil realms.
Having received the dharma of the Three Refuges, he knows the three karmas as they truly are, And practices the supreme path to the three types of enlightenment.
"Though born in a realm of heedlessness, He does not delight in heedlessness;
The Heavenly King sustains the world, And through the practice of Dharma, he remains free from enmity.

At that time, while the sons of the gods from the various regions were praising the Heavenly King with words of supreme wisdom and the like, Śakra Devendra surveyed the assembly of gods, comforted them with kind words, and addressed them, saying:
"O sons of the gods!
Do not act with negligence.
For those who are negligent, there is no benefit."
When the sons of the gods had finished praising Śakra, they ascended into the air with him and proceeded toward the realm of the Many-Portions (Vaijayanta).
With Śakra at their head, the gods followed him as they went to the realm of the Many-Portions.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:

"These sons of the gods are negligent in their conduct and do not understand the suffering of decline. I shall manifest a transformation of the signs of falling away and passing away, so as to cause them to give rise to weary detachment."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for the sake of those devaputras who were indulging in play and negligence.

As the devaputras were sporting in the gardens, groves, mountain peaks, and flower ponds, each of them saw all their excellent ornaments and furnishings fall into ruin; all their instruments of pleasure likewise perished. Terrified and afflicted by suffering, their bodies were bound; they wept in dread as smoke and flames rose up together, encircling their bodies.
Seized by the messengers of King Yama, they are consumed by hunger and thirst and undergo great terror; flames come to burn their bodies as if burning a forest.

The messengers of King Yama are hideous and fearsome, with various evil complexions; in their hands they hold swords, staves, bows, blades, spears, and lances, and they grasp black ropes, red clubs, nets, and snares. Some ascend upward while others descend below.
At that time, the messengers dispatched by King Yama pervaded Mount Sumeru.

Then the sons of the gods saw the messengers of Yama binding the sons of the gods from the heavens, inflicting upon them bitter torments, reviling and beating them, while flames of fire erupted from their entire bodies, blazing with fierce intensity.
At that time, the messengers of Yama, grasping swords and halberds, their eyes blazing with great rage, cried out to one another: "O messengers of Yama!
Bind this negligent deva-son quickly! I shall execute him and cast him into hell, so that he may never again indulge in negligence."
Thus, with a great cry, he ascended into the void and climbed Mount Sumeru, causing all the lands to be utterly destroyed.

Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of Yama’s messengers, the officials who await the end of life, and hideous hell-wardens completely devastated the various lands and the sides of the mountains; they filled the void, moving up and down to torment the sons of gods, saying to them:
"Where now are the five sensual pleasures and the various kinds of music that you enjoyed?"
"You have now been led by the messengers of Yama to the hells to undergo great suffering.
If those devaputras were about to fall into hell, they would see the fires of hell coming to burn their bodies.
If there are devaputras who possess wholesome karma, they see only the hells and do not see themselves being burned by fire.
At that time, the devaputras see for themselves their intermediate state (antarābhava) bound by great fetters.
At that time, the jailer, the King Yama, spoke these verses for the sake of this deva-son:
"You cherished sensual pleasures, Yet you did not perform wholesome deeds;
Therefore, you have obtained bitter fruits, Which have now reached full maturity."
If you delight in heedlessness and act contrary to the Dharma,
then at the time of death, your heart will give rise to the fever of regret.
This fever of regret is like the burning of fire, and it is also like the stroke of a sword or a spear.
Arising from the five faculties, they in turn consume and destroy themselves.
Taking suffering to be pleasure, regarding the enemy of craving as a friend—
observing heedlessness in this way, one should therefore abandon it.
Through the union of heedlessness and craving, one is bound by desire;
these three great enemies are capable of destroying supreme bliss.
Arrogance, association with evil friends, indolence, and a greedy mind—these are the adversaries.
To be far removed from the observance of precepts is the cause and condition for hell.
The touch of keeping the precepts is cool; its retribution is exceedingly cool.
The fool does not practice them, and at the end of life, they give rise to the fever of regret.
Seeing the wives and concubines of others, one gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment;
drinking alcohol and committing robbery—because of these, one falls into hell.
Speaking evil words, befriending wicked companions, holding false views, and lacking right faith.
Their minds are mostly restless and agitated; by this dharma, they lose their human form.
With greedy hearts and frivolous speech, speaking falsely and lacking sincerity, they shall find not even the slightest peace or happiness, neither in this life nor in the next.
Staying far from virtuous friends, Associating with evil associates,
Fundamentally lacking benefit, Not believing in the retribution of karma.
Failing to recognize the retribution of karma, They hold that suffering and pleasure do not belong to sentient beings.
Such a person is deluded regarding cause and effect, and at the moment of death, they give rise to the fever of regret.
If a person constantly speaks falsehoods and, relying on their own intelligence, gives rise to arrogance,
they will later encounter great decline and distress, only then realizing the karmic fruit of their actions.
"If one wanders through the world, Fully experiencing all manner of suffering and affliction, It is entirely due to the power of ignorance; Thus has the Great Sage spoken.
At that time, Śakradevendra manifested himself as such a messenger of Yama to preach the Dharma for the *antarābhava* beings among the devas, subduing and rebuking them.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again manifested transformations for the assembly of devas.

To those sons of the gods who, due to karma from previous lives, were destined to fall among the animals, he displayed immeasurable varieties of karmic signs, like a seal impressing its mark upon clay.
The beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) mutually harm and devour one another, giving rise to great terror; this causes all the devaputras to see them clearly.
If the devaputras have no karma for rebirth as animals, they merely see the animals harming and devouring one another, but do not see themselves taking on animal forms.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further manifested for the sake of the heedless sons of the gods the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

He showed them those sons of the gods who were destined to be born as hungry ghosts (*preta*): their bodies scorched by hunger and thirst, with long hair covering their faces and forms that were hideous and loathsome.
These devaputras saw in the sky crows and various other birds coming to peck at their eyes, ears, noses, and tongues.
At that time, the host of devas, seeing such evil omens manifested before them, were struck with great terror.
When the other devas saw this, they said to Śakra: "King Śakra!
For what reason do you abandon the sons of the gods and dwell here alone?"
All these sons of the gods have been bound; whether by asuras or other wicked men, they are being led away across all the grounds of Mount Sumeru.
"I have also fought with the asuras in the past, yet I have never beheld such evil omens.
Furthermore, neither the asuras nor their hosts have ever come together to this celestial realm; how then has the True Dharma been lost in the world?"
Are you unfilial toward your parents?
Do you fail to revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
Do you fail to honor the elders and seniors?
"O Heavenly King!
Do the people of this world today no longer make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
Are they ignorant of cause and effect, and ignorant of the True Truth?"
"Just as the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings constantly preach this Dharma, why is it not practiced now in Jambudvīpa?
Now the hosts of devas are all being tormented and disturbed.
O Heavenly King!"
Why do you not arm yourself with weapons, mount the great elephant king Eṇa, don your armor and mail, beat the great war drum, and prepare for battle?
There were hosts of devas whose karma was similar to that of the Lord of Devas; they spoke thus to Śakra, the King of Devas.

Furthermore, there were other devas who, beholding this rare and unprecedented event, felt a sense of weary detachment and profound terror; their faculties trembled as they took refuge in Śakra, speaking these words:
"We pray only that the Heavenly King will protect and deliver us."
The lands where these hosts of devas dwell have all been plundered by the asuras.
Never before have we seen such terrifying bodies of asuras inspire such dread.
All the devaputras addressed Śakra in this manner.
Furthermore, there were other devaputras who, having seen these manifestations, rushed swiftly toward the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) to take up various weapons and implements for battle.
Furthermore, there are devaputras who go to the Citraśālā forest and take up various weapons to strike or seize the messengers of Yama, yet they are unable to inflict harm upon them.
It is like the reflections seen in a mirror; they cannot be grasped, nor can they be struck or harmed.
In this manner, the Heavenly King displayed such transformations.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra further manifested to the devaputras—transformed asuras who surpassed Rāhu and the valiant asuras—who were bound, beaten, hacked, pierced, and reviled; they wept and were distressed, just as the transformed devaputras suffered affliction.
At that time, the sons of the gods saw the asuras undergoing intense suffering a hundred thousand million times greater than their own.
Seeing the asuras endure such unprecedented agony and distress, the sons of the gods were struck with great terror.
He then went to the Deva King Śakra and said to him:

"I do not know what kind of man it is who possesses such great power that he is able to bind all the asura kings—the asura king Rāhu and the asura king Vikrānta—and lash them with whips, beat them with clubs, pierce them, and revile them?"
"How is it that such an unprecedented event has occurred, causing the body hairs of all these devaputras to stand on end?
We pray only that the Heavenly King will explain this to us; we too are now struck with fear and have fallen into this distress."
"O Heavenly King! Do you know what this is?
The hosts of devas and asuras have all been defeated; the entire world fears it will be utterly destroyed."
"O Heavenly King, if you know [this], I pray that you will explain it to me.
O Śakra, Heavenly King, if you do not know, then if you do not know, I pray that you will contemplate it well.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 32.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Three.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: Contemplation of the Heavens, Part Nine: The Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the sons of gods, saying:
"These sons of gods, through their heedless conduct, do not understand things as they truly are, and thus they do not practice the True Dharma."
For the sake of such heedless devaputras, wishing to cause them to abandon arrogance and negligence, I have manifested such a transformation.
Now that these devaputras have conceived a sense of weary detachment and their minds are subdued, they will surely be able to believe and accept the Dharma I now preach.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing that the minds of the sons of the gods had been subdued, addressed the assembly of devas:
"Listen attentively; I shall speak for your sake."

Such a man possesses supreme great power; though his physical appearance is hideous, he can destroy others and is difficult to oppose as an adversary. He cannot be subdued by the power of incantations or spells, and none among the hosts of devas can do anything against him.
Furthermore, even superior devas who surpass you are unable to obstruct him, let alone you, whose physical strength has diminished and who lack sovereign power.

This man is called the messenger of Yama and the messenger of the time of death; he binds all sentient beings with the fetters of afflictions and karma, binds them and departs, leading them to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
There are eight dharmas that encompass all sentient beings in saṃsāra. What are these eight?
First, all who are born must return to death.
Second, there is no one who remains healthy without falling ill or being afflicted by distress;
third, all youth and vigor inevitably turn into decay and old age;
fourth, even those endowed with abundant wealth shall encounter poverty.

Fifth, all things arise from karma; there are various worlds obtained through karma, which accord with karma. According to the actions one performs—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one receives the karmic retribution accordingly.
Sixth, all that is cherished and loved must inevitably be parted from; nothing is permanent.

Seventh, the karma one has created oneself will certainly result in retribution for oneself; it is not the case that another creates karma while I receive its fruit, nor that I create karma while another receives its retribution. All phenomena are definitively thus.
Eighth, worldly negligence brings no peace and security, and one will inevitably experience bitter fruits.
These are called the eight dharmas.
Such dharmas circulate through birth and death within the world, arising from causes and conditions.
Such a dharma cannot be resisted by force; it cannot be subdued by the power of incantations.
Likewise, the messengers of Yama cannot be opposed by force, nor can they be warded off by the power of incantations.
Such is the nature of birth and death; all phenomena are thus. If a person commits evil, they will be subjected to immeasurable suffering and agonizing torment.

Devas, asuras, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, and others—all such messengers of Yama—are capable of inflicting harm, causing these sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Then the assembly of devas said to Śakra:
"O Heavenly King!
We have no power over such messengers of Yama."
"I only pray that the Heavenly King, by means of your skillful power, will enable me to escape the messengers of Yama; I shall then follow the instructions of the Heavenly King.
At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the gods, saying:
"There is a great skillful means; if one can practice it, one will not be harmed by the messengers of Yama."
What skillful means can bring about mastery?
It is said: by abandoning one dharma.
This "one dharma" refers to abandoning heedlessness.
Furthermore, one cultivates two dharmas, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, one abandons three faults, namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
One contemplates the Four Noble Truths:
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
One should know the five things to be well-guarded, namely the five sense objects.
Furthermore, there are six things to be guarded, namely the six sense faculties.
One knows the seven right knowledges, namely the seven factors of enlightenment; one practices the eightfold noble path, namely right view and so forth;

one knows the nine abodes of sentient beings; one knows that the ten karmas yield their fruits; one knows the eleven cultivations; one knows the twelve sense bases; one knows the thirteen applications of mindfulness and the practice of continuous mindfulness; one knows the fourteen dhyānas and the well-cultivated mind; one knows the fifteen dharmas; one knows the sixteen aspects of ānāpāna; one knows the seventeen methods of the continuous cycle of rebirth through the intermediate state (antarābhava); one knows the eighteen elements; and one knows the nineteen intermediate states.
One knows that among the beings dwelling in the desire realm there are twenty abodes, and one knows their karmic actions.
One who knows thus attains mastery.
Whether they be devas or humans, those who can know in this way are able to sever the three evil paths, give rise to all wholesome dharmas, and encompass all wholesome dharmas.
Whether gods or humans, those who can sever the path to evil realms will not be terrified by the messengers of Yama upon death.
Therefore, one should abandon heedless conduct; for heedlessness can sever all wholesome dharmas, just like an enemy.

A person who is negligent attains neither worldly happiness nor supramundane happiness. Negligence shrouds a person just as it does an animal; though not asleep, they are as if sleeping. They do not know what should be done and what should not be done, merit and non-merit, friends and non-friends, fields of merit and non-fields of merit, or what should be spoken and what should not be spoken. They do not know benefit or harm, virtue or fault; this is called the first evil.
All lack of benefit is the root of decline and affliction.
One should sever heedlessness; since all the devas practice heedlessness, how could they not be bound by the messengers of Yama?
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Śakra Devendra, spoke in verse:
"If gods or humans are heedless and take pleasure in practicing what is unrighteous,
when the time of their death arrives, they will see the messengers of Yama."
Heedlessness is like a poisonous harm, which the wise abandon;
when one approaches the end of life, there will be no manifold sufferings.
Through heedlessness one suffers at death, while heedfulness is the supreme bliss.
"If you wish to seek happiness, you should always remain free from negligence.
'O sons of the gods!
To sever one dharma means to sever negligence, which has six aspects.'"
What are the six? Having seen forms with the eye, one gives rise to a heedless mind and does not see according to reality.
One may see beautiful forms or ugly forms—whether yellow or black, red or white, long or short, square or round.
Thus, not knowing the world as it truly is, because of negligence, they likewise do not know the supramundane Dharma.

With a negligent mind, although they see forms, they do not see them as they truly are; they are unable to correctly contemplate the form of their own bodies and do not delight in contemplating the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Among all forms, they perceive the unreal as real; because their minds are negligent, they are unable to contemplate worldly phenomena or supramundane phenomena.
Having heard sounds with their ears, they do not understand their meaning—whether it be song or speech, whether meaningful or meaningless—they fail to comprehend such worldly meanings.

Whether it be a sūtra, a gāthā, a geya, a vyākaraṇa, an udāna, a nidāna, a vaipulya, an itivṛttaka, an jātaka, a vaibhāṣika, or an abhūtadharma—having heard such teachings as these, one does not understand their meaning.
Because of negligence, at the time of death, one is bound and led away by the messengers of Yama.
Furthermore, there is negligence:

having smelled various fragrances, the nose immediately craves their scent; one does not recognize that these are the scents of flowers and fruits, nor does one realize that such worldly fragrances were previously offered as incense in acts of worship and charity.
Because of negligence, they do not discern various fragrances.
Furthermore, because of negligence, they do not discern various tastes:
whether a food is sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, bland, astringent, or slippery, they do not know their distinctions.
Because the mind is negligent, one does not know the flavors of such worldly things, nor does one know the flavor of the supramundane Dharma;
this is due to negligence.

Furthermore, through negligence, one does not perceive bodily contact, fails to perform physical actions, does not maintain one's dwelling, does not cultivate one's work, and does not perform various wholesome deeds; thus, this person’s dwelling and possessions are incomplete.

They do not know what should not be done in the mundane world, nor do they know what should not be done in the supramundane; they do not draw near to the elders, nor do they show them respect, pay homage, or inquire after their well-being.
"Because of negligence. 'O sons of the gods!
Furthermore, because of negligence, they do not know the mental phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.'"

Unaware that at the time of death, one will be struck by the staff of death, undergo great suffering and affliction, and be led away at will by the messengers of Yama, a son of heaven should therefore abandon one thing: namely, heedlessness.
The two dharmas to be cultivated are: first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā.
These two dharmas demonstrate the path to nirvāṇa.
Śamatha is that which can sever both arisen and unarisen phenomena and bring about tranquility.
Vipassanā is so named because it involves seeing the two types of bodies: the mind and phenomena.
These two dharmas serve as virtuous companions, capable of severing the three faults:
for those attached to desire, they teach the contemplation of impurity;
for those who harbor ill will, they teach the contemplation of loving-kindness.
If there are those who are deluded, they should be taught with wisdom.
In this way, these three dharmas counteract three [other] dharmas, causing them no longer to give rise to negligence.
When the time of death arrives, they will no longer fear the messengers of Yama.
What are the Four Noble Truths?
The Four Noble Truths are the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin [of suffering], the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Regarding the truth of suffering, there are two kinds of suffering:
The first is physical suffering;
the second is mental suffering.
The Truth of Origination refers to the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), and the sense bases (āyatanas).
The truth of cessation is what is called quiescent extinction.
The truth of the path refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
These are known as the Four Noble Truths.
To well-guard the five objects of the senses refers to form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
What are the six guards?
They are the six sense faculties—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which one well-protects within their respective spheres of objects.
What are the seven dharmas?

They are the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga). Just as there are limbs of a person, parts of a city, or members of a community, these are called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
What are the seven?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
What are the characteristics of the awakening factor of mindfulness?

It is said that mindfulness of the faults and evils of conditioned phenomena, mindfulness of the true realities, and mindfulness of the dharma of nirvana’s tranquility—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What are the characteristics of the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? It is the discernment by means of wisdom. How does it discern?
One discriminates this dharma by means of the dharma of the suchness-characteristic, contemplates its meaning, and brings that meaning to mind, never departing from it moment to moment.
Having thus reflected, one further cultivates diligence; this is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).
Having reflected upon this Dharma, a longing arises; reflecting upon such meaning, one gives rise to joy—this is called the factor of awakening of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Furthermore, having contemplated this meaning with the mind, one truly subdues both bodily and mental phenomena so that they become supple, light, and blissful, and practice without distraction—this is called the factor of awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Furthermore, having reflected upon this meaning with the mind, one takes the settled mind as an object to collect the mind; this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Then, relinquishing the intention toward concentration as well as other thoughts, this is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

In this manner, whether it be the fruits, the wisdom, or the abandonment of afflictions, all are distinct; their fruits likewise differ, becoming progressively more excellent as they ascend. Arising from a single object-condition, their functions are each different.
"Thus it is, O devaputras!
These are called the seven factors of enlightenment; whoever possesses mindfulness is able to abandon negligence. 'O devaputras!'"
How is it that the Eightfold Noble Path can bring about freedom from negligence, fear of the future, and the pursuit of peace and happiness, as well as the path to Nirvana?

It consists of: right view regarding the noble truths as they truly are; right intention regarding the noble truths; right speech regarding the noble truths; right action regarding the noble truths; right livelihood regarding the noble truths; right effort regarding the noble truths; right mindfulness regarding the noble truths; and right concentration regarding the noble truths.
What is right view? To see things in accordance with reality as they truly are—this is called right view.
What is right intention?

To see the specific characteristics and the universal characteristics of phenomena as they truly are, and to maintain the seeds of mental attention toward such phenomena—this is called right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
What is right speech (*samyag-vāc*)?
Reflecting upon the four types of vocal karma, one abandons the four faults of speech and maintains the prohibitive precepts; this is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
What is right action (*samyak-karmānta*)?
One abandons the three types of unwholesome bodily karma and maintains the prohibitive precepts; this is called right action.
What is right livelihood?
Not abandoning the precepts even at the cost of one's life—this is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?
Regarding such a meaning, when the mind recollects it and arouses diligence, this is called right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).
What is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)?
When one recollects and contemplates such dharmas and meanings, without forgetting or losing them, this is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?

Regarding the meaning of such dharmas, to recollect with a mind of true mindfulness, to maintain single-minded recollection, and to resolve upon a single characteristic—this is called right concentration.
This is called the Noble Eightfold Path; if one can keep it in mind, one will not fear the messengers of King Yama.
Furthermore, one contemplates the nine abodes of sentient beings.
“‘O sons of the gods!
Furthermore, observe the ten kinds of dharmas of the great earth. What are these ten?’”
First is sensation;
second is perception;
third is volition.
Fourth is contact;
fifth is attention;
sixth is desire.
Seventh is liberation;
eighth is mindfulness;
ninth is samādhi.
Tenth is wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are called the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), which arise together with the mind, each having its own distinct characteristic.
You should know this!
What are their characteristics?
Such phenomena arise from a single condition, just like sunlight.
Such phenomena arise together with the mind, possessing characteristics that correspond to increase and decrease.
What is called "perception" (saṃjñā)?
It is called perception because it knows the correspondence of distinctions.
What is called "volition" (cetanā)?
The mind takes three kinds as its objects: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
There are further three kinds, namely body, speech, and mind.
It is that upon which volition depends, yet it has no perceptible form.
What is called contact?
Contact arises from the conjunction of three factors, giving rise to the three kinds of sensation; therefore, it is named contact.
O Devaputra, you should know this!
How do the three types of contact give rise to the three kinds of feeling?
Namely: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is called "attention" (manasikāra)?
Because it grasps the dharmas, it is called attention (*manasikāra*).
What is meant by desire (*chanda*)?
Because it recollects what has been done, it is called desire.
What is liberation? It is so called because it is capable of discerning and understanding.
It is also termed faith, because it is capable of believing.
It is also called "power" because it is able to sustain.
What is meant by "mindfulness"?
When the mind does not become confused or distracted regarding the object of focus, this is called mindfulness.
What is called samādhi?
If the mind is focused on a single object, this is called samādhi.
What is called wisdom (prajñā)?
To discern and contemplate phenomena is called wisdom. "O Sons of Heaven!

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of great grounds of affliction; if there are those who accept and practice such dharmas, at the time of their death, they will be bound at will by the messengers of Yama."
What are the ten?
First is lack of faith;
second is indolence.
Third, lack of mindfulness;
fourth, a distracted mind; fifth, delusion.
Sixth, lack of skillful observation;
seventh, liberation through false views;
eighth, lack of self-discipline.
Ninth is ignorance;
tenth is negligence.

These are called the ten dharmas of the universal ground of affliction (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*), which defile the phenomena that arise in existence and serve as the causal conditions for being bound by the messengers of King Yama.
O sons of the gods!
As I have taught, what are the ten kinds of unwholesome universal mental states?
What is lack of faith?
Lack of faith in liberation.
