If one does not have faith in the dharma of liberation, it is called lack of faith.
What is indolence?
Because one abandons diligence, it is called indolence.
What is meant by "non-recollection"?
Because one forgets and loses the Dharma, it is called non-recollection.
What is a distracted mind?
Because the mind is not upright, it is called a distracted mind. What is delusion?
Because there is no mind of skillful means, it is called ignorance (*moha*).
What is meant by "unskillful observation"?
It refers to improper observation, contemplating what is not the Dharma, failing to practice the right path, and perceiving the impure as pure; therefore, it is called unskillful observation.
What is wrong view? To grasp at inverted dharmas, clinging to them firmly and refusing to relinquish them, is therefore called wrong view.
What is an unsubdued mind?
Because it is not tranquil, it is called "undisciplined.
What is ignorance? It is delusion regarding the three realms; therefore, it is called ignorance.
What is negligence? It is called negligence because one does not perform wholesome deeds.
These are known as the ten universal mental afflictions, which are utterly contemptible and evil.
“O sons of the gods!
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of dharmas that defile the ground. What are these ten?
First is anger;
second is resentment;
third is lack of remorse.
Fourth is stubbornness;
fifth is illusion;
sixth is flattery and crookedness.
Seventh is envy; eighth is stinginess;
ninth is arrogance.
Tenth is great pride (*māna*).
These are called the ten defiled mental states (*kliṣṭa-bhūmika-dharma*).
Why are they called "defiled mental states"?
Because it is encompassed by the great earth, it is called "defiled ground" (kliṣṭabhūmi).
What is meant by "hatred" (dveṣa)?
Because the mind is coarse and evil, it is called hatred.
What is called resentment (*upanāha*)?
When the mind is bound and fettered, it further develops into a knot of enmity; therefore, it is called resentment.
What is non-regret (*akaukṛtya*)?
One takes pleasure in committing various evils and feels joy after having committed them; therefore, it is called "unrepentance.
What is meant by "firmness"?
To perform various evil deeds and cling to them without relinquishing—this is called "firmness."
Why is it called an illusion?
Because it deceives sentient beings; because one is deluded by the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is called an illusion.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
What are the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?
They are as follows: internally there are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the internal bases.
Externally there are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; these are called the external bases.
There are two kinds of conceptualization:
first, that of characteristics;
second, that of the magnitude of the self-substance.
As for what is called "characteristic":

eye-consciousness arises due to the causal conditions of the four great elements; this is termed the "eye. One should know that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind likewise each have their own specific characteristics as they differentiate their respective objects.
How should one know its intrinsic nature?
That which is called "intrinsic nature" is termed "non-erroneous.
Visual consciousness arises by means of five causal conditions.
What are these five?
Because there is the eye, visible forms, light, space, and mindfulness, visual consciousness arises.
It is not so with the ear; the arising of auditory consciousness perceives both light and darkness, as it does not depend upon light.
The nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise.
Regarding consciousness and clarity, sometimes it is functional and sometimes it is not.
In what way is it functional?
What is meant by "not functioning"?
If the eye-consciousness sees a form and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) discerns it, this is called "functioning.
What is meant by "sometimes functioning and sometimes not functioning"?

When visual consciousness perceives forms, if there is no light, nothing is seen; yet what is known by the other sense faculties does not depend on light—this is called the element of consciousness (vijñāna-mahābhūta).
O sons of the gods!
Furthermore, there are four great elements that depend upon one another.
How do these four great elements mutually depend on each other, increasing or decreasing?
The eye increases the fire element;
The nose increases the earth element;
the body increases the wind element;
the tongue increases the water element.
The ear increases the element of space.
This dharma being predominant, the space-element within the ear enables the mind to apprehend sound.
Therefore, one should know that there is indeed increase and decrease.
Furthermore, one contemplates the sense bases (āyatana):
which are proximate conditions,
and which sense bases are remote conditions?
The three faculties of the nose, tongue, and body perceive their objects only upon contact.
That which is seen by the eye is neither near nor far.
That which is heard by the ear is not clearly perceived when distant, but can be known when near; it is even heard internally.
What is smelled by the nose is known when it is near, and it is also understood internally.
For instance, if there is a disease within the nose, one smells the odor oneself; likewise, if there is the sound of wind within the ears, one hears it all oneself.
Such consciousness is comprised of two types: visual consciousness and mental consciousness.
These encompass it entirely; for example, just as a single fire is given names according to what it burns—being called either a "wood-fire" or a "grass-fire."
All consciousnesses are likewise; they each differ according to the mental consciousness.
O Devaputra, you should know this!
Having understood these sense bases as they truly are, do not be negligent.

Those who practice heedfulness and are free from greed, hatred, and delusion—such virtuous people, at the time of their death, do not fear being bound by the messengers of King Yama; they do not see the terrifying and malevolent forms of the hell-wardens, nor do they encounter the evil realms of King Yama.

They shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but shall constantly experience peace and happiness until reaching nirvana, accomplishing immeasurable joy and bliss because they are free from negligence.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Contemplate the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; contemplate their basis, arising through causes and conditions.
Having contemplated them thus, one becomes free from negligence."
Contemplate the arising of eye-consciousness as being like an illusory phenomenon: empty and non-existent, neither solid nor real, a nature subject to disintegration.
Once eye-consciousness has ceased, ear-consciousness arises; it too is empty and non-existent, lacking solidity and subject to destruction.

Thus one contemplates the six internal bases and the six external bases as either arising or ceasing, characterized by conflict and attachment to flavor, subject to decay and impermanence, and produced from causes and conditions.
Knowing it as it truly is and having seen it thus, one does not crave form.
Even if one sees a pleasing form, no defiled attachment arises.
For one who is heedful, even the five desires of the devas do not give rise to craving, let alone human desires.
At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra spoke in verse:
"Deluded regarding the elements and sense-bases, One obstructs the path to Nirvāṇa;
Because of such negligence, One loses all wholesome dharmas."
If there are these three faults, they are the messengers of the great evil realms;
delusion is the foremost evil, for through heedlessness one wanders in saṃsāra.
For those who act with the heedlessness of ignorance, death is ever held in the palm of their hand.
If one delights in heedlessness, everything will be utterly destroyed.
If a person transcends one dharma, contemplates two dharmas,
and understands the characteristics of three bases, that person shall experience happiness.
If a deva’s merit is exhausted, destroyed by heedlessness, and they fall, deceived by delusion, no one can provide protection.
One dharma is always supreme: the practice of patience.
If one is endowed with patience and compassionately regards all sentient beings,
then at the time of death and fear, one shall obtain such great power.
Therefore, abandon negligence and practice all deeds with diligence.
If one can abandon ignorance and constantly guard wise understanding,
knowing clearly the difference between wisdom and ignorance, then negligence shall not destroy them.
If a person abandons negligence, they will certainly attain great benefit.
Thus, through heedfulness, one can benefit oneself;
bound by the net of negligence, one is liberated through diligent practice.
These characteristics of bondage and liberation—I shall now explain them in brief.
"O Son of Heaven, you already know this: if one acts with negligence, it is only at the time of death that one realizes its retribution.
Thus did Śakra, Lord of the Devas, extensively explain the characteristics of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) to subdue those sons of the gods who were negligent.

If there are sons of the gods who have previously planted roots of goodness and have practiced little heedlessness, upon hearing this Dharma, their minds will awaken of themselves and they will no longer be heedless; their faculties being matured, they will all be able to receive and practice it.

If there are sons of gods whose faculties are not yet mature, it is just like lancing a festering boil; once the boil has been lanced and the area washed and treated, no benefit whatsoever is gained—this is exactly the same case.
"Furthermore, Śakra, King of Devas, gradually increased [the teaching] from one up to twelve, sequentially explaining the dharma of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Having displayed miraculous powers and rare wonders before the great assembly of devas, he caused them to enter [the path] in succession, binding their minds in right mindfulness, awakening them to the characteristics of causes and conditions, causing them to abandon negligence, and bringing them benefit."
Seeing these transformations, his mind gave rise to weary detachment.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, through skillful means for their benefit, extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the assembly of devas:
"O sons of the gods!..."
What is meant by "deceit and crookedness"?
When the mind is not upright and is firmly attached to birth and death, it is called deceit and crookedness.
What is meant by "envy"?
To feel vexation and distress toward others is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
What is called stinginess (*mātsarya*)?
It is the arising of greedy attachment out of fear that one's own possessions will be exhausted; therefore, it is called stinginess.
These are called the defiled dharmas of the three realms; they exist through conceptual differentiation and are subsumed within the three realms.

Anger, resentment, stinginess, envy, and deceit are bound to the desire realm. The single dharma of guile pervades both the desire realm and the Brahma heavens. Arrogance and extreme arrogance pervade all three realms.
O sons of the gods!
These are called the ten types of unwholesome universal mental factors (akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma).
Furthermore, there are ten types of wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma).
What are the ten? They are:
non-greed, non-delusion, a sense of shame, a sense of dread, faith, self-mastery, heedfulness and diligence, relinquishment, and the absence of malice.
These are called the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). These ten dharmas each have distinct characteristics.
That which is non-attachment is the root of all wholesome dharmas, just like a pillar or a beam.
The wholesome root of non-delusion is likewise.
Shame (*hrī*) consists in maintaining one's own integrity;
remorse (*apatrāpya*) consists in feeling shame before others.
The faithful have a mind that is pure regarding all phenomena.
Those who are disciplined have their bodies and minds well-tamed, having departed from unwholesome dharmas and relying upon the dharma of coolness.
Heedfulness consists in diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas.
Equanimity consists in the mind remaining detached amidst the causes and conditions of both action and non-action.
Non-affliction consists in not harming sentient beings.
These are called the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas of the great ground.
If there is one who brings such dharmas to mind, at the time of death they will not fear the terror of dying, nor will they fear being bound by the messengers of Yama.
Why is this? Because they subsume wholesome dharmas.
These are as previously explained: the mental states and their concomitants, the universal wholesome mental factors, and the universal defiled mental factors.
To speak of their individual characteristics collectively, these are called the ten dharmas.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is meant by practicing the eleven dharmas?"

"If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates his own body, seeing his own body without attachment or delusion, and with a mind that does not cling firmly to it—this is called the first stage of cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

If there is a bhikṣu who, having previously experienced sensual desires, disparages them, does not relish them, does not cling to them, and does not dwell upon them, but instead gives rise to a mind of weary detachment—this is called the second cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
If there is a bhikṣu who is constantly heedful, who does not cling to sense objects, and who exhausts all fetters and latent tendencies, this is called practicing the conduct of heedfulness."
This is called the third cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
If there is a bhikṣu who recollects wholesome dharmas and practices wholesome dharmas."
“Such wholesome dharmas can produce a pleasant retribution; with pleasure as their cause and pleasure as their condition, such is the pleasant retribution.
I shall experience it and abandon unwholesome dharmas.”
"This is called the fourth cultivation.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods, one cultivates the arising of pleasant feelings."
What power does sensation have? How does it arise?
What are its causes and conditions? What is the nature of those causes and conditions?
How does it arise? Such arising as this—do not create obstacles for it.
Contemplate sensation as it truly is: it is neither firm nor substantial; it is empty and devoid of anything existing.
This is called the fifth cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates the understanding that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and that nothing exists independently, but arises through mutual causes and conditions rather than being produced by a single power; [this is the sixth cultivation]."
Practicing in this manner, and having practiced thus, the mind feels no attachment or delight; this is called the sixth cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
If a bhikṣu should think, "I have produced a wholesome thought;
I have produced wholesome causes and conditions," once this thought has arisen, it is destroyed by other thoughts.
"I am now focusing my attention on unwholesome thoughts of arising and ceasing, which destroy my wholesome thoughts and obstruct my wholesome dharmas.
To constantly maintain mindfulness of the object in this way is called the seventh cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates the eighth practice—the mark of phenomena, the mark of equality, and abiding in their own marks—then his understanding of phenomena will not be inverted, because the nature of all phenomena is inherently stainless."
In this way, the bhikṣu further observes himself:
"Since I have been born, I am certain to die.
Among conditioned phenomena, there are none that do not possess these three characteristics."
"Practicing in this manner, one realizes that all phenomena are entirely impermanent; this is called the eighth cultivation.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the ninth cultivation?
It consists of the three roots of affliction and their three types of antidotes.
These are: greed, hatred, and delusion.
For those with greedy desires, teach the contemplation of impurity;
for those with anger and hatred, teach them a mind of loving-kindness;
for those who are ignorant and deluded, teach them to contemplate causes and conditions.
This is called the antidote.
To cultivate contemplation in this manner, with the mind constantly mindful of it, is termed the ninth cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the tenth cultivation?
It is to cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha’s merits, which bring peace and happiness to the world; thus, this practice benefits oneself and is therefore named the tenth cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the eleventh cultivation?

It is hearing from others, in successive order, that all phenomena are impermanent and do not abide from moment to moment; that from the time of dwelling in the womb, there is arising and ceasing without abiding, just as it was when first in the womb, and so through childhood, youth, and even until old age."

When a bhikṣu or others have practiced in this way, having completed their cultivation, at the time of death they will not fear the messengers of King Yama; they will maintain self-mastery and will not see the loathsome or terrifying signs.
This is called the eleventh cultivation.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is meant by the thirteen applications of mindfulness that are well-cultivated for the sake of benefit and happiness, even unto nirvāṇa?
What are the thirteen? They are:

mindfulness of heedfulness; mindfulness of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and mindfulness of non-distraction. Having cultivated such mindfulness, whether one sees a beautiful form, an ugly form, or a woman, one contemplates the interior of the body as a dwelling place for pus, blood, and impurities, and as a locus of the impurities of feces and urine.
In this way, one maintains mindfulness so as not to allow the mind to become distracted.

If one enters cities or villages to beg for alms, one must not wander through places of sensory objects that are improper to frequent; for if one does not maintain mindfulness, one will become attached to sensual desires.
By these causes and conditions, one binds the mind so that it does not scatter; this is called the first binding of the mind through mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the second binding of the mind:
one contemplates and observes external objects such as lovely gardens, lotus ponds, and delightful rivers and springs for recreation. Having seen them, one forms this thought:
"Such a delightful place for play, through a mind of delusion, gives rise to attachment; it will inevitably decay and perish.
The leaves of the trees wither and turn yellow, losing their original appearance; they shed and fall until they resemble dead wood, and the shade becomes sparse."
"In this way, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, empty, and non-existent; how much more so the objects of craving!
Thus one should apply the mind with focused mindfulness. Having formed this thought, the mind will not be greedily attached to internal or external objects, and Māra will be unable to disturb it.
This is called the second application of single-minded attention.
"Furthermore, what is the third application of single-minded attention for the sake of benefit and happiness?
How does one apply the mind?"
With reference to what phenomena?
Whether it be food or sleep, or having previously seen beautiful forms, one does not engage in conceptualization or fixate the mind upon them, but reflects thus:
"Foolish worldlings are attached through their sense faculties and do not know contentment."
To maintain mindfulness in this way is called the third application of single-minded mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the fourth application of single-minded mindfulness is as follows:
wherever one receives offerings and benefits—whether robes, bedding, seats, or medicinal requisites—one’s mind does not feel joy; one neither delights nor takes pleasure in them."

Why is this? The benefit of making offerings results in a wound of gain that is deep: it cuts the skin and destroys the flesh; it destroys the flesh and severs the tendons; it severs the tendons and breaks the bones; it breaks the bones and injures the marrow.
The manner in which gain and offerings can destroy wholesome dharmas is likewise so.
This is called the fourth application of single-minded mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the fifth application of single-minded mindfulness is as follows:"
If he travels through cities, towns, villages, or camps, he does not dwell in those cities and towns.
If many people come to where he is, he does not engage them in much conversation nor take pleasure in speaking at length.
Why is this? If a person wanders through cities, towns, and villages, their mind becomes distracted and they are unable to benefit themselves.
Thus, to maintain single-minded focus and contemplate things as they truly are is called the fifth [practice]: single-minded focus.
"Furthermore, the sixth single-minded application of mindfulness is as follows:

seeing such faults [in worldly life], one dwells among burial mounds, beneath trees, at the edge of grassy thickets, by mountain streams, or in empty dwellings; free from attachment and devoid of affection, not associating with others, one increases wholesome qualities, attains personal benefit, and keeps far away from the crowds."
This is called the sixth application of one-pointed mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the seventh application of one-pointed mindfulness is:
upon hearing the description of celestial retribution, the mind feels no attachment or delight, but instead gives rise to weary detachment."
He delights in hearing the discourse on the bitter fruits of the hells, his mind never wearying of it, and he reflects thus:
"When a deva declines and passes away, he is led away at will by the messengers of Yama."
"I shall no longer create karma for the hells, nor shall I rejoice in it.
Should I see others doing so, I shall instruct them to abandon it.

Thus, when a bhikṣu hears of the celestial realms without delight, and hears of the sufferings of hell without fear, he is free from both sorrow and joy, constantly mindful of wholesome dharmas; this is called the seventh application of single-minded attention.
"Furthermore, the eighth is one-pointed concentration of mindfulness:
'I shall give rise to wholesome thoughts, abandon unwholesome dharmas, cause them all to be utterly destroyed, eliminate their remaining traces, and give birth to other wholesome dharmas.'"
One fixes the mind upon wholesome dharmas; if unwholesome thoughts obstruct wholesome thoughts, one thinks, "I have already abandoned unwholesome thoughts.
Thus taking them as objects of focus, one counts the sequence of these thoughts, fixing the mind with single-minded attention to subdue the heart.
This person is able to cause the mind—which is like a turbulent whirlpool with surging waves and an enemy—to abide within its objective domain.
This is called the eighth application of one-pointed mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the ninth application of one-pointed mindfulness is as follows:

One should practice mindfulness of the merit of the Buddha, mindfulness of reverence for the Dharma, and mindfulness of reverent faith in the teacher; follow the conduct of a virtuous teacher, practice with right intention, gaze straight ahead for the distance of one fathom, benefit all sentient beings, and keep in mind their deliverance.
To maintain such focused mindfulness so that one attains the fruits of practice without fail, up to and including Nirvana, is called the ninth application of single-minded mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the eleventh application of single-minded mindfulness is as follows:
one correctly cultivates virtuous conduct, mindful of the arrival of the four great terrors—namely, decline, old age, sickness, and death."
Fearing the enemy of death and taking no pleasure in dwelling upon it, one perceives four phenomena that flow and are impermanent: the security of life, youth, and the possession of all faculties.
These four kinds, as previously described, are constantly accompanied by fear.
By thus cultivating the perception of impermanence, one does not delight in the five desires and is no longer driven by craving or anger.
By constantly practicing right mindfulness, one is able to shatter the great mountain of afflictions.
This is called the eleventh application of mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the eleventh application of one-pointed mindfulness is as follows:"
Not giving rise to discrimination that "this is diligence" or "this is indolence"—
if such thoughts arise, one brings harm upon oneself.
Not vexing others, with a pure mind, maintaining mindfulness and self-mastery, one does not afflict sentient beings.
This is called the eleventh single-minded application of mindfulness.
"Furthermore, the twelfth single-minded application of mindfulness is:
constantly listening to the true Dharma; having heard it, receiving and upholding it; and having received and upheld it, holding it firmly without forgetting."
This person knows both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; such a person is like a great lamp of light in the midst of thick darkness.
Being able to fully comprehend all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas within the Buddha-dharma is like a bright lamp; this is called "binding the mind to mindfulness."
Thus, to single-mindedly fix the attention in this way—neither for the sake of attachment nor anger, and not acting as an agent for Māra—is called the twelfth single-minded fixation of attention.
"Furthermore, the thirteenth single-minded fixation of attention:
one fixes the attention on the body, feelings, and mind; one fixes the attention on such objects, knowing their specific characteristics, with a rectified mind, free from heedless conduct."
Being thus free from negligence, they will not be helplessly led away by the messengers of Yama.

Because they possess self-mastery, they do not lose mindfulness; they do not act at improper times, do not go to improper places, and do not frequent unwholesome environments, keeping their attention fixed on everything.
This is called the thirteenth: single-mindedly fixing the attention.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods, there are fourteen ways to well-cultivate the mind, to well-subdue the mind, and to well-purify the mind, thereby remaining free from negligence."
What are the fourteen?
First is contentment;
second is diligence.
Third, tranquility;
fourth, associating with virtuous teachers;
fifth, distancing oneself from evil associates.
Sixth, practicing the Buddha-dharma;
seventh, skillfully observing and practicing;
eighth, relinquishing arrogance.
Ninth, one has faith in cause and effect, as well as in what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;
tenth, one maintains mindfulness of wholesome desires;
eleventh, one does not gaze upon the forms of women.
Twelfth, not associating with kinsmen;
thirteenth, dwelling correctly within all objective spheres;
fourteenth, fearing birth and death.
This is called the fourteen dharmas for well-cultivating the mind.

By means of these causes and conditions, one tames the mind; at the time of death, one does not fear the evil realms or the jailers of Yama, the gates to the evil realms do not open, one does not sever the True Dharma, and one is not bound by the messengers of Yama to be led away against one's will.

One who does not commit evil deeds and is able to attain all wholesome dharmas is one who skillfully subdues the mind, causing it to cultivate wholesome karma; such a person can lead sentient beings to the realms of humans and devas, open the gate to nirvāṇa, and subsequently attain nirvāṇa.
Therefore, O sons of the gods!
You should skillfully subdue your minds.
Because the mind is subdued, one does not even see the messengers of Yama, much less being led away by them.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke to the assembly of devas about the terrors of the evil realms and the dread of seeing the messengers of King Yama:
"I have thus explained these fourteen dharmas to you, increasing them one by one in succession; now I shall explain the fifteenth dharma to you."
As I heard it from the Buddha in the past, I shall now speak of it.
What are these fifteen?
If a renunciant śramaṇa violates the rules of discipline and causes others to do so as well.

Regarding the method of donning the *kāṣāya*: though they wear the *kāṣāya*, it arouses desire in others; they delight in fine *kāṣāyas* to adorn themselves. Their voices are coarse and harsh like the bray of a donkey, yet they walk with mincing steps and deliberate gait, maintaining a dignified and solemn deportment—all for the sake of sensual desire, adorning their bodies.
Thus, a śramaṇa who does not apply himself with diligent effort, who delights in seeing women, who is arrogant and conceited, whose mind is fickle and restless, and whose desires are dissolute—
such a person wears the robes merely to ward off cold and heat, just enough to cover the body, without giving rise to greedy attachment or passionate clinging.
"Deceived by negligence, one does not give rise to a mind of regret at the time of death;
this is called the first dharma. 'Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the second dharma? He knows contentment.'"
What kind of precepts does he maintain?

Whether practicing as a renunciant or cultivating wisdom, having gained self-knowledge, he accepts and possesses bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites offered by donors with contentment; he accepts gifts in accordance with what is appropriate and receives gifts in accordance with the Dharma.
Receiving such offerings does not obstruct the dharma of the renunciant śramaṇa; this is called knowing the second dharma.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the third dharma?
He does not think of bedding and requisites with a mind of craving.

If he enters villages or towns—which are places devoid of merit—merely for the sake of food, drink, and clothing, he abandons the forest hermitage (āraṇya). This hinders the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and causes him to lose his contentment.
Among the dharmas of a śramaṇa, the foremost and most excellent are contentment and heedfulness.
If a person delights in craving and does not delight in contentment, they will be deceived by craving and bring harm to wholesome dharmas.
Such a person is like a foolish dog that eats its own vomit.
This is called the third dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the fourth dharma?

Regarding the sūtras he studies, he does not say that he has read many; he fears that the donors might provide him with excessive offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine, and he fears that these might be difficult for him to digest, thereby obstructing the way of the renunciant.
"It is not for me to pursue; I know contentment.
This is called the śramaṇa’s knowledge of the fourth dharma.
Furthermore, there is a fourth dharma of having few desires:
If there is a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content, in what matters should he practice heedfulness?

Such a śramaṇa, whether acting as an envoy for the Saṃgha or going to a donor’s house to beg for goods on behalf of a sick person, if he drinks even a single sip of water at that donor’s house, it hinders the wholesome Dharma; his mission is a mere waste of effort, and his labor is in vain, yielding no merit.
Why is this? Because of their craving for flavors, they go to the homes of donors, causing those donors to feel contempt.
Such bhikṣus do not benefit themselves, nor do they benefit the sick, nor do they benefit the Saṃgha; this is the first cause and condition for contempt.

That is to say, when one goes to the home of a donor and is greedy for the flavors of food, is flighty and restless, and speaks improperly—these three kinds of conduct are despised by both the worldly and those who have transcended the world.
"Therefore, one should practice contentment and heedfulness, abandoning these [other] dharmas.
This is called the fourth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does one know the fifth dharma?
It is to have few desires and be content, to rely on alms-gathering, to uphold the dharma of renunciation, to accept only a single meal a day, and not to store food overnight.

If one harbors leftover food, the mind becomes attached to it; one takes no pleasure in meditation or recitation, becoming greedy for the flavors of food and fearing that one might not obtain more later.
Such slight greed already hinders the dharma of a śramaṇa, let alone when a bhikṣu is excessively greedy for offerings.
If one maintains this dharma, one will be firmly bound by the net of craving.
This is called the fifth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the sixth dharma?
If there is a śramaṇa who has gone forth from a great clan and is one of few desires and contentment,
he does not say of himself after having gone forth:
"I am [Name], who has gone forth from a great clan.
He also instructs his disciples not to proclaim this; whether they be disciples who have received the Dharma or disciples who have gone forth, he instructs them not to speak of it.
"I fear that the donors will provide many offerings of bedding, clothing, food, drink, and medicine.
If I accept them, it will hinder my wholesome dharmas;
if I do not accept them, it will disappoint the disciples' hearts. Should they give rise to anger, it will obstruct their wholesome dharmas and cause them to receive no benefit in future lives."

Such a person, being content and receiving alms without being gripped by craving, with a mind undistracted, gives rise to right mindfulness within the True Dharma. They delight in practicing meditative contemplation in the forest, observing the body as it is, observing the mind as it is, observing feelings as they are, and observing phenomena as they are.
In this way, a bhikṣu is able to transcend the prison of conditioned existence by practicing the conduct of few desires and contentment.
This is called the sixth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the seventh dharma?
He has few desires and is content, and he fears great gain and offerings."
Having renounced gain and honor, what kind of dharmas does he know?

If there is a bhikṣu who has many acquaintances, who delights in many affairs, who delights in many disciples, who receives much gain and offerings, who greedily enjoys invitations to meals, and who frequently visits old friends.
A practitioner such as this bhikṣu should not go into a village together with him as a traveling companion.
For what reason should one not follow along with him?
Fearing the occurrence of negligence, [the Buddha taught]:

"In this way, a bhikṣu who delights in gain and offerings becomes known to the public; because he associates with others in the same community, people will also say of him that he is full of greed and lacks contentment."
Because of making offerings, one respects the person; thus, both [parties] create obstacles.

If a busy monk accepts the offerings of others, yet this practitioner does not accept his things, it causes the busy monk’s mind to become resentful and angry, saying: "This monk is sycophantic and insincere, deceiving the various donors in the village," thereby implying that the monk’s inner heart is greedy and turbid.
For this reason, those who see him will suffer internal injury.

Therefore, a bhikṣu who is content with few desires and knows satisfaction should not dwell together, reside with, or associate in coming and going with a bhikṣu of many affairs, for it gives rise to transgressions.
This is called the seventh dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the eighth dharma?
A bhikṣu with few desires fears birth and death, stays far removed from gain and honor, and constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness.
How does he know the Dharma?
When he was a householder, he possessed various skills; having gone forth, he no longer speaks of them himself.
Regarding medical arts, crafts, music, swordsmanship, and various such technical skills, one does not speak of them oneself.
Why is this? It is for fear that donors, knowing of one's technical skills, would provide excessive offerings, thereby obstructing the dharma of a śramaṇa.

Or, by delighting in the practice of such worldly arts and techniques, they destroy wholesome dharmas; they fail to attain single-mindedness or meditative concentration, their minds remain impure, and they obstruct the dharma of the śramaṇa. Consequently, both self-benefit and the benefit of others are diminished, and they are unable to benefit or discipline their disciples.
Therefore, one should abandon the failure to explain technical methods; this is called the eighth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the ninth dharma?
A bhikṣu of few desires and wise person remains far removed from offerings.

He may see a monastery within a stūpa-temple, or within a city, or within a village, or near a village, or within a walled town, or near a walled town. There he sees a monastic dwelling belonging to the Saṃgha.

If there are many bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, who are full of desire and never satisfied, who store up much food and drink, who consume impure food, who drink alcohol and are dissolute, who engage in livelihoods such as buying and selling impure goods or managing property, who associate with worldly people as their friends, who take no pleasure in dwelling in the monastery, and who instead mostly delight in staying at the homes of donors.
A bhikṣu of few desires should not dwell together with this bhikṣu of many desires in the same monastery.
If one wishes to attain a mind of tranquility and desires to be free from the bonds of Māra, one should not reside in such a place.

Why is this? It is because he fears that the people of the city, or those of the villages, or those of the market towns might learn that the bhikṣus have broken their precepts and committed evil deeds, and thus think, "I alone am foremost in upholding the precepts," and consequently offer him abundant gifts and support.
"If I were to accept these offerings, I would not be called one of few desires.

Yet, if I do not accept such gains and honors, the multitude will harbor resentment and cause many people to feel anger toward the donor, asking: 'Why does he give his goods to only one person and not to many?'"
Having recognized this fault, a bhikṣu of few desires should not dwell in the same place as an impure bhikṣu; this is called the ninth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the tenth dharma?
If there is a bhikṣu who has attained mundane supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and can manifest extraordinary signs, a bhikṣu of few desires should not proclaim them."

Why is this? I fear that those who hear of it might think I am an arhat and provide excessive offerings; this would obstruct the dharma of the śramaṇas, cause me to lose my supernormal powers, and destroy the practice of having few desires.
This is called the tenth quality of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods,
how does a śramaṇa know the eleventh quality?

If there is a bhikṣu who carries the Buddha’s relics from city to city, from village to village, from town to town, and from district to district, manifesting them to the world through his true supernatural power.
In this way, the Śrāvakas are a great field of merit and should be provided with offerings.
Likewise, a bhikṣu who has heard little and lacks wisdom may praise and extol a bhikṣu of few desires, saying: "This bhikṣu is learned and wise; he can expound the True Dharma for you all."
Having heard this, the donor will revere the śarīra and the learned bhikṣu, making extensive offerings.
If this bhikṣu accepts these offerings, it is not the practice of one with few desires.
A bhikṣu of few desires should not travel or dwell together with this wandering bhikṣu.

Why is this? Because when various donors see that this bhikṣu does not uphold the prohibitions and precepts, they will assume that even those who claim to have few desires have likewise broken the prohibitions.
Therefore, one should not walk, stay, sit, or lie down with those who have broken the precepts, for fear that the messengers and wardens of Yama will bind them, and for fear of negligence.
This is called the eleventh dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the twelfth dharma?
It is the practice of receiving alms-food, the merit of the dhūta ascetic virtues."
"Wandering for alms in places devoid of learning, not practicing negligence, and relinquishing attachment to flavors—this is called the twelfth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the thirteenth dharma known by the śramaṇa?

A bhikṣu who is content accepts robes made of discarded rags; being content with the robes he receives, he keeps them even when they are old and worn out. Being thus content with material things—this is called the thirteenth dharma of the śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa bhikṣu of few desires know the fourteenth dharma?
A bhikṣu who is contented is able to destroy the hosts of Māra; this is called the fourteenth dharma of a śramaṇa."
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
How does a śramaṇa know the fifteenth dharma?
A bhikṣu with few desires wanders alone without companion; he abandons evil associates and shatters the firm mountain of beginningless afflictions."

Thus, one who is content attains the foremost happiness; at the time of death, they will not be bound by the power of the messengers of Yama, nor will they behold the hideous and terrifying forms, and their mind shall not be afraid.
At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, spoke these verses:
“The dharma of few desires and contentment is what those who have left the home life should practice.
A person who maintains the precepts in this way draws near to the path of Nirvāṇa.”
Acting without expectation, diligently seeking the path to nirvāṇa,
one is not bound by the realms of Māra and does not fall into the domain of Māra.
If a person constantly practices in this way, they will not give rise to a mind of expectation.
If one practices with diligent vigor, there will be no manifold sufferings.
Having brought forth fear through mindfulness and reflecting upon the present,
as well as knowing the future, one shall be liberated from the bonds of affliction.
Always delighting in heedfulness, fearing those who do not believe in the Dharma,
and cultivating stainless, pure wisdom— one then dwells near Nirvana. Even the gods,
while experiencing happiness, still give rise to heedless conduct.
How much more so for the foolish person, who is driven by heedlessness!
One who acts with heedlessness is already as good as dead;
one who acts without heedlessness is a person who dwells eternally in wisdom.
"The mind of negligence and indolence can be severed through diligent effort;
negligence is the root of all suffering—abandon it as one would cast away death.
Thus did the Heavenly King Śakra, for the sake of the assembly of devas, manifest the messengers of Yama to terrify the sons of the gods and preach the Dharma for them.
At that time, Śakra, knowing that the sons of the gods had conceived faith and delight in the True Dharma, saw that the messengers of Yama were gradually being extinguished.
Having witnessed this, he went again to the presence of King Śakra; furthermore, there were other gods who, out of fear, had been hiding in the groves, and they all went to where Śakra was.

At that time, Śakra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these devas, gradually extinguished the transformation [of the city] in accordance with the increasingly purified minds of the assembly of devas.
*The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Fascicle 33.
*The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Fascicle 34.
Translated by the Bāhman Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen on Contemplating the Heavens, Section Ten on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven:

"At that time, the assembly of devas gave rise to a heart of profound reverence and further listened to the essential Dharma taught by Śakra. With palms joined above their heads, they addressed Śakra, saying:"

"I now clearly perceive the power of this Dharma: as the Heavenly King preaches the Dharma according to our minds, we attain pure faith; the messengers of Yama likewise gradually diminish, and upon hearing the power of the Tathāgata’s preached Dharma, they are all immediately extinguished. How much more so for those who practice—should they practice, they shall reach the state of non-extinction."
At that time, Śakra, his heart filled with joy, spoke these words:
"I have now accomplished what was to be done.
For the sake of these negligent devas, I have severed their negligence and brought them to non-negligence, causing them to rejoice."

I shall now preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for this assembly of devas—just as I heard the essential points of the True Dharma at the abode of my Great Teacher concerning the gateway to the city of liberation: the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, ānāpāna.

Having heard this sequentially from the ancient devas of old, and having now heard it further as the World-Honored One has proclaimed it for me, I shall therefore now expound for the sake of the devas the Dharma of the mixed Four Noble Truths, with fourfold analysis within each single truth.

I shall now speak for the benefit of all these hosts of devas, to benefit myself as well as others—those beings wandering in the cycle of birth and death—teaching the Dharma to them through various skillful means so that the minds of all sentient beings may reach full maturity.

I have thus explained these fifteen dharmas; I shall now, for the sake of the assembly of devas and others, explain the sixteenth dharma: the method of ānāpāna, the inhalation and exhalation of breath, which analyzes the four noble truths and the characteristics of the causes and conditions of skillful means.
What is meant by "teaching in successive order"?
It is this practitioner who contemplates his own bound mind as a monkey, [saying]:
"O sons of the gods!..."
How does one bind the monkey-like mind of vitarka and vicāra?
What kind of mind is bound?
It is the consciousness that is bound.

In this way, with a single mind, one sequentially contemplates the characteristics of the body: contemplating the body as the body, contemplating it as defiled, undefiled, or neutral; contemplating feelings as feelings—contemplating painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings; contemplating the specific characteristics of feelings; and contemplating phenomena as phenomena—contemplating them as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral according to their specific characteristics. These are called the four foundations of mindfulness.

The practitioner enters into such dharmas and, with single-minded observation, perceives that all conditioned phenomena are quiescent in their own characteristics; he contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness, which are the marks of the Four Noble Truths.

Thus, the foundations of mindfulness pervade all places; that is to say, their sequential aspects are: the permanent and the impermanent, conjunction and dispersion, emptiness and the absence of an agent, emptiness and the absence of a self, and destruction, decay, and affliction.
Having thus contemplated suffering and impermanence and perceived the four foundations of mindfulness, one contemplates the specific characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.
By observing them as they truly are, the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) arises; from this stage of Heat, wisdom is born.
It is like drilling for fire: first the sign of smoke is seen, and only afterward is the fire seen;
as with the drill and the fire-stick, first heat is generated, and only afterward is fire produced.
Because of this faith and delight, just as future noble dharmas and vinaya can arise amidst all afflictions and states of ignorance,
so it is likewise through the sixteen modes of contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
"How does this Dharma of Heat arise?
How does one contemplate the Four Noble Truths?
O sons of the gods!..."

That which is called the Noble Truth of Suffering: because it has causes and conditions, it is impermanent; because it is subject to decay and destruction, it is suffering; because it is devoid of a person, it is empty; and because it lacks self-mastery, it is non-self.
In this way, one contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering through these four kinds of discrimination.
Having contemplated the Noble Truth of Suffering, the practitioner contemplates the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering through four kinds of discrimination.
What are these discriminations?

This is because the formations proceed in a continuous succession; because they accumulate similar fruits that flow through the various states of existence (*bhava*); because they flow through existence by means of all natures as causes; and because there is the continuity of conditions through forces that are not identical.
The practitioner further contemplates the fourfold analysis of the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
O sons of the gods!
How does the practitioner analyze and practice the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

Because it abandons all decline and affliction; because it extinguishes the fire of the defilements through detachment; because it is the supreme quiescence of all phenomena; and because the pure dharma emerges from birth and death.
The practitioner further contemplates the fourfold analysis of the Noble Truth of the Path.
O sons of the gods!
How does the practitioner analyze and observe it?

This is because it is the attainment of the state of non-retrogression; because the path is not inverted; because it is the dharma in which all noble ones abide; and because, through unimpededness, one transcends the world by severing the decay and afflictions of birth and death.

These are called the sixteen methods of practice, which I have now explained. You, members of the celestial assembly, should cultivate with diligent effort and observe the present dharma of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*). Teach one another in succession: from the inhalation and exhalation of breath, the dharma of warmth arises; from the dharma of warmth, the dharma of "summit" (*mūrdhan*) arises. By fixing the mind through faith upon the accumulation of merits of the Triple Gem and other such qualities, this surpasses the previous observation.
"How does such a practitioner observe so that it is called the path of the 'Summit Dharma' (*mūrdha-dharma*)?
Just as on a mountain peak the Summit Dharma increases, one successively gives rise to the roots of goodness of the 'Patience Dharma' (*kṣānti-dharma*)."

Because one has attained patience (*kṣānti*), one dwells in the third stage, which is called "the manifestation of birth" (*upapatti-sākṣātkriyā*), not the "patience of the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-kṣānti*).
Because one manifests the dharma of patience, it is called the "dharma of patience" (*kṣāntidharma*).
Because patience has increased, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
At the moment of a single thought, the mind and its mental factors are said to have attained the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
One attains the stage of Srotāpanna through these successive stages.
Such is the Dharma that I have realized for myself.
If a person can realize such a Dharma, they will not see the terrifying messengers of Yama, nor will they feel any fear.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
It is by means of non-negligence that one attains such dharmas as these.
Therefore, O sons of the gods, do not be negligent.
At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra spoke in verse:
"If one well understands the sixteen stages of abandonment regarding inhalation and exhalation,
The stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) and its summit (mūrdhan), And the stage of Patience (kṣānti) through both progressive and regressive contemplation."
Knowing the Dharma Supreme in the World, one knows the True Truths in succession;
knowing the True Dharma in its proper order, one does not lose the path of goodness.
Liberated from the three fetters, one destroys the eight kinds of existence.
Valiantly severing the evil paths, one is therefore called a *srotāpanna*.
Having abandoned all tainted and unwholesome dharmas that would certainly lead to the evil paths,
and flowing toward *nirvāṇa*, one is therefore called a *srotāpanna*.
At that time, having spoken these verses, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of devas:
"I have thus fully explained these sixteen kinds of mindfulness of ānāpāna; you should reflect upon them."
This path is tranquil and leads into the city of Nirvana; it is free from all fear and is cherished by all the noble ones. Therefore, you should resolutely practice this path.
If you fear the messengers of Yama, you should sequentially recollect these sixteen modes of ānāpānasmṛti.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
There are seventeen kinds of dharmas pertaining to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); you should fix your mindfulness upon them and practice the path of tranquility.
Whether one is a deva or a human, if they keep this path in mind, they will never fear the harm inflicted by the messengers of Yama.
What are the seventeen types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
They are as follows: at the time of death, one perceives visual forms.
If one dies among humans and is to be reborn in the heavens, one then perceives signs of pleasure.

In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he sees what resembles a white woolen cloth, hanging down as if about to fall, fine, soft, white, and pure; having seen this, he rejoices, his countenance becoming serene and joyful.

At the time of death, he further sees gardens and groves that are exceedingly delightful; lotus ponds are likewise lovely, as are the rivers and the forests. He successively hears various songs, dances, and laughter; next, he smells various fragrances; and he experiences the infinite varieties of agreeable objects and their subtle tactile sensations, all of which he finds pleasing.
In this sequence, they are immediately reborn in the heavens; by virtue of their wholesome karma, they presently enjoy celestial bliss.

Having attained this joy, they smile with serene delight, their countenances pure and radiant. Although their kinsmen and brothers weep and wail in grief, because of these auspicious marks, they neither hear nor see them, nor do they even think of them in their minds.
Due to their wholesome karma, at the time of death, they achieve great bliss within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

They are born in a joyful place, resembling celestial bodies and resembling the celestial hosts; such are the signs of their birth and their environment, like a seal being impressed upon its clay. Their physical forms are like those of all the celestial hosts, like the enjoyment experienced by the six heavens of the desire realm, like the realms they traverse, and their tactile sensations as well as their celestial colors are likewise similar.

Furthermore, while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one perceives that the birthplace among the devas is superior; thus, a mind of grasping arises, and because of craving for that realm, one immediately assumes a celestial body. This is what is called the first intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the intermediate state of existence (*antarābhava*) of the second kind?
If a person from Jambudvīpa dies and is reborn in Uttarakuru, they will perceive the lovely color of fine, soft, red cotton cloth."

Seeing it, he felt affection and joy, immediately giving rise to a mind of craving; he reached out his hand to grasp it, but as he lifted his hand to seize it, it was like grasping empty space, leading his kinsmen to say that he was "feeling for the air with both hands."
Furthermore, there is a wind that blows:

if this patient is during the cold of winter, a warm wind comes to blow; if it is during the heat of summer, a cool wind comes to blow, removing their stifling heat and distress, and causing the mind to feel joy and happiness.
Because their minds are focused on other objects, they do not hear the sounds of lamentation and wailing.
If their karma is stirred, their minds are also stirred; they then hear the sounds of that wailing and weeping, and the winds of karma blow them to be born in another place.
Therefore, when one's kinsmen and brothers weep and wail at the time of death, it constitutes a severe hindrance.
If there is no such hindrance, one will be reborn in Uttarakuru.
In the interim, auspicious signs appeared in succession:
he saw a pond of blue lotuses, filled with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, all present in abundance; upon seeing this, the person immediately ran toward it.
Thus, having generated a wholesome mind during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), at the moment of death one sees a pond of blue lotuses and enters it to sport therein.
If one is to enter a mother’s womb in Uttarakuru, one emerges from the lotus pond, walks upon dry land, and beholds the parents in union through lustful passion.
Due to impurity and perverted views, they perceive their father’s body as a male goose and their mother as a female goose.
If a male is to be born, he perceives himself as having the body of a male goose;
if a female is to be born, she perceives herself as having the body of a female goose.
If a male is born, he feels aversion toward his father and attachment toward his mother.
When one is born in Uttarakuru, this is called the second intermediate state (*antarābhava*). "Furthermore, O sons of gods!
What is the third intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
If one dies in Jambudvīpa and is to be reborn in Aparagoyānī, then certain signs appear.
At the time of death, one sees houses that have all turned yellow, like the color of gold, covering everything like clouds.
He sees the appearance of a yellow cotton cloth in the void and raises his hands to grasp it; his kinsmen and brothers say, "The patient is grasping at empty space with both hands.
At that time, the person's wholesome existence is about to be exhausted; he sees his own body as an ox and sees herds of oxen as if seen in a dream.
If a male is to be born, he perceives his parents in a state of passionate union engaged in impure conduct.
He sees himself as having a human body and many dwellings; perceiving his father’s form to be like a bull, he drives away his father and unites with his mother.
The men born in Godānīya possess such characteristics.
If women are born in the realm of Godānīya, they perceive their own bodies as being like milch cows and think to themselves:
"For what reason does the bull mate with her and not with me?"
Having formed this thought, they receive a female body; this is called the birth of women in the country of Aparagoyānī.
This is known as the third intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the intermediate state of existence (antarābhava) of the fourth [continent]?
If a person from Jambudvīpa dies and is reborn in the realm of Pūrvavideha, then certain signs appear."
He sees the appearance of blue woolen cloth, entirely blue and pervasively covering the void.
He sees his house as being entirely like the void; fearing that the blue woolen cloth might fall, he shields it with his hand, whereupon his kinsmen and brothers say, "He is shielding the void."

At the end of his life, he was reborn in the country of Pūrvavideha; he perceived his intermediate state body (antarābhava) as being like the form of a horse. He saw his father as a stallion and his mother as a mare, and they were joined together in union through the bonds of passion.
If a male is to be conceived, he forms this thought:
"I shall unite with this mare.
If a female is to be conceived, she perceives her own body as having the form of a mare and forms this thought:
Thinking, "Why does this stallion not unite with me?
he immediately assumes a female body.
This is called the fourth intermediate state (antarābhava).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the fifth [realm]?
When a person of Uttarakuru is approaching the end of life, they perceive signs of ascending."
"O sons of the gods!
If one possesses great karma and a great mind, with mastery over the activities of the mind, they will be born in the heavens.

At the time of death, they grasp at space with their hands as if it were a dream-mind; they see various beautiful flowers within that dream and rejoice upon seeing them. Furthermore, they smell a supreme and most exquisite fragrance, and all manner of supreme, wondrous colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—are fully present as the highest adornment. A supreme scent remains within their hands."
When this person sees the flowers, a mind of craving arises, and they think:
"Now that I see this tree, I shall climb it.
Having formed this thought, at the time of death, they are born within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where they see lotus trees of blue, yellow, red, and white in immeasurable varieties.
Again he thought to himself:
"I shall ascend a tree.
Having formed this thought, he immediately climbed a great tree; it was, in fact, ascending Mount Sumeru, the Mountain of Jewels.
Having ascended this mountain, he beheld the celestial world adorned with flowers and fruits, and thought to himself:
"I shall wander through such places; now that I have arrived here, groves of flowers and fruits are found everywhere."
"This is called the inferior mode of rebirth for the people of Uttarakuru;
this is called the fifth intermediate state (antarābhava).
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the sixth [realm]?
If a person from Uttarakuru, due to their intermediate karma, is about to be reborn in the heavens at the time of death, then signs appear.
At the time of death, one sees a lotus pond that is exceedingly lovely and delightful, adorned with many peaks, all of which are fragrant.
One ascends this lotus; having ascended, in a mere moment, one flies through the air as if in a dream.
Born in the heavens, they see a wondrous lotus flower—lovely, sublime, and supreme—which brings them this thought:
"I shall now go to that excellent lotus pond and gather this lotus flower."
"This is called taking birth as a person of middle capacity among the inhabitants of Uttarakuru;
this is called the sixth intermediate state of existence (antarābhava).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the seventh intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
Due to their superior karma, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru are born in thirty-three places, such as the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*).
When one from Uttarakuru approaches the end of life, they see a magnificent hall, exquisitely adorned; at that moment, the person ascends that superior palace.
In reality, it is not an ascent to a palace, but rather an ascent into the void, reaching the celestial realms.
Seeing its palaces, his mind immediately inclines toward them, and he is reborn within that palace as a deva-king.
This is called the case of one from Uttarakuru who, after death, is reborn in the heavens and receives a superior birth.
This is called the seventh intermediate state existence.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the eighth intermediate state, the continuity of the path?
When a person from Uttarakuru approaches the end of their life, certain signs appear.
O sons of the gods!
That person sees rows of gardens and places for recreation that are fragrant, pure, and lovely; hearing them, they experience joy and pleasure, and suffer little distress.
Because they are free from suffering and affliction, their minds are not turbid; with a pure mind, they relinquish their life-span and receive an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
Seeing the celestial palaces, they think to themselves:
"I shall ascend to these palaces to sport therein."

Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended to his palace and saw the hosts of devas traveling through the air, some running and some staying amidst the mountain peaks, their bodies touching one another as they frolicked everywhere.
Abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), he perceives his own body as ascending to the heavens as if in a dream.
Seeing the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as supremely wonderful and delightful, with all five objects of desire fully present, he thinks:
"I shall now go to such a place."

Having formed this thought, he was immediately reborn in the heavens, taking existence through causes and conditions; such is the "existence-component" (bhava-aṅga), which is divided into superior, middling, and inferior grades.
Having been born in the heavens, he beheld various magnificent groves and gardens and desired to possess them; thus, dying in Uttarakuru, he was reborn in this celestial realm.

Thus, once all these people from Uttarakuru have been born into this heaven, their remaining karma gives rise to a mental body; they delight in sensual pleasures, craving the objects of the five desires, engaging in song, dance, and play to experience the joys of passion; they take pleasure in roaming the mountain peaks, indulging extensively in sensual delights, and are fond of all forms of desire.
Why is this? Because of former habituation, the habituation of craving increases.
Thus it is, O devaputras!
This is called the death and rebirth in heaven of a person from Uttarakuru; it describes the habitual play and the signs at the time of death for one born in this celestial realm.
This is known as the eighth intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the ninth intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
If a person from Godānīya dies and is reborn in the heavens, there are two kinds of karma."
What are these two? First, residual karma;
second, generative karma.
Regarding those born in the heavens, how do they undergo birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
At the time of death, a sign of rebirth appears.
When the retribution of the present life is about to end, if there is to be an intermediate state existence, a sign of rebirth arises, turbulent and like a dream.
O sons of the gods!

When the people of Godānīya approach the end of their lives, by virtue of their wholesome karma, as they are about to relinquish their life-force, their breath is not turbid, their pulses do not cease or fail, and their faculties remain pure.

Then, in succession, he saw a great pool of water like beryl; entering the pool to cross over, the water was temperate—neither cold nor hot—and flowed gently as he floated toward the opposite shore, thus drawing near to his place of rebirth.
Having reached the other shore, he saw celestial maidens of supreme beauty, adorned with various ornaments, laughing, singing, and dancing.
Upon seeing them, his mind was filled with desire and he approached them; as he stepped forward to embrace a woman, he was immediately reborn in heaven, where he experienced celestial bliss.

Just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) in a dream immediately perishes, so too, upon birth with immeasurable distracted minds, one immediately awakens to see various wondrous forms and receives a supreme and sublime body.
This is called the ninth intermediate existence.

The people of Aparagoyānī have three grades of birth—superior, middling, and inferior—based on their karma; yet they share the same radiance, the same intermediate state (antarābhava), the same views, and the same modes of rebirth, being entirely similar to one another, unlike the people of Uttarakuru who exhibit three distinct types of birth.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the tenth intermediate state of existence (*antarābhava*)?
When a person from Pūrvavideha is approaching the end of life, they perceive the signs of death."

Seeing the signs of one's own karma or the karma of others, or seeing palaces adorned with magnificent banners and streamers and decorated with railings, one gives rise to joy within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and wanders about everywhere, desiring to approach rebirth.

Outside the hall, he saw that their karmic results corresponded to their deeds: he saw many court ladies and men singing and enjoying themselves, supremely adorned, dancing, singing, and laughing in play.
While in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one forms this thought:
"I shall emerge from my palace to see the ladies-in-waiting and the men, and together with them, engage in play, song, dance, and laughter."
"Why is this? Because these court ladies engage in the foremost amusements of singing, dancing, and laughter with these men.
Having thought this, he immediately went out and entered the assembly of those engaged in play.
At that time, the person realizes they have entered [the womb], just as one awakens from sleep, and is immediately reborn in the heavens.
This is called the tenth intermediate state (antarābhava).
"This is called the intermediate state within the four continents."
Within such radiance, there exists the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of birth; I know it with subtle discernment, whereas others cannot comprehend it.
No other non-Buddhists are able to know it, and even among worldly phenomena, no one is able to see it.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the eleventh intermediate state of existence?

When various hungry ghosts, having been born among the hungry ghosts due to unwholesome karma, have exhausted that evil karma and receive the influence of remaining wholesome karma—namely, the wholesome karma and agreeable karma previously performed in other realms that are like parents—they then manifest signs of desiring to be born in the heavens.
How is it that while existence is exhausted, the mental characteristics still manifest?
O sons of the gods!

If one dies among the hungry ghosts (preta) with the desire to be born in the heavens, while still among the hungry ghosts, their bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst; they are destroyed by envy and constantly crave food and drink. They always think of water and spirits, focusing only on food and drink, knowing nothing else.

When his life was about to end, he no longer gave rise to thoughts, and all former thoughts were extinguished. His body was without fever, becoming supple and cool; long hairs grew upon it, and all the malevolent insects covering his body fell away. His facial complexion became pure and clear, and a cool breeze touched his body.
As they approach the end of their lives, they are entirely free from hunger and thirst, and their sense faculties are pure and clean.
Although hawks, vultures, crows, ravens, and various other predatory birds and beasts constantly peck at their eyes, at the time of death, none of them draw near.

They see rivers of food and drink overflowing and full; entering the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), due to past habits, although they see the food and drink, they neither drink nor eat, but merely look upon them with their eyes—just as when a person sees food in a dream, they neither drink nor eat;
or like eating in a dream, where though one eats, one is not satiated.
Although they see this, they are not yet fully satisfied; they merely give rise to joy.

Seeing the heavens as lovely, as if perceiving forms upon waking, a thought immediately arises in their minds. They run toward them, longing to go to that place; having formed this thought, they proceed and are born in the heavens.
This is called the eleventh intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the twelfth intermediate existence?

This is a rare karma: because of ignorance, one receives the body of an animal; through immeasurable varieties of causes and conditions for delusion, and due to the ripening of that karma, one undergoes the bodies of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of births and deaths as a result of residual karma.

Because their karma is fully accomplished, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; for immeasurable eons, the karma they have created causes them to revolve through the worlds, which is inexhaustible and inconceivable.
From beginningless time, they have been crooked and perverse, failing to perform beneficial deeds and instead afflicting and harming sentient beings, transmigrating without end.

Among the animal realm, there are immeasurable varieties of species, immeasurable kinds of food, immeasurable paths, immeasurable types of bodies, and immeasurable lands; there, with immeasurable seeds of various mental states, they create immeasurable karma, or they teach others to lack faith and commit various evil deeds.
When the retribution has been fully experienced, it is like a drop falling into the waters of the great ocean that causes the ocean to dry up.

A drop is produced from the ocean of karma; when the karma of the animal realm is exhausted, one dies among animals due to remaining wholesome karma and is reborn in one of two celestial realms—either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

When the retribution for suffering in the evil realm of animals is about to end and one is on the verge of attaining liberation from that body, signs will appear; the objects of these signs are of immeasurable kinds and cannot be described in full detail.
To die among the animals and be reborn in the heavens is extremely rare; this does not apply to those in the realms of hungry ghosts or hell-dwellers. Why is this?

Because due to a deluded mind, one performs many evil deeds and falls into the animal realm. The evil karma committed in a single lifetime is not exhausted even after hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes; for one kalpa or up to hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Bound by the shackles of karma from birth to birth, one transmigrates through the world, receiving the body of an animal.
Therefore, it would be better to fall into the realms of hell or hungry ghosts than to receive the body of a foolish animal.
For this reason, among the various forms of existence, it is exceedingly rare for one to be reborn in the heavens after death while in the state of an animal; this is not the case for those in hell.

Thus, when facing death in the realms of suffering as animals, they perceive the manifestation of light; due to residual wholesome karma, their deluded mind becomes thin and diminished, their innate wisdom slightly increases, and their faculty of wisdom gradually sharpens.
At the time of death, one sees signs of light; one may see mountains and valleys, various groves of trees, diverse flowing waters, various rivers and ponds, as well as food and drink.

If, through recollecting the perception of worldly knowledge, one sees a place of pleasure—whether it be in the mountains, in the forest, or by recollecting food and drink, or seeing a pleasant place—one immediately runs toward it; just as one runs toward what is seen in a dream, so too does one approach the place of rebirth.

Immediately they receive a celestial body, like awakening from a dream and beholding various forms and appearances; among hundreds of thousands of billions of places of rebirth, they have never before seen such forms as these, and having seen them, they rejoice and give rise to a sense of wonder.
What is this thing? How does it exist?
By what cause does it exist?
Because they have not practiced [such deeds] and because their various consciousnesses are dull, they give rise to a sense of wonder, thinking:
"I shall go there and fully take possession of these things.

Due to other wholesome karmas, they conceive such a thought; through these causes and conditions, they form such an intention, and at the moment this thought arises, they are immediately reborn in the heavens.
This is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) among the twelve; it is foremost in its difficulty of occurrence, foremost in its rarity, and foremost in its difficulty of being known.
Among all forms of play, karma is supreme.
"In various spheres of karma, the great illusionist that is the mind sports within the realms of birth and death across the various paths, deceiving sentient beings.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, the gods conceived deep faith and spoke in verse:
"The Heavenly King is like a father and mother, Benefiting the world of devas."
The Heavenly King benefits us, both in this world and in the future.
By preaching the Dharma for us, he cuts off the mind of negligence;
we shall surely attain the path to Nirvana, where suffering is exhausted.
By means of the retribution of present karma, you have proclaimed it for us;
by means of the dharma of birth and death, you have shown it to the world so that it may be understood.
O Heavenly King, having seen the true reality, you bring benefit to us.
Because of our ignorance, you have shown us wisdom.
While we were greedy for and attached to court ladies, constantly seeking sensual pleasures,
the Heavenly King has shown us the causes and conditions of birth and death.
The King is like a guide for the blind, a great and excellent medicine for the sick;
he expounds the path of the True Dharma and benefits the hosts of devas.
Since the Heavenly King is thus, he benefits others by preaching the Dharma.
"May the jailers of Yama be completely extinguished and no longer appear.
When the assembly of devas had spoken this verse, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the sons of the gods:
"What is called the thirteenth intermediate state of existence?"
It is rare and difficult for beings in the hells to be born in the heavens due to the remaining causes and conditions of their karma,
as well as the causes and conditions of their merit.
When such karma ripens, it is the foremost cooling and the foremost benefit.

Having first fallen into hell, virtue serves as the condition for escape; once one has been liberated from within immeasurable suffering and affliction, one is born in a place of immeasurable happiness.

As for the sentient beings in the hells, these include the Sañjīva (Reviving) Hell, the Kālasūtra (Black Rope) Hell, the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell, the Raurava (Wailing) Hell, the Mahāraurava (Great Wailing) Hell, and the Pratāpana (Greatly Heating) Great Hell; as well as various separate locations and places of great suffering—places of supreme terror that cause one's hair to stand on end—where blazing flames surround them on all sides.
