When these hell-beings, due to the exhaustion of their karma, are about to be liberated from this hell, signs appear at the time of their death.
How is it that there can be an intermediate state (antarābhava) leading to rebirth in the heavens?
By reason of their karmic causes and conditions, they abandon great suffering and experience supreme bliss.
O sons of the gods!

When the time comes for those in hell to end their lives because their evil karma is exhausted, even if the hell-wardens cast them into cauldrons, they vanish like bubbles on water and are not reborn there again.
If struck with a staff, one dies immediately upon being struck and is not born again.
If placed within an iron chest, one dies as soon as one is placed therein and is not born again.
If one is placed in the Ash River, once submerged, one dissolves away and is not born again.
If struck by an iron club, one dies instantly upon being struck; having perished, one is not reborn.
If they are devoured by iron-beaked birds or iron crows, once consumed, they are not reborn.
If they are seized and devoured by lions, tigers, wolves, or various other evil beasts, once consumed, they are not reborn.
When the evil karma of these hell-beings is exhausted, after their lives have ended, they no longer see the jailers of Yama.

Why is this? Because they are no longer reckoned among the number of sentient beings; just as there is no lamp when the oil and the wick are spent, so it is when karma is exhausted—they no longer see the jailers of Yama.
Just as when the light of the sun appears over Jambudvīpa, there is no longer any darkness, so it is with the wardens of Yama’s hells when one's evil karma is exhausted.

The foul mouths, evil eyes, and terrifying forms that correspond to the characteristics of sentient beings are all completely obliterated; just as when a painted wall is broken, the painting vanishes along with it, so too is the "painted wall" of evil karma, such that one no longer beholds the terrifying forms of the wardens of Yama’s hells.
Because the Tathāgata has said:
"Since the wardens of the Yama hell are not reckoned among sentient beings, it is called 'hell.
Sentient beings, having escaped from hell, are born in the heavens."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke in verse:
"Just as a person encountering an enemy May escape without any further hardship,
So it is when one gains many wise friends, Benefited by every skillful means."
Having already escaped from the realm of the powerful hell-wardens and their evil karma,
one has now attained wholesome karma and been born into the heavenly world.
Having been born in the heavens, one possesses immeasurable adornments.
They constantly enjoy celestial pleasures until their wholesome karma is exhausted.
When that person lacks self-mastery and their karma is spent, they fall back into decline;
just as when the oil and wick of a lamp are spent, the light likewise fades away.
Blown by the winds of karma, one descends from above;
turned by the power of the winds, one wanders through the world.
If a person possesses wisdom, they will not be bound by karma.
All karmas cannot bind him, nor does he wander through birth and death.
It is as if one were to try to tie Mount Sumeru with the fibers of a lotus root;
such a person crosses the wilderness free from sorrow, decay, and affliction.
"The wise do not transmigrate, Just like Mount Sumeru.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having spoken this verse for the sake of the assembly of devas, further described the characteristics of the intermediate state (antarābhava) within the hells.

"Having never seen such things before, they suddenly behold in the midst of empty space the most exquisite singing, dancing, play, and laughter; fragrant winds touch their bodies, and they experience supreme bliss."
Various wondrous sounds refer to the sounds of musical instruments and diverse voices; they hear such wind-blown music.
They smell delightful fragrances and behold exquisite forms—gardens, groves, flowers, and ponds—and they hear a multitude of wondrous sounds.
He suddenly beheld his own physical form manifesting a wondrous color, with supreme majesty and virtue.
He saw his body fragrant and pure, adorned with flower garlands, unimpeded in all respects.
He saw all of space as clear and stainless, filled with the constellations of the stars.
They hear the sound of flowing rivers and perceive all the various cries of geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.

Likewise, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they hear the music of their future place of birth—the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou* lutes—sounds of various musical instruments that they have never before experienced for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years.
Thus rejoicing, auspicious signs arise throughout; as if seeing oneself among brothers, kinsmen, and friends, one gives rise to great joy in every thought-moment.
Desiring to be born near existence, they are either born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three or the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

Having reached these heavens, they see various groves and gardens, smell fragrant scents, and behold lotus flowers made of the seven treasures; seeing the handsome celestial sons, they think to themselves:
"I shall now go to such a place."
Having formed this thought, it immediately arises; thus there is the *bhava-aṅga* (existence-factor), which takes conditions as its cause for existence.

When the evil karma of such a sentient being is exhausted, they emerge from hell and, passing away from that place of unspeakable great suffering and affliction, are reborn in a place of great bliss; this is called the thirteenth intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the fourteenth continuity of the path of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
and how is it known?
If one dies among humans and is reborn again among humans, what signs are there?
What does one long for?
When such a person is dying, if they are to be reborn among humans, then signs appear; what do they long for?
If one is born among humans, at the time of death, they will see such signs.
They will see a great rocky mountain appearing like a shadow upon their body, and at that time, the person will think:
"This mountain may fall upon my body."
"Therefore, he moves his hands, wishing to ward off this mountain; when his brothers and kinsmen see this, they say he is touching empty space.

Having seen this, he further sees the mountain as if it were white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*); he then ascends this white cloth and sees red cloth. As death approaches in succession, he again sees light. Because of his limited practice, he becomes confused at the moment of death, and all forms appear to him like those seen in a dream."
Because the mind is deluded, one sees one's parents in union through desire; seeing this, a thought arises and one gives rise to perversion.
If a male is to be born, one sees oneself engaging in sexual intercourse with the mother and perceives the father as an obstacle;
if a female is to be born, one sees oneself engaging in sexual intercourse with the father and perceives the mother as an obstacle.

At that time, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) perishes and the consciousness of the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) arises; through the sequential conditions of dependent origination, it is like a seal being impressed: when the seal is destroyed, the impression is formed.
This is called dying among humans and being reborn again among humans; this is termed the fourteenth intermediate existence.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the fifteenth continuity of the path of existence within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
When one passes away from among the gods and is reborn again in the heavens, there is no suffering or affliction."

Unlike other devas who, at the time of their death, suffer the pain of separation from what they love and fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, this deva does not lose his own bodily ornaments, nor does another deva take his seat.
He does not witness various signs of suffering, nor is there the birth of another deva in the place where he sits; rather, upon the end of this life, he is reborn among superior devas.
If, after the end of life in the realm of the Four Great Kings, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one perceives delightful and superior signs;
one hears the sounds of various songs never heard before, and one sees that all objects of the five desires are entirely sublime and wondrous.

Passing away in succession, they perceive the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). There, they hear the various sounds of celestial maidens who hold lotus flowers in their hands; their physical forms are exceptionally sublime, and the rivers, ponds, flowing waters, and groves are wondrous and exquisite—things never seen before, appearing as if in a dream.
In this state, the intermediate existence perceives such things.
If it is near to the existence of birth, it is like waking from sleep and seeing true colors.
It sees the objects of the five sensory pleasures complete and perfect—things never seen before—and exclaims with a cry of wonder: "Aha!"
"How rare is this! Such a place as this has never been seen before; I shall go to such a place.
Having thought this, he was immediately reborn among the devas.
This is called the fifteenth path of continuity for the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the sixteenth path of continuity for the existence of the intermediate state?
How does such existence come to be?

If one descends from a higher heaven to be born in a lower heaven, one perceives that the lotus gardens, groves, and flowing ponds there are all inferior; having seen this, and being afflicted by hunger and thirst while longing with thirsty yearning for what they desire, they immediately go to be born there.
Thus, although they are born together in the heavens, there are two kinds of intermediate existence (antarābhava) and two kinds of birth-marks arise.
This is called the sixteenth path of continuity for intermediate existence.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is called the seventeenth continuity of the path in the intermediate state?
What are the signs when one born in Pūrvavideha is reborn in Aparagoyānī?"
"What further characteristics do those born in Aparagoyānī have when they are reborn in Pūrvavideha?
O sons of gods!
Those born in these two continents as one another share the same single characteristic."
At the time of death, one sees a dark cavern; within this cavern, there is a flash of red lightning that hangs down like a banner, sometimes red and sometimes white.

When the person sees it, they reach out with their hand to grasp it. At that moment, the person's present *skandhas* (aggregates) immediately cease. By catching the banner with their hand, they successively follow the banner and enter this cavern, taking on an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
When approaching the intermediate state of rebirth (*antarābhava*), one sees the phenomena of taking birth, as previously described.

Alternatively, one may see two oxen or two horses engaged in passionate union; immediately, a mind of desire arises, and once that mind of desire has arisen, one undergoes rebirth into the intermediate state.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
This is called the seventeenth intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). "You should know this!"
Having understood this Dharma, do not be negligent.
Why is this? A person who is negligent cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor can they obtain benefit from worldly dharmas.
Such heedlessness brings no peace or happiness at all;
if one wishes to be liberated from suffering, one should exert oneself and abandon heedlessness.
Whether gods or humans, those who possess wisdom should renounce heedlessness.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
This is called the seventeenfold continuity of the path of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which proceeds without interruption. You all should abandon all negligence.
O Sons of Heaven!"
In this way, there is a continuous succession of the path through the seventeen intermediate states of existence (*antarābhava*); you all should contemplate and observe this.
Having observed it, you will know it as it truly is; having known it as it truly is, you shall diligently cultivate vigor.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

Among twenty dharmas, increasing gradually from one, I have already explained to you in succession the seventeen intermediate states (*antarābhava*) through which the continuity of existence proceeds."
Now, for your sake, I shall explain the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
What are these eighteen?
Sentient beings are infinite, their faith and understanding differ, their dispositions (*gotra*) are of infinite kinds, and they fear the three faults.
The three groups of sentient beings, the three kinds of mastery, and subtle inclinations;
their various activities, various natures, various karmas, various paths, various sufferings and pleasures, various forms, and various predominances.

The nature of the mental realm of all sentient beings is vast and manifold; while their physical bodies differ from one another, within these immeasurable mental realms of sentient beings, there are, when briefly summarized in broad terms, eighteen types of evil.
Driven by the transgressions of the mind, and because the realm of the mind is vast, there is the cyclic wandering through the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans.
To summarize all phenomena, they are subsumed within the eighteen [elements].
Within the nature of the first realm, desire is predominant; among devas and humans, the mind of desire is predominant.
Among all female ghosts and female animals, as well as those capable of transformation, pride is predominant and malice is predominant.
Because of their state of anger, their desire is diminished; these are called animals, whose nature belongs to the initial realm of non-humans.

Within the animal realm, there are further those with much desire and an intensified lustful mind, such as the peacock, the *kukkuta* bird, the pigeon, the dove, the chicken, the sparrow, the goose, the duck, the ruddy sheldrake, various bees, fish, and the *kalaviṅka* bird.
Their nature is characterized by much desire; this is called "superior desire.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods, what is the second mental-nature element?
Among animals, which animals are said to have moderate desire?

They are those such as cats, dogs, pigs, oxen, water buffaloes, camels, elephants, horses, mules, donkeys, crows, ravens, eagles, vultures, starlings, and other such birds; these are called those with moderate desire.
This is called the second realm of the nature of mind.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the third realm of the nature of mind?
Among the animals, which animals are said to have inferior desire?

They are the lion, tiger, rhinoceros, wolf, dog, bear, brown bear, jackal, leopard, fox, and wildcat; as well as the makara fish, the kṣayā fish, the kilisamara fish, the makara fish, and the tundamara fish.
Such categories as these, engaging in desire at the proper time and not engaging at improper times, are called "inferior desire.
This is the third realm of the nature of mind. "O sons of the gods!
Among the animals, there are immeasurable kinds, immeasurable places of birth, and immeasurable names; they cannot be fully described and cannot be known by counting.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the fourth element of the nature of mind?
Among animals, which animals predominantly possess a mind of hatred rather than a mind of desire?
This fourth element consists of lions, tigers, wolves, dogs, snakes, yellow monkeys, rhinoceroses, leopards, bears, brown bears, horned owls, crows, eagles, *śiṃśumāras*, wild boars, and the like.
Thus, when sentient beings have a preponderance of anger, this is called the fourth realm of mental nature.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the fifth realm of mental nature?
Among animals, which animals are said to have moderate anger? They are as follows:
oxen, horses, water buffaloes, *kalaviṅka* birds, *sālendraka* birds, *garuḍa* birds, peacocks, chickens, pheasants, cats, mice, and so forth—these possess a nature of moderate anger.
This is called the fifth realm of the nature of mind.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the sixth realm of the nature of mind?
This refers to the nature of inferior anger.

Those who are said to have inferior anger include: geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, fish-eating white birds, *kūṭīra* birds, sparrows, *sāla* birds, donkeys, deer, turtles, tortoises, rabbits, hedgehogs, mountain crows, wild geese, and frogs.
Such as these are called minor anger;
this is known as the sixth realm of mental nature.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the seventh realm of the mind-nature?
Among ghosts and spirits, those who possess supernatural powers and act with desireful minds—
such as the Asura deities, who belong to the category of animals and whose nature of desire is particularly excessive— are termed "those of superior desire."
This is called the seventh realm of the nature of mind.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the eighth realm of the nature of mind?
If one is a hungry ghost who feeds on fragrances, they are called "Moderate Desire.
This is known as the eighth realm of mental nature.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the ninth sphere of the nature of mind?
If one is a *prēta* who craves [food] or a *prēta* who eats discarded food, this is called inferior desire.
This is called the ninth sphere of the nature of mind.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the tenth realm of the nature of mind?
The Garuḍa-footed devas and others are called 'those with inferior desire'; they abound in anger and delight in strife, constantly wishing to fight with the asuras."
Because of that anger, the desire-mind becomes thin.
This is called the tenth realm of the nature of mind.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the eleventh mental nature realm?
It refers to the Māladhara devas, who possess moderate desire, moderate hatred, and moderate neutrality; this is called the eleventh mental nature realm.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the twelfth realm of the nature of mind?
It is the realm of the *Sadāmattas* (Ever-Intoxicated), whose nature is characterized by a predominance of desire and a scarcity of anger, and who do not engage in strife or contention."
The gods of the Yāma Heaven have much anger and little desire.
These are called the twelve mental natures and realms.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the thirteenth realm of mental nature?
It refers to all those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three who predominantly possess a desirous nature and have little ill-will; this is called the thirteenth realm of mental nature.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the fourteenth realm of mental nature?
It refers to the people of Uttarakuru, whose minds have little ill-will and whose nature is predominantly characterized by desire; this is called the fourteenth realm of mental nature."
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the fifteenth realm of mental nature?
It refers to the people of Aparagoyānī, who possess an abundance of both anger and desire; these two natures are equal. This is called the fifteenth realm of mental nature."
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the sixteenth realm of mental nature?
For the people of Pūrvavideha, both the mind of desire and the mind of hatred are present together; this is called the sixteenth realm of mental nature."
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the seventeenth realm of the nature of mind?
It refers to the people of Jambudvīpa who possess various natures, various conducts, and various inclinations; this is called the seventeenth realm of the nature of mind."
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
What is the eighteenth realm of the nature of mind?
Even though all other devas and the inhabitants of hell undergo suffering and affliction, they still give rise to desire when they see women who are illusions produced by karma."
Because they are produced by karma, the desire-minds of such hell-beings are likewise as numerous as those of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
The mental nature of sentient beings—such realms, such supports, and such inclinations—is what is called, in brief, the nature of all eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
In this way, wherever there is desire and anger, there is a mind of delusion; it is through the conditions of delusion that greed and anger arise.
If one is free from a mind of delusion, then greed and anger do not exist.
Due to a deluded mind, one either craves or feels hatred.
Thus, O sons of the gods!
This is called the differentiation of the three kinds of faults; because of reliance on these faults, there are immeasurable differentiations.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods! There are eighteen elements (*dhātu*), namely:

the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element."
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
These are called the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

If gods or humans contemplate these eighteen elements in this way, they will be able to guard against heedless conduct regarding sensory objects; for such [heedlessness] is the cause and condition for the delusion of all foolish, ordinary beings.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!

There are nineteen abodes for those who are heedless, subsumed under two categories. These are: sixteen abodes consisting of the four dhyānas—excluding the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—and three abodes in the desire realm: hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
Those who undergo much suffering are comprised within the hells; this is the nineteenth.
"Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
As previously stated, the persons of the four dhyānas and sixteen bases, as well as those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—this constitutes the twentieth."
"Thus, because birth and death are not subdued, they each differ from one another.
Or it is said that there are ten kinds of restlessness and regret.
At that time, having heard the Lord Śakra, King of Devas, speak this Dharma, the assembly of devas praised Śakra with these verses:
“The Heavenly King has taught this Dharma, The most supreme state of tranquility;
I now receive this Dharma, And practice it out of fear.”
If a person can preach the Dharma for the benefit of others,
that person is like a parent, showing them the city of Nirvana.
If one explains even a single verse of the wholesome Dharma for the sake of another, [the merit is immeasurable].
Thus one becomes a good guide, revered by all sentient beings.
This which has been taught by the Heavenly King is the Dharma of immeasurable value;
through this Dharma one attains tranquility, for it is not for the sake of other worldly treasures.
Material treasures return to impermanence, while wholesome dharmas increase wisdom;
worldly things are subject to destruction, yet wholesome dharmas are eternally firm.
If one practices in accordance with the Dharma, it will follow one through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
Though there be various kinds of precious objects, they cannot reach the next world.
Various kinds of wealth and treasures can be forcibly plundered by kings,
thieves, water, or fire, but they cannot plunder the treasure of the Dharma.
At that time, after the sons of the gods had praised and made offerings to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, they stood before him with reverence.

Then Śakra, having subdued the gods, demonstrated to the sons of the gods that all celestial pleasures are entirely impermanent, subject to transformation and decay, devoid of self, and destined for cessation.

At that time, the assembly of devas all conceived a sense of weary detachment and returned to their respective palaces to enjoy celestial pleasures. Eventually, when the karma accumulated through the pursuit of such pleasures was exhausted, their lives ended and they passed away; yet, they did not fall into the evil realms, but were reborn among human beings. There, they were foremost in accordance with the Dharma, practicing self-cultivation, delighting in wandering through forests and wilds, and fearing future existences.
Having heard the Dharma, they left the household life to study the Path; some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some attained Sakṛdāgāmin, some attained Anāgāmin, and some attained Arhatship.
By the power of the causes and conditions of having heard the Dharma in the past.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 34 [and] Scroll 35.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Fourteen: The Eleventh Section on the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the ground where the Heaven of the Thirty-three resides."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that the twenty-ninth level of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named Mandāra.
By what karma do sentient beings are born in this heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

there is a virtuous person who practices in accordance with the Dharma; with an upright mind, they do not afflict living beings; seeing the reality of karmic results, they maintain the precepts purely, always delighting in upholding them, and are free from flattery and crookedness.
Like refined pure gold, it is clear and free from defilement.
One practices with right view and upholds the good precepts, fearing future lives, practicing generosity, and cultivating merit.

This refers to seeing a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna who seeks to sever the bonds of Māra; when it is the heat of midsummer and he is sweating and parched with thirst, one gives him honey syrup or offers a whisk and fan.

Thus, a virtuous person does not kill living beings. Should they see a hunter using nets to capture various birds such as peacocks and mountain pheasants—whether the hunter has already captured them, is keeping them, is about to kill them, or is using the birds for amusement—they do not participate in such acts.
When such a person sees this, fearing that it might be killed, they ransome its life and release it back to its original place so that it may find peace and happiness.
This is called benefiting sentient beings through non-killing.
What is non-stealing? What is the relinquishing of stealing?
It is to perceive the retribution of even the most subtle karmic actions and thereby give rise to fear.

If this person who maintains the precepts sees willow branches or honeyed syrup by the bank of a river or pond, or in another place, intended as offerings for travelers, they will not take them nor drink from them because of their mind of loving-kindness, even though they are parched with thirst.
This is called non-stealing.
Such a person, at the end of life, will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Having been born there, they will possess all desires in full: the sounds of the five kinds of music, sporting in the gardens and groves, where various birds emit wondrous sounds, as do the bees amidst the lotuses and the cries of the swans.
The various trees in the groves are adorned with the seven treasures.
The lotus ponds are filled with fragrant water as clear as lapis lazuli, wherein they sport and play.
From within the mountain peaks—seven-jeweled flaming light and seven-jeweled stone caverns—and from the gold, silver, crystal, and indranīla blue jewels, various kinds of birds emit wondrous sounds.
Thus these various birds have wings adorned with the seven treasures, and their diverse songs are delightful to hear.
All the hosts of devas accord with one another, and their immeasurable beautiful voices pervade the groves and forests.
Within that grove, delightful food and drink flow from the river; when the gods see them, they give rise to great joy and exclaim, "How marvelous!
Thus, within the forest, there are various colors and various adornments that grace their bodies.
Together with a retinue of hundreds of thousands of jade maidens, he sports and enjoys pleasures, experiencing various delights within the heavens.
His body is radiant, and his majestic virtue is supreme.
Thus, having experienced the karmic retribution of his deeds, the devaputra was surrounded by celestial maidens as he enjoyed pleasures, his heart filled with joy.
Having thus enjoyed these delights, he thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the grove surrounded by railings adorned with Vaiḍūrya jewels."

Adorned with various jewels, the forest was filled with the wondrous songs of diverse birds; all the celestial hosts were filled with joy, enjoying themselves amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments as they sported in the grove together with the gods and goddesses.
Within the grove there is a pond called Clear Water (*Vimala*), pure and lovely.
The hosts of devas sport and enjoy themselves in this lotus pond.

At that time, the newly born devaputra, together with a multitude of celestial maidens, desired to go to this grove. Then, seeing the devaputra from afar as he sang, danced, and laughed while walking slowly, the devas went out to welcome him. They proceeded to the Clear Water Pond, where they enjoyed themselves and took pleasure by the side of the pond.
By the power of the pond, everything appears according to whatever the sons of the gods conceive in their minds.
If they think of color and fragrance, swarms of bees appear in full abundance.
If they think of celestial drink, celestial drink immediately arises.
If one contemplates the *sūtra* [or "the necessary"], its color, fragrance, and flavor are likewise complete; it is soft, pure, and clean, with a color like that of the full moon.

If one contemplates the forest trees, there immediately arise various groves of trees endowed with the foremost merit, covered by nets of bells; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce wondrous sounds like the music of the *gandharvas*.
Furthermore, the host of devas thought to themselves,
"We shall enter the pond.
Having formed this thought, they immediately entered the pond and submerged their bodies, plunging deep within.

He saw that the various kinds of precious jewels formed railings around the pond, adorning the jeweled palace; there were couches made of pure gold, white silver, lapis lazuli, blue gems, crystal, and assorted jewels, spread with celestial garments.
The devas and apsaras sport and enjoy themselves within that pond in countless varieties of ways, never knowing satiety with the pleasures of the five senses.
Free from envy and jealousy, they love and respect one another, sporting, singing, dancing, and enjoying their delights.
Having emerged from the pond water, he proceeded again to the Nyagrodha Grove; within that grove were many birds, and it was fully adorned with lotus ponds and groves.

Immeasurable flocks of birds emit wondrous sounds that fill the entire grove; these trees are constantly endowed with various kinds of radiance, and the forest is replete with manifold merits, adorned with numerous lotus ponds.
The hosts of devas possess bodies of radiant light and are fully endowed with various meritorious realms, experiencing celestial bliss.
"The foremost pleasure of foolish worldlings is that which consists of the amusements and enjoyments of deva sons and deva daughters."
Foolish worldlings, ensnared by the net of celestial maidens, wander through the cycle of birth and death, taking pleasure in one another.

After having long enjoyed these pleasures, they proceed once more to the palaces on the peaks of Mount Māta; ascending the summit of Sumeru, they climb the mountain peak together with the heavenly maidens.
A gentle breeze blew upon their robes, and they turned to follow the wind, all ascending together to the peaks of Mount Māta.

At that time, the devaputras beheld this palace, exceptionally wonderful and exquisite, adorned with lotuses and mountain peaks resplendent with the light of the seven jewels, perfectly corresponding to the fullness of the mountain's merits.
The peaks of Mount Māta are lofty and precipitous, wondrously magnificent and beyond all comparison.
Upon these peaks, they frolic, sing, dance, and enjoy themselves in pleasure.
Having already experienced such pleasure, they behold a great radiance that surpasses their original appearance.

Within the mountain peaks, which were previously endowed with a brilliance like that of the sun, there now appears a different light that shines upon the peaks; once this light has shone, it exceeds [the former] by a hundred thousandfold.
When the Son of Heaven saw this, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he immediately closed both eyes and remained with his head bowed.
Why was this? Because he had never before seen such radiance.

That light illuminated them, but before long it vanished; just as when the people of Jambudvīpa see a celestial fire descending, all sentient beings are filled with great terror, so too were the sons of the gods when they beheld this radiance.
Not long after their fear subsided, their minds returned to a state of tranquility; once the fear had vanished, they all deliberated together upon this matter:
"For what reason has there appeared such a rare phenomenon that caused all of us gods to feel fear, yet it was extinguished before long?"
At that time, the assembly of devas, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall and went with the celestial maidens to where Śakra was.
Upon seeing the Lord of Devas, they prostrated and made offerings, surrounding him on all sides as they stood there in reverent attendance.

At that time, the assembly of devas dwelling near Śakra, the King of Devas, engaged in song, dance, and play, adorning themselves with various lotuses; they rejoiced and laughed as the entire host of devas performed song, dance, and play before Śakra. However, the assembly of devas on the Mandāra grounds neither sang nor danced nor played, nor did they offer songs of praise to Śakra, nor did they engage in conversation or discourse with the other devas.
At that time, Śakra addressed the host of devas dwelling in the Mandārava grove: "O sons of gods!
For what reason do you not sing, dance, or sport?"
At that time, the assembly of devas dwelling in the Mandara realm addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"In our abode, we have seen an unprecedented and marvelous event, the likes of which we have never heard before."
At that time, the Heavenly King addressed the devas dwelling in Mandarava:
"What rare and extraordinary thing have you seen such that you say it is the first you have ever seen or heard of?"
At that time, the gods of the Mandara realm said to Śakra:
"O Heavenly King!

While we were sporting upon the peaks of Mount Mādhava and had ascended those mountain heights, we saw a great radiance descend from above, and all the mountain peaks were set ablaze with great flames."
"Having seen this matter, I find it strange and unprecedented.
I do not yet know what causes and conditions there shall be.
Upon hearing this, Śakra, after reflecting for a short while, addressed the assembly of devas:
"Such a thing indeed exists!
I have already heard of such a matter before.
Having heard this at that time, I immediately asked the World-Honored One:"
“By what causes and conditions has this extraordinary and rare event occurred?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed me, saying: “Kauśika!
"You have already closed the gates to the evil realms; do not give rise to fear.
All conditioned phenomena are encompassed by birth and death, which is to say, they are impermanent.
Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you."
These are the gods of the Yāma Heaven who have reached the end of their lives.

The physical dimensions, forms, and the pleasures experienced by the gods of the Yāma Heaven exceed those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by more than a hundred thousand times; yet, because their karma is exhausted, they pass away and fall from above, descending through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas from this place.
Their light becomes thin and sparse, like a lamp about to go out, its radiance faint and meager.

Even when the devaputras of Yāma fall from the midst of the sky at the time of their decline, their light is still faint and meager in this way; how much more so is it for the great manifestations of light of the devas of Yāma, which cannot be fully described?
The radiance of the Yāma Heaven cannot be beheld by the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Why is this? Because it is not within their sphere of experience.
Kauśika! The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven cannot behold the radiance of the Yāma Heaven.
Because the hosts of the Yāma Heaven possess three kinds of karma, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven speak only of two kinds of karma.
"I have heard such words from the World-Honored One; what you now perceive is likewise so, and I shall now speak for your sake.
When the assembly of devas heard these words, they conceived a sense of weary detachment toward the five desires.
"This is the sign of the passing away and death of the gods of the Yāma heaven.
Their light has departed from here by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas and descends from the sky; do not be afraid."
At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, spoke these verses for the assembly of devas:
"According to such great pleasure, And likewise according to such wealth and joy,
One will certainly fall, And undergo such great suffering."
Karma yields a corresponding fruit; thus has the World-Honored One taught.
Because the karma is superior, its fruit is likewise so.
The dharma of successive excellence is obtained just as the karma was acquired.
The supreme continuity of bondage, its fruit is likewise so.
Because this majesty is supreme, one knows that karma is decisively victorious;
because karma is superior and preeminent, one obtains a superior life, form, and strength.
All the hosts of devas, because their karma is exhausted, must eventually fall back;
they are like scorched and withered seeds that, though sown, will not sprout again.
Contemplate the continuity of the mind-nature: every thought-moment is like the flame of a lamp.
The mind perishes moment by moment, and all karmas are likewise.
Because the causes of karma are impermanent, they must inevitably perish;
as for that which is called "eternal bliss," such a thing cannot be found.
If pleasure were not impermanent, it would neither arise nor cease.
One who possesses wisdom should depart from the realm of craving;
one who is weary of and detached from sensual desire shall attain the joy of freedom from craving.
"All phenomena subject to outflows are impermanent, suffering, and unreal;
if one attains the state of no-outflows, it is then called the bliss of immovability.

Having thus spoken truthfully to the gods of the Mandara realm, Śakra, Lord of Devas, further comforted those gods of Mandara, causing them to return to their own abode, and addressed the assembly of devas:
"You gods, at all times you must not be negligent.

At that time, the gods prostrated to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and returned to their respective dwellings. Having reached their own abodes, they experienced the pleasures of the five senses; amidst gardens adorned with various kinds of ornaments and the sounds of the five musical instruments, they enjoyed celestial delights.
Until their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they die and fall back, wandering according to their karma into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they are born in places of peace and happiness; they may become great men who are loved and remembered by all, free from illness and affliction, and born into noble lineages or the families of great elders, constantly experiencing peace and happiness until old age and death.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
The thirtieth abode of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is called Upariṣṭha.
By what karma are sentient beings born in this heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who practice in accordance with the Dharma, who believe in the retribution of karmic actions, who conduct themselves with right view, who practice giving to cultivate merit, and who observe a portion of the precepts;
at first they observe many portions, and later they observe them all.
While traveling on the road, he gave alms of boots and sandals to the Sangha and offered a water flask.
He refrained from killing and stealing.
When some frontier tribesmen captured a person intending to kill them, this observer of the precepts ransomed that person and caused them to be released.
If one is a king who, upon seeing wealth acquired through the conquest of wildernesses, fears that he would be committing theft and therefore does not accept his share,
this is called non-stealing. What is non-killing?
Whether such a person upholds the precepts or is a king, if they see an evil person wishing to come and harm them, because they uphold the precepts, they do not take that person's life.
Such a person, fearing the retribution of karmic results, is reborn after death in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the stage known as "Higher Conduct."

Having been born in this heaven, by virtue of his wholesome karma, he is attended by three thousand celestial maidens. These hosts of goddesses adorn their bodies with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments; holding various musical instruments such as lutes and zithers, as well as various perfumes, they sing various songs and praises to the deva-son, approaching him with hearts full of desire.
When the sons of heaven saw this, they too felt a sense of joy toward each other and the celestial maidens, and together they proceeded to the Garden of Constant Joy (*Nityapramuditavana*).
That grove was adorned with trees of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, gold, and silver, and its park was beautified by various flowing springs, lotus forests, and ponds.

It is adorned with immeasurable rivers, covered above by various nets of bells, and completely graced by immeasurable flocks of birds that produce immeasurable varieties of exquisite, harmonious, and elegant sounds.
Thus adorned in various ways, the celestial sons and daughters within the groves illuminate one another, increasing their exquisite beauty.

Within the grove is a mountain named *Vihāra* (Play), composed of the seven treasures. There are countless species of deer made of various colored jewels, upright and magnificent: their flanks are of red lotus-jewels, their backs of pure gold, their bellies of white silver, their crests of pure gold, their hooves of coral, and their horns of crystal.
There may be some of one color, namely golden; or there may be two colors—golden and silver—all various colors serving as adornments.

All the deer within the forest trees followed the movements of the celestial hosts, emitting various exquisite sounds like the songs of celestial maidens; thus did the multitude of deer sing with these manifold wondrous voices.
After these hosts of devas have experienced such immeasurable pleasure, they proceed once more to the summit of Mount Sumeru. Upon that summit there is a great river named Valley.

Riding upon various celestial palaces, accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments and the five kinds of music, endowed with supreme desires and the highest joy, and possessed of majestic power, they proceeded to the mountain peaks, valleys, and rivers of Mount Sumeru.
Amidst these various riverbanks, they sport and enjoy themselves.

Amidst flowing waters, within lotus groves, and in the midst of gardens and forests, their songs are pleasing to the ear; they experience sensual pleasures and all give rise to joy, mutually loving and respecting one another.
There are many sons of gods and hosts of goddesses, their bodies anointed with fragrant flowers and their heads adorned with flower garlands.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they experience celestial bliss; by the power of that karma, they sport in accordance with their inclinations.

As is appropriate for a deva, he experiences celestial bliss that is beyond analogy; I shall now describe but a small portion of it, for all the people of the world cannot fully describe it. Why is this?
It is beyond analogy, for such celestial pleasures have no counterpart.
By means of the causes of virtuous karma from observing the precepts among human beings, one experiences such pleasure.

Within this heaven, one enjoys the pleasures of the five senses until the beloved roots of virtuous karma are destroyed and exhausted; at the end of life, one falls back and wanders according to karma, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If born among humans, one will experience supreme peace and happiness in a land near mountains and marshes, abounding in rivers and forests; there, one will become either a great king or a high minister, possessing the highest majesty and virtue.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The thirty-first stage of the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods is named Majestic Virtue and Countenance.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

There are sentient beings who possess the foremost pure mind; they practice giving to cultivate merit, uphold the seven types of precepts, and do not associate with evil friends. Their observance of the precepts is untainted as they protect and maintain their merit, always being diligent and energetic, with a single-minded and straightforward heart like refined, genuine gold.
How many kinds of precepts does one protect?
They are namely: non-killing and non-stealing.
What is meant by non-killing?

If a land is in turmoil and its people slaughter one another, this person who upholds the precepts, out of fear of breaking them, would rather give up their own life than harm others or incite others to kill; this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?

If a kingdom is devastated by ruin and chaos, and all the people compete to seize the property of others, this person who upholds the precepts—fearing the breaking of his vows—even when starving and on the verge of death, would rather sacrifice his own life than take another's property.
What is giving? To what field of merit does one give?
One gives by making offerings to the Buddha or at a place where the Dharma is being taught.
First, as for the cultivation of the mind: one whose intention is characterized by right view will, at the end of life, be reborn in the celestial realm of Majestic Virtue and Radiance (Tejovatī).
Having been born in this heaven, they will be completely encircled by a halo of majestic light, possessing the most supreme and excellent form.
They experience corresponding causes and effects due to their virtuous karma:
their ears are delighted by the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments;
their noses are delighted by the constant fragrance of māndārava flowers, kūsṇaśeya flowers, blue lotuses, and flowers of the seven precious gems.
The tongue obtains various kinds of most excellent and sublime flavors and drinks from the Sudharmā Heaven;
the eyes behold various kinds of most excellent and sublime forms of seven-jeweled mountains and valleys;
the body obtains various kinds of supreme and wonderful celestial garments that are without warp or woof.
Their bodies were anointed with the fragrance of *utpala* flowers.
Thus, by virtue of their wholesome karma, these sons of gods achieved such excellent fruits.
They were surrounded by a retinue of a thousand celestial maidens, and the gardens were magnificently adorned; those groves were so exquisite and wonderful as to resemble molten gold.

Precious bells were suspended from branches of gold and silver; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced exquisite sounds for their enjoyment. Furthermore, they heard various songs and praises, experiencing the highest bliss.

Adorned with celestial garlands and celestial garments, they sport among the mountain valleys, beholding immeasurable varieties of colors: beryl jewels, gold, silver, blue gems, and the great king of sapphire gems.
Upon the crystal mountain peak, he sees his own body as clearly as in a bright mirror.
At that time, the newly born deva, surrounded by celestial maidens, enters the precious mountain peak and beholds hundreds of thousands of bodies, with a joy increased a hundredfold.
The hosts of celestial maidens were likewise filled with joy and exclaimed in wonder:
"How upright and magnificent is my body!
Now I shall constantly delight in the sounds of the five kinds of music and enjoy the bliss of the five celestial sensual desires."

The hosts of celestial maidens felt great joy in their hearts; they went from one mountain peak to another mountain peak, and from one mountain valley to another mountain valley, sporting and enjoying themselves throughout them all.
“Intoxicated by the poison of craving, their mental activities are as distorted as those of one suffering from madness; thus it is with these celestial hosts, ruined by negligence.

Together with the celestial maidens, they roam upon the mountain peaks, partaking of various foods and the flavor of *sudhā*, listening to the songs of diverse birds, and experiencing immeasurable pleasure within the groves.”
Delighting in one another, they roam together with a single mind, their thoughts fixed upon each other.
Thus sporting, adorned with celestial garments, garlands, and necklaces, they all go together to the Saṃkalpa Garden, or to the rivers, streams, and lotus ponds.
In this river, red *utpala* flowers cover its surface entirely, adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
At that time, the hosts of devas on the riverbanks eat the nectar of the flowers, or drink the supreme and exquisite celestial beverages, sporting and enjoying themselves with the celestial birds.
Beholding them brought joy to their eyes.
At that time, the various devas were intoxicated by the poison of craving; drinking celestial wine again, they grew a hundredfold more so.
The fire of craving burned the fuel of the five desires; parched by sensual longing, they knew no satiety, all of them bound by the net of desire.
For example, it is like a person who has violated the laws of the state and is bound by the king;
meanwhile, all the hosts of devas behold immeasurable hundreds of thousands of objects of desire and, seeing them, go toward them and sport therein.
Having finished their play on the banks of the Pāṇḍuka river, various birds take delight and enjoy themselves among the lotuses, padmas, utpalas, and kumudas within the river.
“In the pond there is a bird named Crimson Water (*Citravāri*), whose body and two wings are made of the seven treasures and whose body radiates light.
Seeing that the hosts of devas delight in heedless conduct, he spoke this verse for the sake of the sons of gods:
‘The hosts of devas are constantly heedless, And the celestial bird is likewise so;’”
The celestial hosts and the flying birds are neither superior nor inferior to one another.
If those in the heavens delight in unrighteous conduct and do not seek the bliss of liberation,
then such celestial hosts are no different from birds.
If one is free from heedlessness and practices in accordance with the Dharma,
one becomes supreme in the world through that very heedfulness.
Whether it be celestial beings enjoying their play or even the birds, it is the same for them.
The celestial hosts are equal to the birds, without distinction;
yet because their karma is superior, the manner of their rebirth is also superior.
If one enters into unwholesome states, one cannot be born in a favorable realm.
If one does not realize that birth and death, and all things, are impermanent,
then even if one belongs to the host of devas, such a person is as ignorant as a beast.
The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and likewise the suffering of death are all thus.
Through union and separation, one undergoes suffering in succession.
If a person possesses wisdom and beholds the stainless Dharma, they shall excel in this world; such is not the conduct of your negligence.
If a person awakens to suffering and distress, and thereby gives rise to pure wisdom,
that person is called a "deva," not you who are attached to desire.
Friends and brothers repeatedly experience the pain of separation through love.
If one does not weary of birth and death, one is no different from the birds.
Though the transgression of drinking alcohol is grave, one may still sober up from intoxication;
yet heedlessness cannot be awakened from—therefore, one should distance oneself from it.
Heedlessness destroys a person, causing them to revolve through the five realms of existence;
therefore, freedom from heedlessness is the foremost and most excellent means.
Even a single day of drunkenness causes a person to lose their clarity of mind.
Those who are heedless and intoxicated wander through hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
if one is free from heedlessness, one attains the state of non-extinction;
if a person delights in heedlessness, they will constantly undergo birth and death.
If a person seeks their own benefit, they should abandon heedlessness;
for heedlessness gives rise to afflictions—this is what the Great Sage has taught.
When birds act with heedlessness, it is because of their frivolous minds as animals.
“O gods, why are you negligent and unable to abandon it?
Thus, by virtue of their past wholesome karma, these celestial birds teach and benefit all the gods.
These celestial birds are like parents, providing benefit and instruction;
yet because these hosts of devas have minds of negligence, they do not perceive the beneficial Dharma spoken by the birds.
"At that time, the devas again proceeded to the Mātala Forest.
With various sounds of music and mutual affection and respect, they went to the Mātala Forest to sport and enjoy themselves."

That grove consists entirely of trees made of the seven treasures, their branches and leaves touching one another; upon these trees, amidst celestial jewel flowers, immeasurable swarms of bees sport and play.
When the hosts of devas saw this, they all gave rise to joy and sported, sang, and danced together with the throngs of celestial maidens.
The songs of the celestial maidens pervaded the groves, and as their echoes resounded throughout the groves, they were all like the original singing voices.
The voices of birds and bees were perfectly harmonious, pervading Mount Sumeru.
Since the nature of Mount Sumeru is inherently delightful, with these sounds present, it became twice as magnificent.
At that time, whenever the hosts of devas see or hear [this], they all experience bliss and their great desires are fulfilled.

Together with the celestial maidens, they sport and enjoy pleasure; adorned in various ways and endowed with exquisite forms, they engage in play, song, and dance, experiencing celestial delights. This continues until their wholesome karma is exhausted, at which point their lives end and they fall back, transmigrating according to their karma into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Having residual wholesome karma, if born among humans, they experience the foremost pleasure.
Their minds are constantly joyful, their countenances are upright and handsome, and they are loved and respected by all people; they may become kings or great ministers.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
There is a celestial abode in the thirty-second stage called Majestic Radiant Wheel (*Tejorāśicakra*).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

These sentient beings cultivate merit with a virtuous mind; they are without flattery or deceit, contemplate the true Dharma, benefit all sentient beings with a mind of right view, and place their faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
With a mind that is supple and gentle, he practices meritorious deeds.
If he sees that a monastery or a Buddhist stupa has fallen into ruin, he repairs it for them.
Or if a stupa or monastery is consumed by fire, he exerts all his strength to rescue and protect it, not begrudging even his own life.
Or, seeing the precious treasures and property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha being consumed by a great fire, they sacrifice their own bodies to save them.
Or, seeing someone being burned by fire, they enter the flames to rescue them.
Out of compassion, one is able to perform such meritorious deeds that are difficult to accomplish.
What is meant by not killing and not stealing?
If one sees items left behind by the road—whether gold, silver, or other treasures—one should take them and proclaim:
"Whose property is this? If someone says, "This is my property," one should question them regarding its characteristics; if they are correct, it should be returned to them.

If no one claims it, one should carry it about for seven days, proclaiming it day after day. If there is no owner who claims it, these precious objects shall be entrusted to the king’s ministers, the governors, and the magistrates of the prefectures and counties.
If kings, ministers, governors, magistrates, or local officials see a person of merit and do not take these goods, but instead later present them to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,
this is called non-stealing.
What is meant by "not killing"?
If, while traveling on a road, one sees various insects, ants, earthworms, moths, shrimp, frogs, or other small creatures, one should avoid these creatures and take a distant path.

Because one protects sentient beings with a mind of compassion, believes in the retribution of karmic results, understands the faults of birth and death, and contemplates the dharma of arising and ceasing—
this is called non-killing.

This person who maintains the precepts, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a good destination, in the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods where they dwell upon the wheel of majestic splendor and radiance.

Having been born in that heaven, by virtue of their foremost wholesome karma, they enjoy bliss adorned on all sides by that wheel of majestic splendor; it cannot be fully described, but I shall now speak of a small portion of it.
His body is pervasive with majestic power and blazing radiance like the shining sun, yet it does not dazzle the eyes due to his virtuous karma.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, he experiences pleasure within palaces made of gold, lapis lazuli, and blue indranīla gems, where he sports, dances, and sings.
Furthermore, there are gardens and groves where flowers are always in full bloom, and many birds emit wondrous sounds; both the sights and the sounds are delightful to behold and hear.
There is also another grove named Opening-and-Closing, wherein in every part of the various groves, whether eyes are opened or closed, one constantly perceives radiant light.
In this grove, he sports and enjoys pleasures together with various celestial maidens, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
He then proceeds to the Citra grove, where he sports upon mountain peaks with hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens amidst the sounds of song and dance.
Because of the sound of the singing, all the various resonant voices produced were like that singing itself.
If there were other devas sporting and enjoying themselves among the groves who heard this singing, they would immediately leave those groves and say to one another,
"What kind of sound is this?"
"He is just like a second Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Having emerged, he immediately beheld the newly born deva-son; seeing him, the celestial host gave rise to a heart of joy and went out to welcome the deva-son, conceiving a sense of wonder.
Having seen the Son of Heaven, they all felt great joy and addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, O Son of Heaven!
Come to our place."
"You are the most excellent among the host of devas;
within this celestial realm, you are like a second Śakra, King of the Devas.
At that time, all the other devas quickly went to where the son of the deva was, and having arrived, they surrounded him.

At that time, the sons of the gods sang, danced, and laughed in play; with hearts full of joy, they surrounded the lord of the gods and all went together to the Nandana Grove to sport and enjoy themselves.

Surrounded by various celestial maidens who sang, danced, and sported with him, the deva-son turned his gaze back for a moment and saw that the entire host of devas was following behind him. His heart filled with joy, he asked the celestial assembly:
"Where do you wish to go?"
Then the assembly of devas said to the newly born son of heaven:
"Now you should go to the delightful place of the Nandana Grove, where you may enjoy supreme pleasures through the merits of the five senses."
At that time, the devaputra, having never before seen such a marvelous grove, proceeded at a leisurely pace toward the Nandana Grove.
That grove was resplendent, its radiance shining everywhere like the solar orb; upon seeing this grove, the newly born devaputra felt further joy and entered within it.
He saw that this forest was of infinite varieties and exceedingly delightful.

Within a single grove, it possessed fourfold majestic splendor, and there were the sounds of countless hundreds of thousands of birds; some produced subtle and exquisite melodies, while others called out, saying:
"Welcome, O Devaputra!"
Some [birds] circle about, leaping for joy; thus are the gardens and groves adorned by these celestial birds.
Furthermore, in another place, amidst the mountain valleys, the sound of the river issues forth as various wondrous melodies, with banks made of pure gold.
Within those waters, there are many various geese, ducks, and flocks of birds that emit exquisite sounds.
Having seen this river, he sports and enjoys pleasures with immeasurable celestial maidens on its banks, delighting in the music of the five instruments and experiencing joy.

Having thus experienced pleasure, they proceed again to the forest of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*). There they see such trees whose radiance is like that of the moon, or perhaps like that of the sun.
Beneath these trees, the newly born deva-sons enjoy the pleasures of the five senses in a manner that cannot be fully described.
Having experienced such immeasurable bliss, they proceeded toward the lotus pond.
Upon reaching the lotus pond, the celestial hosts surrounded them as if attending upon Śakra, and all were filled with joy.

Having enjoyed themselves in the lotus ponds, they proceed once more to the summit of Mount Kūṭāgāra, where they dance, sing, and sport; there the devas and apsaras entertain one another, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
Reaching the summit of the peak, he saw a lotus pond atop the mountain where immeasurable flocks of birds and hosts of devas together enjoyed supreme bliss.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they possessed the highest majesty and splendor.
Together with the hosts of devas, they sport and enjoy pleasures within the groves, the *cintāmaṇi* groves, and the groves of supreme flavors.
Many varieties of birds adorn these forests, wherein they play and experience delight.

At that time, after the deva-son had long enjoyed pleasures with the hosts of devas upon the High Peak, he again beheld a newly born deva-son on his own level; struck with wonder, he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deva-hosts.
Furthermore, together with the host of devas, he proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall and beheld Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
At that time, the newly born devaputra arrived at the Sudharmā Hall.
He saw that the Sudharmā Hall was adorned with various kinds of precious jewels, with railings made of many jewels, as previously described.
At that time, Śakradevendra, seeing this devaputra, felt joy arise in his heart and spoke these verses:
"By the fruit of wholesome karma, you have now been born in this place;
yet within this celestial world, when your life ends, you shall surely fall."
When karma is exhausted, one falls back down, being born again according to the nature of that karma;
if you now cultivate wholesome karma, you will have no cause for regret later.
Through heedlessness and attachment to sensual pleasures, one exhausts all wholesome karma.
Because time is sovereign, when karma is exhausted, one falls into the evil realms.
Seeing other devas fall and perish, how can you not feel weary of it?
I too shall surely fall; of this there is no doubt.
If one fears the future, one should practice in accordance with the Dharma;
when such a person’s life comes to an end, there will be no fear of the evil realms.
But for those who are heedless and devoid of dread, whose minds engage in what is unwholesome, [there is only suffering].
Later one will experience great anguish, And at the end of life, the fever of regret.
All the hosts of devas must inevitably decline and pass away;
Knowing that desire is impermanent, Do not act with negligence.
The five desires deceive sentient beings; they are deluded by desire and ensnared by the net of desire, constantly falling into hell.
Having understood these decays and afflictions, one should act for one’s own benefit.
Because the mind has been tamed, at the end of life there is no regret.
Bitten by the serpent of desire, like the surging waves of the ocean,
the deluded person walks the path to death, consumed by the fire of desire.
Loved ones and brothers, dear friends—all are parted;
at the time of death, a multitude of sufferings gather, which cannot be fully described.
Once the time of death has arrived, it is like falling from a mountain cliff.
Great power is unavoidable; it leads people into evil realms.
Great power seizes and holds men, capable of destroying the world.
Having understood this, the hosts of devas should abandon heedlessness.
The various sense faculties give rise to craving and attachment, yet one knows no satiety;
the heart of love constantly increases, like clarified butter poured into a fire.
Through such various gateways, the world exists because of craving.
They revolve through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
agitated by birth and death, their minds are deluded by suffering and affliction.
Once one knows how to leave behind craving, one shall reach the supreme path.
The courageous one cuts off craving; free from sorrow and without affliction, they attain peaceful sleep because they have been able to leave craving behind.
If a person’s mind is always joyful and practices wisdom, [they shall likewise find peace].
Not bound by the net of craving within birth and death,
if a person’s mind is signless and they grow weary of and renounce sensual desire,
they will leave behind defilement and the wilderness to reach the shore of peace and bliss.
If a person does not loathe suffering, And does not rejoice even upon attaining pleasure,
Such a person is liberated from both suffering and pleasure, And is able to reach the city of Nirvāṇa.
If there is one who practices cultivation, Constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion,
One who understands cause and effect can thus escape the net of suffering.
If a person does not engage in conceptual discrimination, they will be free from the faults of mental discrimination;
being free from all such faults, they can attain the unsurpassed path.
Where there is union, there is separation; where there is flourishing beauty, there must be decay.
All who possess life return to death; such is the nature of all phenomena.
As the gods are about to fall away, the thought of their own demise manifests before them in every moment.
One should know such dharmas as these: do not practice negligence.
The fool lacks skillful means and constantly seeks sensual pleasures;
it is like seeking oil from sand—it simply cannot be obtained.
If a person delights in heedlessness, they shall find no peace;
through heedlessness they undergo great suffering, as firm as the roots of a tree.
I have spoken this truth for you: the meaning of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
You should reflect well upon this, lest you later feel regret.
If there is a foolish person who does not accept the instruction of a virtuous teacher,
when the distress of the end of life arrives, their heart will surely give rise to the fever of remorse.
Billions, trillions, and countless *koṭis*, nayutas,
and *asaṃkhyeyas* of devas— All have been deceived by heedlessness.
Even the great kalpa-fire of impermanence Shall burn this king of mountains.
How much more so for the bodies of the gods, Which are like foam on water or the trunk of a plantain tree.
All conditioned phenomena are subject to change; The nature of all that is born is impermanence.
Within such phenomena as these, Happiness cannot be found.
"In this way, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, skillfully taught the Dharma for the benefit of the newly born deva-son; yet, because of his negligence, the newly born deva-son did not accept a single word."
At that time, Śakra, knowing that he would not accept [the invitation], remained silent.

Then the newly born devaputra joined his palms above his head, paid homage to Śakra, and together with the hosts of devas, engaged in song, dance, and play; groups of hundreds and thousands returned to their own abodes, sporting everywhere in gardens, groves, and flower ponds.

Surveying his dwelling place, he beholds streams, flowering ponds, and sites adorned with various birds whose songs are delightful, as well as various mountain valleys with wheels of jewel-light and flames; together with the hosts of devas, he experiences immeasurable bliss.

With the mind shrouded by heedlessness and the heart attached to desire, one is consumed by the fire of lust; from the five sense-faculties arise five kinds of flames, yet dwelling within the cave of the mind, one does not realize that one is burning oneself.
Together with the celestial maidens, they indulge in heedless play, concealing their enemies within what they call friends.
Thus they experience pleasure until their wholesome karma is exhausted; then, driven by the flow of karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If one possesses wholesome karma and is born among human beings, they will constantly experience peace and happiness, possess supreme physical beauty, and be endowed with immeasurable merit. They will be born into a great lineage and be cherished by all people; whether becoming a king or a high minister, they will live a long life in whatever place they are born, experiencing unbroken bliss until the end of their lives.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:"
The thirty-third level of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is named Pure.
By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that heaven?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:

Because these sentient beings possess a virtuous mind, they have faith in cause and effect, observe the sevenfold precepts, give rise to compassion toward all sentient beings, do not associate with evil friends, do not converse with wicked people, and always place their trust in the Triple Gem.

Their mind is tranquil, free from hindrances, and undistracted; they do not engage in unwholesome dharmas, nor do they associate with base or evil persons; toward all sentient beings, they always speak words of love and words that are beneficial and timely.
One should make offerings to the Dharma teacher, constantly listen to the True Dharma, and practice giving according to one's ability.
Even when on the road, one should not take another’s grass or leaf with a thieving mind; this is called non-stealing.
What is meant by not killing?
Whether it be a frog or a *tuṇḍuka*—a two-headed snake—even when seeing them with one's own eyes, one does not give rise to the intent to kill. Why is this?
All sentient beings cherish their own lives; for this reason, one should maintain single-minded mindfulness, look with clear awareness while walking, and not harm any living being.
How does one refrain from killing?
If one has a disease and fears losing one's life, one might purchase meat to treat the illness.

If, during hot weather or after a long period of time, worms have developed within the meat, one would rather lose one's own life than remove these worms, for the sake of protecting the lives of the insects.
In this way, such virtuous persons feel dread even upon seeing a minor transgression;
how could they ever steal?
Such virtuous persons bring peace, happiness, and benefit to all sentient beings.
If there is dried cow dung in a field, marsh, or grove that he knows belongs to another, he will never take it intentionally, fearing he would commit theft.
Such a person abandons the intent to steal; upholding the precepts, he is free from defilement, untainted and unclouded, remaining aloof from chaff and straw.
This person who maintains the precepts, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a happy realm called the Ground of Purity.
Thus, having been born in this heaven, the devaputra experiences supreme bliss.
The radiance of his body surpasses that of the sun; his majestic virtue is blazing and intense, and he experiences immeasurable celestial bliss.
By virtue of his wholesome karma, he enjoys such happiness.

Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with divine garlands and celestial garments, they sported within groves of the seven precious gems together with those maidens, experiencing the foremost pleasures.

He then proceeded to the Mṛgadāva (Deer-Park) grove; seeing that this garden was lovely and extraordinary, he felt great joy and asked the gods, "For what reason is this grove superior to all other gardens?"
The mountain caves, ravines, valleys, and cliffs were adorned with flowers and fruits; there were rivers, springs, lotus ponds, and flowing streams, where countless birds emitted wondrous sounds.
Throughout that mountain, there were many deer made of various jewels, exquisitely adorned and most excellent.
At that time, the elder and former devas addressed the newly born deva-son, saying:
“Devaputra, you should know!
As we have heard in succession in the past, the deva-sons of previous ages spoke thus:”
"There was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Mūrdhaja, who ruled over the four continents and enjoyed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pleasures, yet he never felt satiated with his desires."
By the power of their sovereignty, they have come to this deva realm.
Proceeding from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, they have successively arrived at this heaven.
Measured by human reckoning, they have spent immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years here, experiencing sensual pleasures without ever reaching satiety.
Having arrived at this heaven, he sat sharing a seat with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and together with Śakra, they went out to play.
Perceiving the immeasurable merits within this grove, they entered the grove to enjoy themselves and experience pleasure.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, this grove remains exceptionally sublime even to this day, surpassing all other groves.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja sat together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in this celestial realm; however, because his own karma was exhausted, he fell back from the heavens.
"I have previously heard this matter handed down from the ancient devas; it was not something I saw for myself that this grove remains complete even until the present time.
Having heard this, the newly born deva-son rejoiced, became free from doubt, and experienced immeasurable pleasure of the five desires through the sounds of the five musical instruments.
“In the forest there is a bird named *Abhirati* (Delight). By virtue of its past wholesome karma, it speaks these verses for the sake of the sons of the gods:
‘Because of the conditions of craving, The mind of desire knows no satisfaction.
Much desire arises from craving; The heart and mind can never be filled.’”
For all classes of sentient beings, the law of death is ever present;
even by means of every possible expedient, one cannot obstruct this law.
Having long enjoyed immeasurable pleasure, one will inevitably decline and pass away.
Therefore, O sons of the gods, you should practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Only the Dharma can save; it can lead one to the good realms.
Through the Dharma one attains life; without the Dharma, there is no life.
If one can love and delight in the Dharma, And practice in accordance with the Dharma,
One will attain a state of happiness from that happiness, And shall no longer behold manifold sufferings.
If one does not love and delight in the Dharma, But delights in practicing what is contrary to the Dharma,
Then one falls into hell, constantly undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Such is the realm of the heavenly kings; among all the places described, there is none other than this for those dwelling in the remaining lands.
In these Trāyastriṃśa heavens, there is not even the slightest place where one can escape the realm of death, due to the nature of impermanent karma.
One should understand this causal condition: all various phenomena are impermanent.
The Dharma taught by Śakra could not be received by the gods.
The wise Kauśika, whose body was like a wondrous treasury,
who loved the kunda flower, and who had abandoned the evil multitude;
“As a parent to all the devas, I have well expounded the True Dharma;
yet the foolish devas do not accept my instruction, because their minds are distracted by negligence.

When the celestial bird had thus spoken this verse for the sake of the sons of the gods, at that time the sons of the gods—being by nature negligent—did not give rise to a sense of weariness. Negligence shrouded their minds, and they did not accept his instruction, returning instead to attachment to sensual pleasures.
They contemplate only the present and do not contemplate the future.

While experiencing the pleasures of the five desires within this heavenly realm, they remain until their wholesome karma is exhausted; at the end of life, they fall back and, driven by the flow of karma, descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
