If there remains further karma, one will be born among human beings, constantly experiencing happiness, delighting in the practice of wholesome dharmas, being foremost in physical beauty, and being loved and cherished by all people.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; apart from these thirty-three grounds, there are no other grounds.
He thinks to himself:
"There are only these Trāyastriṃśa gods and no other lands.
This is the realm of Śakra, King of the Gods; it is through the power of the King’s merit and the King’s sovereignty that there is nothing else."

Thus he contemplates that the multitudes of the second heaven arise through a continuity of similar causes and effects; the mirrors of karmic results are entirely congruent, with each and every stage being distinct from the others.
Having completed this investigation, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment toward the terrors of immeasurable birth and death.

Seeing immeasurable suffering within the perilous realm of saṃsāra—a place oppressed by the pain of separation from the beloved, the pain of encountering the hated, and the pains of old age, sickness, and death; a place where beings are swept away by violent torrents—he conceives a mind of weary detachment.
Alas! The world is subject to great suffering; within this place of immense peril—birth, old age, sickness, and death—one is submerged and remains unaware, knowing not how to seek deliverance.
Thus, in this cycle of birth and death, there is not the slightest happiness; it is a phenomenon characterized by impermanence, decay, and transformation.

Sentient beings, out of ignorance and delusion, fail to know or perceive this, and due to the conditions of their bodies, they commit many evils. Although the body is destroyed, the bondage of karma does not perish.
At that time, having contemplated these matters, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"Though one provides various internal offerings— Couches, mats, and bedding— This body must inevitably perish; No one can protect it."
Failing to acknowledge kindness, they seek to harm whenever they find an opportunity;
such wise ones regard themselves as their own enemies, and thus do not create evil karma.
It is the dwelling place of decay and illness, where all manner of sufferings converge.
An impure and foul accumulation—therefore it is called the "body.
When observed by the wise, the sign of death is ever-present;
life does not abide for even a single thought-moment, but in an instant returns to annihilation.
This body grows old with every passing thought; it never increases.
Deluded by ignorance, one relies on youth to give rise to arrogance.
Relying on wealth to give rise to arrogance does not benefit oneself.
All wealth and possessions are lost; one's evil karma burns oneself back.
If one does not practice giving, there will be no reward of happiness;
though wealth eventually comes to an end, one guards it out of the madness of greed.
If one gives away cherished wealth to teachers and elders, that wealth shall be secure; for the miser, wealth is like grass.
One who gives with a pure mind is like a guide for the blind.
In this world and in future worlds, it can protect those who are timid and weak.
The seven kinds of merit from upholding the precepts are indestructible words;
the precepts can protect a man and cause him to be reborn in the heavens above.
The one of foremost supreme wisdom constantly desires to slay the afflictions;
such a person is liberated from all bonds and reaches the state of non-retrogression.
There is a sea of great peril and difficulty, and these three are the sturdy rafts.
"If one attains the stainless mind, / Then one can reach the other shore.

Thus the bhikṣu contemplates the fruits of giving, morality, and wisdom; seeing them as they truly are, desiring to reach the ultimate truth, he undergoes these three contemplations and attains the eighteen stages.
Within all cycles of birth and death, his mind attained weary detachment; he practiced with diligence to seek nirvana and did not dwell within the realms of Māra.
When the terrestrial yakṣas learned of this matter, they informed the celestial yakṣas.

The Ākāśa-yakṣas informed the Four World-Protectors; the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings informed the Trāyastriṃśa devas; the Trāyastriṃśa devas informed the Yāma devas; and so on, successively passing up to the Ābhāsvara devas, as previously described.
The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Thirty-Five;
The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Thirty-Six.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
3. Yāma Heaven (36–63), Chapter 15: Surveying the Heavens, Part One: The Yāma Heaven.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma and with unshakable diligence, having already observed the Heaven of the Thirty-three, further examines what other heavens exist above those Thirty-three, where beings dwell with more excellent and wondrous radiance, power, and longevity, and whose karmic rewards surpass those of the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
He sees, hears, and knows:
above those Trāyastriṃśa gods, there is further a hall called Yāma, which excels all others in its dharma, its karmic fruition, and its sublime radiance.

By means of three kinds of precepts, one is born in that Yāma Heaven; these three are namely: abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. These are well-cultivated, without deficiency, without flaw, and without breach—firm and inviolable.

The precepts beloved and praised by all noble ones yield a reward that is eternally cool; they lead progressively until one attains nirvana. They are like a virtuous kinsman and serve as a bridge for crossing the ocean of birth and death.
If there are those who ascend that bridge of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they will be able to cross the great ocean of birth and death and reach the further shore.

That practitioner further contemplates and perceives with precision: that monk observes the seven types of ethical discipline, wherein the karmic fruits and laws of retribution are categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, as previously described.
Having observed this correctly, he further observes the realm of the Yāma devas upon Mount Sumeru: what constitutes their abode, and what is their radiance?
To what height does it extend?
Examining in this manner, he perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowledge:

those who delight in and frequently practice such virtues as refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, and refraining from sexual misconduct; who are able to maintain the precepts themselves and teach others to maintain them, thereby benefiting both themselves and others—such beings are born in that heaven.
"How high is that Yāma Heaven?
He perceives, hears, and knows:
"It is sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas high."
That Yāma Heaven is twice as high and distant above Mount Sumeru.
How many grounds does that Yāma Heaven have,
and how high is it in total?
"What constitutes earth?
He perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowing:
"That entire earth consists of thirty-two [parts], each five thousand yojanas in height."
Those gods of the Yāma Heaven dwell in the void, just as masses of clouds in the sky are sustained by the wind.
Likewise, these terrestrial roots are sustained below by water, and that water is sustained by the wind called Yāmavāyu, which sustains the Yāma Heaven just as it sustains the masses of clouds.
What are the thirty-two stages? First is named Power;
second is named Traveling by Means of the Vehicle.
The third is named Wandering in the Clouds;
the fourth is named Accumulated Burden;
the fifth is named Mental Characteristics.
Sixth is named Endowed with Mountain Trees;
seventh is named Vast Conduct;
eighth is named Accomplishment.
The ninth is named Victorious Radiance Enclosure;
the tenth is named Right Practice;
the eleventh is named Constant Joy.
The twelfth is named Increasing Dharma;
the thirteenth is named Constant Joy;
the fourteenth is named Joyful Practice.
Fifteenth is named Various Mixtures;
sixteenth is named Adornment of the Mind;
seventeenth is named Blown by the Wind.
Eighteenth is named Sublime;
nineteenth is named Whirling Foam;
twentieth is named Bank of a Hundred Radiances.
Twenty-one is named Mountain-Gathering Practice;
twenty-two is named Moon-Mirror;
twenty-three is named Measure of Recollection.
Twenty-fourth is named Cchagalaśīrṣa;
twenty-fifth is named Vimokṣadhyāna;
twenty-sixth is named Mānamānottara.
Twenty-seven is named "Descending into the Lower Realms";
twenty-eight is named "Staircase Practice";
twenty-nine is named "Mirror of One's Own Body."
The thirty-first is named Pride-of-the-Body Radiance;
the thirty-second is named Superior Practice;
the thirty-third is named Forest Radiance.
These are the realms of that Yāma Heaven, where the King of the Yāma gods is named Mūśalūta.
Just as the Great King Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, is named Kauśika, so too is the King of the Yāma gods there named Mūśalūta.

The King of the Yāma Heaven follows the practice of the Dharma; compared to the extent of the divine power and pleasures of Śakra, the King of the Devas, that of the King of the Yāmas is a thousand times superior.

The body of the King of the Mūśalūta Heaven measures five yojanas, and its radiance is most excellent; the body of Śakra, the King of the Devas, measures one krośa—such is the bodily measure of the King of the Yāmas, Mūśalūta.

The power of a single part of the body of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, cannot be matched by even a hundred thousand combined efforts of Śakra, the King of Devas; such is likewise the case with the causal relationship between karma and its fruit.
Having thus observed, the bhikṣu spoke these verses:
"Just as one who carries but a small burden does not sink when crossing water,
so too a person with little evil karma ascends upward and does not sink down."
"Just as a bird’s wings are firm and strong, it travels through the sky without obstruction;
so too, those whose observance of the precepts is steadfast are reborn among the devas.
Thus that bhikṣu contemplates the causes and effects of karma regarding the fruits of pleasure in that Yāma Heaven.
In that Yāma Heaven there are four great mountains, all of which are ten thousand yojanas high.
What are the names of these four great mountains?
The first is named Pure (Vimala).
The second is named Stainless;
the third is named Greatly Pure;
the fourth is named Inner Image.
These are called the four great mountains.
Furthermore, there are various other distinct mountains, of immeasurable kinds, with immeasurable colors, immeasurable forms and shapes, and immeasurable merits.
Thus, possessing many thousands of diverse mountains and abounding in celestial flowers, the Yāma heaven is adorned in this manner.
Within its thirty-two grounds, there are various mountains, various adornments, and numerous rivers; it is surrounded on all sides by lotus ponds and hundreds of thousands of groves.
A certain kind of tree possesses fragrance, color, and flavor;

its lotuses have various tastes. Just as the superior and wondrous things found among the mountains, rivers, lotus ponds, and gardens of Śakra and the Thirty-three Heavens cannot be matched by the mountains, rivers, forests, or lotus ponds of the human realm, so too the superior and wondrous things of that Yāma Heaven cannot be matched by those of the Thirty-three Heavens.
Why is this? Because causes and effects are manifold.

He possesses immeasurable wholesome karma and merit; the fruits of the causal conditions of his hundredfold meritorious deeds and the transformations produced by his wholesome karma cannot be fully described.
For what reason is it impossible to describe?
Because the movements and transformations of the various powers of karma are so manifold.
Such karmic fruits cannot be described by any sentient beings.
Through all wholesome karmas, one attains birth by transformation in the Yāma Heaven; such various [details] cannot be fully described here.
Of the celestial retributions of that heaven, only one part in a thousand can be told.

Why is this? If one upholds the precepts, one will certainly attain the fruit; this is the truth as it is spoken. If a person who upholds the precepts hears this, their mind will advance; if a person who cultivates wisdom hears it, they will advance with tenfold strength.
By what causes and conditions is it known that there are such distinctions in the observance of the precepts?
Those who observe the precepts are born in those heavens, while those who cultivate wisdom attain nirvāṇa.
Thus the merit of wisdom and ethical discipline has been explained. If one already knows such fruits of ethical discipline and such fruits of wisdom, they will give rise to this thought:
"If even the mere upholding of ethical discipline yields such results, how much more so for cultivating wisdom? I shall attain it in this way."
Having heard this, that person practices with diligent effort and speaks thus:
"There is the fruit of karma within existence.
Furthermore, through various causes and conditions, he explains the existence of phenomena in different ways:
"Those devas dwell thus for a long time in the heavens, experiencing supreme bliss without any hindrance; yet in the end, they still undergo decline and do not attain mastery."

Moreover, sensual desires among humans have many faults; they offer little joy and little flavor, are unstable and shifting, and are never peaceful or secure. They are capable of destruction and bring about immeasurable punishments, terrors, and calamities.
"Regarding those deities spoken of through such causes and conditions, I shall further explain them through other distinct causes and conditions:
Those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) hold this view:
'All things are created by Maheśvara; they are not obtained through karma, and no one else knows this.'"
To refute those non-Buddhists, he thus taught the existence of karmic results.
Karmic results truly exist; they truly arise from causes; they are not produced by another, nor do they exist without a cause.

All causes and effects yield results that correspond to them; cause and effect are similar. One does not obtain a dissimilar result from a dissimilar cause: a wholesome karmic cause does not produce birth in hell, nor does an unwholesome karmic condition produce birth in the heavens.
Nevertheless, because they have cultivated the karma of giving, morality, and wisdom through such causes and conditions, they are certain to be born among the gods.

Thus it is said that the two kinds of experience—suffering and pleasure—among the gods cannot be fully described; as for the pleasures in the heavens, even a single portion of that karma is beyond analogy, and what has been stated here is but a small fraction.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, next observes the Yāma heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
within that Yāma heaven there is a region called Power (Bala).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows through vision and hearing:

if there is a person who maintains the precepts, who feels fear upon seeing even the slightest evil as small as a mote of dust, whose mind is upright, who is neither sycophantic nor deceitful, who does not afflict others, who possesses right view and is not perverse, and whose thoughts are free from delusion.

Contemplate that all things in this world are impermanent, suffering, and without self, and maintain mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; refrain from killing and stealing, as previously described.
Furthermore, one does not engage in sexual misconduct:

the mind remains detached, finds no pleasure in it, does not practice it, and does not perform it; even regarding the sexual acts of birds such as pigeons, one does not look upon them, nor does one entertain such thoughts even when about to sleep.
If a person acts in this way and also instructs others, that person speaks to them regarding the fruits of karma, saying:
"Do not act in this way; if you do so, you will certainly enter hell."
Thus, that person truly perceives the results of karma and, fearing karma, refrains from violating the wives of others and so forth.
By virtue of such wholesome karma, that person is born in that place, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.
As soon as they are born there, those celestial maidens immediately sing with heavenly voices at the moment of their birth.
When the devas suddenly hear this, it is as if they have awakened from sleep; thus they are born by transformation at the very first moment that the musical sounds emerge.
Regarding pleasant sounds, one attains mindfulness in this way:
that vocal music possesses eight qualities, complete with all virtues;
the first is speech.
Second is appropriateness;
third is sweetness;
fourth is harmonious blending.
Fifth, it is consistent;
sixth, it is profoundly excellent;
seventh, it is universally cherished.
Eighth, the sound reaches a million *yojanas* without obstruction; it accords with the words of the Dharma and is pure, untainted.
Thus, endowed with these eight qualities of merit, this sublime and wondrous voice awakens those who perform wholesome deeds.
“He emits a wondrous radiance from his own body, extending five yojanas in width, in colors of blue, yellow, red, and white like a rainbow in the heavens.
At the moment that celestial son was first born, there was a swirling radiance, as majestic as the halos surrounding the sun and moon.”
Once he has arisen, he is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who follow him; thus, he possesses a heart of supreme joy.
The devaputra and the celestial maidens follow one another as they proceed in this manner to enter what is called the Forest of Radiance (*Prabhāvana-vana*).

Furthermore, in that realm of the Yāma Heaven, there are flowers that do not wither; those flowers are named Eye-Amitābha (Eye-Nectar) Flowers, Unfading Fragrance Flowers, and Exquisite Color and Fragrance Flowers.
Upon hearing the names of these flowers, the mind experiences joy; such is the power of those flowers.

Wherever their names are spoken, from the midst of the empty space in those very places, those fragrant flowers emerge—namely, the Moon-Surpassing Flower (*Candraprabha*) and the Constantly Revolving Flower (*Nityaparivartin*).
When those devas think of it, flowers emerge from the celestial trees with a sound and grow; they move according to the devas' actions, following wherever those sons of gods intend to go.
Thus, that devaputra, while upon that tree, travels through the air; within those flowers, he proceeds according to wherever his mind inclines.
Just as a second deva of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven moves about in its celestial hall, so too does that Yāma devaputra move about within the flowers.
Its radiance blazes brilliantly as it constantly surveys all places; in a single instant, it perceives everything everywhere without ever becoming weary.
Furthermore, in that place there is a tree called "Delightful to Behold," which is most lovely.
Within that tree, what is there that is delightful?
Having entered its interior, one experiences celestial bliss.
Amidst the groves and lotus ponds, there is a tree known as "Accordant with All Desires."
By the power of that tree, whenever those devas call it to mind, all the most excellent things within the entire realm of the Yāma Heaven appear upon that ground.
By the power of those trees, they experience bliss within them; the eightfold musical sounds are beyond measure or calculation.
Among them is a tree named Gandhavāsin (Fragrance-Drifting); it possesses such power that whatever fragrance the deva-son recollects, such fragrance issues forth from that tree.
Furthermore, there is a tree there called the Flower-Fragrance Tree; within that tree, they enjoy themselves as if in a chamber, no different from being at play.
There are excellent groves and lotus ponds, where those gods of the Yāma Heaven experience pleasure.
Those Yāma devas dwell within those trees, which possess the wondrous colors of blue, yellow, red, and purple, and are fully endowed with all varieties of fragrances and hues.
When those gods enter [the trees], every kind of exquisite color arises, and the bodies of those gods likewise take on such colors.
The color of his body and garments completely vanished, and only the colors of the trees appeared.
Furthermore, there was a tree named "Moving Through Space" (*ākāśagāmin*).
In the blink of an eye, it traveled hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* through the sky, proceeding according to its thought.
The radiance of those trees was no different from that of the sun.

Yet those devas, riding upon those immeasurable and variously wonderful trees, traveled through the air, surrounded and followed by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who adorned their bodies with garlands, incense, and ointments.
That deva’s body possesses a supreme radiance.

Before that deva stand various celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with diverse and exquisite garments; they laugh joyfully and perform songs and dances, the sound of their singing pervading and filling immeasurable yojanas in every direction.
Among those celestial maidens, the celestial son is handsome; let me describe him briefly.
As he has obtained his state through virtuous karma, like the moon among the stars, so too is the celestial son handsome.
"Yet that deva-son, possessing a thousandfold superior merit, enters the fragrant grove accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments, singing, dancing, and sporting.

Hundreds of thousands of species of birds pervade that forest, which is adorned with immeasurable rivers, ponds, and exquisite lotuses; it is exceedingly delightful, surpassing the radiance of hundreds of thousands of suns. This is merely a partial illustration based on perceptible phenomena."
It is just as if a lovely garden, flowing stream, pond, or lake among humans, adorned with lotuses, were not even one-sixteenth part of the splendor of the celestial realm of the Four Great Kings.
Thus, even the delightful groves of the abodes of the Four Great Kings do not equal even a sixteenth part of those in the abodes of the Thirty-three Gods.
Thus, the delightful groves of the Heaven of the Thirty-three do not equal even one-sixteenth part of the delightful groves of the Yāma Heaven.
Thus, in this sequence, because virtuous karma is preeminent, and because there exists ever-increasingly superior and excellent virtuous karma, the groves and gardens are so lovely.

Even if a person among all sentient beings possessed excellent wisdom, were single-minded and focused without any other activity, and were endowed with skillful means and corresponding eloquence, they would still be unable to describe even a fraction of them.
Why is this? Because it is not within the sphere of experience of all people.

In that place, it is likewise not within the sphere of the minds of all people; even if the second Heaven of the Thirty-three, together with King Śakra, were to speak for a hundred thousand years, they could not describe the matters of the enjoyment of pleasure experienced by a single level of the Yāma devas.
Why is this? Because it is not within their sphere of experience; as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have never seen it nor heard of it, they are unable to describe it.
Regarding those virtuous deeds, I shall speak of but a single portion, for it is impossible to describe them all in their entirety.
All these wholesome karmas, when fully accumulated, will certainly result in inconceivable happiness.
Of the matters of experiencing such happiness and of that delightful joy, I have described only a single portion.
For example, suppose a highly skilled painter or his disciple were to paint either the moon or the sun upon a wall or similar surface.

Yet that painter would ultimately be unable to depict its radiance or its majestic power; he could not make it move, nor cause it to shine, nor make it cool, nor make it scorch—he could only paint the circular form.

The same applies to the description of the Yāma Heaven; it speaks only of pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), yet it cannot describe the nature of that desirable pleasure, nor can one grasp its actual power.

Whether it be those radiances, those groves, those sublime virtues, the songs or music, that beauty, the pleasures of sensory objects, the circles of light, or the various enjoyments shared with the nearby celestial maidens, one can only describe them by way of faint analogies and partial comparisons.

Furthermore, in that celestial realm, within the places of play and delight, that deva-son possesses an infinite variety of sensual pleasures, immeasurable provisions for sustenance, and gardens adorned with splendor.

Having thus observed these regions, his mind is drawn by the merits of the objects of the five desires; moved by the power of those objects, the mind fails to remain steady, turning toward defiled conceptualization and being swept away by the river of craving. Everything seen by his universal eye appears entirely attractive.

Having seen this, that deva-son then proceeded toward the forest named Endowed with Immeasurable Desires, which was adorned with various lotuses in flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, and filled with the songs of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of birds.
Having reached that grove, they beheld within it various wonders such as they had never seen before.
Once they and their celestial maidens had arrived there, they saw within those lotus ponds and rivers sands of pearls and birds of gold and silver, whose wings were all the color of blue beryl gems.
On that riverbank, various exquisite trees adorned the shore, and within them the devaputras sported and enjoyed themselves.
Having thus experienced such pleasures, the devaputra next proceeded toward the forest named Ratnatīra, surrounded by a great multitude of devas and apsaras.
He beheld that excellent grove, a region of ground radiant with the seven precious jewels, where, at every mountain peak, flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, there were lovely lotuses.
Hundreds of thousands of peaks adorn the mountain valleys, and every portion of that ground is embellished with exquisite jewels.
By the power of their virtuous karma, those devas behold the celestial maidens and sport together with them, wandering about and experiencing pleasure.
Due to their virtuous karma, as a result of those roots of goodness, they obtain corresponding fruits in immeasurable varieties; thus they experience immeasurable and diverse pleasures.
Having enjoyed such superior delights through the merits of the five sensory desires, those devaputras then proceed toward the place known as the Realm of Śakras’ Discourse.

"Having experienced various celestial pleasures in that place, their minds are again drawn by beloved objects; their intellects, deluded by the power of conceptual discrimination, do not abide in those perceived objects."

That mind-monkey, having eaten the fruit of celestial pleasures, becomes intoxicated by that fruit; because it perceives the celestial maidens and gives rise to craving and delight, it moves constantly without ceasing.
By what wind is it blown, causing it to revolve perpetually?
Among those hosts in the Yāma Heaven, their faculties are never satiated.
The pleasures of their sensory realms are of infinite varieties, exceedingly lovely, and can never be seized or plundered by others; others have no share in them, nor can they be destroyed by others.
Furthermore, exquisite jewel lotuses sprout everywhere; in such and such ways they engage in various sports, and in such and such ways they experience various recollections.
Within each of those jewel lotuses, these are obtained as the fruit of wholesome karma.
If that Lord of Gods, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, thinks thus:
"I shall sit upon that lotus and travel through the air together with the hosts of devas."

As soon as that thought arose, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with the host of devas, flew away through the air; all the devas likewise flew in this manner, their bodies remaining perfectly still.

At that time, all the devas sat upon lotus flowers in the void, amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, singing, dancing, and joyful laughter; thus they wandered about, experiencing celestial delights and the merits of the five desires.
Seated thus within the lotus flower, that deva experiences celestial pleasures.
Just as when the sun is about to rise or has just set, the sky over the human world becomes magnificent and entirely crimson, so too is the magnificent radiance of that deva’s lotus flower.

All those gods experience supreme pleasure; having experienced that pleasure, they next proceed toward the mountain named Sliṣṭaka within the grove named Kovidāra-vana, ascending its summit for the sake of experiencing further delight.
When those celestial hosts have reached the mountain peak, there are immeasurable rivers, ponds, and lakes adorned with the seven treasures, whose radiance surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns.
There are many handsome devas and devīs; the trees of that heaven, adorned with the radiance of immeasurable seven-jeweled gems like the sun, beautify it.
Having reached Mount Slightha, they sport and enjoy themselves upon that supreme mountain, wandering together.
Descending from that lotus, he ascends once more to the mountain named White Peak for the sake of play and pleasure.
Only then does he reach the abode of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, where he is accompanied and surrounded by various celestial maidens as he approaches the assembly of devas.

Upon seeing him, those hosts of devas came forward to welcome him; their hearts filled with joy, they sang, danced, and played as they proceeded together toward Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

"One obtains the fruits of one's own karma; because those wholesome karmas are of inferior, middling, or superior grades, the pleasures of the devas are likewise of inferior, middling, or superior grades. Likewise, their exquisite forms are of inferior, middling, or superior grades; their food is likewise of inferior, middling, or superior grades; and their happiness is likewise of inferior, middling, or superior grades."
In this manner, even the pleasure experienced by Śakra, King of the Devas, does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the pleasure experienced by the most inferior and lowly among the Yāma devas.

The pleasures enjoyed by that King Śakra are already beyond description; how much more so, then, can the pleasures resulting from a hundredfold performance of deeds and the cultivation of threefold meritorious karma be described?
Those devas possess only such abundant wholesome karma.
Such wholesome karma brings constant joy to the minds of those who observe the precepts, and it is of immeasurable kinds.
Thus it is said that they experience great happiness within the Yāma Heaven because they still harbor longing for existence.

Furthermore, in this way, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, possesses hundreds of thousands of various distinct recollections and is endowed with immeasurable varieties of merit; being beyond all analogy, he experiences every form of happiness.
On Mount Sligh-kau on the night-ruling Yāma Heaven King Mūśaludha, having experienced pleasure within those lotuses made of the most excellent seven jewels, he again beheld a lotus and thought thus:
"I shall enter into that great lotus; once I have entered it, all the celestial hosts shall together experience pleasure."
At the very moment of that thought, those lotus pedestals expanded and grew vast; due to their virtuous karma, there were many such great lotus pedestals, and they all entered within them.
Within that flower pedestal there are many hollows, and from within those hollows a great radiance issues forth.

Inside that lotus there is moreover another deity never seen before, whose radiance extends beyond a hundred yojanas in all directions, and whose light is endowed with immeasurable varieties of color.
When the Yāma Heaven King Mūsuludha and the assembly of devas saw the radiance, they were struck with wonder and thought,
"What is this radiance that issues forth from within this lotus pedestal?"
At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"Do you see such power and light as this being emitted?"
The celestial hosts replied:
"Indeed, we have seen it.
Such radiance is truly rare."
At that time, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven spoke again:
"All you celestial hosts, now all enter the lotus pedestal with me through the lotus gate; having entered, observe it."
At that time, the entire assembly of devas spoke with one mind, saying:
"Just as it is the wish and desire of the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, so too is our own intention; we also wish to enter the great lotus flower, together with all the celestial maidens."

"At that time, Mucilinda, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, together with the hosts of devas and the hosts of devakanyās, all entered together into the center of that lotus flower, desiring to behold this rare and marvelous event."

At that time, as they were about to enter through the opening together, there was a radiance—like sunlight shining upon a mass of molten gold, which in turn generates a further sun-like light—that illuminated the bodies of the devas and filled the entirety of space.
The radiance within that great lotus pedestal shone forth in such a manner that all the devas beheld it; they all turned their eyes toward it, yet could not endure its brilliance.
Having entered that great lotus, they gave rise to a heart of joy and a heart of wonder.
"For what reason is there such an unspeakable radiance that I have never beheld before?
At that time, the celestial lord Mūsuludha, the King of the Yāma Heaven, entered while the celestial hosts followed behind him.

The mind of the King of the Yāma Heaven was also filled with joy; having entered together, he saw hundreds of thousands of immeasurable precious gems, with hundreds of thousands of radiances shining with brilliant splendor. There were many immeasurable places for recreation, adorned with groves and gardens, and hundreds of thousands of palaces magnificently decorated, filled everywhere with light, and graced by immeasurable trees in their hundreds of thousands.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable groves and gardens adorned with trees made of the seven precious substances; there were immeasurable birds of various colors and diverse forms; there were many delightful, wondrous mountains for recreation; there were immeasurable lotus ponds and waters for adornment; there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite halls for adornment; and there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flowing streams, rivers, ponds, and valleys for adornment.
As it is said, even Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, cannot see all those forms, sizes, and shapes adorned with the seven jewels, let alone the other devas.
"In that place, within such a lotus pedestal, there flow rivers of clear water.

Both banks of those rivers are made of crystal; some have golden banks, some have silver banks, some have jewel banks, some have banks of blue precious gems, some have banks of red lotus-jewels, and some have banks of various interspersed jewels."

Furthermore, there are most excellent and wondrous lotus ponds with waters adorned by various kinds of precious lotuses; some are adorned with lotuses of a single color, while others are adorned with wonderful petals of various colors, namely lotuses adorned with colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
If those leaves are green, they are called "blue-colored precious leaves";
if they are yellow, they are called gold;
if they are white, they are called silver.
Those that are red in color are called "red jewels.
In this manner, there are immeasurable varieties of lotuses within such a great lotus.
In this way, those gods take delight in one another’s hearts as they behold those lotuses adorned within by hundreds of thousands of various kinds of bees.
Having seen this, the devas proceed once more to another place, to a sporting ground within an exceedingly lovely garden.
There are many various musical sounds; upon hearing these sounds, their minds are filled with great delight and they give rise to a heart of joy.
The hosts of devas and devīs, with hearts full of mutual joy, approached one another with a sense of wonder and entered that grove.

It resounded with the songs of many various birds and was adorned with the seven treasures; the ground was so soft that it yielded when the foot was set down and rose back up when the foot was lifted.
All of them gave rise to hearts of universal joy; looking everywhere, they saw what was increasingly superior and more excellent than before.
Those devas’ minds were filled with mutual affection and delight as they sported and experienced pleasure.
Having enjoyed themselves for a long time, mutually delighting one another, and having thus experienced such play and pleasure, they proceed again to other places to experience joy in succession.

That place is named Various Jewel Grounds (*vicitraratnabhūmi*). Having gone there, they enjoy themselves with music; they receive joy and pleasure from various sounds, and their minds delight in beholding the objects of the six desires. Experiencing much sensual pleasure, they act with negligence, frolicking and wandering about.
In that place, they behold various extraordinary merits: infinite varieties of blue, yellow, red, and white, all of which are utterly lovely.
In this manner, those devas proceed from that place toward the mountain named Kīḍāśaila (the Mountain of Play).
Experiencing the pleasures of their sensory objects, they were still not satiated.

On those mountains of play, adorned with the seven treasures, there were many various kinds of birds of diverse exquisite colors and diverse forms; they were further adorned by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable trees, flowing streams, rivers, ponds, and lotuses, as well as groves and pleasure grounds.
In places where the mountain valleys and precipitous cliffs reach their utmost height, herds of deer provide adornment.
There, the celestial hosts sport upon the mountains, enjoying the pleasures of the five sensory desires and cherishing one another with mutual affection.
The bodies of those devas are adorned with various kinds of radiance, and they enjoy themselves together with many, immeasurable, and diverse celestial maidens of supreme beauty and excellence.
"In that place, they thus experience great pleasure for a long time without yet knowing satiety.

Next, they proceed toward the multi-storied pavilions and the assembly halls, moving toward those delights without yet knowing satiety; even the pleasures of the five sensory qualities do not bring them satiety."
With immeasurable conceptualizations and immeasurable varieties of desire, their craving increases further and grows great; they again experience immeasurable and manifold pleasures.
Those hosts of devas and hosts of devī-s mutually delight and enjoy pleasure with one another, and likewise together with Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, they joyfully experience pleasure.
The radiance of those lotuses outshines the light of a hundred thousand suns; it is superior and yet not hot.
Within each of their roots, they take mutual delight, experiencing pleasure through the five sense faculties; they are supremely handsome, and all who see them find great joy.

The precepts beloved by the Noble Ones yield a result that is virtuous, pure, and supreme; they possess immeasurable varieties and immeasurable distinctions, with immeasurable spheres of experience through which one enjoys various pleasures.
With a single-minded harmony, their minds do not obstruct one another; they respect each other and maintain mutual purity of heart, enjoying bliss for a long time within those lotuses.

At such a time, not yet knowing satiety amidst these sensory objects, they exit through the gates of those lotus pedestals according to their recollections; because they enter in such a manner, they likewise emerge in such a manner.
When he was about to depart, there was a bird named *Tijñā* (Discerning Vision) dwelling upon that Mount Sliṣṭagiri.
Seeing that the deva was about to leave, the bird spoke this verse for the sake of the deva:
"The physical form and color of this deva are empty, And his youth is likewise so."
Pleasure tends toward exhaustion at every moment, yet through folly one does not perceive it.
All such celestial beings, with their immeasurable and wondrously auspicious marks,
are split and severed by the wheel of time, causing their bodies to be scattered and destroyed.
Just as that celestial body and life, though possessing immeasurable hundreds of marks,
are slain by the King of Death because their karma is exhausted;
so too this deva, having long enjoyed pleasure, remained constantly heedless in mind.
Bound by the noose of self, one is about to destroy one’s happiness.
Happiness, peace, strength, and life itself can cause separation from what is loved;
the power of the King of Death is exceedingly great, and he stands near, on the verge of arrival.
If one is excessively heedless, the celestial snare is about to descend;
it will surely come to snatch away the life of pleasure, swiftly destroying and exhausting it.
This long-term ruin awaits those gods who constantly practice heedlessness.
Attached to supreme pleasure and remaining unawakened, they are deceived by that very pleasure.
These devas lose their radiance; their faculties and minds grow weak and diminished.
Falling into the realm of Yama, it is only then that they realize the fruit [of their actions].
This body changes from moment to moment; pleasure is impermanent from moment to moment.
Yet the gods, whose minds remain stained, do not see this because they lack the eye of wisdom.
From craving to even greater craving, they constantly experience the pleasures of conduct.
When the King of Death arrives, one cannot reach a place of bliss.
Not knowing of birth, death, and old age, the mind feels no fear;
later, when facing death, one will feel regret for one's own karma.
One is never satiated with sense objects, and the same is true for the faculties;
if one is illuminated by the lamp of wisdom, then the darkness of attachment to pleasure is dispelled.
Constantly habituating oneself to sense objects, one gives rise to immeasurable kinds of thoughts.
Just as fire, when fanned by the wind, blazes up and grows ever greater,
so too the power of sensual desire is exceedingly great, constantly increasing the flames of craving.
The wise, through careful and thorough reflection, are thus able to subdue their sensory objects.
If one’s mind is constantly deluded and always delights in sense objects, it is entirely due to the power of ignorance that one thus experiences such playful pleasures.
Because of ignorance, one takes pleasure in approaching them; thus, the fire of sense objects increases.
Like fire joined with fuel, when fanned by the wind,
One who is attached to desire and remains unsatisfied Is constantly driven by that very desire;
Such a deva falls from heaven, deceived by celestial desires.
When the former body experiences pleasure, that body accumulates merit;
yet moment by moment, life does not abide. When it perishes, where does it go?
Just as that human body perishes, so too will the celestial body perish—of this there is no doubt.
Though one has lived long, death must inevitably come; even a celestial body will surely perish.
Though one is constantly attached to the pleasures of this divine realm and never parts from them, one will inevitably fall from this place, yet remains unaware of the suffering.
Such is the pleasure of the fivefold sensory qualities enjoyed by these devas;
it does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the suffering experienced by other devas.
Just as a fish in the water never suffers from thirst, so too do they [in their own realm] lack such want.
One who is content with what they love never experiences desire again.
If a person does not contemplate the mind, but constantly craves sensual pleasures,
they will sleep through the long night for a great duration, and their suffering and affliction shall never be extinguished.
Out of delusion, one delights in pleasant feelings and fails to perceive suffering;
only when later encountering decline and affliction does one realize what fruit has been obtained.
Desire appears virtuous at first, but in reality it is exceedingly evil.
These are the messengers of hell, whose sole purpose is to bring no benefit.
The blind believe in this desire, while those with the eye of wisdom remain aloof;
like a perilous precipice, such [desire] leads one to fall into hell.
Heedfulness is the foremost friend, always able to bring benefit;
heedlessness is the foremost enemy; therefore, one should draw near to virtuous friends.
Desire pervades the entire body, like the most virulent poison.
The foremost guide to the evil realms is what is called heedlessness.
If one acts with heedlessness and further becomes attached to sensory objects,
that person, with a mind of delusion, will constantly undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
If one does not know this is suffering, and does not know how to contemplate it, then one is equal to a sheep; those who delight in the heavens are likewise so.
As for the pleasure of food and the pleasure of desire, even sheep possess such pleasures.
If a deity were likewise [subject to such conditions], they would not differ from a sheep.
Because the power of the mind is superior, karma is likewise superior;
apart from the merit of karma, superiority cannot be found.
The gods do not fear and thus sport; for this reason, they dwell amidst death.
Once the time of death has arrived, one finally realizes the evil of its fruit.
Until that death comes, let the mind never be confused or distracted.
The wise who delight in the Dharma all act in accordance with the Dharma.
All life is lost; all pleasure is exhausted;
there is separation from all that is loved—the time of your death is at hand.
Death is the foremost evil; when one reaches the great road of the wilderness, there is no refuge like the Dharma. Therefore, one should follow the Dharma.
There is another phenomenon called death, which is what is known as the heedless mind.
First, heedlessness destroys; thereafter, death kills.
Because one attains life and happiness through the Dharma, the Dharma is said to be supreme;
the Dharma is non-heedlessness, the guide to the heavenly realms.
Benefit and non-benefit are not different; bondage and liberation are likewise so.
Heedlessness and heedfulness, merit and fault are equal.
Because of that deluded mind, it causes the devas to have no knowledge.
"Playing and sporting together with those who are enemies, the wise abandon such things.
Having thus observed with true insight, the bird named Satyadarśin (Truth-Seeing) rebuked that deva for his manifold faults.
The devas do not yet perceive this, for their minds are shrouded by negligence; they delight in sense objects and the qualities of the five desires.
Because of their attachment to pleasant sensations, they do not awaken to the True Dharma, and thus they do not realize their impending decline.
Thus, even these celestial realms must inevitably return to impermanence; all the worlds shall likewise be impermanent, yet those gods do not perceive this.

Furthermore, while seated upon a lotus flower atop Mount Sliṣṭagiri, together with their lotus thrones, they depart for the place of renunciation without their bodies moving, heading toward the pond named Vistīrṇa. There are five hundred halls there, adorned with the seven jewels, surrounded by railings, and decorated everywhere with immeasurable variegated ornaments, where other gods likewise enjoy pleasures.
Furthermore, within those halls there are recessed chambers situated upon high towers, many stories in height.

Moreover, various devas, their hearts filled with joy, fill those halls; with immeasurable food, drink, clothing, and bedding, they love and respect one another, their minds free from obstruction, constantly wandering about to enjoy pleasures. Their desired food is ever abundant, and at all times there are the sounds of the five kinds of music.
There, all the celestial maidens and the hosts of devas enjoy such pleasures.
King Mucilinda, Lord of the Yāma Heaven, sits upon a lotus pedestal; accompanied by all the celestial hosts, he proceeds toward that vast pool and arrives there in an instant.

Having arrived there, the resident devas, upon seeing the King approach, all descended from their towers; some left their lotus seats, some emerged from their halls, and some left the railings. All came forth from their dwellings, giving rise to hearts of joy, and together they went to welcome Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven. They all ran toward the King, conceiving hearts of reverence and hearts of joy; seeing the Heavenly King in the midst of the void, they joined their palms above their heads.

Having paid homage to the King, Muxuloutuo, the Night-Moving Heavenly King, stood before the host of devas, while all the other devas followed behind him; singing and dancing, he approached that vast pond.

That place is replete with all virtues; its immeasurable, wondrous halls are all constructed in rows and adorned in various ways. There are various birds with various songs, and it is beautified by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable trees. Its radiance surpasses that of hundreds of thousands of suns.
In that place, there are vast numbers of immeasurable celestial hosts who constantly experience happiness upon the sublime ground of the Yāma Heaven.
When the King of the Yāmas arrives and enters, all those devas feel joy in their hearts and praise the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda.

Mukhulinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, first comforted him with gentle and exquisite words; they then proceeded to the vast pond, and having arrived, he ascended the magnificent hall named "Joyful Heart-Sight."

The precious jewels of that hall radiate light, illuminating the area all around; interspersed with various wonders, it is adorned with thousands upon thousands of marks of excellence and immeasurable sublime qualities, and is surrounded by all the hosts of devas.

After the King of the Yāma Heaven had ascended that hall, he sat upon a lion throne of exquisite light, the foremost of all superior manifestations, adorned with the seven treasures. This wondrous seat was endowed with every pleasant tactile sensation. Seated there, the king was surrounded by a host of preeminent and long-standing celestial beings appearing before him, while a vast multitude of countless celestial maidens first performed songs and dances.
Thereafter, in due order, those ancient devas questioned the Heavenly King, saying:
"In what place did Your Majesty mount the lotus throne, that you have now come here?
We have not seen Your Majesty for a long time."
At that time, among the elder devas, there was one who held the King of Devas in the highest respect.
Then, the Lord of Devas, Yāma, King Mūsuludha, replied to the assembly of devas:
"I have just witnessed a rare occurrence within that lotus pedestal. I entered that lotus pedestal, and once all the devas and celestial maidens had entered together with me, everyone beheld it."
Then that heavenly king, regarding the rare and marvelous events he had witnessed, recounted them all in full for the former devas.
He described every detail of the various merits within the lotus flower in their entirety for the former devas.
At that time, because those former devas had already previously seen such various superior sights and had heard of them, they did not give rise to a sense of wonder;
for they had already clearly seen those various excellent things within the lotuses in the past.
Then that former deva spoke of the ancient laws to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, saying:
"May the Heavenly King listen: I have previously heard that this great lotus possesses great power."
Within this lotus, those of great power possess all manner of ornaments of merit, complete according to their mental recollections.
Among all the locations in this Yāma Heaven, there is no place of such bliss as that within the lotus.
Thus he had previously heard:
"The World-Honored One Kāñcanamuni, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, has appeared in the world."

The Dharma he taught was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it was excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing. It was a unique teaching, complete, pure, and pristine, as he expounded the True Dharma, namely:
"This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form, and this is the path leading to the cessation of form."
"In this way, this Dharma is [perfect] in its beginning, middle, and end.

Having spoken thus, within that Buddha-dharma there were many hundreds of thousands who had already seen the Truth; there were those who had attained the fruits, such as those who had successively attained the stage of Anāgāmin, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Srotāpanna. Furthermore, there were those who had attained the fourth dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the first dhyāna.

After that Buddha had established such people in this state, he further caused others to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) and act in accordance with the Dharma. Having led many people, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions, to practice wholesome deeds, he then observed: "Who are there among these people whom I should now guide and discipline?"
With his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he saw: "In the Yāma Heaven, I should exercise mastery.
At that time, there was a king of the Yāma Heaven named Priyadarśana; though that king possessed the seeds of virtue within him, he acted with negligence.
That king’s retinue consists of immeasurable hosts of devas whose roots of goodness are fully matured, yet they are largely negligent and practice heedless conduct.

Out of compassion for them, the World-Honored One Kāñcanamuni has come up to this celestial realm of the Yāma devas to benefit them, to bring an end to their suffering, and to eliminate the negligence of those devas.
Surrounded by five thousand bhikṣus who had exhausted all outflows, he went together with them to the realm of the Yāma devas, where a most excellent radiance pervaded everywhere.
At that time, the various devas beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
If there are devas who, from the very beginning, have not seen the Buddha, they will think that the Buddha is a deva, the most excellent among devas.
Those devas will conceive a sense of wonder toward the Buddha, yet they will not know that he is the Buddha.

Furthermore, the physical form of this Buddha is the most preeminent among all the celestial hosts; he is fully endowed with every merit, without peer or equal, and his radiance pervades the entire world of the devas.
When those devas saw the śrāvakas accompanying the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they too gave rise to a most excellent and rarefied sense of wonder, thinking:
"Who are these people?"
"Thus, with such forms and attire, they followed this deva, never parting from him, as they moved about in a circle.
Then that devaputra took various kinds of exquisite and wonderful lotuses and approached the World-Honored One, Kāñcanamuni.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the devaputra approaching, ascended into the void and manifested various kinds of sublime and wondrous supernatural powers, discerning immeasurable merits according to his thoughts.
Water issued from his body, complete with color, fragrance, flavor, and texture; the water of the celestial realm did not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
From the crown of his head, tongues of flame blazed forth, and immeasurable kinds of light of immeasurable colors filled the void, namely blue, yellow, red, and purple, and so forth.

Furthermore, he manifested various and diverse, supreme and wondrous supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), namely: making one body into many bodies—whether a thousand bodies, a hundred thousand bodies, or a hundred million bodies—with all their radiance filling every celestial realm and the world; and then making those many bodies into a single body once again.
The World-Honored One further manifested such supernormal powers:

he took every location on the ground within the Yāma Heaven, grasping each one with his hand and placing it in the palm; together with its groves, gardens, flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, he cast them into the void beyond the range of vision, and then returned them to their original places of residence.
The World-Honored One further manifested great supernormal powers:

he took that great mountain with his hand and hurled it into the midst of space, along with its gardens, groves, ponds, rivers, streams, valleys, and the host of celestial maidens; they were no longer known where they had gone, until he returned them all to their original locations.
The gods therein were not aware of any movement or change; they remained exactly as they were before, no different.
The World-Honored One again manifested extraordinary supernormal powers:
in immeasurable varieties of colors, he assumed immeasurable forms and garments, possessing immeasurable kinds of meritorious qualities.

Manifesting great power, he caused those hosts of devas to have various different perceptions: some saw the Tathāgata on a mountain; some saw the Tathāgata in a grove; some saw the Tathāgata in a lotus forest; some saw the Tathāgata walking in a hall; some saw the Tathāgata beneath a tree; some saw the Tathāgata in a river or pond; some saw the Tathāgata in pleasure gardens; some saw the Tathāgata in all places of meditation; some saw the Tathāgata sitting in meditation, pervading the entirety of space; and some saw the Tathāgata seated upon a seat suspended in mid-air.
Furthermore, in the midst of the void, he would sit or walk, or again perform walking meditation, and then return once more to sit in dhyāna.
“The World-Honored One further manifested supernatural powers, preaching the Dharma with such and such voices; the sounds of these five kinds of music were superior to those of the Yāma Heaven.”
The sounds produced by the gods of the Yāma Heaven are like the cries of birds in Jambudvīpa; all those gods are thus inferior and diminished.
Once those gods have heard such sounds, they completely abandon their prideful thoughts regarding their ability to sing.
“Furthermore, the World-Honored One manifested another supernatural power: within that very space, he created a multitude of devas and conjured celestial maidens of exquisite and peerless beauty.”
The forms of the Yāma devas and Yāma goddesses are like fireflies;

their radiance, color, size, appearance, attire, ornaments, and the pleasures of their gardens and groves are all so exceedingly sublime that when the Great Heavenly King and his assembly of gods behold these manifested devas, they feel shame and remorse, seeing their own physical radiance and sensual desires as no different from blades of grass.
Then, those gods born in the Yāma Heaven conceived this thought:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their faculties were mature, knowing their profound intentions, and knowing the retribution of causes and effects, possessed unobstructed vision."

Out of a desire to benefit all the world with a mind of supreme great compassion, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, then proceeded toward King Sunetra, the King of the Yāma Heaven, and manifested extraordinary supernormal powers; just as he had previously manifested them, he displayed every supernormal power for Sunetra’s sake, all of them appearing a hundred times more magnificent than before.
At that time, the celestial king of the Yāma heaven, Rati-darśana, completely abandoned all prideful thoughts.

"Then the celestial king of the Yāma heaven, Rati-darśana, likewise sat upon that great lotus flower, sporting and enjoying pleasures within it just as the celestial king of the Yāma heaven, Mucilinda, had previously done."
“At that time, the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers within the great lotus flower, and then spoke again to the gods of the Yāma heaven and others, saying:
‘Everything you now behold is all brought about by the karmic retribution of Sukhānta.’”
The World-Honored One, for the sake of transformation, causes them to abandon arrogance.
You see their inner places of play—gardens, lotus ponds, rivers, valleys, mountains, as well as exquisite halls—and perceive immeasurable varieties of such realms and environments.
King Priyadarśana abandoned his prideful mind.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the great lotus and manifested all things; furthermore, before the abode of the Yāma King Priyadarśana, a lotus arose with billions of petals upon which the Tathāgata sat on the pericarp, while his śrāvaka disciples sat upon the petals, manifesting various kinds of sublime and wondrous supernormal powers.
Some flew up into the midst of space and then returned again to the lotus.
Furthermore, they manifested various and diverse supernatural powers.
At that time, the Yāma King Sunirmita thought to himself:
"Who is this person? What virtuous karma do they possess?
By what power are they able to perform such a marvelous feat?"
"Whatever forms, light, and so forth I possess, whether much or little, are exceedingly inferior;
theirs, however, are superior. *The Sutra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Fascicle 36 [and] Fascicle 37.

Chapter Sixteen: Observing the Heavens, Part Two: Yāma Heaven.
"At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that their minds had been tamed and fully ripened, immediately commanded a śrāvaka to tame them through the power of his divine eye."
At that time, the śrāvakas said to Pramuditanayanajagadvirocana:
"Pramuditanayanajagadvirocana, you should know!
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the teacher of all the world—including its devas, humans, māras, śramaṇas, and brahmins, as well as all devas, humans, and asuras."

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows all and sees all; he constantly preaches the Dharma for the sake of the entire world—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; a unique teaching that is complete, pure, and pristine; he proclaims the supramundane Dharma of tranquility, leading even unto Nirvana.
That is to say:
"This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form, and this is the path leading to the cessation of form.
I have now come for the sake of preaching the Dharma to you, the assembly of the Yāma devas; I have come for the purpose of bringing benefit, peace, happiness, and great advantage.
“Then, having heard this from the śrāvaka, that Yāma Heaven King, Priyadarśana, called out:
‘Great Sage!’”
"I am now going to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; I do not know how I should make offerings to the World-Honored One.
At this moment, I do not understand the proper ritual procedures—how should I make offerings?"
When that śrāvaka heard this, he replied:
"The Heavenly King Sunirmita is approaching the World-Honored One.

Having heard this, Sunirmita removed his crown and ornaments; with a mind well-subdued and his faculties tranquil, he focused his mind on right mindfulness, adjusted his robe to bare the left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, joining his palms toward the Buddha.

Having heard this from the śrāvakas, the entire assembly of devas cast off their ornaments, focused their minds with right mindfulness, stilled their faculties, and all proceeded to sit upon lotus pedestals.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was surrounded by his assembly of śrāvakas, like the moon encircled by all the stars; again, he was like Sumeru, the king of mountains, surrounded by all other mountains; and again, he was like the ocean surrounded by all the great rivers.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch is surrounded by eighty-four thousand minor kings, and just as the sun is surrounded by its radiance, so too is he surrounded by the assembly of śrāvakas.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possessing the most supreme, wondrous, and immeasurable majesty and radiance, sat upon a great lotus pedestal.
At that time, the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Pramoda, wearing Dharma robes and arranging one shoulder of his garment, joined his palms toward the Buddha and stood respectfully to one side.
The World-Honored One said,
"I cause you now to abandon and leave behind negligence.
At that time, after Roca had sat down in one place, the World-Honored One Kanakamuni uttered a courageous, supreme, and fearless voice that pervaded the entire realm of Yama, saying:

“Nandika! I now teach the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing—a unique, complete, and pure holy life. Thus do I speak.”
"Listen now attentively, maintain right mindfulness, and reflect well; I shall now explain this thoroughly for you.
Then, Nandika said, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Then the World-Honored One spoke to the assembly of devas, such as Nandika, saying:

"There are nine causes that give rise to negligence. By delighting in and frequently practicing such negligence, one destroys the foolish worldlings; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms—among the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals."

Due to the causes and conditions of birth, one undergoes great suffering and affliction; bound by the cycle of birth and death, one fails to attain the peaceful bliss of nirvana and fails to obtain benefit.
What are these nine causes?

The first is as follows: they delight in negligence, practice negligence, and constantly engage in negligence; they do not draw near to sages, nor can they restrain the actions of body, speech, and mind. They fail to govern their sensory faculties and cannot rectify their own body, speech, and mind, causing them instead to act within unwholesome spheres. They always take pleasure in hearing unwholesome teachings and have no delight in the Buddha’s True Dharma.
This is the primary cause of heedless conduct, which gives rise to heedlessness.

If one acts heedlessly, foolish sentient beings engage in unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind. Because of these unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind accumulates.
Fools, deceived by negligence, at the dissolution of the body after death fall into evil destinies, being born in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
If one abandons negligence, such a person is a true noble being who always remains free from negligence.
If one seeks what is wholesome, one should abandon negligence;
this is the first cause that gives rise to negligence. Furthermore, Nandika!

Furthermore, there is a second cause for heedless conduct that can give rise to heedlessness; having given rise to heedlessness, it can destroy one's roots of goodness, namely: acting with a mind that lacks careful discernment.
Having seen it with his eyes, he gives rise to conceptual discrimination; he repeatedly recollects and contemplates in this way, taking delight in that form and no longer attending to other objects.
Constantly engaging in such unwholesome conduct, which is not virtuous thought, his mind and intentions become deranged.
Because of that negligence, those who are negligent, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and are born in hell.
This is the second cause of negligent conduct, which gives rise to negligence.

“Furthermore, there is a third cause for heedless conduct that gives rise to heedlessness: namely, that which is unreal, unseen, unheard, and never before experienced, yet is merely conceived by the mind and mentally discriminated, whether based on desire or based on delusion.”

Thus he reflects and thus he contemplates; his mind constantly takes that as its object and his mind constantly dwells upon it. He improperly contemplates the foremost Dharma, thereby disturbing his own mind.

This is the third cause of heedlessness, which gives rise to negligence, binds all sentient beings, and deceives them, causing their body, speech, and mind to engage in unwholesome conduct; at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into evil realms and are reborn in hell.

“Furthermore, there is a fourth cause of heedlessness that gives rise to negligence and causes all heedless sentient beings, upon the dissolution of the body after death, to fall into evil destinies and be born in the hells.
Thus it is, Nandika! What is the fourth cause of negligence? It is this:
constantly delighting in beholding women, delighting in beholding their unreal, adorned forms, and giving rise to a mind of craving and attachment toward those unreal forms.
Seeing their singing and dancing, he gives rise to conceptual discrimination and his mind becomes joyful.
Such discrimination of body, speech, and mind does not constitute the performance of wholesome karma.
Those who are thus heedless, when their bodies perish and their lives end, fall into evil realms and are reborn in the hells.
This is the fourth cause of heedlessness that can give rise to negligence.

Furthermore, there is a fourth cause of heedlessness that can give rise to negligence, namely: delighting in various gardens and groves, enjoying lotus ponds or various flowered forests; having seen them, the mind finds pleasure therein, playing and wandering within them, failing to contemplate wholesome matters, and failing to rectify the mind.
Engaging in negligence and deceived by negligence, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell.
This is the fourth cause of negligent conduct that gives rise to negligence.
"Furthermore, there is a fifth cause of heedlessness that gives rise to negligence.
It is this, Sukha-darśana:
associating with evil friends, joining together with them, violating the pure precepts, engaging in unwholesome conduct, harboring improper thoughts, and committing evil deeds."

In this way, sentient beings who associate with evil friends and engage in heedless conduct will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into evil destinies and be born in the hells.
This is the fifth cause of heedless conduct, which gives rise to heedlessness.
Furthermore, Nandika! There is a fifth cause of heedlessness that can give rise to heedlessness.
This refers to sentient beings who, with immeasurable kinds of conduct and immeasurable kinds of intentions, lack a resolute intention when performing wholesome deeds.
In this way, sentient beings do not have fixed karma; in this way, sentient beings perform indeterminate actions, and all their performed deeds are utterly lost.

Regarding worldly and world-transcending karma, they do not bring those various karmas to completion; they cannot practice giving, they do not perform meritorious deeds, and they lack wholesome reflection. Due to the fault of negligence, they thus transgress the precepts.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one falls into an evil destination and is born in hell.
This is the fifth cause of heedlessness that gives rise to heedlessness.
Furthermore, there is a sixth cause of heedlessness that gives rise to heedlessness.
It refers to sentient beings who abandon the true Dharma and abandon the noble truths, even abandoning the eightfold noble path, and engage in activities without skillful discernment.
Thus it is, Sukha-darśana!
Because the minds of such sentient beings are distracted by heedless conduct, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into evil destinies and are born in the hells.
This is the sixth cause of heedlessness that can produce heedlessness.
Furthermore, there is a seventh cause of heedlessness that can produce heedlessness, namely, craving for flavors.
Wherever those various flavors are placed, there the mind finds delight and constantly dwells upon them, acting in accordance with that mind.

Thus, these sentient beings have no other thoughts; they do not perform wholesome deeds nor maintain right precepts. Their minds always delight in being invited by others for food, and because they are constantly greedy for flavor, they are deceived by flavor.

Failing to perform wholesome deeds, they do not contemplate even one among these four—suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self—but instead contemplate only unwholesome and inverted dharmas; thus, everything they do is not for their own benefit.
Thus, when such beings undergo the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
This is the seventh cause of heedless conduct, which gives rise to heedlessness.
"Thus it is, Sukha-darśana! Furthermore, there is an eighth cause of heedlessness that gives rise to negligence.

That is to say, when sentient beings have obtained various immeasurable pleasures, they take delight in those pleasurable things and become greedily attached to them, claiming they are eternally unchanging, eternally secure, and indestructible."

Constantly recollecting such pleasures, they perpetually engage in unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; they do not know what should be done and what should not be done, nor do they know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma. They fail to perceive or understand their own ruin and suffering, and they do not keep in mind the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of distinct sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
One does not attend to anything that should not be attended to, yet one attends to it.
Thus, one does not attend to the dharma of death and extinction; amidst all the birth and death of the world, death is able to cause disturbance, yet one remains unaware and fails to attend to it.

Thus, these sentient beings are deceived by pleasure; thus, these sentient beings who are evilly attached to pleasure later face the arrival of death, at which point they give rise to regret. Burned by the fire of their own regret, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born within the hells.
This is the eighth cause of heedless conduct that can give rise to heedlessness.
"Furthermore, Nandika, there is a ninth cause of heedless conduct that can give rise to heedlessness."
That which is called the mind that delights in various pleasures is deceived by craving among gods and humans;

they do not know how to take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they do not uphold the prohibitions and precepts, do not listen to the Buddha’s teachings, and do not abide by the noble discipline;
they do not perform what ought to be done, yet they constantly delight in hearing about what ought not to be done.

Not entering into the True Dharma, their minds do not fear the retribution of future lives; they do not perceive the suffering of the next world after death, thereby losing their own benefit, deceived by a heart of resentment.
"When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
This is the ninth cause of heedless conduct that gives rise to heedlessness.
'O Nandika, you should know this!'"
This wealth and pleasure are impermanent, non-eternal, and subject to destruction.

Countless past kings of the Yāma Heaven have already fallen from this state; where have they gone?
It is because they have thus brought about the fruition of their own karma; bound by the snares of wholesome and unwholesome karma, they transmigrate through birth and death.

Therefore, Ānanda! If there are those who wish to obtain a human body, do not practice heedlessness. Why is this?
The body and life are impermanent, and wealth and pleasure are likewise; one should reflect in this way and not act with negligence. Why is this?
Because many hundreds of thousands of celestial beings have fallen away due to their negligent conduct.
Thus, do not follow the path of heedlessness.
Those who travel this path are fools; they are not true sons of noble family.

All who are born must inevitably return to death; death stands before them, and so it is with old age, and so it is with illness, and likewise with separation from those one loves; the same applies to virtuous and non-virtuous karma, as well as wealth and pleasure.

The objects of old age, sickness, and death Constantly dwell upon them. Yet,

because one is liberated from faults, one attains unsurpassed bliss.

Having reflected well upon this and made various distinctions, [one should practice accordingly].

whether it be the gods enjoying their bliss or any other minor phenomena—

Thereupon, in that place, Maudgalyāyana, the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with him, was able to hear the True Dharma from the presence of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

"Just as you now behold these rare wonders within the great lotus, so do I speak of them to you now.

At that time, having thought thus, those eighty thousand devas went together toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There they beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with incomparable countenance; his body was adorned with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, like a mountain of gold, blazing with majestic virtue.
All sentient beings received benefit; everyone saw [the Buddha] surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers as he preached the Dharma in accordance with the Four Noble Truths.
"At that time, the night-moon king of the Yāma Heaven named Mucilinda, together with a multitude of eighty thousand devas, went to the place where the Buddha was.

Mukhulinda! You have already heard the discourse spoken by the Buddha Kāñcanamuni; having heard it thus, you have come to this place.
At that time, the Yāma Heaven King named Mucilinda thought to himself:

Having thought this, Mucilinda was filled with joy, and the entire assembly of eighty thousand devas all together prostrated once more before the World-Honored One.
Having paid homage to the World-Honored One, they stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke thus: "Maudgalyāyana!

I shall now preach the Dharma for you—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; a unique teaching, complete, pure, and immaculate."
"This Dharma gate is called the Joy of the Celestial Vehicle; you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well, for I shall speak it for you.
Having received these instructions, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"What is the dharma-gate called 'The Joy of the Celestial Vehicle'?"
