There are twelve of these, Maudgalyāyana!
What are called the twelve paths to the heavens?

If a son of good family abides in that path, that true person is able to ascend to the celestial realms; just as one who enters a royal highway in this world is able to enter the city, becoming free from fear and free from doubt.
In this way, by not violating body, speech, and mind, and practicing the twelve paths, one attains rebirth in heaven; such a person enters among the devas.
What are these twelve?
The first is called the Path of Reality.
If one clings to that path, one will attain rebirth in the heavens, Mucilinda!
That person who possesses the true path has five merits. What are these five?
First is truthful speech; when one speaks the truth, all people believe the man.
Second, it is indestructible; at all times, no one is able to destroy it.
Third, it is pure; at all times, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is pure.
Fourth, it is worthy of veneration; at all times, it is held in high esteem by the devas.
Fifth is rebirth in the higher realms: when the body perishes and life ends, one is born in the heavens.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"By speaking truthful words and always practicing self-restraint, One is constantly honored by the devas."
"Because of their love for all the world, they will later be reborn in heaven. "Mukhaliṭa!
This is the first path to heaven."
Mukhaliṭa! What, furthermore, constitutes the second path to heaven, by following which one attains the celestial realms?
It is the purity and stainlessness of giving—unbroken, unimpaired, and free from expectation of karmic reward.
Through such perfumed reflection, this is called the second path to the celestial realms; a person of virtuous karma attains rebirth therein.
This second path possesses three merits.
The three are as follows:
being loved by all people;
constantly perfuming one's thoughts so that joy arises in the mind; and...
With the breakup of the body and the end of life, he is reborn in the heavenly realms.
This is the second path leading to the world of the devas.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“‘Giving is beloved by all; it also increases one’s merit.
In the future, one will be reborn wealthy in heaven. Such is the fruit of giving.’”
“Mukhulinda! What, moreover, is the third path to heaven, by following which one reaches the celestial realms? It is patience.”
A person capable of endurance possesses five merits, namely these five:
they do not quarrel and do not harbor resentment; this is the first merit.
No one is able to steal their possessions; this is the second merit.
Being loved by all people is the third merit;
having great compassion is the fourth merit;
and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, attaining rebirth in the heavenly realms of the good destinations is the fifth merit.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“Practicing in accordance with patience, With a compassionate heart and free from fear,
One is beloved by all people, And upon the dissolution of the body, attains rebirth in heaven.”
“Mukhaliṭa! What, moreover, is the fourth path to the heavens, by which one clings to that path and attains the celestial realms?
It is called ‘pleasant speech.’”
Mukhaliṇda! Such pleasant speech possesses six merits:
first, it is beloved by all people;
Second, being free from fear;
third, having a face that is always pure;
fourth, attaining a good reputation.
Fifth, one acts without deliberation;
sixth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens. Muxuloudu!
These are the six kinds of merit of pleasant speech.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"Beloved by all people, Increasing one's good reputation,..."
"With a universally handsome and most dignified countenance, one will be reborn in heaven upon the dissolution of the body. "Mukilinda!
What, furthermore, is the fifth path to heaven, by which one adheres to that path and reaches the celestial realms?"
That which is called having compassion for all sentient beings—this son of good family shall eventually attain even nirvana; I say that such a person possesses incomparable merit.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“Toward all sentient beings, With a heart of compassion like that of parents—
Such a person, a treasure of pity, Dwells forever within the mind.”
“Mukhulinda! What, moreover, is the sixth heavenly path, by adhering to which one reaches the heavens?
It is called the upright mind.”
One who rectifies the mind is able to perform wholesome deeds;
one with wholesome reflection speaks wholesome words.
This is a brief summary of the merit of rectifying the mind.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“If one possesses a virtuous and upright mind, Always observing in accordance with the Dharma,
One will not be driven by transgressions, Just as sunlight dispels the darkness.”
“Mukhulinda! The root of all dharmas is what is called a virtuous and upright mind. Mukhulinda!”
Furthermore, what is the seventh heavenly path by which one, being attached to that path, attains the heavens?
It is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
A person of right view can reach *nirvāṇa*, let alone the heavens.
If they possess even a slight amount of physical, verbal, or mental karma, all such [actions] benefit sentient beings, enabling them to be born in the heavens or even attain nirvāṇa.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says: "Right view alone is supreme; Whosoever possesses it in their mind..."
“Ordinary people are also like this, attaining liberation from the bonds of birth and death.
“Mukhila! What, furthermore, is the eighth path to heaven, by which one adheres to that path and reaches the celestial realms?”
This means that by distancing oneself from unwholesome associates, one is free from the three kinds of faults; virtuous people do not abandon such a person because they share the same precepts.
Consequently, all evil causes and conditions fail to arise, and other superior, great transgressions can no longer be incurred.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"One who associates with evil friends will not obtain happiness;
having associated with evil friends, one will extensively incur what is disadvantageous."
“Mukhila! What, furthermore, is the ninth heavenly path by which one, by adhering to that path, reaches the heavens?
It is the hearing of the True Dharma.”
Briefly stated, hearing the Dharma encompasses seven merits:
first, one hears teachings not previously heard;
second, what has been heard becomes firm and is not lost.
Third, abandoning all evil karma;
fourth, being pleasing to behold for all the noble ones;
fifth, possessing deep-seated faith and reverence for the Tathāgata.
Sixth, one will increase in lifespan;
seventh, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one will be reborn in the heavens.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“‘Those who have not heard shall hear, and those who have already heard shall become firm;
abandoning all evil deeds, they shall be reborn in heaven when the body perishes.’”
“Mukhaliṭa! What, furthermore, is the tenth heavenly path, by adhering to which one reaches the heavens?
It is called the supple mind.”
Mukhulinda! That supple mind possesses four merits:
first, one does not give rise to resentment or aversion toward others;
Second, although they perform [meritorious deeds], they are not steadfast;
third, they are not afflicted by anger;
fourth, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
“If one is well-purified and stainless, With no faults adhering to the mind, The stain of anger cannot defile them; After death, they shall be reborn in heaven.”
“Mukhila! What, furthermore, are the eleven heavenly paths, by adhering to which one attains the celestial realms? They are:
faith in the results of karma.”
One who has faith in the fruits of karma completely abandons all evil deeds; they do not give rise to even so much as a speck of dust of evil, but feel only fear upon seeing such evil karma.
That person knows all the fruits of both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Having known this, they perform wholesome deeds and abandon unwholesome ones.
That person constantly practices and performs wholesome deeds; when the body perishes and life ends, they attain rebirth in the heavens.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"If one understands the fruit of karma, One always perceives the subtle meaning."
"He is not defiled by evil, just as the sky is not stained by mud.
"Mukhaliṭa! What, moreover, are the twelve paths to heaven, by which one adheres to those paths and reaches the celestial realms?"
This refers to having deep-seated faith and reverence for the Triple Gem with an undistorted conviction.
Because one possesses such deep-seated faith and reverence for the Triple Gem with an undistorted conviction, there are immeasurable merits.
There are immeasurable hundreds upon hundreds of merits, yet this single merit surpasses all other merits.
That is to say, such a person first experiences human happiness and ultimately attains nirvana;
whereas for gods and goddesses who practice non-negligence, there is neither worldly pleasure nor supramundane pleasure for those gods who are negligent.
For this reason, Muxulou-tuo!
Just as that Great Sage, the World-Honored One named Kāñcanamuni, preached the Dharma for the sake of Suyāma, the King of the Yāma Heaven, in this manner.
Such is this Dharma; the Dharma of all Tathāgatas is exactly thus, and not otherwise than what you previously heard from the former devas.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"Deeply believing in the Triple Gem, Diligently practicing for immeasurable eons,"
"First one attains birth in the heavens, and finally one attains the fruit of Nirvāṇa.
"These are the twelve paths of the gods; by practicing them constantly, one will certainly attain the fruit as described, without doubt."
At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda and eighty thousand devas, having heard this Dharma-gate from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, all attained the fruit of Srotāpanna upon hearing it.
At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
“I have escaped the evil realms, Relying upon the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
All the solitary devas Are rescued by the Dharma of the Tathāgata.”
"Today I have attained the fruit; having entered into the Buddha-dharma, I shall enter together with the devas and pass beyond the realm of fear—the cycle of birth and death.
Having spoken thus, Mucilinda ascended into the void and, together with the host of devas, proceeded toward the abode of the Yāma devas.
All those devas arrive there in this manner; having reached the celestial realm, they continue to experience pleasure, wandering and sporting about.
Once the karmic merit of their single lifetime is exhausted, they decline, yet the gates to the evil realms remain closed.
Born among humans, they possess the foremost wealth and happiness, the foremost physical beauty, and a superior, great mind; in all lands, they are preeminent therein.
If there are those who are not *srotāpannas*, once they have passed away from that heaven, they will be born in hell, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, according to their karmic actions.
If, due to other residual karma, they are born among human beings, they likewise obtain great wealth and happiness,
adorned with various ornaments,
because of that residual karma. Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, next examines all the regions within the Yāma Heaven.
He perceives through vision, hearing,
and knowledge that within the Yāma Heaven there is another region called Carrying-About-the-Vehicle (Vāhanavikramaṇa).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that region?
He sees, hears, and knows: if a person possesses a virtuous mind, a virtuous and profound upright mind, and refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, that person,
through their wholesome karma, will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in that place.
At the very moment of their birth there, they immediately behold various groves of trees, clear flowing rivers, and lotus ponds within the heavens—exquisite, extraordinary, and most delightful.
The sounds of the various birds, as well as their fragrances, tastes, textures, and so forth, are all superior, lovely, and delightful.
Upon seeing those exquisite forms and hearing those wondrous sounds, they speak thus:

"These various groves of trees now seen, these various lovely, clear-flowing rivers and lotus ponds, with their diverse and marvelous colors never before encountered—these are exceedingly lovely and exceedingly delightful. They exist in infinite varieties, beyond compare, such that the mind can never be satiated."

The various songs and the calls of the birds now heard are all exquisite and wonderful, unlike anything experienced before; they are exceedingly lovely and delightful, existing in infinite varieties, beyond compare, and such that the mind can never find satiety.

The fragrance now perceived is unlike anything experienced before; it is exceedingly lovely and exceedingly delightful, possessing immeasurable varieties that have no equal, such that the mind can never be satiated.

This flavor is likewise so: it has never existed before, and it is both exceedingly lovely and exceedingly delightful; it possesses immeasurable varieties, with nothing comparable to it, such that the mind can never be satiated.

This touch is likewise so: it has never existed before, is exceedingly lovely, and is exceedingly delightful; it possesses immeasurable varieties, with nothing comparable to it, such that the mind can never be satiated.
Thus that deva internally contemplates the spheres of the five desires, constantly seeking them with longing.
Amidst such exquisite pleasures of the five sensory objects, he sports and wanders about, his mind never reaching satiety.
Upon hearing this, all the celestial maidens there said:
"In this heavenly world, such is the constant nature of phenomena; all objects of experience are eternally thus, with no place that is not delightful and no time that is not delightful."

Such superior marks are found everywhere and in all places; they are fully endowed with the merits of the five desires, and one attains immeasurable varieties of recollections, constantly experiencing celestial pleasures beyond compare.
When the devas behold this grove, they conceive such a sense of wonder; how much more so when they enter within it!
Even before the presence of King Mucilinda, it surpasses all else.

In that place, nine billion nayutas of thousands of celestial maidens of various adornments and youthful beauty, fully endowed with song and dance and with joyful countenances, offered worship through the merits of the five desires.
In this way, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, experiences such pleasures; the celestial son Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, will certainly see him. Why is this?

In this realm, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, is its sovereign; all these devas belong to that king, and we rely upon him as if he were our parents throughout all the regions within this entire Yāma Heaven.
"Once that newly born deva had heard this, he was surrounded by various celestial maidens and entered that forest.
Having entered the forest, he saw devas of inferior and middling beauty, adorned with various forms and garments, all of whom were enjoying the merits of the five sensual pleasures."
They partake of food together in joy, and all possess the five virtues of their sustenance.

Beholding them at play, one sees many immeasurable hosts of celestial maidens conversing with melodious voices alongside other devas, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various merits.
Furthermore, there are magnificent trees made of the seven precious gems as adornments, and various rows of trees as adornments.
In that place, there are many wish-fulfilling trees; whatever the gods think of, they obtain from those trees—such are the jewel-trees endowed with perfect qualities.
That newly born deva is fully endowed with immeasurable kinds of supreme and wondrous merits, and is likewise fully endowed with the pleasures of the five sensory objects.
Having seen this, his eyes become intensely attached to that great joy; he gives rise to a superior love and delight, looking everywhere throughout.

Having seen this, they entered that great forest together with the celestial maidens. Having entered the great forest, it was adorned with hundreds of thousands of rivers of abundant food and drink, and filled with birds of various colors and various songs.
The songs of those celestial maidens resounded everywhere; hearing their music with one's ears, it blended with the calls of the birds.
That newly born deva, furthermore, saw in another place a forest of lotuses, rare and exquisite, three yojanas in length and two yojanas in breadth.
He saw in that great forest golden lotuses with immeasurable forms and adorned with immeasurable colors;
it was just like the sky in autumn, adorned by the various celestial bodies. Thus it was, even so.

There, hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens abound in abundance; they engage in song, dance, and play, enjoying various pleasures amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments. Thinking of one another with their minds, drawing near to one another, never parting for even a single moment, they are always of one mind, loving and delighting in each other.

He saw that throughout the groves there were many hosts of *nirmāṇarati* devas; he also saw many flocks of various birds, which played and delighted together, cherished one another, and stayed close to one another, never parting for even a single thought-moment, always remaining single-mindedly and loving one another.
In this way, the gods and others sport and enjoy pleasure, and the birds do likewise.

There are immeasurable varieties of such birds—geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, and so forth—as well as countless flocks that sport everywhere along the banks of those rivers within the pure waters of the lotus groves.
In that place, there are devas who pluck golden leaves to drink celestial wine; they dance, sing, and sport together with hosts of celestial maidens, experiencing various pleasures.

Furthermore, they pluck silver leaves to drink red wine, the color of which is like the hue of a precious lotus flower; its fragrance and flavor are cool and refreshing, possessing every excellence, as they enjoy themselves singing and playing with the celestial maidens.
This is brought about by the power of their own virtuous karma.

Furthermore, there are other devas who also dwell in that lotus grove in an exceedingly delightful place; these devas enjoy the pleasures of the five sensory realms, plucking the leaves of blue-jewel-colored lotuses and drinking celestial wine together with the heavenly maidens.

Furthermore, other devas entered beneath those trees, covered by celestial flowers; having drunk the celestial wine, they were filled with joy and happiness. Within the groves, they wandered about with various celestial maidens in heedless indulgence, drinking the exquisite juices of celestial fruits possessing color, fragrance, and flavor, and singing and laughing in delight.

Furthermore, there are other devas who take shelter beneath the branches of trees made of gold, silver, crystal, and blue jewels; together with various celestial maidens, they sing, laugh, and frolic, experiencing heavenly bliss.

Furthermore, there are other devas who dwell by the riverbanks in places filled with the sounds of birds; they stand upon soft ground and land of exquisite texture where flowers bloom, and they pluck those flowers.
The flowers are five colors, appearing both individually and in clusters.
Together with the celestial maidens, they take them up and smell them; those celestial maidens draw near to the deva-son, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing.
Furthermore, there are other devas upon grounds made of various precious gems—namely blue beryl, crystal, gold, and silver—who sport, wander, and experience every pleasure upon such terrains.
This continues until the accumulation of their wholesome karma of craving is exhausted; once that wholesome karma is exhausted, they pass away from that place.
Having passed away from that place, they fall into the evil realms, being born in hell, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

If there remains further karma such that one is born among humans, one will always be born in a pleasant place; one will possess the foremost degree of physical beauty, a great mind, and great wealth, and shall become a sovereign of a kingdom.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, next examines all the locations within the Yāma Heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
Furthermore, there is another region called Cloud-Ranging (Megha-cāra).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that region?
They perceive, hear, and know:

If a person possesses a straightforward mind and is upright by nature, has faith in the Triple Gem, refrains from killing and stealing, and does not engage in any unwholesome or perverse conduct—neither delighting in it, nor practicing it, nor performing it frequently.

Upon seeing women, he does not give rise to even a thought of desire; he does not dwell upon lust, abandons the mind of lust, and makes no further discrimination regarding it, just as one would discard poison.
When this son of good family’s body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Yāma Heaven, in that place of wandering within the clouds.

Having been born there, the radiance of his body was no different from the sun; he experienced the bliss of virtuous karma and incomparable joy, enjoying all manner of pleasures within immeasurable realms.
Immediately upon birth, he was filled with great joy and thought to himself: "Why am I alone here?
As this thought arose, he saw various celestial maidens within the grove of trees.
The various branches of the trees are fully adorned with precious bells, which produce exquisite sounds.

The color of the ground is like refined gold from a molten furnace; in some places, the ground has the hue of silver or crystal, and it is further embellished by many hundreds of thousands of wonderful lotus ponds.
In that region, the forest trees are soft and supple, and hundreds of thousands of birds emit exquisite sounds.

As those celestial maidens sport and enjoy themselves in such a grove, at the very moment a thought arises in the mind of a celestial son (*devaputra*), wonderful ornaments appear instantly from within the woods to adorn him.
Adorning their heads with garlands of lotuses and wearing garments of various colors upon their bodies, they approached the place where the devaputra was.

Having arrived nearby, they surrounded him with all manner of ornaments, singing various songs with exquisite voices that were deeply captivating to the heart, thus providing entertainment for the devaputra.
Possessing an abundance of immeasurable articles of pleasure, those celestial maidens thus provide various forms of entertainment for the deva-son.
Having never seen these celestial maidens before, once he has beheld them, the deva-son reflects: "Who are these people?"
From where have you come?
To whom do you belong?
For whose sake have you come?

"Once they had come and seen him, they beheld that he was arrayed in garments of various colors and his body was adorned with various jewels; in his hands he held immeasurable musical instruments—of which this is but a partial illustration."

In no place whatsoever can the sounds of song and music of the celestial maidens of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven be compared to this, much less to the fruit obtained from immeasurable wholesome karma endowed with the three kinds of merit.

The celestial maidens of the Yāma Heaven surpass those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the excellence of their singing and voices; they are superior in their physical appearance, power, stature, vocal melody, and sensory enjoyment; they excel in their groves, trees, flowing streams, ponds, and rivers; and they are superior in all respects regarding *sudhā* food, magnificent palaces, and places for recreation and pleasure.

In each successive stage upward, even unto the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), all such matters as the degree of physical form, the power of the body, the stature of the body, and the enjoyment of vocal song are increasingly superior.
Why is this? Because the fruit of karma is weighty;
because the precepts of mind are pure and free from defilement.
These celestial maidens of the Yāma Heaven are beyond compare and possess every excellence.
Yet, in that place there are two kinds of faults, namely impermanence and desire; only a small measure of subtle pleasure can be spoken of.
If a foolish person observes the prohibitive precepts while longing for existence, forming such a thought as,
"May I, by observing these precepts, be reborn in the heavens," I speak [this teaching] in order to turn their mind away from that.
There are such faults as impermanence, decline, and separation from what is loved. Why is this?
If one gives rise to even a slight thought of longing for existence (*bhava*), all wholesome dharmas will utterly perish.
Within all of existence, there is no place where anything is eternal.
Whether below, above, or in the intermediate directions, it is impossible for anything to be eternal, unmoving, and indestructible.
"There is no conceptualization that is not non-conceptualization; for this reason, it is said that the retribution of those heavens is not a desirable place.
At that time, the goddesses there surrounded the newly born deva-son, engaging in various entertainments such as singing, dancing, and sporting.
At that time, the devaputra, having never seen such a sight before, thought to himself:
"To whom does she belong, that she approaches me?
As soon as the devaputra had this thought, by the power of his own wholesome karma, the celestial maiden spoke:
"The Deva is my lord; why does he not speak with us?
The Deva is my husband; whatever he requires, I shall serve as his attendant to bring him joy."
At that time, having heard this, the deva spoke thus:
"If you belong to me, you may now come near here into this grove. Why is this?"
"This celestial realm is a land of enjoyment;
those born in this heaven experience pleasure here.
Then, that goddess embraced the deva-son, and they experienced immeasurable and manifold pleasures.
The goddess rose again and spoke these words:
"I have wandered together with the deva-son throughout this grove.

Within this grove there are many and immeasurable varieties of celestial hosts; whatever the eyes behold is lovely, and there are the delightful sounds of various birds. There are many streams, rivers, and ponds adorned with lotuses, and many hundreds of thousands of various mountain peaks."
Its peaks are lofty and steep, adorned with various kinds of the seven treasures and many radiant splendors.
The various mountain valleys are everywhere magnificent and beautiful, filled with the songs of many diverse birds.
Everywhere upon the ground there are ponds for adornment, and it is fully endowed with such merits as these.
I wander and play together with the devaputra, experiencing all manner of sensual pleasures.
At that time, having heard these words from the celestial maiden, the newly born deva spoke to her, saying:
"I shall follow your will and do exactly as you say."
Having spoken thus, he rose from his seat for the sake of pleasure.

Together with all the celestial maidens, the deva-puṃgava wandered through the groves, holding various musical instruments made of celestial jewels in their hands, sporting and indulging in sensual delights with that deva.

"At that time, the devaputra wandered about and indulged in negligence together with those celestial maidens; furthermore, other devaputras and celestial maidens were also meeting and engaging in play together."

At that time, the two devaputras, upon seeing one another, felt mutual affection and conversed together; the celestial maidens likewise did so, their hearts filled with mutual love as they all united and proceeded toward another grove.
Such a grove is named the Grove of Playful Delight; that grove measures three thousand yojanas in extent, and it contains immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas [of trees].
The hosts of devaputras fill that grove, no different from the Venuvana grove in the wilderness; thus, being endowed with various merits, it is named the Grove of Playful Delight (Kridāvana).
The celestial realm of wandering is fully endowed with all varieties of excellence.
Both groups of devas behold that place together; it has never been seen as such before, nor has it ever been heard of, and it is beyond all analogy.
Having seen that grove, he gave rise to a heart of joy; his face, eyes, and all his features bore expressions of delight.
Then the newly born deva and his celestial nymphs spoke to him, saying:
"Such things as these have never been seen before."

Having spoken thus, the sons of gods and daughters of gods from both factions—wearing celestial garlands upon their heads, their bodies anointed with sandalwood paste, and seated in the celestial palace—ascended into the void. There they sang, danced, laughed joyfully, and sported together, proceeding as one group toward Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

As they ascended in this manner, there were yet other devas together with their celestial maidens, holding lotus flowers in their hands as they sat in their heavenly abodes; ascending into the void, they sang, danced, laughed joyfully, and took pleasure in one another’s company as they proceeded together toward Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

It is likewise as they ascend; furthermore, there are other devas who can move with subtle agility, holding lutes in their hands, able to pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of mountains without obstruction as they travel.
Together with the celestial maidens, they sang, danced, and sported, and furthermore proceeded toward the palace where the night-ruling Yāma king Mucilinda dwells, their hearts filled with joy.

It was likewise as they ascended; furthermore, other devas in the midst of the sky rained down various celestial flowers, and together with their celestial maidens, they sang, danced, and sported as they proceeded toward the palace where Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, resides.

It was likewise as they ascended; those newly born devas beheld all such infinite and diverse distinctions and infinite amusements, and they also moved together, proceeding in this manner before the celestial maidens.
Those immeasurable devas all conversed with him in pleasant speech.
At that time, the newly born deva-son saw from afar a supreme radiance exceeding a hundred thousand suns, which the eyes of ordinary beings cannot behold.
Furthermore, one hears immeasurable sounds from that place; these sounds are of four kinds:
first, those that are harmonious;
second, those that are authentic and true.
Third, harmony; fourth, equanimity.
Having heard these sounds, those devas felt joy arise in their hearts and asked the celestial maidens:
"Now I see that place as supremely wonderful and lovely; there is a great radiance present there, which I behold from afar.
There, such superior sounds are heard—exquisite, harmonious, and perfectly blended songs—and furthermore, there is dancing and play. How can this be so?"
At that time, the goddess immediately spoke to the newly born deva-son, saying:

"The King of the Yāma Heaven enjoys pleasure there, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of immeasurable devas and immeasurable hosts of celestial maidens, all of whom are praised by the entire assembly of devas."
"It is just like the Tranquil King (Śāntideva) of Tuṣita Heaven, who experiences celestial bliss.
At that time, having heard these words, the newly born son of heaven felt a sense of supreme wonder and thought to himself:
"Aside from the Tranquil King, where else could there be such an experience of bliss as this?"
Then, having reflected thus, that newly born deva spoke to the celestial maidens, saying:
"Who is named Śānti? Where does she dwell?"
"Having seen this, I shall go to see him.
At that time, having heard his words, the celestial maiden reflected and thought to herself:
"Because he has only recently been born, he does not know that there are others of greater power; therefore, he speaks in such a manner."
"I see tranquility. Then, that goddess spoke to him again:
"The Tuṣita Heaven is above me; it is superior to mine by a hundred thousandfold."
All the enjoyments and pleasures I possess, as well as all the fruits of my karma, are entirely superior.
In this place, his majesty, power, and all other various qualities surpass mine in every respect; he dwells above me.
None of the ordinary devas can go there; it is not within their realm.
All those devas are superior to me; only those devas who possess the power of merit and great supernormal powers can reach that place—it is not accessible to all devas.
The Sutra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll 37;
The Sutra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll 38,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: Observing the Heavens; Part Three: Yāma Heaven.
"At that time, the newly born deva-son had this thought:
'The great bliss of those devas is superior even to that of the King of the Yāma Heaven here.'"

Reflecting thus, for a brief moment his mind became restless and unsettled; he conceived a sense of affection and delight toward the pleasures of the sensory realm and became even more deeply attached as he contemplated those places of joy. He beheld all the various ways in which the hosts of devas experienced pleasure, and he proceeded to wander through those regions with calm composure. In this manner, he gradually drew near to the dwelling place of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

There, the king enjoyed pleasures, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of celestial hosts, while a vast multitude of countless goddesses, holding lotuses in their hands, attended upon him in worship.
The physical form of that celestial king is beyond comparison; there is no one whose form equals his. He is fully endowed with majestic power, radiance, and merit.

That king’s splendor surpasses all the light of the entire host of devas, just as the sun, surrounded by a multitude of stars, excels all other luminaries. The King of the Yāma Heaven is likewise preeminent in majesty and virtue as he sits upon his lion throne.
The seats are soft to the touch, not made of silk or similar materials, but consist entirely of exquisite jewels. Adorned with rare colors, forms, and garments, they are replete with majestic power.
There are sounds of immeasurable kinds of song and music, and various playful diversions; hearing these qualities of desire, their superior minds experience bliss.
Within the Yāma Heaven, there is no realm more excellent than this.
It surpasses all the merits possessed by Śakra, King of the Devas:
from the body of Mucilinda, the Heavenly King of the Yāmas, fifty clusters of exquisite light emerge, each of which blazes forth with flames.
King Śakra emits light from two places upon his two shoulders, but the mass of that radiance is inferior to this.

The assembly at the gates of the six sense-faculties of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, through the power of their virtuous karma, are thus harmoniously united; they surpass all the merits of King Śakra by a hundredfold.
Because it is thus supreme, it cannot be compared to anything else.
That form is such that no analogy can be found; likewise, its bliss and its objects are so superior that they are beyond comparison.

The majesty of that king’s retinue, though inferior, still surpasses that of Śakra; how much more so, then, is the majesty of the heavenly king Mucilinda, which is pure both internally and externally?
Since that is the case, how can it be illustrated?
"At that time, when the newly born deva-son saw King Mucilinda from afar, [the king's] physical beauty, pleasure, and majestic virtue were all slightly inferior."
Having seen the Heavenly King and observed his own body, he reflected thus:
"My body is inferior to that of the Heavenly King by a hundred thousand million times, even a hundred thousand billion times."
Because he performed the foremost and most excellent wholesome deeds, he obtained this sublime body as the Heavenly King Mucilinda.
He possesses such extraordinary majesty and virtue; how much more so, then, for those who have heard the name "Tranquility," which surpasses even this king.
"Mañjuśrī, all the majestic virtues possessed by Mucilinda are fully complete; the karmic fruits of the higher heavens increase in excellence, becoming progressively more subtle and sublime.
Having reflected thus for a short time, he again focused his attention on listening to the sounds of singing and other music.
At that time, this newly born deva-son proceeded further, advancing calmly and slowly toward the abode of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

The Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda was surrounded by many of the most excellent and wondrous physical forms; he was supremely adorned, with a handsome countenance and peerless majesty. Possessing a beautiful body and a sublime voice, seven thousand celestial maidens attended him closely, singing, dancing, laughing joyfully, and strolling about.
As for the other celestial maidens who were slightly further away from his person, they were beyond counting.
They engaged in playful amusements and all drank the celestial wine, their minds and intentions being mutually aligned and one with each other.
Each of those celestial maidens, together with King Mucilinda, enjoys sensual pleasures, and in their hearts they think:
"The King loves me alone; he does not love any others."
‘May I obtain pleasure from her, and not from other women;
may my desire alone be supreme, and that of others not so.
In the desire of the Yāma Heaven, it is accomplished by verbal expression alone; there is no physical union.
All those celestial maidens harbored this thought, each thinking individually that the Night-Ranger King Mucilinda loved her alone.

At that time, the newly born son of heaven again approached King Mucilinda of the Yāma Heaven; he saw him surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, and how he, possessing immeasurable varieties of supreme and wondrous merit, subdued the celestial hosts with his eloquent speech.
The Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda universally recognizes all the devas—whether those who have been born there for a long time or those who have only recently been born.
When Mucilinda saw the newly born deva, his eyes did not even blink; the other long-established devas then spoke to that newly born son of heaven, saying:
"Great King, you are looking at him now in this manner; why do you not kneel?"
At that time, having heard this, the newly born deva-son knelt immediately.
Seeing him kneeling, King Muxilinda addressed him, saying: "Great Seer!
You have now been born for the first time in the Heaven of Yāma.
You may now abide in the foremost place of delight within the Heaven of Yāma and experience its pleasures there.
It is by practicing the three kinds of wholesome karma that you have attained birth in this place; welcome, well come!
"By virtue of your own wholesome karma, you experience pleasure here; dwell for a long time in this celestial realm and do not act with negligence.
Then, the Night-Mover (Mauṣḷudha) King of the Yāma Heaven spoke these verses to the newly born deva:
"If the newly born son of a deva Should cherish the pleasures of this birth,"
The suffering of falling back from that state is not even one-sixteenth part of it.
Its flavor is slight while its terrors are many; it constantly deceives and deludes men.
Just like a city of the Gandharvas, so too is the flavor of sensual pleasure.
"This desire is extremely evil, for it can destroy sentient beings;
therefore, the wise always have hearts that do not trust in desire.
Thus did Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, instruct that newly born deva. The newly born deva then addressed Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, saying:
"It is truly so, Great King!
At first, I did not know that there were such faults within this heaven; I did not know what the practice of the Dharma was like among the gods.
Whatever other gods practiced and performed, I likewise practiced and performed, being myself unaware of it."
At that time, the Deva King Mūśalinda spoke again in verse:
"When the time of death arrives, there is no other companion;
after death one departs for another place, and there is no one who travels along with you."
The minds of sentient beings are manifold; according to their various mental dispositions and desires, they perform diverse karmas that create the bonds of birth and death.
Even at the very moment of birth, one is already inevitably subject to death.
With minds shrouded by various forms of delusion, they do not perceive the terror herein.
When the time for their downfall has arrived, though they could destroy even the highest existence (*bhavāgra*),
those with deluded minds fail to realize the dreadfulness of the suffering of death.
Joy gives rise to negligence, and one undergoes birth and death again and again;
the deluded do not perceive this, for sensory objects can deceive the gods.
The serpent of sensory objects bites; craving for sensory objects engenders delusion.
The gods are constantly unaware, yet they face great terror at the time of their decline.
The suffering of birth is the greatest; the suffering of decline is not like this.
Such great suffering as that of birth is found only among the gods.
Blown by the winds of karma, one revolves and undergoes great suffering;
led away at death by the man, the mind is deceived and lacks autonomy.
Neither father nor mother, neither friend nor relative [can save one].
When the time of death arrives, there is no one to accompany you.
Such is the nature of this deception: all are without companions.
Only the mind is thus malevolent, each deluding the other in turn.
Neither others nor even one's own kin can act as a savior;
once the time of death has arrived, kin are just like those who are not kin.
If you were to see that even those who are not kin could experience great happiness [in such a state], [you would realize the futility of worldly ties].
The King of Death’s power is sovereign; he forcibly snatches away great bliss.
His realms cause the mind to become deluded, and one is constantly driven by desire.
Though one has not yet awakened to this suffering and affliction, it will certainly be obtained—of this there is no doubt.
“Mukhānanda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, taught that newly born deva with such true dharmas as these.
Having heard them, the deva felt a sense of weary detachment;
yet in an instant, he returned to dancing, singing, play, and laughter, once again becoming immersed in attachment.”

Because the minds of all ignorant, ordinary worldlings are impermanent, because their minds are unstable, because the power of pleasure overcomes and obscures their minds, and because they are driven by craving, their minds fluctuate a hundredfold.
For this reason, the devas engage in heedless conduct.
Because of this, not even the slightest dharma remains within their minds.

At that time, the newly born deva-son, in the presence of King Mucilinda’s palace, indulges in various amusements together with his own retinue; thus they sing, dance, and engage in all manner of play, possessing every excellence of the five sensual desires.
Experiencing pleasure within his realm, he returns after his gathering; following the path by which he came, he arrives at his own dwelling place.
He wanders through the region of clouds, returning to his original abode.
Having returned, they again enjoy various pleasures together with the other devas, frolicking and wandering toward the hall named Vistīrṇa.
That hall is lovely; I shall now describe it in full detail.
Within it are twenty nayutas of palaces, where various colors, diverse forms, and the gathered radiance of jewels shine; there are many hosts of devas and multitudes of celestial maidens.
In this manner, regarding such a wondrous palace, everything is obtained according to what the deva thinks.
Just as that son of heaven conceives in his mind, so shall it all be obtained—of such color and such form.
The gardens, groves, and flower ponds are adorned by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flocks of birds, as well as peaks of the seven precious gems.
Such is that palace, due to the virtuous karma of the devas.
When a deva remembers the desire to travel, the palace, along with its gardens, lotus ponds, and various celestial trees, flies through the air like a bird, no different from such.
If a deva thinks,
"This palace moves away, and I shall experience pleasure," at that very moment of thought, it flies away.
If a deva recollects and gives rise to such a thought as,
"May food and drink be fully provided according to my needs," then there appear rivers of celestial food,
complete with immeasurable varieties of every kind. These appear according to his thought, flowing forth from the river, replete with color, fragrance, and flavor.
Because of that deva’s original wholesome karma, such a realm would not exist if his karma were unwholesome.
Furthermore, this deva gave rise to this thought:
"This palace of mine has become even more spacious and vast, extending for one hundred yojanas."

At the very moment of that thought, there appeared many immeasurable varieties of delightful flowing rivers, exquisite lotus ponds, and mountain torrents; they were fully provided with dwellings, various groves, and wonderful lotuses—all of these being perfectly complete.
Seeing such vastness and breadth, those devas become even more joyful and give rise to this thought:
"I shall roam and sport for pleasure in this place; my heart is filled with joy, and I shall further enjoy myself here together with other devas."
"Furthermore, I shall cause other devas to sport and enjoy themselves with me in this palace; if the celestial hosts of King Yāma come here, I shall experience pleasure together with them.
As soon as that son of the gods conceived this thought, the celestial hosts belonging to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāmas, came toward the interior of his palace to sport together with him.
At that very moment of recollection, those devas set forth:

some were riding geese, some riding peacocks, others riding domesticated birds, some riding flowers, some riding ducks; furthermore, there were other devas riding ruddy sheldrakes, some riding jīvaṃjīvaka birds, and some riding trees.

Thus, arriving by various and diverse vehicles with hearts of supreme joy, they sport amidst the sounds of music; furthermore, together with various celestial maidens adorned with diverse forms and garments, they laugh, sing, and dance, their bodies draped with exquisite lotus garlands, experiencing the highest bliss.
With hearts filled with supreme joy and praised by celestial maidens, they travel through the air toward the pleasure palaces of the gods.
Having arrived there, they mutually experience various delights; because they thus engage in such playful and heedless conduct, their minds become unsettled.
The Yāma Heaven King Mūsuludha, seeing their negligence, observed them.
Just as with the negligent devas, he contemplated their negligent conduct and gave rise to this thought:
"What skillful means can I now employ to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to these heedless devas?
At that time, King Mūśalinda again reflected with a subtle mind, deeply contemplating:
"I shall now have the other devas who are *srotāpannas* follow me, so that we may deliberate and discuss together."
In those regions—within those various places of wandering—where they experience manifold pleasures and act with negligence, how do wholesome dharmas encompass those devas?
Benefiting both self and others, one acts for the sake of both; this causes both myself and others to be free from faults and transgressions.
Acting as a virtuous friend to bring benefit to others and teaching the Dharma to aid them is what constitutes a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"If one teaches evil karma, that person is an enemy who can cause one to accumulate the evil karma of the hells.

At that time, King Mūśalinda, having deliberated together with the Srotāpanna, used his own supernormal powers to manifest a wondrous palace; they ascended that palace together and departed for that destination.
The first [level] is fully endowed with rivers and ponds, and possesses all manner of gardens and trees; there are immeasurable varieties, all of which are delightful.
Possessing such supreme and wondrous things, they proceed together toward that place.
The palaces of the Cloud-Cloud Wandering Grounds are inferior, being a hundredfold and a thousandfold less excellent. Why is this?
Because of the power of virtuous karma; among all the gods in the Yāma Heaven, the virtuous karma of the Yāma King Mūśaludha is the most supreme.
Because his wholesome karma is superior, his supernormal powers are also superior.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, his palace is superior; it possesses a wondrous radiance that surpasses all the palaces belonging to the gods of the Yāma Heaven.
Just as the sun palace surpasses all other palaces by even the slightest degree,
so too that palace is most preeminent, such that the palaces of other devas do not equal even a fraction of it.

That palace, fully endowed with its own merits, travels through the void toward that region—the place where the clouds wander and where one experiences pleasure—and the *srotāpanna* devas follow along together.
Because the heavenly beings who are *srotāpanna* noble ones have few indulgences in heedlessness, they accompany him toward that place.

At that time, when the heavenly beings indulging in heedlessness there see King Mūśaludha, they conceive a heart of reverence and quickly advance; they all turn toward King Yama Mūśaludha and together welcome him.
Whether by the hundreds, the thousands, or by the hundreds of thousands, all of them came forth to welcome the Heavenly King.

At that time, once the Heavenly King Mucilinda had arrived at that palace, he immediately exercised his supernormal powers; through the power of his transformations, he caused those welcoming deities to suddenly become invisible to one another, so that each saw only themselves approaching the Heavenly King alone.
As for the musical sounds, they heard none of them, and as for the various exquisite forms, they saw none at all.
By means of the king’s supernormal powers, he caused each of those gods to have this thought:
"I alone am here; where are all the other gods?"
"He has always sat with me in this palace; where has he gone now, that we can no longer see him at all?
Having thought thus, those gods each approached the Heavenly King Mucilinda.
They saw only the Heavenly King and the *srotāpanna*, but saw no others.
Each of those gods conceived a sense of wonder and felt fear in their hearts, and they all addressed the Heavenly King Mūśaludha, saying:
"The various gods who dwell together with us in this palace do not know where they have gone now."
At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda addressed those devas, saying:

"All such devas as these, being heedless and practicing heedless conduct, shall—due to the exhaustion of their karma—fall away into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, or be born among human beings."
If a heedless deva practices heedlessness and is ruined by it, he will be destroyed by craving for sense objects.

Because his mind delights in the merits of the five desires, his mind’s conceptualizations regarding the fire of sense objects cause him to blaze up of his own accord; this fierce fire is produced from the flint of his own mind.

Blown by the winds of karma into what is called the Hall of Vast Palaces, their hearts remain unsatisfied; having already been scorched by the five tongues of flame, they are further incinerated by the great fires of hell, undergoing various kinds of suffering.
Deceived by their own minds, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the hells.
This fault of negligence is the most preeminent among all faults. Why is this so?
Those who are destroyed by the fault of negligence lose all wholesome dharmas.
Such gods deceive themselves with their own minds;
these deluded gods will later feel regret in their hearts.
At that time, all the devas there, having heard this from King Mucilinda, each conceived a sense of weary detachment and fear in their hearts. They each addressed King Mucilinda, saying:
"O Great King, Lord of Devas!"
"How is it that in a single moment of thought, all the devas pass away?
This is unprecedented.
In a single moment of thought, all the devas thus pass away, until the places where the various clouds once roamed are entirely empty."
"This is extreme suffering; by what means can I ensure that I do not fall back, that I do not undergo affliction, and that I do not experience the suffering of separation from what is beloved?"
"How may I avoid falling into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and the like?
At that time, King Maudgalyāyana (Mūśalinda) spoke these verses for that deity:
"One who walks the path of heedlessness Shall not behold the noble and virtuous."
Just as one who drills into ice will never obtain fire, so too, where there is no cause, there can be no fruit;
and where there is no cause, the fruit cannot be found.
Thus, those who seek merit through negligence shall ultimately find nothing at all.
Heedlessness destroys one's life; thus do those who wander among the gods lose their wholesome karma through delusion and fall into the realms of evil destinies.
If one possesses such a deluded mind and seeks pleasure in sensual desire, [they will likewise fall].
After later encountering decline and affliction, their minds will give rise to regret.
Those burned by the fire of desire, deceived by sensory objects,
shall not attain the path of tranquility or any of the supreme states of bliss.
Whether it be the pleasures of the world or the joy born of sensual love, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the internal bliss born of tranquility.
This bliss born of tranquility is supreme; it is a pure dharma that transcends birth and death.
The exhaustion of craving is the foremost bliss; it is the ultimate bliss from which there is no falling back.
One who is fearless and contented does not seek such bliss through this practice;
there is no other bliss that can compare to the bliss of such meditative concentration.
Those who are not bound by craving and cannot be destroyed by doubt,
they cross the ocean of existence and constantly experience all happiness.
Those whose minds dwell upon desire do not experience such happiness.
These are all instruments of suffering, leading one into the realms of hell.
Constantly bound by the snares of karma and dragged away by them,
no one at all can rescue or liberate one from this suffering.
The phenomena of the past and future that are perceived arise from karma, through which birth and death occur;
both the past and the future are thus obtained through the cause of karma.
Due to ignorance, there is craving and desire, continuing even until the time of final decline.
They undergo the great suffering of birth and death, yet are unable to perceive it.
Because they are shrouded by ignorance, they experience pleasure without ever feeling satiated;
because they lack contentment, they are thus constantly destroyed.
Neither in the beginning, the middle, nor the end; neither in this life nor in future lives—those who constantly cultivate desire flow on because of ignorance.
Because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they will inevitably fall away from this state.
Those who consume the poison of heedlessness do not perceive it because of their delusion.
This body changes moment by moment; yet, due to delusion, one does not realize this, and only when one is about to decline later on does one perceive the suffering.
"If one fears suffering and fears death, one should mindfully reflect upon the True Dharma; in this way, one will surely attain happiness.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Heavenly King Mucilinda, those devas temporarily turned their minds away from heedless conduct and again addressed the Heavenly King Mucilinda, saying:
"O Great King, Lord of Devas!
None of these gods can be seen; have they all been destroyed in a single moment?
Have they all perished?"
"I pray that the King will speak truly.
At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda addressed him, saying:
"The virtuous karma of the Tathāgata departs in this very manner."
Because karma is exhausted, all phenomena of karma are necessarily thus.

All sentient beings are separated from one another, giving rise to distress in their hearts; such are the three relative phenomena as aging, sickness, and death, in contrast to life, youth, and health.
If any man—whether human or divine—whose mind is not negligent and who practices non-negligence, he will be able to perceive these three kinds of terrors.
These three kinds of life—longevity, freedom from illness, and vigor—are all liable to be lost through negligence; such is the ultimate fate of all devas before death arrives.

One should practice with diligence and employ various skillful means; the three kinds of diligence are giving, ethical discipline, and wisdom, and these three are able to eliminate these three great fears.

Immeasurable discursive thoughts constantly pursue one’s conduct, never departing for even a moment; if one does not fear them, then later, when facing death, one’s mouth and face will be distorted, the eyes will roll, and the sense faculties will dry up. All kinsmen, brothers, wives, children, and retinues will abandon one, at which time one will be scorched by the fire of the suffering of separation from loved ones and die in extreme agony.

At all times, those gods engage in immeasurable conceptualizations; as the five sensory desires manifest before them, they sing, dance, play, laugh, and wander about in joy, thus experiencing pleasure and indulgence in the realms of the groves and gardens.
"Just as one might see the face of a virtuous friend or a spiritual mentor yet fail to perceive the fruit [of that connection], they will later be consumed by the fire of regret, thinking:
'Why did I not perform wholesome deeds?'"
Why do you not practice giving?
Why do you not maintain the precepts?
Why do you not cultivate wisdom?
"Why did I not practice these three kinds [of virtue]?
Due to negligence, I am now dying alone, separated from my kin and brothers, and seized by death."
"Thus being led away, one is separated from this world’s foremost place of love and the realm of immeasurable enjoyment.
Thinking thus, later on, remorse and distress arise in the mind; in this way, it can even destroy the gods.
Before the powerful King of Death arrives, you must by all means refrain from negligence.
By abandoning negligence, you will surely attain peace; at the time of death, you will not be consumed by the fires of remorse—this path is the foremost in security.

For all those who are afflicted by every kind of decline and distress, if they joyfully practice and frequently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, they will at that time rely upon these to receive rescue and attain liberation; these are their refuge, their protection, and their powerful allies.
"When the time of death arrives, it is certain that one cannot escape it;
it will inevitably bring about destruction. When it comes, it cannot be restrained nor avoided; it can snatch away the lives of all sentient beings."
Regarding such an evil death, why do you not skillfully apply yourself with diligence and exertion so that it does not come?
While all forms of negligence have not yet arrived, it is most excellent to remain virtuous.
Just as there is great poisonous fire, so too is heedlessness.
You gods are all driven by heedlessness;
furthermore, all gods are subject to heedlessness, and that enemy of heedlessness follows them, never letting go.
Wandering and sporting upon the mountain peaks within the groves, he perceives all phenomena—which are entirely impermanent—as being permanent, and gives rise to this thought:
"I shall always enjoy pleasure together with these hosts of celestial maidens; such celestial maidens are eternally youthful and never age."
"This celestial maiden has always accompanied me, and I can never be parted from her.
Thus, he is constantly deluded by the pleasures of various sensory objects; yet, there is a supreme power capable of destroying them.
“Once the King of Death has arrived, neither the celestial maidens can obstruct him nor save one;
even the calculating mind cannot save one, nor can the ever-discriminating mind save one.”
All that they contemplate is entirely empty; all is impermanent, unstable, and fragile. Having been destroyed by negligence, they are reborn in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Ruined by delusion, they have brought about this great suffering.
Furthermore, those devas, revolving through birth and death since beginningless time, repeatedly experience anguish; constantly deceived and deluded, they remain ignorant and fail to awaken.

At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, having spoken these words consistent with the Dharma and consistent with its meaning, those gods present who possessed wisdom received his speech—like nectar, stainless and pure—into their hearts; they abandoned negligence and felt profound revulsion for sensual desires.
Having thus established right mindfulness in his mind, that deva addressed King Mūśalinda with these verses:
“If what is beneficial and true, Is consistent with reality and not otherwise—
When a deva speaks such words, It is the cause of benefit.”
One who can collect the mind in tranquility, such a person attains happiness;
proceeding from happiness to the state of bliss, they will certainly attain joy without doubt.
But if one is inverted regarding this, heedlessness destroys the devas.
"One with such a deluded mind will surely fall into hell.
Having spoken thus to the Heavenly King, the deva gave rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Those sons of the gods again questioned the Heavenly King, saying:
"We now have a doubt.
Where have all the celestial hosts within this palace gone?"

At that time, King Mūśalinda, seeing them thus subdued, gave rise to a sense of weary detachment; having abandoned his negligence, he immediately withdrew his supernormal powers, and those hosts of devas were able to see one another once more.
Once they had seen one another, they each gave rise to hearts of mutual joy.
After those hosts of devas had become joyful, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, addressed them, saying:
"You all were obstructed from seeing one another; it was because you were hindered by my supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) that you were unable to see each other."
Now you shall once again see one another as before.

If that powerful King of Death were to arrive and destroy you, for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas you would never see each other again; he would cause you all to fall back into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where it would be impossible to meet in such a manner once more.
"Therefore, you should maintain mindfulness and not act with negligence; do not give rise to divergent thoughts, but always restrain the mind and take no pleasure in sensory objects.
When many gods had heard this, they felt profound revulsion and renunciation.
Because his mind was weary of and detached from [sensual existence], he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, King Mūśalinda, having understood this, was filled with great joy and gave rise to this thought:
"I have now accomplished what was to be done; my own purpose is fulfilled. I shall leave this place and proceed to the Realm of Play."
“The hosts of devas who roam in the Cloud Abodes possess a supreme state of wholesome mind; among them, those who have already attained the stage of Srotāpanna practice with heedfulness.”
If they do not obtain [these things], their minds become light; they thus practice heedlessness, delighting in heedless conduct and the pleasures of heedlessness.

In this way, amidst groves, flowing streams, ponds, rivers, mountain peaks, and valleys, they enjoy various pleasures together with celestial maidens, disregarding the fear of death. Even as they experience pleasure and sport in those places, singing, dancing, and laughing, the collection of their lovely and wholesome karma is completely exhausted.
When their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fail to perform what ought to be done and fall again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If there remains residual karma, they are born among humans, always possessing the foremost joy and pleasure, the foremost physical beauty, and the foremost abundance of wealth and goods. Loved by all people, naturally joyful in heart, and acting in accordance with the Dharma, they enjoy various delights through play, song, and dance; they take pleasure in visiting monasteries and dwelling by lotus ponds, flowing streams, and rivers.

Whether they be kings, ministers, or wealthy persons such as rulers, all their acquaintances shall be their virtuous friends; their kinsmen and brothers shall all love and delight in them; they shall never speak falsely, their minds shall always be upright, and they shall always take pleasure in associating with all virtuous people; they shall not violate their dignified deportment and shall be fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
In this way, that person’s aggregate of the body is fully endowed; such is the body they obtain due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates all the grounds and abodes of the Yāma Heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
In that Yāma Heaven there is another place called Saṃcita-bhāra (Accumulated Burden).
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows this:

if a virtuous person constantly fears the fruits of karma, possesses an upright nature, maintains right view without deviation, practices right action, abandons evil associates, and at all times recollects the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; if they feel deep dread toward even the slightest evil deed and refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and even improper conduct on the road.

If he sees women singing or dancing, or hears the sound of their ornaments, upon hearing them, he does not become attached; his mind does not harbor affectionate thoughts, but observes them skillfully. Without unwholesome thoughts or delight, having seen their faults, his mind does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
If he thus refrains from unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will be reborn in a good destination—the realm of the Yāma devas, in the region known as Saṃcitavistara.

Once this person of wholesome karma has been born there, he experiences uninterrupted bliss; he is constantly endowed with his own natural radiance and enjoys the pleasures of the five sensory objects.
In that place there is a mountain named Accumulated Cliffs, adorned with trees made of the seven precious gems that fill the entire mountain.

There are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various flocks of birds; these birds, adorned with immeasurable varieties of wondrous colors, beautify that mountain. Dwelling in that mountain region, they produce various sounds and move through various places; to behold them is truly delightful.
There are many immeasurable varieties of exquisite colors, moving through various places, with infinite forms and shapes filling those mountains.

Furthermore, there are flowing streams, rivers, and ponds; amidst various lotuses and mountain ravines, there are many trees of various names known as "Recollection Trees" (Smṛti-vṛkṣa) serving as adornments. Their interlacing branches form dwellings, and they are fully endowed with all kinds of flowers and fruits.

That mountain measures three hundred yojanas in extent; it abounds everywhere with hosts of devaputras and hosts of devakanyās, and throughout that entire mountain range, all is delightful and pleasing.
In the various locations within those mountains where the hosts of the first heaven dwell—
every such auspicious spot throughout— all seven ridges and seven enclosures are interspersed with various groves and gardens.
"In that realm of excellence there are seven kinds of jewels, and each of these seven kinds of jewels constitutes a distinct section.
In one section, the radiance of blue jewels extends throughout sixty thousand yojanas; likewise, this radiance pervades the entire void with a universal blue hue."

When the devas recall their desire to ascend the mountain, they themselves adorn their entire bodies with various interspersed jewels; thus arrayed, they travel upon the galleries of blue jewels on that mountain of accumulated cliffs, proceeding through the air.

The various ornaments of jewels upon his own body have no color or radiance of their own; they take on the same color as the mountain, appearing entirely blue with a blue luster, identical in appearance to the mountain itself.
The blue color and its radiance are both supreme.
On one side of Mount Saṃcita, there is the color of such blue jewels.

Furthermore, on the second side of Mount Saṃcita, everything is made of crystal (*sphaṭika*). When the gods, having adorned their bodies with various ornaments, traverse that side in all their diverse array, moving through the air, the various jewels adorning their entire bodies lose their own brilliance and become the same color as the mountain—namely, the color of crystal.
The radiance is likewise equal to the mountain.
The light from the bodies of those devas is as if they have entered a pool of water.

Furthermore, at the third flank of this mountain of accumulated cliffs, everything is made of silver; its color and radiance extend for five hundred yojanas, a supreme white light that brings great joy to those who behold it.
If any deva travels along that side of the mountain, departing by way of the sky, the various colors of their bodily ornaments all become white, due to the power of the light from that mountain side.
Furthermore, the fourth side of Mount Kūṭāgāraśikhara is composed entirely of Jambūnada gold, its radiance and color like that of the sun.
The radiance of that side forms a circular wheel of flames extending for a thousand yojanas.
Whatever deva travels upon that side, moving through the air, their body likewise becomes the same color.

Furthermore, at the fifth terrace of this mountain range known as Heap of Cliffs, all is the color of the true jewel padma; it is entirely crimson, and its radiance extends everywhere for a thousand yojanas.
If a certain deva travels through that region, moving through the air, his body becomes the color of vermilion.
If that deva is adorned with red jewels, his natural red color fades away, and he becomes a hundred times more intensely red.

By the power of the radiance of those precious chambers, furthermore, the sixth chamber of this mountain of accumulated cliffs is entirely the color of genuine diamond-jewels; its light extends everywhere for five thousand yojanas, and the colors from its edges appear like the hues of a celestial rainbow.
If any deity travels through that side, moving through the air, their body likewise becomes the same color as it;
this is due to the power of the mountain’s radiance.

Furthermore, on the seventh side of this mountain, Heap-of-Rocks (Citrakūṭa), all is composed of various colors of the seven precious gems, and its radiance extends throughout hundreds of thousands of yojanas.

If any deity travels through that region, departing by way of the sky, all the colors of their various ornaments become even more excellent as they follow their bodies, and the colors of their diverse garments become increasingly superior.

"Thus, this Mount Saṃghāṭa, with its supreme and wondrous majesty, is universally victorious; if one were to compare it to Mount Sumeru, the king of wonderful jewel-mountains, the lovely light and the radiance of its exquisite jewels would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of that of Mount Saṃghāṭa."
Such is the majestic power of that Supreme Mountain. Why is this?
Because their virtuous karma is supreme, the radiance of that mountain is likewise supreme.
Because the pure precepts of those gods in the Yāma Heaven are superior and their virtuous karma is superior, by virtue of these excellent causes, that mountain is universally supreme and lovely.
Furthermore, that mountain is completely covered on all sides by nets of genuine pearls; it is foremost in purity and foremost in radiance, such that all the gods who behold it obtain benefit.
That net of pearls thus covers the mountain, making it exceedingly magnificent and endowed with great radiance.
There is a great city there named *Yathāmanasikāra* (As One Wishes), adorned with exquisite pearl necklaces; such is its brilliance, which is vast and expansive.
There are many immeasurable varieties of birds named *Vicitra-hāra* (Diverse Necklaces) dwelling within that net.
When the gods become heedless and act with negligence, those birds speak these verses as a teaching of admonition:
"Because of various karmic causes, You have now been born in this celestial body."
Having attained heaven yet not knowing the Dharma, one later feels regret in the heart.
This grove is delightful, adorned with branches and railings;
for those born in this place, it is entirely the fruit of wholesome deeds.
Whatever karma a person creates— whether they perform evil deeds or virtuous deeds—
they shall be established accordingly, and the fruit shall likewise be obtained.
You gods, behold for yourselves the inferior, middling, and superior pleasures.
Whatever the actions one performs, such are the various fruits one receives.
Adorned with manifold forms of delusion, the person who follows the path of delusion is bewildered by that very delusion and fails to see the great terror.
If one is deluded and negligent, they do not act for their own benefit;
delighting in various desires, they long for various fruits.
Because the gods are shrouded by delusion, they do not perform any meritorious deeds.
If a celestial being craves mixed fruits, that celestial being does not maintain the precepts.
Just as one might discard a lamp while wishing only to take its light, so too is it with those celestial beings: they seek a fruit apart from its cause.
If one seeks the fruit by means of its cause, one will then constantly experience happiness;
without seeds, fruit cannot be obtained, and without a lamp, how could there be light?
Without precepts, there is no heaven; apart from wisdom, there is no liberation.
If one has attained liberation, then there is nothing to be hoped for.
If one is free from sensual craving, then wisdom is no longer "mine.
Any pleasure obtained through karma is entirely defiled and turbid.
If one attains the bliss of total cessation, one is entirely free from defilement;
if one does not attain the bliss of total cessation, one will undoubtedly remain defiled.
Even after passing through a hundred kalpas, such a person remains unsatisfied with sensory objects.
Because they delight in the pleasures of sensory objects, they know no satisfaction in their enjoyment.
If one constantly draws near to desire, it increases again and again;
that increase is like poison, which brings suffering in the end.
Sensual desire can cause destruction and is a constant cause of decline;
if one cannot renounce desire, that deva is utterly indolent.
To know both the virtues and the faults [of desire] is the mark of wisdom.
Not knowing the nature of merit and fault is the mark of ignorance.
If one knows the characteristics of merit, one likewise knows faults;
truly knowing merit and fault, one is never separated from happiness.
"The wise man knows this desire, that its objects surpass all merit;
O Deva, why would you abandon wisdom to indulge in the pleasures of sensory objects?
Thus did that bird, within the pearl net, speak these verses for the benefit of the devas.

Furthermore, that mountain is encircled by a universal wheel of light; various jewel wheels revolve and wind around the summit, their diverse radiances resembling the colors of a rainbow over Jambudvīpa.
When the various devas see those revolving wheels, their hearts give rise to joy, and then revolving wheels arise surrounding their bodies.
All those devas, seeing each and every side, conceive a sense of wonder, as their celestial bodies are adorned with immeasurable jewels.
In each of these quarters, they sport and enjoy pleasures because they have cultivated various kinds of superior wholesome karma; thus do they experience such bliss.
Furthermore, within all the palaces on those mountains, there are four gardens and groves, like Mount Sumeru.

What are the four? The first is named Prāsādika-vyūha (Adorned with Beauty), the second is named Śikhara-vana (Forest of Peaks), the third is named Amṛta-prāsādika (Adorned with Nectar), and the fourth is named Citra-bīja (Various Seeds).
These are called the four types of groves.
There are flowing streams, rivers, and ponds with exquisite lotuses; in various mountain ravines dwell diverse birds whose songs are subtle and wondrous.
The flowers bloom upon all the trees, and the songs of the birds among the trees are entirely delightful.
With railings and multi-storied pavilions, various halls and palaces arranged in orderly rows, there is a mountain named Sarvadāna (All-Giving), rare and most excellent.

Having reached that mountain, they next arrive at that grove, which is like a region for wandering amidst clouds; there, the devaputras, together with hosts of celestial maidens, enjoy the bliss of the five celestial sensual pleasures.
That grove was most delightful; within it, one forest consisted entirely of Jambūnada gold, its leaves being made of vaidūrya gems, exquisite lotus-gems, and flowers the color of musāragalva.
Furthermore, the second grove is a silver grove with leaves of genuine gold.
The flowers of that grove are of immeasurable varieties and possess a supreme fragrance that perfumes a hundred yojanas.
When those devas smell it, having smelled the fragrance, their hearts are filled with supreme joy.
That third grove is made of *vaiḍūrya*, its leaves are of silver, and its flowers possess various colors and various fragrances.

That fourth grove is named Citraratha; it possesses immeasurable varieties of colors, with countless rivers and ponds containing wondrous lotuses, and is endowed with hundreds of thousands of merits, including the various songs of diverse birds.
