Within those forests, there are various sounds, just like those of Śakra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, in his second heaven.

Thus, in that place, the Suyāma Heaven is endowed with the majesty of light and all virtues; there, amidst mountains, immeasurable beings who have performed many wholesome deeds dwell, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, enjoying happiness and endowed with the virtues of diverse sensory realms.

That Suyāma deva of great merit possesses the foremost supernatural powers, the foremost radiance, and the foremost might; manifested by his own karma, he is fully endowed with the merits of the five desires, all objects of the five desires are utterly delightful, and his six sense faculties experience bliss.
In that place, such is the Suyāma Heaven; it is the most excellent among those heavens due to the power of virtuous karma.
That mountain is likewise endowed with all that is lovely, and within it there is a bird named the "Always Joyful at All Times" bird.
Thus that bird, with speech corresponding to its own karma and its aspirations, spoke these verses:
"Not through the thought of wisdom, nor yet through aspiration, Is it that karma alone can grant happiness;
Happiness is obtained through the performance of action."
The most excellent among the excellent, the most desirable among the desirable—
the virtuous fruit of observing the precepts— is attained by a man through his own actions.
The gateway of sensory objects wavers like the current of a winding river.
If one can discipline the mind, that deity is an instrument of happiness.
Having performed meritorious deeds oneself and practiced them with one's own body, one experiences suffering or pleasure; thus does one experience it within one's own self.
One who commits evil deeds has their own body as an enemy;
when the body is virtuous, it is like a good friend. Thus one acts with the body.
Just as the speed of a river flows on, so too does the transformation of the body proceed.
Therefore, one should perform meritorious deeds and maintain stainless, pure precepts.
If the mind is inclined toward what is unwholesome and constantly delights in sensory objects,
it is like being in a place of great darkness, performing actions that bring no benefit.
Shaken by the objects of pleasure, constantly following the course of desire, those who harbor such unrighteous thoughts will suffer affliction.
All sufferings are the work of Māra; the joy of the Dharma pervades everywhere.
Such are the characteristics of suffering and pleasure; thus does the wise person know them.
If the mind seeks happiness, one should practice in accordance with the True Dharma;
if there is a longing for suffering, that mind is practicing what is contrary to the Dharma.
Without causes, one does not obtain happiness; the same applies to all various forms of suffering.
Through the distinction between the causes of suffering and happiness, you shall know the practice of self-benefit.
If there were immeasurable conceptualizations, then there would be immeasurable varieties.
All those karmic fruits lead one thus to birth and death.
If one does not delight in the Dharma, this life’s body will pass in vain;
the Dharma can lead one to heaven, and the practitioner of the Dharma attains happiness.
If one protects the Dharma, they will thus be well-provided for;
those who abandon the Dharma are not virtuous and will certainly enter hell.
A good person would rather die than practice what is contrary to the Dharma.
Those who abandon the Dharma will perpetually wander through birth and death.
Those who lack the eye of the Dharma have their minds shrouded by delusion;
they delight in what is false and profitless, like one with diseased eyes looking upon what they perceive as pleasure.
The Dharma-sprout takes the mind as its field; without the mind, it does not arise.
If the mind that upholds the precepts is dull, one will practice exclusively what is contrary to the Dharma.
Having relied upon the path of unrighteousness, one is driven to perform unwholesome deeds.
Having long wandered through birth and death, one becomes weary of the mind.
Within every moment of thought, this mind revolves in immeasurable ways;
its essence is extremely light and restless, like a phantom or a gandharva city.
That mind is bound; yet wisdom and ethical discipline are not bound, possessing great power and transforming in immeasurable ways.
Though sensory objects and desires abound, they are driven to act by the influence of craving.
Therefore, they deceive and delude the devas, causing them to engage in heedless conduct.
They do not realize that there is eventual decline; at the end of life, there is certain destruction.
All things are impermanent and shifting; when their time is exhausted, one must inevitably lose their bliss.
All the pleasures of the heavens, the deluded gods do not perceive;
through delusion, craving, and heedless conduct, they take such sensual delights as their joy.
Because the hosts of gods are ignorant, they perpetually revolve in birth and death.
What was not previously existent comes into being at a later time; what has already existed returns to non-existence later on.
The gods are certain to fall; such is the nature of worldly phenomena.
Only those possessed of wisdom do not cling to worldly pleasures.
"Thus that bird, while traveling through those mountains, spoke in this manner, in harmony with various dharmas.
If a deva had previously performed virtuous deeds over many lifetimes, upon hearing the bird’s words, his mind would embrace them."
If one has practiced wholesome dharmas for only one or two lifetimes, rather than many, then even upon hearing the cries of birds, one will not perceive even a single phrase.
Therefore, you should practice with diligent effort, constantly perform what is beneficial, and cultivate the light of wisdom; apart from this, there is no such salvation and no such medicine.
This wisdom can obstruct all evil destinies; it is the seed of the foremost happiness.
The wise person should take delight in the True Dharma with their mind, cultivating the mental faculty through right mindfulness and reflection.
If one cultivates the mind, one will possess such meritorious qualities in harmonious conjunction, proceeding by stages even unto Nirvana.
When the devas hear the voices of those birds, they momentarily cease their negligence for a brief interval.

Furthermore, on the peaks of that mountain garden, which are composed of the radiance of immeasurable jewels, those devas—amidst the manifold assemblage of the fivefold sensual pleasures of that celestial realm—sport, wander, and experience various forms of delight.

Until finally, when all the accumulated agreeable and wholesome karma has been exhausted, they pass away from that place and, according to their karma, are born in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

When born among human beings, they constantly experience happiness throughout their entire life; they attain mastery over their own bodies and are not dependent on others. They possess the greatest wealth, their minds are always fond of wisdom, and they are endowed with the most excellent and upright physical form. They are a joy for all people to behold and are respected by all. Born in a lovely land of abundance and prosperity—whether in a city or a populous region—they are supported by their kinsmen and brothers. If they become kings or ministers, their minds are upright, they act in accordance with the Dharma, and their view is correct and not deviant.
Due to that remaining karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 38.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 39.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Eighteen: Observing the Heavens, Part Four: Yāma Heaven.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes all the grounds and locations of the Yāma Heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
within the Yāma Heaven there is another region called Saṃcita-bhāra (Accumulated Burden).
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that region?
He sees, hears, and knows this:

if one practices wholesome deeds with diligence, maintains the precepts, and never harms others; if one’s observance of the precepts is harmonious, accomplished, without deficiency, without flaw, and without breach—firm, unbreakable, and capable of closing the gates of all evil destinies; and if one can provide cooling relief from the burning afflictions of all evil destinies and act as a refuge like parents in future lives.
Acting in accordance with this is endowed with three kinds of merit.
What are these three? They are:
refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, and refraining from sexual misconduct.
Not killing and not stealing are as previously described. Regarding non-sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*):

whether walking along a road or through a crossroads, moving from street to street—whether on an alms-round or for other purposes—if one sees women adorned with various songs, dances, and ornaments, one does not give rise to thoughts of attachment, nor does the mind take pleasure in them. Seeing what others do, one does not rejoice in it; instead, one celebrates the good deeds of others, instructs them to repent, and speaks of their faults, saying: "This woman’s foremost cause of transgression is sexual misconduct; by this cause and condition, she can cause sentient beings to fall into hell."
Maintaining the precepts in this way and keeping the holy life pure, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the region known as Saṃjñāprabha.
Having been born there, by the power of one's wholesome karma, one experiences bliss therein.

It refers to Mount Kūṭaśaila, five hundred yojanas in extent, filled with the lovely sounds of various birds; the cries of the *vavaka* abound within the mountains, and throughout that entire mountain range, the sounds are delightful.

However, when that deva is first born, he is thus produced beneath a tree made of the seven precious gems; just as a person sleeping in Jambudvīpa awakens upon hearing the sound of another clapping their hands, so too does that deva awaken because he hears the lovely sounds of the birds.
The radiance of that deity’s body surpasses the radiance of the sun rising over a mountain peak in autumn;
the light of that sun is not even a small fraction of a likeness compared to it—the celestial radiance is superior.
When that deva suddenly awakens, by the power of his wholesome karma, the bird causes him to hear these verses corresponding to wholesome karma:
"Released from the binding of sinews and snares, From places of excrement, urine, and spittle— Such is the body of a woman; Therefore, one is born here."
Deceptive and crooked, not straight; seeing a man, the heart rejoices;
the mind is deluded and does not abide. You have come because you do not recognize [the truth].
With false speech you deceive others; your adornments bring pleasure to men.
She is skillful at deceiving women and adept at deluding men.
Like a bee that delights among various flowers,
she thus gives rise to love and pleasure for various kinds of men.
Just as a bee, having sipped from a flower, then departs for another place;
so too are women: they sip from a man and then go elsewhere.
Though they may acquire wealth like the virtuous, they are ever-angry and impossible to tame.
Having deceived the man, she then goes elsewhere.
With her deceptive and illusory implements, which are no different from virulent poison,
this woman kills the man and brings about his misfortune.
Just as wind, space, and fire cannot be grasped or held,
so too women cannot be guarded by any number of various means. They bring no benefit,
yet they lead to death and disease, and cause the commission of unwholesome karmas and the like.
Women are the primary cause that can destroy the practice of Nirvana.
Whether in various places or in narrow, terrifying locations,
the suffering that men in this world encounter is entirely due to women.
Neither in youth nor middle age, nor in the tranquility of old age, does the female mind remain still; it is like the radiance of the sun.
A woman is no constant friend; she is like the flickering flame of a lamp.
Such a person is a constant enemy, like an inscription carved in stone.
They associate only with the wealthy; when one has nothing, they treat one with disdain.
When one possesses wealth, women draw near; when one has nothing, women abandon one.
Giving things and making offerings, performing all manner of meritorious deeds,
his mind is like a flame that cannot be grasped.
When a man thus conforms to this, he acts according to whatever the mind desires.
Such women as these constantly deceive men;
like a snake covered by flowers, or like fire covered by ashes and dust,
so do their outward forms conceal their hearts— women are just like this.
Just as seeing a poisonous tree is pleasing to the eye yet not wholesome, so too are women like poisonous flowers; the wise should abandon them.
To long for the sight of women and to take pleasure in their sensory realms—
He never attains happiness, neither in this world nor in the next.
If one universally delights in heedlessness, is indolent, fickle, and deceitful,
associates with evil friends, and is greedy for food, he shall not see the noble ones.
Diligent, of great strength and valor, Virtuous, having renounced women, Respectful and believing in cause and effect— Such a person attains goodness for themselves.
The net of all faults is women; They move about within the world.
"If one can distance oneself from women, one will be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.

Thus, having heard the voice of that bird—like something heard in a dream—the deva, fully endowed with immeasurable and various kinds of sublime merits, spoke this verse, performing a virtuous deed that benefits both parties.
When the newly born deva hears this sound and has heard it thus, knowledge arises through those conditions.
By means of that knowledge, he is able to recollect from where he came to be born:
"I have come here having well maintained the three kinds of lovely precepts."
Recalling his place of origin, and having recalled it, he spoke this verse:
"By upholding the precepts, one is born here; yet women cannot be abandoned.
O brave one, by leaving women behind, you shall reach the city of Nirvana."
Neither fire nor sword, neither fire nor sword nor saw, can sever the bonds of women; there is no other expedient means.
I have already long since abandoned them, having come here with a diligent mind to revile and loathe them.
By relinquishing [the former], one attains this bliss in the superior realm of the Yāma Heaven.
Beyond this bliss, there is yet another great bliss;
one shall attain the stage of non-retrogression and will surely reach Nirvāṇa.
At that time, having heard the birds' speech and beheld their colors, the newly born deva-son felt joy in his heart as he gazed upon that celestial realm.

The mountain of Accumulated Fragrance is filled with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of trees surrounded by radiant light; one also sees hundreds of thousands of flowing streams with manifold adornments and hears the various songs of the celestial birds.
Those birds possess wings made of various jewels.
There are many exquisite ponds, adorned with various lotus flowers, from which swarms of bees emerge like smoke; they are thus magnificent and upright in their beauty.
All such things as these were originally unseen and have no resemblance to anything else.
Having thus observed the realm of the Yāma devas, they rejoice according to what they have seen and heard.
Having rejoiced, he rose from beneath the tree; having thus arisen, he observed his own body.
Having observed his own body, he saw that the majestic splendor and radiance belonging to his body were of various and immeasurable kinds.

Having seen the majesty and the various radiances of his body, he immediately gives rise to pride regarding his physical form; subsequently, he further gives rise to a second kind of pride, thinking thus:
"I have no equal; whatever I recall, I obtain it all."
"This is the second pride.
Next, there further arise five other types of prideful mind, namely, the five faculties becoming attached to the five objects of experience.
Because such seven kinds of pride arise, they cause the mind to be destroyed; the dharmas originally practiced cannot continue, and one becomes indifferent to everything."
Because their minds are stirred and they are largely negligent, those negligent minds act with negligence;
bound by the snares of the five sense objects around the necks of their craving, they ascend that Mount Accumulated Burdens for the sake of experiencing pleasure.
"That mountain has three levels, namely: the lower level, the middle level, and the upper level.
On that lower level, there are five groves:
the first is named Fragrance-Drifting;..."
The second is named Jvālā-vijaya;
the third is named Prabhāsa;
the fourth is named Nitya-sukha.
The fifth is named High Mound (*Uccaya*).
Whatever grows in that Forest of Floating Fragrance (*Gandhavahana*) possesses a fragrance superior to all others, and its scent permeates five thousand *yojanas*.
In that Forest of Supreme Flames (*Jvālābhāsvara*), there are immeasurable kinds of flames and various colored radiances, all of which surpass the light of a hundred thousand suns.
In that Forest of Radiance, the celestial bodies emit light, and therein they enjoy the five objects of desire, all of which are fully provided.
In that Forest of Constant Joy, there are flowing streams and lotus ponds, complete with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial fragrances, tastes, and colors.
That highest peak of the High-Heap Forest possesses the radiance of the seven jewels.
Thus has been described the grove and forest of the lower level.
Now, for the second, the middle level:

In those hundreds of thousands of vast wildernesses, there are immeasurable seven-jeweled lotus ponds filled with hundreds of thousands of lovely birds of various kinds uttering diverse songs; their touch, taste, color, and fragrance are exceedingly delightful, pure and stainless, filling that entire land.
The third higher realm is the summit of the mountain peak; there is a city there measuring one hundred yojanas, filled with devas.

The city is named Jewel Forest (Ratnavana), and it contains various rivers. Within these rivers, flowing water is filled with food and drink. There are many celestial trees and exquisite lotus ponds, and the trees are fully adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flowers and fruits.
There were many joyful hosts of celestial maidens, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, filling that city.

When Suyāma and Maudgalyāyana arrived at that city, they experienced celestial pleasures within it through the fivefold qualities of desire; the harmonious union of lovely sounds, tastes, forms, and fragrances increased the fire of craving.

In this way, those devas experience various pleasures upon Mount Citrakūṭa; they roam, sport, and enjoy diverse sensory realms, experiencing manifold delights according to the distinctions of cause and effect.
"At that time, this newly born deva, because his mind yearned for the pleasures of sensory objects, went toward that mountain alone, without a companion.
An elder deva, seeing this newly born deva, felt joy arise in his heart; he immediately approached him and spoke thus to the other elder devas:
'This deva is one who has just been born.'"
The other elder devas asked,
"How does this deva now know how he was first born?
Then that great deva answered the other devas:
"This newly born deva possesses five characteristics: first, his body is covered in radiance, yet he has no clothing;
he thinks to himself, 'May other devas not see me naked.'"
At the very moment of that thought, others see him as having clothes when in reality he has none; this is the first sign.
Furthermore, for a newly born deva, there is a second sign, namely, seeing objects and giving rise to a sense of wonder.
In the gardens and groves, he has never seen them before; upon seeing them, he gazes at them all around—this is the second sign.

Furthermore, for the newly born deva, there is a third sign: seeing the celestial maidens with their delicate countenances, he feels bashful and ashamed; doubt arises in his mind, and he does not dare to look directly at them—this is the third sign.

Furthermore, there is a fourth sign of a newly born deva: when he sees other devas, even though he approaches them, his mind gives rise to doubt and his will becomes unsettled; this is the fourth sign.

The newly born deva-son further possesses a fifth sign: when he wishes to ascend into the void, fear arises in his mind; even if he flies, he does not go high, moving with composure rather than speed, traveling no great distance as he wanders near the earth, either alongside city walls or clinging to them—this is the fifth sign.
"The newly born deva possesses these marks; let us go together to visit him.
At that time, the host of devas surrounded Mahādeva, and they all went to the newly born deva. Having arrived, they said:
"O Great Sage, you should know!"
We gods, seeing you at your birth, have come here together.
Because of your wholesome karma and because you have well cultivated the training in the precepts—unbroken, unimpaired, unblemished, unpierced, stainless, and pure—you have attained rebirth here.
Having spoken these words for the sake of the newly born deva, and because of his negligence, he next ascended that mountain and departed, flying through the air.
In the midst of the various musical sounds in the void, their hearts were filled with joy as they mutually experienced pleasure together.
At that time, having seen this, the newly born deva-son thought to himself:
"I shall now go alone on foot to Mount Saṃghāta."

Having reflected thus, he immediately proceeded on foot to that mountain. There he saw a great multitude of celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with immeasurable garments, singing to the accompaniment of countless varieties of musical sounds.
When those celestial maidens saw the newly born deva, they each rejoiced and vied with one another to run forward toward him.
Having seen his eyes, they were struck with wonder and gazed upon him; they further thought to themselves:
"I ought to make offerings to him; I ought to become his wife."
Approaching him yet again, and seeing him for the first time since never having seen him before, he was filled with a sense of wonder and said to the Devaputra:
"I now delight in beholding the Devaputra; I have come for the sake of the Devaputra."
"Today, O Devaputra, because of the fruits of your own karma, you enjoy pleasure together with me.
Within these gardens are various groves; within these various groves are various mountains, high peaks, and mountain valleys."

Furthermore, there are various and diverse celestial abodes, adorned with the seven treasures and surrounded by radiance; trees, flowers, and fruits fill the mountains, and in every place there are pavilions formed from tree branches.
Within that hall, there are many various sounds of song and music; the color of its ground is like molten gold, and they experience pleasure upon such a ground of exquisite beauty.
Furthermore, there is another place adorned with various lotuses in flowing streams, rivers, and ponds.
Moreover, in the void of space, there are hundreds of thousands of halls, adorned in every way and most lovely to behold.
"I shall enjoy various pleasures together with you, O goddess, in such a place as this.
Then, by the power of his former wholesome karma, that newly born deva spoke thus to the celestial maiden:
"I shall now enjoy pleasure with you in this manner."
"In this realm of heaven and earth, one can never be satiated with any sensual pleasures.
At that time, the host of celestial maidens there went together toward another grove named the Grove of Variegated Palaces (Vicitrāyatana-vana).

In that forest, amidst the various sounds of music, hearing those melodies, their hearts give rise to joy; through the fulfillment of their wholesome karma, they experience the retribution of pleasure.
That forest is endowed with realms of exquisite form, which are exceedingly delightful.

Thus there are immeasurable delightful tastes and various superior flavors; thus there are immeasurable delightful fragrances; and thus there are immeasurable delightful tactile sensations—these tactile sensations exist because the ground is soft and supple.
Not made of thread, these various celestial garments are soft and smooth to the touch.
All such things are exceedingly lovely.
There are various birds with exquisite songs, and various melodies that are most delightful; amidst immeasurable kinds of sounds, they experience the pleasures of these five sensory objects.
Together with various celestial maidens of exquisite and diverse adornments, they experience manifold pleasures.
At that time, that grove was thus endowed with such merits, filled with immeasurable hosts of devas and celestial maidens.
When those devas see this, they give rise to a sense of supreme wonder.
Having seen these various things, they travel everywhere; throughout all those gardens and groves, the ground is adorned with musaragalva, blue jewels, and other such gems.

Furthermore, there is a green ground where birds move about; these birds possess bodies variegated with the colors of various kinds of the seven treasures. These birds take delight in playing together, uttering the sound "bakku," and enjoy themselves with their mates upon that green ground.

Having seen the green ground in this way, he further sees various birds within the water—many mandarin ducks, geese, ducks, and the like—adorned with a variegated array of diverse colors; those birds all possess the most excellent of sounds.

Having seen this, he further saw a deva together with various devī-s in a grove; in those groves and forests were flowers of the six seasons, all blooming at once, and from each tree there vied to produce the most excellent blossoms.
The radiance of those trees was withdrawn and emitted like the opening and closing of eyes; when the sons of gods and the hosts of goddesses saw this, they were filled with joy.
Furthermore, seeing in another place rows of green forests of various colors, their hearts were stirred; because their hearts were stirred, they experienced manifold sensual pleasures.

Looking up at the void, he saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens filling the sky, adorned with the finest garments that pervaded space in various intermingled patterns, like the various colors of a painting on a wall, or upon silk or cotton cloth; they were seen in all their diversity, singing, dancing, laughing joyfully, and engaging in manifold amusements.
When those devas see this, their minds become stirred and they engage in various forms of conceptualization.

Having seen it in the air, they turn their faces back and immediately behold a grove of lotus ponds; the ponds are filled with various kinds of lotuses of diverse shapes and exquisite colors—blue, yellow, and red—and there are various birds within those ponds.
Having observed this, those devas gave rise to a heart of joy.

At that time, the hosts of devas were seen everywhere; there was no empty space between them, filling the void of space entirely. There was no place where birds and deva-hosts were not present, pervading both the waters and the sky, with no gap as small as a mote of dust left unoccupied.
By the power of having cultivated wholesome karma in the past, upon seeing this, he spoke these verses:
"This great ocean seen here can never be filled;
so too is the craving of the tongue for flavors— there is no time when it is satisfied."
The nose greedily smells various fragrances, like seeing them, it can never be satisfied;
the body clings to pleasant touches, and its lack of contentment is likewise.
The ear is greedily attached to exquisite sounds, and it too never knows satisfaction.
The mind conceives of various phenomena, none of which can ever be fully satisfied.
Moving within the six sense-objects, it departs from the light of contentment;
driven by the affliction of thirst, it perpetually revolves through the immeasurable varieties of the realm of desire.
The gods who do not know contentment are like fire fed with fuel;
if they do not know contentment, they have no place for their own bodies to abide.
Thus, these six fires of evil, fanned by the wind of arising thoughts, [consume them].
This [fire] constantly burns the world, yet the deluded do not perceive it.
This is the realm of the heedless; it is not the path of practicing the Dharma.
Now that heedlessness has destroyed me, I have entered the sphere of sensual pleasure.

"Thus, that deva, recollecting his former wholesome karma, having finished speaking the verse because he remembered that karma, by the very nature of things (dharmatā), once again becomes attached to sense objects. There are many lovely sounds, touches, tastes, smells, and forms, associated with immeasurable varieties of merit, which increase moment by moment."

Once they have grown, they roam about together with hosts of celestial maidens in various places, experiencing immeasurable kinds of sensual pleasures through the five objects of desire, with infinite distinctions and manifold enjoyments.

Furthermore, together with the celestial maidens, they went to various gardens and groves; within the mountains and valleys, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of birds emitting exquisite songs, adorned with the seven treasures and most delightful to behold.
Having arrived at another celestial realm, desiring to experience pleasure together with the other hosts of devas and celestial maidens there, they reached that place.
There, they addressed one another with beautiful voices, conversing in this manner; thus, with single-minded focus, they frolicked together, wandering about and enjoying themselves.

If there are other inferior devas who are surrounded by ten thousand celestial maidens, constantly enjoying sensual pleasures without ever knowing satiety, those maidens always delight in play and are also able to provide for hundreds of thousands of countless other devas with their desires.
Thus do these celestial maidens delight in sensual pleasures.
For what reason is it that in those heavens there are many women and few men?
There is a cause for this:
In the heavenly world, desire-taint is the most powerful and delusion is middling.
If one is born there, while dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one already sees the celestial maidens of that place in their full splendor.
Having seen her, his desire increased; becoming attached to that celestial maiden, he immediately turned his mind toward taking her body.
Because that being in the intermediate state (antarābhava) yearned for pleasure and grasped with the mind, he immediately assumed the body of that celestial maiden.
For this reason, among the gods, the goddesses are many while the male gods are few.

Thus, there are some gods who have ten thousand goddesses; others have twenty thousand; others have thirty thousand; others have forty thousand; others have fifty thousand; others have sixty thousand; and so on in succession up to hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of goddesses. Among them, some are more powerful, and thus the number of their goddesses varies accordingly.
"The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings engage in the practice of desire just as humans do, without difference.
Their sexual desire is such that the male and female bodies mutually unite and press against one another; yet there is no emission of impurity."
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three engage in sexual desire, they embrace one another, yet their organs do not touch.
When the gods of the Yāma Heaven engage in sexual desire, it is accomplished through speech and laughter.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, desire is fulfilled by mutual gazing.
In that Nirmāṇarati Heaven, desire is fulfilled by speaking, hearing voices, and smelling fragrances;
for those dwelling at a distance from one another, if they smell each other’s fragrance or hear their voices, their desire is then completely and fully accomplished.

In this way, the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) and those of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*) are not different in one respect:

if a single son of heaven is loved and cherished by all the celestial maidens and held in great esteem, his mind knows no weariness nor any illness; he is free from flesh, bones, insects, sweat, and all such things.
Within each and every day, there is the conjunction of superior power; at all times, that power is ever indestructible, fully endowed with both potency and radiance.
For these reasons, a single deva-son, together with many hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who are intensely fond of one another, constantly engages in amorous acts.

That deva’s mind does not dwell upon only one maiden; rather, his heart delights in beholding all of them. He acts according to his will, and all the celestial maidens likewise possess the highest degree of sensual passion. They mutually enjoy pleasure without hindering one another, experiencing such bliss exactly as their minds conceive it.
Furthermore, those gods, together with those goddesses, experience whatever they desire in infinite varieties and infinite distinctions;
these correspond to their celestial status and accord with their own past karma.

In the region known as Accumulated Burdens, for a vast duration of time, they sport and enjoy pleasures through immeasurable varieties of the five sensory qualities, while numerous hosts of devas and celestial maidens proceed in succession along the paths.
They proceeded further to another forest named Vāyu-vyūha (Forest of Adorned Winds), where they wandered and sported in pursuit of pleasure.
There they saw other sons of gods whose original merit had been exhausted; among the hosts of celestial maidens, the time for their downfall had arrived.
When those devas are about to fall from their celestial realm, signs appear that resemble the symptoms of illness.
These signs are as follows:
if those devas approach a lotus pond, the flowers do not bloom; this is the first sign.
Furthermore, as for the second sign of that falling deva: whether near forest trees or lotus ponds, the bees leave the forest and depart from the lotuses; this is the second sign.
Furthermore, the third sign of that deva’s decline is this: when that devaputra is sporting with the celestial maidens, he feels revulsion upon hearing their songs; this is the third sign.
Furthermore, the fourth sign of that deva who is falling away is this: when he approaches a grove of trees, all the flowers of those trees wither;

this is the fourth sign. Moreover, the fifth sign of that deva who is falling away is this: when he wishes to go for recreation through the palace halls, he is unable to travel through the air; this is the fifth sign.

These five signs are the omens of impending decline for those in the Yāma Heaven; they are just like those of the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, when they are about to fall, where one knows it by the presence of flies and the breaking out of sweat.
Such are the omens and signs of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three when they are about to fall from their station.
Because the wholesome karma of these gods in the Yāma Heaven has been exhausted, these various signs appear; thus one knows that they are about to fall.
"He possesses twelve great signs of death, through which these signs of impending death appear in succession.

When that deva is about to fall, the signs of death manifest; that is to say, when that deva intends to emit light, the light does not emerge but instead returns into his own body, just like the setting sun."
Furthermore, signs of decline appear: that is to say, those devas see flower garlands and fruits and their hearts no longer find delight in them.
Again, signs of decline appear: that is to say, when those devas place flowers upon their heads, they immediately fall away.

Furthermore, signs of decline appear; that is to say, when those devas look at their own bodies in the water, they see their own reflections not as celestial bodies, but as the bodies of those into whose realm they are about to be born—whether seeing the form of a hell-being, a hungry ghost, an animal, or a human. Upon seeing such diverse visions, they fall from there, and signs of being reborn as distinct beings in the hells and other realms manifest.

Furthermore, signs of decline appear; that is to say, those devas look at their own bodies in the water. Having seen their bodies, they give rise to fear, and once fear has arisen, the hairs on their bodies all stand on end.
Furthermore, signs of decline appear: that is to say, those devas perceive their own abodes as ugly and lacking in majesty.

Moreover, signs of decline appear: that is to say, in whatever place those devas sit—whether in a beryl region, a gold region, a silver region, a crystal region, or a blue-jewel region—in all such places they sit unsteadily and with agitation.
Furthermore, signs of decline appear: when that deity is blown by the wind, he trembles violently, and its touch is harsh and rigid.
Again, signs of decline appear:
the touch of that deity’s garments becomes as heavy as diamond.
Having seen this, his mind becomes sorrowful; once the mind is sorrowful, it finds no pleasure in desirable sounds, tastes, touches, forms, and fragrances.
Having become thus, he immediately draws near the fire of impermanence.
Furthermore, there appear other signs of regression, namely:
in various places—such as within walls made of lapis lazuli or stone, or in mirrors, or in other locations—one looks at one's own reflection and does not see one's head.
Furthermore, signs of decline appear:
they may see their own head upon the ground; seeing such a sign, they know that death is near and not far off.
Having realized this, those celestial maidens feel weary of it, loathe it, and abandon it.
Those devas are filled with sorrow and give rise to thoughts of separation; such is their suffering.
The suffering experienced from birth until death does not equal even one-sixteenth part of this suffering.

Furthermore, the twelfth sign of decline appears: namely, the mind of those devas becomes disordered and unstable, like a whirling firebrand; they cannot fix their attention on a single point as their minds are extremely agitated. Because of the sorrow of impending decline, their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) appears on the verge of extinction, just as the light of a lamp grows faint when its oil is exhausted.
Thus, that deva perceives and sees that he is about to fall away; when the celestial maidens who constantly attend him see him in such a state, they all abandon him and depart.

Just as when a fire burns a tree, birds see it and depart without considering the merits it previously possessed, so too do those celestial maidens abandon and depart from a deva who is about to fall, while the other sons of gods follow him along.
At that time, having seen the women depart with such an appearance, the deva calmed his mind, endured it with patience, and spoke these verses:
"Because of their own karma, they receive such retribution;
seeing that my desire is fading, the women abandon me from afar and do not approach."
Because their own karma is exhausted, they are separated from immeasurable bliss;
seeing the deva falling, the celestial maidens then depart for other heavens.
This pleasure is not constant, and the nature of the mind is likewise so.
Women delight in evil; friends are untrustworthy and evil.
These four great sufferings constantly oppress one at all times;
therefore, one should abandon them, just as one would cast away poison or fire.
Through karma one obtains happiness; through karma one obtains suffering.
By means of karma there is destruction, and through karma such things are seen.
Such is the great bliss of these gods, as they enjoy the five sensory qualities.
Later, when their meritorious karma is exhausted, they fall from heaven and lose their sovereignty.
Thus it is said that birth and death are entirely an illusion of karma;
the path to liberation is that which the Buddha has revealed as the ultimate truth.
If one’s mind is agitated, one does not perceive various faults;
being possessed by delusion, one thus draws near to women.
The sun is not the cause of darkness, nor is fire cold because of it.
Women lack a loving heart; having little love, they do not abide [in it].
Like the earth, they remain unmoved; like the wind, they move and do not abide.
The nature of women is ungrateful; therefore, such faults exist.
For a long time a husband may provide much for his wife, but when he sees her decline, he abandons and distances himself from her, like a bird leaving a dried-up pond.
One who practices the higher path does not fall; even stones cannot fly.
Mountains cannot be traversed; women lack virtuous friends.
They constantly create obstacles, destroying the reputation for Dharma and meaning;
they provide no benefit to the treasury and give rise to every fault.
Diamond may be made pliant, and even the sun may be freed from its heat;
yet a woman does not abandon her deceit—such is the nature of things.
It is not through various kinds of affectionate speech, nor through offerings, nor through material wealth.
Yet they can captivate women, whose hearts are like fire, difficult to approach.
When they obtain pleasure, they act together with them; when they encounter suffering, they abandon them.
They do not reflect upon their boundless kindness, but harbor a single transgression in their hearts.
"In the gardens and mountain ranges, one achieves immeasurable pleasure;
yet once decay and affliction have arrived, women grow weary and abandon him.
Having seen the celestial maidens thus forsaking his body, that deva reflected that all worldly phenomena are like this, and having spoken these verses, he departed.
The women’s hearts were firm; though their original deities wished to die, they immediately departed and took refuge with other deities.
It was just as when a lotus flower withers in winter and swarms of bees, seeing it thus, immediately abandon it and go elsewhere.

At that time, the goddess who had been a deva fallen from desire departed for another heaven. There, amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, she engaged in song, dance, and play, experiencing various pleasures in gardens, groves, and lotus ponds. Amidst the songs of various birds and beneath the *dhāraṇī* trees adorned with hundreds of thousands of ornaments, she forgot the devaputra with whom she had previously shared her pleasures, and instead enjoyed various delights together with other devaputras.

In an instant, she forgets as if it were hundreds of thousands of lifetimes; seeing the former husband fall from his station, she forgets his virtues in a single thought-moment—thus do women abandon kindness and fail to remember it.

The nature of women is such that they have no attachments or longings; it is only because of external objects that they feel love or desire, or because they have some need, that they draw near to men.
Yet its essential nature is not fully realized in any respect; there is no one throughout all the past, future, and present who is able to know its essential nature.
Because the mind is in motion, it is like a whirling firebrand, a city of the Gandharvas, or a mirage—incapable of being grasped.
The essential nature of women is likewise thus, incapable of being seized.
Thus, appearing before him, the deva abandoned his celestial realm and departed for another heaven.
Because of the karmic impressions of his former deeds, that deva about to fall spoke this verse:
"If a deva’s mind wavers, Like one intoxicated by sensual pleasures,"
Feeling no fear regarding decline, one will certainly fall from the celestial realm.
If one is born in a heavenly abode, there will inevitably be a subsequent fall;
just as when the day comes to an end, night is certain to arrive.
"During the day it is as if advancing; during the night it is as if retreating.
Having understood these two states, one should contemplate that there is neither birth nor death.
Thus those gods reflect upon their former births; having formed this reflection, they take human time as a metaphor rather than celestial time for illustration.
Why is this? Because there is no day or night for the gods; since they possess their own radiance, it is perpetually day.

At that time, having thus observed for such a long duration those gods who were about to fall from their state, he returned to the natural law of the gods and definitively experienced the karmic fruition of his wholesome deeds.

Furthermore, those devaputras sport and enjoy themselves amidst groves and forests to the sounds of the five kinds of music, whether by rivers, embankments, streams, and valleys, within lotus groves, or upon mountain peaks.
In such places as these, together with hosts of celestial maidens and other various devas, they experience all manner of pleasures.

Relying upon their original wholesome karma, they enjoy the retribution of happiness until the wholesome karma they have performed is exhausted. Once that wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall away from that celestial realm.
Once they have fallen from the heavens, they come and go according to their past conduct, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If, after falling, they are born among humans, they are always born in pleasant places, dwelling in lands where they practice the Dharma in accordance with the True Teaching. They are intelligent and wise, beloved by all people; whether they become kings, ministers, or rulers, their kingdoms need not fear the military forces or enemy armies of other nations, and they constantly experience happiness.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, again examines all the various regions within the Yāma Heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
In that Yāma Heaven, there is another region called Mind-Aspect (Citta-lakṣaṇa).
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that region?
He sees, hears, and knows:

If one practices good deeds with a good mind and a straightforward heart, possessing right view and not being perverse, always clearly understanding the causes and effects of good and evil with the mind, and refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Not killing and not stealing are as previously described.
Regarding non-sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*):

one does not give rise to such thoughts in the mind nor take pleasure in them; that is to say, even upon seeing a painted woman, one does not dwell upon her or contemplate her, harboring no unwholesome thoughts. One does not delight in the sight of her, does not savor it, and does not become attached to it. One observes her with a mind free from lustful desire, and likewise teaches others to do so, restrains others from doing so, refrains from doing so oneself, and does not instruct others to do so.
He is able to benefit himself and, furthermore, to benefit others.

That person who upholds the precepts attains liberation from feverish affliction; they constantly practice all manner of goodness and always remain mindful of their own body. Seeing the impurity of the body, they maintain constant mindfulness of their own physical form without delusion. They do not crave women and attain liberation from the snare of women, becoming free from desire for women.
Trusted by all people, one who currently maintains the precepts in accordance with harmony and assembly attains such happiness.
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, one takes no pleasure in it, does not practice it, and neither contemplates nor thinks of it.
That person, being thus able to extinguish the fire of desire, applies the foremost effort and practices the foremost joy.
At the dissolution of the body after death, that virtuous being is reborn in a good destination—the region of Mind-Aspect (*cittākāra*) in the Yāma Heaven.

"Once beings of virtuous karma have been born in that place, they experience immeasurable celestial pleasures and engage in joyful conduct. Free from the impurities of flesh and bone, their own bodies emit radiance as they constantly enjoy supreme bliss. They perpetually partake in the merits of the five sensory desires, and all their wishes for pleasure are fully accomplished."
Having accomplished such merits therein, they experience celestial bliss.
Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of goddesses, like Mount Sumeru encircled by the stars, they adorn themselves with supreme and wondrous radiance.
Transformed by virtuous karma, they are majestic and beautiful, encircled by a wheel of supreme radiance, with immeasurable light streaming forth from their bodies.

The hosts of celestial maidens there are exceedingly numerous; they enjoy themselves and experience pleasure through the sounds of the five musical instruments, as well as desirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances, thus partaking in happiness.
He thinks thus: "I shall go once more to other delightful and sublime places.
At that very moment of thought, by the power of his wholesome karma, those celestial maidens perceive his mind; having perceived it, they say:
“O Son of Heaven!
How can I remain here now? Beyond this place of delight there is another place of delight; you may now follow me as we proceed toward that other place called the Thousand Palaces.”
Upon the mountain peak are various kinds of precious ornaments and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial dwellings.
You should now follow me together toward that place.
At that time, having heard these words from the goddess, that deva was filled with extreme joy according to his own thoughts and spoke thus:
"Now, as you intend, so shall I act."
At that time, having spoken thus, that deva flew through the air toward the mountain named Thousand Palaces.

Upon its peak was a place adorned with immeasurable jewels, where there were immeasurable devas and immeasurable celestial maidens. Their various wondrous voices and songs could be heard from afar for five hundred yojanas, pervading the entirety of space.

Numerous devas and celestial maidens sang songs by the wayside, causing this son of heaven to give rise to a heart of joy as he ascended swiftly toward the summit of the mountain peak named Thousand-Peaked Palace.

From afar, they hear the sounds of the gods and goddesses in that place—their singing, dancing, and the tinkling of their ornaments; having heard these, they give rise to a sense of rare wonder and joy, and quickly draw near.
Then, that deva-son immediately approached the mountain named Thousand Palaces; having arrived, he beheld various kinds of excellent and delightful places, existing in immeasurable varieties.

These are adorned with seven precious jewels, exquisite gardens, and magnificent lotus ponds; they are delightful to behold, where beings enjoy pleasures together, amidst the sounds of flowing water from the most pure and pristine pools.
He saw various excellent birds flying up and down within the groves, and rows of pavilions made of the seven precious gems interspersed in every variety.
Adorned with a diverse array of different jewels, those halls were exceedingly delightful; the mountains, valleys, cliffs, and banks were likewise magnificently adorned by various rows of forests.
There are many exquisite geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks; the various calls of these waterfowl are all delightful.
Various banners and streamers, blown by the wind, form a lovely adornment that excels all that is seen.
In the midst of the void, there were moving celestial palaces that came and went, joined and separated, adorned with luminous jewels.
Furthermore, they heard the exquisite sounds of one another singing, dancing, and so forth; they heard the sublime sounds of mutual play, laughter, and the like.

There are level and uneven accumulations of the seven treasures, adorned with immeasurable varieties of supreme and wondrous ornaments, and situated amidst immeasurable varieties of sublime mountain peaks.
There are immeasurable thousands of kinds of exquisite flowers, possessing diverse forms, colors, and fragrances.
Whether walking, standing, running, or playing, or embracing one another and so forth—engaging in such various activities in that celestial realm, the assembly of devas and devīs surrounded him.
Standing upon the summit of Mount Sahastrakūṭa and dwelling in the midst of space, he looked down at that palace.
Having thus beheld that mountain peak, he gave rise to a heart of joy and addressed the celestial maidens, saying:
"All of you, behold this Mount Sahastrakūṭa! This palace is exceedingly lovely; everything of every kind here is truly delightful."
When those goddesses had heard his words, they said to that deva:
"O Deva, you should know this!
We have already seen it; we have seen it thus many times—whether a hundred times or a thousand times—but the Deva has never seen it."
"O gods, now look well upon this supreme place; it is most excellently to be beheld.
After those celestial maidens had spoken thus, the god descended from the sky with them and drew near to that palace.
In that palace, there were gods experiencing pleasure who, upon seeing him arrive, gave rise to a heart of joy.

Some gods went forward to welcome him; drawing near to gaze at him, because this devaputra had just been born, they rejoiced with such intensity that they embraced him with their hands and spoke these words:
"Now our celestial friends have thus increased, and by this means the hosts of gods shall possess great power."
At this moment, you are enjoying happiness together with many devas.
There are many devas and much radiance.
In the abode of King Mūśalinda, there are many hosts of devas and many hosts of celestial maidens who sport and enjoy themselves.
"Furthermore, other devas see the newly born deva and join their palms in worship.
Having made their offering, they say to him:

'You have now arrived at the summit of this mountain peak. Within this place, there are now immeasurable hosts of Suyāma devas and hosts of celestial maidens surrounding one another to enjoy pleasures; furthermore, there is the Heavenly King.'"
"By virtue of your wholesome karma, you now sport together amidst immeasurable, wondrous lotus flowers.
By the power of your wholesome karma, you experience pleasure in this place.
This is a sublime realm; you have come here now, having been born in heaven for the first time."
When the newly born deva-son heard these words, he spoke thus to his own celestial maidens:
"Where does the King of the Yāma Heaven sport, enjoying the pleasures of the fivefold qualities of desire?"
Having heard this, the goddess replied to the deva-son:
"I shall now go with you toward the dwelling place of the Great Lord Mucilinda, where we may enjoy happiness."
Having heard these words, that newly born deva immediately went with the celestial maidens toward the place where the Heavenly King enjoys his pleasures.
Moving along with the host of celestial maidens, singing and dancing, they soon saw from afar Mucilinda, the Night-Ranger King of the Yāma Heaven, dwelling within a grove of red *utpala* lotuses.
The red utpala lotus has one hundred petals; within each petal is a dwelling like a cave, inside which resides a celestial maiden of supreme fragrance, sporting together with various flocks of birds.
Those birds are water-faring birds, possessing excellent voices and various wondrous melodies;
in that place, such red utpala lotuses thus adorn that Great Heavenly King.

The bodies of these women were entirely adorned with various exquisite garments made of precious jewels; because those jewels possessed manifold radiances, and specifically due to the radiance of red *utpala* jewels, they appeared as one uniform crimson color.
Because that *utpala* is thus red, it causes the radiance of all jewels to become red.
Such a supreme and wondrous red lotus jewel surpasses the exquisite redness of the sun when it first rises in autumn.
Furthermore, amidst the various petals of those red utpala lotuses, they sport with bees, thus fully experiencing the bliss of the five sensory qualities.
If a deva or a devī within those red utpala lotuses should have this thought:
"I now wish to drink celestial wine," [they proceed accordingly].

As soon as he thought this, from within the petals of those red utpala-jewel flowers, celestial liquor—possessing superior, virtuous color, fragrance, and cool, refreshing touch—flowed forth in immeasurable varieties; he drank it together with that lord of gods, Mucilinda, and thus experienced such bliss.
Furthermore, that deva had another thought, desiring that the sound of song should issue forth from within the red utpala lotuses.
At the very moment of that thought, a wind blew, causing the petals of the red utpala lotuses to strike against one another and produce various sounds.
All other various sounds of the five kinds of music do not equal even one-sixteenth part of this sound.
Having heard that sound, they give rise to a heart of joy.
Having heard that sound, they experience a hundredfold joy, together with the lord of gods, Mucilinda, enjoying happiness upon those red *utpala* lotus petals.
Furthermore, if the mind of that deity recalls sporting and enjoying pleasures, they form this thought:
"I am now dwelling amidst these exquisite red utpala lotus petals made of wonderful jewels; while sporting thus, I now wish to cause this red utpala to travel through the sky."
At that very moment of thought, that *utpala* flower flew through the air like a swan;
within it, the deva looked down upon the various gardens and groves elsewhere, where other devas, by virtue of their own good karma, were sporting and enjoying pleasure.
At that time, that deva-son again sported and enjoyed pleasures together with the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, upon the exquisite jewel-petals of an utpala lotus, wandering from place to place.

The pleasures they experience are immeasurable and manifold; because they have well maintained their precepts, they obtain fruits corresponding to the nature of those precepts and thus enjoy happiness.
Since their observance of the precepts is categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, the pleasure they receive is likewise categorized as inferior, middling, or superior.
Having experienced such pleasures there for a long duration and having seen various sights, they proceed again toward the Thousand-Palace Mountain Peak, the realm of mental characteristics.

At that time, having witnessed such inconceivable various sights, the newly born deva felt joy in his heart and approached the red, exquisite jewel *utpala* flower of Mucilinda, the Lord of Devas; there, together with a vast multitude of countless celestial maidens, he engaged in song, dance, and play.
In that Yāma realm, they fully experience the supreme pleasures of the five sensory objects.
The red light of the red *utpala* lotus belonging to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāmas, illuminates the body of the Great King Mucilinda, the Lord of Devas, making it likewise red.
It was like the color of red *aśoka* flowers; even sixteen parts of the red hue present upon the body of the Heavenly King could not equal one part of it.
In this way, he fully experienced immeasurable varieties of bliss.
At that time, the newly born deva-son advanced further, gradually approaching the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, with palms joined in prostration, his head bowed and not yet raised.
The King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūśaluta, then spoke these verses:
"The wholesome karma performed in the past, And the observance of the three kinds of precepts—
By that karma this retribution is obtained, And now one experiences happiness."
Do not act with negligence; you will vainly exhaust the fruits of past karma.
You should apply yourself to further wholesome deeds; practice them diligently and do not be negligent.
One should perform wholesome actions and abandon unwholesome ones.
Through wholesome conduct one experiences supreme happiness; through unwholesome conduct one experiences suffering.
If one exerts oneself without ceasing and thus performs virtuous deeds, one will always experience happiness and later attain nirvāṇa.
If one practices heedless conduct, that is not a wholesome course of action;
because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they will go to hell.
If one practices pure deeds and is always diligent and energetic, [they shall attain liberation].
Then one attains the foremost state, where there is no suffering or affliction.
But if one is driven by the sense-faculties and further impelled by sensory objects,
bound by all fetters, one will perpetually wander through birth and death.
One who is not defiled by unwholesome dharmas is like refined pure gold;
having escaped the wilderness of existence, they are secure in every place.
For one who acts with heedlessness, this is the root of disadvantage.
If you renounce them, it will be auspicious; you shall dwell in peace and bliss, free from decline and affliction.
Now that you have just been born, you are fit to experience pleasant things;
give rise to such a mind and be careful not to become attached to defilements.
Heedlessness can lead even the gods astray, and women do likewise;
scorched by the fire of women, one constantly undergoes suffering.
Therefore, O gods, you ought to diligently abandon women.
Those who are greedy and deluded are bound by their own minds.
Thus, regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, they do not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Such men, possessing little merit, remain very far from Nirvana.
Truly knowing what is light and what is heavy, practicing the Dharma without remainder,
longing for the Dharma and longing for the fruit of the Dharma— one who is thus attains happiness.
Those who are dragged by the mind do so because the horses of their faculties are untamed.
If contentment draws the mind, one will courageously reach the supreme state.
Contentment binds the mind with a cord; as is the sphere of the mind, so it is—only the courageous can cause it to abide, for they possess worldly wisdom.
In the celestial realm of Immeasurable Love, one attains immeasurable varieties of bliss;
if one does not greedily cling to sensual desires, one will reach a virtuous destination.
Having performed wholesome deeds, you have attained this lovely realm.
Now that you have attained this realm of Yāma, let not your mind be attached to negligence.
Thus, having been newly born in heaven, the hosts of devas and celestial maidens, numbering in the hundreds of millions of *padma*, experience the fruits of their own karma.
The rope of karmic fruit is difficult to untie; it emanates from the mind.
Sentient beings are deceived by ignorance and act in accordance with it.
The twelve sense bases are like enemies, skillfully able to delude the mind.
Placed within the wheel of birth and death, it causes the world to revolve.
In the past, present, and future, all beings in the celestial realms fall away;
yet the mountain of the celestial realm remains ever as it is, while sentient beings continue their wandering course.
The peaks of Vaiḍūrya mountains, the gardens and groves so delightful,
and the mountains themselves ever unmoving, while the gods revolve without ceasing.
The gardens and groves are exceedingly lovely, and the grounds are likewise.
Ever remaining and indestructible, the various heavens revolve without ceasing.
With lapis lazuli for its stem and pure gold most lovely, this lotus flower is eternal; the various heavens revolve without ceasing.
The rivers and ponds are delightful, adorned with many birds;
always thus without lack, the gods pass through them without ceasing.
The halls and palaces are ever unchanged, and the railings are likewise so.
Constantly thus, never ceasing, the heavens revolve without stopping.
Deceived by sensory objects, the world revolves in this manner;
why, then, do the gods here not give rise to a mind of weary detachment?
The mind wanders through birth and death; because it has been habituated for so long, it is firm.
Thus one undergoes great suffering, yet remains unaware of it.
It is like a butcher who binds a sheep and places it within a pen.
"Taking them one by one and killing them, the rest feel no fear.
*The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Scroll 39;
*The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Scroll 40.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen on the Observation of the Heavens, Part Five: Suyāma Heaven.

After Mucilinda, the King of the Suyāma Heaven, had thus rebuked them, he and an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of devas all followed him out from that red utpala lotus toward another mountain peak.

The peak is named Sarvadarśana (All-Observing) and measures five hundred yojanas. It is adorned with the seven treasures, graced by flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, as well as groves, various flowers, and flocks of birds, and is fully endowed with immeasurable kinds of merit.
For the sake of sporting and enjoying pleasure, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, ascends that mountain peak.

He observes all the various lovely features of that mountain of exquisite jewels, namely, at its base there is a wonderful pond called "Beloved Sight" (Priyadarśana) which encircles the mountain peak.
In that pond, there is a peak named Corner Peak (Vijayakuṭa) which rises out of the water; it is composed of the seven treasures, with joints like armlets.
Those joints of the seven treasures emit a supreme radiance, appearing like upraised arms, extending for five hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, there are seven-tiered railings surrounding its summit; as for these seven, they are:
first, golden railings; second, silver railings; [and so forth].
The third railing is of lapis lazuli;
the fourth railing is of sapphire;
and the fifth railing is of musāragalva.
The sixth railing is made of red lotus jewels;
the seventh railing is made of the wondrous jewel of vajra.
Thus, these various jewels are interspersed as adornments, and it is surrounded by such exquisite jeweled railings, which are majestic on all sides and most lovely to behold.
There were many hosts of devas and many hosts of deva-maidens of supreme beauty and lovely voices, adorned in such a manner and so exceedingly wonderful.

At that time, King Mucilinda, together with many hosts of devas and many hosts of deva-maidens, as well as an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, thus proceeded together to the place of the Peak of Universal Observation.
Having arrived there and seen the hosts of devas upon those mountain peaks, he spoke these verses:
"In every place of Yāma Heaven, These heights are as if one’s arm were raised;
At all times, They abound with hosts of devas."
The Mountain of Radiant Rectitude is adorned with the seven treasures;
there are pure flowing streams and lotus ponds surrounding it.
Its gardens and groves are most lovely, abounding with many birds and deer.
Emerging from the pond within this peak, it rises exceedingly high, piercing the void.
In this place, the devas always enjoy bliss; adorned with celestial garlands, they dance and sing with joyful hearts, surrounded by a vast multitude of celestial maidens.
The sounds of the five musical instruments are lovely; those who behold them find joy in seeing them.
This peak is exceedingly delightful, surrounded on all sides by radiant light.
Through the performance of wholesome deeds and the three causes of upholding the precepts, [one attains this].
The hosts of devas rely upon this peak, sporting and enjoying happiness.
I have long relied upon this peak, sporting and experiencing various pleasures;
this is the ground of sensual delights, manifested by virtuous karma.
In this place, the foolish devas who have fallen from their former state and are now born here—
beings who act with heedlessness— are slaughtered like sheep by the butcher.
They do not perceive their own death and feel no fear, just as sheep do not tremble.
"If a deva perceives death, he should not indulge in negligence.

Having thus observed all the wondrous mountain peaks, Mūśalinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, beheld many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of devas and hosts of celestial maidens, their minds experiencing pleasure amidst various sensory realms.

Having clearly perceived the karmic retributions of the various devas, he further observed that the devas engage in heedless conduct, being swept away by craving and never knowing contentment, consumed by the blazing fires of sensual desires.
Having seen such foolish devas, he gave rise to a heart of compassion and spoke these verses for them.

He then proceeded further into the midst of the mountain peaks of Universal Observation; there, they experience pleasure through their own karma, yet are drawn by their fixed karma because their minds are wavering.
Furthermore, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, he thus entered that place of bliss together with them.

When the resident deities there saw King Mūśaludha, they immediately came forward to welcome him: some remained in the air; some anointed their bodies with various perfumes; some stayed within pavilions upon the backs of birds; some traveled through the sky on celestial chariots alongside other sons of gods to welcome King Mūśaludha, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven; and others welcomed him with the sounds of the five kinds of music. In these various and diverse ways of adornment, each group came forward to welcome King Mūśaludha, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven.
At that time, all these devas and others, remaining in the sky above, scattered various flowers and perfumes down upon Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven; having scattered them, they drew near.
Furthermore, other devas produced exquisite sounds with golden musical instruments and sang praises as they likewise approached Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.

Furthermore, there were other devas holding flower garlands in their hands; the fragrance of those flowers aroused desire in those who smelled it. Remaining in mid-air, their robes fluttered as they were blown by the celestial winds, as they gradually drew nearer to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.
Furthermore, other devas dwelling in the midst of space praised Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, with exquisite voices as they gradually drew near.

There were such immeasurable and diverse devas, adorned with various and distinct, sublime ornaments and possessing various colors—since their karma at the time of its performance was categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, their physical forms and adornments likewise possessed these three grades—and all of them came individually to welcome Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.
At that time, all these hosts of devas praised Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven; having welcomed him, they all proceeded together to the summit of the mountain peak called Sarvadarśana.

By the power of the Heavenly King, all the qualities of desire and the pleasures of the five sensory objects become infinite in their varieties and increase in every way through the force of his virtuous karma.

At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, together with the hosts of gods, was in a garden by a wonderful lotus pond where they enjoyed immeasurable and diverse desires; they then gradually ascended further to another location atop the mountain peak known as Sarvadarśana.
Having arrived there, by the power of their wholesome karma, they immediately see the gates of the evil realms opening. They see celestial maidens whose time has come to descend from heaven.
Because they are about to descend, nine signs first appear, namely:
first, their skin becomes slack and excessively soft because it has become wrinkled.
Second is bodily movement.
Because of this bodily movement, the flowers upon his head become disarrayed and fall away.
Furthermore, a third sign of decline has already appeared, namely:
When red flowers appear on his head, they turn yellow.
Furthermore, the fourth sign of decline has already manifested:
namely, when a wind comes and blows upon his garments, those garments without threads appear as if they were made of threads, just like the touch of a person's clothing.
Furthermore, a fifth sign of decline has already appeared, namely:
when flying through the air, one becomes fatigued, and the same occurs when walking upon the ground.
Furthermore, a sixth sign of decline has already appeared, namely:
The sweat on his body, which was originally clear, has now become turbid.
Furthermore, the seventh sign of decline has already appeared:
when he goes beneath the trees to gather flowers or fruit, the branches lift themselves high so that they cannot be reached, and thus he is unable to take them.
Furthermore, the eighth sign of decline has already appeared, namely:
when a celestial son comes to engage in desire with them, they see that the celestial maidens have become ugly in appearance and lack charm.
Furthermore, the ninth sign of decline has already appeared, namely:
A wind arises that scatters their hair, making it lose its softness; when touched, it is coarse and rough.
This sign of decline appears, and though ten days have passed by celestial reckoning—equivalent to two thousand years by human calculation—it still does not subside.
"When those celestial maidens who are to fall back manifest two further signs of their impending decline, they have reached the time of their descent.
The first is this: their desire becomes excessive, and they can no longer remain still for even a moment."
The two things referred to are these:
while wandering upon the ground, the earth was not soft; when she set her foot down, it could not be accommodated, and when she lifted her foot, it did not rise.
Being unable to remain there alone, she called out to the other celestial maidens, saying:
"I am distressed; stay here with me.
Yet another sign of that celestial maiden's impending fall appeared:
her lips quivered incessantly, moving without cause for speech and refusing to cease.
Furthermore, another sign of decline appeared for those celestial maidens who were falling away; that sign was this:
they had previously been skilled in song and dance, yet now they forgot all their melodies.

When they first took birth there, they possessed knowledge of song and dance and melody without anyone teaching them and without learning from others; through the power of their wholesome karma, they naturally knew them all. Now, however, they had forgotten them.
When they thus fall, because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they forget everything.
Furthermore, signs of that falling goddess's imminent decline appear; these signs are as follows:

when she goes near a lotus pond or a river, she sees within the water the place where she is destined to be born, and according to whichever realm she is to be reborn, she sees her own reflection there.
Furthermore, another sign of decline appeared for those goddesses who were falling away; that sign was this:
the ornaments they wore—whether they were necklaces, bracelets, or any other kind—all became heavy.
Furthermore, other signs of decline appear for those goddesses who are falling away; such signs are as follows:
wherever they sit, that very place undergoes transformation.
Whether they sit upon gold, or on *vaiḍūrya*, *indranīla*, or similar precious substances, all those jewels transform into wood.
That falling goddess further manifests signs of decline; that is to say, the features of the ground and other things she previously saw now appear entirely different.
That falling goddess further manifests signs of decline; that is to say, the features are as follows:
The entire body breaks out in a profuse sweat.
Furthermore, within these humans, signs of retrogression have already appeared; such signs are as follows:
when they look upon the celestial hosts, everything appears to spin like a turning wheel, and they no longer see the bodies of the devas.
All their faculties find no pleasure in sense objects, and their minds think:
"I have now no refuge. Because their lives are about to end, they see their place of rebirth in the realm of desire as if it were already there, seeing those forms as if they were already present.
As previously described, when that celestial maiden’s life has ended and she is about to fall away, at the very moment her life ceases, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises within her mind.
Having thus seen that celestial maiden fall away, Maudgalyāyana, the King of the Yāma Heaven, conceives a sense of weary detachment. Seeing the celestial maiden thus fall away, he speaks this verse:
"Women bind the world, Deceiving it into long strife and resentment."
Unrighteousness can destroy the Dharma; it is the source of all faults.
Driven by the desire for women, this celestial realm is bound;
when the army of Death arrives, they will be shattered and carried away.
With various kinds of play, women skillfully deceive men;
they cause them to fall away later, departing according to their own karma.
Whether in lotus gardens, groves, or mountains, or within rivers and valleys, [they lead them astray].
After many kinds of playful delights, the celestial maidens then withdraw;
the celestial maidens must inevitably withdraw, and there will surely be separation from those one loves.
Seeing this, a man still pursues desire without ceasing.
It causes the world to lose its way, it greatly increases craving;
bound by women for this reason, one cannot attain liberation.
The bond of sensual passion is the greatest, for it binds this world.
Through various and diverse reflections, there is no further such bondage.
Where has the celestial being gone who was wounded by the immeasurable arrows of desire?
Let the women's desires enslave you!
"Having defeated the women, he has attained victory.

Thus did Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, observe; he felt fear regarding his own impending fall, for there was no means by which he could rescue or liberate the celestial maidens who were about to descend.

Having observed the various infinite gateways of universal phenomena and determined that [the gods] would inevitably fall, he further observed the other devas enjoying various pleasures through the merits of the five sensory desires; yet they felt no fear regarding their impending fall, being like mere beasts. He then reflected:
"Why is it that those devas feel no terror when the time of death approaches?"
Having reflected thus, fear arose within his own mind, yet he was unable to speak of it to the other devas.
Why was this? Because teaching the Dharma at an improper time causes the Dharma to be held in low esteem.
Furthermore, because those other devas experience pleasure within their own realms and are thus attached to such objects of enjoyment, it is impossible to speak to them at such an improper time.
