Having contemplated the fear of death, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, nevertheless continues to engage in play and enjoyment with those devas, experiencing various kinds of games and pleasures for immeasurable durations.
Within all these mountain peaks of such universal observation, there are many various exquisite gardens and lotus ponds, where they sport and enjoy pleasures together with the hosts of devas.

In six ways, they take delight in objects of pleasure within those gardens, lotus ponds, and other countless locations; there, they dance and sing together, sharing food and drink, and experiencing touches, fragrances, and flavors.
Thus experiencing such pleasure, they find the sound of singing to be exceedingly lovely.
Experiencing such pleasure, they proceed to sport and wander upon the railings at the summit of that mountain peak.
Those railings are made of beryl; when the gods enter within them, the radiance of their own bodies is completely eclipsed.
Adorned with those jewels, because of the light of that beryl, everything becomes a single color—namely, blue.
When the devas saw that everything was uniformly blue, they were struck with wonder and each said to one another:

"Though we have previously seen many kinds of palaces and hundreds of thousands of palaces arrive, we have never before seen a mountain peak such as this, with the lapis lazuli jewels emitting such radiance."
At that time, after this deva had spoken thus, there was among the devas an elder deva who addressed all the other devas born later, saying:
"According to what I have heard through successive transmission, I shall now tell you for what cause and condition this radiance appears."
In the distant past, during a long-elapsed age, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven descended to Jambudvīpa and made offerings with a sincere heart to the Truly All-Pervading and Truly All-Knowing One.
Having made these offerings to the Buddha, he passed through this place, amidst the peaks of the Sarvadarśana mountain, and out of compassion for the Yāma devas, left behind a single jewel.
When these Yāma devas see the radiance of the jewel, they recognize that among the various karmic fruits and retributions of the Yāma devas there are both light and heavy;

thus, they abandon their prideful minds. If a Yāma deva has acted contrary to the Dharma, upon seeing this jewel, he realizes that the Yāma devas may be superior or inferior to the Tuṣita devas, and his mind understands thus:
"What kind of happiness have I now accomplished?"
The radiance, color, size, and form that I delight in are inferior in Tuṣita; my lifespan is also inferior, my dwelling place is also inferior, and the fruits of my karma are also inferior.
When those gods behold that supreme radiance of the precious jewel, they give rise to a state of unsurpassed and sublime joy.
If they act with negligence, they abandon their pride;
if they act in accordance with the Dharma, they cause that Dharma to increase.
"For this reason, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven has left this jewel here.

At that time, when the various devas heard these words from the elder devas, they gave rise to a supreme and most excellent heart of joy; they conceived a sense of wonder toward that precious jewel and desired to see it.
All those gods together, within that entire mountain peak of universal observation, searched for that jewel.
Because of their searching, they saw it in one place, from which a hundredfold superior radiance issued forth, able to overwhelm the other jewels so that they would no longer appear.
If it is still like this when it has not yet been uncovered, how much more so when it is not covered at all?
As for what is meant by "covered":
the jewels of the Yāma Heaven cover such a great luminous jewel as this.

When those gods of the Yāma Heaven set aside their other precious jewels and bring forth this single jewel, the gods of the Yāma Heaven, upon seeing all the radiance of this single jewel, their minds become free from pride.
Furthermore, all the natural radiance of the Yāma devas themselves completely vanished.
Looking again at that jewel, there appeared within it golden inscriptions in the form of characters, and among those characters was a verse:
“Pure and free from defilement, Always acting in accordance with the Dharma,”
Because they are heedful, they constantly experience happiness.
Whether in pleasure or in suffering, whether old or young,
whether of high birth or low birth— the King of Death can kill them all.
Whether handsome or ugly, whether powerful or weak,
whether solitary or with a protector— the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether a king or a servant, whether a layperson or one who has gone forth.
Whether firm or soft, the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether rich or poor, whether possessing merit or lacking it,
whether man or woman— the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether walking or staying at home, whether on water or on land,
or dwelling upon mountain peaks— the King of Death can kill them all.
Whether sleeping or waking, whether eating or fasting.
Capable of traversing the chaotic world, the King of Death can slay all.
Whether one is below or above, or dwelling on the side, the Wheel of Time faces no obstruction; the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, whether one acts according to the Dharma or contrary to it,
whether sick or healthy— the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether evil or good, whether stingy or generous—
Whether one is heedless or not, the King of Death can slay all.
Whether in the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or humans, the King of Death—
possessing great power and never resting— can slay them all.
Whether they be the various devas of the desire realm, or the devas of the form realm and so forth—
though those gods possess great power, the King of Death can slay them all.
Even the devas of the formless realm, born through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), [are not exempt].
Though those gods possess great power, the King of Death can slay them all.
All that is born is impermanent; everything must perish.
There is no doubt that all conditioned phenomena will be destroyed.
Seeing the power of death thus, and seeing the faults of desire;
having seen the speech of passionate attachment, one then leaves the ocean of birth and death.
At first, its flavor is firm, and one becomes greedily attached to the realm of desire.
By this one enters hell, like a snake’s tongue licking its own face.
Seeing that once fallen from this state there is no returning, and knowing the great power of the King of Death,
the mind is well-subdued, for it recognizes these faults of the mind.
Whether dwelling among gardens, mountains, or within celestial halls,
all devas shall eventually fall away, consumed by the fires of time.
If one is shrouded by sensory objects and acts with negligence due to delusion, [one will likewise perish].
"Bound by the snare of craving, this deva is being led away into the evil realms.
At that time, within the great Vaiḍūrya jewel, those devas saw those verses written in gold; having seen them, they read them, and having read them, they heard them.
If there are devas whose minds possess the seeds of goodness, upon seeing or hearing these verses, they will momentarily give rise to a sense of weary detachment.

However, as for those devas who are deluded by sensory objects and mired in ignorance, even though they likewise see and hear them, they remain attached to their environments, engaging in play and wandering about, enjoying the pleasures of the five desires, and no weariness arises in their hearts.

At that time, when those devas saw such radiance from the precious gem, and heard within it the verses explaining the many faults and afflictions of all worlds, they were filled with a sense of wonder upon seeing and hearing this.
"This supreme jewel possesses such radiance; it is truly rare.

Yet those devas, by their very nature prone to negligence, engage in various diversions and enjoyments, indulging in countless conceptualizations and experiencing the pleasures of immeasurable sensory realms.
That bliss was profound and supreme, beyond all analogy.

At that time, those devas again engaged in heedless conduct, frequently playing various kinds of musical instruments as they headed toward a river named Swift Flowing (Kṣiprasravā), remaining firmly attached to their negligence.

Seeing various sensory objects, their minds become firmly attached; bound by the net of craving accumulated since beginningless time, they are dragged toward that river. Bound by the sounds of various pleasures, their minds are fettered as they take turns playing together and experiencing delight.
That swift-flowing river is lined with many groves of trees and covered with lotuses; the sounds of various birds are most delightful, and the fragrance of the lotuses perfumes its waters.

On both banks of that river there are many *nirmāṇarati* devas, whether singing or dancing; with hearts filled with mutual and supreme joy, they experience various pleasures on those riverbanks. The sounds of the five musical instruments are perfectly harmonious and exquisite, and they enjoy happiness through immeasurable varieties of the qualities of the five sensual desires.
Because the waters of that river flow swiftly, it is called "Swift Flow.
Between the branches of the trees on both banks of the river dwell birds; those birds are thus named "Dwelling in the Intervals of Tree Branches."
Due to their wholesome karma, the birds, with hearts of mutual and supreme joy for the sake of benefiting the devas, spoke these verses:
“The mountains and rivers pass so swiftly, And the devas thus lose their pleasures;
Yet through delusion they do not perceive this, Thus proceeding in heedlessness.”
For all sentient beings, life and pleasure pass swiftly without ceasing;
yet the deluded do not perceive this, like those born blind upon a path.
It would be better to be blind and sightless than to be attached to desires and mired in folly.
To pursue pleasure according to one's desires leads one toward the hells.
It is not because one is blind that one goes to hell, but because one does not know the Dharma;
therefore, it is better to be physically blind than to be driven by desire.
Desiring to act for one's own disadvantage, they constantly deceive and delude the ignorant;
because their own minds are deluded, they do not feel weary of or seek to renounce desire.
Those who pursue such desires lack wisdom and possess no true knowledge.
Failing to recognize the suffering inherent in the arising of desire, one constantly delights in it.
Seeing desire as an enemy yet regarding it as a friend— like the pāka fruit—
it leads one toward the place of death and causes one to repeatedly fall into the evil realms.
"Just as all rivers flow onward without turning back, so too is the pleasure of the heavens; once gone, it does not return.
Having spoken this verse, that bird remained in the tree according to the reality of its karma.
At that time, those devas, whose minds had been cultivated through wholesome karma, having heard the recitation of the verse, felt profound revulsion and reflected thus:
"It is now only among these animals that we have heard such a teaching; therefore, we know that our own conduct was negligent and that we are certain to enter the evil realms."
At that time, having given rise to such thoughts and reflected upon them,
one among those devas moved away from the riverbank, stood in a certain place, and spoke this verse:
"The lives of all sentient beings Are no different from bubbles on the water."
Like the surging waves of a river, so too is youth.
All sentient beings without exception are subject to old age and death;
yet you possess no mindfulness, neither reflecting nor considering this.
"Those whose bodies have not yet perished, those who are pure within the world—
if their minds all act in accordance with the Dharma, they shall not enter the evil realms.
Thus did those devas, each in turn, speak these verses and contemplate the Dharma in mutual accord with one another’s minds.

Before long, their faculties became weak and powerless, and they ceased further reflection. Seeing immeasurable varieties of desirable and delightful objects of the five sensual pleasures, and having become attached to them according to their inclinations, they proceeded toward other heavens in order to experience those pleasures.

Thus deluded by sensory objects, those devas—driven by the five sense objects which constantly increase their celestial desires—experience heavenly bliss in that place, enjoying pleasures corresponding to the most desirable objects of the five senses.
When this wholesome karma of craving is exhausted, they are again driven by karma to be born in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

If they fall from their celestial state and are born among humans, they will be born in the foremost place of happiness, free from all decline and affliction, possessing supreme wealth and pleasure, and arising within the most eminent lineage. All will revere and love them, and all will offer them worship. They will be without fear or illness, possessing supreme intelligence; whether it be others, slaves, servants, or laborers, all will love them and always maintain a heart of veneration toward them. They will be born in a foremost, virtuous land, not in a border region, but in a place where people know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; their five faculties will be complete, and their wisdom will be sovereign.

Because those wholesome karmas were performed and further accumulated— dear to the noble ones— and because of these three meritorious karmas, they will certainly be born in heaven due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates all the various realms within the Yāma Heaven.
He sees, hears, and knows:
In that Yāma Heaven there is another region called "Endowed with Mountains and Trees.
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that region?
He perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowledge as follows:

if there is a person who practices wholesome karma with a straightforward mind and a correct mind, acting in accordance with the Dharma; whose majestic deportment is neither impaired nor deficient; who stays far away from evil associates and constantly gives rise to wholesome thoughts;
and who feels deep dread upon seeing even the slightest evil, as small as a mote of dust; [he perceives that such a person will attain this samādhi].
Possessing right view and not being perverse, they constantly practice right view; at all times they believe in the retribution of karma, their minds being upright;
they perform wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, guarding the threefold precepts, namely: non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct.
Not killing and not stealing are as previously described.
Regarding non-sexual misconduct:
if one sees the form of a woman during the day, no thought of desire arises in the mind.
Having seen [these things] by day, one does not give rise to thoughts of them at night. One gives rise to contentment in the mind;

while walking during the day, one skillfully restrains the mind, binding the sense faculties with the rope of contentment. Walking with mindfulness of the body, one skillfully guards the mind, constantly delighting in observing the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and aggregates (*skandha*). One does not delight in much speech; one does not enter the houses of others at improper times, nor frequent evil marketplaces. One does not travel at improper times to any location, does not approach vicious dogs, and does not habitually enter villages, cities, or crossroads.
One does not delight in frequently seeing old acquaintances or friends, nor does the mind dwell upon them constantly.

Constantly and diligently practicing the sphere of wisdom, always observing correctly, maintaining perpetual right mindfulness, honoring elders and superiors, and always attending upon them with service—

such a practitioner of good deeds, by thus upholding the precepts, at the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in a happy destination, in the region of Mount Saṃjñāyana within the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where trees and groves abound.
Having been born there, they experience immeasurable pleasure; as if like a seal, they fully obtain all kinds of immeasurable delights.
Two wonderful mountains surround that land, and within those mountains are four groves of trees:
the first is named *Snigdha-chāyā* (Glossy Shadow);...
The second is named Immeasurable Burden;
the third is named All-Surpassing;
the fourth is named Pure Burden.

The forest of glossy blue shadows consists of blue-colored wondrous jewels and blue trees, fully endowed with leaves of gold and silver; it is so upright, majestic, and sublime that it is beyond all comparison.
From the palatial halls within the grove, a blue light and shadow emerge, extending far away to fill five hundred *yojanas*, its color like that of blue clouds.

Beyond those are three further groves—the Immeasurable Burden Grove, the All-Surpassing Grove, and the Pure Burden Grove—each of which contains immeasurable kinds of trees, immeasurable colors, immeasurable shapes, immeasurable characteristics, and immeasurable kinds of leaves; immeasurable kinds of birds frequent these groves.
In that forest, there were such immeasurable varieties of trees as these, along with many other kinds of trees: namely, many golden trees with silver leaves;
silver trees with lapis lazuli leaves; coral trees with white silver leaves;
and various jewel trees with leaves made of various jewels.
Because the trees are variegated, their shadows are also variegated; the branches cover the ground everywhere, and in every place there is water.
Those various locations are exceedingly beautiful, adorned with swarms of bees and filled with exquisite sounds, while many celestial birds grace the grounds.
Such is the exquisite beauty of that second grove.

Furthermore, the third grove contains many immeasurable streams, rivers, and ponds; these rivers abound with countless birds of various kinds, such as peacocks and *kukila* parrots, whose voices are lovely and who dwell in delightful places.
Furthermore, in the fourth grove there are many various trees of diverse colored jewels, as well as gardens, ponds, and various lotuses, where the shadows of the forest shimmer with light.
All those trees are like mica and lapis lazuli; when a deva enters therein, they see their own bodies appearing as the color of mica and lapis lazuli.

Furthermore, that mountain possesses a unique power such that when a deva is about to fall and the time of death is approaching, he sees everything regarding the place where he will go according to his karma.
Having seen this, he becomes weary of and detached from existence, practicing with heedfulness because he perceives his own state as that of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
That meritorious deva is born in such a ground of merit due to the power of immeasurable kinds of wholesome karma.
At that time, the deva who has been born there is born upon a mountain named Gaṇa.
When this deva is first born, he engages in heedless conduct; however, having seen his own decline and the fact that he was born in an evil state, the newly born deva begins to practice heedfulness.
Having thus concentrated his mind, before long he again became attached to the pleasures of the five sensory desires within the realms of objects.

In a most delightful place within a lotus pond in a grove, where all the qualities of the five desires were fully present, he was surrounded by a vast multitude of celestial maidens amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music; there were immeasurable varieties, immeasurable distinctions, and immeasurable thoughts.
In those mountain forests, as previously described, by virtue of the former wholesome karma of those devaputras, they thus experience various kinds of the pleasures of the five senses.
Having thus experienced such sensual pleasures, through the power of their wholesome karma, they then behold five kinds of rare and wonderful forms within those mountains.
What are these five? They are:
seeing from which place of birth one has come to be born here, and seeing that place of origin;
By what karmic causes did they come to be born here? He sees those karmic causes.
At what time will they fall away? He sees that time of their falling away.
Having seen them fall away, he sees in what place they will be reborn.
They see themselves being born in that place, and having been born there, they experience suffering and pleasure.
Having seen their own suffering and pleasure, they likewise perceive the affairs of other bodies in the same way.
Those celestial beings further see events from other times—whether of a hundred kalpas or a billion kalpas—and perceive their own past deeds, knowing them thus:
"I was once born among these gods; though I know the number of my births, I do not know the number of years.
Why is this? Because my wisdom is slight, I am unable to fathom the power of that mountain."
"It is by the power of the force of wholesome karma that they see things in this way.

Thus, having seen those immeasurable kinds of rare and wonderful things, that deva-son fears the faults of birth and death and grows weary of and detached from wholesome karma; how much more so would he grow weary of and be detached from non-meritorious karma? He likewise becomes detached from mixed karma.
Because they all possess the fault of suffering and affliction, and because those [mountains] are interspersed with many evils and faults;
having seen this, and having seen those rare wonders within the mountains, one becomes fearful, weary, and detached from the realm of birth and death which is fraught with such faults and evils.

At all times, they increase immeasurable and manifold forms of decay and affliction; having seen the beams and ropes [of their own bodies], their minds turn away from other pleasures and find no delight in them.
What are called "pleasures" are the desires, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances within the heavens.
Thus, having seen touch, taste, form, and fragrance as they truly are—like seeing poisoned rice—they do not take pleasure in them.
Having thus seen the pleasures of the immeasurable celestial realms in their true light, they feel aversion and find no delight in them.
Having thus become weary of and detached from desire, he speaks to the other devas, causing them to perform deeds that bring benefit and happiness.
Those devas, in this manner, practice well through body, speech, and mind, and thus carry out virtuous karma.

"If a Dharma-preacher is able to expound the True Dharma for others, he shall preach the Dharma to those heedless sentient beings by being fully endowed with the Buddha's words, out of fear of their heedless conduct."
Sentient beings who are heedless enter into immeasurable realms of evil states; for those beings, he preaches the five kinds of fear, namely:
the fear of birth, the fear of old age, the fear of illness, the fear of death, and the fear of one's own karma.
Because these sentient beings perform such actions, they thus obtain objects of attachment and dread separation from them.

If one can demonstrate these various fears to others—not out of greed for material things, nor with a deceitful mind, nor for the sake of seeking offerings—but can correctly expound the Buddha-dharma for others; [this is true teaching].
Furthermore, there are those who preach the Buddha-dharma to others in a mixed manner:
they provide analogies corresponding to what they have heard themselves,
yet fearing that their own learning and reading of the Buddha’s words are meager, they defer to later times and employ various causes and analogies [instead].

Having heard it from others and spoken it after one's own deliberation, with a mind full of various kinds of greed for manifold speech, one pushes the time [for practice] to the future and teaches the Dharma in such a manner.
Through such causes and conditions, one creates the fear of birth and death.
Within that mountain, he saw various karmic activities.
Among all such phenomena, there is yet another that is superior:
namely, preaching the Dharma for one's parents and elders.
Furthermore, there are those who preach the Dharma for the sick;
who preach the Dharma for those with wrong views in order to cause them to give rise to right view;
and who preach the Buddha-dharma for those about to die.
If one perceives that birth and death exist spontaneously, without cause and without condition, for such a person he explains the Dharma of causes and conditions.
If there are those who have not yet heard the Dharma since their birth, for them he expounds the Dharma.

Whether they are traveling through wildernesses, or voyaging upon the great ocean in large ships, or those who act with negligence, or kings, or royal ministers, or youths who indulge in desire, negligence, and various forms of pride—he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation from these states.

If there are those who are valiant and capable of killing many, or those who kill many living beings and act with negligence, he explains their transgressions to them and restrains them from taking life.
If there are those who delight in strife—hoping to be reborn in heaven by seeking death in battle through perverted views—he preaches the Dharma for them and restrains them so that they do not act.
If there are those who constantly hunt, he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to renounce that practice.
If there are women who are envious and jealous, he preaches the Dharma for them, restraining their envy and jealousy.

"If there is anyone who can preach the Dharma for these twelve kinds of people, that person, having preached the Dharma in such a truthful manner, will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three among the regions of the Tree-Abounding Mountains."

Once he has been born there, he perceives within the mountain walls and other such places the karma of birth and death; having perceived this, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment toward all birth and death.

If one does not teach the Dharma to others in this manner and is nevertheless born there, all of one's past actions will become invisible; thereafter, one will experience various sensual pleasures, wandering about and sporting, fully endowed with the manifold merits of the five desires.

In that place, one hears the sounds of singing and the calls of various birds; within lotus ponds endowed with diverse colors and fragrances, there are immeasurable bees producing hundreds of thousands of sounds and various blended melodies.

Having experienced various pleasures in that place, they proceed again toward the mountains; there, upon a level plateau in the midst of the mountain range, they experience pleasure. Possessing the foremost beauty and all manner of virtues, the celestial maidens sing divine songs that are exceedingly delightful, and as they are fully endowed with color, flavor, fragrance, and so forth, they give rise to great joy.
They further drink celestial wine; having drunk the wine, their pleasure in heedlessness increases all the more.
After they have long practiced heedlessness and experienced various delights, they proceed once again toward that mountain named the Forest of Play (*Vihāra-vana*).
The railings were made entirely of beryl; the halls and residences were adorned with ornaments like molten gold, and these places of adornment were composed of various kinds of the seven treasures.
Having arrived there, they find that place abounding in many birds of supreme beauty.

Once they have reached that place, they sport and enjoy themselves with the merits of the five desires; yet they do not know contentment, their minds constantly longing for more, never able to be satiated.
Just as fire that has obtained fuel is fanned by the wind, so too is the ordinary person defiled by craving, never knowing contentment.

Why is this? Because from time immemorial, foolish ordinary persons have thus transmigrated, deceived by craving; within their own spheres of experience, their faculties know no satisfaction, for from the very beginning they have never known contentment.

That hall possesses the most excellent and lovely railings endowed with all virtues; therein, the gods enjoy together the pleasures of the five sensory desires, which consist of various and immeasurable distinctions and are accomplished through immeasurable kinds of recollections.
At that time, the deva who practices heedfulness and lives with vigilance, seeing such a practitioner of heedlessness, felt compassion in his heart and spoke this verse:
“As one acts with the mind, so one receives the fruit;
Right mindfulness cuts off craving and desire, while unwholesome states cause them to increase.”
Those who seek tranquility view sensual desires as a blade or poison;
those whose minds are undisciplined through delusion perceive desire and give rise to passionate attachment.
Whether it be the sense faculties or their objects, these conditions arise within the mind.
Because the afflictions perfume the mind, there is a corresponding flow of conditioned existence.
Regarding such defilement and purity, the courageous one is not stained;
since they ultimately perceive form as constant, how could there be any distinction?
All things are thus: objects are what the mind itself conditions.
To discipline the mind is the foremost task; to be mired in various faults is most base.
It is like a single species of rice, whose colors and forms differ from one another.
Through the combination of various elements, birth arises; the mind likewise revolves in this way.
Like a mechanical waterwheel, because it turns, there is activity;
through the causes and conditions of the mind, speech arises, and thus this world revolves.
Heedlessness ruins sentient beings; their minds are greedily attached to the flavor of desire, and they constantly delight in forms, unaware as the continuum of existence revolves.
Just as the colors of mountains and forests appear within a reflection, so too does one perceive a body due to karma.
How can one, having seen this, become greedily attached to the realm of desire?
Since desire is ever-present, it ends in the pain of separation from what is loved;
such craving for desire is not something the wise delight in.
How much more so for impermanence and emptiness? When one's own body is likewise empty, how could a fool find joy within those bitter retributions?
Once the devas have fallen from their celestial realm, they are led away by their evil karma.
“Deceived by sensory objects, tranquility cannot be attained.
“If a deva does not act with such negligence, he practices non-negligence.”

When the gods who are heedful have finished speaking thus to the heedless gods, having seen their true forms due to their own karma, they feel fear toward that karma; furthermore, out of compassion, they have spoken as follows.

Thus, the devas dwelling in that place on the mountain, which is replete with trees, experience immeasurable varieties of pleasure; in a region of lapis lazuli, they see their own bodily forms reflected within it.
Furthermore, among the gods dwelling in that region of mountains and trees, there are other forests of *vaiḍūrya* or silver.
Those forests have names; some are named "Constant Shadow" (*nityacchāya*) and some are named "Shadowless" (*acchāya*).

That Forest of Constant Shadows is made of lapis lazuli; within such a forest, the ground is soft and supple, adorned with the songs of various birds and hundreds of lotus ponds. There are flowing streams that beautify the place, where the gods roam, sport, and enjoy manifold pleasures.

In that Forest of Constant Shadows (Nityapratibhāsa-vana) there are five great ponds, filled with lotuses, geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks; they are filled with the various calls of *bakra* birds, which utter their voices together in a most lovely manner, as they enjoy manifold pleasures.
In that water, winds blow, creating various waves that cause the bodies of those birds to touch one another and then separate.
That water is pure and free from turbidity.
In this way, these various birds roam together among the lotus petals, experiencing manifold pleasures.
As for the five flower-pools:
the first is named Delightful to Behold;
The second is named Water-Basis;
the third is named Bird-Delight;
the fourth is named Constant-Joy.
The fifth is named Celestial Music.

Within those lotus ponds there are many bees of immeasurable forms and colors, possessing hundreds of thousands of various hues; they drink the nectar of the lotuses, which possesses immeasurable exquisite flavors.

Once the swarms of bees have finished drinking, they emit a most excellent and sublime sound; when the devas dwelling in the region of the mountain and its lush forests hear this sound, they hasten toward the bees.
Within the lotus pond, the water of that pool is foremost in purity, foremost in color and fragrance.
Having seen that water, the hosts of devas, together with the hosts of celestial maidens, enter the pool to sport and enjoy themselves.
Having entered the pool, they sport in the water together with the celestial maidens; endowed with all varieties of the merits of the five desires, they further indulge in sensual pleasures.
In that place, there are such various forms of play and delight.
Furthermore, there are yet other supreme sounds of various kinds, namely the sound of song, the sound of music, and the sound of water.

There are also the various calls of diverse birds; these various sounds, though distinct from one another and following one another in sequence, do not disrupt the phrasing, but merge into a single harmony. Thus delightful, the hosts of devas together with the hosts of celestial maidens experience such pleasure.
Once these various sounds have issued forth, the sporting and enjoyment of the gods in other mountains are not like this.

When deer and birds in other places approach their food and drink, if they hear these sounds, they immediately cease eating; they remain still with their ears erect, listening to these blended sounds.
It is the same when they drink: they stop and do not drink, remaining there to listen to those sounds.
When the celestial hosts dwelling in other realms hear this sound, they give rise to a sense of wonder; how much more so for the other animals.
Thus, they experience various pleasures in these five places.

At that time, the devas dwelling in that region of mountains and trees, having enjoyed pleasures for a long duration in the five lotus ponds, proceeded toward other groves for the sake of drinking wine and experiencing sensual delights.
The grove is named Pānīya (The Drinker). It is filled with celestial wine, and for this reason it is called the Pānīya Grove.

By the power of the virtuous karma of those devas, when they arrive at the Pānīya Grove, all the clear, pure pools that were previously full vanish. Instead, celestial wine—endowed with the most excellent fragrance, color, and flavor—is produced and fills those rivers. The fragrance of that wine pervades an area of five *yojanas* in every direction; whether moving upstream or downstream, the wine arises exactly as the devas desire, just as such things occur in this world.
"The foremost pleasure is the pleasure of recollection; that which is attained through the mind’s mastery of mindfulness is the supreme pleasure.
This alone is pleasure; there is no other pleasure beyond it."

This joy of following one's own thoughts is the foremost pleasure; how much more so the pleasure of being fully endowed with the merits of the five desires, experiencing delight together with hosts of celestial maidens amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments!
Furthermore, there is the pleasure of sovereign freedom according to one's will, wherein they engage in various diversions and experience manifold delights.
That wine is free from the faults of intoxication; once drunk, it brings such supreme satisfaction that it is beyond description.
Thus those devas experience various pleasures and act with negligence; together with hosts of celestial maidens, they drink divine wine, their minds shrouded by craving for a vast period of time.
Having accumulated [suffering] since beginningless time, they accumulate it further in this way, unable to abandon it, deceived by craving.
Those gods are thus never satisfied, like a fire that has obtained fuel.
Thus, among them, the devas dwelling in that region of mountains and groves think to themselves:
"I shall now ascend this mountain peak.
Those devas thus call one another to mind, and their minds arise as one.
Thus, with one mind and all together, their hearts harmonious and joyful, they proceeded toward that mountain; having arrived, they ascended it.
By virtue of their own wholesome karma, emitting the most brilliant radiance, they soared through the void and climbed that mountain.

Having ascended that mountain by means of the first supernormal power, the sounds of the five kinds of music all harmonized together; the sounds of all songs and music pervaded the mountain, while superior fragrances wafted everywhere across the mountain, and wondrous light filled the void of space.
In the midst of the void, the Victorious Radiance and other lights ascended that mountain.

Having ascended the mountain by means of celestial supernormal powers, they saw upon its summit immeasurable varieties of flowing streams and lotus ponds, filled with lotuses and complete with all kinds of gardens and flowers.
In that place, there are the songs of many birds and the fragrance of the foremost celestial incense.

The summit of that mountain is entirely level; once the light has shone everywhere and the celestial hosts have ascended, they experience the foremost pleasures together with the hosts of celestial maidens.
Among the gods on the mountain, there are those with one hundred celestial maidens, those with two hundred, and others with three hundred celestial maidens;
due to the results of their own karma, they have few, middling, or many.

Furthermore, there were other devas—some few, some moderate, and some many; some numbering one thousand, some two thousand, some three thousand, and so on up to twenty thousand—who enjoyed themselves through various songs, dances, and games, wandering from place to place through each of the groves, sporting and taking pleasure.
Thus, within that most excellent and wondrous grove of lotuses, adorned with swarms of bees, they sport and enjoy pleasure amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.
That mountain is extensively adorned with many varieties of exquisite jewels, and throughout its slopes, they wander, sporting and enjoying pleasure.
The stones of that mountain are entirely composed of jewels, exquisitely interspersed and radiating a brilliance surpassing the sun.
The ground is as soft as the finest cotton bedding or down found in Jambudvīpa and Aparagoyānī, such as *tūla* cotton or other varieties of cotton;
it is like other types of soft down, sinking when the foot is placed upon it and rising level again when the foot is lifted.
The summit of that mountain is thus soft;
whether it be the jewels, the ground, the trees, the forests, or the mountain peaks, every place there is supremely soft.
The touch of Sukhāvatī is such that everything seen by the eye is delightful.

Thus, this mountain is exceedingly lovely; there, the hosts of devas and celestial maidens sport together, mutually enjoying various pleasures. Possessing every excellence of desire, they experience celestial bliss.
Having thus enjoyed pleasure for such a long time in that place, those gods experience various delights through harmonious music of the highest quality, singing, dancing, and sporting.
Then, a great radiance appears in the sky, like a celestial fire-dog (*śikhin*), which all those gods behold together.
That supreme deva, seeing a great radiance such as he had never before seen or heard of, was struck with wonder.
The deva of the middle realm, unable to look upon it with his eyes, covered his eyes with his hands and entered beneath a tree.
The gods of the lower heavens, seeing this, could not endure it; because they were struck with fear, they entered their own jewel caves together with the celestial maidens.

Furthermore, there were other gods of great majesty and virtue who, having seen it with their eyes, were able to endure it; they observed it closely and, giving rise to a sense of wonder, thought to themselves:
"What kind of light is this?"
Who possesses such supreme and wondrous radiance?
This mountain has such wondrous jewel-light; it is so replete with the light of this mountain that this other light is eclipsed and no longer appears, like a mirage in the sky.
"I have never seen anything like this before.
He looked again with keen scrutiny and saw the great celestial dog (Mahāśvāna) thus descending, its great radiance pervading the void of space like a blazing flame as it fell downward.
Looking up at that celestial realm, it was like a great celestial dog falling from the sky; he contemplated its length, breadth, and dimensions in this way and that, and then said:
"The size of that celestial dog is five thousand yojanas."
"All of space is ablaze, beyond all analogy.
"In this way, in this way," they descend in succession, gradually drawing closer below.
Even that Great Heroic Deva was unable to look. Why?
Because it was not within the range of his divine eye; he could not behold that supreme, great radiance, and so he covered his own eyes with his hands.

Before long, they conceived a sense of wonder and withdrew their hands again to open their eyes and look; gazing upward into the void, they saw that celestial dog gradually drawing closer and lower. All the hosts of devas were filled with doubt and anxiety, and they said to one another:
"What thing is this up in the empty sky?"
"It is most extraordinary that it falls from the sky.
At that time, the host of devas was unable to reach a decision and spoke thus: "What is this thing?"
At that time, before long, the celestial dog (śyāma-śunaka) thus vanished into the sky, and its whereabouts were unknown.
When the timid deva realized it had disappeared, he emerged from his cave; freed from fear along with the celestial maidens, they turned toward one another and said:
"This rare phenomenon—what kind of thing is this?"
"My mind is deeply suspicious; were I to see it, fear would arise within me.
Having spoken thus, they were unable to reach a resolution with one another.
After a long time had passed, they spoke to each other in turn:
"What is that thing? It gives rise to a sense of wonder and inspires fear.

Thus, while sporting on the mountain and experiencing pleasure, their minds were further stirred; they continued to experience pleasure, experiencing the pleasures of sensory objects (*viṣaya*), experiencing various pleasures in immeasurable ways and with immeasurable distinctions, including the sounds of the five musical instruments.
In the groves, there are many hosts of devas together with hosts of celestial maidens;
hundreds of thousands of such deva hosts experience pleasure.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Volume 40 [and] Volume 41.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: Observing the Heavens; Section Six: Suyāma Heaven.

"At that time, King Mūśalinda of the Suyāma Heaven, together with the assembly of devas and the assembly of devakanyās—consisting of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of thousands of deva multitudes and devakanyās—all proceeded toward the place on Mount Gaṇa within the Realm Endowed with Mountains and Trees."
All the hosts of devas, seated upon lotus thrones, pervaded the entirety of space as they ascended that mountain.

There they beheld those celestial hosts, adorned with immeasurable varieties of forms and garments, possessing immeasurable colors and immeasurable merits, and surrounded by a retinue of celestial maidens.
The devas on that mountain experience various pleasures through the merits of the five sensory desires.

At that time, having seen this, King Mucilinda was filled with great joy; together with the host of celestial maidens, he immediately and swiftly proceeded toward the place where the celestial assembly dwells amidst mountains and trees.

When the assembly of devas there beheld the celestial king Mucilinda, they immediately and swiftly went forth together with the host of goddesses to welcome him. Amidst the sounds of drums and music, various songs and dances, and the arising of joyful hearts, they drew near to one another and united in harmony.
Throughout the mountain peaks, they performed various songs, dances, and hymns of praise to the celestial king Mucilinda, and together they ascended the mountain.
Upon that mountain, they took delight in one another’s company, enjoying themselves with various sounds and music.
While those hosts of devas were thus enjoying such pleasures for a long duration,
they saw a celestial dog (ulkā) descending from the upper void of space.
The radiance and other attributes of this celestial dog were as previously described.

At that time, having witnessed such a rare occurrence, the host of devas gave rise once more to a mind of doubt and suspicion, and being seized by great fear, they immediately approached and drew near to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven.
Some gazed directly upward into the void;
others, having previously heard of that celestial dog, abandoned their heedless conduct and together with the lord of gods, Mucilinda, paid sincere homage to the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were those who feared and entered golden caves, and those who took refuge under trees; these two kinds of devas lacked both courage and strength.
There were devas who fled toward Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, seeking him out in the hope of finding refuge and rescue.
"This vision is most extraordinary; it gives rise to a mind of doubt and uncertainty.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, having seen this, addressed the host of devas, saying:
"Do you, members of the deva host, know or not whether this radiance in the void is about to fall to the earth?"
"All of you, come here!
Among them, there were devas who had not previously known this, and they said to King Mucilinda:
"We truly did not know."
"Now that I behold such a rare phenomenon as this, I truly do not understand it.
At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda called to all the devas and addressed them, saying:
"All you hosts of devas, listen all of you; I shall now explain it for you."
"Because the flames of light from the void have fallen to the ground, you members of the celestial host who feel fear and possess rare resolve, listen!
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, spoke for the sake of all these celestial hosts, saying:
"All of you, listen!
Far above my station, there are further hosts of devas;
in every respect—measure, color, form, and the karmic causes for long life—they are a hundred times superior to me. This is the foremost, most excellent, and pure abode of the Bodhisattvas.

While among humans, they maintained the five precepts without breach or flaw; being firm and unviolated, and because they engaged in immeasurable kinds of superior practice, at the dissolution of the body after death, they were reborn in the heavenly worlds of the good destinations.
That celestial world is named Tuṣita.

Within Tuṣita, whether it be the pleasures experienced, the various gardens and groves, the celestial maidens, the various radiances, their physical forms or strength, their sharp wisdom, their long lifespans, their immeasurable joys—whether of body or mind—their requisites for livelihood and enjoyment, or the beauty of the celestial maidens; even sixteen parts of these do not equal one part of those in this Yāma heaven.
The merits of those devas are beyond my power to describe.
The radiance and form of those devas compared to the light of the Yāma Heaven where I am now are no different from a firefly compared to the sun.
Whether it be their radiance or the various articles of life they enjoy, nothing can compare to them.
For a long time, those gods experience immeasurable and manifold pleasures.

The bliss of those devas is supremely delightful; they experience pleasure through various objects and the manifold realms of the five sensory qualities, which surpasses the bliss found here in the Yāma Heaven.
After a long period of time, when their wholesome karma is finally exhausted, they are shattered and destroyed by the vajra of impermanence.
This dharma of impermanence is certain to exist for all sentient beings; it is their inevitable seed.
All sentient beings possess indeterminate seeds.
When impermanence arrives, their life is exhausted; because their wholesome karma is spent, they immediately descend from that Tuṣita heaven.

All conditioned phenomena are as fleeting as a lamp, characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing; throughout the three realms, there is nothing that is not subject to motion and yet remains eternal.
All things are subject to movement; all things come to an end. They are not eternal phenomena, and nowhere is there permanence.
All conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are inevitably subject to decline and loss.
Therefore, one must eventually fall away from that Tuṣita Heaven, just as a lamp is extinguished when its oil and wick are exhausted.
Once the lamp has been extinguished, darkness arises;
as the lamp arises, darkness ceases, and as the lamp is extinguished, darkness arises.
It is like how, once the seed has ceased, the sprout arises.
In this way, and in this way, because that karma is exhausted, their life-span comes to an end.
Because the gods in the Tuṣita heaven thus pass away from that place, you now see that those devas have died; by the power of karma, such signs appear.

The body itself is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); yet, even though it has died, it possesses such radiance—how much more so the radiance emanated by immeasurable wholesome karmas, and the radiance emanated by the most supreme and definitive wholesome karmas!
O Yāma devas, from this day forward you should know that such are their characteristics: if they have not yet died, what radiance do they possess?
What majesty do they possess?
What adornments do they possess?
What kind of karma did they possess?
It cannot be described, for there is no analogy for it.
That heaven was produced by fourfold superior karma; when even that comes to an end, how much more so this [heaven] of mine, produced by threefold observance of the precepts and meager karma?
"All of you have been born in the Yāma Heaven, yet it is fragile and impermanent, a defiled residue of conditioned existence; therefore, this heaven is utterly distinct from that [ultimate state].
If even such a heaven as that is subject to destruction, how much more so will you not be destroyed?"
At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda spoke these verses:
"The impermanent heavenly firebrand flashes, Burning the Tuṣita Heaven;
Through lack of self-mastery it perishes, Like a lamp when its oil and wick are spent."
Driven by the power of karma, the wheel of karma— with its twelve spokes of great force— revolves, never pausing in its ascent or descent.
It grasps at various objects of perception, adorned with immeasurable gateways.
Because time is fulfilled, darkness recedes and lacks autonomy.
Because the seasons possess autonomy, grasses and trees grow in this manner;
yet once their time has arrived, they wither and dry up once more.
When such a time comes for a deva, they then achieve celestial bliss;
yet when such a time comes again, they fall back and lose their sovereignty.
When the time for karma arrives, one wanders through the world.
Because time is sovereign, those who experience pleasure will again experience suffering.
Whether one experiences pleasure or suffering, do not trust that sensory objects are permanent;
it is due to all these causes and conditions that pleasure and suffering are thus differentiated.
All things are devoid of pleasure; all karma is sovereign.
Suffering is likewise impermanent, for it arises entirely from the cause of karma.
As various distinct fruits are produced, conditioned phenomena continue to flow and revolve.
If you wish to know the causes and conditions of this, you should know the Four Noble Truths.
If one knows the Four Noble Truths, they will surely attain liberation;
but those who delight in the realm of delusion revolve in the world like a wheel.
One who well understands meaning and knows the truths will attain liberation;
for one who does not know meaning and the truths, there is no prospect of liberation.
If one understands in this way that the world is impermanent, [one attains liberation].
"Then one gives rise to the intention for liberation and restrains the mind from unwholesome karma.
Thus do the gods of the Yāma Heaven feel such fear; in the Suyāma Heaven, there are immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions [of suffering].
The King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, being in accord with the Dharma, spoke thus of the path.
At that time, having heard the words of the wise King of the Gods, the minds of those devas were each individually transformed.
There are those who feel weary and detached, those who loathe birth and death, and those who fear birth and death; yet their minds again turn toward delighting in sensory objects.

In Mount Gaṇa, there are various groves and various places for play, many adorned with flowing waters, lotus ponds, and the like. Covered by tree branches and adorned with treasures, there are the lovely sounds of various birds, lotus ponds of manifold adornment, and mountains adorned with the seven great precious jewels.

There are many immeasurable and desirable objects of the senses—various realms of sound, touch, taste, form, and fragrance—where they enjoy these realms together with hosts of celestial maidens; having attained such delights, they forget their previous weariness and no longer remember it.
Furthermore, all sensory objects are pleasant at first but bitter in the end; yet, together with hosts of celestial maidens, one experiences various pleasures through such objects.
Because of that mountainous realm, the monkey of the mind, by its own sovereign power, experiences pleasure therein.

Furthermore, the hosts of devas all returned together with their lord, Mucilinda; some traveled through the air, some sat upon lotus flowers, and some rode in vehicles adorned with infinite ornaments.

There are those among the devas who ride peacocks, those who ride white elephants, those who ride geese, and those who ride mandarin ducks; there are such various and diverse vehicles. Surrounded by celestial maidens who sing and dance, they enjoy all manner of musical sounds in harmony with the heavens.
Before that lord, the Great King Mūśalūta, they proceeded toward the Mūśalūta Heavenly King’s abode in the Forest of Playful Delight.
With various deep intentions, they gave rise to conscious awareness; among them were those who felt weary detachment and those who were heedless.
In this manner, they experience pleasure within various realms of play.
Within the grounds of the Forest of Playful Delight (*Kūṭāgāra-vana*), the gods are distinguished by such diverse and manifold differences.
Furthermore, those gods dwelling in that region of mountains and groves reside upon the summit of Mount Gaṇa;
with various intentions, they sport and enjoy themselves.
Among them, some gods naturally develop weary detachment.
Thus, through various and immeasurable conceptualizations and immeasurable objects, they experience pleasure.

Though they experience such immeasurable pleasure within these realms, their minds are never satisfied; this continues until the causes of their wholesome karma—the source of their pleasure—are exhausted, decayed, and lost, at which point their karma being spent, they fall away from that celestial realm.
Having thus fallen away, they are bound by the various ropes of karma and are born in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If they are born among humans, they always dwell in pleasant places, possess complete sensory faculties and virtuous wisdom, have the foremost great mind and the greatest wealth, are constantly venerated by all people, and are handsome and of excellent complexion; they may become kings of men or high ministers.
"Due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the various regions of the Yāma Heaven.
He then hears and knows:
Furthermore, there is a place called Vast Conduct.
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He sees, hears, and knows:

If a son of good family associates with virtuous friends, believes in the retribution of karmic actions, maintains an upright mind, accords with the practice of the Dharma, upholds the prohibitive precepts, possesses right view without deviation, cultivates the conduct of right view, constantly stays near the elders, gives rise to pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, believes in birth and death, always at all times skillfully restrains the sense faculties, does not cling to sensory objects, and fears birth and death;
if he understands the suffering of separation from what is loved, and knows all about birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the meeting and parting of those one holds dear;

and if he recognizes the faults within the five aggregates of grasping, is constantly diligent and energetic, practices wholesome karma in accordance with the truth, and distances himself from evil associates—then [he shall attain liberation].

At all times, one always delights in hearing the true Dharma; having heard it, one contemplates it; having contemplated it, one understands its meaning and holds it in mind, knowing the flavor of detachment from desire;
one always refrains from killing and always refrains from stealing, as previously described.
Furthermore, he abandons sexual misconduct:
his eyes do not delight in gazing upon the private parts of women;
and having heard their songs, dances, ornaments, and voices, he does not relish them.
Whether seeing or hearing of women depicted in paintings, one harbors no unwholesome thoughts;
upon dreaming of a woman, one feels no pleasure upon waking and does not give rise to thoughts of craving;
one does not indulge excessively in desire, constantly practicing right observation, abandoning sexual misconduct, and discarding sensual matters as if they were nothing other than poison.

That person, thus endowed with such merit, constantly performs wholesome deeds, always maintains virtuous thoughts, remains free from defiled minds, upholds the precepts with universal purity, and carefully guards the prohibitions.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas, in the Vast Conduct region of the Yāma heaven.
Having cultivated and frequently practiced those three meritorious qualities, delighting in pure precepts and attaining the fruit of upholding them, they are born in that place.
As soon as they are born there, they hear the various sounds of celestial birds, which are supremely lovely, like the call of the *barku* bird.
As for the fragrance smelled by their noses, it is a supreme celestial scent never before experienced; having smelled that fragrance, they experience the highest bliss.
The tactile sensations experienced by the body are such as have never been attained before; the mind and its mental factors are pure and free from turbidity or confusion.
Because they accord correctly with the turning of the mind, joy arises.
Flavors are likewise; there are various flavors that they have never experienced before.
After those gods have thus first experienced pleasure with their six-fold bodies of consciousness, they think to themselves:
"What kind of world is this?"
"In what place do I dwell?
This place is entirely lovely and entirely delightful; it is different from before in every respect.
Here, one sees all forms of the world, including immeasurable beautiful colors."

Furthermore, he sees that all the light of his own body surpasses the light of the sun; it is free from the impurities of flesh and bone, free from all forms of uncleanness, free from shadow and glare, free from veins and sinews, free from large and small joints, and free from any sensation of hardness.
The body is supple, and all its various parts are entirely soft.
Free from fatigue and weariness, there is no obstruction whatsoever in whatever movements one intends, whether coming or going.
Free from seeking and free from physical deformity, they do not harbor mutual hatred or envy toward one another.
The hairs on their bodies and their hair all curl; each individual hair curls, and there is no obstruction whatsoever in the range of their vision.
Their sensory domains are not inferior, being free from all obstacles of sound, touch, taste, and fragrance.
Their bodies neither increase nor decrease; they do not change or age, and they are always possessed of strength.
They are entirely free from the jealousy of celestial maidens and from all fear or timidity.
His body is naturally perfected; he is free from seeking adornments and free from seeking wealth, and regarding the celestial maidens, he is free from the fault of attachment.
Furthermore, what does he abandon?
He wanders everywhere through the groves and gardens without fear—free from the fear of enemies, free from the fear of impurity, and free from the fear of [not] being content.
Upon seeing their own bodies, they give rise to love and delight, which increases with every passing thought.
They obtain all the pleasures of the various immeasurable realms of the heavens, exactly as they had hoped for.
Having desired happiness, because of his limited wisdom, his mind thus doubts:
"From where have I come? What kind of body is this body of mine?"
"What place is this? What is the name of this location?
Thus he doubted and reflected within his mind.

For example, suppose there is a drunken man or a sleeping man who, when three-quarters of the four parts of the night have passed, awakens from sleep and, after a long while, his mind becomes filled with doubt, thinking: "Who am I?"
"Where did I dwell?
After reflecting for a short while, he then came to know.
In this manner, after the newly born deva had contemplated with his mind for a long time, he finally knew: "I died among humans and was reborn here."

In that way, those devas, having cultivated their thoughts through the observance of precepts during their time as humans, are born into the celestial realm in a manner corresponding to that practice.
Just as those in Jambudvīpa do not delight in sensory objects, so too, at the moment of their initial birth in that celestial realm, they do not yet experience joy.
Why is this? Because of the habitual perfuming of thoughts from the past, at that time it was thus.
After a long while, the newly born deva-son thus realizes: "I am in the celestial realm; by virtue of my wholesome karma, I have been born in the world of gods."
If a person is thus, dying among humans and being reborn among the gods, they maintain their precepts and, as before, remain unattached to sense objects.
Later, when they pass away from the heavenly realm and are reborn among humans, because of the habitual perfuming practiced while in heaven, there are corresponding characteristics.
Likewise, due to the perfuming of thought while among humans, when they die later and are reborn in the heavens, they do not delight in sense objects nor do they approach sexual desire.
At that time, because he had maintained the precepts in such a manner, although this newly born deva was reborn in that celestial realm, he did not draw near to sensory objects.
Due to the influence of his residual karma, his mind remained thus unattached to and disinterested in those objects.
"If one emerges from hell to be born among the devas, it is because of their remaining karma;
while it was difficult to emerge from within hell, due to other wholesome karma and a slight aspiration, they have emerged from hell and been born among the devas."

Having come from such places of suffering and affliction, they are born among the gods and, upon attaining pleasure, become attached to it; their minds give rise to joy, yet they are also prone to much anger.
They take delight in gardens, flowing streams, rivers, ponds, and various lotuses, wandering and sporting with hearts full of superior love and attachment.
Regarding food and drink, their craving and delight are strong because their mental continuum has been permeated by such tendencies.

If, after emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they are born among the devas due to residual karma, their mental continuum remains permeated; thus, their desire for food is strong, they crave food and drink, they constantly dwell in coolness, and they take great pleasure in women.
Because that [karma] perfumes the mind.
"If one emerges from the animal realm and is born among the devas due to residual karma, then they consume much food and drink.

Just as those in the animal realm eat and drink much, so too those born among the devas likewise eat and drink much; whether drinking little while eating much or eating little while drinking much, their desire-mind is powerful."
It is because of the continuous perfuming of mental impressions (*manas-saṃtati-vāsanā*) that it is thus.

"If one has fallen from the four levels of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in those heavens—having previously attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), one is thus born within the four stages of the formless realm; when karma is exhausted, one falls and is reborn in those heavens—it is because of such continuous perfuming of the original mental impressions that, having thus obtained such pleasant contact, flavors, forms, and fragrances, one nevertheless finds no further delight."
Because the mind is tranquil and not greatly distracted, it perfumes the mind.
This applies whether one relies upon the first dhyāna in the form realm, or likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.

Because that dhyāna is exhausted, he regresses and is reborn in the desire realm; yet, due to the continuous perfuming of his original intention, there are lower, middling, and superior degrees, and his mind delights in sitting in meditation.
His mind finds joy in the meditative object, though it is slight and not extensive.
"If those in the heavens of the desire realm fall away from the desire realm and are reborn again within the desire realm due to the karma of their birth,

and likewise those who have performed various wholesome deeds in these two paths— whether as gods or humans— these two types, having fallen away from the heavens of the desire realm, are reborn again among the gods of the desire realm."
Because they perform wholesome karma, this occurs only within the Desire Realm.
For all the devas, two types of karma ripen, with the exception of the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) devas.
Those Śuddhāvāsa devas do not experience the ripening of karma that leads to rebirth, nor do they experience the ripening of other [kinds of] karma.

In this way, the winds of karma constantly blow upon all sentient beings in the world, causing them to wander in saṃsāra. Bound by the snares of the mind and further fettered by various snares of karma, they possess immeasurable hundreds of thousands of diverse inclinations and beliefs, as well as immeasurable conceptual discriminations; these continue in succession, and they perpetually wander through the five destinies.
"At that time, having observed in this way and reflected in this way, the newly born deva-son then came to know:
'I have passed away from such-and-such a realm and have been reborn here.'"
"I have passed away from among humans and come to be born here because of the karma for rebirth.
Thus he knows that he was born due to that karma; if he was born due to other karma, he likewise knows it.
By what causes and conditions is it known that this devaputra was not born from other karma?
If it were from other karma, its causal conditions would have existed for a long time—perhaps a hundred kalpas—and could yield its retribution;
or perhaps a thousand kalpas, or even a hundred thousand kalpas, such that those with inferior divine eyes could not perceive or know it themselves.
Regarding those born from the karmic causes and conditions of long-distant past lives, they know their place of origin.

Having thus contemplated the causes and conditions of birth, conceit arises in their minds; yet before long, due to the permeation of wholesome karma, they develop various kinds of attachment toward sense objects.
That deva then reflects and knows thus:
"I have now been born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the place called the Ground of Vast Conduct.
At the very moment this thought arises, hosts of celestial maidens appear before him.
Due to the power of their wholesome karma, those celestial maidens quickly come to surround him.
By the force of that deva-son’s wholesome karma, the celestial maidens arrive.

If those celestial maidens have been born there for a long time, they feel no shame; desiring to embrace him, they approach and circle around that deva-son, enjoying various pleasures together within the groves.
By the price of their virtuous karma, they obtain those celestial maidens endowed with various merits, who are most lovely, and together they enjoy pleasures.

In that place, there are beautiful mountain forests, lotus ponds and rivers, mountain torrents and flowing streams; there are fine level plains and excellent golden caves, dwellings among the branches of trees, and hundreds of thousands of various birds with diverse songs.
Surrounded on all sides by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, they engage in song, dance, and play in such places.
In those gardens, deer made of the seven precious gems roam about everywhere.
All such various things seen by the eye are entirely lovely.

In that place there is a mountain named Vistīrṇālpa; its peaks possess the radiance of the seven precious gems, are adorned with various ornaments, and are interspersed with a multitude of diverse jewels.
There are lotus groves composed entirely of the seven treasures, and within these gardens there are many rivers and ponds; such are the various places of adornment.
Due to their virtuous karma, they are adorned with exquisite colors, and in such places they enjoy various pleasures through singing, dancing, and play.
After those devas have thus enjoyed such pleasures together, some sport within the waters.
In this way, through various desires, they arrive at the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Due to their virtuous karma, their playful delights never cease.
Those gods themselves manifest within their own bodies the names and characteristics of all the karmic deeds of the other gods.
As for what kind of virtuous karma each god performed in a previous life:
With what state of mind is karma performed?
At what time is it performed?
By what causes and conditions is it performed?
"What birth-place was created?

Regarding such matters as these, one performs wholesome karma by providing for those who possess the excellence of superior, middling, or inferior fields of merit, as well as the excellence of material wealth.
All those characteristics appear within one's own body as their respective names.
For example, just as a skilled calligrapher or painter, working in various separate locations, produces each piece with distinct clarity according to his work—
just as those names [indicate], so it is with this deva.
The master painter of virtuous karma, within the realm of karma, paints all manner of virtuous deeds everywhere.
The pigments of these virtuous deeds are pure and radiantly luminous; they are exceedingly lovely to behold, and when he paints those celestial realms, all beings delight in seeing them.
Just as the colors of a skillful painting produced by that good karma arise,
so too does the body of that deva manifest with such inscribed marks, appearing a hundred times more magnificent and superior.

For example, just as the finest gold refined a hundred times, or other such precious gems like red lotuses or blue jewels are exquisite and lovely among various superior treasures, the physical form of that deva is a hundred times more exquisite and lovely than those.
Such a mark, though painted, cannot be seen by one's own eyes.
Why is this? Because it is located on the mark beneath the jaw and above the throat; therefore, it is not seen.
If those devas have not yet become heedless in mind, they will see these signs as they look upon one another;
furthermore, due to the causes of their wholesome karma, they see these signs as they look upon one another in this way.
The gods of that Vast Conduct Stage are thus rare and marvelous.
Those gods possess yet another rare characteristic: just as they have a mark upon their throats, so too do they have one upon their foreheads.
Due to the power of wholesome karma, there are such signs.
It is a painting of various karmas, with various colors and forms.
As for what these signs are:
How does one fall back?
At what time does one fall back?
Having thus fallen back, where will one be reborn?
Those various colors and various painted forms are all clearly visible upon the foreheads of those gods.
This wondrous appearance is produced by karma.
Upon the bodies of those gods, there are such variegated garlands of letters, so beautiful and majestic.
Just as the various gods in other places have their bodies and heads adorned with diverse flower garlands, making them exceptionally beautiful and sublime, so too is this array of ornaments.

Furthermore, those devas, as the fruit of their virtuous karma ripens, have their bodies painted by their own karma; together with the celestial maidens whose bodies are likewise adorned with various exquisite paintings, they experience every pleasure.
Within immeasurable and diverse groves, amidst the vast expanse of the Ground of Extensive Practice, they sport and enjoy pleasures.
Having thus enjoyed these pleasures, they proceed once more toward a river named Well-Mixed (*Su-vyūha*).
That river flows forth from the peak of Mount Citraratna and thus is named Sucitrā.
That river is adorned with various jewels; it possesses the diverse songs of immeasurable flocks of birds and is graced by many, immeasurable, and various kinds of extraordinary trees.

There are various flowers, their petals of manifold colors, with hundreds of thousands of distinct hues, adorning the riverbanks; there, immeasurable celestial maidens draw near those banks to sport and enjoy themselves.
Furthermore, there is another exceptionally wonderful river called the Variegated River (*Citra-nadī*).
This river flows from mountain peaks with variegated-colored cliffs and banks; therefore, it is named the Variegated River.
When a deva approaches such a river of mingled waters, he is able to remember his place of origin.
If that deva has come from the hells to reach the banks of that river, he then remembers it.

Having recollected this, they find themselves fully endowed with all the most desirable qualities of the five objects of desire; there, the celestial maidens are filled with great joy as they sport and experience pleasure.
Because they remembered with their minds the suffering they had previously endured, they forgot all pleasant things; thus, weary of desire, they spoke these verses:
“In the blazing fires of hell, The agonizing pain was most extreme.
Now that our evil karma is exhausted, We have all come to this place.”
Wholesome karma yields wholesome fruit, adorned with all manner of merits;
because karma is evil, its fruit is suffering, which one must inevitably experience.
Amidst this suffering and pleasure, I wander through the realms of birth and death.
Driven by the winds of karma, they roll like waves upon the ocean.
If one has a mind that commits evil and delights in wicked deeds,
because of those unwholesome actions, one will fall into hell due to such causes and conditions.
Having escaped from that hell, one is born here in this celestial realm;
having forgotten the suffering of that place, one again indulges in sensual pleasures.
This flow of wandering through realms is like the ropes on a balance scale, where pain and pleasure shift back and forth.
Yet their minds are exceedingly firm and stubborn, never wearying even as they undergo suffering.
Bound by the snares of craving and deceived by the sensory faculties,
they wander through the cycle of birth and death, joining this shore with the other.
Emerging from hell, one is born as a hungry ghost; emerging from ghosts, one is born as an animal;
emerging from other animals, one becomes a dragon; emerging from dragons, one is born into three realms.
As karma thus constantly functions, the world revolves like a wheel.
Because of long-standing habituation, they do not yet grow weary;
they delight in the palaces of the nāgas, finding no pleasure in the sufferings of hell.
They wander through the prison of existence, seeking pleasure in places where there is no true joy.
The suffering of a thousand padmas, and that of ten billion padmas—one undergoes such suffering for this long, yet through delusion, one never grows weary of it.
There is no pleasure whatsoever in the three realms; they are pervaded entirely by suffering.
Sentient beings are deceived by ignorance, yet they feel no weariness or revulsion.
Having thus experienced suffering, they create the causes of suffering because of their ignorance;
from these causes, results arise, just as fruit comes from a seed.
The mind is deluded by its objects; with courage and great strength, one should discipline that mind of sentient beings and cause it to become tranquil at that time.
Once that mind has been subdued, all realms will proceed in transformation.
Cycling through the three realms of existence, they are unable to perceive the ultimate truth.
Just as the wind, acting as a condition, causes the waters of the ocean to surge;
so too does the mind, acting as a condition, cause the world to revolve perpetually.
Sentient beings are attached to women and are seized by suffering and pleasure;
they do not reach the auspicious realm where there is no place for affliction.
When one recollects and understands suffering, then the mind of weary detachment arises.
Having forgotten those sufferings, they again become attached to pleasure and negligence.
If there were one who could remember and know the sufferings of hell,
then such pleasures in the heavens would be like a tiny speck of dust.
"Those devas all remember their former places of birth.
Those who remain near that mountain peak with its variegated cliffs and banks where the mixed-colored river flows, all remember and know their former places of birth;
however, those who have departed from there forget everything regarding their former place of birth."
Furthermore, once they have forgotten their suffering and forgotten their place of birth, they become attached to various sensory objects.
