They experience pleasure through immeasurable, diverse, and similar types of delightful celestial realms—such as sounds, tangibles, tastes, forms, and fragrances—which are exquisite and beyond compare. Thus do they enjoy these pleasures.
Having experienced that pleasure, they proceed once more toward the mountain named Cira-kāma.
That mountain Cira-kāma is entirely lovely; it possesses a supreme river and lotus ponds, its waters pure, which encircle the mountain.

Geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks adorn those rivers and ponds; the two banks of the rivers are composed of various kinds of gold and jewels, and the sound of the flowing water produces all manner of melodies.
Within that mountain, there are ten thousand such rivers, adorned with various groves of trees and diverse flocks of birds.
Among those rivers, four are the most excellent; these four are as follows:
The first is named Swift Flow;
the second is named Golden Garland;
the third is named Lapis Lazuli Water.
The fourth is called Delightful Drifting. These are the four.

At that time, as the fruits of their own karma ripened for the host of devas, they all gave rise to hearts of joy; adorning their bodies with various garments, they sported and enjoyed pleasures as they headed toward the River Swift Flow.
Near that riverbank, there is a vast and magnificent forest of flowering trees called Immeasurable Joy (*Anantasukha*).
Its flowers are in full bloom, and its branches are so densely interlaced that no space remains between them; it is filled with hundreds of thousands of various kinds of flowers in countless colors.
There is a flowing pool where various kinds of birds dwell; the bodies of these birds are composed entirely of various mixed jewels, and the cries of the multitude of birds fill every place.
On the second bank of that swiftly flowing river, there is a lotus pond named *Matta-bhramara-paricāra*.
Just as when the sun first rises, red lotuses serve as an adornment within that pond, so too do these lotuses possess a supreme fragrance that pervades the waters of the pond.
On both banks of that river, one side has groves of trees and the other has flower ponds.

That river is five hundred yojanas in length and five yojanas in width; its waters are universally clear, and flowers growing within the water completely cover the surface. The petals of these flowers are of various colors and diverse kinds, possessing the most excellent fragrance.
The fragrance of that [incense] pervades five yojanas.
At that time, in that place, those various devas follow whatever they think of in their minds; some devas are in the groves and gardens, while others are within the lotuses.
Just as they had intended in their minds, they sported and experienced pleasure, mutually rejoicing with hosts of celestial maidens.
Possessing their own radiance,
they were born in that place through the power of their virtuous karma.
On both banks of that Swift-Flowing River (Āśu-srotas), the gods of the Vast Conduct (Vipula-cārin) engage in various sports and enjoy pleasures.
Such is one river. That Golden Garland River (Suvarṇa-mālā) flows forth from a mountain peak; that mountain is named Vastra.

Furthermore, this river flows out from the peaks of the Vastra mountain; this Suvarṇamāla River is exceedingly lovely, for as it courses through the Vastra mountain, it resembles a golden garland, and thus this river is named Suvarṇamāla.

Such are the merits of that Suvarṇamālinī River: its waters are entirely celestial wine, free from the faults of intoxication; it possesses the most excellent fragrance, and its taste, color, texture, and so forth are all exactly as one desires, with everything fully provided.
Whatever they recollect, it does not hinder them nor cause confusion.
At that time, those devas, together with their celestial maidens, drink such wine and further experience superior pleasures.

Each and every one of those devas is surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of celestial maidens; their minds are attached to the realms of the five desires, and the sounds of the five musical instruments are exquisite and harmonious to their hearts' content.

Together with the celestial maidens, they enjoy every wish as it arises with sovereign ease; by the banks of the Golden Garland River, they achieve immeasurable varieties of supreme pleasures, never feeling satiated amidst these sensory realms.

Furthermore, they engage in various amusements such as singing and dancing, experiencing every kind of pleasure; they go from one mountain pass to another, from one mountain peak to another, from one riverbank to another, from one lotus pond to another, from one grove to another, and from the foot of one tree to the foot of another.
Having thus experienced various kinds of pleasure in those places, they next proceed toward the third river of Vaiḍūrya water.
Within that third river of Vaiḍūrya water, the water is as pure and clear as Vaiḍūrya; there are many Vaiḍūrya trees, and furthermore, many Vaiḍūrya birds are present within that water.
The waves of that water form garlands, and its foam appears like a smile; the pure, clear water flows slowly and not with haste.
The water is exceedingly deep and possesses wondrous sounds.
By the power of virtuous karma, the lapis lazuli water flows thus gently.
When the devas desire to experience pleasure and give rise to such thoughts, they go to that river; because of their thirst for sensory objects, they harbor various forms of craving and greed.
Those devas do not experience pleasure in a single location: some experience pleasure on the riverbanks, while others experience it within the water.
Together with the celestial maidens, they experience the supreme pleasure of dalliance.
All those hosts of devas ride upon birds, traveling from one wave to another, wandering everywhere; they enter one whirlpool after another, and pass from one eddy to the next.
Some enter the water; having entered, they emerge again and enter once more into the swift currents.
Furthermore, those gods pass from one lotus flower to another lotus flower, and again from one *utpala* grove to another *utpala* grove.
Thus they wander, arriving there hundreds and thousands of times, attaining a state of bliss that is beyond all analogy.
Furthermore, by the power of their virtuous karma, those gods perceive the ripening of karmic fruits in a tranquil realm of pure *vaiḍūrya* waters.

If there are devas whose purity of precept-observance is superior or whose wisdom is superior, they are able to see the original causes and conditions; thus they see everything regarding how this karma was performed to result in birth in that deva realm of pure Vaiḍūrya water.
By what causes and conditions does such a mind give rise to recollection of past events?
It is because in a previous life, one gave rise to a pure mind and deep faith toward the field of merit.
Each and every one of those gods thought to themselves:
"The power of my own realm moves and shifts in this way; the waters of the five desires within the river of craving thus carry me away, causing me to remain unaware."
Impermanence has arrived; I shall certainly fall away from this state.
The signs of the karma performed in past lives—the causes for my birth here—appear upon my own throat.

Because those devas see such signs, they know that due to the causes and conditions of having performed such virtuous deeds in past lives, they have been born in this place and thus experience such pleasure.
When their karma is exhausted, they will certainly fall from this heavenly realm.
Having reflected thus, they address one another.

Furthermore, seeing the terrifying places of the five realms of existence, and having seen those terrors, all those gods give rise to weary detachment and speak these verses on the banks of the Vaiḍūrya river:
"If one cultivated virtue in the past, one is loved by virtuous people;
yet now, while receiving the fruits in this celestial realm, every moment moves toward exhaustion."
When that is exhausted, one then falls away; the rewards of heaven, all causes and conditions for pleasure—all such things are utterly extinguished.
Having fallen into the grasp of impermanence, everything is destroyed.
If phenomena were impermanent, they would cause all to be greedy.
Such impermanent phenomena can give rise to all greed;
those who are foolish and of little wisdom become greedily attached to the flavor of desire.
Delusion prevents one from perceiving faults, just like the pāka fruit;
bound by forms, sounds, and the rest, one suffers affliction because of craving.
Evil karma deludes sentient beings, depriving them of self-mastery.
Because they are deluded by evil karma, they undergo the fruits of that evil karma.
Those who are attached to the flavors of desire find that desire harms them like a poisonous fruit;
being attached to desire without knowing contentment, they fall into the hells.
Always delighting in the practice of giving and precepts, When the merit of giving and precepts is accomplished,
If one always practices in this way, Then one will be born in the heavens.
Constantly practicing the observance of the precepts, One abandons unwholesome karma.
Those who reverently cultivate dignified conduct will be reborn in the heavens.
Those who compassionately comfort sentient beings, have deep faith in the Buddha’s Dharma,
and maintain a tranquil, collected mind will be reborn in the heavens.
If, toward one's enemies, one maintains a mind of loving-kindness free from the stain of hatred and remains ever tranquil in heart, such a person shall be reborn in the heavens.
If there is no hatred within the mind, that person is virtuous and free from affliction.
The brave who are well-disciplined will be born in the heavens;
those who always speak truth, uphold the precepts, and do not speak excessively,
knowing what is firm and what is not, will be born in the heavens.
If one does not delight in the world, but grows weary of and seeks to leave behind the nature of old age and death,
always rejoicing in nirvana, such a person will be born in the heavens.
Whether beneath a tree, in a cemetery, or likewise in mountain valleys and the like—
Those who always practice single-minded meditation will be born in the heavens.
Those who know the proper time to honor their parents, avoid evil associates,
and constantly practice a heart of loving-kindness will be born in the heavens.
One who does not delight in villages or cities, nor in places of amusement or on the road,
but dwells in one place with contentment, will be reborn in the heavens.
If one skillfully observes one's own body and constantly perceives its impurity, [one will attain liberation].
Knowing oneself to be thus, one will be born in the heavens.
If one can understand the net of phenomena, knowing the various nets of phenomena,
and takes no delight in birth and death, one will be born in the heavens.
If one realizes that all phenomena arise in infinite varieties,
and though seeing them, feels no delight, such a person will be born in the heavens.
The mind, moment by moment, is like an illusion, like a city of the gandharvas.
If one tames this mind, one will be born in the heavens.
If one truly knows the single characteristic, or skillfully knows the two characteristics,
and the mind becomes weary of and detached from desire, one will be born in the heavens.
Regarding the wives of others as one’s own mother, and regarding all beings as one’s father—
if one is thus impartial, one will be born in the heavens.
If one constantly refrains from divisive speech and always delights in bringing others together, [one will likewise be reborn in the heavens].
With a mind free from stinginess and straightforward, one will be born in the heavens.
Regarding all things belonging to others as being like clods of earth,
and naturally finding joy in contentment, one will be born in the heavens.
If, whether by night or by day, one is always able to remain free from indolence and practices with diligent vigor, such a person will be born in the heavens.
If one is free from pride, greed, and hatred, and further remains free from indolence, [they shall likewise attain that state].
Those who thus renounce and abandon [the world] will be born in the heavens.
Those who never take pleasure in the five sensory objects, and whose precepts are not broken by those five objects—
those wise ones who constantly guard their precepts will be born in the heavens.
If one can understand the four graspings, and likewise the Four Truths— if the wise know them in this way,
they shall be born in the heavens. If one knows the suffering that is the retribution for suffering, and also knows the cessation of suffering, [one shall be born in the heavens].
One who sees thus with clarity will be born in the heavens. If,
even when encountering decline and affliction, one does not abandon the Dharma,
such a person who upholds the Dharma will be born in the heavens.
If one wears robes of dyed color, or even wears rag-robes from a dust heap,
and with a virtuous mind does not commit evil, such a person will be born in the heavens.
If one practices meditation at all times and always maintains a mind directed toward transcendence, [they shall likewise be reborn in the heavens].
Those who always delight in secluded places will be reborn in the heavens.
Whether things are pleasant or unpleasant, whatever they may obtain from others,
those whose minds feel neither joy nor anger will be reborn in the heavens.
If one wears coarse and shabby garments, or clothes of dust and rags,
and is thus content with such clothing, that person will be born in the heavens.
Whether on a bed, on the ground, or on a terrace, or even in any other place, [one remains content].
One who gives rise to neither thoughts of suffering nor pleasure will be born in the heavens.
Regarding the forms seen by the eye— whether blue, yellow, red, white, or otherwise—
if one views them according to reality as they truly are, that person will be born in the heavens.
If one hears neither pleasant nor unpleasant sounds, taking no delight in these two kinds of voices,
and the mind remains upright, unmoving, and undisturbed, that person shall be born in the heavens.
Having subdued the six sense faculties and taking no pleasure in sensory objects, one attains liberation.
One who gathers the mind so it is unmoved and undisturbed will be born in the heavens.
Through such great benefit, one constantly experiences happiness;
if one performs all these [practices], one will be born in the heavens.
Just as all karmic actions exist, this is indeed the most supreme:
those who practice the stainless Dharma will be born in the heavens.
If one understands the retribution of karma, one can accordingly perform karmic actions that lead to such retribution.
"Those who are constantly fearful of suffering will be reborn in the heavens.
Having thus observed these signs in his neck and throat, that deva, overcome with extreme terror, spoke this verse.
On the banks of the river, together with the hosts of devas, they are by nature heedless; due to their past karma, [the results] appear within their throats.
If they go elsewhere, they no longer see them.
If there are causes and conditions, then one sees it;
if there are no causes and conditions, then even though it exists, one does not see it. Why is this?
Because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, those devas, being by nature heedless and habituated to heedless conduct, departed from Mount Longed-For and proceeded toward another mountain named Jewel-Encircled.

Due to a joyful mind, they are adorned with various ornaments; as sensual desires arise in the present, they are able to captivate their hearts. Not reckoning the various fears of the future, because their faculties are agitated and lack tranquility, they experience the foremost pleasures within those heavens.

With song, dance, joy, and laughter, they engage in various diversions by the riverbanks, where various tree branches are laden with all kinds of flowers; in that place, there are many birds known as "Ever-Joyful."
Furthermore, there is a mountain of jewels surrounded by a mountain of supreme jewels, possessing hundreds of thousands of distinct sections in their entirety, interspersed with various gems.
Because those devas long for such pleasure, they desire to go and see it.

At that time, the host of devas saw from afar that mountain encircled by flames and light, appearing as if piercing through space; the flames and light shot upward, a sight never before seen by the devas.
Suddenly they beheld it: the radiance of that mountain was blue, yellow, red, and purple, pervading ten thousand *yojanas*.
Furthermore, the radiance of these various jewels surpasses the radiance of all other immeasurable jewel mountains.
Just as the radiance of Mount Sumeru can eclipse the radiance of all other mountains,
so too does the radiance of this Jewel-Encircling Mountain eclipse the radiance of all other jewel mountains.
When those who look upon that Jewel-Encircled Mountain with their eyes, it brings joy to their sight.
Furthermore, it provides a second kind of pleasure for the ears:

namely, the sounds of various rivers and ponds, the diverse calls of peacocks and other birds with wings made of the seven precious gems, and the manifold vocalizations of such immeasurable species of birds.
There are jewel trees there, upon which are nets of bells; when the wind blows, they produce sounds so exquisite and beautiful that they are beyond comparison.
By means of such sounds, the Great Mountain Jewel-Enclosure brings joy to the ears.
Furthermore, that Jewel-Encircled Mountain is able to provide pleasure to the third sense organ; yet those celestial hosts have not yet reached the mountain.
That is to say, within that mountain, immeasurable fragrances issue forth from immeasurable flowers, bringing delight to the celestial noses.
In this way, that Jewel-Encircling Mountain brings pleasure to the third faculty;
furthermore, that Jewel-Encircling Mountain can also provide pleasure to the fourth faculty, namely, enabling the tongue faculty to obtain pleasure.
Forms, fragrances, tastes, and wines can make them abundant; various exquisite fruits all cause them to be satiated.
Furthermore, that Jewel-Encircled Mountain enables the bodies of the gods to obtain the touch of seamless garments.
The immeasurable garments are all exceedingly soft; furthermore, there is a cool breeze that, according to their thoughts, provides a pleasant touch as it blows upon their bodies.
That great mountain of jewels is thus able to bestow such celestial bliss.
Those devas experience pleasure through their five sense faculties in this way.
Just as they find pleasure through the five faculties, so too does the mind attain the supreme bliss.
This Jewel-Encircled Mountain causes all faculties to obtain pleasure, thus benefiting the entire host of devas.
"At that time, having reached that Jewel-Encircled Mountain (*Ratnavicitra-parvata*), it was surrounded by the radiant flames of jewels, emitting an immeasurable variety of flaming light.

It was adorned with many hundreds of thousands of lotus ponds and flowing rivers, and embellished with various hundreds of thousands of ornaments made of gold, lapis lazuli, blue precious gems, white silver, and other such diverse treasures."
Once those devas have seen such mountains, their innate nature is one of joy; because they see those mountains, they experience a hundredfold pleasure.
Together with the celestial maidens, they mutually and individually enjoy one another’s company, giving rise to hearts of delight, with ever-increasing longing and a profound desire to behold them.
In every cave and valley of those Jewel-Encircled Mountains, there are lotus ponds and groves everywhere;
from one mountain peak to another, from river to river, wherever the *srotas* flows.
From one jewel grove to another, they see everywhere flocks of various birds and hear their voices, which sound like the music of the five instruments as they sport and enjoy themselves.
Those five types of sensory objects—those of the divine eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—are all desirable.
Each of those faculties—the sounds, tangibles, tastes, forms, and scents—is individually excellent and sublime; thus, each of these faculties experiences pleasure within its respective object.
"Because of craving for such objects and due to negligence, one completely forgets both suffering and pleasure in the present life, as well as suffering and pleasure in past lives."
Just as one forgets all the various characters of the fruits of previous karma that were previously seen within one's throat,
so too, by sporting and experiencing various pleasures, one completely forgets the actions originally performed.
"On that celestial mountain peak, surrounded by exquisite jewels, is the place named Pure and Stainless (*vimala*).
In such a stainless and pure location, one sees the dust of the moving palace.
As the deity moves within the palace, there is the dust of exquisite jewels where the palace travels."
In those pure realms, one can even see the dust within the palaces, let alone other things such as the bodies of the devas.
Their various ornaments and lovely bodily colors are produced by the exhaustion of karma, and they appear in diverse and manifold ways.

If these celestial hosts, their lives having come to an end, are to fall away, by what karma is it wrought that they see such characters and inscriptions within their throats through the power of their wholesome karma?
Having seen this for the first time, they do not yet give rise to revulsion or renunciation.
Why is this? It is because of ignorance.
Having first experienced the flavor of desire, one immediately becomes attached to it and fails to give rise to a sense of revulsion.
If that dull-witted deva is shown [the truth] by another or realizes it himself, he perceives the faults of sensual desire and immediately becomes aware of the approaching terror.
Thus, while that deva is so deeply attached to the flavor of desire, upon seeing its dangers, he will later be consumed by the fire of remorse.
"How is it that I have not yet abandoned these desires, which are like poison, swords, or fire?
These desires are the very cause of rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, and as animals."
"Because of these causes and conditions of desire, I shall surely fall into the evil destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Thus, at a later time, he will be consumed by the fire of remorse.
If one cultivates the mind, one will not produce a relish for the flavor of sensual desire;
seeing the faults and perils of desire, one will neither relish nor be attached to that desire.
Because one knows the faults of desire and perceives those faults through wisdom, one will have no regrets later.
If one does not crave or delight in those sensual realms and does not grieve over their loss, it is because of having originally cultivated the mind.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 41; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 42.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-One: Observing the Heavens; Section Seven: The Yāma Heaven.
"At that time, those devas proceeded in succession upward to that mountain peak, to the first ground, which is stainless like a mirror."
Those hosts of devas see their own bodies within the mirror of the karmic ground, clearly manifest in every detail.

Among those devas, those who have previously cultivated body, speech, and mind are able to see themselves within the mirror of the karmic ground, wherein the fruits of karma—the cycle of birth and death—are manifested upon their foreheads.

He sees all such things as at what time, in what place, in what country, for what cause, for what condition, and with what signs of decline [they occurred]; he also sees the signs of others—namely, the signs that they are about to fall away.

Whatever marks of residual karma—such as the characters inscribed upon the foreheads of certain devas—or whatever marks of karma for future birth there may be, all such signs appear clearly to them within the mirror of the realm of karma; thus they fall from the Yāma heaven.

If it is due to other karma, or karma pertaining to birth—whether it be evil karma of body, evil karma of speech, or evil karma of mind—and through such causes and conditions one has fallen away, one will be born in a certain hell, among certain hungry ghosts, or among certain animals;
having already escaped from the animal realm, because one is deceived by the pursuit of sensual desires and negligence, one is blown by the winds of karma and is reborn in another place.
Furthermore, when such a desire arises beyond the proper time, he sees everything depicted within the inscriptions and drawings upon his forehead.

Within those forehead drawings, he likewise sees the emergence of the desire beyond the proper time; he perceives that for each specific type of desire there is a corresponding antidote, namely, the cultivation of the contemplation of the lack of radiance regarding desire, whereby he cannot be deceived by that desire.

Furthermore, there is another specific antidote for that desire: namely, seeing this form as a false perception; having thus accorded with the view regarding such form, one observes it with a correct mind, so that the heart of longing no longer increases.
In this way, and in this way, one should contemplate the faults within the five sensory objects just as they are; when that deity contemplates thus, there will be no more delight or craving.

Since a mind of delight and craving cannot cause obstruction or hindrance [to liberation], and because such craving is the seed of birth and death, that deity thus attains deliverance from the midst of desire.
Within the characters drawn upon his forehead, he sees everything. Having seen this, he either excels in the cultivation of the body or excels in the cultivation of the mind.
He is able to renounce desire because he perceives the faults and perils of desire;

having understood the escape from them, he perceives the faults and perils of the previously experienced objects of pleasure as being like eating poisonous jujubes, and he views the desires currently experienced in the same way.
Why is this? Because by experiencing sensual pleasure within sense objects, one falls into the evil realms.
By practicing in this way, one abandons and leaves behind sense objects.
If, among the characters inscribed upon the forehead, one perceives the karma of the evil realms—falling into the evil destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Having seen those karmas, all such karmas are entirely lost;
and all karmas for rebirth in the happy realms arise,
by the power of wholesome karma.
Having seen this, those devaputras conceived deep faith, performed virtuous deeds, and in this manner even cultivated the seeds of virtuous karma that lead to nirvāṇa.

"If there are other devas of lesser wisdom whose minds are inclined toward desire, and who are subject to the sovereign power of the net of karma—their own prior actions—once they have seen the marks of the written characters of that karmic painting, they give rise to this thought:
'When I eventually pass away from this place, may I be born among humans or among devas.'"
Having thus seen their place of birth, those devas feel no alarm or fear; instead, they enter once more to be washed in the river of craving, which has the five sensory objects as its waves.
Because of their negligence, they engage in negligent conduct.

Such a deva, having never studied nor heard [the Dharma] and possessing little wisdom, does not understand desire and is unable to leave it behind; thus, wholesome dharmas perish, and he further creates other karmic actions for future births—namely, the karma of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Why is this? Because all their wholesome karmas have been completely exhausted, and being deceived by desire, they further fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
At that time, there was a bird named Wise-Speech (Kalyāṇavādin) who, seeing the heedless devas engaging in heedless conduct, spoke these verses by virtue of the devas' own past wholesome karma:
"If one's mind is drawn toward what is good, One will thus obtain what is good;
If one follows after what is unwholesome, One will thus obtain what is unwholesome."
The mind exerts great effort, like earth, wind, water, and fire;
according to the causes and conditions it encounters, the mind thus moves and turns.
The mind can move with great speed, and it can also turn back with great speed.
It swiftly leads one to the heavens; it swiftly causes one to enter the evil realms.
If the mind swiftly practices goodness, and if one can guard the mind, all dharmas can be accomplished and all karmas can be severed.
The master of all mental activities is this very mind; for this reason, it is called "mind.
The mind constantly seeks opportunities to exploit one; one should never place trust in it.
Its essential nature is extremely fickle and restless; its great power cannot be restrained.
In one moment it performs good, and in another moment it performs evil;
likewise it performs the indeterminate—its course is unfathomable.
The coming of the mind cannot be known; the going of the mind cannot be discerned.
It was non-existent before and exists later; having existed, it returns once more to non-existence.
The mind has no fixed location, and its aggregation cannot be apprehended.
Because it has no physical body, it cannot be grasped or held.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, it arises thus moment by moment;
like the meeting of a fire-drill and cow dung, fire is produced through causes and conditions.
Thus, with the sense faculties, forms, and so forth, all conditions together give rise to the mind;
it is not a single factor that can produce the mind, but rather the mind arises through their conjunction.
Having understood the mind in this way, one knows that the mind is difficult to subdue.
"Let the mind follow the practice of the True Dharma; be careful not to delight in sensual desires.
Having heard this verse, those devas cultivated their bodies and their minds—practicing these two ways of training the heart.

Having thus cultivated the mind, they take no pleasure in sensory objects and practice in accordance with the Dharma. They may descend from the Yāma Heaven and be reborn in a superior realm, never departing from the celestial abodes.

If they are born among humans, they may become a king or a high minister; at times, they may plant the seeds of liberation and attain any of the three types of enlightenment according to their vows, or, endowed with virtuous karma, they may become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
"If those gods, despite seeing such rare karmic signs as clearly as if looking into a mirror, do not discipline their minds, they will fall again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."
Furthermore, as that bhikṣu contemplates these signs of the karmic retribution of rare paintings and written texts, he perceives this:

if a person diligently and with focused attention and deep resolve paints an image of the Tathāgata, or if they transcribe the scriptural texts of the True Dharma with a mind of faith, tranquility, and mental stillness.
When that person is born in heaven, they see [the image] on their throat or upon their forehead and give rise to faith.

Furthermore, there are those whose minds lack right faith, yet whether by royal decree, at the behest of others, or for the sake of obtaining goods as a means of livelihood, they write out the scriptures or paint images of the Buddha; these too will be born in heaven, though they do not believe upon seeing it and mostly engage in heedlessness.

They too have cultivated the seeds of wholesome karma and thus attained birth among the devas; yet, although they see [the truth], they do not believe, because they come without faith and come without reflection.
Thus, where there is no cause, there is no karmic fruit; in this way, all things arise from causes and conditions corresponding to their respective karma.

Furthermore, if there is a certain class of devas who by nature delight in negligence and practice negligent conduct, experiencing the pleasures of the five sensual desires within their celestial realm without ever being satiated; and having for a long duration enjoyed the merits of the five sensual desires amidst the mountain ranges of increasing immeasurable desire surrounded by jewels—

Having thus engaged in various kinds of play and enjoyment with the hosts of celestial maidens, he later departed from that mountain adorned with the excellence of the five desires and proceeded toward the third mountain, the Jewel-Encircled Mountain (Maṇiparivāra).

Giving rise to a heart of joy, they sport upon the path amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music; having fully accomplished all supreme and wondrous matters, they experience complete bliss in an instant, enjoying various realms of sensory objects exactly as they desire.
Having thus experienced sensual pleasures upon the mountain slopes by the riverbanks, they proceed to the third mountain, which is encircled by jewels.

In this manner, as they experience the delightful realms of the devas, their craving increases further and further; because they are not liberated from that craving, they are consumed by the fire of desire. They know no satiety regarding sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances, nor do they find satisfaction within the river of sensory objects, like the mīna fish.

Thus, the third is named Mount Maṇimaya (Jewel-Encircled). One side consists of blue jewel-gems; the second side consists of red lotus-gems; the third side consists of musāragalva-gems; and the fourth side consists of white silver-gems.
Having seen this, those devas give rise to a heart of joy and, turning toward one another, speak thus:
"O devas, behold these immeasurable, manifold, upright, and exquisite varieties of light!"
The radiance of these jewels pervades a million yojanas; entering that light, they cannot be distinguished.
This supreme radiance has immeasurable varieties, including blue, yellow, red, and white.
After those hosts of devas had spoken thus, they proceeded toward another grove named Ghanavṛkṣa (Dense Trees).
Those hosts of devas and celestial maidens, their hearts filled with joy, delighted in beholding the various places accompanied by immeasurable music.

Next, they arrive at that forest; as their wholesome karma ripens, they wander about adorned in various ways and experience manifold pleasures. Thus, for a long time, they engage in heedless conduct, driven by craving.
At that time, those devas beheld a dense forest of trees; within that grove, they saw two rivers made of the seven precious jewels.
The first river was of fragrant water with excellent taste and touch, which filled to the brim according to whatever one thought in one's mind.
The waters of that river flow according to one's thoughts.
On its silver banks, there are many various and diverse kinds of birds.
That single river is named "Mixed Waters."
Next, the second river is named Water that Grants Wishes (*cintāmaṇi-vāri*).
As for those mixed waters, they are its inherent nature and essence.
Such mixed waters are supremely pure, and the flow of water fills it to the brim.
Those various waters are free from the fault of intoxication due to the causes and conditions of wholesome karma.
These waters possess immeasurable varieties of color; therefore, that river is named "Variegated Water" (Citrapānīya).
Furthermore, the second river is named *Yathā-īpsita-jala* (Water According to Wish). In accordance with the various mental intentions of those devas, such water arises.
If they think of *sudhā* (ambrosia), then *sudhā* flows—supremely white and pure, with supreme fragrance and flavor—and the stream of *sudhā* fills [the river].
If those devas think of celestial wine, then exquisite celestial wine, complete with color, fragrance, touch, and flavor, flows forth from within, filling the space.
If they think of various extraordinary flowers of the mountains and marshes, then such wondrous flowers, complete with color, fragrance, and touch, flow forth from the river, filling it;
within those flowers, various bees serve as adornments.
The names of those flowers cannot even be spoken;
thus, the second river of wish-fulfilling water is filled with various flowing streams.
In that place, within such a dense forest of trees, there are such flowers, beautiful and adorned.
The gods there sport in various places within the two rivers, experiencing manifold pleasures.
Through their virtuous karma, they enjoy diverse delights such as desirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances; together they drink celestial wine and experience various forms of bliss.
Hearing the sounds of music, they experience various delights for the ear and manifold joys; according to their hearts' desire, they fully enjoy all manner of pleasures.
They are far removed from sorrow and lamentation, far removed from hunger and scarcity, and free from fear; yet within the realm of sensory objects, they are never satisfied.
It is like drinking salt water, which only increases one's thirst.
There are immeasurable kinds and immeasurable varieties of conceptual distinctions, and there are immeasurable kinds of celestial pleasures to be experienced.

After those gods have thus enjoyed their pleasurable activities among the groves and rivers, there is a bird there called River-Walker (*Nadīcara*), who, seeing the gods' negligence, speaks this verse:
"Just as this stream flows, so too do celestial pleasures;
life does not abide for even a single moment, yet through delusion one does not perceive it."
Because of old age, sickness, death, and the like, one’s karma can be exhausted and one may fall;
even the gods cannot escape this law, which constantly pursues their desires.
Life is not eternal, and the pleasures of the three realms are likewise so.
The fool is deluded by desire and thus fails to perceive this:
just as drops of water in the air must fall and cannot remain, so it is with all pleasures; they are no different from falling raindrops.
Like wind blowing upon dust and soil, They push and shove against one another, Whirling through the midst of space; The turning of the body is just like this.
This pleasure is not a supreme pleasure; It is deceptive with craving and lacks constant stability.
Combined with the poison of craving, it is like food mixed with venom.
That which is eternally supreme bliss is what is called the deathless state,
the place where there is no separation from those one loves, and the place where there is neither cold nor heat.
That place is eternally peaceful and secure, as taught by the wise;
where there is no birth-and-death, there is no suffering.
All pleasures derived from women are accompanied by suffering.
With craving as their seed, they are born again in the hells.
That which they take for pleasure can only produce suffering; how, then, can it be called pleasure?
It is the very essence of suffering, and in time, it becomes like poison.
When these sentient beings are born, they are blown by the winds of their own karma;
shrouded by the net of ignorance, they take delight in whatever place they are born.
Whether their actions be wholesome or unwholesome, they always follow them and move together with them.
Everywhere they are pursued and driven away, like fragrance that does not leave the flower.
You enjoy such pleasures now, but later you shall lose them;
just as when the day is full and the sun sets, its light follows in its disappearance.

"Having thus spoken for the sake of all those gods who act with negligence due to their past good karma, that water-faring bird, if there are among the gods those who act negligently and are given to negligence, will hear these verses spoken by the water-faring bird and say:
'This bird speaks well; he has awakened me.'"
"This bird speaks thus, and I shall surely attain what it says.
This bird speaks the truth; yet because of my own negligence, I have practiced negligent conduct and am still unable to abandon it."
"In the future, we will certainly be destroyed and shall encounter great terror.
From this day forward, we should cultivate a virtuous mind, counteract negligence, and abandon negligence."
"Thus, for a long period of time, that deva, with a focused and virtuous mind, having abandoned negligence and understood the faults of desire, reflected upon them with his mind;
yet, because of the movement of the mind, the great power of the mind, or because he had long practiced desire over many eons, he returned once more to attachment to pleasure."
In that celestial realm, there are thus immeasurable distinctions and immeasurable spheres of experience, a place replete with various desires and the enjoyment of pleasure above and below.
There are the songs of various birds and exquisite gardens containing lotus ponds.

The peaks of the seven-jeweled mountains are adorned with many immeasurable and wondrous lotus ponds, where countless hundreds of thousands of swarms of bees produce various sounds, adorning the exquisite pools.
In that place there is a river filled with food and drink.

There are hundreds of thousands of trees whose branches form a canopy over the river according to one's thoughts; among the branches are flowers, which serve as pavilions, complete with every variety of excellence.
Those devas possess wondrous radiance from their own bodies and are free from all sorrow and affliction; they obtain such retribution due to their own virtuous karma.

Whether in the lower, middle, or higher heavens, they are all free from envy and jealousy, loving one another with a single mind and a single desire; they do not obstruct one another, and thus they wander about and experience pleasure in this manner.
"At that time, having experienced pleasure, those devas deliberated together and said:
'As we have heard before, there is a sovereign of all the devas in this realm of Yāma named Mucilinda, who sports and enjoys pleasures; let us now go there together.'"
"The gods there, five hundred yojanas away from that lord of the gods, Mucilinda, heard the sound of singing from afar; because it was so distant, they heard it indistinctly."
Because their voices pervade all celestial realms, they are not clearly distinguished.
If it were the sound of birds, such as this song endowed with every excellence, even though that singing is heard indistinctly, one would give rise to extreme delight and could never be satiated.
Because their minds were stirred, they conceived a resolute intention, and all the hosts of devas proceeded toward the place of sport and pleasure belonging to the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda.
That forest was endowed with every excellence.

Those gods of the Heaven of Desire, together with their celestial maidens, were adorned with various ornaments and possessed every merit, including all kinds of garments. Their entire bodies were graced with heavenly robes that required no thread for weaving. Holding various musical instruments in their hands, they cherished one another and gave rise to hearts of joy.
Some ride upon the void, some ride upon lotus flowers;
others again ride upon *utpala* lilies, which possess a supreme fragrance and swarm with many bees.
Furthermore, there are those who ride upon *kubjaka* flowers; these *kubjaka* flowers are in shape, size, and color exactly like the lunar disc.

Those devas, together with such celestial maidens, engage in play, song, and dance as they travel through the air, experiencing various pleasures within the realm of the five desires, never knowing satiety.
The gods, through the transformation of their own virtuous karma and their own minds, mount such vehicles.

These transformations produced by their own karma are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior; likewise, their forms are also inferior, middling, and superior; and likewise, their pleasures are also inferior, middling, and superior.
Thus they experience pleasure; likewise, their wisdom is of three grades—inferior, middling, and superior—and their lifespans are likewise of three grades—inferior, middling, and superior.
All things are thus.

Pervading the entirety of space, they proceed toward the Forest of Playful Delight (*Kūṭāgāra-vana*), a place endowed with immeasurable varieties of desire, the palatial abode where the celestial king Mucilinda dwells.

As he traveled along that path, before reaching the Grove of Playful Delight, he saw from afar in the sky what appeared like a mirage; furthermore, in one place he saw the color of blue jewels, in another place the yellowish-white color, and in yet another place the color of fire.
When those devas have thus seen this in the sky, they give rise to a sense of supreme wonder and say to one another:
"O devas, behold this rare phenomenon within the void, like various garments of wondrous colors arrayed in the sky."
"I have never seen such a thing.
After those hosts of devas had spoken thus to one another, they were struck with wonder and remained still for a short while.
Before long, they again heard a sound—a most subtle, exquisite, and beautiful melodic song. Having heard this sound, they once more gave rise to joy and a sense of wonder.
From those dwelling on the ground up to all the celestial hosts throughout space, together with their respective goddesses, all in their hearts longed to see them and desired to go and behold them.
As it was for these gods, so it was for all those seen in the air;
even the gods in the terrestrial regions, complete with mountains and trees, likewise saw these gods from afar.
The devas from the mountainous regions, where trees abound, also approach the Heavenly King Suyāma.

King Suyāma sits upon a throne of the seven precious gems within a cave of the seven precious gems, adorned with necklaces of great blue jewels; he further adorns himself with the colors of exquisite lotuses and the most sublime and wondrous gems.
Furthermore, there was another supreme banner of wondrous jewels of foremost radiance, its light pervading a thousand yojanas, with white flames of light filling the void of space.
"Just as one wearing various kinds of exquisite and wonderful garments remains in the void, so too is it with the banners.

When the gods of this Vast Conduct Stage see this, they give rise to a sense of wonder and remain for a short while; after a moment, they realize that the gods of the Stage Endowed with Mountains and Trees are also proceeding toward the Grove of Play where the Lord of Gods, Mucilinda, dwells, and they conceive this thought:
'They depart in such a manner, just as I am departing.'"
The gods of the superior and vast abodes deliberated and said:
"We shall now join with the gods of that mountainous region endowed with trees; all together in harmony, we shall go toward the place where Mucilinda, the Lord of Gods, dwells."
Thus they remained for a brief moment.
At that time, the gods dwelling in the region of Mounts Endowed with Trees saw the celestial hosts of the region of Vast Conduct and were struck with wonder, saying:
"We shall now join with all the gods of that region of Vast Conduct, and together we shall go to the Grove of Playful Delight where King Mucilinda dwells."

"At that time, the devas from the region of the mountain filled with trees and those from the region of the vast earth all gathered together as one assembly. Pervading the entire sky, they rode upon jeweled palaces atop the backs of birds, adorned with immeasurable banners and streamers. Fully endowed with the sounds of the five kinds of music and the merits of the five desires, they proceeded toward the Great Forest for Play in the Suyāma Heaven."
They are fully endowed with immeasurable and manifold qualities of desire, beyond all comparison.
They proceed toward that grove to experience the pleasures of the sensory realm and the merits of the five desires, never knowing satiety.
They never tire of all matters of merit, wealth, and pleasure; as they draw ever closer to one another, they can never be satiated.
Thus, they all experience sensual delights, never knowing contentment.
Then that bhikṣu, having seen those devas and thoroughly understood the fruits of their immeasurable karma, spoke these verses:
"Just as when rain falls from the heavens, The rivers thereby increase;
So too, because of the rain of desire, The devas increase the fire of lust."
The mīna fish is born in the water, yet it is constantly afflicted by parching thirst;
likewise, pleasure increases one's craving, and thus the gods know no satisfaction.
Just as space is boundless, it is likewise inexhaustible and never ceases.
Desire is thus boundless; the cravings of the realms can never be exhausted.
Though the waves of the ocean swirl and fill it to the brim, one might find a semblance of satiety;
yet those who long for sensual desires will ultimately never know contentment.
When the gods have not yet attained their realm, they are foolish and lack contentment;
their minds constantly long for pleasure, and even when they have attained it, they remain unsatisfied.
Once they have encountered decline and affliction, immeasurable loss follows.
Because of the feverish affliction caused by sensory objects, one should therefore abandon desire.
Having been deceived by craving, those who possess the desire for faith can be ruined;
yet when they encounter decline and distress, the gods do not perceive it.
Sense objects can never bring satisfaction; there is no happiness for one who lacks contentment.
Thus, the wise are able to abandon such lack of contentment.
Tranquility is the root of happiness, while suffering arises from sense objects.
Therefore, one should cultivate tranquility, remaining far removed from the sphere of sensory objects.
Constantly abandoning the afflictions, one practices unsurpassed wisdom;
through wisdom one attains liberation, whereas by the afflictions one is bound.
Sickness, death, and bondage, The terrors of sensory objects—
Transmigrating through birth and death, All arise because of sensory objects.
Whether meeting or parting, Whether arriving by the hundreds or thousands,
Wherever one is born, it is always thus; only the Sugata knows this with certainty.
The immeasurable pleasures of birth and death, and the immeasurable sufferings of birth and death—all arise from objective spheres (*viṣaya*); they exist wherever one is born.
Such objects of experience destroy those with deluded minds;
because they are ignorant and lack the eye of wisdom, they take pleasure in these objects once again.
One should abandon enmity and not draw near to them; even hearing their names gives rise to anxiety.
Sense objects are like enemies, yet out of delusion one never abandons them.
If one is scorched by sense objects, then that person is a fool;
deceived by their own karma, they cannot escape due to their delusion.
Just as one who fears fire yet still remains near it;
so too those deluded by sense objects likewise delight in being near them.
It is like one who eats poison, who does not thereby experience happiness for himself.
Attachment to craving is likewise; there is never any state of peace or security.
Just as a thirsty person licking salt does not alleviate their thirst, so do objects darken the eye, leading one to know no satisfaction in craving.
"The realm of heaven is insufficient; deceived by the mind of desire and blown by the winds of karma, one arrives at the places of the evil realms.

Thus, that bhikṣu, having clearly understood the births of sentient beings according to their karma in immeasurable realms of existence and knowing them all in succession, spoke this verse out of compassion for those devas.

Furthermore, those devas, harmonizing with one another and acting in complete accord, their hearts filled with joy, proceeded toward the Forest of Playful Delight, the abode of the celestial king Mucilinda.

At that time, those devas proceeded in this manner: with immeasurable finery, immeasurable pleasures, and immeasurable karmic transformations, they enjoyed themselves amidst immeasurable groves, gardens, ponds, and the like, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens as they went along.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of other devas seated within celestial palaces above, traveling through the void. Their radiance pervaded and illuminated the entire sky as they engaged in song, dance, and play, accompanied by the sounds of the five musical instruments. Their bodies were adorned with flower garlands, their forms sprinkled with fragrance, necklaces hung from their throats, and they wore celestial crowns. As the wind blew upon their robes, they moved like clouds, while celestial maidens embraced them, their hearts filled with profound joy and delight.
Furthermore, there were other devas who, upon hearing the sounds of celestial maidens singing and the lutes being played, felt love and delight arise in their hearts.
Such beings of various kinds, experiencing manifold pleasures, remained in the air toward the Forest of Playful Delight (Kūṭāgāra-vana), longing for enjoyment.
All the devas of that realm turn toward the abode of King Mucilinda.

Generally speaking, those devas—whether in play, in movement, or with their ornaments—are accompanied by sounds that pervade and fill the ten directions; they all come close to the king’s palace hall.
Among all those hosts of the Yāma devas, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma devas, is the most preeminent.
Just as the body corresponds to one's karma, because his karma is superior, his fruit is likewise superior.
Thus, cause and effect are not dissimilar, just as a seed and its sprout.
All the celestial hosts approach the hall where the Heavenly King Muxulou (Mucilinda) resides; those other devas are all inferior, and only the Heavenly King Muxulou alone excels among them.
Among all the heavens, within the realm of celestial desires, the desires of the heavenly kings are supreme and fully perfected.
Their bliss is beyond analogy; here, only a small portion shall be described.
"There are birds made of the seven precious gems upon the forest trees, appearing everywhere all around.
They hold the heart-wood of the trees in their beaks and remain suspended in mid-air without any support for their bodies.
Furthermore, in another place, there are many rare bells whose sounds are exquisite; when the devas hear them, they all come toward them."
Because their minds were thus filled with joy through such conceptualizations, they moved about within that forest.
Furthermore, there were birds made of the seven precious gems with variegated wings, which surrounded the exterior of the forest on all sides, flying around it while carrying garlands in their beaks.
Furthermore, there are many rare peacocks, each with a lotus pond upon its back.
Within those ponds abound various kinds of birds, and hundreds of thousands of bees dwell amidst the lotuses in that water, their wings producing melodic sounds.
The pond is named Clear Water.
Its lotus petals are of various different kinds; some flower petals are made of lapis lazuli, while others are made of the seven precious gems.
There are other lotuses whose fragrance extends for five yojanas.
Thus, upon the backs of those peacocks, which are magnificent and exquisite, they sing, play music, and frolic, their movements in harmony with the birds of the pond.
The backs of those peacocks are also exceedingly rare.
Furthermore, there are many other most extraordinary birds; the peacocks carry garlands, meaning that upon their backs there are great lotus flowers.
The devaputra sat upon that lotus pedestal, surrounded by a hundred celestial maidens, enjoying pleasures through various amusements and exquisite songs.
Furthermore, there are many most marvelous birds, such as peacocks bearing garlands.
These are manifested by the power of the karma of those gods who experience pleasure; upon the head of each and every peacock, a wish-fulfilling tree grows spontaneously.
There are various flowers, and these flowers are exceedingly abundant; upon the trees dwell many birds with wings made of the seven precious gems.
Once those sons of gods have ascended those trees, they drink celestial wine together with hosts of goddesses, enjoying themselves through song, dance, and play.
Furthermore, there are many other most marvelous birds, such as peacocks bearing garlands.

Within the dense plumage of each individual peacock, many hosts of devas together with hosts of celestial maidens sit and enjoy happiness; they take delight in one another, frolicking, singing, and dancing, experiencing celestial pleasures.
When the devas saw this rare occurrence of the peacock holding the garland, they were struck with wonder.
Furthermore, they beheld another marvel: the lotus pond holding the garland.

Those lotus ponds number twenty thousand; free from the turbidity of mud, they contain sands of gold and silver, and are filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities. Geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks abound within those ponds.
Due to their wholesome karma, the swans spoke these verses:
"Having long endured this pleasure, one must realize that this pleasure is not an eternal dharma;
all things are impermanent, yet the devas do not perceive it."
This pleasure continues for a while, yet it must inevitably come to an end;
deceived by the mind of desire, one does not perceive its ruin.
This pleasure is intermingled with suffering, and because it is concealed, it is not perceived.
Just as a venomous snake cannot be seen within a garland of lotuses,
or like poisoned rice that kills the one who eats it—
so too is all such pleasure; one will inevitably fall into hell.
Just as a snare made of sinew appears very lovely to the eye when seen, so too is the snare of sensory objects;
though it looks good, it is in truth most evil. It is like the *kimpāka* fruit:
at first sweet and full of delicious flavor, yet [ultimately] poisonous.
Later, one will be able to kill; worldly pleasures are just like this.
Like a flying insect that sees a lamp and its heart is filled with great love and delight, yet upon entering it is burned—these pleasures are also like this.
Foolish worldlings do not understand that sensual play is like a lamp;
they long for pleasure as if touching fire, yet in the end they find no joy.
Like a deer tormented by thirst, it runs after a shimmering mirage.
Just as one can never ultimately eliminate thirst, so too is this pleasure.
Not satisfied with the past or present, the future shall be the same;
therefore, one should renounce all celestial realms.
The root of happiness is tranquility; this is what the wise have taught.
Those who lack a mind focused on the faculty of happiness will constantly suffer.
The Brahma-realm is the foremost excellence; patience is the supreme tranquility.
One wisdom illuminates this world; one loving-kindness gives rise to supreme bliss.
Not harming others is the greatest auspiciousness; right view is the foremost goodness.
A straightforward mind is the most excellent virtue; so too is the relinquishing of evil karma.
If one stays close to the elders, always respects and honors the Dharma,
makes offerings to teachers and preceptors, and has faith in karma, that is virtuous.
Constantly making offerings to the Triple Gem, with a correct mind free from defilement—
Furthermore, honoring one's parents is the path to the city of Nirvana.
The Buddha has taught that among all dharmas, going forth from home is supreme;
it is the most excellent among the practices of the holy life (brahmacarya) and can bring about all happiness.
Among all forms of giving, the Buddha taught that the gift of Dharma is supreme;
among all forms of diligence, meditative concentration is foremost, for it leads to Nirvana.
Among generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, wisdom alone is considered the most excellent.
Through wisdom one reaches Nirvāṇa; through giving and morality one gains only happiness.
Seeing with the eyes is not supreme; seeing with wisdom is superior.
The Buddha has taught the Eightfold Path, the most tranquil among all paths.
Among the truths, the Four Noble Truths are supreme; this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
Among the five powers, the power of wisdom is the foremost.
Proclaimed throughout the four directions and the eight intermediate points, there is none superior to it.
Only the Tathāgata is supreme, for he can reveal the true Dharma.
Among all assemblies, it is said that the assembly of noble ones is most serene;
by relying on the Triple Gem as a field of merit, one is able to give rise to happiness.
Equally honoring one's parents, and for the third time, the preceptor,
who by means of the realm of Dharma can open one’s eyes so that one may see—
that which is neither visible nor graspable— thus has the Tathāgata spoken.
All these are grounds of pleasure; it is not the objects themselves that are pleasurable.
If one can practice this Dharma, then one walks the stainless path.
Walking this path brings peace and security; the Yāma realm is not true pleasure.

"Thus it was with that bird; because of his wholesome karma, when he was formerly a human being, he sustained his life by means of the Dharma, obtaining goods by selling the Dharma to support himself."

Due to such karmic causes, he became a bird in that place; because of his original wholesome karma, although born among birds, he remembered the Dharma without forgetting it and spoke these verses accordingly.
Therefore, one should diligently recite and constantly uphold the Dharma.

Due to the causes and conditions of past karma, even though one may be born as an animal, because of long-standing habituation, one will be well able to preach the Dharma, and the fruit attained shall not be in vain.
Furthermore, all those Yāma devas proceed toward that pond of twenty thousand lotuses, which is adorned with various distinct and diverse ornaments and surrounded by exquisite celestial maidens.

Within that pond, there were previously various and diverse assemblies of devas and assemblies of devī-s, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, billions, and trillions, who experienced manifold pleasures.

Together with the celestial maidens, amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, some enter into the lotuses, some sit upon the pericarps of the lotuses, some rest upon the petals of the lotuses, and some dwell among the filaments of the lotuses.
In accordance with their mental intentions, whether for coarse or subtle bodies, they are able to come and go across hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* in the mere blink of an eye.
Just as what is seen by the eye has neither distance nor proximity, all occurring within a single thought-moment, so too is the coming and going of those devas.
Just as when many eyes look at the surface of a single finger, it is not hindered nor does it suffer from the sight;
so too, those devas—whether there be a hundred or a thousand—all gather together upon the filaments of a single lotus flower, sitting together without hindrance, neither cramped nor confined.
Due to their virtuous karma and by the power of their own actions, that lotus pond possesses such strength and such merit.
Within those lotuses, those gods thus sport, whether by the hundreds or by the thousands, drinking to their heart’s content the delicious celestial wine.

Within those lotuses, the devas who had long resided there joined with those who had arrived later to frolic and play together; possessing their own radiance that surpassed a hundred thousand suns, they all experienced sensual delights.
Having enjoyed pleasure in such places for a long time, they then proceed to the grove of the heavenly king Mucilinda.
As they wish to enter that grove, it abounds with immeasurable varieties of colors that are exceedingly delightful.

Mukhulinda, according to the thoughts in his mind, manifested that forest; just as he conceived various things within his own heart, so did he manifest various and diverse groves of trees, such as had never existed before.
Due to the power of the virtuous karma of the King of the Yāma Heaven,
at that time the celestial hosts, seeing such a grove as they had never before existed and never before seen, gave rise to a sense of wonder.

Having conceived this thought, he desired to enter that grove and gradually drew near it. That deva had adorned his body in various ways, anointed himself with celestial sandalwood, and donned various garments appropriate for a deva that made him resemble one; yet as he passed by the lotus pond and reached that tree grove, upon seeing it, he was filled with shame.
Because their karma is thus, there exists such a grove, variously sublime and wondrous.
When those hosts of devas see other groves approaching, once they have seen them, they examine them thoroughly and in detail.
Having observed this thoroughly, they speak to one another and point it out to one another, and only then do they enter within.

Once they have passed that pond and entered the forest, they see a flock of parrots, all of whom hold various kinds of jeweled garlands; every single parrot has a precious gem tied around its neck, and these gems are strung together as garlands that encircle the entire forest. Then they speak this verse:
“Beings revolve in saṃsāra, Driven and pushed by their own karma.”
Within the beams and ropes of old age and death, sentient beings feel no weariness or detachment.
Whether gods, humans, or asuras, because they do not know the truth, they are driven by their own minds along that path and the paths leading to it.
The wheel of worldly activity, though pushed by the hand, does not turn swiftly;
yet the wheel of sentient beings, driven by the hand of karma, turns with extreme speed.
With its twelve spokes joined together, it is gathered within the hub of ignorance.
"Driven by causes and conditions, the wheel of saṃsāra turns, yet the world does not perceive it.

Having heard these verses spoken by the parrot, that deva focused his mind with wholesome mindfulness and examined his own past karma. With great earnestness, he recollected his former karmic actions and spoke thus:
"That parrot has surpassed me; I am not equal to that parrot."
"Reflecting on my past deeds, I was ruined by craving and indulged in pleasure and play.
When those gods had spoken thus, desiring to go and see the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, they passed beyond the Śuka-gati and proceeded toward the forest named Khaṇḍāvataṃsaka.
Within that grove there is yet another grove named Mandāra, adorned with flowers of a hundred thousand colors.
That grove is filled with various flocks of birds, and its radiance surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns, yet it is free from the affliction of solar heat.
The trees of that forest possess a supreme radiance. Beholding those groves produces joy for the eyes;

hearing the songs of the birds produces joy for the ears; smelling the fragrance of lotus roots produces joy for the nose; tasting the flavor of the fruits produces joy for the tongue; and the touch of the seamless celestial garments produces joy for the body.
Because the faculties are at ease, the mind gives rise to joy and happiness.
The five faculties bind the mind, causing it to comply and contemplate all phenomena.
By means of these two types of mental engagement, one knows in accordance with reality.
Thus he beheld the Mandāra grove.
Each and every Mandāra tree was filled with throngs of celestial maidens.

These celestial maidens were adorned with various garments of exquisite beauty; they spoke in diverse tongues, performed various songs and dances, and experienced manifold pleasures—things that those hosts of devas had never seen before.
"Thus, in all those grounds, the gods who traverse the earth saw those celestial maidens within the groves.
There were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of hosts of gods and goddesses, filling the forest beyond all comparison."
There was not a single deva or a single celestial maiden whose heart did not long to see the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda; all of them desired to go and see him.
With hearts full of joy and longing to see the Heavenly King,
they come together as described above by the power of that Heavenly King’s merit and virtue, and proceed through that forest.
That forest abounds with flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, and is fully endowed with groves of various lotuses; every part of the ground is adorned in every way.
The earth is soft and entirely golden in color, interspersed with various jewels.
Having seen this, they experience sensual pleasure.
In this sequence, they gradually advance toward Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven; with one mind, they all long to see him, their hearts filled with mutual affection.
Beyond those various distinct vehicles described above, one further enters a different stage.
Within that stage there are lovely mountains; in this manner, there are five hundred such lovely mountains within the stage, which serve as places for recreation.
All those mountains are made of lapis lazuli, and their trees are all of red lotus jewels, adorned with golden leaves.
Furthermore, there are jewel-trees adorned with silver leaves.

In that place there are many coral-colored birds, and furthermore, it is adorned with other extraordinary features: it is embellished by countless various jewel-like deer and birds, and graced by diverse rivers, ponds, and flowing streams, where interlacing branches form natural dwellings.

Throughout all places there are dwellings with universally adorned interlacing branches; their fruits are golden, their branches are made of gold and jewels, their fruits are all the color of lapis lazuli, and their leaves are made of gold and jewels.
There are hundreds of thousands of bees, whose humming is exquisite and pleasing to the ear.
The river is filled with various flavors, textures, and foods, and it is adorned by many jewel-birds.
In those regions, contact gives rise to pleasure.
Furthermore, the hosts of devas behold various jewel mountains; one mountain is named *Vikrīḍita* (Play).

Some see level ground, some see mountain peaks, and some see the openings of caves. Moreover, some devas see pavilions among the branches of trees, while others see everything within lotus ponds; all these devas and their celestial maidens are filled with joy.

Some were singing and dancing together with celestial maidens; some gods entered lotus groves with hosts of celestial maidens to sport and enjoy themselves; some drank wine with joyful hearts; some scattered celestial flowers upon the level ground; some fashioned flower garlands to adorn their bodies; and some used jeweled crowns to mutually embellish one another along with the celestial maidens.
They possess their own radiance, and their bodies are free from defilement.
Furthermore, there are other devas who travel through the void together with various celestial maidens.
Still others stand upon level ground, holding musical instruments in their hands and singing hymns with their voices.

Whether by the hundreds or by the thousands, the bodies of those devas are adorned in such various ways and emit such various radiances—blue, yellow, red, purple, and light of mixed colors—all of which issue forth from their bodies.

"At that time, having already experienced such pleasures upon those mountains of play, that deva desired to see the celestial king Mucilinda and proceeded further inward to enter that celestial realm."
Furthermore, he saw the King of the Yāma Heaven named Saṃkusumitarājendra (Flower-Garland-Abode), and immediately entered therein.

It was a land of mountains and trees, a vast realm of activity, where all the gods were adorned with the foremost ornaments; together with those in the Saṃkusumita stage, the gods of all three stages conceived a heart of profound respect for the Heavenly King Mucilinda.
This is due to the power of that celestial king’s virtuous karma; it is brought about by the immeasurable wholesome karma he cultivated and accumulated in the past.
Within the Maṇicūḍābharaṇa-bhūmi (Flower-Garland Land), there are ten thousand palaces, adorned with pillars of various kinds of gold in immeasurable colors.
That palace is lovely, with walls made of gold and jewels, interspersed with pillars of *vaiḍūrya* and blue gems.

There is another palace with walls of *vaiḍūrya*, featuring railings of gold, jewels, and blue gems, with windows made of *indranīla* gems; furthermore, it is filled with many various pillars of diverse jewels interspersed throughout.
Furthermore, there are other palaces with walls of lapis lazuli, doors of gold and jewels, and panels of lapis lazuli, all interspersed in various ways.

There are also towers and palaces most delightful to behold, with pillars made of red lotuses mixed with gold, doors of gold and jewels, windows of coral, and floors inlaid with various kinds of precious gems.

Furthermore, in that place, various blue jewels were interspersed as walls, red gold formed the doors, and white silver served as the pillars; throughout that entire palace, a garland of radiant flames shone forth.

Furthermore, in that place, within the palace of the celestial king Mucilinda, there is a supreme palace of red-colored gold jewels, transformed by various karmic powers. It is interspersed with diamonds, its pillars are made of red lotus jewels, and its windows are fashioned from the seven precious gems; its multi-storied towers and processional palaces are mutually illuminated by their supreme radiance.
Having seen such various and manifold adornments, those devas turned their eyes to look all around.

They further beheld the jewel mountains, and with one mind shared among them, they gazed upon the mountain palaces, facing toward the great king Suyāma, before finally entering the palace of the heavenly king Mucilinda.
Having thus entered, they behold ever-surpassing and diverse visions, all manner of lovely things, and the full possession of the most rare and immeasurable merits.

When those devas have seen the Arrayed Garlands, they long to see Mucilinda, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven; all the hosts of devas proceed together with him and enter another place, the domain where the King dwells.
He saw the Great Heavenly King surrounded by seven thousand devaputras, all of whom were supremely and exquisitely adorned.

Their bodies emitted radiance, and each devaputra possessed majesty like a mountain; their celestial robes fluttered, they wore jeweled crowns upon their heads, their elbows and upper arms were adorned with exquisite jewels, and their chests were embellished with magnificent flower garlands.

Seven thousand such devaputras surrounded King Mucilinda, just as various mountains encircle Sumeru, the king of mountains; as various rivers encircle the great ocean; and as the luminaries and stars encircle the moon.
Thus, all those gods surrounded the Yāma King Mucilinda as he stood there.
The Yāma King was handsome and exquisite; his radiance and majesty surpassed all other hosts of devas.
The palace of the Heavenly King has hundreds of thousands of pillars, each and every one of which is made of the seven treasures and adorns the palace.
There is a great sapphire throne for the celestial Indra.
The celestial palace of that king possesses such power and such magnificence.
As the devas enter that palace, it becomes increasingly vast and expansive, and it is likewise adorned with the seven precious jewels.
Within the palace there is a tree called the Palace-Adorning Tree (*prāsāda-vyūha-vṛkṣa*).
Such a tree is always in bloom throughout the six periods of the day, never lacking in flowers, and at all times it constantly bears celestial fruits.
What is the name of that palace?
It is called "Delightful to Behold.
Its walls are made of the seven precious substances, interspersed with various varieties.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 42 [and] Scroll 43,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Twenty-Two: Yāma Heaven, Section Eight.

"At that time, those devas gradually drew closer to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, singing and dancing, engaging in various amusements, and together enjoying the foremost fruits of their superior karma."
All those gods, having offered various kinds of worship to Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, sat down in one place once they had finished their offerings.
When everyone was seated, they spoke with joyful conversation.
Having finished speaking, the Heavenly King addressed them, saying:
"All you devas, you have indulged in heedlessness and followed one another here.
From this day forward, protect your lives and protect the Dharma; practice with diligent vigor."

"Because they protect the Dharma, they constantly experience happiness; even after attaining nirvana and casting off the body, they shall forever be free from suffering and affliction, constantly enjoying celestial bliss.
At that time, all the hosts of devas there gathered together, and the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke these verses for them:
"In the various realms of the world, Beings have mastery over their diverse karmas."
The various paths of the devas come; through wholesome karma one is born in this place.
Thus one comes within the realms of existence, and thus one departs from them;
as was the karma when they came, so too is it when they depart.
All things that come together, and all those whose minds are undistracted, are the result of virtuous karma;
therefore, exert yourself and do not be negligent.
One may enjoy happiness for a long time, but after this, one will inevitably decline.
Falling away is the foremost suffering; when it occurs, there is no doubt.
Regarding this meaning, I call upon you to explain it;
all of you listen, just as the Tathāgata has taught.
"Having thus spoken these verses for the sake of the universal harmony and benefit of all those devas, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed the celestial hosts, saying:
'You are deluded by the objects of your pleasurable realms, yet you do not perceive that the heavens are diminishing and not increasing.'"
This pleasure of the sensory realm is entirely impermanent; it shall not bring tranquility and will result in disadvantage.
What is this? Listen all of you!
As you have seen, these six Perfectly Enlightened Ones possess stūpas and temples adorned with various kinds of the seven treasures.
As for those six, the first is the Perfectly Enlightened One Śikhin;
2. Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One;
3. Viśvabhū, the Perfectly Awakened One;
4. Kanakamuni Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One; 5. Krakucchanda Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Sixth, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One.
These six stūpas were long ago established among the devas; having heard of them in succession, I now make offerings to them.
For what reason? All such things as these have never been seen by me, because my mind was immature.

Those Blessed Ones, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all the world, came to this world in past ages; I have heard of them in this sequence and have thus attained this Dharma.
"That Krakucchanda Buddha brought great benefit to the Yāma devas. As for that benefit:
