he manifested a stūpa, which is a most rare realm of the Tathāgata, and caused it to abide here."
If the people of this world do not show respect to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the faction of the devas will diminish.
Within the radiant flames of this stūpa, I clearly perceive all these signs of decline and inferiority; whether they diminish or regress, I alone behold them.
"You all are negligent and abound in negligent conduct; therefore, you do not see me, because you are attached to sensory objects and indulge in sensual pleasures.
I have summoned you with this song for the sake of your benefit."
"You are all negligent; to act with negligence is itself death and decline.
Fearing that you might exhaust your wholesome karma and fall into the evil realms, I have summoned you here."
Because the six Buddha-Bhagavāns have benefited immeasurable sentient beings, they have already spoken various sūtras.
All those Tathāgatas have inscribed them within this stūpa, and I have already mastered them through recitation.
"O Deva, listen well now; I shall speak for you, lest you later feel regret when it is too late.
At that time, that deva, with the utmost reverence and single-minded attention, remained entirely silent. There were two kinds of reverence: first, reverence for the Heavenly King;
[the second was reverence for the teaching].
2. Reverence for the Dharma.
With minds fixed in truth and dwelling correctly, their hearts remain unshakable.
Having seen that the celestial hosts were thus well-disciplined, the Heavenly King addressed them all, saying:

"You have now entered for the first time this stūpa of the Tathāgata; here, the Tathāgata Śikhin inscribed scriptures upon the walls, for the benefit of the assembly of devas, for the welfare of the assembly of devas, and for the happiness of the assembly of devas."

Then that most excellent deva, together with King Mucilinda, was the first to enter the stūpa. There he beheld the Vaiḍūrya image of the Buddha Śikhin, sitting cross-legged upon a bed of blue jewels. Upon its walls, the sūtra was inscribed by himself, saying: “O bhikṣus!...”
Whether gods or humans, there are eight things that obstruct wholesome qualities.
What are these eight? O bhikṣus!

What is called "the one" refers to whether it be a deva or a human, being ruined by negligence and thus unable to perform wholesome deeds—whether worldly wholesome deeds or supramundane wholesome deeds.
Regarding worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*): if the mind is indolent or if the mind is negligent, and one engages in negligent conduct, all those worldly phenomena will utterly perish.
One who is negligent cannot look after virtuous friends and thus becomes a neutral person;
if they are an enemy, that enmity increases as the enemy seeks an opportunity [to harm them].
This is negligence, which obstructs worldly dharmas;
those who are indolent and practice negligence cannot accomplish such deeds.

When that person's karma is exhausted, their friends and associates are also lost; enemies flourish and increase their great power, they lose their entire household, become impoverished and destitute, and are held in contempt by others.
The foremost of all base and vulgar conditions is poverty.
In those base and vulgar men who are impoverished, their unwholesome friends and associates, as well as their kinsmen and brothers, cause greed, hatred, and wrong views to increase in every way.
That deluded person is most vulgar and base.
Why? Because of their unwholesome conduct.

Abandoned by the gods, they are assailed by all manner of misfortunes; others may invade them or even cause their death, or they may lose their wealth in trade—all because of their negligence and their negligent conduct.
If monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen are thus negligent; if they constantly and diligently practice neutral meditative concentration (*avyākṛta-dhyāna*) yet fail to exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*);
and if they crave only the taste of food, divining its signs and timing, thereby obstructing and distracting their minds.

Thus, those who are negligent and practice negligence are at all times impure in mind; they are greedily attached to the taste of food like animals that eat what has been vomited, their minds are like dogs, and they are like those who observe the "crow-dog" precepts.

Such persons as these constantly act with negligence; they do not recite the sutras, and among their kin and among those of great learning, they are of little wisdom and are vulgar and base. They are held in contempt by all donors and are deprived of fearlessness.
The foremost fearlessness is that which consists of extensive learning and the ability to contemplate the Dharma;
the foremost base and vulgar state is that of meager learning.
Those who have heard little are despised by others, yet they do not recognize their own faults, and instead harbor much greed, hatred, and delusion toward others.

Toward those who are learned, those who possess true knowledge, or toward elders and donors who possess roots of goodness, one may give rise to the wound of a mind of anger due to ignorance and excessive negligence.
Due to unwholesome karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell.
Those who practice heedlessness, by practicing heedlessness among human beings, create obstacles to both worldly and world-transcending goals.
“Monks! How is it that negligence among the devas destroys these devas? By their very nature they practice negligence;

being negligent, these devas delight in their hearts in tactile sensations, tastes, forms, and fragrances as they practice negligence. They do not see old age approaching, they do not see destruction, and they do not see their own decline. Their minds do not contemplate the exhaustion of their wholesome karma; they do not cultivate the Dharma, nor do they revere the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.”
Having abandoned the virtuous mind, he indulges in negligence; when the Buddha appears in the world, he neither sees nor knows him, and no faith arises in his heart.
Fear approaches, ruin and calamity approach, the suffering of death approaches, and the pain of separation draws near before long, as the celestial maidens abandon him.

Great terror is approaching, like one who is about to fall from a precipice; one no longer perceives the pleasures experienced in former realms, fails to act in accordance with them in other worlds, and at the moment of death, they provide neither joy nor consolation.
Such objects of experience are all utterly destroyed and possess no power; when one departs for another place among the various states of existence, they do not follow along with one.
If one acts with negligence—that is, through negligent actions—those [consequences] will pursue and follow one within those states of existence.
Thirsting for those sensory realms and with their minds unsatiated, they die in negligence.

Abandoned by all the gods, fear arises in their hearts; thus, deluded by sensory realms, they die. At that time, in accordance with their karma, they may be reborn in the three evil states of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
"Therefore, all gods and humans should not practice heedlessness.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śikhin spoke these verses:
"If at all times, O gods, You achieve the pleasures of sensory realms..."
Once that heaven has been destroyed, all karmas follow one wherever one goes.
Pleasure cannot be maintained forever; the accumulation of karma is never lost.
Deceived by pleasure, the deluded devas lack sovereignty because of their karma.
Sensual objects manifest pleasure in this life, yet later they bring about decay and affliction.
Devas who are stained by attachment to these objects have minds that are constantly distracted and unstable.
They do not know that wholesome meritorious deeds are the medicine for the disease of birth and death.
Just as medicine and lamps are likewise, they serve as both refuge and protection.
Among all things in existence, wholesome karma follows sentient beings;
therefore, the wise should always exert themselves with diligent vigor.
Cultivating merit brings auspiciousness; abandoning sensory realms is wholesome.
If one possesses the eye of wisdom, they know to fear future lives.
The wise develop dread beforehand; the foolish fear only when it is too late.
The wise know this and their minds are constantly wary of destruction.
If the mind is perpetually deluded, it will delight in sensory objects;
being infatuated by these objects, remorse will later arise in the heart.
"Whosoever possesses a body in conjunction with the world, whose wisdom is ever untainted, performs meritorious deeds; without merit, there is only suffering.

Having thus shown those hosts of devas the first teaching—the verses spoken by the Tathāgata Śikhin inscribed upon the wall—Mukhila, the King of the Yama Heaven, proceeded to show them the remaining seven teachings, speaking as follows:
"I shall further explain to you another seven dharmas.
The next is arrogance, which knows no time for tranquility.
One who acts with arrogance is never tranquil; among gods and humans, they are constantly an obstacle, always hindering all mundane and supramundane dharmas."
What is meant by obstructing worldly meaning and supramundane meaning?
One who is arrogant in body disturbs the mind;
for all dharmas and their meanings, the mind is the precursor, and thus they proceed accordingly.
With a distracted mind, they frequent unwholesome places and improper locations; they act at inappropriate times, travel through remote and dangerous regions, and associate with evil companions.
They lack self-reflection and do not understand others; they are ignorant of their own strength and unaware of the strength of others.
Because of his arrogance, he was unable to perform his duties; he lacked the capacity for prudent deliberation regarding his own household affairs and was no different from a madman.
He did not practice right conduct and was the most vulgar among all the people, and furthermore, the lowest among all his kinsmen and brothers.
He does what should not be done and fails to do what should be done.
He is entirely ignorant of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and likewise he does not know what has been done and what has not been done.

They are unable to discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; furthermore, they do not know what should be spoken and what should not be spoken, nor what should be practiced and what should not be practiced, and they likewise do not know what is possible and what is impossible.
Thus, they are entirely ignorant of all these things.
Because of their arrogance, they are unable to understand the dharma of upholding the precepts.
Furthermore, due to their haughtiness, they do not know the proper time, they do not know the place, and they do not know whether the mind is abiding or non-abiding.

Because of their arrogance, they do not know the proper time for pleasure; they do not know what is significant or trivial, nor do they distinguish between the true and the untrue. They walk about with their faces held high, devoid of any sense of awe or restraint.
"Furthermore, regarding how this pride obstructs the meaning of the supramundane Dharma: in what way does it obstruct the supramundane meaning?

One who is obstructed and distracted by this pride does not know the causes of karma, does not know the retribution of results, does not know the path of goodness or the path of unwholesomeness, does not know proper decorum, does not know place, does not know the proper time, does not know how to judge what is sufficient or insufficient, and does not know the great assembly."
Although they have heard the Dharma, they are unable to practice it;
regarding the Dharma they have not yet heard, their minds have no desire to hear it, nor do they have the intention to seek it out.

Wicked and obstinate, they have no fear; their speech does not accord with reason, and their minds are as agitated and scattered as dust blown by the wind in every direction. Thus, their minds are constantly distracted and unstable.

Those whose minds and intentions are distracted and who act with arrogance do not cultivate meditative concentration and are unable to collect their thoughts. Upon seeing forms, they become attached and delight in sensory objects.

At times they are obsessed by desire; their eyes are constantly flickering. Such a person, because of their improper vision, acts with arrogance—whether due to attachment to desire, or being intoxicated and confused, or at times by calamity or madness—at all times it is thus, and nothing else.
Because he is thus, he is pointed out with derision by all the world.
Being pointed out in this manner, he is held in contempt by everyone, yet he does not recognize his own faults.
That is neither beneficial nor advantageous, nor is it peaceful; it does not accomplish any of the true goals.
"In what way does arrogance act as an obstacle to the supramundane Dharma and Vinaya?
Furthermore, how does it constitute an obstacle among those who are arrogant?
It is because among such people there are renunciants whose conduct of arrogance is most base and inferior.
This Dharma-Vinaya can eliminate arrogance and bring about all forms of dignity;
without abandoning arrogance, one lacks dignity.

Those who are arrogant cannot cultivate meditation and do not know how to abide; they constantly wander through cities and villages rather than frequenting virtuous places, unable to preach the Dharma to discipline donors, but instead craving only food, drink, beds, and bedding, and failing to observe with skillful discernment.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falls into the evil realms, being born among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Such a person finds no security in either the mundane path or the supramundane path.
"There are seven types of pride:
first, pride in physical appearance;
second, pride in wealth;..."
Third, pride regarding birth;
fourth, pride regarding clothing and ornaments;
fifth, pride regarding royal offerings.
Sixth is pride due to intimacy with women;
seventh is pride due to a distracted mind because of another's wife.
These constitute pride in its general form, whether in its diminished, residual, or complete expressions.
All these phenomena are obstructed by that conceit.

Thus, among human beings, there is little wealth or pleasure, a meager span of life, and only slight conduct; yet they still practice arrogance. How much more so in the heavens—this, indeed, is conceit.
Those devas, fond of sounds, touches, tastes, fragrances, and forms, increase their arrogance from moment to moment.

Because they act with such arrogance, their lifespan gradually diminishes; yet they do not perceive the movement of their life-force, nor do they know when their life is ending, nor when their conduct is exhausted, nor do they distinguish between virtuous and non-virtuous karma.
At all times and for all eternity, until the end of their lives, they do not cease their arrogance.

This continues in succession until their wholesome and beloved karma is exhausted; when that karma is exhausted, they fall back. It is only as they approach the time of their downfall that they finally realize it, giving rise to this thought:
"The sensory realm has deceived me, causing me to give rise to defilement."
Thus, through such pride and deceit, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the evil realms, being born in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.
In this way, arrogance obstructs the path of the world.
"Furthermore, because the celestial hosts are arrogant, they obstruct the path to transcendence.
All those gods were born here in this Yāma heaven because they cherished wholesome karma and because of the True Dharma."

Due to their practice of divine pride, they do not understand their own karma; they do not associate with those who possess even slight pride, nor do they associate with any gods who are free from pride. They take no pleasure in seeing the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, and they lack faith and fail to enter into the True Dharma.
Because they do not accord with the True Dharma, they travel upon evil paths;
they are unable to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not revere their elders, nor do they draw near to wise devas.
Deceived by desire, they become greedily attached to sensory objects.
Only when they are about to fall from this celestial realm does remorse arise within them.
Therefore, devas and humans should abandon negligence and distance themselves from arrogance.
If one does not abandon them, it is like a blazing fire burning sesame seeds and the like.
At that time, Śikhin Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Negligence brings about destruction; One is deluded by pride."
Whether one be a deva or a human, one shall not obtain the bliss of tranquility.
If one delights in heedless conduct, this is what is called death;
the transgression of delighting in heedlessness leads to falling into the hells.
Transgressing by practicing the unrighteous path is what is called negligence;
negligence deceives the celestial mind, and one then enters hell.
Delighting in the unreal and not delighting in the real—
Because of the darkness of the defilement of heedlessness, the gods are deceived by desire. The gods,
deluded and infatuated by desire, as well as by heedlessness and pride,
are unable to see reality, like those born blind upon a path.

“Thus has the World-Honored One Śikhin already explained how negligence and arrogance obstruct both mundane and supramundane dharmas; furthermore, he now demonstrates the third [fault]: the transgression of breaking the precepts.”

Such matters as these, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows completely and without exception; having realized with perfect truth the faults and afflictions of violating the precepts, he inscribed them in sequence upon the walls within the stupa.
"At that time, King Mūśalinda showed the celestial assembly the inscribed words on the wall within the stupa regarding the transgressions of failing to uphold the precepts:

'Those who do not uphold the precepts have this as their third affliction among all devas and humans; it is not beneficial, nor is it the worldly path, nor the supramundane path—it is entirely contrary to both the worldly and supramundane paths.'"
Why is this? Because failing to maintain the precepts among human beings obstructs the worldly path.

Specifically, those foolish people who have received the precepts, once they have received them, do not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; furthermore, they do not know what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
Having committed these transgressions, they conceal them within their hearts.

Due to the influence of brothers and other relatives, they thus break the precepts; being solely intent upon their kinsmen and old friends, they disregard the precepts or do not even accept them. Having received them, they then violate them, showing no sense of caution or difficulty.
Because of this, all their kinsmen, relatives, brothers, and associates will treat them with contempt, saying: "This person does not maintain the precepts;
they are not diligent in vigor; they do not observe any restraint of body, speech, or mind."
Thus, their relatives, down to their brothers and others, came to despise, loathe, and treat them with contempt.
Because of this contempt, they no longer observed auspicious times or occasions for them, nor did they maintain any social interaction with them.

At assemblies for auspicious or inauspicious occasions, such persons are neither invited nor summoned, neither trusted nor respected, because they do not receive the precepts, do not uphold the precepts, and do not maintain the precepts.
Those who were originally good friends become neutral persons;
those who were formerly enemies seek out one's vulnerabilities;
and those who are neither enemies nor kin do not take one into their circle as companions.
Such a person is like a tree whose roots have been severed; blown by the wind, it falls to the ground. Having fallen thus, they lose all possessions and are abandoned by their kinsmen.

Because that person’s own mind is by nature light and restless, due to this restlessness, they harbor malice within. Toward all people, they are excessively greedy and excessively angry; their minds are filled with perverse doubts and suspicions, and through discrimination and longing, they seek to cause disturbance. Their hearts are constantly enraged toward all sentient beings; their facial expression is unpleasant, they lack majesty and virtue, their minds are disordered and unstable, and they are perpetually impoverished.
Because such a person has neither received nor maintained the precepts, at the dissolution of the body after death they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell.
Therefore, one should constantly be mindful of performing beneficial acts, receiving and maintaining the precepts, without obstructing worldly dharmas.
"Because this person who upholds the precepts has a mind made firm by the causes and conditions of morality, they maintain constant right mindfulness and place their trust in virtuous friends.

Consequently, kings and high ministers, out of faith in that person, entrust to them all manner of precious items—gold, silver, and various other valuables of great worth. Whether it be confidential words spoken in trust or property entrusted by kings and others, they do not misappropriate the goods nor reveal the secret words."
Because they protect the precepts, they are trusted by others.

Furthermore, at all times, their kinsmen, brothers, and retinue trust, love, and provide offerings for them; everyone respects them even more than their own elders. Upholding the seven types of precepts, even kings make offerings to them, as do their acquaintances, relatives, and all others.

Such a person is trusted by all people and loved by all; they are fully endowed with wealth and never suffer from poverty, and no one can cause them harm—they are the foremost among the great wealthy.
Because of great wealth, one is able to practice generosity and perform meritorious deeds; with right intention and firm abiding, one’s wisdom remains unimpaired.
By these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavenly realms of the good destinations.
"If such a person has thus broken even a small portion of the precepts, they are already inferior and weak; how much more so when it comes to practicing the supramundane path?
Such a person’s mind is restless and unstable, and regarding the retribution of karmic results, they are blind, lacking the eye of wisdom."
Whether they do not observe the precepts, or have broken many of them, or possess only a single precept, or have no precepts at all, others call such a person a bhikṣu, saying:
"That person possesses only the physical form and robes of a bhikṣu, like the sound of a conch shell."
With a mind constantly crooked and deceitful, they mislead various donors by saying, "I uphold the Buddha's precepts.
Such a person does not truly uphold the precepts; they have not truly accomplished the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones.

They are deceptive thieves who deceive the world, including the devas, Māra, all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the multitudes of gods and humans; they deceive both themselves and others, for they do not act according to their words.
Such a person is empty and void within, unreal and insubstantial, like a mass of foam that deceives all people; they are the foremost in deceit and crookedness.
This person constantly seeks out bedding, seats, medicinal requisites for illness, and other necessities, taking much from various places.
That person is constantly submerged in the mire of birth and death, or is born in the hells, or within other such evil destinies as the hells.
Because that person has violated the precepts and taken what should not be taken, due to their violation of the precepts, they are categorized among the unwholesome.
Such a person should not even take a single step upon the grounds of the Saṃgha, because they are unsuitable and unworthy of being there.
For what reason is this so?
The donors cultivate and prepare that ground for the sake of bhikṣus who maintain the precepts, not for bhikṣus who lack precepts or have broken them, nor for anyone who lacks a virtuous mind.
Such a person ought not even to take a single step upon that ground, let alone use bedding, medicines for illness, or any other articles of necessity or enjoyment.
“At that time, Śikhin Tathāgata spoke these verses:
‘If a bhikṣu lacks precepts, he is a thief among thieves;
Within him is filled with putrid pus and the like, Yet on the outside he wears the saffron robes.’”
All things are empty and unsubstantial, like a mass of water bubbles;
one who is thus empty and lacks precepts, yet falsely claims to be a bhikṣu,
is a breaker of the precepts who belongs to hell and is not encompassed by the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Deceived by the mind, one falls into hell when the body perishes.
Having abandoned the Dharma and Vinaya, one falls due to one's own karma;
shrouded by the darkness of defilement, one constantly undergoes great suffering and distress.
Not wearing the garment of wholesome dharmas, one is naked and abandoned by the virtuous;
because of being separated from wholesome karma, evil will lead one to hell.
Accumulating unwholesome karma, the gates of suffering then open wide.
The bonds of birth and death are firm; it is because of breaking the precepts that they are thus.
Burned by the fire of broken precepts, one is utterly consumed;
such a person who lacks the precepts will certainly enter the evil realms.
Because one intends to uphold the precepts, the teacher is able to bestow them;
If one receives the precepts with a mind of deceit, one will certainly enter hell.
Such a person, day and night, constantly increases their unwholesome states.
If one can uphold the jewel of ethical discipline, one will then be able to destroy transgression of the precepts.
If a person is empty of dharmas and possesses nothing but a gathering of darkness,
there will not be a single moment when that [darkness] does not momentarily break apart.
Caught in the snare of broken precepts, they are abandoned by the virtuous because of their defilement;
the snare of broken precepts constantly drags down those who have renounced the precepts yet remain unwholesome.
Lacking precepts or having broken them, they associate with evil friends.
If one associates with sensual desires, this is the cause and condition for hell.
A person who lacks precepts and is deluded, or one who is fickle and restless,
or one whose actions correspond to evil karma— such a person is not far from hell.
Karma has corresponding fruits; how can one not know this?
Out of delusion, one brings suffering upon oneself, yet remains attached to the pleasures of play.
Day by day it increases; the river of evil cannot be crossed.
Suffering fills it to the brim, and thus it sweeps away sentient beings.
Such a person does not give rise to goodness; such a person possesses no virtuous mind.
One who abandons the Dharma thereby embraces unwholesome dharmas.
If one gathers wholesome dharmas within the body, this is the foremost path of goodness;
the person who practices these words will reach the state of non-retrogression.
Those who uphold the precepts, study the scriptures, and delight in wholesome dharmas—
Those who always discipline themselves through right practice are free from suffering and affliction.
Those who do not maintain the purity of their precepts will be defiled;
because they have ruined their training, they are seized by the hells.
"One who knows all this should diligently take up the precepts with a focused mind;
for in the entire ocean of birth and death, the absence of precepts is the causal condition.
"Thus, for all such people, the supramundane path described above is obstructed by the lack of precepts."
Why is it that the absence of ethical discipline constitutes an obstacle within the heavens?

This world is a realm of karmic fruition; if one maintains the sevenfold precepts here, gathering and accumulating their merit, one will experience pleasure in the heavens. Yet, having practiced heedlessness for a long time, once that pleasure is exhausted, one subsequently falls away.
"Just as when the oil of a lamp is exhausted and the wick is spent, the light is also extinguished.
'What is it that obstructs the supramundane path? It is the failure to maintain ethical discipline.'"
That person who observed the precepts is born among the devas; having been born there, they think to themselves:
"In the human realm, I observed the seven kinds of precepts, and thus I have been born here, equal to the devas."
Because this newly born deva is attached to sensory objects and craves sensual pleasures, he forgets everything.
If other devas who have not forgotten their observance of the precepts are present, they will show this deva the karmic results of observing the precepts and say to him:
"In your previous human life, you were fully endowed with the observance of the precepts; it is for that reason that you have been born here."

Because that newly born deva’s mind was stirred, he became attached to the pleasures of sensory objects; failing to hear the voice of the teaching, he did not enter into it, did not grasp it, and lacked faith in the observance of the precepts; therefore, he was unable to take up the karmic fruit of wholesome deeds.
Because their minds are moved by the power of sensory objects, they do not maintain the precepts nor do they practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Such devas destroy wholesome dharmas; therefore, they fall away and decline.
Maintaining the precepts in this manner leads to rebirth among the devas, whether in the mundane world or the supramundane realm.
Regarding that mundane realm, such is one type resulting from the observance of the precepts.
That which transcends the world is bodhi.
This third dharma does not obstruct the upholding of precepts.
"What is the fourth obstacle for devas and humans?"
What is called indolence:
those who delight in indolence or those who are attached [to it], such persons do not achieve success in any way whatsoever regarding all phenomena existing throughout the entire world.
That indolent person is inferior in seven ways.
What are these seven?
If a person is indolent, they lack superior fruit; this constitutes two forms of inferiority.
Because of this inferiority, their offerings are inferior, their wealth is inferior, and their wisdom regarding their spheres of experience is inferior.
Being thus inferior, they are not approached by the true persons of the world, and the inquiries of worldly people toward them are likewise inferior.
Such a person is inferior in all matters of this world; therefore, being dull and obtuse, everything they undertake is utterly ruined.
In this way, among the worldly dharmas and principles of human beings, laziness acts as an obstacle.
"How can one among human beings obstruct the supramundane Dharma?
It is because of indolence.
Such indolent persons fear all domestic affairs and labors; therefore, they leave the household life and speak as follows:"
"Since I have gone forth, I have many bedding and requisites, including medicines for illness; my food and drink are abundant and pleasant.
Day and night, I have nothing to do.
Because of such indolence, he has thus gone forth.

Having already left the household life, they do not recite the sutras, cannot cease from evil, do not practice wholesome dharmas, do not cultivate meditative concentration, and do not maintain the prohibitive precepts; they are constantly shrouded and obscured by indolence.
That person gains great profit and receives abundant offerings and sustenance; yet, they take no delight in upholding the precepts nor do they delight in wisdom.
Due to the fault of their meager wisdom, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are reborn in hell.
"At that time, Śikhin Tathāgata spoke these verses:
'One who is indolent has little merit; Delusion can destroy the mind.
When all kinsmen and associates are thin, The path of goodness cannot be attained.'"
Laziness and evil deeds, or being shrouded by delusion,
obstruct the path to Nirvana and result in unwholesome and evil fruits.
Lacking shame and a sense of propriety, one is agitated by evil associates.
All these are causes of suffering and affliction; the wise therefore abandon them.
Whether they be wrong views, pride, great pride, or the like, such as the conceit "I am," one should always relinquish all these, which are the conditions for experiencing suffering and affliction.
If one is shrouded by indolence, Failing to maintain mindfulness and exertion, One's breath is like that of the dead; Though one lives, it is in vain and fruitless.
For those afflicted by indolence, Though they possess life, they are the same as the dead.
For such a person of indolence, it is better to keep death in mind.
If one is mired in the mud of indolence, one sinks into the ocean of suffering and does not emerge;
but if a person exerts diligent effort, they will cross the ocean of birth and death.
Those of little strength and indolent people are like sheep craving food and drink;
though their lives are not yet ended, they are as if dead, and if they die, they enter hell.
Poor and deluded like sheep, they are either seized by suffering, or...
If a person eats the food of others, laziness is the cause and condition.
Those who are lazy mostly depend on others for their livelihood;
they are deeply attached to delicious flavors, and their minds are deluded, always delighting in sensual desires.
They do not know the Truth, but are merely attached to the taste of food;
when the time of death has arrived, the fire of regret burns their own hearts.
Those who endure cold and heat, even hunger and thirst, and so forth—
Thus the body undergoes suffering, yet in the future one attains tranquility.
Do not give rise to a mind of indolence; for indolence leads to weakness, making one unable to endure birth and death, and failing to escape from suffering and affliction.
"Though one may exist in this world, if one is indolent, one is base among virtuous people;
the future life will likewise be empty, and one shall never attain tranquility.
"Furthermore, for an indolent person who has not abandoned these faults, there is another distinct fault: namely, being far removed from the supramundane path."
A person who is indolent is an unwholesome person; they are one who has fallen away and perished.
[The Buddha asked: "How do the devas lose the mundane and supramundane Dharma, Vinaya, and discipline?"
How do the gods obstruct the path of the world?
It is said that this indolence has further consequences: although they may have been born among the gods due to virtuous conditions, those gods are again ruined by indolence.

Their minds find no delight in any sounds, touches, tastes, fragrances, or forms; they take no pleasure in groves or the lovely abodes of the gods; they neither fly nor run, they do not listen to songs, nor do they perform them themselves.
They do not fly through the void, nor do they travel from mountain peak to mountain peak; they do not stay within rivers, nor do they wade through waves or ride upon birds for sport.

Such are the pleasures of the King of the Yāma Heaven, yet those indolent devas do not go there, nor do they experience any of the sensory delights belonging to the realm of the King of the Yāma Heaven.
All of these are like poison and like enemies; all are defilements.
This is the laziness that obstructs the mundane world.
"How does laziness further obstruct the supramundane path?
Furthermore, other devas who constantly hear the True Dharma and delight in the True Dharma cannot approach them.

They distance themselves from the True Dharma; regarding the Dharma they have not yet heard, they have no desire to hear it. Even if they do hear it, they do not uphold it, nor do they practice it. They do not draw near to their elders, nor do they study the learning of wisdom. They are alienated from all dharmas and alienated from all that is wholesome; they constantly delight in birth and death, and constantly undergo suffering and affliction.
Why is this? Because they have departed from the Path, they cannot attain liberation within existence (*bhava*).
Since they are ruined by indolence, they are born in the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Such a person is constantly ensnared by birth, old age, death, and the like, undergoing various sufferings and wandering through the world.

For one who is thus indolent, such indolence constitutes every kind of non-beneficial matter; it is the root of all evil destinies and the seed of saṃsāra. Therefore, all the sufferings and afflictions in the world arise from this.
Therefore, if there are those in the world who wish to be liberated from the bonds of birth and death, they should apply themselves with diligence and abandon indolence.
All things that are not beneficial have this as their root; through such forms of indolence, one cannot cross over the ocean of suffering.
This indolence possesses immeasurable faults.
"Furthermore, beyond these four kinds of faults, there is a fifth fault that obstructs the mundane and supramundane paths for all devas and humans, namely, evil greed."
All mundane and supramundane dharmas act as universal hindrances.
How do gods and humans encounter the hindrance of evil craving regarding the mundane path and the supramundane path?

It is said that because worldly people act unrighteously out of greed, they constantly delight in wealth and possessions; their craving for material things is like the swirling of a river and also like a monkey.
Because of attachment to objects and the desire to acquire them, one employs various skillful means; in this way and that way, evil greed increases. One thinks thus:
"What skillful means or what deceptions should I now employ to delude and mislead others?"
Their minds are constantly thus fraudulent and delusive, and they further teach others in such a way as to be fraudulent and delusive.
"Such people commit many unrighteous acts, and by means of such teachings, they instruct others as well."
Such a person possesses great greed and thinks to themselves:
"All that belongs to others shall belong to me.
Having thought this way, they further instruct others to do the same.
Having instructed others, they then follow one another in practicing deception and delusion; employing various expedient means, they deceive and mislead others to take their wealth.
Having thus deceived them, their hearts give rise to joy, and they think to themselves:
"I am truly skillful!"
"I am able to deceive and delude others to obtain their wealth and property.
What originally belonged to them now belongs to me.
Giving rise to such thoughts, he feels joy and finds gratification therein; thus, in this sequence, he delights in practicing it frequently, causing others to suffer.
With their minds shrouded by malicious greed, they destroy cities, towns, villages, and populous settlements, or set fire to cities, towns, villages, and populous settlements.
He is abandoned by all people and despised by all virtuous persons.
He is a great thorn to these lands, a thorn to cities, and a thorn to villages.

They destroy the land, ruin cities, devastate villages, and demolish dwellings; they destroy other lineages, constantly and at all times delighting in such evils, causing others to suffer decline and distress.
Thus, when such evil persons die and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
These are the people of evil greed in this world; these people of evil greed obstruct the world.
Once wicked greed has accumulated, it further increases, like fire obtaining fuel.

In this way and that way wicked greed grows; in this way and that way one employs the means of wicked greed; in this way and that way one acquires the wealth and property of others; and in this way and that way it increases all the more.
Therefore, those who practice the cultivation of merit should diligently abandon evil greed.
Why is this? The foremost defilement is the greedy mind that seizes the wealth and property of others.
Those who are defiled and corrupt fall into hell.
At that time, Śikhin Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"If a person acts with deceit, And by crafty means takes the property of others,"
This is a mind of great greed, constantly engaging in unwholesome conduct.
Such a person, throughout day and night, remains perpetually impure in heart;
with their mind shrouded by greed, they are always longing for the possessions of others.
Such a person is like the fire at the end of an eon;
their very nature is inherently evil, and they are feared by all, just like a venomous serpent.
If a person is driven by evil greed and constantly shrouds their mind with it, [they shall suffer].
Constantly entering the hells, as well as among the hungry ghosts and others;
once they have escaped the heat within the fires of the great hells,
if they are born as humans, they will remain impoverished for five hundred lifetimes.
With faces disfigured and mouths contorted, they constantly undergo suffering;
those whose minds are ruined by greed all experience such pain.
If a person abandons greed and always seeks after wisdom, [they shall not suffer thus].
Constantly possessing the power of supernormal knowledge, one then proceeds upon the path of goodness.
To eliminate greed from the mind is like closing off a snake’s den;
if one is bitten by the serpent of greed, one will certainly suffer affliction.
If one harbors a mind of greed, it increases with every passing thought,
like fire finding dry fuel that blazes and grows ever fiercer.
One who delights in wealth and possessions constantly craves more.
When the time of death has arrived, one must abandon all things;
yet if one has committed evil deeds, they can never be cast off.
Bound by greed, that person shall be led away to enter hell.
Wealth belongs to others, yet one defiles oneself with evil karma;
what is not wealth is seen as wealth, and what is not pleasure is called pleasure.
When wicked greed dwells in the mind, one views an enemy as a virtuous friend.
The fire of greed can burn a person; therefore, the wise do not accumulate greed.
Those burned by greed will enter hell in the future;
the wealth of the world is like a mountain, yet all is impermanent.
"What kind of wealth is it that leads one to commit such evil deeds? Only those who are foolish can commit such evils.
"Do not commit such evil greed yourself, nor cause others to do so."
In this way, evil greed obstructs the world.
For one who accumulates evil greed, it increases day by day, like fire obtaining fuel; in this manner and that, it blazes forth and grows ever greater.

Because such evil greed acquires wealth and property, it increases in this way; together with greed, stinginess, and envy, it grows and blazes forth. Therefore, those who possess merit and virtue should abandon it.
"You hosts of devas, you should know this:

there are those who make their living by buying food, drink, or other goods at low prices, and then giving them as offerings during ritual assemblies to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, so that others may recognize them as meritorious people who are truly trustworthy;
having gained the trust of others, they subsequently sell their own goods to them at high prices."

Although this is an act of giving, it is not done with a pure mind; rather, it is for the sake of inspiring faith in others, for the purpose of managing livelihoods and seeking profit, buying low and selling high.
By such means, one gives a small amount of goods yet receives much more in return—perhaps tenfold or eightfold.
Virtuous people thus abandon such evil greed.
Furthermore, one should abandon evil greed.

What is called "evil greed" refers to a Dharma teacher taking material goods while preaching the Dharma; obtaining such things for purposes other than those of the Triple Gem is evil greed, and should therefore be relinquished.
Furthermore, one should abandon evil greed.

As for what is called "evil greed," it refers to a renunciant selling images of the Buddha made of ivory, embroidered images, images painted on cotton cloth or similar materials, or images carved from wood or cast in copper and other metals.
That is evil greed; having already acquired wealth, one employs it in ways that are contrary to the Dharma.
Among humans, such evil greed obstructs both worldly and world-transcending dharmas; it is censured and reviled by the wise, and abandoned by the wise.
"What is meant by 'evil craving among the gods'?
You gods possess such great bliss, yet you still harbor evil cravings.

Thus, you see before you these mountains of gold and silver, mountains of lapis lazuli, mountains of blue gems, mountains of great blue gems, and mountains of crystal; within each of these, you individually sport and enjoy pleasure. Having already enjoyed yourself upon one mountain, you proceed to another mountain to experience various pleasures together with the celestial maidens, surrounded by hosts of gods."
All this occurs because of greed; it is not caused by anything else.

You hosts of devas are bound together by the fetters of craving; you fall into evil realms without realizing it, feeling no fear, fearing neither the suffering of death nor the separation from beloved kinsmen and attendants.
They do not perceive the time of their decline, nor the various sufferings of decay.
You, the hosts of devas, because of your greedy minds, neither fear nor perceive this.
Such greed as yours, O devas, is immeasurable and boundless; it is the greedy mind of Māra’s work—never knowing satisfaction, fearing neither separation nor the suffering of death.
Thus, evil craving obstructs the mundane path.
"How does the mind of craving within the heavens obstruct the supramundane path?
It is this love for sound, touch, taste, form, and fragrance, and the delighting in and experiencing of pleasure."

The gods with greedy minds do not approach other gods with little greed to listen to the Dharma; though they hear the Dharma, seek the Dharma, and study the Dharma, they do not wish to hear it so as to purify their minds.
The supreme root of all wholesome dharmas is what is called the awakening to dharmas.
The awakening to all dharmas must depend upon hearing the Dharma; if one does not hear the Dharma, one will not awaken to the dharmas.
Why is there no awakening?
It is because of negligence.
Furthermore, by what dharma is negligence rooted?
This is what is called a greedy mind.
Therefore, one should abandon the greedy mind; if one abandons the greedy mind, one reaches nirvana.
Those who are shrouded by greed transmigrate through birth and death.
“‘O celestial hosts, you should know!
Among gods and humans, evil craving obstructs the supramundane path; therefore, the wise should always be diligent and abandon evil craving.’”
There are three kinds of giving:
first, the giving of material requisites;
second, the giving of fearlessness.
Third is the gift of Dharma.
While that gift of material requisites produces the fruit of rebirth in the heavens as its retribution, it cannot lead to true giving;
this person surpasses the devas, for it is not the devas who surpass humans.
Thus, a human body is the most difficult to obtain; if one obtains a human body but does not practice giving, it is a life lived in vain.

It is like a merchant who happens upon an island of jewels but, failing to take any treasure, returns empty-handed; likewise, it is the same for one who obtains a human body but does not know to renounce wealth through giving.
"What, furthermore, is the gift of fearlessness?
How many kinds of gifts of fearlessness are there?
There are, in general, three kinds of gifts of fearlessness: [text continues]"
First, saving lives by bestowing fearlessness;
second, employing skillful means to rescue and protect wives and children who have been seized by others, thereby bestowing fearlessness;
and third, protecting those who fear the loss of their possessions, thereby bestowing fearlessness.
Those who save lives will be reborn among humans or devas, receiving as their karmic reward a long life.
Those who protect lost property will be reborn as great wealthy persons; whatever wealth they possess cannot be seized or destroyed by kings, thieves, water, or fire.
If they become kings or great ministers, it is due to that karma that they possess great power and great renown, remaining perpetually wealthy in every place of birth.
Those who rescue their wives and children will, if reborn among humans, properly care for their wives and children;
when descending from the heavens, the celestial maidens will not abandon them.
Such are the three kinds of fearless giving.
"What is the gift of Dharma? There are two kinds of gifts of Dharma:
first, giving by means of worldly dharmas; [second, giving by means of supramundane dharmas]."
Second, giving by means of supramundane dharmas.
As for giving by means of mundane dharmas, it refers to giving through the synthesis of the four dhyānas and mundane wisdom.
One experiences worldly pleasures among humans and devas; yet, being born among devas and humans, one may give rise to wrong views.
One who practices giving through the supramundane Dharma, by virtue of freedom from anger, is reborn among devas and humans, either in the desire realm or the form realm.
If one is born in the desire realm, one may be born upon any of the one hundred and ninety-eight stages, being born there according to one's vow.

If one is born in the form realm, one attains liberation; because the fruit is superior, because of great wisdom, and because the basis is superior, one attains liberation and is born in the Pure Abodes.
If, through the power of his vows, he becomes a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, he possesses the precious golden wheel.
There are fourteen such treasures, namely the seven jewels and the seven secondary jewels.
By the power of his virtuous vows, he extinguished all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained the path of a *pratyekabuddha*.
Because his vows were supreme, he then became a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān.
Because the causal conditions for the gift of Dharma are superior,
these three kinds of giving are entirely absent among you,
the assembly of devas. For this reason, humans are superior.
Heaven is the ground of retribution; humanity is the ground of karma—the fruit arising from the causes and conditions of karma.
Thus, among humans, those born through heavenly causes and conditions possess superior karmic fruits.
Such people as these are superior; the gods are not their equal.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Volume 43. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Volume 44.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-three: Observing the Heavens; Section Nine: Yāma Heaven.
"Furthermore, regarding the divisions of karma: if a person is born in heaven without having ever practiced giving, yet has maintained the precepts, they shall be born among the gods."
They possess only one kind of merit, and their fivefold sensual pleasures are inferior to those of other devas.
Due to these karmic causes and conditions, humans are superior and the devas are inferior.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha spoke this verse:
"Having given alms among human beings, one is then reborn in the happy realms;
it is not gods who can give alms, because that is the ground of such karmic fruit."
The human realm is the ground of karma; the celestial realms are the ground of its fruit.
All fruits have karma as their cause; without a cause, there is no fruit.
Life does not abide for even a single moment; thus it revolves without turning back.
When the fruits of karma are about to be exhausted, one should cultivate merit.
All things are the power of the mind; it is able to cause the life-force to flow on.
Therefore, the wise do not commit evil for the sake of their own lives.
None fear at all the various sufferings of the future;
such people are tormented by suffering because they are bound by the snare of delusion.
Yet within their deceitful hearts, there lies the treasure of generosity and ethical discipline.
Whether one be a deva or a human, one will reach the auspicious realms;
yet because all conditioned phenomena arise, abide, and perish, they are entirely impermanent.
All conditioned pleasures are likewise impermanent in this same way.
"Though it perishes, craving arises; moment by moment it stirs and does not rest.
Life and pleasure are all like this; therefore, one should abandon them.
"In this way, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self."

Throughout all worlds, immeasurable decay and affliction are omnipresent; there are five kinds of bonds that bind gods and humans, who are blinded by the eye of ignorance, whose hearts are ruined by evil desires, and who give rise only to craving and attachment.
All foolish, ordinary worldlings are bound to one another by mutual affection, like birds in a cage; all humans and devas thus constantly wander and transmigrate within the cycle of birth and death.

For this reason, whether among humans or devas, one should not conceive the notion of permanence regarding life or pleasure; rather, one should not conceive the notion of permanence toward any phenomena within the world, nor engage in immeasurable varieties of conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, they are endowed with twelve kinds of giving; such generosity does not exist among the gods, but exists only among humans.
The gods subsist solely on fruits; once their fruits are exhausted, they wither, perish, and fall from that celestial realm.
What are the twelve perfections of giving?
First, perfection of place;
second, perfection of time.
Third, the perfection of merit;
fourth, the perfection of what is desirable, namely, beloved objects;
fifth, the perfection of the field of merit.
Sixth, giving to those who are hungry and thirsty;
seventh, giving with a mind of faith;
eighth, giving without being asked, thereby becoming fully endowed with merit.
Ninth, giving with a joyful heart to one’s wife, children, and others;
tenth, discerning and giving to those individuals (pudgala) who are respected and superior;
eleventh, giving to those in the world who are not held in contempt.
Twelfth is giving without expectation of reward.
These are the twelve kinds of giving.

Furthermore, there are those who possess the merit of observing the precepts and thereby attain birth among the gods; yet once their [merit] is exhausted, they fall back. For this reason, the gods should abandon heedless conduct.
These twelve types of stainless giving lead one to become a wheel-turning monarch with abundant wealth and treasures, or to be born among the gods or as one similar to a god.
"Furthermore, there are twelve types of impure giving."
What are the twelve kinds of defilements?
First, within a large assembly of people gathered together, or within the Saṃgha, where all members equally possess the merit of precepts, wisdom, and conduct, one gives unequally.
This is a defiled gift that yields meager fruit.
Second, if a man or a woman, motivated by desire, gives to a woman or a man respectively—this is the second type of defiled and evil giving.

Furthermore, the third defiled form of giving is that which is done out of fear: one gives away possessions to the gatekeepers or teachers of royal households—namely, those such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—with this thought:
"If I should suffer decline or distress at the hands of the king, they will be able to save me."
This is not given because of the cultivation of the causes and conditions of reflection; it is called a defiled gift.
Furthermore, the fourth defiled gift is that which is given by relinquishing objects with a deluded mind, such as the offerings made at sacrificial assemblies by non-Buddhist Brahmins and others.
This is the fourth defiled and evil form of giving.
Furthermore, regarding the fifth defiled giving: it refers to seeing another person who is practicing giving, yet not knowing whether that person maintains the precepts or not.
I do not know whether that person possesses wisdom,
whether they possess tranquility,
or whether they possess meditative concentration.
Seeing only that others perform such giving, one gives away things in this manner solely due to the influence of others, while internally harboring no intention of one's own;
this is the fifth defiled and evil form of giving.
Furthermore, the sixth defiled form of giving refers to giving only after the previous petitioner has begged with great difficulty;
this is the sixth defiled and evil form of giving.

Furthermore, the seventh defiled form of giving refers to knowing that another possesses something and, in order to inspire confidence in them, employing skillful means to steal it and then giving that object away, intending later to commit various evils and inflict harm.
Giving things for the sake of seeking an opportunity—this is the seventh defiled and evil form of giving.

Furthermore, the eighth defiled giving is when one gives away goods in order to destroy the harmony between others; by giving to two people who are friends, one causes them to separate, and subsequently, seeking their vulnerability, one inflicts upon them ruin and affliction.
This is the eighth defiled and evil form of giving.
Furthermore, the ninth defiled giving refers to giving away one's possessions to others for the sake of establishing a marriage alliance—either a man giving to a woman, or a woman giving to a man.
This is the ninth defiled and evil form of giving.

Furthermore, the tenth defiled giving is as follows: namely, engaging in trade by purchasing in large quantities various provisions for food—such as millet, beans, fruits, vegetables, and all manner of miscellaneous goods—and then waiting for the day of a religious assembly to sell them at a high price to seek profit; taking the proceeds for one's own use and providing only a meager amount to others.
This is the tenth defiled and evil form of giving.
Furthermore, the eleventh defiled giving is to relinquish material things as an offering for the sake of reputation;
this is the eleventh defiled and evil form of giving.
Furthermore, the twelfth defiled form of giving is when one’s wife and children are hungry and poor, and one gives them things without any virtuous intention within.
This is the twelfth defiled and evil form of giving.
This universal giving is free from thought and without thought; because it is without thought, it is empty and without karmic fruit. If thought increases, one is then able to leave behind defilement.
For example, just as a soiled garment becomes pure when washed with alkaline lye,
so too is the perfection of giving accomplished through the cultivation of reflection.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha spoke these verses:
“Endowed with twelve virtues and free from twelve kinds of defilements, one accomplishes pure giving;
if these are contrary, it is turbid and defiled.”
Whether as a deva or a human, one who practices giving attains great power;
by abandoning giving, one falls into the evil realms, while through giving, one is born in the happy destinies.
Tainted by greed and envy, one cares only for wife and children.
This person falls among the hungry ghosts, longing only for food and drink;
yet if they untie the bonds of greed, cut down the tree of pride,
and eliminate the mass of darkness, it is because this person has practiced generosity.
Generosity goes before; the donor follows behind.
Generosity can show the way as one travels to the next world.
One who bathes with the water of giving anoints themselves with the fragrance of ethical discipline.
Wisdom is vast and stainless; through it, one reaches the far shore beyond suffering.
A man has three lamps which he kindles for the sake of benefiting others:
namely, generosity, morality, and wisdom. These are able to eliminate all faults.
Craving is exceedingly deep and vast, and the waves of doubt are extremely turbulent;
by upholding the precepts and cultivating wisdom, one crosses over such an ocean of suffering.
When the mind is neither disciplined nor swift, it becomes attached to all things.
The dharmas of generosity and ethical discipline can bind this mind.
These three physicians are able to eliminate the disease of afflictions;
generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom constantly bestow peace and happiness.
The mind has the fault of negligence; it discriminates with crookedness and lightness.
Generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom—these three can bind the mind.
These three faults are like a blazing fire that burns all the world.
"Once the fire has been extinguished by the water of wisdom, one attains the quiescence of nirvāṇa.
"In this manner, the scriptures of that Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Vipaśyin, were inscribed within that stūpa."
"This practice of giving can only be performed by humans; the devas cannot.
For this reason, humans are superior and the devas are inferior.
Since you know such giving, do not let your minds become lax regarding all sensory objects; you should maintain your minds well."
Having well sustained the mind, one ensures that the great evils and afflictions do not arise within it.
Should they arise, the fire of wisdom can burn them away;
once burned by the fire of wisdom, one reaches the supreme state of non-retrogression—a place that is without birth or aging, and without death or exhaustion.
One should abandon heedlessness as one would an enemy.
Furthermore, there are other matters for the celestial hosts that cause their minds to diminish and lead to injury, humiliation, and shame;
namely, at the time of eating, they feel ashamed because it is witnessed by others.
Because the power of karma has inferior, middling, and superior degrees, its fruits likewise have inferior, middling, and superior degrees.
Those gods are unable to give even the slightest thing to another god; they cannot, by means of their own karma, transfer it to another.
That is to say, when one gives alms at the time of eating among humans, or observes the precepts at certain times, one obtains food in this way.
When the devas see others enjoying food endowed with superior color, superior fragrance, and superior flavor, having seen this, their hearts feel ashamed.
When they sport in gardens or within lotus ponds, they experience all manner of pleasures according to their karma, accomplishing joyful affairs.
Having seen the faces of other gods and experienced such happiness, they feel shame within their hearts, and their own status diminishes.
“In the heavens, there are five kinds of shame. What are these five?
First, when eating, if one sees another deva’s food is pure white like *sudhā*, while one’s own food is soiled or sometimes reddish.”
When eating together with others, if one sees [another] and feels extreme shame, this is the first shame.

As for the second shame, it refers to seeing other devas who possess exquisite beauty and fine complexions, whose forms and attire are majestic, and who are attended by many celestial maidens of peerless and sublime beauty as they offer service to other devas; having seen this, one then feels shame.

The third shame is this: seeing other devas within lotuses, flying through the air, and moving through groves, mountain peaks, lotus ponds, and jeweled pavilions made of gold and lapis lazuli where they sport and enjoy themselves.
Because their karma is superior, they travel by flight with great speed.
Those gods of lesser karma do not move so swiftly; they cannot travel together in the same places and always remain behind them, feeling ashamed before the hosts of celestial maidens.

Regarding the fourth type of shame: when a deity enters a lotus pond, because that deity originally possessed such karma, there arises a lotus pond with corresponding color, fragrance, texture, and magnitude.
When the inferior gods see this, they feel shame among their retinue.
This is the fifth shame: as was their karma, so is the retribution they receive; as was their karma, so is their seat.

If one has performed great wholesome deeds in a previous time, there will be a magnificent seat of vaidūrya or a seat of blue gems; or at times, one may sit upon a superior seat with the color of a red lotus.

If other inferior devas sit in that place, because their karma is meager, such exquisite seats may transform into gold, silver, or crystal; once those devas see that their sitting places have transformed, they perceive their various mixed karmas—the light and heavy karmas and so forth.
Once they have seen and known this, they feel shame.
Because shame has arisen, their majesty and virtue diminish.
Thus, the facial complexion of those gods deteriorates, while the majesty and facial complexion of the other gods increase.

When the host of celestial maidens sees him in this way, they abandon him and depart; leaving behind such a minor-merit deva, they resort to other devas of great merit and sport there, experiencing pleasure.
When the celestial maidens, being of one mind, all go together to other deva-sons,
those devas with little merit feel extreme shame.
This is the fifth kind of shame among kinsmen in the heavens.
"In this way, one does not delight in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), for those conditioned phenomena are capable of deception and delusion, giving rise to a mind of craving.

Just as the leaves of the *liàn* tree are extremely bitter in taste even when mixed with other sweet flavors, so too is celestial bliss; it is a mixture of suffering and pleasure. How much more so for those beings in the realms of other paths—whether in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, or among animals—whether born of fixed karma or unfixed karma—who suffer constantly without ceasing, and in whom immeasurable kinds of powerful suffering arise."
For example, just as there are various kinds of mixed waters in the ocean, with diverse rivers flowing in and various streams entering it, so too is the mind of sentient beings:
it is a continuous river where various karmas arise based on the river of karma, which, having attained great power, gives rise to all manner of suffering and affliction.
O assembly of devas, such is the measure of this; you should know that all varieties of distinct sufferings are likewise described.
In brief, there are three causes for all suffering; when they combine and correspond, all sufferings are fully realized.
These three kinds of suffering have three remedies that can eliminate them.
What are the three?
They are wisdom, ethical discipline, and generosity.
"At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha spoke this verse:
'If the mind does not rely upon the three— wisdom, ethical discipline, and generosity—
those sentient beings will suffer constantly, and happiness shall not be attained.'"
Just as through various causes and conditions, whatever karma of how many kinds sentient beings perform, such results are accomplished.
All things are caused by conditions; there is nothing that does not have causes and conditions.
Conditioned things are indestructible, yet their causal conditions cannot be seen.
Because one is deceived by the mind, one feels shame and embarrassment when giving;
such a giver of gifts will not obtain the fruit of happiness.
Generosity through harmony is supreme; by abandoning the stains of stinginess and envy, one constantly enjoys bliss as a deva and thus harbors no such [negative] thoughts.
Hunger and thirst are like a great fire that can burn all hungry ghosts.
All the fruits of stinginess and envy are as described by those of true wisdom.
If one constantly practices giving, they will certainly attain happiness;
since the fruit of happiness is obtained through giving, therefore giving is supreme.
It creates light for the world and follows one constantly;
through giving, one reaches heaven, where the gods serve as attendants.
Giving is a state free from deception—thus has the Tathāgata spoken.
Because this is the truth, one should always practice giving.
Having abandoned stinginess, envy, and resentment, one should skillfully cultivate the mind;
if one can practice giving, one will cross the ocean of birth and death.
Bestowing gifts upon the Triple Gem, the field of merit— All three aspects are pure;
having resolved this at the three times, The three eyes behold that fruit.
First, one constantly practices giving; Next, one diligently guards the precepts.
Wisdom can sever craving; this is the path to great bliss.
If one does not eliminate and cut off craving, it will bring no benefit to the world, and such a person cannot reach that supreme state beyond birth and death.
Always remaining free from the thought of not giving, one should constantly delight in practicing generosity.
Due to the absence of giving, one suffers from hunger and thirst, with the body scorched among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Through giving, one attains great wealth, even among the gods and *gandharvas*.
Through giving one becomes a king; through wholesome Dharma, a Wheel-Turning King.
Relying on the ground of generosity, the wise are able to maintain ethical discipline.
Those who maintain ethical discipline know the proper time; through wisdom, they attain liberation.
The essential path for escaping suffering is praised by all Buddhas;
once those who are courageous and steadfast have understood it, they constantly practice giving.
Without practicing giving, one is not born in heaven; even if born among the gods, the enjoyment of pleasure there is meager.
Through giving, one is born among humans, and from birth, one experiences wealth and joy.
Even if born among animals, one constantly experiences the fruit of happiness;
all such joys result from giving—this is what the wise have taught.
If one is among the hungry ghosts, they likewise possess food and drink;
because they gave little in their past lives, they obtain such a result.
If one is born in the hells, hunger and thirst cannot burn them.
Because of giving, all such fruits are obtained.
Those born into the miserable realms are the result of their own karma;
yet through giving, one attains peace and happiness, as if seeing one's own parents.
"Abiding thus on the ground of giving, constantly practicing generosity, and always delighting in the giving and upholding of precepts, one shall be liberated from all evil realms.

Having thus instructed the host of heedless devas, the Night-Mover (Mauśalīta) King of the Yāma Heaven, the devas understood; they all directly perceived the karmic fruit of abiding in the precepts and embraced the upholding of them.
"Furthermore, those celestial hosts possess a sense of shame; that is to say, due to their karma, they feel manifest shame and feel ashamed upon seeing the food.

They roam through gardens and lotus ponds in every direction, surrounded by many celestial maidens. Amidst various musical sounds, they move about among the heavens and upon the earth, their minds delighting in the objects of the five sensual desires. These are the foremost and most excellent pleasures, beyond all analogy, as they achieve these blissful states."
"Thus proceeding through the grounds where food and drink are found, he arrives in succession at various beautifully adorned and exquisite celestial maidens.
Surrounded by such celestial maidens, that deva enjoys himself, sporting amidst the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments and singing."
That divine ear-consciousness knows no satiety; its objects are lovely, and for this reason, the enjoyment of pleasure can never be satiated.
Furthermore, those gods see various forms that are entirely lovely, upright, majestic, and exquisite; they perceive forms according to their wishes, and upon seeing them, joy arises.
Seeing various radiances, various distinct colors, and various forms—whether dwelling far away, nearby, or in between—that deity, having seen them, has this thought:
"Those forms dwelling afar may come forward and draw near."
As soon as he thinks of them, those lovely forms immediately come near;
or the forms dwelling at a medium distance come according to his thought.
If he thinks of those nearby, those nearby then come.
If one thinks of what is near, that which is near will come;
if one thinks of what is distant, that which is distant will come.
Because the fruit of karma is supreme, it occurs according to one's will in this manner.
Because those karmic causes are categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, the celestial retribution is likewise inferior, middling, or superior.
Thus, those gods are bitten by the poison of craving; they know no satiety, for like fire encountering fuel, there is never a time when it is satisfied.
Those who possess a heart of craving can never find satiety regarding sensory objects; likewise, they can never find enough of the countless varieties of pleasure within the heavens.

Furthermore, the members of the celestial host experience an immeasurable variety of fragrances through their olfactory consciousness, namely the exquisite celestial flower scents found within the gardens and groves.

Furthermore, flowers grow upon the branches of those trees, which hang down to the ground; they possess various colors and various forms, diverse and distinct in their many parts, with all kinds of flowers blooming simultaneously at all times.

The celestial maidens take such flowers as these and present them to the deva-son so that he may smell them; or, the fragrance is wafted by the wind to the deva-son, and when he smells it, desire arises, and he experiences sensual pleasure.
"Furthermore, the celestial bodies in this heaven are adorned with such exquisite splendor as befits the gods.
The ornaments upon their heads, such as jeweled necklaces and the like, all manifest according to the gods' thoughts."
The various garments possess various fragrances; these threadless celestial raiments correspond in measure to their wearers.
Because those devas thus give rise to thoughts of attachment, they know no satiety.

"Furthermore, if those devas have a thought in their minds, by virtue of their own karma, they obtain everything they require in full; thus, there are foods and drinks that are foremost in their loveliness."
In the heavens and on earth, there is *sūdā* food.
Because there were inferior, middling, and superior [offerings] at the time of its original giving, the *sūdā* likewise has inferior, middling, and superior qualities.
Furthermore, it possesses various celestial drinks, which also have inferior, middling, and superior qualities.
Because karma is thus, one's own karma is like a seal.
It is just as among humans, where the length of a person's body follows the position of the sun, and the shadow likewise becomes long or short according to the body.
In this way, and in this manner, when those devas were formerly in the human realm, they performed such karma that such food arose for them.
When they eat that food, celestial maidens appear before them, and they feel shame.
Thus, seeing a superior celestial maiden within the heavens, one experiences great suffering and affliction.

In this manner, all things within existence are impermanent; there is not a single pleasure that does not perish. One should know that it is evident that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are exactly like this.
Furthermore, when that deity’s former wholesome karma is exhausted, suffering arises at the time of their decline.

If the deity was negligent, delighting in celestial pleasures and sensual desires, then at the time of their decline—when they are separated from what they love and the moisture of their attachment is spent, and as they are about to head toward another realm—signs will appear.
Because he was about to fall away from his state, his body and mind experienced great suffering;
such great suffering arose that its pain was beyond all analogy.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha spoke these verses:
"Amidst various pleasures of negligence, deceived by sensory objects,
when the time comes for desire to exhaust and fade away, there is no one to accompany one."
If one has practiced heedlessness in the past and failed to practice generosity and other virtues,
then at the time of death and decline, one’s heart will be scorched by the fever of regret.
Therefore, at all times— beginning, middle, and end— one should constantly act for the benefit of others.
Those who are constantly disciplined for their own benefit will not be afraid or terrified at the time of death.
There is birth, and there must be death; there is also the separation from those one loves.
The fool does not reflect upon this, being deceived by sensory objects.
At the moment of death, in every successive thought, the realm that destroys the gods arrives;
yet the gods do not perceive it, because their minds are attached to desire.
If the gods could know this, they would experience the suffering of separation from what they love.
Even for a mere moment, the mind does not abide in desire.
Desire is impermanent and fearsome; it constantly brings about what is disadvantageous.
Yet such a foolish person still draws near to desire.
Foolish gods are always like this, consumed by the fire of desire;
once they have been scorched by desire, they continue to indulge in it without ceasing.
If they contemplate the True Dharma, they will find no pleasure in sensory realms.
Those who delight in desire are constantly weeping;
this entire triple world revolves like a wheel.
Bound by the snares of all karma, the gods do not perceive its true nature.
Amidst various paths, they undergo birth and death in every place;
sentient beings, deluded by craving, constantly suffer all manner of afflictions.
Desire is like a whirling firebrand of lightning; it cannot be found to abide even for a moment.
Like a dream or a gandharva-city, sentient beings grasp at what is false.
Desires are like these; even greater than them is the fear of desire.
Within impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, do not give rise to the thought of "mine."
This wheel of old age and death is extremely evil and difficult to subdue;
it is like sentient beings without rescue, sightless and lacking awareness.
The Muni taught that the five faculties are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
There is much impermanence and suffering; the very self is a locus of disease.
Having seen and known this, one should abandon desire;
through that tranquil wisdom, one dwells near Nirvāṇa.
When those gods who are about to fall from their celestial realm, their faculties and minds become utterly agitated;
at that time, suffering arises such that no simile can describe it.
Just as they experienced great bliss, so too do these hearts of love and hatred [now suffer].
When those gods are about to fall away, they experience such great suffering.
For all those for whom death has not yet arrived, and for all those who have escaped the eight difficulties, one should perform beneficial deeds; this path is able to bring about happiness.
