"Descending from their place among the gods, Dying upon the earth among humans—
Who is there that knows this And does not grow weary of and seek to leave birth and death?
"When one's karma in the heavens is thus exhausted and they descend, bound by the cords of karma, they are dragged away and led toward other realms, giving rise to great terror."
Therefore, there are gods who are just like animals.
If the minds of gods delight in sensory objects and engage in such pleasures, it does not lead to their own benefit.
For this reason, O hosts of gods, do not act with negligence; lest at a later time, remorse and feverish distress arise in your hearts.
"Thus did the Yāma Heaven King Mūsuluta [Mukhila] describe for those devas dwelling in the realm of the mountain trees and groves the stūpa built by the Buddha Vipaśyin."
Having seen that stūpa, he subdued the host of devas for their benefit, demonstrating the faults of sensual desire.
For those devas who were subject to the four inversions, he preached the True Dharma; and before death had even arrived, he revealed to them death and its terrors.
In that place of fear of death and place of immeasurable suffering, he reveals the path of equality; with a mind of tranquility, he brings benefit to others and subdues the hosts of devas.
This concludes the second discourse among the six sūtras composed by the Buddha Vipaśyin.

Furthermore, when that Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, comes together with his celestial host to the region of Mount Pārijāta, he gathers in all those who have cultivated their minds as well as those who have not.
Diligently practicing deeds that benefit others, he removes their negligence, causes them to clearly perceive the results of karma, and makes their minds supple;
because their minds have become supple, great faith arises;
once faith has arisen, he demonstrates to them the faults of desire.
Having demonstrated the faults of desire, he spoke of the impermanence of life;
having spoken of impermanence, he spoke of the suffering of birth and death.
When the devas heard this, their minds became supple; because their minds were supple, the Heavenly King addressed them, saying:

"All you hosts of devas, behold this great stūpa of the Tathāgata Kakutsunda—a stūpa of the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān. The light of this exquisite jewel stūpa fills all directions; its golden pearl balustrades seem as if they were piercing through space, rising high above. All see it as most lovely and delightful, supremely pure, and all the hosts of devas who behold it find joy in their hearts."

Among these deities, it rises high like a banner, firm and immovable as if established in meditative concentration; with the radiant splendor of various excellent jewels, it is as wondrously sublime as the teaching of the True Dharma and most beloved.
The devas saw it thus:
"You, O assembly of devas, follow along with me to that stupa to offer worship and prostrations, or to make offerings by anointing it with incense and scattering flowers."
"What wonders does this stūpa of the Great Sage contain?
Let us go there together now.
If it brings me benefit, even until my parinirvāṇa, may both my body and my life find peace and happiness."
Why is this? Although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, preaches the Dharma but briefly, he is able to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings.
All sentient beings will certainly obtain this benefit; of this there is no doubt.
"We shall now all go together for our own benefit.
When the celestial hosts had heard these words from the Heavenly King, their minds became pure; they placed faith in the Heavenly King’s words and said to him:
"We shall all go to offer worship and prostrations for our own benefit and our own peace and happiness."

At that time, the devas of that region of Mount Gandhamādana, with the celestial king at their head and the host of devas following behind, all went together toward the stūpa of the World-Honored One.
Having arrived, he beheld the stūpa of the Tathāgata Kakudha; conceiving a heart of reverence, he prostrated, made offerings, and circumambulated it.
At that time, the radiance of the various jewels within the stūpa made the light of the sun appear like the glow of a firefly.
The splendor of those jewel radiances was thus supreme and wondrous.

Within that Buddha-stūpa, one saw hanging jeweled plaques of foremost brilliance; upon these plaques were the words of the sūtra, produced by the supernormal powers of a deva. Therefore, they were not lost, nor broken, nor destroyed, and could not be wiped away or erased.
Why is it not lost?
It is because the Tathāgata Kākaṇḍaka Muni, for the sake of benefiting all devas and humans, preached this sūtra and taught the Dharma in such a manner among the devas and humans.
Why is this? For the celestial realm is the virtuous path for humans, and the human realm is the virtuous path for devas.
When devas are about to fall from their state, they long for the virtuous path of humanity.
When a person dies, they hope for the heavenly realms and good paths.
Thus, gods and humans alternately serve as good paths for one another; gods and humans take delight in each other.
"If one maintains the precepts without violation, one will be born among the gods."
There are two kinds of those who uphold the five precepts.
Among them, the one who upholds the precepts does so because of ignorance, and thus their practice is not yet matured.

It is only the ignorant who act in this way; though they are ignorant, they possess faith. Because of this mental faith, they place their trust in the Buddha and others, practicing virtue of body, speech, and mind, and are not possessed of wrong views.

Until the end of their lives, they believe in the retribution of karmic actions; they obtain goods in accordance with the Dharma to sustain themselves, do not afflict others, revere and honor their parents, provide for them, draw near to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and constantly hear the True Dharma.
Such a deluded person possesses only faith.
Although he is dull-witted, he fully practices wholesome karma corresponding to body, speech, and mind; yet, by his very nature, he does not receive the prohibitive precepts.

Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas; because their final thoughts were virtuous, they attain birth among the gods.

If they are born in the realm of the Yāma devas, they find themselves inferior to the other devas in physical form, color, attire, and ornaments, and in the assembly of celestial maidens, as well as in their conduct and sustenance—all of which are inferior—and thus they feel shame.
Their radiance is also slight, and all their sensual enjoyments, though complete, are inferior.

Because they lack wisdom, they do not know how to adopt the precepts; thus, compared to those among the gods who possess the precepts, who have wisdom, and who know how to adopt the precepts, they are diminished and inferior.

"Furthermore, because of that delusion, they do not know how to undertake the precepts to practice the conduct of morality, nor do they give rise to pure faith toward the Buddha and others; they are even unable to undertake the one-day precepts, nor can they perform good deeds of body, speech, and mind, nor can they fully accomplish all practices within body, speech, and mind."

Regarding wholesome conduct of the body, it refers to refraining from killing and refraining from sexual misconduct, as well as not committing theft; yet this is not the entirety of bodily cultivation.
Regarding wholesome conduct of speech, it consists solely of refraining from false speech, while all other defilements of speech are not avoided.
In this way, one practices only a portion of wholesome conduct and is unable to fulfill all wholesome conduct.
Regarding mental wholesome conduct, one may only believe that life will end, or that there is remaining karma, or at times believe in nothing at all.

Those born in the Yāma Heaven who are inferior to those previously mentioned are further diminished compared to other devas who have practiced cultivation, received the precepts, and fully maintained them; in terms of physical stature and complexion, superior ornaments, food and conduct, retinues of celestial maidens, the length of lifespan, and all aspects of sound, touch, form, and fragrance, they are entirely inferior.
Because they perceive themselves as inferior, they feel extreme shame and are ashamed before other devas who uphold the precepts.
Furthermore, there are those who are foolish and do not know how to take up the precepts or how to practice in accordance with them.

Possessing the right view that all is but mind, they are able to hear the Buddha-dharma and reverently believe in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—even if they do not observe the precepts for so much as a single day.
One hears of it through the observance of precepts, or hears it through the instruction of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), or refrains from theft out of fear of the consequences.
One hears of it in successive order; for instance, one hears the Buddha say:
"Due to residual karma, one is born into poverty."
Such a person, fearing the present life and fearing future lives, does not steal.
They do not speak words that cause division nor do they engage in mutual antagonism; rather, they bring those who are divided back into harmony, out of their love for wholesome karma.
At times, one hears the words spoken by the Buddha:
"Due to the residual karmic conditions of that divisive speech, all one's relatives, friends, acquaintances, wives, children, servants, and slaves will be torn asunder."
Due to these karmic causes, when their body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
Because of these two kinds of causes and conditions, such a person refrains from double-tongued speech.

Due to these causes and conditions of karma, when that person’s body perishes and life ends, because their mind possesses faith, or due to other karma, or due to the karma of rebirth, and because they have faith in the field of merit, they are born in the Yāma Heaven.

Their physical dimensions, forms, and characteristics are all inferior and diminished; the assembly of celestial maidens is inferior; their movements throughout various places, as well as their food and drink, are inferior; their sounds and tactile sensations are also inferior; their tastes, colors, fragrances, and life spans are all inferior, and even their radiance is inferior.
In the presence of other devas, they feel shame.
Because they have failed to adopt the precepts due to such negligence, these three types of beings are born among the gods with varying degrees of excellence and inferiority.

It is solely because of faith in the Buddha that one may think thus: either because his merit is superior; or because his fundamental nature is at times superior; or because the essence of his mind is superior in its suppleness; or because his right view and profound faith are superior, being free from flattery, crookedness, and causing distress to others;
or because his honoring of parents generates a sense of reverence and respect; or because his aspiration is superior.

In this way, that person’s mind, which accords with their karma, continues in constant succession; within the field of merit, the power of their deep resolve and the qualities of their intention exist in lower, middling, and superior degrees.
Such superior karma leads to rebirth among the gods; one will certainly experience a fruit corresponding to that karma, which is never in vain.
Do not doubt that it will not be obtained; thus it is certain to be attained.
How much more so regarding the taking of precepts, up to and including Nirvana, which will certainly and inevitably be attained, never being false or deceptive.
"In how many ways are the precepts taken?
To speak briefly, there are the fourfold assemblies and their followers; these are the four ways of receiving the precepts, all of which encompass the fruit."
What are these four?
They are the bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās—the fourfold assembly receiving the precepts.
"For such a person as that, how many distinct types of receiving the precepts are there?
"There are briefly four types of upāsakas. What are these four types?"
1. One who practices for a portion;
2. one who practices for half;
3. one who practices repeatedly.
Fourth, regarding all practices:
those who practice a single portion observe only one precept;
those who practice half observe three precepts and act according to those three precepts.
Those who practice intermittently do not constantly receive the precepts.
Those who practice universally receive and uphold the five precepts.
Furthermore, there are another four kinds of upholding the precepts; what are these four?
First, observing precepts out of aspiration;
second, observing precepts partially;
third, observing precepts with regret.
Fourth, the combined observance of the precepts.
That upāsaka gradually takes up the ocean of training rules in successive order; first, he takes the three refuges and becomes an upāsaka.

As that person cultivates the mind and further observes them well over a long period of time, he takes up one training rule and firmly maintains it without deficiency, without breach, and without perforation.
“What is it that is not broken?
What is it that is not pierced?
What is it that is not perforated?”

That which is "unimpaired" means that until the end of one's life, one upholds it without abandoning it, never giving rise to even a single thought of breaking the precepts; regarding others who act [contrary to the precepts], one does not rejoice in their hearts, but rather restrains others from such actions or establishes them in the Dharma—therefore, it is called "unimpaired."

Regarding "not piercing": it is like one who has received a certain training precept (śikṣāpada) but later abandons that training precept, and subsequently takes it up again; to abandon and take it up repeatedly in this manner is called "piercing."
That person thus studies the phrases without piercing them, remaining free from such grasping.
"What is it that is not pierced?
What constitutes a piercing?"
Regarding these points of training, at first one’s mind is pure and one grasps them by way of knowing their limits.
Having grasped them, later on the mind feels regret; one is unable to maintain them, and doubt arises in the mind.
Doubt draws his mind, and with a turbid mind he acts, rather than acting with much reflection.
Later, that person is consumed by the fire of regret; having been thus consumed, he abandons the precepts (*śikṣāpada*);
having thus abandoned them, he does not take them up again—this is called a "hole."
If a person does not abide in such a manner, they are called "uncorrupted.
Furthermore, those upāsakas who practice with aspiration abide in the precepts of training that are deficient, pierced, and perforated.
What is meant by "deficiency"?
This mind is neither extinguished, nor broken, nor destroyed; yet once a wholesome mind has arisen, it grasps at the precepts like a plantain leaf or like a flash of lightning.

Thus, having moved the mind with joy and taken up the precepts with faith and reverence, one later hears the teachings of non-Buddhists and the mind then gives rise to regret; with the mind defiled by the impurity of delusion, one therefore abandons the precepts.
Furthermore, at a later time, having heard the True Dharma, they revert to and resume [their former ways]; this is called "deficiency.

Moreover, as for deficiency: this upāsaka has doubts regarding the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). While observing such morality, making offerings to the devas, and recollecting the True Dharma, he forms this thought:
"Do I now attain purity through the Buddha’s word, or do I obtain the power of grace from the devas?"
Because of such a state of mind, one makes offerings to both.
Such a state of doubt, while maintaining the precepts according to the Dharma, is called "pierced.

Furthermore, as for a "hole," it means that while there is a hole within the inner mind, one performs virtuous conduct outwardly; because of being seen by others and for the sake of receiving offerings, one accepts and upholds the rules of training—this is called a "hole."
The wise person thus relinquishes everything.
"Regarding the rare upāsaka who maintains the practice of ethical discipline: why is he called a rare upāsaka who maintains the practice of ethical discipline?"

This upāsaka takes up one precept, and after a long period of time, he then takes up another precept; proceeding in this sequence, it is not at one time, nor does it arise from a single mind, nor does it come from a single teacher; in this manner, over a long duration, he hopes to take up the precepts.
This is called the lay follower (upāsaka) who practices the rarefied training precepts.
"Furthermore, there is the second type, the 'Half-Precept' upāsaka.
Having observed one half-precept, or having observed two, they subsequently take up three; [and so on]."
Or, having first taken three, one subsequently takes two;
or at a later time one then takes three;
or after a long period of time one finally takes two.
This is called "half-practice.
Within each half, one practices by increasing from the lower [level] and practicing by decreasing from the increased [level]. Why is this?

Taking the precepts by combining them half by half, and thus practicing and upholding them in this combined manner, is called the second type of *upāsaka*: the one who practices the half-and-half combination.
"What is the third type of lay follower who regrets [not taking the precepts]?
Previously, they did not take the precepts solely because of a deluded mind, yet they have merely developed deep faith in the Buddha and others."
When that upāsaka hears from a bhikṣu about the fruits of observing the precepts and their immeasurable merit leading even to nirvāṇa, once he has heard this, the fire of regret burns his heart;
only then does he give rise to reverence and respect, maintaining the precepts without forsaking them until the end of his life.
This is called the third type of repentant upāsaka.
Furthermore, there is the fourth type, the compliant upāsaka,
who maintains the precepts and practices all of them in full perfection.
What is meant by an upāsaka who maintains the practice of the precepts?
This upāsaka, having heard the True Dharma, attains the True Dharma.

In every phrase and every passage throughout the sūtras, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), he understands these twelve factors of dependent origination as they truly are. Having given rise to this thought in his mind and having thus gained faith, he relies solely upon the faculty of the tongue to fully embrace and maintain all the precepts.

At one time, they received the five precepts and maintained them firmly—without deficiency, without breach, and without flaw—until the end of their lives, always upholding them in this manner; these four upāsakas were as previously described.

"Furthermore, among those who are inferior, middling, and superior in this sequence, all are supreme within their respective categories; yet even one who fully upholds the five precepts is considered the most inferior of all if they merely aspire to uphold them."

As for the lowest level of upāsaka who maintains the precepts, even within a single thought-moment they encompass the observance of the precepts; thus, the devas cannot equal them, nor can the Māras and others.
Why is this? Because the dharma of the city of nirvāṇa is capable of encompassing all.
Yet, none of these devas aspire for or seek after that city of nirvāṇa.
"When the earth-dwelling yakṣas see one who upholds the precepts, they make offerings and pay homage.
When the space-dwelling yakṣas see this, they likewise make offerings and pay homage."
Because such a person follows the practice of the Dharma, they are able to repay kindness and are able to be disciplined and compliant.

Thus, when a yakṣa speaks to a deva regarding such a person, that person will obtain fruits in the present life: kings, ministers, or lords of lands will make offerings to them, or bestow wealth and goods upon them; subsequently, as they follow the devas, their supernatural powers will increase and they will possess great influence.
Various non-Dharmic yakṣas and other evil spirits will be unable to harass or destroy them.

Whatever they require according to their hearts' desire, all their various mental aspirations shall be fully realized; they shall experience joy in accordance with their wishes, and all their undertakings shall be completely successful. They will suffer little illness, their facial complexion will be pure and clear, their sleep will be peaceful and restful, and they will be joyful upon waking.
His wife, children, servants, and other guests will remain with him, never parting from him.
When his body perishes at the end of his life, he will be reborn in a good destination; among the gods there, his size, complexion, and physical form will all be superior to others.
Because the observance of precepts is supreme, such a superior rebirth occurs.
By the power of such karma—specifically through the observance of precepts—one attains this great fruit.
However, the wholesome karma accumulated during one's previous existence as a human being is entirely exhausted here in the Yāma Heaven due to the practice of negligence.
Because the minds of sentient beings are bound by the net of karma, they subsequently fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Therefore, all should practice with diligent vigor; until the seal of the noble ones is attained, one should thus exert such diligence.

If one acts with heedlessness despite having mastery over the mind, that deity will feel regret at the time of their decline; because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Therefore, one should abandon heedlessness.
In this way, the fourth virtuous upāsaka attains happiness in the present life; if he can proceed by stages with uninterrupted diligence, he will reach nirvāṇa.
"Such a person as this is an upāsaka, a member of the Buddha’s retinue.
Furthermore, what constitutes an upāsikā, a member of the Buddha’s retinue?"
Generally, how many kinds of Buddhist upāsikās are there?
There are four kinds of upāsikās:
the first is those who possess faith;
Second is the sequence conforming to the spiritual lineage;
third, the practice of discipline;
and fourth, the practice of proximity.
Regarding those who possess faith: that female lay follower (upāsikā) has her mind perfumed by noble lineage; her mind is supple, and she has skillfully cultivated it.

That female lay follower has heard little of the Buddha’s words, yet having heard them, she is able to understand them; having understood them, she finds their flavor; having found their flavor, she enters into them—meaning she enters the Dharma and Vinaya.
Once that upāsikā has established herself in a virtuous mind, she then receives the precepts.

A woman’s mind cannot be constrained; having heard the words of non-Buddhists, her mind does not accept them, nor does she abandon the Buddha-dharma, even to the point of not conversing with non-Buddhists.
"Only those who give rise to a pure mind toward the Buddha and others and fully receive the five precepts are called faithful upāsikās.
What is meant by an upāsikā who follows the sequence of the [noble] lineages?"

Of noble lineage, virtuous, and compliant with the practice of the Dharma, they enter the Dharma and have faith in the Dharma—finding refuge in the Dharma, taking the Dharma as their home, being firm in the nature of the Dharma, and steadfast in the Dharma; they do not engage in unwholesome actions, and teachers of other paths cannot destroy them.
They are born into the lineage of perpetual upāsakas and develop supreme faith toward the Buddha and his equals.
If they are born as women within that lineage, those women are able to follow the proper sequence; from birth, they have constantly heard the Buddha’s words and have made offerings to śramaṇas.
This upāsikā constantly hears the meaning of the Dharma.
This upāsikā, at all times and continuously, perfumes her mind with the precepts she has received and maintains.
She is an upāsikā who follows the sequential order of the spiritual lineage.

"As for that female lay follower, Vinītamati, she originally had no faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and so forth; however, because she came into the proximity of virtuous spiritual friends, she came to have faith in the Buddha and the others."
Relying on external conditions, she is made to have faith by others; seeing that their merit consists in the complete observance of the precepts, she repeatedly takes up the precepts herself.
Such a female lay follower is called "tamed."
“Regarding that female lay follower who dwells in proximity:
if there is a woman who constantly associates with non-Buddhists, knows their doctrines, and observes their deportment;”

Having understood their deportment, one subsequently approaches the disciples of the Buddha, the śramaṇas; there one observes their deportment, hears the Dharma from them, and beholds their physical appearance, manner of eating, gestures, and movements, as they wear the saṃghāṭī robe and come and go in tranquility.
Having seen this, she then gradually abandons the non-Buddhist paths and places her faith in the Buddha and his teachings.
Because she has drawn near, she becomes disciplined and compliant; by receiving the precepts from him, she is called a *upāsikā* who dwells in proximity.
"Thus, regarding these four kinds of upāsikā assemblies and these four kinds of upāsaka assemblies, it is briefly explained as follows:

Because of their faith and understanding, because of the continuity of their minds, because of external conditions, and because of their sequential proximity—just as were the causes and conditions for the upāsaka assemblies previously described, the upāsikā assemblies likewise all enter into the Dharma and Vinaya."
Just as with all the causes and conditions pertaining to the upāsikās, the assembly of upāsakas likewise enters [this state].

Because of the continuity of the mind, the assemblies of upāsakas and upāsikās practice together without distinction; they are entirely subsumed by all that is wholesome, possessing right view and right conduct.
Because those minds all possess inferior, middling, and superior qualities, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are all born in the heavenly realms of the good destinations.
Among them, some are born in the Yāma Heaven; according to the precepts they have accumulated and the differences in their right conduct, they are likewise born among the other heavens.
Having been born in heaven by virtue of properly maintaining the precepts and practicing in harmony with others, they act with negligence and fail to apply themselves with diligent effort.
Those who have not yet attained the state of an *ārya* find their merit and karma exhausted, and they are reborn again in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Because their merit is exhausted and due to the fault of negligence, they fall;
however, those gods who practice without negligence reach the most delightful of pleasant places, owing to their observance of the precepts and their virtuous cultivation.
Therefore, one should not give rise to a heedless mind; this heedlessness is no different from poison.
All foolish worldlings, deluded by craving, engage in all manner of unbeneficial actions and remain bound by the fetters of birth and death, never escaping them.
Therefore, devas and humans should abandon negligence.
Whether as a deva or a human, by thus observing the precepts, one attains birth in the foremost of excellent realms.
Yet, due to the fault of negligence, one's merit is exhausted.
"Such a person as that deceives themselves excessively; they will either fall into the evil realms or wander through birth and death for a very long time.
With such a virtuous mind, Mucilinda, the King of the Yama Heaven, showed the heavenly hosts the script on the wooden boards within that Buddha-stūpa, and spoke these words:
"That Blessed One, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and for the benefit of the devas, manifested this through his supernormal powers."
Having heard this, that deva developed a supreme mind of renunciation toward birth and death, abandoning heedless conduct as if it were nothing other than poison.
This concludes the account of the laymen (upāsakas) and laywomen (upāsikās), along with their retinues.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 44 [and] Scroll 45.
Translated by the Brahamana Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four of the *Devatā-darśana-parivarta*: The Tenth Section on Yāma Heaven.
"What are the two kinds of retinues—the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs?
How many types are there?"
What are its merits?
What are its practices?
How does one maintain the precepts?
How many kinds of observance of the precepts are there?

Such a śramaṇa—a disciple of the Blessed One—whether he be a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, seeking the practice for nirvāṇa, exerts himself with diligence day and night, able to cause the hosts and retinues of Māra to tremble with fear.
There are some bhikṣuṇīs who are wise and practice correctly, acting in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya, their minds free from fear as they seek the true reality toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
Because they seek the true reality, they maintain the precepts without transgression; in this way, they are able to enter the city of Nirvāṇa.
What kind of practice should be cultivated to correspond with merit?
There are two merits regarding all women’s love and desire and their proximity to desire:

first, all virtuous ones should thus truly observe the male body as their own; seeing that male body as being either equal to their own body or larger than their own, and having seen it thus, they conceive the notion of him as a brother, a father, or a mother.
One should cultivate the mind in this way:
"This woman has sensual pleasure as her foundation; if one draws near to her, the mind will constantly harbor longing.
Whether by day or night, whether sitting or lying down, whether asleep or awake, or whatever else one may be doing.
Whether young, old, or middle-aged; whether dwelling in a favorable place or an unfavorable place;
whether in suffering or in happiness; whether ill or healthy; whether protected or unprotected; whether restrained or unrestrained;
whether born of a noble lineage or a lowly lineage; whether beautiful or ugly; whether dwelling by the roadside or within a house.
Whether dwelling in a village or in a secluded place; whether adorned or unadorned;
whether bound in prison or not in prison; whether beloved by her husband or not beloved;
whether near elders or in the presence of elders; whether near those of low status or near the young, or near the elderly.
At all times and in all places, the desire of all women constantly binds the mind.
This desire abiding within the mind is like the heat of fire, the solidity of the earth, the light movement of the wind, and the moisture of water.
Just as the specific characteristics inherent within the four great elements are never inverted and never depart from them at any time,
so too does desire for women constantly follow and bind one, never departing for even a moment.
Such women further have two defilements, namely envy and jealousy.
These two defilements are further accompanied by another defilement that arises together with them and does not depart from them, namely flattery and deceit.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, deceit.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, arrogance.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, the state of decline and affliction.
Regarding the state of decay and affliction: one approaches wealthy men and engages in sensual desire with them.
Furthermore, there is a defilement that pursues and never leaves such a person, namely agitation, whereby the mind is constantly unsettled.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, falsely accusing one's own relatives, friends, brothers, and kinsmen.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, being able to ruin one's dignified deportment in the midst of a great assembly.
Furthermore, there is another stain that follows him and does not leave him, namely, double-tongued speech.
Furthermore, there is another stain that follows him and does not leave him, namely, private gossip.
Furthermore, there is another stain that follows him and does not leave him, namely, greed for food.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, the ability to engage in sexual desire for those with whom one should not engage.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, being untrustworthy.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, the ability to speak of the misconduct of other women.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that follows him and does not leave him: namely, a love for quarreling.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that pursues and does not leave him: namely, insulting others.
Furthermore, there is another defilement that pursues and does not leave him: namely, causing disruption, which can bring ruin and disorder to villages, hamlets, and settlements.
Furthermore, there is a defilement that follows him and never leaves him: namely, by reason of his association with these women, he falls into hell.
Such women are like excrement, like poison, and like a sharp blade; they are similar in every way to falling over a precipice, to a great fire in a wilderness, and to a venomous serpent.
"The hearts of women are all like this.
When women who possess such minds as these behold the Triple Gem, praise and extol it, and hear the Buddha’s words, their female hearts then become supple."
Furthermore, there is another extraordinary quality: the application of such remedies against such stubborn, defiled, and evil minds.
There are two kinds of remedies: those arising from one's own mind or those prompted by the instruction of others, through which one leaves the household life out of faith.
That which arises from oneself is due to the mind being well-perfumed;
that which is taught by others is due to proximity with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These cause the mass of darkness consisting of all faults—which has resided in the mind since beginningless time—to be dispersed and eliminated.
When one first leaves the household life with such aspirations for the bhikṣuṇīs, they draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Why is this?

It is because, as has been taught, these are the remedies for all defilements; knowing what should be said and saying it, they cause others to dwell well therein, skillfully providing liberation from the bonds of suffering and affliction, so that they may attain deliverance and abide in peace and happiness.

A virtuous friend provides consolation and guidance; they cause the darkness from beginningless time to be extinguished and show one the path of goodness. They extract the thorns of evil desires and the like from beginningless time, and are able to rescue and deliver one from places of attachment and aversion, showing the place of eternal non-birth, non-death, and non-aging—a state of peace and security.

Regarding those points for the antidotes to such defilements, I shall now explain them; as they are explained in sequence, according to each defilement and its respective antidote, they bring about tranquility—all of which is thus.
Women possess more envy and jealousy than men; thus, through such mutual oppositions and harmonies as antidotes, one departs from birth and death.
"Because women have many desires, impurity is the antidote, as seen by observing the body as it truly is."
The body is a storehouse of disease and a collection of unwholesome things; it is a locus of all manner of impurities, such as excrement and urine.
Regarding this body—whether one's own or that of another—one observes its fundamental nature by examining it according to its own specific characteristics.
From where did this body originally arise?
He sees that it is produced from the impure combination and accumulation of semen and blood, like a broth; the foul fluids of two families unite to form a single body.
Such a body is born from impure seeds. Furthermore, that woman contemplates the body in this way:
"If this body is produced from impure seeds, then within this body there is not even the slightest pure dharma."
That bhikṣuṇī further carefully seeks and contemplates the nine kinds of foul sores from which impurities flow from the body.
As it is with the female body, so it is with the male body; both women and men have these nine kinds of sores from which [impurities] flow.
The female body has three great defects.
What are these three? They are:
the width of the urinary opening, and the flowing of milk from both breasts; these are called the three.

"Furthermore, wounds flow equally from both males and females; both nostrils discharge tears, both eyes shed tears, and from both ear canals there may issue wax, blood, or pus. The breath from the mouth is foul, either naturally so or due to eating; saliva flows out; and from the lower parts come impurities such as feces, urine, and blood."
Having thus observed this body as it truly is in its various impurities, one reflects:
"Within this collection of the body there is no pure thing; not even so much as a speck of dust flows that is not entirely an impure thing."
“Regarding such a body as this, what dwells within it?
What is its support?
Even if pure things come near this body, the body remains impure.”
Because the body is impure, even such pure things as these become equally impure.
Whatever object was originally pure, if it comes into contact with the body, it then becomes impure.
Regarding what is called the inherent purity of things: if one consumes the most pure food, once that food enters the body, it becomes excrement.
In this same way, when this body drinks pure substances, they enter the body and become urine.
When external objects touch the body, because of this body, all pure things become impure.
That which is called "pure"—such as all kinds of fragrant garments—if they are worn on the body and sweat is produced, they then become foul-smelling.

Furthermore, just as a flower, though originally possessing every fragrance, becomes withered and foul-smelling when it comes into contact with the body, that bhikṣuṇī further contemplates the body: "From where has such a body come to abide?"
That is to say, [the embryo] originally resides within the mother’s womb.
As for the mother’s body, is it pure or impure?
That bhikṣuṇī observes in this manner:
“My mother’s own nature was likewise of this same kind of impurity.
Furthermore, that bhikṣuṇī observed the body: “In what place does such a body abide?”
In what place does it move?
Is that place pure or impure? Having observed in this way, one sees and knows it as it truly is.

In all places that are pure, wherever such a body may be—whether dead or alive—if it remains in that location, then that place will become filled with worms, filth, hair, and bones, causing that entire spot to emit a great stench.
Because such a body exists in that place.
"That bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of severing desire, further contemplates the body:
'Of whom is such a body eaten?'"
How does one observe it? One sees it as it truly is:
namely, that it is devoured by rākṣasas, various evil spirits, and other impure beings, and not by pure creatures such as geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.

“Furthermore, after that bhikṣuṇī has truly observed this body in such a manner, she sees that this body is comprised solely of what is perverse, characterized by inverted discrimination and improper observation; with the eye of darkness appearing before her, when a man draws near, her mind becomes bound by desire and she does not see its impurity.”
Through such definitive observation, he brings about the total eradication or at least the attenuation of these long-practiced, firm desires from time immemorial.
Among all defilements, the defilement of delusion is the most evil.
Among all women, desire is the most evil.
Due to the causes and conditions of the defilement of desire, other defilements arise in turn.
If one eliminates the defilement of desire through its antidote, all other defilements will be extinguished without remainder.
Just as when the sun sets its radiance completely vanishes, so too, because the root of defilement—desire—is severed, all remaining defilements are extinguished.
"That bhikṣuṇī extinguishes desire through this path; because that desire is extinguished, all other co-arising defilements are entirely extinguished."
What arises simultaneously?
It is envy and jealousy.
Whatever envy and jealousy men or women possess, all arise because of desire.
Regarding the two defilements of envy and jealousy, desire is their root.
Because that desire is severed or rendered faint, those two are extinguished.
Furthermore, those two defilements are pursued and bound by other remaining defilements.
What are the remaining defilements?
They are flattery and deceit, which arise from envy and jealousy.
Because envy and jealousy are extinguished, flattery and deceit are also extinguished.
From the defilement of flattery and deceit, further defilements arise that pursue and bind one, namely, deception.
Because flattery and deceit are extinguished, there is no deception.
From the defilement of deception, further defilements arise that pursue and bind one, namely, arrogance.
Because deception is extinguished, there is no arrogance.
From the defilement of arrogance, further defilements arise that follow and bind one, namely, the states of decline and affliction.
Because arrogance is extinguished, there are no states of decline and affliction.
From the state of decline and affliction, further defilements arise that pursue and bind one, namely, agitation.
When the state of decline and affliction ceases, there is no agitation.
From the defilement of agitation, further defilements arise that pursue and bind one, namely, false accusation.
Because agitation and disturbance are extinguished, one does not commit deception or injustice.
From the defilement of deception and injustice, further defilements arise in succession that follow and bind one, namely, the violation of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Because there is no deception or injustice, one does not violate dignified conduct.
From the violation of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), further defilements arise that follow and bind one, namely, divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
All women destroy [relationships] through divisive speech.
If one does not violate dignified deportment, there will be no divisive speech.
From the defilement of divisive speech, further defilements arise that follow and bind one, namely, backbiting—speaking of others in private.
Because divisive speech is extinguished, one does not engage in backbiting.
From the defilement of private speech, further defilements arise that follow and bind one, namely, the craving for food.
Within the wombs of women there is much food and drink; all women constantly crave food and drink, placing much within their bellies to nourish their own bodies.
Because one does not engage in private conversation, one does not crave food.
From the defilement of craving for food, further defilements arise that pursue and bind one, namely, the practice of improper desires.
Because all women consume the food of lust, improper and wicked desires arise.
When their craving for food and the impurities of their consumption are extinguished, those improper and wicked desires will no longer exist.
From that unwholesome and improper desire, further defilements arise which follow and bind one, namely, being untrustworthy.
If there is improper desire for a woman, all people will harbor suspicions regarding her, and she will be disliked by everyone.
That discordant impurity of wrong desire ceases, and the lack of trust likewise ceases.
From the impurity of lack of trust, other impurities arise again that follow and bind one, namely: the ability to speak of the misconduct of other women that destroys their dignified demeanor.

Because one cannot trust [the other], and thus does not speak of their own violation of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), further defilements arise from speaking of the other's impurities; these follow and bind one, namely, the quarreling of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
By speaking of the cessation of others, quarrels arising from craving cease.
From the defilement of quarrels arising from craving, further defilements are produced that follow and bind one, namely, the insulting of others.
Because quarrels arising from craving have ceased, one does not insult others.
From the defilement of insulting others, further defilements arise that follow and bind one, namely, the act of causing disorder, which can bring ruin and chaos to villages and settlements.
Because the insult is extinguished, there is no longer such disorder.
All these defilements, which abide and support one another in successive order, are entirely extinguished.
Such is the fundamental bondage of their own nature; regarding the minds of women, there is no dharma whatsoever capable of making them supple, except for the Buddha’s word.
Having heard this oral teaching from the mouth of one who has attained knowledge, that woman, having thus heard it,
renounces her dwelling place and household affairs— which are so difficult to abandon— and goes forth into homelessness.
If one is unable to completely extinguish all outflows (*āsrava*), then one should single-mindedly uphold the precepts and practice.
At the outset, one practices non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct; one does not engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech.
Having thoroughly cultivated all virtues, constantly practicing them repeatedly, and delighting in their frequent cultivation, such women,
upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in the happy realms among the devas of the desire realm.
If one does not grow weary of sensual desires and the mind is dominated by karma, one will be born among the celestial trees and grounds of the Yāma Heaven and obtain the body of a man.
Having thus maintained the precepts without deficiency and obtained that celestial body, one then indulges in negligence.

Because the wholesome karma of these gods who act with negligence is exhausted, they fall again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, and are further reborn in such a body as that of an exceptionally foul and wicked woman.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Desire is the ground of envy and jealousy; The mind is like a wheel of lightning-fire.
It is the treasury of greed and arrogance; The wise do not place their trust in it.”
The essence of the mind is a snare of desire, like a sharp blade or fire;
the mind is like falling down a precipice, its depth more unfathomable than the sea.
The mind constantly conditions objects like a net, deceiving and deluding others.
Like a vajra fire that burns, and like poison that kills;
though they are filled with every kind of fault and a multitude of evils gathered together,
women have no heart for even a small portion of practicing the precepts.
"Because of the power of desire, women do not maintain their precepts;
if they were free from the power of desire, they would be able to maintain them.
Thus did Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, speak of his own past life regarding the maintenance of precepts, and addressed them, saying:
"You male devas, you were female bodies among humans who maintained the precepts and were thus born in this celestial realm.
Due to the wholesome karma of maintaining the precepts while in your original female bodies, you have now been born as males."
Having been born thus, you will be exhausted through heedlessness.
You, the assembly of devas, deceive yourselves in this way; from now on, be careful not to act with such negligence.
“The World-Honored One has thus tamed the world and brought benefit to it.
Such are the fourfold assemblies of all those who are Perfectly Awakened Ones and Perfectly Omniscient Ones.”
Among those retinues, the second retinue consists of women and sisters who follow in succession; the retinue of bhikṣus follows that same order.
These bhikṣus maintain the precepts, being foremost and most excellent, and have well-cultivated their minds.
In this way, a bhikṣu who sees that he and others are afflicted by turmoil gives rise to fear; he develops weary detachment toward the path of birth and death within the world.
His mind fears all of birth and death, such that even the slightest evil, as small as a speck of dust, fills him with dread upon seeing it.

He observes his conduct with discernment, harboring no expectations, possessing the foremost profound resolve and the foremost spiritual lineage. He maintains right conduct through the precepts, perfumes his mind with generosity, and correctly contemplates the Four Noble Truths with mindfulness.
How many kinds of bhikṣus are there?
How many kinds of dharma-practice?
A bhikṣu does not transgress four kinds of true dharmas.
What are the four?
First, one who does not travel alone on the path; this is the first type of bhikṣu. Why is that?
When a solitary bhikṣu wanders through a village, he is treated with contempt.
Or again, he may act with self-will; because of this self-will, he violates the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).

Whether in a village or a city, among crowds of people, he acts according to his own whims and shows no restraint toward other bhikṣus. Seeing many women, he gives rise to doubt and suspicion; his mind becomes agitated as he gazes upon those women.
When worldly people see this, they give rise to criticism and disdain.
Seeing others criticize and disdain him, he gives rise to anger and resentment; in this way, a second fault of anger arises within the bhikṣu’s mind.
In this way, because the bhikṣu is shrouded by the desire for anger, his mind becomes deluded.
Thus, when a renunciant who wanders alone practices the life of a śramaṇa among people, these three faults increase.
Therefore, one should not walk alone among people; this is the first kind.
"Furthermore, the second is the non-transgressor monk.
Such a monk walks while maintaining mindfulness of the body."
When this bhikṣu walks on the road while practicing desirelessness, he maintains focused mindfulness upon his own body, thinking thus:
"As I lift this foot, my mind and mental factors observe that foot."
In this way, the bhikṣu observes every part of his body from the feet to the head.
Whether he lifts his right foot or his left foot, he constantly contemplates how this body is bound by a network of vessels, and how the ankles are bound by fat, bone, skin, and sinews.
Driven by the winds of karma, the mind does not cease; whether lifting or lowering, extending or contracting, when the foot is raised it is gathered, and when the foot is lowered it is relaxed.
Such as this foot is, it is bound together by a network of tendons; the five fingers, both large and small, are joined to form the foot, and the old nails and new nails combine to form the instep.
Having observed the instep, one next observes the shank, which is like the stalk of a sugar-cane with its juice condensed.
It is sealed and smeared with flesh-paste, bound together by sinews; the cavities within the bones are long, and the sinews wind around their exterior.
Born from prior causes and conditions, it is covered with hair upon the skin.
Externally there is a mass of hair, and the skin, like the wing of a fly, covers the exterior of the shank.
He thus contemplates that shank as it is, being raised and lowered, as he walks back and forth along his place of practice, causing the body to come and go.
"Next, one further observes that this body's two thighs are a composite of sinews, blood, fat, flesh, bones, and so forth.
Observing in this way, one sees that the mind and its mental factors are moved and set in motion by the winds of karma."
"Furthermore, he observes these two thighs of his body: they are thicker than the calves, with abundant muscle tissue intertwined and bound together.

They are smeared with flesh and plastered over with flesh; blood has rotted into a liquid, and this liquid fat fills their interior. Seeing only the outer skin, the mind gives rise to attachment and defilement."
When lifting one foot to step forward, observe it as it truly is; then lift the second foot. Observe the second foot in the same manner:
when the foot is lifted, it is drawn in; when placed upon the ground, it is extended; and it may be either stretched out or bent.
In this sequence, one observes everything—the solid parts and the hollow parts—whether they are about to move or have already moved; all such various phenomena are driven by wind.
Above the two feet, there are things like vessels containing the internal "cooked organs," namely the impure foul fluids of excrement and urine.
All that is seen is neither solid nor pure.
Because it moves on two feet, that jar follows along, and all the various objects contained within it likewise follow.
As he walks, he thus maintains mindfulness in accordance with his practice.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, shaking his body against that upper jar, observes as he walks and reflects:
"How do I walk? How does my upper body move as I walk?"
He contemplates the large and small intestines.

He sees that when he lifts his foot, the breath moves along with the intestines; the large and small intestines all shift and turn, sometimes moving from the left side to the right side, and sometimes moving from the right side to the left side.
In this way, within the intestines there are wind, bile, and cold; they are filled with excrement, urine, and worms, and the intestines themselves are in motion.
Furthermore, having observed the movement, that bhikṣu observes the area above those intestines as it truly is.
The entire stomach is bound by a net of sinews, with networks of vessels entwining it from above, below, and on all sides; within it are putrid froth, food, drink, and fluids.
That food is like freshly vomited cold froth, covered by the stomach and filling its interior, possessing a supreme stench; it connects upward to the throat, supported by sinews, vessels, and bones.
"Only the wind of karma, together with the mind and mental factors, accompanies and sustains its movement.
"Thus, having observed the body in this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the movement of the body."
"The parietal bones, dental bones, cranial bones, and so forth within my body combine to form the head.
There are two eye-balls, which together constitute the head."
"The fat in her eyes is abundant, and her eyelashes never cease their blinking.
As I now observe this woman’s body, its sinews and skin are bound together like a wooden post entwined with ropes.
Moment by moment it arises and perishes; it recedes and vanishes, only to emerge once more.
He goes for alms among villages, towns, and cities to maintain the casket of his body, as one would maintain a casket for a snake.
Thus he maintains his body, not for the sake of desire, nor out of greed for food, nor out of attachment to flavors.
Thus does that bhikṣu practice; thus does a second bhikṣu of diligent effort not transgress against the Dharma.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu enters among the many people dwelling in villages, towns, and market settlements to beg for alms.
Having finished begging for alms, he contemplates his body in this manner, observing all women and men in this same way.
As he is able to thus skillfully cultivate and practice, he exerts diligent effort; his mind desires detachment, and [sensuous thoughts] do not enter his mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu has well-tamed faculties; he is superior and not inferior.
In this way, a bhikṣu aspires for benefit and does not transgress the practice of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the third type of practicing bhikṣu is one who constantly cultivates right mindfulness.
A bhikṣu who possesses right mindfulness has a mind that is not distracted; he is a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), always possessing a benevolent mind and an undistracted mind.
Such a bhikṣu is constantly followed by the devas, and the celestial Māras cannot create obstacles or disturbances for him.
What is right mindfulness?
It refers to knowing the movement of desire.

When mental states and their concomitants have already arisen or are about to arise, one is thus able to know with an undistracted mind, understanding all that should be attended to and all that should not be attended to.
Regarding all mental states and mental factors—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—he knows them all, and his mind reflects thus:
"These various wholesome dharmas of mine arise due to causes and conditions; that is to say, they shall bring me benefit, peace, and happiness, even unto nirvāṇa."
I shall now destroy other unwholesome dharmas; because my wholesome dharmas serve as the causes and conditions for the arising of the mind and mental factors, they thereby destroy the unwholesome.
If these unwholesome dharmas were not destroyed, they would cause me disadvantage and lack of peace at a later time.
"In this way, one knows wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they truly are; having known them, one reflects upon them.
Such phenomena, known by the mind and intellect, are examined in their various aspects."
“There are five kinds of mindfulness that are not relished and not clung to, wherein the mind does not engage in discrimination, and one neither recollects nor delights in what was previously done.
What are these five kinds of mindfulness?
This refers to mindfulness of the eye and forms.

If a desirable object comes before one—the form that is the domain of the eye, whether near or far, beautiful or ugly, previously seen or brought by others—these various kinds of forms [are to be observed].
Having seen this, the bhikṣu does not relish it; his mind does not contemplate what causes and conditions brought it about.
He abandons those causes and conditions, no differently than a person who, fearing being burned, avoids fire.
Thus, a bhikṣu fears being burned by the fire of desire; at the time of initial attachment, there is much joy and delight, but later there is much suffering.
He no longer dwells upon the sensory objects he formerly relished; his mind does not dwell on them, his mind does not discriminate them, and they do not abide in his mind.

Regarding the forms one has personally cherished since the beginning, one no longer thinks of them nor discriminates between them; likewise, regarding the forms of others that are either loathed or cherished, the mind does not dwell upon them, nor does it attend to others.
Regarding the forms contemplated by others, his mind does not seek them either.
Thus, he restrains both himself and his disciples; by preventing attachment and the arising of sympathetic joy, he causes them to abide in the Right Path.
Such a bhikṣu is called pure; with right mindfulness and free from greed, he practices in accordance with the dharmas that are undefiled.
Thus, the bhikṣu’s eye does not cling to forms.
"Furthermore, monks, the second mindfulness refers to the mindfulness of the ear and sounds.

Thus, a monk observes with right mindfulness: if the ear hears sounds that are extremely pleasant—such as the sounds of singing or dancing, or the sounds of drumming, clapping hands, and various forms of entertainment."
Regarding what has been heard in the past, one does not dwell upon it nor savor it; the mind neither delights in attachment nor discriminates regarding the causes and conditions of having heard it.
One abandons those causes and conditions no differently than one who fears being burned abandons fire.

In this way, the bhikṣu abandons those sounds—whether sounds heard from others or from his own brothers—and restrains them all, establishing them in the wholesome path, while his mind feels no approval for them.
In this way, a bhikṣu benefits both himself and others, and does not crave sounds.
Because of his superior mindfulness, he is not attached to sound.
This is called the second right mindfulness of a bhikṣu; thus, the bhikṣu’s ear is not attached to sound.
"Furthermore, the third mindfulness of a bhikṣu is the arousal of diligence.
With right intention and tranquility, he maintains the holy life and observes the precepts; in this way, the bhikṣu does not dwell on them nor relish them, and no such thoughts arise in his mind."

Whether it be natural fragrance or incense smoke, whether fragrant or foul, pure or impure, distant or near—one does not think of any of these. Having no mind toward fragrance, one asks: "By what causes and conditions has it come? and thus abandons those causes and conditions.

Whether it be another person or one's own disciple, if they should smell a fragrance and give rise to attachment to its flavor, such a bhikṣu shall immediately restrain them and not rejoice in their minds.

Practicing wholesome karma oneself and causing others to abide in wholesome dharmas, one’s mind is constantly well-attentive; one practices correctly without greed and does not crave fragrances with the nose.
Such a bhikṣu is called one who has removed defilements, who skillfully cultivates and maintains the precepts, and whose mind gives rise to wholesome thoughts.

"Furthermore, monks, as for the fourth mindfulness: regarding various flavors previously experienced—whether pleasant or unpleasant, whether long-standing or recent—one does not dwell upon those flavors, does not savor those flavors, and the mind does not discriminate as to what causes and conditions brought them about."
He abandons those causes and conditions, no differently than one who fears being burned would abandon fire.
If he observes others or his own disciples becoming attached to the taste [of sensory pleasures], such a bhikṣu shall then restrain them and not rejoice in their minds.

This is called a bhikṣu who is not attached to flavors, who maintains right mindfulness and right conduct, who abandons all evils, who practices virtuous precepts, and who benefits both himself and others.
"Furthermore, the fifth mindfulness of a bhikṣu is as follows:

Regarding the tactile sensations previously experienced and encountered in the past—those sensations that give rise to defilement through pleasure, softness, and smoothness—one does not become stained by or relish those objects of desire;
the mind does not conceptualize what causes or conditions have brought them about.
One should abandon those causes and conditions, no differently than one who fears being burned abandons fire.
If another person’s body is greedily touched or defiled by attachment, do not give rise to sympathetic joy, but skillfully contemplate the nature of touch.

This is called a bhikṣu who is pure through detachment from contact; he is said to be one who well maintains the precepts, practices wholesome dharmas, and is rightly established, proceeding by stages even unto nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, that bhikṣu has five further recollections which he should practice. What are the five?
First, the recollection of time."
2. mindfulness of youth;
3. mindfulness of birth and death;
4. mindfulness of the complete loss, decay, and disintegration [of all things].
5. Mindfulness of Nirvana: desiring to reach Nirvana.
How does such a bhikṣu practice mindfulness?
It means that this bhikṣu constantly practices with focused mindfulness at all times; he is not deluded by sense objects, is not destroyed by sense objects, and does not lose or scatter his mind.
The bhikṣu does not attend to this day or this night; likewise, he does not attend to or know such divisions of time.
At the time of awakening, his exhalations and inhalations are associated with the mind and are never separated from it.
Just as with the inhalation and exhalation, he knows with certainty down to even a single thought-moment:
"The two breaths, inhalation and exhalation, are within my belly; therefore, my belly either expands or contracts."
"Because of the two breaths, my aggregates, bases, and elements are maintained.
All conditioned phenomena do not abide for even a single moment; the aggregates, elements, and bases emerge from warmth.

These arise together with the vital energy and perish together with the vital energy; they are destroyed and utterly decayed, yet at a later time they arise again through different causes and conditions. Thus, the vital energy arises and perishes simultaneously, not abiding for even a single moment.
When that mindful bhikṣu reflects in this way, his mindfulness becomes focused and integrated.

Thus observing for himself the elements, aggregates, sense bases, and so forth, as they are gathered and assembled, he sees that they do not abide for even a single moment, but consist of nothing but suffering and affliction.
All parts of the body have no agent and no experiencer; they arise together in equality through mutual causes and conditions.
Such a body flows on from moment to moment; within each moment, the various formations of birth, death, and aging decay accumulate.
In this way, the bhikṣu’s practice is not in vain.
When a bhikṣu practices mindfulness in this manner, by virtue of that mindfulness, he will certainly and inevitably attain four kinds of purity: the purity of single-mindedness.
Because the mind is pure, the facial complexion is pure; because wholesome karma is pure, there will be future benefit, proceeding in succession until reaching nirvana.
Furthermore, when others see that he maintains the precepts, those donors will experience supreme joy and give rise to a pure mind.

“Thus, for these four kinds of bhikṣus who uphold the precepts, when they contemplate this true meaning with purity, because all such things are universally pure, they shall obtain peaceful sleep, see auspicious dreams while lying down, and remain in accordance with the Dharma.”
He constantly practices in this way with non-negligence; because of this non-negligence, he attains seven kinds of qualities. What are the seven?
First, he is unimpeded regarding the Dharma; as he contemplates wholesome dharmas, his mind rejoices in those wholesome karmas, and that joy increases.
Due to the causes and conditions of joy, the body becomes robust and flourishing.
Because the body is robust and flourishing, the two phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serve as reciprocal causes and conditions;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, the body becomes robust and flourishing, and the body is free from illness.
When body and mind rely upon each other in alternation, one becomes wise and intelligent.
Regarding what is called wisdom and intelligence: it consists in recollecting one's original actions; because of such recollection, wisdom and intelligence increase.
Because one contemplates wholesome dharmas, they thus increase.
Having reflected in this way, joy also increases;
because joy increases, strength also increases.
Because these seven qualities thus increase, one sleeps peacefully at night;
because one sleeps peacefully at night, one cultivates the body and cultivates the mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu reflects during the night.
“How does a bhikṣu attend to the daytime?
In this way, a bhikṣu attends to the opening and closing of his eyes:
‘I am mindful that when the eyes are closed, the time has passed; thus he is mindful that it has passed.’”
In this manner, the temporal factors, together with the mind and its mental concomitants, perish simultaneously and are all utterly dispersed and destroyed.
Thus, these temporal factors successively vanish; whether perishing or arising, within the duration of a single exhalation, life has already come to an end.
The time of my old age is now approaching in due course; my youth has already been exhausted.
As I draw near to the remainder of my existence, I am gradually and inevitably approaching the time of death.
Before long, I shall lose all my life; no skillful means can prevent this.
All sentient beings are enemies without cause or condition, seeking to destroy one's life.
It is like lighting a lamp: the fire consumes the ghee and oil, extinguishing them moment by moment.
In this very way, the fire of old age and death burns the ghee and oil of life, extinguishing it moment by moment.
Thus, having fixed one's mindfulness and realized impermanence, one diligently cultivates wholesome dharmas.

These internal phenomena are likewise swift: moment by moment they are impermanent, moment by moment they perish and cease; they deceive those who give rise to craving, for moment by moment they utterly decay.
As it is with internal phenomena, so it is with external ones; all conditioned phenomena in the world are swift and impermanent, perishing moment by moment.
Thus, these mountains, rivers, cities, towns, villages, medicinal herbs, gardens, and groves—within the realms of all humans and all devas—must inevitably be lost and destroyed.
"In this way, these groves, lotus ponds, and rivers have already been lost, are now being lost, and will continue to be lost by all the devas who act with negligence."
Because he was ruined by negligence, he fell into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where his own karma matured. "In this way, bhikṣu!"
Regarding all such immeasurable fluctuations and movements of the world, which are characterized by destruction and impermanence, one does not allow the mind to become distracted.

Even for a single moment, the mind remains constantly undistracted; with firm mindfulness, right mindfulness remains undisturbed, and with single-minded, discerning observation, the correct intention remains undistracted.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu maintains right mindfulness at that time:
"With such deportment and such correct conduct,
I shall rise at this time."
"At this time I practice meditation.
"At such a time I approach the Venerable One. "At this time I eat."
"At this time I shall put on my robes;
at this time I shall go to the house of the donor and preach the Dharma for them;
at this time I shall leave the house of the donor and proceed in such a manner."
"Thus, a bhikṣu reflects upon the time of walking.
How does a bhikṣu reflect upon youth?
It means that this bhikṣu reflects upon himself, even down to the time he was within the womb, reflecting on such youth."

In successive continuity, this small body proceeds thus without ceasing from moment to moment: first as the *kalala*, then the *arbuda*, then the stage of the flesh-mass (*peśī*), then the stage of limbs (*ghana*), then infancy, then childhood, then middle age, and finally old age.
Such is the nature of phenomena: it does not remain still for even a single moment, proceeding through a succession of subtle bodies.
During these moments of thought, foolish ordinary beings fail to perceive or understand this; they are ruined by negligence and, adrift on the river of craving, are swept away by the waters of doubt.

Having been thus swept away, one falls again among a multitude of beings with similar karma in another place; bound by the shackles of karma, one continues to flow and transmigrate, being born yet again in other places.
Furthermore, through the performance of one's own karma, it binds itself to its own body and mind, and within the mother’s semen and blood, it becomes an *aṇḍa* (embryonic stage).
Next, during the stage of the flesh-mass, it gradually unfolds until the limbs and parts are fully formed.
Having been born into the human realm, one passes through the stages of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, until death.

In this manner, for a single individual, such successive transitions occur; throughout all the desire realms and across all paths, each with its particular distinctions, it is the wind of karma that drives those sentient beings, causing them to sequentially attain states from youth onwards.
Such are the distinctions of one's own karma.
In this way, the bhikṣu reflects upon youth.
Furthermore, the third reflection of the bhikṣu is that through diligent practice, he will certainly attain it.
Upon what phenomena does he reflect?
Namely, on birth and death.
Whether by day or by night, he constantly practices [this reflection]: "All sentient beings, until their very end, possess life and must die."
All sentient beings within the three realms are subject to the impermanent laws of birth and death; they are afflicted by conditioned phenomena, suffering, and the separation from those they love.
Having declined from the heavens, they fall into hell.
Emerging from the hells, they are born in the heavens.
If they die among humans, they are born in the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or among devas and humans.
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are born within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.

Thus, blown by the winds of karma—moving upward, downward, or sideways—they revolve and proceed; their own karma having brought them to fruition, they wander and circulate within the ocean of birth and death.

In this way, a bhikṣu cultivates the mindfulness of birth and death, whether by day or by night. Having cultivated it thus, if he should harbor conceit—which constantly causes people to be deluded and delights in the false—[he will not attain liberation].
By means of right mindfulness, this conceit becomes either thin or is entirely extinguished.
The foremost and supreme mindfulness is that which contemplates arising and passing away; therefore, those who wish to enter the city of Nirvāṇa should practice this mindfulness.
Why is this? Because of the conceit of "I," the mind is constantly deluded; seeking permanence through inversion, one perpetually wanders in transmigration within birth and death.
Bound by the snare of craving, that state of permanence can never be attained.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Having attained liberation from the fear of craving, Free from all expectations,
The courageous one who has abandoned doubt Is able to attain the eternal abode."
If one sinks into the waters of existence, with a mind always delighting in desire, that person’s mind is delusory; how can they attain a permanent abode?
If a person possesses a delusory mind and finds delight within the sensory realms, [they shall not escape].
That person, deluded regarding the path of the Dharma, will be born within the hells.
Heedlessness obstructs and confuses the mind, preventing one from seeing reality as it truly is.
Heedlessness is like fire; therefore, one should abandon it.
Through heedlessness, one can lose the treasury of all wholesome dharmas;
though one exhausts every means, one will not see the Eightfold Path.
All ten qualities are ruined for one who delights in the poison of heedlessness.
Furthermore, because of negligence, one loses all four dhyānas.
Negligence binds sentient beings; it can bind though it is not material.
That which is constantly present is pleasure; by abandoning negligence, one attains it.
"If a person’s mind is not deluded and always fears birth and death,
they shall escape the evil realms and attain peaceful tranquility.
"Practicing in this way, one maintains mindfulness of birth and mindfulness of decline."
Having thus practiced the mindfulness of birth and death, one is never deluded.

Having observed that all conditioned phenomena in the world are subject to arising and passing away, one becomes weary of and detached from birth and death; having performed various contemplations, one observes that the suffering of birth and death has immeasurable varieties.

Regarding all these various kinds of negligence among the sentient beings of the world, whenever one abandons such negligence, one is able at all times to contemplate impermanence and contemplate exhaustion and cessation; having seen exhaustion and cessation, one contemplates mindfulness of the Buddha.
Such a person is then able to exhaust suffering.

Furthermore, monks, the fourth mindfulness is as follows: it is the practice of reflecting that all forms of prosperity are subject to total ruin, and thus one contemplates the destruction of all such prosperity.
This mindful bhikṣu does not delight in gain and offerings, nor does he crave the coming and going of donors; he likewise does not delight in seeing kings or great ministers.
Even if he should see a king, he does not give rise to a mind of attachment, and his love cannot obstruct him.

Furthermore, throughout day and night, they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination; regarding the bedding and other requisites possessed by others, their minds do not discriminate, nor do they conceive a longing for them as their own property.
"Having seen this, one does not give rise to envy, but thinks in one's mind:
'Such sentient beings are certain to die; all that they possess will inevitably perish.'"
In this way, as they fully increase, craving likewise increases.
Furthermore, because such fullness is lost, one longs for it to be regained; thus, through immeasurable kinds and immeasurable conceptualizations, the mind gives rise to suffering and distress.
"The suffering of that person is beyond analogy.

"In this way, bhikṣu, one observes the complete ruin [of such states]. Having observed this, one thereafter no longer aspires to the rank of a celestial king, much less to that of a human king or a wheel-turning monarch."
Why is this? Because one sees the suffering of immeasurable kinds of ruin and destruction.

Even if a king, a high minister, or a great elder of a prominent Kṣatriya clan is endowed with all manner of prosperity, yet another who possesses greater power may destroy it; thus, all that was fully possessed is lost, and wife, children, servants, guests, and others abandon them.
Because they have lost their wealth and property, they suffer great decline and distress;
because others are powerful and victorious, they become inferior and diminished.

Wandering everywhere through the four-way streets, their hands and feet are cracked, their lips are parched, and their clothes are tattered; famished, thirsty, and emaciated, with bodies withered and dry, they travel from city to city, from village to village, from mountain to mountain, and from one borderland to another, undergoing such immeasurable varieties of suffering.
Having thus observed this, the bhikṣu further reflects and develops a sense of weary detachment toward the realm of birth and death, seeing it as a place of immeasurable precipices and evil states.
