"In this way, a bhikṣu further observes how all manner of things among human beings, though once complete, are subject to ruin. Seeing this, he reflects by analogy upon the celestial realms: 'If such immeasurable and manifold fears exist among humans—where one lacks self-mastery and suffers from the afflictions of swords, thieves, water, fire, and kings, and where even abundant wealth and prosperity are lost—how much more so must it be for those born in the celestial realms that are free from flesh, bones, and impurities? "

They are adorned with celestial flower garlands upon their heads and surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas. Many countless hosts of celestial maidens engage in play, singing, and dancing, laughing joyfully as they enjoy themselves. In the celestial gardens, lotus ponds, and mountain peaks, there is the radiance of the seven treasures; they gather to perform music, enjoying the sounds of the five musical instruments and various celestial songs. The halls and palaces, interspersed with the seven treasures, emit light at all times. Their bodies possess immeasurable varieties of ever-surpassing, sublime qualities that are beyond all analogy.

Within the celestial realm, they achieve the enjoyment of bliss; they love one another and are free from strife; whatever they desire or think of, they obtain it all; and through the sounds of the five musical instruments, their hearts experience joy and happiness.
If such enjoyments are thus lost and destroyed, one will experience suffering and affliction;
because one's karma is exhausted, one falls again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

As they are about to fall, their successive births proceed without interval; having long since performed immeasurable kinds of actions, they experience suffering and affliction in all of them, and are born again in other places, undergoing various forms of suffering and affliction.

If such a deva is born in hell, the powerful and blazing fires within that hell will burn his body on all sides; he will suffer from extreme hunger and thirst, experiencing great agony beyond all analogy.

Having performed the karma of the hells and completed the path of such action, they see themselves falling into the seven great hells—namely Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, and Pratāpana—excluding only the greatest hell, Avīci.
Being separated from the means of livelihood gives rise to great suffering and distress; seeing such matters of suffering and distress, that suffering and distress cannot be fully described.
Thus, a bhikṣu constantly at all times, day and night, practices with such right mindfulness.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates how such wealth and the necessities of life are subject to loss and destruction; practicing this mindfulness, he reflects that such things exist among gods and humans, whereas in the other three realms there are no such material resources or means of subsistence—how could there even be any loss?"
That which is called hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm contains but a small measure of pleasure comparable to that found among humans, yet it is not sovereign.
"In those human states, there are five kinds of perfections that may be lost."
What are the five? They are:
regarding forms with the eye, if there is craving or delight, one seeks them upon seeing; having sought them, one becomes attached to their flavor; and for the sake of pleasure, one grasps them.
One who is thus inverted and lacks benefit does not find delight; seeing impure forms, their mind feels aversion toward those forms, and for this reason, there is no joy.
Thus, this fulfillment and that ruin share the same root.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, in accordance with his focused mindfulness, possesses ruin. What is this fulfillment?

What is ruin? It refers to hearing sounds with the ear; having heard the sounds with the ear, one complies with those sounds, associates with them with craving and delight, and gives rise to joy in the mind—thus it is fully present.
Furthermore, there are distinct causes and conditions for the sounds one hears, namely the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Regarding sounds produced by these four great elements, if the mind does not find delight in them, if joy is not born, if they are contrary to the mind, and if they do not benefit the mind, this is called "ruination."

"Furthermore, that bhikṣu hears the fragrance of fine flowers, blended powdered incense, and various mixed perfumes; smelling these and other such diverse fragrances, he experiences pleasure in accordance with his mind."
Due to those fragrances as conditions, a mind of pleasure arises, which is able to cause desire to manifest.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, binding his mindfulness in contemplation, contemplates that recollection of fragrance by reflecting on how that person’s nose smells various scents.

Each of those various odors is of immeasurable kinds; that is to say, there are putrid stench and odors contrary to the mind, such as the countless foul smells of excrement and urine, which the mind finds neither pleasant nor joyful.
In such a way, that person’s things are lost and destroyed.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, with a concentrated mind and focused mindfulness, perceives another kind of complete destruction within the world.
What is the binding of mindfulness?

Regarding the attachment to the taste of flavors in the human world, one experiences mental delight and joy; the flavors are easily digested, and once digested, they bring comfort. One obtains life, physical luster, strength, happiness, and eloquence, whereby joy arises in the mind.

Furthermore, if there are other flavors that are not pleasing, which are contrary to one's heart and unpleasant, and which are difficult to digest and cause mental discomfort, they will be of little benefit to life, complexion, strength, well-being, eloquence, and resources, and will produce only suffering and affliction.
"For that person, these things will thus be lost and destroyed.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu again contemplates bodily contacts that are lovely and delightful: obtaining warmth when it is cold, obtaining coolness when it is hot, and experiencing pleasure in accordance with his mind.
In this human world, such things are fully present.

Due to other causes and conditions, they further cause the body to encounter what is undesirable and unpleasant, so that the mind finds no joy; when it is hot, there is no coolness, and when it is cold, there is no warmth. Contrary to one's heart, one undergoes suffering, feeling neither delight nor pleasure, but giving rise only to distress.
Among the people of the world, these five kinds of perfections are thus ruined.
A bhikṣu should practice with mindfulness, whether by day or by night.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 45.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 46, translated by the Uighur Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part 25; Yāma Heaven, Section 11.

"Furthermore, that bhikṣu again contemplates the desirable objects within the heavens, which arise from the conjunction of the sense faculties, are blown by the winds of conceptualization, increase repeatedly, and are consumed by the fire of craving."
Ordinary people of the world, craving the pleasures of that realm, give rise to such thoughts as:
"The heavens are exceedingly joyful.
In this same way, a bhikṣu binds his mindfulness and reflects:
"Those devas have perished.
Thus, the bhikṣu does not give rise to craving or delight toward those lovely objects, and his mind is free from feverish distress.
In this way, with the foremost wholesome intention, the bhikṣu sees that all six classes of desire-realm devas have utterly perished.
"In those four celestial abodes, there are twelve kinds of calamities:
first, inferiority of strength;
second, constant fighting with the asuras, wherein those asuras suddenly arrive in the darkness and enter their midst."
Third, it means that during the battle, they strike the armor and mail worn upon the bodies of those gods by the asuras;
fourth, it means that during the battle, they seize the helmets and crests worn upon their heads and cause them to fall into the ocean;
fifth, it means that once [the enemy] has been defeated, they feel shame and remorse.
Sixth, it is that at the time of fighting, upon seeing Rāhula, they give rise to alarm and fear;
seventh, it is that at the time of retreat, those celestial maidens abandon them and depart toward other sons of gods;
eighth, it is that at the time of eating, due to their own karma, upon seeing inferior food, they give rise to shame and embarrassment.
Ninth, regarding the size, color, shape, and ornaments of their military hosts, which correspond to their own karma, they feel shame when others are inferior;
tenth, when those gods are at play, the birds born in that celestial realm also treat those who are inferior with contempt;
eleventh, inferior gods must travel on foot toward the places of recreation.

12. Regarding the tactile objects of desire experienced by inferior devas, these correspond to their own karma; however, the ornaments of others are superior and exquisite. Because they see the superiority of others, they give rise to shame and embarrassment.

In the realm of the Four Great Kings, there are these twelve kinds of ruin; thus, a bhikṣu who has well-cultivated his mind does not crave celestial pleasures, but observes those heavens with an undefiled mind.
Having observed this, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and reviles celestial desires.
If there is someone who practices the holy life (brahmacarya) out of a longing for heaven, such a holy life is not the cause of the holy life.
Such persons as these are held in contempt by those bhikṣus. Why is this?
Because they lack self-mastery.
"Furthermore, that bhikṣu observes the destruction of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
He sees eight kinds of destruction within the Heaven of the Thirty-three. What are these eight?
First, they are inferior in armor; when fighting against the asuras, impurities fall from them.
Second, during battle, upon seeing their enemy leader, the courageous asura, their hearts become weak with retreat.
Third, at the time of eating, the inferior one feels shame and embarrassment.
Fourth, the inferior deva is not recognized by Śakra, the King of Devas.
Fifth, the color, strength, and physical form of the inferior deva are all inferior.
Sixth, the inferior devas possess inferior sounds, tactile sensations, forms, tastes, and fragrances, which do not equal those of others.
Seventh, when inferior devas fall from their celestial realm, the celestial maidens abandon them.
Eighth, when inferior devas ascend to the halls for recreation, their supernormal powers (ṛddhi) become deficient, and they are unable to proceed swiftly.
These are the eight ways in which the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three suffer loss and ruin.
"In the Yāma Heaven, there are six forms of ruin. What are these six?
First, when it is time to eat, those who are inferior feel shame."
Second, the goddesses do not accept the commands of inferior gods.
Third, because inferior gods possess little merit and karma, even though the host of goddesses makes offerings to them, it is not as [efficacious] as making offerings to those with great merit.
Fourth, when the inferior devas hear the Dharma being taught by Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, their minds do not find delight in it.
This is the greatest failure among them.

Fifth, because the karma of inferior devas was meager, their radiance changes; however, if a deva practiced many wholesome deeds in a previous life, that deva will sit upon a great sapphire throne and rise again after sitting.
The gods of inferior karma sit there, and their seats transform into silver.
Due to the variety of their karma, they undergo such ruin; the sixth [type of ruin] is diminution of stature.
These six kinds constitute the matters of ruin for the Yāma Heaven.
“The Tuṣita Heaven has four kinds of decline. What are the four?
First, when the inferior devas hear the Dharma in Tuṣita, their hearts do not rejoice; they do not delight in the sound of the Goose King preaching the Dharma—this is called a decline.
Within Tuṣita, the king of geese constantly dwells in the ground of untainted bliss.
That king of geese is a bodhisattva who has taken birth by his own will; therefore, he manifests as a king of geese with a color that appears at will.
The body of the goose was filled with the radiance of the seven treasures, its color beyond all comparison; the light from its body pervaded five thousand *yojanas* and displayed various hues.
The radiance of the Tuṣita Heaven could not compare to that of the Goose King, who surpassed them all and caused the hearts of those devas to be filled with wonder.
“After that Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, had caused those [gods] to give rise to a sense of wonder, he immediately preached the Dharma to them in verse, saying:
‘When the karma of merit is exhausted, Life then swiftly diminishes;
One should always act thus in Tuṣita: Diligently apply effort and gather the Dharma.’”
If one abandons the Dharma and is ruined by negligence,
failing to accumulate meritorious karma, one will later feel regret.
Even before old age arrives, and while neither sickness nor death has yet come, [one must practice].
All should cultivate merit; do not harbor regrets later.
If one does not gather merit but is ruined by negligence, then because of being ruined by negligence, one will suffer in hell.
Having obtained the full endowment of the faculties, yet practicing what is not the Dharma—
what use are life and wealth, or kinsmen, relatives, and brothers?
Constantly cultivate merit and virtue, and let the mind be receptive to the Dharma.
Or else one may cease from evil deeds, or at times draw near to virtuous people.
With the sharp sword of wisdom, one cuts away the branches and leaves of evil;
one destroys the accumulation of faults and sever the continuity of transgressions.
Valuing wisdom, precepts, and merit, the mind harbors no desire for material things;
one should always associate with virtuous men who show the path of truth.
If, while observing the precepts, one is reborn in heaven yet remains deluded by sensual desires, [one will not attain liberation].
Those who do not cultivate meritorious deeds always wander within the realms of existence.
Those who ever delight in wisdom and are adorned with the jewel of the precepts,
and who fear the serpent of desire— they are the Gods among Gods.
Those who constantly practice the Dharma are worthy of the devas' prostrations;
those who act with perversion fall into the evil realms.
This shore and the far shore are distant, but once the bridge of Dharma has been obtained—
If one does not cross over swiftly, one shall not be liberated from existence (*bhava*).
The fire of wisdom can burn the immeasurable fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*);
for what purpose are you bound by afflictions, clinging to those objects of craving?
The heavy and thick defilement of desire obstructs the eye of wisdom;
the Buddha’s word is like a potent medicine, capable of removing those obstructions.
The great general of the True Dharma can destroy the army of the thieves of desire.
I shall speak words of the sublime Dharma; you should listen and receive them with diligence.
There are four kinds of perversions that can constantly deceive and delude;
there are eight worldly dharmas that can cause all things to be lost.
Within the great river of craving, one cannot cross over a hundred doubts;
yet one who possesses the raft of superior wisdom crosses over and reaches tranquility.
If a deva is close to desire, that desire can cause the mind to become deluded.
Constantly dwelling in the five realms, there is no time for liberation.
Desire is difficult to obtain and easily destroyed; like lightning, what use is it?
The suffering born of desire is like a sword, like the *kimpāka* fruit, fire, or poison.
In this way, as they draw near, they likewise increase;
desire can never be satisfied, just as fire consumes fuel.
Foolish devas long for sensual pleasure, unaware of the fear of being consumed by their transgressions.
If one is free from unwholesome desire, one will attain great happiness later on.
But the deluded, having become stained by desire, are firmly bound by it;
like lightning, desire does not remain the same, and then it departs for another place.
If one associates with desire, then desire becomes ever more intense;
scorched by the fire of desire, one reaches the place of burning.
If a deva draws near to desire, this mind is utterly deluded.
Not longing for dharmas that lack intrinsic nature is the greatest bliss among all pleasures.
For those possessed by desire, there is no nirvāṇa; there is neither bliss nor liberation.
Therefore, do not draw near to desire; to draw near to desire is most evil.
If one draws near to the realm of desire, the senses will never know contentment;
without contentment there is no joy, and tranquility cannot be attained.
One should fear the conditioned state, this great ocean of birth and death.
Because of great and evil desire and craving, which are ever-present within sentient beings,
he dwells upon such mountain peaks where various lovely trees stand;
relying upon them, he practices dhyāna and contemplates the arising and ceasing of desire.
The wise who skillfully practice the tranquility of the four truths, Fearing birth, old age, and death, reach liberation on the far shore.
Those of deluded mind do not reflect; bound by the desire for pleasure, They remain in bondage.
Once sensual pleasures have been exhausted, one will surely be freed from birth, old age, and death.
If one reflects upon this great suffering, one will not grow weary within the ocean of existence;
yet, pierced by the arrows of desire through delusion, one falls into the evil places of hell.
Because of delighting in delusion and desire, one ultimately abandons peace and happiness;
not knowing fear toward evil, the time of death arrives like fire.
Even when the time of death arrives, it is able to destroy everything.
Because this can destroy, it destroys the seeds of life.
All that is beneficial and brings peace—therein a man should be diligent;
having attained happiness and being free from sorrow and grief, he should constantly perform wholesome deeds.
"If one removes the storehouse of desire, Leaves behind the fever and attains coolness,
With such wisdom and freedom from delusion, One will have no longing for desire.
Thus did the King of Geese speak these verses because he was taming the devas.
If a deva is negligent and acts with negligence, though they hear [the teaching], they do not keep it in mind nor contemplate it with their thoughts.

However, if a deva delights in hearing those verses of discipline spoken by the goose, they will swiftly proceed toward the state of outflowlessness (anāsrava-bhūmi), desiring to hear the True Dharma.
Having heard the true Dharma, they conceived a sense of reverence.
Thus, once these celestial hosts had heard the true Dharma and their minds were filled with reverence, they ran swiftly and hurriedly back toward the Hall of Practice.

All the devas within that Hall of Practice, because they have heard the True Dharma and their minds are filled with reverence, see their radiance increase a hundredfold and a thousandfold; the radiance of the other negligent devas, by contrast, is inferior.
Thus, within that celestial realm, one obtains the fruits of the present life.
For those who delight in celestial desires, the splendor of that heaven diminishes; their physical forms, attire, and all manner of adornments become inferior.
In this way, the Tuṣita Heaven is the first to fall into ruin.
"Furthermore, this is the second loss of Tuṣita Heaven.

When the assembly gathers to hear the Dharma, there is a great congregation numbering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions. At the place where five hundred bodhisattvas reside, the King of Tuṣita, named Śānta, preaches the Dharma for the assembly, namely: 'Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations,' and so forth."
When those hosts of devas listen to the True Dharma, they focus their minds with single-minded devotion, listening attentively and hearing clearly.
Because they hear it in this way, their majestic power and adornments all become superior by hundreds of thousands of times, increasing further and further.
If the mind of a deva wavers, that mind is like lightning and like the great waves stirred by a mighty wind blowing across the waters of the great ocean.

Due to the causal conditions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the mind thus wavers, delighting in sensory objects. Although the deva’s majesty, physical form, and ornaments remain as they were without change and do not further increase, he feels shame and humiliation in his heart upon seeing the superiority of others. This is called the second failure and ruin of the Tuṣita Heaven.
"Furthermore, this is the third destruction of the Tuṣita Heaven:
if the devas hear the Dharma, they conceive a heart of reverence; they understand according to what is taught and recognize it according to the characteristics of the Dharma."
Having understood this, his mind remains correctly established.
The celestial majesty, physical form, and adornments of that deity all become a hundred thousand times more excellent than before, increasing ever further.
If those devas do not keep the Dharma in mind, their divine majesty, physical forms, and ornaments will not increase; this is called the third ruin of the Tuṣita Heaven.
"Furthermore, this is the fourth failure regarding the Tuṣita Heaven.

When those devas hear the True Dharma, they give rise to a mind of reverence, recollect it with single-minded focus, embrace it in accordance with the Dharma, uphold it with concentrated attention, and practice accordingly."
Having reflected for a long time, they subsequently engage in practice.

Because those devas thus revere and honor the Dharma, by virtue of these superior causes and conditions and the power of hearing the Dharma, their majestic radiance, physical appearance, and attire become hundreds of thousands of times more excellent and sublime than before, increasing ever further in excellence.

If those devas hear this but are unable to practice accordingly, they see that the majesty, radiance, physical appearance, and adornments of others have increased and surpassed their own; consequently, they perceive that their own majesty, radiance, physical appearance, and adornments have not increased.

When those devas see the majestic power, radiance, and the excellence of the attire and ornaments of others increasing and surpassing their own, they feel shame and humiliation; this is called the fourth ruin of the Tuṣita Heaven.
“Furthermore, that bhikṣu thus observes the four kinds of destruction of the Tuṣita Heaven; having seen their destruction, he then observes the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and again sees its destruction.”
He sees that even such superior and wondrous pleasures of the devas are still subject to four kinds of ruin. What are these four?

Regarding the first point: because their wholesome karma is exhausted, their feet cast shadows while all other parts of their bodies are radiant with light, yet there is no such light upon the feet themselves.
Thus, those gods have shadows on their feet; when the gods of lesser radiance see the surrounding mountain-like brilliance of the other gods, they avoid and depart from them.
When the Victorious One of Radiance saw him, he smiled and spoke these words:
"This deva is base and inferior, for his wholesome karma has been exhausted.
Upon hearing this, the deva Foot-Shadow felt ashamed and was filled with sorrow, thinking to himself:
"Because my karma is exhausted, it is now thus.
All that is fully possessed must ultimately perish and be destroyed.
Just as in the human world, because there is day, there must inevitably be night, so too within this [realm], all that is fully possessed must ultimately perish and be destroyed.
If a person has life, they must inevitably face death; likewise, that which is fully possessed must inevitably be lost and destroyed.
Thus, in this world, there is nothing that is fully possessed and yet does not undergo loss and destruction.
This destruction is the first destruction of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*).
"Furthermore, there is the second destruction of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.
For example, the cotton and other fibers found among the people of Jambudvīpa are extremely soft; when stepped upon, they sink, and when lifted, they spring back up."
The ground in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) is likewise soft and supple.

When a deva’s retribution for their wholesome karma is exhausted, the ground is no longer soft; when they step upon it, their foot does not sink, and when they lift their foot, it does not rise. When other devas see this, they know that his karma has been exhausted.
A certain deva saw this and said to the other devas:
"The karma of that deva is exhausted; the time for his decline is approaching.
This is the second destruction of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
"Furthermore, this is the third destruction of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
When those Nirmāṇarati devas engage in play, if they go beneath a tree to enjoy themselves, the tree then rains down flowers upon them in that celestial realm."

These flowers are found everywhere upon the grounds of the pleasure groves; yet when a deva’s wholesome karma is about to be exhausted, the tree-flowers do not fall, nor do they scatter upon the ground.
When other devas see that the tree-flowers neither fall nor scatter on the ground, they say:
"This deva’s karma is exhausted; the time of his decline is approaching."
Having heard this, those devas were ashamed, distressed, and troubled, thinking to themselves:
"I am now about to fall; thus shall I be ruined.
This is the third ruin of the Nirmanarati devas.
"Furthermore, this is the fourth destruction of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
That realm of the Nirmāṇarati devas will certainly be destroyed; the excellence possessed within those heavens will certainly be destroyed.
What is the fourth excellence of those Nirmāṇarati devas that is destroyed?

That is to say, in each of the places where the devas dwell upon jeweled grounds, such jeweled grounds are pure and stainless, no different from a mirror; the body of a single deva appears in immeasurable locations, manifesting various reflections, various forms and garments, and various ornaments.

Just as the sun-disk in the world of humans is one, yet appears in countless places within lotus ponds across hundreds of thousands of various locations, so too does this celestial body appear everywhere throughout hundreds of thousands of jewel grounds, appearing exactly like the body itself.
If there is a deva whose wholesome karma is exhausted, his celestial body appears as a mere reflection within a single jewel-ground and does not appear everywhere.
Having thus perceived such ruin and destruction, other wise devas, seeing this, say:
"This deva, because his wholesome karma is exhausted, is about to fall and perish."
"This is the fourth destruction of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
'When the world is fully possessed of pleasures, One does not perceive their impending destruction.'"
Whatever is possessed will inevitably be lost, just as there must be night when the sun rises.
So too, such pleasure of possession will surely perish;
for one who knows no satisfaction in desires, craving lasts but a short time.
If the mind is fully possessed by craving, or if one constantly hopes for pleasure,
yet abandons that very craving, one will thus always obtain happiness.
Since the pleasures of celestial desires are never sufficient, one falls into the midst of hell.
"All things arise from craving; this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
If a person enters hell, whether a hundred times or a thousand times, it is because they were deceived by the net of craving that they incur such evil."
“Furthermore, those gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven undergo these four kinds of destruction.
Moreover, that bhikṣu further contemplates the four kinds of ruin within the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.”
When the wholesome karma of those devas is about to be exhausted and they are on the verge of falling away, there occurs a state of ruin.

In that celestial realm, many kinds of exquisite garlands serve as adornments; celestial flowers do not wither and cover the ground everywhere, their supreme and excellent fragrance being beyond comparison.
Those garland-adornments possess various colors and exquisite radiance; even the light of jewels does not equal one-sixteenth part of their brilliance.
Those garlands abound with seven-jeweled winged bees that constantly produce celestial songs at all times.

Likewise, in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, when the celestial karma is exhausted and the gods are about to fall, those jewel-winged bees emit unpleasant sounds and, abandoning the various flower fragrances of such gods, depart for other places.
Other devas of wisdom, knowing that this deva was about to fall from his station, said to him:
"Because of your negligence, the time for your downfall is now approaching, yet you do not perceive it."
Having heard this, the deva whose karma was exhausted saw that bee abandon its place and go elsewhere.
That deva knew within himself that he possessed such a thought:
"My meritorious karma is exhausted."

Thus, the sorrow and suffering that arose in the mind of this deva were beyond all analogy; because he saw that his own pleasures were about to end, his mind was so inflamed with heat that it was no different from the fires of hell—indeed, there is no such fire as this except in hell.
This is the first destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Furthermore, there is the second destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations.
The bodies of those gods possess a supreme smoothness to the touch and are surrounded by radiance; their forms are like the sun among men, yet appear like fireflies.

The radiance from the necklaces, as well as all other various ornaments worn by those devas, was reflected upon the jeweled walls and mountain peaks, appearing no differently than if they were being seen within a mirror.
When that deva is about to undergo his fall from heaven, the necklaces, ornaments, and other decorations adorning his body no longer appear within the mountain peaks or cliffs.
Having seen this, other wise devas spoke to that deva whose karma for remaining was exhausted and who was about to fall, saying:
"Your conduct has been heedless; the time of your downfall is at hand.
The necklaces and ornaments adorning your body no longer emit light, and the jeweled walls and mountain peaks are no longer visible within it."
That wise deva had previously seen other devas when they were about to fall from their state exhibit such signs.
This is the second destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations.
"Furthermore, this is the third destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

That is to say, when those gods are about to fall from that realm, those whose karma is not yet exhausted ride upon various precious and wondrous luminous palaces, capable of traveling through three locations: namely, through the sky, on land, and through water."
When walking, they are swift and unimpeded, neither wavering nor shaking.
However, when their celestial karma is exhausted and they are about to fall, those palaces waver and their movement becomes slow.
The other devas, seeing their palace tremble, said to them:
"The time for your downfall has now arrived; I have previously seen such signs when other devas were about to fall."

Having heard this, those devas whose karma was exhausted, about to part from their celestial realm, had their hearts consumed by the fire of sorrow, no different from being scorched by the fires of hell.
This is the third destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Furthermore, there is the fourth destruction within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations:

if the wholesome karma of those devas has not yet been exhausted, the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments and the sounds of their ornaments are all exquisite and beautiful; all their songs are lovely and pleasing, such that upon hearing them, their hearts rejoice.

If there is a deva whose wholesome karma is exhausted, the five kinds of musical sounds of that deva will no longer be exquisite, nor will the voices of song; they will be no different from those of a mute.
When that deva hears them, joy does not arise in his heart because of his own karma. Then, from among his ornaments, sounds emerge saying:
"Your wholesome karma is now exhausted and extinguished because of your negligence and your negligent conduct."
"Now you are about to depart for another world, bound by the power of karma.
Because of his own past actions, that deva heard the sound of these ornaments and his heart was filled with extreme grief, saying:
"Now my enjoyment of sensory realms and my meritorious karma are exhausted."
The turban adorned with various kinds of jewels immediately fell off; having seen this, they were overcome with great suffering and distress.
This is the fourth calamity within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
“Within the three realms, there is no place or thing that is permanent; all things are impermanent.
Thus, these six heavens are places of ruin and destruction. Because their wholesome karma is exhausted, those gods dwelling in such heavens will inevitably fall away from this state of ruin.”
"Those who hope to be born in this heaven by maintaining the precepts will certainly meet such a fate when their wholesome karma is exhausted.
Thus did the Night-Moving Lord (Mauśaladhara), King of the Yāma Heaven, show the scriptural words contained within the stūpa of the World-Honored One Kākaṇḍa to that assembly of devas, speaking thus:
"You, assembly of devas, abandon negligence; do not act with negligence!"
"The flavor of negligence is bitter; it is experienced within the hells. The flavor of all desires is exactly like this.
When those hosts of devas had heard the sutra spoken by the third Buddha, the negligence of those devas who were negligent and who delighted in negligence was diminished.
"Among the six scriptures, this concludes the third scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Kakacuṇḍa.
At that time, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, perceiving that the minds of the celestial hosts had conceived a sense of weary detachment, addressed them, saying:
'You celestial hosts have already heard the True Dharma spoken by the Great Sage, which can exhaust all sufferings and eliminate negligence; it is the teaching of tranquility for gods and humans.'"
“You hosts of devas have now heard the Dharma of the third Tathāgata.

Having now heard this Dharma and its discipline, you should practice with diligent effort. Furthermore, listen to the Dharma preached by other Buddhas; having heard it, take it up, and you will obtain benefit. Once you have passed away from this heaven, you shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.”
After Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, had spoken thus, all the celestial hosts addressed the Lord of the Gods, Mucilinda, saying:
"We pray that the Heavenly King may benefit us and bring us peace and happiness."
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:

"All of you, devas, behold this fourth stūpa of the Tathāgata. It is adorned with various precious jewels, radiating immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lights; it is interspersed with diverse gems of wondrous beauty, adorned by immeasurable merits. Its light universally covers this celestial world, pervading it entirely."
At that time, the assembly of devas said to the Heavenly King,
"We have now seen it.
Then, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"You all should now come together with me to visit the stupa of the Tathāgata.
The celestial hosts replied,
"So be it, O Heavenly King!"

At that time, the Lord of Devas Mucilinda, together with the host of devas, followed one another and proceeded until they reached the Buddha’s stupa. Their minds were purified, and they prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata’s stupa with their heads and faces touching it; their hearts became cool and serene. Having paid homage, they arose and gazed upon the stupa of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.
The various exquisite jewels of that Tathāgata’s stūpa radiate light and brilliance, as previously described.
Upon the jeweled walls within that Buddha-stūpa are the words of the Dharma, which benefit devas and humans, stating:
"If there are those who can accomplish seven dharmas, they shall be reborn in the heavens."

What are the seven? First, there is a son of good family who hears the Dharma and its meaning; hearing the Dharma, he practices it; hearing the Dharma, his mind is well-disposed. According to the Dharma he has heard, he grasps it with his mind; having heard it, he becomes firm; having heard it, he receives and upholds it; having heard it, he cherishes it, and joy arises in his heart.
This son of good family is close to a spiritual friend who is endowed with seven kinds of merit.
What are the seven kinds of merit that this spiritual friend fully possesses?
They are as follows: first, acting according to what one says; [and so forth].
Second, associating with those who practice as they preach;
third, being able to act according to what they have preached and firmly embracing it;
fourth, attaining firm reflection upon the Dharma.
Fifth, abiding in right mindfulness;
sixth, associating with those who perform wholesome deeds;
seventh, not adopting the evil teachings of others.
One should associate with a spiritual friend who is endowed with these seven kinds of qualities.
What is meant by "practicing according to what has been taught"? Such a spiritual friend acts and performs deeds well;

whatever they say is measured and spoken sparingly for the sake of benefit. They speak at the appropriate time and in the appropriate manner; neither too hurried nor too slow, they convey much meaning with few words. Their speech is elegant, easy to understand, and consistent with the Dharma, benefiting both themselves and others. It is in this way that they speak.
As it has been taught, so one should practice.
How does one draw near to those who practice as they speak?
One constantly and correctly cultivates body, speech, and mind; with the internal and external mind purified like pure gold, such a person practices in accordance with what has been taught.
What is meant by "acting according to what one says" and "firmly grasping"?

If there is anything to be done, one performs it with universal purity; having thoroughly examined those three types of actions and purified them well, one is reborn among gods and humans, and even attains nirvana.
Such a person, whether through their own reflection or by hearing it from another, [perceives] that this karmic retribution is happiness;
they firmly take up this joyful pleasure and firmly grasp such knowledge.
How does that son of good family attain firm contemplation of the Dharma?
It is by means of a well-purified and firm grasping that brings benefit to both worlds; having seen it thus, he engages in firm contemplation.
One whose mind thus possesses firm contemplation, having either heard from others about the fruits of firm wholesome karma or having reflected upon it themselves, takes delight in the true reality.
Thus, for one who delights in the knowledge of the true reality, how does one dwell with a settled mind?
Having heard this much, the mind is no longer distracted; this is called dwelling with a settled mind.
What constitutes association with those of similar virtuous conduct?
This means that when one sees others possessing merits equal to one's own, having seen this, one draws near to those people.
How does one not adopt the faults of others despite their instruction?
One cannot be led astray by others who act contrary to the Dharma or who practice what merely resembles the true Dharma.
One who thus associates with a son of good family—a spiritual friend endowed with these seven kinds of merit—will be reborn either among humans or in the heavens.
This explains the first teaching.
“What, furthermore, are these other six dharmas by the accomplishment of which one is born in the heavens? They are:
being well-versed in the teachings (*bahuśruta*), undertaking and practicing them, being free from indolence, mindfulness, not causing distress to others, and not being deceitful—these six.”
These seven dharmas have thus been explained.
One who accomplishes these seven kinds of dharmas, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, will be reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas.

Just as when a king or a great minister mounts one of the seven great palaces, accompanied by the sounds of the five kinds of music, singing, dancing, and joyful laughter, adorned with exquisite garlands, they proceed in this manner toward a place for recreation.
If a person accomplishes these seven dharmas, they will proceed toward the celestial realms.
"What constitutes being 'learned' (bahuśruta) and being named 'the learned'?
It means hearing the true Dharma; having heard it, one becomes disciplined and does not give rise to arrogance."

In accordance with what one has heard, one increases one's learning, practices without negligence, and never tires of wisdom; one constantly consults others, yet does not speak of one's own virtues to others, nor recite one's own name.
This person of much learning, upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas.
This is the second dharma that accords with right entry and leads to the accomplishment of practice.
"What is the third way of embracing and practicing?
It refers to embracing and practicing after having heard the Dharma.

Furthermore, if there is someone who, having heard the Dharma, embraces and practices that which is not the True Dharma and Discipline—merely hearing the Dharma, they shoulder the heavy burden of the Dharma, yet do not cultivate it, do not practice it, and do not attain the fruit of the Dharma."

Furthermore, if there is a person who maintains the precepts through the hook of wisdom, yet their wisdom is not tranquil, then that maintenance of the precepts is like a lamp by day: it possesses no light, being neither firm nor substantial.
If one’s observance of the precepts is conjoined with wisdom, that person is like the light of a lamp; being firm and substantial, they will attain the fruit without fail.

One who cultivates the Dharma may be said to be "firm," yet this firmness does not consist merely in verbal declarations. Such a person’s bodily, vocal, and mental actions are all entirely tranquil; when the body perishes at the end of life, they are reborn in a good destination, within the heavenly realms.
This is the third dharma.
"What is the fourth, called 'non-laziness'?
As for laziness, it refers to non-action."
What is meant by "not doing"?
It refers to failing to bring a practiced dharma to completion after having initiated it; such a dharma cannot be perfected.
If one applies oneself with diligence and without interruption, that dharma can be brought to completion; however, if one is indolent and lacks diligence, it cannot be perfected.
Those who lack initiative do not practice fully regarding worldly matters or supramundane goals.

If one is indolent, all that they undertake will be weak and inferior; they will be held in contempt by all people, reviled, despised, and slighted. They will suffer affliction for themselves, and at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into evil destinies, being reborn in the hells.
Such a person is ruined by indolence.
This indolence should be abandoned as one would [fear] fire, a sword, falling over a precipice, or a venomous serpent.
If one is destroyed by indolence, they will lack diligent effort and possess no majestic power, being no different from a sheep. Such a person lacks wisdom;

they do not understand any of their various activities—whether it be knowledge or ignorance, the Dharma or non-Dharma, or what should be practiced and what should not be practiced—they know nothing at all.
Why is this? It is because they have not read the sutras, have not heard the Dharma, and are indolent.

Furthermore, if there is another person who discusses and opens their mind, they will know everything regarding what is known by wisdom—whether it be the Dharma or non-Dharma; they will know all that should be done and what should not be done, and all that should be practiced and what should not be practiced.
Such dharmas as these are known through wisdom; all are known by him.
Wisdom and diligence do not exist in the indolent.
That indolent person is no different from one who is blind; when the body perishes and life ends, he falls into an evil destination and is born in hell.

Such a person is inferior in every worldly sense; they undergo the foremost suffering, begging at the houses of others, constantly relying on the doors of others in hope of alms, always looking to the faces of others, possessing the most wretched appearance—with hair covering their eyes, parched eyes, and skin on their feet and nails all withered and shriveled—they wander from house to house through the four-way streets to beg for their livelihood, enduring hardship and being despised by all.
For this reason, one should abandon all laziness.
"Conversely, for those who apply themselves with diligent effort, everything they undertake will be fully accomplished, even up to Nirvana, let alone other worldly dharmas."
At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will be reborn in a good destination, within the world of the devas.
For these reasons, whether one is a deva or a human, all should abandon indolence and diligently exert themselves with vigor.
Then, that Blessed One, Vipaśyin Buddha, spoke these verses:
"Laziness of mind and illusion, Or pride, or harsh speech,
Or the abandonment of wisdom and so forth— These are the grounds of ruin."
Associating with evil associates, abandoning virtuous friends,
or furthermore holding wrong views and the like— these are the causes and conditions for failure.
Not knowing what is wholesome or unwholesome, speaking at an improper time,
Or if one places trust in women and the like, this is a ground that brings no benefit.
Whomever one associates with, wherever one eats,
if one does not benefit oneself, this conduct will cause others to look down upon one.
One who is ruined by lack of courage, or lacks mindfulness, or is detested by kings,
or possesses a stubborn mind— such persons do not die before their time.
This is because they do not truly understand the fruits of karma, nor what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Those who distance themselves from virtuous friends will fall into the evil realms.
Whether through excessive indolence or sleepiness, or through attachment to various flavors;
whether through anger or intentional lying, or through the utterance of harsh speech;
Excessive greed or arrogance causes the mind to waver and abandon the Dharma;
if one associates with sensual desire or praises the ways of lust,
there are these three faults, of which indolence is the root.
If one exerts diligent effort, then there will be no faults of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
All who exert effort will certainly achieve the fruit;
as one should exert effort, so shall the karma certainly obtain its fruit.
"Thus, these three kinds of karma can produce three kinds of fruits;
through the three aggregates and the three roots, one is certain to undergo the activities of the three realms of existence.
When the celestial hosts saw these verses inscribed upon the wall of the stupa of the World-Honored Buddha Vipaśyin, which thus censured indolence, they spoke as follows:
"We shall certainly abandon indolence.
From this indolence, there arise various secondary faults, as the Buddha has taught.
"For one who is indolent, whether they be a deva or a human, all their undertakings at all times are diminished and inferior."
Whether they be devas or humans, those who do not become indolent will, in due course, reach even nirvana.
This fourth dharma is one that brings much to be done and great benefit among both humans and devas.
"Furthermore, the fifth quality is one that accomplishes much and brings great benefit, namely mindfulness (*smṛti*).
That which acts as an obstacle to all dharmas is laziness (*kausīdya*)."
Regarding all such worldly dharmas that encompass nirvāṇa, mindfulness is their root.
Whether one is a renunciant or a householder, if one maintains mindfulness and practices heedfulness, everything one undertakes will be fully accomplished.
Such a person repeatedly performs actions, performing them in accordance with the Dharma, diligently exerting vigor, and acting with right conduct according to their aspirations.
That person guards the five sense faculties against the five objects of experience, so that the mind is not deluded.

Having seen forms with the eye, one does not give rise to lustful defilement toward those forms, nor does the mind take delight in them; one sees forms as they truly are, knows their root, and perceives that such forms arise from specific causes and conditions, seeing what those causes and conditions are.
When that person has thus known and seen forms, their mind is not turbid or distracted; thus, those forms cannot draw them away, because they see such forms as they truly are.

Whether they be those who have gone forth or those who remain at home, or gods and humans alike, knowing the fault in the arising of forms and having extinguished the fault in the desire for the arising of forms, they thus mindfully know that in a certain direction and at a certain place, the mind takes that form as its object; by reason of such objective conditions, consciousness arises together with the eye.

"From those objects, fear has already arisen within me; this stainless mindfulness can eliminate the afflictions, and by means of this mindfulness, I have already removed such dread of these objects."
Such fears arise from causes and conditions.
By means of right mindfulness directed toward the supreme aspiration regarding all objective spheres, one is able to dispel fears concerning immeasurable varieties of forms and objects.
Mindfulness as a condition can eliminate [defilements]; within each moment of thought, they are slightly eliminated and gradually removed.

It is like a skilled copper-smith of the world who places a fine copper vessel into fire and then refines it; thus repeatedly entering the fire and refining it, he works diligently without rest until the dross is gradually removed and it becomes smooth and pure.
In this way, through the repeated application of wholesome mindfulness, one gradually removes defilements until they become pure.
It is also like a potter: when the necessary conditions assemble, through long-standing practice, a lump of clay is fashioned into a jar.
Such a person applies diligent effort and gives rise to mindfulness, cultivating and accumulating the necessary conditions, just as a jar is produced through dependent origination.
They observe with right mindfulness, like the garment they wear.

From the very beginning, proceeding step by step through every moment until the end, they thus give rise to wholesome thoughts in succession until all faults are exhausted, and they attain the vision of the Seal of the Noble Truths, which stamps the mind.
When those signs of transgression are exhausted, because those signs of transgression are exhausted, people will know it.
Therefore, if one wishes to attain what is wholesome, one should maintain right mindfulness in accordance with reality at all times.
If the eye encounters forms, mindfulness acts as a tether to bind the mind, preventing it from wavering, just as one tames a wild horse.

Thus, through wholesome mindfulness, one first maintains control over past objects; having focused the mind upon them, one likewise restrains the present visual field with mindfulness in ninety-eight ways.
"What is the application of mindfulness?
It means that when the wind of improper contemplation, which gives rise to the defilement of desire, arises, it cannot cause [the mind] to waver.

Such application of mindfulness involves contemplating reality as it is: 'This form and that form have immeasurable kinds and immeasurable shapes. One contemplates the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—thereby causing all that defilement of desire to become entirely stilled, or to be completely extinguished, or at least attenuated."
What is the power of these wholesome dharmas?
It is said that the binding of mindfulness is their root.
All wholesome dharmas rely upon the foundations of mindfulness; such a mode of engagement is the manifestation of mindfulness in the present.
"How, moreover, does one recollect dharmas of the future?
Since the future has not yet come to be, has not yet arisen, and has not yet been seen, how can one recollect the characteristics of its objects?"
If an object is already attained, it can be recollected.
Since objects in the future have not yet come into being, how can one recollect them?

That which is recollected, although it belongs to the future, perceives the characteristics of its causes and conditions and takes the future as its objective support; in this way, recollection is achieved.
That is to say, when one sees someone who has cultivated their body, speech, and mind and practices wholesome deeds, upon seeing them, one thinks:
"Such a person will certainly be reborn in heaven.
If one sees a deva who practices unwholesome deeds, upon seeing them, one then thinks:
"Such a deva will certainly fall into hell.
Thus one should reflect upon and know this fifth dharma; it is of great utility and brings much benefit among humans and devas.
"Furthermore, the sixth quality brings about much activity and great benefit among gods and humans.
As for this sixth quality, it is not to cause distress to others."
If one does not disturb others, their mind remains tranquil and free from discrimination, thinking:
"This person possesses the holy life; this person lacks the holy life.
Seeing others' requisites for bedding, medicine, or other necessities, they do not give rise to contempt or disdain; they do not claim superiority for themselves, nor do they speak thus:
"I am able to uphold the precepts.
Even if one upholds the precepts only slightly or recites the sutras only sparingly, one does not boast of this to donors.

One regards enemies and kin with an equal mind, constantly recollects the Triple Gem, does not associate with those who break the precepts, and does not trouble those who uphold them. One does not frequently visit donors to seek provisions, but keeps the mind supple and moist. One repeatedly requests instruction from Dharma teachers and elders, always dwells in secluded places, and at all times remains close to those who practice pure conduct.
A person endowed with such merit does not cause distress to others; because they do not distress others in this way, their actions are many and their benefits are great.
"Furthermore, the seventh quality brings much benefit and accomplishes great deeds among gods and humans; it is namely, non-deception.

One conceals one's own merits, eliminates evil karma, maintains a straightforward mind, and remains content with robes and alms-bowl while constantly begging for food. Dwelling in mountain valleys, rock caves, or forest groves, one practices moderation in eating and maintains an equanimous mind free from partiality. One does not wander among people without a proper cause or occasion;
nor does one walk where there may be insects."
He does not damage the banks, riverbanks, or ditches within marshes, out of fear of killing insects;
he does not cast spells upon thunderbolts, lightning, rain, and the like to cause them to fall and injure or kill;

nor does he predict the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the stars, the sun, the moon, eclipses, or the various planetary movements in order to seek wealth, food, drink, or offerings to sustain his own life.
One should not constantly frequent the home of a single donor;
nor should one walk with a haughty expression, looking up with the face turned upward;
nor should one move the lips to feign the recitation of scriptures.
One should not speak in a loud voice nor in private whispers;
one should not wear mixed or variegated boots, shoes, or sandals;
one should not bind the body with variegated cords, nor should one wear variegated scented pouches on one's person.
He does not keep bedding and other such items;
lacking the merit of precepts, he does not enter into great assemblies;
nor does he cause others to go to cities, towns, or villages to proclaim that he maintains the precepts for the sake of seeking gain and offerings.
One does not allow various places to distract or disturb the mind; one is neither greedy nor seeking, and does not dwell near a village;
one does not enter the homes of former acquaintances, relatives, and kin with a sense of entitlement to bring them under one's own influence;
one does not proclaim the faults of others nor conceal their virtues, and even when seeing the actual transgressions of others, one does not speak of them in private.
He abandons women as he would a venomous snake; he does not converse with them nor travel in their company.

"He does not approach any trees laden with flowers, nor does he wander through lovely groves, for he fears hearing the songs of lovely birds, fearing that hearing those sounds will stir his lustful mind; therefore, he does not wish to hear the voices of those birds."
One should not sit in meditation near noisy rivers or streams, for fear that hearing those sounds will cause the mind to become agitated and distracted.
One should likewise not sit in meditation near places where many incense and flowers are being offered, nor should one walk about there.
Why is this? Because he fears that his mind will be stirred by the nose smelling fragrances.

Furthermore, he does not look at various birds or birds of various colors—such as geese, ducks, jīvañjīvaka birds, peacocks, and other highly lustful birds; he does not look at them, does not see them, and does not approach them, for he fears his mind will be stirred, and fears that the causes and conditions of seeing animals or women will give rise to lustful thoughts.

One should not sit in meditation near various forest trees such as the coconut tree, the *panasa* tree, the *moca* tree, the *āmra* tree, the *vīra* tree, the *kapittha* tree, the *piluṣa* tree, or the *kharjūra* tree, for fear that a mind of craving for their flavors might arise.
Having abandoned fruit trees, he dwells in a secluded forest where there is nothing desirable to crave and no large crowds.

Practicing meditation within such a pleasant grove, he exerts diligent effort, overcoming faults and adversaries; his mind remains ever undisturbed, to the point that he would not even take soil from a plowed field for the sake of building a monastery.
"Thus having severed craving, he uses a worn-out iron bowl joined together with cords to receive food and drink, yet his mind does not think of bowls made of copper or silver;
he does not keep three bowls;
and as for all his *kāṣāya* robes, he wears them without turning them inside out."
During the summer months, except for the times of relieving oneself, he does not take even a single step further, out of fear of killing insects;
when eating *śami* fruits, he eats only the good ones and does not eat those that are rotten.

When eating small jujubes and the like, one does not eat them without looking; likewise, when eating pears, *kharjūra* fruits, soft dates, peas, or rotten beans and the like, one does not eat them without looking, for fear that there may be insects within them.
He never removes the insects that have appeared on the walls of his own dwelling, for he fears harming them and fears their death.
While seated, he does not look at the bowls of others, for he fears the desire for food.
When walking on the path, one should not walk too close to others, for fear of causing them obstruction.
In places abounding with insects, one should not defecate or urinate, out of fear of harming the insects and fear of killing them.
When walking for alms, he looks only a fathom’s distance before him because of his upright mind;
he constantly associates with those who possess an upright mind.

Such a bhikṣu does not accumulate material things, has no longing for any objects, and his heart takes no pleasure in seeing rare or extraordinary things. He is always diligent in seated meditation; such a virtuous bhikṣu is thus non-deceptive.

That virtuous bhikṣu thus maintains the precepts with purity and commits no transgression; his livelihood is thus pure, and his inner mind is thus pure and thoroughly refined; such a bhikṣu, according to the training rules as they have been taught, upholds them firmly and commits no violation.

As that virtuous bhikṣu contemplates in his mind, so does the path arise; because he maintains a constant pure livelihood, wholesome intentions arise within him. He takes no pleasure in inferior births and aspires to be born in the good realms.
Then, that Blessed One, Vipaśyin Buddha, spoke these verses:
“The person of pure livelihood, Whose body, speech, and mind are tranquil,
Who sits in meditation and is free from craving— For such a one, Nirvana is not far away.”
The dhūta practitioner, free from heedlessness, Dwells constantly in such places as cemeteries and groves; He is not far from nirvāṇa.
His bedding consists of dust and earth, And his single alms bowl is even broken.
Content with roots and fruits as food, that person lives in peace and happiness.
One who seeks liberation from desire and always delights in contentment—
a person of noble mind and courageous vigor— is not far from Nirvana.
"One who is without flattery or deceit, far removed from worldly dust and defilement,
whose mind is like space— such a person is not far from Nirvāṇa.
Thus did that Blessed One praise the bhikṣu Sukṛtakārī for being without flattery or deceit.
"A person who accomplishes these seven dharmas is a true son of good family;
if one indulges in desires and sinks into the sea of birth and death, they are but a beast—though their form is human, they are in reality not human."

One who is able to accomplish these seven dharmas will be praised by virtuous people; at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will be reborn in the heavenly realms of the happy destinies.
Having experienced celestial pleasures, they subsequently take birth among humans and attain *nirvāṇa* due to the remaining karma.

These seven kinds of dharmas are the foremost virtues: namely, from the beginning, approaching a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), followed by extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), undertaking practice, being free from indolence, mindfulness, not causing distress to others, and not deceiving. These seven dharmas are not deceitful methods; by means of these seven treasures of dharma, one attains birth in the heavens.

If, after attaining these seven dharmas among the gods and others, you do not act with heedlessness so as to exhaust your merit, you will not fall from the celestial realms into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.

Therefore, O Deva, you should not practice heedlessness, thereby bringing about your own destruction; for among all states of existence, there is no one who attains happiness through heedless conduct.
If one accomplishes these seven dharmas among human beings, one will be reborn in the heavens.
However, there are three causes and conditions by which, after falling from the heavens, one will descend into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
The three are as follows:
not hearing the True Dharma;
and associating with evil associates.
"They do not believe in the ripening of karma.
If they do not accomplish these seven kinds of dharmas, they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"All of this you have already heard. That Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of a heart of compassion and for the benefit of sentient beings, has already spoken thus.
At that time, the entire assembly of devas addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"We have now heard this sutra spoken by the Tathāgata.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the world, has already brought about benefit; he has spoken thus in order to eliminate negligence."
Mūsulinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"Having heard this sutra, do not act with negligence.
Because of negligence, devas are reborn in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals."
For what reason?
You have acquired this birthplace among the gods by means of highly valuable and precious things; you should not now allow it to be rendered empty and exhausted through negligence.
"As the Buddha has taught, such sutras and dharmas embrace right practice and abandon negligence.
Thus ends the fourth sutra spoken by Vipaśyin Buddha among the six sutras.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 46 [and] Scroll 47,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Six: Contemplation of the Heavens; Section Twelve: Suyāma Heaven.

"At that time, the third Suyāma Heavenly King, Mūśaludha, showed the heavenly assembly the scriptural texts of the Buddha’s stūpas. Having caused the minds of those heavenly beings to become fully matured, he further showed them the realm of birth and death—a place filled with hundreds of thousands of immeasurable faults, including the suffering of decay and affliction, the separation from loved ones, and the proximity of the unloved. That is to say, it is filled with all manner of faults such as old age, death, grief, sorrow, and lamentation; it is completely possessed of ruin and destruction. Birth and death are indeed the locus where all forms of decay and affliction are fully present."
At that time, having seen that the hearts of the celestial hosts were well-disciplined, the Heavenly King, out of compassion and for the benefit of sentient beings, spoke to them thus:

"O celestial hosts, you should now know that because all devas engage in heedless conduct, they will inevitably encounter decline and affliction. When the time of death arrives, their hearts will give rise to regret; they will suffer extreme heat and distress, meeting with great calamity."
At that time, there is no skillful means by which one may escape.
Bound by the cords of karma, one is led away thus, alone and without companion—

whether human, nāga, or denizen of hell— as one enters the hells, ensnared by the net of death and without any partner, save for wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, which accompany all beings within the ocean of sentient existence.
Then those hosts of devas again addressed the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, saying: "It is so, it is so!
At that time, there shall not be a single companion, except for Dharma and non-Dharma."
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"You, members of the deva assembly, should know this: there is no other companion for you."
Again, he addressed them, saying:
"O you hosts of devas, if you wish to increase the seeds of faith, and desire to attain peace and happiness, and ultimately eliminate suffering."

Furthermore, within this celestial realm, there is yet another wondrous stupa made of Jambūnada gold, covered with nets of pearls and adorned with pillars of the seven precious gems; it is embellished with various kinds of jewels and various radiances—this is the stupa of Kāñcanamuni Buddha.
I shall now go with you and all the hosts of devas to that stūpa.
Having reached that stūpa, we shall pay homage and make offerings, and enter that Buddhist stūpa.

Once inside, we shall examine thoroughly all the dharmas contained within that stūpa; having seen them, we shall grasp them; having attained them, we shall practice them for our own benefit, emerging from birth and death, and proceeding by stages until we reach nirvāṇa.

At that time, having heard these words from the Lord of Gods, Mucilinda, the celestial hosts conceived a sense of deep reverence; they abandoned their heedlessness, their faculties became tranquil, and together they proceeded toward the great seer’s stūpa named Kāñcanamuni Buddha.
The radiance of the stupa was as previously described.
At that time, the entire host of devas, together with Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, proceeded to that Buddha-stupa.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s stūpa, the Yāma King Mūsuludha addressed the celestial hosts, saying:
“That Tathāgata Kanakamuni taught that all phenomena are entirely impermanent; he benefited the world out of his compassion for sentient beings.”
Within this stūpa, there is a transformation manifested upon the wall; if you, the assembly of devas, should behold it, you will give rise to weary detachment.
Seeing the nature of impermanence, one will inevitably give rise to weary detachment.
"What that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught and manifested has been miraculously displayed upon the walls within this stūpa.
When the Heavenly King had spoken thus, he entered the stūpa together with his retinue of devas.
That Buddha-stūpa was ten yojanas in width; within that stūpa, all of saṃsāra is entirely impermanent, and everything that exists is subject to decay and destruction.

Due to the operation of their own karma, they lack autonomy; being diverse and distinct, the differences among the five realms of existence are each manifested within the walls of the Buddha-stūpa like a mirror. Those forms are clearly manifest, just as with right view, and are distinctly discerned in every place, like a painting of various colors.
"On one side of that place, eight hells are seen, namely: Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and so on, up to Avīci."

Seeing a deva falling into [the hell], blown by the winds of his own karma with his head downward and feet upward, his entire body ablaze; the color of the fire upon his whole body is like that of a *kiṃśuka* tree. Descending from the celestial realm, he falls in succession into the midst of the hells, crying out in a loud voice.

Deceived by their own minds because their wholesome karma is exhausted, and deceived by the enemy of negligence, they—having previously attained the foremost pleasures among the gods—now enter the places of great suffering in hell. Alone and without companions, separated from their friends, relatives, and brothers, they fall into hell with no one able to save them.
"Those hosts of devas first clearly see within the walls of such a stupa that the Cāturmahārājika devas have fallen into hell.
The Cāturmahārājika devas have committed the transgression of killing and the transgression of stealing."
How do the gods of the Four Great Kings take life?
When those celestial hosts engage in battle with the asuras, they kill the asuras.
When the gods achieve victory and the asuras are defeated, they seize their crowns, their iron swords, and take whatever else they possess.
Due to these karmic causes and conditions, or perhaps due to other karmic causes and conditions, they fall into hell, having performed such actions while deceived by the mind.

In that celestial realm, whenever one passes away, at the moment of passing, when the aggregates (skandhas) are extinguished, one grasps onto the intermediate state (antarābhava) and is born in hell. Continuing from that place of pleasure, one receives an intermediate state body and experiences immense suffering and distress.

In such an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their suffering and affliction are unbearable; how much more so once they have entered hell, where they undergo immeasurable kinds of extreme suffering and affliction.
This is a great enterprise; in this manner, these sentient beings are thus deceived.
Having fallen from the celestial realms, they are born within the hells.
All those hosts of devas, within the Buddha-stūpa, saw in this way all that was manifested by the World-Honored One.

Furthermore, in another part of that stupa, those celestial hosts again see the gods of the Four Great Kings who, having fallen from their celestial abodes, have been reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Having thus lost their enjoyment of food and pleasure, they are reborn in the wilderness and once more undergo the torment of hunger and thirst.
After wearing such celestial garments for a long time, their hair later covers their faces and bodies, and they are born with eyes shrouded in darkness.

Their bodies appear like scorched trees, naked and without clothing; some have bodies clothed in garments of flaming fire. In the midst of the wilderness, their bodies are consumed by hunger and thirst as they cry out in lamentation, unable to find even a drop of water as small as a dewdrop. Thus they are born into one of the thirty-six realms of hungry ghosts.
The hosts of the Yāma Heaven see within the walls of that Buddha-stūpa crows, ravens, and jackals pecking at their faces, eyes, mouths, and so forth; they see them in such a place.

In such celestial realms, the ground is soft and smooth to the touch; having sported and wandered there, they are later reborn in the land of hungry ghosts (*preta*), where the ground is composed of a mixture of hot fire, hard earth, and scorching dust, abounding with black insects that have diamond-like beaks.
The hosts of the Yāma devas see this within the walls of that Buddha-stūpa; those ghosts wail as they fall back from their celestial abodes.

Furthermore, while in heaven they smell exquisite fragrances—various superior scents such as māndārava and kausuma, and hundreds of thousands of kinds of perfumes—they smell them all; yet at a later time, they must travel through impure places filled with the stench of excrement, urine, corpses, and the foulness of cemeteries.
Thus, these hungry ghosts smell various kinds of impure things and foul, putrid odors; within their nostrils there are flaming ants, and those flaming ants fill their nostrils.
Those hungry ghosts, having been born among the hungry ghosts, see this within a certain section of the wall inside that stūpa:

"Furthermore, in a previous life, they enjoyed immeasurable varieties of sudhā-food in the heavens, complete with desirable colors, tastes, fragrances, and textures; yet now they have received the body of a toy-like hungry ghost."

Having been born thus, this is the foremost impurity, the foremost stench, and the most difficult-to-obtain flavor of excrement; within a hundred years, one has never once obtained such food of feces.
Within a certain section of the wall inside that Buddha-stūpa, it was seen in this manner;
just as he had eaten excrement, it was seen thus within the wall of the stūpa.

Furthermore, the garments worn by those devas were supremely soft and possessed a supreme smoothness to the touch; they were composed of an intermingling of immeasurable jewels, appropriate for devas, and were exceedingly lovely.

Having already donned such garments while among the devas, celestial winds further blew various flowers to sprinkle their bodies; yet later, when their wholesome karma was exhausted, they were born among the pretas, naked and without clothing, with hair growing upon their own bodies.
The hair is extremely thick and coarse, hard and yellowish, covering his entire body.

Hundreds of thousands of black insects devour him all over; likewise, many various fire-insects consume his body. Born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), his body is scorched by hunger and thirst; he is perpetually emaciated, and because of his constant weeping, both his eyes and face are rotted away.
Having long endured immeasurable suffering as hungry ghosts, deceived by their own negligence, they fall from the celestial realm and descend into the land of hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, the devas of the Yamāvatī heaven, in the region known as Mount Śākavati, see within that stūpa, on various parts of the walls, the successive accounts of how the devas of the Cāturmahārājika heaven fall and descend into the various realms of animal existence.
Briefly stated, these various regions are born in three places: those that move in water, on land, and through the air.
Among them, those that move in water prey upon one another, undergoing great suffering and affliction—either suffering from cold or suffering from heat.

Those who travel on land are scorched and burned by the sun, undergoing great suffering and affliction; their bodies are consumed by hunger and thirst, and they kill one another. Some suffer greatly out of fear of being bound. They undergo hundreds of thousands of such types of suffering that cannot be fully described.
Thus, these animals, driven by the winds of karma, undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
Among those that move through the air—whether small, coarse, or large-bodied birds—they constantly delight in killing one another, undergoing great suffering and affliction.
When those devas have fallen from that state, they are born among the animals, for they were deceived by the enemy of negligence.
"In this same way, if other devas are not negligent, practice non-negligence, perform superior wholesome deeds, and cultivate merit..."
Having passed away from the heavens, they are born among human beings and experience retribution according to their own wholesome karma.

If one with unwholesome karma is born among humans, it is likewise in every respect: through various activities, they enter into decline and affliction, experiencing inferior, middling, or superior conditions, and being either poor or wealthy.
According to the directions, times, and methods, whether they be ugly or beautiful, good or evil, such forms are seen upon the inner walls of that Buddha-stūpa.

If there are those with virtuous karma who delight in cultivation and practice extensively—whether practicing the precepts or the path of the Eightfold Noble Way—and whose conduct is unblemished and without holes, firm and unviolated; who have well-disciplined their minds and possess great power in the three karmas, then by the force and momentum of their virtuous karma, they will certainly receive and experience desirable retributions.

By the power of the causes and conditions of taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one may at times bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings through material giving, or provide the gift of Dharma through the force of such causes and conditions;
