or again, by performing other various similar virtuous deeds, one perfumes the mind with pure dharmas through the power of a tranquil mind.

Next, one engages in verbal action; with a pure mind, one exhorts and encourages one's parents to practice generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom. Because one’s own body already possesses the power of wholesome karma, one is able to exhort one's parents.

Or they give to the sick and the poor; or they provide food and drink to the sick; or they bestow medicinal herbs upon those who lack physicians and require medicine for their ailments—all by the power of their generosity.
Or they may refrain from killing, refrain from stealing, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from drinking alcohol, and so forth.
Or, in desolate wildernesses or remote places, they may with a virtuous mind construct wells, ponds, or the like, providing what is needed to others; such is the power of this karma.
Sometimes they make offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; this is due to the power of such karma.
They perform acts of wholesome karma by prostrating and joining their palms.
Or, in places where many people are destroyed and where many fear—such as fearsome wildernesses or those who fear the sword—they bestow upon them fearlessness.
Or, due to such karma, one gives beds, bedding, seats, and whatever medicines and necessities are required to pratyekabuddhas and arhats;
or one bestows happiness upon one’s wife and children while properly protecting them.
Or, during times of famine, one may give food and drink to the hungry to nourish them.
This karma is most excellent; it leads even to Nirvana and the three types of Bodhi, yielding fruits according to one's wishes—how much more so for rebirth in the heavens!
If they decline from the heavenly realm, they are reborn again among the gods.
They further observe the transitions occurring within the heavens; thus, those gods see [these events] upon the walls inside the Buddha’s stūpa.

"In those celestial realms, there are various nets of karma and immeasurable causal conditions; the ropes of karma bind and seize immeasurable sentient beings, spreading them out within the cycle of birth and death. Once sentient beings enter therein, they become bound."

"At that time, the assembly of the Yāma devas within that stūpa, having seen the various ways in which the Cāturmahārājika devas suffer immeasurable decline and great distress—just as manifested by the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kanakamuni—they, having seen this, further observed the Trāyastriṃśa devas."
Having seen the Four Great Heavenly Kings thus afflicted within the walls of that Buddha-stūpa, he then further reflected: "Are the Gods of the Thirty-three likewise so?"
Then, the Yāma devas went to another place within that Buddha-stūpa and beheld the World-Honored One upon a pure wall.
They saw him as he truly is in the cycle of birth and death in this world—bound by the shackles of karma, experiencing pleasure and pain, appearing like a magical transformation.

In this manner, he next saw that it was likewise with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; they experience pleasure according to their karma and act according to their own karmic deeds—whether those deeds were wholesome or unwholesome. Those devas experience pleasure or suffering according to their karma, and whether they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, or as humans or devas, there are various distinctions. Bound by the snares of immeasurable karma, they continue to wander and transmigrate within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Within the realm of birth and death, driven by the winds of karma, there is no place within the three realms where karma does not bear its fruit; how much more so in the abode of the Heaven of the Thirty-three?

"In that Yāma Heaven—within the pure walls of that Buddha-stūpa—he further beholds the five realms of existence created by their own karma and bound by the snares of their own karma; furthermore, at a later time, they enter the seven great hells—Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, and Pratāpana—excluding only the greatest hell, Avīci."
Why is this? Because one does not commit the karma of Avīci while in the heavens.
For this reason, those in the heavens are not born in the Avīci hell; they are born only in the seven great hells.
"When those from the Heaven of the Thirty-three fall and are reborn in the Saṃjīva Hell, it is due to the karma of killing or other such deeds.
When gods and asuras engage in battle and the gods kill the asuras, this constitutes dwelling within the sphere of the hell of killing."

All devas commit killing; among the Cāturmahārājakāyika and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, both [types of beings] engage in killing and both engage in stealing, whereas from the four heavens above, it is not so.
The gods dwelling in that earth element—the Cāturmahārājakāyika and Trāyastriṃśa heavens—perform such actions.
The Trāyastriṃśa heaven consists of subtle karma; the other heavens are not so.

In this way, within the walls of that Buddha’s stūpa, the celestial hosts in the region of Mounts and Trees Endowed with Delights behold the subtle karma for birth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, as well as the process of birth and decline.

"In the Nandana Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, within the Pāriyātra Radiant Forest and amidst the various celestial palaces, they indulge in manifold diversions and experience the pleasures of sensory objects; yet, because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they are bound by the noose of insatiability and enter into the hells."

The suffering experienced by those who fall from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings into hell is ten times greater than that of those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three who fall into hell. Why is this?
Whatever pleasures of the sensory realms exist among the various devas, if those pleasures are superior, the suffering of separation from them is likewise superior.
It is an extreme great suffering that flows on in succession; by such karma, it becomes increasingly more intense.

Just as all parts of the body of a celestial being are soft and supple in every respect, so too, because the eyes and other faculties are soft and supple, the suffering experienced therein is both extensive and intense.
Thus, the pleasure experienced by the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is surpassed by the pleasure of the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
likewise, when the realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is lost or destroyed, their sorrow and suffering are both greater and more intense.
The mental affliction is great; the mental affliction is manifold. The two types—suffering and pleasure—are exceedingly numerous and preeminent, beyond all analogy.

"In the heavens there is supreme bliss, yet in hell there is extreme suffering. Bound by the snare of karma, one is like one fallen from a precipice, undergoing immeasurable varieties of most grievous torment."

The hosts of the Yāma devas saw within the walls of that Buddha-stūpa the Trāyastriṃśa devas ruined by negligence; having seen this, the hearts of those Yāma devas were filled with extreme grief and distress.

Furthermore, within the walls of another section inside that same stūpa of the Yāma Heaven, he again saw how those from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having fallen away from that celestial realm, were reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta).

In the Nandana Grove, the Ābhāsvara Grove, amidst the Varṣakāra palaces, and in places of recreation, they experience celestial bliss, partaking of divine *sudhā* food that fully sustains their bodies; having been satiated and enjoyed such pleasures for a long time, they then consume impure food of excrement and feces, and various impure worms infest their entire bodies.

Having thus observed the gods of heedless conduct falling from the Heaven of the Thirty-three into the realm of hungry ghosts, the gods of the Yāma Heaven, having seen this, were overcome with extreme grief and distress.

Furthermore, in another part of the wall within that same stūpa of the Yāma Heaven, he again beholds the following: certain gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having fallen from their celestial state, are reborn in the realm of animals. In the great ocean they become *miṇa* fish, or shellfish, *makara* fish, or *śuśumāra* fish; born among such evil creatures, they kill one another, and with their bodies scorched by hunger and thirst, they undergo immeasurable suffering.
Likewise, there are sky-dwelling birds and other such animals that kill one another, constantly living in fear, their minds perpetually dreading death as they endure various afflictions.
Similarly, there are various beasts in the marshes who kill and eat one another, undergoing all manner of suffering and distress.

"Having spoken thus, the gods of the Four Great Kings, by virtue of their wholesome karma, are born among human beings; likewise, in due order, the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, by virtue of their wholesome karma, if born among humans in places of similar karma, undergo various sufferings and are bound by birth and death."

When a deva falls from that state, they undergo immeasurable kinds of suffering and affliction within the celestial realms; such suffering and affliction are beyond description, let alone the suffering experienced within the womb in the human realm.

In the human world, when one is about to emerge from the womb, one undergoes various sufferings and afflictions. There is the suffering of infancy; when one has emerged from the womb onto the ground and is unable yet to walk, there is the suffering of falling over and so forth, as well as the suffering of crawling on hands and knees. With the body lacking strength, one knows nothing of what should or should not be done; thus one suffers through foolish weeping and lamentation.
Such various matters of suffering and affliction cannot be fully described.
They are seen upon the walls inside that Buddha-stūpa as clearly as if seen in a mirror; all the celestial hosts see the entire region, complete with its mountains and trees.

"Those hungry ghosts, thus afflicted by hunger and thirst, are bound to others and lack autonomy; they experience cold and heat, are buffeted by the wind and scorched by the sun, and wander everywhere through the wilderness."
Such sufferings as these are of infinite varieties; they are experienced in their entirety and cannot be fully described.
Thus, the celestial hosts in that region of the mountain and forest-filled land saw them within the walls of that Buddha-stūpa.
Having thus seen the various sufferings and the immeasurable kinds of worldly birth and death within that wall, as if in a skillfully executed painting,
those hosts of devas, having witnessed such wonders, conceived a sense of weary detachment and gave rise to this thought:
"The devas are superior to humans."
“The foremost path for humans is what is called the heavenly realm;
the foremost path for devas is what is called the human realm.
When a human is about to die, they wish to be reborn in the heavens.”
When the gods are about to fall from their realm, they wish to be born among humans.
Humans delight in the heavens, and the gods delight in the human world; thus they are reborn within these two paths of gods and humans.
If such is their suffering and affliction, how much more so for those in the other evil realms, who are toyed with by the power of karma?

Furthermore, in this manner, the celestial hosts dwelling in the region of Mount Gandhamādana behold within the walls of another part of that same Buddhist stūpa the Trāyastriṃśa gods of the Sudharmā Hall as they fall from that celestial realm and, according to their karmic conduct, are reborn within the five destinies.
As for those devas who fall, it is as previously described: due to the causes and conditions of their karma.

Even if they fall from one heaven and are reborn in another heaven, they still do not escape suffering; just as when they originally fell from birth, they experience the pain of separation from what they love and harbor fear regarding their own decline.

Thus fearing such decline and its immeasurable varieties of suffering, that deva, having already witnessed those countless afflictions, next further observes another part of the wall within that Buddha-stūpa. There he sees the body of Śakra, who has fallen from that celestial realm, adorned with exquisite jewel-garlands and celestial robes, and radiating manifold lights.
Those ornaments were the color of gold refined by fire, possessing a supreme radiance beyond all analogy.
Having fully mastered superior desires and being endowed with the five sensory pleasures, he renounced them all.
Drawn by their own karma, the gates to the evil realms open; driven by heedlessness, they fall into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.
By the workings of their own karma—whether drawn by wholesome karma or unwholesome karma—they thus undergo such decline.
Within the pure jewel walls of that Buddha-stūpa, he saw the former Śakras who had previously descended from their positions in past ages;
those Śakras numbered thirty-two. The first Śakra was named Aṃśumat.
Having served as the king of the Thirty-three Heavens, because his own merit was exhausted, he was reborn in the great ocean as a makara fish of immense body.
In his previous life among humans, he had been a fisherman who constantly killed many fish, yet he also regularly paid homage to the Buddha.
By virtue of the karma of worshipping the Buddha, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as King Śakra;
by the causal conditions of killing, he became a fish in the ocean; and due to residual karma, he was born among the animals.
Furthermore, the celestial hosts in the realm of Mount Trees Abounding (Pārijāta-vana) on Mount Yama saw, in succession, another place within the walls of that same Buddha-stūpa.
There they saw the second Śakra, named Trāyastriṃśa, who had formerly been among human beings and performed virtuous deeds by giving food to the sick, or with a pure mind giving food to bhikṣus.

Due to those karmic causes and conditions, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as King Śakra; later, when his merit was exhausted, because of the remaining causes and conditions of unwholesome karma, he became a lizard insect.

In a previous life, because of a mind of wrong views, he killed a lizard during an outsider’s ritual; due to those causes and conditions, he was born in hell, and after emerging from hell, through the remaining karmic causes and conditions, he became a lizard.

Furthermore, within the celestial assembly on the ground of the Tree-Abounding Realm in the Yāma Heaven, they again saw them in succession within a different section of the wall inside that same Buddha-stūpa: the third was Śakra, whose name is Pālakasva.
Having experienced the celestial realms and the pleasures of the five desires, he was about to pass away from that state.

Because in his previous life as a human he had made offerings to his parents and tended to them when they were ill, through the causal conditions of those deeds, he was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as King Śakra.
When their primary karma is exhausted, they fall from that celestial realm and are reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

In a past life, having been born in another place during a time of famine, they had stored up much grain and other goods; they sold them at high prices to others, deceiving them, and with their minds further harboring the hope for a great scarcity in the future.
Due to those causes and conditions, he was born in the Black Rope Hell; because of the remaining karma from that, he was subsequently born among the hungry ghosts with needle-throats.

Furthermore, the celestial hosts in the realm of Mount Trees Abounding in Fragrance within the Yāma Heaven saw within the walls of another part of that Buddha-stūpa the immeasurable varieties of the decay and affliction of birth and death, and they gave rise to a sense of rare wonder.
Having thus seen these various immeasurable sights, he next saw the fourth Śakra, named Kāmadarśin, who, having fallen from his celestial abode, was reborn among pigs.
Having seen this, he examines those wholesome karmas: by what karmic causes and conditions did he become King Śakra?
In a previous life, when another person—a Brahmin of wrong views—was suffering from illness and on the verge of death, he gave him medicine to take, speaking out of a heart of compassion:
"You should take this medicine."
By the causal conditions of this karma, he was born in the good realm among the Trāyastriṃśa gods as King Śakra.
When his wholesome karma was exhausted, he fell into hell; having emerged from that place, due to the remaining karma, he was born among pigs.
That deity further contemplates such karmic results: by what causes and conditions is one reborn among the swine?
In a previous life, he constantly delighted in hunting, killing many sentient beings—either killing many deer or killing many swine.

Due to the causal conditions of that karma, after his life ended, he was reborn in the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva-naraka*). Once that karma was exhausted, by the power of residual karma, he was born among pigs.

Furthermore, within the mountain grove of the Heaven Endowed with Trees and Mountains (*Pārijāta-khaṇḍa*) in the Yāma Heaven, the celestial hosts, in another section of the wall inside that same Buddhist stūpa, successively saw a fifth Śakra named Sumati.
By what karma was he born in that place as King Śakra?
In a previous life, he saw another person about to kill a lion; out of compassion, he rescued it and brought it home, providing various kinds of food and drink for many days.
By reason of those karmic causes and conditions, he was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as King Śakra, named Sumati.
After passing away from that place, he was reborn within the Great Hell of Intense Heat.
By what causes and conditions is one born in that hell?
It is because in a previous life, amidst a royal assembly, one spoke false words; through the causal conditions of that karma, one falls into that hell.

"After the Śakra Suyāma has passed away from that place, another Śakra is born in succession, named Kauśika; he is seen by the celestial hosts in the realm of Mount Trees Abounding in Delights within the Yāma heaven, upon a different section of the wall inside that Buddha-stūpa."
What were his wholesome karmas?

It is said that in a previous life, while he was a wealthy Brahmin with vast treasures, he established a residence for Brahmins within his home, organized a great assembly for offerings, gathered honored guests, provided them with food and drink, and bestowed wealth and goods upon them.
By reason of those karmic causes and conditions, he shall in the future become the King Śakra, named Kauśika.
Furthermore, having previously performed immeasurable meritorious deeds, he shall become the King Śakra, named Kauśika.

Furthermore, within the mountain groves of the Yāma Heaven, the celestial hosts saw within the walls of another section of that Buddha-stūpa the realm of the gods and the abode of Śakra, the King of Devas. Therein they beheld the power of the Dharma-teaching of the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, which causes Śakra to block off the evil paths; having passed away from the heavenly realms, he is reborn among humans, and thus undergoes this course of existence for seven such cycles.
When the various Yāma devas saw this, they were struck with wonder and thought:

"All the other Śakra-devānām-indras have seen their own future births in the evil realms within the walls of various places inside that Buddha-stūpa; yet alone among them, Śakra Kauśika has not been seen to fall into an evil realm."
For what reason was this?
At that time, all the hosts of devas there addressed their lord, Mucilinda, saying:
"We see the evil destinies of all other Śakras; why do we not see the evil destiny of that Kauśika Śakra?"
"By what cause and condition do we see that he returns seven times, yet there is no eighth?
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, having heard this, replied:
"Listen now, all of you; I shall explain to you the path of that Kauśika."
For this reason, because I now wish to speak for your sake, I have brought you all into this Buddha-stūpa.
Having entered this stūpa, I shall preach the True Dharma for you.
For what reason?
All of you act with such negligence because you are deceived by celestial desires; your minds are deluded and confused, and thus you do not hear the True Dharma.
Therefore, for your benefit, I have brought you all into this Buddhist stupa so that you may manifest freedom from arrogance.
Your conduct has been heedless, and this life has passed in vain; later, when you fall away, remorse will arise in your hearts.
For these reasons, I now exhort you all to listen to the True Dharma.

"By what causes and conditions does it come about that here, among the two paths of birth for Kauśika, one is born only in the higher realms and not in the evil destinies, and furthermore, there is no eighth rebirth?"

Within this stūpa, one does not see such things as the former heedless conduct and great indulgence of that Kauśika; rather, when his life was about to end, the signs of the exhaustion of his wholesome karma and the signs of his decline appeared. Then, a spiritual friend spoke to him, saying:
"Kauśika, the signs of your decline have already manifested and you are now about to fall; therefore, use your pure mind for your own benefit."
When he had spoken thus, Kauśika said:
"Show me the path so that I may hear the Dharma and not fall back from this state.
At that time, the seer, his virtuous friend and spiritual mentor, spoke thus to Kauśika:
“Kauśika, listen! There is a skillful means that will prevent you from falling back from this state.

In this Jambudvīpa, there is a Buddha who has appeared in the world; he was born into the lineage of the Ikṣvāku clan, he knows all things and sees all things, he has universally realized all karmic fruits, and he guides all sentient beings toward the right path.”
The Unsurpassed Dharma King has preached the Dharma for you, so that you shall not fall away from this state.
Having heard it thus from that spiritual friend, and having heard it, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, proceed with speed!
"Quickly! Go to Jambudvīpa to where the World-Honored One is.

Then, in a single moment of thought, Kauśika arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was. He beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who was preaching the True Dharma for him, speaking words of consolation, and enabling him to gain benefit upon hearing them; he pointed out the city of Nirvana.

The Dharma he taught was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it was excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing. It was a unique teaching, complete, pure, and pristine—namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the realization of the path to the cessation of suffering; that is, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its accumulation, its cessation, and the path.
Having heard this, Kauśika again addressed the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, saying:
"Great Seer Gautama! I now face an obstacle;
the signs of decline have already appeared, and I shall soon fall away from this state."
When he had thus questioned him, that Blessed One said: “Kauśika, it is so, it is so!
Just as you have conceived in your mind, the signs of your decline have appeared.

Because your celestial merit has been exhausted, because of your heedless conduct, and because you cherish the sovereignty of your own body and mind, you wish to go elsewhere; yet, within this vast wilderness of great saṃsāra, it is impossible to cross over, and the further shore cannot be reached.

All the foolish, ordinary worldlings of this world, lacking the power of the feet, are beset by birth, old age, sickness, and death; they wail and cry out in lamentation, filled with grief, sorrow, and distress, finding nothing to delight in. They encounter the separation from loved ones and the meeting with those they hate; they are surrounded by various terrifying things such as venomous snakes and lions filling that wilderness. These foolish worldlings are scorched by the sun of ignorance, shrouded in the darkness of delusion, and obstructed by boundless sensual desires.

The forest of manifold hundreds of thousands of distinctions is filled with various beasts, obstructed and congested; there is no water of the True Dharma, and one is far removed from virtuous friends.

The right path that has been taught is crowded by countless heterodox practitioners of false views and those with deviant intentions on divergent paths, who fill that wilderness, making it impossible to escape.
The past, the future, and the intermediate present are vast and far-reaching; the sufferings of the five realms of existence are unbearable, and the darkness of suffering covers the earth.
O Kauśika, within this wilderness of saṃsāra, you have conceived fear in your heart, yet you cannot escape it.
In the past, you were stained by and attached to sensual pleasures; for this reason, you did not perceive them. Now, because those sensual pleasures have come to an end, you understand them.
When the time of your decline arrives, sensual pleasures cannot save you; as the moment of decline approaches, you are about to fall into another realm.

“Having heard what the Buddha had said, Kauśika adjusted his robes to one side, removed his celestial crown from his head, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed him, saying:
‘World-Honored One!’”
Is there any skillful means by which I might not fall away from this place?
Is there any way that I might not fall away, but instead continue to reign as king over these Trāyastriṃśa gods?
That Buddha said: "I have a skillful means that will prevent you from falling back. Why is this?"
There is no other person capable of performing such determined deeds as to be born here, to sit upon your seat, and to become the king of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Such are the causes and conditions as I have perceived them.
Now that I see you sitting here, remaining for a long time without departing, I perceive a cause and condition today: that you shall not regress, namely, by hearing the Dharma I preach.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Kauśika placed his palms together at his forehead, and with a heart full of joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain this well for me; I shall now listen attentively.”

When Kauśika had spoken thus, that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, for his sake explained the defects and the transcendence regarding the flavor of desire, expounding at length such a superior sūtra.
Having heard this, Kauśika immediately attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Once Kauśika had attained that fruit, he gradually passed away and was reborn, having closed off the evil paths.
For this reason, within the inner walls of this stūpa, the assembly of the Yāma devas does not see that eighth birthplace of Kauśika.
Because that King Śakra has attained nirvāṇa, after seven returns, an eighth return to birth can no longer be found.
"Such are the causes and conditions that I have explained for you, the assembly of devas.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, spoke these verses:
"Desire is not material wealth, For it provides no real sustenance or benefit."
The wealth of ethical discipline and faith is supreme; it leads ultimately to nirvāṇa.
This desire is not true wealth, for it causes one to enter the wilderness of existence;
if one brings about liberation from desire, that indeed is true wealth.
If one does not rescue others from evil states, and if one delights in what is not tranquil,
it is solely because of great delusion that what is not wealth is called wealth.
Thus, while such things may be termed "possessions," the desires they indicate are not true possessions.
If one abandons non-material desires, one attains that true wealth.
If one speaks of the path of tranquility, that is shown to be the foremost path.
What, then, is this superior path?
The wise are able to reach it.
If one does not draw near to sensual desires, and if one is not deceived by craving,
they will travel upon the path of goodness and remain far from the fire of desire.
Desire can never be satisfied, and desire is not tranquility;
it unites with craving like a flame finding fuel.
Whether gods, humans, or nāgas, those who do not know contentment shall fall.
"Being burned by the fires of hell—this loss is indeed a true loss.
Thus did the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, instruct the assembly of devas with such immeasurable kinds of teachings, protecting, rescuing, and gathering them in.
At that time, the host of devas felt profound revulsion; having become weary of desire, they again addressed the Deva King Mucilinda, saying:
"O Great Heavenly King!..."

"I have already observed the various realms of rebirth where others will be born in future lives; now I shall further observe for myself which realm I am destined to be born in during my own future life.
King Mūśalinda replied, "It is thus that you should observe."

Having heard this, the celestial hosts looked within the walls at another location inside that Buddha-stūpa and beheld the Yāma devas falling away into the hells—namely, Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and so forth.
He sees immeasurable varieties of beings falling into that hell; some fall with their heads downward, while others fall into it with both arms outstretched.

While his celestial body has not yet perished, he thus foresees the place of birth in hell and also sees the time when his karma in the heavenly realm is exhausted and he must retreat. There, within that hell, bodies are rotting and cooked; upon the ground of glowing iron, immeasurable crows and vultures fill the area. In that place, there are various immeasurable terrors; the ground is covered with flaming sand, and the sentient beings of the hell are scorched and roasted intensely upon the hellish earth.

When that deva thus falls into hell, his head is positioned downward as he undergoes such suffering—the most urgent suffering, the most intense suffering—experiencing immeasurable varieties of various torments.
The messengers of Yama rebuke them in various ways; having rebuked them, they inflict various sufferings upon them.
All those devas see themselves undergoing such suffering.

Having seen this, he further beheld within another part of the wall inside that same Buddha-stūpa the former King of the Yāma Heaven, undergoing immeasurable kinds of harsh and evil suffering within the hells.
Regarding those who, with minds already agitated by desire, have previously delighted in sense objects and thereby committed various evil deeds: how did they act,
and what were their characteristics?
The messengers of Yama explained everything in detail and said to him:
"Because you formerly craved all sensory objects, you committed evil deeds; now you must undergo their retribution here."
"In this way, what were the names of the past kings of the Yāma Heaven?

There was one named Mahākarma, one named Samantabhadra, one named Tejasvin, one named Abhedyamati, one named Manoratha, one named Suvarṇa, and one named Samantasukha. These and others who were lords of the Yāma Heaven fell into the seven hells."

Just as one experiences the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma, having already experienced the pleasures of the supreme realm, the mind remains unsatisfied; ruined by craving, one thus falls away and declines.
"As for that one of great karma, what deeds did he originally perform to be born in the Yāma Heaven and become the King of the Yāmas?
In his former life as a human, with pure faith, he gave food to a pratyekabuddha."
Due to the causal conditions of their karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they were reborn in a happy destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven within the realm of the Yāma devas.

There, they experienced immeasurable varieties of sensory pleasures and desires, yet remained unaware of satiety. When they eventually fell from that celestial realm, because of their original act of stealing, they descended once more into the Black Rope Hell.
In his previous life, he served as a physician who failed to treat other patients properly, instead seizing their wealth.
Due to that evil karma, he was born in the Black Rope Hell.
Having observed the past karma of that Great-Deed King Yāma, he next further examines the various merits and demerits of those who possess them.
By what wholesome karma was he born in the Yāma Heaven and become the King of the Yāmas?

Within another part of the wall inside that Buddha-stūpa, he further beholds that past life: with a pure mind, he gave away his own wealth as an offering to a sick bhikṣu, perfuming his heart with such intention.
Due to those karmic causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn in a happy realm as a celestial king among the Yāma devas.
Yet, being further drifted by the river of sensory objects, because his wholesome karma was exhausted, he fell back down into the Great Hell of Screaming.

Furthermore, in a previous life when he was among humans, he served as a lord of the land; acting with negligence and conceit in his heart, he encountered a practitioner on the path who was extremely thirsty and sweating profusely. Upon seeing him, the king gave him sugarcane wine.
Because he drank alcohol, he lost his fundamental faith and immediately transgressed the precepts, thereby forfeiting his own benefit.
Due to such unwholesome karma of providing liquor, at the dissolution of the body after death, he fell into the Great Hell of Screaming (Raurava).

Having thus observed the evil karmic conduct of the second Yāma Heavenly King, those gods perceived all conditioned birth-and-death as no different from a flame. Facing one another, they said to each other:
"This Great Heavenly King has shown us, in accordance with the fruits and retributions of immeasurable kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karma."
"Today, the benefit we have received from this Heavenly King is no different from the benefit we receive from our parents.

After those devas had spoken thus to one another, they proceeded further within the Buddha-stūpa to another location, where upon a jeweled wall they beheld the manifestation of the supernatural power of the World-Honored One Kāñcanamuni: the Heavenly King of Yāma named Tejodhipati, and by what original karma he was born in the Yāma Heaven to become its king.
When he saw those people of former times among men, they did not harm others to acquire wealth;
and during the darkness of night, at places where the Dharma was being taught, they lit lamps for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Due to those karmic causes and conditions, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Yāma Heaven as a celestial king named Majestic Virtue (Tejas).
Having served as king for a long time, at the conclusion of his lifespan, his body perished and his life ended, and he was subsequently reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Having passed away from there, he was born in Uttarakuru; having finished his life there, he was next born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Having passed away from there, he was born in Jambudvīpa, becoming a king of men endowed with great majesty and great supernormal powers.

Having been born there, because they act with negligence, are deceived by desire, and possess a fickle mind, they further commit the three unwholesome karmas: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Due to the causal conditions of having committed such evil karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the Great Hell of Scorching Heat.
It is beyond comparison, for there are immeasurable kinds of distinct and diverse hells resulting from hundreds of thousands of varieties of karmic actions.
"Having experienced all manner of sufferings within the hells, they have thus been deceived by their own mental enemies.

At that time, the celestial hosts again beheld the infinite abundance within the heavens, and then beheld its destruction—whether in pleasure or in pain. Having seen this, they addressed one another with these verses:
"Exceedingly evil and even more terrible, A great force, unbearable to endure."
Having created these karmas with a deluded mind, one thus falls into hell.
All karma arises from the mind; through causes and conditions, one exists within *bhava*.
Because they are destroyed by delusion, all beings transmigrate and undergo suffering.
Various great sufferings of intense power afflict them everywhere, unbearable;
yet, bound by karma within this world, they feel no weariness or revulsion.
When gods fall, they are born among humans; when humans die, they enter hell.
From there they emerge to be born as animals; from the animal realm they emerge to be born as ghosts.
Thus, within this wheel of karma, blown by the winds of worldly action, they transmigrate through the world, yet due to their delusion, they do not perceive it.

"In this way, the celestial hosts in that mountain region of abundant trees and lands recounted to one another how the Blessed One Kāñcanamuni had truly manifested immeasurable kinds of karma, which were clearly visible within the walls of the Buddha’s stūpa."
"Having observed those karmas, he next further examines the immeasurable varieties of birth resulting from the wholesome and unwholesome karma of the King of the Yāma Heaven.

Within another section of the wall inside that Buddha-stūpa, he again sees the King of the Yāma Heaven in a beautiful form; he wonders by what karma he was born in the Yāma Heaven to become its king."

He saw that in his previous life as a human being, he was born into a Brahmin lineage; he held right view without deviation, did not cause distress to others, and skillfully practiced the precepts. Toward those suffering intensely in prison, those who were without a protector, or those who were hungry during times of famine, he gave much pure, excellent food and drink.
With a pure mind, whether on a fast day or not a fast day, they receive and uphold the precepts;
by reason of those causes and conditions, they rescue those who are bound so that they may attain liberation, or they redeem them with material goods so that they may be set free.
By virtue of those causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven in the Yāma realm, named Suvarṇa (Good Color).
For a long period of time he served as that celestial king, possessing great majesty and great supernormal powers.

Having served as that king, when his body dissolved and his life ended, he was subsequently reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where he experienced immeasurable kinds of great happiness until the end of his time there.
Passing away from that realm of the Thirty-three Gods, he was subsequently reborn among the asuras, possessing a massive body and great supernormal powers.
When his retribution among the asuras came to an end, he was born among human beings as a great householder, endowed with great majesty and virtue.
When his life there has ended, he is reborn among humans in Aparagoyānī.

When his life there has ended, he is again reborn among humans, but in a frontier region; because his mind is light and fickle, he again commits killing, hunting various beasts and slaying them with various means such as swords and arrows.
Due to those karmic causes and conditions, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in hell.
There he was scorched by the great fires of hell and underwent immeasurable kinds of harsh and evil suffering, because of having committed unwholesome and evil karmic deeds.

Having thus observed those karmic retributions, and having likewise seen the various immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, the celestial hosts in the realm of Mount Pārijāta proceed further within the Buddha-stūpa to another location, where they behold within the walls the manifestations of the World-Honored One Kāñcanamuni.
Having arrived there, he further beheld other rare wonders within that wall. He wondered:
"In a past age, there was a King of the Yāma Heaven named Universal Joy (Samantapriya). By what karma was he born in that celestial realm to become the King of the Yāmas?"
He perceives thus:

"In a former life, while in the human world as a human being, I once possessed wholesome intentions; I constantly paid homage to my teachers and elders, giving rise to a mind of reverence, rising when seeing them, and joining my palms in worship."

Furthermore, as for other deeds: sweeping the ground of a Buddha-stūpa, having swept it, smearing it with mud, scattering flowers and burning incense; and at all times, according to one's power and according to one's means, giving alms to śramaṇas or brahmins; and constantly providing gifts and offerings to those who are sick and to those who are non-returners (anāgāmin), making such offerings with pure faith.

By the power of the causes and conditions of these wholesome karmas, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he was reborn in a happy realm as a celestial king among the Yāma devas, named Universal Joy (Samantapriya).

The entire body experiences bliss; that body’s radiance possesses various colors, bringing joy to the hearts of those who see it, providing peace, security, and coolness. This radiance pervades five hundred yojanas and consists entirely of the colors of all precious gems.
This radiance is supremely majestic and exquisite, surpassing all else and beyond comparison.

Just as among the people of Jambudvīpa the moonlight is the most majestic and exquisite, so too, among all the hosts of the Yāma devas, the light of the Heavenly King Samantatopaśobhita is the most supreme.

After experiencing the pleasures accomplished through the five objects of desire for a long period of time, he passes away from that place; by the remaining force of that karmic power, he is born among humans in Jambudvīpa as a king, ruling over a territory of five hundred yojanas with sovereign authority therein.
Having been born in that place, because their minds were fickle and restless, they hunted and killed various beasts.
Due to the causal conditions of those karmic actions, when their bodies dissolved and their lives ended, they fell into the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Having emerged from that place, due to the residual force of their unwholesome and evil karma,
they are born among birds. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 47 [and] Scroll 48.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-seven: Contemplating the Heavens; Section Thirteen: Yāma Heaven.
"Having thus seen the retribution of karmic results, those hosts of devas further examined another section of the wall within that Buddha-stūpa, seeking rare and marvelous dharmas."

Within that wall, he further beheld the celestial king Mūśalinda acting in accordance with the Dharma; he did not associate with sensual desires but delighted in the practice of the Dharma, performing deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings, and was well-acquainted with all karmic actions, both wholesome and unwholesome.
Having understood this regarding karma, he practices without negligence; though he is the king of gods, he does not become negligent.
When those hosts of devas observe the karmic retribution of the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, they think to themselves:
"By what original karma was this Great Heavenly King born in this celestial realm to become the king of gods?"
"I saw that in a past life, when he was in a human body, he practiced wholesome dharmas and heard the Buddha-dharma from Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
having heard the Dharma, he grasped and upheld it, contemplated and practiced it, and dwelt accordingly as he had heard the Dharma."
Having heard this, his mind was not distracted for even a single thought; with right faith he went forth from home, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned the dharma robes.
Once he had gone forth, he felt great dread toward even the slightest evil, such as a speck of dust, and practiced the holy life.

By virtue of that karmic cause, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn in the heavenly world of the good destinies, specifically as the king of the gods in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), named Abhedya (The Indestructible).
Having passed away from that place, he is born among human beings as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who rules over the four continents.
Once that karma is exhausted, at the end of his life, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Having passed away from that place, he is born among human beings and again becomes a king; the territory over which he rules is one thousand yojanas.
After his life there ends, he is born in Pūrvavideha and becomes its king, possessing a most excellent body.
After his life there had ended, he was next reborn among the asuras, possessing supreme supernatural powers and great might.

When his life there ended, he was again born as a wealthy householder who constantly practiced the foremost of great gifts; furthermore, he was fully endowed with ethical discipline, wisdom, and so forth. In whatever place he was reborn, in each and every location, he remained complete in these three matters: generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom.

When his life there comes to an end, because he has practiced generosity, morality, and wisdom without interruption, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, in the realm of the Yāma devas as the Yāma king named Mucilinda.

"Because those dharmas continue in succession without interruption, and because his mind is virtuous and well-disciplined, he does not become heedless when encountering the objects of desire; his mind remains uncorrupted, and as he practices in accordance with immeasurable wholesome karma for the benefit of himself and others, there are many among the celestial hosts who are not bound by desire."
At that time, the assembly of the Yāma devas spoke these verses:
"By practicing in accordance with the wholesome Dharma, one shall always obtain what is good;
throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, one's virtuous karma shall never be lost or destroyed."
Constantly increasing and upholding ethical discipline, Practicing and cultivating wisdom,
Giving at all times, With mindfulness ever uninterrupted.
Cultivating the three [perfections] beginning with giving, One eliminates and severs the three kinds of faults.
Because they have abandoned those faults, they diligently cultivate meritorious qualities.
Although they possess all celestial desires and their pleasure in sensory realms remains unimpaired,
because they are not heedless, they do not fall into hell.
The Dharma is eternally uninterrupted; those who follow it practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Those who do not follow the Dharma are utterly deluded.
Drawing near to those who possess the Dharma and precepts, they diligently cultivate the practice of wisdom.
One who can extinguish the suffering of all existences, like the sunlight dispelling darkness,
and who can cause the Dharma to flourish, is honored by devas and humans;
such a person is reborn in other realms and shall eventually reach Nirvana.
If one knows the Dharma in this way, and contemplates the characteristics of phenomena with discernment,
they will be liberated from existence and shall reach the further shore.
Possessing wisdom, patience, and constant kind speech, they take pity on all sentient beings.
Or one may give various kinds of gifts; this path leads to nirvāṇa.
The wicked draw near to evil, or they associate with the indolent;
strengthening their resolve in unwholesome dharmas, they travel the path to hell.
Seeing whomsoever one feels joy, seeing whomsoever one feels anger,
and being greedily attached everywhere— thus it is called delusion (*moha*).
Deluded by unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*), one abandons wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
Through delusion one enters hell, Suffering the afflictions of unwholesome dharmas.
By practicing the Dharma and seeking what is good, And constantly abandoning desire,
One dwells in the stainless realm of Mucilinda, Abiding among the gods.
Thus did those hosts of devas in the region of Mount Trees Abounding in Delight in that Yāma heaven speak to one another, giving rise to fear toward their cherished sensory realms.

Having directly perceived all these decays and afflictions, they further went together with King Mucilinda into another section of the wall within that same Buddha-stūpa to observe in succession: after the Night-Mover King Mucilinda and the assembly of devas have passed away from this place, where will they be reborn?
"In which realm do they dwell?

At that time, the assembly of devas all saw themselves within that wall, together with their lord, Mucilinda. Having passed away from their celestial abodes, they were born in Jambudvīpa; at the time when the World-Honored One Maitreya appears in the world, they will all have their faculties complete, and all will be born into great clans as companions. They will share the same land, cherish one another, and be born into great clans—all being wealthy, honored, and of noble lineage.
Thus, within the walls, they all saw their own selves.

Muxulou-tuo was born in that land into a great kṣatriya lineage; he was immensely wealthy and powerful, honored by all people, and his house was filled with hundreds of thousands of billions of jewels. Born as the eldest son of a kṣatriya family, he was named Shanjie (Good Precepts).

At that time, there the World-Honored One Maitreya taught the Dharma of tranquility leading toward the city of Nirvāṇa—namely, the Four Noble Truths—which are complete in merit, good in the beginning, middle, and end, excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, a unique teaching that is perfectly pure and pristine.
That is to say: "This is form; this is the origin of form; this is the cessation of form; this is the path leading to the cessation of form."
"In this same sequence, he briefly explains the general characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He teaches the Dharma to all worlds in such a way that all sentient beings may dwell in peace, leave behind turbidity, and proceed toward the city of Nirvana without any obstacles."

"At that time, the Kṣatriya prince Śīlavat—the king’s eldest son—heard by report that Maitreya, the World-Honored One, was preaching the Dharma; having heard this as previously described, his companions likewise heard it."
Due to the causes of virtuous karma cultivated in previous lives, they all deliberated together and proceeded toward that son of the Kṣatriya clan, Sudarśana.
Twenty thousand people went to that prince Sudarśana, as previously described.

At that time, having heard those words, Kuśalamati—due to his past roots of goodness—felt great joy in his heart and gave rise to a mind of profound reverence. His countenance became pure and serene; all his faculties were harmonized, and they rose up together at once to go to the place where the World-Honored One, the Buddha Maitreya, was staying.
Thus the multitude circumambulated Śīlavat, just as the second Heaven of the Thirty-three deities surrounds Śakra.

On the road, they saw from afar the World-Honored One Maitreya, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, extensively preaching the sublime Dharma to benefit all the world of devas and humans, as well as the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; he was thus teaching the Dharma for entering nirvāṇa, excellent in its beginning, middle, and end.
That Dharma is pure like a pool of water; it can exhaust all suffering and remove all the fetters of birth and death, leading progressively even unto Nirvana—such is the Dharma he teaches.
At that time, the assembly was as vast as the ocean, and the World-Honored One Maitreya was preaching the Dharma therein.
Then, seeing from afar the person of Good Precepts surrounded by a multitude, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"This is the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Musulinda, together with his great retinue."
This Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, has practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) and previously planted the seeds of wholesome dharmas; now, their roots have matured.

The bonds of this Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, have become loose; his many unwholesome karmas are all extinguished, and he has abandoned desire. The time when all sufferings are exhausted is now approaching.
Having heard these words spoken from the mouth of the Tathāgata, that person gives rise to joy in their heart and a sense of profound reverence; they shall be entirely freed from all of saṃsāra.
“The form of the Tathāgata is most rare and beyond all analogy.
Having beheld such a rare Buddha, Muxuluotuo prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
‘World-Honored One!’”
"I have been wandering through the cycle of birth and death in this world and am weary of it;

I seek renunciation. At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma according to their needs, and ten thousand people who had long been close to the king and had always traveled with him—his former companions—attained the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
"All future [beings] will see Maudgalyāyana, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, just as he was manifested within the wall by the World-Honored One Kāśyapa, appearing in succession."

The various and wondrous deeds manifested by the Omniscient One are of infinite kinds; they are not within the domain of others, including the worlds of gods and Māras, nor can any śramaṇas or brahmins perceive them, except for those who are near to the True Being and those who dwell with the Tathāgata.
"Associating with virtuous friends is the foremost way to transcend birth and death.
At that time, all those heavenly hosts collectively gave rise to a heart of joy and developed a mind of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Then that Heavenly King, together with the assembly of devas, again prostrated before the Buddha and departed from that stupa.
"Among the six sūtras, the fifth transformation by the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāñcanamuni, is now complete."
At that time, Mucilinda, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, gave rise to a heart of joy; yet, seeing the faults and perils of desire, he again felt fear.
Together with the host of devas, he proceeded to observe the region of the Ground Endowed with Mountains and Trees, where the celestial assembly moved about in delight.
In that place there are many various hosts of devas and many groves; lotus ponds fill that region, with immeasurable varieties of lotuses covering the pools.
There are various birds with lovely voices; those who hear their sounds experience great joy.

In that region, where mountains and trees abound, there are many hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who engage in various pastimes of singing, dancing, and joyful laughter, possessing immeasurable merit.
There are trees made of the seven precious substances, complete with flowers and fruit; there are many mountain peaks composed entirely of exquisite jewels, filling that region as an adornment.

According to the retribution of their own karma, there are inferior, middling, and superior [levels of experience]. The celestial hosts, through their own karma, enjoy only the pleasures of desire; they fill that region, acting as companions to one another without mutual interference, and trusting each other.
There are many sons of gods and hosts of goddesses who cherish one another with mutual affection.
There are many rivers, and within these rivers are drinks whose flavors are exceedingly delightful.

Furthermore, there are various exquisite jewel-palaces arranged in rows, lovely with their variegated colors; they are fully endowed with the merits of the five desires, and the radiance of the various jewels mutually adorns them.
Those various jeweled palaces vied with one another to emit surpassing light, like gold refined by fire.
With coral, musaragalva, and many blue jewels as well as mountain peaks, they adorned the ground.
The mountain regions, complete with trees and lands, are adorned in such a way as to be so lovely.
Having observed this, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, addressed the host of devas:

"O devas, behold those devas acting with hearts full of joy; from mountain to mountain, from one peak to another peak, they sport in delight, with the sounds of the five kinds of music, singing, dancing, and play."
"You all should now behold those celestial hosts.
Having thus seen various things within the Buddha-stūpa, the celestial hosts replied to the Heavenly King,
"We have already seen them."
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
“The Tathāgata has already spoken; he has spoken in accordance with reality concerning the decline and afflictions within the heavens.”

For the deva who acts with negligence, his life is about to end, his wholesome karma is about to decay, his time of decline is approaching, and the fruit of his precepts is about to perish; yet, as his karmic actions are like a magical illusion, he remains deluded and does not perceive it.
The gods who practice heedlessness do not perceive nor understand that they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
These immeasurable kinds of suffering, decline, and affliction, as well as the cycle of birth and death, all arise from their fundamental karma.
Why is this? Because those life-processes (jīvitasaṃskāra) flow on from moment to moment and cannot be turned back;
because the power of karma is great and cannot be escaped.

Thus, all conditioned phenomena possess these three characteristics; because of the three defects of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there are many immeasurable matters of decline and affliction, and not even the slightest flavor of true satisfaction.
Yet the hosts of devas neither know nor perceive this; they consider themselves to be in great bliss, though moment by moment they draw near to death.
When the time of death arrives, they have already entered the gateway of death, yet they remain unaware of it.
Thus, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not cease for even a single moment; all that possesses life is impermanent and subject to destruction, and youth swiftly changes.
When those gods fall from their celestial state, they experience suffering and affliction, undergoing immeasurable kinds of separation from those they love.

At that time, having seen the Heavenly King, the assembly of devas felt great joy in their hearts; they quickly, very quickly, adorned their bodies, draping celestial garments and adorning themselves with jeweled crowns, necklaces, and exquisite celestial garlands.

With their own bodies radiant and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens adorned with various ornaments, the sons of gods enjoy the highest pleasure amidst diverse musical sounds, songs, dances, and laughter.
Due to their own virtuous karma, they were thus adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of colors as they proceeded toward the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda.
At that time, having seen them thus, the Heavenly King looked upon them with favor and drew slightly closer; there he saw them sporting and enjoying various pleasures.
"At that time, because the Heavenly King accords with their minds, he briefly enters among the hosts to sport and enjoy pleasures;
it is not out of his own delight. While among the other devas, he sports and laughs for but a moment."
The mind of that deity was stirred, and he took delight in sensual desires. Having finished his playful enjoyment, he went to another mountain peak.

That mountain peak was adorned with various coral, gold, silver, and other trees of immeasurable hundreds of kinds of exquisite colors; it resounded with the songs of immeasurable varieties of birds, was illuminated by immeasurable kinds of radiance, contained immeasurable varieties of distinct thoughts, and was graced by immeasurable kinds of celestial, wondrous jewel-natures.
That deva went to such a mountain peak; having reached the peak, his heart was filled with love and he experienced pleasure.
That Lord of the Yāma devas traveled together as one with those devas who had previously seen the stūpas of the Buddha, proceeding with that host of devas who delight in immeasurable realms of joy.
Then, the Lord of the Yāma Heaven addressed the celestial hosts, saying:
"I shall go together with you all.
By abandoning sensory realms for the sake of one's own benefit, one will indeed attain that benefit."
"If we do not abandon sense objects, there will be no benefit.
We shall resolutely follow the practice of the Dharma until we ultimately reach nirvana.
Having spoken thus to that assembly of devas, they all proceeded together with those devas toward the place on the mountain where trees abound, their minds serene.
Having arrived there, in one part of that place, there was a wonderful lotus pond with various flowing waters and groves of lotuses, adorned by many kinds of birds.
Furthermore, there were various jewel-bees as adornments, all appearing like flames.
In that lovely place, there stood the sixth stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha; upon seeing it, the Lord of Devas was struck with wonder.

Among the radiance of all precious jewels, the light of the Buddha-stūpa is most supreme; it pierces through the void and emerges, adorned with various wondrous gems, its brilliance surpassing that of hundreds of thousands of suns.
The radiance was tranquil, and from a vast expanse, they beheld that Buddhist stūpa.
At that time, having seen this, the host of devas addressed their lord, Mucilinda, saying:
"What kind of wondrous jewel-light is this?"
"It was just as I saw it before.
At that time, having heard these words, the Lord of the Gods, King Yama, addressed them, saying:
"Listen, all you hosts of gods!
What is now seen—this manifold, supreme, and wondrous radiance—is just as it was previously seen.

This is the stūpa of the Great Sage, the sixth Tathāgata—the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, the God among Gods—Kāśyapa Buddha.
As for this stūpa, it is the manifestation of the pure conduct cultivated through the original karma of the devas, and of the mind they once cultivated for the sake of benefit and welfare;
these appear clearly manifested upon the jeweled walls within this stūpa.
Just as it is appropriate for other Tathāgatas to bring benefit, so too shall it be within this Buddha-stūpa.
Together with you, the great assembly of devas, I shall generate a mind of reverence for the Buddha’s true Dharma and thereby accomplish our own benefit.

After the Lord of the Yāma Heaven had spoken thus, he went together with the assembly of devas toward the Buddha-stūpa. Upon arrival, they beheld it replete with the radiance of various exquisite jewels, just as previously described.
"At that time, it was thus: the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, together with his celestial host, entered that Buddha-stūpa and immediately beheld the image of the Great Seer Kāśyapa.

It was an image made of Jambūnada gold, adorned with garments of exquisite jewels and immeasurable radiance. A lion throne was fashioned from Vaiḍūrya gem, and upon it sat the Buddha-image in the very same manner as when he was currently preaching the Dharma, without any difference whatsoever."
That image possesses an incomparable color; such a color surpasses the color of those heavenly beings.
Just as a firefly is no different from the sun, so too is the Buddha’s color of majestic virtue (tejas) thus preeminent and sublime.

At that time, the Heavenly King and his celestial retinue, having beheld the Buddha’s image, were filled with supreme joy. With deep reverence and faith, they prostrated themselves in homage. They removed their crowns, necklaces, garlands, and ornaments; they cast off pride regarding physical form and ceased attachment to the pleasures of the senses. Freeing themselves from pride in radiance, they abandoned all arrogance. Their minds purified of the stains of desire, they bowed their heads to the feet of the World-Honored One, repeatedly prostrating themselves as they gradually shed their pride.
Having thus paid homage, all the devas arose with single-minded concentration and remained unmoving.
Due to the causes of their karma, they saw inscriptions upon the side walls of the Buddha-stūpa, beside the images of the Buddha.

This sūtra is a manifestation produced by the Buddha’s spiritual power; it benefits devas and humans, bringing benefit to all the world. With its correct words and phrases, excellent meaning and flavor, it proceeds in sequence until it reveals nirvāṇa. It is the great preceptor for all those who have left the household life, teaching according to the Vinaya as follows:
"Bhikṣus, there are thirteen things that act as obstacles, such that one cannot practice dhyāna or recite the sūtras and Vinaya; they hinder one's own benefit and prevent the attainment of nirvāṇa."

If bhikṣus do not abandon these thirteen dharmas, then amidst sickness, old age, death, lamentation, weeping, grief, suffering, and distress, they shall find no liberation. They are base and vulgar among men; they have not truly left the household life; their body, speech, and mind constantly engage in improper conduct, and they lack diligent perseverance.
In this way, if a bhikṣu accepts bedding, medicine for illness, or other necessities from others for even a single day, he will be unable to digest them.
Such things become an impediment to him; as for what constitutes an impediment, they cause the body to become emaciated, lead to indolence, engender fear, and result in a lack of understanding.
Such a person cannot cross the great river of immense power, swift force, valor, and profound depth.

Such a person is physically emaciated and lacks diligence; their mind is unsubdued and constantly indolent; they do not know how to practice seated meditation or recite the sutras and vinaya; they are fearful and ignorant, their very being shrouded by nescience.
Therefore, one cannot cross the five rivers; because one relies upon sense objects, one cannot cross them.
Driven by sense objects, one is swept away in the river of craving; once swept away by the river of craving, one enters the ocean of birth and death, wandering and revolving incessantly without end.
“What are the thirteen? They are:
delighting in much talk; and treating illnesses;”
Practicing painting;
hearing and singing praises of evil and wicked matters;
counting stars and engaging in such contemplations.
Contemplating omens;
craving only food and drink;
and seeking various precious substances.
Associating with kings and the like;
hoping for invitations;
and not inquiring of others.
Delighting in many acquaintances;
dwelling together with the wicked.
These thirteen dharmas are hindrances for a śramaṇa engaged in seated meditation and recitation.
Because of such hindrances, one loses one's own benefit, and the benefit obtained is meager.
Due to this loss of benefit, one is reborn in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; thus, one's renunciation is in vain.
Such a person is neither a renunciant nor a householder; having abandoned wholesome dharmas, they are held in contempt by their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
Possessing nothing but empty fame, which resembles the sound of a conch shell, they neither hear nor know the practice leading to Nirvana.
Whatever they recall and contemplate does not accord with their wishes;
the deities who protect their bodies abandon them and depart.
"As for that first obstacle, it hinders seated meditation and can cause great turmoil."
That which is the initial delight in much talk is pleasant at first, but later leads to regret and feverish distress.
All who have gone forth should abandon this practice, namely, the delight in engaging in much speech.

Because one delights in excessive speech, the mind is not subdued; one is unable to practice correctly or maintain the precepts. The mind is constantly agitated and distracted, and because the mind is agitated and distracted, one is caught in a dense web of doubt.
Such a person delights in associating with wicked people; those wicked people are what is called "disturbed minds.

They constantly take pleasure in watching actors, singers, and dancers, traveling incessantly from region to region and place to place—whether to cities, villages, or various settlements—never stopping in their wanderings as they watch such spectacles for amusement.
They constantly observe spectacles on festival days and visit all places of assembly; they associate with such people as their companions and identify themselves with their own minds.
Their minds are constantly agitated and they always delight in speech; day and night it is ever thus, without rest.
With such distracted minds, they neither hear nor understand, and are perpetually held in contempt by their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Having recognized another as lowly, one gives rise to anger and resentment toward that other person who maintains the precepts and practices the path.
Because of these karmic causes and conditions, when that person’s body breaks up at the end of life, they fall into the evil realms—among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Furthermore, for those who delight in much talk, there is yet another great fault.

Those evil bhikṣus have not heard much of the Dharma and have violated the prohibitions and precepts; they delight in much talk, exalting themselves and being fickle. Even though they have seen the Buddha, their hearts lack shame and remorse; because they lack shame and remorse, they do not revere the Buddha."
When the donor sees him, he does not give rise to respect.
Because others treat him with contempt, he abandons the precepts and returns to secular life.
Furthermore, there is another great fault for one who delights in excessive speech.
What is the fault?
It is that, being personally fond of much talk, they further teach other renunciants to cause them to retreat from the True Dharma.
They destroy themselves and are likewise able to destroy others.
Because that person has thus brought ruin upon himself and others, his ill repute spreads far and wide; for the Saṃgha knows this, they expel and abandon him.
These bhikṣus who properly maintain the precepts, fearing that such an evil person might cause them to fall, all say, "Abandon this bhikṣu," and declare, "This bhikṣu is a bad friend."
Fellow practitioners of the holy life thus despise them as evil.
Furthermore, there is another great fault for those who delight in much speech:
having previously heard various kinds of talk, their minds take pleasure in it, thinking, "This is joy. Once that wicked śramaṇa has heard it, his mind gives rise to great delight.
Because that mind is so inclined toward pleasure, one believes in what is not the Dharma and believes in the meaning of what is not the Dharma;
one regards the Dharma as non-Dharma and non-Dharma as Dharma, and likewise believes in other practitioners who follow what is not the Dharma.
Because this person delights in those who speak excessively, they fall into wrong views; due to the causal conditions of those wrong views, they engage in false speech.
By reason of these unwholesome karmic causes and conditions, when their body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms, being reborn in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.
"Therefore, because of the faults of excessive speech, there are further many faults.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke in verse:
"Accumulating many words of frivolous chatter Can cause the mind and intentions to become disordered."
They destroy the holy life and obstruct the path to Nirvana.
Always delighting in much talk, vulgar and lacking in moral discipline,
such people are forever shunned by those who sit in meditation and know the Truths.
Lack of self-control is the root cause; it can cause one to lose wholesome thoughts and can also cause one to lose the holy life.
It makes the path to Nirvāṇa dark, obstructs the path to the heavenly realms, and furthermore leads one toward the evil paths.
It causes one to head toward the realm of hungry ghosts and leads one to be born in the realm of animals.
That which is called "delighting in much talk" is the mother of birth and death;
monks who practice meditation and recitation should abandon it if they desire peace and security.
"Thus has that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, the Great Sage Kāśyapa, already spoken: there are great faults in delighting in much speech.
Furthermore, he next spoke of the merits of not delighting in much speech, namely:

'A bhikṣu who rightly rectifies his mind delights only in the True Dharma and knows only the True Dharma; he speaks correctly in this way, contemplates only the True Dharma, reflects upon the True Dharma, practices only the True Dharma, and constantly pays homage to the Buddha.'"
These various bhikṣus were able to see places they had never seen before, because they were able to abandon the existence of much speech and practiced only right conduct, fearing birth and death.
That speech has its fruit, namely, when one speaks the words of the Four Noble Truths;
that body has its fruit, namely, when one pays homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and exerts oneself with diligence and vigor;

that bodily exertion has its fruit in the mind, for when the mind is constantly diligent, the marks of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are contemplated—these are the fruits thereof.
There are three kinds of diligent application that bring one close to nirvāṇa.
If there is a person who employs every means and every form of diligence to abandon excessive speech, distance themselves from evil associates, and never remain in their company;
A mind that is upright, a mind that is straight, and a mind that is undisturbed—these three lead to nirvāṇa.
As for the threefold path, what are these three?
What is called the mental application of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) consists of contemplating the realm of impurity as impermanent and subject to destruction.
All these paths can be attained through a right mind, not through a wrong mind.
Delighting in excessive speech and lacking right mindfulness obstructs these three paths; this is indeed the conduct of the evil realms—of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
This noose binds people and leads them away into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; such sentient beings are thus deceived and deluded by excessive speech.

Therefore, delighting in much talk and discourse is like poison, like a sword, like fire, like a snake, or like falling over a precipice; a wise bhikṣu practicing dhyāna and reciting the scriptures should always abandon it.
“Because he was able to deceive many people with his various languages, he caused them to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

If, through the remainder of his karma, he is born among humans, he will become a professional entertainer who constantly performs for others—such as a tightrope walker, a trapeze artist, a wrestler, a dancer, or one who sings various songs;
he will wander from place to place, begging at the gates of others' houses.”
Some again pursue a livelihood through commerce, seeking profit as merchants;
others are blind, constantly staying in busy marketplaces and thoroughfares to trade for their own sustenance.
Those who delight in excessive speech are bitten by venomous snakes;
those who delight in excessive speech are consumed by great fires. Having fallen into such a perilous state of excessive speech, they are stung by the poisonous venom of much talking.
Such deluded people delight in excessive speech and are bewildered by its various branches. All such bewilderment arises from excessive speech.
Delighting in excessive speech is a mass of great darkness;

those who fear the evil realms should abandon it entirely in this way. Having abandoned it, they should practice with diligent effort in succession, and thus they will attain the vision of the Truths.
"Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:

In empty, vast, and secluded places—places free from obstructing sounds, free from the sound of shouting, the sound of singing, or the sound of drums; in places for cultivating wisdom such as mountain valleys, rock caves, and the roots of trees; in meritorious places free from the interference of noise; sitting alone with no other person, with a single-minded and right mindfulness, one shall destroy the Māra of afflictions."
Thus practicing well, they tame the mind and bring it to stillness, remaining free from all excessive speech.

Whether relatives, friends, acquaintances, or brothers come and go or meet them, they remain detached from conversation; their minds harbor no expectations, finding peace and happiness only in solitude. They constantly engage in meditation and recitation, remaining free from the four inversions.
He fully attends to and understands these sixteen types of ānāpāna; day and night, he exerts diligent vigor, so that within the bonds of birth and death, he is able to escape and flee.
One who is able to act in this way will attain the state of excellence.
If one has not yet seen the place of eternal peace and security, that person should distance themselves from excessive speech.
A person of wisdom and virtuous intent practices with firm resolve; such a śramaṇa abandons indolence and relinquishes this one practice, namely, the delight in much talk.
"Furthermore, one must abandon the second obstructive dharma that should not be practiced, as it is subsumed under killing. What is the second?
It refers to a bhikṣu who acts as a physician for treating illnesses, such that he is unable to practice seated meditation or engage in recitation."

A bhikṣu who acts as a physician administering medicine in this manner pursues a heterodox path and performs heterodox deeds; constantly seeking out the sick and constantly striving to cure their illnesses, he engages in such activities and greatly increases his greed.
Out of a greedy mind, he thinks to himself:
"I hope that sentient beings will have many illnesses, all manner of countless ailments.
When those sick beings provide me with much support and give me many things."
Therefore, as I travel among many people, I constantly experience happiness, going from village to village, from city to city, and from one remote region to another.
Once that evil bhikṣu has formed such thoughts and reflections, his greed increases.
When the greed of such a bhikṣu has thus increased, defilement arises in his mind; he is unable to practice dhyāna or recite the scriptures, and this is not a virtuous practice.
