"Furthermore, treating illnesses results in the fault of defilement.
Those wicked bhikṣus, while claiming for themselves the title of 'bhikṣu,' will, when sentient beings are afflicted by illness, prescribe medicine to them, saying:
'Quickly bring oil; if there is no oil, then press sesame seeds.'"
Because sesame seeds are pressed, many insects die; this is what is called the fault of treating illness.
They falsely act as śramaṇas, merely saying with their mouths: "I am a śramaṇa."
"They are not truly śramaṇas.
Furthermore, upon seeing a sick person, they command their attendants to provide meat, saying:

'It must be freshly slaughtered; it must not be fatty, nor must it be from an animal that died of itself, nor one that died of disease, nor one killed by poison, nor one killed by a snake, nor must it be dried, nor must it be lean.'"
Having been thus instructed,
because of that instruction, he then takes life;
because he has taken life, he incurs the offense of taking life.
Whether one instructs another to kill or kills oneself, both types of persons share the same karmic act of killing and will fall into the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Therefore, one should not perform medical treatments out of a greedy mind.
"Furthermore, there is yet another fault regarding the treatment of illness: they can only say with their mouths,
'I am a śramaṇa,' yet in reality they are great thieves and great evildoers."

Because those sentient beings were afflicted by much illness and pain, he went everywhere to gather various medicinal herbs—whether trees, tree branches, or tree fruits—and for the sake of material wealth, he collected them all.
All those medicinal herbs are inhabited by various insects, serving as their dwelling place, with insects filling every part of them.
Because they desire to obtain these things out of greed, they uproot them from the earth or cut them down.
Because of uprooting it, one kills the insects dwelling in the ground or destroys the place where those insects reside.
If one cuts it off, one kills the internal insects, and the insects in that location die.
This is the fault of treating illnesses: when the mind thus delights in impure livelihoods, how can there be the practice of meditation or the recitation of scriptures?
Such a mind constantly takes pleasure in treating illnesses.
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu who treats illnesses harbors such evil thoughts, there is a great transgression.
Such a bhikṣu contemplates unwholesome dharmas with a mind that desires many people to fall ill, thinking:
'If there are many sick people, I will receive abundant offerings of wealth, food, drink, and bedding; such are my great gains.'"

With a mind intent on destruction, he does not contemplate wholesome dharmas, takes no delight in meditation or recitation, does not draw near to his elders or virtuous friends, nor does he pay homage to the Buddha; thus, he performs unwholesome deeds.
When his body perishes and his life ends, he falls into an evil destination and is born in hell.

Having emerged from that place, due to the remainder of his karma, even if he is born among humans by virtue of those wholesome karmas, he will constantly suffer from illness and pain, and will be poor and short-lived.
This is because of their evil and unwholesome practice of treating illness.
Furthermore, there are faults in treating illness; even treating illness according to the Dharma has its own faults.
Since beginningless time, there have always been three types [of humors]: wind, heat, and cold. When these three are balanced, the body is at peace and one does not fall into the evil realms.
Because this body is a composite of parts and because the body perishes, those three [qualities] are also lost.
Yet these foolish, ordinary people, having never heard the truth and lacking wisdom, though they are not truly śramaṇas, claim of themselves: "I am a śramaṇa."
To remedy those three types [of faults],
for what purpose and by what cause did he shave off his hair and beard, don the dharma robes, and go forth into homelessness?
For what reason did he renounce this world?

Since beginningless time, desire, hatred, and delusion have not been comprised within the body; if one were to burn the body, those three would not be burned, nor lost, nor extinguished, but would continue to pursue and bind one, accompanying one everywhere throughout the five realms of existence.
Why is it that one does not first treat these three great faults—desire, hatred, and delusion—but instead treats wind, heat, and cold first?
"This false renunciant, a foolish and ignorant person of vulgar character, is deceived by his own mind.
It is as if there were a foolish man who was without a master, without companions, poor and possessing nothing, yet who had a powerful enemy who harassed and disturbed him day after day."
If that foolish person gives wealth and goods to a powerful enemy, he cannot be warded off; even by means of his own power, he cannot prevent it.
Because such an enemy possesses great strength, he constantly watches for an opportunity, desiring to come and kill him.
This foolish person does not fear that enemy, yet knowing that others have even minor grievances, he becomes terrified of such minor grievances and takes such a foolish person as his companion.
Then the fool says to his companion,
"I shall now act on your behalf to eliminate that enemy.
That powerful enemy, perceiving the fool's stupidity and knowing him to be acting with negligence and indolence, goes and kills him once he has recognized this.
Why is this? Because that deluded person performs tasks for others.
In this very way, those who call themselves śramaṇas and who claim to stand as śramaṇas abandon the great powerful enemy that is their own self and instead perform tasks for others.

Those [afflictions of] desire, hatred, and delusion follow one through immeasurable lifetimes without ever departing; they manifest the path of birth and death, possessing great power yet having no fixed location. They cannot be sought out and are known only by wisdom; they move in tandem with delusion.
In order to eliminate such causes and conditions for great enmity, he abandons his own kin, friends, wife, and brothers to shave his head and leave the household life.
Having already left the household life, he fails to recognize these powerful enemies; for the sake of wealth and possessions, he says to others:
"Your enemies—wind, heat, cold, and so forth—I shall eliminate them."
Thus, for such a person of distracted mind and delusion, when the King of Death arrives, these three kinds of enemies pursue him without ceasing.
Those powerful enemies are desire, hatred, and delusion.

That person is bound by the ropes of desire and acts with extreme heedlessness; as they are about to depart for the next world, they delight in pursuing worldly affairs with great greed and a distracted mind.
Therefore, if one recognizes these faults, one should not employ such means to treat the illness.
"If a person wishes to cure their illness, they should eliminate desire and the like; then they will be forever free from disease.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"The faults of wind and the other humors are not many, But the faults of desire and the like are many.
Wind and the like do not lead to evil realms; it is desire and the like that cause one to fall into hell.
Mental transgressions are the greatest of faults, for they constantly cause one to wander through evil paths.
Therefore, their removal brings true happiness, whereas the mere removal of wind and the like does not.
If one abandons one's own work and delights in the work of others,
that person will quickly come to ruin and be mocked by the wise.
Because of the destruction wrought by the winds and other elements, sentient beings lose their bodies.
Desire and the like have never been lost; through birth and death, there is immeasurable perversion.
The cessation of that desire and the like is bliss; the cessation of wind and the like is not bliss.
Because desire and the like are extinguished, one ultimately attains supreme bliss.
"To treat the mind is called treating the disease; to treat the body is not treating the disease.
To treat the diseases of the mind is difficult to understand; to treat wind and other [physical ailments] is easy to comprehend.
For this reason, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, thus prohibited those who have gone forth from treating diseases.
"Furthermore, for a renunciant to treat illnesses using medical prescriptions involves immeasurable faults, namely, the arising of a greedy mind.
Upon seeing other physicians, arrogance arises in their hearts, and they disparage those other physicians with unwholesome speech."
They obstruct and abandon their work, giving rise to envy and jealousy; they accumulate the karma of hungry ghosts and thus create the causes for rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts.

With such a mind of envy and a restless mind, they give rise to great greed. Because this greed arises, when they see women, they fail to observe them properly and thereby bring about their own obstruction and confusion.
That person, with a deluded mind, sees another’s wife and gives rise to a corrupting desire.
While he treats others' ailments of wind, cold, and heat, he himself increases the various diseases within his own body—namely, the diseases of desire, hatred, and delusion.

Because they increase desire and the like, these causes and conditions cause the various sufferings of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals to grow; thus, they are destroyed by desire and the like.
An unskilled physician possesses wrong views and is bound by great transgressions, destined for hell.
Therefore, all those who have left the household life should always be diligent in eliminating the diseases of desire and the like, rather than treating ailments such as wind-disorders.

This is the second rule: a śramaṇa who seeks nirvāṇa should not treat illnesses with medicine in such a manner as to obstruct or neglect sitting in meditation and the recitation of the sūtras and the vinaya.
"Furthermore, one should abandon the third obstructive factor, which is not to be practiced.
What is the third? It is the painter."
To paint the deeds of one who has left the household life is improper.
Why is this so? Having abandoned the home and gone forth from the household life for the sake of eliminating desire, one instead gives rise to other desires.
Having understood that the world is a painting produced by the mind’s karma, one then creates its various other painted colors.
If there were those who did not know that the world is a painting produced by the mind’s karma, they might instead create paintings of various physical colors.
That renunciant should always thus discern and examine this painting:
the five great colors are used to paint the five destinies, because the seeds of the mind are manifold. What are these five?
This refers to painting the five destinies using primary colors.
The painter of the mind uses the supreme, pure color of great white karma to paint the heavenly realm;
because of his faith, he delights in practicing great generosity and remains free from stinginess and envy.
The first pure dharma is the mountain-arising of generosity and precepts; the mind as a painter paints the various devas and paints the heavenly realms.
Furthermore, those who have left the household life should further observe and understand the painting of karma: through the many-colored pigments of karma, the human realm is painted.
Human beings are differentiated into three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
If a wealthy person is able to maintain the precepts, that person is one who has been painted with the colors of the foremost white karma.
If a person is very wealthy yet cannot maintain the precepts, that person is one whose karma is painted with the colors of black and white.
If a person is poor yet can maintain the precepts, that person is one whose karma is painted with the colors of red and white.
If a person is impoverished and unable to maintain the precepts, that person is painted with the dark black hues of karma.
If a person is indolent and moreover full of desire, that person is painted with the dark yellow hues of karma.
If a person is handsome and born into a great lineage, that person is one painted with the colors of pure white karma.
If a person is born into a middle-ranking lineage, that person is one painted with the colors of reddish-pink karma.
If a person is born into a low caste, they are one whose form is painted with the dark pigments of defiled karma;
yet the painter of the mind uses the pigments of wholesome karma to paint them as a human being.

"Even if one is born among humans as a king or a great minister, yet continues to perform unwholesome deeds, such a person’s white karmic seeds will perish, while the color of their black karmic seeds will increase and come forth."

Furthermore, if a person is born into a lowly family or is extremely impoverished, yet constantly practices generosity and upholds the precepts, such a person’s dark karmic seeds will be extinguished, and the colors of their white karmic seeds will increase and flourish.
Furthermore, if among human beings one belongs to a noble lineage and possesses beautiful form, or performs middling deeds, that mind-painter paints them with the pigments of red and white karma.

In this way, the master painter of immeasurable variegated karmic colors creates the diverse and differing distinctions of the various types of worldly activities through the application of these mixed pigments.

"Furthermore, the renunciant further contemplates other realms, namely, he again contemplates the sentient beings in the hells, who are painted by the artist that is the mind with the pigments of two kinds of karma—namely, yellow and black."
Yellow signifies fire; black signifies envy. Those born in the lower realms are born in hell; thus they are depicted with these two colors.
Having observed these painted colors of the hells, that bhikṣu further observes the black karmic colors of the hungry ghosts whose bodies are scorched by hunger and thirst.
"All those ghosts are each individually painted by the colors of their own karma.
Furthermore, he observes: by what karmic colors are animals painted?
They are the colors black and red."
If they experience the foremost suffering and the foremost terror, it is a black drawing;
if they kill one another, it is a red drawing.
Such colors are drawn by the mind-painter in this manner.
"Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are three abodes of animals where they mutually fear one another—fearing slaughter, fearing bondage, and being eaten by others.
Those that move through the air are birds such as peacocks, pheasants, and geese;
those that move on land are livestock such as oxen, water buffaloes, pigs, and horses."
Those that move within the water are the so-called fish and such.
That which is painted black is [the elephant] that does not fear slaughter;
that which is painted red is the elephant among the gods.
"Thus, regarding these five realms and their five kinds of colors, that person is unable to reflect in this way:

'The various sufferings and afflictions of all the world—the five signs in the heavens, the toil of human beings, the mutual slaughter among animals, the hunger and thirst of hungry ghosts, and the great suffering endured within the hells—are all painted by the colors of such diverse karmic actions.'"

Being foolish and lacking wisdom, they neither exercise restraint nor reflection; therefore, they are indolent, unable to practice seated meditation, unable to maintain the precepts, and unable to recite the scriptures, yet they fail to understand that the mind is a painter and instead produce other paintings.

The first painting refers to the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death within the world; the meeting with those one hates and the separation from those one loves; cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; mutual destruction and the disparagement or honoring of others; the suffering and joy of servants and masters; and the karmic forms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas—thus depicting the various aspects of birth and death.
Being distracted by various things, they are unable to practice or to contemplate; though their minds recognize this, they do not give rise to weary detachment.

Thus, those bhikṣus abandon the practices of seated meditation and recitation, and instead direct their minds toward creating the outward appearance of the śramaṇa’s dharma, making meditation and recitation merely a matter of form.

"Furthermore, there is another phenomenon: one cannot contemplate the paintings of the places of birth and death, yet one instead contemplates other paintings, namely, the various sense faculties, conditions, and objects."
If there are sentient beings who delight in sense objects, they will wander for a long time through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
What is this dharma? It is said:
when the eye sees a form, one takes pleasure in that object and gives rise to a mind of desire, becoming firmly attached and stained by that form.
That person then gathers the pigments of black karma—the colors of the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth—and paints them in this manner.
"If those sentient beings, having seen a form with their eyes, reflect thus:
'This form is impermanent; it moves, transforms, and changes.'"
When that person is thus neither delighted nor pleased, neither covetous nor attached, they thereby gather white karma and will be reborn among gods or humans, even unto nirvāṇa.

In this way, when a person has seen forms with their eyes, they do not delight in them, do not take them as objects, do not long for them, and do not dwell upon them; they do not mentally enjoy them and do not give rise to a mind of desire. Such a person, by means of the finest white karma as if using pigments and skilled craftsmanship, experiences happiness among gods and humans.

"Those evil bhikṣus, with such deluded minds, neither contemplate nor reflect, neither practice dhyāna nor recite the scriptures. When their eyes see forms, they take delight in and become attached to those objects; thus bound, they are like painters using black ink as their pigment."
A person of wisdom is able to abandon that painting of black karma and the colors of evil mental actions; they should instead sit in meditation and recite the sutras and vinaya.
Furthermore, one should observe what kind of image the śramaṇa-painter creates when he contemplates and paints.
That is to say, when the ear hears sounds—whether pleasant or unpleasant—one contemplates them as they truly are:
"Such sounds are impermanent and unstable; they are not solid and are subject to destruction."

Having understood this, his mind finds no delight; he does not give rise to joy, nor does he dwell upon it or take pleasure in it, nor does he listen to or contemplate it—thus is the white karma painted by the master artist of colors.
That white painting results in birth among gods or humans; having been born among the gods, such a painting is the foremost and most excellent of all varieties.

Yet that painter-monk of evil intent, though calling himself a monk, never once gives rise to the thought to contemplate sound or painting; instead, he produces other paintings, neglecting meditation and recitation, abandoning dhyāna and study, and failing to cultivate pure karma.
"Furthermore, that śramaṇa of deluded mind, having never heard this before, being foolish and lacking wisdom, thinks thus:
'This sound is lovely; it can gladden the heart and bring me pleasure.'"
That evil śramaṇa, failing to observe correctly, perceives that sound and gives rise to longing; because of this, desire arises, and within his mind toward that sound, he conceives joy and pleasure.
This painter of the mind, with its dark pigments, paints out the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Having recognized that these are paintings produced by karma, that wicked śramaṇa creates other paintings, abandoning such activities as meditative concentration and recitation.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 48; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 49.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Observing the Heavens, Part Fourteen: Yāma Heaven.
"Furthermore, the wicked bhikṣu, having finished the various paintings of diverse colors, proceeds to create other paintings."
What are the remaining drawings?
That which is called "the remainder" refers to the bondage of birth and death caused by the sense faculties and their objects.
Those sense faculties and objects may be either attractive or unattractive; this refers, for example, to the nose smelling odors.

Having observed and understood this, regarding what is smelled by the nose—whether fragrant or foul—he does not take pleasure in fragrance and does not fail to observe it well; thus he is unable to let it disturb his mind, reflecting:
"This fragrance is impermanent, not abiding from moment to moment, unstable and subject to destruction."
"Such genuine fragrances were originally non-existent and later came to be; having existed, they return to non-existence.
Regarding such fragrances, though they may be foul and unpleasant, his mind does not waver.
Because of those paintings of white karma and virtuous karma, they are born among humans and devas.
Yet that painter-monk, harboring evil intentions, abandons such karma to create other paintings, departing from the practice of meditation and recitation.

"Furthermore, by smelling other fragrances and taking delight in them, the mind becomes deluded; thus, being bewildered by longing and failing to observe correctly, the mind is destroyed—this is black karma."
Because they constantly collect such pigments of black karma, they paint the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where they undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

Those evil śramaṇas abandon such karmic pigments for painting, yet fail to contemplate them; instead, they create other paintings, thereby obstructing and neglecting their seated meditation and the recitation of the sūtras and vinaya.
"Furthermore, there are various mixed karmas represented by diverse colors and forms, namely the flavors of the tongue, which may be either pleasant or unpleasant.

When that virtuous bhikṣu obtains a pleasant flavor, he feels neither delight nor aversion; he does not dwell upon it nor take pleasure in it. He constantly observes this delicious flavor skillfully, never failing to observe it properly."
"Regarding such a taste: it was originally non-existent and later comes to be; having existed, it returns to non-existence.

When one grasps that food with the hand and places it within the mouth, the tongue touches it; once the tongue has received the food, that food is called sweet, and a delicious flavor immediately arises."
The putrid brain and nasal mucus flow down from within the forehead and bridge of the nose, emerging from the gums.
When the tongue encounters flavor, it mingles with saliva; held between the teeth and jaws, one chews and grinds it. In this manner, the foolish worldling is bound.
When that person thus contemplates and correctly observes the taste of the tongue, it is a white painting.
By means of this white painting, one experiences supreme bliss among humans or among devas.

“Those evil śramaṇas are unable to contemplate such karmic paintings; instead, they create other paintings, thereby obstructing and abandoning their practice of seated meditation and their recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya.”
When that foolish person eats the food, the flavor remains on the tongue; once the tongue has made contact with the sweetness, he perceives the taste and thinks to himself:
"This food is of excellent flavor—the foremost, most superior, and most delicious of flavors; it is perfect in color and fragrance, and is the most pure."
Because of the pride of attachment to food, one performs evil karma through body, speech, and mind.
These paintings of black karma are clearly manifest in the three realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Those wicked śramaṇas, who claim to be śramaṇas while being ruined by improper observation, bring about their own obstruction and confusion; having abandoned the painting of their [proper] work, they instead create other paintings, thereby obstructing their meditation and recitation.

"Furthermore, there is the painting of karma; karma paints the world. This means that there is only the attachment between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and there is the consciousness of bodily contact (*kāyasparśavijñāna*).

Regarding that actual contact, one should skillfully examine it with the mind: this contact that arises is of three kinds—it is impermanent and unstable, it is subject to disintegration, and it possesses nothing but a thin skin.
One perceives it and gives rise to craving, yet it is merely the locus of the sense faculties."
It is not pure, nor is it permanent, nor is it blissful, nor is it a self-existent dharma; it is merely a provisional combination, and is therefore called a "body.
The four great elements are like a chest or like arrows piercing the body—constantly obstructive and constantly diseased, the locus of all faults.
When one observes the contact of the body in this manner of true reality, that contact does not constitute an obstruction.
This contact is merely adventitious and capable of causing hindrance; it is not one's own inherent substance.
If one can observe skillfully in this way, the white-painted karma will lead to rebirth among gods or humans.
“Those wicked śramaṇas who claim to stand as śramaṇas do not engage in such reflection and observation.

The mind is a painter whose various and diverse karmic deeds paint the world; yet those wicked bhikṣus abandon this observation and instead create other paintings, thereby obstructing and neglecting their practice of sitting meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya.”
"Furthermore, foolish ordinary persons do not observe correctly; they fail to examine this contact properly and give rise to such a thought:
'This contact of mine is the foremost pleasant contact; my body is robust and flourishing, thus accumulating the causes of pleasure.'"
"Having obtained this pleasant touch, I shall experience pleasure.

Thus do foolish, ordinary persons fail to examine and fail to reflect properly upon this touch; through this black karma, they paint themselves into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Those wicked śramaṇas, who merely claim to be śramaṇas, abandon those karmic paintings and fail to contemplate them; instead, they create other paintings, thereby obstructing and neglecting their sitting meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, those who are evil śramaṇas, though claiming to be śramaṇas, delight in worldly dharmas and not in supramundane dharmas; they do not contemplate or reflect upon supramundane dharmas."
The supramundane dharmas refer to the Four Noble Truths.

Yet, regarding the sixteen aspects of cessation and the path, as well as mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the four dhyānas, the four brahma-vihāras, and the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, he neither cultivates nor practices them.

Having abandoned these dharmas, one performs other base activities; the mind is not tranquil, seeking only minor pleasures and superficial colors, thereby obstructing and neglecting seated meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya, while further pursuing various other colors and non-tranquil paintings.
Because he did not observe correctly in this way, at the dissolution of the body after death, he fell into an evil destination and was born in hell.

Furthermore, that painter has another great transgression which serves as the cause and condition for entering the evil destinations and hells: namely, painting beautiful women adorned with various exquisite and charming colors.

Out of ignorance, they give rise to delight in their hearts and cause others who see them to likewise feel attachment and desire, thereby provoking a distracted mind; how much more so for the one who actually commits the act!
Such a person causes both themselves and others to give rise to desire, and when the body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"If one does not paint with the colors of karma, But instead creates other painted images,
One will be burned by the fire of those paintings And enter into the hells."
Not contemplating the untainted dharmas, yet delighting in tainted dharmas—that person’s mind is defiled by delusion; they stand on a precipice, about to fall.
Whether one should practice meditation and recitation, or whether one should dwell in the forest—
Through delusion one abandons what should be done, and thus falls into hell.
Through delusion one engages in evil thoughts, creating a powerful painted snare;
deceived by that painting, one is led away toward hell.
Colors are not what is variegated; it is the mind’s painting that is variegated.
A painted image perishes with the rain, but the mind’s painting cannot be lost.
If a person does not paint with the mind, that [external] painting is not equal to the mind.
Karma is the great painter, painting within the realms of the three worlds.
The various forms of sentient beings, transmigrating through the five destinies—
all these are the paintings of karma, created by the mind as the master artist.
This mind-painter paints the net of karma,
binding all sentient beings and causing them to wander through the three realms.
Rain, heat, dust, smoke, and the like cause the painted colors to fade and vanish.
The paintings created by that mental karma will not be lost for billions of kalpas.
Even if all the earth were to perish and the waters of the ocean were to dry up,
what is produced by the paintings of the mind would ultimately never be destroyed.
"The deluded do not observe the various paintings of their own karma;
for the sake of life and wealth, they instead engage in other painted works.
'The monk-painter thus obstructs and abandons sitting meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya. Such discrimination involves immeasurable faults."
Those who delight in painting are not loved by the virtuous, but are delighted by the unvirtuous; therefore, a bhikṣu should not engage in painting.
Painting disturbs the mind, preventing the attainment of nirvāṇa, and even rendering one incapable of skillfully observing conduct or cultivating a single wholesome dharma.
Therefore, one should train correctly in this way:
if bhikṣus desire to seek nirvāṇa and dread unwholesome karma, they should not even hold a painting brush with their own hands.
I now censure these three kinds of dharmas, which are not to be practiced by those who are śramaṇas, because I know that such dharmas possess these faults.
"Furthermore, there is a fourth dharma which is not to be practiced by those who are śramaṇas."
What is the fourth?
It is the recitation and chanting of songs and verses concerning false teachings, evil, and unwholesome dharmas.

Such a bhikṣu has abandoned wife and children, relatives, friends, parents, and brothers; desiring to sever the afflictions, he sits in meditation and engages in recitation, and for this reason he has gone forth from the household life.
If one’s mind is not distracted and remains constantly single-minded, one can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and nothing will be able to obstruct or distract them.
If one composes songs or chants in praise of evil deeds, or engages in various kinds of recollections, the mind and heart will become distracted.

Because their minds are distracted, they obstruct wholesome dharmas; they are unable to practice meditation or recitation, do not draw near to teachers and elders, do not hear the True Dharma, take no delight in making offerings to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, fail to maintain dignified deportment, and are unable to properly uphold the precepts of decorous conduct. They constantly engage in singing and chanting, their hearts giving rise to attachment and delight therein.

Such singing, based on what is thus chanted—various teachings previously heard that are not subsumed under the Dharma—is done merely for the pleasure of hearing those sounds; it is not subsumed under or gathered by skillful investigation, and is associated with frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).

Such teachings as these are those in which wicked śramaṇas place their faith and delight; having heard them repeatedly, they travel those evil paths, and by traveling those evil paths, they return once more to the life of a layperson, thereby destroying the true Dharma themselves.

Because they delight in singing and chanting, they constantly engage in singing and chanting; consequently, they become indolent and lack diligence in meditation and recitation. They should not even enter among the assembly of monks, nor should they consume any food or drink whatsoever.
If this is so even for one who is merely indolent, how much more so for one who has broken the precepts?

Such a person should not even enter among the community of monks, let alone receive bedding, mats, or the requisites for illness and medicine, nor should they accept the prostrations and respect of others; these things are not to be received by an indolent person.
Therefore, monks, those who constantly sing and chant, because of that singing and chanting, take no pleasure in sitting in meditation or reciting the Sūtras and Vinaya.

Those who delight in singing and chanting constantly apply their minds with diligence to the practice of singing, always taking pleasure at all times in relying upon song. Through various means, they distract their minds and are destroyed by various forms of delusion, praising that singing as having many flavors.

Such a person thus confuses their own mind; their life is gradually coming to an end, and the time of old age and death has arrived. On the verge of departing for a place never known before, they travel alone without a companion, separated from the supramundane Dharma.
If one constantly engages in singing and chanting, such a foolish person fails to perceive that death has arrived; this is a profound form of self-deception.

A human body is difficult to obtain, and the full complement of faculties is difficult to possess. Although one has managed to leave the household life, to do nothing but sing and chant is to achieve nothing at all; one dies in vain and falsehood, losing one's own true benefit.
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu composes songs, because he is destroyed by delusion, with a defiled mind and defiled conduct, he performs the karma of composing songs.
Among all forms of delusion, delusion regarding women is the greatest."
Women are deluded; a bhikṣu should not [associate with them].
That women are deluded means that though they are few, they can burn much, just as fire, though small, can consume a great deal.
That woman is deluded; yet she is thus able to incinerate the host of the ignorant, and throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of births, she is able to incinerate them all.
In that song of praise, women are extolled at the outset.
Women come first.

Those women, through delusion, destroy the bhikṣus; they engage in various and immeasurable improper observations, their minds corrupted by ignorance. They praise the female body as an object of offering, hold it in their hearts, and declare it to be pure.

Those evil bhikṣus fail to correctly observe their own entire selves and further cause others to observe incorrectly; because they have failed both themselves and others, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell.
"Because of the fault of being bound by singing and praising those evil and unwholesome teachings they have heard.

Furthermore, there is a great fault in hearing and then singing and praising false doctrines; that is to say, when wicked śramaṇas hear such evil and false doctrines and sing and praise them, they cause their minds to become ignorant and darkened."

Furthermore, if that person has never heard it before, has never seen it before, and has not previously heard or seen it from another, yet out of a greedy mind they intentionally compose songs themselves and further teach others to sing various songs, claiming "I have seen it" or "I have heard it," they shall therefore be bound.
Because others know that such a person has neither previously seen nor heard of [the truth], they say of him, "Such a person is unwholesome.
Thus, through false speech, he composes songs based on his own mental deliberations.
Because that person has committed such false speech, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell due to the transgression of singing.

Furthermore, there is a great fault in hearing and singing in praise of false teachings; that is to say, one who delights in singing what they have heard falsely conceives an evil mind toward the person from whom they first heard it, speaking words of hatred and envy: [text continues]
"I excel at singing," he said,
disparaging the ancient masters of long standing;
though they were truly great in ability, he declared them to be unskilled.
That evil śramaṇa thus abandons seated meditation and recitation, increasing his anger and fully augmenting his unwholesome, defiled karma.
Wholesome, pure karma—which is capable of bestowing peace and happiness in future lives—is extinguished by him.
Those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) despise such people who sing and chant upon hearing false and evil teachings, for the minds of such people are not upright.
Furthermore, there is a great fault in hearing false teachings and singing praises and hymns to them.

Those who thus sing and chant based on false learning—whether by day or by night—possess minds that are not upright; they do not contemplate the Buddha-dharma but delight in singing and chanting, constantly offering praises, neither reflecting upon the True Dharma nor being able to practice seated meditation, nor diligently striving to eliminate afflictions.
Such a person is not a true śramaṇa and lacks the intention of a śramaṇa.

The True Dharma is difficult to encounter; even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is difficult to encounter the True Dharma. Yet those wicked śramaṇas, who merely claim to be śramaṇas, having obtained such a Dharma, do not practice it correctly and do not embrace it.

"Furthermore, there is another great transgression in hearing and chanting songs of false teachings; that is to say, those evil persons greedily compose songs and offer praise for things they have never heard before, or they even utter falsehoods."

That person constantly associates with those of improper conduct; like a madman, because his mind is agitated, he wanders everywhere, praising and singing songs, bound by perverse speech and extolling those who speak falsehoods.
Whatever various things they speak, all their verbal karma is entirely false speech; not once is it truthful.
Such people have their minds shrouded by song and chant, and they further associate with other wealthy and noble evildoers; because they rely upon them, they commit unwholesome deeds.
Because such a person associates with evil people, they receive offerings of alcohol; due to drinking alcohol, they do not perform a single virtuous deed.
Their minds become agitated and disturbed, and they lose their own benefit; because of drinking alcohol, the gates to the evil realms open.

Because that person is intoxicated, they are capable of committing all manner of unwholesome and evil deeds; because they gaze upon women, they fail to observe correctly and thus lose their right mind.

That wicked śramaṇa practices non-celibacy, burning away his merit like a rotten and foul-smelling substance. He is like a *viṭula* tree that has flowers but no fruit, like a lamp by day that lacks illuminating light, or like the moon by day that lacks the sensation of coolness.

In this way, in this manner, those evil bhikṣus merely cover their bodies with the kāṣāya; they possess only the outward appearance and form of śramaṇas. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into evil destinies and are born within the hells.
"Because he has heard evil teachings and sung them, and because he has praised them,
for this reason a śramaṇa, upon hearing unwholesome teachings, should not sing them nor should he praise them."
If one composes the true Dharma through hymns and praises, the true Dharma will increase.
If there is such hymning and praising, it does not harm the true Dharma; whether one extols the Buddha or praises the Triple Gem, it causes the true Dharma to flourish and makes the Dharma radiant.
For one who praises in this manner, such merit will lead, in succession, even unto nirvāṇa.

As for the person who diligently cultivates the fruit of such verbal karma, when they are praised by others, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will be reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas.

Because that person thus praises in accordance with reality, they cause the True Dharma to increase; such eulogizing is what ought to be done, for if one does not act in this way, one will enter hell.
"Furthermore, there is a fifth dharma that obstructs and causes one to abandon sitting in meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya. What is this fifth?
It is when a bhikṣu counts the stars while practicing contemplation; though he is not truly a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa."

One should not engage in such contemplation as counting the stars; for a bhikṣu who does so violates the dharma of a śramaṇa and obstructs or abandons practices such as sitting meditation and recitation.
Having engaged in that [unwholesome] contemplation, his merit, lifespan, and vital formations (āyuḥ-saṃskāra) will be lost without his even realizing it.
What is the purpose of going forth?

If one does not attain that Dharma, then at the end of life, when all existence is exhausted, one's task remains unfulfilled; one fails to escape old age, sickness, death, lamentation, wailing, grief, suffering, and despair, and such a person continues to wander and transmigrate within the path of birth and death.
One who merely counts the stars gains no benefit; by contemplating the stars, one cannot save oneself, nor can one save others.
Why is this? Only by counting the stars of one's own karma can one save both self and others.

Why is this? Among those born under a single star, there are those with suffering and those with happiness; those who are ugly and those who are beautiful; those of great lineage and those of humble lineage; those who act in accordance with the Dharma and those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma; those who are poor and those who are wealthy; kings and commoners; the noble and the lowly; thieves and non-thieves; the clever and the dull; the ignorant and the wise; men and women; some who observe the precepts and some who do not; those who are diligent and energetic and those who are not; those who are loved by others and those who are not; and those who are loved by all and those who are not loved by any.
If there is but one kind of star yet humans of different kinds are born with differences,
then if it were due to the causal conditions of the stars, why would those born from that same single star not all be of one kind?
As previously stated, one is entirely ignorant of the faults and virtues of others;
one does not count their karmic stars, but instead counts the stars in the sky. Such foolish people neither know nor reckon the merits and transgressions of others.
The two fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma cannot be counted; they would be like counting the stars in the sky.
Furthermore, though that person counts the stars and reflects upon them, in reality, it is neither wholesome nor peaceful.

Regarding what is called a single star: it may be born as a human, or born as an animal, or born as a hungry ghost; these differences are not equal and do not arise from the power of the star, but rather from the power of karma, whereby beings are born in various distinct ways.
Contemplating these stars, one sees that they are thus unwholesome and not tranquil;
contemplating the stars of karma, one sees them as wholesome and tranquil, proceeding in sequence until reaching nirvana.
"Furthermore, those people who calculate and contemplate the stars do so in a manner that is neither truly skillful nor tranquil.
This is because the power of those stars is not constant or fixed; there are further obstructions, and there are variations of superiority and inferiority."
This constellation is further eclipsed by another superior constellation, and that constellation, at a different time, is in turn eclipsed by yet another constellation.
Therefore, one should know that the contemplation of the number of constellations is inconsistent with the true meaning.

If there were someone who, calculating and contemplating the stars, claimed that suffering and pleasure exist because of the stars as their cause and condition, rather than arising from one's own self,
then since those stars are themselves eclipsed by other stars, how could they possibly bestow suffering and pleasure upon others?
Thus, one should know that [the results] are obtained through karma.
Such fruits of the wholesome and unwholesome are not bestowed by the stars.
If they were determined by the planets, there would be further planetary afflictions.
Thus, the first luminaries undergo suffering and affliction; just as the sun and moon suffer when Rāhu eclipses them, they are beset by distress.
If these very sun and moon cannot save themselves, how could they possibly save others?
Therefore, a śramaṇa, or one who stands as a śramaṇa, may count the stars and contemplate them, but he should not contemplate them by counting the stars in this manner:
"There are three great luminaries—namely, illness, old age, and death—which are the greatest and constantly abide in the world."
That wicked śramaṇa does not contemplate this, but instead contemplates other worldly luminaries.
That person is deluded and lacks the wisdom derived from hearing; he contemplates the twenty-eight lunar mansions of the world.
To contemplate in such a manner is a fault.
However, if one contemplates those twenty-eight lunar mansions that transcend the world, and if one can contemplate them with true observation, one will enter the city of Nirvāṇa.
The twenty-eighth is that which refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five aggregates of clinging (*upādāna-skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.
By contemplating these, one reaches nirvāṇa.
Because one attains nirvāṇa through observing reality as it is, through detachment from desire, and by upholding the precepts, one cannot attain it by merely counting stars in one's contemplation.
"Furthermore, there are other practices of those who are evil śramaṇas, yet claim to be śramaṇas—namely, the counting of the twelve months.

Having counted them in this way, they gain no benefit and are unable to sever their afflictions; they continue to wander within the realm of existence and fail to understand the counting of the twelve bases (āyatana)."

If one can contemplate and enumerate the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and, having understood their true meaning, develop disenchantment with sensual desires, then through that tranquility, one attains *nirvāṇa*.
Those wicked śramaṇas who merely claim to be śramaṇas, because they cannot enumerate or contemplate [the truth], instead contemplate the defilements of others while enumerating external matters.
“Furthermore, there are other kinds of defilements of evil reflection belonging to those who are wicked śramaṇas or who claim to be śramaṇas—they reflect upon the six periods of the day.

Having reflected thus, they fail to attain liberation from sickness, old age, and death; they are disturbed by the defilement of impermanence and do not reflect upon the thirty-six components of the body.”
If one contemplates this, through such genuine observation, one will be able to relinquish it and attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, when a wicked śramaṇa or one who merely claims to be a śramaṇa reflects upon the world and contemplates that time, he speaks thus:
"This time is good; that reflection is not good."
"At such a time it shall be obtained; at such a time it shall not be obtained.
Such evil thoughts and evil reflections are not tranquility; they do not lead to happiness, they do not approach nirvāṇa, and they do not attain nirvāṇa.
When one contemplates the mind, the characteristics of the mind involve objects of perception that may be wholesome or unwholesome, and determinate or indeterminate.
When contemplating the world, the mind does not conceptualize these three types of time.
If one can contemplate that wholesome or unwholesome minds have objects of attachment, one should contemplate thus:
"Since I have generated a certain mind with wholesome objects of attachment, I shall be reborn in a happy realm in future lives, and I shall attain nirvāṇa in the future."

"I have given rise to a certain unwholesome state of mind, an unwholesome object of focus, and a defiled mind; that will not lead to happiness, it will not lead to peace, it will not lead to Nirvana, and Nirvana will not be attained."
“I have given rise to a certain indeterminate thought with an indeterminate object, and thus receive an indeterminate retribution.

Furthermore, there are evil śramaṇas who merely resemble śramaṇas; they contemplate worldly paths and reflect on worldly time. They focus only on a single moment of thought, without much leisure, whether it be for a day, a half-month, or a month, regarding the fruits of good and evil. When contemplating the exhaustion of the life-process among humans, they do not reflect: “My life-process is exhausted in every moment of thought;

it is exhausted in the snap of a finger, without much leisure, whether it be for a day, a half-month, or a month. My life-process perishes in every moment of thought and cannot be avoided; there is no expedient means by which one can avoid the time of death.”

"Furthermore, there are evil bhikṣus who again contemplate various other dharmas at improper times, thereby obstructing and abandoning their practice of seated meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya; that is to say, they contemplate worldly defiled dharmas—namely, they contemplate the stars and the timing [of the seasons]."
That person contemplates this with pleasure and practices it extensively; keeping it in mind, they declare:
"Thus, such-and-such a star and such-and-such a planet have come to cover [the heavens]; they can cause obstacles and bring misfortune; within this world, they can bring both good and evil."

If one contemplates those matters, one will still be unable to escape old age, sickness, death, lamentation, weeping, grief, suffering, and despair; nor will one sever the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, one should not contemplate in such a manner.
Just as it is covered by the stars and planets, there is another phenomenon, covered by yet another phenomenon; that is to say, one is covered by the star of birth and the planet of death.
The star of health is covered by the planet of illness.
The star of a youth is eclipsed by the planet of old age.
The star of union through craving is eclipsed by the planet of separation from craving.
The star of rebirth in heaven is eclipsed by the planet of decline.
The star that gives rise to birth among humans is covered by the planet of affliction.
The star of pleasant sensation is covered by the planet of painful sensation.
The star that gives rise to wholesome states of mind is covered by the planet that gives rise to unwholesome states of mind.
The star of impurity is obscured by the planet of desire.
The star of loving-kindness is obscured by the planet of hatred.
The star of contemplative wisdom is obscured by the planet of delusion.
Those wicked śramaṇas, who merely claim to be śramaṇas, are unable to contemplate their own reflection, nor do they contemplate supramundane contemplation.

This is the contemplation of supramundane stars; as previously described, it is the contemplation of the stars of the true Dharma through observing reality as it is, yet it is obscured by false luminaries.

As previously explained, having thus reflected and observed the eight factors of the noble path as such luminous stars, one attains the fruit through contemplation—tranquility, bliss, and even nirvana.

"If foolish, ordinary people contemplate such celestial bodies of the world—whether contemplating the *yōs* (planets) or the *seikyō* (stars)—it causes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings to enter the evil paths, being born in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."
This is the causal condition for birth and death in the world, which gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.

If one contemplates the path that transcends the world—contemplating the seasons, the constellations, the times, and the luminaries—and having contemplated these, practices while observing them as they truly are, then this will cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people to attain liberation from old age, sickness, death, lamentation, weeping, sorrow, suffering, and distress. They shall reach the non-retrogressive state, the supreme Nirvana where there is no aging, no sickness, no death, and no exhaustion.

If one trains in this way, a bhikṣu who is a śramaṇa or one who stands as a śramaṇa, desiring the exhaustion of suffering and the exhaustion of the suffering of birth and death, yet practices contemplation on the stars and contemplation on time as previously described, this is considered base and defiled.
Having understood this, one knows that it is not ultimate, not tranquil, and does not constitute the attainment of nirvāṇa; it merely obstructs a bhikṣu’s practice of meditation and recitation.
A bhikṣu should not contemplate by counting the stars; to contemplate by counting the stars is not conducive to the path.

"Furthermore, there is a sixth thing that should not be contemplated: namely, that śramaṇas and those who claim to be śramaṇas obstruct and neglect sitting meditation and the recitation of the Sūtras and Vinaya."
What is the sixth thing that should not be contemplated?
It is the contemplation of omens and signs.
A śramaṇa should not contemplate worldly defiled dharmas, which increase desire, hatred, and delusion.
To contemplate those signs obstructs and causes one to abandon wholesome dharmas.
If any śramaṇas or those who stand as śramaṇas recognize the signs of an earthquake—the signs of worldly defilement—whether by day or by night, they reflect thus:

"The earth is about to shake; now we see the signs. That is to say, when the earth remains level and stable, it moves when blown by the wind, yet though it moves, it does not become turbid; however, because the earth is about to shake, it becomes turbid when blown by the wind."
When rain is about to fall, ants carry their eggs away.
When a lunar eclipse is imminent, oil sinks in water and birds fly low in the sky near the earth.
When a solar eclipse is imminent, all directions turn crimson.
If one desires peace and security, when the oily-moist wind arises and all directions are free from defilement,
and one perceives such signs as moving in a clockwise direction, then one knows that there will be peace and security.

If there is to be misfortune, the various directions will appear reddish-yellow, dry and lacking luster; a parched wind will arise, and a halo of reddish-yellow and blue colors will appear in the sky.
When the sun is about to be eclipsed, all directions turn crimson.

There will be auspicious signs: from that direction, a moist and oily wind will blow—pure, stainless, and free from dust, mist, and the like—and one will further behold auspicious omens, such as the appearance of clockwise movement and signs of harmony.

When unwholesome states arise, one sees the various directions as reddish-yellow and dry without any oily luster; or one sees a wind blowing from those directions that is without oiliness, and sees a reddish-yellow-blue haloed sun rising in the midst of space.

Those evil śramaṇas, who claim to be śramaṇas, practice such divination and hold such views; because of this, they neglect and abandon sitting in meditation and the recitation of the sūtras and vinaya, and instead engage in speculation and prediction. They long for wealth, profit, and various offerings, and contemplate whether one king or another is superior or inferior.
Because he seeks victory and non-victory in this manner, desire, hatred, and delusion arise within his mind; these three are the roots thereof.
Thus, a bhikṣu incurs three kinds of faults; he is neither a śramaṇa nor a layperson.
If one is a true śramaṇa or one who stands as a śramaṇa, they do not rely on divination or physiognomy, because seeing such signs increases defiled desire.
"Furthermore, there is another evil reflection: suppose there is a diviner whom the king consults regarding the timing for an impending military expedition, and he gives a definitive prediction:
'At such-and-such a time and date, you shall engage in battle with them and defeat all your enemies.'"
If all people were to desire to engage in battle, in what place would they slaughter countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, utterly destroying them or capturing and binding them?

In this way, within cities, villages, or kingdoms, or in places where many people gather, they engage in mutual strife and contention against that king; they destroy one another and bring about ruin, causing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to undergo suffering.
Those wicked śramaṇas act as astrologers for the king and as diviners of auspicious times for him, saying:
"Such-and-such a day is favorable; such-and-such a time is most excellent. Your Majesty will surely achieve victory and be able to defeat all other kings."
Having observed these signs, that wicked śramaṇa thinks to himself:
"If this king is victorious, I shall obtain much wealth and much honor from him; I shall receive such things from the king."
“‘Those evil śramaṇas who claim to stand as śramaṇas cause wholesome dharmas to perish—namely, sitting in meditation and reciting the sūtras and vinaya;
instead, they sometimes increase unwholesome dharmas because they discriminate between what is superior and what is not.’”
Because he contemplates such dharmas, at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into an evil destination and is born in hell.

For this reason, a true śramaṇa or one who stands as a śramaṇa does not contemplate the characteristics of the world, for such contemplation gives rise to three kinds of faults that obstruct the wholesome dharmas.

If one does not contemplate the characteristics of this world but contemplates other dharmas, one remains free from the three kinds of faults; this is supramundane, comprised of right mindfulness and contemplation.
What is this dharma?
It is like knowing the signs of an earthquake: whether by day or by night, one thinks, "The earth is about to shake.
Why does such a person, by night or by day, not likewise reflect:
"The mind-ground shall move; just as when the earth shakes, all the world—including mountains, rivers, gardens, groves, trees, villages, and cities—shakes everywhere?"
"In this way, as this way, because the ground of the mind moves, all other great earth-like wholesome dharmas and other dharmas likewise move everywhere.
Therefore, a śramaṇa—or one who stands as a śramaṇa—should first observe that this ground of the mind is about to move."
The movement of the mental ground is like an earthquake.
This mental ground is moved by three factors—namely, desire, hatred, and delusion—which cause the mental ground to tremble.
Just as when the earth is about to shake, there must first be signs: for example, water is originally clear, yet it becomes turbid when blown by the wind.
In this way and that way, when desire, anger, or delusion are about to arise in an ordinary person, their facial complexion becomes either dark or flushed; thus they first become turbid.
Therefore, a śramaṇa, or one who stands as a śramaṇa, should contemplate this mark, which is the mark of encompassing nirvāṇa.
One who contemplates this mark shall not experience suffering or affliction.
This characteristic of the mind-ground is a supramundane characteristic.
Furthermore, next, one contemplates the characteristics of worldly phenomena: because rain is about to fall, the ants carry their eggs.
In this way, the śramaṇa who stands as a śramaṇa observes the characteristics of the supramundane.

It is like seeing in a village or city—a place crowded with people—donors, various śramaṇas, various brahmins, and various elders, who, out of faith in the Buddha and for the sake of hearing the Dharma, go to where the Buddha is.
Regarding this true reality, those virtuous śramaṇas and those who stand as śramaṇas, seeing such signs, immediately declare:

"At this moment, there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, in that place, wishing to preach the True Dharma; thus, these donors, as well as the various śramaṇas, brahmins, and householders, have all arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling."
"That Buddha definitely intends to preach the True Dharma; seeing this sign now, it is no inferior sign. We now know that this sign is the sign of the rain of Dharma.

Furthermore, when wicked śramaṇas or those who merely claim to be śramaṇas see the radiance of the moon, they know for certain that the moon will surely be eclipsed, because when oil is placed in water, it sinks to the bottom.
Such signs as these are neither virtuous, nor auspicious, nor peaceful.
Such signs as these are not the signs of a śramaṇa, nor are they the signs of tranquility; those signs of a śramaṇa are inconsistent with the supramundane sign.

Observing the corresponding signs, one notes that when the moon of the world reaches its end, it becomes malevolent; one knows that the moon of the True Dharma is about to be eclipsed, as the oil of the True Dharma sinks into the waters of the hearts of those with false views.
"This sign is neither auspicious nor refreshing; this first sign is not a sign of a lunar eclipse in the world.

Furthermore, a wicked śramaṇa or one who merely claims to be a śramaṇa observes another extraordinary sign of a lunar eclipse in the world: when the moon is about to be eclipsed, birds fly low in the sky, close to the earth."
This is a characteristic inconsistent with being a śramaṇa or one who establishes himself as a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, there is another excellent characteristic, a supramundane characteristic, namely: observing the lunar eclipse of the True Dharma. This is the practice of the path of the śramaṇa’s True Dharma; it means that when a śramaṇa frequents inferior acquaintances, inferior donors, and other inferior persons—descending like a bird flying low, walking at the gates of those laypeople who practice improperly and hold wrong views, and engaging in base conversation—it is like a bird flying in the sky that descends close to the earth due to the fault of having passed its [proper] time.
All śramaṇas and those who stand as śramaṇas should not observe this mark—the foremost and most excellent mark—but rather that mark of a lunar eclipse is not a favorable mark.

"Furthermore, there is another sign: if a wicked śramaṇa or one who merely claims to be a śramaṇa observes the signs of the world through the sign of a solar eclipse—when the sun is about to be eclipsed, the various directions turn crimson;

yet when there is to be something auspicious, that direction will be blown by a smooth wind, becoming pure, stainless, and free from dust and mist. Seeing such an auspicious sign, characterized by a clockwise movement and corresponding features—"
That good śramaṇa who stands as a śramaṇa possesses an improper view, for it obstructs the practice of sitting meditation and recitation.
These worldly characteristics are neither tranquil nor peaceful.

In this way, in this way: if a true śramaṇa or one who stands as a śramaṇa desires to attain tranquility, he should observe the supramundane signs; he should contemplate that the sun of the bodhisattva will surely encompass omniscient enlightenment—whether in one eon, two eons, or three eons.

Thus the śramaṇa beholds the marks of a world-transcending bodhisattva, namely: diligence, generosity, and the wisdom of learning; a square mark of crimson color; and a heart of loving-kindness that has compassion for all sentient beings.

That the Bodhisattva’s body is crimson signifies that he shall be secure; it means this Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the foremost merits, his marks of omniscience will certainly be perfected, and he will certainly preach the Dharma. That there is no defilement or dust-fog in all directions signifies that he is free from the calamities of evil times; there shall be the excellence of the Tathāgata’s renown, wafted by the fragrant breeze.
Just as those worldly physiognomists observe, so too does this supramundane physiognomist perceive the signs of the future—the marks of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats;
the mark of turning to the right refers to correct observation.

"Furthermore, that physiognomist perceives only such signs of birth and death within worldly phenomena; when there will be misfortune, he sees in all directions a reddish-yellow color, a parched appearance devoid of luster, or he sees in those directions a wind blowing without moisture, and a sun with reddish-yellow and bluish halos rising in the midst of space."
That evil śramaṇa observes such signs, which obstruct and cause him to abandon meditation and recitation.
If a virtuous śramaṇa who is a worldly prognosticator were to give such a prediction for the sake of faithful people, saying:
"There shall be misfortune."
What is unwholesome? It is that which obstructs the True Dharma.
Seeing such signs is like seeing a reddish-yellow hue in that direction.

Regarding such signs: when the True Dharma is about to perish, there are such signs as these—namely, that people in all directions take pleasure in harsh speech, false speech, divisive speech, killing, and stealing.
When that person is struck by the "wind of dryness," it refers to ill repute.

If there are sentient beings who do not practice the True Dharma, the wind of ill repute will blow, and their infamy will be heard throughout the eight directions, the four cardinal points, and the four intermediate directions, pervading them all.
Because sentient beings do not practice right conduct and perform unwholesome deeds, the wind of ill repute blows, and thus it is heard everywhere:
"The world's prognosticators see a sun with red, yellow, and blue halos rising in the midst of the sky."
Such a teacher is a worldly physiognomist.
A transcendent physiognomist who sees a sun surrounded by halos of red, yellow, or blue regards such individuals as wicked śramaṇas and wicked brāhmaṇas.
Such an assembly is not composed of those with all-encompassing wisdom; because they give rise to the pride of wisdom, they say of themselves, "I am an omniscient person.
These people of false views are not the true sun; they do not establish omniscience through actual omniscience, nor do they come from a noble lineage, but rather from an ordinary lineage.

When such a person’s sun of false views rises, all medicinal herbs, groves, and tree leaves wither and dry up; likewise, all the medicinal herbs, groves, and forests of virtuous people and right view are utterly parched.
In this way, in this manner, when this sun of the supramundane True Dharma rises, it increases meditative recitation, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the light of supreme wisdom.

Having thus observed the characteristics of the supramundane, and having first made such an observation, he then makes a declaration for the sake of those faithful śramaṇas, brahmins, householders, and others, declaring as follows:

"All who encounter the rising of the sun of the True Dharma should diligently perform all wholesome deeds; do not let the time come when all True Dharmas have utterly vanished and the sun of false views has risen, where those who are not śramaṇas claim themselves to be śramaṇas."
Those who are not brahmins claim to be brahmins;
those who are not omniscient claim to be omniscient.
When these evil śramaṇas and evil brahmins appear like the sun eclipsed by a halo, you will suffer decline and affliction.
"One who thus records and proclaims the Dharma of omniscience is then in accord with it; such a person is a true teacher of the marks and possesses a great, superior intention.
One who is able to contemplate such marks will not be hindered from practicing dhyāna or reciting the Sūtras and Vinaya."
Furthermore, to engage in further conceptualization regarding the characteristics of the world obstructs meditation and recitation.
Such is the distinction between the superiority and inferiority of the worldly path and the supramundane path.
Worldly dharmas encompass birth and death;
"The supramundane dharmas proceed in succession until one reaches nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"Abandoning seated meditation and recitation, They always delight in divining signs and omens;
Having abandoned the wholesome Dharma, one cannot attain nirvāṇa.
If one abandons one's own Dharma and delights in the Dharma of others,
both dharmas will be lost and ruined, and one will arrive at the realms of evil destinies.
If a person abandons their own home and takes pleasure in another’s house,
they will be lightly ridiculed among men and swiftly fall into poverty.
Such a foolish and evil-minded person, arrogant in their wisdom, claims to be superior.
Having abandoned one’s own Dharma, one practices the Dharma of others;
living as a renunciant with a wrong livelihood, one loses both the Dharma and one’s reputation.
Despised among men like a blade of grass, one enters the evil realms in the future.
Having abandoned the peaceful Dharma and practicing evil deeds,
that person will before long hear [of their downfall] and thereby lose the Buddha-Dharma.
With a mind longing for detachment from desire, they have no other longing.
Diligent, energetic, and content—this is called practicing meditation.
If the mind delights in desire and is constantly greedy for food and drink, such a person is a thief wearing the kāṣāya; they are not called a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu engages in divination, constantly contemplates the stars and planets,
associates with kings, or acts with negligence, he is not a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma.
One who practices as a physician or a painter, or who listens to and recites evil teachings, [is likewise not a bhikṣu].
Dwelling together with those who are evil, one loses the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Hating and envying meditation and recitation, delighting in much talk,
and craving offerings and material gain— one then loses the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Seeking after various precious gems, delighting in many acquaintances,
and further craving other wealth and goods, they fall away from the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Craving only food and drink, they are arrogant and do not inquire of others.
One who hopes for praise from others falls away from the dharma of a bhikṣu.
If one does not associate with anyone, abandons evil crowds,
and is content with whatever water and grass for food one receives, such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
Having encountered various sensory objects, one casts them aside as if discarding fire;
having severed the fault of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"), such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
With both internal and external states in perfect tranquility, adorned with the radiance of wisdom—
One who wears the robes of ethical discipline covering the body is called a true bhikṣu.
One who remains far removed from worldly dharmas, as immovable as Mount Sumeru,
and free from all worldly cravings is called a true bhikṣu.
Dwelling for three nights within a city, wherever there are many people—it is the same everywhere;
yet one who dwells amidst mountain valleys is called a bhikṣu of liberation.
Fearing evil, he does not draw near others; practicing rightly, his mind is unmoving.
One whose wisdom is discerning and tranquil is a bhikṣu who wanders alone.
One who does not crave constant pleasant speech, who has abandoned evil associates,
and who does not delight in much activity is called a liberated bhikṣu.
Such a bhikṣu as this has attained liberation from existence and faults;
knowing both the world and nirvāṇa, his mind is equanimous and free from longing.
His heart always delights in wisdom and in sublime tranquility.
"From the terrors of birth, old age, sickness, and death, one attains liberation.
"In this way, a bhikṣu becomes an arhat; were it otherwise, he would merely be called a bhikṣu by name, being hindered by himself and falling into a precipice."
This sixth dharma is likewise an obstacle; a virtuous śramaṇa should not perform it.
Furthermore, a śramaṇa, or one who stands as a śramaṇa, should not perform this seventh dharma.
What is the seventh? It is that which consists solely in filling one's storehouse with gathered food and drink.
Such a person abounds in greed and anger, abandons all activities such as meditation and recitation, and does nothing more than sit idly upon a large couch.
They falsely enjoy the bedding, mats, and medicinal requisites provided by the Sangha.

Having been indolent and lazy when formerly living as householders, they feared manual labor; therefore, having gone forth, they crave only the flavors of food, constantly waiting for assemblies to seek out and hope for meals, or else delighting in sensory objects.

Such a bhikṣu is a "dead bhikṣu," meaning a bhikṣu who is unable to practice seated meditation or recite the Sūtras and Vinaya, and who has violated the pure precepts; as for all other types of death, it is merely the discarding of the body.

A bhikṣu who violates the precepts destroys all wholesome dharmas; he is capable only of sitting upon a seat, conceiving arrogance in his heart and considering himself excellent, possessing nothing but the outward form and robes of a bhikṣu. In reality, he has no precepts and is far removed from the true precepts.
“Regarding what is called ‘precepts,’ it refers to the precepts of the mind; they cannot be maintained by him, nor can they be performed by him.
Those precepts are of seven kinds. What are the seven?
This is what is called the precept of speech.
A bhikṣu who observes it thus does not engage in conversation with other bhikṣus or with laypeople, except for matters concerning the Dharma.
Nor does he engage in conversation with women, except when on his almsround; even then, he may speak such words as those used for offering blessings and prayers.
"May you obtain happiness and attain nirvāṇa and so forth.
When seeing one's mother or seeing one's sister, one should look only at her feet, not at her face, nor at her clothing or ornaments.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"Like the touch of the hand or a gust of wind, this fire burns only after a long time;
but when the fire of seeing women arises, it burns swiftly without waiting for long."
"Therefore, monks, fearing the burning of desire, one should not engage in speech with any woman;
this is the first precept.
Furthermore, the second precept is as follows: one should not associate with unwholesome friends."
He does not dwell for a long time in a single place;
he does not accept excessive profit;
he relinquishes abundant offerings, yet does not abandon the sick.
He does not see his wife or children;
wherever there is great gain and offerings, he abandons that place and departs, fearing the arising of greed;
and he stays away from those who break the precepts, not dwelling together with them.
These seven kinds of bhikṣus are not restrained;
they crave only food and drink, and upon seeing or hearing of the wealth and offerings of others, they give rise to distress and anxiety, thinking to themselves:
"By what means shall I now obtain those gains and offerings?"
Reflecting in this way, a mind of craving arises; with such mental turbidity, the mind of craving increases.
That wicked śramaṇa destroys all wholesome dharmas; day and night he is constantly sorrowful, his mind never at peace.

When that bhikṣu sees other bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and practice wholesome conduct being honored by others, he gives rise to envy and greed, and consequently goes to the house of those donors.

With a deceitful appearance and attire, speaking little and walking slowly, his mind is not tranquil; yet he outwardly manifests the marks of dignified composure and tranquility. Clad in hempen robes, he further associates with many who do not uphold the precepts; possessing only the sound of a conch shell while practicing evil dharmas, he follows along with such companions to visit donors, manifesting the appearance of one who upholds the precepts.
In this way, in this way, they act according to their minds.
Thus, that lay patron, perceiving those bhikṣus to be observers of the precepts, thinks to himself:
"These bhikṣus are foremost in observing the precepts."

Those wicked bhikṣus manifest the appearance of observing the precepts to inspire faith and reverence in the minds of those donors; having done so, they frequently go together with their companions to the homes of those donors.

In this way, a bhikṣu, having heard [the teachings] himself and possessing a limited knowledge of the Buddha-dharma, speaks of that known dharma to his companions for the sake of a donor. By such means, he intends to cause the donor to divert the gains and offerings received by those other bhikṣus and bestow them instead upon him.
A monk with such outward appearance is the foremost thief among śramaṇas.
Having gone to the house of a donor, he employs skillful means to plunder the wealth and offerings of others.

In this way, when a bhikṣu sees the wealth and profit of others or the offerings made to them and gives rise to greed and envy, he will not, for even the briefest moment—the mere blink of an eye—practice even a small portion of wholesome dharmas.

Those evil bhikṣus and precept-breaking śramaṇas abandon such practices as seated meditation and recitation; there is not a single moment when they do not encompass the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 49; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 50.
Translated by the Brahamana Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Twenty-nine: Yāma Heaven, Section Fifteen.
