Furthermore, that bhikṣu, together with his companions in the house of a donor (*dānapati*), speaks of the faults and evils of a previously acquainted bhikṣu who maintains the precepts, doing so with a mind of flattery and deception; or, out of jealousy, he speaks of his breaking of the precepts; or, out of jealousy, he speaks of his lack of learning; or, out of jealousy, he speaks of his conduct, saying to the donor:
"This teacher of yours has violated the prohibitions and precepts."
Or they may speak of indolence, lack of learning, and lack of wisdom, being as foolish as birds with little hearing and little knowledge.
Such wicked bhikṣus speak thus maliciously to other donors; constantly associating with unrighteous spheres of activity, how could they cultivate practices such as meditation and recitation?
"That emptiness is devoid of substance, neither firm nor real; when the body perishes and life ends, one falls into the evil realms and is born within hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"The one who speaks false words Afflicts all sentient beings."
Such a person is always as if in darkness; though possessing life, they are no different from the dead.
The sword of speech cuts its own tongue—how could the tongue not fall?
If one speaks with false words, one loses true merit.
If a person speaks falsely, there is a venomous snake within their mouth;
a blade dwells within their mouth, and a blazing fire burns within their mouth.
The poison in the mouth is true poison; the poison upon the snake is not.
Poisonous speech destroys sentient beings; at the end of life, one falls into hell.
If a person speaks falsely, pus issues from their own mouth;
their tongue becomes turbid mud, and their tongue is also like a blazing fire.
This kind of snare and bond is the precursor to hell;
destroying the bridge of Dharma and the like—all these are the faults of false speech.
For that person who speaks falsely, there are no parents.
Nor can they maintain the precepts; they fall into the evil realms.
If a person speaks falsely, that person will quickly be held in contempt and abandoned by the virtuous; the devas will not protect them.
Failing to restrain one's speech, being quick-tempered and full of anger,
with a restless mind and excessive talk, one constantly undergoes various sufferings;
always harboring hatred and envy toward others, one brings evil upon all sentient beings.
"By intentionally harassing others, one enters hell because of this.
Thus did that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, speak regarding these seven kinds of evil dharmas that obstruct and cause the abandonment of meditation and recitation.
"Those evil bhikṣus bring harm to those who uphold the precepts; for this reason, the devas abandon them.
A sword grows within their mouths; for the sake of minor gain, they claim that others possess no real merit, and they attribute faults to those who are truly without fault."
Such a person is a wicked śramaṇa who merely calls himself a śramaṇa and speaks with false words.

Because that person constantly possesses evil intentions, evil conduct, and evil dharmas, the donor, having later come to know this, regards him with contempt and recognizes his deceitful crookedness.
This is the seventh dharma.
Therefore, a bhikṣu should abandon this seventh unwholesome dharma, namely: the longing for offerings of food and drink, desiring them all for oneself.
"Furthermore, the eighth obstructive and evil dharma hinders and causes the abandonment of a bhikṣu’s practice of seated meditation and recitation; therefore, a śramaṇa should abandon it.
What is this eighth? "
This refers to gathering various kinds of precious substances to create all manner of jewels.
In the same way, a bhikṣu, fearing birth and death, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the dharma robes, and leaves the household life out of faith.
Within that cycle of birth and death, there are many sufferings and afflictions; to speak briefly, there are two kinds of suffering.
Based on the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), they exist within the three realms; broadly speaking, they extend throughout the five destinies.
Furthermore, as for the extensive [suffering], there are the eight great hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals;
within the desire realm, there are the six heavens of the desire realm, which further possess various subsidiary sufferings;
and within the form realm, there is furthermore the suffering of the mind.
In the formless realm, there is the suffering of regression; therefore, when one is about to regress, samādhi becomes disturbed.
Such a mind experiences immeasurable kinds of suffering arising from conceptual discrimination.

Having contemplated suffering and affliction, that son of good family gave rise to a mind of weary detachment; fearing such immeasurable faults and evils, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and left the household life out of faith.
"Furthermore, that śramaṇa contemplates other forms of suffering and gives rise to fear in his mind, namely, bodily suffering.
Bodily suffering exists in two realms, namely, the desire realm and the form realm; wherever there is a body, one experiences suffering and affliction."
In that realm of form (rūpadhātu), how do they experience suffering?
It is said that because they become weary within meditative absorption (dhyāna), they emerge from it; having emerged from that absorption, their bodies then become weary.
When they are about to fall away [from that state], the majesty of their bodies diminishes, and winds touch their bodies.
Such winds are originally non-contacting; therefore, when they touch the body, one experiences suffering and affliction.
With the sole exception of visual contact, which experiences pleasure and no pain, that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thus, one discriminates that the various sufferings experienced exist in dependence upon the physical body.
Having heard this, that son of good family understands that all afflictions within birth and death—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—are suffering through their very combination.
"Having contemplated such immeasurable and boundless suffering of birth and death, he then renounces the household life.
Once he has renounced the household life, he associates with unwholesome people."
Because he associates with those people, he engages in their activities and hears of the methods for obtaining precious gems.
Out of fear of what kind of nature [the world] possesses, he leaves the household life out of faith.

Yet, upon hearing of other natures—whether hearing of the nature of gold, or silver, or precious gems—he gives rise once more to a greedy mind. Having heard such things, he knows no satiety, being consumed by the fire of craving.
Once they have been burned, they wander together with evil associates through the mountains, going from mountain to mountain and from one peak to another, thus roaming everywhere in secluded places.
Burned by the fire of greed, one suffers constantly day and night, with no time of happiness.
For what reason and by what causes does one thus go forth?
One does not contemplate that nature, but contemplates a different nature; that is, as previously described, one abandons the nature of the body and fails to contemplate it.
Such a person possesses an improper mind; because their mind is distracted, they obstruct and abandon meditation and recitation, thereby losing wholesome dharmas.

They are neither a true śramaṇa nor a layperson; having left the household life for the sake of seeking nirvāṇa, they are possessed by a demonic nature and thus give rise to greed. Bound by the snare of greed, they enter hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"One who observes the nature of the body Is [observing] the nature of all things.
Those who wish to attain nirvāṇa Should discipline the nature of the body, and nothing else."
If one abandons the nature of the body and becomes greedily attached to other natures,
that person is deluded regarding true nature and shall not escape from suffering and affliction.
Even the nature of gold cannot eliminate all suffering and affliction.
One who truly knows the real nature will undoubtedly attain liberation from suffering.
All sufferings arise from suffering; this suffering is difficult to escape.
Regarding wealth, kings, thieves, and fire—there is fear of them all.
Therefore, one should relinquish material things as if they were originally non-existent;
by renouncing them, one experiences happiness, whereas by grasping at them, one experiences suffering.
One should truly know the nature of the body, and furthermore, truly know its characteristics.
Delighting in meditation and recitation, one can burn away the mountain of afflictions.
Therefore, the wise person observes the nature of the body;
when sentient beings know their own true characteristics, they attain the bliss of nirvana.

“A person of wisdom who thus diligently contemplates the nature of this body will take no pleasure in the pursuit of the nature of gold, silver, and the like; for these are the very root of fear for all householders, let alone for those who have left the home life.”
One who has gone forth from the household life renounces everything;
those material possessions are all objects of fear.
By not selling such possessions, one attains happiness in this way.
Such wealth is not material wealth; it is not of the nature of material wealth.
What is that which constitutes wealth?
It is the contemplation of the nature of the body.

If one abandons the nature of the body and takes pleasure in other natures—being neither diligent nor persevering in meditation and recitation—such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, will fall into hell.

Therefore, those who have left the household life should constantly cultivate and accumulate the wealth of meditation and recitation; they should not seek after the ordinary things of the world, for by reason of such things, craving is increased.
Therefore, contentment is the foremost of riches; other riches can lead to decline and affliction.
This eighth quality obstructs meditation and recitation, and the renunciant śramaṇa should abandon it.

"Furthermore, there is a ninth obstructive and unwholesome dharma that hinders and causes the abandonment of a bhikṣu’s practice of sitting meditation and recitation; therefore, a śramaṇa should relinquish it.
What is the ninth?
Regarding what is called "associating with kings":
one who has left the household life should not associate with kings. Why is this?
When a śramaṇa associates with a king, all people of the world despise him and refuse to make offerings.
That evil śramaṇa who is intimate with a king covets wealth; whether it be from cities, villages, or populous places, he constantly seeks riches and knows no satiety.
If one does not seek [such things], merely associating with kings will obstruct and cause the abandonment of meditation and recitation.
Thus, a bhikṣu who has resolved to practice the path to liberation yet instead returns to the path of bondage—therefore, a bhikṣu should not associate with kings.
"Furthermore, what does a bhikṣu not associate with?
It is said that a bhikṣu does not associate with evil persons. Who are they?"

This refers to evil associates, or those who at times become attached to the five sensory objects—namely, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—and fail to examine them wisely; those who are indolent, ignorant, or dwell in villages and the like—all such persons should be abandoned.
Do not associate with those who are indolent; do not associate with those who are deceitful and hypocritical;
do not associate with those who are greedy for the taste of food; do not associate with merchants;
do not associate with those who live by evil livelihoods, such as butchers and hunters; do not associate with those who are inherently envious; do not associate with...
One should not associate with those who hold any false views; one should not associate with those who are not discerning or truthful;
one should not associate with those who are arrogant; one should not associate with those who have suddenly attained wealth and status;
one should not associate with those who gamble; one should not associate with those who sell alcohol; and one should not associate with those who are addicted to drinking alcohol.
One should not frequent places where liquor is sold; one should not associate with those who take pleasure in looking at women;
one should not associate with the proprietors of brothels; one should not associate with those who store and sell miscellaneous goods;
one should not associate with cooks and butchers; one should not associate with jailers and the like.
One should not associate with any bird-catchers, nor with any persons given to frivolous debate,
nor with any who place their faith in non-Buddhist paths, nor with any who are detested by the multitude.
A bhikṣu should not associate with such a person—whether by dwelling together, conversing, or traveling along the same path—in any way whatsoever. Why is this?

Because many people harbor doubts, neither those who have left the household life nor those who are pure and free from all faults should associate with them. Those who give rise to such doubts will think that the bhikṣu is likewise the same, because that bhikṣu either associates with such a person or dwells in the same place as them.
In this way, monks, one is defiled by the faults of others; therefore, one should not associate with such as these, let alone with kings.
Those who associate with kings are the most vulgar and base.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
“A bhikṣu should dwell in the forest; to live near a king is most base and vulgar.
To wear the kaṣāya while being close to others is like a slave who depends on his master’s commands.”
A bhikṣu should not associate with others, nor even with the devas;
a swan should not associate with a dog, because of its purity.
Being without self and without expectation, his mind seeks nothing at all.
For one who fears birth and death, it is not good to draw near a king.
Dwelling in groves or cemeteries, whether on level ground or in the mountains—
one is a virtuous bhikṣu.
"To be near a king is not good.

"In this way, through various and immeasurable skillful means, one should abandon proximity to a king; for if one is near a king, all fellow practitioners of the holy life will censure and revile him."
The one who should be approached is none other than the King of Wisdom; approaching him in this way leads to ultimate tranquility.
By approaching the King of Wisdom, one will certainly attain nirvāṇa, and wherever one may be, one shall never fall back.

To draw near to that King of Wisdom, one must possess skillful means; that is to say, one should be firm and diligent in meditation and recitation, refraining from other activities that would obstruct or neglect them; one should attend upon elders and cultivate contentment, with a mind that is disciplined and ever free from greed. By attending upon elders, one should inquire of them at the appropriate times, receiving and upholding their teachings without forgetting them; furthermore, one should not seek to see or hear of rare things, nor should one give rise to feelings of wonder or marvel.
"One who draws near to a wise king possesses this skillful means.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke in verse:
"Draw near to and make offerings to one's elders; At all times, diligently inquire and question them."
Practicing the wisdom of generosity and ethical discipline, he further draws near to the King of Wisdom.
Among gods, humans, and the world, he is the one who can show the way to peace;
he is not bound by the suffering of existence like an ordinary worldly king.
"One who is free from suffering and affliction is truly called a king;
one who constantly undergoes suffering and affliction cannot be called a king.
A bhikṣu should draw near to such a wise king and not to an ordinary king, for by drawing near to a worldly king, one’s meditation and recitation will be hindered and abandoned."
If one does not practice meditation or recitation, one will again fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
This is the domain of worldly, ordinary kings; therefore, having understood this fault, a bhikṣu should never associate with kings.
"For one who dwells in the forest, it is not appropriate to associate with kings; therefore, they should be abandoned.
This is the ninth factor that obstructs meditation and recitation.
Furthermore, there is a tenth obstructive evil factor that hinders and causes a bhikṣu to neglect sitting meditation and recitation; for this reason, a śramaṇa should abandon it."
What is the tenth?
It is when a bhikṣu longs for invitations and craves the flavors of food.

Having already practiced correctly regarding sense objects, he later wanders among people, abandoning the lovely places of the forests and wilds, and instead roams from place to place amidst human society.

In this way, a bhikṣu who is close to negligence wanders from house to house, from village to village, from city to city, and from one populous place to another; thus traveling everywhere, he delights in much talk, acts falsely among people, enjoys worldly conversation, and delights in seeing his old acquaintances.
When these old friends and associates invite him with great hospitality, he obtains fine food and drink.
Having obtained various kinds of delicious food, they falsely abandon meditation and recitation in the forest to wander about with negligence, longing for more food.
Because they are constantly attached to various foods, they do not perceive the exhaustion of their bodies; thus, clinging to flavors and hoping for invitations, they consider this to be pleasure.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu acts contrary to the Dharma regarding sense objects, because his mind finds delight in seeing beautiful forms with his eyes, he gives rise to defiled desire; longing to see them again, he becomes increasingly attached."
In this or that place, he gives rise to delight and pleasure.
Thus, as a bhikṣu wandering among human beings, he loses his own benefit.
Having lost such practices as meditation and recitation, he constantly craves the flavors of food and frequently goes to the houses of others.
Because the eye sees forms, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight; following this sequence, when the ear hears sounds, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight;
and when the nose perceives odors, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight.

Thus, delighting in and clinging to all sensory objects, they are bound by every fetter and ensnared by every net; pursuing all desires wherever they lead, they are neither householders nor renunciants.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, will fall into an evil destination and be born in hell.
Therefore, one should not delight in being invited by others; to delight in being invited by others carries such faults as these.
"Therefore, monks, you should contemplate this fault and not constantly wander among people.
If you must travel among them, there are five causes and conditions by which one may do so:
first, for the sake of seeking medicine and provisions for the sick, one may travel among people."
Second, by virtue of benefiting one's elders and superiors, one attains rebirth among human beings.
Third, by virtue of repairing and restoring Buddha-stūpas and one’s own dwellings when they have fallen into ruin, one attains rebirth among human beings.
Fourth, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, one may enter among people.
Fifth, when another king has destroyed one's kingdom, one may enter among people for the purpose of converting that king and saving one's life.

For these reasons, one should practice among human beings; if one were to practice among humans without these five kinds of causes and conditions, that would be a false practice, obstructing and abandoning meditation and recitation.

A practitioner who acts in this way cannot escape old age, sickness, death, lamentation, weeping, grief, suffering, and despair; such a wicked śramaṇa, a mere pretender to the status of a śramaṇa, has left the household life in vain.

"Therefore, monks, if a bhikṣu desires to sever craving through his mind, he should contemplate correctly, quiet his sense faculties, rely upon his elders, draw near to the Triple Gem, and practice with a restrained mind."
"Because they uphold the Three Jewels, they uproot and sever the very roots of all afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke in verse:
"Abandoning the practices of meditation and recitation, They cling only to the flavors of food."
Such a person is not a bhikṣu; his mind is like that of a hungry ghost.
"Apart from dhyāna there is no joy"—thus the wise have said;
apart from the bliss of meditative concentration, no other joy can be found.
The fool abandons supreme bliss, clinging only to various sensory flavors;
such a deluded and evil person will encounter decline and affliction.
If a person delights in sense objects and constantly relies on the pleasure of those objects, [they will suffer].
Increasing unwholesome dharmas, one falls into evil realms at the end of life.
If a person abandons meditation and recitation, forsakes the precepts and generosity,
and remains stubborn, fierce, and unsubdued, though they possess life, they are as good as dead.
If one acts in accordance with the Dharma, one does not die while in the world;
one who is devoid of the Dharma is perpetually deluded, and though possessing life, is as if dead.
Though covered by human skin, such a fool is no different from an animal.
Because they do not illuminate their own minds with the light of the lamp of wisdom;
those who uphold the precepts may be called human beings,
while all those who break the precepts are no different from dogs.
If one is greedy and does not practice giving, and if one’s evil conduct remains unsubdued, then such a person is not called human; they are reckoned among the hungry ghosts.
If a person lacks both ethical discipline and wisdom, and furthermore lacks the jewel of generosity, [they are likewise not human].
Although such a person possesses life, they are no different from the dead.
But if one practices precepts, generosity, and meditation, upholds them, and maintains samādhi—
such a person is truly called a human being and should be honored by the gods.
One who possesses merit is a human being; one without merit is like a sheep.
He who knows merit through merit—that person is called a deva. "Such is merit; those with merit know it."
One who possesses merit finds joy in all places;
if one lacks merit, they constantly experience suffering.
Therefore, monks, having heard of such supreme merits, you should not crave flavors.
"This tenth dharma obstructs and causes the abandonment of meditation and recitation; those śramaṇas who fear birth and death should regard it with dread.
Furthermore, the eleventh obstructive evil dharma hinders and causes the abandonment of a bhikṣu’s sitting meditation and reading/recitation; therefore, a śramaṇa should relinquish it."

The eleventh is as follows: because of a mind of pride, a deluded bhikṣu does not inquire of others; his internal wisdom remains unopened, yet externally he declares himself to possess all-knowledge, saying:
"Because I possess all-knowledge, I am able to speak, I am able to explain the meaning, and I am able to recite."
The entire collection of all dharmas is that which I uphold.
Hundreds of thousands of dharma-meanings are those I teach to my disciples.
There is no one else who can equal me.
Having grasped this within their own minds, they further speak thus to others:

"That person possesses only the pride of wisdom while actually lacking wisdom; that person constantly speaks of his own virtues to all sentient beings, and for this reason, all who hear of him in the world regard him with esteem. All people in the world say:
'This virtuous bhikṣu possesses all-encompassing knowledge (sarvajñā); there is no one equal to such a bhikṣu.'"

"All the people of the world speak thus, yet that bhikṣu understands nothing at all; he is inwardly empty and void, possessing no knowledge. His mind is as insubstantial as an empty vessel or an autumn cloud; having abandoned meditation and recitation, he is merely supported by those of little wisdom."

“‘To practice meditation and recitation, uphold the precepts, and practice giving; to cultivate diligence with vigor, take hold of wholesome dharmas, and adorn oneself through wisdom and discipline (*vinaya*); to dwell peacefully in the Buddha-dharma, exerting oneself without rest, and to have great compassion permeate the heart—this is the dharma that a śramaṇa ought to practice.’”
“Those evil bhikṣus are internally empty and devoid of wisdom; they think to themselves:
‘If I were to see that bhikṣu now, he would show me the Dharma.’”

In this way, that bhikṣu would despise me; yet that donor’s family constantly makes offerings to me. If he were to study under them, then that donor would no longer make offerings to me and would despise me.
Therefore, I now proclaim for others whatever I have known and understood to the best of my ability; whether those who hear it understand it or not, I can never learn from them in return.

Thus, regarding internal emptiness, out of fear of being despised by others and due to pride, they neither understand it themselves nor inquire of others, fearing that people will look down upon them.
“Such a person with a haughty mind and who speaks falsely loses the five precepts of training.
What are these five? They are as follows:
namely, false speech.”
Because he does not know this, he speaks falsely to others; this constitutes that person’s violation of the first precept.
Furthermore, next is the violation of the second precept, namely, stealing.
He should not accept the offerings of others; yet that donor provides goods for the sake of wisdom, while that foolish person, possessing little wisdom, takes those goods for himself.
Such a deluded person is a thief; this is called the breaking of the second training rule.

Furthermore, there is the breaking of the third training rule: namely, when a bhikṣu first leaves the household life, he receives the training rules and dwells relying upon the precepts. Taking the observance of the precepts as his condition, he gives rise to this thought:
"I have now left the household life."
If that bhikṣu does not engage in study and inquiry, how can he possess moral discipline?
Yet he says to others, "I am one of great knowledge. This is called breaking the third precept.
"Furthermore, there is another way of violating the fourth precept, namely, through contentious questioning.
Out of fear of being despised by others, one slanders the Dharma and declares what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma; this is the first violation of the precepts."
This is called the violation of the fourth precept.

Furthermore, next is the violation of the fifth precept: because that person does not understand the Dharma, regarding the True Dharma spoken by their fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), they declare it to be not the True Dharma, saying:
"None of you understand the profound Dharma; what you have spoken was not spoken by the Buddha."
That person thus slanders the Saṃgha, saying:
"Only I know; you members of the Saṃgha know nothing at all.
Slandering the Saṃgha in this way out of fear of being disparaged by others, he says to the Saṃgha:
"You speak what is not the Dharma," yet that which the Saṃgha speaks is indeed the Dharma.
"That evil bhikṣu thus loses the merit of the True Dharma; having uttered the greatest falsehood, at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into an evil destination and is born in hell."
He does not inquire of others because of the causes of his evil karma.
Furthermore, there is a great fault in not inquiring of others, namely, the mind of pride (*māna*).
Because of this pride, he does not enter the forest; fearing the contempt of others, he does not inquire of those who show the path.
"What is the path? How does the mind take its object?
What is it that serves as the focal point?"
"How can this be forgotten and yet again brought back into the mind?

Thus, because of the fault of pride in not being invited or questioned by others, and because he was unable to attain such a path, his mind became weary. He sat down cross-legged, but immediately rose again, thinking:
"This Dharma is false; those bhikṣus are performing these practices in vain."
"This is not the Path; truly there is no dhyāna, no samādhi, nor is there any fruit of dhyāna or fruit of samādhi.
Thus they slandered out of a mind of self-conceit, fearing the contempt of others.
"Those with such wrong views, when their bodies perish and their lives end, will fall into the evil realms and be born in hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke in verse:
"Knowing the proper time and free from conceit, One should inquire of one's elders."
The bhikṣu who exerts diligent effort will swiftly attain nirvāṇa.
Whatever he has heard from others, he explains to others as well;
knowing for himself that he is free from the conceit of "I," that bhikṣu knows with clarity.
Free from pride and free from great arrogance, knowing what is the path and what is not the path—
thus knowing oneself and others, such a one is a bhikṣu who knows contentment.
But for one whose mind of self-conceit is very firm, whose heart is wavering and dull-witted,
If one hopes for wealth, profit, and offerings, then one shall not attain tranquility.
"Because he does not thus inquire of others, his mind is hardened by pride, and he is unable to practice meditation or recitation."
In this way, a bhikṣu constantly consumes the food of others merely to sustain his life.
Such a person possesses only the outward form and robes of a bhikṣu and the name of a bhikṣu; when his body perishes and his life ends, he falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell.
Or perhaps, out of mental pride, one does not inquire of others.
Therefore, a student should always inquire of others for as long as their life remains.
In this way, a bhikṣu’s mind is constantly at peace; when his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas.
Having been born in that place, they will proceed in succession until they reach nirvana, because they have abandoned pride.
"Furthermore, the twelfth obstructive and unwholesome dharma hinders and causes the abandonment of a bhikṣu’s practice of sitting meditation and recitation."
The twelfth is: delighting in many acquaintances.
To have many acquaintances is called "bringing no benefit"; such a bhikṣu merely increases craving.
If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances, there will be much distraction and much activity; because of these, his mind becomes distracted and disturbed.
Because the mind is distracted, one cannot achieve meditative concentration or recitation.
For those who have left the household life, enemies and kin are equal; they should not even rely upon a single spiritual friend, let alone many.
If one is indolent, they are merely called a bhikṣu by name.
Upon entering another’s house, as soon as they see with their eyes, the mind becomes agitated.

Because of seeing forms with the eyes, the visual consciousness deviates from its original state; the mind does not take hold of the dharma of tranquility, does not contemplate or observe, is not upright, and is full of idle talk.
Having seen forms and known objects, one subsequently hears sounds; the mind then becomes distracted by various conditions, giving rise to diverse observations, and the mind is not tranquil.
Because it is not tranquil, there is non-tranquil observation, which involves grasping at objects of perception.
If even seeing a single acquaintance for a moment is an obstacle, how much more so is it to see acquaintances over a long period of time?
Therefore, a śramaṇa should not have even one acquaintance, let alone many.

If there is a bhikṣu who associates with acquaintances and frequents places where many people gather, traveling from such places to other such places, wandering in this manner, he will not realize that his life is ending moment by moment; thus, he loses his share of merit.
If one loses the portion of the wholesome, it is the ultimate self-deception, such that one cannot practice meditation or recite the scriptures for even a single moment of thought.
Therefore, monks who train in this manner increase their defiled attachments; they should not associate with worldly acquaintances.

"Furthermore, if one can bring about future peace and security by showing the path to nirvāṇa—such as a guide, a spiritual friend, or a fellow practitioner of meditation—one should associate with them."
What is meant by "practicing together"?
It refers to the one who eliminates all afflictions and leads one to the city of Nirvana; this is the foremost and most excellent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Any other spiritual friends are merely enemies and not true spiritual friends.

Because they are not real, they do not constitute true knowledge; if one sees them conversing together, acting together, or engaging in common activities, it will obstruct and cause the abandonment of wholesome deeds.
If one gains strength from them in future lives, they are called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Whether they demonstrate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), cause one to practice it, or teach one to fear—showing one to fear the future lives of birth in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm—they are called a virtuous spiritual friend.
"Do not associate with anyone who causes one's body, speech, and mind to commit evil deeds and leads one to the miserable realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"If they can show you the way to future lives, they are true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)."
If one can ward off evil states and further rescue others from calamities,
constantly preaching the Dharma of benefit for the sake of future generations—
such a person is a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), providing the benefits of friendship.
"This so-called 'superior spiritual friend' possesses immeasurable kinds and immeasurable varieties of conceptualization, teaching various doctrines.

One does not become known as a spiritual friend by providing abundant food and drink, by entering one's home to receive prostrations, nor by displaying affection toward sounds, touches, tastes, fragrances, and forms; such a spiritual friend is not a true spiritual friend."
A virtuous bhikṣu should abandon them; he should not even associate with such a single companion, let alone many such companions, for doing so gives rise to immeasurable faults.
If there is a "good friend" who brings no benefit in future lives, though they are called a good friend, they are in fact an enemy.
If a bhikṣu associates with such a person, it will obstruct his own practice of meditation and recitation.

"Furthermore, the thirteenth obstructive and unwholesome dharma hinders and causes the abandonment of a bhikṣu’s practice of seated meditation and recitation; therefore, a śramaṇa should relinquish it.
The thirteenth is as follows: a bhikṣu dwelling together with evil persons."
When all bhikṣus dwell together with the wicked, it hinders and causes the abandonment of meditation and recitation.
There are five kinds of dwelling together with the wicked; what are these five? They are as follows:

a bhikṣu who well maintains the pure precepts—the foremost wholesome dharma—and possesses an upright mind, yet dwells and resides together with a foremost person of broken precepts and evil conduct, thereby losing his autonomy.
This is the first instance of dwelling together with evil.

"Furthermore, the second instance of dwelling together with evil is as follows: when a bhikṣu, whether through his own lack of self-mastery or by the influence of others, associates with those of wrong views, traveling and residing together with them in villages, cities, or populous places."
This is the second instance of dwelling together with evil.

"Furthermore, the third instance of dwelling together with evil is as follows: a bhikṣu constantly delights in frequenting former acquaintances and friends; he desires to go to them, desires to draw near to them, and accompanies them to the houses where they lived when they were still laypeople."
This is the third instance of dwelling together with the wicked.

"Furthermore, the fourth instance of dwelling together with the wicked is as follows: a bhikṣu, out of fear of being despised by others and desiring to acquire knowledge and views, goes to the abode of a teacher of false doctrines who dwells in an evil place and associates closely with him."
This is the fourth instance of dwelling together with evil.

"Furthermore, the fifth instance of dwelling together with evil is as follows: a bhikṣu whose mind is agitated and unable to practice correctly, who dwells upon his previous food or bedding, or what he previously ate, or what he previously drank, or where he previously slept, or his proximity to women; or who recollects and contemplates various things such as the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles formerly enjoyed—thus, by dwelling on these objects and recollecting them, he is destroyed by those very objects."
All other places may be avoided, but this realm cannot be avoided, for it is the foremost and most evil of all places;
it is the greatest obstacle to all practices such as meditation and recitation.
All other evil realms can be avoided, but this one realm—the pleasure of sensory objects—is the most impossible to avoid.

The evil realms arising from the conceptualizations of one's own mind are the most difficult to avoid; they can only be avoided through the bliss of seated meditation (*samādhi*), through right observation, and through mindfulness. Only by such means can one avoid them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, spoke these verses:
"The wind that is not properly observed Blows upon the blazing fire;
But when it is correctly observed as rain, It can extinguish it without remainder."
The long-standing darkness of ignorance that sentient beings have previously given rise to can be extinguished without remainder by the lamp of wisdom.
The fires of desire and delusion burn the foolish people in the hells.
The wise are not thus; therefore, they attain nirvāṇa.
These thirteen factors can be eliminated by the light of wisdom;
therefore, those who fear transgression should always diligently uphold the precepts.
"Uproot the three kinds of faults from within yourself,
and with the great fire of wisdom, burn the fuel of manifold afflictions.
"As previously stated, regarding dwelling together with evil, one should employ skillful means to remain entirely detached from them."
A renunciant śramaṇa should rather walk alone; do not harbor many recollections, nor be indolent.

Do not recall or take pleasure in past delights from your former villages, cities, or populous places. Do not think of former times of festivals and gatherings where people were abundant, nor recall with longing the desire to see them again, nor grasp after them.

Do not associate with wicked disciples or evil associates; do not take pleasure in or crave sounds, touches, tastes, fragrances, or forms; do not give rise to defiled thoughts, nor engage in improper conduct; let your mind not be agitated, and do not harbor expectations for food, drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites for illness.
Do not wear saffron robes of various mixed colors, nor use expedients such as pressing or pounding them to make them flat;
when bathing, do not rub or scrub the body with your feet;
and do not engage in various kinds of miscellaneous chatter.
In this way, the mass of beginningless darkness is incinerated.

"The most wretched cycle of birth and death has the five realms as its gateway; within the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, the flames of conceptualization regarding the objects of the six sense-fields constantly burn and scorch."

All the foolish worldlings of the various realms wander here and there, scorched and ruined, entering the ocean of suffering; yet they continue to revolve through birth and death without ever feeling weary or seeking liberation.

Abandoning the practice of upholding the precepts, if a person is born in heaven, they will become supremely heedless; later, when they fall from that heaven, they will be separated from their former superior companions and be reborn in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, where they undergo supreme suffering.
Burned by the fire of regret, there is no one to save them.
Ruined by negligence and scorched by the fire of remorse, they are reborn in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"For these reasons, all those who fear future decline should practice the True Dharma and never let it be interrupted."
Such is the Dharma and Vinaya: all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas establish it in order to eliminate negligence among negligent devas.
If a person is born in the heavens, it is entirely due to the power of observing the precepts.

If there is one who has well-cultivated and well-tamed the mind, such a person cannot be said to have died; at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will be reborn in a good destination, within the world of the devas.
“O you hosts of devas, none of you know the causes for being born in this heaven, nor the lightness or gravity of precepts.
For your benefit, I shall demonstrate those karmic actions to you; therefore, I have taught these thirteen dharma-gates.”
In the worlds of humans and devas, they serve as causes for one another.
In the human world, one is able to maintain the precepts; in the heavenly world, one is unable to do so.
When a human dies and is reborn in heaven, if they are not negligent, they may later decline and be reborn among humans.
"For this reason, I preach this sutra.
"That Blessed One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, benefited devas and humans, providing them with benefit, welfare, and peace, even unto nirvāṇa; in this way, he benefited the entire world."

"At that time, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with his celestial host, gave rise to a profound sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*). Although they remained within the realm of desire, they did not act with negligence (*pramāda*) amidst those desires, and all fully accomplished the practice of non-negligence."
They prostrated before the stūpa of the World-Honored One, Kāśyapa Buddha, their minds purified.
All those devas departed just as they had originally come.
"The sixth sūtra of the World-Honored One Kāśyapa is finished."
"This teaching is called the Six Sūtras; it circulates in a place endowed with mountains and trees.
At that time, the entire host of devas emerged from the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha and addressed the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, saying:
"O Heavenly King, how do you know this Buddha-stūpa?"
When the host of devas had thus questioned him, the Lord Mucilinda replied:
"All you hosts of devas, listen attentively."
I have a karmic connection by which I previously beheld this stūpa.

Long ago, when I was first born into this deva realm, I acted with negligence, delighting in sensory objects and being bound by the five snares; I wandered throughout these regions of the Yāma heaven, sporting and enjoying pleasures amidst the merits of the five desires, traveling from place to place.

From one grove to another grove, from mountain to mountain, from crag to crag, from cliff to cliff, from one flower pond to another flower pond, and from one peak to another peak, there were many hundreds of thousands of countless devaputras, surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens.
Those hosts of celestial maidens, adorned with countless hundreds of thousands of ornaments and finery, stood before the prince, dancing, singing, laughing joyfully, and playing as they circled him.

At that time, I surveyed this celestial world in its entirety; I was attached to the objects of the five sensual pleasures and their merits, my heart filled with delight, and I was led away by the bonds of craving.
My movement through three locations was entirely unimpeded: namely, being upon the back of a goose, moving from the back of one goose to the back of another;
next, being upon the back of a ruddy sheldrake, moving from the back of one sheldrake to the back of another.
Next, he again mounted a duck and traveled from the back of one duck to the back of another.
Then he was upon lotus flowers, traveling from one lotus flower to another;
amidst the waves of water, he went from wave to wave.

They sport everywhere, proceeding as they please without any obstruction; indulging in all manner of play, song, dance, and laughter, their hearts experience the utmost bliss as they wander in this way.

"Having thus engaged in various diversions, I further thought of other amusements: namely, traveling upon the land while riding in celestial palaces, surrounded and followed by hundreds of thousands of goddesses, going from mountain to mountain, from one peak to another peak, from one valley to another valley, from one grove to another grove, and from one mountain cave to another mountain cave."
At that time, I moved through such places without obstruction.

Thus, in succession, I traveled through the void, riding upon celestial palaces, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of devas. As they played various celestial instruments producing wondrous sounds, they proceeded with song, dance, joyful laughter, and play throughout this entire world of the devas.

One sees various unspeakably diverse locations, many of which are places of supreme excellence, brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of the seven treasures; such mountain peaks are seen everywhere throughout.

There were hundreds of thousands of trees adorned with the seven treasures; following this sequence, he further beheld a river, upon whose banks hundreds of thousands of lotuses gathered, with exquisite lotuses everywhere.
I, together with the hosts of devas, see it all thus: looking down from the midst of the sky, we behold all the perfections of every desire.

"In this world of devas, hundreds of thousands of kinds of palaces abound everywhere; I constantly move through them without obstruction—whether in water, on land, or in the air—thus sporting and experiencing various pleasures."
"I further recall a time when I saw six mountains from which six rays of light pierced through the void and emerged; their blazing colors were distinct, yet I did not know what they were."
Having seen this at that time, I gave rise to a sense of wonder and focused my mind in contemplation:
"What is this that I have seen? Such a thing has never occurred before."
Having thought thus, I immediately proceeded with the celestial palace; all the hosts of devas quickly went before me to the Six Radiant Lights.
Once I arrived at the place of those Six Radiant Lights, both I and the palace fell together, and all the radiance and majestic power I previously possessed were entirely diminished.
At that time, I thought to myself: "What is this?
What power is it that causes my own body and all these celestial hosts to fall, and diminishes all our majesty and radiance?"
“At that time, having finished my reflection, there was among the host of devas an elder deva named Vimalavipula.
That deva had previously seen these six mountains and their six kinds of radiance, and he said to me:
‘O Heavenly King, do not be afraid now; you are without fault.’”
"There is nothing inauspicious for the Heavenly King; I pray that Your Majesty will now listen.
By what causes and conditions has the Heavenly King, together with this assembly of devas, now fallen from the sky?"
In the past, there were immeasurable heavenly kings who, while traveling through the void at this place, were unable to pass and all fell in this manner.

Because the heavenly kings had never heard of this before and did not know of it, they attempted to pass through as they were, immediately falling downward; their majestic power and radiant light were all about to be extinguished.
I shall now explain the causes and conditions for this.

At this place, there have always been six Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, perfected in knowledge and conduct, gods among gods, who possessed true knowledge and vision of all worlds; they erected six Buddha-stūpas within these mountain trees and lands to benefit devas and humans.
This stupa is worthy of veneration and worthy of offerings.
Through prostration and making offerings, there is nothing that does not yield its power. Why is this so?
"Because there is nothing superior to it, such a Buddha-stūpa is impossible to encounter.
For this reason, O Heavenly King, you have now fallen so low.
At that time, I spoke these pure and extensive words to him:
"Where is the Buddha? Vimalavistara replied to me, saying:
"At this time he is nowhere; throughout the entire world, he is entirely absent."

He possessed all-knowledge and saw all things; having understood the faults and evils of desire and realized the various sufferings within birth and death, he diligently practiced the six *pāramitās* for a full three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, attained all-knowledge, and entered *nirvāṇa*.
This is a brief explanation; if you wish to hear it in detail, you shall see this Buddha-stūpa, which will explain it further.
These six Buddha-stūpas now reside within the region known as the Land Endowed with Mountains and Trees.

“At that time, having heard those words of the long-standing deva Vimalavistṛta and having witnessed his power, I conceived a sense of wonder. Together with that long-standing deva Vimalavistṛta and the assembly of devas, I went to the site of the six stūpas. Having arrived, I reflected that for the sake of hearing the Dharma and crossing over birth and death, I should enter the Buddha’s stūpa.”
"Having entered the Buddha-stūpa, they heard this Dharma as proclaimed by that Blessed One, the World-Honored One.

When the assembly of devas had heard these words from the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, they each took leave of the Heavenly King and departed for their own realms; Mucilinda, the Night-Wandering Heavenly King (Yama), likewise returned to his former dwelling place.
The discourse on the Buddha-stūpas is concluded.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 50. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 51.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty: Observing the Heavens; Section Sixteen: Yāma Heaven.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, observes the seventh station of the Yāma Heaven, named Vast Conduct (Vipula-caryā). By what karma do sentient beings take birth in that station?
He knows through seeing, hearing, or inference, or sees it with the divine eye:
that if a person has previously known how to maintain the precepts with a virtuous mind—refraining from killing and stealing as previously described—and furthermore abandons sexual misconduct.
It is said that there may be someone who goes into a forest and approaches the birds of wondrous song.

Because those birds of wondrous song give rise to lustful thoughts toward one another, they emit lustful sounds; the female bird goes before and the male bird follows behind, traveling together in this manner.
The wings and feathers of those birds are of various colors, such that all who see them feel joy in their hearts and sensual desire arises within them.
Yet, having seen them, they do not give rise to thoughts of desire; they do not even contemplate it in their minds, let alone engage in sexual acts.

That person, thus maintaining pure precepts and abandoning wrong desires, being pure in their observance of the precepts, at the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas, arising in the region known as Vistīrṇacarā.
Having been born there, all manner of sensual merits converge, and they experience various pleasures.

There are superior groves and gardens, adorned with trees of silver, lapis lazuli, and blue gems, as well as trees of great sapphire and various jewel-trees the color of lotuses; there are various jeweled ponds filled to the brim with flowing water.

If there are people who have come here having performed wholesome deeds in the past, they experience various pleasures while walking through this grove. As for what is called this grove, it is named the Crimson Grove (*Raktavana*); within that grove dwell hosts of devas and hosts of celestial maidens.
If one enters therein, the radiance of those trees increases and becomes even more excellent, adorned with various wonderful jewels and producing various garments.
When the hosts of devas enter that forest, the radiance of those trees becomes entirely red in color.
The color of those groves is entirely like that of red lotus jewels, or they take on the hue of karketana jewels.

The colors of the trees are soft and supple, and canopies of pearl-bell nets cover them above. Fruits appear according to one's thoughts, wine flows according to one's thoughts, and everything proceeds exactly as one desires.
Wherever the gods intend to experience pleasure, the branches and leaves of those trees immediately produce various kinds of exquisite and wonderful musical sounds as they travel in this manner.
Accompanied by many celestial maidens and the hosts of gods, these trees fly through the air; wherever their hearts desire, they move no differently than birds.
Once those trees have flown into the midst of space, they all appear like the rising sun, universally adorning and beautifying the entire void.
Furthermore, those trees are called "Red Trees"; water issues from them like rain, and they are exceedingly delightful within the sky.
The sounds of those bells, the songs of celestial birds, and the music of divine instruments—such various and sublime sounds filled the void of space.
At that time, the celestial hosts saw the tree flying before them, surrounded by throngs of celestial maidens, and their hearts were filled with a single sense of joy.
Accompanied by the singing voices of many hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, they fly through the void.
The trees stand before them like guides showing the way, while the hosts of devas follow behind, keeping pace with the trees.
As the hosts of devas thus followed their thoughts, they gave rise to this intention:
"I shall now ascend that tree.
At the moment they thought this, the tree turned over, and the devas immediately ascended it.
There are those who sport upon the branches; thus do those gods sport everywhere upon that tree.
When those gods dwelling on the branches think of it in their minds, lotus ponds immediately arise upon those very branches, where the gods and goddesses sport and enjoy themselves within the pools.

Thus, the devas dwelling upon the branches of these trees sport and enjoy themselves with hosts of celestial maidens in the Crimson Grove; all according to their own inclinations, they experience such pleasures.
Furthermore, there are other devas who dwell within the leaves; whenever they have a thought, a magnificent hall immediately emerges from within the tree leaves.
At the moment of that thought, such halls appear, adorned with various exquisite jewels interspersed and arrayed, and covered by networks of bells.
That Hall of All is adorned with lotus ponds, and its doors and windows are draped with nets of pearls.
Devas dwell therein, sporting together with various celestial maidens through song and dance; they do not obstruct one another, but cherish and care for each other.
Thus, by the power of their wholesome karma, these devas are mutual friends, harboring neither enmity nor indifference.
This abundance of friends is the fruit of wholesome karma; indeed, having many friends is the fruit of great wholesome karma.
At that time, those devas, with one mind toward each other, engaged in various amusements within the Crimson Forest.

In that Crimson Forest, all manner of sensual pleasures were fully provided for those devas; by virtue of their great and superior karma, they traveled through the air according to their every thought, experiencing immeasurable bliss.
Furthermore, those devas do not travel through the air, but return to their original abodes.
In various lotus ponds filled with flowing water, they sport and enjoy themselves, surrounded by celestial maidens in such places.
Furthermore, they proceed next toward the grove named Ghanavṛkṣa.
That Ghanavṛkṣa grove is exceedingly delightful; within the grove there is a river, and milk flows through it.
Such a river of milk adorns that grove, and by the power of that milk, if a deva drinks from it, they remember where they were born in their past lives and how they passed away to come here.
Falling away from this state, one is born elsewhere.
If one has acted with negligence, having recollected those various sufferings and immeasurable kinds of suffering, the mind gives rise to grief and distress;
because such grief and distress arise, one then abandons negligence.
Having abandoned negligence, they practice in accordance with the Dharma.
This great benefit is brought about by the power of drinking that essence of milk.
Having drunk such milk of powerful essence, they then enter that grove known as Ghanavṛkṣa.
The forest was adorned with various flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, in which dwelt many kinds of birds.
These birds were exceedingly numerous, and the branches of the trees were laden with flowers; because of the weight of the blossoms, they all hung downward, creating a magnificent adornment.

There are bees made of the seven precious substances, their colors uniform; they drink the nectar of those flowers to enjoy themselves, traveling from lotus pond to lotus pond and from beneath one tree to beneath another.
All those trees are made of vaidūrya, and their lotus-jewel leaves bear golden fruits.
Such fruits as these surpass even the exquisite sudhā nectar found among the gods.
Such fruits are fruits of recollection; whenever they desire flavor, such delicious fruits arise.
Having eaten those fruits, they further dance and sing, proceeding toward other places with hearts full of joy.
They then proceed toward the Forest of Drinks; from the trees of that forest flows celestial wine, which is of exquisite flavor, fragrance, and color, most delightful and beyond description.
It is free from the faults of intoxication.
Such superior wine flows from the trees like rain falling from the clouds; having drunk it, those gods give rise once again to even greater hearts of joy.
Having thus experienced such joy, those gods hear various sounds, drink celestial fine wine, and enjoy manifold pleasures.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable lights adorning their own bodies, and the celestial maidens played, sang, danced, and laughed joyfully with one another.
"Moreover, they proceeded next toward the Lotus Dragon Forest."
That forest measures five hundred yojanas in extent; it is adorned with lotus flowers made of the five precious gems, which are exceedingly fragrant.
Within the Lotus Dragon Forest there is nothing else at all, except for the lotuses and the various dragons.
Within those lotuses, these nāgas arouse mutual desire toward one another.
They consume those lotuses, and with a single mind, the many nāgas act as companions for one another, surrounded by nāga maidens amidst the clear water.
The water possesses seven virtues: it is free from the fault of clinging garments, free from the fault of muddy turbidity, and free from the fault of being too deep or too shallow.
Within that touch, one experiences pleasure according to one's own mind.
In whatever way the nāga himself conceives in his mind, in that very way water arises according to his will.
When that nāga sports and enjoys himself among the nāga maidens therein, it is no different from the way the devas enjoy pleasure together with the deva maidens.

At that time, the hosts of devas, seeing the various nāgas sporting and enjoying themselves within that Lotus Nāga Grove, descended from the sky toward the Lotus Grove with the sounds of chanting and singing, as well as the adorned voices of the celestial maidens.
The dragon, dwelling within the pool, utters a voice like thunder that pervades that celestial realm as if it were a single song.
Because this song from the celestial realm causes all the mountain valleys to resound, the gods in other regions hear its sound and all come together toward the Lotus Dragon Grove.
Adorned with various kinds of radiance upon their bodies and surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, they thus proceeded together toward the Lotus Dragon Grove (*padma-nāga-vana*).
At that time, those gods who were already there in the Lotus Dragon Grove were sporting in various ways, while other gods arrived from diverse locations such as mountain valleys and other places.
Once those gods have seen one another, their hearts of joy increase all the more.
Thus, these gods together with their hosts of goddesses, as well as those nāgas and their nāga-wives, sport and enjoy themselves together within the waters.
Those devas, goddesses, nāgas, and nāga maidens experience such pleasure for a long time, thus sporting, singing, dancing, and laughing with joy.

As those devas thus act with such negligence, because their wholesome karma is exhausted and their lives are about to end, when the merit and wholesome karma of those devas and goddesses are on the verge of being spent, if they ascend upon a lotus flower, the lotus cannot support them;
thus the lotus sinks into the water and immediately breaks apart.
In this way, one should understand the signs of the exhaustion of merit for these gods or goddesses.

Furthermore, the signs of the exhaustion of merit for those gods or goddesses are as follows: while those gods or goddesses are playing, they mount the backs of nāgas; the nāgas cannot endure it, and [the gods] fall from the nāgas' backs.
This is the sign that the merit of that deva or that celestial maiden has been exhausted; it is the appearance that arises when a deva who acts with negligence is destroyed by his own negligence.
At that time, if there is among those devas one who has not been excessively negligent from the beginning, he perceives that sign beforehand. Knowing that sign, he speaks this verse:
"A long time has already passed; The moment for the end of life is approaching."
When the time of death is about to arrive, the deluded devas do not perceive it.
Their minds know no contentment; they are greedily attached to the pleasures of sensory objects.
Because the senses lack contentment, their desire for sensory objects increases.
The five faculties delight in their objects, seeking to destroy the mind;
as the karma of the field of merit is about to be exhausted, the deluded gods do not perceive it.
This great wheel of the cycle of time constantly severs the lives of all beings.
As it turns swiftly and approaches its arrival, the deluded deva does not perceive it.
This fire of death is most terrible; blown by the winds of karma, the time for the end of life is drawing near, yet the deluded deva does not perceive it.
Within the conditioned realm of birth and death, there is neither kin nor stranger;
yet the snare of death is most terrifying, and none can grant exemption from it.
For all beings before death has arrived, and for all whose life-force is not yet exhausted—
All should abandon heedlessness and act for their own benefit.
Before long, the staff of death will surely shatter one's life;
once its great power arrives, it can cause life to perish and be destroyed.
Blinded by delusion regarding the realms of existence, they are far removed from the lamp of the Dharma’s light;
thus they do not see or know the great and terrifying snare of death.
The deluded cannot understand this, yet they must face the dread of the time of death.
Because the mind clings to sense objects and is deceived by craving,
beings fall back again and again, passing from one state to another.
Destroyed by ignorance, sentient beings thus undergo the fruits of their own karma.
Extremely terrible and exceedingly swift, it can destroy all worlds;
why then, at the time of death, do you not give rise to fear?
Do sentient beings lack a mind, or are they simply fearless?
Thus, through delusion they do not know, and they fear the time of death.
When the signs of decline appear most vividly, as if seen before one's very eyes,
they will soon realize this and fall from among the gods.

"Having thus seen the signs of decline, that deva clearly recognizes those signs; his mind becomes sorrowful and distressed, and he does not speak of them to other devas who have not yet declined, nor to those who are about to decline."
Because those who have not yet fallen back experience various sensual pleasures within the five sensory realms, one fears they might not believe that they will later fall. Why is this?

Because they are heedless and deluded regarding the sensory realms, or because their minds are confused; therefore, one should neither speak to nor show [the truth] to those among the celestial hosts whose lives are about to end or who are heedless.
At that time, having understood this, that deva remained silent and spoke no word; he left the lotus pond and departed for another place.
Later, that deva again took pleasure in sensory objects and experienced the delights of those objects.

When he is about to fall away, signs of great shame appear and signs of great fear appear; yet, being deluded, he does not perceive them, nor does he feel dread or fear. He continues to sport among the nāgas, dwelling together with the celestial maidens in the lotus ponds, and there he experiences pleasure for a long time.
Furthermore, together with a multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, they proceeded toward another mountain called Mount Constant Delight Garlands (*Nitya-rati-mālā-giri*).

Having arrived and wishing to ascend, they beheld that mountain adorned with hundreds of thousands of magnificent halls featuring exquisite gates made of celestial gold, silver, celestial lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and celestial lotus jewels; it was further embellished by hundreds of thousands of most excellent and wondrous lotuses.

Thus, within this mountain, there is the foremost and most excellent bliss, complete in every respect; hundreds of thousands of musical sounds are freely heard by the ears, and they wear various kinds of celestial garments without thread, their own bodies emitting radiance.
They gaze at one another’s faces, experiencing pleasure according to their hearts’ desires through exquisite forms, sounds, touches, tastes, and fragrances.
Acting according to their own mental inclinations, they fully accomplish an ineffable bliss.
The flowing waters of the celestial river and the adornments of the groves bring joy upon being seen.

Thus, those gods proceed in succession further up Mount Constant Joy-Garland (*Nitya-sukha-mālā-giri*). Having ascended the mountain, some sit upon couches within halls, some ride upon geese, and some gods sit cross-legged upon the pedestals of lotuses.

The devas dwell together with their celestial maidens amidst the leaves of the kumbhāṇḍa tree; they engage in various diversions, such as singing and dancing, and sit enjoying happiness to the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments.

Their minds desire to travel through the void of space, together with the celestial maidens, looking everywhere throughout those heavens; wherever they find delight, they proceed according to their hearts' desires and to their satisfaction.

In some places, there is the brilliance of gold, silver, lotuses, and exquisite jewels, resembling flickering flames; in some places, there are many green, glossy shadows of *kubjaka* leaves; in some places, there is the blue radiance of celestial *vaiḍūrya* gems; and in some places, there is the lovely luster of silver, crystal, and pearls.
"Next, there is another river with sands of genuine pearls, flowing from the peaks of jewel mountains. It carries clear, cool water possessing seven merits.
Upon seeing that mountain peak and river, one observes whirlpools of water whose shapes resemble strings of genuine pearl necklaces."

Having observed and seen that place in this manner, he flew into the air and saw another location: a pond adorned with lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems, where countless swarms of bees graced the blossoms.
Having seen this, he further observed another place where there was a grove with ponds that were exceedingly lovely.

He saw birds and beasts; the beasts were of various colors—some were silver-colored, some were gold-colored—with lovely jewel-like horns, lotus-jewel eyes, backs of true gold, flanks of white silver, hooves of crystal color, and backs and feet that were even and level.

Furthermore, there were other beasts that followed one another in herds; possessing the wondrous colors of the seven treasures, they were entirely without fear, frolicking in groups and enjoying happiness for themselves.
Because they are produced by karma, their forms and bodies are exceptionally sublime; by virtue of that same karma, they all consume celestial food.

Furthermore, in other parts of the groves, one sees peacocks, *jīvañjīvaka* birds—also known as *anantāśaya* birds, *pralāpa* birds, *mahānetra* birds, and *calapakṣa* birds—and such birds as these travel in flocks among the mountain peaks, entering and exiting the groves, which are seen within the gardens.
Having arrived at such Mount Nitya-sukha-mālya, as he was about to ascend it, he saw such birds.
One side of that mountain consists of blue jewels; its second side consists of lotus-jewels; its third side consists of gold jewels; and its fourth side consists of silver jewels.

Within the chamber of blue jewels, there is a sublime jeweled hall named Variegated Reflections (*Citra-pratibimba*). Inside this hall stands a lapis lazuli tree, its flowers hanging down like great parasols. It is adorned with flowing streams and lotus ponds; there are hundreds of thousands of lotus groves, and hundreds of thousands of birds of various colors provide further adornment. Many celestial maidens, exceedingly beautiful and upright, reside within that hall.
In that second enclosure, at the place of Lotus Jewels, there is a grove named Smiling Forest.
In that forest, the trees are of silver and their leaves are of gold; there are swarms of red bees and the sounds of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flocks of birds.
There is a river of flowing water whose waters possess a fragrance; as a gentle breeze stirs it, the entire forest of Smiles is thus universally adorned.
In that third enclosure, amidst the place of gold and jewels, there is a wondrous jewel forest named the Forest of Delightful Jewels.

It is adorned with crystal trees; these trees have golden branches, and their lattices of branches cover everything. There are immeasurable birds with hundreds of thousands of melodic voices, and it is further adorned with flowing rivers.
In that place, there are many hosts of *nirmāṇarati* devas and *nirmāṇarati* goddesses who sing and dance therein; it is adorned with the full perfection of all excellent sensual qualities.

In that fourth enclosure, where silver jewels abound, lotus-jewel trees are adorned with branches of blue-colored jewels; there are many birds of various exquisite songs, numerous immeasurable devas and devīs, and it is further embellished by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lotuses.
There are immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions; there are immeasurable kinds that follow what the eyes behold, and upon seeing them, one experiences joy.

Those forests, those trees, those rivers, those waters, those jeweled branches, and so forth—those lotus ponds, those birds, those beasts, and those lotuses—possess various colors and fragrances, and their various forms and characteristics are exceedingly magnificent.
Throughout the Mount Nityapriyamālā, there are such gods and hosts of celestial maidens everywhere; they ascend into the air and travel across that entire mountain range.

All see this Mount Superior-Mindfulness (Śubhamati) emitting variegated lights; having seen it, those devas’ eyes become delighted and attached, and they all desire to ascend the mountain to experience pleasure together with hosts of celestial maidens amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music and the merits of the five desires.

Diligently performing wholesome deeds, delighting in cultivation and practice, possessing lovely and virtuous karma, and holding the precious jewel of ethical discipline— the fruit beloved by the noble ones—
they experience such joy as they all desire to ascend that Mount Nityasukhamālā.
As they were about to ascend, the bird named Satyavādin spoke this verse for them:
“The waters of this river flow swiftly, and so too does the pleasure of wholesome karma;
the deluded do not perceive this, being deceived by their craving for sensory objects.”
Just as time comes and goes, death likewise comes;
because they are deluded by pleasure and intoxicated by negligence, the gods, in their folly, do not perceive it.
Because the foolish lack wisdom, they do not realize that their lives have already passed away.
They are likewise deluded regarding wholesome karma, yet their craving remains inexhaustible.
Sentient beings do not escape craving; they follow its course within the realms of existence.
Those sentient beings, mired in ignorance and craving, do not perceive what is wholesome or unwholesome.
The fruits of goodness are most lovable, like the bliss experienced by the gods;
likewise, one sees the unwholesome as it exists in the painful realms of the evil paths.
If one abandons both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and is further able to leave behind all faults, [one attains liberation].
Thus one reaches the state of non-retrogression, the realm where there is neither birth nor death.
That joy is the attainment of liberation; sensual pleasure does not yield liberation.
Even the Yāma gods and other celestial beings attain liberation only when their karma is exhausted.
"What is impermanent does not abide; what is permanent is the foremost.
To long for the pleasures within existence is to fall into that which is not to be enjoyed.
Thus did the bird of True Speech speak to those celestial hosts who wished to ascend the mountain.
Having heard this, among that assembly of devas, those who were not excessively heedless would hear it;
however, those who were heedless, due to the fault of their heedlessness, did not hear it, remaining instead attached to their sensory objects.
Those heedless devas did not accept at all what the celestial birds had said; yet such was the true benefit of the birds' words.
Then, with hearts full of joy, that host of devas proceeded toward the first mountain, where there was a hall upon a peak at the summit of the mountain, and they sat within that hall.
As previously described, that single mountain peak is named Mount Universal Vision (*Samantadarśana*).
Among the one thousand mountains, Mount Universal Vision is the highest and most supreme; therefore, that mountain is called Universal Vision.

Together with hosts of celestial maidens, they ascend that mountain peak, enjoying themselves with various musical sounds, songs, and dances. Many hosts of devas and celestial maidens ascend those mountain summits and behold a pool of radiant water, manifesting in infinite colors through the power of their virtuous karma.
In that Pond of Radiance there is lovely water, pure and clear, within which are golden fish that bring joy to the eyes of those who behold them.

The ripples of the water move in agitation, and there are flocks of birds such as geese, mandarin ducks, and ducks; these various birds produce delightful songs, and they are very numerous in the water.

Furthermore, within that water there are many lotuses—kubjaka, kumuda, nīlotpala, and kaṭamāra flowers—and such blossoms as these completely cover the pond waters, while various bees produce all kinds of sounds.
Furthermore, there are many *mandārava* flowers, interspersed with many golden pearls, and the water is pure and clear.
Moreover, within those lovely ponds, there are lotuses called *mukhamandita*, each having a hundred petals, and from each individual petal emerge immeasurable further petals.

There are lotus petals the color of blue jewels; there are lotus petals the color of crystal; there are lotus petals the color of golden-yellow; there are lotus petals the color of white silver; there are lotus petals made of musāragalva; there are lotus petals of karketana; and there are diamond flowers of the most excellent fragrance.
Within each of those variously colored leaves, there is a pericarp, the radiance of which is like that of the newly risen sun.

Those various pericarps possess immeasurable colors, and leaves of immeasurable colors fill the entire pond—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and black. The pericarps are white and red; their fragrance is lovely and fills a single great pericarp.
At that time, the host of devas descended from the void toward the Radiant Pond; having descended, they entered the pond.

There were golden birds in the pond, and once the devas had entered, some sat upon the backs of the birds, while others stayed upon the pedestals of lotuses, sporting and enjoying themselves together with many celestial maidens.

There were devas upon the *kubalaya* lotuses, others among the waters, some who had mounted the backs of swans and entered the water to sport, and others on land sporting with hosts of celestial maidens; they were fully endowed with the merits of the five desires, laughing and playing together as they experienced delight.

There are those who, together with various celestial maidens in the halls, sport in different locations; they drink the celestial wine together, free from the fault of intoxication, manifesting the merit of bliss, wherein taste, touch, color, and fragrance are all fully perfected.
Among them, some of the devas drink wine from jeweled vessels, namely various kinds of jeweled vessels such as those made of blue gems, silver, gold, lapis lazuli, lotus-colored gems, and crystal.
Some, together with celestial maidens, drink wine from the petals of golden lotuses.

Some drink divine liquor from blossoming *kubjaka* flowers that are neither pierced nor broken, while they sing songs that give rise to joy. There are those who enjoy the food of *sudhā*, in which color, texture, fragrance, and flavor are all perfectly complete.
Each and every one, together with their respective retinues, experiences various pleasures.
In other places, they sport with celestial maidens, surrounded by the sounds of the five kinds of music and various songs and dances, as they play about the Pool of Radiance.
There are those who sport in the water together with celestial maidens.
