The taste of that water changes according to the thoughts of the devas; if the deva’s mind intends for this water to possess such-and-such color, fragrance, flavor, or texture, whether cold or warm, it appears exactly as intended through the power of their wholesome karma.
The retribution for wholesome and unwholesome karma is thus; there is no agent.
Furthermore, if those gods should think:
"This water is wine; let me drink it."
At the very moment they think of it, these become celestial wines, fully endowed with touch, flavor, fragrance, and color, yet free from the fault of intoxication.
Once the gods have drunk them, their supreme bliss increases; by the power of their virtuous karma, their hearts are filled with joy.

Nevertheless, by the power of their own karma, those devas experience such pleasure; they are transformed by their own karma, and all that they do is never lost, for the teacher of the snare of karma treats the human body as a mechanical puppet, playing with it in various ways within the three realms, while ignorant ordinary beings neither perceive nor understand this.
Thus, these devas are fully endowed with the merits of the five sensual pleasures and experience great happiness.
Within that celestial realm, there is a bird named Satyavādin (Truth-Speaker) who speaks this verse for them:
"Just as a lamp goes out when its oil is exhausted, so too do the body and life come to an end."
Because their original karma is exhausted, they will certainly fall from the heavens.
Just as when a wall crumbles, the painting upon it perishes;
so too, because karma is spent, celestial pleasures cease to exist.
When the merit of those gods in their celestial realm is exhausted, they fall away;
all phenomena are impermanent, and all sentient beings are subject to destruction.
All things are impermanent and unstable; life passes swiftly and does not endure for long.
"The power of death is exceedingly great, yet the gods do not perceive it.
Thus did that bird of Truth speak for the benefit of the celestial hosts, having already explained this by virtue of the power of those gods' own wholesome karma.
If those devas have not been indulging in negligence for a long time, upon hearing the birds' speech, they will contemplate it with correct attention for a short period;
however, those who are negligent are as if they did not hear it at all, for because their minds are distracted, they do not receive the teaching even though they hear it.

"Having thus enjoyed the pleasures of the sensory objects at that lake for such a long time, each mounted upon their respective conveyances, they fly through the air toward the mountain peak together with the celestial maidens."
Furthermore, he sees other places with immeasurable mountains of various forms and appearances.

Among all these mountains, Mount Nityarati-māla is the most elevated; there is another mountain named Samatā-niketa, and another named Samantadarśana; the dimensions of these three mountains are the greatest and highest among all the mountains in the realm of Yāma.
As the celestial hosts thus observe that mountain, its radiance pervades that celestial realm.

Having seen it, the celestial hosts ascend Mount Nitya-sukha-mālā; once they have ascended, they behold various interspersed, wondrous jewel trees—trees of gold, trees of silver, and trees of *vaiḍūrya*—adorned upon that mountain.
The roots, stems, joints, branches, and leaves of those trees are all exquisitely adorned with the seven treasures.
Their roots and stems are embellished with the seven treasures, while each successive joint is distinguished by a different jewel.

One joint is of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, one joint is of lotus-colored jewel; the next joint is of silver jewel, the next joint is of gold jewel, the next joint is of crystal (*sphaṭika*) jewel, the next joint is of musāragalva jewel, and the next joint is of *karketana*; thus, each joint of that tree is adorned differently.
From the roots and stems up to the leaves, everything is adorned with the seven treasures.
Not far from those trees, there are rows of jeweled halls arranged without disorder, all of a single color, like the radiance of the sun in the human world.
For the sake of play and pleasure, those hosts of devas proceed next toward that hall.
There are hundreds of thousands of such halls, which exist according to the measure of their minds, according to the movement of their thoughts, and according to the creation of their intentions.

Within that celestial realm there are such halls; near those halls are lotus ponds, equal in number to the halls themselves, each of which is adorned from section to section with the seven precious jewels in successive order.
Furthermore, in that place there are also birds with three types of meritorious conduct. What are these three?
First, those that move through water; second, those that move on land; [and third, those that move through the air].
Third are those that move through trees.
As for those that move through water, they are called ruddy sheldrakes (*cakravāka*), *nilapaṇa*, large gourds, geese, ducks, *majūra*, and so forth; these are the birds that move through water.

Regarding those that travel on land: from the summit of that mountain, wondrous sounds emerge—namely, the sound called "The Two Skills," the sound called "Joy," and the sound called "All Endurances. There are birds named "Sound of All Birds" and "Always Constantly Experiencing Bliss at All Times"; such birds as these are the land-traveling birds.
Among all celestial sounds, the voices of these birds are the most exquisite and beautiful.

As for those that dwell in trees, they are known as the *kūṭāhara*, the *jīvajīvaka*, the peacock, the parrot, the *viśvākṣa*, the *animiṣākṣa*, the *viśvacārī*, the *satyavādī*, and the *kāla-vid*—such birds as these are the tree-dwelling birds.
What exists only half among humans exists in its entirety among those gods.
Within those heavens, there are such immeasurable flocks of birds with various sounds; thus, these three kinds of birds that move through the heavens produce exquisite melodies.
Furthermore, atop the great mountain peak of Nityapramada-mālya, there is another bird that travels through the void, its body composed of the seven precious jewels.
When those devas engage in heedless conduct and are ruined by that heedlessness, the bird speaks a verse to rebuke them, saying:
"The devas ruined by heedlessness Are deceived by sensory objects; They do not know their own end, Nor do they perceive the arrival of Death."
Deluded by the mind of craving, the King of Death approaches.
Because they are stained by attachment to sensual pleasures, they do not know what is wholesome or unwholesome.
All sentient beings are ignorant, deceived by the desires of their sensory realms.
"Traversing various paths, performing various karmas, driven by various minds,
they wander through the five realms of existence. Thus,
seeing the heedless devas engaged in heedless conduct, that bird spoke this verse to rebuke them, just as parents discipline their children.

Although those devas hear this, they do not accept it nor take it to heart; they continue to experience pleasure, sporting, singing, and dancing, until finally all their wholesome karma is exhausted, at which point they later fall from that celestial realm.
Having fallen from the celestial realm, they descend into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm according to their own karmic actions.

If, due to residual karma, they are born among humans in a place of common karma, they will be born in a region of supreme wealth and happiness; possessing superior intentions and a mind constantly filled with joy, they will be born in a noble family within excellent lands such as the continent of Kāñcana or the wealthy and happy regions of Siṃhala.
This is due to the remaining karma.
"The Seventh Stage, the Ground of Vast Conduct, is hereby concluded.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates all the grounds and places of the Yāma Heaven.
He perceives through seeing, hearing,
and knowledge that within the Yāma Heaven there is another region called Accomplishment (Siddhi).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that region?

He sees: there is a person who has faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and maintains the precepts with a virtuous mind; they refrain from killing and stealing as previously described, and furthermore, they abandon sexual misconduct, no longer dwelling upon thoughts of the women with whom they previously engaged in sexual relations.

That son of good family, having thus maintained the precepts and perfumed his mind with wholesome intentions, at the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in a happy destination, in the realm of the Yāma devas, on the ground of the Accomplished Stage.
Having been born in that place, they receive retributions corresponding to their own karma.

That is to say, there are groves, lotus ponds, and waters; the ponds possess the exquisite songs of various birds and diverse adornments; they are surrounded by celestial maidens with wondrous bodies. Born in such places of celestial bliss, they enjoy the sounds of the five musical instruments and engage in various diversions. They experience pleasure through incomparable, supreme, and wonderful sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances.
It is like a reservoir with five water channels, all of which contain water; situated at the edge of the reservoir, the water flows into the pool without obstruction or hindrance.
In this very way, the five faculties are attached, and the body of the five cravings constantly follows the five locations, never knowing contentment.
It is, for example, like placing fire in all five locations, so that everything blazes up and spreads everywhere as the wind blows.
If one were to take dry wood and add it to those five fires again and again, those fires would thus blaze forth and increase in intensity.

In this way, in this manner, this craving of the sense-faculties increases like a fire: fanned by the wind of recollection, with the flames of improper observation and the dry fuel of sensory objects, the five sense-faculties blaze forth.
In this way, in this manner, when these fires of the five sense-faculties obtain the fuel of their objects, in this way, in this manner, the fires of the faculties blaze up.
Just as in the world, a moth that enters a fire is consumed by it, so too, if anyone enters the fire of the objects of craving, they are consumed by it.
All attachments are like flying insects, which neither perceive nor understand.
All the devas are like those flying insects; scorched by fire, they fall into the five sensory realms.

Together with hosts of celestial maidens, they wander through the groves, from lotus pond to lotus pond, from place to place of *sudhā* nectar, from drinking hall to drinking hall, and from place of beautiful sounds to place of beautiful sounds.
Having smelled the fragrance of the flowers in the Fragrant Flower Grove, he next proceeds to the Exquisite Fragrance Flower Grove.

Moving from one grove to another, he beholds groves that delight the eye, and proceeding further, he sees groves that delight the eye; in this manner, he enters entirely into the fires of various sensory objects.
"That mountain is as if alive; those devas see it as if they were seeing a living being.
Those hosts of devas see the mountain in this way, and as they look everywhere in this manner, it blazes forth like a fire that has obtained clarified butter."
Thus, when the newly born deva-son beholds that place adorned with the seven treasures and perceives its immeasurable varieties, joy arises in his heart.
He sees there, upon the mountain, hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.

In this way, the celestial maidens are exceedingly numerous and abundant; in all those places, there are many celestial maidens adorned with various ornaments who fill every spot. The hosts of devas are likewise, filling those places, singing, dancing, sporting, and mutually enjoying themselves, delighting in play amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments.

If it is an inferior deva, he may have ten thousand such variously adorned celestial maidens; likewise, in succession, there may be thirty-two thousand, and in further succession, forty thousand, fifty thousand, and so on, up to as many as one hundred thousand celestial maidens.
At that time, these hosts of celestial maidens were mutually enamored with one another, and no weariness arose in their hearts.
Each and every celestial maiden thought to herself:
"The celestial son loves me."
Thus those devas, craving sensual pleasures and never knowing contentment, blaze like a fire that has obtained clarified butter.
Those sons of gods who act with negligence enjoy happiness together with lovely celestial maidens in the groves, among the trees, in the lotus ponds, and within the river waters.
In this sequence, at a later time, he entered the Haṃsa Forest together with those celestial maidens.
Such a forest is already rare even within that heaven, let alone in any other place.
It is said that in that forest there is the adornment of swans; such swans dwell in that forest.
Those swans have silver wings, some have golden wings, and their feet are made of lotus-jewels.
Furthermore, there are other geese with lotus-blossom jewel beaks and bellies variegated with gold and jewels.
There are geese with golden bodies whose backs are of silver and *kācāndana*—a supreme jewel—and whose feet and beaks are likewise made of *kācāndana*.
Furthermore, there were other geese with backs of crystal, flanks of musaragalva, bellies of blue gemstone, and feet of gold.
There were also other geese whose bodies were composed of a mixture of the seven jewels, as well as geese of a single color, such as the color of silver.
Some have the color of crystal, some are pure gold, some have the color of musāragalva, and some have the color of blue gems.
Furthermore, there are other geese with the color of great blue gems.
Furthermore, there are other geese with the color of the supreme jewel kācāndana;
they experience such pleasure as their karma and mental states permit.
These geese, moreover, sport together with exquisite and beautiful female geese in various places, or engage in such play within the lotus ponds.

In this manner, they subsequently dwell among groves of lotuses, within mountains and rivers, or upon soft ground in terrestrial lotus groves where various flowers abound; there, together with those female geese, they thus experience pleasure.
At that time, the devas entered that Goose Grove, which abounded with various celestial maidens adorned with many ornaments; they sported and enjoyed themselves together with those celestial maidens.
Having seen such geese as these, the devas felt a sense of wonder and their joy increased even further; they turned their eyes to gaze all around at this most excellent grove.
Those celestial maidens, acting in accordance with the minds of the devas and perceiving that the mind of the deva-son was filled with joy, spoke to him, saying:
"O Deva, you should now know!
This is called Haṃsavatī Forest.

Thus, this Haṃsavatī Forest is exceedingly delightful; the various jewel trees possess wondrous and sublime radiance, and this forest is adorned with diverse jewels, fully endowed with all rare and marvelous qualities.

It is adorned with various kinds of lotus flowers and embellished by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable mountain peaks; that forest is further adorned with diverse blossoms, and its manifold varieties are such that even their names are difficult to recount.
A lotus pond adorned that grove, and within that grove dwelt a king of geese named Śubhakāla.

Just as the lord of gods, Mucilinda, dwells in this celestial realm, so too did that Śubhakāla, the king of all geese, dwell in this forest, sporting and enjoying pleasures in the lake known as Viśāla.

The Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda constantly comes to this king of geese and engages in various sports with him, enjoying pleasures that surpass those experienced when sporting with all the other hosts of devas.
"Playing with all the other gods is not at all like playing with the geese. The deva said,
"By what cause and condition does the King of the Yāma Heaven constantly play with that Goose-King, Kālaka?"
The goddess replied:
"Regarding such causes and conditions, none of the celestial hosts know them at all.
Since you, O Devaputra, have now thought this in your mind, let us go together now to that place where the Goose-King Supratiṣṭhita dwells; we shall enter that forest and proceed even unto the pond."
Having seen the entire grove, he saw that celestial king Mucilinda as well as the king of geese.
Having heard this from the host of celestial maidens, the newly born deva spoke thus:
"I shall now go together with you to where that king of geese and King Mucilinda dwell."
"At that time, this assembly of celestial maidens, together with the newly born deva, proceeded toward the king of geese in the pond within that forest.
Before they had even reached the king of geese, they saw various exquisite celestial groves, abounding in diverse flocks of birds and herds of beasts of many different colors and kinds."
The male birds dwell with their females and the male beasts with their mates; their various foods differ according to what they require.
They consume the roots and fruits of the heavens, and all possess bodies made of the seven treasures, adorned with supreme excellence.

In the midst of level ground within forest groves, in caves and hollows, or on level terrain; or by riverbanks and the shores of lotus ponds, or within the pools themselves, or amidst mountain valleys, they frolic in groups or utter various sounds.

Upon seeing this, the newly born deva felt joy and conceived a sense of wonder at such an unprecedented sight; his eyes twinkled as he was surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens who sang songs, and thus sporting, he entered that Goose Forest.

Furthermore, in another place, he saw a flock of peacocks in a grove; some of those peacocks had their necks raised, while others rubbed their necks against one another, thus sporting in various ways in that open space.
Furthermore, there were peacocks with bodies made of the seven precious gems, sporting in secluded places within the dark forest.
Some played together with the hearts of trees.
Having seen these various peacocks, which were as they should be for the gods, the newly born deva, together with the celestial maidens, desired to enter the Haṃsa Forest.

He saw many hundreds of thousands of billions of celestial maidens in the Haṃsa Grove, and he further saw other groves that were exceedingly delightful; namely, there was a river of the finest clear water, along both banks of which there were many devas and celestial maidens, and the river was filled with water possessing the seven qualities.

As for what are called rivers, they are named the River of the Water of Desire, the River of the Water of Tranquility, and the River of the Flow of Joy; they are named the River of Flowing Wine; there is a river named the Flow of Grape Wine; there is one named Following All Names, which is the Water of All Recollections; and there is one named the River of Delightful Bird-Songs.
In that great forest, there is such a river; when birds traveling on its banks have drunk the cool water, they speak this verse:
"Do not let past karma be exhausted, But repeatedly create new karma.
Because one's original karma is exhausted, One then falls away from the celestial realm."
If one creates new karma, it arises in three ways during three periods;
therefore, as long as one has not exhausted [past karma] while creating new, one will not fall into the evil realms.
If one fears future lives, one should not be greedily attached to the present.
Those who do not delight in the past will soon attain liberation.
If the mind does not waver and neither suffering nor pleasure passes through it,
that wise one, having cast off the body, shall find happiness in another realm.
If one experiences the pleasure of past karma, yet does not create new karma,
then once that past karma is exhausted, the fool will know it at the time of death.
If that foolish-minded deva experiences the pleasures of his sensory realm, [he will suffer when it ends].
If one exerts oneself in the virtues of the Buddha, one will not be driven by desire.
If there is one who attains such a state— that body which is subject to great calamities—
and is able to remain unattached to present pleasures, that person is truly wise.
If one is not enslaved by desire, fears transgression and does not crave attachments,
and further fears the evil realms, then such a person is truly brave and strong.
But if the mind craves pleasure and does not fear the evil realms, [it is not so].
This practice of delusion and craving leads to decline through that very craving.
Clinging to various sensual desires, one rejoices at having obtained them;
yet practicing desire yields no power, and in the end, one falls into the evil realms.
"Like lightning, like a mirage, like a city of the gandharvas—
thus are the evils of desire described, for they can delude everyone.
Thus did the bird of the Far Shore speak these verses upon seeing the newly born devas engaging in heedless conduct.
Because that newly born deva was newly attached to sensual desires, he did not accept what he heard despite having heard it.
At that time, having failed to accept the words of the bird, the deva entered the Goose Grove once more and experienced the pleasures of immeasurable sensory realms.
Because they have begun to conceive desire and because the Haṃsa Grove is so superior, they do not accept what they hear.
Thus, because the branches of the Haṃsa Grove are covered by a net, they know nothing at all—neither the real nor the unreal.
"In that Haṃsa forest, he beheld a grove of jewel-trees; from afar, he saw a supreme radiance, and moreover, hundreds of thousands of nets of light overspread that place."
Even the gods themselves cannot gaze upon it, let alone the gods of the lower realms—the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven—how could they possibly look upon it?
Such is the radiance of that forest of celestial jewels; if the gods so desire, these precious gems form palatial halls for them as they travel through the midst of space.
Within the jewel there is a hollow, and a deva sits therein, flying through the void and sporting in pleasure.
By virtue of his wholesome karma, the jewel serves as a palace as he travels through space.
Within this jewel, there are celestial gardens, lotus ponds, and various groves; in every region there are many mountain peaks, abounding with the sounds of birds.
Thus, those devas, dwelling in the midst of the void, enjoy themselves with vocal music; all the merits of the six desires are fully accomplished as they sport and experience pleasure.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 51. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 52.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Thirty-One: Yāma Heaven, Section Seventeen.

Furthermore, if those devas have the thought in their minds that they wish to descend from the void, at the very moment of that mental thought, they descend from the sky together with the hosts of devas; having descended, they return to dwell in their own respective abodes.
Thus the jewel returned to its original state and emitted a great radiance.
After those celestial maidens had spoken thus to the newly born deva,
at that time, the newly born son of the gods— bound by the snare of desire and longing for sensory realms— proceeded toward the Jewel Forest.
Not far away, he saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various lights—yellow, red, and white—filling the Pearl Forest; not far from that Jewel Pearl Forest was a forest of swans.
At that time, having heard this from the celestial maidens, the newly born deva turned toward the Jewel-Cluster Grove and proceeded there together with them.
Having arrived there, he saw that the radiance of the jewels was immeasurable; at that moment, the newly born deva thought to himself:
"Just as those other devas enter the jewel-grove and travel through the air, seeing all the celestial realms, I too shall likewise enter the jewel-grove and proceed in this manner."
At the very moment of that thought, according to his mental intention, the jewel became a palace suspended in mid-air.
Having seen it from the sky as soon as he was born there, he entered the jeweled palace together with the host of celestial maidens.
According to their own virtuous karma, they see within that hall various delightful things.
Inside those precious jewels are flowing rivers, lotus ponds, groves, and mountain peaks that fill the interior of the hall; these are seen with the eyes and bring joy to the mind.
Furthermore, in various places he saw birds whose songs were lovely.
In those areas there were flowers of diverse colors, shapes, forms, and fragrances.

He also saw various birds and beasts in other locations; there were rivers with level banks and rivers with steep banks, all of which were delightful. Along the banks of those rivers, in yet other places, he saw many devas and apsaras singing, dancing, laughing joyfully, and sporting in pleasure.

In those various groves and parks of that place, all were exactly as previously described; when the deva-son first saw them, he sported and enjoyed pleasures with the host of celestial maidens, acting with heedlessness and never knowing satiety in his craving.
Moving again to another place, he next arrives at the place where *sudhā* food is served for the purpose of eating.
He receives food that corresponds to his own virtuous karma.

Having eaten that food, he is scorched by the fires of sensory objects and proceeds toward the River of Wine. There, together with the celestial maidens, he is swept away by the waves of passion and heads toward the drinking grounds of that river.
Having arrived there, they drink wine from vessels made of jewels.

Once they have drunk the wine, their hearts of joy increase even further; burned by the fire of attachment to sensory objects and deluded by the five sense realms, they again engage in singing, dancing, and sporting together with the celestial maidens.
"Having thus experienced celestial pleasures in that place, they proceed toward the lotus grove by the pond.
Desiring to sport within that pool and enjoy various sensual delights together with the hosts of celestial maidens, they head toward that lotus pond grove."

Having arrived, they further experience the pleasures of sensory objects, sporting in the water with various celestial maidens; this supreme pleasure is beyond analogy, and they experience such bliss.

Furthermore, desiring to arouse longing for sensual pleasures, wishing to hear sounds, and greedily attached to sensory objects, his mind yearned to hear the songs and chants of the hosts of celestial maidens amidst the five kinds of musical sounds.
Having heard the sounds of the five kinds of music, their hearts experience an ineffable joy that no other phenomenon can serve as a metaphor for.
Experiencing such various and supreme pleasures derived from the five objects of desire, they know no satiety.
Because there is craving, one is never satisfied by that craving; it is like fire obtaining fuel, for which there is no time of satiety.
Thus, as for desire, desire can never be satisfied; constantly through immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions, one experiences various pleasures.
Having enjoyed themselves for a long time, they again sat upon a jeweled pavilion within the Haṃsa-vana grove.
Together with the celestial maidens, they descended from that jeweled pavilion and once more beheld unprecedented wonders within the Haṃsa-vana.

Having seen that place in such and such a way, the mind gives rise to joy and pleasure in such and such a manner; yet, having seen various things in this way, one still finds no satisfaction with the sensory objects.
In such places as flowing streams, lotus ponds, and groves, when gods and goddesses behold the sounds of immeasurable varieties of the five kinds of music, they thus engage in play.
Furthermore, the king of geese dwells in a vast and spacious place, where gods together with celestial maidens go toward that abode of the goose.

Thus, one sees various gods in that place, enjoying celestial pleasures through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of songs, dances, and games; there is nothing else that can serve as a metaphor for it.
In comparison to the world, that day is like the light of a firefly; apart from its radiance, there is no other analogy.
In that place, such is the bliss experienced in a realm beyond analogy; for those gods who experience such bliss, no metaphor can be found.

Among all the finest flavors in the human world—namely honey, medicinal wines, sugarcane, meat, and so forth—these are the foremost in Jambudvīpa; yet when all these are combined with red *sudhā*, they become no different from the taste of extreme bitterness or turmeric.
The supreme flavors among humans are thus inferior and diminished compared to the flavors of those heavens.
While such flavors may serve as a slight analogy for their superiority, the flavors within the heavens are beyond all comparison.

The fragrance of those devas is likewise beyond comparison; even if one were to combine all the finest fragrances found in the human world—such as sandalwood incense, aloeswood incense, powdered incense, and unguents; the *campaka* flower, the *nikuścindika*, and the *sumana* flower; and likewise the *gandhapālīśaka*, the *utpala*, the *kumuda*, the *nicula*, and so forth—even the union of all these flowers would still not equal the flowers found among the devas.
Among those heavenly flowers, even the *rava* blossoms do not equal one-sixteenth part of its splendor; likewise, the fragrance of that heaven is beyond all analogy.
Furthermore, the tactile sensations in that celestial realm are likewise beyond analogy.

Even if one were to combine all the most excellent and refined tactile sensations found throughout every land in the human world—such as *kauśeya* silk, *uṇṇa* wool, or *karpāsa* cotton—and even if all such various human tactile sensations were united, they would still be far inferior to the subtlest tactile sensation in that celestial realm. For instance, gold is the hardest of substances, yet it is still surpassed by the superior tactile sensations found among humans.
Among all tactile sensations in the world, they do not equal even one-sixteenth part [of those in the heavens]; thus, the various tactile sensations found in that heaven are beyond all analogy.
Furthermore, the sounds in that heaven are likewise beyond all analogy.

Regarding the foremost sounds in the human world—namely those of the lute, the zither, the flute, the harp, the cymbals, the drums, and songs—even when all such sounds are combined, they still do not equal the sound of the ornaments in that celestial realm.
The sound of the ornaments in that celestial realm does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it; thus, all the sounds within that heaven are beyond analogy.
Such a metaphor can only serve as an analogy for the gods of the Four Great Kings; it is not an analogy for the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, nor is it an analogy for the Yāma heaven.
The sensual pleasures among humans can only serve as a comparison for the sensual pleasures experienced by the gods of the Four Great Kings.
The sensual pleasures experienced by the gods of the Four Great Kings can only serve as a comparison for the sensual pleasures experienced by the gods of the Thirty-three.
The sensual pleasures experienced by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three can only serve as a comparison for the sensual pleasures experienced in the Yāma Heaven.

Following this sequence, because the power of their karma is superior, the six heavens of the desire realm become progressively more excellent; the same applies to the sensory domains of these gods, such that their celestial pleasures become increasingly superior.
The pleasures of the mental plane are of immeasurable kinds, all of which are combined therein.
"Thus, O Devaputra, sporting and enjoying pleasure in that Swan Grove, he gradually advances and eventually draws near to the king of swans."
He saw that king of geese sporting in various ways within a vast pond, dwelling together with his female companion in a forest of lotuses, surrounded by hosts of celestial beings.

There was a lotus flower, one yojana in size, a lotus made of the seven precious gems with filaments of diamond; its touch was exceedingly soft, and its fragrance, color, and other qualities were beyond comparison. Immeasurable light radiated from the flower, which possessed a hundred thousand petals.
That great king of geese dwells within such lotuses as these.
On festival days— on those festival days—
the Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda, together with the hosts of devas, has the goose preach the Dharma to them.
That king of geese, by the power of his vows, was reborn among the Yāma devas.
Having been born in the Yāma heaven through such beneficial merit, he preached the Dharma in this manner to the Yāma devas, causing them to abandon negligence.
"At that time, the newly born deva-son proceeded step by step toward the vast pond.
Upon seeing this newly born deva-son, the Goose-King Kāla spoke these verses for him:
'Because of the existence of craving and thirst, One knows no satisfaction in sensual desires.'"
Driven by the mind, the senses move, yet one does not realize that time has already passed.
That which is cherished as sensual pleasure is encompassed by the law of impermanence;
because one delights in beholding women, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Deluded by craving, they are bound to birth and death;
such fools do not realize that time has already passed.
Because their minds are dragged away by desire, they sink into the darkness of ignorance.
Those bound by hatred do not realize that time has passed;
bound in hell, they do not give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Deluded by the poison of heedlessness, they do not realize that time has passed.
Lacking self-control and shame, relying on one’s lineage to give rise to arrogance,
the mind is greedy and knows no contentment, unaware that time has already passed.
Bound by the snares of the five cords and deluded by the six dharmas,
Constantly deluded throughout the three periods of time, one does not realize that the time has already passed.
Not knowing the path to the evil realms, one is destroyed by the noose of evil;
if one possesses such a mind, one does not realize that the time has already passed.
At first, the attainment of desire is pleasant, but later it brings no benefit;
because the mind is attached to desire, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Unaware of the suffering of previous lives, one delights in and clings to celestial pleasures.
Unaware of the suffering of parting from what is loved, One does not realize that time has already passed.
Bound by the net of karma, like a fish in a net,
Thus one loses the path of virtue, Failing to realize that time has already passed.
The foolish have no mindfulness; they do not know of the existence of faults and calamities.
Immersed in the darkness of delusion, they do not realize that time has already passed.
Bound by the snare of sentient beings' karma, they are alone and without a companion.
Deluded by beholding celestial maidens, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Mounted upon the horses of the sense-faculties, one loses the way to the virtuous path;
craving the flavors of the three realms, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Not knowing what is precept and what is not precept, or being prone to excessive anger,
one loses both the mind and the Way, unaware that time has already passed.
Not knowing what is beneficial or not, one is deluded regarding what should and should not be done.
Like a child at play, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Like the swift flow of a river, because one constantly indulges in sensual pleasures within gardens,
groves, and ponds, one does not realize that time has already passed.
Within the mountain peak hall, as if in a grove of lotuses,
because one constantly experiences sensual pleasures, one does not realize that time has passed.
Amidst karma and its retribution, there has never been any understanding or insight.
Clinging only to the taste of food, they do not realize that time has already passed.
Blown by the winds of karma, they constantly remain within these three realms, revolving like a wheel;
because of their delusion, they do not perceive this.
Constantly dwelling in evil places, upon high beams and ropes—
such are the foolish who do not diligently abandon their transgressions.
If one can abandon desire, that is the foremost diligence.
Free from all hope, one is then without afflictions.
Having attained the Buddha-dharma throughout the beginning, middle, and end,
because of practicing in tranquility, such a person is one who is free from afflictions.
If one obtains sensual pleasures, those pleasures will inevitably perish;
because of desire, one reaps the fruit of suffering—knowing this, one realizes that desire is not the supreme Dharma.
Therefore, the wise do not delight their hearts in desire.
"He shall then be able to sever the causes and conditions of the suffering of birth and death.
Thus did the Great Goose King speak these verses for the sake of the newly born devas, disparaging the nature of desire as he spoke.
That newly born deva gradually advanced, drawing near to the king of geese.

Although that newly born deva had heard the sublime Dharma, his mind did not accept it; because he was deluded by sensory objects, he drew closer to the king of geese without grasping the Dharma, remaining attached to those objects and experiencing various sensual pleasures.
He saw the King of Geese sporting in the water, entering the lotus grove, plucking lotuses, and tossing them about in play with the host of celestial maidens.
The Goose King Kāla addressed him, saying:
"You refused to accept these words of peace; what will you obtain for yourself in the future?"
“At that time, the newly born deva residing in the bird realm again heard a sublime and wondrous sound from afar, surpassing the sounds of the heavens.

Having heard that sound, his heart gave rise to love and delight; it was a sound that pervaded with various lovely tones such as those of the lute, the harp, the *kinnara* drum, the flute, and so forth.”
At that time, those devas were sporting in various ways by the edge of the vast pool; having heard the sound, they all turned their faces toward it to listen.

Then, from afar, they saw hundreds of thousands of halls surrounding them on all sides, where the sounds of celestial songs were exceedingly lovely, such that those who heard them were moved to desire.

Exquisite and magnificent, like stars surrounding the moon, they thus encircle the pavilions in procession, or move in circles with their bodily radiance; all the hosts of devas behold them with joyous hearts, while hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens sing with melodic voices.

The Lord of the Yāma Heaven sat upon a lotus pedestal made of the seven precious gems with a hundred thousand petals, surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens; for the sake of hearing the Dharma, he proceeded toward the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Kālika, the king of geese.

At that time, the Goose King, the Bodhisattva Kāla, having seen him, quickly went out to meet him, accompanied by other female geese and male geese whose bodies were adorned with countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite, intermingled seven-jeweled ornaments. Simultaneously, they all flew through the air toward the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, while other geese sang songs in melodic tones.
Thus these two kings—one a king of geese and the other a king of devas—mutually respected one another and exchanged elegant words as they greeted each other.
Because of his original vow, the goose king, Supraśānta, was born in the Yāma heaven in order to eliminate the heedlessness of the Yāma devas.
King Kṣemadatta said: "Your Majesty, it has been a long time since you have come here to this Great Pond. From another deva, I heard these words:

'The Night-Wandering King of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, practices heedfulness and, together with the hosts of devas, visits the place on that mountain where trees abound to behold the six Buddha-stūpas—worshipping and making offerings to them—and through his power of transformation, he writes out scriptures; at those stūpas, he reads and recites those scriptures, showing them to the hosts of devas.'"
"For this reason, I have now come to welcome you.

While you preach the Dharma there, I shall also remain here by the side of this vast pond, preaching the Dharma as is appropriate for the gods who sport therein—namely, the ultimate truth of tranquility and peace, which can eliminate heedlessness and bring about ultimate benefit."
"For this reason, I have now come thus to welcome the Heavenly King.
Out of love for the Dharma and free from pride, I have come out of deep respect.
At that time, having heard these words, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, spoke as follows:

"The King of Geese, for the sake of universally benefiting all the gods of the Yāma Heaven and for the benefit of all the gods of the Yāma Heaven, has been here; now let us return together to the site of the Great Pond."

Having spoken these words, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, surrounded by an immeasurable host of devas and celestial maidens, and the Goose-King Kāla, surrounded by an immeasurable hundred-thousandfold host of geese—these two kings, each together with their retinues, harmoniously joined one another in the midst of various sounds in the sky. Their minds were entirely stainless like precious jewels; though in a realm of heedlessness, they practiced non-heedlessness. Possessing great majesty and virtue, they proceeded together toward the Vast Pond.

Having arrived at the vast pond, all the celestial hosts there, upon seeing the Heavenly King, momentarily ceased their heedlessness; they made no sounds, did not amuse themselves with one another, and no longer engaged in various sports within the water, but gave rise to a heart of reverent devotion.
Knowing that the minds of those celestial hosts were well-disciplined and compliant, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed the Goose King, saying:
"O Goose King of Auspicious Time!
This is the most excellent moment; you may now preach the Dharma."
"When the celestial hosts see me, their minds will all be freed from pride; likewise, the entire assembly of celestial maidens will be free of pride, and I may then preach the Dharma to them.

At that time, the Goose King recalled his past lives, remembering that in a former age there was a Buddha named Kakudha, from whom he had heard various Dharma gates. Among all the teachings he had heard, he chose to expound only a single Dharma for the sake of the celestial hosts.
He spoke to the Heavenly King, saying:
"May the Heavenly King listen well; I shall now explain for you.
There are five kinds of dharmas which constitute the fundamental fault for those among gods or humans who practice with negligence."
What are these five? They are as follows:
the mind of one who is heedless becomes distracted; his thoughts dwell on improper things, and his speech proclaims improper words.
Whatever he says is untrue and meaningless, contradictory from beginning to end, unstable and wavering, and thus others do not accept it.
Why is this? Because their minds are agitated by negligence.
They do not know for what purpose it was spoken or for whom it was spoken; they then disparage it and do not accept it.
Because of this, one comes to disparage oneself in all things; this is the fault of negligence.
Due to the fault of negligence, one falls into the evil destinies, being reborn in accordance with the three lower realms as appropriate.
This is the first fault.
"Furthermore, that negligence has a second fault. What is the second?
This refers to not knowing what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
because of a heedless mind, one does not know what is to be performed, nor does one know what is not to be performed.
They do not know what karma is, nor do they know what its fruit is; because they do not know karma, they do not know its fruit.
Those deluded ones, being confused about karma and its fruit, fall into evil destinies after the dissolution of the body and the end of life, being born in hell.
Because of negligence, one incurs such faults; this is the second fault.
"Furthermore, that negligence has a third fault. What is the third?

Whether they be humans or devas, because of their heedlessness, they associate with evil friends; they do not revere the Triple Gem, they do not seek wisdom, and they do not honor their elders and superiors;
regarding faults and virtues, they neither perceive nor understand them;
and toward the suffering of birth and death, they do not give rise to weary detachment.
Not knowing miscellaneous karmas— that is, various kinds of karma—
and being unable to exert diligent effort, they constantly delight in sleep and cannot maintain the precepts.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into evil realms and are born within the hells.
Because of negligence, one incurs such faults; this is the third fault.
Furthermore, that negligence has a fourth fault. What is the fourth?

That is to say, whether among the gods or among humans, at the very moment of birth, the formations of life do not remain still; they arise and perish instantly, and so too does one's wholesome karma.
Having been born, it is immediately exhausted; when the King of Death is about to arrive, with whom can one indulge in negligence?
They will certainly be separated.
There are four things that inevitably lead to separation;
what are these four? First, youth.
Second is peace and security;
third is longevity;
fourth is fulfillment.
These four things are inevitably separated; the wise constantly contemplate these four, whereas those who are heedless cannot understand them.
Whether gods or humans, those who act with heedlessness know none of this, and because they do not know it, they fall into the evil realms.
Because of negligence, one incurs such faults; this is the fourth fault.
"Furthermore, that negligence has a fifth fault. What is the fifth?
This means that one places trust in a first place that is utterly untrustworthy.
Among all things most untrustworthy, there is none more so than women; yet the foolish place their trust in women.
Although that fool places his trust in women, those women place no trust in him; until the end of their lives, they do not depart from deception.
All women are full of flattery and guile, full of illusion and hypocrisy, defiled and destructive; their minds are full of pride, and their hearts are turbid due to the breaking of precepts.
All women are never free from such faults; as heat is inseparable from fire, all women are inseparable from these qualities.
If a foolish person places their trust in such a woman, it is merely words, for there is not a single truth in them.
Because of craving and greed, one is led by desire and therefore draws near to it.
Thus, in brief, these five kinds of faults of heedlessness have been explained; since these five faults do not exist apart from heedlessness, gods and humans should abandon heedlessness.

This practice of negligence obstructs the gateway to Nirvana; those who act with negligence, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into the evil realms, being born in hell, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
Because of negligence, one incurs such faults; this is the fifth fault.
"Therefore, the wise person should abandon negligence. If one relinquishes negligence, there are five merits."
What are these five? They are: practicing correctly;

having right faith in one's mind; performing what ought to be done and refraining from what ought not to be done; constantly applying the mind; and always acting for the benefit of others at all times.
Abandoning heedlessness is no different from avoiding poison; one thus comes to know the three periods of time well.
This is the foremost merit of heedfulness; it is through heedfulness that this merit is attained.
"Furthermore, there is the second merit of non-negligence.
What is the second? It is the knowledge of what is light and what is heavy."
Associate with virtuous friends and constantly practice wholesome deeds;
distance yourself from evil associates and refrain from committing unwholesome deeds, for such unwholesome deeds are despised and condemned by the virtuous.
If one sees an evil person, one abandons them entirely; if one sees a person of merit, one draws near to them.
By practicing such wholesome mental conduct in this way, one does not enter the evil realms.
This is the second merit of heedfulness; because of being heedful, one attains this merit.
"Furthermore, there is the third merit of heedfulness. What is the third?
This is what is called being cautious:
even at the cost of one's life, one does not submit to women nor place trust in their words.
At all times, one’s conduct must be visible to others; for all women possess two kinds of fetters that bind the world.
One sees only their physical form and does not believe their words; thus do the wise observe women according to reality.
Having observed them correctly and according to reality in this way, even upon seeing dancing, singing, joyful laughter, play, and ornaments, the mind does not become attached.
All negligence is caused by women; all women constitute half of negligence.
If one can distance oneself from the negligence associated with women, one will be able to cross the great ocean of birth and death.
In the world of humans, everyone says:
"One who is heedful is called a good person.
This is the third merit of heedfulness; it is through heedfulness that one attains this merit.
"Furthermore, there is the fourth merit of non-negligence. What is the fourth?

It is that one who is conscientious and non-negligent does not place faith in wealth, pleasure, desires, and the like; observing and knowing them to be impermanent, they understand it thus: [text continues]"
"This desire is impermanent, shifting and unstable; it cannot be relied upon, for it will soon be destroyed and soon perish.
Thus, because one does not place trust in matters of security, one practices non-negligence.

All that is secure is destroyed by illness; thus, one should not give rise to confidence in youth. All that is young is destroyed by old age; therefore, one should not give rise to arrogance regarding youth.
In this way, one should neither place trust in life, nor give rise to arrogance, nor commit evil deeds.
Why is this? Because one will inevitably be plundered by the King of Death.
Therefore, one does not place faith in any conditioned phenomena of birth and death; because of this lack of faith, one practices without negligence.
This is the fourth merit of non-negligence, which is obtained through the practice of non-negligence.
"Furthermore, this is the fifth merit of non-negligence. What is the fifth?

It is that by constantly associating with noble ones and delighting in wisdom, one takes refuge in the Triple Gem, hears the Dharma, and contemplates its meaning; thus, at the time of death, one will not give rise to fear."
Because he knows the signs of death and knows the signs of decline, he does not give rise to fear.

The Devaputra Śrutārtha knows the signs of decline; when a person is about to die, he knows the signs of death. Knowing thus, he knows of birth in the evil realms and knows of birth in the good realms, and he forms this knowledge:
"I am born in a good realm."
“I shall be born in the evil realms.

If, at the time of death, the signs of the evil realms appear, one can then employ skillful means to purify the mind; because the mind is purified, the signs of the evil realms vanish and the signs of the good realms manifest.
This foremost and most excellent fruit of heedfulness is extremely difficult to attain; among all kinsmen and friends, it is likewise the most supreme.
This is the fifth merit of heedfulness: because of being heedful, one attains this merit.
At that time, the Goose King Kāla there recited these verses spoken by the Tathāgata Kakutstha: "The Tathāgata,
who has already transcended desire, Praises heedfulness and censures heedless conduct,
Which leads to the realms of birth and death."
Heedfulness leads to liberation; through heedlessness one suffers.
This bond of heedlessness the fool cannot sever.
The virtuous person who is heedful is born among the gods.
Because of heedlessness among the gods, the mind regrets at the time of falling away.
All those who are heedless cannot escape birth and death;
heedlessness is the foremost snare, capable of binding one and causing one to wander in saṃsāra.
Doing what should not be done and failing to do what should be done—
those who are entirely heedless act in a manner that is completely inverted.
They do not even practice the mundane dharmas, let alone the supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, the wise do not praise heedless conduct.
For this reason, one should not engage in heedless behavior;
such heedless conduct is the first messenger of the evil realms.
"If there are those who can abandon and leave behind the storehouse of suffering and affliction,
such courageous and steadfast ones are able to cross the great ocean of existence.
Thus did the Goose King Supratiṣṭhita explain the ancient laws of the past for the sake of the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, and the assembly of devas, thereby benefiting the gods and humans.
Furthermore, that king of geese, manifesting as the celestial lord Mucilinda, again preached the Dharma, speaking these words:
"There are five kinds of dharmas that serve as antidotes to the heedless conduct of śramaṇas."
What are these five? They are as follows: all those who act with negligence undergo suffering and affliction.
Such persons, according to whatever form of negligence they indulge in, will bring about suffering and affliction.
Having abandoned that negligence and recognized its faults, one cultivates meritorious qualities; because of having relinquished that [negligence], there is nothing that does not bring benefit.
One does not undergo suffering and affliction, unwholesome and evil karma does not increase, and one practices the right conduct.
This is the first remedial method for a śramaṇa, the remedy for heedlessness.
Furthermore, the second remedial method for a śramaṇa is the remedy for heedlessness.
What is the second? It is the vision of the true meaning.
One who possesses true vision is entirely resolute in all mental states and perceives things as they truly are.
Because one sees things as they truly are, one does not engage in negligence, for one sees the faults of negligence as they truly are.
This is the second antidote to negligence.
"Furthermore, the third antidote of the śramaṇa is the antidote to negligence."
What is the third?
It is to associate with those who are heedful, receiving and upholding the precepts;
acting exactly as they act and performing exactly as they perform.
One should always dwell together with those who uphold the precepts and abandon and stay far from those who violate them.
Consequently, all forms of negligence will be absent.
This is the third remedy for negligence.
"Furthermore, the fourth remedy of the śramaṇa is the remedy for heedlessness. What is the fourth?
It is that, for the sake of seeking wisdom, one constantly associates with the wise and always delights in the wise, thereby abandoning heedlessness."

Associating with those who are heedful and thus being cautious and heedful oneself brings happiness near and suffering far; such a son of good family constantly practices this heedfulness in this way.
This is the fourth antidote to negligence.
"Furthermore, monks, there is a fifth antidote that counteracts negligence. What is the fifth?

That is to say, if there is a king or a royal minister who apprehends one who is heedless, they may inflict punishment upon them, or even deprive them of life; or at times they may confiscate all their wealth, or administer a flogging, or cut off their hands.
Having seen these various and diverse punishments for those who are negligent, their hearts give rise to fear.
Because of this fear, they abandon negligence and practice non-negligence.
In this way, one abandons negligence through its antidote, because one gives rise to fear upon seeing others receive such punishments.
Following the practice of the Dharma, one fears that practicing negligence will lead to falling into hell; therefore, one does not commit any evil deeds.
"This is the fifth antidote to negligence.
Such negligence brings no security, whether for devas or for humans.
Having heard this discourse, that great multitude of devas abandoned their negligence.

Having heard the sutra spoken by the Goose King, Mūśalinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; he then ascended into the void together with the host of devas and departed just as he had originally come.
As for the other devas, some continue to experience pleasure in the vast ponds, while others seek pleasure in the groves.
Having entered the gardens and groves, they enjoy various pleasures in this manner until their wholesome karma is exhausted.
When their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall away from that place.
Having fallen away from that place, according to their own karmic conduct, they may fall into hell, or fall among the hungry ghosts, or fall into the animal realm.

If, through other karma, one is born among humans, one will be born in a place of supreme wealth and happiness; being clever and of sharp faculties, possessing extensive knowledge and vision, and endowed with the life-force of wisdom—one is greatly wealthy because of this wisdom and is beloved by kings.
"Due to residual karma.
[The "Stage of Accomplishment" concludes.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates all the abodes belonging to the Yāma Heaven.
He perceives through seeing, hearing, and knowledge:
there is another region named Ābhāparivāra (Encircled by Light).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
He knows this through seeing, hearing, or learning, or he sees it with the divine eye:

if a son of good family has previously heard the meaning of the Dharma, received and maintained the precepts, possesses right view without deviation, does not harass or disturb others, and is upright in mind; if he refrains from killing and stealing as previously described, further abandons sexual misconduct out of fear of improper conduct, and does not even gaze upon painted images of women; and if he constantly performs wholesome deeds and skillfully cultivates a pure livelihood.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the gods, in the region called *Prabhāsa-maṇḍala*.

Having been born there, by the power of their wholesome karma, they experience various pleasures of the five objects of desire within the sublime realm of the gods; impelled by their six sense faculties, they take delight in beholding the gardens and groves.
In such and such a manner they perceive various phenomena, and in such and such a manner their six sense faculties become predominant.
Because these faculties are predominant, they are able to command that the ground be level and even, supremely soft, interspersed with the seven treasures, and exceedingly delightful.

If there are trees growing upon that ground, they are extremely soft and smooth to the touch; they bear golden fruits with silver leaves, fully endowed with superior textures, fragrances, and flavors.
Such celestial fruits emit fragrance at will and produce flavor at will.

“If the devas there have the thought that they wish for wine to emerge from those fruits according to their desire, then divine wine—endowed with touch, fragrance, color, and flavor—flows forth from the fruits and remains beneath the trees.”
Then those gods, together with the hosts of celestial maidens, took up jeweled vessels and drank from them.
Such celestial wine has inferior, middling, and superior qualities in terms of fragrance, flavor, texture, and so forth.
Because karma is immeasurable, just as its causes are, so too does one obtain wine in inferior, middling, or superior degrees.

Furthermore, other devas experience immeasurable varieties of the five sensual pleasures; consumed by heedlessness, they delight in seeing gardens, singing, dancing, and joyful laughter. They wander together, playing everywhere, heading toward those groves.
In this way, as they travel along their respective paths, they behold various kinds of subtle and exquisite forms.
As for the flavors they obtain, there are immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions among these various superior flavors.
The fragrances they smell are of immeasurable kinds and immeasurable varieties, consisting of various sublime scents that correspond with the mind.
As for the touches they recollect, there are immeasurable kinds and immeasurable varieties of celestial, exquisite touches associated with the experience of bliss.

The celestial beings hear the wondrous sounds of the gods, which consist of immeasurable varieties and correspond to immeasurable distinctions of mental delight; having heard them, they rejoice, due to the preeminent and virtuous karma of their supreme observance of the precepts.

Fully endowed with all the qualities of the five desires, they experience pleasurable conduct; because those devas thus experience such pleasurable conduct, they pass a long time enjoying them, never knowing satiety.
Looking further yet, he saw the forest named Mind-Delight (*Cittaratāvana*), adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewel trees.
That Forest of Mind-Delight was so lovely that its branches, leaves, roots, and trunks were each distinct from one another.
One grove is of silver, as white as snow, named the Silver Tree Grove; its radiance is like the light of the moon in Jambudvīpa.
Each individual tree is majestic and exquisite; if the devas behold them, their hearts experience joy.
Furthermore, one side is red like *kāñcanana*, an incomparable crimson with a red radiance; its leaves are also red.
Such leaves and other elements combine to form a forest, and this red forest is exceedingly lovely.
Because that forest is red, it illuminates the entirety of space, making everything red.
Furthermore, one side is named the Forest of Constant Joy (*Nitya-sukha-vana*); on that side of the forest there is a blue grove, which is entirely blue with a blue radiance and light.
One side of that grove was thus radiant, majestic, and exquisite, no different from the sky of Jambudvīpa; this was the light of vaiḍūrya jewels.
Thus, that place is named the Forest of Constant Joy (*nitya-sukha-vana*).

Furthermore, one side consists of a crystal forest (*sphaṭika-vana*), whose roots, stems, branches, and leaves are pure and luminous, and which is fully endowed with countless flowing waters, rivers, and ponds.
Furthermore, adjacent to that great forest is another section, a grove of blue-jewel trees, whose roots, trunks, branches, and leaves emit a blue radiance.
Amidst the tree branches dwell various kinds of birds that utter diverse songs, and it is further adorned with many ponds of exquisite lotuses.
The gardens and groves of those devas possess such radiance, being upright, majestic, and sublime.
At that time, all the devas within the circle of light there, desiring to sport and experience various pleasures, proceed toward the Forest of Mental Delight (Cittaratavana).
In that grove, they sport and enjoy themselves, bound by their attachment to the forest; experiencing celestial pleasures through the qualities of the five desires, they know no satiety.
Furthermore, sporting and enjoying various delights, they enter the Forest of Mental Joy (*cittasukha-vana*).
Within that forest, there are various colors, various flavors, and various fragrances; it is fully endowed with flowers and fruits, and many exquisite bees adorn the grove, pervading every place.

Furthermore, there are many flocks of lovely birds, various exquisite lotus ponds of great beauty, and various delightful arbors formed by tree branches; flowers are strewn across the ground, which is soft to the touch and exceedingly pleasant.
There are many hundreds of thousands of immeasurable hosts of devas; therefore, that place is so exquisitely adorned.
There are tree-branch dwellings, many lotuses, flowing streams, ponds, and rivers, as well as various mountain valleys filled with many trees.
With songs, dances, joyful laughter, and various playful sounds from their ornaments that resonate like the melody of song;
with gentle breezes stirring the forests and flowering branches swaying and drooping—
therefore, that forest is so exquisitely adorned.
At that time, those devas entered that forest, becoming even more exceedingly joyful; they further engaged in singing, dancing, sporting, and laughing, mutually enjoying pleasure together.
At all times their minds delighted in sensory objects, and their hearts were constantly preoccupied with heedlessness.
“Those hosts of devas enjoy such pleasures for a long time, and then they enter again the Mandārava Forest of the Seven Jewels.
That forest is lovely and most excellent among forests, like a king of mountains.”
All its radiance surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns, and it encircles the lotus pond as an adornment.
In the Mandārava forest there is a peacock king named Variegated; his plumage is a mottled blend of various seven-jeweled colors, and the sounds he produces resound throughout that forest.
In truth, it is because of his power of aspiration that this bodhisattva was born among those devas in order to remove their negligence.

Seeing that those devas were being consumed by the fires of the five sensory realms, he remained within the branches of a tree, courageous and fearless, and giving rise to a heart of compassion, he addressed those devas, saying:
"These devas engage in much negligent conduct and do not consider their future downfall."
This desire for pleasure ends; it is impermanent and does not abide.
All celestial pleasures pass away with great speed, like a mountain river whose swift current flows by unnoticed.
"The mind is constantly attached to pleasure because of its evil craving.
At that time, the King of Peacocks of Variegated Colors spoke these verses:
"What is done is like a dream; The dwelling place is like a mirage."
The city is like that of the gandharvas; thus do the gods cling to desire.
Born of craving, the gods will ultimately be destroyed;
thinking that pleasure can never be exhausted, the gods thus cling to desire.
Pleasures do not last long and are lost, passing away as swiftly as a flowing river;
deceived by the city of desire, the gods are thus attached to sensual pleasures.
Like water stirred by the wind, they see the moon reflected within that water.
Like a whirling circle of fire, so do the gods cling to desire;
like the flickering of lightning, like the shimmering mirage of a deer,
like the insubstantiality of water bubbles, so do the gods cling to desire.
Like the trembling leaves of a plantain tree, and also like the ears of an elephant—these are what unwholesome people love; thus do the gods cling to desire.
It is like the fruit of the *kimpāka*, or like one who has swallowed an iron hook.
Like an illusion, impermanence is such that the gods thus cling to desire.
All is empty, deceptive, and devoid of substance; it does not abide for even a moment.
Its flavor at first is sweet; the gods thus cling to desire.
Only the single flavor of heedlessness is the cause of bondage;
it swiftly causes one to enter the evil realms—such is the attachment to desire among the gods.
They love what is loathsome, calling it good; it is ever fearful and ever obstructive.
"Like poison, like a sword, and so forth—thus do the gods become attached to desire.
Thus did the peacock named Citrarāja, the King of Variegated Colors, who delights in that forest, speak this verse to discipline the gods.
Because of his wholesome aspirations, he was born among the gods.
That King Peacock used things from the human realm as metaphors to teach the assembly of gods. Why was this?
Having caused the devas to hear this, they will remember their past lives;
by remembering their past lives, they will understand the fruits of karma and thus practice impermanence;
by practicing impermanence, they will act with heedfulness.
Therefore, the peacock king of variegated colors uses human analogies to teach the Dharma to the devas.
What Dharma does he teach?
It is the dharma of impermanence.
He spoke of the faults of desire and the impermanence of desire.
At that time, there was a deva who, having heard the Dharma being taught, recollected his former lives.
Because he recollected his past births and understood the retribution of karma, he practiced non-negligence for a short while and gave rise to wholesome thoughts.

For a short time, that deva gave rise to wholesome thoughts and practiced non-negligence; for a short time he benefited himself and for a short time he was at peace, planting the seeds of wholesome karma for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of peaceful rebirths in future lives. For this reason, the Bodhisattva, the King of Variegated-Colored Birds, preached such a Dharma.

At that time, the celestial hosts, still attached to pleasure, entered that grove; adorning their bodies and heads with lotus garlands and beautifying themselves with the radiance of their own bodies, they experienced various delights through the sounds of the five musical instruments.

In that forest, immeasurable rivers and ponds were filled with flowing water and perfectly adorned; having seen this, the celestial hosts moved about with negligence, feeling no fear toward birth, old age, or death, and never knowing satiety in their singing, dancing, and play.
They further entered another forest, named Mālya-vana (The Garland Forest).

In that Garland Forest, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of trees; the branches and flowers of these trees were of various different colors, interspersed and distinct from one another, possessing immeasurable varieties of shapes, forms, colors, and fragrances—various exquisite flowers complete upon every branch.
Thus these wondrous flowers were equal in both size and beauty, a rare and fitting sight.
Within that forest were bees made of the seven precious gems; their sounds were lovely as they sported together with the devas amidst those flowers.
Those devas take those flower garlands and, together with the hosts of celestial maidens, toss them about in playful sport.
The devas and celestial maidens were already naturally handsome, but because they wear such wondrous flower garlands, they become ten times more beautiful than before.
With single-minded focus on one another, they sport and enjoy themselves within that forest, plucking flowering branches.
The fragrance of those flowers pervades five yojanas, and extends for ten, twenty, or even thirty yojanas.
Thus, that celestial grove was fully endowed with divine fragrances and possessed a collection of immeasurable varieties of flowers.
At that time, having thus sported and experienced various pleasures, those gods proceeded toward a river of wine called "Joy."
That river is exceedingly vast; its wine is endowed with all excellent sounds, textures, tastes, fragrances, and colors as it flows.
Having seen it, those gods sit upon the riverbank, take it up, and drink.
There is another bird there named Constant Joy (Nityapriya). Seeing those gods drinking wine in the River of Joy (Nandana-nadī), it spoke this verse for them:
"Submerged in the ocean of heedlessness, Greedy for all sensory objects— This wine can delude the mind; Why drink wine again?"
"Burned by the fire of sensory objects, they do not know what should or should not be done;
their minds give rise to craving for gardens and groves—what use is there in drinking wine again?
Thus did the bird Nityapriya speak these verses to subdue the gods who delight in wine as they drank it in the river.
Having heard this, those devas nevertheless continued to drink wine, neither ceasing nor stopping, their hearts filled with joy.
The radiance of their own bodies surrounded them like garlands, and they further adorned their bodies with flower garlands, drinking and sporting without knowing satiety.

Amidst the merits of the five desires and the sounds of the five musical instruments, they engage in song, dance, and play; proceeding in succession toward the forest of Flower-Branched Dwellings (Puṣpaśākhāvāsa), they go to that grove out of hope for sensual pleasure, where they sing, dance, and laugh joyfully together with the hosts of celestial maidens.
"At that time, seeing that grove of trees fully adorned with various flowers, that deva felt great joy in his heart.
Because he had heard of it previously, he rejoiced upon seeing it."

In such a supremely wonderful and lovely grove, adorned with bees made of the seven precious gems, the celestial hosts, having seen it, gave rise to a sense of wonder; they turned their eyes to gaze everywhere, never feeling weary or satisfied.

Those hosts of celestial maidens were all likewise; they beheld five thousand kinds of hundred-thousandfold distinct flower-palaces in their full splendor, and upon seeing them, the celestial maidens entered within, singing, dancing, sporting, and enjoying bliss.
The branches and leaves of those trees are exceedingly lovely and pleasant, densely covering them like a house.

Those various tree branches are composed of diverse jewels; that is to say, there are beryl branches covered with golden leaves, or golden branches covered by a canopy of beryl leaves, and they are fully endowed with exquisite, beautiful-colored fruits of *kakkatana*.
The branches of the *karketana* blue-jewel trees are covered with silver-colored leaves;
the crystal trees are fully endowed with golden fruit.
If there are trees there whose branches consist of *karketana*, they are covered with blue-jewel leaves and fully endowed with golden fruit.
If it is a crystal tree with a crystal branch-house, its leaves are densely covered in gold and it is fully endowed with fruits of great blue jewels.
Adorned according to one's thoughts, all are utterly lovely; swarms of bees surround it, their exquisite sounds echoing around the flower-branch houses.
The interior of those branch-houses is thus adorned and magnificent; when the devas wish to enjoy pleasure, they enter therein because of their virtuous karma.

Furthermore, outside the branch-houses, all manner of things are fully provided: there are lotus ponds with lotuses that have golden leaves made entirely of *vaiḍūrya*, blue jewels for stamens, and pedestals of white silver. Surrounding the exterior of the grove, they are adorned by immeasurable swarms of bees.
Geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, and *kādamba* birds emit exquisite sounds, which bring joy to the hearts of those who hear them;
for this reason, that grove is exceedingly subtle and wondrous.
Outside that lotus grove, there are flower ponds like garlands, no different from them, and dwellings of precious flowering branches surround that grove, pervading it everywhere.
"Outside the lotus wheel there is further a grove of trees; in such a grove dwell birds and beasts whose hearts are all filled with joy.
Some sit beneath the trees leaning against them, some wander about, and some within the forest eat the exquisite fruits, flowers, roots, and other delicacies of the devas."
Fruits, flowers, roots, and so forth, possess a primary perfection of the combination of color, fragrance, flavor, and touch.
Likewise, among birds and beasts, males and females, bulls and cows, all follow one another accordingly.
Furthermore, when those birds and beasts hear the celestial songs, they open their eyes and prick up their ears; their feathers all bristle with joy, and their hearts are filled with delight.

Moreover, those birds and beasts—whether male or female, stallion or mare—follow one another, resting beneath trees on ground of soft touch, gazing into each other's faces as they experience pleasure or engage in play together.
The various beasts chew and swallow their food; males and females dwell together, gazing at one another’s faces as they enjoy mutual pleasure.
Their bodies are all interspersed with the seven treasures, and they thus experience such delights within the forest.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 52; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 53.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Two: Observing the Heavens; Part Eighteen: Yāma Heaven.
Furthermore, those birds possess various forms and appearances that those who see them find delightful; they evoke various thoughts and bring about various pleasures.
As for what is called "pleasure":
there are those who carry lotus flowers in their beaks and wander about listening to the sounds of songs, with males and females following one another as they play.

There are also flocks of birds that dwell together, lowering their bodies and huddling close to listen to the sounds from within the leafy houses on the branches, listening with single-minded attention.
Some, with their beaks holding jewels of supreme radiance, travel everywhere;

some possess bodies made of the seven precious substances and, having heard the sound of singing from within the mountains, spread their wings and fly there to listen to the music, heading toward the pavilion of flowering branches, adorning the entirety of space and filling those who see them with joy.

Furthermore, there are other birds in other groves whose two wings are adorned with various exquisite jewels; they pluck various blooming flowers with their beaks and carry them back toward that house of flowering branches.
Furthermore, having heard the singing of other birds, they together carry jeweled garlands of various colors and exquisite radiance;
thus they come toward the dwelling of flower-branches, adorning the entirety of space with such splendor as they approach.
Thus, the birds and beasts within and without that forest possess various colors, various forms, and various endowments, all of which are delightful.
That forest is exceptionally wonderful and magnificent; in this way, those hosts of devas experience various pleasures within that forest.

"At that time, those devas sported for a long duration in that grove to the sounds of the five kinds of music; yet, consumed by the fire of craving, they remained unsatisfied and proceeded toward another grove."
That forest is named Bird-Sound Music; surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens, they thus sing, dance, laugh, and play, strumming lutes with their hands as they fly through the air.
