Some travel in this manner upon the backs of geese; others are gods riding peacocks; some travel thus seated upon lotus pedestals in mid-air; and yet other gods ride seven-jeweled birds through the void, all of them heading toward the Forest of Bird-Sounds and Music.
As he traveled in this manner, before he had yet reached his destination, he was endowed with all kinds of supreme delights as he drew near that forest.
A bird named Satyavādin (Truth-Speaker) spoke these verses for him:
"Among vehicles, the vehicle of karma is supreme; other vehicles are not so."
By means of the vehicle of karma, beings are able to travel throughout the three realms.
Who, in what place, by what karma, and in what manner acts—
that person, in that very place, experiences pleasure or pain according to what was done.
Karma is manifold and diverse, produced through the conditions of the mind;
though no substance can be found therein, after a long time it will inevitably be experienced.
All manner of various pleasures arise from the causes and conditions of karma.
Because the causes of karma are exhausted, various pleasures also cease to exist.
As long as one’s previously performed wholesome karma has not perished,
those who wish to constantly obtain happiness should all perform further meritorious deeds.
If the mind is constantly indolent, oppressed by the poison of negligence,
and the gods do not perceive their negligence, they will reach a place of future suffering.
Separated from all pleasure, they arrive at a place of great anguish.
Because it can shatter the aggregates and elements, it is therefore called death.
It approaches with great speed, capable of exhausting and extinguishing life;
deluded by the celestial realms, one thus fails to perceive it.
"Because that Bird of Truth possesses a virtuous mind, he feels compassion for the celestial hosts and thus speaks these verses on the true Dharma to benefit those devas."
Yet the devas do not perceive this, for their minds are shrouded by craving; instead, they become even more joyful and advance further into the Forest of Bird-Sound Music.
All the hosts of devas delight in seeing this Forest of Bird-Sound Music; since the forest is named thus, it possesses such musical sounds from the birds.
All the trees in that grove are made of jewels; that is to say, there are trees of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli, as well as trees of white silver, crystal, and blue gems.
In this level marshland is a grove of lotus flowers; those lotuses are like trees of lamps, and all their various kinds are exceedingly delightful.
There are various birds of immeasurable colors and immeasurable forms, with wings variegated by jewels, beyond full description.
Why is this? Because the wholesome karma of the mind is of immeasurable kinds, the forms and characteristics of these birds are likewise diverse.
Because the mind is diverse, one performs diverse wholesome karmas; because wholesome karma is diverse, one obtains such fruits, which cannot be described in full detail.
Because the mind is subtle and flows with such rapidity, for these reasons it cannot be fully described; all the dharmas of the heavens are likewise ineffable.

I shall now describe but a small portion of the karmic fruits of the heavens: there are exquisite and wondrous objects of desire and indulgence, including groves, flowing streams, lotus ponds, various mountain peaks, lotus forests, birds, jewels, and other such things, as well as lovely celestial maidens.
Due to the fruit of karma, such manifestations appear within the celestial worlds.

These causes and conditions are described as the "loveliness of the heavens"; just as the retribution produced by those wholesome karmas is neither lost nor extinguished, so too, if one has not performed the actions, the fruit cannot be obtained.
Furthermore, for this reason, happiness is described in such a way.
Moreover, those devas, with their bodies adorned with various kinds of garlands and their bodies anointed with perfumes, experience pleasure through their own radiance and a heart of supreme joy.

Thus he observes the forest as a pleasure grove through the sounds of birds; thus he beholds the trees made of the seven precious gems, their radiance like flames, with various kinds of birds surrounding that forest.
When those birds sing and chant, if the gods hear it—a sound such as they have never heard before—their hearts rejoice and they experience pleasure upon hearing it;
all those gods likewise find delight once they have heard it.
Among those birds, some dwell within trees and sing; some dwell within groves of lotuses and sing; some dwell among flowers and sing; and some dwell within lotus ponds and sing.
Having heard this, those devas felt joy and happiness in their hearts.
Whether it be devas or devīs, they all ceased their mutual harmonious union and their various songs, and instead listened to the singing of the birds, their hearts filled with love and delight.

Thus, the melodic sounds of that bird’s song resounded throughout the mountain peaks; all the various beasts dwelling among those peaks, whose very nature delighted in the sound of song, heard that singing and, numbering by the hundreds or thousands, all approached it.
Having already drawn near, their ears were alert and unshaken as they listened to the sound of the singing.
Some stood at the foot of the trees listening to the song; others, facing the celestial grass, had no desire to eat it, remaining instead to listen to the melody.
In that grove, the songs of the birds are so lovely; the forest is thus delightful through the music of the birds' voices.

Furthermore, the fragrance in that grove is exceedingly lovely, consisting of the scents of various flowers of diverse colors, all appearing according to one's thoughts; fragrances, colors, sounds, and so forth, are all obtained according to one's wishes.

The various beautiful sounds of the *konghou*, *qigu*, *zhen*, and *dizi* lutes and flutes, as well as songs—these are the sounds of the devas; yet the voices of those birds surpass even those celestial sounds within the domain of a single sense faculty. Because they are so superior, that forest is lovely.
Furthermore, within that grove, there is another sense-object of delight, namely celestial flavor.
According to whatever one desires in thought, one obtains the taste of superior fruits, or the taste of celestial wine, or the taste of celestial medicinal herbs.
In this way, in that forest, flavors are obtained according to one's thoughts; thus, within that forest, all flavors are fully present.
Furthermore, in that forest there is another superior quality, namely, the presence of mountains.

They sport upon that mountain, which is entirely covered by a network of branches; the various multi-storied pavilions are all made of this branch-network, arranged so that they do not obstruct one another as they move.

There are immeasurable varieties of walls adorned with the seven treasures, and immeasurable varieties of colorful paintings cover them everywhere. Many celestial maidens, adorned in various ways, reside within these multi-storied pavilions.
That forest is thus adorned in various ways;
furthermore, that grove possesses further adornments.
The merits of that forest have already been fully described.

Now, furthermore, the characteristics of the mountain’s delightful and perfect adornments will be described: namely, that the mountain is adorned with lapis lazuli, and the mountain is endowed with seven kinds of meritorious qualities.
What are these seven? They are as follows:
one obtains whatever one recollects, whether forms, sounds, touches, tastes, or fragrances; there is a tree of recollection that is endowed with these seven qualities.
When the gods there behold those merits, they become deluded and confused, neither seeing nor hearing the birds preaching the Dharma.
"The Dharma-preaching birds speak with the same certainty as their parents;

yet the devas, being attached to sensory realms, neither hear nor perceive them. Because they are deluded by these realms, they do not accept the birds' words and wander through the wilderness of craving."

Again he turns toward the great forest, where he is scorched by three kinds of fire; driven by the five enemies, deceived by craving and delight, and deluded regarding the true path, there is for him only suffering and pleasure.

Suffering resembles pleasure; because they are attached to such false pleasure, they do not perceive or understand it. Though the beneficial teaching of the Dharma is offered, they neither accept nor take it up, but instead listen to the sounds of the birds singing as they move through the other three realms.

These are the water-faring birds, whose colors and forms are lovely to the gods, with bodies made of the seven precious jewels interspersed in various ways—such as geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks. With their manifold songs and the sounds of the water, those gods delight in hearing such exquisite melodies and songs, always indulging in pleasure and heedlessness.
All the gods cherish those sounds; yet, although those gods hear various other sounds from other birds, they do not hear the sound of the Dharma.

Specifically, there are various forest-dwelling birds—peacocks, white pigeons, tree-adorners, and birds that dwell in mountain valleys and rock caves—which produce exquisite voices. All these bird sounds are matched by birds of similar wondrous voices—birds with bodies of the seven precious gems—who adorn the mountains, flying in pairs side-by-side through the void, together producing their songs.

Beholding those birds as if seeing a magnificent adornment, the light of those birds brings constant joy to those who see them, giving rise to a mind of attachment; such are the increasingly sublime songs of the various birds.

Those gods delight in hearing the sound of speech, the sound of song, and the sound of resonance—such immeasurable and variously distinguished sounds of *vakra* [melodies], diverse and wonderful to hear. With minds possessed by desire and surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens (*apsaras*), they listen to those sounds; for a long time they experience pleasure in hearing these sounds, their hearts further shrouded by superior passion.

Furthermore, they drink celestial wine, which is endowed with the foremost flavors and fragrances, flowing forth from within the rocky caves just as befits the gods; many exquisite bees all gather upon the wine.
Those devas, with single-minded intent toward one another, drink the celestial wine together without obstructing each other.

Furthermore, there are other devas who go toward the lotus groves; within the petals of the lotuses there is much celestial wine, endowed with the supreme flavors, fragrances, and textures, providing exquisite tastes according to their thoughts.
The gods and goddesses drink to their hearts' content, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing; with single-minded devotion toward one another, they share common desires.

Those gods sport and enjoy themselves within the Supreme Forest (Vana-viśeṣa), yet their minds find no satiety amidst such sensory objects, and they proceed further toward the mountain adorned with Vaiḍūrya jewels.
That mountain abounds with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, all of which cast a pervasive blue reflection for ten thousand *yojanas*.

The mountain rises three hundred *yojanas* high and is filled with many groves and gardens, as well as numerous lotus ponds where flowing waters overflow. There is a supreme bird there, whom all who see it love.

Within that mountain there are excellent level plains, excellent valleys, excellent rocky caves, and springs and grottoes; there are many groves of trees, and lotus ponds complete with every kind of flower.

There are three kinds of swans that cry out from the shore: some are the color of crystal, interspersed with the seven precious gems; others are white by their very nature. Such swans abound in the mountains, adorning that mountain.
Throughout the Vaiḍūrya mountains there are flowing streams, the color of whose water is as pure and clear as precious jewels.
Those mountains abound with various fragrant flowers and many hundreds of thousands of diverse birds; these various birds adorn the lotus ponds.

Those various objects are increasingly marvelous, each more rare than the last; lovely and wondrous colors adorn that mountain, and it is adorned with immeasurable kinds of things such as sounds, textures, and fragrances, providing pleasure to the six sense faculties and adorning the entire mountain.

Those hosts of devas, desiring to experience pleasure, go to that mountain and everywhere engage in singing, dancing, and play; they adorn their bodies with lotus garlands and necklaces, enjoying themselves at all times, their minds always joyful and always filled with delight.
The five sense objects are enemies like five fires that burn; craving binds their throats.
For the sake of experiencing pleasure upon that mountain peak, they long to see, and thus harbor various recollections and various conceptualizations.
Gradually drawing near, as they approached that mountain, they saw a mountain cave made of lapis lazuli.
That mountain cave was blue in color and radiant with light, adorned by ten thousand such features, and was filled everywhere with the most supreme, exquisite, and wonderful radiance.
If the mountain-dwelling devas enter that cave, they engage in various forms of play.
Whenever those devas enter the cave, the cave becomes wider and more expansive in accordance with their minds; as they conceive various thoughts, all of these are fully realized within the cave.
That cave is named the Cave of Attainment According to Thought; the devas dwelling in that cave, together with hosts of celestial maidens, constantly experience pleasure without ever knowing satiety.

Those celestial maidens are adorned in various ways, and because of their virtuous karma, the devas behold them with hearts of extreme affection and delight. Their forms and attire are magnificent, their beauty is peerless, and they enjoy celestial pleasures through singing, dancing, and joyful laughter.
"For the sake of benefiting the devas, the Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda had these verses spoken by the Buddha inscribed upon the door of a jeweled cave on that mountain. The verses say:
"The King of Death swallows sentient beings; Decay and old age drink up the youth.
When sickness arrives, it destroys vigor; Yet in this world, none recognize it."
There are immeasurable kinds of birth, and there are immeasurable kinds of decline;
as it is with birth, so it is with old age—yet in this world, none understand this.
Not for even a single thought-moment, nor for a single instant, nor for a single day, [does this cease].
Death dwells without fixed time or place, yet none in the world understand this.
Having undergone birth again and again, and likewise having fallen away again and again, the deluded devas are bewildered by sensory realms; yet none in the world understand this.
This wheel of existence is like a cage; clinging with craving to sensual desires, bound by the ropes of love and led away, the world remains ignorant.
Amidst the swirling waves of the excesses of craving, there are many birds of conceptual discrimination.
"This river of craving is vast and wide; no one in the world understands it.
Such was the method by which those gateways to the jeweled caves were inscribed with the Buddha’s verses for the benefit of the devas.
A deva saw this and immediately began to read it; having read those verses, he recollected his own past lives and practiced heedfulness for a short time.

By virtue of that wholesome karma, through right reflection for a mere moment, he increased the happiness of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of future births, increasing the pure portion and diminishing the defiled portion.
When that deva maintains right mindfulness for even a brief moment in this way, he can extinguish the measureless hundreds of thousands of births he has undergone.
If there are those who see the verses inscribed above the entrance of that jeweled cave, they will give rise to world-weariness and detachment, and practice without negligence;
however, if a deva enters the cave without reading the verses, his entry is in vain.
"If one sees that all who do not enter [this state] act with negligence,
they may see within a single place a heap of jewels— a heap of diamonds, a heap of blue gems, a heap of magarata gems, and a heap of great blue gems."
Furthermore, the very nature of that jewel cave is inherently luminous; because of the precious gems, its radiance becomes even more superior.
Thirdly, because devas enter within it, the radiance of their celestial bodies causes the light of that jewel cave to become even more brilliant. Thus, that cave is exceedingly lovely.
Within that jewel cave, the hosts of devas and devīs enjoy the merits of the five sensual pleasures; they experience various delights, dwelling in peace and free from affliction.
Being free from burning distress and far removed from sorrow and lamentation, by virtue of their own wholesome karma, they experience immeasurable kinds of sublime celestial bliss.
Once those devas have beheld that jeweled ground, they give rise to a heart of joy; they dance, sing, and sport, experiencing pleasure through the sounds of the five kinds of music.
Furthermore, those who enter the jeweled caves therein see rivers filled with celestial wine, endowed with the most excellent fragrance and touch.
On both banks of that river of wine, there abound birds that drink wine, serving as its adornment.

Such birds are named Joyful, Constantly Delighted, Constantly Sporting, No Different Flavor, Seeing What is Lovely, and Discerning Mind; there are also birds named Not Delighting in Other Places and Fragrant Drink Joy—these and other such birds.
Furthermore, there were other birds at that river of wine, sporting and drinking the wine.
Due to the virtuous karma of the devas, the birds spoke these verses:
"First one drinks the delicious wine; having drunk it, one commits many evils."
In the future one will obtain evil fruits, dwelling within the hells.
Having drunk [of this], it causes delusion; because of delusion, one creates evil karma.
Because of creating evil karma through delusion, one enters into the hells.
At first there is joy, but later one receives an evil retribution;
at first it can quench thirst, but later it brings great heat.
At first one loses control of speech and mind, and later one loses happiness.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom should not drink alcohol.
One who drinks constantly is no different from a bird;
drinking brings about delusion, for alcohol is said to be a great poison.
If one views liquor as poison, that person sees the state of non-retrogression;
if one drinks liquor without relishing its flavor, it is as if drinking molten iron.
One part of all evils is said to be liquor.
These are the transgressions committed by the mind; the mind is the root of all precepts.
When the mind is unsettled by drinking alcohol, one cannot contemplate the Dharma.
Because a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, he does not practice as an araṇya-dweller.
Drinking wine causes the mind to become disordered; it leads to lack of self-control and a failure to recognize shame.
One loses the Dharma and becomes empty of merit, forfeiting both the present and the future.
Such a person does not know how to cultivate dignified deportment, nor do they understand the proper time or place.
Obstructing the True Dharma, they speak only words devoid of meaning;
not knowing it themselves, they do not know what they are saying.
Their own speech is like excrement, and they themselves cannot even recognize it as such.
It causes one to be held in contempt by the world and prevents the Dharma from flourishing;
seeing a poor person drinking alcohol is like witnessing a blazing fire.
One forgets all past events and becomes utterly deluded regarding present matters.
How much more so when contemplating the future: drinking alcohol causes loss during the three periods of the day.
It can destroy name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) or cause the loss of one's sentient body;
it can give rise to immeasurable faults, for drinking alcohol obstructs the Dharma.
"Thus, the birds dwelling in that mountain cave are constantly joyful in heart; by the causal conditions of their karma, they speak verses for the sake of the devas.
Having heard them, those devas who were born there due to wholesome karma and conduct in accordance with the Dharma remember their previous lives.
Because they remember their former births, they understand the faults of alcohol."
Knowing the faults of alcohol, they do not drink it and practice without negligence.

The remaining hosts of devas, however, do not accept the bird's verse; they continue to drink alcohol, giving rise to hearts of joy, and enjoy themselves with the sounds of the five musical instruments, singing and dancing, for a long time within that mountain cave, experiencing various pleasures.
Having experienced pleasure, they emerge by the same path through which they entered.
Having thus emerged, they remain unsatisfied with their objects of perception and continue to act with heedlessness.
Delighting in the sight of groves, they together with hosts of celestial maidens engage in various diversions within all the gardens, along riverbanks, and in mountain valleys.
Thus do these gods experience such pleasures by virtue of their wholesome karma.
That place is thus beyond analogy, replete with celestial delights.
Those devas experience various sensual pleasures within their realms, never knowing satiety because of their vast and manifold cravings.
That which is called "vast" is so because its own nature is vast; it is never contained and is perpetually expansive, and for this reason it is called vast.
Furthermore, there is no knowing of satiety regarding objects, because all objects are vast and immeasurable, and because the sense faculties are constantly thirsty and never cease.

In this way, the fivefold sensory pleasures and merits of those devas increase further and further, uninterrupted and unceasing; they constantly experience sensual delights, giving rise to a sense of wonder, for their lovely merits are beyond all analogy.
Therefore, those gods do not know contentment; just as the ocean swallows rivers and never reaches satiety, so too the gods are never satisfied.

At all times, they experience such pleasures in that celestial realm, wandering through various groves and gardens, drifting upon the waters of desire, sporting and enjoying themselves together with the celestial maidens.

That deva remains in such a state until his accumulated store of beloved wholesome karma is exhausted; subsequently, he falls from that celestial realm, bound by the ropes of karma according to his own past actions.
When their karma in such pleasant realms is exhausted and they decline, they fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.

If there remains some residual wholesome karma, they are born among human beings in the great wealthy and joyful regions of Jambudvīpa, within the foremost of castes. They constantly experience pleasure through various games of song, dance, and laughter; they possess exquisite complexions and are adorned with dignified attire and ornaments, dwelling in such superior lands.
They may become kings or ministers, or reside in the peaceful islands of the Kāśī kingdom or the Kośala kingdom.
This is due to their remaining karma.
Thus ends the ninth stage, the Garden of Supreme Radiance (*Vijayaprabha*), within the realm of the Yāma Heaven.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates all the various grounds of the Yāma Heaven.
Through seeing, hearing, and knowing, or by means of the divine eye,
he perceives that there is another place called *Samyak-caryā* (Right Conduct).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?

He sees that there are those who practice in accordance with the Dharma correctly; being supremely pure, their retribution is also pure, and because their karma is pure, they experience pleasant karmic results, which are cherished by the noble ones.
One who practices excellent and virtuous generosity but possesses little wisdom,
by virtue of that generosity, is reborn among the devas and experiences the fruits beloved by the devas.
Regarding these celestial realms, what kind of person attains the retributive fruits therein?
It is said that there are those whose virtuous minds are pure, who give rise to a mind of reverence and a mind of gentleness, and who refrain from killing and stealing as previously described.

Furthermore, they abandon sexual misconduct; that is to say, having heard with their own ears that in the past someone once engaged in sexual desire with a woman, upon hearing this, their hearts find no pleasure in it. Regarding such prior acts of desire, they do not dwell upon them in thought, they do not give rise to discursive reflection (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*), and they are further able to restrain others, not permitting them to think of such things.

Having thus accomplished pure karmic conduct, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in a happy realm, in the region of Right Conduct within the Yāma Heaven, where they experience the fruit of the wholesome karma previously cultivated.
Having been born in that place, they take delight in various immeasurable objects of the senses—such as fragrances, tastes, and textures—and roam within the groves and gardens.
There, they are honored by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens amidst divine lotus ponds.
They roam through groves, lotus ponds, and flowing streams, never pausing for even a moment.
They experience all manner of celestial delights—unprecedented, beyond analogy, and impossible to describe in full—and enjoy those immeasurable varieties of pleasure to their heart's content.
Within those sensory objects, the mind knows no satisfaction.
Furthermore, in that place there are immeasurable kinds of exquisite celestial gardens; thus, when a newly born son of the gods arrives, he is surrounded by a multitude of young women.

In other gardens, there were hosts of celestial maidens sporting therein; upon seeing the newly born deva, desire arose in their hearts, and their conduct became altered from its former state. Adorned with various celestial garments and garlands, they immediately approached the newly born deva.
When the newly born deva beholds those celestial maidens, his desire is aroused fivefold, and he immediately approaches them.
Those celestial maidens and the newly born deva mingle with one another; together they experience immeasurable varieties of pleasure, their hearts and minds unified, never at variance.
Thus all those celestial maidens sang together, rejoicing, dancing, and laughing; those goddesses gave rise to this thought:
"This newly born deva is my husband."
When the newly born deva-son first conceives such a thought as,
"These celestial maidens are my wives," the deva-son and the celestial maidens trust one another, harbor no doubts or suspicions, and delight in mutual affection through laughter, song, and dance.

Within the groves, he went from one grove to another, from one mountain peak to another, from one lotus pond to another, from one bower to another, from one thicket of trees to another, and from one pool to another.
Such a pond possesses the color of blue jewels.

In that pond, there are many geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, with their various calls; there are the diverse sounds of such immeasurable birds that when heard by the ear, they bring joy to the heart, just as one desires in one's mind.
Thus they were born from the water, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.
Within that pond, there were immeasurable varieties of singing, dancing, and play, as they experienced various pleasures.

Having enjoyed these delights, they again saw other hosts of devas in another place joyfully wandering about; upon seeing them, the newly born deva immediately went toward them and, together with the host of celestial maidens, proceeded in this manner, singing, dancing, and playing amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.
At that time, having seen the newly born deva-son in this manner, that deity spoke these verses:
“Within mountain gardens and groves, or by the lotus ponds, and in all the multi-storied palaces,
he enjoys pleasure together with the celestial maidens.”
Whether amidst golden mountains, or on peaks of lapis lazuli,
or within groves of trees in gardens, they enjoy pleasures together with celestial maidens;
according to their wishes, they dwell among lovely trees or by flowing rivers.
Sometimes in vast ponds, they enjoy pleasure together with celestial maidens;
amidst places interspersed with the seven treasures, or within mountains and rivers,
or on level ground in beautiful spots, they enjoy pleasure together with celestial maidens.
In the groves of *mandāra* trees and blue *utpala* forests,
amidst the songs of various birds, they enjoy pleasures together with celestial maidens;
in various regions of the earth, or within groves of jewels, they dwell.
Sometimes they are in the Hall of Delight, enjoying pleasure together with celestial maidens;
sometimes the sounds of the five musical instruments bring their hearts joy and cool serenity,
as they constantly sing, dance, and play, enjoying pleasure together with the celestial maidens.

When those devas had spoken this verse for the sake of the newly born deva, the newly born deva-son, having heard the verse, was further addressed by the birds there known as "Truth-Speakers," who, for the purpose of benefiting him according to the Dharma and causing him to practice correctly,
spoke this verse: "Amidst mountains and gardens, or within lotus groves, Deluded by ignorance and infatuated by craving, One falls together with the celestial maidens."
Sometimes amidst golden mountains, or on peaks of lapis lazuli;
once their good karma is exhausted, they fall together with the celestial maidens.
Following their thoughts toward lovely trees, or by flowing rivers, they descend.
When the merit of their playful deeds is exhausted, they fall together with the celestial maidens.
Amidst places interspersed with the seven treasures, or within mountains and rivers,
they are deluded by sensory objects and fall together with the celestial maidens.
In the groves of mandāra trees and the blue utpala forests,
those blinded by attachment to pleasure fall together with the celestial maidens;
in various regions of the ground, or within the jewel groves.
Failing to practice wholesome dharmas, they fall together with the celestial maidens.
Or, by the sounds of the five kinds of music, their minds find delight and coolness;
yet because of their greedy attachment, time passes them by, and they fall together with the celestial maidens.
Thus did that Bird of Truth speak these verses for the benefit of the devas, in order to accord with their welfare, to bring them peace and security, and to lead them toward right conduct.
Although those gods hear this, they do not accept it due to their negligence; even the long-established gods do not take it to heart, let alone the newly born gods.

Because both the new and old gods have been wounded by the poison of negligence, they all sing and dance, their hearts filled with joy as they sport everywhere within the groves, experiencing the pleasures of sensory objects.
Their own bodies emit radiance, requiring no other light.
All those gods, together with their hosts of celestial maidens, proceed toward another mountain called Mount Mālyavat.

That Mount Mālyavat abounds in countless varieties of precious substances and is adorned with diverse jewels; its entire mountain is illuminated by hundreds of thousands of lotuses, which serve as an adornment like the rising sun, and it contains hundreds of billions of flowing streams, springs, and ponds.
On the four sides of that mountain are four groves: the first is named Hundred Pools and Flowing Streams; the second is named Great Radiance;
the third is named Adorned Mountain; and the fourth is named... [the name is omitted in the source].
The four are named Universal Fragrance (*Samantagandha*).
These are known as the Four Groves, situated on the slopes of that mountain.

On one slope of that mountain, amidst a hundred ponds, flowing streams, and dense forests, there are wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*). There are hundreds of thousands of ponds, filled everywhere with fish of various jewel colors—gold, silver, blue gems, and *kācāndana*.
The water of that pond is pure, cool, and refreshing, filling the pond with water that appears according to one's wishes.
Many groves and gardens surround that pond; the cries of geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks are lovely, bringing joy to the hearts of those who hear them.
There is a bird called "Ever-Joyful" who, seeing those celestial hosts, spoke this verse:
"All life is impermanent; youth does not remain.
This celestial realm is likewise so, yet the gods do not perceive it."
All phenomena are momentary and do not abide; they perish one after another in succession.
Bound by the cords of karma, the world remains unaware of this.
Billions of celestial hosts roam and wander through the gardens and groves.
When the time of decline is about to arrive, the world does not perceive it.
The gods of the six heavens of desire, indulging in negligence and enjoying their pleasures, shall all perish; yet the world does not perceive it.
"Pleasures are like a mass of foam, like objects obtained in a dream;
they perish quickly and do not endure for long, yet the world does not realize this.
When those gods there wish to ascend the mountain, at all times that bird of constant joy, out of a mind intent on their benefit and due to the gods' own wholesome karma, speaks these verses.
Because those devas delight in their sensory realms, they do not listen, do not grasp, do not perceive, and do not know; they are unable to see the Truth and do not look at that bird.
Like one born blind, they do not see the path that exists.
"At that time, that deva proceeded next toward the second great grove of radiant forests. The radiance of that forest surpassed the light of a hundred suns.

The trees of that forest possessed supreme brilliance—whether the light of the trees themselves or the light of their jewels—endowed with all manner of sublime and wondrous merits, blazing with radiance."

In that Great Radiance Forest, three kinds of light pervade everywhere; such a forest is entirely delightful, adorned with flowing streams, rivers, and ponds, and features wish-fulfilling trees that grace its grounds.

Thus, in these various forest regions, each distinct from the others, those hosts of devas dwell in different places, enjoying various pleasures through the sounds of the five musical instruments, singing, dancing, and sporting, as their wholesome karma gradually comes to an end.
On that mountain, in yet another place, they experienced sensory pleasures like a great intoxicated elephant; thus they enjoyed themselves in that forest for a long time.
Furthermore, because their own minds were stirred, those celestial hosts proceeded in succession toward the forest of rocky mountains.

Within that state, they further experience the pleasures of the five sensory objects; deluded by the enemy of heedlessness, they do not know to fear or withdraw, and there is no expedient means by which they may be liberated.
It is pleasant only at the beginning, but later leads to decline and distress.
Because their minds are distracted by craving for sounds, flavors, forms, and fragrances while experiencing various sensual pleasures, they wander from place to place.

Again, he sees another grove; surrounding the exterior of that grove is a lotus forest, which encircles it entirely. Within that grove are wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) as adornments, beautified by hundreds of thousands of kinds of flowers.
There were other great trees, adorned with exquisite and wondrous fragrances; furthermore, it was further adorned with many flowing streams, rivers, and ponds.

Moreover, there were many various birds and beasts, and dwellings with branches made of the seven treasures served as adornments; furthermore, there were many rivers of various fragrant and delicious foods and drinks.

When those hosts of devas reach such mountains—whether arriving in groups of hundreds or thousands—they sing, dance, and sport, acting as companions to one another with a shared desire. Together they enter that grove and enjoy pleasure for a long time with the host of celestial maidens, each mutually longing for the sensory realms of the other.
Furthermore, those devas, still not yet satiated, see in that mountain region another most delightful forest called Universal Fragrance (Samantagandha). That forest is exceedingly fragrant;
the branches and flowers emit a sweet scent, and golden branches and flower-canopies cover the forest above, where there is the supreme, exquisite fragrance of kucela sandalwood.

Furthermore, in that grove, the *mandārava* flowers possess a supreme and wondrous fragrance; its scent spreads throughout a hundred *yojanas*, and when the gods smell it, they give rise to a sense of wonder.
Those hosts of devas, smelling such immeasurable and exquisite fragrances, enter that forest.
Those devas take mutual delight in one another; with a single mind and desire, they experience the pleasures of sensory objects without knowing satiety, wandering everywhere in countless ways.
"Thus those devas wander from place to place, moving about in play, gradually heading toward the summit of Mount Mālādhara.

Eventually, having advanced to hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of those mountain peaks, they see a great city; the city is most lovely, measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."

Throughout that city, there were multi-storied towers and pavilions made of various precious gems—pavilions of gold and jewels, pavilions of silver and jewels, pavilions of lapis lazuli, and pavilions of musaragalva; it was thus adorned with such diverse and wondrous jeweled pavilions.
The streets are well-proportioned and the gates are lovely, all fashioned from exquisite jewels; throughout that city, lotus ponds abound.
When the hosts of devas enter such a city, their hearts are filled with joy, and they experience bliss endowed with every kind of merit.

Within jeweled houses, in jeweled groves, or again in lotus ponds; within bowers of branches and flowers, or in flower forests; or again in lotus ponds, or in places abounding with flowers, or within mountain caves, or in mountain valleys, or on the slopes of mountains—those devas, thus situated either within cities or elsewhere upon mountain peaks, experience pleasure in every place together with the celestial maidens.
They enjoy immeasurable kinds of pleasure and manifold delights, fully endowed with the merit of the five musical sounds, thus sporting and experiencing various forms of bliss.
When those gods experience pleasure, the birds, seeing them, speak these verses:
"The wholesome karma of the gods will inevitably come to an end;
only when they later undergo suffering and affliction will they realize the fault of heedlessness."
Those whose minds delight in sensual desires experience only a slight pleasure;
before that pleasure has long endured, it will inevitably perish later on.
Those who find joy in sensory objects always harbor a heart of longing.
Seeing women’s heedlessness, one knows they will surely perish later.
The gods, attached to the pleasures of sensory realms, do not consider the suffering of their decline;
only when the time of destruction arrives do they realize the torment of falling away.
If a deva draws near to women and indulges in heedless conduct together with them,
then when the time for his final decline arrives, they all abandon him.
When a deva is about to fall from all his desires, there is no one who will accompany him.
Only all karmas follow after and accompany one.
One should always cultivate wholesome karma, always abandon unwholesome karma,
always remain free from heedlessness, and always practice non-heedlessness.
Heedlessness is the root of existence; heedfulness is tranquility.
Regarding heedlessness and heedfulness, their characteristics are as they have been described.
The hero constantly reflects upon them and delights in the practice of wholesome deeds.
"Those who constantly practice the Dharma will not undergo any suffering.
Having thus spoken this verse for the benefit of the devas, that bird—
Because those devas act with negligence, they do not listen or accept [the teachings], and are further blinded by their sensory objects.
They wander through the groves and gardens, engaging in various diversions; whether in the parks or within lovely jewel-cities and the like, they experience manifold pleasures.
Having experienced pleasure on Mount Mālyavat, that deity then proceeds further toward the Thousand-Peaked Mountain (Sahasraśikhara), desiring to behold that mountain of jewels.
Delighting in celestial realms, they proceed there next; due to the causes of their wholesome karma, they experience happiness.
Seeing those jewel mountains, they give rise to a heart of supreme attachment, for all sensual pleasures are fully provided therein.
At all times there are many flowers and fruits, and flowing streams, rivers, ponds, and groves of lotuses are fully present.
All those devas experience pleasure upon seeing that delightful place; they experience pleasure while walking about, and they experience pleasure while eating.
Beholding that supreme mountain, they conceived a sense of wonder, calling it the Mountain Garland (Girimekhala).
That great and supreme mountain is further surrounded on all sides by various other mountains, all of which are made of jewels; for this reason, that mountain is named the Mountain Garland.
That mountain abounds with groves, flower ponds, flowing rivers, and many precious bees; it resounds with the various songs of immeasurable flocks of birds.
All these birds possess jewel-like bodies, and their diverse forms and features are entirely lovely, adorning the mountain peaks.
Throughout all those mountain peaks, light pervaded everywhere; those lights were of hundreds of thousands of kinds.
Thus, among all the mountains, that jewel mountain was seen with its summit piercing the void, possessing a great radiance, subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
Those devas ascend such mountains and, together with hosts of celestial maidens, enjoy themselves amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.
With hearts full of joy, they ascend those mountain peaks and move about according to their wishes;

some travel through the air, while others, sharing the same desires as the celestial maidens, experience various sensual pleasures within the five sensory realms, drifting upon the river of craving without a moment’s pause.
If it were the bliss of tranquility, it would be eternal bliss.

Yet, they abandon such future benefits and peace of tranquility to delight in celestial pleasures; these celestial pleasures are like honey mixed with poison, yet the hosts of devas give rise to attachment and delight in them.
At first it seems virtuous, but later it is not good; in reality it is not pleasure, though it resembles pleasure.

Those devas do not realize this, and with hearts full of attachment to joy, they sport together with hosts of celestial maidens amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, following their desires as they ascend to the summit of that mountain.
In this manner, as they ascend that mountain, so do they behold its various locales; wherever they look, it becomes increasingly beautiful and lovely.
Such a jewel-mountain is entirely delightful, with groves of trees, rivers, and ponds, and all kinds of birds filling the gardens throughout that mountain region.
Countless hundreds of thousands of various gardens adorn that mountain, surrounded on all sides by the radiance of the seven treasures.
All those celestial hosts, together with their goddesses, ascend that mountain slowly, singing, dancing, and sporting as they walk side by side and gaze at one another.
The devas and their goddesses, adorned with various forms, garments, and garlands, possess no other thoughts; their minds always delight in pleasure, and they move about in heedlessness.

Those hosts of devas, possessing natural radiance, proceed together with celestial maidens—adorned with immeasurable forms and garments—who are surrounded by their own light. Moving with ease and composure, they ascend that mountain according to their hearts' desire.
By the power of their wholesome karma, having performed wholesome deeds themselves, they personally receive the retribution of happiness, which they must certainly experience for themselves.
They sport, sing, and dance within rivers and ponds, experiencing all manner of immeasurable pleasures.
Gradually ascending that mountain, amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, free from illness and without weariness, their hearts give rise to joy as they thus sport.

As they travel in this manner, they see immeasurable varieties of mountains, valleys, and ravines, each distinct from the others; they proceed according to their own will, and wherever they go, they are entirely without fear.
In this manner, they gradually ascended the mountain.
On that Mount Mālyavat, there was another place where a great king of geese resided.
That king of geese had a body adorned with jewels and was named Śubhakāla; he beheld those gods engaging in heedless conduct.
Because of their superior and wholesome karma, those gods have obtained such pleasant lives; yet, at a time when they ought to feel fear, they instead laugh with joy.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva, the Goose King Suśamaya, for the sake of benefiting all those gods, dwelt within a mountain cave. Following the practice of tranquil and wholesome deeds to benefit the gods, and in order to eliminate their negligence and ultimately benefit them, he—possessing the most supreme courage and various subtle, exquisite voices beloved by all the gods—overwhelmed all the other sounds with his speech and spoke these verses:
"Stained hearts by desire and delusion, Always delighting in and attached to sense objects,..."
Those devas do not realize that they are benefiting future generations.
With only this meager remaining merit, when the time for their decline approaches and they have already fallen to another place, they will experience the retribution of their own karma.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, one is bound by the shackles of karma;
since this karma binds sentient beings, one must gather the provisions for the Path.
Even if a deva constantly experiences pleasure, if they perpetually perform unwholesome deeds, [they will fall].
Because that cause is dissimilar, the deluded dwell within the mind.
Deluded by desire, they merely eat while awaiting death;
if one cannot know this with clarity, one cannot benefit sentient beings.
Deluded by desire, one merely eats while awaiting death;
to destroy the Dharma for the sake of bodily pleasure is folly.
At all times, with a single mind, always diligently cultivate wholesome deeds.
To abandon what is unwholesome—this is the mark of wisdom.
If one is heedless and does not maintain the precepts, the fruit of one's former karma will be exhausted;
because of such heedless conduct, one will before long fall from the celestial realm.
With such a mind as this, he is constantly driven by time;
later, he will be consumed by the fire of regret, and there will be no one able to save him.
Evil cannot be avoided; sentient beings must inevitably undergo its consequences.
"When one later arrives at the time of death;
knowing this, one practices tranquility.
Thus did the King of Geese, Supratiṣṭhita, preeminent in valor, with such a naturally exquisite voice, speak these verses for the sake of those celestial hosts.
In this way, the Bodhisattva, as the King of Geese, manifested immeasurable kinds of immeasurable sounds and phrases for all the devas, all of which were perfectly harmonious.
The voice of the Bodhisattva was exquisite, powerful, courageous, and supreme, eclipsing the sounds of the heavens.

There, all those hosts of devas likewise heard a great sound from afar, [emanating] from a most wondrous and magnificent jewel palace surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens and adorned with every kind of ornament.

It is fully endowed with flowers and fruits of every season; immeasurable lotuses cover the entire place. The songs of many celestial maidens are lovely to hear, and the radiance of exquisite jewel necklaces shines brilliantly. Adorned with groves and ponds interspersed with the seven treasures, it is further embellished with various banners, streamers, and railings.
A hundred thousand celestial maidens sang with exquisite voices, and those who heard the sounds of the five kinds of music felt joy in their hearts.
Adorned with pillars of *vaiḍūrya* gem, great blue gems, and pure gold, and further embellished by great lion thrones, such a jeweled palace traveled through the midst of space.

Upon that palace, the King of the Yāma Heaven was attended by many hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who made offerings to the king; hundreds of thousands of them joined their palms in reverence and praised the king.
In the midst of the void, appearing as clearly as a painting, their hearts filled with supreme joy, they turned toward Mount Mālyavat, desiring to go and see the king of geese, Kālīṅga.
Thus, by the power of his great vows, this king of geese was born in the Yāma heaven for the benefit of the devas, and he remembered his former lives.

Therefore, the Heavenly King has conceived a heart of reverence and respect, coming toward him for the sake of hearing the Dharma; for the benefit and happiness of himself and the celestial hosts, to bring profit to both self and others, so as not to fall into the evil realms and to remain free from negligence.
"At that time, they sported and enjoyed themselves on that mountain, the Wreath of Mountains (Girimekhala),
in various places among its mountain gardens and groves; some stayed in level plains,
some in mountain valleys, some in lotus forests, and some in the waters of ponds."
Some were on the upper terraces of palaces; some were within jeweled mansions;
some were among mountain peaks; some were at the riverbanks;
some were upon mountain summits; some were in flowering groves; and some were in fruit orchards.
As for those in the middle, some reside among the trees of recollection (*anusmṛti-vṛkṣa*); some reside among the trees of beryl and gold recollection;
and some reside within the groves of the "Immeasurable Attainment of Number" trees, which are lovely upon sight.

All of them, together with hosts of celestial maidens—whether in large groups or small—quickly gave rise to hearts of joy; they sang, danced, played, and laughed as they gazed upon that Heavenly King.
Seeing the Great Heavenly King seated upon the Victorious Palace, attaining incomparable celestial bliss, they ran toward him with haste; all the hosts of devas ran with their utmost strength.
Having seen the celestial king Mucilinda, they all ran toward him together; their minds and eyes were filled with joy, and gazing at him without turning away, they drew closer and closer.
Those hosts of devas thought to themselves:
"The Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, has come to the King of Geese, Kāla, because he wishes to hear the Dharma."
"I shall now go to see and make offerings to the Heavenly King.

Having thought thus, all those hosts of devas approached the Heavenly King of Yāma; they were fully endowed with the pleasures of the sensory realms of the five desires, adorned with celestial garments and celestial garlands.
All those gods turned forward toward Mucilinda.
As the King of the Yāma Heaven traveled through the sky,

the gods who were sporting and enjoying themselves on the Thousand-Peaked Mountain, seeing him thus adorned with celestial garments, all approached the presence of the Heavenly King to prostrate and make offerings.
Having made these offerings, they became even more joyful and engaged in singing, dancing, and laughter as they approached the presence of the king.
All of them joined together with the King of the Yāma Heaven and proceeded toward the place where the Bodhisattva Swan King resided.

"That Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, is foremost in intelligence and possesses great wisdom; by the power of his original vow, he was born in the Yāma heaven in order to eliminate the heedlessness of those devas."
All those gods went to the place where the Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, was.
Upon seeing the Bodhisattva, the King of the Yāma Heaven conceived a heart of reverence; out of respect for the Dharma, he descended from his palace together with the host of goddesses.

The Bodhisattva Goose King constantly expounds the Great Dharma and constantly utters the lion’s roar of the Dharma; upon seeing the celestial king Mucilinda, he then utters the roar of the True Dharma.
Because of the power of that Great Goose King’s Dharma, he is the most excellent and sublime among all the devas, his radiance being peerless due to the majestic might of the Dharma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 53; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 54.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
The Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Three: Suyāma Heaven, Section Nineteen.
At that time, the Goose King, seeing the Lord of the Gods, Mucilinda, spoke these words: "Welcome now."
Having offered various greetings and provisions with diverse words of inquiry, and having completed the offerings, he praised him, saying: "Excellent!
It is truly rare that the King of the Yāma Heaven is able to practice such heedfulness."
That one can thus refrain from negligence and practice non-negligence in this first place of negligence is truly rare.
Furthermore, there is another rarity:
that all the lords of the gods, though experiencing a hundredfold pleasure within the heavens, do not practice negligence; this is most rare indeed.
"Separated from the causes and conditions of happiness, it cannot be obtained.
Thus did the Bodhisattva, the Goose King Suśīma, recollect his own past life and the Dharma he had previously heard from the Buddha Śikhin.
Having recollected that sutra, he spoke thus to the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda:
"O Great Heavenly King, you have attained a sublime benefit; it is most rare indeed that you have come here out of heedfulness to hear my voice."
Listen well now; I shall speak for you.
I shall speak just as that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śikhin, spoke.
At that time, I was a king of men, and having heard what the Tathāgata said, I shall now speak it for you exactly as I heard it originally.
Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well.
There is a dharma-gate called "The Practice of Royal Law," and this dharma-gate can benefit a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration and ascended the throne.

When a king attains this Dharma, he constantly enjoys peace and happiness in the present life, always gains benefit, rightly protects his kingdom, and is able to protect himself; he is praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.

"What karma must a consecrated Kṣatriya great king have accomplished so that, in this present life, he constantly attains peace and happiness, always brings benefit, rightly protects the world, possesses great wealth and great power, is able to protect himself, is praised by virtuous people, and at the breaking up of the body after death, is reborn in a good destination, becoming a Yāma King in the heavenly world with great supernormal powers, great wealth, and great power?"

It is said that this king, being fully endowed with thirty-seven qualities, constantly attains peace and happiness in the present life and always brings benefit; he rightly protects the world, and by protecting the world, he possesses great wealth and power such that no other kings can destroy him. He is able to protect himself, is praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly realms, as a King of the Yāma Heaven.
“What are the thirty-seven dharmas?
First, the entire military host is completely pure;
second, taxes are collected in accordance with the law.”
Third, they constantly maintain patience and refrain from anger;
fourth, they adjudicate matters with impartiality and integrity, without bias;
fifth, they constantly make offerings to their elders and superiors.
Sixth, to follow established custom and bestow gifts according to precedent;
seventh, to practice generosity with a mind free from stinginess;
eighth, not to associate with those who engage in unrighteous conduct.
Ninth, one does not associate with unwholesome friends;
tenth, one is chaste and prudent, not becoming attached to women;
eleventh, upon hearing various words, one does not believe them all.
The twelfth is to cherish a good reputation and not covet material wealth;
the thirteenth is to abandon wrong views;
and the fourteenth is to practice constant generosity.
Fifteenth, speaking with loving words and elegant discourse;
sixteenth, speaking words that accord with reality;
seventeenth, among the assembly of ministers, neither promoting nor demoting anyone without cause or reason.
The eighteenth is to know the preferences and aversions of others;
the nineteenth is to regularly fix a specific time to see people frequently;
the twentieth is not to sleep or lie down excessively.
Twenty-first, he is always free from indolence;
twenty-second, his virtuous friends are steadfast;
twenty-third, he does not associate with any friends who are unbeneficial.
Twenty-fourth, being unmoved by anger or joy;
twenty-fifth, not craving food and drink;
twenty-sixth, having a mind of skillful reflection.
Twenty-seventh, he acts with composure without waiting for a later time;
twenty-eighth, he benefits the world through the Dharma;
twenty-ninth, he constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action.
The thirtieth is to have faith in causes and conditions;
the thirty-first is to constantly make offerings to the devas;
the thirty-second is to properly protect the kingdom.
Thirty-third, he correctly protects his wife and children;
thirty-fourth, he constantly cultivates wisdom;
thirty-fifth, he does not delight in sensory realms.
Thirty-sixth, he does not allow wicked people to dwell within his realm;
thirty-seventh, regarding all subjects, whether in terms of emoluments or rank, he bestows them according to the former laws.
These are called the thirty-seven dharmas.

If one accomplishes these thirty-seven dharmas, one is named a Kṣatriya Great King who has received his consecration; in the present life, he constantly attains peace and happiness, always possesses benefit, great wealth, and great joy, has abundant treasures, is able to protect the kingdom and protect himself, is praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in a good destination, becoming a Yāma King in the heavenly world.
Because of such thirty-seven factors as these, which serve as the causes for wholesome karma.
"What is meant by the purity of the military host of a Kṣatriya great king?
It refers to a virtuous mind that benefits others."
When adjudicating disputes according to the Dharma, he does not contravene the laws; he provides righteous protection in accordance with the Dharma, not violating fundamental principles.

With a loyal heart, he remonstrates with his sovereign; when the sovereign acts for the benefit [of the people], he complies with and accomplishes it, praising what is virtuous and protecting the nation according to the Dharma.
The teachings established are intended for benefit according to the proper measure; one should first give rise to a straightforward mind and not cause distress to others.
One should serve the master in accordance with the Dharma, rather than doing so merely out of fear of punishment.
His mind is free from greed and pride;

he accords with and does not oppose any phenomena. For the sake of future lives, he acts in accordance with the Dharma, fears birth and death, believes in the retribution of karma, abandons the three evil karmas, does not delight in excessive desire, takes no pleasure in inflicting punishment, and maintains right mindfulness without distraction.
In this way, both self and others can be delivered, and one is able to benefit the king.
If it is thus, such is the king’s army.

Since such an army is in harmony with the king, it causes the king to always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; it is able to protect the kingdom and protect his own person. He is praised by virtuous people, and when his body perishes and his life ends, he is reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
Because the entire host of troops is completely pure, it prevents the king from giving rise to evil thoughts; this is due to the cause of his wholesome karma.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has ascended the throne should diligently practice a second dharma, which, when accomplished and mastered, brings constant benefit in the present life, protects the kingdom, and protects himself. He is praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
What is the second?
It is the receiving of taxes in accordance with the law to provide for food and clothing.
How does one act in accordance with the law?
Whether it be a kingdom, a city, a village, a town, or a place where people gather, at all times he always takes [revenue] according to established custom and in accordance with reason.

Such being the king, when the kingdom is in ruin or during a celestial famine, he does not levy taxes; when he does take them, he does so with justice, without coercion or punishment, using the weights, measures, and cubits that have been traditionally used since ancient times, ensuring they are equitable and standard.

Receiving taxes in this manner—acting in accordance with the Dharma without contradiction, without coercion or punishment, and without encroachment or seizure—a king such as this is one who has compassion for all sentient beings.

If a king thus receives [taxes] in accordance with the Dharma, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he shall always attain peace and happiness and constant benefit in this present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is because of the cause of wholesome karma resulting from always receiving taxes and tributes in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has received his throne has a third dharma which he should diligently cultivate; when it is accomplished and correspondingly practiced, he will not oppress the realm, bringing benefit to both the present and future worlds.
What is the third?
It is to constantly maintain patience and remain free from anger,
thinking in one's mind as follows:
"Whatever causes or conditions may provoke my anger and resentment, I shall relinquish them all.
Although he possesses mastery over his own body, when he perceives the faults of others, he neither censures nor rebukes them.
Regarding ministers, kinsmen, and servants who have committed offenses, he does not impose severe punishments.
Toward those who are his enemies or those who are his friends, he does not speak of their faults nor of their evils.
If, when anger arises toward the military host, one then recollects patience;
because of recollecting patience, the angry mind is extinguished.
One speaks pleasant words and further utters other words, causing that military host to feel neither sorrow nor fear.

One is always patient toward all phenomena at all times; this patience is the patience of the true nature itself, not produced by causes and conditions. Thus one is without hatred and thus one is without resentment.

If a king maintains such a mind of patience, by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life and constantly receive benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
This is because he has cultivated the causal karma of always maintaining patience toward others.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has received his throne should diligently practice a fourth dharma; when it is accomplished and realized, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
What is the fourth? It is to adjudicate matters with impartiality and rectitude.

With a virtuous mind, the king treats all his subjects like his own parents; he does not adjudicate based on material gain, nor for the sake of utility, nor out of kinship, nor out of gratitude, nor out of friendship, nor because of the influence of the powerful or those who have made requests. Without employing any such motives, he adjudicates according to the Dharma, remaining unbiased and without partiality.
Toward those engaged in disputes, one should maintain equanimity toward both enemies and kin, speaking words that are beneficial and speaking words that are truthful.

If a king thus adjudicates matters with impartiality and integrity, by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life and always receive benefit. He shall not lose his kingdom nor his reputation; none among his entire army shall be subject to punishment. He will be able to protect his realm, need not fear the arguments of others, and other kings shall not prevail over him. He will rule as king for a long time, governing the kingdom and protecting himself. Praised by virtuous people, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly worlds, as a King of the Yāma Heaven.
Because one judges matters with a mind that is impartial and upright, due to the cause of wholesome karma.

"Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has ascended the throne possesses a fifth dharma which he should diligently cultivate; when it is accomplished and realized, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives, and likewise leads even unto Nirvāṇa."
What is the fifth?
It is the constant making of offerings to one's elders and superiors.
Who are these elders and superiors?

This refers to a venerable elder who perceives things as they truly are, upholds the precepts, acts with wisdom, and benefits sentient beings; who constantly performs wholesome deeds, remains perpetually serene in body, speech, and mind, and, being free from defilement in his own heart, causes others to gather merit.
The king should personally attend upon such elders and superiors.
Having attended upon them, he should listen to and hear the Dharma, constantly go to make offerings, receive what they have taught, and accept their instructions.
As it has been taught, the King should uphold it and act according to what was said.

By virtue of the merit from making offerings to one’s elders at all times, he will always attain peace and happiness in this present life and constantly experience benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a Yāma King in the heavenly realm.
This is due to the causal conditions of the wholesome karma of making offerings to one's elders and superiors at all times.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has received his position should diligently cultivate a sixth dharma; when it is accomplished and realized, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
What is the sixth? It is that which conforms to antiquity and is bestowed based on precedent.

Whether it was given by his father, or given by his grandfather, or even given by a more distant ancestor in former times—be it land, gold, silver, or other such things—the king who has ascended the throne receives them with an unclouded mind and a pure heart, following along with joy and delighting in that practice.
Thus, by following the precedent and praising the act as virtuous, he instructs others to give.

If the king acts in this way according to the former custom, through the causal conditions of such merit, he will always obtain peace and happiness in the present life and constantly receive benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
Because he constantly accords with tradition and relies upon the past to provide the causes for wholesome karma.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has ascended the throne possesses a seventh dharma which he should diligently cultivate; when perfected and brought into correspondence, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
What is the seventh?
It is so-called giving, with a mind free from stinginess. What is giving?

A donor is one who gives constantly throughout youth, adulthood, and old age; one who gives everything, giving in every way and at all times; one who benefits all, enriches all, and brings peace and happiness to all, always mindful of the various sufferings such as hunger and thirst endured within all realms of existence, including the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
When practicing generosity, one should make the aspiration that sentient beings in these three realms may quickly attain liberation and be reborn among humans and devas.
If a king acts in this way, he will obtain rewards in his present life.
What is the retribution manifest in this life? It is renown;
furthermore, when one encounters calamity, servants and military forces will not abandon or desert him.

People from other lands constantly come to make offerings to him; when others see this, they are unable to cause harm, and even all his enemies cannot find the slightest opportunity against him, for he is always victorious over them.
Giving in this manner yields rewards in the present life.

If giving even to those who are not fields of merit yields such present rewards, how much more so for giving excellent gifts with perfect intention to a field of merit? It constantly closes off the evil realms and ensures the constant reception of joyful retribution; thus, one bestows gifts in their immeasurable varieties.
What are these immeasurables?
They are the gift of Dharma, the gift of material goods, and the gift of fearlessness.

O King, through such various kinds of giving—whether giving to śramaṇas or giving to brāhmaṇas—the causal conditions of such meritorious giving result in constant peace and happiness, and perpetual benefit in this present life; one is able to protect the kingdom and protect oneself, is praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a good destination, as a Yāma king in the heavenly worlds.
This is due to the causal conditions of that wholesome karma of giving.

Furthermore, there is an eighth dharma that a Kṣatriya great king who has received his position should diligently abandon; by accomplishing its application, he will benefit both the present and future worlds.
What is the eighth? It is that those who do not practice according to the Dharma are not admitted; they are not allowed to remain in the kingdom.
Because the Kṣatriya king himself follows the practice of the Dharma, he does not admit those who do not practice according to the Dharma and does not allow them to dwell in the kingdom.
Who is called one who acts contrary to the Dharma?
It refers to someone who, by various means, plunders the property of others—such as by strangling their throat until they faint—and thereby takes those goods.
Or they may administer harmful drugs to render someone unconscious so as to take their property;
or they may employ various stratagems to steal another's goods;
or they may privately and secretly pilfer another's property.
Whether on the roads or in the marketplace, they employ various expedients to take the property of others;
they purchase the genuine to sell as counterfeit, using all manner of deception to seize the goods of others.

Furthermore, there may be those who are treacherous, deceitful, and unprincipled; they suppress the good and promote the evil, advance what is wrong and retreat from what is right, falsely accuse the virtuous and worthy, and take sides with the unworthy.
Some hold heterodox views, while others hold nihilistic views.
Furthermore, there are some who, through the suffering they inflict by killing sentient beings, hope to attain liberation;
or those who, at the feasts of non-Buddhists, slaughter sheep and other animals within great assemblies, hoping thereby to acquire merit.
Furthermore, there may be those who castrate sentient beings, rendering them impotent;
or those who commit sexual misconduct with men;
or those who are unable to provide for their parents, teachers, and elders.
Such persons as these should not be allowed to reside in the country. Why is this?
Because if they dwell together in the same land, they will cause the minds of virtuous people to become corrupted and lead them to emulate their habits.
Because they dwell together and because virtuous people are corrupted, they cause the king to become powerless and lose his sovereign authority.
Rain falls out of season, while it does not fall at the proper time;
when the five grains should ripen, the five grains do not ripen.
All lands are utterly destroyed because of the transgressions of wicked people.
For this reason, one does not allow wicked people to dwell within the country.
For this same reason, one does not include those who practice all manner of unlawful acts, nor does one allow them to reside in the country.
Those who act in accordance with the Dharma are gathered and brought into the kingdom.

Because the people of the Dharma are gathered, rain falls at the proper times, and the sun’s touch accords with the seasons; therefore, the five grains ripen excellently when their time comes, the land is not ruined, they are free from fear, and no sorrow arises.

Regarding all matters of benefit for the various lands, by the power of the causal conditions of gathering in those who uphold the Dharma, one is able to sever all the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death, causing those with merit to dwell within one's own land.
Because he is in the company of such persons of merit and those who practice the Dharma, he dwells in the foremost holy life, which is called "abiding.

A person of merit associates with other persons of merit and those who act in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, every wise king keeps those who practice the Dharma near him and causes them to dwell within his realm.

If a king does not thus fail to restrain those who act contrary to the Dharma, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he shall always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life and constantly receive benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is because he does not embrace the unrighteous conduct of those who perform such deeds due to the causes of his own wholesome karma.

Furthermore, a Kṣatriya great king who has received the throne should diligently abandon a ninth quality; by accomplishing and corresponding with it, he will benefit both the present and future worlds.
What is the ninth? It is that one does not associate with unwholesome friends.
An unwholesome friend is an evil friend; there are briefly eight kinds of such evil friends whom all kings should abandon.
What are the eight?
First is the view of nihilism, which refers to someone who thinks and says:
"There is no karma, there is no giving, there is no this world, and there is no other world."
This is the first evil friend. Furthermore, the second evil friend is one who thinks and says:
"Engaging in sexual intercourse with all women at the proper time does not violate the holy life (brahmacarya)."
Furthermore, the third type of evil friend is one who speaks with such a mind as this:
"If one burns [something] with fire, one will obtain great merit."
"If one gives to sentient beings, there will be no merit.
Furthermore, the fourth kind of evil friend is one who speaks with such a mind, saying:
"As long as one has not yet died, and while life still remains, one is called a human being."

If, after the body has died, all wholesome and unwholesome karmas are entirely lost—like clouds blown away by the wind such that nothing further can accumulate—then sentient beings would likewise possess neither sin nor merit.
Furthermore, the fifth kind of evil friend is one who constantly instructs others to destroy their parents and likewise refuses to allow them to make offerings to their elders and superiors.
Furthermore, the sixth type of evil associate is as follows: there are those who say that killing is virtuous;

they claim that by taking the lives of the elderly, the blind, those with malignant diseases, or those who have been ill for a long time, one will be reborn in a happy realm because of having deprived them of life.
Furthermore, the seventh kind of evil friend is one who speaks with such thoughts as these:

"By throwing oneself down from a mountain precipice, or by burning one's body with fire, or by starving oneself to death, or by roasting one's body with fires at the five locations [of the sense organs], one attains immeasurable merit through such a death; subsequently, one will be reborn in heaven, where one will be served by immeasurable retinues and immeasurable celestial maidens."
Furthermore, the eighth type of evil friend is one who thinks and says:
"Everything is determined by fate; it is not the result of karmic retribution."
Regarding these eight kinds of evil associates, one shall not permit them to dwell within the realm, nor even cast a glance upon them.
One should instead gather only those who speak words of truth; from such persons as these, one should hear the True Dharma, and having heard it, one should grasp it, uphold it, and practice it.
