If a king does not associate with any unwholesome friends in this manner, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always experience peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is because he did not associate with unwholesome friends due to the cause of his wholesome karma.

Furthermore, there is a tenth quality that a Kṣatriya great king who has received his throne should diligently abandon; when he achieves and accords with this, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
What is the tenth thing that should be abandoned?
What dharma is to be abandoned? It is women.
A person of wisdom does not belong to women; among all those in the world who belong to women, they are the most base and vulgar.
If other ordinary people who belong to women are already considered base and vulgar, how much more so is this true for a king, the foremost among men?
All women are capable of bringing about destruction; all lands, all peoples, and all kings are brought to ruin because of women.
Because of a greedy mind, it causes kings and others to lose all benefit, robs them of their possessions, leads them to practice what is unrighteous, and prevents them from practicing charity.
Because of a greedy mind, it causes kings and others to become entirely indolent.
Because of their lustful desires, they constantly remain close and never depart, causing men to lose their own benefit.
Women are like hailstones, capable of destroying the sprouts of virtue.
All women delight in divisive speech and are repositories of pride and envy.
One who is bound to women acts like a woman;
one who is bound to women loses his kingdom as well.
Therefore, one should not be bound to women, for if one is bound to women, he becomes vulgar and base, since the nature of women is base and evil.
To be dependent on women is likewise base and evil.
One who is dependent on women loses all dharmas;
one who is dependent on women constantly enters into states of suffering.
If they belong to women, virtuous people abandon them.
Because of the faults of desire, such persons are deceived by women.

All women deceive and oppress those who are weak; for such is their very nature. They are ungrateful for kindness received, capable of inflicting decline and distress, and full of greed, envy, and jealousy.
Women are thus entirely untrustworthy.

If one is under the sway of women, that person becomes the most base and vulgar among all people in cities and villages; how much more so for a king, whose loss would be even deeper. Therefore, one should not be dependent upon women.

If a king thus fears the faults of women, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is because he has abandoned the causes of unwholesome karma associated with women.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the eleventh, which you should diligently cultivate and bring to fulfillment; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The eleventh is this: one does not believe everything one hears when it is spoken.
The minds of people in all the world are diverse; they mutually destroy one another, for their nature delights in destruction.
They can be destroyed while being formed, and they can be destroyed once they have been completed.
They are ruined because their intrinsic nature and essence are defiled; they are mutually destroyed because they constantly delight in contention;
and they destroy one another because of their close intimacy.
Their own essence is destroyed due to the faults of their realm; for this reason, they are destroyed.
Because of the causes and conditions of self-deprecation, they mutually destroy one another.
They speak in secret to one another, each seeking to clarify themselves; therefore, they destroy one another.
Desiring to excel themselves and cause others to fall short, they thus engage in mutual destruction.
The King did not believe such words, for they contravene reason and are internally inconsistent.
Because they arrive in succession with malicious intent, and because they speak thus out of partiality for their own faction;

having been previously instructed, or having arrived on a prior commission, or having come as former benefactors, or having come as former enemies, they mutually destroy one another and report it to the king.
These and other such preceding causes and conditions were spoken because of mutual animosity;
since the king does not trust them universally, the kingdom is therefore not destroyed.

Such a king is fundamentally good-natured; he is neither contrary nor disordered, feeling anger only in accordance with reason and never out of caprice. Regarding divisive speech, his mind does not give rise to belief.

That king himself possesses such virtues; he does not rely on others but follows what his own mind delights in. He has little anger, and all sentient beings love and revere him. His mind is skillful in reflection, he acts in accordance with the Dharma, his intentions are upright, and he governs many provinces and territories.

If a king does not believe everything in this way, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is because they do not universally believe in the causes of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another twelfth quality which you should diligently cultivate and practice in accordance with its perfection; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twelfth is as follows: it means loving a good reputation and not coveting wealth or goods.

Because the king’s mind does not covet wealth or goods, he does not clench his fists, does not knit his brows or contort his face, does not glare with anger from his eyes, and does not speak harsh words. His mind never becomes angry without cause, nor does his mind ever become joyful without cause; his mental disposition is firm and stable.
If a king thus attains a good reputation, he will also acquire wealth.
Having acquired it in this way, he does not take great delight in that wealth.
Because he has gained renown, his mind is filled with superior joy; he is not obstructed by royal law, all people love him, and enemies find no opportunity against him.
Because of having abundant wealth, there are furthermore ten causes and conditions by which one attains a fine reputation. What are these ten?
First, pleasant speech;...
Second, the ability to relinquish;
third, thorough discernment; fourth, being visited by people from distant lands;
and fifth, attaining peace and happiness upon approaching it.
Sixth, to provide timely alms to those around him;
seventh, to respectfully honor and offer what is needed to the venerable, to support virtuous people, and to rescue the orphaned and the solitary;
eighth, to practice pure conduct;
Ninth is a benevolent mind, not troubling or disturbing others;
tenth is right view, not giving rise to false views.
Having attained these ten dharmas, one practices such dharmas oneself and further teaches others to practice such dharmas.
Because one attains this Dharma through such conduct, one gains a good reputation.

If a king thus cherishes a good reputation and does not crave wealth and goods, then by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life, always find benefit, and act in accordance with the Dharma. Others cannot overcome him, and when strangers approach him, they too shall obtain peace and happiness.

That person shall serve as a king among men for a long time, able to protect the kingdom and able to protect himself; praised by virtuous people, at the dissolution of the body after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
Because one delights in a good reputation rather than in the causes of wholesome karma, such as the non-greed for wealth and material goods.
"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another thirteenth quality which you should diligently abandon; by achieving its opposite, you will benefit both the present and future lives."
The thirteenth is the relinquishing of false views.
False views are called the root of all sentient beings' lack of peace and security.
This perverted view leads one to have no faith in any causes and conditions whatsoever.
That which is a ground for lack of faith is detested by all and censured by all; therefore, the king should abandon it.
If the king does not abandon it, he practices wrong views; he will be detested by all people, distrusted by all, and no one at all will act in accordance with him.
Because they do not practice in accordance with the Dharma, all people abandon them; when they encounter decline and affliction, even the devas who follow the Dharma completely forsake them.
Once the devas have departed, they are left powerless to act.

Therefore, a king should abandon wrong views. If a king possesses such right view and is not mistaken, by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always attain peace and happiness in the present life and constantly receive benefit. He will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself; he will be praised by virtuous people and perform true benefit at all times. He will be honored by all people and loved by all; the deities who dwell according to the Dharma will never abandon him, and all the people of the land will act in accordance with the king’s intentions. He will fully attain all discernment and all mental aspirations.

That king, his mind naturally undisturbed, was able to rule over the kingdom for a long time in peace and security, free from affliction; at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world as a King of the Yāma devas.
This is because of the wholesome karmic cause of abandoning wrong views.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the fourteenth, which, when accomplished and maintained, brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The fourteenth is the mundane dharma, the supramundane dharma, and the fundamental dharma of kings, namely, generosity (*dāna*).

If a king or his ministers practice generosity, all the people of the nation will respect and love them without abandoning them; they will give rise to reverence in their hearts and will not leave that country to go to other lands.
If people from other countries, because the king is able to practice generosity, all come to take refuge in him— along with their wives, children, and military hosts—
the population of the king’s own country will increase even further due to this influx of many people, such that other nations will be unable to destroy it.
Because there are many people, none are able to destroy it.
Such a giver, through this worldly gift, attains the foremost peace and security within the world.

Furthermore, there is yet another gift that is supramundane and the most excellent of gifts: if a person practices such giving, they will be taken into the care of the devas, possessing great power and great majesty.
By giving to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and others, one adorns the future and possesses a beautiful complexion in the present. Why is this?
Because the mind is pure, the food is pure.
Because one's food is pure, one's facial complexion is pure;
because one's facial complexion is pure, one is upright and pleasing to behold.
All of these are the power of giving, and furthermore, there is a dharma that yields its fruit in the present life.

What is the retribution received in the present life? It is as follows: namely, practicing giving with a mind free from arrogance; being devoid of greed and envy; having faith in causes and conditions; believing in the cause, believing in the retribution, and believing in future lives; making offerings to one's elders and superiors; possessing a supple and gentle mind; reflecting with right intention; relinquishing various kinds of things; gathering the causes for great wealth; gathering the state of being free from stinginess and envy; and having faith in the field of merit, the virtues of the field of merit, and the seeds sown in the field of merit.

If a king thus perfumes his mind with such virtuous speech, through the causal conditions of this foremost merit of a pure mind, he will always attain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself. He will be praised by virtuous people, and as a long-reigning king, he will lead his kingdom for a long time and enjoy happiness. His realm will not be in disorder but will remain perpetually peaceful and secure, free from fear and anxiety. When his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is because of the causal power of the wholesome karma of being able to practice generosity.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the fifteenth, which you should diligently cultivate; when accomplished and mastered, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The fifteenth is the diligent practice of loving speech (*priyavāditā*).
One who is a king of loving speech is loved by all and approached by all.
Even if one were to bestow material wealth, one could not attract and sustain sentient beings in such a manner.
Regarding such pleasant speech, there is nothing else that can bring about such joy and purity as pleasant speech.
It is for this reason and through these causes and conditions that one speaks with pleasant speech toward all sentient beings.
First the mind of love arises, and only then are words uttered; for this reason, one speaks kind words with the mouth.
A king such as this is able to seize the cities and kingdoms of others, while his own kingdom and city cannot be taken by others; he is beloved by all people.
If the King speaks with truthful words interspersed with affectionate speech, even his enemies will become his close friends, let alone neutral persons or those who were originally his kin.

If the King speaks such loving words, by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness in this present life and constantly receive benefit. His enemies will become his friends, and he will not remain neutral; he will be beloved by all people and receive offerings from all. He will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, praised by virtuous men, and shall rule as king over all people for a long time. At the dissolution of the body after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a Yama King in the celestial world.
This is due to the cause of that wholesome karma of pleasant speech.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the sixteenth, which you should diligently cultivate and bring to fulfillment; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The sixteenth is the cultivation of truthful speech.

Truthful speech is called the cause for liberation from all birth and death; it does not require purchase with material goods and can never be exhausted. It is a great treasury that no one can plunder; it arises within the ocean of the mind, is foremost among things difficult to perceive, is praised by all virtuous people, and flows forth in succession throughout all worlds.

This Dharma is the gateway to the city of Nirvana; it can never be exhausted throughout all time, increasing merit and virtue, able to extinguish all faults, trusted by all people, and capable of eliminating poverty.

If one can speak truthful words, then even if they are otherwise ugly or deformed, they will be the most excellent among all those who are handsome and well-proportioned, for they adorn themselves with the radiance of truth.
If those of all low castes can speak the truth, they will surpass all people of high caste.
Such truthful speech adorns one’s lineage; all people will trust them, all people will draw near to them, and all people will look upon them as they would a brother.
Wherever he travels, in each and every place he is honored by people as no different from a father, a mother, or a king.
Even when traveling through wildernesses and perilous, evil places, he still experiences joy.
Whichever country he traveled to, he was honored by the king as if he were the king’s own master.
Whether in villages, cities, or populous settlements, all the people and great elders provided him with offerings.
In all other lands where he does not travel, his fame spreads everywhere; the people there speak thus:
"Whether it be the king or the king’s ministers there, their truthful speech and virtuous conduct are like a tall banner or pennant, and their renown reaches the six heavens."
That son of good family is constantly provided for by devas who follow him; he does not see evil dreams.
As for the foremost and most excellent deva, he honors him as one would a celestial being.
If one becomes poor again, by virtue of truthful speech, one will later become wealthy once more.
One will fully attain all that is remembered.
Though aging gradually with every thought-moment, the faculties will not decline.
Having attained excellent supernormal powers and a body of great strength, one performs the karma of longevity, achieving it in accordance with reality.
In all disputes and confrontations, this shall serve as the standard and this shall serve as the testimony.
If one has been arrested and bound for violating the king’s law, this person alone is the most trustworthy to whom one may entrust goods.
Thus, when the wealthy entrust their property to him, his mind remains unshakable because of his truthful speech.
Neither enemies nor kin can cause them to waver; they find delight solely in the true nature of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), giving rise to a heart of joy.
Sustained by the food of truthful speech, they remain fully satiated.
Constantly contemplating the love of truthful speech, his mind remains unmoved whether by anger or joy.

This king is the foremost of great seers (*maharṣi*); he constantly brings about the two kinds of benefit—worldly and supramundane—and never deviates from what he has undertaken. He is like a true painting; he is always purified by bathing with the water of truth, and he always wears fresh white garments of precious fabric, free of even a single thread of impurity.
The fragrance of their true names is smelled throughout the ten directions.
All those in the world who have not yet met them become their friends; how much more so for those who have seen them? Their good reputation spreads far beyond the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
Although he is young, when the elderly see him, they honor him as if he were their father.

Because he is truly old, he is even able to perform the karma for long life, up to and including the karma for the great wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi; how much more so could he perform the karma for the world of the King of the Yāma Heaven?

If a king practices such truthful speech, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a Yāma King in the heavenly world.
This is due to the cause of having cultivated the wholesome karma of truthful speech.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the seventeenth, which you should diligently cultivate and bring to fulfillment; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The seventeenth is this: regarding his ministers, if there is no cause or reason, he neither promotes nor demotes them.
This is a mark of the king’s gravity; yet if that king does not understand the outward signs of others' discipline nor their inner intentions, then trust will not arise.
The law for a king is this:
he should deliberate with careful attention before acting.
If a king does not first reflect deeply and minutely regarding his ministers and subjects—whether to demote them or promote him—he is no king at all.
If one acts as a king, his reign will not endure for long; he may possess only the title of "king" alone.

Lacking reflection in his actions, his mind moves but little, and his thoughts are frivolous and unstable. When the ancient laws are proclaimed, the multitude does not believe them, claiming instead that the king speaks falsely. Consequently, they do not conceive affection for the king, and may even replace him on the throne with another person.
Therefore, once a king has recognized these faults, he shall not utter false speech.
Such lying brings no benefit in the present or the future; thus, it entails immeasurable kinds of faults in the present life.
Having recognized these faults, one should not speak falsely.
If others do so, it is likewise improper; how much more so for a king? In this way and that way he loses the royal dharma, and in this way and that way he also loses the world.
If a king possesses merit, he excels all worldly people; thus, he excels in every respect.
When a king always speaks the truth, he protects the world; because he protects their happiness, his royal dharma does not cause obstruction.
All wholesome dharmas have truthfulness as their very foundation.
If one does not speak truthfully, then among the assembly of ministers there will be no grounds for either promotion or demotion.
If one always speaks the truth, then among the officials there will be no grounds for either promotion or demotion when such grounds do not exist.
If the king acts in this way, he will remain unshaken and secure in his royal station. When all his ministers know that the king is thus, they will not abandon him to go to other lands;
instead, they will develop deep respect for him as for a father or a mother, finding joy at all times and giving rise to a heart of gladness.
That king possesses a firm mind and a settled mind; he has an unshakable mind and a focused mind, and he delights his assembly of ministers.

If a king is thus—not acting without cause or condition, whether in raising or lowering [his hand]—then by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he shall always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life. He is able to protect his kingdom and protect himself; praised by virtuous people, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world as a King of the Yāma devas.
This is because there is no cause or condition for them to be raised up or lowered, due to the causal nature of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the eighteenth, which you should diligently cultivate and practice in accordance with its fulfillment; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The eighteenth refers to being able to discern the good and evil of others.
Because this great wisdom has been cultivated repeatedly, one who possesses such knowledge is the foremost and most excellent of great kings.
If a king knows whether a person is wise or unwise, and knows them in this way, he becomes a vessel for all the lands of the world; as a ruler, no other kings will be able to destroy him.

If one applies oneself diligently to what is to be done, establishing and directing others according to their appropriate stations, then all such undertakings will achieve success and no wealth or property will be lost.
In the dharmas one performs, there will be progressive increase.
If the king observes that among his subjects there are those who act contrary to the Dharma,

he does not include them in his protection. Those who are greedy for food, those who are ungrateful, those who are hated by many, those with false views, those lacking compassion, those who speak falsehoods,

those who are enemies of other kings, those of evil discipline, those who do not know the proper time, those who are difficult to subdue, those who constantly perform evil deeds, those who are attached to sensory objects, those who speak based on crooked causes, those whose very nature is never satisfied, those who constantly fail to practice beneficial conduct, those who always initiate evil toward others first, those who are arrogant, those who always delight in enmity, those who are impulsive, those whose speech is restless, and those whose minds are restless— such persons as these, the king does not include in his protection.
Whom does it encompass?
It encompasses those who practice in accordance with the Dharma, those who are not deceitful, those who are not arrogant, those who speak truthfully,
those who are wise and intelligent, those whose minds are gentle, those who do not afflict others, and those who...
Deceiving others; [deceiving] those who are able to make offerings to the Triple Gem, those who have attained faith, those who are content,
those who are self-disciplined, those who are not indolent, those who constantly perform their duties,
those who eat little, all those who are beloved, those with a mind of loving-kindness, those with a mind of compassion, and those who are diligent.
Such a person is one of right view, one possessed of wisdom, one who relies on the Dharma and Vinaya, one whose body, speech, and mind have been pure from birth,
one who believes in causes and conditions, one who understands karmic retribution, one who does not drink alcohol, one who does not sleep excessively,
one who associates with virtuous friends, one who delights in giving, and one who possesses the precepts.
Regarding such people—those who possess wisdom—the king should include them among his retinue.
Within this group, the king should discern their relative capacities, both light and heavy, and assign them to whatever tasks they are fit to perform.
That king was such that no other king could destroy him; he was fully endowed with immeasurable wealth, treasures, and prosperity, and he acted in accordance with the Dharma.
Because he acted in accordance with the Dharma, he was able to practice generosity, perform meritorious deeds, and make offerings to the Triple Gem.

If a king thus understands the good and evil of people and the causes and conditions of their merit, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is because it enables one to discern the causes of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the nineteenth, which you should diligently cultivate; when perfected and brought into accord, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The nineteenth [quality] refers to always seeing the multitude at fixed times.

If a Kṣatriya king always sees the multitude at fixed times, such a king will remain king for a long duration; all the people of the land will harbor no resentment against him. He can discern the good and evil of all people and cause all the people of the land to practice the Dharma. The strong do not oppress the weak, and all the people of the land see the king at appropriate times, their wealth and resources being fully provided.

By these skillful means, because his wealth and Dharma riches increase and flourish, he is not subject to other kings; because of his peace and security, he accords with the practice of the Dharma, making offerings to śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, and hearing the Dharma from them.

Having heard the Dharma, their practice of the Dharma becomes increasingly superior; because they see people more frequently at certain times due to their meditative concentration, their cultivation of the practice of the Dharma becomes further enhanced and more excellent.
In this way, through practicing in accordance with the Dharma, their wealth and happiness increase accordingly.
Because of great wealth and happiness, one is able to practice great generosity, extensively perform meritorious deeds, and diligently uphold the precepts.
If a king is difficult to see, he will lack such virtues; therefore, a king should establish a fixed time for being seen by the people at all times.
If a king can regularly fix upon one specific time each day to see his people, he will be able to practice the Dharma; such a practitioner of the Dharma possesses great merit and virtue.

If a king thus regularly fixes upon one specific time to see the multitude, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
This is because, through the power of meditative concentration, he frequently perceives the causes of the virtuous karma of the multitude.

"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma that is the twentieth, which you should diligently cultivate and practice so as to achieve its correspondence; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives."
The twentieth is having little sleep.
Because one sleeps little, the mind reflects well; the intellect is not errant, nor is it deluded or dull. Enemies find no opportunity, and one remains constantly single-minded.
Because his actions are determined and he acts with determination, he acts with wise reflection.
If a king acts with such wise reflection, whatever dharma he pursues will all be swiftly accomplished without taking a long time.
That king, being diligent from the early morning, enjoys a long life because of his diligence.
Because he reflects well, the hearts of all the people in the kingdom admire and delight in him, never giving rise to weariness or aversion.
The people within the realm, all the military forces, all the servants, the officials high and low, and the various great ministers were all exceedingly numerous and flourishing.
Because wealth and resources are abundant and subjects and citizens are numerous, there is an abundance of wealth;
because there is an abundance of wealth, one possesses great majesty and virtue;
because one possesses majesty and virtue, one is able to practice giving and cultivate meritorious deeds, and is able to maintain the precepts well.

If a king thus has little sleep due to the power of his merit, he will constantly experience peace and happiness and always find benefit in this present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is due to the cause of the wholesome karma of having little sleep.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another dharma, the twenty-first, which you should diligently cultivate; when accomplished and mastered, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-first is to be constantly free from indolence at all times.
A king who is not indolent possesses firm diligence; he cultivates his undertakings in accordance with the Dharma, and whatever he does, he is able to bring it all to ultimate completion.
Controlling them according to his will, they all come under his command; others cannot destroy them, nor can others take them away.
All the people of the kingdom love the king’s mind and heart, and they all give rise to reverence and respect for him.
The king’s realm was entirely excellent and fully endowed with all things.
Whether cities, villages, or populous settlements, they filled the entire country, leaving no space empty or desolate between them.
The King who is untiring, firm in his diligence, and possesses great power—whatever he undertakes in such a manner, all those undertakings will be fully accomplished.
Why is this? Because they are free from indolence;
they are fully endowed with skillful means regarding the Dharma, the time, the place, and so forth.
The King of Non-laxity is able to accomplish all mundane and supramundane deeds, even unto the deed of nirvāṇa, let alone other deeds.

If one applies oneself with diligence and without indolence, employing skillful means regarding time and place, and brings all that is to be done to completion, that king will surpass all other people, being fully endowed with every excellence.
That king thus accomplished all that is to be done in the world; through such wisdom, he was further able to perform supramundane deeds, all of which he fully accomplished.
"Supramundane" refers to generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom.

If a king is thus constantly diligent, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always enjoy peace and happiness in the present life and always receive benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, praised by virtuous people. With generosity, morality, wisdom, and so forth being like a fragrant scent, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
Due to the cause of non-laxity in wholesome karma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 54. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 55.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Thirty-Four: Yāma Heaven, Section Twenty.

"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the twenty-second, which you should diligently cultivate and bring into correspondence; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives. What is this dharma? It is the practice of constant mindfulness toward all sentient beings."
Twenty-second: firmness in virtuous friends.
A king whose friends are firm acts with wise reflection; having long served as king, he remains far removed from all faults and cannot be undermined by others.

Just as a tree with many roots that grow long and penetrate deep becomes firm, well-established, unshakable, and cannot be destroyed by the wind—just as that sturdy tree cannot be destroyed by the wind, so too is the king:
his friends are steadfast, possessing good hearts and kind intentions; he is beloved by all people and is held in common reverence.
“Within the worldly dharmas, there are thirteen kinds of qualities possessed by a virtuous friend who is firm and indestructible.
What are these thirteen?
First, they possess excellent knowledge; if the king commits any wrong, they are able to purify him.”
Second, he is capable; though the task be most difficult, he is able to perform it for the king.
Third, he possesses wisdom; if that good friend has other good friends, he causes them to become his friends as well.
Fourth is the exhaustion of the mind: all of one's wealth and possessions are known by virtuous friends.
Fifth is the exhaustion of intention: knowing that there is beneficial work to be done for virtuous friends, one applies oneself with diligent effort.
Sixth, the mind is expansive; upon suddenly meeting [the object], one does not restrain one's deportment.
Seventh, it is ultimate; even if one encounters decline and affliction, or even the loss of life, one does not abandon it.
Eighth, being agreeable: according to what the mind requires, one acts in accordance with that mind.
Ninth, being non-concealing: whatever the household possesses, nothing is hidden; according to what is required, one does not begrudge those who ask.
Tenth is shared intention: if one sees that a virtuous friend possesses many excellences, one gives rise to joy.
Eleventh: if one encounters suffering and affliction, one shares in that suffering; even if the other becomes greatly angry, one’s own mind does not change;
whatever food is available, one eats it all together, and one plays and sports together.
Twelfth, regarding all possessions, one does not seek them with inferior faculties;
if one possesses things oneself, one gives them away without seeking to do so with hardship.
Thirteenth, if one knows the news within the household—whether good or bad, even including disputes—one speaks of all such matters completely, without hesitation or reluctance.
They speak exhaustively of all matters, from domestic affairs to disputes.
A virtuous friend endowed with these thirteen merits is thus a true friend in the world.

"Thus, the world possesses thirteen such virtuous friends endowed with merit; if a king achieves even one, he will possess great power, let alone many. Therefore, O Wise King, you should diligently cultivate and gather such virtuous friends."
If the King diligently associates with such virtuous friends, all his desired undertakings will be fully accomplished.
Furthermore, by means of these virtuous friends, he will also be able to achieve the supramundane path.
To speak briefly, there are ten qualities possessed by a virtuous friend.
What are these ten? First, they are able to restrain one from unrighteous conduct.
Second, they are able to teach the practice of giving;
third, they are able to teach the receiving and maintaining of precepts;
fourth, they demonstrate wisdom and are able to teach the cultivation of wisdom.
Fifth is a benevolent mind, which prevents one from associating with evil friends;
sixth is right faith, which demonstrates the retribution of karmic actions;
seventh is, when seeing others deluded on evil paths, teaching them to abide in the good path.
Eighth, when seeing those who have violated the precepts, one is able to eliminate their transgressions;
ninth, one instructs them to make offerings to their parents;
tenth, one constantly and repeatedly provides them with instruction and admonition.
These ten kinds of supramundane spiritual friends can protect one from all evil realms, just like parents.
They are steadfast spiritual friends who always remain as such spiritual friends.
If one has virtuous friends, one does not give rise to a mind of arrogance.
Such virtuous friends belong not to the present life, but to future lives; therefore, a king should remain steadfast in his friendship with the virtuous.

If a king is thus firm in his virtuous friends, then by the causal conditions of the merit of cultivating wholesome deeds, he will constantly obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is because of the causes of firm, wholesome, and virtuous karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another twenty-third quality which you should diligently abandon; by being accomplished in its opposite, it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-third is what is called not associating with unbeneficial friends.
Those who are said to be unbeneficial are all those who are deceptive and delusive.
One should not associate with any gamblers or those who lead others to perform evil deeds.
If one engages in evil reflection and acts upon it, associating with such a person brings great disadvantage and results in immense loss.
Among all losses, the greatest is that of being deceived and deluded.
There are two kinds of deception:
first, that which is private;
second, that which is public.
That which is "public" refers to various forms of deception, such as gambling and the like.
That which is "private" refers to the fraudulent assumption of appearances and dress, resembling an evil person; those who lack discernment perceive this as being good.

Such persons as these are categorized among the heterodox; they are true heterodox practitioners, thorns to the heterodox fold, who deceive their own kin and likewise deceive others. Having no fear of future worlds, they manifest the appearance of virtue while being, in reality, great thieves.
One should not even look upon such persons, nor should one speak with them, much less associate with them as friends;
virtuous people should abandon them.
Such individuals cannot even benefit themselves, let alone others.
A king should abandon such unwholesome teachers and useless friends; he should not associate with any who are deceptive or delusive, nor with any who are addicted to gambling.
One should not associate with such persons; rather, one should act with right mindfulness and act with right reflection.

O King, if you associate with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), practice their conduct, and are perfumed by them, through the causal conditions of these merits, you will constantly obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in this present life. You will be able to protect the kingdom and protect yourself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, as a Yāma king in the heavenly world.
This is because of the karmic cause of not associating with those who are unbeneficial friends.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another twenty-fourth quality which you should diligently cultivate; when accomplished and mastered, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-fourth is what is called being unshakable by anger or joy.

If a Kṣatriya king can maintain equanimity toward both anger and joy, his kingdom will be firm and indestructible; all the people of the nation will be devoted to happiness, feeling no weariness or aversion, and no one will be able to destroy it or find an opportunity for harm.

If the king does not act out of anger, but acts after careful reflection, he will not dismiss a person from their position without due consideration or without cause, nor will he promote them to office or grant them wealth and benefits without cause.
Because he is without anger, his secret words are not revealed.
He does not disparage others without cause;
even in a state of joy, his mind does not become arrogant.
Such a king possesses sincerity of heart; he commits no evil deeds, does not harbor wicked people, and maintains a mind of impartiality and gravity.
Thus, within the laws of the world, that king remains unmoved by anger or joy, and attains peace and security.
How, furthermore, can one remain unmoved by anger and joy regarding the supramundane path and thereby attain tranquility?
If a king does not become angry, he is able to maintain the single defilement of birth and death;
if a king does not become joyful, he is able to maintain the defilement of power.
That king was thus able to maintain the stain of power and the stain of birth-and-death.
If a person can maintain these two stains, that person is then able to maintain the stain of the power of delusion.

If a king is thus able to maintain these three purities, possessing wisdom, patience, and firm resolve, and having a determined mind, then through the causal conditions of such merit, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
Because of the causes of wholesome karma that remain unmoved by anger or joy.
"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another dharma, the twenty-fifth, which you should diligently cultivate and bring to fulfillment; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives."
The twenty-fifth is what is called non-attachment to the two things of food and drink, and not being excessively greedy for them. Why is this?
Because if one is excessively greedy for food and drink, it is an impediment to a king, as he would constantly be mindful of food and drink remaining within his belly.
The people of those lands and the troops on both sides felt revulsion and contempt, thinking to themselves:
"That king’s mind is just like that of a beast; apart from eating and drinking, he has no other intention and no other karmic intent."

Constantly thus craving and delighting in food and drink, because his mind is always attached to the flavors of food and drink, he does not contemplate what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; he is unable to deliberate upon or calculate the affairs of the kingdom; he does not contemplate the people, nor can he discipline the various military forces of his inner and outer retinues; he cannot bestow official ranks and titles upon his ministers and all the citizens in due order according to their merit; and he lacks knowledge of the relative importance of the tasks at hand.
The king's wealth and possessions will only diminish.
Because his wealth diminishes, he will have little property.
Because his property is meager, his food and drink will be exhausted.
Because they lack food and drink, all people despise them.
Because of their craving for food and drink, they fall into poverty.
By craving excessive food and drink and failing to exercise self-restraint, kings thus obstruct the welfare of the world.
What, furthermore, constitutes an obstacle to the supramundane?

It refers to a mind that is greedily attached, delighting in abundant food and drink, constantly craving various flavors, and engaging in improper reflection; such a mind is unable to maintain mindfulness of the body, unable to maintain mindfulness of feelings, unable to maintain mindfulness of the mind, and unable to maintain mindfulness of phenomena; it fails to contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and is likewise unable to contemplate anything else whatsoever.
Thus, those who are greedily attached to the objects of food and drink are no different from animals; there is no distinction between them.

Therefore, one should act in accordance with the principles of reason: consume food and drink appropriately, engage in appropriate conduct, speak appropriate words, purify the sense faculties, move about as is fitting, and contemplate the Noble Path—the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena, and suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Thus, with the mind well-tamed within these dharmas, one is able to contemplate and reflect.
Because the mind possesses right mindfulness, the faculties become increasingly pure; through appropriate food and drink, the body becomes balanced;
and because the body is balanced, the mind also becomes harmonious and compliant.
Because the mind is disciplined and compliant, one is able to recollect wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, one should not be attached to various flavors.
If food and drink are taken into the body, they will lead to peace and security when they are balanced and appropriate; thus, one should always practice in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, that king is able to subdue his mind; with a subdued mind, he possesses right mindfulness. Because his mind is possessed of right mindfulness, he is able to perform wholesome deeds.

If the king is thus free from greed for food and drink, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will constantly obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, praised by virtuous people. When his body perishes at the end of life, the wholesome karma he has cultivated will be like a fragrance as he is reborn in a good realm, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is due to the cause of wholesome karma consisting of non-attachment to the two flavors of food and drink.

"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another dharma, the twenty-sixth, which you should diligently cultivate; when accomplished and brought into correspondence, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives."
The twenty-sixth is called "skillful reflection.
A king who practices skillful reflection will attain all matters of security, both mundane and supramundane.
Why is this? It is because of the merit of the mind.

One who practices right reflection will always obtain supreme happiness in the present life or in future lives; whatever matter they undertake, if they act with right reflection, there will be no faults.
He thought thus: "The defilements such as greed constantly lead one along evil paths; they must be completely extinguished.

One should eliminate the defilement of greed by means of the dharma of impurity, the defilement of hatred by means of the dharma of loving-kindness and compassion, and the defilement of delusion by means of the dharma of contemplative wisdom."
Thus, all these are extinguished by means of wholesome mental reflection (*citta-saṃkalpa*), and cannot be extinguished by unwholesome intention.
If one engages in evil reflection, one cannot accomplish even worldly dharmas;
it is only through wholesome reflection that one can achieve accomplishment.
Therefore, you should know that all phenomena are accomplished when one practices them with right reflection.

If a king reflects well in this manner, through the causal conditions of such merit, he will always attain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
This is because of his skillful reflection on the causes of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another twenty-seventh quality which you should diligently cultivate and bring into accord with yourself; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-seventh is to act with composure without waiting for a specific time.
Whether performing worldly or supramundane beneficial deeds, if one acts only after a long delay, it is not possible to accomplish them.
That which ought not to be done yet is done will not succeed.
It is like having an illness that is not treated promptly; if it is treated only after a long delay, it becomes incurable.
Because it is incurable, it can kill the person.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable ritual procedures that are not performed promptly, but are instead delayed for a long time; such acts are difficult to perform, impossible to perform, and cannot be accomplished, and they thus obstruct the supramundane path.
Even minor afflictions are like that illness; because they are not treated promptly, the afflictions are not severed.
Because they are not severed, one enters the evil realms.
This becomes a great calamity over a long period, thus obstructing the supramundane path.

Because even minor afflictions are not severed at the proper time, they gradually increase like the sprouts of poison; over a long period, they grow until they consume the entire body and cause sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. Therefore, one should not wait calmly for a long time before acting.
Thus, whether it be a king, other persons, monks, laypeople, the very wealthy, or the poor, none should wait calmly for a long time before acting.

If a person waits for a long time before acting, that person commits a transgression and swiftly incurs decline and affliction; even after a long period has passed, they cannot eliminate it, cannot destroy it, and cannot sever it;
because it is not severed, they themselves undergo decline and affliction.
If a person does not contemplate [the nature of things] but acts only after a long time, they will quickly fall into ruin, with their very roots utterly uprooted.
Because such a person is free from those faults, they will ultimately attain happiness, abiding in both the worldly path and the supramundane path.
If such a person passes beyond their initial birth, they will be able to eliminate [these afflictions] immediately, just as one who sees a sprout of poison can remove it as soon as it appears.
That sprout of poison is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*); if left for long, they increase, and once born, they become numerous.
Therefore, if one eliminates the fault of beginning anew, that constitutes true knowledge; such a person attains peace and security and dwells in constant joy.

O King, if you act with such composure and without waiting for a later time, through the causal conditions of this merit, you will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life. You will be able to protect the kingdom and protect yourself; praised by virtuous people, that person dwells in constant joy, and at the dissolution of the body after death, they will be reborn in a good destination, as a Yāma king in the heavenly world.
Because they perform wholesome karmic causes with composure, without waiting for a specific time.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another twenty-eighth quality which you should diligently practice and bring to fulfillment; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-eighth is what is called benefiting the realm through the Dharma, rather than through that which is not the Dharma.
Such a king of abundant Dharma is able to benefit himself and is able to benefit others.
Benefiting oneself means that if a king maintains the precepts, he is able to protect his kingdom; it is not by failing to maintain the precepts that one benefits oneself.
Benefiting others means that when one sees someone who does not act in accordance with the Dharma, one causes them to abide within the Dharma.
When a king thus correctly protects his realm, by virtue of protecting the realm, he attains the harmonious convergence of the three: Dharma, wealth, and reputation.
Since he is already able to cause others to act in accordance with the Dharma in this way, how much more so should he himself follow the practice of the Dharma?
Such a king shall obtain wealth. How does he obtain it?
It is by taking one-sixth of all the wealth within his realm as a fixed tax.
Therefore, the kingdom becomes greatly wealthy because it is protected by righteousness.
If the kingdom is very wealthy and the king encounters an emergency, all the people, out of their love for the king and knowing that he has urgent need of wealth and goods, will all give him much.
This is the second sovereign virtue, fully accomplished by the king.
Thus, as the king rightly protects the realm, his surrounding military hosts revere and love him, and his excellent reputation is proclaimed in all directions.

If a king acts in this way, he will possess the perfect integration of Dharma, wealth, and reputation; in this present life, he will constantly enjoy peace and happiness and always experience benefit; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself; he will be praised by virtuous people; and after the body perishes at the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
This is due to the causes of wholesome karma that benefits both oneself and others.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the twenty-ninth, which you should diligently cultivate and practice in accordance with it; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The twenty-ninth is the constant cultivation of the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).
These ten paths of wholesome action yield the foremost retribution of happiness; to state it briefly, they consist of three types: namely, those of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the body, there are three:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Regarding the mouth, there are four:
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
On the mental level there are three:
greed, hatred, and wrong view.
These ten kinds of unwholesome paths of action, when inverted, are called the ten wholesome paths of action; they are called the path of wisdom and the right path.

Since unwholesome paths of action possess no wisdom while the wholesome paths possess wisdom, they are called the path of wisdom. They encompass birth among humans and gods, and lead progressively even unto nirvāṇa.
When that king is thus able to abide himself and further causes his army and retinue to abide likewise, such a king is like a father or mother to all sentient beings and is able to reach nirvana.
According to their own wishes, they shall attain success in any path whatsoever.

That king will have all his thoughts thus fully realized; he will be constantly protected by the devas, free from fear of swords, enemies, and the like; his entire realm will never suffer ruin or disorder, and all five grains will ripen well in their proper seasons.
Just as when the seasons are favorable and the sun and moon shine in harmony upon all things, such that everything required for the kingdom is fully provided and the population is abundant—

so too, when that king thus rightly protects his kingdom, he will, at the time of his impermanence, with the breakup of the body and the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, in the world of the devas.
"What karmic retribution do they receive?
What kind of bliss do they experience?
To speak briefly, in the Yāma Heaven, because of the karma of non-killing, their lifespans are long; such heavenly lifespans are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior."

In the six heavens of the desire realm, because they did not steal, they are immensely wealthy among the gods, possessing all seven treasures; in such places as gardens, groves, and mountain peaks, which are variously delightful, they sport and enjoy happiness.

Because he refrains from sexual misconduct, the hosts of celestial maidens do not go to any other sons of gods; until his merit has declined and his life has ended, they do not approach him nor draw near to him.
All those celestial maidens are perfectly upright and of exquisite beauty; their radiance is sublime and wondrous, bringing joy to the eyes and the heart.
If a person has engaged in misconduct, yet is born among the gods, all the celestial maidens will consort with other gods instead.

Thus, through the accomplishment of various karmic retributions, one who thus practices such bodily wholesome karma—guarding it well without transgression, delighting in its cultivation, and performing it frequently—is born among the devas and experiences the retribution of celestial bliss.
"Next, the second [category]: one who joyfully cultivates and frequently practices the four wholesome karmas of speech is born among the devas.
What kind of vocal karma leads to birth in the celestial realms?"
What kind of pleasant retribution does one receive?
It is said that it results from cultivating the fourfold precepts of right verbal conduct.

Because of refraining from false speech, one’s words become fulfilled and beautiful; one speaks various kinds of truthful words at all times, which are the most excellent and sublime speech. Whatever is spoken from the mouth, those words bring joy, and through such speech, one attains everything accordingly, because of refraining from false speech.
Because he refrains from divisive speech, his military forces are never divided, and they always follow and provide him with offerings.
Because he refrains from harsh speech, he constantly hears the sounds of exquisite song, dance, play, and laughter—the most delightful and beautiful of sounds.

Because they do not engage in frivolous speech, they always utter words that are meaningful; all the devas delight in their speech and all believe their words. Thus, within the heavens, they achieve such a karmic fruition of their verbal actions.
"What is the mental karma by which such heavenly beings receive these fruits of happiness?

Because they are free from greed, all that they think of and all that they require are obtained simply by their thought; once obtained, they are not lost, and no other gods can seize them away, so that they enjoy them solely for themselves."
This retribution results from non-greed in one's karma.
Because of non-anger, he is beloved by all the devas, possessing supreme physical beauty and a delightful, wondrous complexion.
Because they are free from wrong views, they obtain everything they seek; as they obtain it through their seeking, it remains unchanging and not otherwise.
As they obtain it through their contemplation, there is never a failure to obtain it; they always obtain it in its full perfection.
Thus have the fruits and rewards obtained through the ten paths of wholesome action been briefly explained.
"If one practices giving, one obtains superior retribution;
because of that giving, wealth and happiness become increasingly more excellent."
Because their wisdom is supreme, they surpass all devas.

All pleasant sensations have aspiration as their root—what is pleasurable through delusion is not true pleasure—due to mastery over the mind, the power of the field of merit, mastery over time, mastery over objects, and the power of resolute faith.

Because of the power of sovereignty, even a single instance of wholesome karma can lead to rebirth among the devas, and there are even sentient beings who enter nirvana, let alone those born in the heavens.

Such karmic retribution is supremely subtle; if anyone does not understand it, they will be deluded regarding karma and its results. Because they are deluded regarding karma and its results, they fall into hell.

As for these ten paths of wholesome action as they have been described, if a king practices them, then whether it be the people of his realm or his military forces, they will all practice the ten wholesome actions by reason of the king.

If a king thus cultivates the ten wholesome courses of action, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial worlds.
This is because of the causal conditions of the wholesome karma of practicing the ten virtuous actions.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the thirtieth, which you should diligently cultivate and bring into correspondence; it will bring benefit in both the present and future lives.
The thirtieth is the belief in causes and conditions.

Believing in the king or ministers who understand causes and conditions, they are not deluded regarding karmic retribution; their minds are always in right mindfulness, and they act without negligence amidst sensory objects.
That cause is called the causal seed of the fruit, which, through the complete convergence of time and place, is termed the "cause of faith.
If one has the cause of faith, one also has faith in the fruit; thus, by perceiving the cause and fruit with such clarity, one does not commit unwholesome deeds.
Just as a seed is the cause for a sprout, so too, by seeing the truths and having faith in dependent origination, one is not deluded regarding karmic retribution.

Such karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—causes the continuity of birth and death to proceed without interruption; through various forms of suffering and pleasure, it enables sentient beings to take birth in all places and to circulate within the realms of existence.
In this way, there is a continuous cycle of rebirth among the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans.
There are three kinds of karmic conduct: first, meritorious conduct; [second, non-meritorious conduct; and third, immovable conduct].
2. Actions of sinful karma;
3. Immovable actions, which refer to the practices of the four dhyānas.
Among these, the practice of meritorious karma is the cause for [rebirth as] devas and humans.
Those unwholesome karmic actions are the cause for the hells and other realms;
those imperturbable actions are the cause for the realm of form.
Regarding these three realms, O King, if you understand their causes with perfect clarity, that king will not be deluded in the wilderness of saṃsāra.
All such things as these exist within this realm of the conditioned; that is to say, cause and effect.

Your Majesty, because you believe in cause and effect, past transgressions cannot destroy you. Since you are able to fear transgression, you do not commit unwholesome deeds but constantly perform wholesome ones.

If a king thus places his faith in the power of the merit of dependent origination, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven within the celestial realms.
Because of the causal conditions of faith and the causes of wholesome karma, the foremost and most excellent dharma for all sentient beings is the causal condition of faith.
Therefore, a king should diligently cultivate this dharma and uphold this dharma; that is to say, the causal condition of faith.
"Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another quality, the thirty-first, which you should diligently cultivate, achieve, and correspond with; it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The thirty-first is the offering to the devas.
For what reason does one make offerings to those devas?
Because of the practice of wholesome karma, one is born among the devas and possesses great supernormal powers; they are able to restrain me if I should commit unwholesome courses of action.
Whether by night or by day, they constantly make offerings; all that they do can bring about subduing, and they are able to manifest what is wholesome and unwholesome within dreams.
When all lands are not being benefited, they are able to act as protectors, causing beings to enter into wholesome dharmas.
That deity is thus able to ward off unwholesome states, constantly providing protection by night and by day, just as parents protect with immeasurable skillful means in various ways.
One should make offerings to the devas, for they are capable of performing wholesome deeds.
Therefore, when a king makes offerings to those devas out of love for the Dharma, he abandons unwholesome karma and refrains from harming others, as he is free from wrong views.
There is no such thought as:
"Apart from heaven there is no karma; it is this heaven that creates.
No one in the entire world has such a mind.
"All suffering and happiness are created by the gods.
They do not have such a thought as:
"By making offerings to the gods, through such offerings, it will benefit me and I shall not lose any profit."
"It is not a denial of cause and effect, nor is it a mind of wrong view; because that king thus makes offerings to the devas, he receives offerings from others.

If a king constantly makes such offerings to the devas, by the causal conditions of that merit, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, as a Yāma King in the world of the devas."
This is due to the cause of the wholesome karma of making offerings to the devas.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the thirty-second, which a king should practice;
when accomplished and applied correctly, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The thirty-second is: at all times, he correctly protects the kingdom.
As a king who correctly protects, he accords with the practice of the Dharma like a father and mother, bestowing fearlessness upon all who are in states of dread.
Because he bestows fearlessness, his wholesome dharmas increase constantly day and night; all military hosts respect and love him, their hearts never turning away from him.
The people within the realm either present him with wealth and goods or offer praise, extolling the king’s virtuous reputation.
At times, day and night, his mind constantly contemplates how to bring that person peace and happiness.
Because that king thus benefits all sentient beings, it causes the king’s sovereign power to increase.
Because of his great sovereignty, the five grains ripen, the kingdom flourishes, and all the military forces increase.
The elders within the realm pray that the King may reign with ever-increasing splendor.
When such a king thus rightly protects his kingdom, his three assets—dharma, wealth, and fame—increase day by day in harmony and accord.

If a king thus rightly protects his kingdom, benefiting it at all times, free from hatred and free from greed, then by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he shall always enjoy peace and security and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body and the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, as a Yāma King in the heavenly world.
This is due to the causes of wholesome karma for protecting the kingdom.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another thirty-third quality that a king should practice; when accomplished and applied correctly, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The thirty-third is as follows: at all times, one correctly protects one's wife and children.
Because one protects one's wife and children, they attain happiness; and for the king or a great minister, immeasurable merit and various kinds of merit are gathered and increased.
If one possesses wealth or any kind of property—whatever object, wherever, or whenever it may be—one gives it to one's wife and children without begrudging it.

Whether it be wealth, food and drink, bedding and seating, or clothing; or perhaps by holding them in one's arms, speaking with affectionate words, and placing trust in them, one causes their hearts to rejoice and bestows upon them fearlessness.
If one gives according to one's means to one's wife and children, one gains merit within the household;
by performing immeasurable kinds of meritorious deeds within the home, this protection of one's wife and children brings great merit.
If there is another person who lacks a heart of compassion, or who, being shrouded by greed, does not cherish his wife and children,
that person’s mind is worse than that of a predatory beast that kills and eats living beings, or a scavenger that eats excrement.

If a person is unable to leave the household life to dwell in the Dharma, that person should, according to their strength and capacity, properly protect their wife and children so that they may attain peace and happiness.
If one possesses the ability yet lacks a compassionate heart and fails to protect their wife and children, such a person is called neither a householder nor a renunciant.
Therefore, one should provide gifts of the necessities of life and other material goods, or instruct them in the observance of the precepts.

If a king or a great minister can cause his wife and children to receive and maintain the precepts, instruct them in giving, and instruct them in the cultivation of wisdom, he should further protect their well-being through these successive stages according to his capacity.
If a king or a great minister acts in this manner, they will enjoy happiness for a long time and possess a long life.

If a king thus correctly protects his wife and children, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, as a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial worlds.
This is due to the causal conditions of the wholesome karma of protecting one's wife and children.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another quality, the thirty-fourth, which you should diligently cultivate; when accomplished and realized, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
The thirty-fourth is the constant cultivation of wisdom.
The cultivation of wisdom is called the extinction of all suffering and the departure from all causes of birth and death.
It is well if one can resolutely cultivate wisdom.
That wise one is named:
a lamp that illuminates those who have entered great darkness and fallen into obscurity, undergoing immeasurable kinds of ruin and affliction;
the provisions for the perilous paths through the wilderness of birth and death.
The eyes for the blind;
strength for the weak;
a companion for the solitary.
A savior for those without refuge;
a potent medicine for the sick;
a guide for the lost.
It is the clear, cool water and the food and drink for those traveling far on the perilous paths through the wilderness of birth and death;
it is the cause for escape from those bound in the prison of saṃsāra;
and for those who have no kin or friends, it acts as a beneficial friend.
It acts as a luminous eye for those who are sightless;
it can serve as a powerful companion at the time of death.
When the messengers of Yama approach and at the moment of passing away, it becomes a companion of great strength.
It can block off all evil realms;
for those about to fall into great precipices, it is like catching them with one's own hand.
If one takes it as a companion, one shall obtain all happiness.
To those who are naked, it is excellent clothing that cannot be plundered.

For those who are terrified by the transgression of precepts or oppressed by the heat and affliction of fire, it can become a tree endowed with immeasurable branches, leaves, flowers, and cool, refreshing shade.
All sentient beings who behold it with their eyes give rise to love and joy.
Therefore, wisdom is supreme.

Among all sentient beings wandering through the worlds since beginningless time, there is no other dharma capable of providing happiness in the present and future lives as effectively as this single wisdom.
One should always recognize and cultivate various practices, causing the mind to proceed upon the right path, to engage in wholesome reflection, and to abide securely within the heart.
When the mind moves together with other dharmas through immeasurable kinds of mental activity—whether initially unwholesome or otherwise—wisdom can eliminate them and reveal the true path.
This is peace and security; it can accomplish all benefits and reveals the city of Nirvāṇa, and should be constantly practiced.
Because of such practice and because of thorough understanding, one will be born among humans or devas, becoming a king or a superior being.

The fire of wisdom can burn away all afflictions, leading eventually to the attainment of the bliss of nirvana; there is no other dharma capable of bringing about liberation from all birth and death like this wisdom.
Therefore, those who aspire to all stages [of realization] should contemplate and cultivate this wisdom and explain it to others.

If a king thus constantly cultivates this wisdom and explains it to others, delighting in its frequent practice, then by virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, he will always attain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after passing through the cycle of existence, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, he will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world as a King of the Yāma devas.
Because one is able to cultivate the causes of manifold wisdom, one will ultimately attain nirvana.
Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another dharma, the thirty-fifth, which you should diligently abandon; by accomplishing its opposite, you will benefit both the present and future lives.
The thirty-fifth is what is called not delighting in any sensory objects.
If a Kṣatriya king delights in sensory objects, such a king will not attain peace and security.

If a king delights in sounds, touches, tastes, fragrances, and forms through any means whatsoever, he will find no peace and security; furthermore, he will be unable to properly protect his kingdom, nor will he be able to properly protect himself.
Because he constantly delights in sensory objects and is perpetually attached in mind, he loses his Dharma, his wealth, and his reputation—all three of which decline and perish.
A king who delights in sensory objects can be overthrown by other kings;
because he is thus destroyed by others, his own army and retinue develop aversion toward him and no longer love or cherish him.
Because of such wearying detachment, one loses the royal throne and encounters decline and distress;
because of encountering decline and distress, one may even lose one's life.
Therefore, a king should not indulge his mind or become attached to sensory objects.

If he does not indulge his mind in the realm of great pleasure, that king will be able to correctly protect his own Dharma; at times his mind will be pure, and he will correctly restrain forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles so that they cannot disturb his mind.

Having been king for a long time, he ruled over the kingdom and its entire military host without weariness or abandonment; therefore, other kings were unable to destroy him, his life endured for a long duration, he was free from affliction, and he enjoyed happiness for a long time.
Now that you have experienced pleasure, you will be reborn in a place of happiness in the future.

O King, if you do not delight in such sensory objects, by reason of these meritorious causes and conditions, you will constantly obtain peace and happiness and always receive benefit in this present life; you will be able to protect your kingdom and protect yourself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the body perishes and life ends, you will be born in a good destination, becoming a Yāma King in the heavenly world.
Because he does not delight in sense objects due to the cause of his wholesome karma.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya king, there is another thirty-sixth quality that a king should not practice; yet when it is accomplished and maintained, it brings benefit in both the present and future lives.
