The thirty-sixth is as follows: one must not allow wicked people to dwell in the kingdom.
Those who are unsubdued shall not be permitted to reside in the kingdom.

If a king allows various wicked people—those of evil karma and broken precepts—to dwell in his realm, that king will not remain sovereign for long, and he will surely suffer calamity at the hands of those very people.

Because of those great transgressions, the people of the land are ruined, his sovereignty diminishes, the five grains do not ripen, and the people cease their labors; the king is then unable to properly protect the realm, and all the people take no pleasure in the king.
The devas who dwell in that land do not give rise to compassion, because evil people reside within that country and because there are unruly persons in that land.
Even those who are disciplined fail to remain disciplined; for even a person of supreme cultivation and merit suffers loss by associating with evil people.
Therefore, a king shall not allow those who are unsubdued to dwell within his kingdom.
If a king does not permit those who are unsubdued to reside in his realm, then those who practice unwholesome dharmas will not dwell in the kingdom.
Because he does not allow [evil persons] to dwell within the kingdom, there are no superior transgressions; furthermore, he is always able to correctly protect the land.

All the people of the country know that the king does not permit evil persons to reside within the realm, and thus they do not commit evil; all the people of the country practice the Dharma and do not engage in what is contrary to the Dharma.
When that king thus practices in accordance with the Dharma, all his intentions are fully accomplished; all the people of the country understand the law and act in accordance with it;
and whatever else is unbeneficial neither arises nor occurs.
Thus, that king takes the Dharma as his refuge and the Dharma as his companion.

If a king thus makes the Dharma his foundation, he will not allow wicked people to dwell within his realm; by virtue of these meritorious causes and conditions, he shall always enjoy peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life, being able to protect his kingdom and protect himself. He is praised by virtuous people, and when his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial world.
This is because he has abandoned the causes of unwholesome karma associated with evil people.

Furthermore, O Kṣatriya King, there is another thirty-seventh quality which the king should diligently cultivate; by doing so, he will acquire great merit, all the people of the nation will not loathe him, he will achieve harmony and correspondence, and he will benefit both the present and future worlds.
The thirty-seventh is as follows: relying on the ancient laws of the past, one does not interrupt what was previously obtained, but bestows it according to the law.

To those people, military hosts, and all citizens who first came to obtain it—whether land or goods—one does not interrupt or seize their possession, but continues to grant them these things as they were originally.
If there is anyone who has previously obtained [the throne] through the successive order of their lineage, they should be granted it according to what is appropriate.
Then all the people will not feel aversion toward that king, and none among the surrounding military hosts will be able to obstruct one another.

The king felt no anxiety or regret, nor did he give rise to feverish distress; his royal station remained unshaken and his realm was not thrown into disorder. He always abided in rectitude, and none of his officials adjudicated cases with partiality. The strong did not oppress the weak, and there was no violation of the laws and regulations. All the people of the country performed their duties according to their own karma, their hearts filled with joy.

Because the mind of Heaven is joyful, it sends down rain in due season; cold and heat follow their proper times, there is constant abundance without scarcity, there is no kalpa of war, and the dragons' minds are free from anger.
All the virtuous devas do not abandon their realm to travel to other lands.
Because that king’s kingdom practices the Dharma, it is not destroyed by other devas.
It is due to human causes and conditions that there are devas.
Because of human effort, the gods possess power.
Once that king has recognized such faults, he grants according to ancient custom, neither interrupting nor seizing.

If the king practices the foremost practice of the Dharma, he shall grant to the people within his realm in accordance with their sequence and as is appropriate, granting what is due to them according to the succession of their ancestors.

If a king causes the Dharma to endure long within his realm and protects it correctly according to the Dharma, bestowing [rewards] upon those who follow the sequence and their respective portions, then that king who thus acts in accordance with the Dharma will find no opportunity for harm from any of the celestial hosts; they will protect his realm, and that great king shall possess abundant wealth and a complete kingdom.
Because of great wealth, one practices generosity to create merit, observes the precepts, and cultivates wisdom.

If a king thus follows and acts in accordance with the Dharma, through the causes and conditions of such merit, he will always obtain peace and happiness and constant benefit in the present life; he will be able to protect his kingdom and protect himself, be praised by virtuous people, and after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in a good destination, becoming a King of the Yāma Heaven in the celestial realms.
Because it is due to the cause of wholesome karma that does not contradict the Dharma.
"If a king accomplishes these thirty-seven dharmas such as these, and grasps those dharmas and abides in those dharmas, he will be fully endowed with all merits."
"From that state of happiness, he shall further attain a state of happiness.
At that time, the goose king named Kāla (Good Time) recited for them the verses spoken in the past by the Tathāgata Śikhin:
"If a king’s army is pure, And he practices the Dharma to restrain his senses,"
He possesses the wisdom of the Dharma and is reborn in the celestial realms.
If, when he was a king, he collected taxes in accordance with the law,
he will abandon greed and become the King of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king is patient and speaks with loving words, remaining unmoved by anger or joy,
he protects his kingdom and is reborn as the most excellent among the gods.
If a king does not take sides in disputes, nor regard others as friends or enemies, [he likewise attains such excellence].
He whose mind is equanimous shall become supreme among the hosts of devas.
If a king is diligent in honoring the aged and makes offerings to his elders,
his will shall be firm and free from greed, and he shall become a king among the devas.
If a king relies on the ways of former ages and bestows gifts according to the laws of his ancestors,
he does not seize the property of living beings and shall become a king among gods.
If a king cultivates generosity and morality, and teaches the Dharma to restrain his sense faculties, [he shall likewise attain such sovereignty].
Those who protect the kingdom and its people are noble within the world of devas.
If a king abandons what is unrighteous and embraces those who practice the Dharma,
he will uphold the True Dharma and observe the precepts, thereby being reborn as the most excellent among the devas.
If a king stays away from women and associates only with virtuous people,
his mind will be free from defilement and he shall be reborn as a king in the heavens.
If a king does not place his trust in everyone but only embraces those who are virtuous, [he shall likewise attain such a state].
When he passes away from that life, truly seeing the truth, he will be preeminent among the gods of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king loves a good reputation and does not crave or cling to wealth and goods,
because he is free from the defilement of greed, he shall become the King of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king is free from wrong views and his heart delights in right view,
his pure vision remains unshakable, and he becomes the King of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king is diligent in generosity and morality, and also constantly practices wisdom, [he shall likewise attain that state].
He shall obtain various lands and later be born as a celestial king.
If a king always speaks with loving words, he brings the greatest joy to others;
he shall obtain pure and cool lands and be born among the most excellent of the gods.
If a king speaks truthful words, as immovable as Mount Sumeru,
he ascends the stairway of truth and stands like a banner among the hosts of devas.
If a king, without cause or reason, does not mobilize his military forces, [he shall prosper].
If that king’s subjects do not weary of him, he shall become a celestial king at the end of his life.
If a king knows what is good and evil, and also knows who possesses strength and who does not,
that king, possessing the power of wisdom, will be born as a king in the Yāma heaven.
The most supreme in the three realms are what are called the Three Jewels;
if a king can make offerings to them, that king shall be reborn in heaven.
If a king at any time sees a person who is able to benefit the land, [he should honor them].
He who is free from pride and stinginess is reborn as the most excellent among the gods.
If a king is free from the defilement of sleep, he is then free from the fault of delusion;
through union with the realm of wisdom, he will certainly become a celestial king.
If a king abandons indolence and is always firm in his diligence,
he can exhaust the ocean of transgressions and become a celestial king in a future life.
If a king has steadfast friends who always follow the practice of the Dharma, [he too shall attain such a state].
Surrounded by virtuous friends, he is born in heaven as a celestial king.
If a king distances himself from evil friends and always abandons them without drawing near,
he will be free from the poison of flattery and be born in heaven as a celestial king.
If a king maintains freedom from anger and malice, and does not delight in performing evil deeds, he shall,
because he is free from the defilement of evil, always be a king among the gods. If a king is not greedy for flavors,
but loves and delights only in wholesome dharmas, [he shall likewise attain such sovereignty].
He can show the good path, and through wisdom one is born in a superior realm.
If a king reflects well and practices in accordance with the wholesome Dharma,
seeing the path according to the Dharma, he will reach the abode of the Yāma devas.
If a king acts with speed and practices according to this Dharma,
he will swiftly be freed from all suffering and become a king of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king benefits the country through the royal law, or protects it by means of the royal law, [he shall likewise attain such a state].
He is praised by men, and when born in heaven, the gods praise him as well.
If a king practices the ten wholesome paths of action, as taught by the Tathāgata,
he follows the Dharma of practice and will be born in heaven as a celestial king.
If a king believes in causes and conditions regarding what is the path and what is not the path,
he will be free from the defilement of views and, through his wisdom, be reborn in a superior heavenly realm.
If a king makes offerings to the deities, he should do so as is appropriate.
He who receives the offerings of the gods is born as the most excellent among the gods.
If a king protects his wife and children, and his mind remains unturbid and undisturbed,
he is content with his own wife and is born as the most excellent among the gods.
If a king stays far from those objects of sense that are cherished by the foolish,
he is one who upholds the precepts and shall be born in heaven as a king.
If a king abandons evil men and draws near to those who act in accordance with the Dharma, [he is one who upholds the precepts and shall be born in heaven as a king].
He is a Dharma King of virtue; he ought to be the King of the Yāma Heaven.
If a king acts in accordance with the Dharma, he is a lord who protects the land;
he is fit to be a sovereign of all lands and is worthy to be the King of the Yāma Heaven.

"Thus, that one named the Goose King Suśamaya, by the power of his vows, was born in that heaven as the king of geese. Having seen the celestial lord Mucilinda, he recalled the sūtras and dharmas he had heard from Śikhin Buddha during his previous life. In order to gladden the heart of the celestial lord Mucilinda, after speaking thus, he addressed the heavenly king, saying:
'O Heavenly King, you should know!'"
Because their karma was thus, they have attained this celestial realm; because the Great Dharma is supreme, they have obtained this place.
If, having attained this place, they practice with heedfulness, then when they later fall away, no regret will arise in their minds.
When life comes to an end at the time of death, the messengers of hell—with their hideous and terrifying countenances—will not appear before you.
You, King Yāma, must be careful not to be negligent; do not engage in heedless conduct.
Because you heard my voice there, you have come here.
Having abandoned all sensory objects, you have come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
If those who suffer follow the practice of the Dharma, it is not extraordinary;
however, if one who enjoys celestial bliss practices without negligence, that indeed is difficult.
O Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, if you are not attached to desire, that shall be great bliss.
Furthermore, other devas will draw near to you, love you, and follow after you.

Those who belong to the military host have attained a favorable place of birth; because they have been able to draw near you, their spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they constantly experience happiness.
By drawing near to evil associates (*pāpamitra*), such happiness cannot be found.

"You, Maudgalyāyana, Lord of the Yāma Heaven, have brought great benefit to this multitude of devas; because these devas are close to you, they obtain two kinds of happiness: namely, happiness in the present life and the happiness of nirvāṇa in the future."
"You hosts of all the celestial armies, each of you return to your respective abodes.
I now wish to proceed further to the other realms of the heedless devas in order to eliminate their negligence."
After the Goose King Kāla had spoken thus, those hosts of devas ascended into the air from the mountain peak.

Having heard this teaching, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, rejoiced and praised it; he then ascended to his celestial palace, surrounded by the host of devas, amidst a retinue of both male and female devas, as they all rose together into the sky.
Furthermore, there are other devas dwelling amidst the thousand peaks of Mount Śailāṅga, sporting and enjoying themselves; thus they are negligent, acting with negligence.

Bewildered by sensory objects and delighting in those objects, they are destroyed by craving. Within the groves, lotus ponds, and wish-fulfilling forests, they sport and enjoy themselves together with their companions in this manner.
The sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments and the music of the devas are beyond all analogy; there they sport and enjoy pleasure along rivers of food and drink.

It is fully endowed with flowers of every season, fruits of every season, and the songs of various birds; in these places abounding in lotus ponds, they experience the supreme bliss that is the fruit of their own karma.

In this way, until their craving for wholesome karma is exhausted, their accumulated karma is exhausted, and because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall according to their own karmic actions—either into hell, or into the realm of hungry ghosts, or into the animal realm.

If, through other residual karma, they are born among humans in a place of shared karma, they will possess the foremost wealth and happiness—either near the seashore or in other places abundant with flowing water—becoming great wealthy men with extensive commerce;
or they may become kings, always by the seashore, possessing full fleets of ships, abundant wealth and property, and large retinues, beloved by all people.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 55; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 56.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Thirty-Five: Yāma Heaven, Part Twenty-One.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the fruits of karma, contemplates the ground where the Yāma Heaven resides.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,
he sees that in the Yāma Heaven there is another realm called Constant Joy (Nitya-sukha).
By what karma do sentient beings are born in that land?

He sees that if a person does not kill or steal as previously described, and always abstains from sexual misconduct— even upon seeing a painted image of a woman— does not harbor thoughts of desire, and does not give rise to notions of excellence regarding that painted woman.
When seeing a painted woman, one does not give rise to the thought, "She resembles such-and-such a woman.

No thought of attraction arises in the mind; one does not contemplate her in this way, nor does one view the image of the painted woman with a lustful mind. The mind is not deluded, for it relies upon the True Dharma.
By means of right mindfulness, he abandons the mind of desire and keeps himself far removed from women who ruin their own bodies.

Having reflected that he himself does not engage in sexual misconduct, his heart gives rise to joy; regarding the lustful mind that has not yet arisen, he constantly employs skillful means to prevent it from arising.
He exhorts those who engage in sexual misconduct to abide in the Right Path, preaching to them the faults of desire and how it is not to be craved or delighted in.

If one can thus abandon sexual misconduct, this constitutes the foremost purity of bodily action; possessing right view and freedom from greed, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn in the heavenly realms of the good destinations, in the land of Constant Joy within the Yāma Heaven.

Whether in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or in the celestial realms, they all experience pleasure through their five sense faculties due to their wholesome karma; possessing in full the qualities of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, they are born in the heavens in succession.
Within that celestial realm, beings are born through transformation in three places:
first, they are born within the calyx of a lotus flower;
second, they are born within the filaments of a kumuda lily.
Third, they are born from *mandārava* flowers.

If they are born within the filaments of a *kubjaka* flower, their radiance and color are likewise like that flower—whether red, blue, or various colors—and their adornment with the seven jewels is also like the filaments of the *kubjaka*.
What is meant by being adorned with the variegated colors of the seven treasures?

His hair is made of blue *vaiḍūrya*, and his eyelashes and eyelids are likewise; his fingernails and toenails are silver-colored; his teeth are red-white in hue like pearls; his body is like *Jāmbūnada* gold; the hair on his abdomen below the navel is the color of *indranīla* gems; and all other parts of his body are variegated in color in various places.
The mind is like a painter that creates its own works.

If one is born within a lotus pedestal, their complexion is likewise: it is the color of Jāmbūnada gold, with hair the color of blue gems; the lips are the color of red lotus gems or conch shells; the nails are the color of lotus gems; and the hair below the navel is the color of dark-blue conch shells.
This is but a partial explanation.
If one is born among *māndārava* flowers, the body and clothing will possess various colors; because one is born therein, they correspond to those colors.

Regarding "that which is similar": it is as seen in the present case of phenomena; whatever colored fruit there may be, the thing produced by the living being within it will be of that same color, because it is produced therein.
Their appearances are likewise; according to the place of their birth, they assume the same color as those inhabitants, and it is just so.
Because they dwell among the flowers, they resemble them entirely.
Once the deva-sons are born, they constantly possess manifold pleasures that are uninterrupted and unceasing; they always experience celestial delights beyond all analogy.
Within that bliss, only a small portion has been described; it is like a single drop of water in the ocean, and the bliss here explained is likewise so.
If those among humans who perform wholesome deeds hear of this celestial bliss, their minds will become diligent.
Why is this? Because they understand the fruits of karma, they diligently cultivate wholesome deeds in anticipation of these pleasant rewards.

Just as those who exert themselves with diligence for the sake of liberation do so to destroy the immeasurable sufferings within existence and to eliminate the poison of craving, they perceive that there is not even the slightest pleasure to be found within existence.
For these reasons, the fruits of wholesome karma are explained; this description of celestial bliss does not constitute the ultimate fruit.

At that time, having been born in this celestial realm of Constant Joy, the deva-son constantly sports and enjoys pleasures therein through the merits of the five desires, while hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens offer him worship by singing songs of praise.

In the groves and gardens, amidst lotus ponds and rivers, they enjoy themselves together with various songs and dances in such places without hindering one another; experiencing the fruits of their own karma, they constantly enjoy celestial pleasures within the groves, on level plains and mountain peaks, and within the lotus forests.

At that time, the devaputras, surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, experienced divine sensual desires in every single location, in every garden, in every delightful place for recreation, and amidst every peak of the seven-jeweled mountains, never knowing satiety.

They behold various lovely and wondrous lotus ponds, hear exquisite sounds, partake of celestial flavors, and wear fine, soft, and superior heavenly garments; enjoying their beloved fragrances, they long experience the five desires together in mutual love and delight.
At that time, there was a bird named Jāgarita (Awakened at Dawn) who, for the sake of the heedless hosts of devas, spoke in verse:
"Within the assembly of the three realms of existence, All must eventually die;
yet the fool, amidst birth and death, Is unable to give rise to weary detachment."
All must surely die; one should all diligently apply skillful means.
Once the enemy of death has arrived, there is no one who can save.
It can sever all pleasure and inflict manifold suffering and affliction.
Separation from all that is beloved—therefore it is called death.
It can instill fear in sentient beings, it can bring about great suffering and affliction, and it can cause the mind to become deluded; therefore it is called death.
It can sever the life-sustaining mind and destroy all the sense faculties;
because sentient beings cannot break it, it is called death.
Sentient beings cannot destroy it, and no karmic actions can overcome it.
It causes sentient beings to perish; therefore, it is called death.
All sentient beings possess it; it is certain to bring about slaughter and to cause separation from those one loves; therefore, it is called death.
The gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, pretas, nāgas, rākṣasas, and others—the wheel of time can kill them all; therefore it is called death.
It is turbulent and difficult to subdue, like fire toward all things.
Irresistible and unavoidable, it is therefore called death.
It can destroy the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas), as well as the life-force and the mind;
because the power of the law of time is so great, it is therefore called death.
"His movement is exceedingly swift, destroying all sentient beings;
you should diligently cultivate meritorious deeds and must not practice heedlessness.
Thus did this bird of awakening preach the dharma of death to the heedless devas, with absolute certainty and no doubt.

At that time, because the hosts of devas were negligent, although they heard this Dharma, they did not give rise to weariness or renunciation; for the very nature of their faculties is light and restless.
Those who experience much pleasure have faculties that are light and restless, and thus difficult to subdue;
because their pleasure is so predominant, their faculties are light and restless and cannot be tamed.
For this reason, although these hosts of devas hear the truth that is firm and beneficial, they neither perceive nor understand its meaning.
Even if they were to perceive it, being harmed by the poison of craving, they would not accept it despite their perception.
Due to these causes and conditions, although they hear true words and beneficial, authentic speech, they do not accept them.

Because they do not receive the Dharma, they initially become attached to beautiful objects and experience various sensual pleasures—playing music with the five types of instruments, laughing, singing, dancing, and engaging in all manner of diversions.

In the lotus ponds within the groves, together with the celestial maidens—due to their wholesome karma—they constantly experience uninterrupted and unceasing bliss upon lovely mountain peaks adorned with immeasurable seven-jeweled ornaments.
Fully endowed with all celestial desires and virtues, they enjoy themselves together in a land adorned with various precious jewels, constantly experiencing happiness.
Thus sporting and enjoying various pleasures, they travel in succession until they reach the Vast Pond.

That pond was one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; upon it grew a lotus flower, soft and supple, interspersed with the seven treasures, with a stem of lapis lazuli and filaments of diamond, its blossoms fully opened, covering the entire great pond.
These hosts of devas had never seen such things before; upon seeing these flowers, they were struck with wonder and thought:
"This celestial realm is exceedingly lovely; everything we behold here is delightful."

When the devas saw this, they rejoiced a hundredfold; showing it to one another, they all gazed upon it together, surrounding it on one side as they moved about in play. With hearts full of joy, they beheld this lotus flower, and everyone felt a sense of wonder, saying to one another: "Look! Look!"
There were lovely lotuses, never seen before, emitting great radiance and adorned with immeasurable multitudes of bees made of the seven treasures; such were these magnificent jewel-lotuses.
This great lotus flower completely covers the large pond; surrounding the flower on all sides, only a small portion of the water is visible.
Along the broad banks of the pond, it is adorned with pearls interspersed among blue indranīla jewels, red lotus-colored jewels, and white silver-colored jewels.
The great lotus pedestal is five yojanas high and ten yojanas wide.

By the power of their wholesome karma, in accordance with the thoughts of the devas, it becomes large or small according to the mental inclinations of the devas at the time they are sporting and enjoying pleasures.

Just as the mind of a deity conceives, every part of the heart of a lotus within this great pond is fully perfected; therefore, this pond is named the Pond of Recollection, and its flowers are called Recollection Lotuses.
These two matters are both termed "recollection.

At that time, when the celestial hosts first see them, their hearts give rise to a joy a hundredfold greater than before. Due to their virtuous karma, they stand upon the banks of those ponds, singing, dancing, playing, and laughing, collectively enjoying such celestial pleasures amidst the sounds of the five musical instruments.
After the hosts of devas have finished their play, they again drink the supreme ambrosial beverages of the heavens, free from the fault of intoxication.
Having drunk this supreme flavor, they experience the merit of bliss; whatever they conceive in thought is obtained immediately: fragrances as they wish, forms as they wish, and flavors as they wish.
Just as they think of various precious vessels, such vessels immediately appear within that pond, filled with the finest flavors and emerging from the water.
Exquisite celestial wine flows forth from the pond, and these hosts of devas drink this supreme flavor.

Having drunk the supreme flavor, they again proceeded to another place to sport and wandered about, where they saw a mass of *suda* [nectar] fully endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and texture; desiring to eat it, they approached it with joy.
Having arrived at the place where food was provided, they all partook of it together; some ate with their hands and others used precious vessels, according to the similarity of their past karma.
Once they had finished eating the *sūdā* (ambrosia), they returned toward the vast pond from whence they had come.
Mutually giving rise to hearts of joy, surrounded by hosts of devas, they proceed to the vast pond amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, singing, dancing, laughing, and sporting.

One beholds a great lotus whose radiant splendor surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns; the exquisite jewel-light of all those gods does not equal even a sixteenth part of the light of that flower.

At that time, the host of devas, seeing the great lotus flower, were filled with supreme joy; surrounded by the host of devas, they circled the great pond with the sounds of the five musical instruments, singing, dancing, and sporting as they all proceeded together.
In this manner, as he walked all around the pond, following its circuit, he again beheld rare wonders within the pool.

Upon the flower pond, there were many various bees of lovely and wondrous colors made of the seven precious gems; males and females enjoyed themselves in pleasure, drinking together from the floral nectar.
The flavor of the flower juice was exquisite, beyond all comparison; they all drank the flower juice and spoke in verse:
"If one performs various kinds of karma, Then various kinds of fruits will arise;
Those who undergo various births Do so because their karma is manifold."
Because the mind is manifold, it creates various bases;
when various karmas are exhausted, they will soon perish and be destroyed.
This celestial bliss that has been experienced cannot be fully described.
The power of impermanence is sovereign; it will arrive before long, in an instant.
Pleasures are like bubbles on water, or like a mirage that is not water;
all pleasures are likewise, for everything must inevitably perish.
Exceedingly evil and impossible to ward off, all sentient beings tremble with fear;
the King of Death is about to arrive, and his power cannot be destroyed.
He destroys all happiness and severs the life-faculty.
Bound by the fetters of karma, one is led to future lives.
If pleasure has already passed, that pleasure cannot be recalled;
if pleasure is yet to come, it likewise cannot be called pleasure.
If one delights in dwelling in the present, mingling with the realms of craving;
moved by impermanence, all things are destroyed.
If one delights in that which belongs to the three realms, it is not praised by the wise.
How is it that the hosts of devas delight in such pleasure?
This body will not remain for long; the fire of death will surely arrive and burn everything away, just as fire consumes dry wood.
All pleasures swiftly pass away; do not practice heedlessness, lest at the time of death you give rise to a heart of regret.
Through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, the karmic fruits of pleasure have all already passed.
Like a dream, it reaches nowhere; like the wind, thought does not abide.
The fool finds pleasure without satiety, like fire obtaining dry fuel;
therefore, the pleasure to which one is attached is not a permanent pleasure.
One who is liberated from craving, able to leave behind the faults of desire,
and practices meditation with heedfulness, attains stainless, pure bliss.
Only one who attains such bliss may truly be called "happy."
Though all forms of existence are called "pleasure," they are like honey mixed with poison.
Thus, those who are attached to pleasure have minds that constantly seek sensual delights;
yet sensual delight is not true happiness, and therefore it is not tranquility.
"Thus, by virtue of their wholesome karma, these swarms of bees spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of devas.

Although the devas heard this Dharma, they did not take it to heart; instead, they gazed upon the pond, their hearts filled with love and delight, and together with the celestial maidens, they played, sang, and danced, surveying every part of the place."

Having sported and enjoyed pleasures in this place for a long time, they further desire to behold the lotuses in that pond; by virtue of the sovereign power of the light and agile four great elements and the force of their karma, they roam freely through the lotus pond.

Some hosts of devas enter into the flowers and leaves to sport and enjoy themselves; others enter into flower pedestals interspersed with various wonderful jewels, where they experience bliss together with celestial maidens.
Within the flower pedestal, according to what they think in their minds, they ascend upon the lotus petals.
At that time, the lotus petals grow larger and larger in this way; by virtue of their wholesome karma, the lotus grows to two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, or even up to a thousand yojanas.
By the power of the deva’s wholesome karma and mental intention, the terrace likewise gradually increased by two hundred yojanas;
the radiance of that great lotus flower increased in the same manner.
At that time, the hosts of devas each dwelt within other flower petals, sporting and enjoying pleasures together with the hosts of celestial maidens.
As soon as these devas ascended the flower petals, the petals immediately expanded.
At that time, as the hosts of devas were sporting and enjoying themselves, they thought to themselves:
"As we sport and dwell here now, a river of wine and *sudhā* food should arise."
At the very moment he thought this, rivers of wine and *sūdā* food appeared within the lotus petals, all perfectly complete.
He then thought again:
"I shall now drink the wine and eat the *sūdā* delicacies."
Thereupon, they drank celestial wine together with the goddesses and partook of the *sudhā* flavor.
At that time, after the host of devas had long enjoyed their pleasures, they again thought:
"While we dwell and sport here, groves and gardens should arise within these flower petals."
By virtue of their wholesome karma, as soon as they think of it, a grove appears according to their wish.
There are trees made of the seven treasures, with various kinds of birds and various sounds; the shade of the jewel-trees covers them like palaces, and they are fully endowed with flowers and fruits.
Whatever flowers and fruits they think of, they obtain them at all times.

There are various rivers, springs, ponds, and flowing streams that are supremely wonderful and lovely; there are various exquisite sounds, and the ground adorned with jewels abounds in the wonderful colors, fragrances, and forms of flowers—all of which are utterly delightful.

There are three kinds of flowers, namely: the blue utpala flower, the kumuda flower, the amarantha flower, the sūcīra flower, the gandhaparṇa flower, the nirmala flower, the paripūrṇakāma flower, the rāvaṇa flower, and the kuntala flower; such are the water-born flowers.
Within the radiance of these flowers, there are many bees; such flowers as these appear in various colors according to one's thoughts, with the hue of blue jewels arising everywhere.
Thus, these celestial flowers adorn the grove.

Furthermore, various flowers grow upon the land; these flowers possess diverse colors and forms that are similar to one another, being exceedingly lovely and delightful as they bloom within this forest.
The hosts of devas dwell amidst the petals of such lotuses—namely, the *Ratnaprabhāsa* (Light of Joy) flowers—and when the sons and daughters of gods call out to them, they immediately come.

Furthermore, there is a flower named Joy-to-See; another flower named Various Colors; flowers with joyful blossoms and supple petals; the Flower of Supreme Adornment of All Radiance; the Cūḍāmaṇi flower; the Insatiable flower; and the Flower of Recollecting Joy. Such are the flowers that grow on land.
At the moment the gods think of them, all appear before them.

Within those groves there are further various flowers, namely: the *māndārava* flower, the *saṃtāna* flower, the *gandhasparśapriya* flower, the *gandharasapriya* flower, the *citraka* flower, the five-leafed flower, the *nāgavṛkṣajihvā* flower, the *campaka* flower, the forest-garland flower, the *sumana* flower, the radiant flower, the flower that satiates upon smelling its fragrance, the "beloved by all" flower, the mountain-garland flower, and the mountain-peak-garland flower.
Such flowers as these grow beneath trees, and some grow in thickets.
When these devas dwell and sport within the lotuses, through the power of their wholesome karma, these various flowers come into being.
At that time, the hosts of devas, together with the celestial maidens, dwell in the lotus grove, sporting among the flowers and petals and enjoying various pleasures.
Such is the power of those great lotuses that they expand the vast ponds according to their thoughts.
At that time, the hosts of devas within the lotus petals thought to themselves:
"There must now be various mountains in this place.
Various jewel peaks emerge from here, replete with radiance; within those mountain peaks dwell various flocks of birds making various wondrous sounds."
"In rocky caves, rivers, and ponds; on level ground or precipitous banks; on lands adorned with jewels—in such places as these, I should sport. He further thought:
"I now dwell upon this great lotus petal; if there are rocky caves, rivers, and ponds, or level plains and flowing springs here, I shall sport and enjoy myself therein."

By the power of their wholesome karma, at that very moment of thought, there appeared many gardens, groves, flower ponds, mountain peaks, rocky caves, and level plateaus—all of which were delightful to behold, adorned with the radiance of the seven precious gems. The various branches of the trees were exceedingly lovely, and upon seeing them, their hearts were filled with joy.

Beyond a hundred mountains of heavenly flowers and fruit trees, whose branches and twigs provide shelter like palatial chambers—extremely delightful—and adorned by hundreds of thousands of jeweled caves arising within the mountains.

At that time, the assembly of devas left the lotus petals and were surrounded by a thousand celestial maidens; they held exquisite celestial flowers, perfect in color, fragrance, and texture, none of which had withered or changed.
The celestial maidens were adorned with exquisite beauty; their voices were melodious and their songs harmonious, bringing joy to the hearts of all who heard them.
Possessing the five sensory pleasures appropriate for the heavens, they ascended the great mountain with a calm and graceful gait, looking back and surveying the surroundings from every direction.
At that time, the hosts of devas sported and enjoyed themselves, eating from the River of Food and drinking the flowing essences.

Having partaken of immeasurable food and drink, they gathered *māndārava* flowers and *kubjaka* flowers by the riverbank to adorn their bodies, and likewise adorned the celestial maidens, singing, dancing, and sporting.

Having long enjoyed pleasures among the five sensory desires, they experience various sensual delights within lovely objects, never knowing contentment; drifting upon the river of craving, they proceed once more toward a vast pool containing great lotus flowers.

These hosts of devas, surrounded by hundreds or thousands of celestial maidens and adorned with various ornaments, arrive at the great pond and each reach the lotus petals where they dwell; there they sport individually, experiencing delightful and sublime pleasures.
"Just as a seal produces its impression, each receives a corresponding pleasure according to their own karma.
At that time, the celestial hosts again thought:

"In this place there must be various mountain valleys, various flocks of birds, and various forms and appearances; those whose movements, food, and characteristics are similar will find joy in seeing one another."

With a body composed of the seven treasures, they emit wondrous sounds; their movement through all places is entirely unimpeded, whether in water, on land, or traveling through the air, without ever experiencing fatigue.

If such a bird were to come to this place, I would mount it and travel through the air, sporting with the celestial maidens in mid-air, looking down upon the gods in the realm of Constant Joy as they enjoy their pleasures and delights.
Having observed them all, they again experience supreme pleasures together with the celestial maidens.

At that time, as the hosts of devas form this thought, various mountains, mountain peaks, mountain valleys, mountain caves, groves of trees, and flocks of birds—through the power of their virtuous karma—appear immediately according to their thoughts.

Beholding the various forms, the various adornments, the various sublime and wondrous sounds of *vakra* birds, and the various multicolored birds made of the seven precious gems, all the celestial maidens were filled with a sense of wonder.
Their voices were exquisite and filled the entirety of space; they all came toward this place where the devas sport upon the lotus petals, completely covering the sky.
At that time, the hosts of devas and the celestial maidens, having seen those birds, became even more joyful in heart.
Out of joy, they wished to ascend into the void together with the host of celestial maidens.

At that time, the birds, knowing the thoughts of the devas, approached the celestial assembly. Then the sons of the gods, together with the celestial maidens, ascended upon the birds. The birds immediately flew through the entirety of the void; holding lutes (*vīṇā*) in their hands, they sang songs of exquisite melody, accompanied by flutes, pipes, drums, and wind instruments—so exceedingly delightful that those who heard them felt joy in their hearts.

Furthermore, he observes the hosts of devas in his own realm experiencing celestial sensual pleasures; with hearts of attachment, fondness, and craving, they do not think of their eventual decline and fall, and due to their wholesome karma, they experience only celestial bliss.
At that time, there was a bird named Satyavādin (Truth-Speaker). In order to discipline the heedless hosts of devas, he spoke in verse:
"The violent wind gathers and flies, its movement being exceedingly swift;
yet the life of all sentient beings passes even more swiftly than this."
The wind may blow in circles, and birds that have flown away sometimes return;
but once the life-faculty has been destroyed, there is no time for returning.
Because karma is swiftly exhausted, one quickly arrives at the moment of death.
One will certainly depart from the celestial realm, yet the fool does not perceive this.
Irresistible by great power, most evil and hating toward sentient beings, the King of Death is exceedingly fierce and strong; he will certainly arrive in an instant.
The devas often practice heedlessness, deceived by their pursuit of pleasure;
they fail to realize that they will inevitably encounter immeasurable suffering and distress.
All phenomena are impermanent; they are certain to disintegrate.
All phenomena are thus; this is most truly to be feared.
Old age can destroy youthful beauty, and death can take away life itself;
it ruins and breaks apart one's possessions—such is the nature of the law of opposites.
In the face of such great evil, decline, affliction, and great terror,
those who still act with negligence are called mindless people.
If one fears future lives, then one is said to possess the eye of wisdom.
If one acts contrary to this, it is the height of great folly.
Deceived by all mental states, the mind becomes utterly deluded;
when karma is exhausted, one perishes, like a lamp going out when the oil is spent.
"The bliss of immeasurable realms—this bliss is all impermanent;
because the karma originally created has been exhausted, it must inevitably return to extinction.
Thus, by the power of his wholesome karma, this Bird of Truth spoke these verses in order to subdue the minds of the devas.
At that time, because the hosts of devas were negligent, they were deluded and lacked awareness; their minds neither believed nor understood, nor did they accept [the truth].
Furthermore, they beheld such places of eternal bliss—lovely mountain valleys, rivers, springs, flowing waters, lotus ponds, and groves.
In each flower grove, mountain peak, and mountain valley, hosts of devas are filled; they sport in mid-air, and the sounds of their songs pervade the entirety of space.

At that time, the assembly of devas again saw in another place a great multitude of devaputras and hosts of apsaras on the banks of a flower pond, drinking celestial nectar and enjoying pleasure amidst the five kinds of musical sounds from wish-fulfilling trees.

Proceeding further to another place, he saw a palace situated in the void, adorned with celestial sons, celestial daughters, and divine garlands; there, all the five celestial desires were fully provided, and they sported and enjoyed themselves.
He saw two groups of devas merged into a single assembly, sporting and enjoying themselves in the midst of space.
Mounted upon birds adorned with the seven treasures, the Nārada forest-dweller resided in his palace; these two groups of devas were all in harmony, together delighting one another in the sky.

Having sported for a long time in the midst of the void, they ascended again to the mountain peaks; after sporting and enjoying themselves upon the peaks for a long time, they proceeded toward the vast lake, mindful of the flowers, and departed.

Some ride upon birds that fill the void of space, soaring and leaping as they travel while singing celestial, wondrous melodies; these hosts of devas, mindful of supreme bliss, proceed once more toward the vast pond.
Having reached the pond, they descended from the birds and entered the lotus leaves of the vast pool; as previously described, they engaged in various sports and experienced pleasure.
At that time, after the hosts of devas had long enjoyed pleasures within the great lotuses of the vast pond, they again thought:
"Now, in this place of ours, branches and leaves should grow to provide shade for our palaces, adorned with the cries of cuckoos, various exquisite jewels, and groves of flowers."
"Covered by branches and leaves of various jewel colors, they shall serve as my palace; therein I shall sport and enjoy pleasure.

By virtue of his wholesome karma, at that very moment of thought, the area was adorned with the radiance of various exquisite jewels, and covered above by the most wonderful flowers, complete with color and fragrance.

That is to say, there are white silver, *vaiḍūrya* jewels, great sapphire kings, red lotus jewels, crystal-colored jewels, and so forth, even up to golden jewels; these are the most subtle and supreme, bringing joy and delight to those who behold them.
Thus, various kinds of precious branches and leaves provide shade over the palaces; by the power of their wholesome karma, these arise according to their thoughts.
At that time, seeing these branches and leaves shading the palaces, the celestial hosts feel joy in their hearts and enter the palaces to enjoy themselves and experience pleasure.

Surrounded by all the celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with celestial garments and celestial garlands, they possess every celestial desire; their minds are harmonious and do not obstruct one another, and being free from envy, jealousy, strife, and anger, they experience joyful conduct.
Due to their virtuous karma, they experience this celestial bliss.

The sounds of the five musical instruments are all perfectly harmonized; within palace chambers shaded by the coverings of branches and leaves, they enjoy sensual pleasures together with various heavenly maidens. Their minds know no satiety, being consumed by the poison of craving; they experience the pleasures of the five senses without knowing contentment, beyond all comparison.
The branches and leaves provide shade over the palaces, where they enjoy supreme celestial delights and achieve profound bliss.
Such branches and leaves shade the palaces, composed of various jewels; there are trees of *vaiḍūrya* with leaves of pure gold and fruits made of red lotus jewels.
Their branches are made of blue indranīla jewels;
some have leaves of white silver with fruits of crystal,
while others have leaves of blue jewels with flowers and fruits of red lotus.
Some have leaves of various jewels with fruits of various jewels;
some have leaves of pure gold with fruits of white silver;
and those with leaves of gold and fruits of gold are likewise.
Various branches and leaves provide shade over the palace; by virtue of their wholesome karma, everything is fully provided according to whatever the devas desire.
At that time, the deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, feels joy arise in his heart and enters the palace shaded by the branches and leaves, remaining there in profound stillness.
Together with the many celestial maidens, they sport and enjoy various pleasures, like fish in water, never knowing satiety.
Within this palace, sheltered by the shade of branches and leaves, they give rise to a sense of wonder; dwelling within the palace, they frolic, sing, and delight in sensory enjoyment.
Having experienced pleasure, he further thinks:
"In this place of mine, within the palace shaded by branches and leaves, there should arise the foremost forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects."
The supreme flavor of the heavens flows forth from the leaves; together with the hosts of celestial maidens, they drink it and experience joy.

By virtue of their wholesome karma, at the very moment of thought, the celestial nectar—possessing the most excellent color, fragrance, taste, and texture—flows from the leaves, and they drink it together with the various celestial maidens, experiencing bliss.
Their minds were insatiable; with hearts of craving and desire, they engaged for a long time in singing, dancing, and sporting to experience pleasure.

In this state of heedlessness, they knew no satiety—even as their previously performed karma was about to exhaust and they were on the verge of falling away—they continued to sport and enjoy themselves, thirsting for sensory objects and never knowing contentment.
Again, he thought:
"Now, within these flowers and leaves here, there should arise the foremost taste of *sūda*, endowed with fragrance, flavor, and texture.
Due to his virtuous karma, at the very moment of this thought, the foremost *sūda*—endowed with fragrance, flavor, and texture—emerged from within the leaves; having emerged, he ate it.
Then, after the hosts of devas had long enjoyed their pleasures, they again thought:

"Now, from within the branches of the jewel-trees here, there should arise various ornaments for the devas—such as jeweled pearl necklaces, magnificent celestial crowns, and arm-ornaments endowed with full radiance—all these diverse articles of adornment, brilliant and majestic, shall emerge from the tree branches."
While they were thinking thus, by the power of their wholesome karma, various celestial ornaments and radiant decorations appeared.

At that time, the hosts of devas donned these ornaments and enjoyed celestial pleasures for a long duration, never knowing satiety; together with the celestial maidens, they indulged in the pleasures of the five senses, never knowing satiety.
Although they have long enjoyed pleasures, their craving for sensory objects increases further; because their minds are not settled, another thought arises:
"Now, in this place, there must be fragrant breezes blowing upon the tree leaves, which, by rubbing against one another, produce exquisite sounds surpassing even the finest singing."

While he was thinking this, by the power of his wholesome karma, various fragrant winds blew, causing the leaves of the trees to rustle against one another and produce exquisite sounds; the singing voices of the celestial maidens did not equal even a sixteenth part of these.
At that time, the host of devas, together with the celestial maidens, engaged in song, dance, and play, enjoying themselves for a long duration without yet knowing satisfaction.
Then, the host of devas again thought to themselves:

"In this place where we dwell, we should cause various palaces adorned with the colors of the seven precious gems to arise; all celestial desires shall be fully provided and manifest according to our thoughts."
Having been thus born, they pervade the entire circumference of this vast pond;
dwelling in the midst of the sky, they enjoy themselves together with the celestial maidens, singing, dancing, sporting, laughing, and experiencing delight.
As he was thinking this, there immediately appeared various palaces made of the seven treasures, adorned with diverse colors and embellished with pearl necklaces.
On all four sides of those palaces were exquisite railings made of various precious gems, which were lovely to behold.
Upon those railings there were geese, peacocks, or jīvaṃjīvaka birds; various kinds of birds dwelt upon them.
In every place, flocks of birds were perched, appearing before one as various birds according to what the heart desired.
Having seen this, the celestial hosts, together with their goddesses, ascended these palaces to engage in play, song, and dance; they all proceeded toward the vast pond.
From within the palaces, looking down at the great pool, they beheld the various lotuses and were struck with a sense of wonder.

This great lotus is adorned with various jewel petals, various radiances, and various exquisite colors, namely: vajra, blue indranīla, red lotus gem, vaidūrya, the great king of sapphire gems, and gold-luminous petals; beholding it brings forth joy.

At that time, the hosts of devas were within their celestial palaces in the void; furthermore, other devas dwelt amidst vast lotus petals, dancing, singing, and sporting together with their celestial maidens, mutually enjoying themselves.
Some are in celestial palaces within the void, while others are upon the petals of great lotuses; these hosts of devas enjoy pleasures through immeasurable kinds of play that are beyond all analogy.

Such various sounds of playful songs filled an area of five hundred yojanas; all the merits of the five desires were fully present, and amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, they experienced immeasurable bliss.

"Having performed superior deeds, yet not perceiving that the accumulated karma is exhausted, one fails to realize that one's wholesome karma is about to end and the time for decline is approaching; as one wanders to other realms, into which destiny shall one be born?"
What kind of suffering do they undergo?
What kind of happiness do they experience?
By what wholesome or unwholesome karma will they now lead me to which place?
Show me which path it is:
am I in the hells,
or am I among the hungry ghosts?
Are they among the animals?
Are they among human beings?
Or have they been born in places of fear?
Is it not a place of fear?
Because they have sunk into the darkness of negligence, they neither perceive nor understand such things as these.
When the time comes for awakening, their wholesome karma will have been exhausted, and the great winds of impermanence will blow them down into ruin.
Thus, these hosts of devas frequently practice heedlessness; like an enemy feigning friendship, they do not provide true benefit but falsely pretend to do so.
When their wholesome karma is exhausted and they are about to undergo its contrary fruit, it is only then that they awaken and think:
"I committed unwholesome deeds and practiced much heedlessness; it is only at the time of my end that I have realized this."
Because they have long practiced this enemy of heedlessness, they feel no fear or difficulty; instead, they continue to play, sing, and dance by the lotus ponds.
By the power of their wholesome karma, they experience intense delight and take great pleasure in watching these sights.
The gods sporting amidst the petals of the lotuses and the hosts of gods dwelling in palaces in the void unite with one another and together experience pleasure.
At that time, there is a bird named Water-Wave (Jalāvarta); by the power of its virtuous karma, for the sake of the heedless hosts of gods, it speaks in verse:
"The lives of sentient beings do not abide, Just like the surging waves upon the water."
As unsubstantial as a bubble on the water, yet the gods do not perceive this.
If not stirred by the wind, a bubble might endure for a while;
but when impermanent celestial merit is exhausted, it perishes swiftly and does not remain long.
Just as when the oil of a lamp is exhausted, its light also vanishes entirely, so it is when karma is exhausted: celestial bliss likewise ceases.
There is no action performed that does not perish and decay.
Thus all these sentient beings, In their folly, do not perceive this truth:
Of all classes of living beings, Whatever is born must inevitably return to extinction;
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) Are likewise of this very nature.
Sentient beings, due to their own karma, Wander through birth and death;
why is this world So ravaged by heedlessness?
Through heedlessness one loses wholesome dharmas; Heedlessness is a firm bondage.
Because of such negligence, one falls back into the hells.
If there is a single cause and condition, it is said to arise from negligence;
therefore, those who seek happiness should abandon negligent conduct.
If one is free from heedlessness, one attains the deathless state;
by practicing heedfulness, one draws near to Nirvāṇa.
Because of heedfulness, one reaches the realm of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the wise say that heedlessness is the cause of suffering.
All those who are heedless are like madmen;
they are currently despised by others, and at death, they enter the evil realms.
All those who are heedless, within the ripening of karmic results and throughout the realms of birth and death, act without exception in a perverted manner.
The fire of heedlessness blazes fiercely, burning the sentient beings in the hells.
If you wish to escape hell, you should abandon heedless conduct.
If you wish to leave behind heedlessness, you should delight in cultivating wisdom;
then you will be freed from the bonds of affliction and forever attain a state of peace and happiness.
The five faculties give rise to the three defilements, and the mind wanders through the three realms.
For one who has already abandoned negligence, such is the teaching on negligence:
the storehouse of negligence is exceedingly painful, while the storehouse of non-negligence is blissful.
"Therefore, those who seek happiness should abandon heedless conduct.
Thus did the Water-Wave-Wheel bird, for the sake of causing those celestial hosts to abandon heedlessness and because he was well-disciplined, speak these verses.
At that time, because the hosts of devas were negligent, although they heard these teachings of true speech and reality, they were unable to receive or retain them.

Furthermore, within the vast lotus ponds in the sky, they took pleasure together upon the lotus petals, sporting and enjoying themselves, performing celestial music and divine melodies, as well as other sensory objects; they remained stubbornly attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures, never knowing contentment or weariness.
Just as drinking salt water, though one drinks it repeatedly, cannot quench thirst;
so too it is with these hosts of devas, for although they enjoy immeasurable and manifold celestial pleasures, they know no satisfaction.

"At that time, after the hosts of devas had long enjoyed pleasures in the void of space, they again sported and took delight among the broad ponds with those sons of gods and goddesses upon the petals of great lotuses. To the sounds of the five kinds of music, they gathered together in harmony, sharing the same hearts and desires as they enjoyed one another’s company."

Their minds are firmly attached to the realms of the six desires; for a long time they have danced, sung, and laughed here, experiencing celestial pleasures through immeasurable kinds and immeasurable varieties.
Such pleasures as these are fully accomplished according to what the mind contemplates.
Because of their virtuous karma, all manner of pleasures are achieved exactly as they are conceived; through the distinctions of their thoughts, they all come to fruition.
These hosts of devas, being swept away by the great river of surging waves of immeasurable mindfulness, vitarka, and vicāra, gave rise to hearts of joy.
All the deva hosts had long been established in celestial delights within the great lotuses of the vast pool, experiencing the immeasurable pleasures of celestial indulgence.

At that time, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, perceiving that the assembly of devas was attached to the pleasures of negligence, gave rise to a heart of compassion. Desiring to eliminate the heedless conduct of the devas, he manifested a transformation for their sake in order to sever their pride regarding physical form.
Not far from the vast pond, he manifested a great mountain named Pure, which was as perfectly pure as the finest lapis lazuli.
It was adorned throughout with immeasurable gold, silver, and various kinds of miscellaneous jewels.
There is a Forest of Play that encircles it on all sides, containing countless hundreds of thousands of flowing springs, the waters of which are all cool and refreshing.
The mountain’s jewel-peaks radiate light everywhere, and all the forest trees serve as its adornment.
There are many flower ponds, adorned with immeasurable varieties of flowers.
Branches and leaves provide shade in numbers reaching into the thousands, resembling a celestial palace.
Thus, this supreme mountain is universally adorned, and all the hosts of devas dwelling in the realm of Constant Joy within the Yāma Heaven behold it.
The Yāma Heaven King Mūsuludha further reflected and manifested a host of celestial beings who were like enemies of the gods;
their countenances were upright and handsome, and their movements were swift. Their singing, dancing, and playful laughter surpassed those of the Realm of Constant Joy by more than tenfold.
Alternatively, he may further manifest as a most excellent and wondrous celestial maiden, surpassing all the celestial maidens of the Ground of Constant Joy by more than tenfold;
the celestial maidens of this ground are entirely inferior to her.
What is meant by "all"?
It refers to their physical forms being upright and handsome, their complexions being exquisite and wondrous, and their laughter, singing, dancing, and various diversions all being preeminent.
That Mount Qingliang is entirely composed of lapis lazuli mountains, just as previously described.
At that time, the Victorious Deva was on the mountain of transformation, dwelling upon the foremost and highest mountain peak.
Upon this mountain peak, he manifested transformed devas and transformed devīs; their singing and instrumental music were so exquisite that all who heard them became attached to it.
Those manifested hosts of devas and devīs descended in succession from the manifested mountain peaks, playing, singing, and dancing as they approached the real devas.

At that time, the Real Devas heard the sounds of the songs and chants of the Emanated Devas as previously described—ten times more excellent and with exquisite voices—as they sang and played together with the hosts of celestial maidens.
At that time, the emanated devas likewise sang songs of a single melody as they gradually descended, drawing near to the assembly of the actual devas.
When the two groups of devas had seen one another, the singing of the emanated devas became increasingly more excellent.
At that time, because the actual celestial hosts beheld those superior forms, they immediately abandoned their pride regarding their own physical appearance.
Once the pride of the actual celestials concerning their own bodies, garments, and colors was shattered, the emanated celestials then produced sounds and sang hymns of praise.

At that time, the Real Gods were overwhelmed by the songs and chants of the Emanated Gods; in every respect—the fragrance, color, size, and physical form of the Emanated Gods, as well as the size, color, and physical form of the Emanated Goddesses—they all surpassed [those of the Real Gods].
At that time, all the actual deities' sensory realms of the five desires and all their pleasures were eclipsed by the sensory realms of the five desires and the pleasures of those emanated deities.
Through the power of the skillful means of the King of the Yāma Heaven, the various forms of pride among the actual deities were gradually thinned.
At that time, the emanated devas gathered together with the assembly of actual devas, causing the majesty and radiance of the actual devas to be completely eclipsed.
Just as when the light of the sun appears in Jambudvīpa, the light of the stars and the moon all vanish;
so too did the majesty of the emanated devas cause the radiance of the actual devas to be entirely extinguished.
At that time, the emanated celestial hosts produced superior songs, causing the voices of the actual devas to be eclipsed and rendered invisible.
As for the sounds of these emanated devas, they were like the singing of humans in Jambudvīpa compared to the volume of the celestial voices;

likewise, their physical forms, appearances, and all excellent characteristics were such that they surpassed those of humans, just as the celestial form and appearance of the Yāma Heaven surpasses that of humans.
At that time, because the real devas felt shame and wished to conceal themselves, they headed toward the shore of the vast pond.

Meanwhile, the manifested devas were upon great lotus flowers in the middle of that pond, singing, dancing, and laughing; they were fully endowed with all the fivefold sensual merits of the heavens, and their pleasures were perfectly accomplished.
Upon the great lotus in the vast pond, they dance, sing, play, and laugh, enjoying themselves together.
At that time, all the musical instruments of the emanated devas surpass those of the actual devas; with various songs and verses, they speak this stanza for the sake of the actual devas:
"All karmic actions are similar, Yet one receives the retribution of joy among the gods."
When the mandate of heaven and pleasant sensations end, they are lost and destroyed.
Therefore, all the various pleasures still remaining in the heavens arise from the cause of merit; without merit, there is only great suffering.
Life is swift and does not pause for a moment; even the most excellent physical form is likewise so.
Death arrives with extreme rapidity; do not practice heedlessness.
Heedlessness can destroy all the happiness of sentient beings.
Life is extinguished by death; do not practice heedlessness.
The sense faculties cannot be restrained, and objective spheres cannot be blocked;
yet the wise one attains mastery over these very spheres.
Therefore, one should abandon delusion and constantly cultivate wisdom;
one should always remain far removed from all faults, which are the root of lack of benefit.
Negligence gives rise to all desires, and through desire, one creates the causes of suffering.
Birth and death are both suffering; such is the nature of arising and ceasing.
If one abandons negligence, one will find no delight in sensory objects.
By being able to leave behind all faults, one attains the bliss of liberation.
Heedlessness is the tree of suffering, the root of great misery;
heedlessness can destroy all sentient beings.
These things, such as form, are impermanent; they are neither pleasure nor union.
Having gained them, one loses them again; such is the nature of all conditioned existence (*bhava*).
Whatever realms of pleasure one pursues, they are all causes of bondage;
as they are acquired, they further increase, like fire fed by dry fuel.
Thus, to be insatiable is not called happiness;
only when one attains freedom from craving can it be called happiness.
If one leaves behind the pleasures of birth and death, only then does one attain eternal happiness.
"If one is driven by desire, one cannot be said to possess permanence or bliss.

Thus, the Night-Mover King Mūśalinda, through the power of skillful means, shattered the celestial pride of those gods; with such a song of supreme and wondrous sound, never before heard, he enticed the assembly of gods, desiring that the true gods hear his singing so that they might, by virtue of hearing it, come to hear the Dharma.
When the assembly of devas had heard this, because they were permeated by the power of their past cultivation of the mind, they immediately understood the meaning of such songs.
Having understood it, a sense of weary detachment arose in their hearts, and they spoke these words:
"That deva is superior to us in every respect; he has spontaneously distanced himself from negligence to speak these verses, let alone we who are base and inferior yet practice negligence."

At that time, the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Mūsuludha, through the power of skillful means, caused the sentient beings among the devas to feel weary of and detached from [sensual existence]; he provided them with benefit by employing the foremost skillful means for severing negligence.

Because these celestial hosts are intoxicated by their physical beauty and pleasures, they do not realize that they must eventually decline and fall; when the time for their downfall arrives, they are consumed by the fires of regret, and later they are scorched by the great fires of hell.
By these skillful means, the King of the Yāma Heaven causes the genuine celestial hosts to give rise to a sense of weary detachment, thereby attaining benefit.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 56; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 57.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Six: Observing the Heavens; Section Twenty-Two: Yāma Heaven.

"At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsulinda, knowing that the hearts of the celestial hosts had conceived a sense of weary detachment, again manifested transformations to further increase their renunciation. He conjured a host of celestial beings who were sporting, singing, and dancing amidst the petals of flowers—beings whom the actual celestial hosts had never seen before."

In this way, the celestial hosts enjoy themselves and experience pleasure in countless ways and with infinite variations; however, this is for the sake of enabling the actual celestial beings to become free from pride.

At that time, when the actual celestial beings hear the sounds of the songs and music of the manifested devas, shame arises in their hearts. They cease their singing and dancing, can no longer engage in play or enjoy sensual pleasures, and with single-minded composure, they dwell correctly, observing the manifested celestial hosts.

He saw the hosts of devas of the Heaven of Transformation performing immeasurable kinds of song, dance, and playful laughter—immeasurable in their variety, immeasurable in their charm, and beyond all comparison or analogy.
At that time, the emanated devas within the lotus petals danced, sang, and sported, experiencing various pleasures.
Then, King Mūśalinda, seeing that the hearts of the actual deva hosts were free from pride and well-subdued, again caused emanated devas to dance and sing within the lotus petals.

There was a single lotus petal upon which transformation-beings (nirmāṇa-devas) were seated; suddenly it fell into the great pool. Some sank deep and did not emerge again; some surged up to the surface of the water; some floated like corpses; and some, embracing one another, both sank beneath the waves, all crying out these words: "Save us! Save us!"
They called out to one another;
some embraced each other and cried out loudly, while others embraced and then sank away.

As the assembly of real devas stood on the shore of the great pond watching the transformed devas, they saw the transformed hosts retreating, sinking, and falling into disorder and ruin; they were struck with extreme terror and profound sorrow.

"At that time, once a lotus leaf from within the pond had fallen, another lotus leaf—filled with transformed devas—also fell into the great pool. Some sank; some, being weak, floated upon the water and cried out loudly; some sank and were lost; some died and remained submerged beneath the water; and some, having died, floated upon the water like rafts."
Some cry out in distress; others embrace celestial maidens and shriek loudly; still others are tightly embraced by celestial maidens with both hands and sink into the water.
It is just as when people in the human world are in treacherous waters and, upon the destruction of their boat or raft, everyone sinks down.
Just as these transformed celestial beings dwelling within the flower petals fall together with the leaves into the pure water and sink into the great pond, so it is likewise here.
At that time, there was again another lotus petal filled with transformed celestial beings which fell and dropped into the great pond; like a stone falling into water, they did not emerge again.

At that time, there was another lotus petal upon which many transformed devas were dwelling; they then fell down into the great pond, where they embraced one another and all cried out in loud lamentation.
Some have half their bodies submerged, crying out for a long time before sinking entirely.

In this manner, hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of beings of immeasurable kinds fall slowly and calmly into the great pool like sinking stones, so that the assembly of the Real Heavens may all behold them.
"Immeasurable hosts of devas have perished and do not emerge again.

At that time, there was another lotus petal filled with transformed devas who were on the verge of falling; they let out a great cry like the crashing of a great mountain, or like an earthquake, or like the sound of the waves of the great ocean.
When the manifested devas fall, they likewise emit a great sound.

At that time, the real deva hosts on the opposite bank hear such sounds from the manifested devas and witness these various signs of decay and affliction; they all give rise to weary detachment, their hearts filled with great terror. Circling the pond, they observe these manifested devas and feel extreme revulsion, saying to one another:
"Such things as these have never been seen before."
“There are such great afflictions among all these hosts of devas—this great terror never before heard of, never before seen.
Having spoken these words, some reflected and gave rise to an intense sense of weary detachment.

At that time, there was another celestial maiden who had been sitting upon a lotus petal; she fell again into the great pond, and in her terror and seeking mercy, she cried out these words: "Save me! Save me!"
They further said to one another:
"If the devas become negligent, they will suffer such decline, affliction, and calamity, falling and sinking away.
Having thus informed each other, the minds of those true devas became subdued; they all gave rise to wearying detachment, ceased their negligence, and their minds attained compliance.

At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, seeing that the hearts of the assembly of real devas were tamed, for the sake of benefiting others, concealed his own body and entered the lotus pedestal.
Together with the tamed and heedful devas, he entered the lotus pedestal, causing the actual deva hosts not to see the Heavenly King.
With the most excellent and virtuous minds, the King and the deva hosts, for the sake of benefiting the deva hosts, all entered together into the center of the lotus pedestal.
The other real devas do not see their bodies; observing the real devas, they think to themselves:
"How is that deva? Has he been subdued?"
"Have you abandoned arrogance?

At that time, the Heavenly King knew that the hearts of the assembly of devas were well-subdued, and that they no longer entertained thoughts of negligence, but had all given rise to a sense of dread.
"Now is precisely the time; I should preach the Dharma for them and gather them in.
Having understood this matter, he again manifested transformations within a great lotus flower in the middle of the large pond, causing [the beings] to feel fear.
He transformed himself into a lotus flower with immeasurable petals and various emanated deities, which fell into the great pond upon the lotus petals.
As they fell into the water, they uttered immeasurable sounds of terror, and furthermore, he manifested as an infinite multitude of celestial corpses strewn in disarray.
The Yāma Heaven King Mucilinda thought to himself:
"These celestial hosts are filled with extreme terror; they may well flee and run toward other lands."
He then immediately manifested further transformations so that they could not depart; seeing only these transformed devas, they gave rise to an ever-deepening sense of great revulsion and detachment.
Having performed all such various manifestations, he entered the flower pedestal together with the host of devas and observed once more.
Having observed them all, out of the highest compassion and for the benefit of the celestial hosts, he emerged from the lotus pedestal.

Once he had emerged from the flower pedestal together with the celestial hosts, he withdrew his supernormal power, and the manifested transformations all vanished. He then comforted the celestial hosts, saying these words:
"If devas are heedless, they shall all undergo this decline and suffering."
"All fears have heedlessness as their root;
those gods who are not heedless shall have no fear and shall not suffer decline or affliction.
At that time, King Mūśalinda spoke in verse for the sake of the assembly of gods:
"The foolish delight in negligence and constantly suffer various afflictions;
if one is free from negligence, then one attains perpetual peace and happiness."
"All trees of suffering have heedlessness as their root;
therefore, those who wish to be free from suffering should abandon heedlessness.
