At that time, the Real Gods, seeing the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mucilinda, felt their minds become peaceful and secure; with joy, they rushed toward the King of the Yāma Heaven and said to one another:
"I have now obtained a lord—the King of the Yāma Heaven—who sits here upon a great lotus pedestal, surrounded by a host of devas; he is able to protect me and is able to sustain me."
Having thus deliberated together one by one, they all proceeded toward the lotus pedestal atop the Great Lotus.

The lion throne in the abode of the Heavenly King Mucilinda and the lotus pedestal were both of the same color; the Heavenly King Yama, along with the other hosts of devas, dwelt within the flower pedestal.
When the celestial hosts had arrived, they said to the Heavenly King:
"Who has caused the celestial hosts to be thus shattered, thus afflicted with distress, and thus fallen and submerged in the water, crying out in lamentation?"
"Who could inflict such various sufferings and afflictions upon the hosts of devas?
At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"This fault of negligence is certainly present in all sentient beings."
"You, the assembly of devas, do not all know this.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, spoke in verse for the sake of the assembly of devas:
"All sentient beings Are utterly unable to shatter it."
Of all karmic activities, none can surpass it;
it causes the entire world to fall into ruin.
Because it possesses such power, it is called death.
He can destroy the world; he can shatter the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
From this world, the King of Death leads one away to the future life.
There is no power able to resist him, and there is no one who can save.
Only the Dharma can save; therefore, the Dharma is called "salvation.
Life does not endure for long, and youthful vigor is likewise transient.
Death approaches with great swiftness; one should not give rise to negligence.
The pleasures of all sentient beings are all destroyed by impermanence;
life is extinguished by death—therefore, one should not delight in heedlessness.
When wholesome karma is exhausted, one will inevitably fall into the three evil realms.
Having recognized such faults, one should not delight in heedlessness.
The world is subject to impermanence; all possess the thorns of the three poisons.
Since there is birth, there is death; therefore, one should not delight in heedlessness.
Death can destroy life; old age can cause decay and change;
illness can ruin one's well-being; therefore, one should not delight in negligence.
The ropes of karma bind sentient beings, for the mind relies upon these ropes as its walkway.
Wandering through the three realms of existence, one should not delight in heedlessness.
Those who delight [in it] will surely suffer; for those who suffer, suffering becomes ever more intense.
Like a husband serving his wife and children, one should not delight in heedlessness.
A mother may become one's wife, and a wife may become an enemy;
such is the cycle of transmigration—therefore, one should not delight in negligence.
Even when surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens in gardens, groves, and mountain valleys, [one must remain heedful].
The world shall all come to an end; one should not delight in negligence.
All the pleasures enjoyed by the devas must ultimately return to destruction;
they are false and cannot be relied upon—thus, one should not delight in negligence.
All that is born is suffering; it is the vessel for old age and death.
Since this is certain and inevitable, one should not delight in negligence.
The sense faculties are difficult to subdue, and there is no one capable of subduing them.
All pleasures come to an end; one should not delight in heedlessness.
Youth must inevitably grow old, and all desires are like dreams.
Therefore, the wise person should not delight in heedlessness.
Like the leaves of a plantain tree, like lightning that does not endure long, all things are subject to destruction;
one should not take pleasure in heedlessness.
The sense faculties are difficult to subdue, for they delight in attachment to their respective objects.
"Only those possessed of wisdom / Can abide in their own realm.
Thus did the celestial king Mūśalinda, seeing that the minds of the assembly of devas were weary and detached, speak these verses for the benefit of others.
At that time, the celestial king Mucilinda again spoke to the assembly of devas regarding the fault of negligence, saying:
"How is it that you, O assembly of devas, are submerged in the darkness of negligence, failing to see great evil and failing to see great fear?"
"You all have seen how these gods, because of their negligence, were all utterly destroyed and returned to death, with no one able to save them.

All the articles of pleasure belonging to those hosts of gods were superior to yours; their complexion, stature, and form, their wealth and joy, their radiance, the singing of the celestial maidens, and their dancing and play were all superior."
"You all see before your eyes how those hosts of devas have been utterly destroyed due to their negligence.
You, too, as a host of devas, should all reflect upon this and distance yourselves from negligence."
Among all the evil dragons in the world—within the dragon-pools and the pools of heedlessness—the dragons of sensory objects are the most wicked.
Among all the evils of wind and fire, the fire of heedlessness and the wind of recollective thought are the most extreme.
Of all accumulations of darkness—those gathered over immeasurable time and those accumulated since beginningless time—the accumulation of darkness that is heedlessness is the most profound obscurity.
Among all malicious enemies who seek an opportunity, the great enemy of heedlessness, which seeks an opportunity within its objects, is the most evil.
Among all sharp swords, the sharp sword of heedlessness is the most injurious; it is the sword that causes one to fall into the evil realms.
Among all great and wicked venomous serpents, the venomous serpent of heedlessness—the poison of craving—is able to kill all foolish sentient beings and is the most evil of poisons.
Among all enemies who feign intimacy, the enemy of heedlessness that falsely manifests as a friend is the greatest evil, for it gives rise to all forms of attachment and craving.
Among all forms of fetters—handcuffs, shackles, stocks, chains, and even ropes—the bond of heedlessness is the most firm, for it is more difficult to overcome than any other.
Among all wildernesses that are waterless, treeless, fruitless, and without shade, where immeasurable sentient beings encounter suffering, the wilderness of heedlessness is the most evil of all.

Because they are devoid of the water of happiness, lack the trees of virtuous people, and are bereft of the shade of ethical discipline, they can inflict immeasurable suffering and affliction upon all sentient beings in the world.
Amidst all unreal and false views, they take these delusive perceptions to be real, like a whirling firebrand or a city of Gandharvas.
Within the mirage of craving for deer, heedlessness and falsehood are the most unreal.
The pleasures of sensory objects are shifting, neither remaining nor abiding; they lack any reality and are merely false perceptions, like a whirling firebrand or a city of the Gandharvas.
Among the mirages that deceive the deer, heedlessness is the most false and unreal.
Among all precipices from which one may fall, the precipice of heedlessness is the most fearsome, for it inevitably leads to falling into the great evil realms.
"You hosts of devas, you should know!
All sentient beings comprised within these five realms of existence fall into the great evil paths because of negligence, and because those in the three lower realms commit evil karmic actions."
"Therefore, all those who fear suffering and affliction should diligently abandon heedlessness with all their hearts.
This heedlessness is the root of all suffering.
At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda addressed the assembly of devas in verse, saying:
"Through heedfulness one attains liberation; through heedlessness one constantly suffers.
Heedfulness and heedlessness—their characteristics have already been briefly explained."
"Thus, the celestial king Mūśalinda tamed the gods and expounded the True Path for them.
At that time, the assembly of gods listened with single-minded attention; because their minds were tamed, they subdued their sense faculties, and their faculties became tranquil."
The Yāma Heaven King Mūśaludha was seated upon a lion throne on a lotus pedestal, when the assembly of devas addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"We pray that you will speak for us of ultimate benefit and ultimate happiness, so that we may attain this ultimate benefit and ultimate happiness."
"How should I practice?
At that time, the Heavenly King addressed the gods, saying:

"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who possesses all-knowledge; he is a teacher of liberation, fully liberated from all faults, and completely endowed with all virtues. Among all sentient beings, he is the most preeminent. If you can take refuge in him, you will be able to sever and eliminate your sufferings and afflictions."
"The Buddha is free from negligence; you should take refuge in him, for he can rescue you all from the immeasurable and boundless terrors of birth and death.

At that time, having heard the instruction of the Heavenly King, the entire assembly of devas—along with the celestial maidens—knelt on their right knees, gave rise to a heart of reverent devotion, and brought their sense faculties under control.
They conceived a heart of reverence for the Buddha, the World-Honored One; with palms joined in prostration, they received the three refuges.

All the hosts of devas, with sincere hearts, took refuge in the Buddha, took refuge in the Dharma, and took refuge in the Saṃgha. With virtuous and pure minds, they censured their own negligence and sincerely repented their transgressions, seeing that the devas of the Transformation Heaven were subject to immeasurable kinds of decay, affliction, and destruction, and could not endure such boundless suffering and distress.
"At that time, the Lord of Devas, Mucilinda, seeing that the assembly of devas had conceived a sense of weary detachment, further manifested immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
In a mere moment, he was able to manifest a single body as a thousand bodies, and within those thousand bodies, he manifested a hundred thousand bodies."
In an instant, from a single form, they manifest immeasurable varieties of forms.
In an instant, they soar into the void, their bodies adorned with various exquisite jewels and diverse garments and attire.

In an instant, he submerged into the water and manifested a thousand heads, adorned with various jeweled crowns and various jeweled seals upon his arms; the radiance of his body surpassed that of a thousand suns.
In an instant, he manifested a great mountain complete with gardens and groves;
amidst these gardens and groves, he was surrounded by all the hosts of devas, who all beheld him.
Or he may see him situated within a great lotus flower, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens of radiant light, all of whom emit light from their bodies.
At that time, the entire assembly of real devas was unable to behold the body of the Heavenly King or the host of celestial maidens.

Then, the Heavenly King Muxuluotuo again manifested supernatural powers; in order to cause the assembly of devas to abandon negligence, he caused hundreds of thousands of great assemblies of devas to emerge from his mouth.

Some sit within palaces made of the seven precious gems, their bodies radiant with various exquisite jewels and adorned with diverse garments; together with celestial maidens, they are majestic and upright, chanting heavenly songs as they are surrounded by their retinues.
All of these emerge from the mouth of the celestial king Mucilinda.

Some sit upon lotuses, their voices like the humming of bees as they drink celestial wine whose fragrance and flavor are perfectly harmonized; accompanied by hundreds or thousands of celestial maidens, adorned with divine garments and garlands, their bodies radiating light—all emerge from the mouth of the celestial king.

At that time, Mūśalinda again manifested supernatural powers, which issued forth from his mouth; some among the hosts of devas rode upon birds made of the seven precious gems, sporting and singing amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music, enjoying themselves in delight together with celestial maidens.
Emerging from the mouth of the Heavenly King, his celestial adornments were beyond compare, and he was fully endowed with radiant merit.

At that time, the Heavenly King Mūśalinda again used his supernatural power to manifest a celestial being who emerged from his mouth and sat within a *kubjara* lotus. This being performed celestial music, producing exquisite sounds, while surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens; they all drank celestial wine, singing praises and laughing in merriment.

Surrounded by hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial maidens whose incomparable beauty and excellence surpasses that of ordinary goddesses, they sport in various ways within the celestial gardens and traverse the paths through the air;
their singing and chanting are a hundred times more magnificent than those of the gods of the Realm of Desire.
The melodies and the various qualities of the musical instruments were all perfectly complete, causing the assembly of devas to hear them.
At that time, the real devas had never before seen such a rare phenomenon; having seen it, they all gave rise to a sense of wonder.
Some were filled with joy, while others gave rise to doubt and thought to themselves:
"How is it that this deva has emerged from the mouth of the Heavenly King?
This is truly most rare!"
At that time, the assembly of real devas reflected thus, or conversed among themselves, not knowing what to do.
Then, King Mūsulinda again manifested supernatural powers, causing emanated seers of various appearances to emerge from his mouth.

Some have long hair, while others wear their hair in spiral topknots; some wear garments of tree bark, while others hold water jars in their hands; some are adorned with celestial robes and flower garlands, while others wear black deerskin garments.
"Various great sages of such diverse forms and appearances—some hundreds, some thousands—emerged from his mouth; having emerged, they remained in the midst of the sky and spoke these verses:
'The minds of all sentient beings Are like illusory phenomena, never abiding.
All must eventually return to death; Do not be heedless within the realm of existence.'"
Among all things that are lovely, The mind of attachment grows ever more intense;
In the end, they must all return to destruction— Do not be heedless within existence (*bhava*).
Within existence there is no place Where one is born and does not pass away.
All pleasures are fearful; do not be negligent within existence.
Among all that is seen, that which is called the five desirable sensual desires—all these are like dreams; do not be negligent within existence.
Lustful craving is difficult to subdue; it is a constant enemy to sentient beings, swiftly leading them into hell.
Do not be heedless while within the realms of existence.
Though one repeatedly experiences sensual pleasures, having gained them, they are lost once more.
All things must inevitably perish; do not be heedless amidst conditioned existence.
That which is unwholesome in the beginning, middle, and end can destroy the world.
Bound by the shackles of karma, one is like a fish caught on a hook.
Though one employs various skillful means, desiring to sever the fetters of karma, neither any god nor any non-god can sever those fetters of karma.
The fetters of birth and death are exceedingly long; their beginning and end cannot be seen.
This craving is exceedingly firm, binding the deluded person.
Myself and the other hosts of devas, as well as humans and asuras—
all are impermanent, yet those blinded by ignorance cannot see it.
The body of karma pervades all things, constantly transmigrating through the various realms of existence;
when the mind is bound by all forms of craving, only wisdom can sever it.
From the waters of craving, the five fire-drills are produced.
Due to the power of the winds of vitarka and vicāra, one is consumed by the fire of time.
Fools lacking wisdom, who crave false pleasures amidst suffering,
take things perversely due to delusion and wander through the five realms of existence.
Delighting in wife and children, as well as in various forms of wealth and pleasure,
one constantly preserves these delusive joys, only to be led away by the King of Death.
Just as a tiger or wolf kills a deer, slaying it without ever growing weary or satiated.
The Great King of Death possesses immense power; his slaughter is likewise.
Amidst all states of existence, there are immeasurable and manifold sufferings;
yet, deluded by ignorance, the mind never grows weary.
"If a person relies upon evil, they cannot be said to love their own body;
since they do not love their own body, what else in this world could they love?

Thus did the transformed seer, who had emerged from the mouth of the celestial king Mūśalinda, speak these verses for the sake of the real devas to eliminate their negligence, providing them with ultimate benefit.

At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda, further seeking to benefit them, manifested a supernatural transformation; from his chest, he caused a great lotus pond to emerge, most delightful to behold.
The pond was adorned with many geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, and contained the most pure water of eight virtues.
Upon the lotus ponds were hundreds of billions of seven-jeweled lotuses covering the surface, the fragrance of which filled a hundred yojanas.

Upon that lotus pedestal sat the King, adorned with a celestial crown embellished with various exquisite jewels; his body was graced by various radiances and various precious robes, his arms were adorned with various jeweled seals, and he was surrounded by various court ladies as he sat upon a lion throne.
The various court ladies stood in attendance at his left and right, each holding a white fly-whisk.
Furthermore, there were people who praised the king, saying:
"How supremely sublime! You are like Śakra, the second King of Devas; there are hundreds of thousands of such emanated kings."

Out of a heart of compassion and for the sake of benefiting others, and in order to cause all the genuine celestial hosts to abandon negligence, the King of the Yāma Heaven manifested as Śakra, a universal monarch (cakravartin), and countless hundreds of thousands of other kings.
At that time, for the sake of benefiting [beings], the celestial king Mūśalinda further manifested a transformation.
From his navel there emerged a great lotus flower, one hundred yojanas in breadth, with hundreds of thousands of billions of petals.

The lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems have leaves of various jewels, and many bees emerge from them, producing melodic songs; those who hear them find joy in their hearts, and those who see them love and delight in them.

From the navel of the King of the Yāma Heaven, there emerges a manifested lotus flower; its stem is five thousand yojanas long, with a shaft of lapis lazuli interspersed with diamonds and composed of blue Indra-nīla gems, all of which serve as adornments, possessing a brilliance surpassing that of a celestial rainbow and being exceedingly lovely.
"Within a great lotus, there were various emanated beings whose bodies were adorned with diverse garments. Experiencing the most supreme bliss, they plowed the earth with plows and spoke this verse:
'All those who plow the earth Have hearts that hope for fruit;
Because their deluded minds long for profit, They do not realize that death shall come.'"
The fool’s mind covets profit, increasing it moment by moment;
yet he does not perceive that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) perish moment by moment.
When the time for the punishment of old age arrives, it can bring youth and vigor to an end.
When the suffering of illness arrives, it can destroy one's peace and security.
These three kinds of evil punishments destroy both gods and asuras;
the time for their swift arrival is imminent, yet the foolish do not perceive it.
Devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, rākṣasas,
and piśācas— all are destroyed by old age and death.
They cause those possessed by craving to abandon their kinsmen.
Bound by the fetters of delusion and craving, one revolves through the various realms of existence;
from son to grandson, and grandson to son—such is the cycle of seeds.
Deceived by craving, a person shall lose everything.
"Thus did the emanated person speak these verses for the benefit of others.
At that time, having heard these verses, the assembly of real devas reflected and contemplated within their minds, no longer finding much delight in sensory objects."

At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda, for the benefit of the assembly of devas, again manifested transformations; from within all his limbs, there appeared various ornaments, various countenances, and various jeweled crowns, in immeasurable colors, immeasurable forms, and immeasurable characteristics.
Devas, gandharvas, humans, nāgas, asuras, and others, each adorned with their own characteristic garments and ornaments, emerged from the pores of the celestial king’s body.
Each appears in its own natural color, according to its form and characteristics, and according to its own nature.
Together with their female attendants, they sing, dance, laugh, and play, enjoying themselves and experiencing pleasure.

The Heavenly King experiences pleasure similar to that of humans; he is wealthy, joyful, and delighted, loving one another, and enjoys himself through singing, dancing, laughing, and playful merriment.

Furthermore, there were various nāgas, adorned in diverse ways; some had one head, some two, and others up to seven heads. They possessed various colors and various forms, their heads adorned with exquisite and wondrous jeweled crowns. With various sounds, they sang and played, giving rise to hearts of joy as they enjoyed themselves in pleasure.
In this manner, the valiant ones, Rāhu, the asuras, and all others were completely manifested.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, finding delight that surpassed that of the Yāma Heaven, was surrounded by and made offerings to together with his various celestial maidens.
This is the first adornment:
surrounded by and making offerings to asura maidens, they hear the sounds of the five kinds of music, which are delightful to the ear;
the asura king dwells in his palace, emerging from the body of the heavenly lord Mucilinda, and experiences the foremost bliss.

Furthermore, he further manifested as beings of Uttarakuru, dwelling in the ten great mountains such as Meghapaṅkti; they were wealthy, joyful, and sovereign, being only slightly inferior to the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa.
In the gardens, groves, and flower ponds, there are many rivers of various foods and drinks, where they enjoy themselves through diverse songs, dances, and games.
Emerging from the body of the celestial king Mūśalinda, he further transforms into people of Aparagoyānī; their own pleasures are perfected, and they likewise sport with joy in this same manner.
At that time, the assembly of real devas beheld these and other such immeasurable kinds and immeasurable distinctions.
The King of the Yāma Heaven, having accomplished such supreme supernormal powers, performed this transformation for the sake of eliminating negligence and for the purpose of supreme benefit.
It is not without benefit.
By causing the heedless devas to directly perceive impermanence, their minds become supple; therefore, he manifests various transformations of perfect abundance.
First he shows the flavor of desire, and subsequently he reveals its faults, so as to cause them to grow weary of desire.
For these reasons, the King of the Yāma Heaven manifests transformations for the sake of the real devas to demonstrate the flavor of desire.

They experience various pleasures, engaging in song, dance, and play; they are adorned with garments, provided with food, drink, and celestial maidens, and attend upon him with offerings. Their five sense faculties experience pleasure exactly as they conceive it in their minds, obtaining everything in full abundance; this is called the flavor of desire.
What are the faults of desire?

Once one has obtained what is desired, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight; yet when seeking it, one does not obtain it, or it is shared with others rather than belonging exclusively to oneself. There is the suffering of separation from what is loved, as well as immeasurable kinds of suffering, such as being plundered by those who are powerful.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of things that can be seized by powerful forces: namely, kings, thieves, water, fire, and enemies.

There are further sufferings: one is constantly encroached upon by adversaries, constantly fears being robbed by others, and lives in dread of guarding possessions; or one suffers mental grief regarding birth and death, and though craving pleasure, the body and mind are in constant pain.
Such are the perils of desire, which ultimately lead to death and involve immeasurable kinds of decline, affliction, and suffering.
Yet, foolish people do not give rise to revulsion or renunciation toward these perils of desire, these declines, afflictions, and sufferings.
Furthermore, there is the fault of desire; what are these faults?
Because of the causes and conditions of desire, mother and son quarrel and dwell in different places—all of this arises solely from the causes and conditions of desire.
If brothers quarrel and contend, hating and envying one another, whether they strike or bind each other, all this arises from the causes and conditions of desire; this is the fault of desire.

If kings contend over immeasurable territories, attacking and subjugating one another, binding and imprisoning one another, killing or harming one another, and inflicting all manner of suffering—all this is due to the causes and conditions of desire; this is the fault of desire.
Therefore, you should know that all beings in the cycle of birth and death are bound by desire.

At that time, the celestial king Mūśalinda, for the sake of the assembly of true devas, manifested such immeasurable and diverse human failings regarding desire, including kings contending with one another through countless expedients.

Furthermore, when other people enter the great ocean for the sake of desire, whether they engage in conflict, or are imprisoned or bound, or experience sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, or face the fear of strife and harmful matters—all these arise solely due to the causes and conditions of desire.
Among all human beings, none attain peace and security because of the faults of desire.
How is it that among the devas there are also faults arising from desire?
It is said that when the various devas engage in battle with the asuras and destroy one another, it is entirely due to the causal conditions of desire.
It is likewise when the asuras engage in conflict with the devas.
Such things arise due to the causes and conditions of desire; this constitutes the fault of desire.
For this reason, the Night-Moving Lord (Mukhulinda) King of the Yāma Heaven manifests such transformations in order to eliminate the heedlessness of the genuine celestial hosts.
"If dragons and their like engage in mutual conflict and strife, causing the destruction of their lands and the unleashing of thunder and hail—all this arises from the causal conditions of desire.
If various animals mutually fight, kill, bind, or capture one another—all this arises from the causal conditions of desire; these are called the faults of desire."

Among the spirits and deities, they strike one another down or hack each other with knives due to the cause of food or the cause of desire; all of this arises from the cause of desire, which constitutes the fault of desire.
For this reason, in order to eliminate the negligence of the genuine devas, the King of the Yāma Heaven manifested such a transformation,
[showing them] how beings within the hells burn and strike one another, kill one another, and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

While among humans, due to the causes and conditions of desire, they committed evil deeds, engaging in strife, hatred, and envy; because they recalled those past causes and conditions of female form, they harbored mutual hatred and envy, and by virtue of these evil karmas, they fell into the hells, their bodies torn asunder and destroyed.
Thus, these hells all arise from the faults of desire.

For this reason, the King of the Yāma Heaven, in order to cause the genuine devas to abandon desire, manifested such transformations throughout the five destinies to demonstrate the faults and calamities of desire, leading them to weary of birth and death, and showing that all the flavors of desire found among human beings are ultimately lost.

The King of the Yāma Heaven, in order to demonstrate to the celestial hosts both the flavors of desire and the faults of desire, manifested a lotus flower whose hundred petals fell away, decayed, and were destroyed; he further extensively revealed the transgressions of gods and humans.
Having thus demonstrated the faults, he further demonstrates the seeds of liberation and transcendence for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to the assembly of devas.
For the sake of further benefiting the assembly of devas, the King of the Yāma Heaven again demonstrates the faults of desire.
Why is this? Because upon hearing of the faults of various desires, one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment from birth and death due to those differing views.
For this reason, he further demonstrates the faults of desire for the sake of the assembly of devas.

Whether they be devas, nāgas, asuras, or others, after having shown them the flavor of desire, he further shows them the faults of desire, [explaining] that at the time of their downfall and decline, they encounter various forms of decay and affliction.

When these gods, humans, nāgas, and asuras have experienced all manner of immeasurable sensual pleasures in every place, at the time of their decline, they are shown all the various signs of passing away according to what each among the gods and others is destined to undergo.

That is to say, upon high mountains with steep and precipitous cliffs and banks, there are immeasurable varieties of lions, tigers, leopards, wild foxes, pigs, rabbits, oxen, donkeys, elephants, horses, camels, cats, and cattle, as well as species such as the *śiśumāra* fish, the *makara* fish, tortoises, and turtles; some have one head, some two heads, and others many heads, with earth in their mouths and fire held in their hands.
Furthermore, smoke and flames arise simultaneously from their entire bodies; some rain down fire, while others discharge fierce vajra-hail that covers vast areas.
Their roaring and shrieking are most terrifying, like a hundred mountains collapsing at once.

Their bodies were of immeasurable varieties and a dark, murky hue; their heads were like great mountains, and their physical forms were terrifying. Their hair stood erect over their entire bodies, ablaze with fierce flames.
Some had a hundred arms, others a thousand; in their hands they held nooses, or swords and staves, or vajras—those who saw them were struck with great terror.
A multitude such as these, filling the mountains and valleys, emerged from the great mountain and rushed toward the Heaven of Manifested Transformations (*nirmāṇarati*).

With eyes wide open in a great rage, their eyes were red like blood; from their mouths issued tongues of flame in immeasurable varieties of colors—yellow, crimson, vermilion, and purple—like flashes of lightning erupting chaotically amidst black clouds.
Furthermore, he manifested the King of Death, Yama, and his messengers, whose appearance was terrifying; they rushed toward the Heaven of Manifestation, clutching red cords and various weapons.
The tips of the weapons they held were all ablaze with fire.
They let out a great, evil sound like a crashing thunderclap, their bodies blazing intensely for ten *yojanas*.

Among them are messengers of death (*yama-dūta*), some with one hundred eyes, some with four hundred, and even some with a thousand; from all these eyes flames erupt in various colors—blue, red, yellow, pigeon-colored, and other variegated hues—and their fires blaze fiercely for ten *li*.
With various appearances that all sentient beings find terrifying, they were hideous and loathsome as they emerged from the mountain of transformations, roaring and howling.
Their protruding bellies hung down, their flanks were like mountain valleys, and their heads were like mountain peaks.
Some have constricted throats that enter between their two shoulders; some have long hair, all of which stands straight up, with flames erupting from their throats.
Some have long claws, from which flames blaze intensely.
Some had flames erupting from the hair on their bodies, while others were engulfed in fierce, blazing fires across their entire forms, like great mountains being consumed.
All emerged from the mountains manifested by Great Power, raining down vajra-hail.

Furthermore, there are the messengers of Yama, the King of Death, whose heads resemble those of crows, vultures, owls, eagles, jackals, foxes, dogs, and camels; their entire bodies are ablaze with fire, and they cover themselves with malevolent insects to terrify the celestial hosts.

Emerging from the Mount Mahākālāparivarta, they all ran with great speed like a fierce wind, blowing away the great black clouds as blazing lightning arose together, as they rushed toward the gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven.

At that time, Yama, the King of Death, as his executioners drew near the *nirmāṇarati* devas, seized them; with flaming iron cords, he bound their hands behind their backs, and having bound them, he dragged them away.
At that time, when the emanated devas saw other emanated devas whose bodies were bound, they became utterly terrified and each fled in different directions.

Then, the messengers of the Lord of Death pursued and seized them, lifted them onto their heads, and ascended into the sky and departed until they could no longer be seen, having passed beyond the range of sight.
The sound of their roaring and shrieking was most terrifying.
Sometimes the Lord of Death (Yama) would seize a transformed deva, bind his neck with flaming iron cords, and depart into the earth.
Furthermore, the King of Death, Yama, together with his messengers, seizes other devas of the transformation realm, casting them into water where they wail and cry out in distress.
Yet, despite their cries, the bodies of those devas of the transformation realm do not sink; they remain upon the surface of the water. For the sake of these devas, he speaks this verse:
"By a mind of folly and arrogance, Driven by heedlessness,"
The time of pleasure has already passed; now one must face the suffering of death.
In the forest of immeasurable realms, poisonous venom fills its depths;
the fangs of craving are vast and great—one who seeks the good should abandon them.
Having performed no virtuous deeds, yet constantly deluded and heedless,
now that the time of death has arrived, what indeed can one do?
Immersed in the waters of craving, one is unable to cross over the manifold sufferings.
Because one has not escaped birth and death, there is never any peace or joy.
For all who are born, death constantly follows behind;
why then do foolish people delight in heedless conduct?
Difficult to perceive and impossible to obstruct, It always possesses great power;
this mighty army of death Is not recognized by the world.
It is no ordinary force of combat, And there is no means by which one can escape it.
Because sentient beings are heedless, they do not perceive that the enemy of death has arrived.
There are two messengers of death that roam throughout the world:
namely, old age and the decay of illness; yet the deluded do not realize this.

"Thus did Yama, the King of Death, the Lord of the Underworld, and his messengers speak these verses to rebuke the assembly of devas, inflicting various sufferings upon them hundreds and thousands of times."
At that time, having witnessed their decline and suffering, the assembly of real devas abandoned all heedless thoughts and took the three refuges.

Then, the King of the Yāma Heaven, knowing that the minds of the assembly of devas were already subdued, further manifested transformations to cause the assembly of real devas to attain weary detachment.

The celestial crowns worn by these emanated kings, as well as all their desired requisites, all emerge from the body of the heavenly king Mucilinda, who together with his court ladies provides them with harmonious offerings.

As previously described, though one was once endowed with a superior complexion, it is now ravaged by old age: the hair turns white, the face becomes wrinkled, the veins protrude all over the body, and one must walk leaning on a staff. Emaciated and haggard, one can no longer perform any of one's former tasks; dependent upon others for everything, one is mocked and ridiculed by fools. Breath becomes labored and joyless, the faculties mature and decline, and all physical strength is exhausted.
Despised by all, he stumbled repeatedly as he walked.

As the time of his death approached, he went near the pond; his body was extremely emaciated and he had to rely on others for support. His complexion was hideous as he moved along the edge of the pond.

Before long, many various ailments arose within his body, namely: fever, diarrhea, coughing and asthma, severe respiratory distress, swelling of the vessels, carbuncles and ulcers, and leprosy; he drew near to the brink of death, his body becoming exceedingly foul and loathsome.
This is a most grievous illness that cannot be cured.
The signs of death have already appeared; the king, afflicted by such various maladies and undergoing such extreme suffering, shall thereafter pass away.
After death, the body becomes bloated, putrid, and rotten, infested with countless hundreds of thousands of kinds of worms.

At that time, the hosts of devas see this corpse; furthermore, vultures, eagles, and other predatory birds fly down from the mountains, seizing the corpses to devour them, while some take the corpses up into the air and depart.
When the assembly of devas saw this, their minds grew weary of desire, and they became single-mindedly focused on right mindfulness.

At that time, the Heavenly King, for the benefit of the devas, further manifested his divine transformations, showing them that Rāhu the Asura King, Vīrabhadra the Asura King, and all the others were entirely beneath the great ocean waters.
He went to the abode of the Heavenly King in the Yāma Heaven; not far from the King, he stood to one side and cried out with a loud voice.
Having finished his cry, he fell headlong to the ground and immediately died, becoming like wood or stone—motionless and unconscious.
When the various asura kings and their court ladies saw this, they were overcome with extreme anguish; they all surrounded him, wailing and weeping.
While they were weeping, birds flew down and seized the corpses; like wood or stone, the bodies were taken by the flocks of birds without their feeling it or moving.

Once the asura women had finished their lamentation, they all died, and were then vied for and carried away by hawks, vultures, crows, and ravens, which departed through the air so that the hosts of devas could no longer see them.
To benefit the celestial hosts, the King of the Yāma Heaven manifested such weeping and lamentation through his transformative power.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven further transformed himself into a dragon king, as previously described, once again demonstrating impermanence.
There are some nāga kings who are scorched by hot sand, like blazing flames.
Just as khaṭṭhara charcoal thrown into a heap of dry grass, so too are these nāga kings scorched by the hot sand.
Furthermore, there were dragon kings surrounded by dragon maidens who were seized and carried off by garuḍas; the assembly of dragon maidens raised a great cry.
There were also dragon kings being sawn apart, wailing with piteous voices as they hacked at one another with hearts full of resentment, inflicting mutual harm upon each other.
When these manifested nāgas were about to be led away to their deaths,
the hosts of devas, having witnessed this event, felt profound revulsion and renunciation. At that time,
the King of the Yāma Heaven again manifested hundreds of thousands of people from Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī, all of whom were in a state of decay and distress.
It is the same for all women: having reached the extreme of old age in a mere moment, they all return to death.
Once dead, many worms proliferate within them as they lie prostrate upon the ground, utterly loathsome and contemptible.

At that time, the assembly of real devas, having witnessed these various and immeasurable distinctions of great evil and transgression, and having seen the suffering of death, all gave rise to weary detachment and said to one another:
"These sentient beings die amidst suffering."
"These sentient beings, though their aging, sickness, and death come to an end, ultimately do not know where they shall go or by whom they shall be led away.
All requisites are impermanent; all pleasures are intermingled with faults."
"Impermanent and non-abiding, these are phenomena subject to decay and ruin, and cannot be relied upon for security.
All dharmas are utterly destroyed; there is not even the slightest happiness."
Thus the real gods discussed this among themselves, and all felt a sense of weary detachment.

At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, knowing that the hearts of the celestial hosts had become weary and detached, further manifested a man who was sovereign and free from pride, destined for rebirth in a higher realm—specifically a person of Uttarakuru, whose heavenly merit was slightly diminished yet who enjoyed the foremost pleasures—and then manifested him as one who grew old, fell ill, and died.
Once the body has died, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worms devour its corpse; anyone who sees it feels revulsion, as if it were a heap of excrement.
For the sake of benefiting the negligent hosts of devas, the King of the Yāma Heaven manifested such a transformation of a person from Uttarakuru.
At that time, the Heavenly King further created another manifestation to be seen by the actual devas, which they took to be an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*).

Within the transformation of the immeasurable net of existence, beings of the intermediate state (antarābhava) arise; just as when sentient beings die, they are born among the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, or devas due to the causal conditions of their karma.

He manifested beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), causing the assembly of devas to directly perceive the immeasurable and diverse mental activities and karmas, as well as the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births and deaths within the five destinies (*pañcagati*) arising from causes and conditions.
In order to cause the various real devas to attain weary detachment, he manifested such transformations within the great pond— unconceivable and rare transformations,
peerless and incomparable.

He caused the devas to behold within the waters of the pond all sentient beings of the five realms, clearly seeing them transmigrating and wandering due to the power of the causes and conditions of their karma and afflictions.
Dying from one state of existence and being reborn in another, they revolve through birth and death without rescue, without refuge, and without companions.

As they cycle through the various realms of existence—transmigrating through the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, as well as among humans and devas—they cause the assembly of true devas to behold the various intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of birth; having seen them, they are struck with terror and give rise to the utmost weary detachment.
Furthermore, he sees the intermediate-state bodies among the gods of Yāma; he sees the gods of Yāma falling from heaven due to the exhaustion of their karma, consumed by the fires of remorse.
Due to greed and negligence, the celestial body perishes and the intermediate state (antarābhava) body arises, with its feet upward and head downward.
Just as an impression is made from a seal, by means of evil karma, the intermediate state body of hell is produced.
Seeing the karma of birth and death, they were struck with extreme terror and said to one another:
"The causal conditions of this karma greatly deceive the hosts of the Yāma Heaven."

At that time, when the real celestial hosts saw this, they gave rise to a mind of weary detachment. This is called seeing the intermediate state (antarābhava) within hell, not the state of existence at birth (upapattibhava).
Thus did Maudgalyāyana manifest such a transformation.
"For what reason is the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) not shown?

Because the minds of the devas are delicate and cannot endure it; if they were to see the arising of the aggregates—a suffering beyond analogy and beyond description—they would immediately lose their lives."

Therefore, this is a manifested transformation; it does not indicate the actual intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of birth. This is called the true celestial being observing the intermediate state body of a Yāma-deva who has fallen from his realm and is about to enter hell.

At that time, the King of the Yāma-devas further uses a rare and divine manifestation of the intermediate state to show how the Yāma-devas are harmed by the faults of negligence. Because their karma is exhausted, they are about to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, with their feet upward and their heads downward.
Like a seal and its impression, drawn by the ropes of karma, they ripen in accordance with the actions they have performed.
At that time, the real devas again see such a second intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"Furthermore, thirdly, one sees the transformation of the intermediate state (antarābhava): like those in the Yāma Heaven who are harmed by negligence, when their karma is exhausted they fall back; bound by evil karma and about to fall among animals, they appear with feet upward and head downward."

In this way, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is like a seal being impressed; one is born among the various immeasurable species of animals with an intermediate state corresponding to that birth. This is called the third characteristic of the intermediate state within the path of existence.
Seeing this, they were struck with fear and gave rise to weary detachment; filled with alarm and dread, they looked at one another and spoke in verse:
"Subtle and difficult to comprehend, Pervading all places, This karma drives sentient beings To wander through the various realms of existence."
If a person slanders the noble ones, delights in practicing the karma of false views,
and does not believe in the fruits of karma, they will enter hell upon death.
If a person harbors evil within and deceives others with the Dharma through flattery, [they likewise fall].
That which the world does not love— death— then leads one into hell.
If a person is attached to sensual pleasures and constantly performs evil deeds,
their mind being deceived by such pleasure, they will enter hell upon death.
If one attains ultimate bliss, only then can one be called secure;
if bliss entails a bitter retribution, it cannot truly be called bliss.
The negligent hosts of devas fall away from the Yāma Heaven.
If one is fully endowed with the Dharma, they are praised by the wise. Yet,
sporting within the pleasure gardens, delighting in the sight of celestial maidens,
and never satiated by the realm of desire— for these reasons, one falls away.
Because pleasure increases, craving grows ever stronger;
as the wise have declared, the severing of craving is supreme.
Seeing the intermediate state within this world, I now feel profound revulsion.
"Who shall rescue and protect me, so that I may attain liberation?
At that time, the assembly of devas, seeing such various intermediate states (*antarābhava*), gave rise to a mind of weary detachment.

At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, perceiving that the minds of the assembly of devas had been subdued, caused all the manifested devas to vanish and revealed his own body, adorned with the majesty of tranquility.
When the devas saw this, their minds became peaceful and secure; they approached the Heavenly King.
Having arrived, they surrounded him and stood to one side, their hearts filled with reverence and leaping with joy, thinking:
"Now we have found our lord."
At that time, the assembly of real devas, seeing such immeasurable evils, all gave rise to weary detachment.
*The Sutra on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma*, Fascicle 57 [and] Fascicle 58.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: Observing the Heavens, Part Three; The Night-Wandering Heaven (Yāma), Section Twenty-Three.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"Why do you now not enjoy yourselves with singing, dancing, and laughter amidst the groves, flower ponds, and mountain peaks adorned with immeasurable jewels?
Thus did the Heavenly King observe the assembly of devas to see whether they felt weary of or detached from [samsara], or were not yet so weary.
Then, having heard these words spoken by the King of the Yāma Heaven, the assembly of devas addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"In which garden, grove, or among the peaks of the seven-jeweled mountains is there a place of delight?"
I have witnessed the immeasurable decline and afflictions of birth and death, with their countless variations, which are unbearable.
With my own eyes, I have seen that all desires are entirely impermanent and ultimately lead only to suffering.
"This desire is impermanent and unstable; it will soon decay and perish, being neither solid nor pleasurable.
At that time, having heard what the host of devas said, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed them, saying:
"You should now know this!"
"All sensual pleasures ultimately lead to suffering.
Then the assembly of devas said to the Heavenly King:
"We have now understood that desire is a great suffering."
Then, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed the assembly of devas:

"I am able to proclaim all the immeasurable sufferings of birth and death; now I shall briefly explain a small portion of them for you, so that for billions of kalpas you will no longer be negligent, but will constantly practice the two virtuous paths of humans and devas."
To sever heedlessness is wisdom. When conditions for heedlessness arise, one should immediately distance oneself from them.
If one is not driven by heedlessness, then one will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Again, he addressed the assembly of devas:
"I shall now explain for you the three evil realms and the two kinds of good realms.
The two good realms are those of devas and humans."
The three evil realms are those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Such great power of suffering within these five paths of existence I am able to proclaim, though it cannot be fully described; now I shall speak of it briefly.
To state it briefly, there are sixteen types of suffering among gods and humans.
What are these sixteen?
Among gods and humans, they are comprised within the wholesome realms.
First is the suffering of the intermediate state;
second is the suffering of dwelling in the womb;
third is the suffering of emerging from the womb.
Fourth is the suffering of seeking food;
fifth is the suffering of association with the disliked;
sixth is the suffering of separation from the beloved.
Seventh, the suffering of cold, heat, and so forth;
eighth, the suffering of illness;
ninth, the suffering of being employed as a servant by others;
Tenth is the suffering of seeking and laboring;
eleventh is the suffering of associating with evil associates;
twelfth is the suffering of the decline and affliction of one's wife, children, and kinsmen.
Thirteenth is the suffering of hunger and thirst;
fourteenth is the suffering of being despised and reviled by others;
fifteenth is the suffering of old age.
The sixteenth is the suffering of death.

These sixteen are the great sufferings among humans; from birth until the end of life in the human world, along with all other various sufferings within the cycle of birth and death, they are unbearable.
Within the conditioned, there is not even the slightest happiness; all is impermanent, all is subject to exhaustion, and all is subject to decay.
"When first born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), consciousness is like a fragrance; what kind of suffering is there?
Driven by the winds of karma, this is not seen by the physical eye, but is seen by the divine eye without any obstruction.
If one is born among humans, one is born into families of low, middling, or superior caste.
For those who wish to be born through the retribution of generosity, morality, and wisdom, this consciousness and its intermediate state (antarābhava) likewise obtain such food.
If one wishes to be born into a poor lineage, what is eaten is coarse and harsh; color, fragrance, taste, and touch are all coarse and foul, and the physical dimensions are diminished and inferior.
Because they practiced little in the way of giving, they do not obtain superior retribution.
This is called being born among humans and experiencing suffering during the first and second moments of consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
"Furthermore, the second suffering is as follows:

If one is born from a womb, one dwells therein due to the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions; one is born into a poor family, and the mother consumes coarse, harsh, bitter, and sour food. The scanty essence of the food passes through the tube of the amnion and enters the navel of the child in the womb, causing the body of the fetus to be emaciated, ill-favored in appearance, and weak in physical strength.
Because the mother is utterly exhausted, the child within the womb undergoes great suffering; it turns toward both sides, fleeing from its distress.
When the mother eats what is cold or hot, it experiences agony, being powerless and without rescue, unable to cry out.
They fall into excrement and urine, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
This is the second of the great sufferings for those on the path of goodness within the human realm; how much more so for those in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, and as animals.
"Furthermore, the third suffering:

upon emerging from the womb, the confinement of the fetal sac is like being pressed for oil; when the infant leaves the womb, the pressure of the impending fall is likewise so—this constitutes a great suffering."
Furthermore, at the time of birth, his body is as soft as a lump of fresh butter, like a plantain tree, or like a ripe fruit.
When the mother attends the birth, she grasps him with her hands.
Their hands were rough and calloused, cracked and split; they had contorted faces of loathing, long and sharp nails, and hideous countenances.
When grasped by the hand, it was like being burned by fire or cut by a blade.
Thus, the infant’s body is delicate and soft; when touched by its mother, it experiences great distress.
If it obtains new clothing, it is coarse, rough, and heavy.
Or if it obtains old clothing, it is patched and torn, with holes and gaps exposed, narrow and thin, worn only upon a bed of straw.
In cold weather it is bitterly cold, and they suffer the agony of great chill;
in heat it is intensely hot, as if being burned by fire.
Because their past acts of giving were not pure, they undergo such suffering and affliction.
Upon emerging from the womb, one undergoes great suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, due to the karmic conditions of giving impure things, it causes the mother’s milk to be scant and her food to be bitter and astringent.
Because the mother’s diet is inferior, her milk becomes scarce; or because the mother consumes coarse and unwholesome food, it causes the milk to be deficient.
Emaciated and of hideous complexion, their bodies consist of nothing but sinews, skin, and bone.

Due to the afflictions of hunger and thirst, their bodies lack strength; if they have nothing to eat, they must beg from others, being held in contempt by people. Even when they obtain food and drink, it is meager and its color, fragrance, and flavor are faint.
Relying on others for food, they sustain their lives through hardship; thus lacking sustenance, their bodies suffer distress.
Because of the unwholesome giving they practiced in the past, they remain constantly insufficient until the end of their lives.
Because they lack food, they constantly experience suffering and affliction.
"Furthermore, the fourth suffering and affliction:

because of longing for food, they experience suffering and affliction; tormented by hunger, they may become thieves, commit various evil deeds, perform what is unbeneficial, or exert themselves with vigor, thereby losing their lives or facing the suffering that follows death."
"Among all the gravities of suffering, none is equal to hunger and thirst.
At that time, the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Mucilinda addressed the assembly of devas in verse:
"The great suffering and affliction of birth and death Is nothing like that of hunger and thirst."
Sentient beings, through the suffering of hunger, commit various unwholesome deeds.
Fire arises from within their own bodies; therefore it is called the suffering of hunger and thirst.
Hunger and thirst burn these three places, just as the fire at the end of an eon consumes the forest.
The great conflagration of the world cannot reach the next life;
yet the fires of hunger and thirst are difficult to sever, persisting for hundreds of thousands of eons.
Fools create unwholesome karma and travel upon perilous and evil paths.
"All this is for the sake of food and drink," so the wise have said.
Hunger and thirst possess great power, exceeding even that of a fierce conflagration;
throughout the entire triple world, all things revolve due to the conditions of food.
“If, within the human world, there are various kinds of wealth and possessions,
it is all because of food that one achieves the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Thus did Maudgalyāyana, the King of the Yāma Heaven, speak to the devas.
"Furthermore, O celestial hosts, there is a fifth suffering in the human world, namely the sixfold suffering of encountering those one hates.
What are these six? They are:
seeing an enemy with one's own eyes, feeling no affection in the mind, and feeling no compassion."

Seeing the color of his body, his mind and mental factors become disturbed; he gives rise to fear toward the mind and its mental concomitants, which produces what is unbeneficial, and within those minds and mental factors, suffering and affliction arise.
Among all evils, the very first and foremost evil is this: seeing the form of an enemy or an evil associate.
"Furthermore, the second suffering is that of association with the loathed:
if one hears their voice and gains no benefit, feeling neither love nor compliance, but instead the mind becomes disturbed and vexed—this is the suffering of association with the loathed."
The first evil sound refers to the sound of hearing the subversion of the True Dharma.
Because of this loathsome sound, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

If one hears sounds that are unpleasant and unbeneficial, and upon hearing them gives rise to an evil mind, agitation, dislike, and lack of joy, such that the heart feels no compassion—this is the suffering of encountering the hated and disliked among human beings.

"Furthermore, thirdly, there is the suffering of encountering what is hateful and disliked: namely, when the nose smells an odor that is neither beloved nor pleasing, the mind does not accord with it, and upon smelling it, the mind is distressed or gives rise to deep suffering."
This is a great evil, an undesirable conjunction.
O sons of the gods, this is what is called an undesirable conjunction in the human realm.

If a person is foolish and lacks wisdom, whether walking or standing, their mind gives rise to greedy attachment, and they treat [the offerings] with contempt and lack of reverence; if such a person uses a mind of desire to smell the incense offered to the Dharma and the Sangha, then at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

Such evil persons, due to the causes and conditions of their bodies, and because they are greedy for their bodies, remain impure in both body and mind; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.
O sons of the gods!
This is the suffering of being joined with those one dislikes and hates among human beings.

"Furthermore, the fourth suffering of being joined with what is disliked is as follows: the foolish and evil people of the world commit unwholesome karmic actions because of their attachment to sensory flavors."
Due to their evil karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into hell.
Though not true śramaṇas, they manifest the appearance of śramaṇas; internally they are rotten, like the hollow sound of a conch shell.
Whether in a monastic temple or in the home of a layperson, they are not actually śramaṇas yet wear the robes of a śramaṇa; they constantly crave fine food and are bound by its flavor.
Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.
Furthermore, there are indolent bhikṣus who abandon the flavor of dhyāna and wander everywhere for the sake of fine food, their minds always delighting in eating.
Because of this indolence, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.
"O sons of the gods!
This is because those among humans, due to their attachment to flavors, do not delight in meeting [with loved ones] and thus give rise to suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!"

The fifth suffering among humans is the suffering of encountering the unloved; that is to say, the body is contacted by this [suffering], which binds the mind, leading to unwholesome reflection, non-conformity with the practice of the Dharma, and lack of right mindfulness.
Such evil persons, bound by evil objects, fall into hell when their bodies perish and their lives end.
O sons of the gods!
This is the suffering born from encountering what is unpleasant among human beings.
"Furthermore, O celestial hosts!
Among humans, the sixth [cause] of suffering arises from union with what is not loved.

That is to say, there are people whose minds are restless and cannot remain still; their minds are not upright and are largely distracted; they constantly contemplate evil karma, take no delight in wholesome dharmas, and instead delight in unwholesome dharmas and things that are without benefit."
By reason of these causes and conditions, when the body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.
O sons of the gods!
This is what is called the suffering born of union with the unpleasant among human beings; furthermore, they fully experience various other immeasurable sufferings within the human realm.

“Furthermore, there are three kinds of the suffering of association with the hated and disliked: namely, being close to an enemy, fearing for one’s life, and being constantly discordant, like a thorn in the eye.”
This is the first suffering of association with what is disliked.
Furthermore, the second suffering of association with what is disliked is this:
engaging in common activities with evil associates; this is called the second suffering of association with what is disliked.
Furthermore, the third suffering is association with the hated and disliked:
harboring malice within and inflicting injury whenever an opportunity arises; this is called the third suffering of association with the unloved and the hateful.
"O sons of the gods!
These are the immeasurable varieties of suffering among human beings.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, further spoke for the sake of inducing world-weariness and renunciation in the celestial assembly:
"Among the six types of persons, there is great suffering, namely the suffering of separation from what one loves.

What benefits both worlds is called 'love'; separation from virtuous friends is considered great suffering—whether it be separation from parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, kinsmen, or others who are beloved and have been kind."

"The great suffering of separation from those one loves is like falling into knives or fire; it burns the body and mind, causing great anguish and distress—this is the suffering of being separated from what one loves.
Thus did the King of the Yāma Heaven expound this Dharma for the benefit of the celestial hosts.
Then, the King of the Yāma Heaven further spoke to the assembly of devas:
"Among humans in the seventh realm, there are great sufferings, namely the two sufferings of cold and heat.
O sons of gods!
What are the two sufferings of cold and heat among human beings?
It is because their food and drink are unbalanced: when it should be cool, it is hot; when it should be warm, it is cold.
Sitting for too long is suffering, standing for too long is also suffering; drinking too much is suffering, and not sleeping is also suffering.
If one lies on one's right side during the darkness of night, sleeping for a long time is painful; the same is true for the left side, which is pleasant at first but painful later.
In the human world, because of a craving for pleasure, people are deceived by that pleasure and cultivate wholesome karma.
Because they are deceived by pleasure, they enter hell.
O sons of gods!
The pleasures of humans are no different from suffering.
Thus, the Night-Mover King Mucilinda, for the benefit of the assembly of devas, spoke this Dharma:
"O assembly of devas, do not give rise to the thought that you should feel weary of and seek detachment from the pleasures of humans."
‘In order to bring about liberation from birth and death, to benefit them through the teaching of the Dharma, and to remove the negligence of the gods.
Furthermore, the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke again to the assembly of the Yāma devas:
‘The eighth among the great sufferings of human beings is the suffering of illness.’

Innumerable distinctions and innumerable diseases arise, namely: feverish illnesses, diarrhea, dyspnea, coughing fits, and the four hundred and four types of diseases that afflict all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, there is the suffering of illness that afflicts all sentient beings—the diseases of grief, sorrow, lamentation, and distress—which are among the greatest sufferings in the human realm.

At that time, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, for the benefit of the celestial hosts, further explained the ninth great suffering, so as to cause them to leave behind birth and death, demonstrating the great suffering of birth and death within the human realm.
"What is called being compelled by others among human beings is a great suffering.

Though sharing the same path, the same birth, the same faculties, the same age, and the same strength, one is compelled by others due to the inferiority of one's karma; whether by day or by night, one finds no autonomy and constantly undergoes great suffering."
This is called the suffering of being employed as a servant among human beings.
Furthermore, there is the suffering of being employed by others.

Suppose a person belongs to the highest caste, is diligent, possesses physical strength, and is fully endowed with learning and wisdom; yet, because of poverty, they are made to serve those of low birth.
Then, for the sake of benefiting the assembly of the Yāma devas, the Yāma Heaven King Mūsuludha further preached the Dharma to them:
"Because their karma is inferior and they lack the merit of giving, they are despised by others; day and night they toil in hardship, being employed as servants by others."

Lacking the causes and conditions for giving, they constantly suffer affliction: their hands and feet are cracked and split; they are impoverished and without food; their clothing is soiled and tattered; they are tormented by hunger and thirst, and endure the hardships of cold and heat.
Thus, there are immeasurable sufferings and afflictions that are unbearable, with forced labor day and night, without interruption or end.
Furthermore, among human beings, there are those of inferior lineage, appearance, and power who possess great wealth.

Furthermore, there are those whose lineage, physical strength, and wisdom are all superior, yet they are constantly impoverished; because of this poverty, they associate with the lowly, and being deceived by their karma and deceived by their own minds, they undergo great and intense suffering.
O sons of the gods!
This is the suffering of being employed by others among human beings.
Furthermore, there is the suffering of being a servant to others.

If a poor person acts in accordance with the Dharma, yet because of their poverty, they associate with those who engage in evil and unwholesome conduct; by associating with such unwholesome people, they partake in their evil karma. Although they do not take pleasure in it, being compelled by others, they create evil karma. When their body perishes and their life ends, they fall into the evil realms and are reborn in hell.
"Because of being driven by others, one suffers in both worlds.
Furthermore, O celestial hosts!
In the human world, one undergoes great suffering and affliction, namely the tenth: the great suffering of seeking."

For the sake of seeking wealth, they undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction: entering the great ocean, engaging in battle against enemies, undertaking various enterprises, employing eloquent speech, associating with the lowly and base, plowing fields and planting crops, engaging in commerce and trade, raising livestock, and traveling abroad on business errands.
Driven by wealth, they ascend great mountain crags and wander about in every direction, dependent upon others.
All such actions and pursuits are solely for the sake of material goods and the adornment of clothing.
Whether they be impoverished persons or those possessed by craving, they pursue their desires in this manner, bound by the net of attachment until the end of their lives.
Some commit evil deeds or speak falsehoods to deceive others; they use light weights and small measures to cheat people;
they sell liquor, trade sesame seeds, and even sell poisons.
They engage in such unwholesome practices as those of improper discipline, such as seeking a livelihood through trade and commerce;
or they commit various kinds of evil deeds, including the destruction of kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, military camps, and multitudes of people.

For the sake of wives, children, food and drink, bedding, and wealth, the suffering of pursuit is immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of times over—and could not be fully described even in a thousand years.
"O sons of the gods!
This is called the suffering of pursuit among human beings.
Thus, for the sake of benefiting the assembly of devas and causing them to feel weary of existence (*saṃsāra*), the King of the Yāma Heaven preached this ultimate Dharma.
"O sons of the gods!
Do not give rise to longing for the human realm; you should instead cultivate weary detachment. If you crave existence within the various realms of being, you will find no benefit.
For this reason, I speak of all the decline and afflictions found among humans."

If one is born among humans, because of the pursuit [of desires], one performs unwholesome karma; by reason of these causes and conditions, one may fall into hell, or fall into the realm of animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
"Having been born in the evil realms, they undergo various sufferings.
Thus, the King of the Yāma Heaven further spoke of the great sufferings among humans, addressing the assembly of devas:
"The great suffering among humans is this: associating with evil associates brings no benefit whatsoever; it is the cause of all suffering."
By associating with evil associates, there is no evil that one does not commit, creating all manner of unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.
Due to these causes and conditions, when the body perishes and life ends, one falls into the evil realms and is born in hell, where one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
In future ages, they may fall among the hungry ghosts or animals and undergo immeasurable suffering.

Having observed the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals within the human realm, he restrains the celestial hosts from aspiring for human existence and speaks of the single place of nirvāṇa and quiescence.
"Furthermore, the King of the Yāma Heaven, desiring to benefit the hosts of the Yāma devas, spoke of the sufferings among human beings:

'That which is called the twelfth [type of suffering] among humans is the great suffering of the decline and distress caused by wives, children, and kinsmen. This refers to the various afflictions such as being killed, bound, or whipped by one's wife, children, or kinsmen; the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and poverty; and the fact that because those whom one loves undergo suffering and distress, one also undergoes suffering and distress—this is termed "decline and distress. "

Within the human realm, one encounters suffering and affliction due to the causes and conditions of wives, children, kinsmen, and relatives; therefore, do not take pleasure in being born among humans.
All that has birth must inevitably return to death, and wherever there is death, there is nothing but suffering and affliction.
Among the greatest sufferings within the cycle of birth and death are those of birth, old age, and death, which are fully present among human beings.
O sons of the gods!
Since you know that such great suffering in the human realm is unbearable, do not give rise to joy or delight.

"By means of such immeasurable meanings of the sublime, tranquil, and unsurpassed path, [the Buddha] showed the celestial hosts that there is no benefit in the human realm; its various nets of existence are beyond analogy, let alone the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of incomparable great sufferings that fill the three evil realms, which cannot even be compared to those of the human world."
When a deva is about to pass away, other devas who have not been negligent will say to him:
"You shall be reborn in the good realm of humans.
When a human is approaching the end of life, their relatives and friends wish for them to be reborn in the good realm of the heavens.
If even the two types of wholesome realms are thus, how much more so for those in the three evil realms who undergo great suffering and affliction!

Thus benefiting and gathering others, the King of the Yāma Heaven constantly spoke, without negligence, of immeasurable kinds, immeasurable distinctions, immeasurable skillful means, and immeasurable varieties of dharmas—the supreme dharma of Nirvāṇa.
Having finished explaining the sufferings of wives and children, he further spoke to the assembly of the Yāma Heaven:
"The thirteenth among the great sufferings of human beings is the suffering of hunger and thirst."
Due to hunger and thirst, one commits immeasurable evils.
Among all other sufferings, none is like hunger and thirst; because of hunger and thirst, one enters into various evil realms.

Even those of great lineage, for the sake of food and drink, join their palms, shed tears, and approach base and lowly persons with plaintive voices and words of affection; all such things arise solely from hunger and thirst.

Out of fear of hunger and thirst, they disregard their own lives and enter dangerous places, amidst the blades of swords and before fierce elephants and enemies; all of this is due to the suffering of hunger and thirst.

Or they may enter the great ocean, traveling for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas through places of perilous waves and countless evil fish, such as the *timi* and *timitimiṅgila*; there, they sacrifice their own lives and board a leaking ship, only to sink into the great sea.
All of these arise from the fear of the suffering of hunger and thirst;
furthermore, there are immeasurable varieties of such distinctions that cannot be fully described.
Such sufferings as these are all for the sake of food and drink.

If a person is bound and led out through the southern gate, beaten with drums of evil sound, adorned with a garland of death, with the signs of calamity before them, filled with fear and distress, and brought to the place of execution where life remains but for a moment—though this is a great suffering, it does not surpass that of hunger and thirst.
Therefore, one should, with a pure and virtuous mind, practice giving with excellent material goods within the field of merit, complete in both time and place.
Amidst the terrors of birth and death, one should diligently cultivate vigor and give with a wholesome mind.
In the heavens, hunger is rare; yet all who undergo birth and death rely upon food and drink to eliminate hunger and thirst. Therefore, everyone should practice giving.
O hosts of devas!
This refers to the immeasurable varieties of suffering from hunger and thirst among human beings.
In the heavenly realms, suffering is subtle and mild; it is covered by celestial bliss, and because their merit is great, food and drink are easily obtained.
Yet the devas do not perceive this; they are entirely shrouded by the flames of hunger and thirst throughout the desire realm, fearing the fires of suffering.
O sons of the gods!
Thus contemplate the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death among human beings, and do not give rise to delight.

Thus, having observed that the assembly of the Yāma devas had their minds subdued and were for the most part disciplined and gentle, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma devas, further spoke to the celestial host about the sufferings of the human realm, saying: "If one diligently cultivates the benefit of others, one's own benefit will be easy to attain."
"By the power of his uninterrupted resolve, for the sake of benefiting others, Mūśalinda repeatedly expounded immeasurable kinds of Dharma to the hosts of the Yāma devas, saying:
'The fourteenth among the great sufferings of human beings is the suffering of being despised by others; it is unbearable and has various distinctions.'"
