The poor are especially subject to contempt and possess ten kinds of suffering: they are held in low esteem by those of noble birth, by their own kin, by their brothers, and by the wealthy.
Suffering from poverty, they depend on others for food.
Their speech is frivolous and untrue; their words toward kinsmen are empty and meaningless.
Relying on others for sustenance, their clothing is dusty and soiled, and they are held in contempt by others.
When entering cities and towns, or on days of festivals and assemblies, people look upon them with contempt and derision.
Within the realm of human existence, there are such immeasurable great sufferings of contempt and derision.

People of the world harbor a fire within their hearts that requires no fuel; it is called the fire of contempt. This fire, which burns one's kinsmen, acquaintances, and brothers, is the most extreme of all.
Because they lack merit, they undergo these ten sufferings that thoroughly incinerate their bodies.
Great evil and terror burn and dry up their bodies, and their breath rises like smoke.
O sons of the gods!

One should give rise to contentment and not take delight in the human realm; for there is little joy in the human realm, but rather great suffering and affliction, decline and distress, short lifespans, and the defilement of being disparaged and reviled.
It is only among human beings that there is much contempt and disparagement, not within the other four realms of existence.
Within the human realm, contempt and disparagement are most severe.
When one receives such contempt from others, every part of one's body feels as if it were poisoned.
Regarding the places where one previously received offerings, one later treats them with contempt and disparagement.

If a person who formerly constantly received excellent offerings subsequently receives little profit or receives offerings for only a short time, and if a son of good family thus disparages them, it is worse than the suffering of death.
"O sons of the gods!
This is a great suffering, difficult to endure among human beings.
Furthermore, the fifteenth great suffering among human beings is the suffering of old age; I shall now describe to you the suffering of old age among human beings."

Old age causes all parts of the body to become emaciated and debilitated; it brings all the faculties to maturity and destroys youthfulness. One must walk leaning on a staff, devoid of strength, and treats one's dwelling with disdain. With a hunched back and a crooked nose, white hair—the messenger of death—appears, and both body and mind grow feeble.
Although they have not yet reached the end of their lives, they are like animals.
O sons of the gods!
This is what is called the suffering of old age among humans; they are toyed with by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and will surely die before long.
If one sees the suffering of old age and yet feels no fear, it should be known that such a person is called "heartless," being like wood or stone.
Because they lack a heart, although they possess a human body, they are like an animal.
"O sons of the gods!
To be born into the human realm is a great suffering; because there is birth, there is the suffering of old age.
Having understood the suffering of old age, do not give rise to a mind of delight toward the human world."
"Furthermore, sixteenthly, there are immeasurable kinds of rebirth among human beings; once born, there is suffering. What is this suffering?
It is called the suffering of death."
Having died, one is born again; the faculty of the body perishes, the life-faculty is severed and extinguished, and one no longer sees brothers, kinsmen, or friends.
Once the physical body has ceased, one proceeds to another place, sustained by the fruit of one's own karma as one's provisions.
All sentient beings must inevitably reach their end; when life is exhausted and the body is cast off, they undergo the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is called death.
All that has birth ultimately returns to death; it is impossible for one who dies not to be born, or for one who is born not to die!
"O sons of the gods!
Do not give rise to thoughts of pleasure regarding the human realm.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, spoke in verse:
“In the world of humans, all that has aggregates is suffering;
birth inevitably leads to death, and where there is death, there is necessarily birth.”
If one dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one suffers the torments of one’s own karma;
the suffering of this long night of wandering is beyond description.
One sinks into excrement and urine, scorched by the heat of the elements.
Thus, the suffering of dwelling in the womb cannot be fully described.
Constantly craving the flavors of food, the mind is ever full of longing;
yet one undergoes great suffering regarding those flavors—a suffering that is beyond words.
Those who are constantly anxious and ever-hoping, who know no satisfaction in their desires, undergo various sufferings and afflictions; these sufferings are beyond description.
To encounter those one hates and dislikes is like a great fire or a venomous poison.
The various sufferings that arise—this suffering is beyond description.
When beings encounter separation from those they love, great suffering arises;
it is a most terrible affliction, difficult to endure, and this suffering is beyond description.
The great suffering of cold and heat gives rise to immeasurable kinds of pain;
this great suffering is most violent and evil, its bitterness beyond description.
The suffering of illness harms human life; illness is the messenger of the King of Death.
Sentient beings undergo this suffering, a suffering that is beyond description.
Driven by others, they are never possessed of autonomy;
sentient beings undergo this suffering, a suffering that is beyond description.
The poison of craving burns sentient beings; in their pursuit [of objects], they undergo great suffering, continuing until death—this suffering is beyond description.
If one draws near to evil associates, all manner of sufferings will never cease.
When one undergoes the sufferings of the evil realms, these sufferings are beyond description.
When one’s wife and children meet with decline and distress, seeing them gives rise to great anguish;
this suffering exceeds even that of hell and is beyond description.
Hunger and thirst burn the body like a fierce flame;
they can destroy both body and mind, and this suffering is beyond description.
One is constantly held in contempt by others—by one's own kinsmen and friends alike.
Born into sorrow, lamentation, and suffering— this suffering is beyond words.
A person oppressed by old age, body frail and mind debilitated,
walking bent over with a staff— this suffering is beyond words.
Human beings are seized by death; from this world they go to the next.
This death is a great suffering that cannot be fully described.
Sentient beings are unable to see it, and no karmic actions can prevent it.
It can destroy all sentient beings; therefore it is called death.
Its great power is difficult to endure; it causes all sentient beings to wander alone in great terror; therefore it is called death.
Sentient beings exist ultimately; the fire of time cannot be avoided.
It can sever the life-force of all beings, and for this reason it is called death.
Destroyed by the King of Death, it can cut off the life-root of human beings.
When the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are exhausted, it is therefore called death.
Birth inevitably entails separation from one's kinsmen and brothers;
once separated, they do not reunite, and for this reason it is called death.
Before death has arrived, one should cultivate wholesome conduct;
for death is cruel and devoid of compassion, it must be met with virtue while it is yet unapproached.
This death is most sudden and violent, utterly evil and lacking in mercy.
One who is able to cultivate goodness even before reaching it is truly one among the gods.
If wisdom arises within the Dharma, such a person is called one with a virtuous life;
if a person does not depart from the Dharma, this is the life within life.
If a person’s mind recollects the Buddha, they are called one who has a good life;
because they do not depart from the recollection of the Buddha, this is the life within life.
If a person’s mind recollects the Dharma, they are called one who has a good life.
Because they do not depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, this is called "life within life.
If a person’s mind is mindful of the Saṃgha, they are called a person of good life;
because they do not depart from mindfulness of the Saṃgha, this is called "life within life."
If a person’s thoughts are rooted in truth, they are called one who has a good life;
because they do not abandon the truth, this is the life within life.
If a person’s thoughts are set on the Path, they are called one who has a good life.
Because they do not abandon the Path, this is the life within life.
If a person constantly maintains mindfulness and proceeds toward Nirvana,
only then may they be called a "deva," not one who delights in sensual pleasures.
If one constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness and delights in the practice of meditative concentration, this joy can bring liberation from existence;
it is not what is called attachment to sensual pleasure.
Once one knows that existence has these faults, one gives rise to weary detachment toward desire.
“Those who diligently seek nirvāṇa are called true devas.
Thus, the King of the Yāma Heaven benefited the various devas in immeasurable ways, causing the minds of the celestial hosts to attain cool clarity and severing their paths to the evil realms.
At that time, the assembly of devas said to the Heavenly King:
"O Heavenly King!
As the Heavenly King has said, we see with our own eyes those whose physical strength and appearance are ten times superior to ours all suffer decline and affliction; how much more so for us?"
Having heard these words, the King of the Yāma Heaven addressed him, saying:
"As you have seen, these hosts of devas experience but slight decline and affliction."
"You hosts of the Yāma devas shall fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm— hundreds of times worse than this—
because you, the celestial hosts, have practiced what is not the Dharma and have acted with negligence."

If the hosts of devas act in accordance with the Dharma and remain far removed from heedlessness, they will close the gates to all evil realms. They shall constantly experience various pleasures among gods and humans, and shall be freed from the sufferings of sorrow, lamentation, old age, sickness, and death. They will attain an abode of permanence, forever free from the various sufferings described above.
For this reason, do not practice heedlessness.
Such sensual pleasures, compared to the bliss of untainted wisdom and meditative concentration, do not equal even one-hundred-thousandth part of it.
At that time, having heard what the celestial king had said and clearly perceiving all these faults, the host of devas spoke again:
"The Dharma taught by the Celestial King benefits us; we now accept it so that we may not undergo such suffering of birth, death, decay, and affliction."
At that time, the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Mucilinda spoke in verse:
"If one performs actions oneself, It is not another who receives the fruit.
If one disciplines oneself well, One shall attain the eternal abode."
If one performs other deeds, there is nothing that surpasses virtuous karma;
throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, karma constantly follows one’s conduct.
Extensively performing all manner of merit and practicing wholesome dharmas, one shall attain the fruit of bliss.
Then one attains the most excellent state, forever free from old age, sickness, and death.
Such is the result of one's own wholesome karma; thus should the hosts of devas reflect.
If one practices wholesome karma, this is the supreme provision.
After the Lord of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha, had spoken these verses, he addressed the assembly of devas:
"From this day forward, do not become negligent by indulging in the gardens and groves out of attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures."
At that time, having heard these words, the assembly of devas addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"May we, in the future, behold Maitreya Buddha—the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans—appearing in the world."
“Having been born among humans, I saw that World-Honored One at his first assembly; having heard the Dharma many times, I have exhausted all outflows.
Furthermore, there were other hosts of devas who sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; having made this vow, they took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Seventy thousand devaputras and other celestial hosts will surely be reborn among humans; having seen Maitreya Buddha and heard his Dharma, their outflows (āsrava) will be forever exhausted.
Furthermore, there are other devas who, having first beheld the Buddha’s stupa, have made the vow for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there were other devas who conceived the aspiration for pratyekabuddhahood;
all of them vowed that they would attain the fruit in a future life.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven thought to himself:
"I have already brought great benefit to others, causing the hosts of devas to abandon their heedless conduct.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, knowing that the minds of the deva hosts were well-subdued, ordered each of them to return to their palaces.
Then, the hosts of devas, having respectfully surrounded the King of the Yāma Heaven, departed from the pond.
Having brought benefit to the hosts of devas, the Lord of the Yāmas, Mucilinda, proceeded to other regions to bring benefit to the devas there.
The eighth chapter, "The Sūtra on the Transformation of the Mucilinda Heaven in the Ever-Blissful Realm of the Yāma Heaven," is hereby complete.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma contemplates the grounds where the Yāma Heaven resides.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing,
he sees that in the realm of the Yāma devas there is a place named Increasing Dharma (Dharmavardhana).
By what karma are sentient beings born in this place?
He sees that if a person maintains the precepts with a virtuous mind— refraining from killing and stealing as previously described—
and further abstains from sexual misconduct, abandoning even the slightest degree of it, such that they do not give rise to thoughts of lust even upon seeing painted figures of men and women.

Such a person does not observe, contemplate, savor, or cling [to sensual objects]; they do not allow their mental thoughts to become turbid, fearing they might violate pure conduct. They do not dwell upon them nor entertain unwholesome thoughts, thereby blocking faults of the mind. For the sake of others, they explain the karmic fruits of sexual misconduct to restrain their minds, causing those [others] to feel no joy, no affection, and no delight [in such acts].
"This fruit of sexual misconduct should not be cultivated or approached; it is not the path to cessation, it is not to be delighted in, and those who practice virtue should not take pleasure in it.
Thus he proclaims for others the subtle fruits [of karma], upholds the pure conduct of the precepts, and feels dread toward even the arising of a subtle dust-mote of evil views.
Such a person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the devas on the Ground of Increasing Dharma.
Having been born in that heaven, because of their practice of wholesome karma, they achieve the fruition of their desires.
What is called a grove is a mountain peak of golden mountains, adorned with flowing springs, rivers, and ponds made of various jewels, where flocks of birds utter wondrous songs.
The four banks of these ponds are adorned with the seven treasures, and the ground is interspersed with blue lapis lazuli and blue indranīla gems.

There are many peaks, each with various colors, sounds, and characteristics that differ from one another; they are lovely to behold, and their sounds are exquisite, bringing joy to those who hear them, thereby increasing one's delight within the groves.

Furthermore, in another place, where the mountains and valleys were adorned with stones of diamond-blue gems and crystal, they experienced bliss upon hearing the sound of flowing water on Mount Radiance.
Whatever they wish to do, they achieve with complete mastery, experiencing incomparable desires.
Surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, they constantly enjoy sensual pleasures, increasing their delight, and experience immeasurable, diverse, and ineffable bliss.

Amidst various mountains of gold and peaks of lapis lazuli, they travel through the void, their bodies adorned with various garments; surrounded by celestial maidens of manifold exquisite forms, they engage in laughter, song, and dance.
They possess the five celestial desires:
when they see the immeasurable variety of celestial forms, they experience incomparable joy and sport at will; this is called the desire for form.
When they hear sounds, according to their inclinations, they laugh, sing, and dance together with the celestial maidens.
They perceive immeasurable varieties of fragrances:
the scent of lotuses and other exotic flowers wafted by the wind from the flower ponds;
and the various floral scents carried by the mountain breezes that delight their sense of smell.

The tongue obtains immeasurable varieties of celestial flavors, which are fully provided according to one's thoughts; these include salty, bland, bitter, sweet, pungent, sour, and other tastes, consisting of immeasurable kinds of incomparable, wish-fulfilling flavors.

Such tactile sensations of the body, arising from immeasurable kinds of karma, are obtained at will: cold, heat, warmth, and coolness; softness and smoothness; garments without thread or seam, adorned with various colored jewels.
Immeasurable jewel-light illuminates ten yojanas, twenty yojanas, and even up to a hundred yojanas; the gods experience the pleasure of touch through these luminous jewels.
Within the celestial gardens, there may be floral fragrances; when the devas smell them, by virtue of their wholesome karma, they experience rare and extraordinary bliss.
"It is not that what has been done does not arise; it is not that things arise without cause; what is done is never lost.
It is not produced by the mind, nor is it bestowed by another, nor is it something created by another that I receive as retribution."
Due to causes and conditions, karmic retribution arises and the fruits of karma are accomplished.

For this person who upholds the precepts, according to what their mind contemplates and the desires of their heart, the exquisite forms of the celestial hosts—the subtle and supreme colors of the heavens—arise whether near or far, at any time. In accordance with their thoughts, they accomplish immeasurable dharmas of bliss.
Because this man has well maintained the precepts.
Thus, these hosts of devas, their minds attached to the objects of the six desires, wander in play, being swept away by the river of desire.

Each garden and each mountain peak is adorned with the seven treasures; the gardens and flowing springs emit wondrous sounds, and flocks of birds of a hundred colors produce various extraordinary notes.
These virtuous deeds allow one to sport within them;
with their various exquisite colors, various appearances, various merits, and various adornments, they cause the fire of desire to arise.

Surrounded by celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with various mountain peaks, divine garlands, and celestial robes, and further embellished with ointments and powdered incense, they sport and enjoy themselves among the mountain summits with these goddesses, giving rise to immeasurable desires according to their every thought.

Furthermore, accompanied by celestial maidens, he proceeded together to the Level and Uneven Grounds; that land was lovely, with a surface made of true gold, white silver, blue lapis lazuli, blue indranīla gems, and musāragalva, adorned with the sound of bell-nets and various birds.
At that time, there was a bird named *Apramāda* (Heedfulness). Seeing this deva-putra engaging in heedless conduct, it spoke a verse in rebuke:
"Only the fruits of past karma are experienced; No new karma is created. When karma is exhausted, one falls— Such is the nature of all phenomena."
When karma is about to be exhausted, life passes away moment by moment; death arrives suddenly and violently, yet the fool does not perceive it.
Even the sons and daughters of gods do not realize the defilement of desire; though the time for their desires has passed, they do not know that the time of their decline is approaching.
Gain and loss recur many times due to the realm of desire; amidst decay and affliction, why harbor evil intentions?
Through your wholesome karma, you have achieved the enjoyment of happiness; by performing further wholesome karma, you shall proceed to the auspicious realms.
If one delights in sense objects, one is submerged in the ocean of existence;
if one is detached from sense objects, one attains liberation.
The power of the waves of sense objects arises from the river of craving; the wise abandon them.

Proceeding toward the city of Nirvāṇa, the courageous person abandons desire and seeks the true reality; they are able to understand that the objects of craving cause one to revolve within the three realms of existence.
Abandoning sensory objects, do not give rise to mental conceptions; like the *ciñcā-māṇavikā* fruit, their retribution is extremely bitter.
When the human mind clings to pleasure and greedily races toward sensory objects, it accumulates unwholesome karma and wanders through the evil realms.
One should always protect the mind; for it is fickle and coarse, constantly attached to sensory objects and shrouded by the craving for them.
The mind races toward various realms without perceiving decay and affliction; only when decay and affliction have arrived does one finally realize the fruit of karma.
"Having understood these karmic actions and the faults of their objects, one should always abandon the various fetters of the world.
Thus did the bird of heedfulness speak these verses, yet this deva-son neither listened nor accepted them, continuing to enjoy sensual pleasures together with the host of celestial maidens.

These celestial maidens are the causal conditions for birth and death, and the cause of great suffering. They consort with those who lack wisdom, constantly engaging in perilous and evil ways; their love is never stilled as they perpetually seek out men. Their minds are like virulent poison and like treacherous precipices, capable of igniting the fires of desire in the hearts of all men.
Together with such fearsome celestial maidens, they experience celestial pleasures; yet, due to their ignorance, they do not avoid them from afar.
If there were one who was wise, fearing birth and death and desiring to seek true happiness, they would distance themselves from these celestial maidens.

Deluded and confused, because their minds are shrouded by desire, they know that suffering arises from women yet are unable to abandon them, continuing to enjoy sensual pleasures together with various maidservants.
Enshrouded by greed, delusion, and hatred, they are submerged in the mire of birth and death.
Though they sport with celestial maidens and experience pleasure, they fail to embrace immeasurable benefits that would bar them from the evil realms.

Deceived by their own minds and lacking awakening to the Dharma, they sport in the groves and gardens, experiencing the pleasures of the net of desire with hosts of celestial maidens who engage in improper conduct.

They then proceed to another place, which is adorned all over with gold, lapis lazuli, blue indra-nīla gems, and great sapphire kings; wandering through immeasurable regions, they hear the sounds of singing and can understand the lyrics and verses, for the voices are exquisite and beautiful.

The five kinds of musical sounds were endowed with supreme excellence; their incomparable and wondrous tones had never been heard before. Upon hearing these sounds, the newly born deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, hurried toward the grove.
That forest is fully endowed with immeasurable jewel trees; the forest is named Great Joy (Mahānandana), measuring one hundred yojanas in length and thirty yojanas in width.

Such a great forest is replete with various jewels and possesses great merit, where hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of celestial beings engage in singing, dancing, and sporting, enjoying themselves in pleasure.

At that time, the newly born deva-son saw this great forest of *vaiḍūrya* trees emitting a great radiance, with immeasurable fragrant flowers and garlands of merit, possessing immeasurable varieties of colors and diverse appearances.

Having seen this, he further beheld other trees: beryl trees with leaves of pure gold, branches of blue gems, and fruits of white silver, fully endowed with celestial flavors and virtues; they were adorned with indranīla jewels, and their branches were embellished with flowers of various colors.

Furthermore, he saw another tree: a tree made of blue jewels with branches of pure gold and leaves of lapis lazuli. It was adorned by immeasurable swarms of bees of various colors and forms, which produced exquisite sounds; seeing it, he felt joy and delight.
At that time, the newly born deva-son again beheld precious flowers; it was as if opening his eyes, for they were lovely to behold, and amidst the flowers, swarms of bees emitted exquisite sounds.
Furthermore, they see golden branches and leaves providing shade like a palace, with hundreds of thousands of peaks; their sounds are exquisite and most delightful.

Again, they see beryl branches with blue jewels for leaves, shading the palaces; they are adorned with the foremost of precious gems and birds of various colors. The ground is soft, decorated with inlaid jewels, perfumed with celestial incense, and filled with many celestial maidens.

"The newly born son of heaven again beholds rainbow-colored light adorning the ground; it is lovely to behold, covered with the seven treasures, level and beautiful, and he also sees celestial maidens."

The various forms seen by the newly born deva-son are all lovely; the sounds he hears are all delightful; the fragrances he smells are of immeasurable kinds and are all likewise lovely; whatever flavors he obtains cause his mind to feel love and joy, for he possesses celestial flavors of immeasurable variety; whatever tactile sensations he encounters, immeasurable touches cause his mind to feel love and joy; and according to what he thinks of, various phenomena are obtained immediately upon that thought.
Thus, these devaputras, bound by all the fetters of desire and with their craving for pleasure unabated,
enter the great forest together with the celestial maidens, hearing the songs of celestial birds amidst immeasurable lovely sights and immeasurable jeweled grounds adorned with precious inlays.
Furthermore, he saw flower ponds, adorned in various ways with distinct differences.
There were lotuses with stems of lapis lazuli, leaves of pure gold, filaments of diamond, and pericarps made of blue Indra-ratna; all the flowers were soft and supple.
Furthermore, there were lotuses with stems of pure gold, leaves of lapis lazuli, pericarps of white silver, and filaments of ruby; various bees emerged from them, producing exquisite sounds.

Furthermore, there are lotuses composed of the seven precious gems, with petals of pure gold and calyxes inlaid with the seven jewels—namely, indranīla sapphire, red lotus gem, vaidūrya beryl, red lotus gem, musāragalva conch-gem, and mahānīla king of blue gems—with the radiant light of these various colors forming their calyxes.
Just as with one flower pedestal, so it is with immeasurable flower pedestals.
When the devaputra beholds them, he gazes upon them without weariness; according to the various realms he perceives, they increase further and further.
It is like pouring ghee and oil onto a great fire; one never knows satiety.
If there is no satiety, how can there be happiness?
Because it is not happiness, it is also not cessation.
Those who lack a mind of love attain a mind of tranquility; however, as they experience whatever pleasure they obtain, their craving increases. As craving increases, they do not know contentment.
Because they lack contentment, they enter into proximity with suffering, yet within that suffering they give rise to the perception of pleasure, being consumed by the fire of craving.

"Entering the forest once more, he saw immeasurable trees in the mountain valleys and immeasurable kinds of light; gazing intently at them, he knew no satiety amidst the fires of desire for these five sensory objects."
Furthermore, they enter a pond of mani-jewel stones, made of pure gold and crystal, with a color and touch that are soft and supple; it possesses five kinds of softness and is free from aquatic moss.
The songs of various birds are clear, tranquil, profound, and deep.

Furthermore, he saw in another place a lotus pond filled with water the color of crystal; its four sides were lined with precious stones that radiated light everywhere, and it was adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
Adorned with lotuses and surrounded by groves of trees, the forest abounds with birds of beautiful song; thus are the various features of that pond adorned.

When the newly born deva-son beholds these various bees in the pond, their wings made of the seven precious gems, and the fragrant trees growing on the banks, complete in color and form as ornaments, he is filled with wonder.
The newly born deva-son again proceeded forward into the forest and saw a great river filled with *sudhā*.

The newly born deva-son further saw in another place a river of milk-rice and a river of pure drink; the sound of the flowing rivers was like the music of a lute, resonating here and there by the hundreds or thousands.
Many birds drink the wine of supreme flavor and emit wondrous sounds.
At that time, the newly born deva-son again beholds the land, where various flowers are endowed with perfect colors and forms; fragrant bees fill the midst of the blossoms, adorning the great forest.
The fragrance of that grove was already sweet, but because of the flowers, it increased a hundredfold.

The newly born deva, together with the celestial maidens, further beheld within the grove a great mountain peak adorned with various jewels and embellished by immeasurable flowing streams; its tree branches provided shade like a palace, and it was filled with the radiance of diverse gems.
The wondrous voices of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of birds are lovely to behold, like the song of the *kūjita* bird.

Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flowers are universally perfumed, and their radiance is sublime; like the light of the sun and moon in the sky over Jambudvīpa, immeasurable light adorns this celestial realm, its brilliance being most excellent.
Seeing the mountain peaks adorned with immeasurable radiance, the deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, enters among those peaks.
As they enter the peaks, they observe that the groves become increasingly superior; their songs are harmonious and equal in pitch, becoming ever more sublime as they draw closer.
Hearing this song, they quickly went there to see what they had never seen before.
As these hosts of devas looked up, they beheld lovely *śāla* groves and trees—*vaiḍūrya* trees and blue *indranīla* trees—all of which were perfectly majestic.

The newly born deva-son further enters the grove of seven-jeweled lotus stalks; within this grove there are many deva-sons and celestial maidens, endowed with exquisite beauty and adorned with ornaments that appear spontaneously according to their thoughts.

Each of the devas dwells separately, drinking the flavors of the heavens together with various celestial maidens; free from intoxication and confusion, they sport and enjoy themselves amidst groves of diverse precious trees and bamboo thickets.
Entering the ponds of the seven treasures, they join with the various devaputras in singing, dancing, playing, and laughing to the sounds of the five kinds of music, receiving joy and pleasure.
With their minds shrouded by craving, they know no satiety, remaining attached to the five desires.
Entering the lotus grove, they drink the flavors of the heavens from lotus petals without becoming intoxicated or distracted.
Furthermore, there are sons of gods whose minds take pleasure in forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles.
Furthermore, there were devaputras dwelling on both banks of the river who were sporting together.
A newly born devaputra saw a jeweled palace with pavilions as dense as a forest, with railings made of *vaiḍūrya* gemstone.

All share the same desire; by the power of their superior, middling, and inferior wholesome karmas, they obtain exquisite forms and experience incomparable pleasure through the sounds of the five musical instruments, beyond all analogy.
"At that time, the newly born deva-son had never before seen such a celestial host sporting and enjoying themselves.
Having seen this, he approached the assembly of devas with a heart full of joy, accompanied by a multitude of celestial maidens."

At that time, the assembly of devas, beholding this devaputra’s exquisitely adorned garments and his most sublime physical form—something they had never seen before—gave rise to a heart of joy and likewise turned toward the devaputra.

The two assemblies were in harmonious accord, their minds free from obstruction; together with the hosts of celestial maidens, they took delight in every bamboo grove, every golden peak, every flower pond, every river of wine, and every flowing stream—such joys are beyond full description.
In this manner, all the hosts of devas experience pleasure.
After the devas have enjoyed these pleasures for a long time, they proceed once more toward the mountain of Universal Solidity (*Sarvābhedya*).
That mountain is composed of the seven treasures and is fully endowed with immeasurable rivers, ponds, and flowing springs.
The newly born deva is surrounded by celestial maidens, and together with the hosts of devas, he constantly delights in music.

Mountains, rivers, springs, and fountains are everywhere abundant; there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite palaces, most delightful to behold, encircled on all sides by lotus flowers like rows of lamps, and adorned with wish-fulfilling trees. When the hosts of devas see this, they give rise to a sense of wonder.

One side of that mountain is made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel; its second side is composed of pure gold; its third side is of *indranīla* sapphire; and its fourth side is of the great king of *mahānīla* jewels. All four sides are equally adorned, and upon these level and even surfaces, peaks, valleys, thickets, and forests are all fully present.
When they think of the pleasure of touch and desire to sport, they ascend into this grove.

By the hundreds, by the thousands, each individual deva has a thousand celestial maidens as his retinue; with the five kinds of celestial music, immeasurable sounds blending together in harmony, they sing, dance, and sport.

By the hundreds, by the thousands, and by the tens of thousands, they accompany the newly born deva-son within the groves, flower ponds, and flowing springs, where all that is seen is most excellent and sublime.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of trees serve as their adornment.

With the radiant flames of the seven treasures and groves of lotus stalks, these hosts of devas dance, sing, and laugh in these various places; moving with calm and slow steps toward that great mountain, they take delight in one another.

With wholesome karma as their companion and sustained by wholesome karma, because of that wholesome karma, they are free from bone, flesh, and impurities; together they roam upon the Sūdhā food-river and wander by the drinking river.
Due to their virtuous karma, they are fully endowed with excellence in color, fragrance, flavor, and texture; the devaputras eat them and delight in the five sensory realms.
As they eat, desire is aroused, and they experience pleasure everywhere; with all desires fulfilled, they enjoy peerless and immeasurable bliss.
Desiring to ascend that mountain, he beheld its most excellent and sublime features and marveled at such an unprecedented sight.
After a long time, he reached the summit of this great mountain; the mountain retreats were so exceedingly delightful that he took great pleasure in roaming there.

Upon this mountain peak there are many immeasurable places for recreation, adorned with various jewels, featuring groves of trees, ponds, and rivers, where *kumuda* flowers cover the fragrant forests.

Upon the summit of the mountain, all desires are fully provided; whatever one thinks of, all immeasurable kinds of love are obtained according to one's wish, all of which are delightful and cannot be taken away by others.
Thus the deva-son has long enjoyed celestial pleasures; having thus experienced such delights, he surveys them everywhere and proceeds once more to the mountain valleys of the seven treasures.
Covered by forests of the seven treasures, with radiant medicinal herbs, he beholds various celestial birds emitting exquisite songs.
“The Cave of Tranquility is surrounded by lotus ponds; one of these is named the Pond of Tranquil Conduct.
Because they failed to maintain their precepts in previous lives, beings are born within these ponds.”

In previous lives, his mind was firm and he was able to expound the essentials of the Dharma, yet he was unable to practice according to what he taught, being like an actor who speaks of karmic retribution.
Emerging from the realms of hell and hungry ghosts, they are born in this pond, mostly as geese.

Because of their practice of tranquility in their former lives, they are born in this Tranquil Pond; their wings are made of the seven treasures, their bodies emit radiance, and their voices are exquisite. Feeding on lotus flowers, males and females follow one another, delighting in each other's company.
The Bodhisattva Goose King, named Śubhakāla, frequently dwells in this pond.
The Yāma Heaven King Mūśalinda frequently dwells within this mountain cave, preaching the Dharma to the devas.
The king of geese was in the pond, preaching the Dharma to the birds.
At that time, the hosts of devas were sporting, singing, and dancing, having divided themselves into two groups:
one group of devas, by virtue of their wholesome karma, arrived at the location of this pond.
A portion of the celestial hosts entered the Forest of Heedlessness (*pramada-vana*), where they played, sang, danced, and enjoyed themselves in pleasure.
Those of virtuous karma went to the Great Lake, where the geese preached the Dharma to them. Seeing the celestial hosts, the geese spoke these verses:
"If a person, though they preach the Dharma, Is unable to act according to what they have taught..."
This fool speaks in vain and constantly undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction.
If one only speaks for the sake of others but cannot act according to what they say, their words are firm yet devoid of meaning; such a person is called "empty and heartless."
Through negligence desire arises; through desire, anger arises.
Such a person enters the evil realms and rushes headlong into hell.
If pleasure has already passed, it cannot be obtained in the present.
Whether experienced in the present or yet to be experienced, this too is not called happiness.
The fool delights in negligence and craves present pleasure;
deceived by the fruits of his own karma, he then enters hell.
Deceived by craving throughout the three periods of time, it constantly brings about what is not beneficial;
it binds sentient beings in birth and death—wise ones should not place their trust in it.
That which is cherished as a friend by the foolish brings harm like a great enemy.
The fetters that bind the beings of the world—wise ones should not trust them.
Even if one is bound by shackles and chains, they may still be broken;
but for those who constantly seek sensual desire, they cannot sever the bonds of craving.
If a person severs the bonds of craving yet still craves permanence and pleasure,
such a person remains within the realm of craving and wanders in the sphere of wisdom.
Through the light of wisdom one perceives true bliss, while craving is declared to be the suffering of great darkness.
The wise one who holds the light can destroy all darkness.
With the sharp sword of wisdom, they cut down the tree of craving;
the person who can fell the tree of craving attains the state of unsurpassed bliss.
Cut down the forest of the faults of craving, along with its many flowing springs;
having severed the trees of the forest of craving, one attains liberation from all states of existence.
In the great river of craving, where the waters of heedlessness swirl in eddies—
If one boards the ship of wisdom, one reaches the secure shore beyond.
Ascending the peak of the mountain of wisdom, adorned by the valley of ethical discipline,
with the eye of immeasurable knowledge, one perceives all faults within existence.
If a person is far removed from the Dharma, that person is empty within and without;
if a person does not delight in the Dharma, they are as unsubstantial as water bubbles.
If there is a person who is solid and firm, both within and without like a diamond, [they are truly steadfast].
By practicing the Dharma with tranquility, one brings benefit to other sentient beings.
If one sinks into the mire of negligence and delights in the pleasures of sensory objects,
one will be bitten by the snake of those very objects and constantly undergo all manner of suffering and hardship.
Therefore, those who seek happiness should not practice heedlessness;
if one is free from heedlessness, they will draw near to immeasurable bliss.
If there is a person of wisdom, they will have no faith in heedlessness.
"If one is stung by heedlessness, one wanders through the five realms of existence.
Thus did the goose-bird speak these verses to discipline the devas.
At that time, the assembly of devas, being attached to sensual pleasures, did not listen or accept [the teaching], but instead continued to perform songs, dances, and games for their own enjoyment.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 58; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 59.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Eight: Observing the Heavens, Part Four; The Heaven of Yāma, Section Twenty-Four.

"At that time, there was a king of geese among the bodhisattvas named Kāla (Good Time). Leading his flock of geese with a mind of right mindfulness and a heart intent on benefiting all sentient beings, he observed that the flock was experiencing pleasure and remained alone in a cave, contemplating and recollecting the Dharma."
Thus, the Goose King Sucīrṇa, who cherished the joy of the Dharma, delighted others by preaching the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, other geese likewise contemplated the Dharma.

At that time, the hosts of devas, with hearts full of joy and seeking pleasure, came to this place; they beheld this great pond, lovely on all sides, where trees at all times were fully endowed with flowers and fruit.
The hosts of devas beheld this, and the throngs of celestial maidens, filled with joy, sang and danced; their play and enjoyment increased a hundredfold as they surrounded the great pond.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, having seen the hosts of devas, spoke these verses with his perfected wisdom:
“The wise do not indulge in negligence; They are able to sever negligence.”
Then one ascends the terrace of wisdom, attaining unsurpassed peace and security.
If one cuts off negligence, one attains the supreme path of quiescence;
entering this vast and great path, wisdom reaches nirvana.
Heedlessness can obstruct the Path, causing the mind’s transgressions to continue in succession;
because of this heedlessness, it destroys the bridge of the Dharma.
It can ruin wholesome thoughts and cause one to lose the path to liberation.
Because of such negligence, it leads people to the evil realms.
With a mind distracted by negligence, one does not perceive timely benefit;
ignorant of speech and ritual action, one is no different from a dead man.
Though dwelling in celestial bodies, they are no different from animals;
ruined by heedlessness and delusion, they dance, sing, and laugh.
Whether being born or passing away, once born, they must again perish.
All sentient beings within the three realms, because of heedlessness, wander on in transmigration.
They commit every transgression, bound by their evil karma;
deluded regarding all phenomena, they are turned about by the enemy of heedlessness.
Harmed by negligence, they do not understand internal phenomena, nor do they understand external phenomena; unaware, they lose their minds.
What the wise hold in derision, the sons of gods nevertheless practice.
Lacking shame and fearing no human punishment, they are harmed by their own heedlessness;
delighting in play and always fond of song and dance,
they never grow weary of sensory objects and thus fall away from their celestial abode.
"Deceived by heedlessness, they laugh in the midst of terror;
they are like blind and deluded people who do not know the path from the non-path.

Thus, for the sake of benefiting others, the Bodhisattva Goose King Sucīra, having observed the celestial hosts, dwelt among the most lovely birds who delight in preaching the Dharma and spoke these verses on discipline.

Although the hosts of devas heard his words, they did not listen or accept them; instead, they sang, danced, and laughed, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses as they remained around the pond, delighting in their sensory realms.
“In the Yāma Heaven there are three Great Beings who constantly expound the Dharma for the sake of the hosts of Yāma devas who practice heedlessness.
Who are these three?
First was Mūsulinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven;
second was the Bodhisattva Śubhakāla, the Goose King;
third was the Bodhisattva Citravicitra-alaṃkāra, the Peacock King.

These three great beings constantly expound the Dharma for the benefit of others; some cause them to attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, while others cause them to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
"In this way, these great beings transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"These great beings are emptying my realm; they wish to abandon me and depart."

Among human beings, there is the śramaṇa; among the Four Heavenly Kings, there are the four Great Heavenly Kings; among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, there is Kauśika; among the Yāma gods, there are Mucilinda, the Bodhisattva Kāla, and the Bodhisattva Citravicitra; and in the Tuṣita heaven, there is the Heavenly King Śānta along with his retinue. Although these individuals dwell within my realm, they do not belong to me.
"I can cause the six heavens and the humans to be defeated, with the exception of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; though they are within my domain, they possess great power and I cannot disturb them.
I shall now dispatch my wise minister to the Yāma Heaven to go and disrupt their dharma."
Having formed this thought, he immediately consulted with his ministers:
"You should go to the presence of the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Mucilinda, the Bodhisattva Kāla, and the Bodhisattva Citravicitra, and destroy them."
"You three are skilled in speech, skilled in transformations, and possess great power—these three being:
first, Joy; second, Heedlessness."

"Three are deluded by desire—go, you shall go to the presence of Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, the Bodhisattva Kṣemaṅkara, and the Bodhisattva Citravicitra; preach the Dharma there and defeat them."
At that time, having heard these words, the three great ministers immediately descended and went to the assembly of the Yāma devas, arriving at the place where the Goose King Kāla was.
Upon arrival, they beheld this Goose King’s majestic power and heroic vigor, his supreme appearance free from fear, and his voice subdued as he spoke a verse for the host of devas:
"This is no time for negligence; One should not give rise to joy."
These two dharmas give rise to delusion, and at the time of death, they possess great power.
The fire of heedlessness, with joy as its smoke, burns an immeasurable multitude;
deluded by sensory objects, those without eyes do not perceive it.
"Able to sever the continuity, as well as the activities of sentient beings,
yet deluded by objects of perception, they do not realize what is beneficial.
When the three great ministers heard these words, they spoke in verse:
"Those who delight most in heedlessness, for whom all objects of pleasure revolve,
and through whose heedlessness craving arises— how can you speak thus?"
The Goose King Kālika replied in verse:
“Delight arises from heedfulness, And all pleasant conditions unfold.
Heedlessness gives birth to suffering; Therefore, I speak of the lotus pond.”
Then the minister of Māra, Pramadaka, spoke again in verse:
"Pleasures and their objects, The heedless celestial maidens,
And all the various arts— These are the foremost of delights."
The Goose King Kāla replied in verse:
"If any phenomenon gives rise to negligence, It is entirely suffering;
it can destroy all roots of goodness And cause one to wander through the three evil realms."
At that time, Negligence spoke again in verse:
"Whether dwelling in a grove, Or by a lotus pond,
Or within a multi-storied pavilion, One experiences pleasure through negligence."
The Goose King Kālika replied with a verse:
“In mountain groves and gardens, in the solitude of the wilderness,
through heedfulness and tranquility, one can sever the bonds of Māra.”
"Through negligence one enters hell, Or falls among the animals,
And is further reborn as a hungry ghost, Because of a negligent and deluded mind.

When the Goose King Śuklapakṣa had spoken these verses in response to Negligence, Mucilinda practiced meditative concentration within the golden cave, free from negligence, and the other devaputras likewise practiced meditative concentration, free from negligence.
Having learned of this matter, Mucilinda came toward the great lake.

Surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who filled the void of space, they sang, danced, and played music, producing a multitude of wondrous sounds as they drew near to the Heavenly King.
The gods of heedfulness neither sing nor dance; they arrive suddenly when it is time to answer difficult questions.
At that time, Mūśalinda, having heard all the verses spoken by the king of geese, recalled and understood them, thinking:
"The minister of Māra is named Heedlessness; he has three companions, and I have heard from other gods that they have arrived here."
The first is named Heedlessness, the second Joy, and the third Delusion of Desire; these increase heavy delusions within those who are ignorant.
I shall now expound for this minister Heedlessness the Dharma-gate of the Eleven Dharmas for Answering Objections, in order to shatter this host of Māras.

At that time, the King of the Yama Heaven reflected upon this matter; having deliberated with the Goose King Kāla, he descended from the sky and sat upon a lotus pedestal, surrounded by immeasurable devas who engage in heedless conduct. He spoke these eleven kinds of supreme methods for answering difficult questions to the assembly of devas, saying:
"Listen now attentively to the faults of heedlessness."

In the past, I once saw the devaputra named Kṣema, who was free from negligence; he expounded this teaching for me, enabling me to hear such a Dharma as this, which was originally proclaimed by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Listen now attentively and reflect upon this well.

All the hosts of devas, the flocks of birds that preach the Dharma, the Goose King Kāla, the host of Māra, the ministers of heedlessness, those who teach perversely, those who bring no benefit to the world, and all those who dwell in the faction of Māra—listen all with careful attention.
Eleventh, the Question and Answer on the Supreme Dharma-Gate: namely, the eleven pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) that sever the eleven defiled dharmas.

Those who seek the truth, seek nirvāṇa, and wish to leave the realm of Māra; those who fear the bonds of birth and death, dwell in the tranquility of an araṇya, remain solitary and without companion, and desire to seek the ultimate reality and extinguish the darkness—listen attentively with a single mind.
What are the eleven superior Dharma-gates that sever the eleven dharmas?
First, one severs arrogance through self-discipline;
second, with a right mind free from distraction, one eradicates the two kinds of broken precepts.
Third, diligence can extinguish indolence;
fourth, pure dharmas can sever defiled dharmas;
fifth, pure dharmas can sever unwholesome dharmas.
Sixth, through contentment, one can sever excessive desire;
seventh, by dwelling in seclusion, one severs attachment to kinsmen and neighbors;
eighth, through right speech, one severs meaningless talk.
Ninth, through right abiding, one abandons restlessness;
tenth, through generosity, one abandons poverty;
eleventh, through wisdom, one abandons ignorance.
Thus, these eleven defiled dharmas bind a person to the branches of the tree of heedlessness; those who wish to leave the realm of Māra should sever them.
Those who fear birth and death should abandon heedlessness.
Heedlessness is the root of birth and death;
heedfulness is the cause of liberation.
At that time, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, wishing to cause all sentient beings to leave birth and death behind, preached this Dharma.
In the past, I heard this Dharma taught by a former elder deva; likewise, that deva had heard this same Dharma from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and proclaimed it for my sake.
I shall explain to you that which has been handed down through successive tradition. "By what dharma is pride subdued?
One who is subdued is loved and respected by all sentient beings; because they abide in submissiveness, they sever this coarse and evil dharma of pride."
There are five kinds of arrogance; what are these five?
They are as follows: when entering a village or a city, or while traveling on a road, one walks with excessive haste and fails to maintain proper decorum.
Whether walking on a path or off the path, whether shaking out their robes or feigning a limp, those of upright mind see them and give rise to anger, thinking:
"Why does this person act contrary to the Dharma?"
"Are you drunk?
Are you mad? This is called the first form of arrogance.
How is such arrogance to be severed?

One should walk with upright conduct, neither turning nor looking back, gazing straight ahead for the distance of a yoke (four cubits). One’s deportment should be perfectly composed: one does not shake one's robes, nor does one lift the feet too high—keeping them at a limit of four finger-widths. One does not let the robe drape over both shoulders, but ensures the saṃghāṭī is evenly adjusted; while walking, one does not swing the arms.
This heedfulness can sever heedlessness.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of heedlessness that bhikṣus and others should sever and abandon: namely, speaking useless words while the mind does not reflect upon them, being unaware of their quantity;
entering a donor's house uninvited and abruptly, without even snapping one's fingers, and sitting upon [the seat] while speaking immeasurable and meaningless words without realizing it.
Producing loud sounds while in a place of quiet meditation;
looking at women with anger for no reason;
glancing left and right without observing what is before or behind.
Arrogant toward their kinsmen;
they enter the homes of others as thieves.
Such bhikṣus are not loved by any people in the world; those who practice tranquility call such bhikṣus "arrogant," whether they be householders or renunciants.
How are such faults as these to be eliminated? One should speak words of the True Dharma to donors and others that are coherent from beginning to end;

one should speak observing the person, speaking with awareness of their mind, speaking according to time and place, speaking without contradiction, speaking with gentle words, speaking so as to be easily understood, and speaking in accordance with the Dharma. One should act as one speaks, not gaze at women, enter after snapping the fingers, know the proper time for entering and leaving, and understand the appropriate signs. One should not shake one’s robes, nor walk with swinging arms; one should not spit high, nor use a loud voice. One should preach the Dharma with beautiful speech, speaking only when questioned, not interrupting the speech of others, speaking little yet beautifully, and speaking only words of the Dharma.
This is called the Vinaya’s severing of pride.
"Furthermore, the second method of subduing can sever pride.
What is this subduing?

What is meant by a bhikṣu or those similar to bhikṣus entering the homes of others? If they hear musicians performing music, laughter, or play amidst diversions, they do not listen to or take pleasure in the speech and laughter of others; they do not savor it nor desire it. They do not engage in excessive talk, nor do they speak of the faults of others. They do not adorn themselves when going to the homes of others; they do not enter frequently, nor do they constantly beg for alms.
In this way, a bhikṣu enters the homes of others—whether to the original patron’s house or to another household—and through such self-discipline, he cuts off arrogance.

"Furthermore, thirdly, a bhikṣu goes to a patron’s house and, avoiding words of the Dharma, speaks worldly talk, discusses matters of the state, speaks of rebirth in heaven, speaks of games, songs, and dances, or recounts past matters of sensual passion; he sits near women and wears variegated garments when entering the homes of others."
If bhikṣus and others thus allow such arrogance to blaze and increase, what discipline (*vinaya*) can sever and extinguish it?

It is as follows: when bhikṣus and others enter the homes of others, they should speak of the Dharma of renunciation; speak on the discourse of giving; speak on the discourse of upholding the precepts; praise the merit of wisdom; speak of the dharma of impermanence and decay; speak of old age; speak of sickness; speak of separation from loved ones; speak of the performance of one's own karma; speak of death and parting; speak of the dharma of contentment; speak of the dharma of gentleness and flexibility; speak of suffering and its origin; speak of cessation and the path; speak of the stages of progress and retreat; speak of the faults of breaking the precepts; speak of the dharma of wearying detachment; and speak of the dharma of severing stinginess.

For those who are conceited regarding form, he speaks of the faults of form, speaks of the faults of food, and speaks of impermanence and destruction; he speaks of the faults of youth, explaining that it inevitably returns to decay through old age.
Observing the deep intentions of others, he speaks in accordance with them.
Thus, through such self-discipline, the bhikṣu destroys arrogance.

"Furthermore, the fourth discipline is the severance of arrogance: one does not frequently partake of various foods and drinks. If there are others who are greedily attached to the flavors of food and know no satiety, taking pleasure in visiting the homes of others, he does not associate with them."

Whatever robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine he obtains—whether much or little—he accepts and keeps them with contentment; he does not dwell on the pleasures of others nor does he relish them, and he gives rise to no discursive thought or investigation, but acts with single-mindedness, acts with self-mastery, and acts with upright deportment.
Regarding the taming of bhikṣus and others, the method of taming is as follows: one should eradicate pride through the method of taming.
All forms of pride arise from heedlessness; with heedlessness as their root, they provide no benefit whatsoever regarding any spiritual virtues.
"Therefore, those who seek nirvāṇa should sever heedlessness.

Thus did the Night-Mover King Mucilinda and the Goose-King Supratiṣṭhita proclaim before the ministers of Māra, such as Heedlessness and others, recounting what had been heard in succession from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa by former devaputras, and speaking it for the sake of the hosts of Māra.
"What is the second question and answer?

It refers to the manifestation of right mindfulness to sever and eliminate non-observance of the precepts. There are two kinds of precepts: [the precept of restraint and the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas]."
Regarding the mundane and supramundane, it is briefly stated that the mind is the sustainer.
Precepts are of many kinds, but briefly stated there are two types:
first, those of natural gravity; [second, those established by formal decree].
Second is being free from immoral conduct.
If one violates the fundamental precepts of essential gravity, one is no longer a disciple of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.

The precepts of essential gravity refer to: killing; unchaste conduct; stealing to the extent of filling three *pātra* bowls, or stealing property belonging to the Buddha or the Dharma, and having stolen it, consuming it without feeling regret, without making restitution, and concealing it without confession.
Such a bhikṣu is not a disciple of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa; he is rotten and decayed, not called a vessel of the Dharma, but merely adorns his robes with false speech.
"This is what is called violating the gravity of the precepts regarding one's nature.
Because of negligence, Kāśyapa Tathāgata told the bhikṣus that they should abandon negligence.

Thus did the King of the Yāma Heaven preach the Dharma for the Bodhisattva Swan-King Suśamaya; the assembly of swans, the host of Māra kings, and the ministers of negligence sat upon the lotus pedestals.
Mukilinda spoke this Dharma:
"Furthermore, there are a second set of abstentions from evil, briefly stated as nine kinds.
What are these nine?"
First, purely cultivating a single practice;
second, constantly and swiftly repenting of transgressions;
third, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, partial practice;
fifth, extensive practice;
sixth, immediately repenting upon committing even minor transgressions;
Seventh, the practice of exhausting the path;
eighth, the practice of destruction;
ninth, the practice of all-encompassing conduct.
This is called the ninefold abstention from precepts.
All foolish ordinary people, or those who are śramaṇas and the like, because of their negligence, are called "unlearned" and "lacking wisdom," and they engage in evil and impure conduct.
What is the single practice?
What is the avoidance of evil?

To disparage others due to wrong views and, because of negligence, to violate even minor precepts; having violated them, to then feel remorse—specifically, such acts as digging the earth or cutting grass—this is called the single practice.
“If there are śramaṇas or those equal to śramaṇas who, having acted with negligence and violated minor precepts, subsequently repent their transgressions;
likewise, if a śramaṇa violates one, two, or three of the minor precepts of the single category of training, and having violated these minor precepts, subsequently repents his transgression.”

To repeatedly perform such acts and repeatedly repent them is called abandoning evil precepts; yet it is not honoring the Dharma, nor is it freedom from negligence, for the mind remains constantly distracted—this is called the practice of repentance for breaking the precepts.
"What is practicing in accordance [with the Dharma]?

It is that while negligence increases, one does not treat the mind or the precepts with lightness; one does not fail to study the precepts with vigor; one can explain and understand the causes and conditions for breaking the precepts; one knows what is real and what is unreal; and within the system of the precepts, one knows that breaking a grave precept incurs a great and heavy offense, and thus one firmly maintains them without transgression."
If, due to difficult circumstances, one breaks a minor precept, fails to maintain it, lacks reverence, and does not hold the True Dharma in high esteem,
this is called a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts and repents.
"Furthermore, how is it that some śramaṇas and those like them are 'half-practitioners'?"

If one studies only the rules of discipline, knowing what is grave and what is light, or whether to uphold them or not, yet directs the mind’s thoughts toward protecting the remaining categories of precepts;
thus restraining the mind to practice only half of the precepts while failing to practice the rest—this is called "half-practice."
A bhikṣu who practices heedlessness, driven by heedlessness and dwelling within the sphere of heedlessness, cannot quickly attain nirvāṇa.
"What is meant by 'practicing much'?"

If a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, or upāsikā fully maintains the precepts, thus practicing in accordance with the Dharma extensively, and extensively upholds the precepts of separation—being without deficiency, without breach, and without voidness—even though they maintain them firmly, they are unable to guard them exhaustively; this is called "extensive practice."
“If a śramaṇa or one who is like a śramaṇa commits a light offense, how should they quickly repent?
Such a bhikṣu, whether due to negligence or because of associating with evil friends, has become lax regarding the precepts; he must quickly repent so as to purify himself.”
Or, fearing the suffering of the hells and evil realms, one immediately repents and purifies the mind, declaring before the Saṃgha:
"I have committed unwholesome deeds."
Not concealing it in one's heart, and having repented, not committing it again—this is called a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense, subsequently repents.
"What is a bhikṣu who speaks of the path and practices it fully?

If a bhikṣu or other monastic should violate or slacken in a grave precept—whether through negligence or by associating with evil friends—they should quickly confess it to their teacher or declare it before the assembly of monks during the poṣadha ceremony, without concealing it in their heart.

Because the assembly of monks has shown them the way and they have been able to hear the Path, they no longer create [new karma]; fearing the three evil realms, they neither break nor slacken [the precepts].
This is called the Goose King Śubhakāla preaching the Path and fully practicing it.
"What is meant by 'corrupting one's conduct'?

It is to be lax and indolent throughout one’s life, abandoning meditation and recitation, and lacking any joy in them; wandering among celestial shrines, traveling everywhere to the homes of donors in search of clothing and food; associating with worldly people and acting as their messenger, seeking only personal comfort and pleasure."
This is called the practice of destruction.
Thus, when such a bhikṣu’s body perishes at the end of life, he falls into hell.
"O Good Time! [Listen!]"
What are all the practices?

Having faith in the *vinaya* of all dharmas and explaining them to others, one may be unable to maintain even one or two minor precepts—either due to one's disposition or a lack of habituation—and thus fail to observe them fully; yet this is not out of a lack of reverence, for having committed such an act, one repents.
Excellent! This is called "all conduct," wherein evil is slight and minimal.
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others have even a small amount of evil or broken precepts, it is entirely due to the fault of negligence.

Thus, the King of the Yāma Heaven, dwelling upon the lotus pedestal, preached this Dharma for the Goose-King Supratiṣṭhita, the assembly of birds who proclaim the Dharma, and the ministers of Māra such as Pramada and others.
At that time, Mūsulinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven,
spoke in verse: “Blinded by heedlessness, Drinking the poison of heedlessness,
Bound by heedlessness, They are about to enter hell.”
If a person acts with negligence, they will be held in contempt by the world;
they will encounter disadvantage in the present life and, at the end of their life, enter hell.
Whether staying still or traveling on the road, such a foolish person, throughout day and night, [remains thus].
All those who are heedless do not obtain even a moment of happiness.
Because of their heedlessness, they wander through the realm of desire,
revolving within the five destinies, or even falling back from meditative absorption.
If one attains worldly meditative concentration and is reborn in the formless realms,
yet continues to revolve through the various states of existence, it is entirely due to negligence.
Within all three realms, one is caught in the snare of craving’s net.
"Bound by heedlessness, the deluded do not perceive it.

Thus, in the past, the King of the Yāma Heaven heard this discourse from the Kāśyapa Buddha in succession from former devas; he has now explained three of the eleven dharmas for the sake of the Goose King Puṇyakāla, the assembly of birds who preach the Dharma, and the Māra ministers such as Heedlessness.
What are the three?
First, subduing oneself to sever arrogance;
second, maintaining a correct mind without distraction to eliminate two kinds of broken precepts.
The first is the precept of nature (*prakṛti-śīla*), and the second is the precept of detachment (*viveka-śīla*).
If one plants roots of goodness and draws near to virtuous friends, one may break the grave precepts of nature;
yet by drawing near to virtuous friends, one attains liberation from birth and death—how much more so for those who possess the precept of detachment!
Therefore, the wise should diligently seek to draw near to virtuous spiritual friends.
Third, there is one dharma to be abandoned.
What is this one dharma?
What is called laziness.

One should abandon laziness and diligently practice vigor; if one can be vigorous, one can extinguish all forms of laziness. Just as negligence brings no benefit regarding any dharma, so too do all wholesome dharmas have the cultivation of intimacy with virtuous friends as their root.
"Furthermore, the fourth pure quality (*śukladharma*) can sever defiled qualities (*mala-dharma*).
What is this pure quality?
It is through diligent vigor (*vīrya*) that one severs indolence (*kausīdya*)."
Just as light dispels all darkness, so too does diligent effort eliminate indolence.
Indeed, indolence is the destroyer of all dharmas.
Following its arising, laziness increases further and further, capable of destroying worldly and world-transcending dharmas, as well as immeasurable, ineffable dharmas of the present and the future.

A person who is indolent possesses little strength and is despised by others; furthermore, they are unable to manage their household affairs, remaining poor, lowly, and base. They are incapable of engaging in livelihoods such as trade, farming, planting, or any other such activities, nor can they draw near to virtuous friends and spiritual mentors.

Because of their indolence, they are held in contempt by others and mocked by all; they do not study wisdom and are so foolish as to know nothing, failing to understand the proper time and place, nor their own strength, nor the strength of others.
If one fails to perform what ought to be done according to the proper time—whether it be in the present or the future—all such duties will remain unaccomplished.

"If a person is diligent, they can eliminate such laziness; they will be beloved by all and respected by the multitude. During the first and last watches of the night, their mind will not grow weary; though they sleep, they are easily awakened. They know the time to rise and the time to lie down, acting in accordance with the proper timing through mindful reflection."
With firm diligence and taking diligence as one’s companion, one washes away the stains of indolence with the water of diligence.
All that is undertaken is accomplished free from defilement.
Should one encounter decline or distress while performing any task, one does not retreat from diligence; one is neither timid nor weary, neither interrupted nor ceasing.
If one undertakes a great task, because of the companion of diligence, it can be accomplished without being ruined.
In whatever one undertakes, one does not rely on others; one recognizes those who are good or evil, and understands the strength of both oneself and others.
Praised by virtuous people and venerated by the multitude, or even venerated by kings and great ministers;
possessing great wealth and great power, no one dares to oppose them in any dispute, and no powerful person can destroy them.
With virtuous friends as companions, one’s knowledge increases; because of having many virtuous friends, one possesses great power and experiences much peace and happiness.
Wherever one travels, even when reaching foreign lands, one always attains security and well-being.
If one travels to other regions, virtuous people will draw near; wherever there are people who draw near, one should pay them respect, make offerings, and treat them with courtesy.

Because one has abandoned indolence, one attains such immeasurable merits as these: donning the great and firm armor of diligence, free from the defilement of indolence, one is able to destroy the armies of Māra, transcend birth and death, and be loved and respected by all virtuous people.
By exerting diligent effort for the sake of companionship, one further attains the supramundane, untainted, and stainless path to nirvāṇa.

Initially, that which is firm and the locus of evil defilements is loose yet difficult to escape; by this, the household binds all worldly beings—the wife, children, and kinsmen; sisters, brothers, servants, fields, houses, wealth, and treasuries; and the great torrential river of craving.
With diligence as one’s companion, one can leave behind the fear of birth and death, renounce the household life to go forth, and don the three dharma robes.

With diligence as one’s companion, by exerting diligent effort within the bonds of the household, one attains liberation and achieves the path of non-abiding; one zealously cultivates meditative concentration, studies and recites the True Dharma, and, desiring to enter nirvana, attains deliverance.

Knowing what is appropriate for the occasion, one exerts diligent effort; one knows as it truly is the emergence and subsidence of body and speech, clearly understands their specific characteristics, and knows as they truly are the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Day and night without ceasing, with diligent effort and without slackening, they draw near to virtuous teachers.
Through wisdom and skillful means, they exert vigorous diligence, practicing the Path to exhaust all faults and severing the bonds of beginningless transmigration in birth and death.
Thus, indolence is entirely without benefit, like utter darkness; it is a firm evil that brings no profit to any sentient being, yet through diligence, one is able to extinguish it.

In this way, according to the path he has attained and according to what he has realized, that person exerts diligent effort; thus, he is able to disperse and extinguish all conditioned combinations and takes no pleasure in the realms of afflictions and defiled fetters.

They deceive all foolish ordinary people, feigning affection and intimacy. Within the realm of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, they are like wicked thieves who plunder the wealth of wholesome dharmas and destroy those very dharmas. They can perform every kind of unbeneficial act; they do not seek desirable karmic results nor desirable riches, but instead afflict and disturb all foolish ordinary people, causing them to become deluded and confused.

Therefore, one should abandon attachment to sense objects and not savor them; one should cultivate the path to liberation so as to purify the mind. As the mind becomes purified, one will be able to exert diligence, possessing right mindfulness and freedom from doubt.
By means of right practice one destroys the enemy; furthermore, by taking diligence as a companion, one is able to sever greed, hatred, and delusion.

Through right observation and abandonment, one does not undergo further existence. Having slain the enemy, one is pure like the sky in Jambudvīpa when it is observed to be clear and free from clouds or mist, with the sun and moon pure and their radiance brilliantly manifest; the purity of that person is likewise thus.

It is like one who has recovered from illness, or like a poor person who has obtained wealth; it is like a blind man traveling through a vast wilderness who, having lost the right path, now finds the way and gains his sight.
Because that person maintains the prohibitive precepts and practices correctly, they realize through practice:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Thus, free from defilement and dust, one attains liberation from all bonds and crosses to the other shore.
Wisdom is courageous and free from defilement and dust; all of this is due to the companion of diligence.
"Therefore, by exerting great diligence, one can sever the bonds of birth and death, namely indolence and negligence.
At that time, Mucilinda, the King of the Yāma Heaven, spoke these verses using the stanzas of Kāśyapa Buddha:
"Exerting the mindfulness of diligence, One always delights in solitary and quiet places."
Having escaped from evil karma, one attains nirvana through wisdom.
With diligence as one's companion, one leaves behind the defilement of sloth;
having escaped the terrors of the wilderness, such a person attains eternal bliss.
Laziness and negligence can obstruct all dharmas;
because of these great faults, they cause sentient beings suffering and distress.
If one seeks happiness in the present and the future, one should abandon laziness.
"Those who are heedless and indolent are no different from dogs.

Thus did the King of the Yāma Heaven speak for the sake of the Goose-King Sucīrṇa and the assembly of Dharma-preaching birds, as well as for the ministers of Māra—Heedlessness, Desire-Confusion, and the rest—reciting the sūtras of that Tathāgata Kāśyapa as they had been heard transmitted from former devaputras.
"Furthermore, the fifth pure quality (*śukladharma*) can sever unwholesome qualities (*akuśaladharma*).
What are these unwholesome qualities?

They are: delighting in entering cities and villages, constantly habituating oneself to clamor and bustle, not delighting in dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*), and thereby destroying the dharma of a śramaṇa."
What is the corruption of the Dharma?
