It is when a bhikṣu abandons the practice of meditation as well as recitation and study, and instead frequents the homes of laypeople in various villages or towns, delighting in staying there; he engages in much conversation with both men and women.
If one converses and speaks with a woman, it can bind one and cause the loss of all benefits, or give rise to a mind of desire. Why is this?
A woman is like fire; the closer one draws near, the more one is drawn in. If one draws near to a woman, she will gradually cause the mind to become distracted.
For this reason, a bhikṣu should not enter among the villages and towns.

If he engages in conversation and talk with men, he loses all matters of his own self-benefit, and his mind becomes impure regarding the outflow-free Dharma (anāsrava-dharma); such a bhikṣu destroys his own Dharma.
Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu who delights in entering villages and towns, he incurs many faults.
What faults does he incur?

By entering the homes of others, his mind becomes agitated and disturbed; seeing the wealth, pleasure, food, drink, bedding, and furniture in the houses of laypeople, greed and attachment arise in his heart.
It is like eating vomit.

Having departed from the *āraṇya*, they wander among humans; having abandoned the Path to enter secular life, they forsake the joy of seclusion and are bound by their households, practicing greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because of these faults, they fall again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
By what causes and conditions do they undergo such suffering?
It is because they delight in entering cities, towns, and villages.
Therefore, monks, if you wish to attain the ground [of realization], you should abandon these faults. "How does one abandon them?
By dwelling in an araṇya, one is able to encompass all the merits of non-abiding."
Subsumed by non-abiding, it is the foremost peace and security.

If there is a bhikṣu dwelling alone in an araṇya, his sense faculties are tranquil and his mind is pure; his intention is like refined gold. Being supremely tranquil, he well guards his sense faculties, is free from fear and free from defilement, and attains the foremost peace and security—the bliss of the outflows-free (anāsrava).
All the sensual pleasures within the six heavens of the desire realm arise from the performance of wholesome karma.
The bliss of even a single heaven is lovely and peerless; how much more so, then, are all the various pleasures of the six heavens combined?

If one attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the bliss of even a single thought-moment cannot be illustrated by any analogy; it cannot be compared through any calculation or conceptual deliberation.

Therefore, if one seeks the bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should leave behind clamor and bustle, not enter villages, and seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and right reception (*samāpatti*).

One should always wander alone in mountain valleys, rocky caves, forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), or at the edge of grassy thickets, traveling solitary and seeking the bliss of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

One should distance oneself from acquaintances, kinsmen, and retinues, and contemplate that the pleasures of acquaintances and kin are impermanent and unstable; they are subject to separation, lack a fixed abode, are turbid, defiled, and agitated, devoid of sovereignty, and fraught with much fear.

Therefore, if there is a foolish person of meager wisdom who abandons the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and delights in seeking tainted pleasure—which is called "semblance-pleasure"—that person is like one who turns away from light to seek darkness.
Foolish people fall away because they do not know the characteristics of merit and fault.
Therefore, one should abandon the pleasures of villages and cities, and always dwell alone in an araṇya.

Thus, having departed from villages and towns to dwell among the forest trees, one attains the bliss of non-abiding; this is called the fifth method of severing defiled karma through pure and white dharmas.
"If you wish to seek happiness and desire to leave the realm of Māra, you must eliminate defiled dharmas by means of pure and white dharmas.

Thus, knowing that the hearts of the assembly of birds who had heard the Dharma were well-tamed, the Bodhisattva Suśīma, with a mind intent on benefiting others, preached the Sūtra of Kāśyapa Buddha as it had been successively transmitted from former devaputras, speaking for the sake of the ministers of Māra such as Pramada and others:
"Among the eleven dharmas, five have already been explained; there remain six dharmas which shall now be explained in succession."
Gather your mind in single-mindedness; now is precisely the right time.
Having now attained freedom from hardships and all that is necessary, it would be a great deception if you were neither to preach the Dharma nor to listen to it.
Therefore, having already attained freedom from calamities and the perfection of the sense faculties, one should preach the Dharma for them.
How can one preach the Dharma among the three evil realms—namely, hell, hungry ghosts, and animals?
How does one listen to the Dharma?
Among animals, they harm one another; among hungry ghosts, they suffer from hunger and thirst; in the hells, they are oppressed by suffering—how could they hear the Dharma?
Only those among humans and devas who practice without negligence are able to hear the Dharma.
I am free from negligence, and you possess a virtuous mind of faith.
Listen attentively now, for I shall speak for you.
The Dharma is difficult to hear, and to be born free from calamities and endowed with all favorable conditions is likewise exceedingly rare.
"Furthermore, the sixth defilement is deception.
What is the defiled phenomenon?
It is called excessive desire."
Now, having many desires is the foremost defilement and the abode of evil greed.
How can it be extinguished?
It should be extinguished by means of contentment.
Whether they be householders or those who have left the home life, those with many desires cannot attain peace and happiness.
If, whether as householders or those who have left the home life, their minds are full of desire, they will never find peace and happiness by day or by night.
If, after having acquired wealth, one’s mind is not tranquil and one knows no satiety regarding the riches obtained,
then while such excessive desire in a householder may be considered a minor hindrance,
for an ordained person it is otherwise: if an ordained person has excessive desire, they are neither called a householder nor are they called an ordained person.
What is it to be called one who has left the household life?
It is to sever pride, jealousy, and excessive desire.
To state the essential point: those with excessive desire are universally despised and reviled.
If there is a bhikṣu whose mind harbors many desires and constantly longs for wealth and goods, such a bhikṣu’s mind will not be pure regarding wholesome dharmas.
Because the mind is impure, his faculties are impure, and his conduct is also impure.

If one walks upon the grounds of the Sangha out of pride and arrogance even for a single step, one will enter hell; how much more so for using bedding, furniture, or medicine for the sick—if these are done without fault, they are purely acts leading to hell.
If one breaks the precepts, has many desires, and practices unwholesome dharmas, they are in truth not a śramaṇa, yet claim to be a śramaṇa.
They are like a jackal wearing a lion’s skin, or like a counterfeit jewel that sounds like a conch shell while being empty and void within.
If a bhikṣu of excessive desire claims,
"I am a disciple of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa," having gone forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, he is consumed by his excessive desire even more so than by a great fire.
Excessive desire causes confusion and distress; its harm entering the body exceeds that of poison.
Excessive desire injures people more than old age and decay.
Excessive desire is a sharp blade that fells the tree of goodness; its injury exceeds that of a physical weapon.
The affliction of excessive desire exceeds that of a malignant disease.
A mind of excessive desire constantly seeks out opportunities to end another's life, surpassing even an enemy who seeks an opportunity to harm others.
Therefore, one should know this:
these faults of excessive desire destroy both worlds; one ought to abandon this defilement of excessive desire.
Even if one contemplates it day and night, one will ultimately find no happiness.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, Mūsuludha (Maudgalyāyana), recited these verses spoken by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa:
"Excessive desire is like a sharp blade, Cutting and harming the foolish person;
Abandon it as one would a sword, For it slays those who are blind and ignorant."
Excessive desire is a great malignant ulcer;
if it arises within the heart, because of that person’s greed, they find no joy day or night.
The fire of desire has recollection for its fuel and is fanned by the wind of craving.
A fierce fire blazes intensely, burning the hearts of sentient beings.
Because greed obscures the mind, it causes the human heart to be light and fickle;
because of attachment to wealth and goods, one loses one's own life.
If a person in this world Commits various evil deeds, It is all due to greed and pride; Thus the wise have said.
If a person’s mind is courageous and resolute, They would be able to enter a great fire.
All arise from a greedy mind, which brings about one's own lack of benefit.
Whether it be the suffering of being harmed by weapons or various forms of strife and contention,
all stem from the causal conditions of the mind and from associating with foolish people.
"You should know that these miseries and afflictions all arise from the fault of craving;
the wise have thus declared that one should not associate with craving.
Thus did Muxuluotuo (Mukhulinda) speak for the sake of the Goose King Shanshi (Kāla), the assembly of Dharma-preaching birds, and the ministers of Māra named Pramāda (Heedlessness) and others.
"How is this great fault to be eliminated?
It should be done through the white dharmas (kuśala-dharma). What are the white dharmas?"
This is what is called having few desires.
Now, having few desires is termed the dharma of all peace and happiness.
If a person has few desires, they will constantly attain peace and happiness; such a person does not fear kings, thieves, water, or fire.
Because those with many desires love wealth and property, they associate with the families of others to seek wealth and property, and they associate with base people to seek wealth and property.

If a person has few desires, they will not go to the doors of evil people; they do not utter false speech, nor do they engage in deceitful singing, dancing, or frivolous laughter; they do not engage in ornamental speech or commit evil deeds. They are not burned by the fire of craving for wealth and desire; seeing others obtain happiness, they do not give rise to distress; they do not associate with evil spiritual friends out of greed for wealth, and they do not harbor doubts.
If one travels on the road, one will not fear bandits or thieves and will be free from enemies.
People will not seek to take advantage of one, nor will one fear punishment or execution.
If those living at home can act in this way, they will have nothing to fear, be free from all terrors, and enjoy complete peace and security.
How much more so for one who has left the household life, who is far removed from faults and fears, who has abandoned the ways of the laity, and dwells among the forest trees.
If such a person should again come to the abode of householders and have many desires, you should know that this person is no different from one who eats vomit.
Among śramaṇas, the foremost offering is that which consists of having few desires.

A bhikṣu with few desires is contented and pure; his fame is heard everywhere. He accepts only one meal a day, wears only rag-robes from refuse heaps, and wanders alone without companion through mountain valleys, rock caves, and thickets of grass. He dwells only among cemeteries and, of the three portions of food, he eats only two.

When begging for food, he avoids acquaintances from afar and does not approach his own kin; he keeps only a single bowl and carries a mendicant’s staff, accepting whatever offerings he receives with wise reflection, and then departs.
When traveling on a road, one looks ahead only a fathom’s distance and does not glance left or right; one abandons delicious flavors and does not eat leftover rice.
Within a village, one stays for no more than three nights; within a city, for up to seven nights.

He does not sit upon seats adorned and embellished with jewels; he abandons his former kinsmen, relatives, and acquaintances and does not go to visit them; he does not think of the king’s savory delicacies, fine meals, couches, or bedding; and he does not speak of noble lineages.

Associating with virtuous friends, those of similar character and conduct, and engaging in conversation and discussion with those who share the same precepts—in this way, a bhikṣu remains free from evil and free from turbidity; possessing few desires and being content, he is able to sever the bonds of Māra.
If there are lustful and precept-breaking bhikṣus who wear the kāṣāya, they are a continuous great evil to the devas and the world, like a disease or a thief.
A bhikṣu who is content, whose faculties do not wander among the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and who dwells in the open air, is able to benefit all sentient beings.
One who restrains the mind, cultivates the dharmas of the body, practices the mindfulness of feelings and the mind, and restrains the mind to guard the sense faculties amidst birth and death—
because of such contentment, one is called a bhikṣu.
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to practice fewness of desires, he will be able to do so through non-negligence;
however, due to negligence, much desire arises. This is true for both householders and those who have left the home life.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke in verse:
"If one is not heedless, Then one attains the fruit of liberation;
If one is heedless, Then one falls into hell."
Heedlessness and heedfulness—these are said to be their respective superior fruits;
as is the difference between light and darkness, so too are liberation and bondage.
The meaning of heedlessness and heedfulness is likewise thus.
Few desires bring peace and happiness; many desires bring suffering and distress.
Such are the characteristics of suffering and happiness as taught by the wise.
If sentient beings have many desires, their minds are always like fire.
Few desires are like a cool pond, where those who bathe therein leave greed behind.
Just as fire finds no satiety when consuming dry fuel,
so too is the insatiability of a person with many desires who covets wealth.
The greedy person, day and night, never possesses peace or happiness;
because they take such great pleasure in desire, the arrows of craving pierce their heart.
Countless kings of the past were insatiable in their greed for wealth.
"The future shall be likewise; all things will utterly perish.
Therefore, the wise declare that having few desires is the supreme happiness.

Thus did the King of the Yāma Heaven, while seated upon the lotus pedestal, preach the sixth discourse of Kāśyapa Tathāgata for the sake of the king of geese, Supratiṣṭhita, the assembly of preaching birds, and the ministers of Māra, such as those named Heedlessness.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 59; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 60.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-nine: Observing the Heavens; Part Twenty-five: The Nightmotha Heaven.

Furthermore, the King of the Yama Heaven—accompanied by the Goose-King Suśamaya and the assembly of birds who preach the Dharma—manifested before them to subdue the arrogance of the ministers of Māra and others. For this purpose, he preached the Sūtra of Kāśyapa Tathāgata, as it had been transmitted from former devaputras.
"I have already explained the six kinds of white dharmas that sever dust and defilement; I shall now explain the seventh defiled dharma, which white dharmas are able to sever.
What is this defiled dharma?"
This refers to one who, upon seeing their place of birth, gives rise to a mind of attachment;
they delight in seeing their kinsmen and relatives, and thus distance themselves from severing such ties.

Regarding their circle of acquaintances and kin, their mind constantly delights in seeing them, always thinking of being near them, never parting day or night. They take no pleasure in cultivating dhyāna or practicing their duties, do not draw near to virtuous teachers or make offerings to the Triple Gem, and do not contemplate future karma.
Among the three types of action, he neither speaks of them to others nor performs them himself; he thinks only of his kinsmen, desiring to see his relatives, acquaintances, and old friends.
[He wonders: "How shall I manage my livelihood?"
"By what means shall I sustain myself?

Having had this thought, he was overwhelmed by sorrow; although dwelling among the trees of the forest for the sake of liberation, he did not practice in accordance with it. This is ignorance, and his mind entered an ocean of grief.

Having already entered the ocean of sorrow, they further enter the incomparable great ocean of sorrow consisting of birth, old age, sickness, and death; desiring to see their kinsmen, relatives, and acquaintances, they fall into the net of Māra.
Because of seeing their kinsmen, their affectionate love increases; when invited for meals from house to house, they give rise to greedy thoughts and conform to worldly customs.
Hearing what householders say, their minds become attached to it with pleasure.

Because their minds are so enamored with it, they lose their own benefit through whatever they do; out of folly, they regress, fearing not the suffering of the evil realms in the future, nor do they contemplate the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, or other places of birth. They likewise do not contemplate the terrors of the present: the suffering of old age, sickness, and death; the suffering of separation from the beloved; the suffering of encountering the hated; nor do they contemplate that all that is dear must inevitably be parted from.

If one leaves the household life out of fear for one's relatives, friends, and kin, yet returns to associate with them again, taking pleasure in those relatives, friends, and old acquaintances; if one craves the food and drink of others and frequently visits their doors, then at the dissolution of the body after death, one will fall into an evil destination—whether born in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal—and whatever purpose one had for leaving the household life will be entirely lost.
Once one has fallen into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals and undergoes great suffering and affliction, one's relatives and friends are unable to provide protection or rescue.
Therefore, all bhikṣus who fear the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals should not take pleasure in seeing their birthplaces, relatives, or acquaintances.
Because they draw near to this, they fail to obtain any benefit.
They have gone forth into homelessness for the sake of realizing the exhaustion of craving and severing the web of attachment;
yet, out of ignorance, they instead cultivate intimacy with that very web of attachment—like a person who, fearing fire, abandons it and flees, only to enter a great conflagration once more.
Thus, having feared the household and abandoned it to go forth into homelessness, to return again to a place of fear is likewise so.

To abandon one's kinsmen and enter among the forest trees, only to return once more to their company—this is to be obstructed by lack of vision and ignorance, with the sense faculties untrained; this is called the defiled dharma.
"How is it severed? If one cannot sever it through wisdom, or cannot obstruct it, or cannot maintain it, one should avoid and obstruct it by remaining far away for a long time."
If a person lacking wisdom cannot sever craving through other skillful means, they should keep their distance from it.
All human affection is severed by not seeing [the beloved];
all phenomena of attachment must inevitably be parted with.

When the time of death arrives, no one can provide salvation except for one's own wholesome karma; among the countless hundreds of thousands of places of rebirth, it is the karma of virtuous dharmas that is most capable of saving. Neither kinsmen nor brothers can save a person.
In this way, a bhikṣu who has abandoned his relatives and dwells alone in seclusion is able to sever defiled dharmas.
At the time of old age, sickness, and death, it is not one's kinsmen who can provide protection.
When a bhikṣu reflects in this way, he severs all craving or renders it faint; this is called a bhikṣu severing craving for kinsmen.
"Furthermore, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, they sever the eighth defiled dharma.
What are the defiled dharmas?
They are so-called meaningless speech, which is severed by right speech.
If a householder engages in empty and meaningless speech, he will be held in contempt by all people, like mere weeds.
Words of meaning are the foremost wealth, which no other forms of wealth can equal;
words devoid of meaning, though accompanied by riches and pleasure, are still called poverty.

Vain and meaningless speech is empty and without substance; such a person is held in contempt by others, like a white sheep that possesses no wealth of eloquence. To the wise, such a person is viewed as nothing more than a beast—the most base object of derision.
Regarding such dharmas as these, how does one sever empty and meaningless speech?
It is what is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
There are two kinds of right speech; what are the two?
The first is silence;
the second is the four kinds of right speech. What are these four?
First, not speaking falsely;
second, not using harsh speech;
third, not engaging in divisive speech.
Fourth is speech that does not cause destruction;
this is called right speech.
Whether one is a householder or a monastic, if one can act in this way, one will not be disparaged or reviled.
Whether lay or ordained, there are six causes and conditions by which one is quickly held in contempt by others.

What are these six? They are: speaking meaningless words; intruding into people's homes; coveting the food of others; sitting in seats reserved for those of higher status; and speaking falsely without substance.
These six dharmas are objects of ridicule by others; whether as a householder or one who has gone forth, one should abandon these practices.
"Furthermore, the ninth defilement is that which pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) can sever."
How does the white dharma sever the defiled dharmas?
It is said that the state of right abiding can sever the dharma of restlessness.
The dharma of restlessness obstructs all dharmas.

The nature of the mind is light and fickle; because of this agitation, one lacks faith and lacks awareness, being ignorant of worldly affairs, ignorant of speech, ignorant of the proper seasons, and not associating with virtuous friends.
Because of restlessness and heedlessness, one cannot thoroughly comprehend worldly phenomena.
Such defilements of restlessness can ruin both the present and future lives, preventing the attainment of benefit.
Whether lay or ordained, one should eliminate restlessness by abiding correctly in the white dharmas.

If lay or ordained persons abide correctly with body, speech, and mind free from restlessness, they will be honored by all; through right precepts, right knowledge, and right intention, they will transcend the realm of Māra, fulfill the wholesome dharmas, and ultimately attain Nirvāṇa.
Regarding worldly dharmas, they are praised by the wise.
They are able to accomplish all that is undertaken in the world and are honored by the multitude.
Wherever they go, they always obtain peace and happiness, and their endeavors reach fulfillment.
"In this way, both householders and those who have left the home life, being free from frivolity and agitation, are praised by all people.

Furthermore, the Yāma Heaven King Mūsuludha, for the sake of the assembly of birds who preach the Dharma, the king of geese named Śubhakāla, and the ministers of Māra such as Pramādaka, recounted the sūtras of Kāśyapa Buddha—having previously heard them in succession from former devas—and spoke them for the celestial hosts.
"Furthermore, the tenth defiled dharma is one that may be despised and reviled, and is abandoned by the wise.
What is this defiled dharma? It is poverty."
There are two kinds of poverty:
first, poverty of precepts;
second, poverty of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, poverty in giving;
second, poverty in wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, poverty of lineage;
second, poverty of view.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, poverty of material wealth;
second, poverty of teachers and masters.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, impoverished kinsmen;
second, impoverished old friends.
All who are impoverished—whether male or female—are subject to contempt.
How may this be severed? It is through giving.
All poverty can be severed through generosity, just as the light of a lamp can extinguish all darkness.
All ignorance can be extinguished by wisdom.
All heterodox views can be severed by right view.
Such unrighteousness can be severed by the Dharma.

This is the foremost and most supreme, cherished and embraced by all those who possess omniscience; it cuts off the various evil realms and brings peace and security in both the present and future lives.
What is giving? Giving is of many kinds, namely:

the gift of wisdom, the gift of morality, the gift of Dharma, the gift of consolation, and the gift of showing the right path; the gift of showing the way to those who have lost their way, the gift of providing water to those traveling on the road, the gift of life, the gift of requisites, the gift of fearlessness, the gift of truthful speech, the gift of severing doubt, the gift of the five precepts, the gift of the monastic precepts, the gift of the full ordination precepts, the gift of medicine for the sick, and the gift of eyes and so forth.

Various forms of giving such as these can benefit both the present and future lives, just like parents; having constantly contemplated and practiced them, one severs all poverty, abandons the evil realms, and experiences peace and happiness among gods and humans.
Having experienced such pleasure, one ultimately attains nirvāṇa.
Thus, giving can sever poverty; for this reason, the wise should practice generosity.
"Furthermore, the eleventh dark dharma binds one to birth and death, obscuring all dharmas with darkness."
What are the dharmas of darkness?
They are what is called lack of wisdom.
From immeasurable ignorance up to the darkness of nescience, they bind all living beings.
The entire mass of darkness binds its neck; ignorance is like a sword, like fire, and like poison.

Ignorance is also like all forms of nescience (*avidyā*); arising from the causal conditions of all nescience, it causes one to wander through all the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. It binds sentient beings and causes them to transmigrate.
How are such enmities and defilements to be severed?
They are severed by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Like a bright lamp, it serves as a rescue and a refuge; toward all sentient beings, it is like a father and like a mother.
It is like a physician and like excellent medicine; it severs the bonds of ignorance so that they do not arise again, just as when the root of a tree is severed, the tree does not grow.

It is like fire consuming wood, which does not arise again, or like flowing water, which does not flow back; likewise, the incineration of ignorance by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is such that it does not arise again.
Therefore, one should at all times diligently cultivate vigor and sever ignorance through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
"These eleven dharmas thus described are the root of negligence."
One pursues heedlessness, and because of heedlessness, [suffering] arises; therefore, one should sever all heedlessness.
All roots of heedlessness are entirely without benefit, for they are capable of producing further heedlessness.

For example, it is by depending upon the great earth that all medicinal herbs, trees, thickets, flowing streams, rivers, ponds, embankments, cities, towns, villages, groves, and even Sumeru, the king of mountains, all depend upon the great earth.
"All hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are likewise thus; they all depend upon heedlessness.
Therefore, the wise should abandon it.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke in verse:
“The body of the aged is wrinkled, They walk with staffs, lacking strength;
That the old do not know the Dharma Is entirely due to negligence.”
With a body ruined by illness, lying prostrate upon a bed and mat, one feels no sense of weary detachment; this is entirely due to ignorance.
Whether encountering hunger and thirst, or entering perilous and evil paths, [one remains unmoved].
That one does not give rise to weary detachment is entirely due to negligence.
If one encounters separation from what is beloved and gives rise to suffering and affliction, it is because of all manner of negligence; thus has the Tathāgata spoken.
If within the five realms of existence, One undergoes all manner of sufferings, And sentient beings are constantly afflicted by distress, It is because of their ignorance. Alas!
They do not grow weary of or seek to leave The various worlds of birth and death.
The great wheel of all karma revolves, circling without a moment’s pause.
Within the three realms there is no joy, nor is there even the slightest permanence;
yet such ignorant people do not know to feel weary and seek liberation.
All realms are empty space; the three worlds are like a dream.
All things are entirely suffering, yet those without eyes do not see or know this.
Such foolish people are harmed by their own negligence.
When the fear of death is about to arrive, there is no one who can ward it off or save one.
Because of unwholesome contemplation, the mind and spirit are disturbed;
though the King of Death is about to arrive, people do not perceive it.
The King of Death is about to arrive, Seizing away people’s hearts that cling to life.
These three things are of no benefit, Afflicting and harming all sentient beings.
Sufferings such as old age, illness, and death Arise because of heedlessness.
Among those tormented by craving, the heedless bring harm to the devas;
The hungry ghosts are tormented by hunger and thirst, Those in hell are afflicted by suffering,
And animals are mostly characterized by ignorance, Mutually harming one another.
Such manifold sufferings and afflictions distress all sentient beings because they follow unrighteous conduct due to negligence and folly.
It is just as all medicinal herbs and the like grow by depending upon the great earth.
Heedlessness is likewise thus: it increases all afflictions.
This host of Māra’s army and his foremost ministers are crushed by the vajra of wisdom, just as sunlight dispels the darkness.
Within what has been explained here, one should know both merit and fault:
the fruit of heedlessness is suffering, while the fruit of heedfulness is happiness.
Thus did the King of Yama speak with immeasurable discernment.
The faults of negligence and the virtues of heedfulness:
"The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death; separation from the beloved and encounter with the hateful;
and immeasurable decays and afflictions— these pervade the midst of birth and death."
If a person knows skillful means, they can ward off future suffering;
since evil karma is the cause of suffering, one finds joy in not committing evil deeds.
The extinction of afflictions is the supreme joy—thus do the wise proclaim.
This is the path to Nirvāṇa, as proclaimed by the One of True Wisdom.
Tamed and heedful, dwelling in a secluded place,
Brave and free from a mind of craving— one is not far from Nirvāṇa.
Having abandoned both enemies and friends, extinguishing desire for existence,
and remaining heedful regarding sense objects— one is not far from Nirvana.
If a person abandons evil and cultivates a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, [they are likewise not far from Nirvana].
Those who fear birth and death are not far from nirvāṇa.
By cutting off afflictions with wisdom, their minds become cool through insight;
having crossed over the defilement of indolence, they are not far from nirvāṇa.
In harmony with the Four Noble Truths, Severing the three kinds of faults,
Mastery over the faculties— One is not far from Nirvana.
Knowing ānāpāna, One practices its two aspects.
One who understands what is known by wisdom is not far from Nirvana.
If one is freed from the fear of transgressions, and if one delights in that which does not bind the mind,
being thus able to cross to the further shore— for these reasons, one is called a Muni.
"Thus did the King of the Yāma Heaven, for the sake of the assembly of Dharma-preaching birds and the Goose-King Kāla, proclaim the sūtras of the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Because they were free from negligence, he thus proclaimed the Dharma with immeasurable, sublime, and heroic sounds of the True Dharma that subdue [the mind]."
At that time, having heard the true Dharma, the host of Māra’s army and the minister Praamāda (Heedlessness) thought to themselves:
"We are now unable to overturn such a teaching as this of the King of the Yāma Heaven."
"The profound Dharma is difficult to comprehend and cannot be turned back.
Having formed this thought, he informed his companions in full:
"Now, within this path of the Dharma of Mucilinda, not even a single phrase can be altered or moved."

After the ministers of Māra had deliberated thus, their power being weakened and their original intent to destroy thwarted, they lost their great majesty and flew up into the void; in a mere instant, they returned to the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to the presence of Māra Pāpīyas.
Having arrived, all the Māras asked the messenger:
"Is the task you were commissioned to perform as you intended?
Has it been brought to completion?"
When the three great ministers heard these words, they addressed the Māra King, saying:
"O Heavenly King!
We have lost our power; the Night-Wandering Heavenly King Mucilinda possesses great wisdom, and regarding even a single phrase within the True Dharma, he cannot be moved."
"As for their celestial hosts, it is likewise; I cannot disturb them.
Then, having heard these words, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"As for the gods who practice heedlessness, I am able to cause them to dwell in desire."
"Though they possess great power, because of their negligence, they remain within my realm.
Having thought this, he addressed the hosts of Māras, saying:
"In the future, I shall be able to destroy the Yāma Heaven; do not be in such a hurry."
"I possess great power capable of destroying and disorienting all the hosts of devas; I shall break them later.

When Māra Pāpīyān had spoken these words, he again experienced the peerless pleasures of the six sense-desires, and in that state of heedlessness, his immeasurable attainment of great pleasure increased further.

“While the King of the Yāma Heaven, together with the Goose-King Supratiṣṭhita and the assembly of Dharma-preaching birds, expounded immeasurable kinds of teachings, the hosts of Māra’s army, having become heedless, retreated; at that time, the various celestial assemblies had accomplished what was to be done.”

"At that time, the newly born devas, sporting and enjoying themselves, came from within the groves toward the place where the Heavenly King was teaching the Dharma, as well as toward the Goose King Kāla and the assembly of birds who teach the Dharma."
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven, seeing this host of devas, said to Kāla:
"Observe these devas who act with such negligence; they are now coming toward this place."
"I shall now roam in the tranquil groves.
Having spoken these words, he soared into the void and entered the Tranquil Forest.

"These hosts of devas wander about in negligence, fully possessed of the five desires, finding delight in the gardens, groves, and ponds; yet, until the karma accumulated through their craving is exhausted, they will flow according to their karma and fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."

If there is remaining karma that causes birth among human beings, one will possess abundant wealth and become a great person in the world—either a great king or a high minister—in a place of great happiness, beloved by all people.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who understands the retribution of karma perceives through his wisdom derived from hearing that the dwelling place of the Yāma Heaven is named "Constant Joy."
By what karma are sentient beings born in that place?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees:
there are virtuous people who uphold the precepts, refraining from killing and stealing as previously described, and furthermore, they abandon sexual misconduct.
Not committing sexual misconduct is the foremost of difficult disciplines; one is able to renounce it and refrain from doing so.
Even upon seeing male and female birds or beasts in union, one does not give rise to thoughts of desire, abandons the wish to look, and does not dwell upon them in thought.

Conceiving a sense of dread toward the retribution of misconduct, they therefore abandon those who hold wrong views and exhort them not to engage in such acts; they explain the retribution of misconduct and cause others to abide in the path of virtue.
For this reason, I have spoken these words of Dharma:
"This sexual misconduct results in an undesirable retribution; it is certain that its retribution is falling into hell.
Since one does not commit it oneself, one teaches others not to do so.
Such a person, benefiting both themselves and others, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Yāma), in the realm of Exclusive Bliss.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, their happiness will never cease, and all manner of immeasurable joys will increase.
"In this place there are various groves which one finds delightful upon seeing.
There are wish-fulfilling groves where all desired pleasures are obtained simply by thinking of them; within these groves, one experiences delight and enjoyment."
The newly born deva-son possesses various gardens and groves:
the first is named Light Delight;
the second is named Flowing Water Delight.
The three mountains are gathered in bliss.

There is a lotus pond called the Variegated Pond (Citrapuṣkariṇī), from which fragrant scents flow; furthermore, there are groves, mountains, and ponds, as well as extraordinary peaks. Endowed with countless celestial merits, the forests and ponds are most lovely.

The newly born deva-son sports and enjoys pleasures with a thousandfold merit. These include the pond with mani-railings; next, the pond called Music of Various Birds; next, the pond called Joy of the Gods; next, the pond called Constant Play; next, the pond called Enjoyment of Pleasure; next, the pond called Unturbid; next, the pond called Truly Existing; and next, the pond called Seeing What Is to Come. All around these ponds dwell various celestial birds that emit exquisite sounds, their colors and forms perfect, filling the waters. Trees that grant every wish stand along the banks of the ponds, fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
By virtue of their wholesome karma, they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses together with immeasurable celestial maidens.

The forms of these devas appear in accordance with their thoughts and follow their inclinations; they gaze upon them with delight without ever turning away, observing them in succession as they experience the pleasures of the five senses.
Because they maintained the precepts and accumulated wholesome karma, they obtained such a retribution.
They sported, danced, and sang within the flower ponds, experiencing the pleasures of the five desires.
These five desires are like a forest of thorns of craving; furthermore, they were surrounded by celestial maidens in ponds interspersed with mani-jewel ornaments.

They further proceed to other lotus ponds and playfully enjoy themselves upon adorned mountains; with celestial garlands and celestial garments, they experience the pleasures of the five sensory objects, which are lovely to behold with the eyes.
Ascending this mountain, they desire to experience pleasure; the peak they ascend is called Mountain Valley (*Girigahvara*), which is exceedingly delightful.

Upon that mountain there are other devas, adorned with celestial garlands and celestial garments, who descend from the Golden Mountain (*Suvarṇaparvata*) surrounded by hosts of devas, coming down in play, followed by hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands.
When the newly born deva-son saw the assembly of devas, he asked the celestial maidens,
"Do these devas enjoy themselves and experience pleasure together with the celestial maidens, and shall I likewise enjoy myself and experience pleasure?"
The celestial maidens said,
"We wish to follow his will. At that time,

the newly born son of heaven, knowing the hearts of the celestial maidens, sported together with them, surrounded by them in joy beyond compare, with the sounds of the five musical instruments serving as their song of praise.
The two assemblies gathered together, sporting and enjoying themselves without knowing satiety.
On the mountain there was a bird named Śikhin, the Peacock King; for the sake of the host of devas, he spoke in verse:
"The world is adorned by karma, And the devas are likewise adorned by karma."
Because the celestial realms are impermanent, when karma is exhausted, they are destroyed once more.
The world delights in union and finds no joy in separation;
yet where there is union, there must be separation—such is the nature of the world.
The mind delights in various pleasures, deceived by sensory objects;
the lives of the gods end swiftly, like the arising and ceasing of thoughts.
Old age, sickness, and death bring destruction, and one is separated from all people.
This law of death is ever-present, yet the fool does not perceive it.
Old age comes in successive stages, and the time of death is about to arrive;
one is destroyed by the army of disease, yet the fool does not perceive it.
The six ways of losing the human body destroy the five faculties;
like a person who has lost the right path, they encounter obstacles everywhere.
If a person contemplates cause and effect, and constantly maintains this mindfulness without losing it, [they shall not fall].
This person sees the fruit of reality, and later will feel no regret.
If a person, regarding sense objects, sees them as they truly are and does not become attached,
this person will be able to swiftly attain liberation from the realm of craving.
If one is freed from the net of craving, one crosses the treacherous wilderness and can keep far away from the fire of heedlessness; such a person possesses great wisdom.
The five kinds of great terrors destroy all the world.
"Because of their own karma, they suffer old age, death, and separation.

Thus, the Bodhisattva Peacock King, adorned with various ornaments such as mountain-peak feathers, by the power of his vows, assumed the body of a peacock to benefit others and to benefit the peacocks themselves; he preached the Dharma to the devas and severed their heedlessness.

At that time, the host of devas, seeing the newly born son of heaven, felt joy in their hearts; yet, due to negligence, they did not with faith accept the words of the sublime Dharma, but instead sang, danced, and enjoyed themselves in play amidst the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments.

Upon the mountain peaks and in the groves, there are immeasurable kinds of incomparable grottoes of golden light and wish-fulfilling forests that adorn this mountain; it is further adorned by immeasurable flocks of birds, hundreds of thousands of rivers and mountains, and flowering woodlands.
Together with the celestial maidens, possessing all desires and fully endowed with celestial delights, they engage in immeasurable play.
Following this sequence of the celestial host’s amusements, they ascend the mountain variegated with interspersed mani-jewels.
Upon this mountain, there is a grove of wish-fulfilling trees made of the seven precious jewels that adorns the mountain, measuring five yojanas in length and breadth.
Within that grove dwells the King of Peacocks named Citravicitra, who resides in this forest and preaches the Dharma to the devas.

In order to cause the deva kings, the goddesses, and others to abandon negligence and to delight in the preaching of the Dharma, the Peacock King goes to where they roam—within groves and lotus forests, amidst various mixed forests, rivers, springs, and flowing waters, upon mountain peaks, in places adorned with jewels, in places filled with the exquisite songs of hundreds of thousands of birds, in places adorned by all the hosts of devas, and in places adorned by the hosts of goddesses—where many deva kings and goddesses gather in harmony to experience pleasure. It is to these places that the Peacock King goes.

Due to their wholesome karma, they experience various kinds of pleasure and engage in all manner of play; such play has infinite variations that are beyond analogy, and they obtain them all according to their thoughts.

At that time, amidst the mountain peaks inlaid with mani jewels, King Peacock saw the hosts of devas indulging in the pleasures of negligence. In order to cause those devas to abandon such negligence, he spoke in verse:
"In the present or the future, there is no satiety regarding the realm of forms.
Burned by the fire of recollection, they repeatedly seek after sensory objects."
Though one may attain birth in the heavens, once born there, one returns to extinction;
bound by the net of karma, one falls again into hell,
emerging to undergo existence as a ghost or an animal, experiencing immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Sentient beings traverse the five realms of existence due to the causes and conditions of their karma.
The various karmas of sentient beings are exceedingly numerous and immeasurable;
therefore, they obtain various fruits.
When karma is exhausted, one falls back; where there is birth, there is death.
Those who perceive the Truth are able to see the falling away and extinction of the devas.
When this time of death approaches, one's life is then destroyed.
All that can cause affliction and turmoil, the fool does not perceive.
Though disciplined by various means and taught the benefits in diverse ways,
the hosts of devas remain deluded by their pleasures and do not give rise to weary detachment.
Speech that is virtuous and consistent with the Dharma brings peace and happiness in both worlds;
the fool who does not accept it will later feel great regret.
One should discipline oneself through many teachings, and one’s speech should be clear regarding the true meaning.
Yet the devas are addicted to negligence and do not know true benefit.
The enemy of death assails their lives; though they possess great power, none can save them.
With great force it rushes swiftly toward them, for the time of death is about to arrive.
Neither gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, nor piśācas can oppose it; therefore, the power of death is great.
One who knows what is powerful and what is powerless truly understands karma.
Unstained by evil karma, one does not travel upon the evil paths.
Constantly practicing all manner of virtues and remaining far from unwholesome realms,
such a person who acts in this way shall have no manifold sufferings or afflictions.
Acting in accordance with the Dharma, increasing faith and diligence,
and corresponding with the power of samādhi, they benefit others like a mother her child.
These wholesome dharmas can protect all beings throughout the five realms of existence.
Neither by the power of a father nor by the power of a mother can one travel to that place;
it is by faith and compliance with the True Dharma that one can be rescued from the suffering of the evil realms.
Wherever one may go, faith always possesses great power.
As a lamp can dispel darkness, as a sick person obtains excellent medicine,
as a blind person gains sight, as a poor person acquires wealth,
and as water rescues one drowning— faith is the great boat and raft.
If a person acts with negligence, faith is able to eliminate it.
Because one attains faith at the time of death, one can cross the ocean of existence and reach the state of quiescence; so the Munis of ancient times have taught.
Because one has attained the power of faith, it is called the practice of right knowledge;
faith and heedfulness, diligence and knowing contentment,
the accumulation of wisdom and proximity to virtuous friends— these six are the causes of liberation.

Generosity, precepts, and the excellence of tranquility; A compassionate mind benefiting sentient beings, as well as practicing kindness, joy, and equanimity— these dharmas provide the causes and conditions [for liberation].
Those who are flighty and fickle, who associate with evil friends, who are coarse and violent, and who delight in false speech,
Holding wrong views and acting with negligence— these dharmas are the causes for rebirth in hell.
Stinginess, envy, harsh speech, negligent conduct that abandons the good,
and a mind constantly craving the property of others— the Sages declare these to be the causes for rebirth as a hungry ghost.
Being close to delusion and far from wisdom, Lusting after desire and distant from the True Dharma,
Greed for food and delighting in sleep— The Buddha says these are the causes for rebirth as an animal.
If a person, through body, speech, and mind, Commits these three kinds of unwholesome acts, [they will fall into the animal realm].
Such ignorant people will thus fall into hell.
If one creates such causes, the resulting fruits will not fail to manifest;
just as sowing grain yields grain, so it is with wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Beholding this great multitude, who create the causes for the suffering of birth and death—
such ignorant hosts of devas yet remain unaware.
Though heedlessness may seem pleasant at first, it results in great anguish in the end.
If a phenomenon is suffering at a later time, the wise should abandon it.
Until one is liberated, there is never even the slightest happiness;
once liberation is attained, eternal bliss is accomplished.
The pleasure of heedlessness is impermanent; it is not spoken of by the wise.
If one attains eternal bliss, the wise declare that to be true happiness.
Thus, through a continuous succession of higher and higher states, all karmic actions are likewise.
Its fruit is likewise so, arising in ever-increasing succession without interruption.
Having understood the nature of karma and its results, one should abandon heedlessness;
one should give rise to a mind of wisdom—for this bliss is unsurpassed.

"In this way, the Bodhisattva Peacock King used various skillful means to preach the Dharma for the devas, severing their negligence with various fearless and exquisite voices that completely eclipsed the songs and chants of all the devas."
Due to their virtuous karma, their voices pervade twenty thousand yojanas; those who hear them experience joy and delight, which accords with the bliss of the Dharma.
At that time, for the sake of seeking pleasure, the hosts of devas whirl through the air; like the Cāturmahārājika and Kāyikadeva devas, they come and go, and these hosts of devas do likewise.

"At that time, having heard this sound, seventy thousand devas from the Tuṣita Heaven descended from above. Because they revered the True Dharma and their negligence was slight, they proceeded toward the place where the Peacock King, adorned with various ornaments, resided in the Yāma Heaven."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King of Various Adornments, perceiving that the Tuṣita Heaven was filled with joy in their hearts, addressed the devaputras:
"Welcome, true devas!"
Because you have been little negligent, you are able to come here to seek the fruits of the future.
If you wish to hear the various essential points of the Dharma, you should descend quickly; I shall explain for you the teaching of tranquility as I have heard it.
"I have already cultivated and accumulated [the path] that leads to Nirvana.
Regarding the Dharma I heard in the past, it was something none of my former teachers had ever heard.
It was at the place of Kāśyapa Buddha that I was able to hear this Dharma."
"In whatever place I am born, by the power of my vows, I shall never forget [this Dharma] and shall preach it for others.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by King Śuka, the gods of Tuṣita descended from the sky, out of reverence for the True Dharma.

Upon the mountain peaks, where great assemblies gather, there are immeasurable lotus ponds, immeasurable flowing springs, and immeasurable precious natures; immeasurable flocks of birds emit exquisite sounds.
Surrounded by mountain peaks interspersed with mani jewels, they stood on all four sides encircling the Peacock King.
Their majestic power was preeminent, their physical forms were perfect, and their radiance surpassed that of the Yāma Heaven.
Just as the Yāma devas compare to the people of Jambudvīpa, so too do the Tuṣita devas surpass the Yāma devas.

At that time, the Yāma devas, seeing that the Tuṣita devas had destroyed their pride in physical beauty and their attachment to sovereign pleasures, went to the place where the Bodhisattva Peacock King resided.
Delighting in play, they entered the forest; because they had never before seen the Tuṣita Heaven, they stood gazing up at it, or climbed to the mountain peaks desiring to seek out their pastimes.
Furthermore, various devas surrounded the Peacock King, standing on all four sides.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King addressed the assembly of devas:
"There are twenty-two dharmas which I shall now expound."
That which I revere and practice brings benefit to devas and humans, is the foremost peace and happiness, and causes all sentient beings to attain right conduct.
These twenty-two dharmas bring benefit, peace, and happiness, and are the dharma beloved by devas and humans.
Presently and in the future, gods and humans who love the Dharma can sever negligence and extinguish it so that it does not arise again.
If all gods and humans can remain free from negligence, they will constantly attain peace and happiness, even unto Nirvana.
The benefits of this Dharma cannot be matched by the benefits conferred by one's parents.
What are these twenty-two?
The first is a sense of remorse.
Second is fear of the evil realms;
third is patience;
fourth is diligence.
Fifth, preaching the Dharma;
sixth, a compassionate mind;
seventh, a gentle mind.
Eighth, subduing;
ninth, faith in karma;
tenth, not dwelling in places of ruin.
Eleventh, abiding in the mind;
twelfth, fearing ill repute;
thirteenth, not delighting in attachment.
Fourteenth, walking alone;
fifteenth, the mind being undistracted;
sixteenth, mindfulness of death.
Seventeenth, being free from the arrogance of physical beauty, wealth, possessions, and noble lineage;
eighteenth, speaking with gentle words;
nineteenth, giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Twentieth is contentment;
twenty-first is fear of sense objects;
twenty-second is abandoning lack of faith.
If gods or humans practice these twenty-two dharmas according to reality, they will not fall into the evil realms and will swiftly attain nirvana.
"What is called remorse?
How does one attain peace after having felt regret?
Having given rise to regret, one abandons unwholesome dharmas.
How does one give rise to regret?

If one sees another person performing unwholesome actions of body, speech, or mind, and that person performs a physical action which one censures and reviles, one should give rise to a sense of remorse and not dwell together with them.

If, due to certain causes and conditions, unwholesome thoughts and reflections arise spontaneously, one should abandon them immediately upon their arising, not give rise to recollection of them, neither savoring nor clinging to them. One should feel shame within the heart toward others, diligently cultivate vigor so that they do not arise again, refuse to accept such thoughts and reflections, and the mind should revile and loathe these unwholesome thoughts and reflections.

It is like a great pit filled with excrement, filth, dead dogs, and impurities; suppose a pure person enters it seeking purity, but once inside the pit, they are submerged up to the throat by the filth, at which time that person gives rise to a sense of revulsion.
If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts and reflections, the resulting remorse in the mind is likewise.
It is like another person who constantly seeks pure conduct, yet out of ignorance, mistakenly consumes filth and excrement.
Suppose there were a powerful enemy who forced one to eat excrement; having eaten it, one would feel loathing and contempt, giving rise to regret and remorse, and thereafter would never eat it again.
It is the same for a person practicing wholesome karma who feels shame and reproaches themselves for unwholesome thoughts and reflections.
Diligently cultivating vigor to eliminate applied and sustained thought—this is called the first dharma.
Not giving rise to negligence, abandoning negligence, and destroying negligence—for this reason, devas and humans should practice and learn it.

If there is a virtuous person who seeks the true reality and fears birth and death, should even a slight unwholesome thought or reflection arise, they should give rise to a mind of remorse, not a mind of aspiration, and not a mind of negligence.
A person who is heedful can give rise to a mind of remorse, whereas a heedless person cannot.
This single quality is the root of all wholesome karmas.
That which is called abandoning unwholesome thoughts and reflections and giving rise to a sense of remorse is named the first dharma.

Furthermore, the second wholesome dharma that increases wholesome dharmas is what is called the great method of emergence: it is the fear of the evil realms, which extinguishes negligence and is able to sever negligence.
All humans and devas fear the course of the evil realms.

Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others, if they fear the evil realms, they do not commit unwholesome deeds; even if they see others committing them, they do not rejoice in it. Knowing that unwholesome karma leads to rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, they therefore refrain from performing evil and unwholesome actions.
Due to the causes of evil karma, one falls into the evil realms.
Why is this? Because by habitually engaging with and taking pleasure in even minor evil karma, one causes that evil to increase, leading to rebirth in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.

Therefore, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others who fear the evil realms should train themselves in this way: they should always be fearful, for the retribution of unwholesome actions is extremely grave, leading to rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.

If those who are heedless in their conduct and of little wisdom can thus fear the evil realms, they will not be negligent and will not commit the three kinds of unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind. Such persons constantly cultivate wholesome deeds and abandon unwholesome ones; this is called fearing the evil realms.
For example, suppose there is a person who knows their own strength and that of others, and who fears venomous snakes, as well as knives and fire, because they can take one's life;
likewise, those who fear the evil realms also dread evil karma in this same way.
Such a person abandons and refrains from even subtle actions, and does not practice heedlessness.
Because they have abandoned heedlessness, they are born among gods and humans, experiencing great wealth and happiness.
Having experienced wealth and pleasure, one subsequently enters nirvana.
Because it is a supreme bliss, it is without death or change, without decline or exhaustion; therefore, one should always fear the evil realms.
"If there be any śramaṇas, brahmins, or other practitioners who can practice in this way, they shall attain the unsurpassed state.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person fears the evil realms, They should abandon the defilement of heedlessness."
Cultivating goodness and seeking merit, one reaches the city of Nirvana.
If a person fears the evil realms, their mind will be upright;
because of that upright mind, they shall attain a place of happiness from happiness.
If one does not fear the evil realms, one will create much evil karma;
scorched by the fires of evil, one is about to enter hell.
Just as even a tiny spark, though small, can still burn.
The evil realms are likewise; even after passing through kalpas, one still receives retribution.
If a person desires happiness, they should fear the evil realms.
By fearing and seeking deliverance from the evil realms, one can attain peace and joy.

"In this Dharma, whether they be devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons, if they fear the evil realms, they shall immediately repent for even a small unwholesome act; their minds shall not rejoice in it nor dwell upon it, as they keep in mind the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, fearing the fruits of suffering."

Having reflected thus, he fears the three unwholesome paths; he abandons the ten unwholesome actions, ceasing from them and refraining from committing them. He does not instruct others to commit them, nor does he rejoice in their doing so. He does not associate with such persons of evil karma, but cultivates wholesome deeds, relinquishes all evil, and practices that which is pure and stainless. Abandoning negligence, he brings all evil to rest and attains liberation from the cycle of existence within the unwholesome dharmas.
Having attained liberation from all phenomena, one who is freed from all faults can abide in peace and cross over to the further shore of existence.
Therefore, one should always fear the evil realms and train accordingly; if any among gods or humans cherish this Dharma, they shall be able to reach Nirvana.
"Furthermore, that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, taught that freedom from negligence leads to Nirvana, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all devas and humans.
I heard this in a previous life among human beings; remembering it without forgetting, I shall now speak of it for the sake of the assembly of devas."
What is called the third dharma of patience?
Such patience is the foremost wholesome dharma, the foremost purity, and is praised by the Buddha.
There are two kinds of patience:
The first is the patience toward phenomena (dharmakṣānti);
the second is the patience toward sentient beings (sattvakṣānti). What is the patience toward phenomena?

Practicing the path of the conditioned dharmas, one contemplates the pure dharmas—namely, the dharma of firm endurance. Because one is able to endure due to contemplating the excellence of the wholesome path, it is called "endurance" (kṣānti).

For example, just as the great earth endures all the various kinds of mountains, rivers, gardens, and groves in the world without weariness, so too is the patience toward all phenomena (dharmakṣānti).

One who is able to reach nirvāṇa possesses the most supreme and firm patience toward all phenomena (*sarvadharma-kṣānti*), which comprises pure and wholesome dharmas and is subsumed within the path to nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is called "patience regarding dharmas" (*dharma-kṣānti*). Because such a person is firm in worldly patience, they are able to attain nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, there is the second patience.
This refers to when a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or anyone else intends to give rise to anger, one endures it so that it does not arise, because one knows the faults of anger and reflects thus:

'If anger arises, it burns one's own body; the mind becomes stifled by poison and the complexion changes; one is abandoned by others and everyone avoids one in alarm; one is not loved by people and is despised, reviled, and treated with contempt; and upon the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into hell.'"
"Because of hatred, there is no evil one will not do; therefore, the wise abandon hatred as they would fire.
Knowing the faults of hatred, one can benefit oneself; desiring to benefit both oneself and others, one should practice patience.
For example, when a great fire burns down a house, a courageous person extinguishes it with water; likewise, a person of wisdom endures and extinguishes anger in the same way.

One who is capable of patience possesses the foremost virtuous mind; they are able to relinquish anger and are beloved by all people. They are a joy for others to behold, trusted and accepted by all. Their countenance is pure, their mind is tranquil and free from agitation. With a well-purified and profound mind, they are free from faults of body and speech, free from the feverish afflictions of the heart, free from the fear of the evil realms, free from enmity and hatred, free from ill repute, free from sorrow and distress, free from the fear of enemies, free from the insults and abuse of wicked people, free from the fear of regret, free from the fear of ill fame, free from the fear of lack of gain, free from the fear of suffering, and free from the fear of pride.

If a person can free themselves from such fears, they will be fully endowed with all merits, their fame will spread everywhere, they will attain happiness in both the present and future lives, and all people will regard them as their own parents.
Those who possess this patience are approached and relied upon by all people.
Therefore, anger is like a venomous snake, like a sword, or like fire; one must extinguish it through patience, for patience can cause it to be entirely eliminated.
To be able to endure anger is what is called patience.
If there is a virtuous person who wishes to practice goodness, they should form this thought:
"Patience is like a treasure; one should protect it well."
One who possesses such patience is able to destroy anger.
The light of the patience of the True Dharma is like a torch, capable of extinguishing the darkness of anger.
It is as if one who is blind were to regain their sight.
The wealth of those who uphold the True Dharma removes the poverty of wrong views, just as parents benefit their children.
For those submerged by anger, patience serves as a great ship.
For those who have fallen into the evil realms, patience is the means of rescue and deliverance.
Patience is like a great flood that extinguishes the fires of hell; the power of patience can sever the afflictions of stinginess, envy, hunger, and thirst that plague the hungry ghosts.
If one falls among animals and they harm one another, the power of patience can even sacrifice one's own life.
One should delight in practicing patience and constantly cultivate it without abandoning it; if one fears the evil realms, one should apply diligent effort and contemplate the power of patience.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
“If a person is adorned with patience, they possess the most excellent of all adornments.
While material wealth may be plundered, patience can never be lost.”
If a person practices patience, they will be beloved by all beings;
in the future, they will attain peace and security—for patience is the foremost precept.
If a person practices patience, they abandon all anger.
In the present and the future, one shall always attain a state of peace and security.
Patience, ethical discipline, and wisdom—these three kinds of wealth are the most supreme; no precious jewels can serve as their analogue.
If a person practices patience, they should be honored by all;
they are praised by the virtuous, and for this reason one should practice patience.
Patience is the foremost medicine, capable of removing the poison of anger.
Patience can extinguish anger and ensure it does not arise again.
For those obscured by darkness and shrouded in folly, patience is the supreme light;
like a lamp that dispels the dark, patience reveals the true path.
If one is deprived of the wealth of the True Dharma, one wanders through the five realms of existence;
yet if one possesses the wealth of patience, one is the most noble and wealthy in the world.
Anger is a vast wilderness, a profound darkness most difficult to cross.
When the provisions of patience are complete, one can pass beyond all obstacles without hindrance.
If one is lost on the path of the True Dharma, patience can serve as the correct guide;
for those who fear the evil realms, the power of patience provides protection.
Constantly bringing joy to sentient beings, Able to extinguish all suffering and affliction;
Always attaining peaceful and secure happiness, Permanently departing from all fears;
Loved by virtuous people, Able to give rise to the merit of faith.
Harmoniously gathering all that is virtuous and auspicious, Abandoning unwholesome dharmas,
he shows people true liberation; He can extinguish the fear of birth and death,
A stairway for ascending to heaven, And extinguishes the fires of hell.
For those in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, patience is their protection;
Patience can fulfill all merits and bring sentient beings to tranquility.
If you wish to attain auspicious joy, you should practice patience.

“‘Such patience as this is called the foremost dharma; by practicing it, one shall always attain peace and happiness in the present and the future, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one will be reborn in the heavens and later attain nirvana.’”
Therefore, one should practice patience so as to be born among gods or humans through heedfulness.
"Furthermore, the fourth wholesome karma is that which can bring about freedom from heedlessness."
What kind of wholesome deeds do śramaṇas, brahmins, and other virtuous people perform?
They are those called the diligent and earnest pursuit of wholesome dharmas.

Being in accord with what is wholesome, they apply themselves to the path of the Dharma; they are in accord with the proper time, remaining tranquil in time and place. They cultivate the worldly and world-transcending dharmas in accordance with tranquility, and not in discordance with it.

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding worldly and world-transcending dharmas, know the proper time for rest during the first and last watches of the night, and know the proper time, the proper place, and the proper means, then they shall dwell in peace while practicing diligence, and will be able to destroy all laziness.

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, in order to destroy the afflictions, diligently cultivate vigor, and having generated such vigor, do not give rise to a mind of attachment toward the objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
If one obtains the necessary conditions, one should hold the mind so that it remains stable; with a correct mind and diligent effort, these two factors act as companions.
One should collect the mind to cause it to depart from all objective spheres.
If unwholesome forces arise, one should obstruct them with diligence and eliminate them through right mindfulness.
Among all dharmas, diligence is foremost.
Because these two dharmas serve as companions, they cause all wholesome dharmas to be firm and indestructible, thereby attaining their fruition.
By the power of the merit of right-minded diligence, one will ultimately attain nirvāṇa.
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons recognize this merit, they should apply themselves with diligent effort.
In the world, diligence is supreme.
If worldly undertakings are practiced with industry, they become firm;
through diligent practice, one obtains their fruit and reward.
Abiding long in the world, he cannot be destroyed.
If a person is diligent, at the time of death, their mind will be pure and not timid; the mind will be undistracted, without fear or terror.

Although they encounter decline and affliction, they do not cease or rest; by constantly and diligently practicing, all virtues increase, such that enemies cannot destroy them, and no one is able to speak of their faults or evils.
Whatever actions one performs, they are fully accomplished.
Such worldly diligence in wholesome karma is praised by the wise; how much more so, then, would the diligence of supramundane right knowledge not be supreme and wondrous?
Therefore, regarding all phenomena, at all times, and with all-knowledge, one should apply diligence that is integrated with wisdom, knowing the proper time and place, and practice with right view.
Because one arouses diligence, one attains all forms of happiness.
If one acts with perversion, one will instead encounter lack of benefit, decline, affliction, and distress.
If one lacks wisdom, then even though one exerts oneself with hardship, it cannot be called diligence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
"Because of the correspondence of time and place, The performance of karma increases;
If one exerts diligent effort according to the Dharma, Then one will obtain a wholesome retribution."
Though one may perform actions within the sphere of phenomena, if one abandons the true Dharma,
those actions will not reach fulfillment because of a lack of diligence.
By practicing with diligence in accordance with the Dharma, one attains nirvana through wisdom.
Like a spear cast into the air, one is immediately reborn in the heavens.
If a person applies themselves diligently to their work and practices with vigor,
all that they do will be harmonious, and they shall attain vast accomplishment.
Whether it be worldly aims or supramundane aims,
all are accomplished through the power of diligence;
yet if one is devoid of the power of diligence and separated from the True Dharma, [nothing can be achieved].
That person possesses no wealth or joy, like one who seeks a stain within the moon.
By guarding mindfulness of the Noble Eightfold Path,
the person of great power through diligence can reach the supreme state.
Through diligence one attains enlightenment; through diligence one is born in the heavens.
Among all the fruits of the various paths, there is none that is not attained through diligence.
Knowing these merits, one should exert diligence to discipline the faculties.
"By rousing the mind to diligent effort, there is nothing equal to such diligence.
Thus did the Bodhisattva Peacock King preach the Dharma of the Jātaka he had upheld for the assembly of Tuṣita devas and the assembly of Yāma devas.
At that time, the assembly of devas all listened with rapt attention; free from negligence and with their faculties subdued, they listened with single-minded focus.

Then, King Peacock, knowing that the hearts of the devas were filled with great joy and that they had aroused diligent vigor, preached the Dharma for them with a pure mind, leading them to gather in peace, tranquility, and *nirvāṇa*, benefiting and bringing happiness to all the devas.
All Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the Dharma.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 60; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 61.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Forty: Observing the Heavens; Section Twenty-Six: Yāma Heaven.
"Furthermore, fifthly, hearing the Dharma brings benefit and peace to all humans and devas. What, then, is this Dharma? It is as follows:"
What is called "preaching the Dharma" refers to preaching all dharmas of giving and preaching all wholesome dharmas.
Among all that is honorable, hearing the Dharma is supreme, for it can sever the very root of all arrogance.
What is called the teaching of the Dharma can subdue arrogance.

It is the teaching of the Dharma, hearing the Dharma, honoring and revering the Dharma, speaking of faith in the Dharma, speaking of upholding the Dharma, and speaking of how practitioners do not depart from the teaching of the Dharma.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take the Dharma as their teacher, let alone the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
There are ten merits in preaching the Dharma, which bring great benefit. What are these ten?

Complete in terms of time and place, easy to distinguish and understand, and in accord with the Dharma, it is not for the sake of gain or sustenance, but for the purpose of taming the mind. He preaches the Dharma in accordance [with the listeners' needs]: he speaks of the retribution of giving; he speaks of how the phenomena of birth and death involve many obstacles; he speaks of the falling away and passing from the heavens; and he speaks of the existence of karmic results.
If a Dharma-preacher possesses these ten qualities, they cause those who hear the Dharma to gain great merit, benefit, peace, and happiness, even up to nirvāṇa.
Both the listener of the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher will each achieve the fulfillment of their respective aspirations.
Among all various kinds of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme; it can even enable all sentient beings to attain the bliss of nirvana.
"Furthermore, the merit of hearing the Dharma is as follows:
it brings about the fulfillment of the profound mind, purifies the faculty of faith, and leads to a single-mindedly pure heart that places its trust in the Triple Gem."
When one goes to a place for hearing the Dharma in order to listen to the True Dharma, with every single step taken, one generates the merit of Brahmā.
If a person makes offerings to a Dharma teacher who expounds the Dharma, it should be known that this person is making offerings to the World-Honored One in the present.
In this way, according to their offerings, those people’s aspirations will be fulfilled, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they were able to make offerings to the Dharma-preacher.
Why is this? Because by hearing the Dharma, the mind attains subduing;
because it is subdued, one is able to sever the darkness of ignorant transmigration.
If one is apart from hearing the Dharma, there is not a single dharma capable of taming the mind.
As for hearing the teaching of the Dharma, there are four kinds of kindness that are extremely difficult to repay. What are these four?
First, one's mother;
second, one's father;
third, the Tathāgata.
Fourth are the Dharma-preachers who expound the teachings.
If one makes offerings to these four kinds of persons, they will obtain immeasurable merit; they will be praised by others in the present life, and in future lives, they will be able to attain Bodhi.

Why is this?
