It is because by the power of preaching the Dharma, it causes those who are arrogant to become subdued; it causes those who are greedily attached to believe in giving; it causes those who are coarse and wild to have their minds become gentle and supple; and it causes those who are ignorant to attain wisdom.
By the power of hearing the Dharma, those who are deluded regarding cause and effect are led to attain right faith.
By the power of hearing the Dharma, those with false views are led to enter into right view.
By the power of hearing the Dharma, those who delight in the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are led to distance themselves from them.
Through these causes and conditions of taming by means of preaching the Dharma, one ultimately attains nirvana.
For this reason, it is extremely difficult to repay the kindness of a Dharma-preacher who expounds the teachings.
The debt of gratitude owed to one's parents is difficult to repay; because they have given birth to one’s body, the kindness of parents cannot be fully repaid.
If one causes one’s parents to abide in the Dharma, this is called a minor repayment of their kindness.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the most supreme in the three realms, the deliverer from birth and death, and the unsurpassed Great Teacher; his kindness is difficult to repay. There is only one dharma that can repay the Buddha’s kindness: if one possesses deep faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and attains indestructible confidence, this is called repaying their kindness.
"By making this offering, one also benefits oneself.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke these verses of the sutra:
"Through the causes and conditions of preaching the Dharma, One attains the peace of Nirvana."
Able to sever all bonds, the Great Teacher of sentient beings,
By teaching the Dharma of tranquility, he can cut through the net of ignorance.
Such a supreme guide is able to show the path to sentient beings.
If a teaching enables sentient beings to transcend the ocean of all existences, this teaching is most supreme; no worldly dharma can equal it.
If a person can make offerings to these four kinds of fields of merit, [they shall attain great reward].
This person attains a favorable fruit; thus has the Teacher spoken.
Having attained the possession of all faculties and likewise having heard the Buddha-dharma, if one should practice what is not the Dharma, regret will be of no avail.
Giving rise to attachment everywhere, constantly seeking sensual pleasures,
and always craving one's wife and children, one does not realize that death has arrived.
In every thought-moment there is much evil, and one is distracted by all manner of transgressions.
The mind binds sentient beings, leading them toward the three evil realms.
This evil is difficult to subdue; it constantly seeks opportunities against gods and humans.
This mind cannot be trusted; it is the great enemy of sentient beings.
"Through hearing the good and seeing the good, Cultivating them in immeasurable ways,
One tames the mind with the Dharma, Like a horse that has received the bit and bridle.
Thus, this foremost and most profound field of merit, endowed with virtuous qualities, should be honored with offerings.

Benefiting the hosts of devas, he taught such Dharma and explained the paths of karma; honoring and praising the teachers of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Peacock King, through the power of his vows, was born among those devas to benefit them.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the assembly of devas attained purity of mind and all listened with single-minded attention to what was being said, exclaiming:
"What this Peacock King has spoken is consistent and not inconsistent; it is consistent with what the Tranquil Heavenly King of Tuṣita has spoken, without difference or distinction."

Reflecting upon this Dharma, which is good in the beginning, middle, and end, supremely pure, the foremost wholesome teaching, and the ultimate peace, it benefits and brings happiness to all devas and humans, leading them to attain nirvāṇa.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Tuṣita Heaven, King Peacock’s mind was pure and filled with joy; with all-pervading compassion and patience, he brought benefit to all the celestial hosts, even unto nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, it is said that the sixth profound and supreme Dharma-gate leads to Nirvana; such a teaching is foremost in peace and security, and foremost in excellence, beloved by all people—namely, compassion."

Loved by all people, he inspires faith in others; he comforts sentient beings who fear birth and death, brings peace to those whose minds are unsettled, and acts as a protector for those who have no refuge.
If one possesses a heart of compassion, that person is not far from nirvana.
A compassionate heart is supple; it is free from deceit and free from harshness, for it is able to sever the mind of anger due to its moistening nature.
Furthermore, compassion is called the "Great Adornment.
If one gives rise to compassion toward sentient beings in the five realms of existence, it can destroy anger and affliction.
How does one give rise to compassion toward sentient beings in the hells?
How are these sentient beings deceived by their own karma?
Created by the enemy that is the mind, they undergo various great sufferings beyond comparison.

There are iron hooks and iron pestles, glowing molten copper, and devouring by malevolent insects; there are impassable torrential rivers that sweep away sentient beings, and being pecked at by vultures, eagles, crows, and magpies; they enter the forest of sword-trees and the river of ashes, undergoing various sufferings that cannot be fully described.

These are the so-called Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, the Heating Hell, the Great Heating Hell, and so on, up to the Avīci Hell and its adjacent great hells—these one hundred and thirty-six locations.

Sentient beings fall into this place, where they are split, torn asunder, severed, and scorched. Deceived by their own minds, bound by the net of karma, and burned by the fire of craving, they have no rescue and no refuge. They run hither and thither, seeking pity for themselves and striving for protection, crying out:
"When shall I cross over this great sea of suffering and affliction?"
One gives rise to compassion toward these sentient beings.
If one plants the seed of such compassion, one will become a celestial king or a wheel-turning sage king, beloved and esteemed by all sentient beings.
A person of compassionate heart delights in wholesome deeds.

This is called contemplating the sentient beings in the hells who undergo great suffering and distress and thereby giving rise to compassion; thus, one attains an increase of immeasurable Brahma-merit.
"Furthermore, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons seek to benefit sentient beings, they should give rise to a heart of compassion when contemplating the various hungry ghosts."
How do sentient beings fall among the hungry ghosts?

Various forms of hunger and thirst burn their bodies as if burning a forest; they run about in all directions, colliding with one another, while blazing flames consume them until their entire bodies are ablaze. With no rescue and no refuge, they run everywhere in search of protection, yet there is none who can save them.
"When will these sentient beings ever be free from their various sufferings and afflictions?
When will they ever sever the suffering of hunger, thirst, and exhaustion?
This is called contemplating the suffering of hungry ghosts and giving rise to compassion.
"Furthermore, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons contemplate the animal realm and give rise to a heart of compassion,
they see that within the animal realm there are immeasurable sufferings and afflictions, as beings slaughter one another."

There are three abodes for animals: namely, those that move through the air, those that move through water, and those that move on land. The modes of their death are immeasurable; they harm one another and devour one another. When shall these sentient beings ever be liberated from this?
This is called contemplating the suffering of animals and giving rise to a heart of compassion.
If one can give rise to such a thought, one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, because of recollecting all sentient beings with a compassionate mind.

"Having aroused compassion for sentient beings who dwell in the great suffering of the three evil realms—the ground of the fruits of most grievous karma—he further arouses compassion for the various devas of the six heavens of desire."

In the six heavens of the desire realm, they experience celestial pleasures beyond compare; amidst various valleys, mountain peaks, and groves, they enjoy happiness, sporting with celestial maidens in lotus forests and ponds, experiencing hundreds of thousands of kinds of delight.

Once they have experienced pleasure, when their karma is exhausted, they fall back and are born in places of suffering, undergoing great anguish, and falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
In this realm of birth and death, sentient beings are toyed with; bound by the shackles of craving, they run hither and thither, deluded and ignorant, undergoing great suffering and distress.
This is called contemplating the suffering of the devas and giving rise to a mind of compassion.

"Furthermore, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others contemplate those among human beings and give rise to a mind of compassion, [they see that] through various karmas, one is born among humans and experiences the fruits of suffering and pleasure."

Sentient beings of superior, middling, and inferior capacities perform various kinds of actions, possess various kinds of mental natures, and have various kinds of inclinations and understandings. Some are impoverished and dependent upon others; they harbor resentment, create obstacles, and fear being despised by others, thus seeking out various occupations to sustain their own lives.
Observing the human world in this way, one gives rise to compassion; such compassion is the foremost pure dharma (*śukladharma*) and can lead to nirvāṇa.

"Having thus observed the five kinds of suffering of sentient beings in the five realms of existence and giving rise to compassion, such a person attains supreme peace and security, and thereby attains nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke these verses on the Tathāgata Kakutstha:
"If a person’s mind is supple, And they are adorned with a heart of compassion,
They will be protected by all, And praised by the multitude."
With such a supple mind, whose faculties are ever joyful,
this person of right view is not far from Nirvana.
If adorned with a compassionate heart, one becomes a god among men.
If a person lacks a heart of compassion, they will always be poor.
If a person has a supple mind, it is as refined as true gold;
if compassion dwells within the heart, this treasure is inexhaustible.
If a person is always diligent and constantly practices the true Dharma,
the light of that person’s mind and wisdom is like a great, bright lamp.
If a person, throughout day and night, keeps the mind ever-abiding in the Dharma,
This person’s compassionate heart is never absent, day or night.
Their mind is pure, benefiting all sentient beings;
having attained peace and happiness, they shall later achieve nirvana.
Giving with a pure heart of compassion is praised by the Muni;
it can sever all faults, and the wealth of compassion is inexhaustible.
This supreme adornment of merit can sever all faults.
The Sage’s heart is moistened by compassion; therefore, he has reached the state of non-extinction.
Wherever the cause of compassion resides, it is like honey blended with milk;
neither hatred nor feverish affliction can dwell within his mind.
Having already ascended the raft of compassion, with a heart of pity and courageous strength, one is able to cross the ocean of existence and its great whirlpools of the three poisons.
These merits surpass all fortified cities; no adornment excels this.
"Because it is that which is loved by virtuous people, it is called the mind of compassion.

Thus did the Bodhisattva Peacock King preach the Dharma to the devas; it was good in the beginning, middle, and end, consistent with tranquility and cessation, and the entire assembly of devas joyfully gathered to hear and receive it.
"Furthermore, that Blessed One, the World-Honored One, taught the seventh dharma: namely, which dharma, when practiced in conjunction with it, leads to liberation and severs heedlessness."
By what kind of karma?
It is by means of a supple mind that severs the fault of restlessness and gathers all meritorious qualities.
If there is one who can possess a supple and profound mind, free from all defilements, then nirvana and liberation will be as if held in their own hand.
A person of soft mind is like white tin; practicing wholesome deeds, they are trusted by all.
A coarse and wild mind is like a diamond; constantly harboring grudges and failing to let go, such a person acts without self-discipline and is loathed and distrusted by all.

If they give rise to an evil mind and cling to it tenaciously without relinquishing it, their mind will find no peace or joy; they will take no pleasure in meditation or recitation, stay far from virtuous people, and fail to produce wholesome dharmas.

Just as seeds do not grow in saline soil, and just as sesame oil is not produced from sand, so too it is with a person of coarse and wild mind: they do not give rise to wholesome dharmas, being like milk from a horn, warmth within the moon, the son of a barren woman, or flowers in the sky.

Coarse, fierce, and evil karma; deceitful and lacking wisdom; deluding oneself and others; submerged in the five realms of existence; associating with unwholesome people; and abandoning the Triple Gem.

Those born blind who do not behold the sun of the True Dharma and clear wisdom are truly to be pitied; they dwell amidst the mass of sufferings—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction—and enter the great wilderness to undergo immeasurable suffering, far removed from the flavor of the gentle nectar of immortality.
Such evil persons are submerged in the ocean of suffering and remain far from nirvana.
Why is this? Because they do not practice the causal conduct of the path to nirvana.
For this reason, one never attains happiness.

If there is a person who can soften their mind, that person will certainly attain nirvana in every respect. It is, for example, like the nature of sesame yielding oil, the nature of the sun being luminous, the nature of moonlight being cool, fire being hot, earth being solid, wind being mobile, and water being moist; the individual characteristics of these four great elements do not deviate from one another.
One of gentle mind who tames their own mind, possessing faith and diligence with non-perverted views, and who trusts in cause and effect, will find nirvana as if it were present before them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke these verses from the Buddhist sūtras:
"If a person’s mind is supple, Like well-refined gold,
That person is virtuous within and without, And shall swiftly be liberated from all suffering."
If a person’s mental vessel is well-tuned, all things become supple;
such a person sows the seeds of goodness, like a fertile field of rice.
All sentient beings together could never exhaust this treasury.
It can destroy poverty as well as much deception.
Those of sharp faculties who are tranquil and constantly practice meditative concentration do not cling to the realm of heedlessness and are forever free from all suffering and affliction.

When the Bodhisattva Peacock King had spoken these verses in this manner, the hosts of the Yāma devas and the hosts of the Tuṣita devas listened with insatiable delight and, wishing to hear the Dharma once more, joined their palms in reverence and said:
“O Great Sage!
“We pray that you will fully explain the twenty-two dharmas for our sake.
Desiring to benefit others, we shall listen with a sincere mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King expounded the twenty-two most excellent dharma-gates to the assembly of devas; having already explained seven dharmas, he now proceeded to explain the eighth dharma in sequence.
"If there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons who give rise to the thought, 'What is this dharma?
it is the dharma of subduing, which serves as an adornment for all and is in accordance with all vinaya of subduing."

Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or others—whether lay or ordained, whether old or young—if they are disciplined and act in accordance with that discipline, they can be made upright and handsome by means of this adornment.
If one is devoid of self-discipline, one is like a jackal, a crow, a raven, an eagle, or a vulture.
How does a person who has left the household life practice self-discipline?
A person who has left the household life first disciplines themselves by means of the *kāṣāya* robe; they should practice seven matters.
What are the seven?
First, in accordance with the laws of one’s own country, one accepts rag-robes (pāṃsukūla)—those garments discarded by householders in whatever country one resides.
If there is a garment belonging to a deceased person in a cemetery that has been crushed by a corpse, one should not take it;
however, if one obtains a tattered garment in a cemetery, one should accept and use it.
This is called the method of discipline for the *kāṣāya*.
"Furthermore, there is a second method of discipline:

when entering a village, one should walk while observing the ground, looking ahead only a fathom’s distance; one should contemplate the image of the Buddha, maintain single-minded right mindfulness, keep the sense faculties undisturbed, count the inhalations and exhalations, and fix the mind upon mindfulness of the body."

When entering a village, he does not look at any necessary articles, nor at various utensils, nor at the ornate curtains and canopies of others; he does not engage in conversation with women, does not hold small children, does not frequently move his feet, nor move his arms or his seat; he does not rub his head with his hands, does not repeatedly adjust his robes, does not shake out his *kāṣāya*, and neither massages his hands nor snaps his fingers.
This is called the second method of subduing.
"Furthermore, the third method of subduing:
when entering the home of a donor, one should wash one's hands up to the wrists at the time of the meal."

When receiving food, one should not extend the hands too far, but keep them within the span of one cubit; one should neither eat with a mouthful so large as to fill the mouth nor with a mouthful so small as to be insufficient.

When eating, one should not treat the food frivolously or playfully—meaning one should not be insatiable, lose the pure faith of others, or cause others to feel contempt—and should instead observe the minds of others.
When taking morsels of food, they should be neither too large nor too small; one should not open the mouth too wide, nor make a sound while eating, nor exhale heavily.
Regarding the food provided, one should eat only two parts, knowing moderation and contentment, and should not look at the bowls of others and give rise to covetous thoughts.
Regarding the food and drink received, one does not disturb the minds of others; observing one's own bowl, one does not look left or right.

Having finished eating and set aside the bowl, one rinses and cleanses oneself, guarding and collecting the sense faculties, and preaches the Dharma with a correct mind. One’s mental reflections are discerning and precise—neither slow nor fast, neither crooked nor straight—and one does not speak at an improper time, nor too much or too little, protecting the donor's mind and not undermining their faith.
This is called the third method of subduing.
"Furthermore, the fourth subduing:

when at the time of eating, whether in a village or a city, one does not give rise to thoughts regarding food previously seen, nor does one speak of it frequently, nor does one crave the bedding and requisites one receives; one accepts and keeps them according to the Dharma, seeking nothing superior or more excellent."
This is called the fourth method of subduing. "Furthermore, the fifth subduing: in all that one does, one is neither dependent nor attached;

one does not begrudge body or life; one does not amass many provisions for use; one does not travel to remote regions of danger and fear; one does not wear distinctive or eccentric clothing; one does not delight in being invited; and one does not exclusively frequent a single household."
This is called the fifth method of subduing.
"Furthermore, the sixth subduing:
one does not cut grass or trees, nor dig the earth; one does not wear sandals of variegated colors or garments of variegated colors."
If others break the precepts, one does not slander or speak ill of them.
One’s mind does not covet the meals of kings, nor does one associate with bhikṣus who delight in strife.
This is called the sixth method of subduing.
"Furthermore, the seventh is subduing.

If there is a bhikṣu who shares the same intention and the same Dharma, one should associate with and benefit him, ensuring he maintains constant moderation; desiring to abandon the realm of Māra, attain tranquil subduing, and guard and collect the sense faculties—one should associate with such a bhikṣu."
Whether in a mountain cave, a mountain stream, beneath a tree, or in the open air, one should constantly practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is called the seventh method of subduing.
"If there is a bhikṣu who can practice in this way, he will be able to abandon all fetters and attain liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King addressed the assembly of devas in verse, saying:
"Corresponding with the Dharma of subduing, Cultivating the realm of wisdom,"
Fearing the perils of birth and death, one does not leave the household life in vain.
Without violating or neglecting the precepts, and without dwelling on former pleasures,
one should constantly contemplate the aggregates and abide in the forest retreats.
One who speaks with gentle words and dwells in tranquility, manifesting the path toward Nirvana,
whose body is adorned by the observance of precepts, and who is in harmony with the life of renunciation—
if such a person is able to remain undeluded regarding the teachings concerning both self and others, [they shall attain liberation].
Karmic retribution and what is not karmic retribution, as well as the path and what is not the path, are likewise so.
Having departed from the practice of evil karma, one neither fears suffering nor delights in pleasure;
having attained liberation from the household life, one cannot be bound by any suffering.

"Thus did the Peacock King speak upon the immeasurable merits of self-discipline, causing all the celestial hosts to attain faith and understanding; all the celestial hosts listened with single-minded attention."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King preached the Dharma for the hosts of the Yāma devas and the Tuṣita devas without ceasing; because he knew that the celestial hosts revered the Dharma, he further expounded the ninth stainless and pure teaching.
"What is meant by the 'stainless pure dharma'?
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others in the world have faith in karmic retribution, then because they have faith in karmic retribution, they shall attain the Great Dharma."

If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in the world believe in the retribution of karmic fruits, such persons will recognize bodily evil karma; they will not practice or increase such bodily evil karma, nor will they cherish or delight in it, because its resulting fruit lies within the evil realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.

In this way, one does not practice or increase verbal misconduct, nor does one cherish or delight in it, because one will consequently undergo the evil retributions of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
In this way, one does not practice or increase unwholesome mental karma, nor does one cherish or delight in it, because one will thereby undergo the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa has previously committed evil karma, but having reflected upon it, gives rise to remorse, ceases from further action, and draws near to teachers and elders to hear the Dharma from them, how can they be liberated from the retribution of that evil karma?

In this way, when a wise teacher disciplines them, he explains the causes and conditions for them through skillful means, causing them to repent their actions so that their past evil karma is completely extinguished.
Because they thus recollect their wholesome karma, they do not commit unwholesome deeds.

Contemplating from what causes and conditions such karma arises, they observe in this way and refrain from committing unwholesome deeds; they are able to cause all unwholesome karma to gradually be extinguished, or to render light and thin the unwholesome evil karma of body, speech, and mind currently being committed. Because the mind is light, having committed [an act], they quickly repent and do not do it again. If, through such a heart of repentance, the karma is brought to completion, all evil karma will be entirely extinguished.
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in the world understand karma in this way, they reflect:
"Because I have practiced evil, I shall perform unwholesome karmic actions of body, speech, and mind; when their retribution ripens, I will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."
Regarding evil and unwholesome karma that has not yet arisen, he employs right effort to prevent it from arising.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa can thus believe in the retribution of karma, even if they have committed the evil karma of hell that would normally lead to long-term suffering in hell, that suffering will become slight or be entirely extinguished.

Furthermore, because of their diligent application of effort, any evil karma that would otherwise cause them to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts—where they would endure the great suffering of hunger and thirst for a long time, or for a short duration—is either mitigated or entirely extinguished.

In this way, if any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other sentient beings possess evil karma that should cause them to fall into the animal realm—where they would long remain among animals devouring one another—their retribution may be experienced for only a short time, or it may be entirely extinguished.

Except for those karmic habits that have been cultivated to the point of certain accomplishment—such that one will inevitably receive their retribution within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, regardless of which path one follows.
"Furthermore, one believes in the retribution of karmic actions and contemplates the difficult-to-understand, subtle workings of karma.
Having committed the three kinds of evil deeds, one repents them and does not commit them again."
Because of indeterminate karma, one is born among animals.
One should reflect thus:
"Whether it be karma for the hells or karma for the hungry ghosts, by receiving this animal body, my mind of regret becomes pure and can destroy heavy karma."
By the power of the mind, either all [karmic results] are extinguished or a portion is severed.

If there is evil karma that ought to result in rebirth as an animal, it can be extinguished through mental repentance; one’s own karma can thus be extinguished so that one does not receive the body of a long-lived animal nor undergo great suffering, or else one may sever such evil karma through a superior state of mind.
For this reason, one should believe in the fruit of karma.
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others believe in the retribution of karma, they will be able to reach the further shore of birth and death.

Why is this? All existence within the five realms of birth and death exists by virtue of the retributive fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore, one should have faith in the reality of karmic retribution.
All sentient beings receive [their experiences] due to the causes and conditions of all their karmic fruits.

Therefore, whether male or female, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor and contemplate day and night that the retribution of karma is the most firm and enduring within the cycle of birth and death.
"Furthermore, tenth: if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others should reflect, what dharma should they reflect upon?
It is that which is harmed by one's dwelling place."

If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who possess little wisdom dwell in places that cause harm, their minds become attached and they cling to them with longing, unable to let go—whether in a monastery, a monastic residence, a village, a kingdom, a city, or any other location. They constantly delight in indolence and take pleasure in improper places; they do not reach the tranquility of an araṇya, nor do they frequent secluded retreats. Such persons are called neither householders nor renunciants, for they remain in unrighteous places until the end of their lives.
For what cause and condition does such a person go forth into homelessness?
Failing to reach any of the appropriate mountain forests or *āraṇya* hermitages, they instead exhaust their life and limb in an improper place.
Having gone forth from home for the sake of practicing dhyāna, one does not enter and dwell in places that are not quiet and secluded, such as mountain forests.

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas dwell in such improper places, they are despised and reviled by donors; people do not delight in associating with them, do not provide offerings, and do not even wish to see them.
If one dwells in an improper place, one's faults become manifest and one is held in contempt and ridiculed by the common folk, who speak of it among themselves, saying:
"Such-and-such a śramaṇa, such-and-such a brāhmaṇa, and other people as well, delight in dwelling in improper places."

They are neither called householders nor called renunciants; they do not delight in mountain forests or *āraṇya* hermitages, but instead hoard wealth and property, take pleasure in seeing worldly people, and associate with householders like servants, being held in contempt by those who wear white robes.
Therefore, such a person is called neither a householder nor one who has gone forth, because they dwell in an improper place.
Even if they were without fault, they would be slandered by others;
there is not a single person dwelling in an improper place who is not despised by donors.
If one frequently encounters laypeople or those living near the laity, even if one does not treat them with contempt, one may still give rise to various faults.
If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas dwell in an improper place, by dwelling in such an unsuitable location, they will obtain no benefit.

Therefore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not dwell in places of destruction; they should always delight in dwelling in suitable locations, always delight in solitude, and take pleasure in dwelling at the foot of trees, in cemeteries, or in quiet retreats to cultivate meditative silence. Or, they may go alone into mountain valleys to practice until the end of their lives.
"One should avoid improper places; by abandoning all unrighteous locations, one can attain liberation;
those who dwell in improper places do not attain liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
“When a bhikkhu dwells in an improper place, people view him as a servant and treat him with contempt like a blade of grass; thus he also loses his own benefit.”
A bhikṣu dwelling in an improper place, neither as a householder nor as one who has truly renounced,
finds no joy in the practice of meditation and recitation;
a bhikṣu dwelling in an improper place accumulates and hoards wealth and goods.
The greedy mind clings to wealth and treasures, unaware that the time of death has arrived.
Though body and life perish moment by moment, one cannot perceive this;
ignorant of the deeds one performs, yet able to receive their retribution in the future.
A bhikṣu who dwells in improper places, who constantly delights in seeing worldly people,
and who always frequents improper places, will enter the evil realms upon death.
One whose mind has no attachment or delight, and who hopes for nothing at all—
One who is able to liberate oneself from all greed is called a śramaṇa.
If one dwells among the mountains or beneath trees, constantly practicing meditative contemplation,
then one will attain pure wisdom and remain far removed from all faults.
Far removed from all craving, Unbewildered by sensory objects,
one can extinguish afflictions As fire consumes dry wood.
A bhikṣu practicing alone, Restraining and gathering the five faculties,
Knowing the characteristics of the body as they truly are, one attains the path to Nirvāṇa.
By constantly maintaining mindfulness and diligent effort, one remains far removed from all faults;
such a person reaches Nirvāṇa as if arriving at a place of recreation.
"Constantly seeking nirvāṇa and constantly fearing birth and death—with such a pure mind as this, one does not delight in improper places.
"A bhikṣu who dwells thus in an improper place incurs many faults; therefore, a bhikṣu should abandon unrighteous places."

If a bhikṣu dwells in an improper place, he is no different from a worldly person; if a worldly person dwells in an improper place, they incur immeasurable evil, how much more so for a śramaṇa? Because of associating with householders, one comes into conflict with all wholesome dharmas. Therefore, one should keep far away from improper places.
Then, the Bodhisattva Peacock King further expounded the eleventh dharma of the Tathāgata Kakutsunda for the sake of the assembly of Yāma-devas and Tuṣita-devas.
"Such wholesome dharmas are most worthy of being cherished and delighted in, for they lead to Nirvana.
What are these wholesome dharmas?
They are what is called 'abiding of the mind.'"
If a bhikṣu possesses a settled mind, he is able to uphold wholesome dharmas and is praised by others.
The method of settling the mind is to remain detached from all evils that have flowed through beginningless saṃsāra.
The net of mental transgressions and the fetters are pervasive, binding one firmly; they cannot be severed by a small amount of time, a small amount of diligence, or a small amount of concentration.
Such a great and evil net—if a bhikṣu possesses only a meager degree of mental abiding, he will be unable to sever this net of transgressions within the mind-ground.
There is no other dharma capable of severing birth and death like the dharma of abiding in the mind.

Only the practitioner possesses this dharma of abiding in the mind; if unwholesome dharmas arise, they collect the mind to subdue them, take no pleasure in evil karma, and with diligent effort, sever those unwholesome dharmas through courageous and vigorous exertion.
If a mind of sensual desire arises, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity; this is called "conformity.
This mind of evil desire can be severed by impurity, such that one finds no pleasure in it and does not cling to it.
"If anger arises, collect the mind and cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If delusion arises, collect the mind and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
"If one does not delight in dwelling in the mind, but follows pleasure by giving rise to various cravings,
and if one is bound by craving, one will lose the benefits of both worlds."
"In this way, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke to the gods of the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens about the immeasurable faults and evils of a non-abiding mind.
At that time, the assembly of gods, hearing of the benefits of both worlds, listened with joy and without weariness, saying:
'The Peacock King is truly extraordinary!'"
You are thus able to expound for me the profound Dharma, which is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, and leads to Nirvana;
it can engender weariness and detachment toward the various cycles of birth and death, and is the foremost in peace and security.
“We only pray that you will explain this to us in due order; we shall together listen with a single mind for our own benefit and for the benefit of others.

When the Peacock King heard these words, knowing that the assembly of devas was single-mindedly eager to hear, he leaped for joy and was filled with delight. With a most excellent, beneficial, and beautiful voice, he addressed the assembly of devas:
“If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or any other group direct their minds toward the Dharma, and having directed their minds toward the Dharma, diligently cultivate the sense of dread [of saṃsāra].”
What dharma should one cultivate?
It is the fear of an ill reputation.
If a bhikṣu fears an ill reputation, he will remain free from all transgressions.
That is to say: one does not enter places of women’s frivolous amusement; one does not enter taverns; one does not associate with those who sell liquor nor converse with them;
one does not associate with those addicted to wine nor converse with them; one does not associate with thieves;
one does not associate with those who have previously committed great evils; one does not associate with those fond of quarreling; and one does not associate with those who are secretly wicked.
One who harbors malice should not associate with those who lack constancy and abandon the path of the Dharma;
one should not associate with gamblers, nor with performers of music and song, nor with children,
nor with those bound by sensual desires, nor with the fickle and impulsive, nor with those who do not guard their speech, nor with the greedy, nor with those engaged in trade.
One should not associate with those who deceive others, nor with those who are crafty, hypocritical, or worldly traders whom the world detests and despises;
one should not associate with those who dig up rivers and ponds; one should not walk even a single step on the same path as eunuchs or women;
one should not associate with elephant trainers, nor with executioners, nor with horse trainers, nor with those who hold nihilistic views.
One should not associate with those who lack precepts. Such evil persons, monks, one should never associate with at all. Why is this?
By associating with such a person, one loses the dharma of a bhikṣu. People of the world will think:
"This bhikṣu associates with such a person; he must surely act in concert with him, for he has become intimate and walks together with such a person."
All people will conceive such thoughts.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should fear ill repute; you should not walk even a single step along the same path as those who engage in such impure deeds.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke these verses using the stanzas of the Tathāgata: "If a person associates with the unwholesome, They become an unwholesome person themselves. Therefore, one should distance oneself from evil;
Do not perform unwholesome deeds. (Note: The twelfth heading in the aforementioned text appears to be missing;
whether it was merged or omitted, the original source remains undetermined.)
Whomever one associates with, and with whom one repeatedly cultivates intimacy,
through that association one’s conduct becomes like theirs— whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
Since all people seek what is wholesome, one should draw near to those who are virtuous.
In this way one can attain happiness; virtue is not a cause of suffering.
Associating with the good increases merit, while associating with the evil increases extreme suffering.
The characteristics of merit and evil have now been briefly explained in this manner.
By constantly associating with virtuous people, one gains a good reputation;
if one associates with those who are not virtuous, it causes others to quickly hold one in contempt.
One should always remain close to the virtuous and distance oneself from evil companions.
"Because of associating with virtuous people, one is able to abandon all evil karmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King again spoke these words to the devas:
"If a bhikṣu possesses seven merits, he will be free from ill repute."
What are the seven?
First, to stay away from crowds;
second, not to delight in the benefits of offerings.
Third, being content, one can cause the donor to attain a pure mind;
fourth, delighting in dwelling in mountain valleys and quiet places, one gathers all wholesome karmas;
fifth, one remains free from excessive speech.
Sixth, when entering a village, one does not go to taverns;
seventh, one does not engage in buying, selling, or trade.
If a bhikṣu possesses such meritorious qualities and acts in accordance with right conduct, he will be free from ill repute and will be respected by all people.
Therefore, those who fear an ill reputation are foremost.

If there is a bhikṣu who does not fear an ill reputation, the faults he incurs will exceed those of a layperson; acting as he pleases and speaking as he pleases, he has no sense of shame or remorse regarding his broken precepts. When such a person of broken precepts dies and his life ends, he falls into hell.

One who fears ill repute delights in secluded places and does not delight in being near villages or cities; because of contentment, they do not violate the trust of others; they remain far removed from all places of clamor and bustle, and their mind is always filled with dread regarding even the slightest transgression.
"In this way, a bhikṣu who fears ill repute attains worldly goodness.
"Furthermore, the thirteenth quality is one that brings great benefit; what is this wholesome quality?"
This refers to not delighting in or clinging to phenomena—phenomena that are otherwise attractive.

If there is a bhikṣu who is free from attachment and pure, whose mind is entirely unattached, who delights in seclusion, who dwells securely in a pure livelihood, who is free from sorrow and affliction, who possesses the foremost peace and security, and who collects the mind in a single point.
If one encounters suffering or calamity, the mind is not timid or afraid;
if others revile or insult one, one does not give rise to anger.
Meeting with joy, one does not rejoice; facing fear, one is not afraid.
Not associating with one's kinsmen, one loses one’s own benefit.
One brings all undertakings to completion.
One takes no delight in previously committed evil deeds, nor does one take pleasure in watching games, singing, or dancing.
From one village to another, from city to city, from town to town, and from house to house, his mind finds no delight in attachment; he is at ease in sleep and at ease in wakefulness.
Because he does not take pleasure in or cling to them, his pure and right conduct is like that of an elder, such that Māra finds no opportunity.
He does not cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, nor does he take pleasure in or cling to the benefits of offerings;
having received them, he abandons unwholesome thoughts and reflections, applying himself with diligence to sever them so that they do not arise again.
If an unwholesome thought arises, he immediately eliminates it so that it does not afflict the mind.
If a bhikṣu such as this is still able to diligently eliminate unwholesome thoughts, how much more so should he sever and remove gross transgressions!
There are three kinds of dharmas that should be practiced. What are these three?
They are as follows: when unwholesome states have already arisen that obstruct the mind of compassion, one should apply diligent effort in order to eliminate them.
One exerts diligent effort so that unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise;
one applies diligent effort to the cultivation, development, and expansion of wholesome states that have already arisen.

If there is a bhikṣu whose mind does not delight in attachment, whose right intention is pure, and who seeks the exhaustion of craving, seeks disenchantment, and seeks peace and happiness, he must not obtain or become attached to pleasure.
"If there is a bhikṣu whose mind does not delight in or cling to anything, he shall attain the foremost and most supreme bliss.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
"Constantly cultivating meditative concentration, The mind has nothing upon which to delight or cling."
Because the mind is ever pure, the intellect is correct and undisturbed.
If a person maintains right mindfulness, no evils can defile them;
by being able to leave all faults behind, this is called attaining peace and security.
With single-mindedness and right mindfulness, Neither vitarka nor vicāra can disturb them;
Because they have abandoned unwholesome vitarka and vicāra, This is called dwelling in wholesome stability.
If a person’s mind is tranquil, And they always delight in nirvāṇa,
Among all their faculties, those people remain far removed from all that is unwholesome.
If there are practitioners who attain the bliss of dhyāna-samādhi,
it is entirely due to single-minded mindfulness, which is what is gained through practice.
If a bhikṣu delights in solitude, that delight arises from within the mind;
among all forms of delight, this is supreme and peerless.
For one whose mind is focused with single-minded attention, the heart becomes pure.
Having escaped the net of all faults, with mind and heart ever in tranquility,
always maintaining single-minded mindfulness and restraining the five faculties—
such a person’s water of wisdom can extinguish the poisonous fire of craving.
Those who have untied the bonds of craving always attain pure bliss;
they realize the supreme state before them, which is inexhaustible and indestructible.
But those whose minds are distracted by discursive thought and investigation undergo birth and death in every place.
When a single thought accords with its object, the power of samādhi can sustain it.
Therefore, this supreme path can reach the city of Nirvāṇa;
by means of single-minded mindfulness, one can destroy the army of Māra.
With the light of firm wisdom, he has bound the wild horse of the mind and reached the supreme further shore, the stainless and pure state.
The foremost of the courageous, through practice, has reached the further shore.
"By fixing the mind with single-minded attention, one can reach the indestructible state.
Thus did the Bodhisattva Peacock King preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways for the sake of the assembly of devas, bringing them benefit, peace, and happiness.
Furthermore, he continued to preach the Dharma without interruption for the assemblies of the Tuṣita and Yāma heavens, [a teaching] capable of leading to Nirvāṇa. He addressed the hosts of devas:

"Among all wholesome dharmas, the foremost and true dharma is this fourteenth: the bhikṣu who wanders alone, who delights in performing good deeds, who dwells among the forest trees, and who practices the conduct of sublime tranquility."
What is called a solitary bhikṣu is one who is tranquil and self-disciplined, whose mind is free from fear,
and who finds joy in all places— whether in mountain valleys, mountain caves, or amidst heaps of grass— with a mind free from partial attachment and upright in nature.
A bhikṣu who practices alone has seven benefits. What are these seven?
First, he is content and his mind is always joyful;
second, his mind is always pure.
Third, one will be honored by the world and protected by the devas;
fourth, one will be free from the defilement of evil dust;
fifth, wholesome dharmas will increase.
Sixth, with single-minded right mindfulness, one purifies body, speech, and mind, so that liberation manifests before them;
seventh, one leaves behind defiled dharmas and accomplishes pure dharmas.
Because of practicing alone, one is able to destroy the enemies of afflictions—the immeasurable, beginningless cycle of transmigration.

A bhikṣu who wanders alone practices with single-minded correctness; fearing the afflictions, he feels dread even toward minor evils, remaining constantly diligent and energetic, with his deportment serene and tranquil.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King, for the benefit of the devas, spoke in verse:
“Agitation is a firm evil; though possessed of great power, it is difficult to subdue.
One who is courageous and subdues the mind attains the foremost bliss.”
These three kinds of faults destroy all worlds;
when the water of wisdom can extinguish them, one attains the supreme bliss.
If a person does not love the Dharma, though they are human, they are no different from a non-human being.
Not abiding on the true path, one does not reach the city of Nirvana.
Having already obtained this human body, the locus upon which merit depends,
why do you not board the raft to cross the ocean of the various realms of existence?
The lives of all sentient beings are like a whirling firebrand or a city of Gandharvas;
they pass away swiftly without pausing for a moment.
This body perishes from moment to moment, constantly fearing old age and death.
Swiftly perishing and lacking any stable abiding, how could one give rise to pride regarding this body?
This body is a city of disease, a locus of great sorrow and lamentation, and the ground of the wholesome and unwholesome; for these reasons, it is called "the body."
If a person adorns their body with generosity, morality, and wisdom,
they are the most excellent among men and achieve the fruition of wholesome results.
If a person possesses the seven truths, that person is equal to a Buddha.
Through generosity, morality, wisdom, diligence, compassion, patience, and sublime self-mastery,
if a person practices these six perfections throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, such a person is called a Buddha.
If a person abandons desire, they are foremost within the three realms;
because they have relinquished all desires, they always attain great peace and happiness.
If a person is greedily attached to desire, manifold sufferings will constantly manifest before them.
“Desire is the cause of all suffering; therefore, one should abandon it.
Thus did the Bodhisattva Peacock King preach this Dharma for the sake of the devas of Tuṣita and the hosts of Yāma Heaven.
At that time, the Peacock King further expounded the fifteenth dharma of benefit for the assembly of devas:
"If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others in the world do not allow their minds to become distracted, they will obtain benefit."

If the mind is distracted, one should skillfully collect and restrain it, causing the mind to dwell in right concentration; one should always delight in associating with fellow practitioners of the holy life, and always be diligent and energetic in seeking peace and security, thereby remaining far removed from all evil realms.
If a bhikṣu’s mind is undistracted, subdues the six sense faculties, does not cling to sensory objects, fears birth and death, and abandons all unwholesome dharmas;
because he abandons all unwholesome dharmas, he constantly attains peace and happiness.
If a bhikṣu’s mind is not distracted amidst forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, this is called the bhikṣu’s right mindfulness of mind;
because the mind is rightly mindful, wholesome dharmas increase.
One who possesses right mindfulness does not delight in birth and death, but constantly exerts diligent effort and delights in cultivating samādhi.
Because of right mindfulness, one is able to attain the Way;
having attained the Way, one diligently cultivates all practices.
By diligently practicing the Way, initiating all practices, and maintaining right mindfulness, one attains the fruit of the Path.
Because the mind constantly cultivates the Path with right mindfulness, one severs all fetters and extinguishes all latent tendencies.
What fetters are severed?
Namely, the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of pride, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of stinginess—all these fetters are severed.
Which underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are extinguished?

Namely, the underlying tendency of sensual lust, the underlying tendency of aversion, the underlying tendency of attachment to existence, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of pride, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt—all these underlying tendencies are extinguished.
Due to these powerful causes and conditions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one wanders through the various realms of existence, encompassed within the three worlds.
However, if the mind is not distracted and focuses single-mindedly on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), all [fetters] can be extinguished.
Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others, those who desire to attain peace and security find that for all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, the mind is the root.

Therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence to the cultivation of the path, fearing transgressions, and restraining the mind through right mindfulness; for there is no other dharma capable of extinguishing the dense forest of afflictions that has flowed on from beginningless time as effectively as the mind of right mindfulness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke these verses in the meter of omniscience:
"With single-minded mindfulness present before you, And fearing all evils,
you can give rise to the outflow-free Dharma, Just like planting rice in a paddy field."
With single-minded mindfulness present before you, Diligently practice the Path;
Sever all unwholesome dharmas, Just as the sun dispels the darkness.
If single-mindedness is present before you, Always maintain right mindfulness of cessation.
Then one will not fear the multitude of faults, Just as the garuḍa bird [fears] no poison.
Such a distracted mind Is like a wind of great power;
The wise are able to subdue it, Just like a trainer of elephants.
Ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom are like a great, fierce fire;
when combined with the wind, they burn away the forest of all evils.
Therefore, one should cultivate wisdom to sever and eliminate ignorance.
Free from the affliction of old age and death, one attains the unsurpassed, supreme state.
If one can diligently restrain the mind and practice with vigor,
then by means of that mental restraint, one is able to sever all evils.
The mind constantly takes objects as its domain; through courageous effort one can restrain it so that no desires can destroy it, like holding a poisonous drug in one's hand.
Thus, by diligent and energetic application, one is able to subdue the mind.
"In the great river of craving of the three realms, cross swiftly and do not linger.
Thus, King Peacock spoke of virtuous conduct for the benefit of the hosts of the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the hosts of devas were struck with fear of birth and death, and they abandoned all the pleasures of sensory objects.

[The thirtieth dharma: "'Furthermore, if a person possesses these five qualities, they will not fall into the evil realms after death. What are the five? First, they do not abandon the four foundations of mindfulness. Second, they do not abandon the four right endeavors. Third, they do not abandon the four bases of psychic power. Fourth, they do not abandon the five faculties. Fifth, they do not abandon the five powers. These are called the five dharmas. [The thirty-first dharma: "'Furthermore, if a person possesses these five qualities, they will not fall into the evil realms after death. What are the five? First, they do not abandon the seven factors of enlightenment. Second, they do not abandon the eightfold noble path. Third, they do not abandon the four fruits of the ascetic life. Fourth, they do not abandon the four analytical knowledges. Fifth, they do not abandon the four fearlessnesses. These are called the five dharmas. [The thirty-second dharma: "'Furthermore, if a person possesses these five qualities, they will not fall into the evil realms after death. What are the five? First, they do not abandon the four foundations of mindfulness. Second, they do not abandon the four right endeavors. Third, they do not abandon the four bases of psychic power. Fourth, they do not abandon the five faculties. Fifth, they do not abandon the five powers. These are called the five dharmas. [The thirty-third dharma: "'Furthermore, if a person possesses these five qualities, they will not fall into the evil realms after death. What are the five? First, they do not abandon the seven factors of enlightenment. Second, they do not abandon the eightfold noble path. Third, they do not abandon the four fruits of the ascetic life. Fourth, they do not abandon the four analytical knowledges. Fifth, they do not abandon the four fearlessnesses. These are called the five dharmas. [The thirty-fourth dharma: "'Furthermore, if a person possesses these five qualities, they will not fall into the evil realms after death. What are the five? First, they do not abandon the four foundations of mindfulness. Second, they do not abandon the four right endeavors. Third, they do not abandon the four bases of psychic power. Fourth, they do not abandon the five faculties.
"Furthermore, there are wholesome dharmas and dharmas worthy of being cherished that can restrain heedlessness, like an iron hook; you should practice them with mindfulness.
What are these wholesome dharmas?"
This refers to the mindfulness of death.

If a person practices mindfulness of death, constantly and diligently cultivating it without ceasing or resting, they will realize that this peerless and great evil which torments all sentient beings cannot be escaped; there is absolutely no exemption from it.

All who are born must die; this causes the separation from all those one holds dear and brings about one's own destruction, leading to rebirth in another place. Some may pass from a state of happiness into a place of suffering, bound by the ropes of karma and sustained by their own actions, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
At the time of death, one has no companion; only wholesome and unwholesome karma serve as one's companions.
Wholesome karma performed is like parents, leading one to a place of happiness;
unwholesome and evil karma is like a great enemy, leading one to the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.
For this reason, one should cultivate wholesome karma and abandon all evils.
If one can thus practice the mindfulness of death, the mind will not be attached to sensory objects, nor will it be attached to greed, hatred, or delusion.
Out of fear of death, one does not commit unwholesome deeds for the sake of wives, children, or kinsmen.
If all householders cultivate this mindfulness, they will still attain tranquility; how much more so, then, those who have left the home life?
If there is a śramaṇa who cultivates mindfulness of death, he will not transgress the precepts, will not delight in sensory objects, and will not dwell in tumultuous crowds.
If one dwells in tumultuous crowds, the mind becomes distracted; this is the root of much speech and leads to frequently seeing women.
One should abandon all places that give rise to craving and instead contemplate death.

If one dwells in a place of clamor and distraction where the mind is not virtuous, at the time of death, one will encounter all manner of disadvantage, decline, and affliction, and shall find no peace or happiness.

At the time of death, one is severed and cut by the winds of knives and swords; having no refuge and no savior, bound by the cords of karma, one is led to the next world, where neither parents, brothers, wives, nor kinsmen can provide protection or rescue.

If one can thus cultivate mindfulness of the signs of death, such a person will delight in upholding the precepts and wisdom; practicing in this manner, they will cause wholesome karma to increase and unwholesome karma to be extinguished. By virtue of this wholesome karma, they will experience the bliss of humans and devas, and subsequently attain nirvana.
"If any man or woman knows these merits—whether they be householders or renunciants, śramaṇas or brahmins—they should constantly keep death in mind."
Because they are mindful of death, their minds are filled with dread, and they refrain from performing any unwholesome deeds. They reflect in their minds:
"All sentient beings must eventually succumb to death; whether in the realms of devas, humans, hell-beings, or hungry ghosts, there is nowhere one does not die."
If one can thus practice the mindfulness of death and fear future lives, the mind will not be attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects.

Such sensory realms are impermanent and unchanging [in their nature of flux], and are not indestructible phenomena; one should constantly contemplate them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

If one contemplates death in the mind, one will not be troubled or disturbed by various evils. One should constantly and repeatedly cultivate the contemplation of impurity so that skillful observation increases.
By repeatedly recollecting death, cultivation increases, and mindfulness of impermanence is maintained.
"There is no permanent place that is not subject to destruction, nor anything that remains unchanging or indestructible.

Even the hundreds of thousands of millions of beloved mountain peaks, up to and including Sumeru, the King of Mountains, shall all be crushed and annihilated when consumed by the fires at the end of an eon; how much more so the bodies of humans and devas?"

The great ocean is boundless; it is the abode of all great rivers and all dragon kings, as well as the place where all dragons and asuras dwell. Yet when the seven suns emerge, it will all dry up and vanish—how much more so my own body?

To state the essential point: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—all three realms are impermanent, shifting, and destined for destruction; how much more so my own body and life, which could they possibly be permanent, immovable, or indestructible?

If one can thus constantly maintain mindfulness with the mind and observe well with the intellect, cultivating the mind in this way, there will be no place for delight, no place for craving, and no place for anger.

Because greed and hatred are purified, delusion also ceases accordingly; by being free from these three faults, one attains the supreme state, which is neither aging nor death, neither exhaustion nor extinction.
Thus, when one contemplates death, there is no other object of thought; therefore, the contemplation of death is the foremost among all forms of mindfulness.
"Furthermore, there are additional merits in cultivating the mark of mindfulness of death."
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas practice in this way, they contemplate this body as being like a tiger’s cage.
How do they contemplate suffering?

"This body of mine, afflicted by physical and mental ailments, ruined by old age, led away by the King of Death, and bound by the net of death—what can it accomplish? It is unable to practice generosity, maintain the precepts, or cultivate wisdom."
Therefore, while death has not yet arrived, one should practice generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom; for before long death will arrive and destroy the lives of all sentient beings.
“If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa thus binds their mind to the mark of death, their practice will not be in vain, and they will certainly attain nirvāṇa.

“Furthermore, as for the recollection of death, it is this: ‘This body is only impermanent; all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self. They change and decay from moment to moment, swift and unceasing; they are things subject to destruction, empty and non-existent, lacking any solid nature. Like a whirling firebrand or a city of the gandharvas, all conditioned phenomena are likewise so.’”
My own body and life are likewise thus: they possess no solidity, being like water bubbles or a city of the Gandharvas.
Such is the nature of death; it is present in all beings, its arrival is certain, and it is truly terrifying.
Therefore, one should cultivate the firm Dharma, embracing the three wholesome karmas and abandoning the three unwholesome ones.
One should cultivate the perception of death in this manner.
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas cultivate mindfulness within their own minds, by cultivating this mindfulness, they will obtain great benefit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King composed verses using the stanzas of former Buddhas, saying:
"These six evil enemies destroy the world;
Old age, sickness, and death do not cease, Because of the three poisons."
The five sense objects are great thieves, capable of plundering the wealth of virtue;
this enemy feigns friendship while wandering through treacherous and evil places.
With a heedless and unwholesome mind, one remains stubbornly attached to these sense objects.
They can lead all sentient beings swiftly to the three evil realms.
If there are those who can awaken to and know the true truths, such as suffering and the rest,
these people will then attain the state of peace and tranquility.
Uproot all poisonous roots, increase meritorious conduct, and abandon the mind of indolence; do not associate with evil friends.
If a bhikṣu is diligent and zealously cultivates the contemplation of death, [he shall attain liberation].
Then one attains the unsurpassed state, forever free from old age,
sickness, and death. If one can, according to reality, awaken to and know the sense faculties and their objects,
and rely upon right wisdom, then one will be able to cross the ocean of existence.
Constantly mindful of death, one gives rise to fear;
Free from pride and indolence, one draws near to those of wisdom. Multitudes of evils do not defile the mind.
With a diligent and supple heart, One cultivates the Dharma and leaves all evils behind.
One whose mind is unmoved by right view is a person whom one should associate with.
If one associates with evil friends, one will not obtain the wholesome Dharma;
if one associates with the superior, one will have no fear of manifold faults.
In a single thought or for a brief moment, day and night, one should never be parted from it;
the wise constantly contemplate death, for there is no place to escape it.
Contemplation of death is most excellent; among all contemplations, none can equal it.
Through practice one attains tranquility, forever free from all defilements.
If one is mindful of the fear of death, then no evil thoughts will arise;
with the mind free from all faults, one shall attain the state of tranquility.
“The Blessed One has thus declared that the supreme fruit of heedfulness is this:
if one constantly keeps in mind the fear of death, one will be free from all unwholesome states.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King preached such a Dharma to the assembly of devas.
"Furthermore, there is a seventeenth quality that greatly benefits śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. What is this quality?
It is the abandonment of pride regarding physical form, pride regarding lineage, and pride regarding wealth."

If one possesses pride regarding physical form, pride regarding lineage, and pride regarding wealth, that fool performs evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. Wandering through birth after birth in those various places, they undergo immeasurable suffering within the cycle of birth and death, beyond all description.
Having recognized these faults, one does not give rise to pride regarding physical form, pride regarding lineage, or pride regarding wealth.

If there is anyone who can remain free from pride regarding physical form, lineage, and wealth, you should know that such a person does not commit evil deeds of body or speech. They see physical form as it truly is: impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; empty and devoid of anything substantial; lacking any solidity; an impure vessel composed of a combination of hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, and flesh; a mass of countless bones, sinews, marrow, fat, and muscle, filled within with excrement, urine, pus, and blood.

"This physical body of mine is impure in the beginning, impure in the middle, and impure in the end; it is produced by the causes and conditions of immeasurable karma and afflictions, lacking solidity, lacking permanence, lacking reality, and lacking a self."

Now, when this body of mine reaches the time of death, it will not be my companion for even a single step; cast away in a cemetery, or consumed by fire, or devoured by vultures, eagles, crows, ravens, foxes, and dogs.
"If a person reflects and contemplates in this way, pride regarding physical form will either be extinguished or attenuated.
Furthermore, if a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa gives rise to pride of lineage, saying of himself:
'My lineage is superior.'"
If one observes with reality within the true dharma, there is no such thing as lineage; it is merely a false discrimination.
Due to ignorance, one falsely gives rise to discrimination, thinking:
"This lineage is superior."
"This lineage is inferior. This is not so according to reality. Why is that?
Because there is birth, there is lineage, which undergoes such transformation.
Whosoever possesses the actual virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, wisdom, and a mind tamed by meditative concentration—
such a person, even if born into a lowly caste, is called one of great lineage.
Why is this? It is because there is a superior lineage of merit, not a lineage of birth;
it is the causal condition of merit, not the causal condition of birth. If there were no merit, then there would be no causal condition.
Therefore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not give rise to pride regarding their lineage.
Furthermore, they should contemplate pride regarding physical form (*rūpa*).

If a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or any other practitioner contemplates this form of mine during infancy: although it possesses physical appearance, the color of the face when held up and motionless is not the color of when moving; the color of when moving is not the color of crawling; and so on, up to the color of youth is not the color of middle age, the color of middle age is not the color of old age, and the color of old age is not the color at the time of death—just as the color of one recently deceased is not the color of one who has been dead for a long time.

Just as my own corpse, being gnawed by flies and devoured by maggots, blown upon by the wind, scorched by the sun, and soaked and rotted by the rain, is completely destroyed and scattered in a mess across the cemetery—this body disintegrating into countless parts, the joints of the bones spreading apart, the skull in one place, the throat, shoulders, arms, fingers, nails, and various other joints in another place; the vertebrae, the hip bones, the thigh bones, the shin bones, the ankle bones, the foot bones, and the toe bones each in their own place.
Because one contemplates form (*rūpa*) according to reality in this way, one becomes free from pride regarding form.
"How does one contemplate pride regarding wealth according to reality, and having contemplated it, become detached from all worldly things?"
Observing and knowing things as they truly are, one sees that all worlds lack autonomy, and that all phenomena of immeasurable kinds lack autonomy; how, then, could this phenomenon possess autonomy?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are bound by causes and conditions and lack autonomy; they arise from causes and conditions.
For example, a house is called a "house" when various timbers, bricks, and tiles are assembled and joined together, mutually supporting one another.
The body is likewise: when skin, flesh, fat, bone, sinews, and marrow are combined, it is called a "body. It possesses no autonomy, and this physical form has no creator.

In this way, when a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa observes with reality as it is the conceit of physical form, the conceit of lineage, and the conceit of wealth, all such conceits are either extinguished or rendered thin and diminished.

"Furthermore, because of observing what is unreal, one gives rise to pride regarding one's lineage (*gotra-māna*); if one observes according to reality, such a lineage is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and it is only those without eyes who give rise to false recollections."

If one is endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, wisdom, pure conduct, and right view, such a lineage is truly superior; it is not like the deluded who give rise to pride and merely think their lineage is superior.
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others are able to know their own lineage as it truly is, all pride regarding that lineage will be entirely extinguished, or at least diminished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King composed verses based on the sūtra-verses of the Tathāgata Kakutsunda, saying:
"If there is a person who constantly gives rise to pride regarding their physical form, lineage, or wealth, that person is like a drunken elephant;
they do not see the precipitous and perilous bank."
All forms of pride and arrogance, along with negligence that deranges the faculties,
cause one to be despised by people in the present life and lead to rebirth in the evil realms at the end of life.
If a person gives rise to pride, blinded by the arrogance of physical beauty or wealth, [they will suffer this fate].
Such a person finds no joy and, at the end of life, falls into the evil realms.
If one is arrogant, relying on physical beauty or wealth, this is not seeing things as they truly are;
being foolish and lacking wisdom, one cannot cross the ocean of suffering.
Physical form, lineage, wealth, and all instruments of pleasure—all these are impermanent;
the wise should not place their trust in them.
If one is devoid of generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, then there is no true lineage.
If one possesses generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, this is the most excellent lineage.
The fool is not called wealthy; he lacks the lineage of the noble path.
Therefore, wisdom is the cause; without wisdom, there is no lineage.
If there are those who uphold pure precepts, like a pool of cool clarity, such people are of noble lineage; they are called those with superior seeds.
Through generosity, morality, and wisdom, they possess courageous and true diligence.
One who is able to correspond with this is called one of the noble lineage.
If one is devoid of the True Dharma, though they have shaved their hair and claim the lineage of a śramaṇa,
or are called a brāhmaṇa, they are not truly so.
If one cultivates the True Dharma, possessing generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, one is then called a śramaṇa; one is then called a brāhmaṇa.
Old age can rob one of youthful vigor, and death can sever the life-faculty.
Wealth and possessions will inevitably disperse and decay; all phenomena are like this.
Illness can destroy one's vigor and health, causing sentient beings to wander in saṃsāra;
therefore, those who possess wisdom should abandon pride regarding physical form and wealth.
Having understood such evils as these, who would give rise to arrogance?
Therefore, the wise abandon pride in physical form and wealth;
by practicing wholesome dharmas, they shall be free from all suffering and affliction.
"In the preceding manifest text, the eighteenth heading is either merged with another or omitted; its original status remains undetermined.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Peacock King preached the Dharma to the assembly of devas:
'Furthermore, Śramaṇas and Brāhmaṇas have another practice, namely the nineteenth: to give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.'"

If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or any other assembly maintain an impartial mind, they will attain the foremost happiness, be loved and respected by all sentient beings, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in the heavenly realms of the good destinations.
How does one give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?
If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa abandons contentious debate and does not dispute with others, having relinquished strife and turmoil, they attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Therefore, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are able to abandon contentious debate, they attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is a dharma that enables śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings:
observing that all sentient beings are subject to decline and affliction, and regarding even an enemy as if they were a close friend.

"These sentient beings are encompassed by birth and death; as birth exists, there is no cessation of birth and death, and thus there are old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress, as well as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, being beaten, bound, and whipped, the suffering of association with the hated, and the suffering of separation from the loved."
Thus, observing that suffering and afflicted sentient beings have met with great calamity, one cultivates the contemplation of equality toward both enemies and kin.
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas perform this contemplation, they will attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas further form this thought:

"These sentient beings are afflicted by manifold sufferings; that is to say, diseases afflict the bodies and minds of sentient beings, and through the distress of illness, they undergo great suffering."
By reflecting in this way upon enemies and kin, and by forming such a thought, the mind attains purity;
because the mind is pure, the blood becomes pure;
because the blood is pure, the complexion becomes pure, and all the sense faculties likewise become pure.

Observing in this way, one obtains visible retribution in the present life, becoming someone whom all sentient beings delight to see, who are filled with affection, respect, and veneration; by these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavens.
"Furthermore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas observe all kinsmen through another method as being like enemies:
'All sentient beings must die; none escape birth and death; having been born, they die again.'"
"Thus, because of their own karma, these sentient beings fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; such beings are tormented by various sufferings.
Contemplating in this way, his mind becomes pure for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
because the mind is pure, the blood becomes pure.
Because the serum is pure, the complexion is clear;

because the complexion is pure, one is peerlessly handsome, such that all sentient beings delight in gazing upon him. Having obtained this visible fruit of retribution, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavenly realms, the world of the virtuous paths.
