In this way, a bhikṣu cultivates great wholesome karma and gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others in the world cultivate the contemplation of equanimity by means of other methods."
These sentient beings possess karma and the storehouse of karma; they transmigrate according to karma, and whatever they have performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is fully accomplished.
By means of wholesome karma, they are born among humans and devas;
by means of unwholesome karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others—including gods—practice in this way, their minds become pure;
because the mind is pure, the blood becomes pure;
because the blood is pure, the complexion becomes pure.

Because their complexion is pure, all sentient beings love and look up to them with joy; at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in the happy realms, receiving the bodies of devas, and will certainly attain nirvana.
Because the mind is pure, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and attains such a fruit.
"Furthermore, if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas possess another dharma by which they cultivate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings..."
What is this distinct phenomenon?
It is that all sentient beings must experience separation from those they love.

All sentient beings are encompassed by birth and death; there is not a single sentient being who does not suffer the separation from loved ones. This separation from loved ones is an exceedingly great evil.
Practicing in this way, the mind becomes pure;
because the mind is pure, the blood becomes pure;
because the blood is pure, the complexion becomes pure.
Because their complexion is pure, they are peerlessly handsome.
Because of this handsomeness, all who see them find their minds purified and look upon them with love and reverence.

By giving rise to equanimity toward all sentient beings, they obtain this manifest retribution: at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in a good destination, receiving the body of a deva.
Due to the remaining karma, they later attain nirvana.
"Furthermore, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others again cultivate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings by means of other dharmas, [they shall likewise attain liberation]."
What are these distinct phenomena?
They are as follows: this mind is light and shifting, moving swiftly and never remaining still. If a mind of desire arises, one should cultivate the contemplation of impurity;
if a mind of hatred arises, one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness.
If a mind of delusion arises, one should observe and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
These three types of mind are countered by three dharmas: one should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, and cultivate a mind of equanimity among enemies and kin.

Because the mind is pure, one has no doubts or anxieties regarding any sphere of activity; thus, one attains the foremost pure and blissful practice, awakening in peace and sleeping in peace, protected by the devas, such that none can find an opportunity for harm, and possesses great majestic power.
Because the mind is pure, the blood is pure;
because the blood is pure, the complexion is pure;
because the complexion is pure, one is of incomparable beauty, such that all sentient beings love, delight in, and gaze upon them with reverence.

By giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, one obtains immediate retribution: at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in a good destination, within the heavenly realms, receiving the body of a deva.
"By virtue of this karma, one will ultimately attain nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
"If, toward both enemies and kin, One’s mind is always impartial,"
As the Dharma is without partiality, the Muni has taught wisdom.
If one’s mind is pure and not defiled by transgressions,
walking alone among the forest trees— the Muni calls this non-attachment.
With a mind free from the stain of longing, far removed from all turbidity,
and taking no delight in sensory realms— the Muni has taught this tranquility.
One should observe with truthful insight that all things are impermanent and so forth.
One who knows the light and darkness of the world, the Muni calls him courageous.
One who does not grow weary of worldly phenomena, yet practices wholesome dharmas,
remaining equanimous toward suffering and pleasure— the Muni calls him free from defilement.
The mind always knows contentment, Always remaining far removed from all desires;
Not longing for lavish offerings— The Muni has declared this to be purity.
Do not associate with evil friends, And do not frequent places of unrighteousness.
Walking alone with a firm mind, the Muni taught right action.
Far removed from joy and fear, he cannot be destroyed by the power of craving;
all his faculties are utterly tranquil—this the Noble One calls freedom from longing.
With a mind that is perfectly equanimous, And with objects of perception always equal,
Being equal toward all things— The Muni has taught this as wisdom.
Thoroughly understanding all phenomena, As well as the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma,
The Muni teaches people to abandon both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
Through diligence he cuts off all evils, and constantly cultivates the foundations of mindfulness.
Knowing the arising of sensations as they truly are—this the Muni calls wisdom.
"If a person fears birth and death, Always acts with regard to time and place,
And restrains the sense-faculties through the Dharma, The Muni speaks of Nirvana.
In this way, the Bodhisattva Peacock King preached the Dharma to the assemblies of the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens through immeasurable kinds of skillful means.
At that time, the assembly of devas focused their minds in right mindfulness, relinquished all sensual pleasures, and with hearts of gentleness, joyfully listened to the preaching of the Dharma.
Then, King Peacock, knowing that the minds of the assembly of devas were well-tamed, again preached the Dharma for them:
"Furthermore, whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in the world, they should keep the Dharma in mind."
What dharmas should one keep in mind?
They are the twenty, namely, the dharma of contentment.
The dharma of contentment brings benefit and peace and happiness.
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are content in body and mind, taking contentment as their companion and contentment as their refuge, they will achieve peace and happiness.

For one who is content, there is no seeking in any place; this is the foremost happiness. Their eyes do not crave forms; regarding immeasurable forms, they give rise to neither longing nor discrimination.

If one sees the appearance of forms, the mind does not dwell upon them; one does not seek after past lovely forms, nor does one find pleasure or delight in them, nor does one long for them. One does not give rise to a mind of desire, nor does one give rise to recollection, nor does one give rise to attachment.
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are thus contented, they will always attain peace and happiness.

"In this way, when the ear hears a pleasant sound, one does not find it attractive or delightful, nor does one dwell upon it with the mind. If desire arises toward past objects, the mind does not discriminate; rather, one observes them as they truly are:
'This sound is impermanent, not pleasurable, and not self; it is merely a discrimination that harms all sentient beings.'"
"Deluded ordinary beings engage in false conceptualization; when sounds reach the faculty of the ear, they cause the mind to become distressed and distracted.
To observe this as it truly is, to observe it skillfully in this way, and to be content with things as they truly are.
One contemplates sounds as they truly are: empty and non-existent, lacking solidity or reality, being nothing but conceptual construction.
Observing in this way, one does not give rise to craving or attachment toward any beloved, beautiful sounds or any beloved objects.
"Because of contentment, one attains such bliss.

'If a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or any other person, upon smelling an odor with the nose, does not give rise to discrimination, does not produce evil thoughts, and does not engage in discursive reflection;'"
Having smelled an odor with the nose, one contemplates it as it truly is:
"Such an odor is impermanent and subject to decay; it is changing, unreal, empty, and non-existent."
"If one is attached to this fragrance, one will be unable to escape evil thoughts and a distracted mind.
This is called contentment.
If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not take pleasure in such things, they examine all such objects in this manner.
Because of contentment, one attains the foremost pure happiness; by cultivating and expanding this, one attains the supreme bliss.

"Furthermore, if recluses, brahmins, or others do not become greedily attached to tastes with their minds, do not dwell upon them, and do not discriminate them; if they do not dwell on past tastes nor reflect upon them, do not recall them with attachment nor crave them, yet are not lacking in contentment—[this is the path]."
One contemplates taste as it truly is:
"This taste is impermanent, subject to decay and change; yet through discrimination one gives rise to craving and attachment, deeming it something to be grasped."
If one observes according to reality, one will find no delight in flavors, the mind will not be greedily attached, and craving for flavors will not arise.
If one can thus be content with respect to flavors, one will attain peace and happiness.
"Furthermore, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others in the world contemplate contact as it truly is:

'Such contact has no intrinsic nature; it is impermanent and subject to decay, a phenomenon of change. Such contact is empty and non-existent; it is without solidity and without reality. It did not exist before but exists now, and having existed, it returns to non-existence.'"

If one can thus contemplate contact as it truly is, one will not give rise to attachment toward past contact, nor feel craving or delight; one will not seek out contact, and whatever contact comes to touch the body, one remains free from the contact of sensual desire.
This is called contentment.
"Furthermore, if a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa contemplates mental phenomena—whether pleasant or unpleasant—he reflects according to reality:
'I contemplate phenomena as impermanent, subject to decay and transformation, empty and non-existent, lacking solidity and substance.'"
"These phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; they did not exist before but now exist, and having existed, they return to non-existence—all are subject to total extinction.
By recollecting beloved and unbeloved phenomena in this way, one comes to know contentment.

One does not give rise to hatred or envy toward unlovely phenomena, nor does one give rise to delight or pleasure toward lovely phenomena; regarding past phenomena, the mind neither clings to them with recollection nor relishes them with attachment.
Thus, one who skillfully contemplates the phenomena desired by the mind does not dwell upon, savor, crave, or delight in any mental phenomena.
Because of contentment, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas attain liberation from the six types of craving.
At that time, the Peacock King spoke in verse:
"If one can contemplate contentment, And escape the realm of the six cravings,
Without recollecting or desiring them, Such a person shall always attain happiness."
If, with a mind of right mindfulness, one contemplates form as it truly is,
that person’s craving for form will be unable to disturb their mind.
When the nose encounters its object, if one can remain without greedy attachment, [the mind remains undisturbed].
When a person’s mind is pure, the excesses of the nose cannot disturb it.
When a wise person encounters flavors with the tongue, they observe them correctly and do not become attached;
thus, the excesses of flavor cannot defile their mind.
Though the body experiences various contacts, one who attains them without craving or attachment—
because that person understands the nature of contact— always finds peace and happiness.
Toward both agreeable and disagreeable phenomena, their mind remains free from craving and attachment.
"Abiding well like a great mountain—this mind is praised by the world.
"If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas practice the dharma of contentment and are able to abandon these six kinds of craving, they are praised by the Buddha."
In this way, the Bodhisattva Peacock King expounded this true Dharma for the assemblies of the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens:
"Furthermore, if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas contemplate and reflect upon the Dharma, what kind of Dharma do they reflect upon?"
The twenty-first is as follows: fear of sense objects, fear of unwholesome sense objects, and false views, which result in a lack of benefit.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa contemplates the sense object of form as it truly is—just as visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms, and the mental consciousness determines, discerns, and examines it—[he will attain true understanding].
If a sense object arises and gives rise to lust, such that this lustful object comes to disturb and agitate me, I shall give rise to fear.
If one sees an object, one should sever the craving and desire for it and not gaze upon it.
Just as they are conceptualized, so too is the mind; whether it be greed or anger, one knows them all as they truly are.

If afflictions arise, one observes their arising as it truly is, realizing that they yield no benefit: through these afflictions, one fails to attain peace and happiness in the present or the future, and all sentient beings likewise fail to obtain benefit or peace and happiness because of these afflictions.
Such afflictions are capable of binding all sentient beings.
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas can contemplate objects in this manner, any arising thought of greed will be entirely extinguished or rendered thin and slight.

"In this way, one contemplates the eye and forms as they truly are; then one contemplates the ear: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, auditory consciousness arises; based on the ear and based on sound, mindfulness arises, and either a painful sensation or a pleasant sensation is produced."
Observing consciousness in this way, one may further give rise to much greed, hatred, and delusion, or produce other forms of consciousness, just like lighting a lamp.
One observes unwholesome thoughts:
"I have produced an unwholesome thought; I know that it is an unwholesome thought."
Knowing that unwholesome thoughts arise from conditions, one should sever and extinguish them.
If one severs the unwholesome, wholesome dharmas will be fulfilled; by contemplating the objective realm as it truly is, wholesome thoughts will increase.

Unwholesome thoughts—those arising from craving for delight and those arising from craving for existence—are all brought to cessation; because they are thus extinguished, one attains purity, becomes free from turbid and evil defilements, and obtains all happiness.

Therefore, whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in the world, when first observing objects, if unwholesome desires arise, they should immediately sever and extinguish them; by contemplating wholesome dharmas, they should eliminate all that is unwholesome.
In this way, one should understand sounds with respect to the ear as they truly are and give rise to wholesome thoughts.
Furthermore, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in the world perceive odors with the nose, how does consciousness arise?
Dependent on the nose and dependent on odors, nose-consciousness arises.
If unwholesome thoughts arise, one knows those unwholesome thoughts.
If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa forms such a thought:
"If unwholesome thoughts arise within me now, they will bring neither benefit nor peace; I must now sever them.
By observing reality as it is, one is able to sever unwholesome thoughts."

Having formed this thought, he contemplates the fragrance as it truly is, giving rise to wholesome thoughts; because of these wholesome thoughts, he is able to extinguish the craving born of shared delight.
Having observed in this way, one does not give rise to attachment toward any fragrance; by severing such attachment, one attains peace and happiness.
Thus, knowing the objects of experience as they truly are, one attains a state of genuine security.
If one can contemplate fragrance in this way according to reality, although the nose perceives fragrance, one finds no delight in it.

"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, upon obtaining a taste with the tongue, should give rise to unwholesome craving, they should mindfully know it as it truly is: 'Tongue-consciousness arises conditioned by the tongue and conditioned by taste. When they reflect in this way, they find no delight in the taste, nor do they crave or cling to it."
One knows tongue-consciousness as it truly is; if one knows that tongue-consciousness delights in flavors and attains liberation from that consciousness, one attains the foremost bliss.
In this way and that way, by knowing objects as they truly are, one attains unsurpassed bliss and is not destroyed by craving and delight.

"Having contemplated the tongue and tastes as they truly are, one further contemplates the body and tangibles: conditioned by the body and conditioned by tangibles, body-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors gives rise to contact (*sparśa*); and because of that contact, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) arise."

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa contemplates contact as it truly is, they see that this contact is impermanent, shifting, decaying, and subject to change; if unwholesome thoughts and reflections arise, they bring no benefit and do not lead to peace and happiness.
Knowing contact as it truly is, one skillfully observes with mindfulness, remaining undisturbed by craving and delight, and taking no pleasure in sensory objects.
"Having observed bodily contact through various skillful means, one further observes how mental phenomena arise."
With the mind as cause and mental phenomena as condition, mind-consciousness arises—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
If one conditions something unwholesome and gives rise to an unwholesome thought, one understands it as it truly is:
"I have conditioned something unwholesome and given rise to mind-consciousness; I have produced attachment and delight, which brings no benefit, but only agitation and unrest."
Reflecting in this way, one contemplates the emergence and disappearance of phenomena and thus practices in accordance with the Dharma.
By practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one perceives the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, and is not disturbed by attachment or aversion.
Because craving is attenuated, one attains liberation;
because one is liberated from craving, one attains the supreme bliss and realizes that all phenomena are entirely subject to arising and ceasing.
By being able to contemplate all objective realms in this way, right knowledge arises, which can extinguish all fetters and afflictions.
Because the afflictions are exhausted, one attains untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Because one has attained correspondence with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one attains the foremost station.

Therefore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas must not trust in sense objects; all sense objects are like enemies, and the sense objects of all sentient beings are like snakes. If a person has not yet attained untainted wisdom, they must not trust in sense objects.
“Sense objects are fickle and restless, like hostile bandits who feign friendship; such sense objects are capable of binding all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
“If one truly understands sense objects, It is as if holding them with an iron hook.”
Because they are restless, fickle, and volatile, they bring about all manner of harm.
Deluded by their longing for sensory objects and delighting in the discriminating mind,
the snare of death is about to descend, capable of severing the lives of all beings.
Dragged away by sensory objects, the human mind becomes restless and agitated;
deceived by ignorance, it fails to realize this.
Sensory objects have no fixed reality; they are like a city of the Gandharvas.
It can increase all sufferings and serves as the causal condition for hell.
Burned by the fires of sensory objects and deceived by the delusions of desire,
one revolves without ceasing, unaware that one’s own body is being consumed by flames.
From thought arises desire; from desire arises hatred.
Hatred obscures the human mind, and at death one enters hell.
Therefore, the wise person abandons desire and extinguishes hatred.
Swiftly distance yourself from delusion, and you shall reach nirvāṇa.
Knowing that sensory objects are like enemies, restrain them and take no pleasure in them;
the wise grow weary of sensory objects and will certainly reach nirvāṇa.
"This is how the Bodhisattva Peacock King expounded the Buddha’s teachings for the assembly of devas.
"Furthermore, there is a twenty-second dharma that brings great benefit. What is this dharma?"
This is what is called "lack of faith.
Whether it be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other virtuous persons, one should not place trust in them even unto the end of one's life.
Such a mind is flighty and difficult to restrain; its nature is crooked and perverse, failing to abide in a single object while delighting in various objects.
Because of this mind, all foolish ordinary beings transmigrate through the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

This mind is entirely unfit for friendship; it is fickle in its engagement with objects and deludes all foolish ordinary beings, causing them to transmigrate within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Although they constantly transmigrate in this way, they do not grow weary of or seek to leave such evil habits, and thus they undergo great suffering and affliction within birth and death.
Therefore, one should not place trust in this evil mind until one has received the seal of the noble ones and attained the stage of Srotāpanna—which closes the gates to the evil realms.
If one does not do so, one will wander through all realms of existence and undergo all manner of suffering.

Bound by every fetter and ensnared by every net, with the various latent tendencies (anuśaya) combined, one is extremely difficult to subdue; therefore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not place their trust [in such things].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock King spoke in verse:
"Profound, swift, and stainless, Pervading all sentient beings—
This mind is like a king, Wandering through all the worlds."
Difficult to see and most fearsome, The light-minded create evil karma;
If one can restrain the mind, Then one reaches the supreme path.
It can lead to the place of ultimate goodness, And likewise to the evil realms.
If one is tamed and free from defilement, one then reaches nirvana.
The mind can produce suffering and pleasure; by the power of the mind, one wanders through saṃsāra.
It can perform all manner of karmas; if it is tamed, one attains happiness.
Therefore, one should guard the mind; by guarding the mind, one attains happiness.
If a person’s faculties and mind are stilled regarding sense objects, they will be liberated from the sorrows of birth and death and reach the place of non-abiding.
Thus did the Peacock King preach the true Dharma of the Tathāgata Kakutstha to the assembly of devas.
At that time, the entire assembly of devas was filled with joy; surrounding him with reverent hearts, they spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“The Great Being has eloquently expounded the sublime Dharma, excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; he has taught it for the sake of the assembly of devas, so that they may reach Nirvana.
At that time, King Peacock further addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
“In the presence of the Tathāgata Kakutstha, I heard twenty-two dharmas which, through their meaning, benefit and bring peace and happiness to gods and humans, enabling them to reach Nirvana.”
"I have proclaimed this Dharma for the benefit of the assembly of devas; therefore, I have expounded it.
At that time, the assembly of devas rejoiced and praised him; with palms joined in reverence, they paid homage and made offerings to the Bodhisattva Peacock King.

Having performed their prostrations, the hosts of the Yāma Heaven entered the lotus groves to sport and enjoy themselves, while the hosts of the Tuṣita Heaven ascended into the void and returned to the Tuṣita Heaven.

"At that time, the hosts of the Yāma devas sported and enjoyed themselves within the groves until their wholesome karma was exhausted; then, according to their own karma, they fell into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."

If there remains further karma, one will be born among human beings, into a great lineage, always acting in accordance with the Dharma, with handsome features, endowed with abundant wealth, and dwelling in a favorable land as either a king or a high minister.
This is due to the remaining karma.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the grounds where the Yāma Heaven resides.
He sees there a place called Sukhacaryā (Joyful Practice).
By what karma are sentient beings born in that land?
He knows through seeing and hearing:

if a person possesses a great mind and practices wholesome deeds, maintains the precepts with a straightforward mind, refrains from killing and stealing as previously described, and furthermore abstains from sexual misconduct.

If one sees a painting of a woman, one does not give rise to improper thoughts; seeing such an act, one encourages its abandonment and establishes others in the observance of the precepts. One constantly teaches the Dharma repeatedly for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to abide within the Dharma, and explains to all sentient beings the faults of sexual misconduct and the retribution of karmic results.

"If a person commits sexual misconduct, they become exceedingly base and lowly; when the body perishes and life ends, they fall into hell, where they undergo great suffering and affliction as the retribution for this karma.
Having made this observation, one should not engage in sexual misconduct, lest one later regret it."
"The sin of sexual misconduct brings about the retribution of great suffering.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he preached such a Dharma, causing them to abide in right conduct and rescuing them from the ways of the evil realms.

Such a person benefits both themselves and others; they uphold the precepts and rely upon them, maintaining them for as long as life lasts. Their observance of the precepts is unbroken, flawless, and unpierced; it is not outwardly real while inwardly empty. When their body perishes at the end of life, they will be reborn in a good destination, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the realm known as the Ground of Joyful Practice (Nandana).
Having been born in that heaven, they experience incomparable bliss.
There is a great pond named Sukhācara, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are cool, serene, and pure.

Furthermore, there are *mātuṅga* trees that yield sweet drinks; these are entirely made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), with leaves of pure gold and branches of blue gems (*nīlaratna*) encircling this pond for five hundred *yojanas*. Lotus flowers fill it, completely covering the waters of the pond.
Those lotuses have leaves of pure gold, stalks of lapis lazuli, and filaments of crystal.
Furthermore, there are lotuses adorned with the seven treasures.
Various lotuses cover the surface of the pond, and various birds adorned with the seven treasures emit wondrous sounds.

Countless hundreds of thousands of deva sons and deva daughters surround this pond; each deva son has countless hundreds of thousands of deva daughters as his retinue, and they enjoy themselves and experience pleasure with these deva sons due to their own past virtuous karma.
Furthermore, by the side of the pond there is a grove of seven precious jewels called Mind-Delight (*Cittarati*).
Within this grove dwell various kinds of birds; it is adorned with a hundred flowing streams, and its trees are embellished with immeasurable multitudes of jewels.
The sons of gods and goddesses, whether at the pleasure-pools or in this grove, experience the bliss of sensory objects through their five faculties by virtue of their wholesome karma.
Having been born in this celestial realm, they are drawn by the sound of singing toward the groves on the shore.

Furthermore, there are other devas who, having reached the end of their lives in this heaven and passed away, are seen by celestial maidens adorned with divine garments rushing swiftly toward the newly born deva-son to seek service for him.
"These hosts of devas abstain from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; it is as a result of such wholesome karma that they are born in this celestial realm.
Because they refrain from sexual misconduct, until their lives come to an end, the celestial maidens do not leave them to go to other devas; only upon the end of their lives do they depart."

The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three do not abstain from sexual misconduct; before their lives have ended, the celestial maidens desert them and depart as if discarding a lamp lit by day, going instead to other heavens to enjoy themselves with newly born devas through song, dance, and play.

At that time, as that deva was about to die, he saw the celestial maidens deserting him and going to others; jealousy arose in his heart, producing great suffering like the torments of hell, and because of this mental anger, he fell into hell.
In the Yāma Heaven, because sexual misconduct has been abandoned, such retribution does not exist.

For this reason, when the former demigods and their celestial maidens have departed, they all go together to the newly born deva; having arrived, they surround him and enter the great forest to experience sensual pleasures, proceeding toward the assembly of gods.

At that time, seeing the newly born deva-son, the hosts of devas were all filled with joy; together with the various devas and deva-maidens—by the tens of thousands or hundreds of millions—they proceeded to the groves and gardens.

Within those groves, wish-fulfilling trees provide adornment, and there are many various kinds of trees in immeasurable numbers; they are further adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lotus flowers, and geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks fill the ponds.
In a great pond of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits, they long performed celestial music and enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses.

Having long experienced such pleasure, they remained insatiable amidst these sensory objects; they then went with newly born devas toward Mount Universal Radiance to sport and enjoy themselves—singing, dancing, playing, and laughing—by each flower pond, each grove, each flowing spring, each mountain peak, each mountain plateau, each mountain valley, each thicket, each flowering forest, each river, and each mountain cave.

In each of the wish-fulfilling groves, the branches of every tree provide shade for the palaces; all the hosts of devas enjoy the five kinds of sensual pleasure accompanied by the sounds of the five musical instruments, beyond all comparison, as it accords with the similarity of their own karma.
They all proceeded to Mount Universal Radiance, where they sang, danced, and played, delighting one another; they knew no satiety in the pleasures of their sensory realms.
All were filled with joy, their every desire fulfilled, as they headed toward Mount Universal Radiance.
"At that time, there was a long-resident deva on the mountain who, hearing the sound of the singing, felt a sense of wonder and observed the host of devas.
Then, the host of devas all ascended Mount Universal Radiance, and the long-resident deva, seeing them, was filled with great joy."
When they first arrived, the celestial hosts all ascended into the void, adorned with immeasurable ornaments and radiant with majestic splendor, gazing upon one another.

Within these lovely mountain peaks, amidst rivers, springs, flowing waters, lotus ponds, and groves, and within palaces adorned with the radiance of the seven treasures and the majesty of forest trees, the gods who delight in pleasure experienced great bliss.

Sometimes they are in lotus ponds, sometimes on riverbanks, sometimes in groves, or amidst wish-fulfilling trees; sometimes they fly through the air to other places. Some engage in song and dance, while others are surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens; they drink the nectar of the heavens, remaining free from intoxication and disorder.
Having drunk the supreme flavor, their joy increases further; driven by these two factors, they are scorched by the fire of sensory objects, their joy like smoke.
At that time, there was a bird named Real Wisdom (Tattvajñāna) who, seeing the hosts of devas indulging in the pleasures of negligence, spoke in verse:
"The five fires blaze everywhere, Fanned by the winds of craving."
Deluded by various desires, they are consumed by the fire of negligence;
when their past karma is about to be exhausted, yet they do not create new karma,
they fall back once their karma is spent— such is the fate of all the devas.
When the time comes to fall away from that state, the mind is afflicted by suffering and destruction;
there is no one able to save them, except for their own wholesome karma.
Delighting in wealth and pleasure, they are ever enamored with the celestial maidens.
Deceived by one's own mind, one shall go to a place of great suffering;
destroyed by impermanence, how can one fail to realize this?
When life finally comes to an end, all things are separated.
Because the mind covets sensory objects, it is deceived by its own karma;
the days of one's life pass away moment by moment, as the heart is destroyed by craving.
It is like a painted wall that crumbles, where all the colorful designs likewise vanish.
Because their karma is exhausted, the celestial rewards are likewise lost.
The five faculties crave sensory objects and never know satiety;
like pouring clarified butter onto a fire, they burn with insatiable intensity.
"In this way, the bird Real Wisdom (Tattvajñāna) spoke these verses on the Dharma in order to sever the heedless minds of the celestial hosts.

At that time, because they were deluded by heedlessness, the celestial hosts did not accept them; with heedless hearts, they sported together with the celestial maidens—some flying through the void, others ascending Mount Mahāprabhāsa. Having ascended that mountain, the radiance of their bodies surpassed that of a hundred thousand suns."
That mountain was already radiant with the light of the seven treasures, but by virtue of the celestial light, it became even more sublime.
Within the mountain were countless gardens and groves of various jewels; by virtue of the celestial light, they became ten times more magnificent.

Furthermore, there were other devas in the groves or amidst lotuses, or in palatial chambers shaded by branches and leaves and adorned with the radiance of various jewels; while they were sporting, singing, and dancing to enjoy celestial pleasures, they beheld this light and experienced what they had never known before.

At that time, having finished their amusements in the groves, the hosts of devas all proceeded toward the delightful Lotus Pond to play and enjoy themselves. Cherishing one another and free from envy, they ascended the mountain of seven-jeweled light with composure, singing, dancing, and laughing. Free from fear, free from anger, sorrow, and grief, and no longer subject to others, they moved according to their own will, experiencing supreme bliss. They indulged in the pleasures of sound, their songs and dances were performed at will, and they enjoyed the food of *sudhā* and exquisite drinks as they desired; filled with the highest joy, they played and entertained themselves, experiencing the fruits of their own karma.
After having thus enjoyed celestial pleasures for a long time, they proceed toward the Lake of Joyful Vision (*Priyadarśana*).

That lotus lake is ten *yojanas* in length and five *yojanas* in width; it is exceedingly delightful, filled with many birds—geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks—and golden lotuses completely cover its waters. The entire bottom of the lake is paved with blue lapis lazuli, blue *indranīla* gems, great sapphire kings, and red lotus jewels.
All around the banks of this pond grow trees with stems of gold, branches and leaves of silver, or branches of blue beryl and leaves of red lotus.
There are also trees of lapis lazuli with branches of crystal and leaves of gold.
There were great sapphire trees with branches of white silver and leaves of gold;
there were trees of lapis lazuli with branches of great sapphire and leaves made of the two jewels of pure gold and mother-of-pearl.
There are some golden trees with golden leaves and golden branches that surpass the radiance of the sun.
There are also some golden trees with beryl branches and beryl leaves like gathered clouds, adorned and lovely to behold.
There are some golden trees, with golden branches and golden leaves like masses of fire.
There are some silver trees, with silver branches and silver leaves, their radiance upright and magnificent, like the full moon.
Some are king-blue-jewel trees with branches and leaves of king-blue-jewel, their color and form as majestic and beautiful as the smoke of aloeswood.
There are also jewel trees adorned with various kinds of branches and twigs; some have branches of white silver, decorated with king-blue-jewels.
Furthermore, there are jewel trees adorned with gold and silver;
further, there are jewel trees adorned with the three kinds—gold, silver, and crystal;
and further, there are jewel trees adorned with red lotus jewels and white silver.
Furthermore, there are jewel trees of various colors, fully endowed with manifold flowers, adorned with *mandārava* and *kūṣmāṇḍa* blossoms.
There are also fruit trees whose juice possesses a flavor that even the finest celestial nectar cannot equal.
Furthermore, there are flowering trees whose fragrance pervades a hundred yojanas.
There are also sound-trees; when stirred by a gentle breeze, their music surpasses that of the gandharvas.
There are also various trees which bring joy and delight to those who behold them; their colors and forms cannot be equaled by the most exquisite paintings or ornaments.
Furthermore, there is a jewel tree named Fragrant Smoke; various kinds of fragrant smoke issue forth from this tree, and when the devas smell it, they all rejoice greatly.
Many such various jewel trees surround the Lake of Delightful Sight.

At that time, when the hosts of devas beheld this pond, they experienced what they had never known before. Some ate its fruits or drank its juice; some, together with celestial maidens, gathered flowers for adornment; some entered the celestial groves and gardens to drink exquisite flavors, sporting, laughing, singing, and dancing with the celestial maidens; some entered the lotus forests to frolic and enjoy pleasure; some ate *sūdha* food; some sons of gods, together with celestial maidens, soared through the void; and some sons of gods, together with celestial maidens, ascended palaces made of the seven treasures to experience various sensual delights.
Thus, these hosts of devas enjoy the pleasures of the five senses within the lotus ponds, never knowing satiety amidst their sensory objects.

Because of their craving, they know no contentment; it is just as when clarified butter is poured into a fire or dry wood is being consumed by flames—their lack of satiety regarding the objects of sensual desire is likewise so.

At that time, there were many birds in the lotus pond. Among them was a king of geese named Kāla (Good Time), who was a great bodhisattva born in the Yāma Heaven through the power of his vows. He was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of geese, just as the full moon in Jambudvīpa is surrounded by a multitude of stars in the sky.
In this way, the king of geese, surrounded by his flock of birds, did likewise.
For the benefit of the celestial hosts, he spoke in verse:
"Thus they come, go, and stay; They play, sing, dance, and laugh."
There is no greater evil than this: that one does not realize death is about to arrive.
Wherever one may go, the enemy of death cannot be avoided;
yet such foolish people still do not perceive it.
Without distinction between the poor and the wealthy, the young and the old,
whether living at home or having gone forth, there is none who is not destroyed by death.
Whether one is a person of pleasure or a person of suffering, whether possessed of merit or devoid of merit— none escape it.
Whether possessing precepts or lacking them, there is none who is not destroyed by death.
Whether one upholds the precepts or breaks them, whether wise or foolish,
whether a king or a commoner— all are destroyed by death.
Whether in heaven or in hell, whether as hungry ghosts or animals—
whether heedless or heedful— all are destroyed by death.
Whether born in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm, [all are destroyed by death].
Thus, within these three realms, all are destroyed by death.
The net of karma is destroyed by old age; the suffering of illness possesses great power.
This death is like a yakṣa, seizing and binding all sentient beings.
Such is the fear of death, the greatest and most violent of terrors;
yet the gods, deluded by desire, should weep but instead laugh.
Thus they habitually pursue sensual desires, though desire is the cause of suffering and affliction.
Through habitual proximity, [desire] increases further, like ghee or oil poured onto a fire.
Desire can destroy wholesome dharmas; it is sweet at first but leads to unrest later.
Desire is the cause of manifold sufferings, resulting in great decline and affliction in the end.
Sensual desire is initially without peace, and it remains so in the middle and at the end;
it is neither hope nor attainment, nor is it a cause for tranquility.
Regarding the sensory faculties and their objects, beings are deluded and attached to them in various ways.
Fools crave sensual pleasures; for this reason, they fall into hell.
If one shares in pleasure with the deluded, one will encounter suffering in accordance with that experience.
This enemy feigns intimacy; he is capable of harming all people.

"When the Goose King Kāla had thus spoken these verses for the sake of the heedless devas, the host of devas, being deluded by desire, did not listen to or accept this Dharma, even though they heard the Goose King speak it."

Within the groves, the lotus groves, and the orchards of fruit trees, there were fragrant and pure chambers shaded by the overhanging branches. Countless hundreds of thousands of bees produced exquisite sounds, while the hosts of devas and devīs each sang and danced together, emitting wondrous voices beyond all comparison.
Furthermore, there were hosts of devas sitting upon the precious celestial ground, beholding lovely lotus ponds and experiencing the fruits of their own karma.
Surveying the entire assembly of devas, the Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, reflected thus:
"Do these hosts of devas lack consciousness?"
They do not realize that they will certainly undergo great suffering and affliction.
When one is about to fall from the heavens, there are five signs of fear. What are these five?

First, all the beloved, delightful, and cherished celestial maidens, who shared the same karma as the devas, will no longer be united with them; this great suffering of separation from what is loved is the first suffering.
Second, the delightful and pleasurable realms of the devas no longer remain in union, and one is separated from them.
This is the second great suffering of decline and disappearance.

Third, at the time of their downfall, they see other hosts of devas sporting and enjoying pleasures; observing themselves as being like lamps about to go out, blown by the winds of karma and not knowing where they shall go, they experience mental anguish exceeding that of the hells.
This is called the third great suffering of falling away.

Fourth, when one is about to fall away, one clearly sees for oneself the place where one will be reborn—whether it be in hell, as a hungry ghost, or among animals. Because one sees the place of rebirth, a great remorse arises in the mind; scorched by the fire of remorse, one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
This is called the fourth great suffering of retrogression.
Fifth, at the time of retrogression, one undergoes great anguish and distress, thinking:
"In the past, I heard the Dharma taught by my spiritual friends; yet, due to negligence, I was greedily attached to sensory objects and neither listened nor practiced it."
"It is because of negligence and because of craving for sensory objects. He further thought:
"I have committed unwholesome deeds, failed to listen to and receive the Dharma, failed to uphold the precepts, and failed to accumulate wisdom."
"Since my birth, I have been deceived by heedlessness; now the fire of remorse burns my heart, and the ropes of karma bind me and carry me away, all because of heedlessness."
These are the five kinds of great suffering experienced by the devas at the time of their passing away.
Thus, the hosts of devas do not perceive or understand this; they are deceived by heedlessness and destroyed by craving.
The Goose King Śubhakāla reflected single-mindedly, wishing to employ a skillful means:
"By what skillful means shall I preach the Dharma for these devas so that they may attain wholesome karma?"
At that time, after the Bodhisattva, the King of Geese, had reflected for a long while, he spoke these verses of aspiration for the sake of benefiting others:
"Always practicing precepts and generosity, Compassionately pitying all sentient beings,
And accomplishing all tasks— For this reason, one should uphold the precepts."
In harmony with compassion, far removed from longing, one benefits all sentient beings; whatever is undertaken shall surely be accomplished.
With courage and without deceit, one constantly practices the gift of Dharma.
Far removed from stinginess, envy, and malice, one’s undertakings will surely succeed.
One who maintains the precepts and dwells in tranquility, who honors and makes offerings to the teacher,
and who knows what should and should not be done— such a person’s undertakings will surely succeed.
Free from flattery, crookedness, and malice, one always speaks pleasant words;
being sincere and not deceitful, whatever one undertakes will surely succeed.
Knowing the proper place and knowing the proper time, one knows what should and should not be done.
"Knowing what is possible and what is impossible, one's undertakings will surely be accomplished.
Thus, the King of Geese, knowing the Dharma and practicing it, acted as a teacher of the Dharma, benefiting sentient beings through the accomplishment of the Dharma.
"This deva is negligent; how can I preach the Dharma for him so that he may abandon negligence?
Having reflected thus for a long time, he recalled his former birth:
"In the past, when I was born in Jambudvīpa, I heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One Kāśyapa; I should now preach it."
At that time, I was born into the family of a great elder in Jambudvīpa as the son of an elder, named Utpaladatta.

That Tathāgata, knowing that my life had come to an end, foresaw that I would be reborn in the realm of Yāma Heaven, the Land of Joyful Practice, and wished for me to be born as a king of geese to proclaim my Dharma for the sake of the heedless sons of gods. Now is precisely the right time; you should proclaim it for them.

At that time, the goose king, having reflected thus, with a pure mind seeking to benefit the host of devas and out of compassion for them and their aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, went to the place where the host of devas enjoyed the five desires and stayed there, surrounded by his flock of geese.

He saw those hosts of devas sporting in mountain forests, or wandering in flower gardens, or in palace chambers shaded by branches and leaves; or some were seated in precious palaces in the void, while other sons of gods, together with various celestial maidens, partook of the *sudarśana* (exquisite) food.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Goose King thought to himself:
"Now is the very moment; I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of these heedless devas.
I shall now employ my exquisite and beautiful voice to recite verses, thereby eclipsing the songs of the deva sons and deva daughters."

"The devas and devīs, being attached to desire and negligent, do not hear the Dharma; yet upon hearing my voice, their auditory consciousness will find delight, and they will surely come to where I am.

Having formed this thought, he emitted a wondrous sound, recollecting the Buddha’s merits and giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion. He ascended the mountain of seven jewels, surrounded by a flock of geese extending for ten *yojanas*, and with incomparable, sublime tones, he spoke in verse:
"Before the time of death arrives, One should practice and cultivate merit."
Do not seek to preserve your own life, lest you feel regret in a future existence.
To act with negligence is called the place of death;
to act without negligence is the foremost state of immortality.
If one acts with negligence, this path is not tranquility;
by relying on heedfulness, wisdom attains nirvāṇa.
O hosts of devas, do not be negligent; negligence is not tranquility.
Because it is not the practice of tranquility, one falls into hell.
Whether one has already fallen, is about to fall, or is falling now, all such losses are due to the fault of negligence; thus has the Tathāgata spoken.
"Therefore, at all times, one should diligently apply oneself with vigor and remain far removed from negligence; thus, one shall attain the Dharma of tranquility.

Thus did the Bodhisattva Goose King ascend that mountain and, with a sublime voice, recite these verses, completely eclipsing the songs of the celestial maidens so that their voices no longer seemed beautiful.
At that time, upon hearing the voice of the goose king, the hosts of devas all conceived a sense of love and delight.

All the devas throughout the mountain experienced what they had never known before, perceiving it as the sound of song; with minds of craving and attachment rather than reverence for the Dharma, they all came toward the mountain peak to where the goose king was.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Goose King again recited verses as previously described; when the hosts of devas, the devaputras, and the devakanyās heard his voice, their hearts were all moved to accord with it.
"In this way, when he was among humans as the son of a great elder named Utpaladatta, he heard the True Dharma from the presence of the Buddha Kanakamuni and was thus reborn here."

Now, with a wondrous voice, he proclaims and expounds that which is supreme, marvelous, and peerless; the sons of gods and daughters of gods listen with single-minded attention to what the King of Geese says.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-two [and] Fascicle Sixty-three.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on Contemplating the Heavens, Part Forty-two; The Night-Moving Heaven (Yāma), Section Twenty-eight:
"At that time, the Goose King addressed the assembly of devas, saying:"
"One should always listen to the Dharma and not act with negligence; one should draw near to virtuous friends who are able to benefit others and go to them to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the True Dharma, because of one's reverence for it, that person’s wholesome mind will lead even unto Nirvana and the great bliss of the exhaustion of outflows."
There are two kinds of persons born with Brahma-merit:
first, those who maintain it through skillful observation;
second, those who seek the exhaustion of outflows.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, constantly preaching the Dharma;
second, constantly listening to the Dharma.
Such a Dharma teacher is like a parent; preaching the Dharma for others, they enable them to transcend birth and death and attain the ultimate wholesome Dharma.
Such a Dharma teacher is like a parent; as one who preaches the Dharma, they bestow the gift of the Dharma.
The donor of the Dharma causes others to hear the Dharma; once they have heard it, their minds attain purity and they develop a straightforward mind of reverence.
The person who hears the Dharma obtains thirty-two merits.

What are these thirty-two? When a Dharma Master preaches the Dharma, he is like a parent to those who listen; in the midst of birth and death, he is like a bridge. That is to say: hearing what has not been heard before; having heard it, awakening to its meaning; having understood it, reflecting upon it; having reflected, entering into practice;
having practiced, being able to abide securely; establishing others in that state; deliberating together with them; and remaining unmoved in heart even when encountering decline or affliction.
Those who have not yet planted roots of goodness are able to plant them through the power of superior reflection;
those whose faculties are matured attain liberation; those with wrong views are led into right view;
if unwholesome thoughts arise, they are able to extinguish them, increasing the wholesome mind and severing the conditions for unwholesomeness through the practice of heedfulness.
One draws near to virtuous people and abandons stinginess and crookedness;
one makes offerings to one's parents, believes in the retribution of karmic actions, and accumulates the karma for long life;
one is praised by the people of the world and protected by the devas; one’s aspirations are fulfilled, and one attains happiness in accordance with the Dharma.
Being free from indolence, one arouses diligent vigor;
knowing gratitude and repaying kindness;
and constantly cultivating mindfulness of death.
At the time of death, one’s mind will be free from regret, and one will ultimately attain nirvana.
Such are the thirty-two merits of listening to the Dharma.

The teacher who expounds the Dharma is like a parent; they provide ultimate benefit by teaching the Dharma to others. They teach with an unclouded mind, benefiting sentient beings with a pure heart and bringing them to the realization of wisdom.
Having heard this Dharma, they will obtain liberation from within birth and death, just as the Buddha benefits beings.

Those who hear the Dharma have wandered through birth and death since beginningless time without ever hearing it; having now first heard it from the Dharma Master, they give rise to a sense of rare wonder. They are like those born blind whose cataracts are cleared away by a skilled physician, enabling them to see the various forms and images of the world—those various wondrous colors they had never seen before—and upon seeing them, they rejoice.

Thus, these sentient beings, who have wandered through birth and death since beginningless time, blinded by the power of ignorance, now hear the True Dharma. Regarding the various roots of goodness on the stages of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) and the four Noble Truths that are so dear, they have never before heard the light of the meaning of the sutras; seeing this, they rejoice. Just as one born blind rejoices upon seeing forms, so too do they experience joy in their hearts upon seeing the stages of the factors of enlightenment.
This is called the foremost merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the second merit of hearing the Dharma is that,
by virtue of hearing the Dharma, one reflects upon it with internal thought:
"What is the meaning of 'Dharma'?
If one does not understand it oneself, one should inquire of another:
"What is the meaning of such a Dharma?"
This listener hears the Dharma from another and further reflects upon it personally; through this reflection, they cultivate and increase their understanding.

Because they explain the meaning of the Dharma, their words are coherent from beginning to end. They receive and uphold it with a sincere mind, repeatedly contemplating its meaning; through such contemplation, their mind becomes joyful.
"In this way and that way, according to what one contemplates, recollects, and observes, one penetrates the profound meaning.
This is the second merit of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, the third merit of hearing the Dharma is as follows:"
In accordance with the Dharma he has heard, having heard it, he reflects:
"For what purpose was this meaning spoken?
For what causes and conditions was this meaning spoken?"
"This meaning was proclaimed for the purpose of taming sentient beings.
Furthermore, by deliberating together with those of like mind and like practice, contemplating from beginning to end, one attains great benefit and ultimately achieves nirvana.
This is called the third merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the fourth merit of hearing the Dharma is to contemplate the meaning of the teachings given before and after, and to receive them with full understanding."
To thoroughly understand the recipient is called "the meaning as it has been taught.

One should practice by gathering and undertaking the actions of body, speech, and mind; perform the three types of wholesome karma; cultivate and increase [these virtues]; and embrace the teaching of the Dharma.

With a pure mind, having already received and upheld [the teaching], one contemplates each sentence, seeking out its causes and conditions; according to what is contemplated, as one reflects, one attains meanings never before encountered.

Because they have attained the meaning [of the Dharma], they are able to extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), and are fully capable of embracing immeasurable merit, precepts, generosity, and wisdom; this is because their profound resolve is superior and because of their precepts, generosity, and wisdom.
This is called the fourth merit of hearing the Dharma; one should joyfully practice it, cultivating and expanding it.
"Furthermore, there is the fifth merit of hearing the Dharma."
Having properly heard and properly restrained the three types of action, he cultivates them with firmness himself and dwells securely in the Dharma.
Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or householders, they say of this good man: "He dwells in the True Dharma and practices according to what he has heard."

Practicing in this way, one is able to know one's own abiding and further embraces the Dharma; according to that abiding, one can extinguish hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas of birth and death numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of trillions, and can extinguish the immeasurable sufferings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
This is called the great mass of merit from hearing the Dharma; by practicing and drawing near to it, one gains much benefit.
The person who preaches the Dharma shows others nirvana, just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One, causing them to abide within the Dharma.
This is the fifth merit of hearing the Dharma, because one listens to the true Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the sixth merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"

That is to say, while abiding in the Dharma for oneself, one establishes others so that they become vessels of the Dharma, causing them to weary of birth and death and showing them the place of peace. By teaching suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one generates merit through both one’s own body and the bodies of others. Because one benefits others, one attains great merit; as the Dharma one hears increases further and further, the destruction of afflictions likewise proceeds accordingly. Because afflictions are extinguished, one attains Nirvana.
By hearing the true Dharma, one attains these merits; this is called the sixth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what are the merits of the seventh merit of hearing the Dharma, which are cultivated and expanded?
This means that when encountering decline and affliction, one’s mind does not regress.

Because one has heard of karmic retribution, although one encounters decline and affliction, the mind does not sink or retreat; one does not commit evil deeds, does not engage in evil speech, does not harbor evil thoughts, and does not destroy one's courageous vigor.
This is called the seventh merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the eighth merit of hearing the Dharma? It is this merit:

whether seeing others or knowing that others have come to seek the Dharma, or to hear the Dharma, or to seek the precepts, or to seek wisdom, one should set aside pride and provide explanations for them, analyzing the various points according to their inquiries and making them shallow and easy to understand."
This is called the eighth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the ninth merit of hearing the Dharma:
one who hears the True Dharma plants the seeds of roots of goodness; it is like a rice field whose embankments are not broken, where clear water is released and seeds are sown so that sprouts grow."
When one goes to where a Dharma Master resides to hear the True Dharma, it is likewise like sowing seeds of goodness in the field of the ears and within the boundaries of the mind.
When they reach maturity, one harvests many fruits, thereby rescuing beings from the famine and terrors of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Because they rescue those in the three evil realms, all manner of suffering is completely severed and extinguished.
Because they dwell in the wilderness, liberating themselves from all places of fear, they attain entry into the state of unsurpassed quiescence.
Because of the teaching of the Dharma, one attains entry into Nirvana.

A person who teaches the Dharma is like the World-Honored One; therefore, the merit of listening to the Dharma is the foremost among all means of transcending birth and death. One should always draw near to it, listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion, and, having heard it, practice accordingly.
This is called the ninth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the tenth merit of hearing the Dharma?
Having already planted the seed of hearing the Dharma, one should skillfully protect and maintain it so that it reaches maturity."
If a person hears the Dharma and constantly practices it through the seeds of their roots of goodness, they will achieve accomplishment.
It is like a rice field where seeds are sown at the proper time; when illuminated by the sun's light, the harvest ripens as the season arrives.
It is likewise with those who hear the Dharma: they plant various roots of goodness, which the sun of wisdom causes to reach fulfillment.
For this reason, one should always go to places where the Dharma is preached to listen to and receive the True Dharma.
This is called the tenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the eleventh merit of hearing the Dharma, and how is such a merit accomplished?
With the roots of goodness of the mind, one constantly attends Dharma assemblies to hear the True Dharma; having heard it, one upholds it, contemplates it, and internalizes it.
By these causes and conditions, the mind is brought under control and afflictions are extinguished; because afflictions are exhausted, one attains liberation.
Because of liberation, one becomes weary of conditioned phenomena and should reflect thus:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"All these arise from the merit of hearing the Dharma; therefore, one should constantly listen to the True Dharma.
This is called the eleventh merit of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, the twelfth merit of hearing the Dharma has a distinct skillful means; it is a great merit and the cause of liberation."
What are these merits?
They are as follows: causing those with wrong views to enter into right view.

Having been wandering in birth and death since beginningless time, they hear evil teachings and embrace wrong views; because of these wrong views, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If one hears the true Dharma, delights in practicing and drawing near to it, and cultivates it so that it increases and expands, one can abandon wrong views, practice the true Dharma, increase right wisdom, and attain the supreme bliss—the bliss of non-deception.
"Because of listening to the Dharma, one practices and increases [virtue].
This is called the twelfth merit of hearing the Dharma.
'Furthermore, what is the thirteenth merit of hearing the Dharma, and what merit is practiced, cultivated, and expanded?'"
That is to say, if even a slight unwholesome thought arises, one is able to immediately sever it.
If a sensual thought arises, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity to extinguish it.
If anger arises, one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness.
If deluded thoughts arise, one should observe the twelve links of dependent origination as the remedy to sever and extinguish them.
It is through hearing the Dharma that one knows these remedial methods; it is not by not hearing the Dharma.

Because of hearing the Dharma, one can even extinguish such subtle discursive thoughts (*vitarka* and *vicāra*) regarding the three unwholesome roots; how much more so for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Therefore, hearing the Dharma is a great merit.
This is called the thirteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the fourteenth merit of hearing the Dharma:
by virtue of hearing the Dharma, one extinguishes unwholesome thoughts and discursive reflections, just as sunlight extinguishes the darkness."
Wisdom is likewise: it can extinguish all the darkness of unwholesome states, cause the Dharma to increase, and diminish the afflictions.
Apart from hearing the true Dharma, it cannot be extinguished.
This is the fourteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the fifteenth merit of hearing the Dharma is that it is able to cause wholesome states of mind to increase."

By the power of this merit from hearing the Dharma, not only are unwholesome thoughts and reflections extinguished, but wholesome contemplation is further increased; because wholesome contemplation increases, one thereby attains wisdom.
For example, if a small fire is placed among grass and wood, it increases when fanned by the wind;
the arising of even a small root of goodness is likewise, for through wisdom, it attains growth.

If one hears the True Dharma, listens to and receives its meaning, and gives rise to even a single thought of goodness, it can extinguish the cycle of birth and death for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, ensuring that one is not born again.
Having understood that such are the merits of hearing the Dharma, one should diligently listen to the Dharma; for no other dharma can provide this protection as effectively.
By virtue of hearing the Dharma, one becomes a great donor and practices generosity.
Because of hearing the Dharma, one abandons what is not the Dharma.
Because of hearing the Dharma, one attains wisdom.

Having observed that such merits of listening to the Dharma can bring about transcendence from birth and death, one should apply oneself with diligence, listening to the True Dharma with earnest effort until the end of one's life.
Listening to the Dharma in this way is the foremost protection and the supreme refuge; it enables one to emerge from the ocean of existence.
This is called the fifteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the sixteenth merit of hearing the Dharma: what is this merit?
It is the ability to avoid unwholesome conditions.
If unwholesome conditions arise, one contemplates the terrors of the evil realms."
The wise person, having observed this, abandons it and fears birth and death.
If unwholesome conditions arise, they avoid them and do not act upon them;
for the sake of their non-arising, they diligently practice vigor, maintaining ethical discipline and wisdom.
If a mind of greed arises, one should practice generosity.
If a mind of stinginess arises, one should extinguish it by means of non-greed.
With a mind of wisdom, one should destroy delusion.
By seeing things as they truly are, one extinguishes unwholesome contemplation.
By means of a mind of right view, one severs wrong views.
By means of right awakening and contemplation, one severs deluded discrimination.
If the perception of pleasure arises, one should contemplate all things as suffering.
If the perception of reality arises, one should cultivate the contemplation of emptiness.
If the perception of self arises, one should contemplate non-self.
This is the correct antidote for applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*): if they arise through causes and conditions, one should distance oneself from them;
whether they are subtle, coarse, or middling, one should sever and extinguish them.
All that arises from unwholesome causes and conditions can be avoided by hearing the True Dharma; if one does not hear the Dharma, one cannot avoid them.
Hearing all the Dharma is like finding secure concealment.
This is called the sixteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the seventeenth merit of hearing the Dharma?
It is that by means of hearing the Dharma, those who are negligent extinguish unwholesome thoughts and reflections, and practice non-negligence."
A person who is heedful can restrain the sense faculties, and all wholesome dharmas will increase.
A person who is heedful can sever all unwholesome dharmas; such a person is not far from nirvana and shall attain all peace and happiness.
By what causes and conditions is heedlessness abandoned?
It is by hearing the true Dharma.
Because one hears the true Dharma, one understands the faults of heedlessness and is thus able to avoid it from afar.

By hearing the True Dharma, one is able to discipline the faculties; by disciplining the five faculties, one is then able to collect the mind. As wholesome mindfulness increases and unwholesome thoughts and reflections are extinguished, through this skillful contemplation, one attains the supreme bliss.
All afflictions have heedlessness as their root, just as among all wholesome dharmas, the mind of heedfulness is the foundation. Because one hears the true Dharma, one eliminates heedlessness;
therefore, sentient beings should always listen to and receive the true Dharma with a single-minded focus, and having heard it, they should practice, cultivating and increasing [their realization].
This is called the seventeenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is the eighteenth merit of hearing the Dharma? It is this:
by virtue of hearing the true Dharma, one draws near to virtuous friends, makes offerings to noble persons, cherishes and honors them, and reflects upon and deliberates with them.
By associating with virtuous friends, one attains great merit; if one associates with evil friends, one incurs many faults.

There is no other dharma for attaining association with virtuous friends like hearing the True Dharma; because one hears the True Dharma, one attains association with virtuous friends. Therefore, the foremost holy life consists in associating with virtuous friends.
This is called the eighteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the nineteenth merit of hearing the Dharma?
It is that by hearing the True Dharma, one is able to sever the mind of deceit, fraud, stinginess, and envy."
If one associates with virtuous friends, what merits will be attained?
By associating with virtuous friends, one attains superior merits, namely, the ability to sever deceit, fraud, stinginess, and envy.
Because of hearing the Dharma, one is able to believe in karma and its retribution as they truly are.

If there are sentient beings who are deceitful, fraudulent, stingy, and envious, at the dissolution of the body after death they will fall into the evil realms, or into the realm of hungry ghosts, or into hell.

If they have habitually practiced much deceit, fraudulence, stinginess, and envy, by hearing the True Dharma they are immediately able to abandon and distance themselves from them; they cease to practice such things and feel weary of, renounce, and repent for what they previously did.

Seeing others being deceitful and fraudulent, they exhort them not to do so, causing others to feel weary of and renounce such acts, repent for their past deeds, and establish them in the good realms.
By hearing the true Dharma, one attains this merit, which is the foremost and most steadfast among gods and humans—namely, the hearing of the true Dharma.
This is the nineteenth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the twentieth merit of hearing the Dharma: what is this merit?
It is that having heard the Dharma, one makes offerings to one's parents, understands the retribution of karmic actions, and recognizes the field of merit; this is a supreme merit."

The foremost field of merit is one's father and mother; knowing this through the causal conditions of karmic retribution, one is able to provide various offerings to one's parents, such as many kinds of bedding and necessities for medical treatment during illness. According to the offerings made to one's parents in this way, one can generate Brahma-merit.
By virtue of this merit, one shall later attain nirvana.

Furthermore, by making offerings to one's parents through hearing the Dharma, one will be beloved by all people; in the present life, one will be praised by everyone, and after the end of life, one will be reborn in the happy realms, receiving the body of a deva. By the power of hearing the Dharma, one will ultimately attain nirvana.

Therefore, the wise, knowing these merits, should always make offerings to their parents—the field of merit—even at the cost of their own lives; they should practice with right conduct and right intention, honoring them with single-minded reverence.
This is called the twentieth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the twenty-first merit of hearing the Dharma is what is known as knowing the retribution of karmic actions."
Because he understands karmic retribution, he does not delight in heterodox teachings; for by hearing the True Dharma, he is able to know the fruits of karma.

If he contemplates what is unwholesome, he knows that his thought is unwholesome; if his mind contemplates what is wholesome, he knows that his thought is wholesome, thus knowing the fruits of karma as they truly are.

If the mind contemplates unwholesome dharmas, one knows that after such unwholesome thoughts, there will be the attainment of unwholesome and undesirable retributions, leading to rebirth in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal; because of this knowledge, one no longer gives rise to unwholesome thoughts.
"By means of these unwholesome deeds, one can know with certainty that one will receive an undesirable retribution and fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Because of the conditions created by such evil karma, my own body shall inevitably fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals."
"These three types of karma are understood through hearing the true Dharma; apart from hearing the Dharma, there is nothing else by which they can be known.
Therefore, a wise person should always listen to the Dharma, even at the cost of their life."
If one constantly hears the Dharma and cultivates wholesome karma, one will not commit unwholesome deeds.
This is called the twenty-first merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the twenty-second merit of hearing the Dharma: what is this merit?
It is the ability to accumulate and increase the karma for long life."

By hearing the true Dharma, one gains faith in the retribution of karmic actions and refrains from committing deeds such as killing or stealing; by joyfully cultivating and expanding whatever wholesome karma one performs, one is reborn among gods or humans with an extended lifespan.
Because they hear the true Dharma and delight in cultivating and expanding it, they further obtain such merit as this, with their lifespan extended.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma, they are reborn among gods and humans.
If one is born in the heavens, one will have the longest lifespan among the other celestial hosts, enjoying the foremost pleasures of food, drink, and play.

Because of having heard the Dharma, if one is born among humans, one will possess various forms of physical strength, wealth, and long life; one will be born in a noble land, constantly practice right view, and through hearing the true Dharma, delight in its cultivation and expansion, thereby surely attaining liberation from suffering.
If a person can listen to the Dharma with a virtuous mind, it is the foremost merit.
For the sake of listening to the Dharma, even taking a single step generates Brahma-merit.
One who listens to the True Dharma constantly practices listening to the Dharma and thereby attains wholesome bodily karma.
Having heard it, one recites and studies it, thereby attaining wholesome verbal karma;
having heard it, the mind becomes pure, thereby attaining wholesome mental karma.

Because these three types of karma are wholesome, the listener is born among gods and humans, experiencing the foremost and most excellent wealth and happiness, with a long life span, and ultimately attains nirvana.
All such great merits as these arise solely from hearing the Dharma and cannot be obtained by any other means; therefore, hearing the Dharma is the foremost source of peace and security.
This is called the twenty-second merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, the twenty-third merit of hearing the Dharma: what is this merit?

It is that those who hear the Dharma are praised by all people; through the merit of upholding the precepts, extensive learning, self-discipline, and superior wisdom, they are collectively honored, prostrated to, and greeted by all worldly people, and they speak with beautiful words and a straightforward mind toward everyone."
Such a person, endowed with merit, always feels dread toward even the slightest evil;
they are well-known to all and praised by everyone, and if they should encounter affliction or turmoil, all people will come to their rescue and protection.
Such a person who hears the Dharma is praised by the world.
This is called the twenty-third merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the twenty-fourth merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"
This refers to being protected and mindful of by the various devas.
