Those who hear the Dharma are in accord with wholesome karma; they practice wholesome karma through body, speech, and mind. By virtue of these merits, they are protected by the various devas.
Because of this person, the multitude is at peace;
if this person were to die, immeasurable people would be deprived of benefit.
By protecting this person, the hosts of Māra will diminish and the True Dharma will increase.
Seeing these causes and conditions, the devas therefore protect them day and night, constantly following behind them, so that whatever they do is entirely accomplished.
This is due to the power of the devas' grace and the force of their own virtuous karma; thus, they act as causes for one another.
Once those actions he has performed have been accomplished, he further cultivates and expands them according to what was done; thus, all wholesome karmas attain fulfillment.
In this sequential manner, there is benefit for both lifetimes.
Such merit from hearing the Dharma is the foremost treasury of peace and security.
This is called the twenty-fourth merit of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is the twenty-fifth merit of hearing the Dharma?
It is said that all recollections shall be accomplished.

For such a person of wisdom who practices in accordance with the Dharma, through the karmic retribution of present actions consisting of upholding the precepts and practicing generosity, all recollections shall be accomplished; whatever they undertake shall be accomplished, and nothing can rob them of it.

Whatever they do will easily achieve accomplishment; they will enjoy its fruits in accordance with the Dharma; they will be free from the five kinds of obstacles; their livelihood will be pure; they will not be controlled by others; and when the body perishes at the end of life, they will be reborn in a happy realm, receiving the body of a deva.
This is called the twenty-fifth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the twenty-sixth merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"
This is what is called wealth and happiness in accordance with the Dharma.

Those who maintain the precepts together are approached by wealthy people because they share the same observance of the precepts; they mutually bestow upon one another the wealth they have acquired, which is not obtained by harming others nor by oppressing others, but is wealth gained in accordance with the Dharma, bestowed upon those who practice the Dharma.
The merit of that person’s giving increases ever more and more, bringing benefit and peace and happiness in both worlds.
It is by virtue of hearing the Dharma that they attain this merit.
This is called the twenty-sixth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the twenty-seventh merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"
What is called wisdom is the distancing from indolence; it consists in listening to the true Dharma and hearing of the faults of indolence.
Because of indolence, one fails to achieve success in the meanings of both mundane and supramundane dharmas.

By virtue of hearing the Dharma, one abandons indolence; in all that one does, one is always diligent and perseverant, with right mindfulness undisturbed. One who is free from indolence accomplishes all tasks through skillful means with speed; acting at the proper time and in accordance with the Dharma, all things are accomplished for the benefit of both worlds.
If one is free from indolence and constantly exerts diligent effort, all that is undertaken will be brought to completion, and every aspiration will be successfully accomplished.
If one was originally indolent, by hearing the true Dharma and thereby recognizing the faults of indolence, one should swiftly abandon it, just as one would cast away a sword or fire.
Because of indolence, one can ruin all worldly undertakings;
yet by hearing of the faults of indolence, all goals and benefits will be accomplished through the power of the merit of hearing the True Dharma.
This is called the twenty-seventh merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the twenty-eighth merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"
This refers to hearing the Dharma in successive order, giving rise to a mind of gratitude, and recognizing the extent of others' kindness.

Because one hears the true Dharma explain the repayment of kindness, one contemplates repaying that kindness; and because one knows how to repay kindness, all one's relatives and friends become steadfast.
By virtue of such merit, all enemies become like close friends.
If one constantly remembers even small acts of kindness without forgetting them, and recognizes that kindness by repaying it, one will attain great merit.
This is called the twenty-eighth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the twenty-ninth merit of hearing the Dharma? What are its merits?"

What is called the practice of mindfulness of death is the foremost and most excellent mindfulness; that is to say, mindfulness of death. By constantly being mindful of death, one harbors a sense of dread; because of this dread, one does not commit unwholesome karma.
If one sees beautiful forms, one does not engage in conceptualization;
if one hears various pleasant sounds, one likewise does not dwell upon them;
and if one smells various fragrances, one does not crave them, does not delight in them, and does not dwell upon them.
If the tongue encounters flavors, one does not crave them, does not delight in them, nor dwells upon them;
if the body encounters tangibles, one does not crave them, does not delight in them, nor dwells upon them;
if the mind attends to mental phenomena, one does not crave them, does not delight in them, nor dwells upon them—thus severing and abandoning all such nets of existence.
Because such a person fears death, they contemplate that all worlds are entirely without solidity; everything is suffering, everything is without self, and everything is empty.

One who sees reality has no mind of attachment toward anything—whether among gods or humans—let alone toward the hells, hungry ghosts, or animals; having completely severed all longing within the five realms of existence, they attain liberation.
No longer taking delight in any of the sufferings of birth and death, he becomes fearful of them and weary of them.
Through this weariness and detachment, he attains liberation and the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."

If one is separated from hearing the Dharma, one cannot attain such meritorious qualities as the establishment of the holy life (brahmacarya) and renunciation; therefore, one should diligently listen to and receive the true Dharma and attend upon teachers. To provide benefit for both the present and future lives, one should approach spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and hear the true Dharma; through these two dharmas, one attains peace and security.
This is called the twenty-ninth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the thirtieth merit of hearing the True Dharma? What are its merits?"
It is said that by virtue of hearing the Dharma, one will have no regrets at the time of death.
One who cultivates mindfulness of death can swiftly sever any faults that may arise.
If the three defilements—greed, hatred, and delusion—arise as the causes and conditions for birth and death, through mindfulness of death, they can be eliminated.

By severing the three defilements, one neither arises nor dies, neither recedes nor emerges; there is no other dharma capable of severing this dharma, for it is by the power of the merit gained from hearing the Dharma that such a dharma is attained.
"Among all merits of peace and security, the merit of hearing the Dharma is the foremost root.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Goose King spoke this sutra taught by Kāñcanamuni for the sake of the assembly of devas; it accords with the True Dharma. This is the thirtieth merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the thirty-first merit of hearing the Dharma?
It is that at the time of death, one’s mind is free from regret.

If one has heard the meaning of the True Dharma and practiced wholesome deeds, then at the moment of life’s end, no remorse arises in the mind; having heard the meaning as it was taught, one recalls and contemplates it."
Having reflected thus, one’s pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha increases.

Because the mind is pure, the blood becomes pure; because the blood is pure, the complexion becomes pure; and because both body and mind are pure, at the time of death, one beholds the good realms and sees the lovely celestial abodes of white radiance.
Because they see their place of rebirth, their pure mind increases further; following that pure mind, they believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and are reborn in superior realms.
If they have performed the karma for the Four Heavenly Kings, because of their pure faith, they are born in the second heaven;
if they have the karma for the Heaven of the Thirty-three, they are born in the Yāma Heaven.
If there is karma for the Yāma Heaven, one is born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Proceeding in this manner through successive stages up to the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, one attains increasingly superior states by the power of mental purity.
All of this arises from hearing the Dharma; if one is separated from hearing the Dharma, one will ultimately never attain it.
If one listens to the True Dharma, at the time of death, it shall serve as one's salvation and refuge.
This is called the thirty-first merit of hearing the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is the thirty-second merit of hearing the Dharma? What is that merit?"
By virtue of hearing the Dharma, one will ultimately attain nirvana.
The merit of listening to the Dharma is the most excellent and supreme among all merits.
In what way is it superior?
What is called nirvāṇa:

by hearing the true Dharma, practicing and increasing it, practicing according to the teaching, and accomplishing it as it truly is, such a person will certainly be able to sever the afflictions and reach nirvāṇa.

"In this way, the Bodhisattva King of Geese, Kālaśubha, in order to sever the heedless conduct of the assembly of the Yāma devas, expounded the True Dharma with an incomparable voice; the celestial hosts all conceived a sense of wonder."
At that time, because the host of devas had heard the Buddha’s Dharma, their minds attained purity.
All the devas addressed the King of Geese, saying:
"Among these devas, you are the lord of heaven, for you possess the power of wisdom and eloquence."
"We, the host of devas, are like beasts; because of our heedlessness, we delight in sensory objects and constantly harm our own minds through the craving for desire.
The voice of the Goose King is beyond the reach of our singing."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Goose King spoke these verses in accordance with the True Dharma:
"By hearing the True Dharma, one is able to cease unwholesome states;
by being free from unwholesome states, one always attains a place of peace and security."
By hearing the True Dharma, the mind attains purity;
it enables the mind to abide securely, so that one commits no evil deeds.
Hearing the Dharma allows for total retention; hearing the Dharma prevents the creation of evil.
Hearing the Dharma, one understands the fruits of karma, and later attains nirvāṇa.
Through hearing the Dharma, one knows the Dharma; through hearing the Dharma, one gains faith in the Buddha.
Because the wise hear the Dharma, they are able to liberate themselves from all suffering.
Because of hearing the true Dharma, one is able to know the characteristics of reality;
therefore, the wise should diligently listen to the true Dharma.
Hearing the Tathāgata preach the Dharma enables one to transcend birth and death.
Having severed and abandoned the three kinds of craving, one reaches the state of the inexhaustible.

Because of hearing the True Dharma, one understands the causal conditions of the four dharmas, as well as the arising and ceasing of all phenomena; through hearing the Dharma, one is able to know them all.
By hearing the true Dharma, one thoroughly understands the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
these two kinds of characteristics are what the wise should practice.
The fault of the first great power binds all within birth and death.
By hearing the True Dharma, one can know all things;
by the great power of evil, one is bound to all of birth and death;
by hearing the True Dharma, all [afflictions] can be extinguished.
Regarding all phenomena of transition and all phenomena of non-transition,
because they have heard the supreme Dharma, they are able to know them all.
When the time of death approaches, one then undergoes great suffering and affliction.
Because of mindfulness and hearing the Dharma, the suffering of death cannot disturb them.
Because of the wisdom gained from hearing, they burn down the trees of all afflictions;
having been burned by the fire of wisdom, once extinguished, they do not arise again.
Hearing the Dharma without negligence, one attains all happiness;
through hearing the Dharma, one finds peace and security; therefore, one should listen to the Dharma.
Having heard the True Dharma, one draws near to the wise and the elders.
One can reach the unsurpassed state, forever free from old age, sickness, and death.
Because of hearing [the Dharma], one does not commit evil; because of hearing, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Through hearing the Dharma, one leaves suffering behind; thus, hearing the Dharma is the foremost thing.
By hearing the true Dharma, one attains purity of the three karmas;
those who seek purity should diligently listen to the true Dharma.
By relying on hearing the Dharma, one becomes firm and exerts diligent vigor.
This enables one to swiftly cross the vast ocean of the triple world.
The wealth of hearing the Dharma is the foremost in all the world;
yet those with much wealth who do not know its meaning, the wise declare to be poor.
Staying far away from teachers and elders, one loses the wealth of hearing the True Dharma;
such a person reaps no fruit of life and is destroyed by evil.
The heedless and indolent person draws near to evil associates.
Such a person has no fruit of life, like planting seeds in salty, barren soil.
Being far removed from the Dharma of seeing and hearing, they are truly blind.
If a person distances themselves from the Dharma and practices what is not the Dharma, [they will suffer].
Such a person abandons medicine and takes up illness;
yet if one draws near to virtuous friends, immeasurable qualities will increase,
just as rivers all swell when great rains pour down.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma in tranquility, Arising early to mind the True Dharma,
One will certainly attain peace and happiness, And shall not be deceived by negligence.
Having understood the merit of wisdom, The wise person should practice it accordingly.
"It is not those who lack wisdom who can attain peace and happiness.

Thus, for the sake of planting roots of goodness in the various hosts of devas, the Goose King Supratiṣṭhita repeatedly preached the Dharma that brings benefit, severing what is unbeneficial, and expounded the teachings of the Buddha’s sutras.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the host of devas gave rise to a mind of reverence and a mind of joy; their negligence became slight.
Because they shared common karma, they proceeded once more to another place to enjoy celestial pleasures.

After the Goose King Kāla had fully expounded for the assembly of devas the sūtra spoken by Kāñcanamuni, titled "The Sūtra on the Firmness of Hearing the Dharma through the Accumulation of Immeasurable Merit," he proceeded to another place to contemplate and reflect upon the Dharma.

The gods of the Realm of Delightful Conduct enjoy the five desires through the sounds of the five musical instruments; yet, when their beloved wholesome karma is exhausted, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals due to their evil karma.

If there remains residual karma that is similar to that of humans, they are born among men as those who are immensely wealthy and at peace, who strictly observe the prohibitions and precepts, always delight in hearing the Dharma, are foremost in accordance with the Dharma, possess wisdom and right view, and may become either kings or great ministers.
Due to the remaining karma.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, knowing the retribution of karma, contemplates the grounds where the Yāma Heaven resides. With the wisdom derived from hearing, he sees the Yāma Heaven known as the "Ground of Various Mixtures. By what karma are sentient beings born in this place?

He sees: there are people who perform wholesome karma—wholesome in body, speech, and mind; possessing right view and right livelihood; practicing wholesome conduct in its entirety; being straightforward in heart and delighting in truth; refraining from killing and stealing; and staying far removed from sexual misconduct.
If one sees a woman in a dream, the mind does not approach her, nor does one think of her during the day; with a clear mind, one reflects:
"Just as this body of mine has abandoned sexual misconduct, I shall obtain a virtuous karmic result."
"By abstaining from sexual misconduct, one will be reborn in the heavens, surrounded by celestial maidens and enjoy pleasures.
To abandon women while longing for celestial maidens and seeking them out is called a defiled holy life.
Desiring to be reborn in heaven, one abandons sexual misconduct, thinking:
"In the past, I sang, laughed, danced, and played with women; this was unwholesome and will cause me to fall into the evil realms."
For this reason, one does not give rise to desire for what was previously practiced.
As for the mind of vitarka and vicāra, one does not dwell upon former habits of song, dance, play, or laughter; should such thoughts arise in the mind, they are immediately severed and eliminated.
By these causes and conditions, at the end of his life, he is born in various mixed lands.
Having been born in this place, the fruits of his wholesome karma are realized, and the five desires come together.

Once the deva-son is born, by virtue of his wholesome karma, all manner of light from various jewels naturally arises throughout the celestial realm; that is to say, immeasurable diamond mountain peaks of various colors and lusters, such as those of vaidūrya, indranīla, mahānīlaratna, musāragalva, sphaṭika, and padmarāga, as well as hundreds of thousands of other kinds of radiance pervading the entire celestial abode.

Upon first seeing such various kinds of light, the visual consciousness becomes attached to it; having never seen them before, they take delight in seeing them. They hear various sounds, the songs and music of many instruments that are beyond all analogy, and they further smell the various exquisite celestial fragrances.
The newly born deva-son, having first conceived a mind of attachment toward these three kinds of peerless and incomparable realms, departs from the Forest of Radiance (*Prabhāvana*).
When the hosts of celestial maidens see the newly born deva-son emerging from the forest—which is thus adorned with various kinds of radiance—they approach him.
The deva-son, by means of the price of his wholesome karma, obtained these celestial maidens.

At that time, all the celestial maidens were adorned in various ways and were exceedingly beautiful; they possessed various exquisite complexions and sang various songs with the sounds of celestial music.
At that time, because his mind had been drawn by the beginningless love and desire for the celestial maidens, the deva-son approached them with a joyful heart.
Some of the celestial maidens held musical instruments in their hands and performed various kinds of music, singing many exquisite melodies.
Furthermore, there were celestial maidens who, upon smelling the fragrance of exquisite flowers, looked at the sons of gods with eyes of affection and smiling faces.
Moreover, there were celestial maidens on the ground holding musical instruments, producing sublime sounds.
Furthermore, there were celestial maidens holding exquisite flowers who rushed toward the deva-sons.

There were also celestial maidens carrying various kinds of superior celestial drinks, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, and free from the fault of intoxication; they approached the deva-sons and, having offered them celestial drinks of superior flavor, color, fragrance, and taste served on lotus leaves, increased their joy tenfold more than before.

This is the mind becoming attached to the fourth realm: first becoming attached to exquisite forms, then to sounds, fragrances, and tastes; furthermore, the body experiences various pleasant tactile sensations that are obtained the very moment they are thought of according to one's wishes. This is called the newly born deva-son’s attachment to the pleasures of the five desires.
"At that time, the newly born deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, went to the Forest of Universal Accordance with Desire to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
There, surrounded by the celestial maidens, the newly born deva-son observed the various diversions of the hosts of devas."

Some sported in thickets and forests; some sported upon mountain peaks; some sported while producing the sounds of the five kinds of music; some devaputras, together with various celestial maidens adorned in diverse ornaments, sported and enjoyed themselves in palaces in the void; some devaputras, grasping tree branches with their hands, sang, danced, and laughed amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.

At that time, the newly born deva-son, seeing the various hosts of devas thus sporting and playing, felt joy arise in his heart; surrounded by celestial maidens, he entered among the deva hosts and joined them in harmonious play.
The newly born deva-son, together with the celestial maidens, sports and enjoys pleasures; according to his own karma, he experiences the delights of the five senses.

Having enjoyed these pleasures for a long time, he emerges from the grove and ascends again to various mountains adorned with diverse jewels. There, they entertain one another, sporting and enjoying themselves—whether by flowing springs, in gardens, or on mountains adorned with various precious gems, where cool, clear waters provide ornamentation—and they play within them.
At that time, while the hosts of devas were indulging in heedlessness, there was a celestial bird named Flowing Water (Jalavāhana) who, for the sake of those heedless devas, spoke these verses:
"By means of various karmas, one experiences the fruition of pleasure;
having experienced this retribution among the devas, when karma is exhausted, one shall surely fall back."
The fool experiences pleasure in the present, yet does not contemplate the fear that lies ahead;
when decline and affliction arrive, only then does he realize the nature of karma.
Bound by heedlessness, he perceives no difference between suffering and joy.
Because their celestial karma is exhausted, they later give rise to great remorse.
Heedlessness is like a poisonous harm; therefore, one should abandon it.
Heedlessness harms the gods and leads them to enter hell.
Union gives rise to joy, while separation is great suffering;
union must inevitably end in separation—such is the nature of all phenomena.
There is not a single thing in the world that, once born, does not decay.
All phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing; such is the nature of their appearance and disappearance.
According to what they perceive, the various devas experience celestial bliss;
yet, deluded by the poison of heedlessness, they all return to extinction.
All pleasures of heedlessness are initially thought to be lovely,
but when decline and affliction arrive later, one then knows them to be a great enemy.
Heedlessness and attachment to female form— these the wise declare to be a great enemy.
Attachment to sensual pleasures destroys one's body and life; the same holds true for asuras and nāgas.
Indulgence in alcohol and attachment to women, greed for various sensory objects, and a restless and indolent mind—these are the roots and sprouts of heedlessness.
"Thus did the bird Jalavāhana speak these verses to the heedless devas.

At that time, although the host of devas heard these verses, they were unaware of their meaning; overcome by their sensory realms, they sang, laughed, and played as they entered the Forest of Radiance."
That grove was lovely, its branches and leaves providing complete coverage; it abounded with various types of lush and verdant trees, and was exceedingly delightful.
At that time, the hosts of devas, together with the newly born son of heaven, played and enjoyed themselves amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.

In the groves and among the *śāla* trees, there were various flowing streams, lotus ponds, and diverse grounds where the branches of trees formed canopies like palaces. Within these various forests were trees that fulfill every desire, and various mountain valleys with the radiance of the seven jewels. Seeing such magnificent and exquisite palaces, never before seen, the hosts of devas felt a sense of wonder; how much more so the newly born son of heaven.

Thus, the newly born deva-sons surveyed everything thoroughly; sporting with the hosts of celestial maidens amidst the groves, they conceived an intense craving for these new realms, scorched by the fire of desire.
With heedlessness as its smoke, surrounded by celestial maidens, he is burned again and again.

Wandering everywhere within the groves, scorched by the power of immeasurable objects of desire, he enjoys pleasures for a long time while surrounded by celestial maidens, and then proceeds toward various lotus ponds.

That lotus pond was incomparably lovely, featuring various multicolored padma flowers with leaves of beryl, stalks of pure gold, pericarps of red-lotus gems, filaments of white silver, and adorned by swarms of bees made of blue indra-nīla jewels.

Furthermore, there were lotuses with stems of white silver and leaves of blue indra-ratna; others with stems of pure gold and leaves of blue indra-ratna; their filaments were made of red lotus-jewel, their pericarps of white silver, and they were adorned with bees of red lotus-jewel.
Furthermore, there are lotuses with stalks, leaves, filaments, and calyxes that are all entirely red, adorned by red bees.
There are also lotuses with silver stalks, silver leaves, silver filaments, and silver calyxes, adorned by silver bees.
Furthermore, there are lotuses that are entirely blue, like blue lotuses, adorned with blue leaves, blue stalks, blue filaments, blue calyxes, and blue bees.

There are also lotuses of various mixed colors; each individual lotus is interspersed with the seven treasures and adorned with various forms, various exquisite fragrances, and various colored petals—namely, adorned with blue, yellow, red, white, and dark-blue (indranīla) hues—and further embellished by various multicolored leaves and swarms of bees.
Such various lotus ponds have water that is cool and refreshing, with a sweet and delicious taste, and are exceedingly delightful.
They abound with lotuses of celestial hue, exquisite fragrance, and all perfect characteristics.
The newly born deva-son, together with a host of celestial maidens, enjoys the pleasures of the five senses amidst the sounds of the five kinds of music.
On the banks of the lotus ponds of various colors, there are groves of trees surrounding the pools; adorned by these trees, they are a hundred times more magnificent.
Those trees were fully adorned with various flowers; from their roots to their branches, they possessed every kind of flower—blue, yellow, red, white, and deep azure—in complete abundance.
That lotus pond emits a great radiance that fills ten yojanas, and many birds there produce exquisite sounds.
On the banks of the lotus pond there is also a grove of trees called "Palaces of the Sun"; due to the virtuous karma of the devas, they possess great power.
If a deva ascends a tree and thinks of a palace, it is formed immediately according to that thought.

Due to their wholesome karma, the flowers and leaves of the seven treasures transform into palaces, adorned with the seven treasures; there are many rivers, ponds, gardens, groves, and mountains, and everywhere there are many exquisitely decorated palaces.
Ascending this palace, their bodies adorned with various jewels, they engage in song, dance, and play together with the celestial maidens.
Or, flying through the void, they observe the Yāma Heaven and the various grounds upon which it rests, surveying them at will; such are these flowers, owing to the power of the trees on the banks.
Furthermore, there are various lotus ponds of diverse colors, and upon the banks of these ponds stand extraordinary trees called Maṇisvara, adorned with all kinds of birds.

By the power of these trees, when the hosts of devas sport in the flower ponds, a gentle breeze stirs them so that they brush against one another, producing wondrous sounds. Precious jewels fall from the trees like flowers, their radiance pervading the void; just as the light of the sun and moon in Jambudvīpa, so too is the brilliance of these precious jewels in the sky.
"On the banks of the lotus pond there is another extraordinary tree called 'Bestower of Food and Drink.

When the hosts of devas sport in the flower pond, through the power of their celestial good karma, celestial nectar emerges from the fruits of the tree, complete with color, fragrance, and flavor. When the deva sons drink it, their joy increases tenfold; yet they do not become intoxicated or disordered, as they continue to sing, dance, and play together with the celestial maidens."
Furthermore, there are forest trees that produce *sūdhā* food according to what is obtained through one's karma.

On the banks of the pond, there is another extraordinary tree named *Patraghoṣa*; when the hosts of devas sport by this pond, due to their virtuous karma, a gentle breeze blows, bringing them joy and happiness.

The wind blows through the leaves of the trees, causing them to rub against one another and produce wondrous sounds like the voices of celestial maidens, which cannot be distinguished; the sounds produced by all the trees are likewise thus.
"On the banks of the lotus pond there is another extraordinary tree called *Vihaga-rati* (Bird-Delight). By the power of this tree, birds remain upon it.

When the devas enter the pond to sport and enjoy themselves, making music with the five kinds of instruments to entertain one another, they may ascend the precious trees or ride celestial birds. To behold the lovely places of the deva hosts, these birds appear before them according to their every thought."
Upon that bird there was a great palace, fully equipped with many flowing springs, numerous lotus ponds, and chambered halls shaded by branches.
Furthermore, another bird addressed the assembly of devas in verse:
“The person who upholds the precepts dwells in peace; The breaker of precepts shall not live long.”
It is better to receive the body of a lowly person than to enter hell.
The wise practice in successive stages, cultivating gradually and moment by moment,
purifying the defilement of the view of self, just as a craftsman refines gold.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Fascicle 63 and Fascicle 64,
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
7. Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body (64–70). Chapter Seven: The Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body.
At that time, the Blessed One was traveling through Rājagṛha and stayed at the village of the Nālandā brahmins. He addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall now teach you the foundation of mindfulness of the body, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, perfectly complete and pure—a holy life, namely, the Dharma-gate of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.”
“Listen attentively now, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"We wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What is called the Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Body?"

This is what is called "contemplating the body as a body internally. Once a bhikṣu has practiced this contemplation, he no longer dwells within the realm of Māra and is able to abandon the afflictions.
By contemplating the body as it truly is, and having thus attained knowledge, vision, and realization of such a Dharma, I declare that such a person is encompassed by nirvāṇa.

Thus, when a bhikṣu has truly seen the body as it is, he is not disturbed by any evils; he is able to sever the internal defilements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the external objects of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena. By thus contemplating the body in accordance with reality, he is able to reach nirvāṇa.

In this way, a bhikṣu, though seeing forms with the eye, does not give rise to discrimination, nor does he arouse a mind of defiled desire or joy; he contemplates the body as it truly is, [seeing that] this body consists only of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, fat, blood, muscle, tendons, bone, and marrow; the raw and cooked viscera; phlegm, bile, and wind-disorders; the large and small intestines; the impurities of feces and urine; the liver, gallbladder, bowels, and stomach; the fat, marrow, semen, and blood; the mucus, saliva, tears, and rheum; and the skull upon the crown of the head.
Observing the body in this way and maintaining mindfulness accordingly, if one maintains such mindfulness, one will not become attached to external objects of form, sound, smell, taste, or touch.
First, one observes the eye and its forms, seeing the eye as it truly is: merely a lump of flesh, composed of the four great elements.
How does the practitioner contemplate the eye as it truly is?
He contemplates the eye-faculty: this solid portion of flesh which possesses the quality of sentience within is called the "eye-faculty, a mass of flesh, the internal earth element."

Furthermore, one contemplates that within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty there is an internal element of sensation—the moisture of tears and so forth; this is called the internal water element within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty.

Furthermore, one contemplates that within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty, there is an internal conscious phenomenon—possessing warmth and heat; this is called the internal fire element within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty.

Furthermore, one contemplates that within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty, there is a subtle internal wind moving; this is called the internal wind element within the fleshy mass of the eye faculty.

One observes this internal wind element as it truly is, and likewise observes the ear, nose, tongue, and body in accordance with this principle. Having observed in this way, one does not give rise to attachment toward pleasant forms, nor is one destroyed by objects of craving.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body. This body arises and perishes from moment to moment; it is subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.

This body is like an illusion, empty and non-existent, without reality and without solidity, like a bubble on water. It is the locus where all sufferings gather, the basis upon which all sufferings rely, and the treasury of all sufferings. Within such a body there is not even the slightest happiness; everything is suffering, everything is impermanent, and everything is subject to destruction. It is a phenomenon of decay and transformation, characterized by exhaustion and impurity."
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body in its observation.
Of such a body as this, what is its root? How does it proceed?"
"Who is my protector? How do I abide?
Thus the bhikṣu observes according to reality and further reflects:
"Such a body has karma as its root; it proceeds in accordance with karma, and karma is its savior.
If one accumulates wholesome karma, one will be born among gods or humans."
Associated with evil karma, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Such a body is impure and insubstantial, impermanent and unstable.
"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as it truly is, and no longer gives rise to thoughts regarding sensual desire.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the eye as it truly is."
Just as the eye-faculty of the people of Jambudvīpa perceives forms where there is space, is it not the same for what is seen in other directions?
If my disciples, having heard what I have said, or by means of the divine eye or wisdom, observe this:

when the people of Jambudvīpa see forms, they do so because of five causal conditions—the presence of the eye, the presence of form, the presence of light, the presence of unobstructed space, and the presence of mental attention.

The people of Uttarakuru are not like this; even where there is no empty space, they are able to see forms, just as fish and other creatures see forms within water. It is likewise for the people of Uttarakuru that they see through mountain obstructions beyond them without any hindrance.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.

For example, regarding the sounds heard by the ears of the people of Jambudvīpa—whether pleasant or unpleasant—they are clearly perceived when near, indistinct when far, and unheard when very distant;
however, it is not so for the people of Uttarakuru."

This bhikṣu contemplates, according to reality, what the people of Uttarakuru hear with their ears—whether near or far, great or small, pleasant or unpleasant—and because of the excellence of their karmic retribution, they are able to hear them all.
For example, just as the light of the sun illuminates everything— whether near or far, coarse or fine, pure or impure— with its radiance,
so too is it with the sounds heard by the people of Uttarakuru.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:
Is it the same for the people of Uttarakuru as it is for the people of Jambudvīpa regarding what is perceived by the faculty of the nose?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that because of their superior karmic retribution, the people of Uttarakuru perceive only various fragrances and do not smell any foul odors.
It is like placing water and milk together in a single vessel: when a king of geese drinks from it, it drinks only the milk while the water remains.
The people of Uttarakuru are likewise; they perceive only various fragrances and do not smell any foul odors.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
As for the flavors obtained by the tongues of the people of Jambudvīpa, is it not so for the people of Uttarakuru?
Through his wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,
he sees that while the people of Jambudvīpa have superior, middling, and inferior food, the people of Uttarakuru are not like this.

The people of Uttarakuru have no sense of "mine" and always practice goodness of their own accord; their rice grows naturally, and their food has a single flavor, whereas the people of Jambudvīpa are not like this.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:
'Are the various physical forms of the people of Jambudvīpa not likewise [diverse] among the people of Uttarakuru?'"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes that the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa possess bodies of various forms and colors, whereas those of Uttarakuru are not like this; because of their wholesome karma, they have a uniform body-color, identical in their gait and identical in their physical form. Their color is like that of Jāmbūnada gold; their bodies are rounded, upright, supple, and well-proportioned, and their karmic retribution is not comparable to that of the people of Jambudvīpa.
"The people of Jambudvīpa have immeasurable kinds of karma; because their practices differ, they consequently possess immeasurable kinds of bodies and immeasurable kinds of forms.
Thus, having observed the human world of two continents in accordance with reality, the bhikṣu next observes the third continent, Pūrvavideha."
Are the sense bases (āyatana) of the people of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru the same as those perceived by the people of Pūrvavideha?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that the people of Pūrvavideha can perceive various forms even in the midst of darkness, just as cats, tigers, rhinoceroses, horses, horned owls, and their like in Jambudvīpa are able to see various forms in places devoid of light;
the people of Pūrvavideha are likewise able to see all coarse and subtle forms within the darkness of night, just as they do within the range of their vision.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality: how does he contemplate the people of Jambudvīpa?
As previously described, is the sound heard by the people of Jambudvīpa the same as that of the people of Pūrvavideha?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the people of Pūrvavideha hear a terrifying sound, it is perceived by their auditory consciousness only as far as the range of a single arrow; because of their merit, they do not hear terrifying sounds from a great distance.
"Furthermore, having observed the body in accordance with reality, the practitioner observes the dwelling places of sentient beings in the three continents.
Just as the objects perceived by the olfactory consciousness of the people of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru are such, is it not so for the people of Pūrvavideha?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that the people of Pūrvavideha smell the fragrances they perceive during the day with their olfactory consciousness, and do so at night as well, because the fruit of their karmic retribution is superior.
"Furthermore, the practitioner observes the body in accordance with reality:
Just as the people of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru perceive flavors through their gustatory consciousness, is it the same for the people of Pūrvavideha? Do they experience flavors in this way?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that the people of Pūrvavideha eat one *śāli* grain and remain without hunger for three days. Furthermore,
until the end of their lives, the people of Pūrvavideha suffer no physical illness or affliction, because the Dharma is supreme.
If one encounters illness at the end of life, only after five days does one pass away.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:
"Is the physical form of the people of Pūrvavideha not like that of the people of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that the people of Pūrvavideha have bodies as perfectly rounded as the nyagrodha tree.

Furthermore, the practitioner, observing the body in accordance with reality, having thus observed the three continents as they truly are, now observes the fourth continent, Aparagoyānī, and the place where its inhabitants dwell.
How do the people of Aparagoyānī perceive their physical environment?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, they see that for the people of Aparagoyānī, there is no obstruction to the visual consciousness by mountains or walls; just as one sees various forms and images within crystal or lapis lazuli, so it is for the people of Aparagoyānī.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:

Is it not the case that while the inhabitants of the three continents—Jambudvīpa, Uttarakuru, and Pūrvavideha—distinguish between sounds by their hearing, those in Aparagoyānī perceive sounds through the ear-consciousness in the same way?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the people of Godānīya hear sounds with their visual consciousness, just as the species of snakes and vipers in Jambudvīpa hear sounds with their eyes; the people of Godānīya are likewise so. Just as if there were no obstructions, they hear various sounds and see various forms and images; this is because their dharma is superior.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:
Do the people of Jambudvīpa and Purvavideha perceive odors through the nose-consciousness in the same way as the people of Aparagoyānī do?"
The manner in which the people of Aparagoyānī perceive odors is different; their eyes and other faculties have distinct objects of perception.
How do the nose-consciousnesses of the people of Aparagoyānī perceive odors?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, they see:

When the people of Aparagoyānī see forms with their eyes, they simultaneously perceive their fragrances; even when they do not see them with their eyes, they still smell their fragrance, because their dharmas are superior.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How do the people of Aparagoyānī perceive flavors through their gustatory consciousness?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, they see that the people of Aparagoyānī eat millet and drink "ox-flavor" (gomaya-rasa). Just as the people of Jambudvīpa drink honey-wine or grape-wine, so too do the people of Aparagoyānī drink the five flavors of ox [by-products], which likewise cause them to become intoxicated and stupefied.
The people of Aparagoyānī eat millet, just as the people of Jambudvīpa eat rice, being fully satisfied and satiated.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the physical dimensions of the people of Aparagoyānī?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees that the height of the people of Aparagoyānī is half a tāla tree; their bodies correspond to their karma, being the physical forms produced by their own karma.
"Furthermore, the practitioner reflects upon and observes which dwelling places among the four continents have similar natures, similar intentions, and similar conducts."
They observe one another.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, they see that among the sentient beings of the four continents, there is not a single person whose mind is similar [to another], nor a single person whose conduct is similarly equal, nor a single person whose body is similarly equal; in all respects, there is not a single person who is similar to another.
This is called a bhikṣu’s contemplation of the body in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality:
Is there even a single person among the inhabitants of the four continents who is born here without karma and without cause?
Is there no storehouse of karma?
Is there no transmigratory flow of karma?
Is there perhaps one who does not practice the dharma of desire-habituation?

In this way, monks, one does not see a single person who lacks the storehouse of karma; there is not a single person born without karma, nor a single person who transmigrates without karma, nor a single person who does not practice the dharma of desire. According to the actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one receives retribution in accordance with that karma. There is not a single person who is not comprised within the categories of enemies, relatives, or neutral persons.
This is called the practitioner’s contemplation of the body in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the body in accordance with reality:
how does one accumulate karma to obtain a celestial body?
How do they experience the pleasures of the five desires among the devas?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, they observe:

beings born in the realm of the Four Great Kings experience the five celestial desires; their eyes gaze upon beautiful forms without ever knowing satiety, whether these be subtle or coarse. With their own divine eyes, they see for ten thousand *yojanas*, and if they employ transformed supernatural powers, they can see immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.

Thus, the practitioner contemplates the power of the immeasurable wholesome karma of the devas; all the forms and appearances seen by the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings are entirely lovely, giving rise to love and joy in the mind, and no unwholesome forms are seen.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How do the gods of the Four Great Kings hear sounds?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, they see: [the following]"

If the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings hear the celestial sounds, they find them exceedingly delightful. With their karmically ripened ears, they can hear up to three thousand yojanas; if they employ their supernormal powers of transformation, they can hear up to twenty thousand yojanas—all the sounds they hear are utterly delightful.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How do the gods of the Four Great Kings perceive odors with their noses?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, they see as follows:"

The devas of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, by virtue of their natural retribution, can smell various fragrances for two hundred yojanas; if they employ transformed supernatural powers, they can smell fragrances for a hundred thousand yojanas.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How does he contemplate the fullness of the tongue-faculty of the gods of the Four Great Kings?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The gustatory faculty of the gods of the Four Great Kings is neither satiated nor disinterested; according to what is obtained through their karma, because of their wholesome karma, they never tire of flavors.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the bodies of the devas—whether they be coarse or subtle, or whether they move with great speed?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees that the bodies of the devas possess great power and subtle supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*). Within a single hand, he places five hundred devas so that they remain there; yet each of these devas' bodies is without obstruction, nor is there any crowding.

For example, if five hundred lamps were lit in a single room, their radiance would not obstruct one another; likewise, if five hundred deities were placed within the hands of a single deity, it would be no more cramped or obstructed.
"Furthermore, when the various devas manifest great bodies of immeasurable yojanas—whether beautiful or ugly—those who see them may experience either fear or lack of fear.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality."
How does one contemplate the Śīghraga devas?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees that in the time it takes for a single blink of an eye, the Śīghraga deva can travel immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas and return to his original place; wherever he intends to go according to his recollection, there is no obstruction.

Whatever they desire is entirely fulfilled, and none can take it away from them. In all places, whatever they obtain is entirely at their disposal; they have no fear of others and nothing can obstruct them. The bliss of the celestial realm increases moment by moment, and due to their virtuous karma, they experience the pleasures of the five senses.
This is called the practitioner’s contemplation of the body in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the bodies of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
How do they experience pleasure by taking objects as their condition?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
they observe that the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three experience the pleasures of sensory objects just as the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings do.

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three experience desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are one thousand times superior to those of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Why is this?

Because the karma performed by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is characterized by superior, powerful, and delightful objects of affection, whereas the karma performed by the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is not.

Because the karma performed by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is superior, the gods of the Four Great Kings cannot equal those of the higher heaven; thus, the excellence of the pleasures experienced by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is beyond full description.
This is called the practitioner’s contemplation of the body in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the hells?

The bodies experienced by sentient beings in the hells are those of the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Great Conjunction Hell, the Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, the Heat Hell, the Great Heat Hell, and the Avīci Hell.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the karmic actions performed by sentient beings—unpleasant karma, disagreeable karma, and unwholesome karma; that is, the three types of karma created and accumulated through body, speech, and mind, by which they fall into hell.

Because they have accumulated evil karma, they undergo the sufferings of hell; within the hells, they experience various intense agonies and cannot be liberated until their evil karma is fully exhausted.
This is called the practitioner’s contemplation of the body in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects thus:
"What kind of karma causes one to fall into hell?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
these sentient beings habitually engage in killing, delighting in its practice and increasing it; by these causes and conditions, they fall into the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).

Furthermore, they see sentient beings who habitually associate with and take pleasure in killing and stealing; by increasing such evils through these causes and conditions, they fall into the Black Rope Hell.

Furthermore, they see sentient beings who habitually associate with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and who take pleasure in cultivating these acts, thereby increasing such evils; by reason of these causes and conditions, they fall into the Saṃghāta Hell.

Furthermore, they see sentient beings who habitually associate with and take pleasure in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying; by increasing such evils through these practices, they fall into the Raurava Hell due to these causes and conditions.

Furthermore, he sees sentient beings who kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, and encourage others to drink alcohol; by these causes and conditions, they fall into the Great Howling Hell.

Furthermore, he sees sentient beings who kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, drink intoxicants, and hold wrong views; by these causes and conditions, they fall into the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.

Furthermore, he saw sentient beings who, having committed killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, giving alcohol to others, or holding wrong views and lacking faith—and who had even broken the precepts of bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—fell as a result of these causes and conditions into the Great Intense Heat Hell (Mahāraurava).
Furthermore, I see sentient beings committing the five heinous acts (*ānantarya-karma*) and the five kinds of evil deeds; by these causes and conditions, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
What are the five heinous acts?

If there are sentient beings who kill their father, kill their mother, kill an Arhat, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or with a malicious mind draw blood from the body of a Buddha—due to these five kinds of great evil karma, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Reflecting thus upon the karmic retribution of the hells, one gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body in accordance with reality.
How do sentient beings fall into the realm of hungry ghosts?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that immeasurable hungry ghosts, due to their stinginess and envy, have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts, dwelling five hundred yojanas beneath the earth.

Countless hungry ghosts consume foul food, or have no food at all, or eat impure things; they devour one another, oppressed by hunger and thirst, undergoing great suffering and affliction as a rain of great fire falls from above to burn their bodies.
These hungry ghosts, following the force of their evil karma, undergo such suffering.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the body in accordance with reality.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he perceives the realm of animals. He sees immeasurable and diverse kinds of animals, which, in brief, are categorized into three abodes:
First are those that move in water, such as fish and the like;
second are those that move on land, such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, deer, wild boar, pigs, and so forth;
third are those that move through the air, such as the immeasurable varieties of winged birds.
"Furthermore, the practitioner observes the body in accordance with reality.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes how many kinds of births there are among animals.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:"
There are four modes of birth among animals. What are these four?
First is birth from a womb, namely those such as elephants, horses, water buffaloes, oxen, and sheep.
The second is birth from an egg, namely snakes, vipers, geese, ducks, chickens, pheasants, and various kinds of birds;
the third is birth from moisture, such as the class of fleas, lice, and mosquitoes;
the fourth is miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), such as the dragon Dīrghamukha and others.

Having thus observed animals as they truly are, the practitioner sees that whether among devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals, there is not a single place that is not afflicted by the suffering of separation from those one loves. All sentient beings revolve in birth and death, sometimes becoming enemies and sometimes becoming friends; there is not a single place where they do not undergo arising and ceasing.

In this way, a bhikṣu does not give rise to affection for the realm of birth and death; his mind finds no delight therein; thus he becomes weary and detached, does not follow after it, and brings it to destruction. Such is the nature of phenomena that must cease; they cannot endure long within the place of manifold suffering for all sentient beings.

Therefore, monks, within the cycle of birth and death there is much suffering and little flavor; it is impermanent and subject to destruction. You should cultivate weary detachment toward it; through weary detachment from birth and death, one attains liberation.
"In this way, O Nādikas, a bhikṣu practitioner dwells contemplating the body internally, observing the internal body—observing how this body is composed of various impure parts."
Seeing the body as it truly is, one contemplates it moment by moment, observing the body sequentially from head to foot.
This practitioner first observes the crown of the head; through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes that the skull is divided into four parts.

Within the cranial bone there naturally dwell worms called "brain-walkers" (*mastaka-cārin*); they roam within the bones, are born within the brain, and whether moving or stationary, they constantly feed upon this brain.
Within the skull there are further various worms that dwell inside the skull; whether moving about or feeding, they consume the skull itself.
Furthermore, there are hair-worms that dwell outside the bone and feed upon the roots of the hair; because these worms become enraged, they cause the hair to fall out.
Furthermore, there is an ear-worm that dwells within the ear and eats the flesh therein; because of the worm’s malice, it causes the person’s ears to ache or makes them deaf.
Furthermore, there is a nose-worm that dwells within the nose and eats the flesh therein; because of the worm’s malice, it can cause a person’s food and drink to taste unpleasant.
As the brain-fluid flows downward, the worm eats this brain-fluid, and for this reason, it causes the person’s food and drink to taste unpleasant.
Furthermore, there are fat-worms that are born within the fat and dwell therein; they constantly consume human fat, and because these worms become enraged, they cause people to suffer from headaches.

Furthermore, there are continuity-worms that are born between the joints, and there are body-named worms that reside in the interlocking teeth; because these worms become enraged, they cause pain in the person's vessels as if they were being pierced by needles.
Furthermore, there are various worms called *kheṭāśin* (saliva-eaters) that dwell within the root of the tongue; because these worms become agitated, they cause the mouth to become parched.
There are also various worms called *dantamūla-krimi* (tooth-root worms) that dwell at the roots of the teeth; because these worms become agitated, they cause toothaches.
This is called the internal practitioner’s contemplation of the body as a body. These ten kinds of worms dwell within the head.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body.
How many bones are there within the flesh of the head?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the skull of the head consists of four parts:
the frontal bone and the two cheekbones together constitute three parts, while the nasal bone constitutes one part.
The two jawbones are joined together; there is one bone in the chin. Including the teeth, there are thirty-two bones in total, and the roots of the teeth are likewise.
There are two bones in the throat; thus, there are fifteen bones in the neck.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
How is it that the flesh of the head, nourished by food, comes together and possesses sensation?
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes:

Regarding the flesh of the head, there are four portions: two portions consist of the two cheeks; one portion consists of the segment of flesh comprising the throat and the tongue; and four portions consist of the upper and lower lips along with the skin and flesh of the two ears.
As for the tongue faculty, it is called "tendons and flesh"; it craves superior delicacies and delights in the six flavors.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within by following the body with observation.
What kinds of worms are there?
Where do they dwell?
What kind of karma do they perform—whether causing illness or bringing peace?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he first observes the throat.

Within the throat there is a worm called *Kheṭabhakṣa* (Spittle-Eater). When chewing and eating, it is like vomiting; mixed with saliva, as one is about to swallow, it combines with the brain-saliva. The worms of saliva within the throat eat this food together, thereby sustaining their own lives.
If these worms increase, they cause the disease of *mīḍha* (coughing).
If one eats too much fat, or too much sweet, or heavy food, or sour food, or cold food, the worms will increase and cause diseases to arise in the throat.
Having observed the saliva-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
He observes the spittle-worms, which can digest various forms of saliva, or cause illness, or bring about well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *kṣavathu-nāśana* worm dwells within the throat; if a person does not consume the aforementioned fatty substances and the like, the worm remains at ease, able to digest saliva and flow out delicious flavors through the ten vessels, whereby the person experiences peaceful happiness.
If a person spits excessively, the worms become ill; because the worms are ill, they vomit cold froth; because they vomit cold froth, a disease forms within the chest.
Having observed the saliva-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
He observes the vomit-worms: how do they cause a person to be at ease or afflicted by disease?
Where do they dwell?
What kind of food do they eat?
By means of the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives:
It is observed that the vomiting-demon dwells within the human body, residing in the locations where it flows through the ten channels (*nāḍī*).
When a person eats, this demon leaps up from within the ten channels and ascends to the throat, causing the person to vomit and giving rise to five kinds of vomiting.
What are the five?
First, vomiting due to wind;
second, vomiting due to the humors (doṣas).
Third, that which has been spat out;
fourth, that which has been vomited up mixed with other substances;
fifth, that which has been vomited up by a fly.
If the worms are at ease, their digestion becomes harmonious and they enter into the belly.
How does the vomiting-worm arise from wind-induced vomiting?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

If one eats light and cold foods, or food that lacks oiliness, it will provoke wind-diseases (*vāta-vikāra*), causing difficulty in the passage of both feces and urine, and making the eyes unable to sleep.
When the wind enters the throat and agitates the vomiting-worms (*udgārakṛmi*), due to this fault, it is called "wind-induced vomiting" (*vāta-chardi*).
Having observed the *udariya* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by way of contemplating the body.
How do the *udariya* worms cause a person to vomit up the aggregates?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when people consume pungent food mixed with salty and hot substances, it causes them to become feverish and agitates the *udbhijja* worms. These worms move from their place of residence and travel upward, causing the person to vomit up phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Having observed the *udariya* (stomach-worms), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by contemplating the body.
How do the *udariya* cause a person to vomit saliva?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

when a person eats sweet, cold, heavy, or oily foods, or sleeps after eating, it causes phlegm to increase. Because the phlegm increases, the phlegm-worms (*śleṣma-kīṭa*) increase, resulting in throat ailments, making the body feel heavy, and producing cold phlegm.
Having observed the *udariṇī* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by way of mindfulness of the body.
How do the *udariṇī* worms arise from the mixed vomit?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that eating food that is light, cold, and non-greasy;
pungent, sour, or salty food; or food that is slippery, cold, heavy, and greasy, causes the vomiting-worms to move within the throat. By these three faults, they cause a person to vomit.
Having observed the vomit-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by contemplating the body.
How is it that the fly-vomit causes a person to vomit?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that because flies feed on impurities, when they enter the throat, they cause the vomiting-worms to move, whereby one vomits profusely.
Having observed the vomiting worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by contemplating the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The *madhurasa* worm moves from the tip of the tongue to the life-vein (*jīvanāḍī*); within this interval, it moves or remains stationary, minute and legless.
If one eats delicious food, the worm becomes intoxicated and grows; if one eats unpalatable food, the worm withers and weakens.
When these worms eat, they are like bees consuming flowers; they take the subtle sweet essence to produce honey, and the feeding of these taste-craving worms is likewise.
Although what they consume is extremely subtle, they obtain full satisfaction. If the worms obtain flavor, I likewise obtain this food-flavor;
if the worms remember their food, I likewise remember my food.
"If I do not eat, these intoxicated worms will likewise suffer from illness and find no peace.
Having observed the intoxicated worms, he knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the internal body by contemplating the body in accordance with the body.
He contemplates the insect of heedlessness: "How does this insect cause me illness and affliction, or bring about my well-being?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that the insect of heedlessness dwells upon the crown of the head; if it reaches the fontanelle, it causes the person to fall ill.
If it reaches the crown of the head, it causes sores to arise in people;
if it reaches the throat, it is like ants filling the entire throat;
if it remains in its original location, no illness will arise.
This is called contemplating the worm of heedlessness.
Having contemplated the worm of heedlessness, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
He contemplates the worm that craves the six flavors: how does it suffer from illness, and how does it find peace?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
Whatever flavors the six-tasting worms relish, I also relish; whatever flavors those taste-worms do not relish, I likewise find unpleasant.
When a fever arises, the worms also first contract such a fever. Because of this affliction, the food of the patient becomes unpalatable and lacks any sense of flavor.
Having observed the taste-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes the *ucchvāsaka* worms dwelling beneath the crown of the head; he sees them through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye:

The Qi-shu (抒氣) worm, due to its state of hatred, eats away at the brain and creates cavities; it may cause pain in the throat or blockage of the throat, leading to the suffering of death through wind-induced choking in the throat.
This gas-expelling worm, together with all the other worms within the throat, becomes completely disordered, giving rise to various ailments and afflictions.
This gas-expelling worm is constantly covered by saliva; it is short and small, possessing both a face and feet.
Having observed the *śvāsakṛmi* (breath-expelling worm), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The "Taste-Repulsing Worm" dwells beneath the head within the root of the throat.
How does this worm cause me illness and affliction, or bring about my well-being? He sees:
This worm harbors envy toward all tastes and relishes only one; it may relish sweet flavors while loathing all others,
or relish sour flavors while loathing all others,
or relish pungent flavors while loathing all others.
Some relish salty flavors and loathe all other flavors;
some relish bitter flavors and loathe all other flavors;
some relish fermented flavors and loathe all other flavors.
Whatever flavors the worm detests, I also detest; whatever flavors the worm relishes, I also relish.
There is a vessel upon the tip of the tongue that follows after flavors, causing the tongue to become parched.
Because of the worms' anger, they cause the tongue to become numb and swollen, or cause the throat to immediately contract with spasms;
if they do not feel anger, the throat will not suffer from the aforementioned ailments.
Having observed the worms that relish the loathsome, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He sees:

The *svapnaka* worm is minute in form, resembling a speck of dust in a window; it dwells in all the channels, circulating through the sensory objects. It resides within the marrow, or within the flesh, or within the skull; it may be found within the cheeks, or within the teeth and bones, or within the bones of the throat; it may be in the ears, or in the eyes, or in the nose, or in the beard and hair.
This "sleep-craving worm" is driven by the winds and circulates; when this worm is afflicted or becomes utterly exhausted, it dwells within the heart.
The heart is like a lotus flower: it opens during the day, but because there is no sunlight, it closes at night; the mind is likewise.
The worm dwells within it; when it perceives many objects, the sense faculties become utterly exhausted, and the worm then falls asleep. Because the worm sleeps, the person also sleeps.
All sentient beings possess sleep; when these sleep-insects are exhausted by the day, humans also fall asleep.
Having observed these sleep-insects, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner, contemplating the body within the body, sees:

there are swelling-inducing worms that move within the body, dwelling either in the head or in the neck; they move through the blood or through the fat. Their bodies are extremely subtle, and wherever they drink the blood, a swelling arises, accompanied by a tingling and painful sensation.

It may be on the face, or on the nape of the neck, or in the throat, or at the fontanelle, or in other locations; wherever it resides, it causes swellings to arise, yet if it dwells within the sinews, there is no suffering from disease.
Having observed the swelling-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.

Thus, Nālada, the brahmin householder, and the practitioner-monks of the village observe the species of worms within the head, the tongue, the ears, the fontanelle, the pores, the hair, and within the skin, flesh, bones, blood, and sinews; observing them as they truly are, they develop a mind of revulsion toward tastes on the tongue, no longer craving flavors in future births, and are able to develop revulsion for the ocean of craving and attachment to flavors that extends for immeasurable and boundless *yojanas*.

Because of this revulsion and detachment, he is no longer disturbed or troubled by craving for food; he no longer associates with wealthy and noble elders, remains free from excessive desire, is content with whatever food he receives, and takes only what is necessary to sustain the body.

For this reason, one does not envy others receiving offerings and benefits; one does not delight in much talk, nor in dwelling in monasteries; one does not give rise to pride of person, nor give rise to pride of physical form; one does not rely on robes to give rise to arrogance, nor rely on the *kaṣāya* and alms bowl to give rise to arrogance, nor rely on disciples to give rise to arrogance, nor rely on a village to give rise to arrogance, nor rely on kinsmen to give rise to arrogance. Being solitary and alone, free from craving, far removed from dust and defilement, one dwells in a place of tranquility, drawing near to *nirvāṇa*.
If one craves delicious flavors and sinks into the ocean of taste, one will be seized by Māra and remain far from Nirvāṇa.
Having contemplated the various worms, this practitioner becomes weary of and detached from flavors, no longer craving food or drink.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by observing the spine as it truly is.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the spine consists of forty-five bones;
there are fourteen bones in the chest; twelve bones each in the left and right ribs, with the joints being likewise; and the pelvic bones are also thus."
Having thus analyzed and observed the joints of the bones, one further observes how many portions of flesh there are from the shoulder to the hip;
thus, there are twelve portions on each side, left and right.
Having performed this observation, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
How many sinews are there that connect and bind?
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:"
On both sides of the flanks, excluding the skin and flesh, there are one hundred fine tendons that serve as binding cords.
Having observed these binding tendons, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
He contemplates this body from the shoulders to the hips as to how much fat it contains.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees his own body:
that fat increases due to the condition of food.
Due to the causes and conditions of food, the fat is diminished.
A person who is extremely emaciated—such as those from Magadha and other regions—possesses only five *liang* of fat.
Having thus observed this, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes: 'How much water is there in this body of mine?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees for himself:"
Within the body there are ten handfuls of water that emerge from the pores; this is called sweat.
Among the various sense organs, tears emerge from the eyes; this is called the moisture element (*āpa-dhātu*).
Through the condition of food, fat and blood increase.
Having observed the water of the body, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
He contemplates how much excrement and filth is within his body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that within his body there are seven handfuls of feces and six handfuls of saliva.
Having performed this contemplation, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
