"How much phlegm and urine is there within my body?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that within his body there are five handfuls of yellow phlegm and four handfuls of urine, which increase or decrease except during times of illness.
Having observed in this way, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body internally by following the body with mindfulness:
"Within my body, how much fat and marrow, and how much impure, foul semen, is there?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that within his body there are twelve handfuls of fat, one handful of marrow, and one handful of semen.
Having observed it in this way, he knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body internally by way of observing the body.
He observes how many winds are within his body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees them:"
In the body there are three handfuls of wind.
Having observed thus, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
He contemplates how many channels within his body constantly flow so that food and drink are digested.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
there are thirteen channels within his body; when these channels flow, they cause the body to become plump and joyful.
It is like a waterwheel that draws water and pours it out for irrigation, causing growth; the irrigation of the body’s channels is also like this.
What are these thirteen?
First is the channel named Flow of Life;
second is the channel named Flow of Conformity;
third is the channel named Flow of Water.
The fourth is named the sweat-flowing vessel;
the fifth is named the urine-flowing vessel;
the sixth is named the feces-flowing vessel.
The seventh is named the Ten-stream vessel;
the eighth is named the Juice-stream vessel;
the ninth is named the Flesh-stream vessel.
Tenth is the fat-flowing vessel;
eleventh is the bone-flowing vessel;
twelfth is the marrow-flowing vessel.
The thirteenth is the *srotas* (flowing) pulse.
Having observed the flowing pulse, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body within.
As for what those flowing channels take as their root to cause the body to be plump and joyful, and what various worms travel everywhere throughout them—
he, through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
sees that the life-channel has the mind as its root.
The channels through which fluids flow take the two flanks as their foundation;
the channels through which water flows take the stomach, the palate, and the heart as their foundation;
the channels through which sweat flows take the hair follicles and the adipose tissue as their foundation.
The channels of the urinary flow have the bladder as their root;
the channels of the fecal flow have the lower gate of the matured organ (the large intestine) as their root;
and the ten channels of the [other] flows have the throat and the heart as their roots.
The channels through which the fluids flow have the lungs as their basis;
the channels through which the flesh and fat flow have the tendons and skin as their basis;
the channels through which the bones flow have all the joints as their basis.
Regarding the channels through which marrow and semen flow, the testicles and the body-faculty are their basis.
Having thus observed the flowing channels, the practitioner knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the body by way of contemplating the body.
What kinds of worms circulate in what locations, causing either disease or well-being, from the pelvic bones throughout the entire body?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that when ten kinds of worms reach the liver and lungs, the person falls ill.
What are the ten? First is the hair-eating worm;
second is the hole-dwelling worm.
Third are the *cāndramasa* worms;
fourth are the red worms;
fifth are the juice-consuming worms.
Sixth is the Hair-Lamp Worm;
seventh is the Anger-Blood Worm;
eighth is the Blood-Eater Worm.
The ninth is named the *kṣudrakṣudra* (itching) worm;
the tenth is named the *āmla* (sour) worm.
These various worms are minute in form, lacking both feet and eyes; they move within the blood, characterized by sensations of pain and itching.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body, observing each of the various worms within the body and what they do.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
if the *roma-bhakṣa* worm gives rise to anger, it can devour the beard and eyebrows, causing them all to fall out and inducing leprosy in the person."
If the *khuṅ-gyi-hgro* insects become enraged and move within the blood, they cause the body to become coarse, rough, numb, and insensate;
if the *bsam-gtan-du-ma-ra* insects circulate within the blood, or reside in the nose or the mouth, they cause the mouth and nose to become entirely foul-smelling;
if the *dmar-po* insects become enraged and move within the blood, they can cause sores to develop in a person's throat.

If the *rasaja-kīṭa* (juice-insect) gives rise to anger and circulates within the blood, it causes the body to suffer from a bluish paralysis (*pakṣaghāta*), or a paralysis characterized by black or yellow discoloration;

if the *roma-dīpa-kīṭa* (hair-lamp insect) gives rise to anger and flows through the blood, it produces the suffering of disease, such as sores, scabs, feverish jaundice, and the cracking of eczema and leprosy;

if the *rudhira-krudha-kīṭa* (blood-angry insect) flows through the blood due to anger, it may cause blood-related illnesses, such as menorrhagia in women, itching of the body, and the suppurating decay of sores and scabs.
If the blood-consuming worms become angry, they cause diseases of the brain, dizziness with the head spinning, sores to form in the throat and mouth, and sores to appear at the lower orifice;
if the *ṣa-ṣa* worms circulate through the blood, they likewise produce illnesses characterized by extreme exhaustion and debility, such that one has no desire for food or drink;
if the sour-tasting worms (*āmla-krimi*) become enraged, they also cause a person to contract such diseases.
Having thus observed all these worms and their species, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
Contemplate ten kinds of worms moving within the aggregates (*skandha*).
What are these ten? The first is named the ulcer-producing worm (*vraṇakarī-kṛmi*).
The second is named the piercing worm;
the third is named the constricting-tendon worm;
the fourth is named the arterial worm.
Fifth is the *tvagāśin* worm;
sixth is the *medaścalana* worm;
seventh is the *saṃghāta* worm.
The eighth is named the stinking insect;
the ninth is named the moist insect;
the tenth is named the heat insect.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes what kinds of worms dwell within his body, whether they cause illness or bring about well-being."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
there are wound-insects that, wherever a wound occurs, swarm around and devour it; or they may cause a wound-disease to arise in the throat.
Having observed the wound-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes what kind of disease the piercing-worm (*kantaka*) causes.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *śalyaka* worm:

when it gives rise to anger, it causes a person to suffer diarrhea as if by fire, making the mouth dry and preventing food and drink from being digested. Its body quivers violently; water enters the *pakvāśaya* (the receptacle for digested food), and day and night it does not sleep. Within the *pakvāśaya*, it churns the filth and excrement, causing the urine to cool and mingle with it.

Dwelling in such a place, it produces the disease of diarrhea, rendering one unable to recall food and leaving one weak and unwell. If a person is afflicted by grief and distress, the worm rejoices; it gnaws at the person’s blood vessels to cause decay and affliction, resulting in either the discharge of red blood or undigested diarrhea.
Having thus observed the *śalākā-kīṭa* (thorny insect), one knows the body as it truly is.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 64; *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll 65.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Two:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body."
Contemplating the *saṃvartanīya* worm, he sees it through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye:

the *saṃvartanīya* worm travels either through the coarse tendons or the fine tendons. If one is aware of the worm’s movement, the tendons become painful; if one is unaware of its movement, the tendons do not become painful. All the flesh and bones likewise become emaciated, and pain arises within the tendons.
If the worm is full of anger, people cannot eat.
If it dwells within the sinews and drinks human blood, it causes people to lose their strength; if it eats human flesh, it causes people to become emaciated.
Having observed the *snāyu-bhakṣaka* worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes the *sirā-cala* worms:
This worm circulates throughout all the channels; its body is so subtle that it moves without obstruction.
If the worm dwells within the food-carrying channels of a person, it causes illness, making the body parched and causing a lack of appetite for food and drink.
If the worm dwells within the water-vessels, illness arises that causes the mouth to become parched;
if it dwells in the sweat-vessels, it causes all the pores of the body to be without perspiration;
if it dwells in the urine-vessels, it causes the disease of dysuria, or causes the semen to be corrupted, or causes intense suffering.
If these worms become angry and move through the lower gate, they cause the anus to become obstructed and blocked, leading to such agony that one nearly dies.
Having observed the *cāṅku* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes the *tvakkrimi* (skin-eating worm), seeing it through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye:

due to excessive eating, the skin-eating worm becomes enraged, which causes the complexion of the person's face to become ugly; it may cause malignant pustules to arise, or [the skin] to itch, turn red, turn yellow, or break open; it may also cause the beard and nails to fall out, inflict malignant diseases upon the person, or cause the skin to be torn and the flesh to rot."
Having observed the *tvak-āśin* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Observing the *meda-bhakṣaka* worms, he sees them through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye:

The fat-moving worm dwells within the fat-veins inside the body. If one commits excesses in diet or sleeps excessively, this worm becomes enraged; it fails to digest food and drink, causing either scabies or malignant swellings, diseases of the hair roots, goiters, or vein-tumors, or consumption, or bodily odors, or profuse sweating during meals.
Having thus observed the *calā-lipi* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
He observes what kind of activity the *saṃcita* worms perform within his body—whether causing illness or maintaining health.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the two kinds of bodies where the *saṃghāta* insects congregate:
first, the conscious body;
second, the unconscious body.
Skin, flesh, bone, blood, fat, marrow, semen, and so forth are called the conscious body;
hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are called the unconscious body.
These are termed the two bodies in combination.

Because of excessive eating, the worms lose their strength, and the person likewise loses their strength; they are unable to move quickly back and forth, and suffer from drowsiness, mental fog, or frequent parching thirst; their skin, flesh, bones, blood, marrow, and vital essence are diminished.
Having observed the *saṃghāta* worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
By means of wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes:

Foul-smelling insects dwell within the flesh and amidst the excrement and urine; because they have over-eaten, these insects become enraged, causing the body’s flesh, excrement, urine, nasal mucus, and saliva to all become foul. The putrid pus within the nose or the rotting tears become stinking, and wherever these insects travel—whether upon clothing, bedding, or food—all becomes utterly foul and impure.

Residing within the teeth, because of the worms' stench, the food likewise becomes foul; clothing and bedding become entirely malodorous; there is much white plaque upon the tongue that is putrid and filthy, and the impurities of the body are also foul-smelling.
Having observed the stinking insects, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The moisture-moving worms move within the flesh of the back; once they know the food has been digested, they enter the three apertures of the waist. They take up the impure liquid of human excrement, which becomes urine, while the dregs become feces, causing them to enter the lower gate.
Having observed the moisture-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
He observes ten kinds of worms that move within the sense-faculties; from these, all human bodies are produced.
What are the ten? First is the *kṣudrakṣudraka* worm;
second is the *tanutanu* worm.
Third is the insect named Sprout-Flower;
fourth is the insect named Great Deceit;
fifth is the insect named Black.
Sixth is the worm named Great Eater;
seventh is the worm named Warm-Mover;
eighth is the worm named Heat-Producer.
The ninth is named Fire-Worm;
the tenth is named Great Fire-Worm.
These various worms dwell within the yellow of the *dhātu*.
"What are the worms that cause human illness or bring about well-being?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
because of excessive eating, the *kṣudraka* (tiny) worms become enraged; they consume the eyelashes of humans, causing the eyes to itch and producing much mucus and tears."
If these minute worms move within the eyes, the eyes will become frequently diseased or the vision will be destroyed.
If they enter the vitreous humor, white cataracts will form in the eyes.
These worms are red in color and cause diseases of the eyes; however, if the worms are not provoked to anger, these ailments do not occur.
Having observed the *gah-gah* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The *cūcuka* worm dwells within the human body; it moves through the *kalā* (limbs) and travels throughout the entire body without obstruction, while the *kalā* are covered by yellow fluid.
When this worm enters the bones, it causes the entire body to become intensely feverish;
when it moves through the flesh, one is constantly hot day and night, and both hands and feet are heated.
If they enter within the skin, sweat then issues from the body.
Having observed the *cūcuka* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
the *māhuka* insects dwell within the calyxes of the sprouts; they have sharp mandibles and short legs, their bodies are like repositories of fire, and they have no desire for food or drink.

If one eats in excess, the worms move to different locations; wherever they go, that place becomes intensely heated and rotted. The blood in the body increases, and the body becomes so hot that it seems as if smoke is rising from it; the skin of the body is destroyed like a burn caused by fire.
If the worms move in their proper direction, this illness does not occur.
Having observed the sprout-flower worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the Great Deceit Worm dwells within the body, moving amidst the yellow matter of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), sometimes finding rest and sometimes not.
Due to excessive eating, the worm becomes enraged; it moves without obstruction from the crown of the head to the feet, causing all the warm blood within the body to produce hot sores.
If blood or pus flows from the mouth or ears, or if one is near death or has already died, or if the body turns blue or yellow, or suffers from fever and bitterness in the mouth.
If the *krimi* (worm) is not angry, then this disease does not occur.
Having observed the *mahā-māyā-krimi* (the great deceitful worm), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees black insects dwelling within the body, moving through the yellow *śoṇita* (blood/lymph).

Whether they are at ease or not, due to dietary excesses, these insects become enraged; this causes the face to become blotchy or produces many dark spots—whether black, yellow, or red—and may cause the body to smell foul, induce night-blindness (*tittira-akṣa*), or cause sores to break out in the mouth or in the regions of the anus and urinary tract.
If the worm does not become angry, then this disease will not occur.
Having observed the black worm, one knows the body as it truly is.

Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body; through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *mahāśana* worm dwelling within the body, and considers whether it brings about well-being or illness.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that because of overeating, the *mahāśana* worm becomes enraged;

dwelling within the *pitta* (bile), it consumes and digests whatever is eaten. Because its body is powerful, the entire body and its parts—the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—all become diminished and weakened in their respective domains, such that vision is no longer clear.
Because of overeating, the sense faculties do not function with proper objects.
If the worms do not become angry, this disease does not occur.
Having observed the "great-eating" worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the *uṣṇagati* worms constantly crave warm food and loathe cold food."
How does this worm cause humans illness?
How does it bring about well-being?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

Regarding warm-moving insects: if I consume cold food or drink it cold, whether in terms of its substance or its flavor, these insects become resentful and emit much saliva from their mouths. Consequently, one may experience extreme exhaustion, heaviness, or a sense of being crushed; or one may suffer from mental dullness and confusion, physical pain and stiffness, excessive salivation, or ailments of the throat.
If the worms do not become angry, then this disease does not occur.
Having observed the warm-moving worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *ūṣma-krimi* (heat-worms) dwelling within the body, moving among the aggregates (*skandha*). What kind of diseases do they cause?
How do they bring about well-being?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *uṣṇa-kīṭa* (heat-insect) dwelling within the human body;
when one consumes heavy food, because of that excess of food, the impurities of disease increase, obstructing the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

Due to overeating, the body becomes coarse and large, or the throat becomes constricted; the excrement and urine both become white in color, and one has no appetite for cold things or for fermented foods.
Having observed the heat-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The fire-consuming worm dwells within the body, moving about amidst the aggregates (*skandha*). When it is cold, this worm rejoices; when it is hot, it withers and weakens.
Because it rejoices in the cold, the person craves food;
when it is hot, the internal fire increases, and one has no desire for food or drink.
In the cold of winter, when it is cool, the shadow appears; when it is hot, the shadow vanishes. Likewise, fire-eating insects detest fire.
Having observed the fire-eating insects in this way, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He sees the *mahāgni* insect; how does this insect cause a person to fall ill or bring them peace?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *mahāgni* worms:

if a person forcibly consumes what is unwholesome to their nature, because of this excess in eating, the worms become enraged and devour the worms within the body. Due to this transgression, it causes pain in the intestines, or pain in the feet and hands; wherever the worms consume food, there is pain throughout.
If the worms do not become angry, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the yellow *śoṇita-krimi* (blood-worms), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes ten kinds of worms within the bones. What are these ten?
First is the worm called Bone-Licker;
second is the worm called Bone-Biter.
Third, the *saṃdhicchedaka* worms;
fourth, the *raktamukha* worms;
fifth, the *pūtika* worms.
Sixth is the Crimson-mouthed worm;
seventh is the Tatumā worm;
eighth is the Skin-consuming worm.
The ninth is named Wind-Sword Worm;
the tenth is named Knife-Mouth Worm.
Regarding these bone-worms, what illnesses do they cause?
What is meant by "peaceful abiding"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees:

the *asthileha* worms dwell on the exterior of the bones, residing in places where many bones meet, or dwelling upon the thigh bones, shin bones, arm bones, and spinal vertebrae. Moving thus within all such bones or within the channels, because of excessive eating, these worms become enraged; they cause the bones to ache or make them tremble, and cause the person’s complexion to become unsightly.
Feeding upon the nearby marrow and bones, it causes the bones to ache intensely; if the worm does not become angry, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the bone-worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *asthi-daṃśaka* worms (bone-biting worms) dwell throughout all the bones of the body. When these worms bite the bones, the great elements dry up and waste away; their sound is broken and scattered; diarrhea becomes irregular; there is pain in both flanks, nasal congestion, vomiting, and no memory of food or drink."
If these worms do not gnaw upon any of the bones, that person will be free from such diseases as these.
Having observed the bone-gnawing worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within by means of mindfulness directed toward the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *parvaka* worms:

due to excessive eating, these worms become enraged, causing pain in the body or its parts, such as headaches or heartache; or they perceive populous cities and villages as desolate wastes; their noses are congested and their minds are afflicted, and because of this painful affliction, their minds find no pleasure in agreeable forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or textures.
If the Saṃdhicchedaka worms are well-tempered and free from anger, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the Saṃdhicchedaka worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by way of following the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the stinking worm dwelling within the body, causing either disease or well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees this stinking worm:

due to excessive eating, the worm becomes enraged, causing the body to become heavy and hot; it may produce red or black patches of skin disease, causes profuse sweating, prevents sleep, and results in leprosy, such that all parts of the body become putrid and foul-smelling.
If the worms do not become angry, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the stinking worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by way of following the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *pūyāsthi-kṛmi* (rotting-bone worm) dwelling within the body, causing either disease or well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *pūyāsthi-kṛmi*:
due to excessive eating, the worm becomes enraged; for one year, two years, or even many years, or during youth, it may cause wounds and scars that, though healed, recur even in old age.
Such putrid worms emerge after a long time, causing the bones to rot and decay, and producing red sores upon the body that are as foul-smelling and loathsome as the fruit of the udumbara tree.
The sores itch intensely, with much pus and blood flowing from them; they are swarmed by flies and bitten by mosquitoes and gadflies.
However, if the "rotting-bone worm" is well-tempered and free from anger, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the pus-eating worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the red-mouthed worms dwelling within the bones of the body; what kind of diseases do they cause?
What is meant by "peaceful and secure"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one perceives the *rakta-mukha* worm (*rakta-mukha-kṛmi*).

Due to excessive eating, this worm becomes enraged; its color is red, exceeding even the color of fire, causing the person's body to sweat day and night until it produces blood-clotting ailments (*rakta-śoṣa*).
If the red-mouthed worms are harmonious and not angry, then there will be no such diseases as those previously described.
Having observed the red-mouthed worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *tūtthaka* worm dwelling within the bones and moving through them; how does this worm cause a person to fall ill?
What is meant by "peaceful and secure"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees the *tutu-ma* worm:
due to excessive eating, this worm becomes enraged and causes sores to break out all over the person's body.

When these worms move, they cause a person to yawn frequently, the heart to palpitate with agitation, or to feel as if one’s body has been lost; the body trembles and one cannot sleep. There is an itchy sensation throughout the body as if insects were crawling, vision becomes blurred, and one contracts diseases of cold and heat or suffers from swelling of the body.
If the *tutu-ma* worm does not become angry, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the *tutu-ma* worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *tvakkāṭaka* worms dwelling within the body, causing either disease or well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *tvakkāṭaka* worms:
due to excessive eating, the worms become enraged, causing various sores to arise on the lips, mouth, and eyes, as well as sores on both sides of the ribs.

If it moves within the sinews or gnaws at the sinews, it can cause a person’s throat to become parched, or lead to deafness and blockage with pus exuding from the ears; or it may move with a stinging sensation upon the skull, causing premature graying of the hair, a coughing affliction of the throat, or unscheduled sleep; or one may develop a distaste for food and drink, find no pleasure in staying in one place, take delight in wandering through open spaces, experience great mental agitation, or engage in delusional speech of right and wrong.
Because the worms eat the skin, all parts of the body are torn apart and destroyed, and dust covers the body.
If the worms do not become angry, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the *tvak-krimi* (skin-worm), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *vātāstra-krimi* (wind-sword worm) moving within the bones; because of the anger of this worm, there may arise either disease or well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *vātāyudha* insects:

due to excessive eating, these insects become enraged; their bite is like that of a snake, its agonizing venom difficult to endure, occurring at the crown of the head, the throat, the heart, the bladder, and the openings for the large and small intestines, as well as within the nails of the hands and feet, feeling like the pricking of needles.
Because the worms gnaw at them, their noses lose the sense of fragrance and their tongues no longer perceive flavors; their eyes twitch and throb, and they have no desire for food or drink.
Because the worms are enraged, they conspire with the bone-walking worms to ravage their bodies; due to the intensity of this pain, they do not sleep day or night.
If the wind-blade worm does not become angry, then the aforementioned ailments will not occur.
Having observed the wind-blade worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *Kṣuramukha* (razor-mouthed) worm dwelling within the body; this worm sometimes causes disease and sometimes brings about well-being.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

when the *Kṣuramukha* worm first enters the mother’s womb and at the time of initial birth, because it is initially superior by way of its nature (*dharma*), and because it drinks the mother’s milk upon first emerging from the fetal sac, at that time this worm devours all other worms, but later returns to eating mixed food.
Due to these causes and conditions, other worms are born again.
Having observed the *kṣuradantaka* (razor-toothed) worms, one knows the body as it truly is:
"These ten kinds of worms move within the bones; observe them as they truly are."

Having observed it as it truly is, the eye is freed from dust and defilement, freed from the faults of ordinary beings; the mind gives rise to revulsion, becomes free from "I" and "mine," free from doubt and purified, and is free from false views, knowing the body as it truly is, up to and including nirvana.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees ten kinds of worms moving within the excrement. What are these ten?
First is the "Birth-Worm";
second is the "Needle-Mouth Worm";
third is the "White-Jointed Worm."
The fourth is named the footless worm;
the fifth is named the juice-dispersing worm;
the sixth is named the triple-burning worm.
Seventh is the Intestine-rupturing worm;
eighth is the Obstructing worm;
ninth is the Well-colored worm.
The tenth is named the "Worm of the Ulcerous Foul Gate.
Its color is loathsome, and it dwells amidst excrement and filth. What kind of illness does it cause?
How can one find peace and security?
“Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:
there are worms that move within excrement; if the worms are burning with heat, my body also becomes hot.
If the worms suffer from cold ailments, I also suffer from cold ailments; they cause diarrhea with white pus, which causes the body to waste away and the complexion to become withered and yellow.”
If these produced worms are well-behaved and do not become angry, then there will be no such diseases as those previously described.
Having observed the produced worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the Needle-mouthed Worm moving within the filth of excrement;

its body is long and large. It travels from the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) toward the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*), which no other worms can obstruct. It then ascends from the receptacle of undigested food up to the throat, causing both saliva and vomit to be expelled together; it may cause heart pain or bring about a state of unease.
Because its digestive fire is weak, it is expelled along with the feces and dies in an instant.
Having observed the needle-mouthed worm (*sūcīmukha-kṛmi*), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *śvetāṅga* worm moving amidst excrement and filth;

its body is short and white, it consists of many interconnected worms, it is cold and extremely foul-smelling, it destroys human strength, it emerges along with the feces, and it is craved by swarms of flies.
One who has this disease produces even more excrement and filth, and no longer remembers food or drink.
Having observed the *śvetaka* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the footless worms dwelling within the body; how do these worms cause illness in humans, and how do they bring about well-being?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the legless worms:

due to an excess in eating, these worms become enraged and blow all the bodily winds, thereby obstructing the large and small excretions. If they block the stomach (*āmāśaya*), one cannot vomit nor sneeze, cannot yawn, becomes utterly exhausted and restless, unable to sleep, and cannot endure hunger or thirst.
Because of the anger of these worms, many diseases arise.
Having observed the footless worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *visarpa* worms dwelling within the body; for the sake of digesting food, they stir and disperse it at the sites where the fluids flow. They move through the various parts of the body together with these fluids, even down to the feet. Because the fluids flow everywhere throughout all parts of the body, from the feet to the crown of the head, people describe this as having a "good complexion.
If the fluids do not flow, the complexion becomes ugly.
Having observed the *sañjīva* insects, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There are three *jiao* worms that dwell within the body; when I suffer from a feverish illness, these worms increase in their defilement and wickedness, causing the stomach (*janaka*) to become restless and the element of fire to become greatly agitated.
Because of the feverish illness, the worms also contract a fever and run throughout the entire body, tormented by heat and scorched by it themselves.
Because of the anger of these worms, the channels through which flavors flow become completely parched, resulting in thirst, illness, and headaches.
Having observed the three *tāpa* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *antrāśaya* worms residing within the body. How do these worms cause disease?"
What is meant by "peaceful security"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees the *pācanaka* worms (intestine-destroying worms):

because a person consumes excessive food and flavors, these worms are provoked; the worms then become angry and gnaw through the person's intestines, causing either a distension of the heart with pain, or a wind-distension, or a heat-distension, or a cold-distension, resulting in various such forms of suffering and affliction.
This *antraghāta* worm harms the human intestines; if the worm is well-behaved, then there will be no such ailments as those previously described.
Having contemplated the *antraghāta* worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *niruddha* worms dwelling within the body. How do these worms cause illness in humans?"
What is meant by "peaceful and secure"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *niruddha* worms moving within the filth of excrement.

When I consume food and drink, these worms also eat; having eaten, they become obstructed. Due to this excess of food, they injure the flowing channels (*srotas*) and harm the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). The intestines become distended by what has been eaten, causing the intestines to contract and twist, sometimes resulting in pain in the heart and pain in the intestines.
Having observed the obstructing worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *sukra-varṇa* worm dwelling within the body; how does this worm cause disease?
What is meant by "bringing peace and security"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *suklavarṇa* worm:

"When I eat—whether I eat fine meat, coarse meat, or heavy food—this worm brings peace and security within my body; it takes the flavor from the mouth and circulates throughout the entire body, ensuring that there is no illness or affliction, increasing my vigor and strength, eliminating all diseases, and dwelling securely within my body."
By virtue of merit, the worms possess great strength, and the person consequently has a healthy complexion and sufficient energy and vigor.
If the worms lack strength, the person likewise becomes emaciated, and their appearance becomes haggard.
Having observed the *śubha-varṇa* worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *adhovartma-vraṇa-kṛmi* (wound-worms of the lower gate) dwelling within the body; how do they cause me disease?
What is meant by "peaceful security"?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

one sees that when the worms in the lower orifices consume incompatible food, they become enraged and produce various sores— either moist sores or dry sores, sores appearing in the front or sores appearing in the back, or even hot sores.

If the worm is full of anger, it blocks the impure gate, the channels through which excrement flows, the channels through which blood flows, or the channels through which fluids flow; or, due to a deficiency of fire, it fails to digest food and drink.
Because the fire element is deficient, sores arise at the impure orifices.
Because the worms are provoked to anger, they produce various kinds of diseases; if the worms were not provoked to anger, there would be none of the aforementioned diseases.
Having observed the worms in the sores of the gates of filth, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the internal body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees ten kinds of worms moving within the marrow and some moving within the semen. What are these ten?
First is the hair-worm;
second is the black-mouthed worm;
third is the powerless worm.
The fourth is named the Great Pain Worm;
the fifth is named the Distress Worm;
the sixth is named the Fire-Colored Worm.
The seventh is named the Downstreaming Worm;
the eighth is named the Body-Faculty-Arising Worm;
the ninth is named the Recollecting Worm.
The tenth is named the *ānandika* worm.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There is a marrow-worm called the "Hairy Worm" (*roma-kīṭa*); it causes hair to grow upon all parts of the body. If this worm becomes angry, it inflicts injury upon the marrow; having thus committed its offense, it then devours the person's marrow, causing leprosy, making the complexion hideous, causing pain in the bones and marrow, and causing the loss of all physical strength.
If the hair-insects are harmonious and do not give rise to anger, then the various diseases previously described will not occur.
Having observed the hair-insects, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *kṛṣṇamukha* (black-mouthed) worm dwells within the marrow, moving throughout the entire body without obstruction. If this worm becomes angry, it can cause the marrow to melt; because it injures the marrow, it causes the person’s complexion to become ugly, the spine to curve and the body to hunch, the gait to become unsteady, one to walk leaning on a staff, the facial color to grow sallow, and the body to tremble."
If the black-mouthed worm is disciplined and free from anger, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the black-mouthed worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *alpabala* worm dwelling within the body;
this worm consumes the marrow. If the marrow is insufficient, the worm lacks strength; because the worm lacks strength, the person also lacks strength.
Furthermore, there are other worms that also consume human marrow; when they are oppressed by powerful worms, the person experiences suffering and distress.
Having observed these weak worms, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *mahāvedanā* worms (great-pain insects) wander within the marrow, circulating and moving constantly throughout all parts of the body. These worms act as the causal conditions for various diseases; they cause pus and fluids to flow from all the sense organs, and one is unable to sleep."
Having observed the great worm of pain, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
By means of wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The "suffocating worm" dwells within the body, moving through the subtle channels of the mental flow; it creates obstructions for these channels.

Because it obstructs the channels, one contracts a heart ailment: the mind becomes stifled and feels as though one is about to vomit, the complexion becomes sallow and foul, one has no desire for food or drink, or one suffers from a feverish heart pain as if being cut by a blade.
When seeing external worms, the mind becomes distressed and feels as though it would vomit.
Having observed the "distressed" worm, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there are worms called "Downward-Flowers" (*adhaḥsrotas*) that move within the channels of seminal flow; when they consume excellent food or food that arouses desire, they cause the semen to increase. These worms draw the semen out through the channels of urinary flow.
Having observed the insects flowing downward, he knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The root-arising worm dwells within the womb; when the bladder is filled with urine, the worm rejoices. Having rejoiced, by means of the condition of that urine, it causes the body-faculty to arise. This is the unskillful method of contemplation of all foolish, ordinary worldlings.
Having observed the root-arising worm (*mūlotthāna-kīṭa*), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees what disease the joy-remembering worm (*smṛti-prīti-kīṭa*) causes.
What is meant by "peaceful and secure"?

It is when the worms are joyful and strong, and one sees many dreams, whether auspicious or inauspicious; because of the influence of these worms, and because they circulate through the channels of the heart, one perceives various signs in dreams.
Having observed the *smṛti-kṛmi* (mindfulness-worm), one knows the body as it truly is.
"In this way, a bhikṣu practicing in the village of the brahmin householders of Nādikā, having performed this observation, contemplates the body as it truly is."
Regarding such a body, what therein is permanent, immovable, and indestructible?
What is pleasure? What is the self?
What is pure? What can be relied upon?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
Within this body, whether gross or subtle, there is not a single dharma that is permanent, immovable, indestructible, pleasant, pure, or a self upon which one can rely.
For example, it is like a person seeking darkness at midday; whether coarse or subtle, it cannot be found.
The body is also like this: if one seeks its permanence, bliss, self, or purity, these likewise cannot be found. This is called the practitioner’s contemplation of the body as a body internally.

When one practices this contemplation, one remains far removed from the realm of Māra and draws near to the path of Nirvāṇa; craving cannot disturb them, nor can other afflictions act as obstacles. This is called the internal contemplation of the body in accordance with the body.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *cittavivartana-vāyu* (the wind that turns the mind) residing within the body.
How is it that this mental wind is able to move the body?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The mind turns the winds; because these winds are regulated, it is able to move the body—whether walking or standing, bending forward or looking upward, or performing various tasks—and through the power of the winds, it may experience either stability or instability.
Having observed the wind that turns the mind, one knows the body as it truly is; this is called "contemplation of the body by following the body internally.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or imbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the *nakhāṅguṣṭha* (nail-finger) wind resides within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees that the nails of his hands and feet grow by way of the wind-element as a causal condition, continuing until they become worn out with old age; this is called the contemplation of the wind-element in the nails.
In this way, the practitioner contemplates the wind within the body; because the wind provides firmness, the hands, feet, nails, and claws also become solid and grow rapidly.
Thus, the bhikṣu contemplates the nails of the body and knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *pādādhovāta* (foot-bottom wind) residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the *pādādhovāta* is not harmonized, it can produce itching; once itching has arisen, it can cause sores to form; furthermore, when walking, it causes a sound upon treading the ground, makes the bones of the feet firm, and enables endurance against cold and heat.
Furthermore, these foot tendons connect with the channels of the eyes; by pouring oil into the nose and applying oil to the feet, one causes the eyes to become clear and bright.
Having thus contemplated the wind beneath the feet, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *abodhaka* wind residing within the body, whether it is balanced or unbalanced, and what its functions are.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *abodhaka* wind resides within the skin, causing a tingling sensation (*kaṇḍū*); by the power of this wind, it causes a crawling sensation within the skin like that of ants moving, as if one were pressing on a sore with the hand and feeling ants crawling upon it.
Having observed the wind of non-awakening, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes that there is a wind called "Bone-Breaker" (Asthibheda) residing within the body; if it is not harmonized and regulated, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the bone-breaking wind—whether by day or night, whether walking or standing, whether in a grove or a monastery, or at times of extreme exhaustion—causes such agonizing pain in the bones that one cannot sleep; the hands and feet become unresponsive, unable to bend or extend.
Having contemplated the bone-breaking wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
what winds exist, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Destruction of Action" (Kriyā-bheda) residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that if the *bhramaṇa* wind is not harmonized, this wind arises and causes affliction, such that one is unable to walk, go, come, or advance.
Having observed and analyzed the *vāyu* of breaking, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the ankle-breaking wind (gulpha-bhañjana-vāyu) residing within the body and considers what it does.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that when the joint-breaking wind (parva-bhañjana-vāyu) encounters a cold touch, it causes pain in the thigh bones throughout the entire body.
Having observed and analyzed the *parva-bheda-vāyu* (the wind that breaks the joints), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *ūru-asthi-bheda-vāyu* (the wind that breaks the thigh bones) residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *ūru-asthi-bheda-vāyu* is not harmonized, it causes the vessels through which the fluids flow within the thighs to become swollen, coarse, and very robust; it causes the feet to bend and extend, brings the two thighs close together, and causes heavy, swollen masses of flesh to arise.
Having thus observed and analyzed the *prabhaṅgaka* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a joint-wind (*parvanavāta*) residing within the body; what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
this joint-wind [resides] in the four joints of the two shoulders, the two joints of the throat, the two joints of the frontal bone, and the nose.
One joint for the bone of the jaw; one joint for the chin-bone; thirty-two joints for the teeth;
one joint for the upper palate; two joints for the meeting of the jaws; fifteen joints for the neck; two joints for the two shoulders;
two joints for the two elbows; two joints for the two wrists; forty-five joints for the vertebrae of the spine; fourteen [joints] for the chest.
The vertebrae; twelve joints on each side of the ribs; twenty-four cartilaginous bones at the ends of the two sets of ribs;
one transverse bone; two hip bones; one bone of the spinal column;
two bones of the thighs; two bones of the knees; two bones of the ankles; two bones of the heels; and the feet.
The two joints of the knees, the two hands, and the two feet—altogether sixty joints above and below—and the twenty joints of the nails of the hands and feet:
these are the bases upon which the wind-disorders (vāta) depend. If I were to have a disease therein, it might lead to the loss of life or to great suffering.
Having observed the *vāyu* of the joints, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *ūrustambha-vāyu* (the thigh-stiffening wind) residing within the body;

if it is not harmonized, what does it cause? Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *ūrustambha-vāyu* is not harmonized, one cannot bend or extend the limbs, nor can one come or go, due to the fault of this disease.
Having observed the *pāṇḍuka* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
the bodily wind-element resides within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

When the wind element of the body is harmonious and tranquil, one possesses vigor; the breath flows in and out, enabling the digestion of food and drink; the body has a healthy complexion; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are all at ease; and what is consumed is digested.

If they are not disciplined and compliant, their physical appearance will be coarse and ugly, the five sense faculties will be diminished and inferior, food will not be digested, and their complexion will be unpleasant; the eyes and other faculties will be weak regarding their objects, and they will not conceive offspring.
Having thus observed the wind element within the bodily formations, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *pratoda-vāyu* (the "sinew-pulling wind") residing within the body: what does it do when it is not harmonized?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *pratoda-vāyu*:

If the wind is harmonious and balanced, then in all activities—whether sleeping or remaining awake—all bodily colors and complexions will be lustrous; this is entirely the work of the sinews-wind (snāyu-vāyu).
If they are not disciplined and compliant, one cannot engage in cultivation; whether sleeping or remaining still, one is entirely unable to perform any action.
Having observed the *snāyu-vāyu* (tendon-wind), one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives that there is a wind called "Going and Returning" (ānāpāna) residing within the body; if it is not harmonious and compliant, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *vaivarta* wind (the wind of coming and going) becomes unbalanced, it obstructs the flowing channels of the body, causing the disease of urinary obstruction (*prameha*). All parts of the body become painful; there is abdominal pain and pain in the sense organs of the body. One is unable to eat or drink, the vital essence and blood are completely exhausted, and one cannot conceive or give birth.
If the winds are in harmony, then these ailments do not occur.
Having observed the winds of coming and going, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?

With the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives that there is a wind called *parisarpa* (the wandering one) that dwells within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that if the *parisarpa* (wandering) wind is not harmonious, it causes people to develop abdominal tumors or hemorrhoids, brings suffering in the passage of excrement and urine, withers the four great elements, or causes headaches, indigestion, obstruction of downward winds, emaciation of the body, the arising of various sores, or the onset of fevers.
If the *saṃdhika-vāyu* (joint-wind) is harmonious and well-regulated, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having thus observed the *saṃdhika-vāyu*, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
"What winds reside within my body, whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, and what functions do they perform?

With the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives that there is a wind named *roma-nakha-gūtha-bheda* (the hair, nail, and excrement-disrupter) residing within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the wind of the broken hair, nails, and excrement is not harmonized, the sense faculties become emaciated and impaired; or there is a headache, or pain in one eye, one ear, or half the face; or the vision becomes blurred; or the nose is congested such that one cannot distinguish fragrances or stenches; the complexion turns sallow and yellow; one suffers from coughing fits and vomiting phlegm; upon seeing impurities, one immediately vomits; the mind becomes greatly disturbed, and one is unable to engage in meditative reflection.
One should constantly reflect:

"My body and mind are free from illness and at peace; yet within this human existence, the four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which abide within this body and are comprised by it, are all impermanent."
Having performed this contemplation, one understands the phenomena of birth and death.
Having contemplated and analyzed the hair-on-the-body, nails, excrement, and wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the internal body by following the body with mindfulness.
"What kinds of winds dwell within my body and perform what functions?
He perceives this through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye:

there is the *vibhramśa-phena-vāyu* (the wind of disordered seminal froth) which, within the urine, causes a person's semen and urine to be emitted together; they emerge as fine as mustard seeds along with the urine, or it causes pain during defecation.
Such a disease arises, vexing and disturbing the mind so that it cannot be focused; yet if the wind is harmonious and balanced, this disease does not occur.
Having thus observed the *vikṣepa-vāyu* (the wind of distracted energy), one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds abide within the body that either produce well-being or ill-being?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives that there is a "wind of old age" residing within the body; as this wind increases, one gradually becomes decrepit, their physical strength and vigor diminish until they can no longer come or go. When they wish to rise for even a moment, it is utterly contrary to their will. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they are exhausted and utterly depleted as if they were another person, and their mind is drowsy and clouded.
If the winds are harmonious and well-adjusted, then these ailments do not arise.
Having observed the wind of old age, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by way of following the body.
"What winds reside within my body that may cause either well-being or ill-being?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the *garbhastambhana* (embryo-stiffening) wind resides within the body; if it is not harmonized, the flesh of the body twitches, the body becomes weak, the heart pains, excrement and urine are obstructed, and the passage of feces and urine is difficult and painful. This hinders the practice of dhyāna, brings about great suffering and affliction, causes the mind to become distracted, and leaves consciousness unpeaceful, such that one is unable to contemplate the dharmas.
Because the body suffers, one is unable to contemplate the Dharma.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having thus observed the *sai-pao-feng* (the wind that obstructs the womb), one knows the body as it truly is.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Five;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Six.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Three:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within my body that produce either well-being or ill-being?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees the wind of dry excrement (*śuṣka-śakṛt-vāyu*):

"If I eat too much, this wind becomes disordered and causes me affliction; it enters into the channels and sinews of my body, causing the excrement to become parched. After two, three, four, or five days, I then void a stool that is dry, scanty, and foul-smelling, accompanied by extreme pain."
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then these ailments do not arise.
Having contemplated the wind of dry excrement, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
"What winds reside within my body that may bring either comfort or discomfort?
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the lateral winds; if they are not harmonized, what do they cause?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
the two flanking winds move along the sides of the body, causing the blood to dry up; because the blood dries up, one experiences great suffering.
If the winds are harmonious, then these ailments do not occur.
Having observed the lateral winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.
"What winds reside within my body that produce either well-being or ill-being?
With the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes what winds reside within his body and what kind of functions they perform."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives:

there is a wind named "Obstructing the Nine Orifices" that dwells within the body; if it is not harmonious, it can cause the nine orifices—namely, the seven apertures of the head along with those for feces and urine—to become blocked and impassable. Once these nine orifices are obstructed, the body suffers from illness and pain, and the inhalation and exhalation of breath cannot proceed peacefully.

If the winds are harmonious and balanced, they bring peace and stability to the body, enabling one to practice the Dharma; for it is by being sustained by the winds that the body is able to move to and fro.
Having thus contemplated the winds of the nine apertures, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
By means of wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees what winds reside within his body and what functions they perform."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Body-Section-Severer. What does it do when it is not harmonized or compliant?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the Body-Section-Severer wind is neither harmonized nor compliant, the fingers become withered and incapable of action; both hands and feet become withered; the tendons of the thighs are acutely painful; the nine coarse sinews and vessels become taut and strained; the body parts tremble; and one becomes utterly exhausted and powerless.
If the *prabhaṅgana* wind is harmonized, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having contemplated the *prabhaṅgana* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds dwell within my body that bring about either well-being or ill-being?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees within the body a wind called "Fire-Consumer" (*agnighātaka*) that dwells therein; what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the power of this wind can eliminate the heat of the fire, causing food not to be digested. Because the food is not digested, one no longer thinks of food; because one cannot eat, one loses one's complexion.
Why is it colorless? Because the blood has dried up.

As the blood dries up, the flesh wastes away; as the flesh wastes away, the tendons contract and shrink, and fat no longer forms. Because fat does not form, the bones also dry up; because the bones dry up, the marrow also dries up; and because the marrow dries up, the vital essence throughout the entire body is exhausted.
The vital energy within the heart moves because it is blown by the wind.
If the destructive fire-wind is harmonious and tranquil, then there will be no suffering from the diseases mentioned above.
Having contemplated the destructive fire-wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds dwell within my body, and what functions do they perform?
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called the 'wind that produces coldness in all bodily parts. What does it do?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the cold wind pervading all parts of the body causes the body to emit foul-smelling sweat, become stiff and rough, and turn a hideous color; the limbs wrinkle and shrink, becoming emaciated and the hair stands on end; black sores break out on the body, oozing pus and emitting a putrid stench, with fluids flowing from scratching and tearing, or red sores appear, or there is great burning heat;
or white sores arise, coarse and large, covering the entire body.
Or again, their bodies may be like the hide of a white elephant—rough, coarse, and covered in sores;

or their mouths and teeth may be sparse, dark, and blackened, while sores break out on their hands and feet. Like exhausted craftsmen utterly worn out, their bodies are covered in scabs and rashes, their hands and feet are constantly hot, hard, rigid, and coarse;
or they develop festering sores, their nails turn a foul color, the bridge of their nose collapses, and their eyelids fall away.
One is loathed and despised by others, detested by all donors;
flies swarm and settle upon one, and the fingernails fall off.
When sleeping, the breath becomes turbid and foul, and one snores loudly; one has no desire for food, or what is eaten is not digested, and the tongue cannot perceive flavors.
In this way, the cold winds that pervade all parts of the body cause the body to rot and decay.

However, if the cold winds throughout the entire body are harmonious and well-regulated, then one’s complexion will be lovely, fine, soft, and smooth, and one will be honored by all people; warm sweat and vital fluids will emerge from the pores, and thus none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the cold wind that pervades all parts of the body, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
"What winds reside within my body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a wind named *Balaprabhañjana* (Destroyer of Strength) that dwells within his body; if it is not harmonized, it causes the mind to be timid and fearful, brings about pain throughout all parts of the body, or causes the body to become rigid, frequent yawning, and a lack of joy. The inhalation and exhalation are entirely unsettled, the body trembles, one is unable to wear clothes, and suffers from headaches;
if one practices meditative contemplation, one cannot attain single-mindedness.
Or they may see evil dreams, their minds becoming distressed and causing them to vomit;
amidst beautiful forms, they give rise to perverted views, perceiving what is near as distant, becoming parched with thirst and emaciated.
If the *pracaṇḍa* wind is broken, well-regulated, and harmonious, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the *pracaṇḍa* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
"What kind of wind dwells within my body, and what kind of activity does it perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the *sphurana* (trembling) wind dwells within his body; whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what kind of activity does it perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the *kāyaspandanavāyu* (the wind of bodily tremors) is not in harmony, there is ringing in the ears, the flesh of the arms throbs, and all parts of the body likewise throb; one flees hither and thither, finding no pleasure in staying in one place, and there is no other ailment besides this.
If the *sphurana-vāyu* (trembling wind) throughout the entire body is harmonious, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the trembling wind throughout the entire body, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds dwell within my body?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a 'heat-wind' dwelling within his body. Whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what function does it perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that if this hot wind is not harmonious, whatever is eaten and enters the mouth will burn as it is swallowed; for this reason, the four great elements become unbalanced and fail to increase,
or the flavors of what is eaten do not form the two streams [of excrement and urine], becoming turbid, foul, and impure.
If there is a pure flow and the four great elements increase, yet there is only turbidity and impurity, this constitutes the suffering of illness.
If the hot wind is not harmonized, all that is consumed becomes turbid and fails to become pure; therefore, one contracts illness.
If the hot wind is harmonious, and if the two kinds of food-flows—whether clear or turbid—bring the four great elements into equilibrium, then, by virtue of this equilibrium, illness does not arise.
Having observed the hot winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
"What winds reside within my body, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a wind called "Gathering Insects" (*saṃcita-kīṭa*); this Gathering Insects wind pervades all parts of the body, capable of both gathering and dispersing [the bodily constituents], and it obstructs the upper and lower openings.
From the crown of the head to the feet, there are ten kinds of worms:
first, the head-moving worm;
second, the bone-moving worm.
Third is the hair-eating worm;
fourth is the ear-traveling worm;
fifth is the nose-interior worm.
Sixth is the fat-internal-circulating worm;
seventh is the joint-circulating worm;
eighth is the saliva-consuming worm.
The ninth is named the Tooth-root-eating Worm;
the tenth is named the Vomiting Worm.
Furthermore, there are ten worms located in the throat and chest:
First is the worm named Consumer of Food;
second is the worm named Consumer of Saliva;
third is the worm named Consumer of Spittle.
The fourth is named the Vomit-Inducing Worm;
the fifth is named the Ten-Flavor-Flowing-Vessel-Worm;
the sixth is named the Sweet-Intoxication Worm.
Seventh is the worm named Relish-taster;
eighth is the worm named Air-expeller;
ninth is the worm named Taste-averting.
The tenth is named the Sleep-Seeking Worm.
Furthermore, there are ten worms that arise within the blood and flesh and move therein:
the first is named the Hair-Eating Worm;
The second is named the Hole-Dwelling Worm;
the third is named the Chan-du Worm;
the fourth is named the Red Worm.
Fifth, the *āhārāsava* worm;
sixth, the *romadīpa* worm;
seventh, the *krodharudhira* worm.
The eighth is named the blood-eating worm;
the ninth is named the pricking worm;
the tenth is named the vinegar worm.
Thus, ten types of worms are born within the blood; their forms are either short or globular, minute and without eyes.
Furthermore, there are ten types of worms that produce sensations of pain, which are born within the flesh:
the first is named the Ulcer-Taste Worm (vraṇarasa-kṛmi).
The second is named the *chūchū* worm;
the third is named the *bìjīn* worm;
the fourth is named the *dòngmài* worm.
Fifth is the skin-eating worm;
sixth is the moving-fat worm;
seventh is the harmonizing-aggregate worm.
The eighth is named the stinking insect;
the ninth is named the sweat-wandering insect;
the tenth is named the heat insect.
These and other such worms are born from the flesh.
Furthermore, there are ten worms that move within the yellow marrow:
the first is named the Black Worm;
The second is named the Sprout-and-Flower Worm;
the third is named the Great Deceitful Worm;
the fourth is named the Suvīra Worm.
Fifth, the *kṛmika* worm;
sixth, the *mahāśana* worm;
seventh, the *uṣṇagati* worm.
The eighth is named the Great Heat Worm;
the ninth is named the Taste-Eater Worm;
the tenth is named the Great Fire Worm.
Such worms as these move within the aggregates (*skandha*).
Within the various parts of the body, there are ten kinds of worms:
the first is named the Bone-Licking Worm (*asthi-lehaka-kṛmi*).
The second is named the Bone-Biting Worm;
the third is named the Joint-Splitting Worm;
the fourth is named the Foul-Smelling Worm.
Fifth is the bone-consuming worm;
sixth is the red-mouthed worm;
seventh is the *tutu-ma* worm.
The eighth is named the Skin-Eating Worm;
the ninth is named the Knife-Wind Worm;
the tenth is named the Knife-Mouth Worm.
