"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of worms that move within the excrement:
first, the 'birth-worm';
second, the 'needle-mouthed worm'."
Third, the white-jointed worm;
fourth, the legless worm;
fifth, the excrement-scattering worm.
Sixth is the Trijvāla worm;
seventh is the Intestine-rupturing worm;
eighth is the Obstructing worm.
The ninth is named the *śubhavarṇa* worm;
the tenth is named the *gudadvāravraṇa* worm.
Their colors are loathsome; these are known as the ten kinds of worms within the excrement.
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of worms that move within the fat and marrow. What are these ten?
First is the Hair-Worm;
second is the Black-Mouthed Worm;"
Third is the worm named Lost-of-Strength;
fourth is the worm named Great-Pain;
fifth is the worm named Distressed.
Sixth is the fire-colored worm;
seventh is the downward-flowing worm;
eighth is the body-faculty-arousing worm.
The ninth is named the *smṛti-kīṭa* (recollection worm);
the tenth is named the *pramoda-kīṭa* (joy worm).

These and other such worms circulate throughout all parts of the body; they move through the entire body at will, traverse all the elements (*dhātu*), and wherever they go, they commit transgressions and evils.
This "wind that gathers insects" circulates throughout the entire body at will; thus, by means of this wind as a condition, the various insects flow through the body.
Having observed the wind that gathers insects, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds dwell within my body, and what functions do they perform?

With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes that there is a wind called 'Upward-and-Downward' (ūrdhvādhoga) dwelling within the body; whether it brings stability or instability, what does it do?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the upward and downward winds are not in harmony, they move through five locations; what function do they perform?
They produce the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

People call this "vitality" (*āyus*); it moves within the heart and the crown of the head, pervading the entire body with sovereign unimpededness—this is the first division of the power of wind (*vāyu*).
If the wind is not harmonized, it can destroy the body.

This wind also causes excessive salivation in the mouth, makes the body emaciated, and causes food and drink to be regurgitated and ejected through vomiting; this is the second division of the power of wind.
Abiding in the chest, what does it do?
If the wind-energy is in the heart, one experiences either sorrow or joy.

If the wind-energy rises from the throat to the crown of the head and descends into the root of the tongue, then according to one's thoughts, one is able to speak, articulate syllables, and contemplate various meanings; this is the third division of the power of wind.
Furthermore, there is that which is constantly troubled by the fire of the body, causing the body to perspire; this is the fourth division of the power of wind.
This wind pervades the entire body, causing the eyelids to blink and the whole body to move, and it extends its thought throughout the entire body.

Relying on the male and female faculties, one is able to produce offspring; when a man and woman engage in sexual desire, by the power of such winds, they are able to gather the semen and blood, and cause the woman’s pelvic bones to gain strength, so that the combined and gathered semen and blood of the man and woman form the *kalala* body.
At the time when the semen is thin, the wind blows it so that it becomes thick and forms a mass of flesh;
once the mass of flesh has formed, the five *kalalas* subsequently arise;
after the five *kalalas* have arisen, they may be square or round, and according to the length and shortness of the body, consciousness also pervades them, following their various characteristics.

It is like a person churning curd to produce ghee; there is the curd, there is water, there is the vessel, and there is the churning stick. As they churn it, foam emerges; knowing that it has reached maturity, they collect the fresh butter.
In this same way, the wind-force and the karma and afflictions that are able to assemble and form the body are likewise; this is the fifth division of wind-force.

When food and drink are consumed, within the tongue-root and the channels of the throat, the food and drink fill them completely, even extending to the hair roots and fingernails, whereby physical strength increases and the qualities of color, fragrance, and flavor are produced.
If the winds are not in harmony, the downward-moving wind ascends and produces four kinds of evils: the vital breath becomes obstructed and difficult to expel, and the entire body suffers distress.

If they depart from their original locations, all the sense faculties and all forms of consciousness become agitated and disordered, leading to the loss of life and limb. Once the body has been cast off, one loses three things: first, life; [the other two are omitted in the source].
Second, heat; third, consciousness.
Therefore, the verse says:
"When this body is cast off, life, warmth, and consciousness are lost;
there is no further perception or awareness, just like tiles, wood, or stone."
"This is what is called the first evil.

If one does not achieve composure and performs the second type of action, one's breathing becomes coarse and heavy; unable to attain tranquility, one is oppressed by suffering pervading the entire body. When the intensity of this oppression reaches its peak, one then abandons life and limb—this is what is called the second evil."

If this upward-moving wind is not harmonious, it creates the third evil; having afflicted the sense faculties, it causes turmoil throughout the entire body, leading to the loss of life and limb. This is what is called the third evil.

If this upward-moving wind is not in harmony, it produces the fourth affliction: either one breathes with great gasps or breathes very faintly; it may lead to the end of life, or cause the body to simply hunch over without losing life. This is called the fourth affliction.
When one is asleep, the inhalation and exhalation of the breath persist by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Having thus observed the upward and downward winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.

What winds are there that, whether causing stability or instability, perform what kind of functions? Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives: there is a wind called the life-wind (*jīvita-vāyu*) which dwells within the body;

it may cause the body to become stout or emaciated, and it causes the mind to be discerning. If this wind is not balanced, the mind becomes light and restless, one loses all that has been learned, forgets even what was previously heard, does not clearly perceive objects seen, and does not hear sounds. Likewise, the nose does not perceive odors, the tongue does not perceive tastes, the body does not feel tangibles, and the mind does not cognize mental phenomena; one no longer distinguishes between self and others.
Having observed the life-force wind (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra-vāyu*), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
what winds are there, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the wind of the distracted mind abiding within the body; whether it is harmonious or disharmonious, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees this wind:

if there is a fault in my mind, the wind becomes disharmonious and follows the movements of the mind, becoming either agitated or rigid, causing emaciation and delusive confusion. Or, the flavors of what is eaten flow perversely and improperly, thus vexing and disturbing the mind so that one feels no love or joy for wholesome dharmas, resulting in profuse sweating and salivation, and an inability to endure cold contact.

If one perceives the marks of form, because of the presence of illness, one cannot see form as it was originally or as it truly is; the body becomes heavy and difficult to control, and the hairs on the body all stand erect.
If the winds are harmonious, then there will be no such diseases as those previously described.
Having observed the wind of the distracted mind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, whether causing it to be at ease or ill at ease, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a wind called "disturbance" (*vikṣepa*) that resides within the body; if it is not harmonized and subdued, one frequently experiences bad dreams, awakens in a state of startled alarm while sleeping, and although dwelling in warmth, constantly feels cold.
If one sees cities, towns, villages, or people, one perceives them as empty hamlets; or one sees them as yellowish, speaks little, and takes no pleasure in lying down.
One has forgotten all the teachings previously heard;
the four elements are in turmoil, and the flavors of what one eats remain fixed in the heart, such that there is no cause for weariness, yet one falsely perceives them as mounds and heaps.
If the winds are harmonious and well-regulated, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the turbulent winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.
What winds are there, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the *vīkṣaṇa* wind (the wind of blinking) resides within the body; if it is not in a state of equilibrium, one is unable to blink the eyes.
There is no other wind that moves more swiftly than this.
As for the wind of the blinking eye, it travels everywhere, pervading all the sense faculties; if it is not harmonized and regulated, this disease arises.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the *vīkṣaṇa-vāyu* (the wind of looking and blinking), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what karma do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind named Mutual Obstruction (*anyonya-āvṛti*). At the time of death, five winds arise; whether balanced or unbalanced, what karma do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that because the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind have deteriorated, they are unable to perceive or cognize their respective objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. If the wind does not arise, life is not severed; if it arises, life is lost.
Having observed the five obstructing winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
what winds are there, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a "womb-destroying wind" residing within the body. When a person’s initial consciousness enters the mother’s womb, due to the causal conditions of past karma, its life-force is destroyed at the stage of the *kalala*;
if its life-force is not destroyed at the stage of the *kalala*, it is severed at the stage of the *peśī* as a cold wind enters the womb and causes its destruction.
If one takes the flesh while not severing its life, one severs its life only when its bodily parts are complete;
if one does not sever its life while its bodily parts are complete, one severs its life only when all its sense faculties are complete.
According to the lightness or gravity of their karmic offenses from previous lives regarding killing, their lives are terminated within the womb.
If they did not kill sentient beings in previous lives, the aforementioned winds will be unable to cause their death.
Having observed the wind that destroys the fetal store, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds are there—whether balanced or unbalanced—and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "transformer of the embryo" (garbhavivartaka) residing within the body; whether it is turbulent or not, what function does it perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that the *garbhāvarta-vāyu* (the wind that transforms the embryo) uses the deluded karma of this sentient being’s previous lives to transform a male into a female, or to turn them into a eunuch, or cause death within the womb—
all due to evil karma; however, if there was no evil karma in previous lives, it cannot cause such harm.
Having observed the *parivartaka* wind that turns the embryo, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the winds of going, coming, running, and leaping reside within the body; whether they are disturbed or undisturbed, what do they do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the winds of going, coming, running, and leaping are not harmonious, the hands and feet become cramped or paralyzed, the body becomes hunched and the spine curved, one cannot walk or come and go, and for food and drink one must depend on others and cannot eat by oneself; the faculty of the body and wisdom are both entirely impure.
If the wind is harmonious and balanced, the body is able to move, go, come, advance, and stop; it can run, leap, and mount vehicles to ascend or descend.
Having observed the winds of going, coming, running, and leaping, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the specific functions performed by the distinct winds of the five faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and how they are impelled by the karmic winds. One such wind acts in conjunction with the eye."
Because the power of wind is strongest among the four great elements, it is called "wind.
This wind can cause the four great elements of the eye faculty to become pure, enabling one to see various forms and images;
likewise, a single wind within the ear enables one to hear sounds, and the same applies to the nose’s fragrance, the tongue’s flavors, and the body’s tactile sensations.
One should contemplate these five winds as they truly are.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, there will be no obstruction regarding the five sense objects;
if they are not harmonious and balanced, there will be many obstructions, and one will be unable to know the sense objects as they truly are.
Having thus observed the five kinds of winds in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a "sword wind" (śastravāyu) residing within the body, which may be disordered or undisturbed; what functions does it perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that at the time of death, the "sword-winds" (kṣurapra-vāyu) stir everywhere;
skin, flesh, sinews, bones, fat, marrow, semen, and blood are all severed and cut apart, causing everything to become parched as the vital breaths are blocked and cease to flow.
Once the body has become parched, one dies in agony; it is as if a thousand flaming swords were piercing one's body, yet even this does not equal even a sixteenth part of the suffering.
If one possesses wholesome karma, at the time of approaching death, when the "sword-wind" (kṣuravāyu) stirs slightly, there will not be much suffering or distress.
Having observed this sword-wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the *sūcī-vāyu* (needle-piercing wind) residing within the body; whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that at the time of death, the winds become disordered and pervade all the joints of the body, as well as all the channels, all the tendons, all the bones and branches, all the pores, all the flesh, all the bones, and all the marrow. Like flaming needles, they pervade the entire body and press upon the person; it is as if hundreds of thousands of flaming needles were piercing his body, yet this [suffering] does not even equal one-sixteenth part of that [suffering].
If one has performed virtuous deeds in previous lives, then at the time of death, this "needle-pricking wind" will not cause great suffering.
Having observed the needle-pricking wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there—whether balanced or unbalanced—and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called 'Bad Yellow' residing within the body; whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the evil yellow wind (*pīta-vāyu*) becomes unbalanced, it gives rise to jaundice.

The mouth becomes parched, and the entire body turns yellow; the face, eyes, nails, and all other parts become yellow. The abdomen swells and becomes coarse and large, with blue and yellow veins appearing upon its surface. The body lacks strength, food cannot be digested, the mouth is bitter, and the urine is yellow. The body becomes emaciated, and when looking at various colors, they all appear as blue and yellow. One is unable to rise or sit, and the abdomen remains constantly distended.
If the yellow wind is disordered, this disease arises;
if the yellow wind is harmonious and compliant, this disease does not exist.
Having contemplated the malignant yellow wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called 'Intestine-Disrupter' (*antrāpaha*), which, whether balanced or unbalanced, performs certain actions. What does it do?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *pārupaṇaka-vāyu* (intestine-breaking wind) is not harmonized, or if one eats excessively and frequently stretches, it can rupture the intestines; or if bone fragments mixed with meat enter the intestines, they can rupture the intestines, causing food to flow out. The abdomen becomes distended and grows large, giving rise to great agony such that one cannot eat or drink.

Because the strength of digestion is diminished, the body becomes weak and frail, the hands and feet swell, the lower orifices feel a burning heat, all parts of the body are constantly and irregularly hot, the mouth is parched, and one constantly experiences evil dreams.
When the wind moves within the abdomen, not a single thought remains still.
If the *pācanaka-vāyu* (the "intestine-breaking" wind) is regulated and harmonized, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the *pācanaka-vāyu*, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called 'cold-spittle' (*śīta-lālā*). Whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the cold-saliva wind (*śīta-lālā-vāyu*) becomes disordered, the taste in the mouth becomes sweet, the mind becomes restless, and one loses the desire for food and drink. If one wishes to practice seated meditation, doubt and indolence arise; the tongue becomes heavy and speech difficult, or the throat becomes painful. Eructations are foul-smelling, and a foul odor from within the heart surges up toward the throat. The breath becomes obstructed and difficult to expel, and one is unaware of hunger or thirst as the throat becomes constricted.
If the cold wind is harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the cold-saliva wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called *majjā-ghātaka* (marrow-damaging) residing within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that if the *majjā-vedhana-vāyu* (the marrow-piercing wind) is not harmonized, it causes the body to tremble, brings about extreme physical exhaustion, prevents one from traveling far, results in constant illness, makes the complexion unsightly, causes a pricking sensation throughout the body, hinders much speech, and renders the mind timid and weak.
This person suffers from constant pain in the marrow of the bones day and night; the hairs on their body all stand erect, the channels are weak and feeble, and they constantly suffer from headaches.
Because of this wind, the worms in the brain are perpetually agitated; as the worms move, it feels like being pierced by needles.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having thus contemplated the wind that injures the marrow, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?
With the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "Skin-Inflicter" residing within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the *tvak-han* wind (the skin-destroying wind) is not harmonized, it causes the color of my body's skin to become ugly, making it entirely coarse and rough; the skin of the body cracks and splits, and even when anointed with ghee or oil, it quickly dries up;

the limbs and hands and feet all become rigid and straight, making them difficult to bend or extend; in dreams one frequently sees oneself falling over steep precipices; warm food and drink feel cold in the mouth; and the tongue becomes ulcerated and cracked, rendering one unable to eat or drink.
If the *tvak-ghātaka* wind is harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the *tvak-ghātaka* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?
Through his wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees a wind residing within the body called "Blood-Oppressor" (*rakta-ghātaka*). If it is not harmonious, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the *hṛdaya-rakta-vāyu* (blood-harming wind) resides within the body; if it is not harmonized, it moves through the lungs and produces two kinds of disorders—either moving upward or downward.

If the blood flows upward, it causes the blood vessels of the eyes, ears, and nose to become disordered, and the primary elements (mahābhūtas) to become unstable. Because the primary elements are disordered, the body loses its strength, the complexion becomes coarse and ugly, one is unable to come or go, and a constant foul odor emanates from the nostrils;
furthermore, fellow practitioners of the holy life will not associate with such a person or sit together with them.
If the blood flows downward and issues forth with the stool or urine, it produces three kinds of afflictions:
first, hemorrhoids;
second, painful distress.
Third is the discharge of blood.
If the harmful blood-wind (*rakta-vāyu*) is harmonious, balanced, and well-adjusted, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having observed the harmful blood-wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "Flesh-Destroyer" (Māṃsaghātaka) that dwells within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *māṃsaghātaka* wind (the flesh-destroying wind) becomes unbalanced, it causes various abscesses to arise within the human body; the foul odor pervades the entire body, and once they burst, the stench is even more loathsome, with copious amounts of pus and discharge.
Such a person endures cold but hates heat, and cannot tolerate pungent or bitter tastes; they require light, sweet, and cool food.
All bodily movements emit a foul, putrid odor.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having contemplated the *hāyanaka* wind that destroys the flesh, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes a wind called "Fat-Destroyer" (*meda-vināśana*). What kind of karma does it perform when it is not harmonized?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the Fat-Destroyer wind is not harmonized, it causes fat to increase, causing blisters and fleshy growths to arise on the body; these are uneven in height, forming mounds and depressions, sometimes hard and sometimes slippery, or perhaps numb and dull, such that there is no sensation of touch.
If the *meda-hāraka* wind is harmonious and well-regulated, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the *meda-hāraka* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body within.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either harmonious or disharmonious?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives the *hāru-bhaṅga* wind (the bone-harming wind). If it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *asthi-ghātaka* wind (the bone-harming wind) becomes disordered, it causes pain in the bones, their sounds to crackle and scatter, and one to remain sleepless day and night. There is pain in the neck and nape; all tendons and sinews become slack and untended, losing their strength. The body is constantly in pain, exhausted by extreme suffering, unable to rise or sit, and finds not a single moment of pleasure.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the bone-harming wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind residing within the body named *śukra-hārin* (the semen-destroyer). If it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *vāyu* (wind) of "injuring the essence" is not harmonized, it deceives and deludes people; when a person is asleep, it plays tricks upon them, manifesting various evil thoughts and causing them to engage in unchaste conduct through a mind of false imagination.
Because the winds are not in harmony, the night-walking female spirits (yakṣiṇī) deceive and destroy reality; through dreams they commit offenses, causing one to lose the memory of food.
Having observed the wind that harms the semen, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called the "wrinkling wind" (cūrṇaka-vāyu) residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it cause?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes the *valī-vāyu* (wrinkle-wind):

if it is not harmonized, whether in the soles or the tops of the feet, the calves or the thighs, the hips or the back, the ribs or the breasts, the throat or the neck, the shoulders or the arms, the ears or the eyebrows—every part of the body becomes wrinkled and diminished. His body becomes deeply furrowed, appearing as if opening and closing; his feet become cracked and broken.
Even if oil is applied to his body, it dries up immediately, making him resemble an old man.
Having observed the *vāta* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
what winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "White Hair" residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he observes:

if the *śvetakeśa-vāyu* (the white-hair wind) becomes disordered, it can cause the hair of a youth to turn white and his body to become emaciated, making him appear like an old man. If a son is born to a householder, he will age rapidly like his father; because of that son’s illness, the mother will no longer conceive further children.
By the power of the wind, it causes the young to become no different from the old.
This "white-hair wind" arises during an evil kalpa; as sentient beings increasingly fail to practice in accordance with the Dharma, the wind grows ever stronger.
If one possesses merit, the winds will be harmonious;
if one lacks merit, the winds will not be harmonious.
Having observed the white-hair wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds are there, whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called *meda-kṣaya* (fat-depleting) residing within the body. If it is not harmonious, what does it do?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes:
when the *sneha-hārin* wind (the "fat-diminishing" wind) is not harmonized, one loses the memory of food and drink, becomes physically debilitated, and has no appetite for fatty foods;
this disease arises due to sleeping during the day.
When the wind is not in harmony, one does not delight in sweet flavors but craves bitter and sour tastes;
if one does not consume oily foods, the wind becomes harmonious and the body does not become exhausted.
Having observed the *nīlikā* wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body:
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a *śleṣmānila* (phlegm-wind) residing within the human body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the wind of the *śleṣman* disease is not harmonized, there is constant excessive discharge, the body lacks its natural ease, and one has no physical strength; the inhalation and exhalation become coarse, turbid, and irregular; the complexion becomes sallow, and one becomes emaciated and haggard.
If the winds are harmonious and well-regulated, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the *vāta* (wind) disorders, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds are there, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind named "Associated with Food. Whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the wind associated with eating is not harmonious, three-quarters of what is eaten—whether divided into four parts or five—is vomited up; this causes the mind to become distracted, one loses the strength of food, and one is unable to blink the eyes.
Due to the power of the winds, the mind and its objects are not stable.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will occur.
Having contemplated the wind associated with food, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Tooth-Destroyer" residing within the body,
and considers what its function is. Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that if this Tooth-Destroying Wind is not harmonious, the teeth ache, become damaged and fall out, the gums bleed and fester, sores break out on the lips and mouth, sores form on the palate, and the nose becomes congested and blocked.
If the wind is harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the wind that causes the decay of the teeth, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind named *kaṇṭhanāḍī* (throat-vessel) residing within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that if the wind in the throat vessels is not harmonious, it causes pain in the throat and neck, or swelling of the throat, or makes the voice hoarse.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the wind in the throat vessels, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a wind called "Downward-Moving" (adhoga) which resides within the body; what does it do when it is balanced or unbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that if the downward-moving wind (*adhogama-vāyu*) is not harmonious, it causes food to be consumed improperly, resulting in a lack of strength and indigestion.
Because the food is properly digested, the skin, flesh, bones, marrow, vital essence, and blood increase.
If food is not digested, the bodily winds, cold-natured disorders, and jaundice will all become disharmonious.
If this downward-moving wind (apāna-vāyu) is not harmonious, one loses the strength derived from food; because the strength of food is diminished, the complexion becomes haggard.
If the winds are harmonious, then there will be no such ailments as those previously described.
Having observed the downward-moving winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, whether in a state of equilibrium or disequilibrium, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "Upward-moving" (Urdhvaga) residing within the body; what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the upward-moving wind (ūrdhvaga-vāyu) resides at the crown of the head. If this wind is harmonious, it issues forth from the crown like smoke; whether one stays in the sunlight or in the shade, by day or by night, it constantly flows out without interruption, visible to all ordinary people.
If the wind is not in harmony, the breath will not issue forth;
furthermore, once the breath at the crown has been severed and does not emerge for three days, death is certain.
Having contemplated the upward-moving wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that there is a lateral wind residing within the body; whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees this lateral wind:

if it is not harmonious, it obstructs the inhalation and exhalation, causing all the sinews and veins to contract, making them either clump together or disperse, pulling or tugging at them; it causes the nose to twitch or makes a gurgling sound, after which one experiences great suffering.
If the lateral wind is harmonious and well-regulated, then there will be no such ailments as those previously described.
Having observed the lateral wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind named *snāyu-parivartaka* (the "sinew-turner") residing within the body. If it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *vāyu* of convulsing tendons (*tvarana-vāyu*) is not harmonized, it causes the tendons of the hands and feet, the tendons of the large and small excretory tracts, the tendons of the back, and all the tendons throughout the body to contract and coil together into a single mass. They become rigid, tense, and inert, devoid of any sensation or cognition.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the wind of cramps, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within by means of mindfulness directed toward the body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind named *Lomaharṣaṇī* (Hair-raising) residing within the body; what does it do when it is balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the "hair-destroying wind" (*roma-vināśana-vāyu*) becomes unbalanced, all the hairs on every part of the body fall out; the body becomes withered and pale, and even if hair grows back again, it immediately falls out as well.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then there will be no such ailments as those previously described.
Having observed the *vāyu* that destroys the hair, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or imbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called *alpa-sadṛśa* (resembling the small). When this wind is harmonious, what does it accomplish?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that because it resembles a slight wind and is well-regulated, the power of the ten seasonal winds, as well as its form, appearance, physical strength, and the various movements of bending, stretching, bowing, and rising, are all similar in every detail.

If the winds are not in harmony, the channels through which the mind flows within the body will become agitated, giving rise to madness and delusion, and causing the mind to be disordered and unsteady.
If those channels through which the mind flows are harmonious and compliant, one will not become deranged.
Having observed what appears to be the minor wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "fondness for sleep. If it is not harmonized, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the sleep-wind is not harmonized, it causes a person to become drowsy while listening to the Dharma; furthermore, when hearing unwholesome teachings, the mind takes pleasure in hearing them.
Whether by day or by night, when one wishes to engage in correct contemplation, one becomes distracted and takes pleasure in visiting taverns.
If the wind-element is harmonious and balanced, this affliction does not occur.
Having thus contemplated the sleep-wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform?
With wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called the 'wrathful wind' (krodha-vāyu) residing within the body. If it is not harmonized, what does it cause to happen?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the wind of hatred is not harmonized, even due to a minor cause, great anger arises. Impelled by this hatred, all people in the world give rise to intense rage; the hair on their bodies stands on end, their minds become agitated and distracted, and what they see is not clearly perceived—taking the near for the distant.
When they look at the sun and moon, they develop a perverted mind, mistaking the sun for the moon and the moon for the sun.
If the winds are harmonious, then this illness does not occur.
Having contemplated the wind of anger, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind named *nāman* (name). Whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives the wind of names:

if it is harmonious and compliant, it enables speech; conditioned by mental factors, the tongue-wind engages in speech, proceeding in accordance with the mind, capable of articulating immeasurable names, phrases, and meanings.
If the wind that articulates names through the tongue is not harmonious, one will speak little, utter errors, or suffer from muteness and silence.
Having observed the wind of names in the tongue, one knows the body as it truly is.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Six;
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Seven.
Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Four:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Taste-Destroyer" residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the "flavor-destroying wind" (rasa-vināśana-vāyu) becomes unbalanced, it causes the worms within the tongue that crave sweetness to stir. Because these worms stir, one is unable to eat any good food or delicious meals. Due to not eating, the body becomes weak and inferior; one cannot recite, study, practice meditative contemplation, or cultivate wholesome dharmas. Because the body is unbalanced, the mind does not delight in the Dharma. Name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) abide through mutual causal conditions, just as bundles of bamboo stand by leaning against one another.

By the power of this mutual dependence, name-and-form each rely upon the other; thus the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-kalāpa) abides through the causal condition of nutriment, just as water mixed with parched grain flour is called "gruel," where each has its own power so that name-and-form may abide.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then there will be no illnesses such as those previously described.
Having observed the wind that destroys the sense of taste, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called *phupphusa-saṃvāhana* (lung-overturning) residing within the body; what does it do when it is balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the wind in the lungs is disordered, a person suffers pain at night while attempting to digest food; this causes an acidic taste in the mouth that persists until the food is digested, leaving the entire body devoid of strength and the vessels bound like a net.
If the wind is harmonious and balanced, then none of the aforementioned ailments will arise.
Having observed the wind in the lungs, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "Upward-moving Foulness" (*pūti-ūrdhvagāmin*). What does it do when it is balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that the upward-moving wind of stench causes the body, nose, and mouth to all become foul-smelling; it causes the stench to issue forth from the pores, surges upward from the *pakvāśaya* (receptacle for digested food) toward the *āmāśaya* (stomach), and causes the entire body to become rigid and experience great suffering. Food is not digested, one is unable to practice seated meditation, and one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas day or night.
If the upward-moving winds are harmonious, balanced, and well-adjusted, then the aforementioned ailments will not occur.
Having observed the upward-moving winds, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called the "feces-place. Whether it is harmonious or disharmonious, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

if the feces-wind is not harmonious, it causes hemorrhoids within the three types of fleshy swellings; the blood discharged is like the juice of red beans, the body is scorched with heat, one is drowsy and prone to sleep, the sinews and veins become constricted and tight, food cannot be digested, and the tongue cannot perceive flavors.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then these ailments do not arise.
Having observed the wind at the site of excretion, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by way of observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind named *Vismṛti* (Forgetfulness) residing within the body; what does it do when it is balanced or unbalanced?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the *smṛtivibhramśa* wind (the wind of forgetfulness) is not harmonized, it causes mindfulness to be lost; one forgets what has been studied and recited, being unable to retain it in memory. What is seen in the four directions becomes distorted; one forgets and fails to recall events that have already passed. One becomes hungry quickly after eating and is unable to eat further; the body hair becomes coarse and rough, as do the nails. One cannot endure cold or heat, and whatever is thought of is immediately forgotten.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then there are no such diseases as those described.
Having observed the *vismaraṇa-vāyu* (the wind of forgetfulness), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by observing the body internally.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either harmonious or disharmonious?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind residing within the body called "Producer of Strength" (*balotpāda*). What does it do when it is not harmonious?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that if the life-force wind (*jīvitabala-vāyu*) is not harmonious, even though one consumes much delicious food and drink, the body is constantly devoid of strength, as if the body were being destroyed by poison.
Because the wind is not in harmony, this disease arises; if the wind is harmonious and compliant, then this disease does not exist.
Having contemplated the life-force wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind named "Producer of Physical and Mental Strength" residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives the wind of physical and mental strength:
if this wind is harmonious and well-regulated, from the moment within the womb, the body and mind gradually develop, causing the mind to become robust and healthy.

Because his vital energies (*vāyu*) are harmonized, he knows what should and should not be done; he is able to recollect and know all that was done long ago; his coming and going, advancing and halting, are vigorous and without timidity; he endures the manifold sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; his body is full and robust, and the hair on his head does not turn white prematurely.
If one is not disciplined and compliant, one will lose this Dharma.
Having observed the winds of the physical and mental forces that arise, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, what functions do they perform?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind called "Obstructing the Throat and Speech" residing within the body; if it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the wind that obstructs the throat and speech is not harmonious, bodily diseases arise; if it is further disturbed by other factors, one loses their voice, or at times becomes deaf, or suffers from the contraction and lameness of hands and feet, or the body becomes hunched and crooked, or both eyes lose their sight.
Because the winds are not in harmony, such diseases arise.
Having observed the wind that obstructs the throat and speech, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body by following the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body, and what functions do they perform when they are either balanced or unbalanced?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives a wind named the "sleep-wind" (*svapna-vāyu*). If it is not harmonious, what does it cause to happen?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that when the *svapna-vāyu* (sleep-wind) is not harmonized, what is perceived becomes inverted; it agitates and disturbs the flowing channels, causing them to shift and change, so that all the joints and bones experience pain.
Having observed the sleep-wind, one knows the body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What winds reside within the body, whether they are balanced or unbalanced, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Life-Sustainer" (jīvitāvaha) residing within the body; whether it is balanced or unbalanced, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that if the life-sustaining wind (*jīvitendriya-vāyu*) becomes unbalanced, it causes people to lose their lives and abandon consciousness.

It is the second life-force of all sentient beings, capable of sustaining the body and depending upon the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*); because it is unbalanced, it can sever human life. It supports the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) of all sentient beings; if this wind is balanced, then one does not meet an untimely death.
Having observed the life-sustaining wind (*jīvitaka-vāyu*), one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
"What winds reside within the body, whether they are harmonious or disharmonious, and what functions do they perform?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees a wind called "Destroyer of All Limbs" residing within the body; if it is not harmonized, what does it do?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the "body-destroying wind" (kāya-bhañjana-vāyu), which begins its activity from the time of dwelling in the womb; by the power of this wind, his bodily parts are broken and damaged, causing the body to become hunched, the spine to curve, the chest to protrude, and the hips to twist.
If the winds are harmonious and balanced, then these ailments do not arise.
Having contemplated the wind that destroys the body, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body.
What winds reside within the body and what functions do they perform?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives that there is a wind called *tvak-saṃgrāhaka* (the skin-constrictor) residing within the body; what does it do?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,

he sees that when the *tvak-saṃgrāhaka* wind (the skin-gathering wind) is touched by external winds— whether cold or hot, fragrant or foul-smelling, blowing downward or upward, or whether they are powerful or weak— it perceives them all as they come into contact at any given time.
Having observed the *tvak-saṃvāhana-vāyu*, one knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the internal body:
what other winds reside within the body?

Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he becomes free from defilement and turbidity; his object of focus is pure, and he transcends doubt and overcomes uncertainty. Having crossed the wilderness, he understands according to reality without hesitation that within this body there is no other wind.

This wind accumulates, this wind combines; thus, the flow of this wind conditions the sense bases and elements, abiding in conjunction with karma and afflictions, capable of sustaining the body or causing its impairment.

This practitioner contemplates all the winds within the body; having seen them fully, he develops weary detachment from desire, such that craving cannot destroy him. He does not enter the realm of Māra and draws near to Nirvāṇa. With the sun of wisdom, he shatters the darkness of beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, and leaves behind the wilderness of doubt. He is not stained by form, sound, smell, taste, or touch, seeing these objects as they truly are: he sees that all three realms are entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, seeing them exactly as they are.

In this way, monks practicing in the village of Nādikā, brahmins and householders, truly know this joy in cultivating mindfulness of the body; they know the dharma of arising and ceasing, do not dwell on other meditations, contemplate the entire body, and know all fetters as well as liberation.
"Furthermore, the practitioner again observes this body’s disintegration and total destruction through another method.
How does this body undergo disintegration?
At the time of death, how do the winds and parasites destroy this body?"
What is meant by "disturbance"?
At what time does one pass away from all realms?
How are the upward, downward, reverse, and forward winds blown?

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as the body. Through wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that at the time of death, all the internal worms are first afflicted and disturbed;
once the worms have died, the person's life comes to an end. Thus, all conditioned phenomena are inevitably subject to decay and destruction.
Such is the nature of death; it must inevitably possess this firm and great evil.
Thus, a bhikṣu contemplates that within the head there are ten kinds of worms killed by the winds:
the first is named the "worm within the crown," which is killed by the wind of the toe-nails.
The second is named the Brain-Worm, which is killed by the wind of the two flanks;
the third is named the Skull-Bone-Worm, which is killed by the wind of non-perception;
the fourth is named the Hair-Eating-Worm, which is killed by the wind that breaks the bones.
The fifth is named Ear-Internal-Walker Worm, which is killed by the Wind that Treads upon the Ground;
the sixth is named Tear-Flowing Worm, which is killed by the Wind of the Heels;
the seventh is named Fat-Internal-Walker Worm, which is killed by the Wind that Breaks the Shanks.
Eighth is the *saṃkucita-parvaka* worm;
ninth is the *lālā-bhakṣa* worm, which is killed by the wind that destroys the joints of the ankles;
tenth is the *danta-mūla-bhakṣa* worm, which is killed by the wind that destroys the thigh bones. (10)
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of worms that move through the throat and descend into the chest, where they are killed by the wind. What are these ten?
First is the worm named *Bhakṣaka* (the Eater);
second is the worm named *Lālābhakṣa* (the Saliva-Eater), both of which are destroyed by the wind called *Bhagnabala* (Broken Strength)."
The third is the spittle-worm; the fourth is the vomit-worm; the fifth is the ten-flavor-circulating-vessel-worm, which is killed by the *pravāhaṇa* wind;
the sixth is the sweet-intoxication-worm, which is killed by the *sandhi-hantṛ* wind;
the seventh is the six-flavor-craving-worm, which is killed by the *keśa-nakha-nakha-mala-hantṛ* wind.
The eighth is named *śvāsana-kṛmi*, which is killed by the *saṃkramaṇa-vāyu*;
the ninth is named *rasadviṣ-kṛmi*, which is killed by the *bhedana-vāyu*;
the tenth is named *svapnārthin-kṛmi*, which is killed by the *koṣṭha-vāyu*. (20)
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of worms that dwell within the blood and are killed by the winds:
first is the hair-eating worm (*roma-bhakṣa-kīṭa*), which is killed by the dry-excrement wind (*śuṣka-śakṛt-vāyu*);
second is the pore-crawling worm (*chidra-cārī-kīṭa*), which is killed by the two lateral winds (*pārśva-vāyu*)."
The third is the *cānduda* worm, which is killed by the wind that severs the six orifices;
the fourth is the *rakta* worm, which is killed by the wind that cuts the body parts;
the fifth is the *krimimātṛkā* worm, which is killed by the wind of evil fire.
The sixth is named Loma-jvāla-kṛmi (Hair-Lamp Worm), which is killed by the sarva-gātra-vāyu (Wind of All Limbs);
the seventh is named Keśa-bhakṣaka-kṛmi (Hair-Eater Worm) and the eighth is named Krodha-rakta-kṛmi (Angry-Blood Worm), both of which are killed by the bhagna-ganda-vāyu (Wind that Breaks the Jaws);
the ninth is named Sūcī-sūcī-kṛmi (Prickly-Prickly Worm), which is killed by the sarva-gātra-cālana-vāyu (Wind that Moves All Limbs).
The tenth is named the Vinegar-Worm (*āmla-kīṭa*), which is killed by hot winds.

It is born within the blood; its form is short and round, it has no legs, and it is minute and eyeless. It causes itching on the body and moves with a flickering motion. The taste of this worm is salty. When a person dies, these worms are killed by the wind, the blood then dries up, and the person dies. Therefore, people say that a dead person has no blood;
because the blood is about to dry, one experiences great suffering and distress.

At the time of death, one’s mind is filled with great terror and one undergoes immense suffering and distress. Fearing that this body must be abandoned and one will travel to another realm, one must leave behind kinsmen, acquaintances, brothers, wife, children, and wealth. Bound by the fetters of craving and ignorant attachment, devoid of protection and lacking companions in wholesome Dharma, one is utterly alone. All the bodily constituents dry up, and one experiences the thirty kinds of great suffering of both body and mind.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
What kinds of worms are killed by the wind, and what suffering do they undergo?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees ten kinds of worms residing within the flesh."
What are the ten? First is the ulcer-producing worm, which is killed by the moving wind;
second is the piercing worm, which is killed by the upward-and-downward wind.
The three types of *saṃvāraṇa* worms are slain by the life-force wind (*jīvitavāyu*).
Why is it named the "life-force wind"?
Because when it departs from within the body, a person's life is immediately exhausted; therefore, it is called the life-force wind.
The fourth is the Arterial Worm, which is killed by the Opening Wind;
the fifth is the Skin Worm, which is killed by the Disturbed Mind Wind;
the sixth is the Fat-Moving Worm, which is killed by the Afflicting Wind.
Seventh is the *saṃghāta* worm, which is killed by the *vīkṣaṇa* wind;
eighth is the *durgandha* worm, ninth is the *malina* worm, and tenth is the *uṣṇa* worm, which are all killed by the *saṃvṛti* wind—the *pañcasaṃvṛti* wind—at the time of death. (40)
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
How is it that at the time of death, white sweat flows forth?
How do these various worms move within the aggregates (skandhas), and by which wind are they killed?"
This practitioner contemplates ten kinds of worms moving within the yellow of the *dhātu*. What are these ten?
The first is named the *kṣudrakṣudraka* worm, which is killed by the wind that destroys the fetal sac.
When a man or a woman is about to die, this wind severs the channels.
A second [wind] is called the *cūcuka* (faltering) worm, which is slain by the *garbhavivartana* (transforming the womb) wind;
it causes the man or woman to lose their vital strength, or causes a handful of yellow fluid, like the color of gold, to emerge from the mouth.
The three [kinds of worms] named Miao-hua-chong (Flower-Ornament Worm) are killed by the wind that causes coming, going, walking, and staying;

the four named Da-chian-chong (Great Deceit Worm), Wu-ming xing-kong-xue-chong (Worm Moving in Holes), Liu-ming hei-chong (Black Worm), Qi-ming da-shi-chong (Great Eater Worm), and Ba-ming xing-re-chong (Heat-Moving Worm) are killed by the wind that destroys the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body.
In this sequence, the ninth is named the Great Heat Worm, which is killed by the wind of knives;
the tenth is named the Taste-Eating Worm, which is killed by the wind of needle-stabs;
the eleventh is named the Fire Worm, which is killed by the evil yellow wind.
The twelfth is named the Great Fire Worm, which is killed by the wind that ruptures the intestines. Fifty.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body."
Contemplating the bone-worms, at the time of death, by which winds are they destroyed?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees that within the bones of all parts of the body there are ten kinds of worms.
What are the ten? First is the bone-licking worm, which is killed by the bile-excess wind;
second is the bone-biting worm, which is killed by the cold wind.
The third is the joint-severing worm, which is killed by the marrow-injuring wind;
the fourth is the red-mouthed stinking worm, which is killed by the skin-injuring wind;
the fifth is the bone-consuming worm, which is killed by the blood-injuring wind.
Sixth is the Red-Mouthed Worm, which is killed by the wind that injures the flesh;
seventh is the Tūtumā Worm and eighth is the Skin-Eater Worm, both of which are killed by the wind that injures the bones;
ninth is the Wind-Sword Worm, which is killed by the wind that harms the vital essence (*śukra*).
The tenth is named the Knife-Mouth worm; it is killed by the Skin-Wrinkle wind. Sixty.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Contemplating the worms within excrement, one sees with the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye ten kinds of worms that cause death by wind at the time of passing away.
What are the ten? First is the birth-worm (*jāti-kṛmi*), which is killed by the life-force wind (*janana-bala-vāyu*);
second is the needle-mouth worm (*sūcīmukha-kṛmi*), which is killed by the sweat-injuring wind (*sveda-pīḍana-vāyu*).
The third is the white-jointed insect, which is killed by the wind of palsy;
the fourth is the legless insect, which is killed by the wind of excessive sweating;
the fifth is the dung-scattering insect, which is killed by the wind that destroys the teeth.
Sixth is the *trikṣāra* worm, which is killed by the *kaṇṭhanāḍī-vāyu*;
seventh is the *bhedana* worm, which is killed by the *adhovaha-vāyu*;
eighth is the *āhārakṣaya-nirodha* worm, which is killed by the *ūrdhvavaha-vāyu*.
The ninth is named Yellow Worm, which is killed by the two lateral winds;
the tenth is named Worm that Digests Heavy Food, which is killed by the auxiliary-tendon wind.

This wind and these insects cause the excrement to dry up, agitating the various elements so that they mutually excite and strike one another; the winds all move upward, afflict the bodily elements, destroy the vital breath, and churn the body until it is parched, then kill it with violent force.
At the time of death, one undergoes great suffering and affliction that cannot be illustrated by any analogy; all people in the world must die, of this there is no doubt. (70)
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes the worms within the marrow: at the time of death, by which wind are they destroyed?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees ten kinds of worms within the marrow.
What are these ten? The first is named the Hair-Worm (*vālaka*), which is killed by the wind that harms the marrow (*majjā-vināśana-vāta*).
The second is named the Black-Mouthed Worm, which is killed by the Wind of Slightness;
the third is named the Powerless Worm, which is killed by the Wind of Turbulent Sleep-Vision;
the fourth is named the Pain-Afflicting Worm, which is killed by the Wind of Intolerance.
The fifth is named the Mind-Confounding Worm, which is killed by the Name-and-Form Wind;
the sixth is named the Fire-Colored Worm, which is killed by the Tight Wind;
the seventh is named the Slippery Worm, which is killed by the Lung Wind.
The eighth is named the Downward-Flowing Worm, which is killed by the Upward-Moving Foul Wind;
the ninth is named the Body-Organs-Arising Worm, which is killed by the Impure-Orifice-Traveling Wind;
the tenth is named the Mindful-Joyous Worm, which is killed by the Forgetfulness Wind—eighty in total.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body, having already seen it as impermanent, impure, and non-self.
Previously, one type of worm was killed by the *pārśva-vāyu* (lung-wounding wind); likewise, at the time of death, these various worms are killed by the winds."

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as the body; by means of untainted luminosity (*anāsrava-vidyā*), he cuts off the darkness of beginningless saṃsāra, which is ultimately and eternally extinguished. Having attained this Dharma through worldly-like karma, he perceives it directly because he has long cultivated the seven kinds of mindfulness. What are these seven?
First, mindfulness of the Buddha;
second, mindfulness of the Dharma;
third, mindfulness of the Sangha.
Fourth is mindfulness of the precepts;
fifth is mindfulness of the devas;
sixth is mindfulness of death.
Seventh is the mindfulness of impermanence.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes how many kinds of death destroy all karma?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes four types of death:
namely, the disharmony of the earth element, the disharmony of the water element, the disharmony of the fire element, and the disharmony of the wind element.
What is meant by the earth element becoming unbalanced and taking human life?

If the earth element becomes unbalanced within the body, because the earth element is solid, the entire body becomes constricted; the internal winds then strike against one another, afflicting and oppressing each other. It is like two mountains as hard as diamond, between which a lump of fresh butter is placed; when a great black wind blows, these two mountains strike each other together, crushing the lump of fresh butter.

The earth element and the wind element are like those two mountains; all one's life-force, skin, flesh, bones, blood, fat, marrow, and vital energy are contained within the casket of the body, which is like fresh butter. When crushed and harmed by the earth and wind elements, the physical constituents are destroyed, resulting in great suffering. One is unable to recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha; as the present aggregates are about to perish, one is bound by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), with the continuity of existence remaining unbroken.

All foolish ordinary persons arise through the continuity of a mind that resembles its predecessor, like a seal being impressed. Death is likewise; as the present aggregates are about to perish, a similar mind arises from a similar mind. Due to the causal power of the monkey-like mind, they undergo various births and deaths.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
He observes at the time of death: how is it that the water element becomes disordered, causing me and all foolish ordinary beings to lose our bodies and lives?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives the disharmony of the water element:

at the time of death for myself and all sentient beings, the sinews and veins of the entire body, as well as all skin, flesh, bone, blood, fat, marrow, semen, and vital energy, completely rot and flow out as pus and blood; they press against one another and all tremble, like two mountains crushing together, or as previously described, like a ball of fresh butter placed in the ocean, blown by black winds and battered by surging waves, unable to remain still, lacking solidity or stability.

In this way, when the water element destroys the body, it is likewise; one can no longer recollect the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as other thoughts continue to arise in succession without interruption.

All ignorant ordinary beings receive a body of birth that corresponds to their mental objects, just like a seal being impressed. At the time of death, when the present aggregates have ceased, they receive a corresponding birth in exactly the same way; by means of the monkey-like mind, they undergo birth and death and are led into the cycle of existence.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
How does the fire element become unbalanced and sever a person's life?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

At the time of death, the fire element becomes disordered; all the body’s channels, all the major tendons, all the minor tendons, skin, flesh, bones, blood, fat, marrow, and vital essence are all scorched and boiled, as blazing flames fiercely incinerate them.
It is like burning *khadira* charcoal; when a mass of fire as large as a mountain is fed with fresh ghee, flames erupt. In this way, the body is like a lump of ghee cast into it.
The suffering of death is likewise thus: one can no longer recollect the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

As the present aggregates are about to perish, mental formations continue in succession; all foolish ordinary beings, through the mental objects they contemplate, undergo rebirth in accordance with those conditions, like an impression made by a seal.
At the time of death, when the manifest aggregates have ceased, the mind undergoes rebirth in the same manner; by the causal power of the monkey-like mind, one undergoes birth and death.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
How does the wind element become disordered at the time of death and cut off a person's life?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

At the time of death, when the wind element becomes disordered, all parts of the body, all tendons and veins, and all bodily constituents—namely skin, flesh, bone, blood, fat, marrow, semen, and vital energy—all completely disintegrate. They become parched and devoid of moisture, tearing apart from one another; from the feet to the crown of the head, they scatter like sand.

For example, just as a lump of clarified butter, when blown upon by a black wind, is shattered and its oiliness lost, dispersing through the void like sand; so too it is with a person at the time of death: when the element of wind becomes unbalanced and they are oppressed by the suffering of dying, they can no longer bring to mind the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

All ordinary beings arise through the continuous succession of a mind with objective conditions, just like an impression made by a seal; likewise, at the time of death, the arising of the final moment of mind is also just so.
Due to the causal power of the monkey-like mind, one receives a body subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This is called the disharmony of the four great elements; there are four kinds of death. Having seen this, the practitioner contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Having seen this, one does not approach the realm of Māra but approaches the path to Nirvāṇa. One takes no pleasure in nor clings to defiled and lustful forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; one does not give rise to thoughts of love, remains free from dust and defilement, and leaves behind the wilderness. One does not cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; one does not give rise to pride regarding form, does not rely on youth, does not rely on pride in life, and does not delight in much speech. One does not enter cities or towns, remains without partial attachment, constantly contemplates the fear of death, feels dread toward even the slightest transgression, knows the body as it truly is, understands the dharma of arising and ceasing, develops weary detachment from all defiled desires, and delights in practicing the True Dharma with a mind free from indolence.
In this way, the bhikṣu practicing in the village of Nādikā observes his practice.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.

How does one practice the contemplation of the body internally and externally? This means that after having contemplated external phenomena, one contemplates the internal body by following the observation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

One observes the seed: just as from a seed a sprout is born, from the sprout a stalk is born, from the stalk leaves are born, from the leaves flowers are born, and from the flowers fruit is produced; this is called external observation.

"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the internal body: the seeds of prior consciousness, together with karmic afflictions, enter into the impurity and are called *aṇbudha*; from *aṇbudha* comes *kalala*; from *kalala* comes *ghana*; at the stage of *ghana*, it is called a mass of flesh; from the mass of flesh, the five protuberances arise—namely, the two hands, the two feet, and the head; from the five protuberances, the five sense organs arise; and thus, in this sequence, it proceeds until old age and death."
