"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Why is it that grasses and trees which were previously seen as green gradually turn yellow and finally fall away?
The body is likewise: first one sees it as an infant, then it reaches middle age, and gradually reaching old age, it returns to death.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
How do external seeds arise?
They grow from the earth, producing all medicinal herbs and forests.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees this:

These various phenomena arise each from its own causes and conditions and through its own power; this applies to all conditioned things, whether internal or external, with the exception of three types of unconditioned phenomena: namely, the unconditioned through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the unconditioned not through analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the unconditioned space (*ākāśa*).
How do all phenomena proceed by their respective powers? It is said: ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. In this way, this entire mass of suffering arises.

If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if volitional formations cease, then consciousness ceases; if consciousness ceases, then name-and-form cease; if name-and-form cease, then the six sense bases cease; if the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases; if contact ceases, then feeling ceases; if feeling ceases, then craving ceases; if craving ceases, then clinging ceases; if clinging ceases, then existence ceases; if existence ceases, then birth ceases; if birth ceases, then old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering—cease. Thus, there is only the cessation of this great mass of suffering.
In this way, all phenomena—whether internal or external—arise and grow through mutual causes and conditions.

Thus, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body; they contemplate the three external elements of the body in accordance with reality, observing the internal as the external and the external as the internal, examining them as they truly are.

Thus the practitioner contemplates internal and external phenomena. First, they contemplate Jambudvīpa; in order to increase the True Dharma, they cultivate the contemplation of internal phenomena through analytical observation. They observe each one individually, contemplating humans and devas together, and observing separately that which is without sensation. Internal causes depend upon the external four great elements, while external causes depend upon the internal mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); thus there is the growth of internal and external phenomena.
If there are internal phenomena, and one correctly understands these internal phenomena, then when these internal phenomena increase, one understands them upon seeing the external.
How do internal phenomena increase by means of the external?
When bedding, mats, and requisites for the sick and infirm are all fully provided, a bhikṣu is able to increase wholesome dharmas;
however, if there are no bedding or medicines for the sick and infirm, he cannot increase any wholesome dharmas and lacks the intention to seek them.

In this way, the internal and external mutually act as causes for one another, resulting in growth; it does not have a creator, it is neither permanent nor unchanging, nor is it produced without a cause.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body."
How do all sentient beings within the three realms increase by means of external dharmas as causes and conditions?
There is one dharma that increases: all sentient beings comprised within the conditioned possess four kinds of nutriment.
What are the four?
First is the food of morsels;
second is the food of volition.
The third is the food of contact;
the fourth is the food of craving-consciousness.

Regarding the foods of the desire realm, the four great elements as seeds increase by depending on external food; internal excellence and meditative bliss—this is called the first contemplation of how external dharmas increase internal dharmas.
How do external phenomena cause internal phenomena to increase?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes:
what are the causes and conditions by which the food consumed by sentient beings at the beginning of the kalpa is endowed with eight qualities?
What are the eight factors? They are:
attachment to the flavors of forms and sounds; attachment to pleasant and soft voices; a firm and stable physical appearance;
external things such as beds, mats, bedding, and medicinal decoctions that can nourish the body; and the joy of practicing wholesome dharmas.
In this way, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
If mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and the like do not disturb or touch the body, internal qualities will increase; if wind, rain, cold, or heat do not cause hindrance, one may seek internal qualities.
If one hears sounds that are unpleasant, unlovely, or foul, and hears them without obstruction, this is called increasing the internal dharma.
If one smells odors that are not lovely or pleasant, and does not take them as an obstruction, this is called increasing the internal dharma.
If one hears fragrant scents without any obstruction, it is called "benefiting the internal dharma.
The five sense faculties all have internal causes that enter through external objects; there are five internal bases, which is termed the contemplation of the external body.
The noble disciple knows the body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body:
how do the six consciousnesses grasp phenomena?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he perceives external phenomena without obstruction and is thus able to know the dharmas.
What are the six consciousnesses?
They are: visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness.
This is called thoroughly understanding external phenomena by means of internal phenomena; these internal and external phenomena are mutually dependent causes and conditions.
It is like a flying bird roaming through the void: wherever it goes, its shadow always follows its body. The internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) are likewise so.
If all bodies and all internal phenomena increase, the mind also increases.
The mind is the causal condition for all phenomena; each arises in mutual dependence upon one another.
In this way, the practitioner does not perceive even a single dharma that is permanent, unchanging, or indestructible.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality."
He contemplates how the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa diminishes and how it increases.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

At the beginning of the kalpa, the beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to Jambudvīpa and consumed the "earth-skin" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), which was like the flavor of sudhā enjoyed by the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Because the minds of humans were virtuous at the beginning of the kalpa, this earth-skin possessed excellent color, fragrance, and texture, free from all defects. As all people consumed it, their lifespan reached eighty-four thousand years, and they suffered only three ailments: first, hunger;
[the other two being thirst and excrement].
Second is thirst; third is longing.

At the second stage, such people as these, with unwholesome minds, take the surface of the earth, thereby causing the earth's surface to become defiled and impure. That is to say, due to hunger, thirst, and longing, when they are about to die, they pass away from a feverish illness.
Thus one contemplates how the people of Jambudvīpa obtain their life-span through external food, remaining free from disease and affliction.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality."
How is it that during the third period, the people of Jambudvīpa all obtain their physical form and life-span through food?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one observes the third period:

the surface of the earth is entirely destroyed because of the excesses of eating; wind, cold, heat, and so forth become unbalanced, and immeasurable diseases arise. All conditioned aggregates increase due to the external causes and conditions of food entering within, and by virtue of these internal causes and conditions, external phenomena also increase.
One contemplates the external body by means of the internal, and internal phenomena as conditions for the external.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What kind of food do the people of Jambudvīpa eat during the fourth age of strife?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that when the people of Jambudvīpa are engaged in battle, they eat seeds of weeds, or eat jīvaka beans, or eat fish and meat, or eat the roots of vegetables; all excellent flavors have completely vanished, they suffer much illness and pain, and they grow old prematurely.
During times of battle, people lack physical strength.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality:
what was the length of life for the people of Jambudvīpa at the beginning of the kalpa?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that at the beginning of the kalpa, the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa was eighty-four thousand years and their height was five hundred bows; the height of people today is equal to one bow.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
How is it that the lifespan, physical form, and stature of the people of Jambudvīpa are during the second period?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:
During the second period, the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is forty thousand years, and the stature of a person is two hundred bows tall.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the lifespan, physical form, and stature of the people of Jambudvīpa during the third period?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
one sees that during the third period, the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is ten thousand years, and the height of their bodies is one hundred bows.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He contemplates the lifespan, physical form, and stature of the people of Jambudvīpa; through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
when the people of Jambudvīpa are engaged in battle, their lifespan is one hundred years and their height is one bow."
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.

He observes the time of the final eon, when the ten wholesome paths of action no longer exist; when all people merely protect themselves and merit is absent, what will their lifespan be, and how long will that life last?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the time of a degenerate eon when the Dharma has ceased:

all excellent flavors are utterly extinguished—namely, salt, ghee, pomegranate, honey, rock sugar, sugarcane, rice grains, and the sixty-day ripening rice; all such superior flavors in the world are completely destroyed.
The first is called Red Rice; the second is called Bird-Brought Rice; the third is called Flying-Insect Rice; the fourth is called Kaṭapa Rice;
the fifth is called Red-Awned Yellow-Grain Rice; the sixth is called Eḷaka Rice; the seventh is called Spotted Rice;
the eighth is called White-Pearl Rice; the ninth is called Swift Rice; and the tenth is called Iron-Awn Rice.
Rice: next is named *lambita-śūka* (hanging-awned rice), next is named *rakta-śāli* (red rice), next is named *cūṭaka-śāli* (cūṭaka rice),
next is named *vṛkṣa-śāli* (tree rice), next is named *jalam-sthalaja-śāli* (waterland rice), next is named *sthalaja-śāli* (land rice), next is named *samyak-mati-śāli* (right-minded rice),
next is named *samudra-ja-śāli* (sea-born rice), next is named *yugma-śūka-śāli* (twin-awned rice), and next is named *sama-puṭa*.
Rice: next is called *tāpana-rice*, next is called *śuka-avarjita-rice*,
next is called *sūryadṛḍha-rice*, next is called *jīvita-rice*, next is called *sarvatraga-rice*,
next is called *siṃha-rice*, next is called *vimala-rice*, next is called *mahālāghava-rice*, and next is called *sarvaja-rice*.
Next is named Great Power Rice; next is named Born Fragrance Rice; next is named Snake-Cutting Rice;
next is named Kāśmīra Rice; next is named Mountain-Rice; next is named Snow-Mountain-Adjacent Rice;
next is named Bond-Free Rice; next is named Kaliṅga Rice; next is named Mahākaliṅga Rice; next is named...
There is the snow-rice; next is called the great-conch rice; next is called the virtuous-merit rice;
next is called the flowing rice; next is called the non-learning rice; next is called the non-crooked-sindhu rice;
next is called the round-black rice; next is called the lord-of-Persia rice; next is called the much-obtained rice; and next is called the aṅgāri rice.
Next is named *Mātrika-śāli*, next is named *Dīrgha-śāli*, next is named *Miśra-śāli*,
next is named *Amānuṣya-śāli*, next is named *Prājña-śāli*, next is named *Sūryagotra-śāli*,
next is named *Magadha-śāli*, next is named *Phenaja-śāli*, next is named *Kālotpanna-śāli*, next is named *Anāmayaka-śāli*, and next is named...
The first rice was named Warm Rice; next, Han Rice; next, Yellow Rice;
next, Vatsala Rice; next, Baddhākṣa Rice; next, Tongue-Delighting Rice; next, Astringent Rice;
next, Firm Rice; next, Sūda Rice; and next, Wheat-Colored Rice.
Seventy [generations later], the next was named Few Rice; the next, Sixfold Store Rice;
the next, Skinless Rice; the next, Sweet Rice; the next, Black Rice; and the next, Blue Rice.
Thus, within this rice there are two kinds of seeds:
first, those that grow spontaneously, and second, those that are sown;
as well as all other fragrant flowers, which will all utterly perish during the time of the evil age.

Due to this disappearance, the skin, flesh, fat, and bones of the people of Jambudvīpa all diminish; the skeletal structures of their entire bodies become stunted, deformed, and short. Because the flavor of food has become thin, all internal and external factors that arise through mutual causality are completely depleted and wasted away.

"In this way, the practitioner observes externally that all things are impermanent, without pleasure, without purity, and without self; they are also without an agent. They do not arise without cause, nor do they arise from a divergent cause; they are not the work of one, nor the work of two, nor three, nor four, nor five, nor six; they are not created by the false views of non-Buddhist outsiders."
Thus, one contemplates external objects in accordance with the contemplation of the body.
In this way, the practitioner, observing at the initial and subsequent stages as extensively explained above, contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.

How does he contemplate the mountains, rivers, cities, kingdoms, and lands of the four continents; the bodies of sea-fish measuring many yojanas; Sumeru, the king of mountains; and the four great continents—namely, Jambudvīpa, Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, and Aparagoyānī; as well as the eight great hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the various devas of the six desire realms?
Thus one contemplates the external body in accordance with this method.
Furthermore, the practitioner first contemplates the great ocean, mountains, rivers, and lands to the east of Jambudvīpa.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees a great mountain named Unfailing (Aparihāṇa), ten yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in length and breadth.
In this mountain there is the Gaṅgā River and a kingdom named Kāśī.
Furthermore, there are two other rivers:
one is named the Añjumā River; [the second is the Yamunā River].
The second is named the Vitastā River.
In the kingdom of Kośala, there are six territories:
the one named Aṅga and the one named Videha, each being one hundred yojanas in extent.
The country of Aṃśu is three hundred yojanas in extent;
the country of Kāśi has fourteen thousand settlements, and its cities are two yojanas wide.

The country of Kampila has a vast population and is fully endowed with forests and trees; its cities are adorned with nāgavṛkṣa, tāla, and tamāla trees, while there are many *kharjūra* and *panasa* trees bearing abundant fruit.
The practitioner further observes other people, namely:
those who take up garments, the Śabaras who pierce their lips and mouths and adorn them with jewels;
and those with camel faces, whose country is one hundred and thirty yojanas in length and breadth.
Contemplating that land, he contemplates the external body in accordance with the practice; he further contemplates the mountains, rivers, and villages of Jambudvīpa.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:
the Rohiṇī River flows from Mount Khara, three yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long, emptying into the eastern ocean, where it is adorned with many cities and towns and populated by many people.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What are the mountains and rivers within Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees them:"
There is a great mountain named Mijia (Mijaka), one yojana high and one hundred yojanas long.

There is another mountain named Gaoshan (High Mountain), five yojanas high and one hundred yojanas long; upon this mountain is a lake of great power, half a yojana wide, from which flows a river two hundred yojanas long that enters the great ocean.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What are the various extraordinary rivers within Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees them:"

In Jambudvīpa there is a great river named Kapilā, which is adorned with many large flowers; namely, it is adorned with kadalī flowers, pañcaśikha flowers, aśoka flowers, kadamba flowers, nameru flowers, and atimuktaka flowers.
Furthermore, there is a second river named Gomati; because it abounds in cattle, it is called the Cow River.
These two rivers are half a yojana in width and three hundred yojanas in length, flowing into the great ocean. "Gomati" means cow.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What mountains and rivers are there within Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:

In Jambudvīpa there is a mountain named Janman, and on that mountain there is a river named Sārasvatī. Along the riverbank is a city named Kuśinagara; the river flows slowly and expansively. The mountain is thirty yojanas in circumference, and within the mountain there is a man named Cīratha.
The wicked people of the borderlands have no heart of compassion.

On that mountain there are also those who take clothing and dwell therein; they are skilled at traveling by water across the great ocean and can traverse and cross over mountains and waters abounding in fish. Due to their past habits, they subsist solely on flesh and blood to sustain themselves.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
Beyond Jambudvīpa, what other mountains, seas, or islands exist?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There is a mountain of jewels situated by the seashore, ten thousand yojanas in height, composed of various kinds of precious gems—namely, blue gems, great blue gem-kings, vajras, musaragalvas, and red lotus gems—which serve as its adornments.
In the past, there were merchants engaged in the practice of dharma who entered the great ocean; driven by the force of a great wind, they were brought to a mountain of jewels.

Although the waters of that great ocean were ten thousand yojanas wide and filled with many timi fish, timingila fish, śiśumāra fish, and chāyā-grāha fish, they did not encounter any danger from them.

Having crossed the great ocean, he reached the shore of the Golden Wall, where the ground was made of pure gold. Various rākṣasas dwelt on this shore; their forms were terrifying and they possessed great power.

Having passed this island, there is another sea, two thousand yojanas in width. Having passed this sea, there is another mountain named Dvayaika. This mountain has three peaks, seven yojanas high and three hundred yojanas in length and breadth; it is adorned with the seven treasures—blue gems, vajras, blue vaidūrya, śaṅkha shells, and red lotus gems—which embellish the mountain.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
Having passed beyond this mountain, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
There is a great ocean named Black Water, ten thousand yojanas in breadth, wherein the asuras sport and play, and the nāgas and nāga-maidens likewise sport and play.
That Black Water Sea is terrifying to behold; there dwells a rākṣasa ghost named Shadow-Seizer, who seizes the asuras, rendering them weak and causing them to retreat beneath the waters.
As for that Black Water Sea, there are no mountains beneath its waters; the water is like black clouds, and many dragons dwell therein.
Having observed this, the practitioner contemplates it externally according to reality.
The practitioner further observes: beyond the Black Water Sea, what mountains and seas are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a great sea named Crimson Jewel Water, which fills its expanse. On its shore stands a tree named Jambu, the most lofty and excellent among all trees; it is ninety *yojanas* high, and upon it dwells the king of the *garuḍa* birds, whose beak is made of diamond.

One hundred yojanas from the Jambū tree is the sea named Blue Water; in this sea there are various rākṣasas called Manduhaka, ten li in height, and within the sea there are mountains where these rākṣasas dwell.
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Sixty-Seven;
The Sutra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Sixty-Eight.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Five:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond the Blue Water Sea, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

there is a great ocean named Pure (*Vimala*), five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Within this sea is a mountain named Garland of Light (*Prabhā-mālā*), one hundred yojanas high and three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, composed of white silver and adorned with golden lotuses. There is a lotus pond named Good Intention (*Sukhāśaya*), thirty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, adorned by the Mālādharas, the Lohitapādas, and various celestial geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond the Pure Ocean, what other mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There is a great ocean named Mahātaranga (Great Wave), five thousand yojanas in breadth. When winds arise beneath the water due to the causes and conditions of sentient beings, waves emerge from all the great oceans and islands; when these exceed two yojanas in height, the people of Jambudvīpa call them the "sea tide."
In the Great Wave Ocean there dwell large fish with heads like those of dogs.
Furthermore, as the practitioner observes the external body in accordance with reality,
what other great mountain oceans exist beyond the Great Wave Ocean?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

to the north of the great wavy ocean, there is a great mountain named Anumana, fourteen yojanas in breadth, adorned with white silver like a second sun-god, and beautified by mandārava flowers, kauseyaśa flowers, vimala (lapis lazuli) flowers, and celestial groves.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its successive stages.
Beyond Mount Anoma, what other great mountains and seas are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

To the east of Mount Anumana there is a great ocean called Vimala (Pure and Clear). Not far from this water, on the side of Mount Sumeru facing the Vaiḍūrya surface, there is a mountain named Udayana that faces Pūrvavideha;
it produces golden light, yet because of the Vaiḍūrya of Jambudvīpa, its shadow appears blue.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its proper sequence.
Beyond Mount Udayana, what other mountains are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There is a great mountain named Good Intent (Sumanas), adorned with vast golden flowers of Jambūnada gold; it is ten yojanas wide and five hundred yojanas high. It abounds in golden trees, with birds and beasts of pure gold, and *pārasa* trees of the color of purple-polished gold.

There were many devas and gandharva kings—the Māndhātṛ devas and the Tumburu devas—who, according to the characteristics of their karma—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and by virtue of the fruits of their own actions, went to Mount Sumanas to behold Jambudvīpa.
This is called the mountains and seas to the east of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
What are the mountains and seas to the south of Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees Mount Minda, which is eight hundred yojanas wide.
There is a river there named Namada, half a yojana wide and two hundred yojanas long, in which dwells a great venomous dragon; in the river there are also many śiśumāras, tortoises, and karamas.
Furthermore, there is a great river named Tāpā; there is also a great river named Vika, along whose banks there are many forests and trees.
There is also a great river named Kṛṣṇabhinna, three yojanas wide and three hundred yojanas long, which flows into the great ocean.
Furthermore, there is a great river named Mahāluṭā, in which a great venomous dragon dwells. Mount Malaya abounds in sandalwood;

the mountain is five hundred yojanas in breadth and length, and three yojanas in height. There is a great river named Taṅkṣiṇī that flows from Mount Malaya, one yojana in width and one hundred yojanas in length, as it enters the great ocean.
Furthermore, there is a river named Citrā, adorned with various kinds of forest trees and various flocks of birds; it is one yojana wide and fifty yojanas long, flowing into the great ocean.
"Furthermore, the practitioner, following the sequence of observing the external body, contemplates Jambudvīpa.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
there is a land named Mikhalā, a place of various delights, forty yojanas in length and breadth."

Furthermore, there is another country named Cakravāḍa, fifty yojanas in extent, which abounds with various kinds of trees bearing beautiful fruits: *kiṃnaka* fruits, *panasa* fruits, *amra* tree fruits, *bilva* tree fruits, *kapittha* fruits, *plakṣa* fruits, and *patala* fruits; it is adorned by *asana* flowers and *candaka* flowers.
Next is the country named Kaliṅga; its territory is ninety yojanas in length and breadth, with many forests and trees, and many rice fields.
Next is the country named Dambadīpa; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with many groves of trees and many rice fields.

Furthermore, there is another country named Tāṇḍaka; its territory is twenty yojanas in length and breadth. It is desolate and uninhabited, for in the past, due to the anger of a rishi, he caused the land to become empty.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
He observes Jambudvīpa: what other mountains, rivers, and great oceans are there in the southern region?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,
he sees a great river named Gautamī, its waters pure, one krośa in width and two hundred yojanas in length.
Furthermore, there was another country named Oḍra, its land measuring twenty yojanas in length and breadth.
There was yet another country named Andhra, its land measuring forty yojanas in length and breadth.

Furthermore, there was another country named Kila; its territory measured fifty yojanas in length and breadth. In that land there were many cattle and water buffaloes, and it abounded in rice paddies, groves, trees, flowers, and fruits.

Near the shores of the Southern Sea, there is a country named Kākuloma, where all manner of forests and trees are fully present. Its length is three hundred yojanas and its width is fifty yojanas. There is a great river named Kapilī, adorned with various groves of trees; its waters are pure, one yojana wide and five yojanas long. It is beautifully graced by many lovely *kākola* trees and *kīcaka* trees, making it exceedingly delightful.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its successive stages.
Beyond Jambudvīpa, what other mountains, seas, continents, or islands exist?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
There is a great ocean named Apariṇa, covered with lotus petals, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is unmoved by the wind because the water is entirely covered by lotus petals.
Having crossed this sea, there is another island, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, where various rākṣasas dwell; their forms are ugly and extremely terrifying.

Passing beyond the island of the rākṣasas, there is a great mountain named Mahendra, forty yojanas in length and breadth and ten yojanas in height. It is filled with many trees, such as tāla trees and sāla trees, where various asuras, nāgas, and nāga maidens sport; some, moreover, play within its groves and gardens.

"On the six days of fasting in Jambudvīpa, the gods of the Four Great Kings dwell upon this mountain to observe which sentient beings in Jambudvīpa are filial toward their parents and act in accordance with the Dharma."
Who observes the precepts on the days of fasting?
Who among people has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha?
And who among people engages in battle with Māra?
Who practices a straightforward mind?
Who practices generosity?
Which person is not stingy?
Who does not afflict others?
Who recognizes kindness?
Who believes in karma?
Who practices the ten wholesome actions?
Who draws near to virtuous friends?
And who believes in the false views of non-Buddhist outsiders?

In this way, the Four Great Kings observe Jambudvīpa from Mount Mahāmeru; if the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, the Four Great Kings go to the abode of Śakra and address him thus:
"O Heavenly King, you should give rise to joy."
"He shall destroy the armies of Māra, increase the True Dharma and the hosts of devas, and cause all people in Jambudvīpa to practice wholesome dharmas.
At that time, Śakra, King of Devas, and the assembly of devas, having heard what was said, were all greatly rejoiced.

If the people of Jambudvīpa do not practice in accordance with the Dharma, at that time the gods of the Four Great Kings will all become sorrowful and distressed, and they will speak thus to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven:
"The people of Jambudvīpa do not practice in accordance with the Dharma; they increase the armies of Māra and diminish the hosts of the devas."
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in succession.
Beyond Mount Mahāmeru, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that beyond Mount Mahāmeru there is an island, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, where one-legged people dwell. They sustain themselves by eating roots and fruits; their lifespan is fifty years. They use tree leaves for clothing and have no houses, dwelling instead beneath the trees. In this land there are many fierce and predatory beasts such as lions, and these lions all possess two wings. The soil and fields are temperate, being neither cold nor hot. All the women have faces like those of dogs, yet they emit exquisite sounds from their mouths.

Beyond this continent, there is a great ocean two thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. Within the ocean is a mountain named Maṇiratna, composed of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. It abounds with various golden birds, and the *māndārava* and *kūṣmāṇḍa* flowers are present at all times throughout the six periods of the day. Great *asuras* possessing supernatural powers sport and enjoy themselves upon this mountain, experiencing the pleasures of desirable forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. The mountain is five thousand *yojanas* long and one hundred *yojanas* high; it has fifteen peaks, all made of white silver, where celestial maidens (*apsarases*) dwell and enjoy themselves, though they are occasionally harassed by the *asuras*.
For this reason, when the devas first fought with the asuras, all devas and ignorant ordinary beings were enslaved and employed by women.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its successive stages.
Having passed beyond Mount Mahāmeru, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:"

Having passed beyond those mountains, he saw a great ocean five thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within the waters were fish one yojana long. In this ocean there were various aquatic beings, five yojanas in height, who had the heads of oxen, pigs, water buffaloes, camels, lions, tigers, leopards, or monkeys; they bore faces resembling every kind of beast, as if marked by a seal.

Having crossed this ocean, there is a great mountain named Sūryamaṇḍala (Sun-Wheel Mountain), wherein all desires are fully provided for. There are celestial lotus ponds and fruits of supreme flavor; if one eats these fruits, joy arises for seven days. The Kinnara King dwells in this mountain, and by virtue of his own karma, his mind is always joyful; through superior, middling, and inferior karmic actions, they amuse and sport with one another, experiencing delight.

The mountain of the solar disc (Sūryamaṇḍala) is two thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Beyond this mountain is another mountain named Senāma, which is composed entirely of white silver and adorned with lapis lazuli stones like celestial ornaments. On this mountain there is a tree called the "Woman Tree" (Strīvṛkṣa), and among all the trees throughout this mountain range, infants are born when night is about to turn to dawn; by sunrise they are able to walk; by mealtime they have become youths; at midday their physical forms are full and robust; by the time of the afternoon sun, they have already grown old and decrepit, walking with the aid of a staff, their hair as white as frost clinging to a tree; and by the time the sun sets, they have all died.
All sentient beings act through the power of collective karma; according to the actions they perform, they receive retribution in accordance with that karma.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in progressive accordance with reality.
Having passed Mount Kūṭaśaila, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?
Through his wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees to the south: beyond this mountain lies a great ocean.

Five hundred yojanas beneath the waters of that sea is the palace of a Nāga king, adorned with various kinds of jewels. It features railings of *vaiḍūrya*, *indranīla* sapphire, and crystal, adorned with the seven treasures. Its halls are decorated with radiant *maṇi* gems and various precious substances; its multi-storied palaces are like the light of the sun. There are such immeasurable palaces as these.

Due to his own karma, the Naga King Takṣaka dwells in this palace; this Naga King Takṣaka constantly practices mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha, day and night.

Beyond this jeweled hall, five hundred yojanas away, lies a great and perilous sea; all sentient beings who see it are struck with terror, for it is surrounded by many wrathful and malevolent dragons.

Having passed beyond this sea, there is another mountain named Ox-King (Go-rāja). This mountain is inhabited by all kinds of sentient beings, and from within this mountain issues the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood (gośīrṣa-candana).
The second type of sandalwood is called Yellow; its appearance is like the radiance of the sun, such that no ordinary person can see it.

Only if a person accords with the Dharma, and a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, or perhaps a minor king who acts according to the Dharma appears—just as in the case of a Wheel-Turning King—can it be obtained.
The Gandharva King dwells within this mountain, delighting himself with song, dance, and playful merriment.
Five hundred yojanas beyond Mount Ox-King lies a great ocean named Great Water-Foam, which resounds with the roar of mighty winds.
Having passed this sea, there is a great mountain named Three Peaks: the first is called Golden Peak;
the second is called Silver Peak;
[the third is called Crystal Peak].
The third is called Sphaṭika Peak.

On that peak there is a lake named Phena-cakra (Foam Wheel), with its bottom strewn with golden sand and adorned with celestial flowers; it is filled with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks. When the wind blows upon the ocean waters and strikes the three mountain peaks, it kills many large fish.
"Due to their own karma, they were beaten to death.
Furthermore, as the practitioner contemplates the external body in succession:
beyond the great ocean, what mountains, rivers, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,

he sees beyond the aforementioned great ocean the realm where King Yama adjudicates merit and demerit, the place where all sentient beings experience the fruits of their karma— the domain in which King Yama dwells.
King Yama governs all sinful beings according to the Dharma; these sentient beings, deceived by their own minds, dwell in a place of darkness.
Beyond this dwelling, for a distance of one hundred yojanas, there is only empty space. After passing another hundred yojanas, one arrives at the palace where King Yama resides.

That royal palace was constructed of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with every kind of precious jewel; it was embellished with rivers, springs, flowing streams, and lotuses, measuring one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, its radiance like that of a second sun.
Beyond this dwelling place, there is neither the light of the sun nor the moon; it is entirely dark because the ocean is so vast that the sunlight does not appear.
Due to the causes of the evil karma of the sentient beings in hell, everything is pitch black; their eyes see nothing, and they cannot distinguish east from west.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.

He surveys everywhere the dwelling places of sentient beings—whether in the realms of hell, or rivers, mountains, trees, or oceans; whether in the abodes of the devas, or the paths of animals, or the paths of hungry ghosts—in the eight directions, above, and below—is there any sentient being who is neither born nor dies, neither arises nor ceases?"
Is there any affection that does not end in separation?
There is not a single place that is not subject to decay or change; impermanent affection must inevitably end in separation.

Thus, O bhikṣu, you do not see a single place where there is no parting from what is beloved; within the five realms of existence, there is not even a patch of ground the size of a finger that is free from the separation of the beloved. Wherever sentient beings dwell, it is nothing other than birth and death, characterized by the impermanence of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, one should cultivate revulsion toward these conditioned formations of birth and death; they are deceptive, restless, and obstructive, abounding in sorrow and lamentation, swift and unstable, subject to destruction and decay, lost again after being gained, like a phantom or a dream, obtained only to be lost once more.

This realm of affection deceives the ignorant and deluded; it has been a place of beginningless wandering. Lust, hatred, and delusion are like enemies who feign friendship, dwelling within the abode of sensual desire. Therefore, one should abandon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), give rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*), cast off a distracted mind, and take no pleasure in impermanent objects. Do not play with ignorance.

Thus, the practitioner teaches all sentient beings to accord with reality as it is, observing the forty stations of the external body: there is not a single sentient being who is not born in dependence upon karma; there is not a single sentient being who does not transmigrate through the flow of karma; there is not a single sentient being who is not bound by karma. According to the actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one receives their corresponding retribution.

When that bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he does not see a single sentient being who is born other than through karma; there is not a single sentient being who does not have karma as their storehouse, nor a single sentient being who does not transmigrate through karma. According to the actions they perform—whether wholesome or unwholesome—they obtain their corresponding retributive fruits.
Having thus observed karma, that bhikṣu contemplates the external body as it truly is, in accordance with correct contemplation.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
How does one contemplate the mountains, rivers, seas, and islands of the western lands within Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, one sees:

there is a great river named Pūrṇā, adorned with various flowering trees—such as the Bakula tree, the Paricukka tree, the Khañjula fruit, the Cūḍaka flower, the Nārikela tree, and the Tamāla tree—and many such diverse trees beautify that river, which is also filled with many mountain valleys.

On the riverbank there is a country named Kikayī; crossing the borders of this country, there is the river named Sindhu. On the banks of that river is a country named Suvīra, where the people are prosperous and happy, eating red rice; the country is peaceful and pleasant, with mountains, forests, and flowing streams.
Beyond this realm, there is another country named Surasāṭa. Beyond this realm, there is yet another country named Bharata;

its territory is twenty yojanas in length and breadth. Within that country, there are many pomegranates and grapes. There is a city in that country named Mithilāpūga, and beyond this great city, there are five great rivers which flow together as one.
To the west of this place lies a great ocean, abounding with various kinds of evil fish and beasts, which is most terrifying.

This practitioner sees in the western sea a great continent named Kāla, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Various birds dwell upon this continent, and its diverse groves are exceedingly delightful; it is the place where the Vidyādharas reside, sporting and enjoying themselves. The city is named Pṛthivī, and the second dwelling place is called Dīrghakeśa, a location that is lovely.
On this island of Kāla, there are multi-storied pavilions and halls with many flowing streams.

Beyond this dwelling place lies the River Sindhu, which flows into the western sea. There is a great mountain named Sukṛti situated within the ocean; in this mountain there is much coral. If merchants reach this mountain of jewels, they will obtain abundant precious treasures, enjoying inexhaustible wealth and happiness.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its successive stages.
Having passed beyond this mountain, what other mountains, seas, or islands are there?
In what places do the various rākṣasas and others dwell?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees a great ocean abounding in large fish five thousand yojanas long, filled with many conch shells, *makara* fish, *timi* fish, and *timitimingila* fish that churn the seawater; the wind stirs the great ocean, causing the fish to move about in disorder.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this sea there is a great continent named Sarvato-manoratha-siṃhala-dvīpa (the Land of Lions, Universally Delightful). In that country there are snakes, ten li in length, which travel through the air without obstruction; they have a lifespan of a thousand years and do not harbor mutual hatred or envy.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this continent there is another sea called "Lovely" (Priya), five yojanas in length and breadth. Within these waters there are many lotuses, adorned by swarms of bees, with vast flower-bases. There dwell rākṣasas named Kūkarā who inhabit this sea, eating the lotus bases until they are fully satiated.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this dwelling place there is a great mountain named Vana, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; within this mountain there are many white elephants and *kalaviṅka* birds that emit exquisite sounds.
Such is this beautiful voice that none can equal it—whether among gods, humans, kinnaras, or asuras—save for the Tathāgata alone.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond this great mountain, what other mountains, rivers, seas, or islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a great mountain fifty *yojanas* high, upon which there are many forests of *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli). There are lions there, fully endowed with wings, who guard the precious forest, fearing that the *māndeha* rākṣasas might come to seize their place.
"Furthermore, the practitioner observes the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond Jambudvīpa, what other mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands exist?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he further perceives:

The Western Sea is twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth; in that great ocean there are neither mountains nor cities, and within its waters there are only creatures with the heads of elephants and the bodies of fish, or the heads of pigs and the bodies of fish.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this sea there is a great mountain named Golden Mountain (*Suvarṇaparvata*). The radiance of this mountain illuminates the waters of the great ocean, making them appear as if they were golden in color. It adorns the mountain, which is three hundred *yojanas* high and fifty *yojanas* wide. There dwells upon it a *gandharva* named Jambumālin, whose mind is constantly joyful and delighted; his lifespan is two thousand years, though there are also those who die prematurely.

Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gandharvas dwell within this mountain; their bodies are golden in color, and all their physical features resemble those of the devas. They feed on the fruits of trees, and by nature they are courageous and robust. All the asuras who dwell beneath the waters are unable to seize any of the roots or fruits belonging to these gandharvas.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
Having passed beyond this ocean, what other mountains, seas, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

Beyond five-fifths of this great ocean lies the Great Cakravāḍa Mountain, composed of pure gold, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in breadth, with a summit of diamond; upon this mountain dwell the kiṃnaras and asuras.

This Jñāra Garden is lovely, with its rivers, springs, and ponds abounding in flowers and fruits, where monkeys frolic. The river is named Suvarṇavāhinī; it is half a yojana wide, and within its waters many golden fish swim about, their scales shimmering brilliantly.

The practitioner further observes that beyond the Cakravāḍa Mountains there is a great ocean, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within this ocean is an island called Ratnadvīpa; on this island there are various kinds of jewels and no soil or stones, for the entire island is composed of precious gems.
The practitioner further contemplates: beyond this sea island, what other mountains, rivers, seas, or islands exist?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

there is a great mountain named White Mountain (*Sveta-giri*), abounding in forests and trees; its color is pure white, it is encircled by foam, it is one thousand *yojanas* high, and five hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this mountain there is a great mountain named Good Cloud (*Suvana*), one hundred *yojanas* high and sixty-four *yojanas* wide; it is empty and uninhabited, for neither yakṣas nor kiṃnaras dwell there, being terrified of the asuras.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a crystal mountain (*sphaṭika-parvata*) three thousand *yojana*s in height and one thousand *yojana*s in length and breadth, fully endowed with rivers, ponds, forests, and fruits, like a celestial mountain.
Having passed this mountain, there is a great body of clear water, a hundred yojanas in length and breadth, abounding with conchs and shells, and its waters are difficult to traverse.

Having passed this water, there is Mount Gandhamādana, where various asuras dwell; they are constantly afraid of the celestial hosts. There are many celestial maidens, adorned in various ways, and rivers of wine overflow. On Mount Gandhamādana grow the Jambūka fruit and the Tinduka fruit; their taste is exceedingly delicious, yet eating them kills a person.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What other mountains, rivers, seas, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There are sixty thousand golden mountains, surrounded by trees of purple-polished gold. They are filled with birds and beasts, and throughout these mountains there are many golden lotus ponds that emit great radiance. Within them dwells Sumeru, the King of Mountains; upon this mountain dwell the Mālava-holding devas, the Loka-pāda devas, the Tri-vaṃśa devas, and the Cāturmahārājika devas.

Upon this mountain there is a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); whatever the gods think of arises from that tree. All the birds and beasts have bodies that are entirely golden in color. There are many various flowers—*mandārava* flowers and *kovidāra* flowers. On the four sides of the mountain are four great groves:
the first is named the Joyful Grove; the second is named the Grove of Miscellaneous Palaces.
The third is the Citraratha grove;
the fourth is the Pāriyātra grove.

Within the Nandana Garden stands a great king of trees named Pāriyātra; beneath this tree, during the four months of summer, he enjoys the pleasures of the five senses, sporting and delighting himself.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings sport and enjoy themselves in the Garden of Joy (Nandana-vana).
Because the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings take pleasure and delight within this garden, it is named the Garden of Joy.
As for the Forest of Vivid Radiance (*Vicitra-vana*), it is named such because it is adorned with a multitude of brilliant colors.

As for the Forest of Variegated Palaces (*Vicitra-maṇḍapa-vana*), it is named such because various variegated palaces are situated there, wherein the sons of gods ride and sport, experiencing desirable forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
In the Pāriyātra grove and the Nandana grove, all the hosts of devas enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.

On the side of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, facing Jambudvīpa, there is vaidūrya jewel; by the power of the light of that vaidūrya, it causes those in Jambudvīpa who look up at the sky to perceive it as entirely blue in color.
On the third side, in the Pāruṣyaka Forest, when the devas wish to engage in battle with the asuras, they gather in this forest to deliberate together.
The face of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, toward the direction of Aparagoyānī is composed of pure gold; it causes those in Aparagoyānī who look up at the sky to perceive it all as red in color.
On the second side is the Miśrakāvana Grove; within these palaces are stored the various implements for celestial warfare.
The face of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, facing the continent of Pūrvavideha, is composed of white silver, causing those in Pūrvavideha who look up at the sky to perceive it entirely as white.
The face of Sumeru, King of Mountains, facing the direction of Uttarakuru, is composed of crystal; it causes those in Uttarakuru to see the sky as pure and clear, with the color of white radiance.
The practitioner further contemplates: What is the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings?
Taking fifty years within Jambudvīpa as one day and night, their lifespan is thus five hundred full years; there are also those who die prematurely.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What other extraordinary deities dwell upon Mount Sumeru?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

On the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, dwell the Thirty-three Gods, whose enjoyments and activities are beyond full description. Their city is named Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with the seven treasures: sapphire, diamond, musāragalva, ruby, and great soft jewels.

There is a Hall of Good Dharma, five hundred yojanas in width, with balustrades made of lapis lazuli beads and walls of pure gold; all its doors are likewise so adorned, and the entire palace is embellished with every kind of ornament.
The Deva King Śakra dwells in the Sudharmā Hall; by the power of his virtuous karma, he experiences corresponding pleasure.
One hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for the second heaven; such is their lifespan, which lasts for a full thousand years, though there are also those who die prematurely.

On the western side of Mount Sumeru is the mountain named Astagiri (the Sunset Mountain). When the sun reaches this mountain, the people of Jambudvīpa say that the sun has set; therefore, it is called the Sunset Mountain.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its proper sequence.
He contemplates the dimensions of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as to its height and breadth.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he observes:

Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height and breadth; the Asura Kings dwell at its side, residing beneath these waters. Sustained by the karma of sentient beings, it causes the sun to revolve.

There is a great and venerable deity named Swift (Kṣipra), who constantly leads the way; in the blink of an eye, he can travel ten thousand one hundred and fifty yojanas, circling around with the sun as his measure, knowing the length of the lifespans of all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes the places where the inhabitants of the four continents dwell: how great are the dimensions of Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru?"
He saw that Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in extent, Pūrvavideha is eight thousand yojanas, Aparagodānīya is nine thousand yojanas, and Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas.
In accordance with the topographical features of the four continents, the faces of humans are likewise shaped, mirroring those lands.
The facial shape of the people of Jambudvīpa is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom, resembling the configuration of its terrain.
As for the other three directions:
the people of Pūrvavideha have faces shaped like the terrain, resembling a half-moon;
the people of Aparagoyānī have faces shaped like the terrain, resembling a full moon.
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru have faces that correspond to the shape of their land; their faces are square.
Thus, by observing the external appearance, one understands the physical forms of the people of the four continents as they truly are.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
How does he contemplate the mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands of the northern regions within the kingdom of Jambudvīpa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,
he sees that in the northern direction of Jambudvīpa there is a country named Vatsa, its land measuring ten yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the second country, named Mithilā; its territory is twenty yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the third country, named Śrughna; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the fourth country, named Atiri; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the fifth country, named Dhara; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the sixth country, named Kuru; its land is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the seventh country, named Madhura; its land is fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the eighth country, named Gandhāra; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next is the ninth country, named Śākya; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The tenth country in succession is named Badaraka; its territory is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The eleventh country in succession is named Darada; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and within this country there are many mountain crags.
The twelfth, in succession, is named the country of Vakala; its territory is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The thirteenth, in succession, is named the country of Viśākha; its territory is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The fourteenth, next in order, is named the Kingdom of Mahīśa; its territory is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

The fifteenth, next in order, is named the Kingdom of Han; its territory is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and while the combined extent of its administrative districts is one thousand yojanas, the land of the true Han people is only two hundred yojanas.
The sixteenth, named the country of Tukhāra, is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The seventeenth, named the country of Bahlīka, is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Next, the eighteenth is named the Kingdom of Kūpura; its land is fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Next, the nineteenth is named the Kingdom of Kauruma; its land is exactly five yojanas in length and breadth.
The twentieth country is named Kāmamañjarī; its territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Other minor countries and uninhabited lands are not included in this count.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes the northern regions of Jambudvīpa and considers what mountain kings exist there.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

There is a great mountain named Himavat (Snowy Mountain), with various mountain peaks; its surrounding ranges extend for a thousand yojanas. Within the mountains there are many *lodhra* trees, pine trees, cypress trees, *devadāru* trees, *sāla* trees, and *tamāla* trees. There are also many yakṣas, many kinnaras, and many classes of piśāca yakṣas.

That mountain is lovely, and many practitioners of meditation rely upon it; its rivers are sweet, great nāgas and others dwell within the mountains, and there are many Cilātis who reside on this mountain.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He contemplates the northern regions of Jambudvīpa: what other mountains, rivers, seas, and islands are there?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that to the east of the Snowy Mountains lies the mountain named Hanging Snowy Mountain (*Himavat-pralamba*). It abounds in lovely birds and beasts and is filled with pine and cypress trees, as well as celestial *devadāru* trees, *nami* forests, *bakula* trees, and *jāmaka* trees.
Having passed this mountain, there is another mountain named Tamāla, twenty yojanas in length and breadth, with one thousand caves.
Having passed this mountain, there is a vast, desolate expanse of one hundred yojanas, abounding in rivers and ponds, yet devoid of medicinal herbs and trees.
Having passed this place, there is a mountain of white silver named Kīlasa, surrounded by golden peaks, upon which the celestial king Virūḍhaka dwells.
Upon the mountain peaks, the rivers and ponds are cool and clear, abounding with lotuses and blue *utpala* flowers; the pools are further adorned by many geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
Beyond Mount Kīlaśa, there is a great mountain named Śikhara; beneath it dwells the King of the Kiṃnaras, who delights in song, dance, and play.
Upon this mountain there are five peaks of gold, three peaks of crystal, and ten peaks of white silver; there are immeasurable celestial flowers with lovely fragrances.
Within the mountain there is a river named Kumāra that flows forth from the mountain, filled everywhere with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
Having passed this mountain, there is another great mountain named Minaka, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, where many asuras dwell and constantly delight in singing.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes what other mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands exist within Jambudvīpa.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he perceives them as follows:"
Having passed beyond this mountain, one sees a great ocean, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, abounding with great nāgas, timi fish, nakara fish, and various species of conch shells.

Having crossed this sea, there is a great mountain named Good Intent (Sumanas). On the mountain is a pond named Solidified Butter (Navanīta), one yojana in length and breadth. This pond is lovely, and within it dwell many geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, and kalaviṅka birds.
That mountain is fifty yojanas in length and breadth. Within the mountain there is a river named Kauśika, adorned with many water-birds.

Beyond this mountain lies a great ocean, twenty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, which is most terrifying; the sound of thunder constantly roars, and malevolent dragons, filled with wrath, attack one another, sometimes raining down swords and fire, and emitting great, blazing lightning.
Out of a mind of hatred, they spit forth poison and kill one another.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.

Contemplating Jambudvīpa, beyond the sea-dwelling nāgas, there is a great continent named Dambaka, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, where many great and wicked rākṣasas dwell, sustaining themselves by eating fish.
There is a hell there named Dambaka, which incinerates sentient beings.
There is a great river named Kauśika, filled with flowing blood, in which hair, skulls, and bones drift along with the current.
The hells are five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, where beings undergo great and intense suffering.
Having passed beyond the hells, there is a great ocean resembling a hell, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are dark blue-black, and it contains no nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas.

Having passed this sea, to the north there is a sea named Ratnapūrṇa (Treasure-Full), surrounded by various mountains and immeasurable groves of trees—pines, cypresses, sandalwood, and wish-fulfilling trees—and within the mountains there are also immeasurable fruit-bearing trees.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great mountain named Pāra, five thousand yojanas in length and breadth. On this mountain there are many *liṅnara* fruits and *kīra* tree fruits; all seasonal fruits are present throughout the six periods of the day. Its rivers and ponds are filled with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks, and great ṛṣis dwell within the mountains.
The mountain has a thousand peaks, adorned with all kinds of various jewels; upon the mountain are various *vitāla* trees, all of which are golden trees emitting all manner of fragrances.

Having passed this mountain, there is a great river named Śilodaka. Within this river, all sentient beings—whether grass, wood, humans, non-humans, birds, or beasts—are like stones once they enter it. On both banks of the river grow various bamboo groves called Cīcā; when the wind blows and they rub against one another, fire is naturally produced, which burns and kills immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.

The practitioner further observes that beyond this river there is another great river named Sītā, ten yojanas wide and three hundred yojanas long; no one is able to cross it because its water is salt, and if anyone enters it, their body will immediately shatter.

Having crossed this river, there is an island named Jambumā where a gandharva named Nityapriya dwells. He practices extensive giving, purely maintains the precepts, is always joyful in mind, free from sorrow and affliction, and is fully endowed with the fruits of his desires.

On this island, golden trees abound, and lapis lazuli flowers fill the ponds. Near Mount Sumeru, by the power of the mountain, all the river waters and the various birds and beasts become golden in color. There are many and immeasurable *utpala* and *kumuda* flowers, and everywhere flow rivers of wine, overflowing and surging. There is natural rice that requires no sowing or cultivation.
That island is two thousand yojanas in length and breadth; beyond this island, there are no mountains, rivers, or forests whatsoever.
There is a great ocean named Water-Foam Wheel (*udakaphenacakrā*), within which dwell many fire-poisonous and evil nāgas called Lightning-Light (*vidyutprabhā*).

Having crossed this sea, there is a great mountain named Nemisa. Within the mountain is a cave named Dīmiṣa, a cave of darkness. Inside the cave dwell many nāga maidens born by transformation; they are born by transformation during the first watch of the night, perfectly beautiful and adorned with ornaments. Their lifespan lasts but a single night, and at the rising of the sun, they all grow old and die.
Due to the residual karma of taking life, they receive this retribution.
Having passed beyond this mountain, there is another mountain named Sumāgadhī, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

Having passed this mountain, there is a great mountain named Sumerusama, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. To the north of this mountain is a vast forest called Citaka-vana, where a rākṣasa named Pāpaka-svapna dwells. His movement is exceedingly swift; in the blink of an eye, he can travel a hundred thousand yojanas, bringing harm and discomfort to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in its successive stages.
He observes the space between the two lands of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru: what mountains, rivers, seas, and islands are there?"
Is there anywhere at all that is without birth or death, without decline or cessation, not caused by karma, and free from the separation from the beloved and the meeting with the hated?

Therefore, one should develop weary detachment toward birth and death; those who ought to abandon bondage and attachment should seek liberation. One should loathe birth and death, and within birth and death, one must not give rise to craving or delight. Do not sport together with the heart of love, do not entangle yourself with the net of craving, and do not take pleasure in birth and death.

All of saṃsāra is a blazing mass of great suffering; it is ablaze with the fires of grief, lamentation, pain, and affliction, as well as the suffering of separation from the beloved and the suffering of encountering the hated. Within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans, all things are impermanent and subject to decay. Yet foolish people are greedily attached to them, calling them "happiness. You should give rise to weary detachment; do not dwell in the realm of Māra, do not play with the afflictions, lest you feel regret later.

In this way, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality, seeing birth and death as they truly are; they do not dwell in the realm of Māra, remain free from defilement and turbidity, and leave behind the wilderness of doubt.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes the northern region of Jambudvīpa: what mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:"
There is a great mountain named Kūṭaśilā, thirty yojanas in length and breadth and ten yojanas in height; upon that mountain dwell immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kūṭaśilā birds.

The blue *aśoka* trees, red *aśoka* trees, *saptaparṇa* trees, *kunda* trees, *kovidāra* flowers, *nāgakeśara* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *śephālikā* flowers, *tārā* flowers, *pārijātaka* flowers, *kukubha* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *kunduru* flowers, and *bhallātaka* flowers all bloom and flourish of their own accord according to the seasons.
At another time, the hosts of Mālādharas leave their original abodes to sport upon this mountain;
there are also yakṣas dwelling within these mountains who receive joy and pleasure, not troubling the celestial hosts.
In this mountain there are many *kūṭīra* birds.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great ocean shore named Haṃsavāsa (Abode of Geese), where there are many hundreds of thousands of flocks of geese and immeasurable lotuses. On such a seashore there are geese, ducks, ruddy sheldrakes, pearl-beaked birds, *manuṣya* birds, and *kaṇṭha* birds; the color of these lotuses is like a mass of molten gold, extending for ten thousand *yojanas*, and they are completely covered and surrounded by bees.

Beyond this to the north lies Uttarakuru. There is a great ocean, a thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with many large fish such as the timi, śiśumāra, nāgara, śiśumāra, ghaṭa, and tortoises. Its waters are blue like the void, ten thousand yojanas deep, and the mother of conchs and shells dwells within these waters; her body is ten li in width, and beneath the water there are mountains.
The conch possesses great power, equal to the strength of a thousand elephants; when it falls upon a mountain peak, the peak is completely shattered.

Having passed beyond this sea, there is another great sea named the Sea of Milk (*Kṣīroda*), five thousand yojanas in length and breadth, where vast waves constantly rise and great, malevolent venomous dragons roar like thunder.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes the north of Jambudvīpa: what mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:"
There are five hundred great mountains, made of gold, silver, and crystal, each one thousand yojanas in height; near Uttarakuru, there are many lotus flowers like the rising sun.

Having passed this mountain, there is a great kingdom named Kṣīraparivarta. Its mountains, rivers, and groves abound with birds and beasts, where yakṣas dwell in constant joy; it is filled with many flowering trees and possesses all manner of things in abundance.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes the north of Jambudvīpa: what mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands are there?
By means of wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he observes:"
Between the two lands of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru, there is no other country.

The land of Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it contains thirty-six billion delightful villages, and the pleasures experienced by its inhabitants are only slightly less than those of the gods of the Four Great Kings.

The gods have no flesh, bones, impurities, or sweat; they do not blink their eyes. The people of Uttarakuru possess flesh, bones, impurities, and sweat, and their eyes blink as they look about; yet they are free from the notions of "I" and "mine," and lack the conceit of "I am. When they die, they are certain to be reborn in the heavens. Being free from arrogance, flattery, and crookedness, they do not give rise to envy or jealousy. Their minds are constantly joyful, and they fear neither yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, lions, tigers, leopards, nor the likes of evil nāgas and insects. Furthermore, they suffer neither famine, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, nor disease. They remain far removed from all enemies and terrors, loving and respecting one another without causing mutual hindrance, and they have no fear of kings, thieves, water, fire, or weapons.
The radiance of the golden trees makes no distinction between day and night.

There are golden birds, silver birds, and coral birds; whether tree or bird, they are of various colors. They rejoice like humans, and although they lack consciousness, they act according to human ways.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes: what further delightful flavors does Uttarakuru possess?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:"
In Uttarakuru there are ten great mountains. What are these ten?
First is Mount Saṃkha; second is Mount Samakūṭa.
The third is named Mount Dharmavatsa;
the fourth is named Mount Śvetameghadhara;
the fifth is named Mount Uccaya.
Sixth is Mount Universal Garland;
seventh is Mount Seasonal Joy;
eighth is Mount Sustaining Delight.
The ninth is named Mount Yatheṣṭha;
the tenth is named Mount Kūṭaśālmali.
These are called the ten great mountains.
The great ocean surrounding the land of Uttarakuru is like the four great mountains that exist in Jambudvīpa.
What are these four? The first is named the Snowy Mountains (Himavat).
The second is named Mount Minda;
the third is named Mount Malaya;
the fourth is named Mount Kīrasa.
The ten great mountains of the country of Uttarakuru are likewise thus.
*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Volume 68 [and] Volume 69.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Six:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality."
What kinds of rivers, ponds, flowing waters, flowers, fruits, birds, and beasts are there among the ten great mountains?

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that on Mount Saṃkāśa, the Saṃkāśa trees bear flowers during all six seasons; these trees emit a continuous radiance day and night, like a great torch burning in Jambudvīpa, and their fragrance pervades an entire yojana.
Just as there are some forests in Jambudvīpa that resemble one another, so too on Mount Saṃkāśa there are four great forests:
the first is named the Forest of Green Shadows;
the second is named the Forest of Bird Songs.
The third is the Forest of Warmth and Coolness;
the fourth is the Forest of Khaṃbirā.
When one reaches these forests, flowers descend from the sky like clouds, merging and gathering together; therefore, Mount Saṅkāśa is so named, for "saṅkāśa" means "gathering."

As for the Blue Shadow Forest (Nīlacchāyavana), whatever white birds dwell in this forest take on the color of lapis lazuli due to the power of the forest; therefore, it is named the Blue Shadow Forest.

As for the Forest of Bird Songs: if one enters this forest, birds emit wondrous sounds according to whatever one thinks of; when the people of Uttarakuru see this, they experience great joy, and thus it is named the Forest of Bird Songs.
As for the Forest of Warmth and Coolness: if a person is cold, upon entering it they become warm; if they have heat, upon entering this forest they immediately attain coolness.
Within the forest there are birds called *vāyujava* (Wind-Travelers), which are *jīvajīvaka* birds; by the power of these birds, they can travel one thousand *yojanas* in a single thought-moment.
If a person sees this bird and thinks of traveling, they can immediately mount it; in a single thought-moment, one can reach a distance of one thousand yojanas.

This Jīvajīvaka bird understands all the languages of the people of the four continents and can also speak them. It experiences pleasure like a human being and desires pleasure like a human being. Its body is adorned with the seven treasures: its two wings are adorned with blue gems, musāragalva, crystal, and red lotus jewels. Those who see it are filled with joy.

Observing Mount Saṃkāśa, there is a second forest named Śuka (Parrot). The birds in this forest are joyful, and there is a lotus pond that wells up and covers its surface; if a king of geese from Jambudvīpa dies from the heat, he is reborn in this pond.
Just as the king of geese in Jambudvīpa dwells in Lake Anavatapta, so do various kinds of birds dwell within this forest:
