geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, cāṣa-birds, *tāmracūḍa* and *manava* birds, yellow birds, doves and pigeons, *tuṇḍakeśvara* birds, fragrant birds, *tripuṣṭa* birds, *goyeṣṭha* birds, the "joyful-voice" birds, the "six-season-flying" birds, the "delighting-in-the-moonlight" birds, the "rejoicing-at-the-rising-of-the-moon" birds, and the "sun-colored-peacock" birds, which utter joyful cries whenever they see a thundercloud.

There are the Jāta-sukha birds, the few-yellow birds, the Kaurava birds, the Nadi-pṛṣṭha birds, the Niṅgula-ṇḍa birds, the Dābhaka birds, the variegated-bodied birds, and the swarm-swirling bees; their voices can fill an entire yojana, like the bees of Jambudvīpa dwelling in the forest groves.

The crow, the mountain-dancing bird, the first-sound bird, the cock, the *parāvara* bird, the flower-body-covering bird, the lotus-dwelling bird, the blue *utpala* bird, the *cañcā* bird, the *kaṇṭhapuṣpa* bird, the *pratyutpanna* bird, the *rasāla* bird, the constant-voiced bird, the lute-voiced bird, the cloud-sight-delighted bird, the *saṃkrama* bird, the battle-sight-delighted bird, and the white-cloud bird.
Furthermore, there are other birds that are lovely to behold.
The Aversion-Free Bird dwells among the trees of the forest, and when the people of Uttarakuru see it, they rejoice.
Observing those various birds dwelling in the woods, one knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What forests are there on Mount Saṃkassa?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
The third grove is named Khaṇḍilavana; its branches and leaves overlap one another, casting a thick and cool shade. The people of Uttarakuru enter this forest for the sake of recreation.
The grove is named Spotted-Leaf Tree; next is named Dragon-Flower Tree;
next is named Āmra; next is named Kovidāra Tree; next is named Śāla Tree; next is named Delightful Tree;
next is named Bird-Rest Tree; next is named Parāta Tree; next is named Śyāmāka Tree; next is named...
The *niṣka-viḍa* tree, followed by the *cūta* tree, followed by the *kāra* tree, followed by the *vīraka* tree,
followed by the *kiṃnara* tree, followed by the *bakula* tree, followed by the *priyaṅgu* tree,
followed by the *kovidāra* tree, followed by the *vetasa* tree... [and so forth].
The first is named the Tāmarasī tree; next, the Kuraka tree; next, the blue-fragrance tree;
next, the moon-disk tree; next, the radiance-walking tree; next, the ever-blossoming tree;
next, the nikuṇḍala tree; next, the opening tree; next, the aśvattha tree; next...
They are named the *candana* tree, next the *śamālī* tree, next the *tāla* tree, next the *bilva* tree, next the *kapittha* tree,
next the *nārikela* tree, next the *panasa* tree, next the *anivārita-phala* tree, and next the *aśoka-puṣpa* tree.
Next is the *kadambara* tree; next is the *nicula* tree; next is the celestial *agaru* (sandalwood) tree;
next is the *campa* tree; next is the water-born tree flower; next is the *mandārava* tree flower;
next is the *kūṭaśālmali* tree flower; next is the golden flower; and next—
The first is named Silver-Colored Flower; the next is named Vaidūrya Tree; the next is named Peacock-Rest Tree;
the next is named Moving-to-Different-Places Tree; the next is named Island-Born Tree;
the next is named Kaliśāha Tree; the next is named Bakasa Tree; the next is named Mutually Reflecting and Thick Tree; and the next is named Smooth Tree.
Next is the tree named Shoulder-Born; next, the tree named Indra-Long; next, the tree named Bank-Born; next, the tree named Lane-Born;
next, the tree named Coral-Colored; next, the tree named Kumbhāṇḍa-Beard;
next, the tree named Terrifying; next, the tree named Seasonal-Born; next, the tree named Smoke-Colored; and next...
The first is named Lamp-Light Tree; next is named Wind-Moving Tree; next is named Plantain Tree;
next is named Kūṭaśālmali Joy Tree; next is named Scattering-Flower Tree; next is named Flower-Uncovered Tree;
next is named Blooming-Umīra Tree; next is named Recollection Tree; next is named Like-Rice Tree; and next is named...
The udumbara tree; next, the tūtthama tree; next, the bhramarāvarta tree; next, the śikharadhara tree;
next, the śītalavāta tree; next, the cala tree; next, the aśoka tree—there are sixty such species of trees that surpass all others, which are not mentioned here.
Below lies the Kambila Forest, where flowing streams and lotus ponds are most delightful.

The people of Uttarakuru have no fear, sorrow, grief, or suffering from illness; they have no king and no burning afflictions. Free from the calamities of enmity and jealousy, they rejoice and enjoy themselves in the Kambila Forest on Mount Saṃkāśa.
Having observed Mount Saṅkha, one knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner proceeds with the contemplation of the external body.
In the land of Uttarakuru, on Mount Saṅkha, there is a fourth forest named Warm-and-Cool.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,

he sees the various cool ponds of the Forest of Warmth and Coolness, as described above, complete with flowers, leaves, fruit trees, and rivers— namely, the River of Refreshing Coolness, one yojana in width, its waters exceedingly deep.
The first is named the River of Purity; the next is named the River Without Turbidity; the next is named the River of Milk Water;
the next is named the River of Grape Juice; the next is named the River of Soma; the next is named the River of Beautiful Milky Mud and White Water;
the next is named the River of Mindfulness; the next is named the River of the King of Geese; the next is named the River of Ducks; and the next is named the River of Mandarins.
The Aṅga River; next, the River of Wondrous Sound; next, the Flower-Flowing River;
next, the River of Delicate Willow; next, the Wave-Flowing River; next, the River of Swift Flowing Joy;
next, the Kadambarī-wing River; next, the Pearl-Bill River; next, the Abounding-Turtle River; next, the Crimson [River].
The River of Fish-Spirals; next is the River named Kumbhīra; next is the River of Fish-Spirals; next is the River of Flowing Flowers;
next is the River of Bubbles-Wheels; next is the River of Water-Laughter; next is the River of Level Banks; next is the River of Rain-Sound;
next is the River of Melodious Currents; next is the River that Turns According to the Seasons.
The river named next is the River of Powerlessness; next is the Mountain Peak River;
next is the Golden Water River; next is the Silver Water River; next is the Silver Stone River; next is the Pearl Sand River;
next is the Mountain Flow River; next is the Cloud-Turning River; and next is the Musāragalva-Adorned River.
Next is the river named Coral Tree; next is the river named Spring Joy; next is the river named Autumn Clear Water; next is the river named Valley Flow;
next is the river named Peak-Circle Laughter; next is the river named Snow Water;
next is the river named Unillumined by the Sun; next is the river named Swift Flow; next is the river named Whirlpool.
Next is the river named Niguṇḍula; next, the river named Gandhodaka; next, the river named Keta-gandhavāsinī;
next, the river named Pramodyavarṣa; next, the river named Tuṇḍubha; next, the river named Samantaparivartana;
next, the river named Anantapravāha; and next, the river named Udakotsiñcanatīra.
The river, followed by the one named Bakula River, then the one named Water-Diminishing River, then the one named Joyful Whirlpool River,
then the one named Mountain-Destroying River, then the one named Cloud-Walking River, then the one named Song-Sound River, then the one named Drum-Sound River,
then the one named Thunder-Sound River, and finally the one named Dragon-Girl’s Delight River.
Next is the river called Yakṣapriyā, followed by the river called Ṛṣipriyā.

This is the fourth grove of temperate climate on Mount Saṃkāśa; it contains these seventy great rivers, not to mention its countless smaller streams, and is fully endowed with the virtues of forest trees, flowers, and fruits.
Having observed the Cool Grove, he knows the external body as it truly is:

"On Mount Saṃkāśya, the fifth is named Thundering Cloud-Garland and Dragon’s Playful Cloud-Garland. Therein dwell the nāga kings Virūpa-vāsuki, Takṣaka, and Dantaviṣa; they manifest great flashes of lightning and raise clouds that cover everything, acting in accordance with the Dharma."
There are seven thousand such great nāgas who, in Uttarakuru, send down rain at the proper seasons, pouring it upon the level plains.
The people of Uttarakuru are just like the devas.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.

As previously described, whether it be trees, flowers, fruits, or seeds; rivers, stone caves, or various locations on the earth; or grass, mountain valleys, or mountain caverns—in such places as these, there is not even space the size of a needle’s point where sentient beings dwell who are neither born nor die, neither decline nor emerge, yet who have experienced all manner of pleasures hundreds and thousands of times."

Among the various kinds of sentient beings, there are none who have not experienced destruction, separation from loved ones, mental distress, or regret; there are none who have not been enemies, relatives, or neutral parties; there are none who have not been united with others across immeasurable places of birth—whether through hundreds or thousands of lifetimes, whether born in the water or on land, or moving through the air. Within the realm of animals, there is not a single being that has not preyed upon or harmed another, nor is there a single being that has not formed enmity, just as this body of mine has been born in every possible place.
In this way, the bhikṣu does not see even a spot the size of a needle’s point that is not a place of birth and death, as previously described.
Having thus contemplated Mount Saṃkāśya, he knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What other sublime mountain forests are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees them:"
The second mountain is named Samatala-śikhara (Equal Peak), which is like the Nandana Garden in the heavens.
Regarding all the rivers, ponds, flowers, fruits, groves, and trees on the Equal Peak, they are as described in detail previously for Mount Saṃkhaśa; what further excellence does it possess?
As for those mountain peaks, three hundred golden peaks possess a radiance like the sun, and five hundred silver peaks are as previously described, yet their merit is superior to the former.
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru possess bodily radiance like that of the full moon; they are named "Free from Fear" (*abhaya*), for they truly have no fear, and are thus called "Fearless."

The people of Uttarakuru dwell within these mountains; they enjoy themselves and experience pleasure just like the Four Heavenly Kings. During the four months of summer, they experience the pleasures of the five desires in the Garden of Joy (Nandana).
In what ways is it superior?
The gods of the Four Great Kings have no bones and no flesh, and they are free from sweat and impurities; these qualities are beyond the reach of the people of Uttarakuru.
Furthermore, the people of Uttarakuru are far removed from fear, which makes them superior to those in the realm of the Four Great Kings.

The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings dwell in palaces atop high mountain peaks, yet they still harbor fear; the people of Uttarakuru have no palaces or houses and lack the notion of "mine," and for this reason, they are without fear.
When the people of Uttarakuru reach the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the higher realms; therefore, they have no fear. The gods of the Four Great Kings are not like this.
Furthermore, because the people of Uttarakuru possess superior dharmas that free them from fear, they surpass the abode of the Four Great Kings.

In the mountains of Samatā, all the groves of trees are like a second sun. For those who have abandoned fear, whatever they desire appears from the trees: garments without thread or seam, and ornaments of precious jewels. If they think of food and drink, hundreds of thousands of rivers flow forth, brimming with sustenance. The songs of the birds are as lovely as previously described; there are golden-winged birds and blue *vaiḍūrya* ones, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks. There are also countless deer with bodies of pure gold, antlers of coral, eyes of mother-of-pearl (*śaṅkha*), and hooves of blue jade, as well as other various exotic beasts of infinite kinds dwelling within the mountains. The branches of the trees grow intertwined, shading one another like nets of pearls.
There are *kūṭīra* birds and the exquisite calls of peacocks;
it is adorned with hundreds of thousands of flowing streams and immeasurable riverbanks, and all the rivers contain water of the eight meritorious qualities.
What are the eight?
First, possessing flavor; second, purity.
Third, it is fragrant and pure;
fourth, it removes thirst;
fifth, it is cool and refreshing.
Sixth, one never tires of drinking it;
seventh, it is free from defilement;
eighth, there is no affliction in drinking it.
No malevolent fish pass through it.

Within this mountain there are various flower ponds; that is to say, there is the flower pond named Vast Mountain, next the flower pond named Multitude of Sands, next the flower pond named Five Trees, and next the flower pond named Ruddy Shores.
The pond is next called the Swan-Water Flower Pond; next, the Fan-Wing Flower Pond;
next, the Abounding-Hundred-Birds Flower Pond; next, the Great Coral Flower Pond; next, the Bamboo-Tree Flower Pond;
next, the Deep Flower Pond; next, the Moon-Love Flower Pond; next, the Upper-Moon Flower Pond; and next—
The first is named Miscellaneous Water Flower Pond; next is named Whirlpool Flower Pond; next is named Bamboo Grove Flower Pond;
next is named Immortal’s Affection Flower Pond; next is named Fish-Spiral Flower Pond; next is named Trapped by the *tripota* Fish Flower Pond;
next is named Peak-Center Flower Pond; next is named Lake-Garland Flower Pond; next is named...
The revolving flower pond; next, the pure water flower pond; next, the moonlight flower pond; next, the lunar orb flower pond;
next, the stainless flower pond; next, the milk-water adorned flower pond;
next, the cool and refreshing flower pond; next, the moon-loved flower pond; next, the crystal [flower pond].
There is the Revolving Flower Pond; next is the Rapidly Revolving Flower Pond;
next is the Tranquil Flower Pond; next is the Immovable Flower Pond; next is the Heaven-Loved Flower Pond; next is the Joyful Flower Pond;
next is the Exquisite Flavor Flower Pond; next is the Meaning-as-It-Is Flower Pond; and next is the Delightful Flower Pond.
Next is the Lotus Pond named Kikubha; next is the Lotus Pond named Amṛtōttaravāhinī; next is the Lotus Pond named Nāgapuṣpa;
next is the Lotus Pond named Rati; and next is the Lotus Pond named Aśoka.

On the summit of Mount Samantaprabhāsa, there are such as these forty-seven ponds, which are the most excellent among all the peaks of Mount Samantaprabhāsa; all these ponds contain water of eight virtues, as previously described.
That mountain is loftily exalted as if emerging from the piercing of space;

because the mountain is so high, it possesses superior groves endowed with every merit, namely the Cool Grove (*śītalavana*), which is white in color like the moon and extends for one hundred *yojanas*.
There are many silver trees there, white in color like snow. Within these groves, there are lotus ponds.
The first is named Water-Devoid-Raiment Flower Pond; next is named Bee-Covered Flower Pond; next is named Conch-Colored Flower Pond;
next is named Constant-Water Flower Pond; next is named Half-Visible Flower Pond; next is named Joyful Flower Pond;
next is named Kadamba-Puṣpaka Flower Pond; and next is named Goose-Wing Flower Pond.
Next is the Flower Pond named Playful; next is the Flower Pond named Lovely; next is the Flower Pond named Peak-Sight; next is the Flower Pond named Joyful Play;
next is the Flower Pond named Constant Joy; next is the Flower Pond named Constant Lotus;
next is the Flower Pond named Constant Delight; and next is the Flower Pond named Cloud.

This is called the first and most excellent of the sixteen flower ponds; excluding those of inferior quality among the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of unnamed ones, they are all pure, free from mud and turbidity, and devoid of aquatic moss.

The lovely calls of geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks cause the people of Uttarakuru to be constantly filled with joy, while jīvañjīvaka birds and peacocks produce exquisite sounds within the groves and gardens.
Having observed the level mountain peaks, the practitioner knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner, observing the external body in accordance with reality, gains faith and understanding in the Four Noble Truths.
When one observes the peaks of the mountain of equality, is there even a single place that is permanent and unchanging, pleasant, or a self, and not empty?

As previously stated, among all sentient beings encompassed by birth and death, is there anyone who does not die or take birth, and who is never separated from or parted from anything they love, nor ever subject to destruction?
That practitioner contemplates:

upon the peaks of the Mountain of Equality, not a single place is seen that is permanent, immovable, pleasant, self-existent, or non-empty. In all places where sentient beings dwell, there is no exception to birth and death; they are subject to the destruction of being separated from those they love. Thus, all of saṃsāra is impermanent; among sentient beings, there is not even a space the size of a needle’s point where one is neither born nor dead, neither arising nor ceasing.
Having recollected the Four Noble Truths and observed the level mountain peaks of Uttarakuru, one knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, what other delightful places does the practitioner observe in Uttarakuru?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

the third mountain, named Mukilinda, which is fully adorned. Its complete adornments are like those previously described for Mount Saṃkāśa and the peaks of Mount Samataṭa; yet this mountain is even more excellent.

Mount Mukilinda is replete with flowing waters, honey-sweet rivers, and wish-fulfilling trees—namely golden trees—which bear flowers and fruits throughout the six seasons; they flourish and grow luxuriantly, their radiance like that of the sun.

On Mount Mudgaraka there is a forest of radiance, namely the Forest of Revolving Golden Light; next is the Forest of Silver Mounds; next is the Forest of Universal Mountains; next is the Forest of Softness; and next is the Forest of Revolving Golden Light, which is one hundred yojanas wide and consists of trees of pure gold, where many bees abound.

Next is the forest named Silver Cluster, three hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It contains immeasurable silver trees, and the radiance of that forest is like that of a hundred thousand moons. There are many lions and countless birds, whose minds are always joyful as previously described.
On Mount Mukilinda there is a third forest called the Forest of Eternal Joy (*Nityasukha*). In this forest there are birds named Constantly Sporting (*Nityavihārin*), who experience joy and delight.

There are people in that land called Liberated (*Vimukta*) who, within the Forest of Eternal Joy, sport with joy and mastery according to their will; unimpeded by anyone, they enjoy pleasure just like the hosts of devas.

On Mount Mudovaka there is a fourth forest named Mṛdumṛdu (Soft and Gentle), consisting of trees of gold, silver, and coral. It abounds with various birds called Vimukta (Liberated). This forest is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; those who are constantly full of desire dwell in this forest. Its ground is as soft as tūla-cotton, and it is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of bees amidst flowering trees and lotus ponds.
Having thus contemplated Mount Mukilinda, the third mountain, the practitioner knows the external body as it truly is, as previously described.
Furthermore, the practitioner continues to contemplate the external body in accordance with reality.
Contemplating Uttarakuru, what other delightful places are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the fourth mountain, named White Cloud-Sustainer (Pāṇḍukambala), extending for a thousand yojanas in length and breadth, composed entirely of pure white silver. Its radiance surpasses that of the moon; just as when the full moon appears over Jambudvīpa and the stars lose their luster, so too does it appear on the White Cloud-Sustainer Mountain.

Those people of Uttarakuru who dwell in this forest are named "Ever-Aroused Desire. They constantly delight in sporting upon Mount White-Cloud-Holding, their bodies adorned with lotuses. Free from fear, sorrow, grief, exhaustion, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, they always love song and play. They sport and enjoy themselves amidst the lotuses, and upon the mountain peaks they frolic and amuse themselves with hosts of celestial maidens. They constantly indulge in sensual desires and are forever free from sorrow and grief.
On Mount Śveta there are various groves: namely, the Grove of Drum-Sounds, next the Grove of Duck-Sounds, next the Grove of Mindfulness, and next the Grove of Water-Sounds.

As for the Forest of Drum-Sounds, the hosts of the Mālādharas strike celestial drums that produce exquisite sounds; these are like the blended tones of a kōng-hou, a sheng, and a flute. Yet the sound produced by striking the celestial drums surpasses even this, such that the sounds of Jambudvīpa do not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
The bird-beasts, gardens, groves, flowered ponds, and land-tracts, with their flowing rivers of gold and silver—their merit is such as this.

As previously described, there is the sound of the celestial drum; those who always desire hear the sound of the celestial drum and constantly experience beloved forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and textures, just as the Garuḍapāda devas enjoy celestial pleasures in the Nandana Grove.
There is a second grove named Duck-Sound (*Kāraṇḍava-nirghoṣa*). In that grove, there are hundreds of thousands of kinds of flowers and ponds, which cannot be described in detail.
In the Duck-Sound grove, there are deer made of various jewels;
next are the *Vinasaka* deer, then the Jewel-Adorned deer, then the Tamed deer, then the Music-Sound deer, and finally the Fire-Colored deer.
The deer, followed by those called *śāra* deer, then those called *prapātana* deer,
then those called *parvatacārin* deer, then those called *cāpala* deer, then those called *samantacakṣus* deer, then those called *kāñcanamaṇi* deer,
then those called *suvarṇaviṣāṇa* deer, then those called *rūpyapārśva* deer, and finally those called *vāyuvega*.
The deer: next is called the tree-leaf-eating deer; next is called the water-dwelling vocal deer; next is called the forest-wandering deer;
next is called the coral deer; next is called the concave-horned deer; next is called the slender-waisted deer;
next is called the black-skin deer; next is called the *śaṃsuda* deer; and next is called the sun-light deer.
There are deer there, first called the Soft Deer, next called the White Deer, and so forth, numbering twenty-five kinds of deer.

Those who always delight in human company play with these deer; through their various karmic actions, they experience corresponding pleasures on Mount Śveta-abhra-dhara (White Cloud-Sustaining Mountain).

Furthermore, there is a third grove called Recollection; its inhabitants are named Desire-Seekers. Whatever they think of, they obtain from the trees. All the adornments of the gardens and groves are lovely, just as previously described.

On Mount Śveta there is a fourth forest named Jalasvara, where various sages dwell, sporting and enjoying themselves within the woods; if they become weary with heat, they enter the waters of the pool to sport and enjoy themselves.
There were several rishis: the first was named Unobstructed Rishi;
the second, Power Rishi; the third, Slow-Moving Rishi; the fourth, Space-Walking Power Rishi; the fifth, Cloud-Piercing Rishi;
the sixth, Sun-Path-Walking Rishi; the seventh, Measuring-Walker Rishi; and the eighth, White...
The Rishi Varṇa, next named the Rishi Śāṇada, next named the Rishi Kauśika,
next named the Rishi Parvata-vighuṣṭa, next named the Rishi Nityapriya, next named the Rishi Gandhara,
next named the Rishi Gaganagañja, next named the Rishi Dhanapati, next named...
The rishi Antarāvāsin, followed by the rishi Khaṇḍarīka, followed by the rishi Nityabala, followed by the rishi Haṃsāvatīya,
followed by the rishi Nāgāvatīya, followed by the rishi Vidyujjvāla,
followed by the rishi Mālaya-vāsika, followed by the rishi Kīrtimālaka, and so forth.
The first was named the Rishi Delighting in Courtesans; next, the Rishi Delighting in Wine; next, the Rishi Dwelling on Mount Meru;
next, the Rishi Trikaṇa; next, the Rishi Constantly Sporting; next, the Rishi Constantly Rejoicing;
next, the Rishi Adorned with Hanging Ornaments; and next, the Flying Rishi.
The next is named the Rishi Mantradhara.

These are known as the thirty rishis who dwell upon Mount Śvetābhradhara; they sport amidst various adornments, dancing, singing, and laughing by the waters of the Sound-Pool (Svaranirghoṣa), enjoying the fruits of their own karma. By the power of their own karma, they sport and enjoy themselves together with similar celestial maidens.
Having thus observed all the groves and trees of Mount Śveta-abhra-dhara, he knows the external body as it truly is.
Within Mount Śveta-abhra, is there even a single dharma that is permanent, immovable, unchanging, indestructible, and subsumed within nirvana?

In this way, a bhikṣu does not perceive a single dharma that is permanent, blissful, immovable, unchanging, or indestructible; for all dharmas are entirely impermanent, subject to destruction, and perishable, just as the light of the sun dispels all darkness.

The world is impermanent; it is sweet at first but bitter in the end. One flows deeply into it without emerging; the fruit of craving brings no joy. It is like the *kiṃpāka* fruit, like poison, or like a sword. Though pleasant when obtained, its delight lasts but a moment. Like lightning that does not abide, like the swift current of a river, it is impermanent and unstable. It deceives people like a city of the *gandharvas*.

All people are greedy; if they must fall as a result, it will be like food mixed with poison, which brings great suffering when digested, or like a knife smeared with honey, or like a sharp spear. It deludes and misleads immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, just like a large tree on the edge of a steep riverbank; the impermanence of all desires is likewise so.
Thus the practitioner contemplates desire as it truly is, giving rise to a mind of weary detachment, observing with right mindfulness, and eliminating defilements.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What other lovely mountains and rivers are there in the land of Uttarakuru?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

the fifth mountain, named High Mountain (*Giri*), one thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, its radiance shining everywhere. There are trees of pure gold with leaves of lapis lazuli; trees of white silver with leaves of coral; and trees of lapis lazuli with leaves of pure gold, their brilliance like that of lamps.

Furthermore, there are other trees and immeasurable varieties of trees; there are lotus groves, ponds, and gardens for recreation, as well as various kinds of deer and various mountain peaks, all as previously described.
The Mālādhara devas and the Trayastrimśa devas who dwell upon Mount Sumeru come from that mountain to this high mountain to sport and enjoy themselves.
The peaks of this high mountain are all composed of various jewels; there are five great peaks, each fifty yojanas in height and two hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

On the first golden peak, all manner of jewels arise within the mountain valleys, namely: lapis lazuli, coral, mother-of-pearl, crystal, red lotus gems, soft gems, blue indranīla gems, great blue king of gems, and natural celestial garments.

The second is Silver Peak, which is fully endowed with silver trees. Within the peak there is much gośīrṣa sandalwood; when the hosts of devas and asuras engage in battle and are wounded by blades, they apply this gośīrṣa sandalwood and are immediately healed.
Because this mountain peak resembles the head of an ox, and sandalwood trees grow upon it, it is named Ox-Head (Goviṣāṇa).

The third mountain peak is named Joy of the Goddesses (Devīnandana); its groves are made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli, and its ground is soft and supple. There, beings play with joy; yet foolish worldlings, deceived by craving and estranged from hearing the True Dharma, constantly delight in sensual pleasures.

The fourth mountain peak is named Jātarūpa; there the Four Great Kings sport and enjoy themselves in the Pātali grove, while all the birds, beasts, yakṣas, ṛṣis, and people of Uttarakuru likewise experience delight.
The rivers of grape wine overflow and flow, their taste like honey, like rock sugar, or sometimes with a pungent flavor or various blended flavors.

On the peaks and riverbanks, there are many living beings of various colors, namely: water buffaloes, oxen, sheep, pigs, dogs, wild foxes, elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, dragons, tigers, bears, brown bears, lions, rhinoceroses, and leopards; such are the countless jewel-like colors.
The peak is named Jātarūpa; because it produces all kinds of precious substances (*jātarūpa*), it is called Jātarūpa.

On the fifth mountain peak, there is a lotus pond within a *vaiḍūrya* forest, with stalks of *vaiḍūrya*. Its flowers are soft and supple. These are: the pond named Alpa-pūrṇa, followed by the pond named Bahula-padma, followed by the pond named Parivartana, followed by the pond named Puṣpāvṛta, followed by the pond named Sūryaprabha, followed by the pond named Mṛdu-tīra, followed by the pond named Anupama, followed by the pond named Madhuvana, followed by the pond named Gandhavāta, and finally the pond named Nityodaka.
These are called the ten kinds of flower ponds, which dwell within this peak.

Furthermore, great rivers flow everywhere, endowed with the six flavors, adorned by all manner of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and complete with the flowers and fruits of various trees, as well as rivers and ponds, just as previously described.
Having thus observed the fifth mountain and the fifth peak, that bhikṣu knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner proceeds to further observe the high mountain.
He knows the karmic fruits and retributions of phenomena; he knows the karmic fruits and retributions of the phenomena of sentient beings.

Sentient beings possess their own karma and dwell within the flow of their own karma; because of their own karma, they are born upon this mountain. When their wholesome karma is exhausted and due to their unwholesome karma, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If there are those with wholesome karma who are born among gods or humans, the people dwelling on the four sides of the high mountain are called the "Delighters in Goodness"; they constantly long for desires and are never satisfied.
Thus the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"Just as fire finds fuel, and as the ocean receives all streams, so craving is difficult to satiate; therefore, one should abandon it."
"Thus, with the purified eye, the practicing bhikṣu sees:

these sentient beings, in the midst of great sorrow, grief, lamentation, and poison, yet still laugh and smile; these sentient beings do not know that all is suffering, non-self, impermanent, and that all phenomena are empty; they do not know that all is darkness, and that within all birth and death there is no permanence or bliss, no tranquility, and no cessation; they do not know that all requisites must inevitably perish, and that this dharma is unreal, leading ultimately to falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."
Just as when the sun rises it must inevitably set, so it is with all sentient beings: among those born into existence, there is a certain return to death.

It is like the springtime, when the entire great earth—with its mountains, trees, medicinal herbs, groves, and level plains—reaches the autumn season; then the great earth, the mountains, the trees, the medicinal herbs, the groves, the marshes, and the flowering ponds all undergo decay and transformation.
Youth is like the springtime, and old age is like the autumn; the people of Uttarakuru do not perceive this, yet all vigor and youthfulness inevitably succumb to decay.

It is like the summer months when the heavens send down torrential rains and the rivers, possessing steep banks, gather vast waters until they overflow and fill to the brim; yet by the first month of winter, everything has diminished.
Abundance and prosperity are like the summer, while the destruction of that prosperity is like the first month of winter.
It is like a lotus pond where the water overflows, which various bees delight in and enjoy with joy; yet when frost and snow descend, the lotuses wither and rot, and the bees abandon them.
Human beings are likewise: when free from the affliction of illness, they are like a newly blossomed flower; once decay and sickness arrive, they are like a withered and rotten flower.
Surrounded by swarms of bees like a gathering of wealthy and joyful friends, sentient beings are thus deceived by craving and do not realize they are destroying themselves.

In this way, when a bhikṣu has observed the high mountains, gardens, groves, flowering trees, rivers, springs, ponds, seers, birds, beasts, valleys, and mountain clefts, he knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees the land of Uttarakuru; what other lovely mountains are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

the sixth mountain, named Garland-Adornment (*mālā-vyūha*). Upon that mountain there are various adornments; its trees are of vermilion, green, blue, and yellow hues, namely, groves of trees with variegated flowers.
Furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Aśoka;
furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Suvarṇapattrā;
furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Śākhāpraticchanna.
Furthermore, there are flowering trees named atimuktaka, with golden stems and golden leaves, swaying and shaking in the water as the wind blows.
There are also nyagrodha trees with leaves of lapis lazuli.
There is a plantain tree with leaves of coral that blossoms upon seeing the sun.
Furthermore, there is the tilaka tree, which immediately blooms when it sees the moonlight.
Furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Kumuda, which blooms when there is no sun.
There is another flowering tree named Ardhacandra-prīta.
There is yet another flowering tree named Nārakāra.
Furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Tri-saṃpraharṣaṇī;
another flowering tree named Bandhujīvaka;
and another flowering tree that grows by means of smoke.
Furthermore, there are flower trees called *aśoka*; when women touch them, flowers immediately emerge.
There are also flower trees called *kunduru*, which are soft and supple by nature.
Furthermore, there is a flowering tree named Śirīṣa, which grows and flourishes as soon as it is stepped upon by human feet.
There is also a flowering tree named Vītapa, which emits fragrance when it is warm.
There was also a flowering tree named Kujūma, which spreads its fragrance to distant lands.
There was another flowering tree named Ji-xi (Auspicious Sight).
There was also a lotus flower named Shan-yi (Good Intention), beloved by devas and humans alike.
Furthermore, there is a lotus named blue utpala that grows in the water.
There is also a lotus named ever-blossoming.
There is also a flower tree named siṃhaka-tamāla.
Furthermore, there is a lotus named Water-Laughter (*jalahaṃsā*) which springs up when stepped upon by a foot.
There is also a flowering tree named Red-Aśoka; when a woman steps upon it, the flower emerges because she has obtained the woman’s [sensory qualities of] color, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Furthermore, there is a flower tree named Aṭaka.

Of such flower trees, there are twenty-two, adorned all around with garlands of flowers. Some are golden, some are the color of lapis lazuli, or the color of white silver; some are yellow, some are green, or of variegated colors. They are found either in the midst of ponds, or beneath trees, or in thickets of shrubs, or they are found everywhere throughout all places.

Furthermore, there were various birds with bodies of pure gold and wings of white silver, or bodies of white silver and wings of gold; some had bodies of coral and wings of lapis lazuli, or bodies of lapis lazuli and wings of the king of blue jewels; others had bodies of crystal and wings of pure gold.
There are various birds with bellies of pure gold, wings of white silver, and backs of lapis lazuli.
There are also various birds whose bodies are composed of the seven treasures—namely, blue gems, king-makara gems, crystal gems, musaragalva, coral, masāragalla, and red lotus gems.
Thus, through the power of their own karma, the people of Uttarakuru possess bodies of various colors, various sounds, and immeasurable forms.

By the force of their own karma, they have immeasurable varieties of multicolored forests, mountains, rivers, and flower ponds that are exceedingly delightful; adorned with various kinds of jewels, these appear exactly as they have been conceived in their minds.
Through the ripening of their past virtuous karma, they enjoy food and drink, with rivers, ponds, forests, and trees adorning the surroundings everywhere.
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru experience pleasure upon the Mount Mālyavat, which is adorned with garlands.

The mountain-dweller named Nityanandika, on Mount Mālyagandhika, constantly sports like the devas. During the four months of summer, he dwells beneath a Pāriyātra-kovidāra tree, enjoying himself and experiencing pleasure; except for his blinking, his body having bones, flesh, and the presence of grime and sweat, in all other respects he is entirely equal [to the gods].
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the law of karmic fruition.
Sentient beings, through three kinds of arrogance and negligence, fail to perform wholesome deeds.
What are these three?
First, conceit born of relying on physical beauty;
second, conceit born of relying on youth;
third, conceit born of relying on life.

Failing to perform wholesome deeds of body, failing to perform wholesome deeds of speech, and failing to perform wholesome deeds of mind, one may be reborn in the heavens by means of superior wholesome karma; yet from the heavens, one subsequently falls back, descending into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Human affection is like honey mixed with poison; it brings about the foremost suffering, the foremost bondage, and rebirth in the foremost evil realms.
Bound by affection, sentient beings do not know from where they come into birth, nor to what place they go when they depart.
All desires are like the *jambuka* fruit: though slightly sweet at first, they result in great suffering later; they are like sentient beings covered by a net, unaware as they fall over a precipice.
The great suffering of separation from what is loved is like fire consuming itself;
vigorous beauty does not endure, like water cascading down a steep mountain; impermanence does not abide, but changes, decays, and perishes.

Within the five realms of existence, there is not a single place where one is not blown by the winds of unwholesome karma as one wanders through the various states of being; yet, sentient beings still do not give rise to weariness toward this cycle of birth and death.
Having observed the mountain adorned with garlands where people constantly sport, one knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
What kinds of lovely mountains, rivers, and flower ponds are there in the land of Uttarakuru?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye,

he sees that in Uttarakuru there is a great mountain called Seasonal Joy (*Ṛtusrava*), one thousand *yojanas* in breadth and thirty *yojanas* in height, which remains perpetually fresh throughout the six seasons.
First, the first month of winter;
second, the last month of winter;
third, the first month of spring.
The fourth is late spring;
the fifth is early summer;
the sixth is late summer.
In the first season, what flowers are there?

During the early winter, there are trees that bloom perpetually, known as the *asaṃpuṣpa* (Unfolding Flower), followed by the *dṛḍhapuṣpa* (Firm Flower), the *śītapuṣpa* (Frozen Flower), the *bhramarācitapuṣpa* (Honeybee-Covered Flower), the *vakulapuṣpa* (Vakula Flower), the *sugandhapuṣpa* (Fine-Fragrance Flower), the *an-aṅkurapuṣpa* (Sproutless Flower), the *haṃsakūjitapuṣpa* (Duck-Sound Flower), the *prathamapuṣpa* (First Flower), the *priyapuṣpa* (Lovely Flower), the *śītalasampannapuṣpa* (Endowed-with-Coolness Flower), the *gambhīrajātapuṣpa* (Deeply-Grown Flower), the *rātripuṣpa* (Night-Blooming Flower), the *prathamadṛḍhapuṣpa* (First-Firm Flower), and the *divāpuṣpa* (Day Flower).
These are the fifteen kinds of flowers that bloom during the cold season of the first month of winter on Mount Joy.
In the second month of winter, there further arise lotus flowers on Mount Joy in Uttarakuru;
by virtue of their wholesome karma, *atimuktaka* flowers fall down according to one's thoughts, namely the *kaurava* flowers.
Flowers: next is named the *padma* flower, next the *pāṇḍuraka* flower, next the *kurobaka* flower,
next the *bahugandha* flower, next the *bhramarāvarta* flower, next the *samantha* flower,
next the *aśoka* flower, next the *candana* flower, next the *nīla-aśoka* flower...
The *śoka* flower; next, the *asaṃkoca* flower; next, the *kubjaka* flower; next, the *amṛtaka* flower;
next, the cave-born (*guhā-ja*) flower; next, the riverbank-born (*nada-ja*) flower;
next, the *nyagrodha* flower; next, the red (*rakta*) flower; next, the *bhaṇḍīra* flower; next, the bird [flower].
There is the *āhvaya* flower, next the *nityapraphulla* flower, and next the *śatapattraka* flower.
There are twenty such varieties of flowers that bloom during the late winter and early spring; the *atimuktaka* and others bloom during both seasons.

In the mountains of Mount Nandana in the land of Uttarakuru, various flowers bloom during the late spring. These are the campaka flowers; next, the sumanā flowers; next, the varṇasaṃcaya flowers; next, the tamāla flowers; next, the gandhapuṣpa flowers; next, the bhramarapuṣpa flowers; next, the kṣudhāpahāragandha flowers; next, the śirīṣa flowers; next, the raktapuṣpa flowers; next, the samagandha flowers; next, the nityagandha flowers; next, the tāmbūlarasagandha flowers; next, the vātakuṇṭha flowers; next, the śatapattraka flowers; next, the sūryabhīruka flowers; next, the sarvalantika flowers; next, the raktaguṇa flowers; and next, the jātila flowers.
At that time, in Mount Nandana, twenty kinds of flowers such as these bloom during the late spring, due to the power of the wholesome karma of the people of Uttarakuru.
Then, in the early summer on Mount Nandana, there are further flowers: first, those called *citraka*;
next, those called *koṭaja*; next, those called *śatapatri*; and next, those called *kunda*.
The *bāhā* flower; next, the *niculaka* flower; next, the *yūthikā* flower; next, the *sumana* flower;
next, the *nāgavṛttaka* flower; next, the *anantarapriya* flower;
next, the *suvāsa* flower; next, the *sugandha* flower; next, the *sarvapatra* flower; next, the *sarva*... [flower].
The flowers are: first, the Grasping Flower; next, the Transforming Flower; next, the Nose-Object Flower; next, the Five-Petal Flower;
next, the Rain-of-Love Flower; next, the Beloved-to-Behold Flower;
next, the Anointing Flower; next, the Flowing-Water Flower; and next, the Snow-Colored Flower.
There are twenty such kinds of flowers that grow on Mount Nandana during the first month of summer, due to the ripening of the wholesome karma of the people of Uttarakuru.

At that time, in the mountain of Nandana during the late summer season, there were further extraordinary flowers: namely, the *hasita* flower; next, the *sumanā* flower; next, the *nitya-campaka* flower; next, the *vanaja* flower; next, the *gaganavikṣepa* flower; next, the *rātriramaṇīya* flower; next, the *sarvadig* flower; next, the *pravaha* flower; next, the *vihārabhūmi* flower; next, the *nandana* flower; next, the *girigahvara* flower; next, the *sthalaja* flower; next, the *kattamba* flower; next, the *pāṭalā* flower; next, the *haṃsāvarta* flower; next, the *śirīṣa* flower; next, the *tamālapatra* flower; next, the *jalaja* flower; next, the *candra* flower; and next, the *viṣamataṭa* flower.
There are twenty such kinds of flowers that bloom during the late summer on Mount Kālaśaila in the land of Uttarakuru.

The trees, forests, flowers, fruits, lotuses, ponds, and rivers completely pervade this Mount Kālaśaila throughout the seasons; just as all flowers and fruits exist in other mountains, so too do they always exist upon this mountain.
At that time, the person dwelling in Mount Nandana was named Dharīcama (translated into Wei as Jiānyóu, "Wandering Between").
Furthermore, the practitioner understands the karmic retribution of actions.
How is it that sentient beings, once their past karma is exhausted, fail to create new karma and remain unaware of the revolving wheel of time?

Sentient beings subsist on their life-force, yet time is like a great fire that consumes the fuel of life; time is like a fierce hailstorm that destroys and brings about untimely death; time is like a lion devouring human and beast; time is like a swift river that uproots trees and drifts them to distant places. No phenomenon of death can be escaped.
Why is it that sentient beings do not realize, nor see, that old age, sickness, and death mock and destroy all youthfulness, as well as all desires, and shatter all strength?

It is that which all people mock and deride; it is the root of emaciation. It can destroy the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Saliva and mucus flow profusely; the body becomes bent and crooked. The teeth, skull, bones, joints, tendons, and veins all become slack and loose. One is unable to come or go, nor bathe in clear ponds. One is despised and reviled by the young. Desiring to enter the city of death, one loses physical strength and dwells in a place of no peace or wholesome ground, frequently voiding excrement and urine, and taking great pleasure in sleep and reclining.
Why do sentient beings fail to see this old age and yet practice heedlessness?
Because of their heedlessness, they fail to see that illness is certain to occur.

Due to illness, the four great elements become unbalanced, the sense faculties lose their vitality, and all muscles, skin, blood, fat, marrow, and bone-essence completely wither away. They loathe all flavors, are unable to sit or rise, and long for physicians to seek security. All food and drink, once it enters the mouth, seems bitter; they are suddenly exhausted and utterly weary, unable to move or rest. They desire much sleep, their bodies become emaciated until only skin and bone remain, and though their kinsmen, wives, and children cannot accompany them, they remain unaware and unconscious of this terror of death.
Having observed sentient beings who act with negligence, this practitioner gives rise to a mind of compassion.
Because of that compassion, they cultivate the four brahma-vihāras, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Thus the practitioner contemplates the people of Uttarakuru and gives rise to a heart of compassion. He observes that their physical deportment is no different from that of a thief; their bodies are like foam on water, their various consciousnesses are like illusions, and their wealth and pleasures are like dreams. Having made this contemplation, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes Uttarakuru: what other kinds of extraordinary, lovely mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds are there?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

in Uttarakuru there is a great mountain named Nandadhara. On that mountain is a forest named Samantagata, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with all kinds of precious substances—namely, the nature of gold, silver, copper, jewels, wine, honey, the natures of the six flavors, and other various natures.

That grove was entirely encircled by garlands of *vaiḍūrya* flowers; there were lotuses with golden petals and silver stalks, and others with gold and silver petals and *vaiḍūrya* stalks, filling the space like the rising sun.

Various kinds of birds adorn that pond, namely: geese and ducks; next, those called *haṃsa* (swans); next, those called *baka* (cranes); next, those called golden birds; next, those called white-throated birds; next, those called *cañcā* birds; next, those called *mātṛkūṭa* birds; next, those called ruddy sheldrakes (*cakravāka*); next, those called *pāpā* birds; next, those called cranes (*baka*); next, those called *ajaya* birds; next, those called *sarasas* birds; next, those called *timiṅgila* birds; next, those called *vakra* birds; next, those called seasonal birds; next, those called heat-averse birds; next, those called night-wandering birds; next, those called birds that delight in scattering *padma* flowers; next, those called *siṃhapa* birds; and lastly, those called water-dwelling wave-birds.
There are twenty such kinds of birds dwelling in the lotus pond, beyond the Universal Forest and Mount Joy-Bearer (Nandadhara), in the middle of the mountain for five hundred yojanas.

Furthermore, there is another [mountain] five hundred yojanas in extent named Bamboo Shore (*Veṇuka*). People dwell upon this mountain, which has trees called *kuṇḍikā* that produce exquisite musical sounds; when the celestial maidens hear them, they remain in the air to listen. Its groves, gardens, ponds, and rivers, as well as its lotuses, are all fully endowed with every excellence, just as previously described.
The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma,
Scroll Sixty-Nine; The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma,
Scroll Seventy, translated by the Uighur Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body, Part Seven:
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
These beings ought to be weeping; how is it that they instead engage in song, dance, play, and laughter, failing to perceive their own heedlessness?"

Sentient beings suffer in the hells, wailing and lamenting; they do not realize they are bound by the net of craving. Because they have committed evil deeds with body, speech, and mind, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where they undergo the retribution of great suffering. They experience grief, sorrow, and weeping, enduring various forms of misery according to their karmic actions. They fall into the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, and the Intense Heat Hell. Due to the five kinds of craving—craving for form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—they are bound by them and wander through the great ocean of birth and death.
In this way, when the practitioner has observed those people dwelling on the bamboo bank, they know the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Contemplating Uttarakuru, what other delightful mountains and forests are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that in Uttarakuru there is a great mountain named Cittānukūla (Mind-Compliant), one thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
In this mountain range there are always kinnarī maidens who sing various wondrous melodies upon the mountain peaks.
Along the riverbanks, in the groves, on level ground, and in the mountain valleys, there are many lotus ponds and various gardens,
namely the Citrā-citravana forest, followed by the Nāgavana forest, and then the Nalīcīrava forest.
Next is named the Banaśa Grove; next is named the Khara Grove; next is named the Āmra Grove;
next is named the Anivārita Grove; next is named the Kumbhīra Grove; next is named the Kapitha Grove;
next is named the Peacock Grove; next is named the Cakora Grove; next is named the Śuka Grove; next is named...
The River-Pond Forest; next is named the Lotus Forest; next is named the Utpala Forest;
next is named the Siṃhaparivarta Forest; next is named the Kurabaka Forest; next is named the Jīvajīvaka Bird Forest;
and next is named the Tāla Forest.

Thus, within this forest, all manner of precious jewels and exquisite sounds cause all who hear them to rejoice and experience pleasure; yet, shrouded by delusion and craving, their fire of passion increases further. If there are those who hear the songs and chants of these kinnarī maidens, that fire increases a hundredfold.
If there are hungry deer with grass in their mouths, upon hearing this song, they unconsciously drop it;
if there are birds in the trees, playing as pairs and pecking at delicious fruits, upon hearing this sound, they all come to a halt;
and when the swarms of bees hear the voice, they cease drinking the nectar.
If there are sages in the midst of the void who hear the sound of their singing, they immediately halt and do not proceed.
Thus, the sound of the songs and hymns of the kinnarī women in Mount Cittasena is exceedingly delightful.

That mountain is composed entirely of *vaiḍūrya* jewels; its rocks are of gold and silver, its trees are of coral, and its sands are of pearl. The *pāṣāṇa* ponds have *utpala* lotuses made of *sphaṭika* crystal, and there are many white geese whose color is like that of conch shells.
Furthermore, there are various deer adorned with the seven treasures.
Within the groves there are *kūṭīra*, peacocks, and *jīvañjīvaka* birds, whose songs are delightful;
there are also lotus ponds adorned with swarms of bees.

Thus, when all the people in Mount Cittaprāsāda see or hear these things, their hearts give rise to love and joy; throughout the mountain, all the men and women laugh and play with delight, their minds filled with gladness.

Furthermore, there is a second delightful feature of this Anuloma Forest: whereas the light emitted from Mount Sumeru illuminates two hundred yojanas above, the light from the Anuloma Mountains illuminates two thousand yojanas above. That light is pure white; even the radiance of the golden trees turns entirely white due to the power of the light from the Vaiḍūrya mountains.

Just as when the golden radiance of Sumeru, the king of mountains, reaches the grass, it turns all the grass to gold, so too does the mountain’s light follow the mind, causing all birds, beasts, rivers, ponds, flowers, and trees to become white by the power of the mountain’s luminous radiance following the mind.

On this mountain there dwells a person named Śvetapuruṣa (The White Man). His radiance is also white, and he resides upon this mountain with great power and majestic dignity. His mind is always joyful; he is supremely pure, his body is anointed with exquisite fragrances, and he is adorned with flower garlands. He delights in song, dance, play, and laughter, and takes pleasure in sounds. He gives rise to no envy, possesses no sense of "mine," and is free from pride. All his radiances are of a white color, and various powdered incenses are scattered over his body; when one hears his various songs, one finds them delightful.

The wish-fulfilling trees produce fragrant and delicious wine; drinking it brings no harm. According to their thoughts, garments emerge from the trees—garments that are without the distinction of warp and woof threads. There are various kinds of food and drink, and various ornaments. Various birds emit wondrous sounds that cause people to fall into a peaceful sleep;
yet there are also other wondrous sounds, and various birds that cause them to awaken. In various flower ponds, various flowers bloom.

In this way, the person of white radiance experiences the signs of the karmic results according to the superior, middling, or inferior wholesome karma they have performed, thereby achieving the attainment of happiness.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Observe these sentient beings: how is it that they witness others' wholesome karma being exhausted and yet fall into the suffering of death, while remaining unaware?

At the very beginning, when suffering has not yet arisen, at the moment of conception, consciousness enters the womb within the urethra by means of the parents' semen and blood; gathered there by the winds of karma, it is stirred by their union. After seven days, it undergoes a transformation known as *arbuda*.
Within the *ābudha* stage, because one did not commit killing in previous lives, the consciousness-mind does not perish or decay.

During the second week, it is called the *gaṇa-kāya* (the mass-body); the deluded consciousness of afflictions remains unimpaired and undestroyed. Thus, through seven weeks, it is called a *māṃsa-piṇḍa* (flesh-ball), dwelling within the womb amidst excrement and urine; whenever the mother moves her body or consumes food and drink, it is oppressed with suffering, like grapes being pressed.
Furthermore, moved by the winds of karma, the mass of flesh grows and develops five protuberances, namely the two hands, the two feet, and the head.
Again, moved and further developed by the winds of karma, the *kalala* membrane arises; from within this membrane, a tube-like vessel emerges, piercing upward toward the internal organs.

Whether the mother eats cold food or hot food, or whether it is delicious or not, [the food] enters through the opening of the tube into her navel, serving as the life-force for the embryo and ensuring that it does not die.
Thus, within the womb, one undergoes great suffering and distress.

If one does not die or perish within the womb, one is defiled by urine and menstrual blood; dwelling in the womb for ten months is like being in a prison, oppressed by suffering and affliction, with every part of the body as if crushed by a mountain, until finally emerging from the womb.

After birth, when touched by wind and sun, they experience great suffering; they are cast upon the ground and abandoned at will, yet they suck their own fingers, from which milk flows, thereby nourishing themselves and attaining life.

The infant grows, transforms into youth, and gradually reaches old age, extinguished by the winds of time; yet due to the karma of sentient beings, the storehouse of karma continues to circulate, and according to what is performed through karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—all karmic results are brought to fruition.

Thus, these sentient beings, even while directly witnessing the suffering and affliction that are the karmic fruits of their own actions, remain heedless. Within the cycle of birth and death, the root of all painful sensations is what is called birth—the suffering of cold and heat, hunger and thirst, exhaustion and illness, the pain of separation from the beloved, and the pain of encountering the hated.

Within the cycle of birth and death, birth is a great suffering; it destroys the requisites for life, and one wanders through the flow of saṃsāra. It is impermanent, suffering, and empty; it is subject to arising and ceasing, and devoid of self. How is it that the people of Uttarakuru do not realize this?
In this way, these mountain valleys, groves, flowers, fruits, rivers, ponds, and lotuses—all shall become impermanent and perish, returning to emptiness.
Likewise, all sentient beings die; those born in the heavens, when their lives there end, fall according to their original karma into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Thus the practitioner contemplates the karmic fruits of phenomena and perceives the faults of birth and death; toward those beings of white radiance, he gives rise to a mind of compassion.
Furthermore, the practitioner follows the contemplation of the external body.
What kinds of lovely mountains and forests are there further in the land of Uttarakuru?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

In Uttarakuru there is a great mountain named Kūṭaśālmali, one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. There is a lotus pond named Śītala, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, filled with golden lotuses and free from any turbidity of mud. Within this pond there are many bees, and it is adorned with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.

Within the lotus ponds are *tārkṣyayaśas* flowers and *mandārava* flowers; the forest trees with their blossoms and fruits, the river valleys and groves, and the cool ponds are as previously described.

Fifty *yojana*s within the midpoint of Mount Kūṭaśālmali, there are eighty-four thousand palaces, marvelous and lovely. Some have palaces of pure gold with railings of white silver; some have palaces of white silver with railings of pure gold;

some have palaces of crystal with railings of *vaiḍūrya* gem; some have *vaiḍūrya* palaces with railings of crystal; some have palaces of blue beryl with railings of *musāragalva*; and some have *musāragalva* palaces with railings of blue *indrānila* gem.

Thus, these various jeweled railings were interspersed with one another, covered by nets of bells, and filled with the sounds of singing, dancing, laughter, and musical instruments; their hearts were ever joyful. Covered by grapevines, it was just like the Great City of Sudarśana or the Hall of Good Dharma in the heavens; Mount Kūṭaśālmali was likewise adorned, fully endowed with eighty-four thousand palaces, gardens, groves, ponds, rivers, trees, forests, flowers, and fruits.
The inhabitants dwelling on Mount Kūṣmāṇḍa are called Citravarṇa; their minds are constantly joyful because they delight in singing, dancing, playing, laughing, eating, and drinking.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the retribution of karma.
Why is it that these sentient beings do not see the suffering of separation from loved ones?

All sentient beings experience the separation from those they cherish as they travel to different places; they do not know that all must eventually die and perish, receiving retribution according to their karma."
If there is wholesome karma, one is born among humans or devas; if there is unwholesome karma, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

These people of variegated minds harbor negligence and know no contentment; they are attached to the pleasures of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. Bound by craving, swept away by the river of craving, and scorched by the fire of desire, they remain unaware. They do not perceive impermanence and death, nor do they enter into the great darkness; they do not see that the suffering of old age destroys youth, nor do they see the fire of death approaching to burn them, which can cause one to be forever separated from all loved ones.
Death is like a great fire that burns the life-tree of humans and consumes the forest of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality:
by what karma are the people of Uttarakuru born within the ten mountains?
What are the ten mountains?
First is Mount Saṃkha; second is Mount Samakūṭa.
The third is named Mount Mucilinda;
the fourth is named Mount Śvetābhradhara;
the fifth is named Mount Uccaya.
The sixth is named Garland-Adorned Mountain;
the seventh is named Indra’s Joy Mountain;
the eighth is named Joy-Sustaining Mountain.
The ninth is named Mount Anuloma;
the tenth is named Mount Kuśeśaya-alaṃkāra.
Through his wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that these sentient beings were born in this mountain due to their virtuous karma in previous lives:
"By refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and drinking intoxicants, and by practicing the ten wholesome actions, one is born in this mountain range.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the retribution of karma."
By what karma do those sentient beings possess physical strength, appearance, and form superior to other sentient beings?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

these sentient beings practiced giving with right view; their minds were not crooked or deceitful; they did not afflict other sentient beings; they possessed a straightforward mind of compassion; they practiced in accordance with the Dharma; and they drew near to the True Dharma.

By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the happy realms among the gods of the Four Great Kings or the Heaven of the Thirty-three; there, at the end of their life, they are reborn here in this world; and here, at the end of their life, they are reborn in those places.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the retribution of karma.
By what karma do these sentient beings receive such superior retribution?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees: "

In former lives, these sentient beings bestowed fearlessness upon those who were terrified; when they saw people facing execution—led out through the right gate, bound hand and foot, brought to the cemetery, beaten with drums of evil sound, and sent off by caṇḍālas to be deprived of their lives—they ransomed them and caused them to escape.

By reason of these causes and conditions, when the body perishes and life ends, they are reborn in the good realms—whether among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or the Yāma Heaven.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
By what karma do these sentient beings, among the superior devas, surpass other devas in the loveliness of their physical form and receive the offerings of all people?"
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

this sentient being, in a previous life, delighted in hearing the true Dharma and listened to the Buddha’s true Dharma, the noble Vinaya; he recited and chanted even a single verse of the Buddha’s teachings, and by reading, chanting, and contemplating them, through the causal condition of hearing a single phrase of the true Dharma, he became a Wheel-Turning King ruling over the four continents. After his life there ended, he was reborn in the heavens—once, twice, or up to seven times among the six heavens of desire, namely the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. From those heavens, when his life ended, he came to be born in this world.

By virtue of that wholesome mind, one experiences the pleasures of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles, and is reborn in the heavens. When life ends in the heavens, because of having previously heard the Dharma, one attains the first dhyāna-concentration in a future life and is born in the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, or the Mahābrahmā Heaven.

Furthermore, by the power of the causal conditions of the seeds of hearing the Dharma, they will attain the second dhyāna in future lives; upon passing away from there, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Limited Light, the Heaven of Infinite Light, and the Heaven of Radiant Sound.

Furthermore, by the power of the causal conditions of the seeds of hearing the Dharma, they will attain the third dhyāna in future lives and be born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven or the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.

Furthermore, by virtue of hearing the Dharma and practicing it, through inquiry and reflection, one will attain the fourth dhyāna in future lives; with the fire of wisdom that is free from attachment, one burns the tree of afflictions and is reborn among the Immeasurable Virtue Heaven, the Universal Virtue Heaven, and the Vast Fruit Heaven.

Furthermore, by means of the seeds of the causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma—through practice, recitation, inquiry, and reflection—for those with false views, one explains the teaching so that they may abide in right view, exhaust all existence, cross over perils and difficulties, and attain the path of a pratyekabuddha; or, if they resolve upon the vow for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall achieve unexcelled perfect enlightenment: the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
By the power of the causal conditions of hearing the true Dharma—
where "hearing the true Dharma" refers to hearing that generosity and ethical discipline constitute the foundation—
for what reason?
These listeners of the Dharma, whether lay or ordained, having heard of the fruits of giving and having understood them, practice generosity;
knowing the fruits of giving and hearing of the fruits of maintaining ethical discipline, they observe the precepts.
Hearing of the fruit of wisdom and cultivating that wisdom, one attains rebirth in heaven immediately upon hearing it, and ultimately achieves liberation.
This hearing of the Dharma is the seed for rebirth in heaven and for nirvana.
Among all forms of giving—whether the gift of material requisites, the gift of fearlessness, or the gift of ethical discipline—the gift of hearing the true Dharma is supreme.
To listen to the true Dharma is the foremost observance of ethical discipline.
If one hears the true Dharma and explains it to others, causing them to abandon what is unwholesome and causing the Dharma to increase, such a person is a father of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond Uttarakuru, what kind of people dwell there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees that to the north of Uttarakuru there is a country two thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

One is named Kāśavīri, measuring three hundred yojanas in length and breadth; there is a river named Kāśavīri, and the dwelling places of people are also named Kāśavīri. The lotuses in the rivers and ponds, as well as the flowers, fruits, groves, and forests with their branches and leaves covering one another, are as previously described.

Having passed beyond this country, there is a river named Amitā; its banks are seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and it is fully endowed with groves, gardens, and lotus ponds, just as previously described.
Along the banks of the Amida River there are five lands:
the first is named the Land of the Celestial Crown Pond;
the second is named the Land of the Pārasa Pond.
The third is named Maṇicīvara Country;
the fourth is named Mayūrasvara Country;
the fifth is named Parvatastha Country.

The country of Devamakuṭa is one hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth; the country of Pāraśaka is one hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth; the country of Mālyāmbara is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth; the country of Mayūrasvara is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; and the country of Parvataśikhara is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there are ten kingdoms, each territory measuring one hundred yojanas. What are these ten?
The first is named the kingdom of Koṭaṅga;
The second is named Land of Holding Incense;
the third is named Land of Black Bellies;
the fourth is named Land of Turning Eyes.
The fifth is named Mountainous Precipitous Shore Country;
the sixth is named Country of Following the Course;
the seventh is named Four Directions Country.
The eighth is named the Country of the Circle;
the ninth is named the Country of Hair-Covering;
the tenth is named the Country of Saṃghāta.
Furthermore, one observes that this continent is likewise fully endowed with rivers, ponds, gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits, just as previously described.

The faces of the people on the four sides of that continent are also like this: just as the faces of the people of Jambudvīpa resemble the shape of the great continent—broad at the top and narrow at the bottom—the faces of the people of Uttarakuru resemble the shape of their great continent in exactly the same way.
He contemplates the continent of Uttarakuru, with all its islands, mountains, valleys, groves, flowers, fruits, rivers, ponds, birds, and beasts fully present.
Having contemplated thus, he knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in successive order.
Beyond the two countries of Uttarakuru and Aparagoyānī, what mountains, forests, oceans, and islands are there?"

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees that between the two countries of Uttarakuru and Aparagoyānī there is a great ocean called Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus), ten thousand yojanas in width. Within it is a water-eye (udakacakṣus) one yojana in width, caused by the power of the nāgas.

Beyond this great ocean, there is a great mountain named Līlā-mālā, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its color is like a mass of ink because it has been scorched by the breath of the nāgas.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great ocean named Kṛtasmara, one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It abounds with large fish, such as timi, timingila, kuṃbhīra, and nāgara; these and other fish fill the sea. This ocean is exceedingly deep, and those who see it are struck with fear.
Within this ocean there is a dragon who dwells in happiness, free from anger.
Beyond this great ocean is another great ocean named Water-Cloud (Jalamegha), ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Within this ocean, great waves surge forth, measuring ten yojanas, twenty yojanas, or thirty yojanas in height.

Beyond this sea lies a great continent named Pearl Oyster (Muktikāśukti), abounding in pearls; when fish or nāgas die in the water, they are cast upon this continent, which is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

Having passed beyond this continent, there is a great mountain named Jewel Mountain (Ratnaparvata), five thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with peaks of the seven treasures such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), resembling a second King Sumeru.
Having passed this mountain, there is a *candana* (Jintuqia) forest, two thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, fully endowed with various groves, flowers, and fruits.

Having passed this forest, there is a great mountain, five thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, where golden lotus ponds and flocks of geese and ducks emit various sounds from among its many peaks.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great ocean ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with golden water that emits a golden light. In the sea is a golden mountain named Suvarṇodaka, five hundred yojanas in height.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is Aparagoyānī, nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It contains one billion villages and twelve thousand cities; the number of its preeminent great cities is five hundred, just as there are more than three hundred great cities in Jambudvīpa, such as the city of Pāṭaliputra—likewise, Aparagoyānī has five hundred great cities, such as Mahāmeghavana and others.

That city of Mahāmegha-saṃcaya was twelve yojanas in length and breadth; its streets and alleys intersected at four points, and it was filled with houses, mansions, and towers. It stood in the center of the land, containing five great cities: the first was named Śatadvāra, the second Vahittha, the third Nimindhara, the fourth Ālokita, and the fifth Girisānu.
There are such great primary cities as these, which encompass the intermediate cities.

Furthermore, there are great kingdoms: one named Gadāci, next the kingdom of Saṃkhyāta, next the kingdom of Maṇi, next the kingdom of Rūpya, and next the kingdom of Dhvaja; there are such great primary kingdoms as these.
For example, just as among the great nations of Jambudvīpa—namely the kingdoms of Kāśi, Kośala, and Magadha—the kingdom of Aparagoyānī is likewise the foremost land.

Next there is the Middle Country, called the kingdom of Nikīla; next is the kingdom called Cāmara; next is the kingdom called Caṇḍura; next is the kingdom called Kūlanta; next is the kingdom called Vitasaka; and next is the kingdom called Guhācara.
In the continent of Aparagoyānī, there are such foremost central kingdoms; twenty-five countries comprise all the nations, just as there are eighteen great countries in Jambudvīpa.
In the country of Aparagoyānī there are five great rivers:
the first is named the Wide River;
the second is named the Samantaparibhūti River.
The third is named Candrabala River;
the fourth is named Rativāri River;
the fifth is named Saṃjinā River.

Just as there are four great rivers in Jambudvīpa—namely, the Gaṅgā River, the Sindhu River, the Vakṣu River, and the Sītā River—so too in the country of Aparagoyānī there are five great mountains. What are these five?
The first is named Dragon-Flight Mountain;
the second is named Three-Peaks Mountain;
the third is named Pearl-Gate Mountain.
The fourth is named Hundred-Jointed Mountain;
the fifth is named Firm Mountain.
Just as there are four great mountains within Jambudvīpa, what are these four?
First is named the Snowy Mountains;
second is named Mount Minda;
third is named Mount Malaya.
The fourth is Mount Kīṭaka. In the country of Aparagoyānī, there are three great lakes: the first is named Gambhīratīra Lake; [the second is named Śītavana Lake;
and the third is named Mahāpadma Lake].
The second is named the Uninterrupted Pond;
the third is named the Radiant Light Pond.
They are like the Anavatapta Pond and the Cāmara Pond in Jambudvīpa.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes what is enjoyed in Aparagoyānī.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
In Godānīya, there are many cows and calves; all women have three breasts. Just as women in Jambudvīpa give birth after ten months, so it is for the people of Godānīya.
