Just as women in Jambudvīpa have two breasts from which milk flows, so too do women in Godānīya have three breasts from which milk flows.

Just as the groves and forests of Jambudvīpa are complete, with flowers, fruits, rivers, and ponds all fully present, yet their fruits possess only half the flavor, their flowers only half the fragrance, and the river water only half the taste.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
By what karma are sentient beings born in Godānīya?

They are born in Godānīya by means of inferior or middling karma. Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees other places of rebirth where there is little morality, little giving, little karma, and little practice in accordance with the Dharma."

What is meant by "limited precepts"? Because of poverty in a previous life, one maintains the precepts for hire or out of fear of punishment; with a pure mind, one pays homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; one associates with kings and gives gifts to acquire wealth; because of this proximity to kings, one does not recite or study the sutras; one gives to those who are not fields of merit, such as those greedy for wealth or possessed of false views, yet considers them to be fields of merit; and because the ten wholesome paths are defiled and one performs impure karmic causes and conditions, one dies in Jambudvīpa and is reborn in Godānīya.

Thus, because they do not know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, they consume food that is only half-flavored; possessing little knowledge and little wisdom, and due to the karmic conditions of their past lives of being attached to women, they are born in Godānīya.

All sentient beings, because they possess a storehouse of karma, transmigrate by means of karma, through karma, and by way of karmic action; according to the wholesome or unwholesome karma they have performed, they obtain such fruits.
If one performs wholesome karma, one is born among humans or devas;
if one performs unwholesome karma, one falls into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Through the causal conditions of karma, one obtains corresponding fruits, just as with various kinds of seeds.
It is like planting grain and obtaining grain, or planting wheat and obtaining wheat; weeds produce weeds. Just as when seeds are sown in poor soil, the harvest is meager;
yet if seeds are sown in fertile soil, one reaps a bountiful harvest of fruit.
Just as when one sows red rice, nothing else grows; when one sows beans, one obtains beans; and when one sows sugarcane, one obtains sugarcane.

Because the field is superior, the fruit obtained is likewise superior. There are three kinds of fields: first, the field of merit for giving; [the second is the field of suffering; and the third is the field of virtue.]
Second is giving to a field of merit;
third is giving with difficulty.
Giving to a field of merit is called the superior [type of giving].
Giving to a field of merit that is suffering is called middling;
giving to one who suffers while lacking the merit of intention is called inferior.
This is like the three types of external fields: the first is one with many stones and much moss, which is called a middling field.
Second, where the water is abundant, there is no grass or filth, nor is there aquatic moss, and there are no bandits—this is called superior field.
Third, where there is much aquatic moss and filth, the water is irregular, and there are many bandits—this is called inferior field.
If farmers apply diligent effort, they will obtain fruit.

These internal and external phenomena, because they are stored within karma, circulate according to karma; they proceed through the turning of karma, each with its own power, its own causes and conditions, and its own mode of birth.
Because the people of Aparagoyānī do not cultivate pure karma, they are born in this place; at the end of their lives, they transmigrate through birth and death according to their own karma.
Thus, when a practitioner has contemplated the karma of external phenomena, he knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond Aparagoyānī, what mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye, he sees:

Between the two continents of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha, there is a great ocean named Viśuddhodaka (Pure Water), twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with clear water. It abounds with conchs, shells, śambuka fish, timi fish, timingila fish, nakra fish, makara fish, kumbhīra fish, and śiśumāra fish; these fish are also blue in color.
Beyond this sea is a coral mountain, five thousand yojanas in length and breadth, where venomous beings dwell within its peaks.
Beyond this mountain is a sea of hot water, abounding with poisonous serpents; because of the venomous breath of these snakes, the seawater is heated.
Not a single sentient being remains, for all have died due to the serpents' poison and the heat of that venom.

Beyond this sea, there is a great ocean called the Crimson Sea, fifteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Dragons and asuras dwell beneath this sea; for the sake of food and drink, they harbor mutual resentment and are constantly engaged in strife and contention.
There is a nāga named Mātaliṇa and an asura named Saṃghāta.

Beyond this sea, there is a great continent called the Land of Rākṣasī Women, measuring two thousand yojanas in length and breadth. There dwells a rākṣasī named Dīrghakeśī (Long-Haired), who resides on this continent and devours incense, flowers, and flesh scorched by fire. She can travel two thousand yojanas in a single thought-moment; she constantly seeks opportunities to harm others, her mind always dwelling upon such thoughts.
This is the Rākṣasa Island, filled with the scattered remains of bones, flesh, and blood, and reeking with foul odors.

Having passed beyond this island, there is a great island named the Country of the Piśāca Female Demons, five thousand yojanas in length and breadth, where Piśāca demons called Hair-Covered (Keśacchanna) dwell.
Having passed beyond this continent, there is a great mountain named Mount Abundant (Rāva), five hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
abounding in forests. These consist of what are called nārikela trees,
followed by panasa trees, followed by trees with unobstructed fruit (asaṃvṛtaphala), followed by tāla trees, and followed by tamāla trees.
The *rāśa* tree, next the *vīra* tree, next the *kulaka* tree, next the *tāpa* tree,
next the *khadiraka* tree, next the *tilaka* tree, next the *aśoka* tree, next the *kadamba* tree, next the *nīparava* tree, and next—
The first is named the khaśula tree; next, the āmra tree; next, the bimba-paṇḍa tree;
next, the pāṭalī tree; next, the bhaṭa tree; next, the kiṃśuka tree;
next, the nāga tree; next, the aśoka tree; next, the kuraṇṭaka tree; and next—
The first is called the *citraka* tree; next, the *karṇikāra* tree; next, the *atimuktaka* tree; next, the *nāgavallī* tree;
next, the *pāṭala* tree; next, the *pāṭalā* tree; next, the *kapittha* tree; and next, the *bilva* tree.
Next is the tree named Devadāru; next, the tree named Padma; next, the tree named Campaka; next, the tree named Karavīraka; next, the tree named Nīlāśoka;
next, the tree named Kurabaka; next, the tree named Kunduru; next, the tree named Pāṭala; next, the tree named...
There are *kūṭaja* trees and many such various fruit trees; there are springs flowing everywhere, and the Gandharva kings sport in that forest.

Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great ocean, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, called Milk-Water (*Kṣīrodaka*). The color and taste of its water are no different from milk, and there are large fish in the sea, five yojanas long, dwelling within it.
Having crossed this sea, there is a mountain of sand, one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, devoid of forests, trees, and medicinal herbs.

Having crossed this mountain, there is a great ocean named Dragon-Filled (Nāgapūrṇa), six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. In this ocean dwell various dragons called Cāñcārā, who contend with one another and delight in pouring down heavy rain.

Having passed beyond this sea, there is a great ocean named Sumudra, two thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are motionless, pure, and serene, abounding with *jambīra* fish, *nāgara* fish, *śiśumāra* fish, and various species of conchs and shells.
"Furthermore, the practitioner knows the fruits of the laws of karma.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:
as it is said, in places such as mountains, rivers, oceans, islands, forests, and groves, there is not a single spot where [beings] are not born."
Death is neither born nor extinguished; all forms of affection and love inevitably end in separation.
There is no place that is not traversed because of karma, no place that is not a repository for karma, and no place that is not a realm of karmic transmigration.
One undergoes the fruits of one's own karma, being born or dying, such that there is not a single mountain, river, sea, or island where this does not occur.
Throughout the realms of birth and death—across mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands—there is not even a space the size of a needle’s point that has not been my place of birth.
Amidst hundreds, thousands, billions, and hundreds of thousands of such births and deaths, I have experienced the separation from loved ones and the encounter with those I loathe.
In hundreds, thousands, billions, and hundreds of thousands of such places of birth and death, I have fallen into the hells.
Hungry ghosts and animals have neither beginning nor end; bound by the net of greed, hatred, and delusion, they transmigrate through birth and death.
Therefore, one should cultivate weary detachment from birth and death, and not give rise to greedy attachment.

This cycle of birth and death is exceedingly painful and distressing; one endures it for a long time with firm persistence, and its suffering is difficult to bear. Through old age, death, grief, lamentation, pain, affliction, and despair, all who possess life must inevitably fall and return to the gate of destruction.

Within the cycle of birth and death, there is not the slightest permanence; just as when the sun rises, there is not the slightest darkness, so too should one contemplate the cycle of birth and death.
Thus, the practitioner contemplates the external body and attains knowledge of the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
Beyond the Sea of Equality, what mountains, rivers, seas, and islands are there?
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The land of Pūrvavideha is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it has many dependencies and is fully endowed with minor islands, villages, cities, towns, rivers, ponds, forests, trees, peninsulas, mountain caves, rows of groves, flowers, fruits, birds, and beasts—all things are complete therein.
There are six great mountains:
the first is named Mahāpārśva Mountain;
the second is named Navamālika Mountain.
The third is named Mountain of Assembled Peacocks;
the fourth is named Mountain of the Wild Beasts’ Valley;
the fifth is named Mountain of the High Sea.
The sixth is named Mount Pearl Garland (*Muktāvalī*). It extends throughout Aparagoyānī, just as there are four great mountains in Jambudvīpa as previously described.

Mount Mahāpārśva is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within this mountain are three great forests, each of which is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. The first is named the Forest of Sumeru; the second, the Forest of Flowing Water; and the third, the Forest of Valley Garlands (*Gulmavalī*). They are fully endowed with various trees, namely: the harītakī tree, followed by the flat-surfaced tree (*samatala*), followed by the valley-born tree (*gulmajāta*), followed by the branch-equal tree (*śākhāsama*), followed by the bank-born tree (*tīrajāta*), and followed by the stone-born tree (*śailajāta*).
As described regarding the trees of Jambudvīpa, those who dwell on this mountain are called the Mahāmālaka people.

Within the mountain there are rivers: the first is named the Varu River, followed by the Srotasāra River, then the Saṃkucitasrotas River, then the Śīghrasrotas River, then the Nāgavāri River, then the Prabhāvana River, and finally the Ciñcā River.

The second great mountain is named Vanamāla; it is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. On this mountain there is a forest named Koṭaka-vana, followed by Carita-vana, then Devadāru-carita-vana, then Dhūma-vana, and finally Cirapralamba-vana.
Within the mountain there is a river; its first name is Tālāvatī, the next is Śṛṅgāvatī, the next is Priyodakā, the next is Smṛtisaṃgrahaṇī, and the next is Dhūmahāsā.
The inhabitants dwelling within the Vanamāla Mountains are named Kujjara.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the third mountain, named Mayūrasaṃgha, which is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; on this mountain there are four great forests:
the first is named Vanakhaṇḍa.
The second is named Hundred Pools Forest;
the third is named High Roar Forest;
the fourth is named Pearl Rim Forest.
Furthermore, there are great rivers: namely, the Nigūṇḍa River, followed by the Mahānanda River, followed by the Vanavāsinī River, followed by the Pūrvaśrotas River, and followed by the Śubhā River.
On Mount Mayūra-kūṭa there dwells a person named Nīla-kaṇṭha. Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates Pūrvavideha;

there is a fourth mountain named Mṛga-tuṅga. On this mountain there is a forest named Śāṃkara-vana, next a forest named Priya-vana, and next a forest named Megha-vana; they are fully endowed with flowers and fruits, as previously described.
In the forest there is a river named Naimuka; next is named Vihasita; next is named Karāla. In the forest there are beasts named Vinīta;

next is named Viśvachāyā; next is named Romamṛga; next is named Dṛṣṭadhāvin; next is named Aśva; next is named Amārga; next is named Ṛṣimṛga; next is named Tārakṣu; next is named Sukarṇa; next is named Gajamukha; next is named Agryaputra; next is named Priyacchāya; next is named Śaśaroman; next is named Uṣṭragātra; next is named Kṛṣṇavāla; next is named Śvetamūrdhan; next is named Abhirūpa; next is named Sarpajihva; next is named Śvadaṃṣṭra; next is named Gavyaya; next is named Kambala; next is named Ulūkhalaka.
Such beasts as these may or may not exist within Jambudvīpa.
In Mount Mṛgāra, gardens, groves, flowing streams, ponds, flowers, fruits, and trees are all fully present, just as previously described.
All the flower ponds are like those in Jambudvīpa.
The people dwelling in the mountain range of Beast Valley are called Swift Power (*Javavāhin*).

Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the country of Pūrvavideha; there is a fifth mountain named Ocean High (*Sāgaragiri*), one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, complete with gardens, groves, flowing streams, ponds, flowers, and fruits, just as previously described.
On this mountain there is a forest named Tridanda-vana; next is the forest named Kaṇṭhakī-vana;
and next is the forest named Śaila-vana. Within these forests are rivers named Trikoṇā, next Uccairghoṣā, and next Śilāsvarā.
The mountain situated in the ocean is named Cakravāḍa.
Having observed the Cakravāḍa mountain, one knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the external body in successive order.
He contemplates what kind of mountains exist in Pūrvavideha.
Through his wisdom derived from hearing or with his divine eye, he sees:

the sixth mountain is named Pearl Garland (*muktāhāra*), measuring one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is completely endowed with groves, gardens, streams, and ponds, and is fully possessed of various flowers, fruits, birds, and beasts, just as previously described.
From Mount Muktikāvalī issues forth a great river named Anavalokita-tīra, one yojana in width.
There dwells a person on Mount Muktikāvalī named Samantacakṣus.
In this same way, Pūrvavideha is surrounded by six mountains.
Within the kingdom of Pūrvavideha, there are three great cities:
the first is named City of Auspicious Gates;
The second is named City of Joyful Mountains;
the third is named City of Universal Play.
Each of these great cities is three yojanas wide, and there are sixty-three cities of medium and small size.
There is a middle city named Kauṭāha, next is named Mahāpārśva, and next is named Samantaghosa; such are the middle cities among them.
The first and largest among the lower cities is named Sarvabhāra; next is the city named Mahāśabda; and next is the city named Āṭavībilaka.
Among such small cities as these, this is the foremost and greatest.

Furthermore, there were three hundred million, five hundred thousand, three thousand, five hundred and fifty-six villages. The first village was named Kāśmīra; next, Jālaka; next, Mūlagrāma; next, Vṛkṣaruta; next, Sarvamanuja; next, Parṇagrāma; next, Vituḷa; next, Bakagrāma; next, Viṭhagrāma; next, Māmāgrāma; next, Nadī; next, Ghaṭakumbha; next, Tuhaka; next, Vanagrāma; next, Raktāvarta; next, Akṣa; next, Vātāhata; next, Māligrāma; next, Śikharavṛkṣa; and next, Kṛṣṇabhojana.
There are such foremost villages as these.
The faces of these people are full and round, resembling the shape of the continent Jambudvīpa.

The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are adorned with ears and hair; those of Uttarakuru are adorned with eyes; those of Aparagoyānī are adorned with necks and bellies; and those of Pūrvavideha are adorned with shoulders and thighs. Thus, the inhabitants of the four continents are each beautiful in their own natural adornment.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the retribution of karma.
By what karma are sentient beings born in Pūrvavideha?
There are superior, middling, and inferior karmas."
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

these sentient beings in previous lives did not understand the law of karma and its retribution; because they did not understand it, they gave to those who were not fields of merit, or they gave only after being asked in a difficult manner, or they gave only after seeking [the recipient] through great hardship, as previously described.
Due to this karma, it is called birth in the lower grade.
If there are sentient beings who observe the medium-grade precepts, yet do not kill sentient beings merely because they comply with the laws of kings, this is not out of a pure mind.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, when their body perishes and their life ends, they are reborn in the heavens; from there, when their heavenly life ends, they are reborn in Pūrvavideha. This is called birth through intermediate karma.

As for superior persons with superior karma, having heard the True Dharma, they receive, uphold, read, and recite it; they explain it to others, rejoice in it, and practice according to what they have heard.

There is no single dharma capable of crossing the perilous path and wilderness of birth and death like the hearing of the true Dharma; receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining it for others is the most excellent among all forms of giving—namely, the gift of Dharma.
The first is the upholding of ethical discipline, which means hearing the true Dharma; the wisdom that comes from hearing the true Dharma is the most supreme.
As for the true Dharma, it is as previously described.
Having contemplated the karmic fruits and retributions of Pūrvavideha, one knows the external body as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates what mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands exist within Pūrvavideha.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees that eight thousand yojanas beyond Pūrvavideha there is a great mountain named Ayaskānta (Magnet). It is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and ten thousand yojanas on each of its four sides. Even if there is but a tiny amount of iron, it all quickly rushes and runs toward this mountain."
Having passed beyond this mountain, there is a great ocean seven thousand yojanas in extent called Pāriyātra, which encircles the five mountains like a ring.
What are these five?
The first is named Needle-Mouth Mountain;
the second is named Great Treasury Mountain;
the third is named Toṭaka Mountain.
The fourth is named Śeṣa-parvata;
the fifth is named Nandana-parvata.

Beyond these mountains lies a great continent named Dhatākamaṇḍala, three thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Many yakṣas and kiṃnaras dwell on this continent, which is fully endowed with rivers, ponds, groves, flowers, and fruits, and is exceedingly delightful.
Whatever birds and beasts exist in Jambudvīpa and in Pūrvavideha are all present on this continent.
Beyond this continent lies a great ocean called Tārakāvatī; within this ocean is a mountain named Udayana, which has thirteen peaks surrounding this great sea and is not far from Mount Sumeru.
The non-Buddhists say:

"The wholesome and unwholesome karma of the people of Jambudvīpa acts as the predominant condition; through this wholesome and unwholesome wind, [the stars] emerge from the constellation within Mount Udayana."
The various Brahmins and non-Buddhist teachers, having lost their understanding of karmic retribution and being ignorant of the ultimate truth, spoke in the presence of the king, saying:
"All things are produced by the stars and planetary deities; they are not the fruit of karma."
These non-Buddhist Brahmin masters of logic, with their false views, perversely claim that [the world] is created by the stars and planets, and not by the retribution of karma.

If it were created by the stars and planets rather than being the fruit of karma, then because the sun and moon are superior, the good and evil seasons would flow according to them; yet all seasons possess flowers and fruits. If the sun and moon are indeed superior, why then are they eclipsed by other celestial bodies?

That which is called the sun is Śabala, and the moon is Rāhu; all the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) are eclipsed by the planets (grahas), and the planets are themselves eclipsed by others. Because of this quality of being auspicious or inauspicious, the lunar mansions and planets likewise possess both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Therefore, wholesome and unwholesome karma are the individual karma of sentient beings; they are not created by the stars and planets.

Furthermore, the practitioner, in accordance with the external body, contemplates the luminaries and constellations and perceives that the retribution of karma is not produced by the luminaries and so forth.
Having observed the Ocean of Many Constellations and having observed the peaks of Mount Sumeru and Mount Udayana, one knows the external body as it truly is.
Furthermore, the practitioner observes the Ocean of Many Constellations, which is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

Having crossed this sea, there is a continent where various seers and immortals dwell. Its mountains, rivers, forests, and trees, as well as its flowers and fruits, are as abundant as those in Jambudvīpa.
This continent is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is the abode of seers and yakṣas, and is fully endowed with all kinds of wish-fulfilling trees, flowers, and fruits.
Beyond this continent, there is a Great Encircling Mountain and a great ocean three thousand yojanas wide, situated between the two lands of Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha.

Such is the great ocean named Warm-and-Cold Water, three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, wherein dwell many species such as conchs, shells, *timi* fish, *timirapila* fish, *nakara* fish, *makara* fish, *śiśumāra* fish, tortoises, and soft-shelled turtles.
Beyond these mountains and seas, there is a great ocean called the Crimson Sea (*Raktasamudra*). It is not far from Jambudvīpa and measures five thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.

It is filled with crimson water and abounds with large fish; these fish are red in color and devour one another. Because of the blood of these fish, the seawater is made crimson, and for this reason it is named the Crimson Water.

Having passed beyond this sea, there is a great ocean named Clear Water (*Vimala*), seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, complete with mountains and rivers, abounding in large fish, and being exceedingly deep.

Having crossed this sea, there is a great ocean called Jewel Island (*ratnadvīpa*), three thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; all manner of precious gems are gathered upon this island, fully provided with golden sand, conch shells, pearls, coral, *sūmāra* jewels, and various other treasures.

There is a fruit called *mātuluṅga*, known as "mind-confounding poison," which grows upon trees. If a person from Jambudvīpa picks and eats this fruit, they will be as if dead for seven days; if a flying bird eats it, it dies immediately.

Having passed this island, there is a great ocean named Lavana (Salt), seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is filled with many conchs, shells, pearls, oysters, clams, timi fish, timingila fish, kumbhīra crocodiles, and nāga fish; furthermore, various dragons, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśāca spirits all dwell within its waters, and beneath the water there are countless mountains.

"This Jambudvīpa continent is surrounded by five hundred minor islands. To speak briefly of the most prominent among them: they are known as Suvarṇabhūmi Island, followed by Ratnadvīpa, then Dhvajamālī, then Kana, then Śaṅkhadvīpa, then Muktādvīpa, then Parikṣepa, then Prabhāsa, then Aiṣavataka, then Kāñcanaprabha, then Samantabhadra, then Cittavaśavartin, then Kṛṣṇayugandhara, then Gandhamālī, then Triśṛṅga, then Sukṣetra, then Śanāsuta, and finally Aruṇaka Island."
Next is named Laṅkādvīpa, which has twelve mountains and is inhabited by rākṣasas.

Next is named Merupāraka-dvīpa; next, Parvatavāsin-dvīpa; next, Śaṅkhadvīpa; next, Muktikā-dvīpa; next, Hima-āvarta-dvīpa; next, Pāṃśu-parivāra-dvīpa; next, Amārga-dvīpa; next, Pañca-tāmra-dvīpa; next, Āvṛta-dvīpa; next, Śaktila-dvīpa; next, Strī-rāṣṭra-dvīpa; next, Bahuvṛkṣa-dvīpa; next, Icchāpāda-dvīpa; and next, Puruṣa-dvīpa.
Within the realm of Jambudvīpa, such supreme minor continents as these are described.
This Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is lovely all around, just as previously described.
"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the external body in accordance with reality.
He observes where the light of the sun and moon shines.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye, he sees:

The light of the sun and moon illuminates the four faces of Sumeru, King of Mountains, as well as the four continents and the great ocean; it shines upon Sumeru, King of Mountains, for eighty-four thousand yojanas, yet the light falls only on one side of the mountain, reaching only halfway around its circumference.

The Cakravāḍa Diamond Mountains surround [the world] for thirty-six hundred million yojanas. The unbearable fires of karma burn the waters of the milk-ocean surrounding the Cakravāḍa Diamond Mountains; when they approach it, the water turns into curd; as they draw closer to this mountain, it turns into fresh butter (*maṇḍa*); drawing closer still, it turns into clarified butter (*ghṛta*); and as they draw even closer, they are scorched and extinguished by the fires of hell. For this reason, [these mountains] do not fill the Jambudvīpa and the other continents.

This practitioner contemplates the realm of desire and sees it as it truly is; he becomes weary of and detached from the mind of desire, seeing not a single place that is permanent, indestructible, or immutable. Throughout all places within beginningless birth and death, by the power of the causes and conditions of the retribution of one's own karma, and being toyed with by the retribution of one's own karma, there is not a single place where one does not experience birth and death—whether a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand times, through immeasurable and boundless births and deaths without interval.
Contemplating the body internally and externally, he becomes weary of and detached from sensual desire; his mind finds no delight in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles.
"In this way, monks, a bhikṣu practicing in the village of the Nādikas, brahmins and householders, cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body and does not dwell within the realm of Māra."

Having heard this teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, many people have shattered the defilement of the view of self and attained the arising of the Dharma-eye regarding the unsurpassed Dharma.

To teach the unsurpassed Dharma of mindfulness of the body—whether one practices meditative concentration in mountain valleys, in mountain caves, in cemeteries, in the open air, or beside a heap of grass—I instruct you not to be negligent, lest at the time of death you fall into regret. This is my teaching.
At that time, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, all the bhikṣus were greatly delighted.
They conceived a heart of faith and joy toward the World-Honored One’s teaching, and they practiced it with gladness.
The Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma, Scroll Seventy
